en: The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Fascicle One, with Preface, composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang in the Tang Dynasty. Preface:
Past and future are boundless; movement and stillness share a single source. It encompasses all wonders with abundance, transcending words.
That which transcends through contemplation is surely the Dharma-realm.

It dissects the profound and subtle, illuminating the mind and its objects; it exhausts principle and fulfills nature, penetrating the fruit while encompassing the cause. Vast, profound, harmonious, and all-encompassing in its greatness—this can only be the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Therefore, when our World-Honored One’s ten bodies were first perfected and his perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) was initially attained, he employed the practice of his vows to encompass all things, taking the entirety of empty space as his essential nature. He is replete with myriad virtues and utterly free from even the slightest speck of dust; he is the clear ripples of the profound ocean of wisdom, serenely containing the myriad phenomena;
he is the full moon of the luminous emptiness of nature, instantly reflected in a hundred rivers;
and without rising from beneath the King of Trees, he pervades the seven locations throughout the Dharma-realm.
Without contradicting the future limit, the nine assemblies are fully manifested within the initial formation.
The profound principle of vast expansiveness is exhausted, and the inconceivable ocean-like assembly is encompassed;
the perfect voice resounds clearly, pervading the ten lands all at once, while the primary and attendant teachings layer upon layer, singing in unison throughout the ten directions.
Although emptiness within emptiness leaves no trace, the constellations of the Dharma-realm shine brilliantly;
though the profound depths are beyond words, the waves of the ocean of teaching surge in vast and overflowing majesty.
Thus, as a thousand gates flow in secret confluence, they serve as the great source for all the scriptures.
The myriad virtues converge and return [to this source], encompassing all scriptures as its retinue.

Its fundamental purport is to realize the true essence within the realm of myriad transformations and to manifest the marks of virtue at the gateway of profound mystery (*chongxuan*). Through the proliferation of function, it remains eternally as-it-is; through the universal mirror-like reflection of wisdom, it remains ever-quiescent. Where truth and falsehood mutually penetrate, one perceives the Buddha-mind within the ordinary mind;
where phenomena and principle are cultivated in tandem, one seeks Buddha-wisdom by relying on original wisdom.
When principle conforms to the transformations of phenomena, the dependent origination of the one and the many becomes boundless;
when phenomena attain harmony with principle, the myriad differences interpenetrate without obstruction.

Thus, the ten bodies manifest distinctly yet act as one, and the six positions remain orderly while mutually encompassing one another. The vast and great enters directly into the infinitesimal; a single mote of dust contains all within it without exteriority. They appear simultaneously and in perfect clarity, like mustard seeds within a jar, or the totality of existence contained within a single drop of ocean water.
The one and the many are unimpeded, like a thousand lamps in an empty room;
manifestation and concealment both prevail, resembling a crescent moon in the autumn sky;
they reflect one another in infinite layers, like pearls hanging from Indra’s net.
Moment-to-moment contemplation is perfectly interfused, like a dream spanning an entire lifetime;
the dharma-gates are layered one upon another, like clouds rising in the vast sky;
the myriad practices unfold in profusion, comparable to flowers blooming upon brocade.
If the heights are such that they cannot be looked up to, then the Bodhisattvas who have accumulated their practices will expose their gills at the Dragon Gate;
if the depths are such that they cannot be fathomed, then the Śrāvakas of supreme virtue will close their eyes and ears at the auspicious assembly.
With seeing and hearing as the seed, one transcends the eight difficulties and the stages of the ten bhūmis;
with understanding and practice embodied, one perfects the fruit of kalpas of vast antiquity in a single lifetime.
With the lion’s vigorous leap, the entire ocean [of dharmas] is suddenly realized within the forest.
The Elephant King turns in his tracks; within a single utterance, six thousand paths are perfected.
When the dawn breaks at the Eastern Temple, the fulfillment of wisdom is no different from the initial resolve;
when one takes station in the South to seek [enlightenment], the completion of the cause does not exceed a single pore.

To open the sutra scrolls within a single atom is to achieve fruition in every thought-moment; to exhaust the gates of aspiration for all sentient beings is to fulfill practice in every particle of dust. Truly, this may be called the wondrous teaching of eternity, the grand standard that penetrates all directions, the ultimate discourse in accordance with the nature of reality, and the essential path of the One Vehicle.
Seeking this profound principle and then surveying other sutras, it is like the bright sun beautifying the heavens, eclipsing the radiance of all other lights;
or like Mount Sumeru spanning the sea, surpassing the height of all surrounding peaks.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas sought out the secrets in the Dragon Palace, and great sages propagated them throughout the Eastern Land.

Reflecting upon it, even in an era of the True Dharma, its pure radiance remained concealed; yet how fortunate that in this age of the Semblance Dharma, we have encountered these profound transformations! Moreover, having met a sagely sovereign and being present at the Vulture Peak, to exhaust one’s thoughts upon the mysterious source—how could there not be cause for celebration and joy!
The title *Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra* is the collective name for the inexhaustible collection of sūtras (*sūtranta*).
The first chapter, "The Exquisite Array of the World-Ruling Lords" (*Lokendrarājasaṃdarśana*), is the specific heading for this particular category of meaning among the various sections.

"Great" signifies vastness and boundless inclusiveness; "Square" signifies upholding oneself through the True Dharma. "Broad" means to encompass all things according to their essential nature. The Buddha is called "Awakened" because he has realized this profound mystery. "Flower" is a metaphor for the myriad practices of merit; "Adornment" refers to embellishing the Dharma to perfect the person. The *Sūtra* thus pours forth like an inexhaustible spring, threading together the subtle and concentrated wondrous meanings; it gathers the infinite assemblies of the ocean-like congregation and establishes an eternal standard for all time.

Both the Buddhas and the various kings are equally titled "World Lords" (Lokendra); the Dharma-gates, encompassing both the primary and secondary aspects, are collectively called "Sublime Adornment. To distinguish their meanings and categories, these titles are used to manifest the names of the chapters, which stand at the head of all sections as the foremost.
This sutra consists of thirty-nine chapters; as this chapter stands at the beginning, it is titled *The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya*.

I take refuge in the Teachers of the World, who are perfectly luminous throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, The clouds of great compassion and the ocean of great wisdom of Vairocana, Whose merit within the Dharma-realm pervades every atom of the lands.
The profound true dharma-nature wherein they dwell, And the perfect sūtras that flow therefrom;
Within every atom and every direction, amidst the assemblies of Buddhas, Are Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and all the great bodhisattvas.
Now, with the wisdom of a single hair, I wish to measure the emptiness of the boundless Dharma-realm;
may I rely upon the compassion of the Three Jewels as one essence, so that every phrase accords in mystery with the intent of all Buddhas.
May the eye of the Dharma be forever without deficiency, Throughout the entire realm of sentient beings, as vast as Samantabhadra’s;
May this supreme merit be dedicated to all living beings, So that they may swiftly realize the fruit of eternal bliss, Bodhi.
To explain the meaning of this scripture, ten general gateways are opened: first, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching;

second, the collection and teaching to which it belongs; third, the delimitation of its principles and meanings; fourth, the capacities of the beings to whom the teaching is addressed; fifth, the depth and shallowness of the essence of the teaching; sixth, the scope and limitations of its primary intent; seventh, the classification of its sections and chapters; eighth, the circumstances of its transmission and translation; ninth, a general explanation of the title of the scripture; and tenth, a detailed interpretation of the textual meaning.

Regarding the first cause and condition: Generally, when sages establish their teachings, there must be a specific reason or occasion. Just as Mount Sumeru and the vast ocean can only be shaken by a great cause, now that the Tathāgata’s mountain of virtue—refined gold—is being shaken and his deep and expansive ocean of wisdom is being stirred, this cannot be due to a minor circumstance.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "The appearance of the Tathāgata is not accomplished through a single condition nor by a single matter.

Since his appearance is fundamentally for the sake of the Great Avataṃsaka, ten meanings are first presented as causes and ten as conditions, each opening up ten further aspects to manifest its inexhaustibility.
The ten reasons are: first, because it is the nature of phenomena;

second, to repay past causes; third, to accord with the capacity for response; fourth, as the foundation of the teaching; fifth, to manifest the merit of the fruit; sixth, to clarify the stages and positions; seventh, to explain the sublime practices; eighth, to reveal the true Dharma; ninth, to open up the causal nature; and tenth, to benefit both the present and the future.

Regarding the term "dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena): the Way of Kings is broad and level, following the same standard for a thousand ages; the profound gate of the One Vehicle is realized equally by all Buddhas. Therefore, by the very nature of things, all Buddhas constantly turn such an inexhaustible wheel of Dharma throughout infinite worlds, causing all sentient beings to return to their origin and source, continuing without rest until the end of the future.

Therefore, it is clarified in the "Inconceivable Chapter" that all Buddhas are able, within a single body, to manifest as many heads as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; each head manifests as many tongues, and each tongue produces as many sounds, even down to the individual characters, phrases, and meanings, each filling the entirety of the Dharma-realm without end.

Thus, as for its location, it occupies the tip of a single hair yet transversely encompasses the entire Dharma-realm; as for its time, it spans a single kṣaṇa yet vertically exhausts the ocean of kalpas. In terms of location, it arises instantaneously; in terms of time, it arises eternally. It does not depend on any external cause, yet it is spoken of as having an initial formation and distinct nine assemblies according to what is seen and heard.

All those who possess compassion have briefly circulated this within the inexhaustible [Dharma], so that by seeking it here one may perceive the boundless Dharma—just as one perceives the limitless sky through a window opening—and at that very time and place, it is identical to the inexhaustible, because one place is all places and one moment is all moments.
Second, regarding the recompense for past causes: why does the Dharma necessarily evolve in this manner?
It is because past causes are profound.
For when roots are deep, fruits flourish; when sources are distant, streams are long. Since past causes are profound, the arising of the teaching is likewise vast.
What is meant by "profound and vast"?

Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, first trod upon the profound traces and settled his spirit in wondrous stillness; with compassion and wisdom operating in tandem, his practice and vows were equally perfected. Thus, without severing delusive thoughts, he realized the pervasive clarity of the emptiness of nature; without polishing the spiritual mirror, he suddenly illumined the myriad dharmas. By means of unobstructed liberation, he expounded this [teaching].
Although the Śramaṇa’s past causes are many, they are briefly summarized into two kinds: the first is due to the power of great vows.
The "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" states: "Vairocana Buddha, by the power of his vows, pervades the entire Dharma-realm; within all lands, he constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel."
The *Tuṣita-gāthā* says: "The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any nirvāṇa.
By the power of his original great vows, he manifests the dharma of sovereign mastery."
The Buddhas present in the assembly all testify that this is due to the power of vows; furthermore, there are numerous other passages in various texts that serve as proof.
Second, it is due to the power of past practice.
This means that throughout immeasurable eons, one has undertaken practice based on vows; only when that practice is perfected and the fruit attained can one suddenly expound [the Dharma].
Thus, the mountain deity of the former master spoke in verse: "In the past, you cultivated supreme practices without limit; now, you have attained immeasurable supernormal powers.
You have extensively opened up dharma gates as numerous as atoms, causing all sentient beings to deeply awaken and rejoice."

Third, regarding "responding to the capacity for resonance": although the Dharma is inherently able to be eternal and omnipresent due to past causes, its transmission depends entirely upon the resonance of the capacity of beings; for apart from such capacity, there would be no purpose in preaching the Dharma.
It is like the bright moon above reflected in a clear pool below; as the pool is pure, the reflection appears, and as the conditions respond, the perception arises.
Thus, the *Gāthā on Tuṣita* says: "Seeing the Buddha is likewise so; it must depend upon various wholesome karmas."
The Buddhas of the ten directions addressed Gaṇeśvararāja, saying, "This is due to the power of the roots of goodness of you and the assembly of bodhisattvas.

Vimukticandra then said, "This assembly is free from all defilements; their resolve and understanding are entirely pure," and so forth—all of which are responses to the spiritual capacity of the audience.
The extensive manifestation of responsive capacity and its elicitation is as explained in the section on the capacities to be reached by the fourth teaching.

However, this responsive capacity and elicitation extends across both the present and the future: those who were the appropriate recipients in various assemblies were the present [capacity], while those who hear it now are the future capacity.

Fourth, regarding "the teaching as the root": it means that without the ocean there would be no place for the hidden current, and without the root there would be no way to extend to the branches. Desiring to gradually bestow the secondary teachings according to the capacities of beings, [the Buddha] first reveals the fundamental Dharma by expounding this sutra all at once.
Nevertheless, there are also two [reasons]:
first, to open the foundation for gradual [instruction].
As the "Chapter on the Manifestation" states: "Just as when the sun first rises, it first illuminates the high mountains."
The second is the root that gathers in the branches.

This is because "just as when the sun sets, it still illuminates the high mountains," and because "there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm, and nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm."
The *Lotus Sūtra* also states: "As soon as they see my body and hear what I preach, they all believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
This is the basis for the gradual approach.
Next, it says, "except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna," which opens the way for the gradual approach.
Furthermore, it says, "I now also cause them to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom," which signifies the gathering of the branches back to the root.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also points to this very scripture as its basis.

Fifth, regarding the manifestation of the fruit and virtue: this refers to the manifestation of the Buddha’s supreme virtues within this fundamental dharma, so that all bodhisattvas may have faith in, incline toward, and realize them.
If one does not recognize a precious gem, its utility cannot be realized; likewise, if one does not know this virtue, how can one look up to it and seek it?
Nevertheless, the fruition of virtue is twofold:
first, the fruit of reliance, which refers to the Flower Treasury World-Ocean and so forth;
The second is the primary fruit, such as the ten bodies of the Tathāgata.
These two, being unimpeded, constitute the virtues of a Buddha.
Furthermore, based on the non-obstruction between the environment and its inhabitants, there are generally six propositions:
First, the internal manifestation based on the basis (*āśraya*), such as the oceans of lands within a single atom;
second, the correct internal manifestation of the correct [Dharma], such as the Buddhas manifesting from a single pore;

third, the correct internal manifestation of the basis; fourth, the basis manifested internally by the correct [Dharma]; fifth, the basis manifested internally by the basis; and sixth, the correct internal manifestation of the correct basis—their textual instances are not limited to these alone.
Furthermore, there are four propositions:
first, it may be only the basis, because the Buddha is the field;
second, it may be only the primary reality, because the field is the Buddha.
The "three together" and the "four merged" can be understood through reflection.
Whichever single gate one takes up, it encompasses all others, as will be explained below.

Sixth, regarding the manifestation of the stages and positions: this is to reveal that while the Bodhisattva practices the causes of Buddhahood, there are gradations along the single path leading to the fruition.
Now, the great treasure of the Sage is called "position" (*sthāna*); for without this position, practice cannot achieve fulfillment.
This [position] is also of two kinds:
first, the gate of sequential arrangement (*kramavyūha*), because it establishes the distinctions among positions; [and second, the gate of interpenetration].
Second is the gate of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong men*), because a single stage encompasses all stages, and each individual stage being fulfilled constitutes the attainment of Buddhahood.

As it says regarding the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmi*): "Within a single stage, one fully encompasses the merits of all stages; faith pervades the ocean of fruition, such that at the very moment of the first resolve, one attains perfect enlightenment," and so forth.

However, these two are unimpeded because the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) is the provisional designation of the teaching's characteristics, while the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*) is the functional virtue of the rational nature.
Since characteristics are characteristics that are identical to the nature, sequential arrangement does not impede perfect fusion;
since the nature is the nature that is identical to characteristics, perfect fusion does not impede sequential arrangement.
Because perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential manifestation, the one becomes the infinite;
because sequential manifestation does not obstruct perfect interfusion, the infinite becomes the one.
Since the infinite becomes the one, they are subtly and harmoniously integrated.
Because the one is immeasurable, they interpenetrate in layers of profundity.
Thus, Vasubandhu describes them through the six aspects of perfect interfusion;
such passages appear throughout the text more than once.

Seventh, regarding the explanation of superior practice: one who wishes to ascend to the sublime station cannot do so without practice; therefore, the gentleman does not worry about lacking rank, but worries that he himself is not established.
Practice is also of two kinds:
first, accomplishing all practices instantaneously; second, practicing every single practice.
Therefore, the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes" states: "One is many, and many are one," and so forth.
The "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" says: "The severance of one is the severance of all," and so forth.

Second is the universal accomplishment of all practices; this refers to the sequential progression (*xingbu*), meaning from the essential nature, characteristics, and merits of the great bodhicitta up to the practice during the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
These two are unimpeded, as explained according to their respective stages.

Eighth, regarding the demonstration of the true Dharma: to accomplish the stages of practice, one must understand the principles of the Dharma; if one does not realize the identity of principle and phenomena, even one's practice will not be authentic.
Thus, the *Tuṣita Gāthā* says: "Because they do not understand the true Dharma, the Buddhas appear in the world."
This also has two aspects:

first, the manifestation of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle; second, the manifestation of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena. Both are explained according to the *Yifenji* (The Delimitation of Meanings).
Ninth, the opening of the causal nature refers to the fact that the aforementioned causes and effects, as well as phenomena and principle, all exist by virtue of the nature of sentient beings.
If one's nature were not that of gold or jade, it could not be fashioned into a precious vessel despite being carved.

It is precisely because sentient beings take the inherent virtue of their nature as their substance and rely on the ocean of wisdom as their source; yet, through the transformation of appearances, their substance becomes alienated, and through the arising of emotional attachments, their wisdom is obstructed. Now, by causing them to know that the mind unites with the substance and to realize the fundamental source so that emotional attachments vanish, this sutra is expounded to manifest this truth.
There are also two kinds:
first, manifesting through words so that one may know it exists;
second, causing one to practice and realize its manifestation, as in the example of a scroll of scripture being revealed from within dust.

It is also as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "It is solely for the sake of one great cause and condition that I appear in the world; that is to say, to open, reveal, awaken to, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
Because all sentient beings possess [this nature] equally, it is said to be "one.
Regarding the "ten benefits for the present and future": since they all equally possess this portion, they bring vast benefit to the limitless.
This also has two aspects:
The first benefit is immediate, referring to those present before the Buddha;
the second benefit is subsequent, referring to those who see and hear it now.
The "Chapter on Generating the Resolve" states: "We Buddhas shall protect and uphold this Dharma, so that all Bodhisattvas in future ages who have not yet heard it may all come to hear it."
This benefit is further twofold:
first, it causes one to obtain seeing and hearing so that they may become firm seeds.
As the "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "It is like a person who eats a small amount of diamond; it will never be digested," and so forth.
Second, it appears because it causes the arousal of practice and the accomplishment of realization.

It further states: "Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, practiced the six pāramitās and cultivated various factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma). If they have not heard this Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable great majestic power, or if having heard it at some time, they do not believe or understand it, nor follow or enter into it, they cannot be called a true bodhisattva, because they are unable to give birth to the family of the Tathāgata."

If one hears this Dharma and, with faith and understanding, accords with it and enters into it, you should know that such a person is born into the family of the Tathāgata, and even penetrates deeply into the immeasurable realm of the Tathāgata.
This is because cultivation through deliberate effort will ultimately result in ruin after many kalpas;
whereas when the ultimate reality is realized through a mind-free state, one accords with the Buddha’s teaching in a single thought-moment.
As the "Chapter on Worthy Leader" states: "One may serve Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields for the duration of an entire kalpa."
"If one is able to recite and uphold this chapter, its merit is most excellent, surpassing that [of the former]" and so forth.
Furthermore, these benefits, when distinguished in relation to the preceding nine, constitute ten kinds of benefit; namely:
first, by hearing the Dharma as it truly is, one realizes it is eternal and omnipresent, thereby accomplishing the benefit of seeing and hearing.
Second, by hearing of the original practices, one aspires to learn from the Buddha, thereby accomplishing the benefit of generating the bodhicitta;
third, by hearing of the responsive resonance between faculty and teaching, one knows that the Dharma arises from goodness, thereby accomplishing the benefit of cultivation and practice;
fourth, by hearing that [the teachings] are rooted in the fundamental, one realizes their meaning is perfect and complete, thereby accomplishing the benefit of sudden realization.
Fifth, by hearing of the qualities of the fruit, one’s faith, aspiration, and vow become unified, thereby accomplishing the benefit of eliminating hindrances;
sixth, by hearing of the stages, one directs the mind toward realization and entry, thereby accomplishing the benefit of encompassing the stages;
seventh, by hearing of the practices, one resolves to engage in cultivation, thereby accomplishing the benefit of initiating practice.
Eighth, by hearing the Dharma, one must decisively understand it to achieve the benefit of realizing its nature;
ninth, by hearing the causes, one knows that all things are identical to achieve the benefit of transformation;
tenth, by possessing all the preceding nine, one achieves the benefit of swift realization; therefore, the nine preceding causes all serve as the basis for this present benefit.
Furthermore, each of the preceding sections can be understood to achieve ten benefits through the power of one's own mind.
It is because of these ten meanings that this teaching arose.

Within the "Chapter on Arousing the Resolve," there are ten causes, which state: "By the spiritual power of the Buddha, by the power of the World-Honored One’s original vows," and so forth, with various causal conditions intermingled.
The causes and conditions of the assembly can be understood through the mind.

Second, regarding the explanation of the circumstances for preaching the sutra: at the beginning of all sutras, the mention of the time, place, persons, and so forth, constitutes the arising of conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Now there are ten conditions: first, dependence on time; second, dependence on place;

third, dependence on the principal; fourth, dependence on samādhi; fifth, dependence on manifested signs; sixth, dependence on the speaker; seventh, dependence on the listener; eighth, dependence on the root of virtue; ninth, dependence on the requester; and tenth, dependence on the one who bestows empowerment.
Now, first, regarding time:
when the mind merges with the ultimate Way, it unifies the ancient and the modern; the Dharma-realm is unborn and fundamentally devoid of temporal divisions.
As a verse in the sutra below says: "The Buddhas attain Bodhi, yet in truth they do not calculate by days."
How much more so regarding boundless discourse, wherein thought-moments and kalpas are perfectly interfused!
Now, by means of time that is timeless, I shall briefly manifest ten layers of temporal distinctions:

first, a single thought-moment; second, the full seven days; third, pervading the three periods of time; fourth, subsuming kalpas of the same category; fifth, gathering kalpas of different categories; sixth, subsuming kalpas within a thought-moment; seventh, the mutual inclusion of kalpas and thought-moments; eighth, the time of realms of different categories; ninth, the mutual entry of this and that; and tenth, subsuming the derivative within the fundamental.
This means that because non-aeons are treated as aeons, this sutra is constantly expounded during the ten aforementioned periods.

Furthermore, any one of these ten types encompasses the whole; when time is spoken of in this way, it has neither beginning nor end. Moreover, the "initial formation" and so forth are spoken of according to what is seen or heard, as was explained previously in the section on *dharmatā*.
If one relies on this timing, it is vastly different from other teachings, yet the timing of those other teachings does not transcend this.
Some speak of three, seven, six, or seven weeks and so forth; these follow what has been seen or heard, as explained at length in the *Zhiguī* (The Return to the Source).

Regarding the second basis: since wisdom exhausts the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) such that both subject and object are extinguished, it is conventionally said to "rely on the Truth" rather than a physical land. Moreover, as the atoms of the lands enter one another and defilement and purity are mutually integrated, the universal pervasiveness of the perfect teaching makes it difficult to distinguish between separate locations.
However, reality is not external to phenomena; it does not destroy its locus, for it is the timeless time that pervades all non-spatial locations.
Yet some say: "This sutra was preached in a defiled land, as it was situated in places such as Magadha."
Some say: it is spoken while abiding in the Pure Land, because [the Buddha] is within the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*). Others say:
According to the true meaning, the two kinds of bodies and lands have no fixed distinction of location, as they are seen and heard differently even within a single place.
Of the three preceding meanings, the last one accords with our own school’s tenet.

However, regarding the locations where this sutra is preached, purity and impurity are unimpeded, and the universal and the particular interpenetrate, each forming two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First, concerning purity and impurity: it may be exclusively defiled, or exclusively pure—corresponding to the first two meanings mentioned above;
or it may be both, because the Sahā world exists within the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpasaṃbhava-kṣetra*).
Alternatively, they may be obliterated, for when the characteristics of defilement and purity are exhausted, they are one with the single Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, it may be exclusively defiled, as in the case of the Mahāgrāha [ocean] and so forth, where the characteristics of purity are obscured;
or it may be exclusively pure, as in that ground which is adamantine, where the characteristics of defilement have been exhausted.
Alternatively, they may both be present, because there is no obstruction between their concealment and manifestation;
or they may both be absent, because each negates the other, such that both characteristics are exhausted.
Next, to clarify the two sets of four propositions regarding the interpenetration of the universal and the particular: "or it is particular," because this refers to a single realm.
Alternatively, it is pervasive, because it encompasses the ten directions;
alternatively, it is both, because it is identical to this very place and yet all-pervasive;
alternatively, it is extinguished, because the two characteristics are exhausted.
Furthermore, it may be restricted, because this realm subsumes everything;
it may be pervasive, because this entry encompasses everything;
or it may be both, because it both subsumes and enters.
Alternatively, they may be obliterated, for when form is sublated, all characteristics are exhausted.
Furthermore, by taking a single atom as an analogy for a *kṣetra* (world-system), one should understand that there are likewise four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

If we proceed from the narrow to the broad to briefly manifest ten locations: first, this Jambudvīpa consists of seven places and nine assemblies that pervade the Dharma-realm, as described in the "Chapter on Ascending Mount Sumeru."
Second, pervading ten billion similar realms of the same category, as extensively described in the "Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance";
third, pervading various dissimilar realms such as those shaped like trees;
and fourth, pervading the world-systems (kṣetraprakāra).
Fifth, they pervade the Flower Treasury World;
sixth, they pervade the oceans of other lands, whether by their seeds or their lands;
seventh, they pervade the atoms within the aforementioned six classes of lands, each of which contains both similar and dissimilar lands.
Eighth, throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, within the space of each individual hair-tip, there are infinitely many oceans of lands;
ninth, like a net of Indra;
tenth, identical to all other Buddhas.
However, each of these ten categories individually pervades the entire Dharma-realm; yet, among them, the first nine are precisely the locations where Vairocana preaches the Dharma.

Although these locations for preaching the Ten Abodes and so forth each pervade the Dharma-realm down to every mote of dust and hair, they do not become confused because their respective gateways are distinct.

If one considers the ten abodes (*bhūmi*) and the ten practices (*caryā*) as fully encompassing their respective stages, then they are mutually exclusive, each pervading the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) on its own.
If, however, one considers how these various stages support one another, then they are mutually inclusive, together pervading the entire dharma-realm.
Each chapter and assembly should be understood according to this principle.

Regarding the fact that ten or more Buddhas are identical: since this Buddha is thus, so too are all other Buddhas; therefore, in the concluding passages of each assembly, it is universally stated, "We, all the Buddhas, also speak in this way."
"However, the leaders do not see one another, nor do the companions see one another; it is only when the leaders and companions meet each other that they see one another.
If they do not see one another, then each is individually pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm."
Because they see one another, they are equally pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm; yet there is neither confusion nor obstruction among them.

Furthermore, these ten aforementioned locations function together as a single dependent origination, such that the mention of any one encompasses the whole, for each individual location accords with the nature of reality (dharmatā).

Furthermore, at each preceding moment, [the teaching] pervades all these locations, and in each location, it possesses the preceding moments; thus this sutra is taught instantaneously. This explanation is still made in reference to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).

If one considers them in terms of the world of wisdom-awakening and the world of sentient beings, then every single Buddha’s body—down to its limbs, joints, and pores—encompasses infinite, multilayered lands; this is likewise true for each and every sentient being of Samantabhadra, and all are places where Vairocana preaches the sutras.
Third, regarding the "dependent designation" (tatpuruṣa): The true body is vast and empty, its essence unified with the dharma-realm;
it encompasses all without exterior, its function equal to that of the myriad transformations.

When tracing back to the source, there is no duality; yet when clinging to the traces, there are many divergent paths. Regarding the single body and the multiple bodies, the sūtras and śāstras offer differing explanations.
Now, as we expound this sūtra, is the Buddha the True Body (dharmakāya) or the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya)? Is he one or many?
If you say it is the True Body (dharmakāya), why is it called Śākyamuni, dwelling in the Sahā world, and seen alike by humans and devas?
If you say it is the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya), why is it called Vairocana, dwelling in the Lotus Treasury World, and seen only by great bodhisattvas?
If one sees the Buddha’s Dharma-body as being one, why does it manifest separately in many places?
If one says they are different, why is it further said that he does not divide his body?

Therefore, the Buddha who speaks this sutra is not the one previously described; rather, he is the inexhaustible cloud-body of the *dharmadhātu*, in which the true and the responsive are fused and the one and the many are non-obstructive. Since Vairocana is Śākyamuni, he is constantly here while being elsewhere; he dwells eternally here while remaining far away in other realms. His body is neither divided nor singular, for at the same time and in different places, his single body is perfectly and completely manifested—something that all bodhisattvas cannot conceive.
Now, first we shall clarify the ten bodies, and subsequently manifest their non-obstruction.
Regarding the so-called "ten bodies," there are two senses in which they are established.

First, concerning the integration of the three worlds into ten: (1) the body of sentient beings, (2) the body of the land, (3) the body of karmic retribution, (4) the body of śrāvakas, (5) the body of pratyekabuddhas, (6) the body of bodhisattvas, (7) the body of Tathāgatas, (8) the body of wisdom, (9) the body of Dharma, and (10) the body of empty space.

Second, regarding the Buddha himself, there are ten bodies: first, the Bodhi-body; second, the Vow-body; third, the Transformation-body; fourth, the Sustaining-body; fifth, the Body Adorned with Marks and Signs; sixth, the Majestic Power-body; seventh, the Mind-born-body; eighth, the Merit-body; ninth, the Dharma-body; and tenth, the Wisdom-body.
The detailed exposition of its characteristics is as explained in the Eighth Stage and the "Chapter on Transcending the World.
Regarding the term "unimpeded," there are briefly ten meanings:

first, the unimpeded pervasiveness of function; this refers to the fact that throughout the aforementioned realms of recollection, eons, lands, atoms, and so forth, Vairocana Buddha manifests clouds of Dharma-realm bodies, whose karmic functions are boundless and entirely pervasive.
The sutra states: "Just as one sees the Buddha seated here, so it is in all atoms," and such passages occur more than once.
This refers to the non-obstruction of the pervasiveness of the two aspects, meaning that within each of these aforementioned distinct functions, all karmic activities are subsumed.
Third is the unimpeded function of tranquility, because it is accomplished without partiality.
Fourth is the unimpeded arising based on conditions, because it manifests instantaneously without deliberate thought through the power of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi.
Fifth is the unimpeded nature of the real and the responsive, because the responsive is identical to the Dharma, being of one flavor and equal.
Sixth is the non-obstruction of the six parts being complete, because each individual part contains the entire body.
Seventh is the non-obstruction of cause and effect, because it does not obstruct the manifestation of causes.
Eighth is the non-obstruction of the environment and its inhabitants, because it does not obstruct the manifestation of the environment.
Ninth, it penetrates without obstruction into the realm of sentient beings, like the *tathāgatagarbha*, because although it manifests as sentient beings, it does not lose its own nature.

Thus, the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Samantabhadracaryā-nirdeśa*) states: "The Buddha-wisdom penetrates the minds of sentient beings," and further says: "Within the minds of sentient beings, the Buddha attains perfect enlightenment," and so forth.
Furthermore, it also encompasses all sentient beings, skillfully transforming them within a single pore.
As the Heavenly King said:
"You should observe that within a single pore of the Buddha, all sentient beings are entirely contained therein," and so forth.

The ten kinds of unobstructed perfect penetration refer to this Buddha-body being simultaneously principle and phenomenon, one and many, the basis and the supported, the person and the Dharma, this and that, sentient and non-sentient, profound and vast, cause and fruit, and the three bodies and the ten bodies—all constituting a single cloud of the unobstructed *dharmadhātu*-body.
With these clouds of bodies, they constantly preach the *Avataṃsaka* throughout all times and places.
Thus we know that it is sometimes said that the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) resides in Akaniṣṭha, speaking in terms of its encompassing the retributive fruits;
or it is sometimes said that the reward body resides in other pure lands, speaking in terms of its attracting and gathering beings.
Some say that Vairocana sits upon a thousand-petaled lotus;
this is explained according to the second stage (*bhūmi*).
Others say that one sees him only upon ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*); this is taught in consideration of superior faculties.
To divide [the teachings] into three distinct categories based on essence (*tattva*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and function (*vṛtti*) is not the true meaning of this sutra.

Even if one were to distinguish thirty different types, these would still be explained as a pairing of the provisional and the real; if one does not integrate the preceding meanings, one likewise loses the central tenet of the sutra.
Regarding the fourth reliance on samādhi: movement and stillness pertain only to material things; how could this be the case for the Sage?

To demonstrate the path for future disciples and to clarify what is about to be taught, one must first contemplate the preceding principles with a tranquil mirror-like mind and receive the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas.
Upon arising from meditative concentration, he speaks, and his words are invariably true and appropriate.
Because his words are invariably true and appropriate, the minds of those who receive them naturally become profound and sincere.
Therefore, across various assemblies, he frequently clarifies that entering meditative concentration is the condition for preaching the sutras.
As for those who do not enter [this state], it shall be explained when we reach the relevant passage.
As for the meditative absorptions they enter, all exhaust the source of the Dharma;

their functional efficacy is inconceivable. Regarding the fifth point, "relying on manifested signs": although the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is tranquil and devoid of characteristics, these "signs of signlessness" do not obstruct the profusion of activity. The methods for initiating the teaching are manifold, and its manifestations are not uniform. Whether emitting light and shaking the lands, or raining flowers and producing clouds of incense, all serve to give rise to [the teaching].
Therefore, within the various assemblies, when he is about to preach the Dharma, he first frequently emits light; this universally symbolizes that the light of wisdom is used to encompass all beings.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the light that does not disrupt the sequential order, as it increases or diminishes according to the respective stages.
Second is the unobstructed light of perfect penetration, because each and every ray of light is universally connected.
These rays are emitted differently according to their respective locations; in total there are ten rays, each of which symbolizes something specific, as shall be understood from the text itself.
Regarding such phenomena as the shaking of the earth, these mostly occur subsequent to a teaching; thus, they serve merely as celebrations of what has been heard.

For example, in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, although these events celebrate what preceded them, their meaning also encompasses the initiation of what follows, thereby serving as conditions for the teaching.
The sixth point concerns the person who expounds the teaching: the Dharma neither perishes nor arises; its propagation depends upon people.
As the subsequent text states: "If the Buddha-dharma were not expounded by someone, even those with wisdom could not comprehend it."
Now, this "capable speaker" (the teacher) pervades the three worlds; when expanded, they constitute five types: namely, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, sentient beings, and the receptacle world.

These are further expanded into ten categories by adding the three periods of time, atoms (*paramāṇu*), pores, the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), and sentient beings (*sattva*), each of which has both partial and complete aspects.
Pores and atoms are thus explained in terms of their partial aspects.

Because all the aforementioned explanations pertain to the three periods of time, the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" states: "The Buddha speaks, sentient beings speak, and lands speak; thus they speak throughout the three periods of time," and so forth, extensively and immeasurably.
Because the categories [of teachings] in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" are not uniform— just as the *saṃghāṭa* [sūtra] contains the marks of excellence (*anuvyañjana*) taught by the Buddha himself—
while other assemblies consist mostly of teachings spoken by bodhisattvas,
the beginning of the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" contains teachings spoken by śrāvakas.
The various spiritual friends and so forth are spoken of as the many bodhisattvas, and are also called the "speaking of sentient beings.
The Bodhi tree and so forth are the speaking of the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*).
This shall be understood from the text itself.
As for those who can preach it, their methods differ: some employ vocal sounds, while others employ sublime forms and so forth, as explained in the section on the "Body of the Teaching.
Seventh, regarding the listener: when Ziqi heard of his father’s death, he ceased playing the strings of his lute for a hundred days.
If there were no listeners, there would ultimately be no speaking.
As for the various assemblies below, they are briefly categorized into ten types, which shall be clarified in the text itself.
Excluding those who are the primary audience (the *dharmapratipanna*), all others are merely conditions (*pratyaya*).

Eighth, regarding the basis of the root of virtue: a stream does not dry up because it contains pearls, and a mountain becomes more lush because it contains jade; if one lacks the root of virtue within, how can one possibly discourse upon it without?
However, regarding the speaker alone, because this person possesses this dharma,
there are briefly two categories:
first, those for whom wisdom is the foremost.
The Buddhas of the ten directions said to Vajradhvaja:
"And it is because of the purity of your wisdom.
They then addressed Vajragarbha:
"This is also due to the power of your supreme wisdom.
Second is the power of other practices and vows.
The Buddhas of the ten directions addressed Samantabhadra, saying:
"Furthermore, it is by the power of the vows and all practices you have cultivated," the Buddhas of the ten directions said to Dharmamati,
"as well as by the power of the roots of goodness you have cultivated, that you shall enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma."
Whether it be the roots of goodness of those who are moved to respond, or the conduct and vows of the master of transformation, all belong to the category of causes for teaching.
Regarding the ninth point, concerning the person who requests: if one considers the depth of their compassion, there are instances where the Buddha speaks of his own accord without being asked;
however, if one considers the reverence for the Dharma and respect for the person, it is necessary that he speak only after a sincere request has been made.
Those of initial resolve have dull consciousness and do not yet understand how to seek instruction;
those of superior wisdom possess compassion and raise doubts to request clarification.
Furthermore, there are two categories:
The first is the request through speech; the second is the request through mindfulness.
Whether such assemblies exist or not shall be discussed in the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs.

Regarding the tenth [point], which relies on the one capable of bestowing empowerment: the Sage has no fixed response; he responds to sincere devotion. Because the mind merges with the ultimate, one receives the Buddha's empowerment.
However, if the Buddha speaks for himself, there is no need for supplementation.
As in the ninth assembly, because the discourse was delivered by others, it necessarily required the addition of the prefix "supra-.
In the eighth assembly, since the practice is cultivated in accordance with the Dharma and does not differ from what preceded, there is no such supplement.
Because [the Buddha] did not enter meditative absorption during the second seven-day period, there was no additional empowerment; otherwise, all [empowerments] were fully present.

The reason for this additional empowerment is to demonstrate that the empowerment of all Buddhas is identical to their teaching, and that what is taught by one is taught by all; it also demonstrates that while the ocean of fruition is ineffable, its causal characteristics can be explained.

If that were so, the *anuvyañjanas* (secondary marks) of the Saṃghāṭa-sūtra would not be "all-encompassing," because they manifest as subtle and difficult to perceive, and because they transcend [ordinary] causes and effects.
However, since their designations differ, one should not apply a single standard to them all.
There are two kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*):
first, manifest empowerment, which is endowed with the three karmas;
second, hidden empowerment, which merely bestows wisdom so that one may preach.
In the Dharmadhātu of Universal Radiance, there is no manifestation and only obscurity;
all others possess both, because wherever there is manifestation, there must necessarily be obscurity.
The details of the others will be clarified below.
The section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching is complete.
Second, regarding the inclusion within the scriptural collections (*piṭaka*), there are two parts:
first, inclusion by collection; second, inclusion by teaching.
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, the inclusion [of the categories], and second, the subsumption [of the dharmas].
Now, for the first.
The "Pitakas" (piṭaka) refer to the Three Pitakas and the Two Pitakas.
They are collectively termed "Pitakas" because they contain and encompass [the teachings].
Both Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (First Chapter) and the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* (Fourth Chapter) state: "Regarding those three and two, why are they called 'Pitakas'?"
The answer states:
It is by way of inclusion; that is to say, it includes all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
"Inclusion" means encompassing.
Regarding the "Three Piṭakas," they are: first, the Sūtra Piṭaka; second, the Vinaya Piṭaka; and third, the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
Concerning the first [the Sūtra Piṭaka], we shall first analyze its name and subsequently clarify its characteristics.
First: it is also called *sūtra* and also called *sūtrānta*; these are merely variations in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit term.
In ancient translations it was rendered as "Kie-ching" (Scripture of Concordance), and within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is termed the "Sūtra Piṭaka."

"Sūtra" (契) means "conforming to principle" and "conforming to capacity"; "scripture" (經) means "penetrating" and "gathering/transforming. Thus, it is a scripture that conforms to principle and accords with capacity, receiving its name through the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
"Sūtra-piṭaka" (契經藏) is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
It further states:
"The direct translation of the name is 'sūtra' (line).
A line can string together flowers; a sūtra can hold the warp threads."
In this region, the term "sūtra" (line) is not esteemed, and thus it has been retained in the scriptures.

Some say: "According to the five regions of India, the terms used for a line, a weaving shuttle, a well-rope, and the holy teaching are all called *sūtra*; therefore, 'scripture' (*jing*) is precisely its direct equivalent. This refutes the view of ancient masters who claimed that "scripture" is not the direct equivalent.
Now let us examine this in detail.
If the single term "one" (eka) refers to four distinct realities and all function as opposites (*pratipakṣa*), then it would be refuted by the previous argument.

However, if it also carries the sense of "conforming" (*anugama*), then the sūtra itself belongs to the category of *śikṣāpada-sūtra* (sūtras on training rules), whereas its opposite should be termed *āryadeśanā* (noble teaching); thus, the Liang dynasty translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* renders it as "noble teaching."
That treatise states: "There are Abhidharma works that are not the word of the Buddha (āgama); in order to establish them as such, the term 'Sūtra' is added.

Seeing that the Confucians and Mohists both refer to their texts as "Jing" (Classics), the ancients borrowed this term from them to designate the Buddhist scriptures; thus, it encompasses both meanings and accords with both traditions.
Borrowing the meaning to assist the name and further adding the character "qie" (契), it is highly appropriate for distinguishing it from the *xi* (席) and *jing* (經).

Second, regarding the manifestation of its characteristics: although the four names used in the Western Regions differ in their referents, they are similar in meaning and purpose; therefore, they are collectively termed *sūtra*.
Furthermore, the holy teaching is richly imbued with the three aforementioned meanings; thus, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states: "The Sūtra possesses five meanings:
first, a spring; second, a source of birth; third, illumination; fourth, a measuring line; and fifth, a string of garlands."

The surging spring pours forth without exhaustion; that which gives birth increases and multiplies through successive stages. The meaning is the same as that of a well-rope, for there is drawing up and leading forth.
This clearly demonstrates the true holy teaching, as it reveals both phenomena and principle.
The cord and ink-line serve to calibrate and determine what is correct and what is deviant; thus, the cord is also the warp.
It can sustain the woof, sharing the same function as the warp of a mat.
A garland is like a thread: the thread can string together flowers because it forms the garland.

In summary, these five meanings do not transcend the principles of "pervasion" (*gan*) and "inclusion" (*she*). Therefore, the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* states: "It is called a *sūtra* because it can pervade and include; for the holy teachings of the Buddha pervade and sustain the meanings that ought to be explained and the sentient beings who are to be converted."

This [term "pervasion" (*praveśa*)] may refer to the comprehensive inclusion of that which is taught and those who are to be converted; or it may mean to penetrate the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and to sustain those who are to be converted.

Furthermore, Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* explains "penetration" as follows: "That is to say, it is able to penetrate by way of the basis (*āśraya*), the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the phenomenon (*dharma*), and the meaning (*artha*)."
The basis refers to that which is spoken of, the means by which it is spoken, and the purpose for which it is spoken.
The characteristics refer to the characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the characteristics of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

"Dharma" refers to the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), truths (satya), nutriments (āhāra), meditative absorptions (dhyāna), immeasurables (apramāṇa), formless attainments (ārūpya), liberations (vimokṣa), bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), bases of totality (kṛtsnāyatana), factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), the absence of contention (araṇā), and so forth.
"Meaning" refers to that which accords with the intentional terminology (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) and so forth.
The twenty-fifth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the twentieth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* state this in the same way.
The remaining meanings shall be clarified in the section on the twelvefold division [of the scriptures].
Second is the Vinaya Piṭaka; its initial name and subsequent characteristics are as follows.
Within the former, it is also called *vinaya*, which is merely an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term.
This is translated as "discipline" (vinaya), meaning the refinement of the three karmas and the subduing of transgressions and errors.
Refinement pertains to both abstention and performance, whereas subduing clarifies only the cessation of evil.
The name is manifested based on the conduct that is expressed; it is thus the "Treasury of Discipline" (*Vinayapiṭaka*).
Alternatively, it is the "Treasury that expresses" [the discipline], possessing the capacity for discipline; this is an *upapadavigraha* (possessive compound).
In the Sūtra Piṭaka, there are similar explanations of this.
Vinaya is sometimes translated as "extinction" (nirodha).
This extinction has three meanings:
First, the cessation of unwholesome karma; second, the cessation of afflictions; third, the attainment of the fruit of cessation.
It is also called *śīla*; in its full form it is *śītalā*, which here means "cooling," because one abandons the causes of feverish affliction and attains the fruit of coolness.
It is also called *pratimokṣa*, which translates as "individual liberation. This name is derived from its cause, yet it carries two meanings:
first, it is termed "individual" (*prati*) because it distinguishes itself from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*);
second, it is termed "individual" because each of the two types of karma and seven branches separately prevents unwholesome conduct.

It is also translated as "conforming to liberation" (*anuloma-vimukti*), which is established based on its fruit, because it conforms to the two kinds of fruits of liberation: conditioned and unconditioned.
It is also called "virtuous by nature," and as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is also called "keeping one's word," because it truly enables one to maintain what was previously undertaken.
Regarding the subsequent exposition of characteristics: these were already implicitly contained within the names mentioned previously, namely the characteristics of the *vinaya*.
To explain them separately, Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "The *vinaya* has four meanings: namely, by way of the offense, the motivation, the purification, and the renunciation."
The details are as found in that treatise.
Regarding the third, the Abhidharma Piṭaka: *abhi* means "toward" or "in opposition," and *dharma* means "phenomenon" (*dharma*).
There are two kinds of phenomena: first, the ultimate phenomenon (*paramārtha-dharma*), which refers to nirvāṇa itself; because it is virtuous and eternal, it is called "ultimate."
The two categories of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa-dharma) encompass the four noble truths.
"Characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) refers to both nature (svabhāva) and appearance (ākṛti); both are termed "characteristics.
Since there are these two types of phenomena, their counterparts likewise possess a twofold meaning:
First is "confrontation" (pratimukha), which refers to facing toward nirvāṇa;
second is "contemplation" (pratyavekṣaṇā), which refers to contemplating the four noble truths before one.

Those that are capable of such confrontation consist of untainted pure wisdom (*anāsrava-śuddha-prajñā*) and its associated mental factors (*caitta*). These are divided into two types of "confrontation"—namely, confrontation with the fruit and confrontation with the object—hence the designation of two types of confrontation.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is that which is opposed, but it is not itself an object of opposition (*dharma*), because it is not something to be opposed.

That which is called "Abhidharma" (Dharma-against) is so named because it is the opponent of [ignorance regarding] dharmas; therefore, the Abhidharmakośa is specifically termed a treatise on wisdom (*prajñā-śāstra*). It was translated in the past as "Incomparable Dharma" (*anupama-dharma*), because it serves to characterize the excellence of wisdom.
Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* states: "The Abhidharma has four meanings: namely, 'confrontation' (abhi), 'enumeration' (dharmāḥ), 'subduing' (abhibhava), and 'penetration' (abhigama).
The meaning of "confrontation" is the same as previously explained.

"Enumeration" (*saṃkhyā*) refers to the repeated proclamation and explanation of words regarding each individual phenomenon, due to the infinite distinctions such as specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
"Overpowering" (*abhibhava*) refers to the ability to overcome the arguments of others by virtue of possessing the bases of discourse (*vādādhikaraṇa*) and so forth.
"Compendium" (*abhidharma*) refers to its ability to comprehensively explain the meaning of the *sūtras*.
It is also called *upadeśa*, which means "exposition of meaning";
it is also called *mātṛkā*, which means "matrix" (*mūla*), signifying that it takes both the teaching and its meaning as its basis and source.
It is also said that understanding arises based on the Piṭaka; the Piṭaka is the mother of understanding, for the root itself is the mother.
It is also called Mātṛkā, which here means "mother of practice," because one accomplishes practice by relying on the Piṭaka and because it is the mother of practice.
However, regarding these Three Piṭakas, there are briefly two approaches based on what they expound:

first, in terms of their essential nature, the Sūtras expound the three trainings; the Vinaya expounds only the two trainings of ethical discipline and mind; and the Śāstras expound only the training of wisdom, as stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

Second, regarding the distinction between the primary and the ancillary: within the Three Piṭakas, the Sūtras primarily elucidate meditative concentration (samādhi), the Vinaya elucidates ethical discipline (śīla), and the Śāstras elucidate wisdom (prajñā); yet each of these also ancillarily encompasses all three.
Second, the explanation of the two collections (*piṭaka*): first, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
It is precisely because the former three collections elucidate the principles, practices, and fruits of the śrāvakas that they are called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
and because they elucidate the principles, practices, and fruits of the bodhisattvas, they are called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Therefore, the fourth chapter of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (*Śāstravyākhyā*) states: "These three piṭakas, through the distinction between the Lesser and Greater Vehicles, further constitute the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka."
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* agrees with this.
This [classification] combines them because the principles and fruits of the two vehicles are identical.

However, if distinguished according to their teachings and practices, they are opened up as three vehicles to constitute the Three Piṭakas, as in the *Samantaprabhā-samādhi-sūtra* and other such scriptures.

Furthermore, because Pratyekabuddhas generally do not rely on the teachings and appear in eras when no Buddha is present—whereas during the time a Buddha dwells in the world they are subsumed under the Śrāvakas—they are divided into only two categories; that is, the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, or the Half and Full Teachings.

Second, regarding what it comprises: among the three baskets (*piṭaka*), this sutra is primarily comprised within the Sūtra-piṭaka, while it also encompasses the other two, because chapters such as the "Ten Baskets" extensively reveal the precepts (*śīla*), and chapters such as the "Inquiry on Knowledge" (*Prajñāpṛcchā*) clarify the meaning of the treatises (*śāstra*).

If one distinguishes the teaching by its meaning within the Sūtras, it is subsumed solely within the *Daśadharmaka-sūtra*, because it fully possesses the primary and attendant teachings to manifest inexhaustibility and because the teaching and its meaning are fused; thus, among the two collections (*piṭakas*), it belongs exclusively to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
If one distinguishes between the provisional and the ultimate, it is subsumed under only one portion of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, because the provisional is not included therein.
However, if categorized according to this inclusion, even the Śrāvakas are subsumed within this sūtra, for it is capable of encompassing immeasurable vehicles.
The distinction between the provisional and the ultimate will be clarified below in the section on the establishment of the teachings.
Having already analyzed the inclusion within the *piṭakas*, the second part clarifies the inclusion within the teachings. Regarding the teachings, there are two types:

First is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*): the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) is also divided into Great and Small Vehicles, which will be explained below in the "Chapter on the Ten Stores" (*Daśadharmaka-parivarta*).
Second is the fact that the various schools establish their teachings differently; this shall now be briefly explained.

The ocean of his teaching is vast and profound; the clouds of the Dharma spread everywhere. His light of wisdom is boundless, and his wondrous eloquence is inexhaustible. Through words that are wordless, he expounds principles beyond the reach of speech; through transformations that are unchanging, he responds to infinite capacities. What he has inherited from the ultimate station is difficult for ordinary minds to fathom.
Now, relying on the power of principle and teaching, I shall briefly open four gates:

first, the convergence and divergence of the central intent; second, the contradictions and harmonies between the ancient and the present; third, the classification of schools and the establishment of teachings; and fourth, the comprehensive reconciliation and integration.

First, regarding the various traditions that have propagated and expounded [the teachings] in the Western Regions and the Eastern Lands (China) concerning the sacred words of a single lifetime: some establish schools and divide the teachings, while others provide direct commentaries on the scriptural texts; this is because all such approaches contain both merits and shortcomings.
Furthermore, the meaning of non-differentiation consists briefly of five points:
first, because the principle is fundamentally of a single flavor, and though there are diverse paths, they all lead to the same destination; thus, it cannot be divided.
Second, because a single sound universally responds and a single rain universally nourishes.
Third, because the intention of the holy sages of the three origins is for the sake of a single matter;
fourth, because the various interpretations differ according to each individual passage;
and fifth, because the many types of dharma teachings form various branches and streams.
For these five reasons, it is not to be divided.
To divide it would cause the mind to construct heterodox views and lead to the proliferation of disputes over right and wrong; therefore, non-division is considered the attainment.
Regarding the classification of the teachings, there are also several meanings:
first, although the principle is of a single flavor, the explanations vary in depth; therefore, it is necessary to classify them so that one may understand the provisional and the real.
Second, although the Buddha possesses but a single voice, the teachings differ according to the distinctions among those who respond to his call.
Third, because his original intent has not yet been fully expressed, there are differences arising from speech that accords with the intentions of others.
The four statements have both general and specific meanings, as they are explained according to their manifest expression.
Although the fifth is divided into provisional and ultimate, one must skillfully harmonize the Buddha’s intent, for there is an opening toward manifestation.
Furthermore, the King’s esoteric words are intended for a distinct purpose.
Failing to distinguish between the provisional and the ultimate, one regards the profound as shallow and thus loses great benefit;
conversely, regarding the shallow as profound renders one's efforts vain.

This is because the holy teachings are adorned to become profound and vast, because there are naturally distinct divisions within the various holy teachings, and because the great Bodhisattvas have also expounded these teachings.
For these many reasons, to open [the text] results in gaining much while losing little, whereas to close it results in gaining little while losing much.
However, as long as one can empty oneself to seek the fundamental principle, there is no harm in dividing what should not be divided; thus, I have now divided it.
The second section, concerning the agreement and disagreement between ancient and modern [views], is divided into two parts:
first, an account of this land (China), and second, an elucidation of the Western Regions (India).
This is the first part.
Although the Śākyas are numerous, I shall briefly outline several schools and condense them into five categories:
first, the establishment of the doctrine of a single sound (*ekasvara-dharma*), which holds that the teachings of the Tathāgata throughout his entire life do not depart from a single sound.
However, there were two masters:
the first was Bodhiruci of the Later Wei, who said:
"The Tathāgata’s single voice simultaneously responds to the myriad beings, presenting both the Great and the Small teachings together."
The Dharma Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty said:

"The Buddha’s single, perfect voice is equal and non-dual; it responds universally without deliberation, yet sentient beings hear it differently according to their own capacities. This does not mean that the original vocal sounds themselves present [teachings] as either Great or Small."
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own capacity.

Regarding these two masters mentioned above, the former holds that the Buddha’s voice possesses diversity, while the latter holds that the diversity resides in the capacities of the listeners; each arrives at the same meaning of the Perfect Voice (*pūrṇa-svara*). Nevertheless, both views are intended to clarify the underlying unity within the teachings.
The second classification establishes two types of teaching, which itself comprises four schools:

first, the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of Western Qin established the teachings of the "Half" and the "Full," wherein the Śrāvaka Piṭaka constitutes the Half-character Teaching and the Bodhisattva Piṭaka constitutes the Full-character Teaching.
Dharma Master Suiyuan also established this same position.

This is based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which primarily clarifies the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) in contrast to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna); it expresses the general characteristics [of the teaching] but does not yet explicitly distinguish between the provisional and the real within the Great Vehicle, nor does it encompass both the Half-[teaching] and the Full-[teaching].

Second, Dharma Master Huiyuan of the Sui dynasty established the two teachings of Gradual and Sudden. He maintained that with respect to those of gradual enlightenment, the Great [Vehicle] arises from the Small; because the teachings provided therein possess all three vehicles, it is called "Gradual.
If, however, one considers those of sudden capacity, who proceed directly to the Great without passing through the Small, it is called "Sudden."

Although this [classification] is spoken of in terms of the capacities of sentient beings as having gradual and sudden aspects, the teachings expounded do not go beyond the "Half" and "Full" [vehicles].
Third, during the early Tang dynasty, Master Yin also established two teachings:

first, the "Crooked Teaching," which refers to the sutras of Śākyamuni; because they follow the dispositions and calculations of sentient beings to break their attachments, such as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and others.

The second is the teaching of the Equal Way (Samatā-yāna), which refers to the Vairocana Sūtras, because they explain the Dharma-nature through the principle of sovereign mastery, such as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, there are briefly four differences between these two teachings:
first, the difference in the principal [teacher], meaning that Śākyamuni’s transformation body differs from the ten bodies of Vairocana.

First, the difference in location: this refers to the distinction between the wooden trees and grass seats of the Sahā world and the jewel trees and precious seats within the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha).
Second, the difference in the assembly: this refers to the distinction between teachings spoken for both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, and those spoken solely for Bodhisattvas at the ultimate stage.
Third, the difference in the teaching itself: this refers to the distinction between teachings restricted to a specific locality and those that pervade the ten directions.
This is a judgment based on the pedagogical methods of transformation (*nirmāṇa-vidhi*).

However, although the *Avataṃsaka* contains various means of taming individual sentient beings, these are all skillful means that accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), expounded all at once and instantaneously.

Although the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and others speak of the ultimate one, whether by revealing the real through the provisional or by reconciling differences to return to unity, all Tathāgatas may either teach or not teach; therefore, it is said to be "indirect" (*ku-chü*).
If Śākyamuni is taken as the primary subject, the ten bodies (daśakāya) have not yet been revealed; yet where the ten bodies are primary, they necessarily include Śākyamuni.
Where this Sahā world has not yet merged with the Flower Treasury World (Puṣpaka-dhātu), the Flower Treasury World must necessarily merge with the Sahā world.

Briefly stated, there are four differences, though in reality there are many; this is indeed as you have judged. However, it is simply because within the "crooked" (provisional) teachings, the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Dharma have not yet been revealed.

During the Qi dynasty, the reclusive scholar Liu Qiu also established two teachings—the gradual and the sudden—stating that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is called the "Sudden Teaching," while all others are called "Gradual," because they proceed from small to great, beginning at the Deer Park and ending at the Twin Trees.
However, this sutra is like the rising sun that first illuminates the high mountains; this is the meaning of the sudden (sudden teaching).
That Maitreya and Nāgārjuna sent down rain to testify to the gradual (gradual teaching) may well be so from the perspective of principle.
The gradual [teaching] will be discussed in detail below in five periods. Regarding the third point, the establishment of three types of teaching, there are likewise three schools of thought.

First, the various masters of the Southern and Central regions collectively establish three teachings: namely, they add the "indeterminate" (*aniyata*) teaching to the previously mentioned gradual and sudden teachings. Because within the gradual teaching there is a sequence from the small to the great, yet the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* states that [the Buddha] taught [the Mahāyāna] within six years, they established the indeterminate teaching to resolve this difficulty. This means that there is a separate class of sūtras which, while not included under the sudden category, clarify the eternal abiding of the Buddha-nature; these include the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, and others—these constitute the "partial and indeterminate" teaching.
Regarding the gradual teaching (*zhan*), there are differing views among various masters concerning its classification.
Some divide it into only two categories, namely the "half" and the "full";

others divide it into three, such as Master Yi of Mount Wuchuan, who asserts that for twelve years prior [to the Lotus Sūtra], the teaching was seen as one where there is attainment of the Way, and thus it is called the "teaching with signs" (*xiangjiao*).
Twelve years later, reaching as far as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one perceives emptiness and attains the Way; this is called the Teaching of Non-characteristic (*animitta*).

Finally, there is the simultaneous illumination of the Buddha-nature in all sentient beings and the attainment of Buddhahood even by those who have abandoned all hope (*icchantika*); this is called the Teaching of Eternal Abiding (*nitya*).

This is largely identical to the teaching of the three periods established by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty; it will be discussed in detail in the section on the accounts from the Western Regions.

The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, relying on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, established the teaching of the three wheels—turning, illuminating, and sustaining—which is also largely identical to this [system], though with slight differences in their chronological sequence.
This means that the teaching of the Four Noble Truths during the first seven years was called the "Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
During the seven years thereafter, the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* constituted both the turning and the illuminating wheels, because emptiness (*śūnyatā*) illuminates existence.
Thirty years later, there was the complete turning, illuminating, and sustaining [wheel], because the simultaneous illumination of both emptiness and existence sustains the two preceding ones.
