Alternatively, they are divided into four; that is, the Dharma Master Zhòuyí of the Sòng dynasty asserted that between the three preceding periods and the period of eternal abiding following the signless, the *Lotus Sūtra* constitutes the "Teaching of Common Return," because it unifies the three vehicles into one and directs all myriad virtues toward Bodhi.
Alternatively, it may be expanded into five categories, for which there are two schools of thought:

first, Daochang, Huiquan, and others maintain that between the "Teaching of No-Form" (*wuxiang*) and the "Teaching of Common Return" (*tonggui*), works such as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* constitute the "Teaching of Suppression and Elevation" (*yiyang jiao*).

The second is the aforementioned Master Liu, who did not employ the method of alternating emphasis and suppression; rather, at the very beginning of his teaching, he took the *Tiewei jing* (Sutra on the Extraction of the Stomach) as the teaching for humans and devas.

The various masters mentioned above all differentiated their teachings based on time within the gradual approach; however, if the indeterminate teaching were not added, it would give rise to many difficulties, because there was already a "Great" [teaching] at the outset.
Even with the addition of the indeterminate teaching, there still remain obstacles and difficulties.
This briefly demonstrates the contradictions regarding the five periods; the rest may be understood by analogy.
First, to clarify that the period prior to twelve years was characterized by "having signs" (sanimitta) contradicts the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* itself.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "I now precisely clarify the true meaning within the Three Piṭakas; the true meaning is emptiness.
Furthermore, the *Āgamas* state: "There is no aging and death," which refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
"There is no one who ages and dies," which refers to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Within the Tripiṭaka, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is explained as the Great Emptiness; within the Mahāyāna, the emptiness of the ten directions is explained as the Great Emptiness.
This demonstrates that both types of emptiness already exist within the Hīnayāna.
If it is said that emptiness was taught during the second period, then since the extensive precepts were only established twelve years later, how could it have been that he taught only emptiness?
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "From the night of his attainment of the Way until his parinirvāṇa, he constantly taught the Prajñā."
"Did you not previously speak of emptiness?
If you say that permanence was not yet revealed during the second period [of the Buddha's teaching], could the *prajñā* of the true mark (*dharmatā*) possibly be impermanent?

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also states, 'Buddha-nature is also called *prajñā*. From this we know that the *prajñā* of the true mark is the direct cause (*hetu-bīja*) of Buddhahood, while contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*) is the enabling cause (*parigraha-hetu*)."
Furthermore, since the *Prajñāpāramitā* is free from the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*), when has it ever maintained emptiness?
Since the *Prajñāpāramitā* does not destroy the four propositions, how could it lack wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara-bhāva*)?
Thus we know that both the Small and Great Vehicles each possess four gates; yet, to speak only of "existence first and emptiness next" is merely to grasp the meaning of one gate each.

If it is claimed that in the third period there is merely the name of "suppression and exaltation" and that this too is not eternal, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The Buddha-body is unconditioned; it does not fall within the realm of numerical categories."
"Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha likewise"—how could this not mean that [the Buddha] is impermanent?

The *Prajñāpāramitā* also says, "The wisdom of the two vehicles is like the light of a firefly, while the wisdom learned by a Bodhisattva in a single day is like the illumination of the sun. Is this not a case of suppression and exaltation?

If it is argued that the fourth period merely reveals the commonality of ultimate return and does not clarify permanence, how could this be so when the "Chapter on Lifespan" states, "constantly abiding and never perishing," and the "Chapter on Expedient Means" states, "the characteristics of the world are constantly abiding," and so forth? How could these not be permanent?
Regarding the fifth point, that which takes *nirvāṇa* as eternally abiding (*nitya*), it would indeed be appropriate to teach it accordingly;
however, even at the time of *nirvāṇa*, there exists the view of the *Hīnayāna*, as the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa* are described in the *Āgamas*.
If one takes humans and devas as the starting point, although Devadatta preached the precepts and attained the Way,
all [who did so] were included within the three vehicles.

Therefore, that sutra states that Tiwei attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); furthermore, this would contradict the *Guhyakapada-sutra*, which speaks of the three vehicles during the second seven-day period.
However, regarding the aforementioned five periods and so forth, if they were all strictly defined by their temporal duration, there would be contradictions;
yet, if one excludes the indeterminate cases and speaks according to the majority, there is likewise reason for this approach.

Second, the Vinaya Master Guangtong of the Later Wei dynasty inherited and studied the Tripiṭaka of Buddhatrāta and likewise established three teachings: the Gradual (jiàn), the Sudden (dùn), and the Perfect (yuán).

The first is for those whose faculties are not yet mature; one first preaches impermanence and only later permanence, first emptiness and later non-emptiness, and so forth through such successive stages, which is therefore called "Gradual."

Second, for those whose faculties are mature, he fully expounds all aspects of a single dharma-gate—such as permanence and impermanence, emptiness and non-emptiness—and teaches everything at once without further recourse to gradual stages; therefore, it is called "sudden."

Third, for those who have attained the higher stages and are approaching the realm of Buddhahood, the Tathāgata expounds the secret and sovereign Dharma-gate of the ultimate fruit-virtue of unimpeded liberation; therefore, it is called "Perfect" (Yuan).
This also concerns the method of transformation (teaching), and thus speaks of a sequence of before and after.
The intent clarifies that those capable of receiving the sudden teaching at the present time must have previously undergone transformation.
The expressions "mature faculties" and "attaining the supreme" carry meanings that encompass the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi.
To categorize the stages of the Buddha’s realm as being "on the ground" (bhūmi) is also logically consistent. Third,
during the end of the Sui and beginning of the Tang dynasties, the Dharma Master Jizang established three types of *dharmacakra* based on the fifth chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
First, "Upon first seeing my body and hearing what I have taught, they immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata" refers to the Fundamental Wheel of Dharma;
second, "except for those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna" refers to the Branch and Subordinate Wheel of Dharma;
third, "I now also cause them to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom" refers to the Wheel of Dharma that gathers the branches back to the root.
This classification is entirely based on the pedagogical methods of transformation (*nirmāṇa-vinaya*); according to the Dharma itself, there is only the distinction between Great and Small.

However, since the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals the beginning and the end for a specific class of beings, if one were to use it as a definitive criterion to judge the entire body of the Buddha’s teachings, its scope would be incomplete; for even prior to the *Lotus*, there was already the "Great" [Vehicle]. How could it be that the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras are all merely branches and secondary?
Furthermore, the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (Wúliàngyì jīng) states: "The Buddha preaches both the Great and Small [Vehicles] at all times.

Regarding the fourth section, the establishment of the four teachings, there are briefly four schools of thought:

first, Dharma Master Guangzhai of the Liang dynasty, who based himself on the second chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to establish the teaching of the four vehicles; he maintained that the three carts at the gate represent the provisional teaching of the three vehicles.

The "bestowal of equal gifts at the crossroads" refers to the Mahāyāna of the True Teaching (*samyag-deśanā*). This is because the ox-cart at the gate is identical to the sheep- and deer-carts in that neither can be obtained; because they both lack intrinsic substance; and because all the children requested them. Thus, we know that all three were merely empty pointers used as skillful means (*upāya*).
Thus, the former three [teachings] constitute the Three Vehicles and the latter one constitutes the One Vehicle; this does not contradict scriptural authority or logical principle.

If one were to claim that only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the ultimate truth, then one would be disparaging all the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and other Mahāyāna sūtras of definitive meaning. Therefore, we know that within the "Great" [teachings] of the past, there was both the provisional and the real. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* merely reconciles the provisional aspects of the past; thus it says that the three [vehicles] are all empty, pointing toward the reality of the past. Because it does not linger in expedient means, it does not reconcile them [with the provisional].
If one brings together the provisional to return to the real, this is the convergence of three into one.
If one refutes the small to reveal the great, this is the convergence of two into one.
If one opens up the provisional to reveal the real, then the three are the one; there is no separate "one" apart from them.
Therefore, that sutra says: "That which you all practice is the bodhisattva path; what was previously brought forth and internalized is what this son knows.

If one sets aside the provisional to establish the real, it is explained as fourfold in meaning, just as the three dots are gathered to form the letter *i*: the dots are distinct from the *i*, yet the *i* possesses the three dots.
In the past, once the three [vehicles] were distinguished, they did not in fact encompass the provisional authority;
now, as the One Vehicle fully encompasses all, it establishes the four [teachings] without error.

If, according to the past, it had not yet been explicitly taught that all possess the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, then those whose seeds were ruined are now all said to achieve perfection. Thus, there is a difference between the past and the present; this is supported by the textual evidence, and the meaning is also thoroughly established.
Second, during the two dynasties of Chen and Sui, the Tiantai Master Zhiyi, following the Great Master Nanyue Huisi, established the Fourfold Teaching (*caturvidha-deśanā*), which states:

First is the Tripitaka Teaching (*piṭakatraya-deśanā*). This teaching clarifies the principle of the four noble truths of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions; it primarily teaches the Śrāvaka vehicle while incidentally transforming Bodhisattvas.
The second is the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*). "Shared" means common, because the three vehicles equally receive its transmission.

This teaching elucidates the principle of the four noble truths—that dependent origination is itself emptiness and non-arising; it is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna, primarily intended for bodhisattvas while incidentally accessible to those of the two vehicles.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Those who wish to attain the Śrāvaka vehicle should study the Prajñāpāramitā," and so forth.

However, while the teaching, wisdom, realization, severance, practice, stages, causes, and fruits are all common [to all vehicles], they differ in their depth; thus, regarding the shared Prajñā, it is shared only at the shallow level.
Third is the Separate Teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*). "Separate" means not shared; it is so called because it is taught for those who are not common with the followers of the Two Vehicles.

This teaching correctly elucidates the principle of the four noble truths as being infinitely diverse, provisional names based on causes and conditions. It specifically transforms bodhisattvas and does not involve the followers of the Two Vehicles; therefore, when śrāvakas are present in the assembly, they are as if deaf and blind.

The reason it is not termed "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) but rather called "distinct" is that this also intends to exclude what is not the Perfect [Teaching]. This is because, in the distinct teaching, a single cause stands apart and a single fruit is not integrated; one practices through successive stages and thus fails to attain the perfect integration of cause and fruit.
Fourth is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). "Perfect" (*yuan*) takes the meaning of being non-biased.

This teaching correctly elucidates the Middle Way of the two truths of inconceivable *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination), wherein phenomena and principle are complete, neither biased nor distinct. Because it transforms only those of the highest and sharpest faculties, it is called "Perfect."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Manifesting the power of sovereign mastery, he preaches the Perfect Sūtra;
immeasurable sentient beings all receive the prediction of Bodhi," and so forth.
In the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka*), the doctrine, principle, and so forth are all distinct; in the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa*), the doctrine and everything else are all perfect.

Furthermore, these four teachings arise from three types of contemplation: because there is a distinction between analytical and essential [emptiness] when entering emptiness from the conventional, the first two teachings arise;
from entering the conventional from emptiness and entering the Middle Way from the conventional, the Separate Teaching arises.
The three contemplations are attained within a single moment of mind; thus, there is the arising of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Furthermore, these four teachings are not restricted to a single division, for within one division there may be many.
Furthermore, these may be further categorized by means of four modes of teaching: namely, the sudden, the gradual, the indeterminate, and the secret.
The sudden and gradual are the same as those previously mentioned by Master Jue;

the latter two refer to different understandings from a single sound. If they know one another [to be different], it is called the indeterminate; if they do not know one another, it is called the secret.

This master’s established doctrine is perfectly complete in its principles; however, the designation "Three Pitaka Teaching" (*piṭaka-vinaya*) seems somewhat overly broad, as the other three teachings also possess these three [aspects].
The reason for this is that, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the term "Three Pitaka" is frequently used to refer to the Hīnayāna.

The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* itself also states: "Because I now wish to explain the true meaning within the Tripiṭaka, I first address the old physicians regarding their [concepts of] morality, concentration, and wisdom."

These three matters established here are distinct and differ from the latter three teachings: because the intent of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) integrates the three; because the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) manifests the three based upon the single Dharma-nature; and because in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the three and the one are without obstruction.

The reason this is not called a Hīnayāna teaching is that this teaching also contains Mahāyāna elements, for it includes the six perfections of the bodhisattva and the severing of fetters through the thirty-four moments of mind to become a true Buddha.

Therefore, while the meanings of the Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Complete teachings are mutually present across the four teachings, when their definitive reality is scrutinized, the other three do not truly establish themselves; they only establish the meanings within their own respective teachings.

However, it is judged that the *Avataṃsaka* encompasses both the Perfect (Yuan) and the Separate (Bie) teachings; for since the stage above the first bhūmi is treated according to the sequential progression of stages as the meaning of the "Separate," there is no great error in saying that while the names differ, the meaning is the same.
Third, during the early Tang dynasty, the Dharma Master Wonhyo of Haidong also established four teachings:
first, the distinct teaching of the three vehicles, such as the *Catuḥsatya-sūtra* and the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*;
second, the common teaching of the three vehicles, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
First, the partial teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), such as the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and others;
second, the complete teaching of the One Vehicle, such as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and others.

However, that which is studied in common by the three vehicles is called the "Three Vehicle Teaching. Within this, that which does not yet clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is termed the "Distinct Characteristics Teaching" (*biprakṣaṇa-dharma-paryāya*); that which explains the emptiness of all phenomena is termed the "Common Teaching" (*sāmānya-paryāya*); and that which is not shared with the two [lower] vehicles is termed the "One Vehicle Teaching."

Among these, that which does not yet manifest the universal Dharma is called the "Teaching According to Capacity," while that which fully elucidates the universal Dharma is called the "Perfect and Complete Teaching.
This is largely identical to the Tiantai system; however, it combines the Separate and Perfect [vehicles] and adds the category of the One Vehicle.
He himself stated:
"I have provisionally established four types based on the gate of vehicles; this does not mean that these four universally encompass everything. Therefore, there is no fault.
Fourth, Master Wan, a disciple of Xianxiu, established four types of teaching based on the *Ratnagotravibhāga*.
The treatise states: "There are four kinds of sentient beings who do not recognize the Tathāgatagarbha, like those born blind:
first, ordinary worldlings; second, śrāvakas; third, pratyekabuddhas; and fourth, bodhisattvas at the initial stage."
Regarding the four teachings: first, the teaching of delusion regarding reality and divergent attachments, which corresponds to ordinary worldlings;
second, the teaching of one part and a half of reality, which corresponds to those of the two vehicles;
third, the teaching of one part of reality and its fulfillment, which corresponds to bodhisattvas at the initial stage of mind.
"The fourfold complete and perfect teaching refers precisely to that which is called the Tathāgatagarbha within consciousness.
The initial teaching refers to those non-Buddhists who are deluded regarding the true principle and extensively give rise to various heterodox views.

The second refers to the Hīnayāna; within the two-fold meaning of True Suchness (tathatā) as being both conforming to conditions and remaining unchanging, it speaks only of the principle revealed by the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and is therefore called "half," like the "half-syllables" (*ardha-akṣara*) in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Third, it is called "partial" because it attains only the unchanging aspect and does not attain the aspect of following conditions;
yet, because it explains both types of emptiness, it is called "complete.
Fourth, it is called "fully endowed" because it possesses both meanings of following conditions and remaining unchanging.
This is explained in detail as stated therein.
However, when evaluating the sacred teachings today, how can heterodox doctrines be included?

If one were to address the Founder of the Teaching, one should first establish the three teachings according to this region, or otherwise divide them into the Inner and Outer paths, the six teachers, and so forth, as practiced in the Western Regions.

Furthermore, regarding the classification of "half" and "full" based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: since the latter two [stages] are already "full," there should not be any further mention of a "one-part" [attainment];
and if one has only attained a single part of immutability, how can this be called "full"?
Furthermore, regarding the "Half" and "Full" [teachings] in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, how could they pertain solely to the two kinds of emptiness?
How could it be that the Sūtra does not speak of wondrous existence while yet reviling emptiness?
Therefore, what you have established is not tenable.
Fifth, regarding the establishment of the five teachings, there are briefly two schools:
first, that established by Paramārtha Tripiṭaka, which consists of: (1) the Teaching of the Four Noble Truths, referring to the four *Āgamas* and so forth;
and (2) the Teaching of Signlessness, referring to the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.
Third is the teaching on contemplative practice, referring to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;
fourth is the teaching on peace and bliss, referring to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, because it expounds upon permanence and bliss;
fifth is the teaching on protection, referring to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, because it expounds upon the matter of protecting the true Dharma.
This explanation of the name is restrictive, because practices such as contemplation (*guanxing*) are all mutually present [in various schools].
Second, regarding the five teachings established by Xuanzhuang (Xianxiu), they shall be understood below.

Regarding the second section, the account of the Western Regions: this refers to the fact that the two fundamental schools of Nature (*xing*) and Characteristics (*xiang*) originally emerged from that region; hence it is called the Western Regions.
It is said that at Nālandā Monastery there were two great virtuous masters (bhadanta) at the same time:
the first named Śīlabhadra and the second named Jñānaprabha.

Śīlabhadra inherited the lineage of Maitreya and Asaṅga from afar, and followed Dharmapāla and Nanda in his immediate vicinity. Relying on scriptures such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, he established the threefold teaching and took the Dharma-character (*lakṣaṇa*) Mahāyāna as the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). He was the master whom the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty venerated.

This refers to when the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths of the Hīnayāna at the Deer Park, teaching that all conditioned phenomena arise from conditions in order to refute the non-Buddhists' [notions of] causes such as self-nature (*svabhāva*);

furthermore, he taught that what arises from conditions is without self (*anātman*), overturning the external [belief] in a self, yet he had not yet explained the principle of the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). These are the four *Āgamas* and so forth.

During the second period, although he taught that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty based on the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), thereby overturning the views of the Śrāvakayāna, he had not yet taught the existence of the dependent (*paratantra*) and perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures; this refers to the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and others of that class.

During the third period, according to the correct principles of the Mahāyāna, the three natures and the three absences of nature were fully explained; only then was the principle exhausted, as in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and other such texts.
Therefore, regarding those three stages, the first—falling into the extreme of existence—and the second—falling into the extreme of emptiness—are both not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Only at the final stage, where it is fully explained that the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is empty while the other two natures exist, does one accord with the Middle Way; only then is it considered definitive meaning.
This is based on the judgment of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.

The master Jñānaprabha, who inherited the lineage of Mañjuśrī and Nāgārjuna from afar and received the teachings of Candrakīrti and Bhāviveka more recently, likewise established the doctrine of three periods of teaching based on sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and treatises such as the *Madhyamaka*, clarifying that the signless Mahāyāna constitutes the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
This means that when the Buddha first taught at the Deer Park, he spoke of the Small Vehicle, clarifying that both mind and objects exist.

Subsequently, during the middle period, for those of middling faculties, he taught the Mahāyāna of Dharma-characteristics, explaining the principle that while objects are empty, the mind exists as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). Because their faculties were still inferior, they were not yet able to fully enter the equality of true emptiness.

Therefore, in the third period thereafter, for those of superior faculties, he taught the signless Mahāyāna, elucidating that both mind and objects are empty and that their equality is of a single flavor; this is the definitive meaning.

Furthermore, because he first gradually refutes the "self-nature" (*svabhāva*) and other such tenets of the non-Buddhists, he teaches that phenomena produced by causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*) definitely exist.

Next, because he gradually refutes the Small Vehicle's attachment to the real existence of dependently arisen phenomena, he teaches that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) exists as a semblance; for they fear this true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he employs provisional designations (*prajñapti*) to guide them.
Only at the final stage does he speak from the ultimate perspective, teaching that dependently arisen phenomena are themselves empty, equal, and of a single flavor.
This sequence of three periods is as explained in Master Jñānaprabha’s *Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*, which cites the *Mahāyāna-suvikrānta-vikrāmi-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.

However, these two or three periods cannot exhaustively encompass the entirety of the Buddha’s teachings throughout his lifetime, because each has its own scriptural basis and they contradict one another; furthermore, each was intended specifically for a particular class of disciples.

The intent of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* is this: for a certain class of practitioners who consume the *prajñāpāramitā*, having heard of the emptiness of equality, they negate cause and effect; failing to understand that emptiness and existence are non-dual, the Third Turning of the Wheel analyzes the meaning of emptiness and existence within a single phenomenon.

As for the *Sūtra of Sublime Wisdom*, it addresses those who, having heard the teachings on the three natures, remain deluded regarding consciousness-only and are unable to abandon mental activity while contemplating dependent origination; such people insist that things must truly exist as appearances. Therefore, the sūtra causes them to completely forget both mind and objects, so that phenomena themselves are seen as the ultimate reality.

Those who grasp this meaning will find no contradiction between them. Nevertheless, to reconcile these two schools, one must recognize that there are many differences in their established doctrines; briefly stated, these include: first, the distinction between the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles; second, the distinction between the single nature and the five natures; third, the distinction between mind-only as true or false;

fourth, the distinction between the True Suchness that accords with conditions versus that which is immutable; fifth, the distinction between the three natures as empty or existent, and as identical or separate; sixth, the distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas as neither increasing nor decreasing; seventh, the distinction between the two truths as empty or existent, and as identical or separate; eighth, the distinction between the four marks as simultaneous or sequential; ninth, the distinction between subject and object regarding abandonment and realization, and whether they are identical or separate; tenth, the distinction between the Buddha-body as unconditioned or conditioned.
Furthermore, regarding the first two meanings: because there are five natures that differ from one another, the vehicles (yānas) are established as three.

First, concerning the provisional and the real: according to the intention of the Dharmalakṣaṇa school, the One Vehicle is provisional and the Three Vehicles are real. Thus, among the teachings of the three periods in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, in the first period nothing was established, while in the second everything was established; this means that both "excess" and "insufficiency" are not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). It is only in the third period that those with the [Buddha-]nature achieve [enlightenment] while those without it do not, which is then considered definitive. Therefore, it is said: "Universally for those who set out upon all vehicles."
Furthermore, in the first two fascicles, it is stated in all instances that "the One Vehicle is a teaching of intentional meaning (saṃdhāyabhāṣita)"; thus, one knows it is provisional.
Moreover, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* treats the One Vehicle as a skillful means (upāya).
In the five hundred and ninety-third fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Suvīra said:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for us, will fully expound the realm and wisdom of the Tathāgata."
If there are sentient beings whose disposition for the Śrāvaka Vehicle is fixed, having heard this Dharma, they will swiftly realize their own stage of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).
If there are those whose disposition for the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle is fixed, having heard this Dharma, they will swiftly attain liberation by relying on their own vehicle.
Those who are certain of the nature of the Unsurpassed Vehicle, having heard this Dharma, will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

As for those classes of sentient beings whose natures regarding the three vehicles are not yet fixed and who have not yet entered the state of rightness and departure from birth, having heard this Dharma, they shall all resolve their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The general meaning of the second chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* is the same as this.

It further states: "Śrāvaka-lineage individuals (*pudgala*) who are destined for peace, even if they receive the various courageous applications and skillful means (*upāya*) established by the Buddhas to guide them, can ultimately never be made to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Furthermore, the ninth chapter of the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* also states: "The three vehicles are each fixed in their distinctions, for all are determined by the five natures.
Thus, in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the Buddha told Mahāmati:

"There are five kinds of lineages (gotra): first, the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle; second, the lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; third, the lineage of the Tathāgata vehicle; fourth, the indeterminate lineage; and fifth, the absence of lineage."
The *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* both speak in this same manner.
Although the *Śīla-samvara-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* only mention two types of nature—the nature that possesses the lineage (*gotra*) and the nature that lacks the lineage—they also state:

"Because those without the lineage lack such a nature, even though they apply themselves with diligent effort, they will ultimately be unable to attain unsurpassed bodhi; they can only be brought to maturity through the roots of goodness of humans and devas."
Asaṅga’s *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also speaks in this same way.
According to the intent of the Dharma-nature school (Faxiang zong), however, the three vehicles are provisional while the one vehicle is the ultimate reality.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third, except for the expedient teachings of the Buddhas."
It is further stated: "First, one guides sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, and subsequently delivers them solely by means of the Great Vehicle.
Because the nature [of all things] is one and only, it is said: "The Buddhas, the Honored Ones with Two Feet, know that phenomena are eternally without self-nature."
Furthermore, the third [text] states: "A single characteristic and a single flavor; ultimate nirvana, the eternally quiescent mark.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also says: "Buddha-nature is called the One Vehicle."
The Lion’s Roar is called definitive teaching; it definitively proclaims that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Whoever possesses a mind will certainly become a Buddha.

Furthermore, it says in the *Thirty-three [Chapter]*: "All sentient beings equally possess Buddha-nature; they all share the same vehicle, the same liberation, the same cause and the same fruit, and the same ambrosia. All shall attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity—this is called 'one flavor' (*ekarasa*)."

Furthermore, the third chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "After my parinirvāṇa, there will be disciples who have not heard this sutra; they do not know and do not realize the conduct of bodhisattvas. Regarding the merits they have attained, they give rise to the thought that they have entered parinirvāṇa and shall enter nirvana."

"I shall become a Buddha in other lands under different names; although these people harbor the thought of extinction and enter into nirvana, they will seek the Buddha’s wisdom in those lands, hear this sutra, and attain extinction solely through the Buddha-vehicle," and so forth.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 95, also states this; it clearly shows that those who have entered into quiescence (*śama*) will certainly turn their minds [toward enlightenment].

Within the four types of śrāvakas mentioned in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-upadeśa*, because the faculties of both those who are "fixed" (*niyata*) and those who are "conceited" (*adhimānika*) are not yet mature, the Bodhisattva provides them with a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) as a skillful means to cause them to resolve their minds [upon awakening].
Since it is stated that they are "not yet mature," it is clear that they will inevitably become so.
To employ skillful means to cause this awakening is precisely what constitutes the bodhicitta.
One must not fail to follow one's own school’s tenets by judging this to be an error in the treatise.

In the second, fourth, and seventh fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, it is consistently taught that the two vehicles do not possess a real nirvāṇa; rather, by the power of samādhi, they will inevitably attain unsurpassed bodhi in the future.
The intent in the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (*Fahua lun*) is likewise the same: all these are provisional designations for nirvāṇa, and are thus called "samādhi.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* also states: "To say that the two vehicles attain nirvāṇa is the Buddha’s skillful means."
Furthermore, both the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra* and the two treatises, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* and the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*,
state that those of the Two Vehicles who have entered parinirvāṇa undergo further transformation within a realm beyond the three worlds.
In the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*, it states: "The two vehicles are ultimately non-existent; they are extinguished like ashes, forever ceased.
Passages such as these appear more than once in the sūtras and śāstras, making it clear that the Śrāvakas who have attained ultimate quiescence are necessarily [of the nature of] ignorance.

In the ninth chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the "Bodhisattva Chapter," it is explained in detail that icchantikas sever their roots of goodness and are unable to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
The text itself states: "Although those icchantikas possess the Buddha-nature, they are entangled by immeasurable defilements of sin and cannot escape them, like a silkworm within its cocoon."
This means that it exists and is not non-existent.
Furthermore, when it says, "There may be a Buddha-nature that exists in icchantikas but does not exist in those with roots of goodness," one knows that there are no persons who lack the seed-nature.
Moreover, regarding the five natures cited earlier from the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, you have misunderstood the text yourself.
That sūtra states concerning the fifth nature: "The fifth is the natureless (abhāva-dharmatā), namely the icchantika."
This is of two kinds:
first, burning away all roots of goodness, which is to slander the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
second, having compassion for the entire realm of sentient beings, which is the Bodhisattva.
"If there are sentient beings who do not enter nirvana, I too shall not enter.
Mahāmati said:
"Of these two, which one is eternally not entering nirvana?"
The Buddha said:

"A bodhisattva does not constantly enter nirvana, nor do they burn away all roots of goodness, because they know that all phenomena are originally in nirvana and because they do not abandon any sentient beings."
This meaning clarifies that the Bodhisattva enters yet does not enter.
Since it is said that the Bodhisattva never fails to enter, whereas the icchantika does not, this clarifies that the icchantika will certainly enter later on.
Moreover, the Sūtra itself states: "Furthermore, by the power of the Tathāgata, roots of goodness may at times arise.
In the fifth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, it is said that there are two kinds of "limit of time" (*kālaparyanta*):
first, the limit of time [within a specific period], and second, the ultimate limit of time.
This means that "temporary absence" refers to those previously mentioned icchantikas, while "ultimate absence" refers to the Bodhisattvas of Great Compassion.

Thus, one should understand that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and other such scriptures cited above were all spoken prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; they speak of "fixed nature" and "absence of nature" in terms of long durations, not as permanent states or permanent absences.
All treatises establish their positions according to the Buddha’s skillful means;
therefore, they state that [the icchantika] "definitely lacks" [Buddha-nature].

Thus, treatises such as the *Ratnagotravibhāga* and the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* all explain that because the icchantika slanders the Mahāyāna, it is said that they lack Buddha-nature for an immeasurable period of time, but this does not mean they ultimately lack the nature of purity.

If you claim that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* belongs to the second period of teaching, asserting that it teaches "all shall attain Buddhahood" in order to attract those of indeterminate lineage among the two vehicles, yet maintains that those of determinate lineage will not attain it—and thus characterizes it as being of intentional meaning (*ābhiprāyika*) rather than definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)—then why do you yourself judge the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to belong to the third period of teaching?
Who would dare to judge that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is not definitive?

In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (the *Miaozhi jing*) and in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* translated during the Liang dynasty, which establish the True Dharma, the One Vehicle is always placed after the Three Vehicles. Therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha states in his *Record of the Different Tenets of the Schools*: "After thirty-eight years [of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa], he preached the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (*Jiejie jing*)," and so forth.

The *Anantamukha-sūtra* states: "Forty years later, he will preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This makes it clear that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* comes at the end; hence the sūtra says, "when he is about to pass away."

If one does not believe the *Lotus Sūtra* when it is placed last, yet readily believes the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at the moment of death, does this not likewise refute the [distinctions of] the three vehicles and five natures through the One Vehicle and One Nature?
If one considers the *Prajñāpāramitā* as the second period and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the third period, this is logically consistent.

However, it would further contradict the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, which states that during the third period, [the Buddha] universally taught for the sake of those setting out in all vehicles, because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sublates the three [vehicles].

Although one clearly knows the three periods of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, this cannot definitively determine all the holy teachings, because that sūtra does not occupy the final position; rather, it merely divides them into three based on the manifestation of a certain class of meanings.
The meaning is as previously explained.
If one considers this in light of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there should be four periods, because the teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) sublates the preceding three vehicles.
If it is claimed that there are two types of Buddha-nature:
First is the nature of principle (*li-xing*), and second is the nature of practice (*xing-xing*). The nature of principle definitely exists, whereas the nature of practice may or may not exist.

These words are indeed reasonable; thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "There is a Buddha-nature that those with roots of goodness possess, while icchantikas do not. This refers precisely to the nature of practice.
"The Buddha-nature that both persons possess" refers to the nature of reality (li-xing).

Since the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies their equality based on this nature of reality, it states, "All who possess a mind will certainly become Buddhas," but does not say, "All who possess practice will certainly become Buddhas."

If one were to claim that the rational nature (tathatā) definitely exists [in all beings] and yet the attainment of quiescence (nirvāṇa) could not occur, this would contradict both scripture and logic.

Thus, we know that the statement that icchantikas do not become Buddhas is merely a rhetorical device—suppressing and elevating the contemporary situation—based on the fact that becoming a Buddha is not the state of an icchantika.

If it is claimed that those who believe in the One Vehicle after the parinirvāṇa as described in the *Lotus Sūtra* are merely transformational, provisional śrāvakas, then since the provisional must transform into the real, if there were no real ones, whom would the provisional transform?
Furthermore, would this not be a mistake for those of a certain class of timid beings who prefer extinction?
Thus we know that those who incline toward quiescence all represent the prior intention of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Moreover, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "If the Tathāgata teaches through skillful means according to their inclinations, it is simply the One Vehicle; there are no two vehicles. The two vehicles enter into the One Vehicle, and the One Vehicle is the vehicle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-yāna*)."

This intent clarifies that while the two vehicles (dvayayāna) are taught as skillful means according to [the capacities of] those who desire them, it is clearly understood that these are in fact the One Vehicle (ekayāna), and there are not two.

Not understanding this intent, some read the preceding section on skillful means as being continuous with the subsequent section on the One Vehicle, and they arbitrarily conclude that the One Vehicle is merely a skillful means; such is their profound delusion.

Furthermore, that sūtra extensively refutes the two vehicles, stating that there is no nirvāṇa for them; it also says, "This sūtra severs all doubts, definitively establishing the definitive meaning and leading one into the path of the One Vehicle."
"Could it be that the One Vehicle was taught merely as a skillful means?
Even if there were such talk of 'skillful means,' it would still have occurred prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; how much more so when there is none at all?"

The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "This sūtra is difficult to believe and difficult to understand; even while the Buddha is present in the world, there are still many who harbor resentment and jealousy, how much more so after his parinirvāṇa.
Truly profound are these words.
If one believes in and clings to the three vehicles and five natures while disbelieving in the One Vehicle and the single nature, such a person is deeply pitiable.

Therefore, in the second chapter of the *Sūtra of Hundred Parables*, there is the parable of the king changing a village that was five yojanas away to being three yojanas away, which illustrates how expedient means teach three within the One.
This refers to the fact that later generations believe only in the three [vehicles] and do not believe in the one [vehicle].
Regarding the two schools mentioned above, each relies on its own distinct basis, and thus they contradict one another.
If one were to provide an interpretation, there would likewise be no contradiction:

that is to say, from the perspective of the capacities of sentient beings (*yǒuji*), there are three; from the perspective of the Dharma itself (*yuēfǎ*), there is one. From the perspective of newly perfumed seeds (*xīnxūn*), there are five; from the perspective of originally existing seeds (*běnyǒu*), there are none.
If one enters into the principle and brushes both away simultaneously, then the three and the one are both lost;
if one considers the Buddha’s transformative manifestations, then he can be both three and one.
Therefore, those who compete over right and wrong fail to realize that there is no contradiction or dispute.
Although the five sections of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* differ, they do not depart from the Dharma-realm;
in the *Nirvāṇa*, each explains the cause of the body, and the Buddha permitted that all such teachings are correct.
The remaining meanings will be reconciled below.
The discussion on the contradictions and agreements between ancient and modern views is concluded.
Third, the establishment of the teachings and the opening of the school is divided into two parts:
First, classifying the teachings by their meaning; second, classifying the schools based on the teachings.
Now, for the first: classifying the teachings by their meaning.
There are five categories of teaching, which were established by Xianshou (Fazang); they are treated extensively in a separate chapter.
The *Great Commentary on the Tiantai* merely adds the Sudden Teaching (*dun jiao*).
I shall first employ it here, and later synthesize and harmonize all [teachings], making considerable revisions where necessary.
Regarding the Five Teachings: first, the Hīnayāna Teaching; second, the Initial Mahāyāna Teaching; third, the Final Teaching; fourth, the Sudden Teaching; and fifth, the Perfect Teaching.
The first refers to the *Zangjiao* (Tripitaka Teaching) of Tiantai.

The second is the Initial Teaching (*Shijiao*), also called the Partial Teaching (*Fen jiao*). This is because the second and third periods of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* both maintain that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles will not attain Buddhahood; therefore, these are now combined and treated as a single teaching.
Since this has not yet exhausted the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is established as the first [stage].
Because there are those who do not attain Buddhahood, it is termed "partial" (prādeśika).
Third is the Final Teaching (niṣṭhānta), also called the True Teaching (bhūtārtha).

That those of fixed nature among the two vehicles and those of no-nature such as icchantikas shall all attain Buddhahood constitutes the ultimate teaching of the Mahāyāna; therefore, it is established as the final stage.
Because it accords with the true principle, it is called "Real."
The former two teachings both rely on the gradual cultivation and realization of the stages of attainment; therefore, they are collectively termed "Gradual.

As for the fourth, the Sudden Teaching: it holds that the mere non-arising of a single thought is itself called Buddhahood. Because it does not teach by relying on the gradual progression through stages, it is established as "Sudden."
As the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "One who has attained the true nature of all dharmas does not proceed from one stage to another.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "The first stage is itself the eighth, and so on up to the stage of nothingness; what sequence could there be? and so forth.
Because it differs from the gradual stages of practice that precede it and differs from the perfect integration of all virtues that follows it, it is designated as "Sudden.
Since this principle is expounded instantaneously, it is called the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao).
The reason Tiantai did not establish [a separate teaching for] the ineffable is that within each of the four teachings, there is already an aspect of the ineffable.

That it is now opened up [as a distinct category] is to manifest the ineffable all at once, specifically for the sake of those with a type of faculty free from conceptual thought; this accords with the Chan school.

Regarding the fifth, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): it clarifies that one stage is all stages, and all stages are one stage; therefore, the fulfillment of the mind of the ten faiths (shixin manxin) subsumes the attainment of perfect enlightenment across all five stages.

Because it relies upon the Samantabhadra-dharmadhātu with its infinitely interpenetrating net of principal and attendant elements fully present, it is called the "Perfect Teaching" (Yuanjiao), as explained in scriptures such as this one.

If we consider the characteristics of the dharmas taught therein: in the initial stage of the Hīnayāna, only seventy-five dharmas are taught, and only the emptiness of the person (pudgala-śūnyatā) is taught; even when the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) is briefly mentioned, it is not clearly elucidated.

However, by relying solely on the six consciousnesses and the three poisons to establish the roots of defilement and purity, the *Āgamas* state that "greed, hatred, and delusion are the roots of the world," and so forth; yet these do not exhaust the source of all phenomena, and thus much dispute arises as the various schools hold differing tenets.

Within the second, the Initial Teaching (Śāstra), the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are extensively expounded, while the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is expounded to a lesser degree.

The nature of phenomena taught therein is merely enumerated among the characteristics of phenomena; since it teaches that there are one hundred dharmas with clear and decisive discernment, it gives rise to little dispute.

It is taught that there are eight consciousnesses which are exclusively subject to arising and ceasing; based on these consciousnesses subject to arising and ceasing, the causes of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are established. Because the presence or absence of the seeds of dharmatā is eternally distinct, the five natures are determined to be different.

Since the consciousnesses established [by you] arise solely from karma and afflictions, the True Suchness (tathatā) you establish must be permanent, eternal, and unchanging, and you do not allow it to follow conditions.

The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), while appearing to exist, is not non-existent; yet this is not identical to the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), which is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva-śūnyatā).
When the sūtras explain the meaning of emptiness, they do so solely with respect to what is grasped through attachment.

Since it is stated that the three natures and five natures differ, it is said that certain classes of sentient beings will certainly not attain Buddhahood; this is termed "the realm of sentient beings does not decrease."

The two truths, the ultimate and the conventional, are vastly different; they are neither annihilated nor eternal. As the fruit arises and the cause perishes, the four characteristics exist simultaneously, with cessation signifying the absence of subsequent existence.

The fundamental [wisdom] and the subsequently attained wisdom take objects as their conditions and sever delusions; in terms of meaning, they are said to be both simultaneous contemplation and distinct illumination. By means of conditioned wisdom, one realizes unconditioned principle; in terms of meaning, they are not different, yet in reality they are not identical.

Since supramundane wisdom relies upon the seeds of the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), the four types of wisdom-mind (*catur-jñāna-citta-pakṣa*) are subject to transformation by phenomenal characteristics;

thus, the *dharmakāya* of the Buddha’s fruition is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*). There are many such categories of meaning, as extensively explained in works such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

In the third, the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*), there is little mention of the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) and much mention of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Even the characteristics of phenomena that are taught ultimately converge back into this nature. The eight consciousnesses established therein are all permeated by the *tathāgatagarbha*, which, through the conditioning of circumstances, establishes itself as a synthesis of the unarisen and undying with the arising and ceasing; thus they are neither identical nor different. All sentient beings possess an equal single nature, which is simply True Suchness (*tathatā*) establishing itself through the conditioning of circumstances.

The absence of nature in the dependent [nature] is itself the perfected [nature]; as these two principles are equal and uniform, it is said that the realm of sentient beings and the realm of Buddhas neither increase nor decrease.

Ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) encompasses both the true and the false; since the true is not external to the conventional, it is true precisely within the conventional. Thus, although it is empty, it is not annihilated; although it exists, it is not eternal. The four characteristics coexist simultaneously, and their essential nature is itself cessation.
To sever delusions by taking objects as conditions is duality within non-duality;
that there is both the subject who severs and the object severed is non-duality within duality—this is called internal realization.
To illuminate that delusions have no fundamental basis is itself the essence of wisdom.
The essence of illumination has no self-nature; this is precisely the realization of Suchness (tathatā).
It is not that Suchness exists outside of wisdom as an object to be realized by wisdom;
nor is it that wisdom exists outside of Suchness as that which can realize Suchness.

Worldly and world-transcending wisdom both rely upon the Tathāgatagarbha; since the beginning and the manifestation are non-dual, the conditioned and the unconditioned are neither identical nor different. Therefore, the Buddha’s transformation body is both eternal and the Dharma-body, transcending all numerical categories, let alone the case of the reward body.
The wisdom that is the very essence is not subject to transformation by characteristics.

There are many such categories of meaning; their sequential correspondence with the above [points] is as found in scriptures such as the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and treatises such as the *Awakening of Faith*.
If one were to synthesize the two preceding schools, it would be as explained extensively elsewhere.

Within the fourth, the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*), no *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena) are taught at all; rather, only true nature (*zhenxing*) is elucidated. Furthermore, there is no differentiation of the eight consciousnesses; everything that exists is merely deluded thought (*wangxiang*), and the entire *dharmadhātu* is beyond words.

The five dharmas and the three natures are both empty; the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness are simultaneously discarded. One is rebuked for attachment to teachings and exhorted to renounce them; one is censured for grasping at appearances and urged to extinguish the mind. To give rise to the mind is delusion; not giving rise to it is Buddhahood. Thus, there is neither Buddha nor non-Buddha, neither arising nor non-arising—just as Vimalakīrti’s silence manifested the non-dual, such is its intent.

Within the Fivefold Perfect Teaching (*pañca-pūrṇa-yāna*), that which is taught is exclusively the inexhaustible Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Its nature-ocean is perfectly interfused, its dependent origination is unimpeded, and its characteristics are mutually identical and mutually inclusive. Like Indra’s net, it is infinitely layered; the minute and the subtle contain one another, and the primary and the attendant are inexhaustible. Each of the ten-by-ten Dharma-gates encompasses the entire Dharma-realm.
Within the section on the "Delimitation of Meaning" (*arthaviniścaya*), this shall be explained in full.
Second, regarding the opening of the school's tenets based on the teachings, there are ten such tenets, as analyzed in the section on the "Tenets of the Sūtra.
Fourth, the general reconciliation of these points is divided into two parts:
First, I shall generally synthesize the various teachings; later, I shall synthesize the chronological sequence of the methods of conversion.
Regarding the first:
the various masters who established these teachings each had their own specific basis.
Although five categories are established here, they are also derived by synthesizing various teachings; briefly, there are five levels:
first, some treat them as a single whole, meaning that they are solely the Tathāgata’s one great skillful means for gathering in sentient beings, expounded through a single voice.
Thus, the two former masters who establish [the teaching] as a single sound do not lose their logical consistency.
Alternatively, it may be divided into two; furthermore, there are three ways to do so:

first, distinguishing the Small Vehicle from the Great Vehicle, where the former is the "half-word" (ardha-akṣara) and the latter four are all "full" (pūrṇa); in this way, there is no contradiction with statements regarding the two Piṭakas and so forth.

Second, regarding the contrast between the provisional and the real: the former two [teachings] correspond to the three vehicles, while the latter three constitute the one vehicle; thus, this does not contradict the four vehicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Third, although the two teachings—the third and fourth—merge the duality and differ from the preceding ones, they nonetheless manifest a single, specific, and skillful approach that accords with the capacities of beings. The final [teaching] directly reveals the fundamental Dharma as exclusively unique (*asādhāraṇa*). As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this is similar to what Master Yinping described as "the straight path versus the winding path."
Alternatively, they may be divided into three: the first one is the Hīnayāna, the next one is the Triyāna, and the final three are the Ekayāna.

Or, only the final one is the uncommon Ekayāna; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* indicates this as the uncommon [Ekayāna], whereas sūtras such as the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* explain it in common with the two vehicles.
These three [teachings] also accord with the four vehicles.
Furthermore, the eighth fascicle of the *Liang-lun* states: "The Tathāgata establishes the True Dharma in three ways:
first, establishing the Hīnayāna; second, establishing the Triyāna; and third, establishing the Ekayāna."
"Because it is the third and most excellent, it is called 'well-established' (*suvyavasthita*).
This is also the same as the *Sujñāna-sūtra*.
The second fascicle of Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha’s *Samayabhedoparacanacakra-ṭīkā* likewise states this.
Fourth, they may be divided into four; this also consists of two approaches:
first, the three intermediate teachings distinguish the three while subsuming the two, and thus they are opened up into four.
First is the separate teaching of the Hīnayāna, such as the four *Āgamas* and so forth.
Second, the common teaching of the Three Vehicles, such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and others;
third, the common teaching of the One Vehicle, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and others;
fourth, the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle, such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Second, by distinguishing between those who progress through stages and those who do not, and between the gradual and the sudden, four categories are established.
Combining the second and third categories together constitutes the gradual teaching; the remaining [categories] correspond exactly to their names.

Alternatively, they may be divided into five as previously established, because within the gradual [path] there is a beginning and an end; however, this is merely a rough enumeration based on the majority of the sūtras cited, for it is not a definitive restriction, since a single sūtra may contain many teachings.

Second, regarding the sequence of the transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa-kalpa*), I shall now briefly elucidate ten gates concerning the Tathāgata’s temporal teachings throughout his single lifetime:

1) the gate of the distinction between the root and the branches; 2) the gate of arising from the root to manifest the branches; 3) the gate of subsuming the branches to return to the root; 4) the gate of the non-obstruction between the root and the branches; 5) the gate of indeterminacy according to the capacities of beings; 6) the gate of the simultaneous manifestation of the Exoteric and Esoteric; 7) the gate of instantaneous exposition all at once; 8) the gate of silent quiescence beyond words; 9) the gate of universal penetration across the three periods of time; and 10) the gate of infinite, overlapping layers.
From beginning to end, from root to branch, all things occur simultaneously; from start to finish, they remain of one kind, with no divergent teachings.
Nevertheless, there are three stages:

first, within the Hīnayāna, the initial conversion was that of Ājñātakauṇḍinya, and the final conversion was that of Subhadra; in between, he taught only the Small Vehicle to benefit those of small capacity, as seen in the four *Āgamas* and the five collections of Vinaya.

Second, if categorized according to the Three Vehicles, then from beginning to end the teaching speaks of three [vehicles], universally benefiting those of the three capacities, as in the *Guhyakapada-sutra* and others.

Third, if categorized according to the One Vehicle, then from beginning to end it is taught solely for those of the perfect capacity, reaching the ultimate perfection, as in the *Avatamsaka-sutra* and others.
Among these, the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is not included; furthermore, the nine periods of time encompass both the preceding and succeeding [lifetimes], with no other explanation.

However, as for these three categories, those whose faculties and dispositions are fixed within this present life constantly hear the Dharma of one such category. Therefore, what the Buddha expounds is universally applicable from beginning to end, with no distinction between before and after.

Second is the gate of "the fundamental giving rise to the derivative," which has five categories: first, teaching the Great Vehicle to Bodhisattvas; second, to Pratyekabuddhas; third, to Śrāvakas; fourth, to sentient beings with roots of goodness; and fifth, to those of fixed wrongness. This is as described in the "Appearance Chapter" regarding the sun shining upon high mountains and the three thousandfold world system.
In the initial parable of formation, the characteristics are extensively analyzed, all clarifying that the large precedes the small.

In terms of the Dharma, this is called "arising from the root to the branches," because the One Buddha Vehicle is differentiated and taught as three, and because both the eighteen [schools] and the two [vehicles] originally emerge from the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the capacities [of sentient beings], each refers to a specific category of capacity; it does not refer to the progression from small to great within the same individual capacity over time.

As for the "Gate of Subsuming the Derivative into the Fundamental," according to the *Anantamukha-sādhaka* (Wuliangyi jing), at the initial stage the Small Vehicle is taught, followed by the Middle Vehicle, and finally the Great Vehicle is taught.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also says, "The Four Truths were first turned.

Although the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and the *Ghanavyūha* differ regarding the sequence of the two periods and the three turnings, they all agree that the Small Vehicle comes first and the Great Vehicle follows.
Regarding the fourth gate, the Unimpeded Gate of Root and Branch: it means that first, by citing the ultimate teaching of Mount Śailendra, it clarifies that there are no branches without a root;
subsequently, by revealing the various streams returning to the great ocean, it clarifies that there is no root to which one can return without branches.
Therefore, when the fundamental and the derivative mutually illuminate one another, and bestowal and withdrawal support each other, they constitute the skillful means for sustaining life.
Consequently, a general discussion comprises five stages in total:
first, the fundamental One Vehicle, such as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;

Second, the implicit teaching of the Hīnayāna; third, the implicit teaching of the Mahāyāna; fourth, the explicit teaching of the three vehicles—these first three are as described in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*;
fifth, the refutation of the heterodox views regarding the One Vehicle, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The four preceding gates are perfectly penetrating and unimpeded; thus, what is "before and after" is in fact no "before and after," yet it is the "before and after" of that which is without before and after.

Regarding the fifth gate, the Gate of Indeterminacy according to Capacity: among these four aforementioned gates, the first clarifies how three types of capacities remain constantly fixed from beginning to end; the second clarifies how five types of capacities remain constantly fixed despite occurring at different times; the third clarifies how one type of capacity progresses from shallow to deep; and the fourth clarifies two types of capacities: those of initial capacity who hear the sudden teaching, and those of subsequent capacity who proceed from shallow to deep.

Furthermore, there is another class of individuals with indeterminate capacities who may first enter the Small Vehicle, then proceed to the Three Vehicles, and finally enter the One Vehicle; there are also those who enter directly from the Small Vehicle into the One Vehicle. Moreover, various types of capacities may produce different interpretations upon hearing a single phrase.
Regarding the sixth point, the simultaneity of the Exoteric and Esoteric: if those who have heard different teachings know one another's [realizations], this is the indeterminate Exoteric;
if they do not know one another, it is the Secret.
In the simultaneity of the Secret and Exoteric, there is likewise no sequence of before and after.
7. The various gates mentioned above are expounded all at once and simultaneously.
8. From the initial attainment of the Way until Nirvana, not a single word is spoken.
9. All these aforementioned gates universally pervade the three periods of time.
The nine gates within the ten superior [sections] are inexhaustibly layered according to place and time, all of them without before or after.
The final two gates are precisely the realm of the Avataṃsaka; they integrate the preceding eight gates and likewise do not depart from the function of the Avataṃsaka.
Third, the delimitation of the meaning and principles:
Although it is already known that this sutra belongs generally to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the specific delimitation of its "perfect" meaning remains unknown.

However, this ocean of teaching is vast and profound, encompassing all without exception; form and emptiness reflect one another, and its virtues and functions are layered upon one another. To speak of its horizontal inclusion, it fully embraces the five teachings, even including those of humans and devas, leaving nothing uncontained; only thus is its depth and breadth truly revealed.
It is like this: the hundred rivers do not contain the great ocean, yet the great ocean necessarily contains the hundred rivers.
Although it contains the hundred rivers, they share the same salty taste; therefore, even a single drop differs fundamentally from the hundred rivers.
The four preceding teachings do not encompass the Perfect [Teaching], yet the Perfect Teaching necessarily encompasses the four.
Although it encompasses the four, it is the Perfect Teaching that threads them together; therefore, even the ten wholesome acts and the five precepts are included within the Perfect Teaching.
Since it is not even three or four, how much less could it be two or one?

Thus, this Perfect Teaching possesses that which is universally accessible while lacking that which is restrictive; therefore, when speaking of its breadth, it is called the "Infinite Vehicle," yet when speaking of its depth, it reveals only the "One Vehicle."
The One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is twofold:
first, the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching, so called because it is shared with the Sudden and the Real;
second, the One Vehicle of the Distinct Teaching, which possesses only the virtue of perfect fusion. Since the Distinct encompasses the Shared, both are subsumed within the Perfect Teaching.
Now, to manifest the One Vehicle of the Distinct Teaching, four gates are briefly presented:

first, clarifying the substance and phenomena upon which it relies; second, subsuming all back into ultimate reality; third, revealing its non-obstruction; and fourth, its universal pervasion and inclusion. Each of these contains ten gates to manifest their inexhaustibility.

The ten topics for the beginning and middle [of the teaching] are: first, doctrine and meaning; second, principle and phenomena; third, object and wisdom; fourth, practice and stages; fifth, cause and effect; sixth, the primary and secondary [receptacle worlds]; seventh, essence and function; eighth, persons and dharmas; ninth, the inverse and the direct; tenth, response and stimulus.
The "teaching" (jiao) refers to that which expresses, namely the five preceding teachings, extending even to light, fragrance, and so forth.
The "meaning" (yi) refers to that which is expressed, namely all the principles and doctrines of the five teachings and beyond.
"Principle" refers to the principle manifested by the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena, such as the true thusness of non-substantiality.
"Phenomena" refers to the phenomena of matter, mind, body, location, and so forth.
The rest may be inferred accordingly.
The second, subsuming [all phenomena] into ultimate reality, refers to true emptiness that transcends all marks.
As the Sūtra says: "The nature of dharmas is fundamentally empty and quiescent; there is neither grasping nor seeing.
This empty nature is itself the Buddha, which cannot be apprehended through thought or deliberation."
There are also ten meanings, as in the *Dharmadhātudarśana*.
The third [section] clarifies their non-obstruction.

However, while all ten pairs above are entirely unobstructed, we shall now briefly manifest this non-obstruction by way of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*), which likewise comprises ten gates:

First, the gate of the single principle pervading all phenomena: this means that the principle, which is without spatial limitation, completely pervades all phenomena, which possess spatial limitations; therefore, the principle is perfectly complete within every single atom.

The two matters pervade the gate of principle; that is to say, the matter of having parts is entirely identical to the principle of being without parts. Therefore, a single minute particle pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

Because these two meanings mutually encompass and penetrate one another, they are all of a single nature. Thus, the "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives within his own body all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment, and even universally perceives all sentient beings entering nirvāṇa; they are all of a single nature, namely, the nature of non-nature."
Because principle pervades all phenomena, when one is established, all are established;
because phenomena pervade and accord with principle, it is said that nothing at all is established.
As the Sūtra says: "For example, like empty space, there is neither establishment nor destruction."

The single nature and the absence of nature are themselves Buddha-nature; thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Buddha-nature is called the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the ultimate meaning is called wisdom."
Furthermore, the *Samantabhadra-nirdeśa* states: "There is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
That there is none who does not possess it is precisely the meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Third is the gate of establishing phenomena based on principle (*yili chengshi men*). This means that phenomena have no separate essence; they must depend on principle to be established, just as waves are formed by gathering water.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, clarifying that [phenomena] are transformations of consciousness in its entirety (*jufen weishi bian*).
The Bodhisattva Juelin (Forest of Awakening) spoke in verse: "The mind is like a skilled painter, capable of painting all worlds.
The five aggregates are entirely born from it; there is no phenomenon that it does not create."
This clarifies the meaning of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*).
How is it known that this refers to the complete [aspect]?
The following verse states: "As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha; as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings."
"One should know that the Buddha and the mind are both, in their essential nature, inexhaustible.
Since this refers to the mind of the Buddha, it clarifies that it is not merely the deluded mind.
Second, it clarifies that True Suchness (Tathatā) manifests by following conditions.
In the "Chapter on the Inquiry into Clarity," Mañjuśrī poses a challenge:
"The nature of the mind is one; how can there be various distinctions observed?
This is an objection based on the contradiction between the causal condition (*pratyaya*) and its nature (*svabhāva*).
Bodhiruci replied:
"The nature of phenomena is fundamentally without birth; it manifests as having birth.
This is an answer given according to the conditions of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, it says: "All phenomena have no activity, nor do they possess an intrinsic nature.

This clarifies that while following conditions, they do not lose their own nature; this is identical to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*’s teaching that there is birth and death based on the Tathāgatagarbha, and there is nirvāṇa based on the Tathāgatagarbha.

Four matters can manifest the gateway to the principle: namely, because phenomena are established by grasping the principle, phenomena are empty while the principle is real; the absence of nature in the dependent nature is itself the perfected nature, just as the empty characteristic of waves allows water to be manifested.
The *Yamaka* verse states: "How are the aggregates explained?
What is the nature of the aggregates?
Since the nature of the aggregates cannot be extinguished, they are therefore said to be unarisen."
When these aggregates are analyzed, their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent.
Because they are empty, they cannot be extinguished; this is the meaning of non-arising.
Since sentient beings are thus, so too are all Buddhas.
"The Buddha and all the Buddha-dharmas have no self-nature whatsoever.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Ten Endurances" states: "It is like an echo, which arises from conditions."
"And it does not contradict the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The *Sumeruśikhara* verse says: "One thoroughly understands that all phenomena have no self-nature whatsoever."
Passages such as these appear throughout all nine assemblies.

Fifth is the gate of subsuming phenomena by means of principle (*li*). This means that since phenomena are entirely identical to principle, phenomena are exhausted without remainder; just as when water subsumes waves, the characteristics of the waves are completely exhausted. Therefore, it is said that sentient beings and Buddhas neither increase nor decrease.
The "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "For example, like space, whether all worlds are formed or destroyed, it is always without increase or decrease.
Why? Because space is without birth."
The enlightenment of all Buddhas is likewise: whether one attains perfect awakening or does not attain perfect awakening, there is neither increase nor decrease.
Why is this? Because enlightenment is without marks.

...and so on, until it says: "Even if all sentient beings were to attain perfect enlightenment within a single thought-moment, this would be no different from not attaining perfect enlightenment, for both are equal in their lack of marks (animitta)."
The *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-sūtra* also speaks in this same way; it does not mean that there is no increase or decrease because a portion of sentient beings fails to attain Buddhahood.

There are six matters that can obscure the gate of principle (*tattva*): namely, when true reality (*bhūtārtha*) follows conditions to form phenomenal phenomena (*dharma*), it causes the phenomena to manifest while the principle remains unapparent.
Just as water forms waves, where movement is manifest and stillness is hidden, so too does the Dharmakāya flow through the five realms of existence and is called "sentient beings.

As the verse by Vasumitra states: "All that is spoken of in the world is mere conceptualization; there has never been a single dharma that can enter into the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)," and so forth.
