The seventh is the gate of truth being identical with phenomena: that is to say, whatever is true is necessarily not external to phenomena, because this is the principle of the selflessness of dharmas, and because emptiness is itself form.
Principle is itself phenomena; only then does it constitute ultimate truth.
As the seventh dedication states: "The dharma-nature does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena," and so forth.
The eighth is the gate of phenomena as principle, meaning that conditioned collections necessarily lack intrinsic nature, for their entire substance is itself the Truth.

The two preceding sections correctly clarify the meaning that the two truths are not mutually contradictory; they are like moisture not being contradictory to waves and waves not being contradictory to moisture, because their entire substance is mutually identical.
The *Yamaka* (Night-Moving) verses state: "Just as gold and the color of gold are in their nature without distinction, so too are dharma and non-dharma; their essential nature is no different."
This also serves as a metaphor for the fact that the Tathāgatagarbha and the ālayavijñāna are mutually indistinguishable.
Furthermore, because phenomena are themselves the principle (dharma), although they exist, they are not eternal;
because the principle is itself phenomena, although it is empty, it is not annihilated.
Furthermore, because phenomena and their underlying principles are identical, their arising and ceasing are simultaneous.
The *Sumeru* verse states: "The conduct of all ordinary beings inevitably and swiftly returns to exhaustion; yet its nature is like space, and thus it is said to be inexhaustible."

"The wise speak of inexhaustibility, yet there is nothing at all spoken; because its intrinsic nature is inexhaustible, one attains inconceivable exhaustion," and so forth. Thus, the four characteristics occurring simultaneously do not depend on subsequent non-existence, and this brings about ultimate cessation and realization free from subject and object.
The "Chapter on the Ten Grounds" (Daśabhūmika-parivarta) states: "It is neither beginning, middle, nor end; it is not within the reach of words.

The "Chapter on Dedication" (Pariṇāmanā-parivarta) states: "There is no suchness outside of wisdom that could be entered by wisdom, nor is there wisdom outside of suchness that could realize suchness," and so forth.
9. The gate of truth not being phenomena: because the truth that is identical with the false is distinct from the false, just as moisture is not motion.
10. The gate of phenomena not being principle: because the falsity that is identical with the true is distinct from the true, just as motion is not moisture.
The Verses on the Forest of Shame and Remorse state: "Just as form and non-form, these two do not constitute one.
It further states: "Just as the characterized and the uncharacterized, so too are birth-and-death and nirvana; they are distinct when analyzed," and so forth.

The first seven and eighth gates clarify that phenomena and principle are not different; the ninth and twelfth gates clarify that phenomena and principle are not identical; therefore, the conditioned and the unconditioned are neither identical nor different.
The fourth dedication states: "Within the realm of the conditioned, one demonstrates unconditioned dharmas, yet without destroying the characteristics of the conditioned.
Within the realm of the unconditioned, one demonstrates conditioned dharmas, yet without discriminating the nature of the unconditioned."
The ten matters above share a single causal origin; therefore, they are said to be unimpeded.
When viewed from the perspective of principle toward phenomena, there is both formation and destruction, as well as identity and separation.
When phenomena are considered in relation to principle, some are hidden and some are manifest; some are identical and some are distinct.
Whether in opposition or accord, they arise spontaneously and simultaneously, without obstruction or hindrance.
Through profound reflection, one causes contemplation to manifest clearly, thereby accomplishing the contemplation of the perfect fusion and non-obstruction of principle and phenomena.
Fourth is "Universal Containment," which refers to the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena; furthermore, I shall rely on the ancient masters to clarify the ten gates of the Mysterious Portal.
The Chinese text consists of two parts: first, the formal exposition of the profound gates; second, the clarification of their underlying reasons. Now, for the first part, there are ten gates: 1.

The Gate of Simultaneous Mutual Fulfillment and Correspondence; 2. The Gate of Unobstructed Sovereignty over the Vast and the Narrow; 3. The Gate of the Non-identity of the Mutually Containing One and Many; 4. The Gate of the Sovereign Interpenetration of All Dharmas; 5. The Gate of the Simultaneous Accomplishment of the Secret and the Manifest; 6. The Gate of the Microscopic Mutual Containment and Establishment; 7. The Gate of the Realm of Indra’s Net; 8. The Gate of Revealing the Dharma by Relying on Phenomena to Generate Understanding; 9. The Gate of the Formation of Distinct Dharmas through the Separation of the Ten Ages; 10. The Gate of the Perfect Clarity and Endowment of Virtues of the Principal and its Associates.
These ten gates share a single dependent origination that is unimpeded and perfectly interfused; according to any one gate, all others are fully contained.
Now, within the aforementioned ten, we shall take a single phenomenon to illustrate how it embodies the latter ten gates.

As will be explained below, even a single lotus petal or a single atom possesses the ten pairs—such as the teaching (*deśanā*) and so forth—in simultaneous correspondence, complete and perfect; it likewise possesses the nine subsequent gateways, as well as the teachings and other elements contained within those gateways, because it is a totality.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The inexhaustible ocean of all dharma-gates converges within the single dharma-site.
A verse from the *Avataṃsaka* says: "Within every single atom of all the worlds in the Flower Treasury, one perceives the entire Dharma-realm."
"If even a single atom possesses [this nature], how much more so a single petal?

Second, those flower petals universally pervade the Dharma-realm without abandoning their original positions; for the differentiated is non-differentiated, and the non-differentiated is differentiated—thus, breadth and narrowness are sovereign, unobstructed, and unhindered."
The "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" states: "There is a lotus flower that reaches the limits of the ten directions, yet it does not obstruct external objects from being seen.

Therefore, [the object] may be exclusively vast and boundless; or its boundaries may be clearly defined; or it may be both vast and narrow; or both vastness and narrowness may be simultaneously transcended; or it may possess all four of these preceding modes, because these are the objects of understanding (*jñeya-viṣaya*);
or it may transcend all five of these, because these are the objects of practice (*caryā-viṣaya*).
The following sections are all to be understood according to this principle.

Furthermore, this distinction between breadth and narrowness is also termed "pure" and "mixed": because it universally pervades the Dharma-realm, it is pure, singular, and without a second; yet, because it does not destroy its original position, it does not preclude being mixed.
All myriad practices are likewise so.
"Three" refers to these flowers and leaves, which, having unfolded, pervasively enter into all phenomena, thereby encompassing all things and causing them to enter within themselves.
Since this simultaneous unfolding and encompassing is without obstruction, they are thus fused and integrated; one should contemplate the four or six propositions regarding this.
The text below states: "With one buddha-land filling the ten directions, the ten directions enter into one without remainder.

If one and all are contrasted and analyzed, they are subsumed within four permutations each: namely, one entering all, all entering one, one entering one, and all entering all; the same applies to their mutual inclusion.

Fourth: This single flower petal abandons its own identity to become identical with others; its entire substance is entirely those all dharmas, while it constantly subsumes others to be identical with itself, causing all of them to be its very essence.
The identity of the one and the many is intermingled without obstruction; the distinctions between the realms of understanding and practice consist of six phrases, the same as before.
As it says below, "knowing that the one is the many and the many is the one," and so forth: when the five flowers can encompass that [the one], then the one is manifest and the many are hidden;
when all things encompass the flowers, then the one is hidden and the many are manifest.

The manifest does not coexist with the non-manifest, and the hidden does not stand alongside the non-hidden; yet the hidden and manifest, and the manifest and hidden, are simultaneously present without obstruction. They are fully encompassed and simultaneously subsumed; both existence and non-existence are established together. The categories of phrases remain the same as before.

As it says below: "Entering meditative absorption in the east and emerging from concentration in the west," and so forth; like the moon on the eighth day, its appearance and disappearance occur simultaneously.
Within these petals and leaves, subtle lands and all other phenomena manifest vividly and in perfect symmetry.
As it says below: "Within a single atom, all lands abide with vast spaciousness.
Furthermore, it is stated that within the space of a single hair-tip there are unspeakably many Tathāgatas, as well as in the ninth dedication regarding the subtle.

Seventh: Within each and every atom of these flower petals, there appear boundless oceans of lands; within those oceans of lands there are further atoms, and within those atoms there are yet more oceans of lands. Thus, in successive layers, they are inexhaustible, beyond the sphere of conceptual thought and mental calculation.

It is like the jeweled net covering the palace of the Lord of Devas: within a single bright jewel, ten thousand images appear together, and it is the same for every jewel. These jewels are so transparent that they reflect one another’s shadows; these reflections, in turn, produce further reflections without end.
The text below states, "As in the world of Indra’s net," and so forth.
This is also like mirrors and lamps, where light interlaces in successive layers, such that the Buddhas are inexhaustible.
To see these flower petals is to see the inexhaustible Dharma-realm; it is not that one relies upon these [petals] to represent something else.
The subsequent text states: "These flower canopies and so forth arise from the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena)," and so on.

Ninth, since this single flower pervades all places, it likewise encompasses all times; that is to say, the three periods of each of the three [times] are subsumed into a single thought-moment, thus constituting the ten periods of time (*daśa-kāla*).
Since time has no separate substance and is established in dependence upon flowers, as the flowers are unimpeded, time is likewise so.
Therefore, the Jin translation of the sutra says: "Immeasurable kalpas of the past are placed within the future and the present;
immeasurable kalpas of the future are turned back and placed within the past," and so forth.
The *Samantabhadra-caryā* states: "The future is within the past; the present is within the future," and so forth.
It further states: "Immeasurable eons are but a single thought-moment; a single thought-moment is immeasurable eons," and so forth.
Since it has no separate substance at that time, it is not established separately as a support.
(10) This perfect teaching and its principles do not arise in isolation; they must necessarily include their attendants and arise accordingly.
The text below states: "These flowers have as many attendant flowers as there are atoms in ten worlds.

Furthermore, just as one direction serves as the principal and the ten directions serve as its attendants, so it is with all other directions; therefore, the principals do not see each other, nor do the attendants see each other, yet the principals and attendants, and the attendants and principals, are perfectly luminous and endowed with all virtues.
Just as it is with the "Flower" (hua) cited above, so it is with every single phenomenon, such as a mote of dust.

Since these phenomena and flowers already possess the ten meanings such as "simultaneity" and are thus endowed with these ten gates, and since these phenomena and so forth further possess the other ten gates such as "teaching," they constitute one hundred gates.

Since this is the case for the phenomena (*dharma*) and their functions, it is likewise so for the remaining categories such as the teachings (*śāsana*) and meanings (*artha*), which together constitute one hundred [categories];

thus, there are one thousand gates. Just as the teachings, meanings, and so forth possess these one thousand gates, so too do the "simultaneous" gates (*yugapat-mukha*) possess one hundred gates; and by analogy, the other categories such as "extensive" (*vistara*) and "concise" (*saṃkṣepa*) likewise each possess one thousand gates.
If one takes them up layer upon layer, they too will reach inexhaustibility.
When these ten gates are fully manifest and clearly understood, one will constantly enter the realm of the multilayered dharma-realm.
The second [section] clarifies the causes and conditions for such efficacy.
Question:
By what causes and conditions do these various dharmas attain such mutual integration and non-obstruction?
Answer: It is difficult to describe this in full detail; therefore, ten categories are briefly presented:

first, because all things are manifestations of mind alone; second, because phenomena lack a fixed nature; third, because the characteristics of dependent origination are mutually contingent; fourth, because the nature of phenomena is interpenetrating; fifth, because they are like illusions and dreams; sixth, because they are like reflections; seventh, because causes are infinite; eighth, because the Buddhas have realized the ultimate limit; ninth, because of the power of profound meditative concentration; and tenth, because of supernatural powers and liberation. Any one of these ten is sufficient to cause all phenomena to blend and merge without obstruction.
Among these ten, the first six generally take the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as their virtuous characteristics and causes, being so by the very nature of things;
the latter two are both functional activities, their meaning encompassing both cause and effect;
and the seventh concerns the arousal of cultivation, its meaning encompassing both virtuous characteristics and functional activities.
The eighth [category] is defined in terms of the qualities of the fruit (*phala-guṇa*), because it consists solely of the characteristics of those qualities (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*).

The preceding ten gates encompass both the characteristics of the qualities and their functional activities (*karma-vṛtti*); from the perspective of the Buddha, even the activity is a characteristic of the qualities, as it is the functioning of the qualities;
from the perspective of the sentient beings (*sattva*), even the characteristics are termed "activity," as they cause those beings to know the characteristics.

Thus, the characteristics themselves are the fusion of defilement and purity; the function of these characteristics is capable of both defiling and purifying. Therefore, characteristics and function are not divided into two separate entities. Regarding the initial point that "all is a manifestation of mind":

all dharmas are manifested by the true mind, just as the entire body of water in a great ocean manifests as waves. Since all dharmas are none other than the one mind, phenomena such as large and small follow the turning of the mind and immediately enter into non-obstruction.

Regarding the second point, that dharmas have no fixed nature: since they are manifestations of mind alone, arising from conditions, they possess no fixed nature; thus both their substance and their characteristics are transcended.
Because the small is not fixed as small, it can contain the great void with room to spare, for it is identical to the Great in having no exterior;
because the great is not fixed as great, it can enter a minute particle without obstruction, for it is identical to the Small in having no interior.

This is equivalent to placing as many vast lands as there are atoms within the great void; what difficulty could there be? The "Ten Stages Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika*) of the older translation states: "The Diamond Ring Mountains are infinite in number, yet one can place them all upon the tip of a single hair."
"If one wishes to know that the ultimate great possesses small characteristics, it is because the Bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind [of enlightenment] in this way.
Because the one is not fixed as one, it is able to be all;
because the many are not fixed as many, they are able to be one.
The extreme is not a fixed extreme, and thus it can be identical with the middle;
the middle is not a fixed middle, and thus it can be identical with the extreme.
This is true for every instance, such as length and brevity, stillness and agitation, and so forth.

Third, regarding the mutual dependence of the characteristics of dependent origination: within the great Dharma-realm, the gates of meaning for the ocean of dharmas of dependent origination are immeasurable. According to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), ten gates are briefly cited to explain the preceding meaning; that is to say, the dharmas of dependent origination must possess these ten meanings for conditions to arise, for if any are lacking, they cannot be established.

First, the meaning of the distinctness of each condition: within the great dependent origination (*mahā-pratītyasamutpāda*), when various conditions are compared with one another, it is necessary that their essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*kāritra*) be distinct and not confused; only then does dependent origination come to be established.
If they were disordered, one would lose the dharmas that serve as the original conditions, and dependent origination would not be established.
This means that each of the various conditions maintains its own single position; as the text says: "Among the many there is no single nature, and in the single there is also no multiplicity."
Second is the meaning of mutual and pervasive support: these various conditions must mutually and pervasively correspond in order to constitute dependent origination.
Just as one condition pervasively corresponds to many conditions—since each is entirely identical with those many—the single one thus possesses multiple unities.
If this single condition were not endowed with multiplicity, then the support would not be pervasive, and dependent origination would not be established.
Thus, each and every one possesses all; as the subsequent text states: "Know that through the one there is the many, and know that through the many there is the one."

The meaning of the unimpeded coexistence of these three is as follows: whatever constitutes a single condition must necessarily possess the preceding two [aspects] in order to constitute dependent origination.
This is because it must abide in its own nature in order to be universally applicable, and it is only through such universal applicability to multiple conditions that it becomes a single [condition].
Therefore, there is only the one, the sovereign unity of many, unimpededly fused and integrated.
This consists of six propositions:
first, that the entire substance remains entirely present—this is "the one."
Alternatively, if the entire body were to correspond [to each part], this would be "many in one";
or they may both exist, or both vanish, or be merged as a whole, or be entirely separate—all of which can be seen by reflecting upon them.
The text states: "All phenomena have no basis; they arise solely from conjunction.
This concludes the general explanation of the fundamental principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) across the three preceding sections.
Fourth is the meaning of the mutual interpenetration of distinct entities, which refers to how the functional powers of the various gates mutually support one another and mutually negate one another.
The meaning of both having full power and having no power at all must be complete for dependent origination to be established.
As the treatise states: "Because causes do not produce [results], but conditions do;
because conditions do not produce [results], but their own causes do."
If each [condition] possessed only efficacy and lacked inefficacy, there would be the fault of multiple fruits, because each one would produce its own result individually.
If each possessed only inefficacy and lacked efficacy, there would be the fault of no fruit at all, because they would all equally fail to be conditions and thus nothing would be produced.
Therefore, dependent origination necessarily requires mutual dependence, possessing both power and lack of power; if even one condition is missing, nothing at all is accomplished.
It is the same for the others. Thus, one can sustain many; that one possesses power and is able to sustain the many.
The many depend upon the one; being many, they lack power and thus enter within the one.
Because the one possesses power, it cannot coexist with the many who possess power; therefore, there is no single thing that does not encompass the many.
Because the many lack power, they cannot coexist with a single thing that lacks power; therefore, there is no plurality that does not enter into the one.
Just as it is when one [entity] holds many bases, so too is it when many hold one base; reflect on this by reversing the above.

Just as when looking from one toward many, there is that which is supported and that which supports, with full power and limited power, constantly containing the many within itself while secretly entering into the many within itself, simultaneously and without obstruction;
one should know that the same applies when looking from the many toward one.
Contemplate how both coexistence and simultaneous cessation are non-obstructive within these two propositions.

Fifth is the meaning of the mutual identity of distinct entities: this refers to the way all conditions, when compared with one another, mutually displace their total being. Only through the sense that there is both the existence and the non-existence of an entity does dependent origination truly come to be established; for if even a single condition were missing, the remainder could not arise, and thus the very meaning of "condition" would be destroyed.

The attainment of this single condition causes all things to arise; because that which arises is established, the meaning of "condition" is finally established. Therefore, the single condition possesses substantiality because it is that which can cause and can establish; the multiple conditions lack substantiality because they are that which is caused and that which is established.

Since a single existent entity cannot coexist with multiple existent entities, and multiple non-existent entities necessarily cannot coexist with a single non-existent entity, there is no "one" that is not many, and there is no "many" that is not one.
If it is so for the one and the many, it is likewise so for the many and the one; reflect upon this by reversing the above.

For instance, when viewing the many from the perspective of the one, there are cases where [the many] possess an intrinsic nature and cases where they lack an intrinsic nature; thus, they can subsume the other into themselves and discard themselves to become identical with the other, simultaneously and without obstruction.
One should know that the same applies when viewing the one from the perspective of the many; reflect upon this according to the preceding principle.
The simultaneous existence and mutual negation of these two aspects are non-obstructive; this can also be seen through reflection.

Regarding the meaning of the "mutual fusion of essence and function": it means that all conditioned phenomena must involve the interaction of their essential power and function, merging as a single whole, in order to constitute dependent origination.
Therefore, perfect penetration also consists of six propositions:
first, because the essence is not without function, the entire essence is fully functional; thus, there is only the principle of mutual interpenetration and not the principle of mutual identity.
Second, because function is not separate from essence, when one takes up the function as the whole essence, there is only mutual identity (*xiāngjí*) and no mutual inclusion (*xiāngrù*).

Third, the essence that returns to function does not obstruct function, and the essence that is the whole function does not lose its essence; thus, both exist without obstruction, and both inclusion and identity manifest with sovereign freedom.
When the substance that fully employs [all phenomena] is exhausted, its substance vanishes;
when the function that fully embodies [all phenomena] is lost, its function perishes.
It is neither identical nor entering, but a perfectly interfused single flavor.
Fifth, the synthesis of the preceding four phrases: they share a single dependent origination and coexist without obstruction.
Sixth, the dissolution of the preceding five phrases: transcending all dependencies and departing from words, they merge in silent identity with the ocean of nature.
The preceding three gates have completed the exposition of their meanings within the first gate, that of distinct entities.

Regarding the seventh gate, the meaning of mutual inclusion of identical entities: this means that because all the many "ones" belonging to a single prior condition are non-different in essence from that one condition, they are termed "identical entities."

Furthermore, because this single condition should correspond to many conditions, there is this "many-in-one"; since that which is to be conditioned by the many mutually enters [into one another], it causes this "many-in-one" to likewise possess mutual entry.

First, the mutual inclusion [of phenomena] is clarified: this means that a single condition possesses the power to sustain many unities, whereas those many unities lack the power to exist independently and thus rely upon that single condition. Therefore, the one can encompass the many, and the many enter into the one;
that the one enters into the many and is encompassed by them should be understood as the reverse of the above.
Other meanings and other phrases should be considered according to the preceding analysis.

Eighth is the meaning of mutual identity through the same essence (*ekasvabhāva*): this means that the "many ones" contained within the aforementioned "one condition" also possess the sense of having both an existent essence and a non-existent essence; therefore, they too are mutually identical.
Because the many lack intrinsic nature and are established by virtue of the original one, the many are identical to the one;
because the original one possesses intrinsic nature, it can produce the many as one, causing the one to encompass the many.
Just as it is with the multiple emptinesses within a single [phenomenon], so too is it with the single emptiness within the multiple.
As for the remaining meanings and phrases, they should all be considered according to the preceding analysis.

Regarding the meaning of the mutual fusion and non-obstruction of the nine: this likewise refers to the simultaneous fusion of essence and function as previously described, whereby one enters into mastery.
There are also six phrases, which should be understood according to the preceding [explanation].
These three gates above complete the exposition of the principles within the second gate, that of "Identity" (samatā).

Regarding the tenth meaning, the "Perfection of Identity and Difference": this refers to the synthesis of the previous nine gates into one great dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), whereby multiple doctrinal perspectives are simultaneously and fully realized.
Because they abide as a single pervasive unity, there is the gate of mastery over breadth and narrowness.
Because they are considered both in terms of essence and function, there is the gate of mutual identity and mutual inclusion.

Because different essences are mutually compatible, there is the gate of possessing the subtle; because different essences are mutually identical, there is the gate of possessing the hidden and the manifest.
Furthermore, by taking functional interpenetration as manifest, one allows ontological identity to be implicit; likewise, when identity is manifest, interpenetration is implicit.

Moreover, by taking identity through different aspects as manifest, one allows identity within the same substance to be implicit; likewise, when identity within the same substance is manifest, identity through different aspects is implicit.
Furthermore, through the mutual entry of distinct entities and the mutual entry of identical entities, it possesses the gateway of the Indra’s Net.
Because this great dependent origination is none other than the unobstructed Dharma-realm, there exists the teaching method of manifesting the Dharma by relying on phenomena.
Because it is manifested within time, there is the "Ten Worlds" gate (*daśakāla-mukha*).
Because they are mutually related and encompass one another, there is the "Principal and Retinue" gate (*nāyaka-parivāra-mukha*).

This tenth gate, which brings [the teaching] to perfection, explains its meaning and principle based upon the third gate mentioned previously; therefore, the subsequent text states: "The Bodhisattva skillfully contemplates the dharma of dependent origination; within a single dharma, he understands the many, and within many dharmas, he understands the one."

It is also said: "To understand the infinite within the one, and the one within the infinite, and to comprehend their mutual arising—this shall lead to the attainment of fearlessness. All such passages convey this same meaning.
The preceding section on the gate of mutual conditioning through dependent origination is concluded.
Regarding the fourth gate, the interpenetration of the dharma-nature: if one considers only phenomena (*dharma*), they obstruct one another and cannot be immediately entered;
if one considers only principle (*li*), it is of a single flavor and there is nothing to enter.

Now, principle and phenomena are interfused, possessing this non-obstruction: when a single phenomenon that is not distinct from principle fully encompasses that principle, all the many phenomena that are likewise not distinct from that principle appear within that one, in accordance with the principle upon which they depend.
If the principle is not fully encompassed within the one, then the absolute truth suffers the fault of being limited;
if the principle is fully encompassed within the one, yet many phenomena do not manifest in accordance with that principle, then phenomena suffer the fault of existing outside the principle.
Since a single phenomenon now fully encompasses and exhausts all principles, how could multiple phenomena not manifest based upon the Middle Way?
The "Flower Treasury" chapter states: "Within every single atom of all the Flower Treasury worlds, one perceives the entire Dharma-realm."
"The Dharma-realm is precisely the phenomenal Dharma-realm.
This is the general meaning.
Specifically, it also possesses the ten gates of the Mysterious Portal (shixuanmen):

Since the One is the ultimate truth, it is in perfect correspondence with all phenomena; encompassing all principles without exception, it is the simultaneous and complete fulfillment of all gates and all dharmas.

Since these two matters can both encompass all according to principle and pervade extensively without destroying their narrow characteristics, there is the gate of the unimpeded interpenetration of the vast and the narrow, and the pure and the mixed.
Furthermore, because its nature is eternally equal, it is "pure"; because it universally encompasses all phenomena, it is "mixed."
Since the three principles pervade all manifold phenomena, they cause each individual phenomenon to follow those principles as they pervade all things.
When the pervasive principle is fully present within a single phenomenon, then all phenomena follow that principle;
because it resides within a single phenomenon, there is the "gate of the mutual containment of the one and the many."
Since the Four Truths are not separate from all phenomena, one phenomenon is itself the Truth, and the Truth is itself all phenomena; therefore, this one is identical to that totality of phenomena.
That the whole is identical to the one can be understood by reversing the above logic; thus, there is the Gate of Mutual Identity and Sovereignty.

Fifth, because the truths are each complete within their respective bases and do not share in one another's domains, when this [truth] is manifest, that is said to be hidden, and when that is manifest, this is likewise hidden; thus there is the gate of concealment and manifestation.
Sixth, because the principle of universal inclusion encompasses all phenomena and brings those dependent entities instantaneously into a single state, there is the "subtle gate.
Seventh, because this principle of total inclusion can manifest everything, that principle of total inclusion likewise manifests instantaneously in the same manner as this one.
When that manifests here, both that which manifests and that which is manifested appear therein;
when this manifests there, both that which manifests and that which is manifested likewise appear therein.
Because they are thus layered and inexhaustible, there is the "Imperial Net" (Indra-jāla) gate, for True Suchness (*tathatā*) is ultimately inexhaustible.

Eighth, because phenomena and their underlying principle are identical, any single phenomenon that is raised serves as a gateway to the True Dharma; therefore, there is the "Entrusting to Phenomena" gate.

Ninth, because True Suchness (tathatā) is omnipresent—since it is fully present throughout days, nights, days and months, years, and kalpas—it does not differ when it exists in a day from when it exists in a kalpa; thus, there is the "Gate of the Ten Times Formed through Difference."
Moreover, since time exists because of phenomena (*dharma*), how could phenomena be fused while time is not?

Because this phenomenon is itself the principle (*li*) and time is not obstructed by it, being in constant correspondence with all other things, there is the "Gate of Principal and Retinue" (*sahāya-mukha*).
Therefore, as the single principle is harmoniously integrated, the ten gates are fully complete.
Regarding the fifth point, "like illusions and dreams": it is like a magician who can conjure a single object into various forms, or conjure various objects into a single form, and so forth.
The Sūtra says: "Or manifesting a moment as a hundred years," and so forth.
Because all phenomena are produced by the illusion of karma, unity and difference are without obstruction.

To say they are "like a dream" means that, just as what is seen in a dream—though vast in scale—is not removed from one's pillow, and though it spans a long duration, does not pass beyond a mere instant.
Therefore, the treatise says: "In a dream, one may think years have passed, yet upon waking, it is but a brief moment.
Thus, although time is immeasurable, it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa.
Sixth, regarding the likeness to a reflection: all phenomena briefly possess two meanings:
First, all are like bright mirrors containing luminosity, because they are formed by the single mind that realizes its own nature.
Second, they are manifestations of discrimination, like reflected images.

By virtue of the former meaning, they act as the manifestor; by virtue of the latter meaning, they are the manifested. Thus, all phenomena serve as mutual mirrors and images, just as mirrors reflect one another without destroying their original characteristics.
The subsequent scripture states: "Although distant objects and near objects both manifest as reflections, the reflections themselves do not possess distance or proximity according to the objects.

Regarding the seven causes being infinite: this refers to the fact that when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were formerly in the causal stage, they constantly cultivated contemplations such as dependent origination and the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), as well as great vows and dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) practiced in accordance with the *dharmadhātu*, along with other immeasurable and preeminent causes; therefore, the fruits now produced possess these very same unimpeded qualities.
Regarding the eighth, "the Buddhas realize the ultimate": this means that by penetrating the true nature, they attain the functional activity of suchness (*tathatā*).
Thus, a sutra states: "It is because of incomparable merit that they are able to do so.
Regarding the ninth, "the function of profound concentration": this refers to the power of various samādhis, such as the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).

The "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*) states: "Entering into as many samādhis as there are atoms, each giving rise to as many concentrations as there are atoms, yet those atoms do not increase," and so forth.
The ten supernormal powers and liberations refer to the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the inconceivable (*acintya*) and other such liberations.

As stated in the "Chapter on Inconceivable Dharmas" (*Acintyadharmaparivarta*) within the ten types of liberation: "Within a single atom, one establishes all the Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time," and so forth.
By virtue of the ten aforementioned causes,

the ten pairs of preceding teachings and meanings are endowed with the ten gates such as "simultaneity" (*yugapat*), thereby constituting the definitive scope of the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Fourth, regarding the capacity of those to be taught: since the teaching is manifested in accordance with the capacity, there are no words apart from that capacity.
Although the principles explained above are vast and profound, it has not yet been specified for what kind of root-capacity they are intended.

If one is capable of responding through clarity, the ten bodies and their perfect sounds will manifest; here, we directly reveal those who are the recipients, which generally comprise ten categories: the first five distinguish those who are not suitable vessels, while the latter five reveal those for whom [the teaching] is intended.
Regarding the former [two types], first is the one who lacks faith and is not a fit vessel; because upon hearing [the teaching], they give rise to slander and fall into the evil realms.
Second is the one who contradicts the truth and is not a fit vessel; relying on this sutra to seek fame and profit, they preach the Dharma impurely and accumulate perverse goodness.
The subsequent scripture states: "To cultivate various roots of goodness while forgetting the bodhicitta is the work of Māra.

This constitutes a third deviation from reality and renders one unfit as a vessel; that is to say, because one grasps the words literally and fails to internalize the ultimate truth that transcends ordinary cognition.
The treatise states: "To grasp the meaning according to the literal sound entails five faults.
The first three [faults] pertain exclusively to the ignorant and foolish; therefore, the subsequent text says: "This sutra does not fall into the hands of other sentient beings."
"Fourth, those who are narrow-minded and inferior vessels refers to all followers of the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*).
The 'Chapter on the Manifestation' states: 'All followers of the two vehicles do not even hear this sutra, let alone receive, uphold, and recite it.'"
Therefore, although they are seated [in the assembly], they are as if deaf and blind.

"The five who guard the provisional are not vessels" refers to the bodhisattvas of the common teachings of the three vehicles; because they follow the stages of practice and cultivation according to their respective schools, they do not believe in the Dharma that is perfectly integrated and endowed with all virtues.

The subsequent sutra states: "Even if there were bodhisattvas who practiced the six pāramitās for immeasurable billions of nayutas of kalpas, if they do not hear this sutra, or if having heard it at some time they do not believe or understand it, and do not accord with or enter into it, they cannot be called true bodhisattvas. Therefore.

Regarding the five [aspects] that reveal the intended purpose [of this teaching], the first is the primary purpose, meaning it is for those with the capacity of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) in its perfection.
The "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "This sutra is not taught for other sentient beings," which refers generally to the preceding five [capacities];

"It is taught only for Bodhisattvas who ride the inconceivable vehicle," which refers to the primary intended audience. This means that it carries all vehicles in a single movement; its perfect fusion of practice and stages is profoundly inconceivable, and its universal penetration of all teachings is extensively inconceivable. Thus the text says: "It is not known by the realm of others; only those who practice as Samantabhadra can enter it."
The second is that which serves both purposes: although one has not yet realized or entered [the truth] at that moment, one is able to believe and incline toward it, thereby forming the seed.
This is as described in the "Appearance" chapter (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) regarding the simile of the "vajra-consumption."

The celestial son of hell transcends the ten stages instantaneously; even the kalpa-fire of the great ocean cannot act as an obstruction. Because he has not yet attained realization and entry [into the ultimate], it is termed "inclusive.
Third, regarding "drawing forth": this refers to the bodhisattvas of the aforementioned provisional teachings, who do not receive the perfectly interfused Dharma.

Within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the superior state is manifested by relying on provisional positions; it borrows the names of the sequential practices of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) so that others may think, "This is the same as my own teaching. Subsequently, through the influence of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā-paribhāvita*), they come to believe in and enter the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*). This is because, apart from this universal Dharma (*sarvadharma-sāmānya-dharma*), there is nowhere else to turn, and because the ultimate fruits of the provisional teachings lack substantial reality.
The fourth is provisional action, which refers to those of the Two Vehicles; since they have not even heard [the teachings], how much less could they receive and uphold them?

Therefore, various Bodhisattvas provisionally manifest as Śrāvakas, sometimes appearing deaf and blind within the Dharma assembly to demonstrate their lack of affinity for the path, or sometimes manifesting as being on the way to enlightenment to show that their minds can be turned back [toward the Mahāyāna].

The fifth is "acting from afar," which means that all ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and icchantikas possess buddha-nature; although they do not believe in it now, they will certainly enter [the path] later. The "Chapter on Manifestation" states:

"The great medicinal king tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom cannot provide growth or benefit in two places: namely, those of the two vehicles who have fallen into the pit of the unconditioned, and those sentient beings who have destroyed their roots of goodness and are unfit vessels, submerged in the waters of great false views and craving; yet even toward them, he never feels weary or abandons them."
The first three are not suitable vessels because they are submerged in false views; the fourth is not a suitable vessel because it has fallen into a deep pit; therefore, all of these are excluded.

Now, regarding the fourth and fifth [categories], since the Buddha never tires of or abandons them, he reveals the truth to entice them and perfumes them so that the seeds [of enlightenment] may be formed.

Furthermore, within that same section, it is clarified that even those who lack faith and engage in slander plant roots of goodness; for although such slander leads to rebirth in the evil realms, because the teaching has passed through their ears, they will ultimately attain awakening.
Furthermore, it is said: "Just as the sun also brings benefit to those born blind.
Moreover, in the analogy of the hidden currents of the great ocean, it is clarified that there is nothing that does not possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Furthermore, in the analogy of breaking down a mote of dust to reveal a sutra scroll, it is because if one eliminates deluded thoughts, one perceives the Buddha-wisdom in its entirety.

These points all clarify that the *svabhāva-prakṛti-sthita-gotra* (the nature abiding in its own essence) is precisely that which is acted upon; moreover, since the *dharmatā* is perfectly interfused and the resonance between cause and response penetrates one another, there is not a single dharma that is not the object of this influence.

Fifth, regarding the varying depths of the essence of the teaching: the nature of the inexhaustible ocean of teachings is inconceivable; yet, from shallow to deep, ten essences are briefly elucidated:

1. The essence of vocal sounds and speech; 2. The essence of names, phrases, and syllables; 3. The essence that universally encompasses these four factors—these three are all the essence of the expressive (the *vācaka*); 4. The essence that universally subsumes the expressed (the *vācya*);

5. The essence of all phenomena manifesting their meaning; 6. The essence of the subsumption of objects as being Mind-only; 7. The essence of merging conditions into the true reality (*tathatā*); 8. The essence of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena; 9. The essence of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena; 10. The essence of the brilliant manifestation of the Ocean Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
Among these ten, the first five are solely essence (*tattva*), while the latter five are both essence and nature (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, the first four apply to both the Small Vehicle and the Great Vehicle, while the latter six apply only to the Great Vehicle.
The first seven apply to all three vehicles, while the latter three apply only to the One Vehicle.
The first eight [categories] pertain to the Common Teaching (tongjiao), while the latter two belong exclusively to the Distinct Teaching (biejiao).
Within the former three, four factors are universally employed across both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: first, sound; second, name; third, phrase; and fourth, letter.
Regarding the differences in what is accepted or rejected, there are three explanations for each.
As for the three views of the Hīnayāna, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 126) states: "What constitutes the essence of such Buddhist teachings?"
One explanation states:
It should be said that its essence is vocal action (*vākkarman*).
That is to say, the Buddha’s speech—utterances, discourses, vocal sounds, vocal paths, vocal actions, and vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*)—this is called the Buddha’s teaching.
"The names, phrases, and syllables merely manifest the function of the Buddha's teaching; they do not intend to reveal the self-substance of the Buddha's teaching.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* also speaks in this same way.
The second [position] states:

"Name and so forth constitute its essence; that is to say, the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), the collection of phrases (*padakāya*), and the collection of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*). This is because they are arranged in sequence, disposed in sequence, and joined in sequence, and because sound merely relies upon these successive causes."
This means that speech gives rise to names, and names are able to manifest meanings.
The intention of the *pūrvapakṣa* (the critical school) is to take vocal action (*vākkarman*) as its essence.
The *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* agrees with the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The Sage taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*); their essence is either speech or names, and they are subsumed within the aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*) and formations (*saṃskāraskandha*)."

That is to say, if speech is taken as the essence of the teaching, it is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); if it is called the essence of the teaching, it is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
This preserves both of the preceding two positions without preference, which is why the word "or" is used.
Because the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* uses synonymous terms such as "intention" (*abhiprāya*) and so forth.
Having completed the third explanation of the preceding verse, it further states: "Because it expresses the meaning according to reality, it is called the Buddha's teaching."
"Name is that which can express meaning; therefore, the teaching is name.
For this reason, the Buddha's teaching definitely has name as its substance. By taking name as the primary element, it encompasses phrases and syllables.
The third fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā* (Xianzong lun) also states this in the same way.

Third, according to the intention of the *Abhidharmakośa*, the mind is without preference for inclusion or exclusion; if one accepts both [names and phrases], then the four dharmas combined constitute the essence of the teaching.

However, according to the intention of the Sautrāntika school, only sound is accepted; thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles), chapter fourteen, refutes those masters by stating: "You should not establish the existence of the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables," thereby asserting that sound alone is the essence.
The Mahāyāna [explanation] has three parts, the general meaning of which is the same as before.
One view states:
taking sound as the essence by subsuming the conventional under the real, because apart from sound there are no separate names, phrases, and so forth.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, chapter five, states: "The vocal sounds of the Tathāgata are, in brief, of three kinds:
first, the sūtras," and so forth.
Since it says that there are three types of vocal sounds, it is clear that sound constitutes the essence of the teaching.
The *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* states: "Derived sound refers to that which is spoken by the noble ones.
Second, it says:

"In terms of substance following its function, names and so forth constitute the substance, because they serve as the two bases for the expression of the self-nature and specific differences of all phenomena."

Therefore, the *Nirākāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Absence of Nature) refutes the Sautrāntika school, stating: "It is unreasonable for the nature of the phrases of the various sūtras to consist of speech.

The second fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* likewise refutes them, saying: "If names, phrases, and syllables were not distinct from sound, then there would be no distinction between the objects of the two types of unimpeded knowledge—those of phenomena (*dharma*) and those of expression (*nirukti*)."

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Although these three—name, phrase, and phoneme—are not distinct entities apart from sound, they differ in being either conventional or real, and yet they are not identical to sound.

The third [view] asserts that their substance consists of the combination of sound, name, phrase, and phoneme; this is because both of the preceding two explanations are established as definitive by both reason and scripture.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, chapter four, states: "One cannot abandon speech, words, and letters while being able to proclaim [the Dharma].
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "There are those who perform the Buddha-work by means of sounds, speech, and letters."
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The speaker explains by means of two things, and the listener hears by means of two things; namely, excellent sounds and excellent syllables.
According to my own view, both aspects should likewise be adopted.
If one were to select from among the first two [categories] as that which possesses "going" (movement), why rely on names and so forth?
This is because only sound—specifically that which constitutes the Buddha’s own speech—is fit to serve as the substance of the teaching;
when it is transmitted to later generations and inscribed upon bamboo or silk, how could there ever be any sound?
Is it not the case that there is a substantial essence (*śarīra*) of the teaching?
Although the written word is indeed form (*rūpa*), because it also serves as the basis for names (*nāman*) and so forth, it is likewise subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

As for the previous citations from the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Daśabhūmika*, which comprehensively include all four [aggregates], these merely refer to what is employed [in the teaching] and do not explicitly reveal its essential nature.
The *Ratnakaraṇḍa-avadāna* (Renwang jing) states: "These names, phrases, and phonemes are what all Buddhas have taught.

Nevertheless, although the various schools of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna commonly employ these four dharmas, their principles differ. Specifically, the Sarvāstivāda school maintains that all four dharmas possess substantial reality;
the Sautrāntika school holds that sound possesses substantial reality, whereas names and so forth are merely provisional designations.
In the Mahāyāna, there are cases where all four [realms] are not real;
and there are cases where all four are like emptiness, as neither is established.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The nature of words is detached; that there are no words is itself liberation."
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains the analogy of wind within emptiness and so forth, stating: "Wind is a metaphor for sound; painting is a metaphor for names;
neither can be grasped. The *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "If all dharmas were not empty by even a hair’s breadth, then no Buddhas would appear in the world."
Furthermore, it is stated below that "all dharmas are ultimately empty, without even the slightest trace of characteristics.
Some say that all four [principles] are the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle, while others say that all four are mutually interpenetrating; thus, their doctrinal positions differ.
Regarding the fourth point, which encompasses the essence of the signified (*vācya*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (81) states: "The essence of the sūtra, in brief, is twofold:
first, the letter (*vyañjana*); second, the meaning (*artha*)."
"Words are the basis, and meanings are that which depends upon them.
These two together are collectively termed the 'entirety of objects of knowledge.
This means that by relying on the six types of words, the ten meanings are revealed; this clarifies how the teaching and its meaning mutually establish one another.
If it did not express meaning, what would be the use of the scriptural text?
Therefore, by encompassing both the expressed meaning and the expression, the essence of the *sūtra* is established.

Furthermore, the "Ten Stages Chapter" states: "The text follows the meaning, and the meaning follows the text; when text and meaning follow one another, there is no deviation from principle, and only then does it constitute a true teaching."

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others are the speakers; speech is the characteristic of the speaker; and the bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes are the characteristics of that which is spoken."
Therefore, all [dharmas] are universally included; this differs from the previous interpretation which specifically selected only those that are spoken.

Regarding the fifth point, the essence of the meaning manifested by all dharmas: it means that any dharma whatsoever capable of manifesting the principles of meaning constitutes the essence of the teaching.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, chapter three, states: "There are those who perform the Buddha-work by means of light;
there are those who perform the Buddha-work by means of various bodhisattvas;
and there are those who perform the Buddha-work by means of persons emanated by the Buddha."

There are those for whom the Buddha’s bodhi tree, robes, bedding, and even the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction cause sentient beings to become weary; yet the Buddhas perform buddha-work precisely by means of these very things.
Furthermore, the fourth fascicle of the ten-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra* states: "Mahāmati!
It is not the case that all Buddha-fields teach the Dharma through speech.
There are Buddha-fields where looking directly at one another without blinking, and having no words spoken in the mouth, is called 'teaching the Dharma.'"
It continues, saying: "There are Buddha-lands where movement of the body is called speech.

Furthermore, in the world of Gandhavatī, the samādhi is manifested by partaking of fragrant food; in the Buddha-land of Sukhāvatī, right mindfulness is perfected by listening to the wind in the trees. Since the heart can be transmitted through stringed and wind instruments, and the Way can be preserved through a glance, and since both speech and silence, as well as looking and blinking, are all forms of teaching, then seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all listening.
If one can attain the Dharma and harmonize with the spirit, why must it necessarily depend on verbal expression?

Furthermore, in the ocean of nature of the Avataṃsaka, the jeweled nets of the Cloud Terrace simultaneously proclaim wondrous sounds, and the light from every pore is able to preach the Dharma; flowers, fragrances, clouds, and trees are themselves the Dharma-gates of the Dharma-realm, and lands and sentient beings are fundamentally the true essence of the ten bodies—how could anything not be the teaching?
The text below states: "The lands speak, sentient beings speak, and all things throughout the three periods of time speak.
It further states: "All realms within every world are able to cause the Wheel of Dharma to turn," and so forth.
The texts on this subject are not uniform.
Regarding the sixth [category], "the grasping of objects as being solely the substance of mind," this generally subsumes the preceding five [categories] as being none other than consciousness.
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other works state:
"Because all that exists is manifested solely by the mind.
The *Awakening of Faith* also states: "Based on the dharma of the one mind, there are two gates:
first, the gate of the true suchness of the one mind; second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind."
"However, these two gates each comprehensively encompass all phenomena, for these two gates are not separate from one another.
The "Chapter on Holy Conduct" states: "Knowing that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind, they are manifested as mind-only."
However, there are two gates:
first, the correspondence between the original and its reflection; second, the complete inclusion of both speaker and listener.
Regarding the former, generally speaking across the various teachings, four propositions are established:
First, "only the original and no reflection," refers to the Hīnayāna, because they do not understand that all is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Second, "both the original and the reflection," refers to the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna; this is because the Buddha himself declared that both the words and their meanings are manifestations of the pure consciousness associated with the Tathāgata’s wondrously discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), and are thus termed "teachings as original substances."

The first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "According to one interpretation, through the power of the superior conditions of the listener's roots of goodness and original vows, the aspects of word and meaning arise within the consciousness of the Tathāgata."
The characteristics of these words and their meanings arise from the Buddha’s roots of goodness for the benefit of others and are thus called "the Buddha's teaching";
as for the words and meanings manifested upon the consciousness of the listener, these are called "images."

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "By the power of the Tathāgata’s compassion and the dominant condition of his original vows, the aspects of word and meaning arise within the consciousness of the listener.

Although these aspects of word and meaning arise directly dependent on the power of one's own roots of goodness, they are called 'the Buddha's teaching' because of that powerful condition. Thus it is said.
The *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Through the successive power of mutual predominance, the two consciousnesses become determinate.

Masters such as Dharmapāla all establish this principle, yet they also state that the phoneme (*vyañjana*) and the meaning (*artha*) arise together, further explaining the manifestation of the five mental aggregates (*pañca-citta-samnipāta*). This means that when one says, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent" (*sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ*), there are four sounds, four syllables, four names, one sentence, and the referential meaning.
These fourteen characteristics manifest as a collection upon the consciousness of the listener.
Regarding this, there are many explanations in the West; here, I shall briefly cite one.

For example, when pronouncing various syllables, there are two types of mental states—sudden occurrence (*ābhoga*) and seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*)—yet because one has not yet definitively determined which [syllable] they belong to, there is no state of certainty (*niścaya*).

Next, the syllable *kṛ* (行) is explained: through the continuity of prior habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), understanding arises, and three types of consciousness emerge—namely, the sudden (*ābhoga*), the investigative (*paryeṣaka*), and the determinative (*niścaya*)—because by means of determinative cognition, one knows all the formations (*saṃskāra*) to which the various syllables belong.
Upon hearing the syllable "all conditioned phenomena" (*sarvasaṃskāra*), although one knows its phonetic nature, one does not yet know its meaning;

in order to bring about knowledge of that meaning, the syllable "non-existence" (*na*) is further spoken. At this stage, there are only two mental states—namely, the sudden encounter (*ābhoga*) and the seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*)—and no certainty has yet arisen, because it is not yet definitively known to which category the syllable "non-existence" belongs.

When the subsequent character "constant" (cháng) is spoken, through the power of the preceding characters transmitted through successive perfuming, it arises in conjunction with the subsequent character, fully giving rise to five types of mental consciousness: namely, the sudden encounter, the seeking, the determination, the defiled or pure, and the resultant flow.

At the final stage, it is only when the four characters are complete that the meaning can be understood; totaling twelve moments of mind—namely, two, three, two, and five respectively—there are thus fourteen aspects, the meaning of which is as previously explained.
The remainder is as explained in other chapters.
Third, there are only shadows without an original substance; this refers to the Mahāyāna’s ultimate teaching.
Apart from the minds of sentient beings, the Buddha-fruit possesses no qualities of form or sound, but only suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) remain alone.

With great compassion and great wisdom as the dominant conditions, the Buddha manifests in the form and sound of preaching the Dharma within the minds of those sentient beings whose faculties have matured; therefore, the holy teaching is solely an image within the minds of sentient beings.
The *Yamaka* verse says: "The Buddhas have no dharma; how could there be any teaching by the Buddha?
It is merely according to their own minds that they say such a dharma is taught."
The masters of the treatises, such as Nāgasena and Sthiramati, all establish this meaning.
The four [aspects] are neither the original nor the reflection, as taught in the Sudden Teaching (sudden vehicle).

It is not that there are no forms or sounds of the Buddha outside the direct mind; rather, the images within the minds of sentient beings are also empty, for their nature is fundamentally detached [from such characteristics].
To transcend words and sever discursive thought is precisely the teaching of no-teaching.
As the *Sumeru* verse says: "The nature of phenomena is fundamentally empty and still; there is neither grasping nor seeing."
"The emptiness of intrinsic nature is itself the Buddha; it cannot be grasped through thought.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The one who preaches the Dharma has neither speech nor demonstration; the one who listens to the Dharma has neither hearing nor attainment."
The schools of Nāgārjuna and others frequently establish this doctrine.
These first four explanations are combined into a single, perfectly harmonious, and unimpeded whole, as they encompass sentient beings by leading them from the shallow toward the profound.
The second explanation concerns the complete inclusion of both speaker and listener, forming two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First, the four propositions are established based on the *samaya-vāda* (teaching of commonality): that outside the true mind of the Buddha there are no separate sentient beings, because the true mind of sentient beings is identical to the true mind of the Buddha.
Thus, there is only teaching and no listener; therefore, the teachings spoken are manifested solely by the Buddha.
Second, outside the minds of sentient beings there is no separate Buddha, because the true mind of the Buddha is identical to the true mind of sentient beings.
Thus, there is only listening and no speaking; therefore, the teachings spoken are the spontaneous manifestation of sentient beings themselves.
As the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" states: "To know that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind," and so forth.

When the true mind of the third Buddha manifests, because it does not obstruct the manifestation of the true minds of sentient beings, both speaking and listening coexist, and the two teachings stand together.

Since the fourth Buddha is none other than sentient beings, he is not a Buddha; and since sentient beings are none other than the Buddha, they are not sentient beings. When these mutually negate one another and both vanish, then speaking and listening are utterly quiescent.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The one who preaches the Dharma has neither speech nor demonstration; the one who hears the Dharma has neither hearing nor attainment.

Second, regarding the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*), the four propositions are elucidated as follows: because the characteristics are not destroyed, Buddhas and sentient beings are mutually inclusive; and because a single sentient being is entirely present within the Buddha, the gateway of the fruition encompasses all phenomena without exception.
If those yet to be born already abide within the Buddha’s mind, how much more so the teachings he has proclaimed, which are not merely his own manifestations?

Thus, the "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives all sentient beings within his own body attaining perfect enlightenment, and even universally perceives all sentient beings entering nirvāṇa."

Furthermore, the second chapter of the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, the "Tathāgatagarbha" section, states: "All sentient beings are entirely within the wisdom of the Tathāgata; therefore, they are called a 'garbha' (storehouse), because the wisdom of suchness accords with the object of suchness."

All sentient beings are definitively without exception from the realm of suchness (tathatā) and are sustained by the Tathāgata; therefore, it is called a "treasury" (garbha), and sentient beings are the Tathāgatagarbha.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on Manifestation" explains that even all the mental activities, faculties, and desires of sentient beings throughout the kalpas and lands of the three periods of time are simultaneously manifested within a single body; how much more so, then, is the Buddha’s wisdom, which is as vast as space?
Because the two Buddhas abide within the minds of sentient beings, the Dharma is encompassed through the gateway of causes without exception.
If the Buddhas themselves still reside within the mind, how much more so must the teachings they have expounded not be manifestations within the minds of sentient beings?

Therefore, the "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that in every thought-moment of their own minds, there is always a Buddha attaining perfect enlightenment. Why is this?"
Because all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, attain perfect enlightenment without departing from this mind.
Just as it is with one's own mind, so it is with the minds of all sentient beings; they all possess the Buddha-nature through which perfect enlightenment is realized.

This clarifies that the Buddha realizes Buddhahood through the *tathatā* (suchness) within the minds of sentient beings; therefore, original enlightenment (*benjue*) is without distinction. Since the initial [awakening] is identical to the fundamental, it all resides within the minds of sentient beings, arising as function from the essence.
When manifesting as response and transformation bodies, these are precisely the great functioning of *tathatā* within the minds of sentient beings; there is no separate Buddha.
This meaning is extensively clarified in the *Awakening of Faith*, wherein it is shown that these are the essence and function of one's own mind.

Now, because this sutra teaches that there is no difference between the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings, the Buddha realizes the essence of sentient beings and employs the functions of sentient beings.

Thirdly, since the Buddhas of the past and present exist within one another, each being real and not false, cause and effect are mutually penetrating; thus, according to any single sacred teaching, the whole is present within both minds. Therefore, the Buddha within the mind of a sentient being preaches the Dharma for the sentient beings within the Buddha’s mind;
and the sentient beings within the Buddha’s mind listen to the Dharma preached by the Buddha within their own minds.
Fourth, if Buddhahood were entirely present within birth, then it would be identical to birth and not Buddhahood;
if Buddhahood were entirely present within birth, then it would be identical to birth and not Buddhahood.

When these two aspects mutually negate one another, the two positions are equally integrated. Thus, according to any given sacred teaching, neither of the two minds exists: in the Buddha’s mind there are no sentient beings who listen, and in the sentient beings’ minds there is no Buddha who speaks.
Therefore, the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*) states: "That which is produced by causes and conditions has no production; the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is not a body.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Verses of Praise" (*Gāthā-stotra-parivarta*) states: "The Tathāgata does not preach the Dharma, nor does he deliver sentient beings."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 425, states: "Since I attained the Way, I have not spoken a single word; you, likewise, have heard nothing. And so forth.

Therefore, these four [aspects] are perfectly integrated and unimpeded within a single sacred teaching; only then do they constitute the ultimate, profound principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Regarding the seventh point, "entering the true substance by means of conditions": this is because the preceding six gates all enter into that same single reality.
There are also two meanings:
first, subsuming the derivative within the fundamental; second, reconciling appearances to reveal the nature.

In the former case, because all sacred teachings flow from the Truth (tathatā), they are not different from the Truth; thus, in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, they are termed the "twelvefold teaching flowing from suchness."

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, chapter ten, explains the "Tathatā as the Supreme Flow" (*parama-prasava-tathatā*) as follows: "It means that the teaching which flows forth from this Tathatā is the most supreme among all other teachings."

Although that school does not posit that *tathatā* (suchness) undergoes transformation according to conditions (*pariṇāma*), it maintains that the Buddha’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizes the most pure *dharmadhātu*. Furthermore, it establishes that the teachings taught through subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) are called "flowing like suchness" (*yathā-pravāha*); thus, by subsuming the derivative within the fundamental, it also names "suchness" itself as the essence of the teaching (*deśanā-śarīra*).

Second, regarding the manifestation of characteristics to reveal the nature: it means that all those various differentiated teachings, being without intrinsic nature due to their dependence on conditions, are themselves suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, false appearances are fundamentally exhausted and true nature is fundamentally manifest; the Tathāgata’s speech always accords with suchness.
Therefore, the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "As I speak, it is the meaning that is expressed, not the words;
as sentient beings speak, it is the words that are expressed, not the meaning."
The "Chapter on the Two Truths" in the *Renwang jing* states: "Great King!
The Wheel of Dharma consists of the suchness of the Dharmapada, the suchness of the Geya, and so forth, up to the suchness of the Upadeśa," and so on.
This sutra clarifies that the teaching is itself suchness (tathatā), but it does not say that all suchness is the teaching.
If one takes the manifest meaning of all phenomena as the essence of the teaching, then since all phenomena are suchness, there would be no suchness that is not the teaching.

The eighth is the essence of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena: this means that although the entirety of all teachings is identical with the ultimate truth, it does not obstruct the distinct and vivid manifestation of the various characteristics of the twelvefold division of the scriptures and other phenomena.
Although True Suchness manifests its entire substance as all things, it does not obstruct their being of a single flavor, profoundly serene and equal.
Because it is unobstructed, the Buddha’s voice likewise accords with the unobstructed nature of Suchness, for it is entirely in resonance with the wisdom of Suchness.
This has been explained extensively in the previous section on the "Delimitation of Meanings.

As for the essence of the ninth [aspect], the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratighāta*), both its words and meaning are perfect; these words constitute the Perfect Sound (*samyagghoṣa*).
Within this, there are likewise ten profound gateways (*daśa-gambhīra-dvāra*).

The "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" states: "The Buddha utters a single wondrous sound, which is heard throughout the lands of the ten directions; all voices are fully contained within it, and the rain of Dharma pervades everywhere."
"Immediately, one becomes fully endowed with the corresponding essence.

The "Chapter on the Ten Abodes" states: "Desiring to expound upon even a single phrase of the Dharma exhaustively throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), such that its words and meanings each remain distinct—by means of this, the Bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment."
This is the essence that is both expansive and unimpeded; it is also called the teaching of the pure and the mixed.
That a single phrase remains undestroyed is its narrowness and its purity.
That the words and meanings differ is its expansiveness and its mixture.

Furthermore, it is said: "To understand the many within a single dharma, and to understand the one within many dharmas," and so forth; these are all teachings on the mutual inclusion of the one and the many.

The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Manifestation" (*Prakāśana-parivarta*), states: "The voice of the Tathāgata universally enters into all things, just like written characters," and so forth; this, too, is mutual inclusion, which is identical to mutual penetration.
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* further states: "One is many, and many are one; the text follows the meaning, and the meaning follows the text.
This is precisely the mutual identity of the phenomenal aspect (*lakṣaṇa*) and the essence of the teaching (*śāstra-tattva*).
The "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "Throughout the site of enlightenment, all heard [the teaching] without being outside the assembly, each according to their own understanding.
This refers precisely to the essence of the hidden and manifest teachings.
It is further stated: "The vocal expressions of the Tathāgata are of but a single flavor; yet, because the mental capacities of sentient beings differ, they appear in immeasurable varieties.
This also refers to the hidden and manifest bodies of the teaching, as well as the pure and mixed teachings.
Furthermore, it is said: "The Tathāgata, within a single utterance, expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras, like the woman of eloquent speech"; this refers to the subtle teaching.
The "Chapter on Incalculables" (*Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*) states: "Within each and every *sūtra*, the differentiation of all dharmas is unspeakable;

within each and every one of those dharmas, furthermore, the teaching of all dharmas is unspeakable. Since this is the case for a single dharma, it is likewise for all other dharmas; they reflect one another in infinite layers, endlessly and inexhaustibly—this is precisely the teaching of the Indra-net (*Indra-jāla*).
That all encountered phenomena are the Dharma is the teaching that generates understanding by relying on phenomena.
That a single thought-moment suddenly unfolds [the entirety] is the teaching of the ten ages.
That in all assemblies, what is taught here in this world—such as the Ten Abodes—is likewise so in the ten directions is the teaching of the principal and its associates.
If one explains even a single dharma or a single gate, there are immeasurable sūtras that serve as its retinue; these constitute the "teachings of the retinue.
