Although they do not function as the primary subject, they are nonetheless associated as companions.
This is merely stated in terms of verbal expression.
If one considers the categories that pervade all phenomena as the substance of the teaching, they are simply the meanings expressed.
These meanings constitute the Universal Dharma, which possesses the ten mysteries (daśa-guhya-dvāra), as described in the *Yi-fen-chi* (The Delimitation of Meanings).

The tenth [aspect], the essence of the vivid manifestation of the ocean-seal, is as follows: all the aforementioned diverse and inexhaustible teachings are simultaneously and vividly manifested within the Tathāgata’s ocean-seal samādhi.

If the capacity of those to be converted likewise manifests clearly within meditative concentration as a dependent origination, then for this reason, samādhi alone constitutes the essence of the teaching.
As explained in the "Chapter on Manifestation," this refers to the stage of fruition.

If considered from the perspective of the causal stage, even perfect faith can manifest as a seal; as the "Chapter on Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*) states: "All such things are able to appear through the supernatural power of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi."
These ten sections encompass and integrate all things; there is not a single dharma that is not the essence of the teaching.
Furthermore, the final two sections constitute the very core of the sutra’s doctrine, for they harmoniously incorporate the preceding eight without exception.

Regarding the sixth point, the common and specific characteristics of the tenets (*siddhānta*) and their ultimate goals (*gati*): that which is esteemed by speech is called a "tenet," and that to which a tenet leads is called its "goal. First, the common characteristics are clarified; subsequently, the specific ones are revealed.

The preceding section has surveyed the Buddhist teachings of a lifetime; the various divergent theories of the different schools each constitute a distinct sect, as the eighteen fundamental schools and the two [Mahāyāna] traditions differ from one another. Therefore, they are further consolidated by grouping them according to their shared doctrinal principles.
However, the Dharma Master Dayan of the Sui dynasty established four schools in total:
first, the School of Causal Conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), which refers to the Sarvāstivāda;
second, the School of Provisional Names (*prajñapti*), which refers to the Sautrāntika.
The third is the school of non-reality, referring to the various *prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.
The fourth is the school of reality, referring to the teachings on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), ultimate truth, and the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*).

Furthermore, these four schools are designated as follows: the first is called "establishing nature," the second "refuting nature," the third "refuting characteristics," and the fourth "revealing reality."
The first two [periods] belong to the Hīnayāna and the latter two to the Mahāyāna, each being shallow at the beginning and profound at the end.
While this also has its logic, it does not fully encompass the meaning, because among the eighteen schools only two are thus categorized.
Now, summarizing the teachings of all periods throughout the dispensation, they are categorized into ten schools:

the first is the School of the Existence of Both Self and Dharmas, namely the Vātsīputrīya school and others. They establish three aggregates (*skandhas*): *(Note: The original text provides the opening of a commentary on the ten schools of Buddhist doctrine.
The translation reflects the provided fragment.)*
First, the conditioned;
second, the unconditioned;
third, that which is neither of these two aggregates—that which is neither is the self.
Furthermore, five dharma-treasuries are established: namely, the three time periods constitute three;
the unconditioned constitutes the fourth;
and the fifth is the inexpressible treasury, in which I abide, because the inexpressible is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.

However, this particular school was collectively rejected by the masters of all other schools, who labeled it a "non-Buddhist adhering to the Buddha's teachings," because although the calculations of various non-Buddhists differ, they all posit a self (*ātman*).
Second is the school that asserts the existence of phenomena but the non-existence of a self, namely the Sarvāstivāda and others.
They establish that all phenomena are not separate from form and mind; whether they posit the three times and the unconditioned, or divide them into five categories, in all cases there is no self.
Because it is without self, it differs from the calculations of the non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, by establishing correct causes and conditions within the realm of the conditioned, it refutes the false causes and causelessness of the non-Buddhists.

However, although there are ninety-five types of heterodox views in the Western Regions—some calculating that the twenty-five principles arise from primordial darkness (*avyakta*), others calculating that they arise from the combination of six categories, some claiming they are produced by Īśvara or Brahmā, and others asserting they are caused by time, direction, atoms, space, or past karma—all of these are held to be the basis for both the mundane world and *nirvāṇa*.

To summarize all such reckonings, they do not exceed four views: namely, the Sāṃkhya reckoning of identity, the Vaiśeṣika reckoning of difference, the Īśvarakṛṣṇa (Lèshébó) reckoning of both identity and difference, and the Jaina (Ruòtízi) reckoning of neither identity nor difference.
If one calculates that they are identical, it is said that the effect exists within the cause;
if one calculates that they are different, it is said that the effect does not exist within the cause;
as for the third [alternative], it is both existent and non-existent.
The fourth [position] is that it is neither existent nor non-existent.

All other divergent views do not fall outside of these; though they differ in many ways, when their logical faults are examined, they do not exceed two types: either arising spontaneously from space, which is causelessness, or all others, which are false causes.

The two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism in this land do not go beyond this either; for instance, Zhuangzi and Laozi both reckon in terms of spontaneity (*ziran*), stating: "Man models himself on the Earth; the Earth models itself on Heaven; Heaven models itself on the Dao; and the Dao models itself on spontaneity."
If one holds that "nature" (*svabhāva*) acts as the cause capable of producing all things, this is a false cause;
if one claims that all things arise spontaneously—just as a crane is white or a crow is black—this is the absence of a cause (*ahetu*).

The *Zhouyi* states: "In the *Yi* there is the Great Ultimate (*taiji*); from it arise the Two Polarities (*liangyi*); the Two Polarities give rise to the Four Images (*sxiang*); the Four Images give rise to the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*); the Eight Trigrams determine good fortune and misfortune; and good fortune and misfortune give rise to great undertakings. Here, the Great Ultimate is the cause, and it is precisely a false cause.
If one claims that "the union of yin and yang is called the Way" and thus reckons that the transformation of yin and yang can give rise to the myriad things, this too is a false cause.
If one reckons that the One is void, non-existent, or spontaneous, then it is likewise causeless.

However, to hold that there is no cause or to rely on false causes leads to great error; for if things were produced by such means as "spontaneity" or "empty space," they would have to be produced eternally.

Failing to realize that the three realms arise from one's own mind—that beings transmigrate without end due to ignorance and craving—and being deluded regarding the true nature of causes and conditions, various heterodox views proliferate. How could such people know that the nature of causes and conditions is emptiness, and that True Suchness is wondrous existence?

As for those who claim there is a conflation with the teachings of Śākyamuni, these are all merely remnants of the Buddha-dharma; they are like the parable in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* of stealing a cow. Although the color of the milk may be the same, one cannot properly extract the *ghṛta* (clarified butter); how much less could one produce *navanīta* (fresh butter) or *dadhi* (curd) by churning donkey’s milk?

The various divergent views are explained in detail in the sixth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the ninth and tenth fascicles of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the eleventh and twelfth fascicles of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and as set forth in the *Saptati-sāstra*; these views are also extensively refuted in treatises such as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*.
Now, by merely explaining the correct causes and conditions, all speculative views have been comprehensively refuted.
This is such that even the most superficial aspects of the Buddha’s Dharma already surpass the most profound depths of the non-Buddhists.
Regarding the school of the Mahāsāṃghikas and others who maintain that phenomena neither come nor go, they assert the existence of the present and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) alone.
The dharmas of the past and future lack both substance and function.

Regarding the four schools that maintain that the present is both provisional and real—namely, the Saṃmatīyas—it is held that among the dharmas of the aforementioned present, those existing as aggregates (skandha) are real, while those existing as elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana) are provisional.
The masters of the Sautrāntika school who follow the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* belong to this category.

Fifth are those of the school that asserts the conventional is false while the ultimate is real; these include the Lokottaravādins and others, who maintain that the conventional is merely provisional because it is illusory, whereas the supramundane is the opposite.

Sixth, the school that maintains all phenomena are merely names (*nāma-mātra*), namely the Ekavyāvahārikas and others, who assert that all selves and phenomena exist only as provisional designations because they lack substantial reality.

Seventh, the school that maintains the emptiness and existence of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), namely those who assert that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is empty while the dependent (*paratantra*) and perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures are existent.

The eighth is the School of the Eightfold True Emptiness that Transcends Characteristics (*zhēn-kōng jué-xiàng zōng*), which means that both mind and objects are extinguished, directly manifesting the essence.

The ninth is the School of the Non-obstruction of Emptiness and Existence (*kōng-yǒu wú-ài zōng*), which means that they mutually integrate and are simultaneously transcended without hindering their dual persistence, for True Suchness (*tathatā*) follows conditions and possesses virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The tenth is the school of Perfect Interfusion and Endowment with Virtue (*yuanrong jude zong*), so called because all phenomena are mutually unimpeded, principal and attendant are fully present, and there is inexhaustible sovereignty.
Furthermore, among these ten schools, each subsequent one is deeper than the preceding.

The first four belong exclusively to the Hīnayāna; the fifth and sixth pertain to both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna; and the latter four belong exclusively to the Mahāyāna. Specifically, the seventh is the Dharmalakṣaṇa school, the eighth is the Niriṃśana (or Nirākāra) school, and the final two are the Dharmatā school.

Furthermore, the seventh corresponds to the Initial Teaching (Shijiao), the eighth to the Sudden Teaching (Dun jiao), the ninth to the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), and the tenth to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Moreover, the seventh is also called the School of the Coexistence of the Two Truths; this means that because ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*) is truly existent, the conventional (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is not non-existent, and because cause and effect are not lost, it exists. This is as taught in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and other such works.

The eighth is also called the school that transcends both truths simultaneously (*ubhaya-satya-vinirmukta-pakṣa*). This means that because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is free from characteristics, it is not existent; and because conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) is dependently originated like an illusion, it is non-existent.
As the verse in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (*Pāṇilekhā*) states: "In its true nature, conditioned phenomena are empty, for they are dependently originated like illusions."
"Unconditioned phenomena have no reality; their non-arising is like flowers in the sky," and so forth—this constitutes one portion of the meaning within the three treatises of Prajñāpāramitā.

As for the school of the "Non-obstruction of the Two Truths," as found in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and others, its meaning has been clarified as previously shown.
However, the ten schools and five teachings vary in their breadth and narrowness: regarding the teachings (*jiao*), a single sutra may contain multiple teachings;
regarding the schools (*zong*), a single school may encompass multiple sutras, as any given sutra may belong to that school.
If one were to restrictively judge a single scripture as constituting a single teaching, then all other Mahāyāna teachings would be suppressed.

Furthermore, the establishment of a teaching necessarily involves distinctions such as the stages of realization and verification (*pramāṇa*), whereas the establishment of a school merely clarifies the differences in what is held as supreme.
The preceding six schools differ in their adherence to specific doctrines, and are thus divided into six;
however, regarding the stages of realization and the sequence of attainment, they do not deviate from the eight ranks, and are therefore integrated into a single teaching.
Other meanings are as previously discussed in the section on the establishment of the teachings.
Second, regarding the revelation of the specific tenet: while all sūtras each have their own particular tenet, this section now specifically clarifies the tenet and purport of this sūtra.
As for the statement in the *Laṅkāvatāra* that "all dharmas are unarisen, and one should not establish this as a tenet," these words are intended to dispel attachment.
If one possesses a thesis that is itself without a thesis, then both the thesis and its exposition will be fully elucidated.
This shall be analyzed briefly through two gates:
first, an account of divergent interpretations; second, the presentation of the present meaning.
Regarding the preceding section, ten [masters] are briefly cited:
first, Master Yan, who took the unobstructed dharma-realm as his primary tenet;
second, Master Yu, who took the profound dharma-realm and its mental objects as his primary tenet.
This means that within the gateway of the *dharmadhātu*, its objective aspects are taken as the realm; the Buddhas realize it and thereby perfect the Pure Land.

The *dharmadhātu* is itself the One Mind; the Buddhas realize it and thereby perfect the *dharmakāya*. Therefore, the first chapter states: "The inexhaustible, equal, and wondrous *dharmadhātu* completely fills the body of the Tathāgata."
At the end, the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter (*dharmadhātupraveśaparivarta*) is elucidated; therefore, it is known that the sole thesis is the Dharma Realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Thirdly, some say that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the thesis, because the Dharma Realm and dependent origination are mutually identical and interfused.
Fourth, some say that its primary tenet is Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra), because the Sūtra states: "The three realms are manifested by the mind alone; the mind is like a skilled painter.

Fifth, the two masters Min and Yin both hold that cause and effect constitute the primary tenet; they maintain that this Sūtra extensively elucidates the causes of the bodhisattva’s stages of practice and reveals the resultant qualities of merit, as the subsequent text does not depart from these.
Sixth, Dharma Master Yuǎn took the Huáyán Samādhi as his primary tenet, asserting that the flowers of causal practice are able to adorn the fruit of Buddhahood.

Seventh, Tripiṭaka Master Guptadatta took the contemplative practice of the forty-two worthy and sage stages as his primary tenet, explaining their respective practices and positions so as to bring about the realization of contemplation.

Eighth, some say that the *sāgaramudrā-samādhi* is taken as the primary principle; for from the principles and phenomena of the direct and reverse orders up to the Indra’s net, all appear simultaneously like the waves of the ocean when it is serene.

The Vinaya Master Jiuguang took the reality of cause and effect as his primary tenet, because cause and effect constitute the stages of practice to be accomplished, while the reality of principle constitutes the Dharma-realm upon which one relies.

O Worthy Leader, because each of the preceding [masters] was mutually deficient, [Xianshou] took the reality of the *dharmadhātu* as the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—the causal relationship—as his primary thesis.

This means that while the first two masters only attained the *dharmadhātu* as the basis of reliance, the third and fourth masters only elucidated dependent origination, the fifth and sixth only elucidated cause and effect, the seventh only the cultivation of the cause, and the eighth only the function of the fruit; since all were mutually deficient, Xianshou’s intention was to adopt the system of Guangtong and add the terms "dependent origination" and "*dharmadhātu*."

Because Master Guangtong held that cause and effect are identical to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and that ultimate principle (*li-shi*) is identical to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), he did not differentiate them.

Master Xianshou, however, maintained that cause and effect are specific aspects within dependent origination and that ultimate principle is a specific aspect within the dharma-realm; therefore, he added a general name. He did so because the dharma-realm encompasses both phenomena and principle as well as their non-obstruction, and because [cause and effect] are the functional manifestations upon the substance of dependent origination. Thus, he added it.
Second, regarding the presentation of my own interpretation: while relying on the latter two masters, I have made certain modifications.
If one wishes to adopt a concise formulation that encompasses everything, one should state: "The principle of the inconceivable dependent origination of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is the thesis.
If one adopts a more comprehensive formulation, one should add the term "inconceivable" to the tenth master's position.

This summarizes the general title: in principle, it is the "Great" (Mahā); its dependent origination is the "Vast" (Vaipulya); the Dharma-realm (Dharmadhātu) encompasses both of the former; and its cause and effect constitute the "Buddha's Flower Adornment" (Buddhāvataṃsaka). By examining the general title, one already understands these specific meanings.
Furthermore, while terms such as "dharma-dhātu" (the realm of phenomena) may appear in various sūtras, they do not explicitly reveal its unique distinction.
When these are permeated by the "inconceivable" (acintya), then the dharma-dhātu and all else become inconceivable; therefore, this constitutes the central tenet of the sūtra.
Therefore, it is excellent evidence that Nāgārjuna pointed to this as the *Mahā-acintya-sūtra*.

The *Vimalakīrti* merely clarifies the inconceivable liberation of functional activity; this is but a partial meaning, as it does not yet manifest the inconceivability of the interpenetration of the dharma-realm and so forth. Thus, they are not the same.

If one analyzes the essence (tǐ), tenet (zōng), and function (yòng) based on the title, then taking reality as it is (lǐ shí) as the essence, dependent origination (yuánqǐ) as the function, and cause and effect (yīnguǒ) as the tenet; since one seeks the tenet to lead toward the reality of the true essence, the Dharma-realm (fǎjiè) subsumes all three of these.
Now, to explain the preceding meaning, it is briefly divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the names; second, the elucidation of the meanings.
This is the first part.
The name and essence of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) are as extensive as explained in this chapter;
here, I shall briefly set forth two aspects:
first, the phenomenal dharma-realm (sāṃvṛtika-dharmadhātu), and second, the noumenal dharma-realm (pāramārthika-dharmadhātu).
The two dharmas both contain and maintain the two realms; thus, while their natures and divisions differ, they are mutually pervasive in their function.
Within the second section on the manifestation of meaning, there are four sub-sections:

First, the distinct opening of the dharma-realm to establish cause and effect—namely, the dharma-realm of Samantabhadra as the cause and the dharma-realm of Vairocana as the fruit. Therefore, cause and effect are not separate from the reality of the dharma-realm.
Among these, ten matters comprise five pairs, which constitute five cycles of cause and effect:

first, the cause and effect of what is believed; second, the cause and effect of differentiation; third, the cause and effect of equality; fourth, the cause and effect of accomplishing practice; and fifth, the cause and effect of realization and entry. These shall be pointed out in the text below.
Furthermore, cause and effect serve as the mutual thematic focus (*piṇḍārtha*) because throughout the beginning and end of this single sūtra, they are never separated from cause and effect.
While cause and effect constitute the thematic focus, this does not contradict the *dharmadhātu* upon which they rely.
The second assembly integrates cause and effect to unify them within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Within this gateway of the Dharma-realm, there are also ten matters in five pairs that serve as mutual themes and objectives:

first, the relative contrast between teaching (*śāsana*) and meaning (*artha*). This means taking the teaching as the theme and manifesting the meaning as the objective, or taking the meaning as the theme and manifesting the teaching as the objective, so as to clarify the profundity of the meaning and thereby render the teaching supreme.

In the mutual correspondence between the two persons and the Dharma: taking the person as the primary focus is intended to lead one to understand the Dharma; taking the Dharma as the primary focus is intended to lead one to realize the person.
In the mutual correspondence between phenomena (shi) and principle (li): raising up phenomena is intended to lead one toward principle, while raising up principle is intended to integrate phenomena.

Fourth, the relative relationship between object and wisdom: this is because the observed object is presented so as to bring about the observing wisdom, and the cultivated wisdom is presented so as to realize its identity with the true object.

Fifth, the relative relationship between cause and fruit: this is because the causal practice is presented so as to realize the fruit, and the sublime fruit is presented to encourage the cultivation of the cause.
The five pairs specifically clarify the meaning of this doctrine; the identity of these five pairs constitutes the doctrine itself as its meaning.
The preceding five cycles of cause and effect do not depart from these five pairs of dharmas, which are precisely the dharma-realm of phenomena and principle.

How much more so when cause and effect lack intrinsic nature and are, in their very essence, identical with the Truth; therefore, taking the Dharma-realm alone as the central tenet does not contradict cause and effect.
Third, the cause and effect of the Dharma-realm are clearly revealed, and they likewise comprise ten meanings in five pairs:
first, the peerless object, which has two aspects:
First, the dharmadhātu of pure nature while still enmeshed in afflictions is the object of faith;
second, the most purified dharmadhātu beyond the enmeshment of afflictions is the object of realization.
Second, the incomparable mind also has two meanings:
First, the single great bodhicitta, because it is the root of the conduct of Samantabhadra;
second, faith, compassion, wisdom, and so forth, because they arise in accordance with that conduct.
Third, peerless conduct, which also has two meanings:
First, the practice of differentiation, because each is cultivated separately;
second, the practice of Samantabhadra, because the one is identical to all.
Regarding the four incomparable stages (*asama-bhūmi*), there are likewise two meanings:
First, the stage of sequential arrangement, because realization is distinct;
second, the stage of perfect interfusion, because the realization of one is the realization of all.
Fifth, the peerless fruit, which also has two meanings:
First, the cultivation that produces a fruit, because it is only now that it is first accomplished;
second, the cultivation that manifests a fruit, because it is inherently possessed from the beginning.
In these five pairs above, the first phrase of each constitutes the thesis (*zong*), while the latter phrase constitutes the purpose (*qu*).

Furthermore, among the aforementioned five, the first is the true dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the second is dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), and the third, fourth, and fifth are all causes of dependent origination, while the last one is the fruit of dependent origination.
Guangtong fully employs both meanings as his central tenet, without any contradiction.
Fourth, within the Dharma-realm, cause and effect are mutually fused; both are free from essence and characteristics, blending seamlessly in unimpeded sovereignty.
There are also ten meanings:
first, because of the departure from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), cause and effect are not different from the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); that is, cause and effect are neither cause nor effect.

Here, taking "characteristics" as the thesis (*pakṣa*) and "departure from characteristics" as the goal (*gati*), or taking "departure from characteristics" as the thesis and "the vanishing of cause and effect" as the goal.
The following nine points should be understood by analogy with this reflection.
Second, because it is free from [dualistic] nature, the dharma-realm is not distinct from cause and effect; thus, the dharma-realm is itself non-dharma-realm.

Third, because it is free from [dualistic] nature yet does not obliterate its own nature, when the dharma-realm is manifest as cause and effect, the dharma-realm remains perfectly intact; thus, one takes that which is non-dharma-realm to be the dharma-realm.

Fourth, because it is free from characteristics and does not destroy characteristics, when cause and effect are identical with the Dharma-realm, cause and effect remain distinct; thus, that which is not cause and effect functions as cause and effect.

Fifth, because the absence of characteristics is not different from the absence of nature, cause and effect and the dharma-realm both vanish and merge together, utterly transcending words and thought.
Sixth, because they are indestructible, non-different, and do not vanish, cause and effect and the dharma-realm coexist, manifesting vividly and clearly visible before one.

Seventh, because existence and cessation are not distinct from the five and six [aggregates and sense bases], this wondrous Dharma transcends both sight and hearing, yet there is nothing that does not constantly pass through seeing and hearing;
its profound meaning is beyond thought and deliberation, yet it has never been obstructed by words or reflection.

Eighth, because the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is fused and indivisible, the cause and effect of the *dharmadhātu* each simultaneously and completely encompass the entire *dharmadhātu* without exception.

Ninth, when cause and effect each completely encompass the *dharmadhātu*, they follow the *dharmadhātu* and each manifests within the other as cause and effect; therefore, the Bodhisattva exists within the Buddha, and Samantabhadra exists within the Buddha.

Because the two stages of cause and fruit each encompass all phenomena within the *dharmadhātu* according to their respective distinctions, every single phenomenon, every single practice, every single stage, and every single virtue collectively subsumes an inexhaustible ocean of *dharmamukhas*, as vast and layered as Indra’s net. This is called the inexhaustible core teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*.

Regarding the four preceding gates: the first is the function of the essence; the second is the essence of the function; the third is the simultaneous manifestation of both essence and function; and the fourth is the seamless integration of essence and function.

Furthermore, the first [gate] is precisely the causal dependent origination; the second is precisely the ultimate reality of the Dharma-realm; the third clarifies both together; and the last is the inconceivable.

Since the fourth integrates the preceding three, the four gates are of one principle. Thus, illumination is simultaneous with negation, and negation is simultaneous with illumination; this perfect and luminous single contemplation, which illuminates and negates both simultaneously, accords with the essential intent of this school.

Regarding the seventh section, the "Chapter on Categories": since the profound and deep purport has already been understood, it remains to be examined whether the expressive words and phrases are extensive or concise.

This section contains four parts: first, manifesting the primary division; second, revealing the chapter and assembly; third, clarifying the subsidiary categories; and fourth, analyzing the commentary and explanations.

Regarding the beginning and middle [of this work], the explanations of the Ocean of Nature (dharmatā-samudra) are taught constantly and taught universally; their words exhaust the Dharma-realm and are difficult to measure.
Now, from the narrow to the broad, I shall briefly categorize them into ten types:

First, the abbreviated root sūtra—namely the eighty-fascicle version currently transmitted, as well as the sixty-fascicle version of the earlier translation—both of which are abbreviations from among the one hundred thousand verses, for the translation was not completed in its entirety.

Second, the abbreviated version of the sutra refers to the Mahāyāna Piṭaka; this scripture was compiled by Mañjuśrī and Ānanda Sāgara between the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) and subsequently deposited within the Dragon Palace.

When Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna went to the Dragon Palace, he saw that this *Mahā-acintya-sūtra* existed in three versions; the inferior version consisted of one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters.

Nāgārjuna recited it so that it was transmitted to the world; therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls this the "Inconceivable Sūtra" (*Acintya-sūtra*) consisting of one hundred thousand verses.
In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* of the Liang dynasty, it is called the "Sūtra of One Hundred Thousand [Verses]."
The *Xiyuji* states that the complete original of this [text] exists in the kingdom of Cakubana.
Among the three versions of the original sūtra, it is that which was seen there, consisting of four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred gāthās and one thousand two hundred chapters.

The *Caturuttara-pūrvapīṭha-sūtra* consists of as many verses as there are atoms in thirteen thousandfold world systems, and as many chapters as there are atoms in a single four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*).
The two preceding texts cannot be sustained by the mental power of the people of Jambudvīpa; therefore, they were not transmitted.

Fifth is the *Puyan-jing* (Universal Eye Sūtra), which is sustained by Sāgaramegha. Even with ink equal in volume to the great ocean and pens as numerous as Mount Sumeru, one could not record even a small fraction of a single gate within a single chapter of this Universal Eye Dharma-gate—a single method within a gate, a single meaning within a method, or a single phrase within a meaning—let alone the whole. It can only be sustained through the power of the dhāraṇīs of bodhisattvas who have entered the profound dharma-realm.
The various sutras listed below cannot be received through ordinary human power.

Sixth is the *Sūtra of Identical Discourse*, which refers to speaking with vocal sound throughout the entirety of space—even within spaces as small as the tip of a hair—within world-systems shaped like Mount Sumeru, without end.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharma": "Just as a single Buddha-body, by means of its supernormal powers, turns such various wheels of Dharma that no worldly phenomena can serve as an analogy."

"In this manner, throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space—at every location as small as a single hair-tip, and even within each individual transformation body—all are spoken thus; the sounds, words, phrases, and meanings fill the Dharma-realm one by one," and so forth.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*) states: "The Buddhas seen within the light are unspeakable; the Dharma taught by those Buddhas is unspeakable," and so forth, up to: "Within each and every *sūtra*, the analytical distinctions of the Dharma-gates are unspeakable."

This intention merely means that once the Dharma has been taught using a certain type of sound, it cannot be compiled; how then could those of lower capacities maintain it? Seventh, regarding the various ways of expounding the sūtras:

since the worlds—such as those shaped like trees—are diverse, the types of retributive bodies of the sentient beings therein are also distinct. Consequently, the Tathāgata manifests his body and establishes teachings with different arrangements in those places; it is impossible to definitively determine whether they are material or immaterial, speech or non-speech, and so forth. Thus, their categories and varieties are immeasurable.

The eighth is the Sūtra on the Principal and the Retinue (*pramukha-parivāra*). This means that although the teachings of Vairocana pervade the entire Dharma-realm, he and the various Buddhas act as mutual principals and retinues.

For example, when the *Daśabhūmika* (Ten Stages) is taught, those who come from the ten directions to bear witness all say, "In my land, this is also being taught," and so forth; thus, each of the preceding seven sūtras possesses both a principal and a retinue.

The *Nine Retinue Sūtras* (Jiù juànshǔ jīng) refers to those who, due to their remaining faculties, are unable to hear this universal teaching; for them, teachings are expounded according to their suitability to lead them into this gateway. Because these serve as the superior skillful means for this sūtra, they are called its "retinue."

Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "The Universal Eye Sūtra has as its retinue as many sūtras as there are atoms in a Buddha-field," and so forth; thus, each of the preceding eight [sūtras] likewise possesses a retinue.

The *Daśaviśeṣa-sūtra* (Ten Perfection Sūtras) refers to the total integration of all these aforementioned versions into a single, inexhaustible ocean of Mahāyāna sūtras. Since every assembly, chapter, phrase, and word encompasses everything without limitation, the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" states: "The Buddha Vairocana, by the power of his vows, pervades the Dharma-realm; within all lands, he constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel," and so forth. Thus, it is described as the "Wheel of the Perfect Cause" within the seventy-third [chapter]. This is what that means.
Regarding the differences between the second assembly and the others, this clarifies the similarities and differences between the present sutra and the Jin dynasty translation.

The present sutra consists of nine assemblies; however, because the beginning of the seventh assembly of the Jin translation lacks the "Ten Samādhis Chapter" (Daśadharmasvabhāva-parivarta) and its subsequent reassembly at the Universal Radiance Hall (Samantaprabhāsa), it contains only eight assemblies.
There are now thirty-nine chapters, with six chapters in the first assembly;
that scripture had only thirty-four, because within the first assembly there were only two chapters:
the first, the "Chapter on the Pure Eye of the World," which is the present "Chapter on the World Lord" (Lokēśvara).
The second is the "Vairocana Chapter," which comprises the current five chapters beginning with "Manifesting Signs.
Since the first assembly lacks four chapters and is further missing the "Ten Samādhis," it consists of only thirty-four chapters.
The remaining chapters and assemblies are largely the same, with only minor differences in name, which shall become evident in the text itself.
Third, regarding the clarification of the branch categories, there are two parts:
first, the manifestation of the branches, namely the separately circulated sūtras.
The one-fascicle *Tuṣa jīng* (Dharmaguṇarāja-sūtra) among the Tibetan [canon] is the "Chapter on Names and Titles.
The one-fascicle *Púsà běnyè jīng* (Bodhisattvaprāthamakarmika-sūtra) is the "Chapter on Pure Conduct."
The *Shorter Sutra on the Ten Abodes* in one fascicle is the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes.
The *Greater Sutra on the Ten Abodes* in four fascicles, as well as the *Sutra on the Gradual Preparation for All-Wisdom Virtue* in four fascicles, are both the "Chapter on the Ten Grounds."
The *Samādhi Sūtra Asked by the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin* in two fascicles is the "Chapter on the Ten Concentrations" (*Daśadhyāna-parivarta*).
The *Sūtra of Boundless Merits* in one fascicle is the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*).
The *Tathāgatagotra-nirdeśa-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Subtle and Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata’s Nature-Arising) in two fascicles is the "Chapter on Manifestation.
The *Lokottara-parivarta-sūtra* (The Sūtra on Transcending the World) in six fascicles is the "Chapter on Leaving the World."
The *Luo-mo-jie jing* (Rāmāyaṇa Sūtra) in three fascicles is the "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*dharmadhātupraveśa*) chapter.
These [texts] were all extracted from the Great Canon according to the capacities of those who received and upheld them.

Second, regarding the affiliated texts: the *Cultivation of Loving-kindness Sūtra* (one fascicle), the *Vajramālā Sūtra* (ten fascicles), and the *Sūtra on the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata* (one fascicle) are all affiliated with the *Avataṃsaka* but are not part of its main body as separate recensions; alternatively, they may be separate recensions whose transmission remains incomplete. I have not yet ventured to provide a definitive determination.
The remainder is as explained in the *Zuǎnlíngjì*.
Regarding the fourth point, the commentaries and expositions, four examples are briefly cited:

first, after Nāgārjuna obtained the abbreviated version, he subsequently composed the *Mahā-acintya-śāstra*, also consisting of one hundred thousand stanzas, which was widely transmitted throughout the Western Regions.
In this land, there are sixteen fascicles of the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra*, which are precisely the commentary on the first two of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) from that treatise.

The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* as a commentary on the "Ten Stages Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*). During the Wei dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati and also Bodhiruci each translated a version. Later, Sengguang petitioned for these two versions to be collated by the two Tripiṭaka Masters into a single edition consisting of twelve fascicles, which is what is currently transmitted.
Third, Liu Qianzhi of the Northern Qi felt a spiritual resonance at Mount Qingliang and composed six hundred fascicles of treatises, providing a comprehensive commentary on a single sutra.

Fourth, the monk Lingbian of the Later Wei wore this sutra upon his head atop Mount Wutai; after practicing the Way for one year, he finally realized its profound meaning and composed one hundred fascicles of treatises, which have likewise been transmitted to the world.
The eighth section concerns the transmission and translation, as well as the miraculous responses, which is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying the dates of the translations; second, clarifying the accounts of the transmission and miraculous signs.
Within the first part, this sutra has been translated twice in total throughout its history; including supplementary versions, there are four different recensions.

In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra from North India—whose name means "Awakened Virtue" (Jue Xian) in Chinese—translated thirty-six thousand verses from the Sanskrit original at the Si Kong Temple in Yangzhou. This resulted in fifty or sixty fascicles of the Jin version of the scripture, with the śramaṇa Faye acting as the scribe and Huiyan and Huiguan refining the language.
The Xiesikong Temple is the present-day Xingyan Temple in Runzhou, so named because it was established for the sake of promoting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

During the first year of the Yonglong era of the Great Tang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master from India, Śīlabhadra (translated into Chinese as Rìzhào), translated the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter at Dayuan Temple in the Western Capital. Within this work, there were two omissions of text:
the first occurred between the section following Māyādevī and the section preceding Maitreya Bodhisattva, specifically concerning the ten spiritual benefactors beginning with Devendrābhāsa.

Second, from after Maitreya Bodhisattva until before the good spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) as numerous as the atoms in three thousand great thousandfold world-systems, during which interval Mañjuśrī extends his hand across one hundred and ten yojanas to place it upon Sudhana’s crown—this constitutes fifteen lines of the sūtra.

The Vinaya Master Daode Daocheng, the Dharma Master Bocen, the Dharma Master Dasheng Ji, and others translated it together; the Dharma Master Fuli refined the prose, establishing the sixty-fascicle version as the definitive text.

In the first year of the Zhengsheng era, the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda (translated as Xixue, "Delight in Learning") from Khotan retranslated the old text at Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital; he supplemented various omissions, adding nine thousand ślokas, bringing the total to forty-five thousand ślokas across eighty fascicles, thus forming the Tang edition.

Translated together by the Tripiṭaka Master of Great Virtue, Yi Jing; Chan Master Hongjing; Dharma Master Yuance; Dharma Master Shenying; Dharma Master Fabao; and Dharma Master Xianshou; with Dharma Master Fuli composing the prose.

Fourth, although the aforementioned third edition had added passages in several places, it nonetheless omitted the passage concerning Mañjuśrī placing his hand upon Sudhana’s head as supplemented by Tripitaka Master Jiaruo. Consequently, Master Xianshou compared the new and old translations with the Sanskrit original; he then inserted Jiaruo’s supplementary text into the lacunae of the Xi edition, whereby the text was restored and the meaning made continuous.
The essentials of its text will be discussed below.
What is currently transmitted is the fourth version.

Since the third version was already circulated previously, many omissions still remain in the world’s extant scriptures today; this is precisely the third version. I hope that those of discerning knowledge will notice these deficiencies and supplement them.

Second, regarding the transmission, circulation, and spiritual responses: since the subtle words were translated during the Jin dynasty, the two youths manifested auspicious signs; when the ultimate teachings were rendered in the Tang, the sweet dew presented its blessings. These secret protections are clearly evident, as even the Emperor’s own calligraphy was personally bestowed.

When the treatises were established in the Western Regions, the earth quaked and light streamed forth; when their resolve reached Qingliang Mountain, they moved the unseen and attained profound awakening.

As for their transcription, the scriptures shone with five colors and the fragrance of the paper spread in all directions; winter chrysanthemums burst into bloom and auspicious birds carried flowers in their beaks.

When recited, one seemed to tread upon the void and was as radiant as gazing into a mirror; on every occasion, śarīras were contained within them and divine monks appeared in person. They surged from the earth to manifest golden bodies and ascended to heaven to halt the battle arrays of the asuras.

In his contemplative practice, he entered realization through non-arising and praised the void with verses; the sea deity listened and sent down torrential rains, while the celestial youths welcomed him as great waters overflowed.
In his preaching, he harmonized the sounds of both Chinese and Sanskrit, and was followed alike by humans and devas; the floods were cut off at their source, and divine light filled the halls.
It is truly because the wondrousness of a single word encompasses all meanings without exception that the power of a single verse can shatter the hells;
and since even the water used for washing one's hands can rescue living beings, the merit of reciting, contemplating, and practicing is equal to that of the Buddha’s omniscience.
By what good fortune in past lives have I encountered this sublime literature? Its historical accounts are clearly manifest and fully recorded in the biographies.
Within the ninth section, the General Explanation of the Title, I shall first interpret the title of the sutra and subsequently clarify the titles of its chapters.

Now, first: the general title encompasses specific meanings and includes this inconceivable dharma-gate. Within that which is nameless, we provisionally distinguish ten sections: first, a general exposition of how it is named; second, a comparative analysis of its expansions and contractions;

third, a full manifestation of its categories of meaning; fourth, a specific explanation of its naming; fifth, an infinite unfolding; sixth, a complete synthesis through contraction; seventh, the unimpeded nature of expansion and contraction; eighth, the perfect inclusion of all meanings; ninth, the convergence back into the one mind; and tenth, the dissolution into ultimate equality.

First: there are many ways in which various sūtras receive their names. Some are designated by way of persons, while others are named after dharmas. Among persons, there are distinctions such as those who request the teaching or those for whom it is taught; among dharmas, there are differences such as the Dharma itself versus its metaphors. Furthermore, names may refer to essence or function, or to fruit or cause; they may be compound or simple, their categories being vast and manifold.
Now, the titles by which this sutra is known are also diverse and differ in many ways:

first, there are those designated according to their numerical extent, such as in the tenth chapter on "Superior Characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the Liang dynasty’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, which states: "'The hundred-thousand sutras' refers to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, which consists of one hundred thousand verses."
Second, it is named after its metaphor, as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi Sūtra*.
This sūtra is titled the *Saṃpuṣpita Sūtra* because the myriad practices are intermingled and integrated through the formation of dependent origination.

Third, names are designated based on the Dharma [they represent], such as when the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the "Entrusting" chapter (*Parīndanā-parivarta*) by naming this sutra the *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra*.
Fourth, names are received based on their functional meaning, as seen in the ten distinct titles given to each of the "Leaving the World" (*Lokottara*) and "Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva*) chapters.

According to the present Sanskrit manuscript, it is titled *Mahāvaipulyabuddhāvataṃsakasūtra*, which in Chinese means *The Great Vaipulya Sūtra of the Buddha’s Adornments with Various Flowers*; here, the characters for "various" and "adornments" have been omitted.

The three previous alternative titles were largely general and abbreviated in meaning; the two chapters and ten sections mostly followed specific meanings and were limited to their respective parts. Therefore, the present translator has provided full six-character titles, which simultaneously address both the person and the dharma, and equally present both the dharma and its metaphor. Thus, they fully embody both the substance and the function, as well as the fruit and the cause; being exhaustive in principle and perfect in meaning, they are placed at the beginning of the sutra.
Second, regarding the analysis of the opening and closing [of the categories]: within the seven characters of the title, there are ten items arranged in five pairs.

First, the pair of teaching and meaning: the character "sūtra" (經) refers to the teaching as the means of expression (*abhidhāna*), while the six characters beginning with "great" (大) refer to the meanings expressed (*abhidheya*).
Second, regarding the meaning, there is a pair consisting of the dharma and its metaphor: that is, "Great" and so forth are the dharma, while "Flower Adornment" (Avataṃsaka) is the metaphor.

Third, regarding the dharma, there is a pair consisting of the person and the dharma: that is, "Great, Vast, and Wide" refers to the unobstructed dharma to be realized, while "Buddha" refers to the person who realizes it; this is also called the pair of object and wisdom.

Fourth, within the category of phenomena (*dharma*), the pair of "selection" (*jian*) and "retention" (*chi*) is established: the single character "Great" (*da*) is the selection, and "vastness" (*guang*) is the retention. This means selecting the Great as distinct from the Small, selecting the Real as distinct from the Provisional, and selecting the Fruit as distinct from the Cause; it is also the pair of essence (*ti*) and function (*yong*).
The "Great Square" (Dafang) is the essence (*tǐ*), for the Great Square has no corners.
"Vastness" (*guǎng*) is the function (*yòng*).
Among the five [categories], the character "Flower" (*huā*) from below is borrowed to metaphorize its cause; this constitutes the pair of cause and effect, as the Buddha is the fruit (*guǒ*).
Therefore, if the word "flower" (hua) is used alone, it serves merely as a metaphor for the cause.
If combined with "adornment" (yan), it also serves as a metaphor for the four characters above, which shall be clarified below.

Regarding the third point, "the three aspects that manifest the categories of meaning": this refers to the fact that the meanings of the seven characters, beginning with "Great" (Dà), are all immeasurable; they are each briefly explained by way of ten meanings.
First, to clarify the ten meanings of "Great": 1. **The Greatness of Essence** (*tǐ-dà*):
This means that whether in terms of characteristics (*xiàng*) or functions (*yòng*), all are identical to the true nature (*zhēn-xìng*) and are eternally pervasive; thus, it is the character "Great."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which is called 'great' is termed 'permanent.
This clarifies that its essence is unchanging; it is like a person who is called "great" because they are the eldest.
Furthermore, it says: "The 'Great' refers to its nature being as vast and expansive as empty space.
This clarifies the pervasiveness of its essence (*tattva*).

Second is the greatness of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), meaning that it is fully endowed with all the inherent virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, such that they mutually interpenetrate and enter into one another in subtle, layered, and manifold ways.
Possessing the ten mysterious gates (daśa-guhya-dvāra), all are its manifestations; this corresponds to the character *fang* (方) in the sutra.
*Fang* means "dharma" (*dharma*).
Its three functions are great, meaning that its karmic activity is all-pervasive, just as its essence is omnipresent; this corresponds to the character *guang* (廣) in the sutra.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Furthermore, 'great' (da) is that which can establish great significance.
This refers to its function; for since Nirvāṇa has no breadth (guang), its breadth is identical to its greatness (da). Therefore, "breadth" is used to explain "greatness."
"Vaipulya" (extensiveness) does not inherently possess "greatness"; rather, greatness and extensiveness are conjoined, and thus greatness is used to explain extensiveness.
Since this sutra possesses both qualities, they are each assigned accordingly.

The "Greatness" of the four fruits refers to the fact that their wisdom, abandonment, and the reliance and supported [bodies] universally pervade the Dharma-realm; this is precisely the meaning of the word "Buddha" in the sutra.

The five causes are "Great," meaning that by generating the bodhicitta and giving rise to understanding, practice, vows, and realization, one perseveres with diligence without slackening to accomplish the various stages; this refers to the character "Flower" (Hua) in the sutra.

Sixth is the greatness of wisdom (*jñāna-mahattva*), meaning that great wisdom is the sovereign, which directs all myriad practices to universally adorn everything without exception; this is precisely the character "adorn" (*yan*) in the sutra title.

Seventh is the greatness of teaching (*deśanā-mahattva*), meaning that not a single word or phrase fails to connect through and pervade all ten directions and the three periods of time in a重重 (repeatedly layered) and inexhaustible manner; this is precisely the character "sutra" (*jing*) in the sutra title.

Eighth is the greatness of meaning (*artha-mahattva*): this refers to the fact that the dharmas being expounded exhaustively reach the limit of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), leaving nothing out even unto the Indra-net (*indrājāla*). This comprises all six characters.

Ninth is the greatness of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-mahattva*): because these aforementioned dharma-gates are universally inexhaustible, each one serves as the sphere of transformation for beings.

Tenth is the greatness of activity (*karmamahattva*), which means that throughout the three periods of time and across the entire extent of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one constantly benefits sentient beings with this Dharma without rest.
Thus, the seven kinds of greatness found in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts are not separate from these.

Regarding the ten meanings of the two aspects (*fang*): "aspect" (*fang*) means "dharma. That is to say, the aforementioned ten greatnesses are all termed dharmas, referring to the dharma of essence, the dharma of characteristics, and so forth.

Regarding the ten meanings of the three expansivenesses (*guang*): "expansiveness" (*guang*) means "many. Because its functions arise in manifold profusion, it encompasses everything without exception.
Thus, since the preceding ten [categories] are all manifold, it is clarified that "great" (mahā) refers to one encompassing all, while "vast" (vipula) refers to one containing all;
this may also be reversed.
This is an analysis by way of separation.
If one analyzes the two characters "fang" (vast) and "guang" (broad) by way of combination, there are also ten meanings:
first, the meaning of being a vast basis, which means that the verbal teachings are extensive and serve as the basis for sentient beings.
Second is the meaning of extensive exposition, because it proclaims the vast and profound Dharma.
Third is the meaning of extensive refutation, because it destroys all obstacles without exception.
Fourth is the meaning of extensive transcendence, because there are no phenomena that can serve as its analogues.
Fifth is the meaning of extensive treatment, because it serves as the remedy by fully encompassing all boundless methods of counteraction.
Sixth is the meaning of extensive inclusion, because it universally includes all boundless phenomena of diverse categories.
Seventh is the meaning of extensive virtue, because it fully encompasses all the supreme virtues of the two adornments.
Eighth is the meaning of extensive production, because it can produce an immeasurable and vast ocean of fruits.
Ninth is the meaning of extensive transcendence, because it cannot be known by the measurements of the mind and consciousness.
Tenth is the broad knowledge of meaning, which is the perfection of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), destroying the obstacles of false views without remainder.
Thus, these ten meanings consist of the first four from the eleventh chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* and the latter six from the first chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*.
Regarding the four explanations of the ten meanings of the Buddha, these are the ten Buddhas:
"Great" refers to the Dharma-realm Buddha;
"Directional" refers to the Original-nature Buddha;
"Extensive" refers to the Buddha of Nirvāṇa and the Buddha of Accordance with Desire;
"Buddha" refers to the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment;
"Flower" refers to the Buddha of Vows and the Buddha of Samādhi.
"Veneration" is the Buddha of karmic retribution;
"Sutra" is the Buddha of sustaining presence.
In total, they do not depart from the mind; all seven characters are the Buddha of the mind.
The meaning of the ten aspects of a Buddha is explained as it is analyzed in the Eighth Ground (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) and the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*).

Furthermore, the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "A Buddha also possesses ten meanings: namely, possessing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); being free from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); being able to awaken to oneself regarding all phenomena and all their modes and characteristics; and also being able to awaken all sentient beings—like waking from a dream or like a lotus blooming—and for these reasons, he is called a Buddha."
Furthermore, Paramārtha cites the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, which also contains ten meanings; fearing prolixity, I shall not cite them here.

Regarding the five explanations of the ten meanings of "flower" (*puṣpa*): first, the meaning of "containing reality," which signifies that the dharma-realm contains the qualities of its inherent nature.
Second is the sense of luminous purity, because fundamental wisdom is manifest.
Third is the sense of subtlety and excellence, because each and every phenomenon is identical to the dharma-realm.
Fourth is the sense of gratification, because it accords with the capacities of sentient beings.
Fifth is the meaning of drawing forth the fruit: practice serves as the cause for birth because it gives rise to perfect awakening.
Sixth is the meaning of being upright and handsome: practice is conjoined with aspiration, being without any deficiency.
Seventh is the meaning of being undefiled, because each and every practice is conjoined with the gateways of samādhi.
Eighth is the meaning of skillful accomplishment, because the virtuous deeds cultivated are accomplished with skillful means.
Ninth is the meaning of fragrance, because the various virtues are maintained and their sweet aroma spreads far and wide.
The tenth is the meaning of "blooming": because the myriad practices flourish and cause the mind to open and awaken.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of flowers:
first, the flowers of plants and trees, which serve as a metaphor for the causes of the myriad practices.
However, these may either coexist with their results or not coexist with them.

The two types of flowers that adorn the body—comprising gold, jewels, and so forth—are metaphors for the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the various marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and other such qualities; these exist only simultaneously with their results.
Among the ten preceding meanings, one, five, nine, and ten are restricted to grasses and trees, while the remainder apply to both types of flowers.
Regarding the sixth meaning, "adornment," it refers to the aforementioned ten flowers collectively adorning a single Buddha; because the modes of adornment differ, these also constitute ten meanings.

Furthermore, the aforementioned ten flowers adorn the preceding ten Buddhas in sequence; these are the ten meanings, which are both general and specific without obstruction. Moreover, there are another ten meanings:
first, using causes to adorn the fruit so as to constitute a person—this is the Flower Adornment of the Buddha, because the fruit is attained through causes.
Second, adorning the cause with the fruit: this manifests the excellence of the fruit; once the fruit is realized, it causes each and every causal practice to become boundless.

Third, adorning the Dharma with the person to manifest its function: this means that only after the Buddha has cultivated the causes for vast eons does he manifest the essence and function of the Dharma.
Fourth, one adorns persons with the Dharma to manifest its perfection; for if the essence and function of the Dharma are not attained, cause and effect cannot be perfect and subtle.
Fifth, one adorns function with essence to ensure its pervasiveness; for if function does not attain its essence, it cannot be all-pervading.
Sixth, by using the function to adorn the essence, one knows the fundamental source; for if there were no great function, the vastness of the essence and its source would not be manifested.
Seventh, by using the essence to adorn the marks, one knows their wondrousness; that is to say, if the marks possess an essence, they immediately enter into a state of infinite mutual inclusion.

Eighth, they adorn the essence with characteristics to clarify its profound and mysterious nature; for were it not for these characteristics, the depth and mystery of the essence would not be manifest.
Ninth, they adorn the teaching with meaning so that it transcends words and thought; for the expressed meaning is inconceivable, and the expressive words are detached from it.

Tenth, the various causes are mutually adorned through integration and inclusion; for example, meditation cannot exhaust its stillness without wisdom, and wisdom cannot deepen its illumination without meditation, and so forth.

Furthermore, the aforementioned mutual adornments all involve the four propositions of mutual support and mutual identity; here, we shall first clarify this by means of the mutual adornment of principle and practice.
Regarding the four propositions on the initial mutual support: first, because principle is manifested through cultivation, one uses practice to adorn and expand principle.
Second, because practice issues forth from principle, one uses principle to adorn and expand practice.
The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states: "There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm, and there is nothing that does not return to realize this Dharmakāya.

Thus, the three—principle, practice, and their union—are both fused and non-dual, yet dual. Without practice flowing from the True, one cannot accord with the True; without the True that gives rise to practice, the True is not manifested through practice.

It is because when the essence (tǐ) harmonizes with practice (xíng), the cause is perfected; and when practice encompasses the truth (zhēn), the fruit is fulfilled. Therefore, it is designated as the *Buddha-avaivartika-samantabhadra-caryā-prasthāna* (The Flower Adornment of the Buddha).

Herein, both principle and practice are simultaneously obliterated, being two yet non-dual. Because it is the practice of principle, it is not practice; because it is the principle of practice, it is not principle. Thus, subject and object are both lost, transcending emotion and severing all marks. It is neither adorned nor unadorned; this is what is called "Flower Adornment" (*Huá-yán*).

The characteristics are comprised within the four propositions; both principle and practice are fully encompassed. This can be understood through careful reflection, whereby the mutual illumination of the Dharma and its metaphors is clearly evident.
This concludes the seventh of the ten meanings for explaining the sutra.
The five meanings in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (or *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*) have already been seen in the preceding text.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* presents two meanings:
first, to thread together what has been taught; second, to sustain those to be converted.
This is the same meaning as the "Garland" (mālā) section of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*; when combined, the "Garland" section should be excluded, and [the remaining] six meanings are established.
According to this regional interpretation, there are further four meanings:
first, permanence; second, phenomena (*dharma*); both are as previously explained.
The meaning of the three sūtras constitutes the path for sentient beings;
the meaning of the four scriptures causes one to see and hear the True Dharma.
There are also ten meanings within the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*, but fearing prolixity, they are not cited here.
Fourth, regarding the specific explanation of the names, first the names are established and subsequently explained.

First, as for the establishment of the names: "Great" (Mahā) receives its name according to its essential nature, with "permanence" and "pervasiveness" as its meanings. "Permanence" means that vertically there is no beginning; "pervasiveness" means that horizontally it encompasses all without exception.

"Method" (*dharma*) is named according to its attainment; its meaning is "guiding" (*naya*) and "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*). It sustains both essence and characteristic, thereby giving rise to understanding in accordance with the guiding principle.
"Extensive" (*vaipulya*) is named according to its function; its meaning is "encompassing" and "vast. To encompass means to contain broadly; to be vast means to pervade extensively.

The Buddha derives his name from conforming to humanity; "Awakening" (Buddha) is its essential meaning. To "illuminate" means to clarify the profound depths of the myriad dharmas; to "awaken" means to realize the dense darkness of the great night.

The term "flower" (puṣpa) is derived from its metaphorical function; its meaning consists in the ripening of fruits and the adorning of the body. The ripening of fruits signifies the perfect accomplishment of the myriad practices, while the adorning of the body signifies the embodiment of all virtues.

"Strictness" (*yan*) is named for its functional utility, while "adornment" (*zhuang*) takes the sense of providing resources. This means providing the resources for the vast essence and function, and adorning the true and responsive bodies of the Buddha.

"Sutra" (*jing*) is named for its capacity to express, while "retention" (*shechi*) takes the sense of upholding. It upholds the inexhaustibility of nature and characteristics, and encompasses the boundlessness of sentient beings.
Regarding the subsequent explanation of the names: first, within the dharma itself, essence and function are correlated.
"Great" refers to the "Vast" (Vaipulya) because it possesses the characteristics and functions of an essence;
"Vast" refers to the "Great" because it possesses the essence of those characteristics and functions. Both are explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound).
If the characteristics were identical, it would be a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Second, regarding persons, this is a comparison between the fruit and the practice:
the "flower" of the Buddha is not the practice of the causal stage.
The Buddha of the Flower is not a Buddha of other practices;
thus, they are also identical in their universal characteristics.
Third, they are contrasted by way of person and dharma.
The Buddha’s Avataṃsaka of Great Vaipulya is not the same as the Buddhas of the lesser vehicles of expedient means;
the Great Vaipulya of the Buddha’s Avataṃsaka is not a dharma attainable at the stage of a cause.
The characteristics can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the correspondence between the four teachings and their meanings, there are also two interpretations:
the teaching in relation to its meaning, and the person in relation to the Dharma; both possessive compounds (*sādhana*) are applicable, and these may be inferred accordingly.

The fifth, the inexhaustible unfolding, refers to how, at the outset, the most pure dharma-realm is opened into two gates—wisdom and principle—which correspond to the distinction between nirvāṇa and bodhi.
Furthermore, when principle reveals essence and function, it is "Mahāvaipulya" (Great and Vast);
when wisdom reveals cause and effect, it is "Buddhāvataṃsaka" (Flower Ornament of the Buddha).
When these are combined to form the complete expression, it is the character "Sūtra" (Jīng) within the title.
Furthermore, these eyes are unfolded to constitute the first assembly, as this first assembly is the totality.

The ten oceans represent principle (*li*), while the ten wisdoms represent knowledge (*zhi*); within the ten oceans, both essence and function are contained, and within the ten wisdoms, both cause and effect are likewise contained.
Furthermore, within the Flower Treasury World and throughout the pervasive presence of Vairocana, both the primary and secondary fruits are the very character of the Buddha.
The Crown Prince Mahātejas briefly indicates the causal flowers; that which is realized and observed by those two is precisely the Mahāvaipulya.
Thus, they collectively form one assembly, representing the essence and function of the cause and effect that is believed.
Furthermore, this assembly is expanded to constitute the causes and effects of the subsequent eight cycles of four weeks; in each case, the cause is the flower and the fruit is the Buddha.
The essence and function of what is cultivated and realized therein are precisely the Mahāvaipulya (Great Vaipulya).

Furthermore, these nine assemblies extend throughout the ten directions; as it is said in the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance" (*Prabhāsa-bodhi-parivarta*) of the second assembly that one such assembly has already pervaded the ten directions, so it is with all the remaining assemblies.
Furthermore, each of these assemblies has its own principal figures and retinue; as it is said regarding the Ten Abodes, Bodhisattvas from the ten directions all come to bear witness, saying:
"In the lands of the ten directions, this Dharma is being taught everywhere."
Thus, each of the assemblies that pervade the dharma-realm possesses its own layers of primary and attendant figures.

Even extending to the infinite assemblies throughout the various realms of dust-like lands and diverse worlds, none of them ever transcend the pure dharma-realm of the Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka.

Regarding "the sixth fascicle, which summarizes the characteristics to their ultimate limit": this means that from the end one gradually rolls back until reaching no more than the nine assemblies; the nine assemblies do not depart from the first assembly, the first assembly does not depart from the general title, and the general title does not transcend the principle and wisdom (li-zhi).
Because that which is irrational is not wisdom, there is no wisdom outside of principle;
because that which is not wisdom is not principle, there is no principle outside of wisdom. Thus, principle and wisdom are non-dual, and wisdom is likewise subsumed within principle.
When separated from its essence, it has no function; when functions are subsumed back into the essence, the essence-nature is itself detached. Thus, the essence is non-essence.
Primordially pure, it is conventionally designated as the "Pure Dharma-dhātu."
Therefore, from the ultimate to the inexhaustible, even down to a single character or no-character, all are subsumed within the nature-ocean of the Avataṃsaka without exception.

Regarding the seventh point, the non-obstruction between unfolding and rolling up: this means that at the very moment of unfolding the front, the back is constantly rolled up; and at the very moment of rolling up the back, the front is constantly unfolded.
Because that which is extended is immediately rolled up, the ocean of immeasurable and boundless Dharma-gates is exhaustively expounded in a single word;
because that which is rolled up is immediately extended, the Tathāgata expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras within a single utterance.
Eighth, regarding the comprehensive inclusion by way of meaning:

as previously demonstrated, the various preceding sections are either fully subsumed within seven characters, or fully subsumed under teaching and meaning, or under principle and wisdom, or under person and dharma, or under faith, understanding, practice, and realization.

Alternatively, these may be subsumed within the three sages alone: Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and Vairocana. That is to say, the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Vaipulya) is Samantabhadra, because Samantabhadra represents the *dharmadhātu* that is realized;
the *Avataṃsaka* (Flower Ornament) is Mañjuśrī, because Mañjuśrī represents the means of realization;
and the Buddha is Vairocana, because he possesses both the subject and the object.
Furthermore, "Great" refers to Samantabhadra, because the essential body of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is all-pervasive;
"Vaipulya" (Extensive) refers to Mañjuśrī, because Mañjuśrī represents the wisdom that is identical to that essence.
Flowers represent Samantabhadra, because they are the practice of Samantabhadra;
adornments represent Mañjuśrī, because Mañjuśrī gives rise to practice through understanding.
The Buddha represents the perfection of both understanding and practice.
Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī—these Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī who realize the essence and function of the *dharmadhātu*—accomplish the pervasive illumination of Vairocana’s light.
Regarding the ninth point, the convergence into the one mind: all the preceding gates, even unto infinity, do not depart from the one mind, for the one mind is itself the *dharmadhātu*.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings.

The essence of the mind is itself the Great [Vehicle]; the fundamental wisdom of the mind is itself the Vaipulya; contemplating the mind to give rise to practice is itself the Avataṃsaka; and awakening to the nature and characteristics of the mind is itself the Buddha.
Awakening does not come from without; it is entirely identical to that which is awakened to. Therefore, wisdom and principle are not distinct.
When wisdom and principle mutually dissolve one another, both vanish in stillness and illumination; thus, every thought-moment is the ocean of nature of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
The tenth [point], "Merging into Equality," is intended to cause those who have not yet realized it to understand their own mind.
For only when one knows that all objects encountered are mind does one truly realize the nature of the mind.
The "Chapter on the Holy Life" states: "To know that all dharmas are the very nature of the mind is to achieve the body of wisdom without depending on another for enlightenment.

Yet, those who study the Dharma today mostly abandon the internal to seek it externally, while those who practice Chan meditation prefer to extinguish external conditions to illuminate within; both are instances of biased attachment, each stagnating in one of the two extremes.
Once the mind and its objects are in suchness, they are equal and unimpeded.

I once polished two mirrors and placed a single lamp between them, then set a statue of the Buddha before them; the lights reflected back and forth in infinite layers, and the Buddhas appeared without end.

Behold how the mind and its objects mutually illuminate one another, and fundamental wisdom enters both simultaneously: within the mind, one awakens to the inexhaustible realm; upon the realm, one realizes the inconceivable mind. Thus, as mind and object unfold in successive layers, the illumination of wisdom is ever-present.

Furthermore, the Buddha who is the mind itself cognizing objects is the Tathāgata who perceives that objects are nothing but mind; thus, while the Buddhas of the mind are manifold, the nature of original enlightenment is one.
Since they cannot be grasped, both mind and object vanish;
since they cannot be exhausted through illumination, principle and wisdom penetrate each other.
Since the mind and its objects are thus, when objects are compared with one another and minds are mutually investigated, the myriad transformations that unfold in profusion are all of one essence.
Only through realization in accord with this truth is it called the Buddha’s Avataṃsaka.

Second, regarding the explanation of the chapter title: in Sanskrit it is *Sarvalokendravyūhadharmanirdeśavikrīḍita*, which in Chinese means "The Chapter on the Majestic Power of the Dharma-Gate of the Adornments of All Worldly Lords."
The current text preserves an abbreviated version: "world" (*loka*) refers to time, which is to say, the mundane world;
"ruler" (*pati*) refers to a sovereign, meaning various kings as well as the Buddha.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of worlds:
First, the vessel world (*bhājanaloka*) is the place of transformation;
second, the sentient-being world (*sattvaloka*) is the recipient of the transformation;
third, the world of the perfectly awakened wisdom (*jñānasamyaksambuddhaloka*) is the master who performs the transformation.
There are only two types of lords: kings and Buddhas, because they preside over the receptacle world and sentient beings.
A Buddha is not of the mundane world; he receives his title from that which he governs.
"Wondrous" refers to the essence and function of the Dharma-gate, which are profound, vast, and inconceivable; this is that which the Lord has attained.
"Adorned" means embellishment, which carries several meanings:
first, the adornment of the receptacle world, referring to its ground being firm and solid, and so forth.
Second is the adornment of the world of sentient beings, meaning that each assembly within the ocean-like congregations possesses its own dharma-gates and majestic virtue.

Third is the adornment of the world of the perfectly awakened wisdom, meaning that one has attained supreme perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena, such that the three karmas universally pervade and the dharma-gates are inexhaustible.
Therefore, while the prose section describes the majesty of various kings, the verses praise his virtues to manifest the majesty of the Buddha.
If sentient beings were not majestic, they would not move the Buddha to appear;
if the Perfectly Awakened One were not majestic, he could not serve as their sovereign.
If the vessel-world were not adorned, it would not be the true abode of the Buddha.
