the second line is the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*), because the equality of self and other is the very realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
The next phrase refers to the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), because it functions without obstruction regarding both specific and general characteristics;
the final phrase refers to the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), because it accomplishes the task of benefiting others and guiding the world.
Within the second section, the praise of the *dharmakāya*, the first half [of the verse] is identical in both substance and characteristics.
There are two meanings to this identity:
first, the identity of the substance of the *dharmatā-dharmakāya*.
It is called "without support" because it has no basis for abiding.
It is "without distinction" because its essence is non-dual;
once both have realized the identical nature of the dharmakāya, their powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth are entirely without difference.
This is the body of unimpeded wisdom, which does not rely on anything.
Free from all conceptual discrimination, it is without distinction.

The latter half [of the verse] is identical in function: because it can manifest and give rise to the reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdom without duality, it is the formless Dharmakāya that manifests forms in response to sentient beings.

Regarding the three pairs of fetters: the first pair concerns the wisdom of the upper realm; the upper phrase refers to the fundamental [wisdom] and the lower phrase to the subsequently attained [wisdom].

The second pair concerns the phenomena of the lower realm; this merely cites their function, as their essence pervades both [realms]. This is because wisdom accords with suchness, for the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra explains that both suchness and the wisdom of suchness constitute the Dharma-body.
The subsequent seven praises of the response are divided into three parts;
the first concerns the manifestation of the response according to the inclinations [of beings].
"Inconceivable" means that it is boundless in accordance with conditions.
The *Prabhāsa-bodhi* states: "If one were to contemplate for a hundred million nayutas of kalpas, the marks and majestic virtues would become infinitely more boundless," and so forth.

Next, the four bodies emit light to expound the Dharma; the first is the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) expounding the Dharma, which, in relation to the aforementioned response body (sambhogakāya), constitutes a further transformation (punarnirmāṇa);
the next two are the light from the pores expounding the Dharma.
The final [verse] concludes by praising [the Buddha’s power] as immeasurable.
The meaning of "Wheel of Dharma" (dharmacakra) is as explained elsewhere.
The final two verses concern the attainment of the Way and the manifestation of supernormal powers (abhijñā).
The aforementioned [Buddhas] are all perfectly interfused and likewise possess ten bodies; this has been stated merely from one perspective.
Second is the South: the Bodhisattva Dharmaprīti, who was previously named Samantaprabhā-dharmasāgara-mati in the Cloud Assembly; the meaning of his name is the same as before.
"Radiance" refers to the illumination of phenomena.
These ten verses praise the Buddha’s virtue of quiescent activity responding to capacities, answering the previous [verse on] the "objective sphere.
The manifestation of the Dharma-body constitutes the delimited objective sphere (*pramāṇa-viṣaya*).
Non-arising and non-substantiality are the objects of contemplation;
sentient beings and their lands are the realms to be transformed.
This is divided into three parts:
The first four [verses] rely on the ultimate to manifest the conventional; therein they are divided into two parts.
First, one verse reveals that the body of the ultimate Buddha is eternal: it is eternally so from the perspective of the primary truth (*paramārtha*), because it transcends the three periods of time.
Wisdom accords with principle and is serenely and eternally illuminating.
It is "manifest" because it is free from the two obstacles;
it is "present" because it is ever before one, yet this is not the same as the eternal nature of the self-substance of sentient beings.
"Completely filling the dharma-realm" means that each of the sense organs and the marks of excellence is boundless, for they are adorned by limitless merit and wisdom.
The next two phrases mean that his voice is constantly employed universally, for he constantly enjoys the vast dharma-pleasure of self-enjoyment.

The final three verses initiate the manifestation of function (*vṛtti*): the first universally accords with the inclinations of sentient beings, the second describes the mutual resonance between the response and the stimulus, and the last depicts the boundless radiance of the Dharma.
These two [sections] comprise three verses, demonstrating the non-obstruction between essence and function.
Among these, the first two lines concern its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): non-arising yet manifesting arising;
the next two lines concern its nature (*dharmatā*): non-abiding yet abiding;
the final verse concerns its function (*vṛtti*): neither departing nor abiding, yet universally pervasive.
The subsequent verse simultaneously negates both essence and function.

This means that by negating "no-essence," it negates the aforementioned "non-arising," because non-arising constitutes the essence of the Buddha-dharma; thus, the present essence is itself no-essence.

Regarding "having no abiding place," this negates the two lines concerning nature, and furthermore, since even non-arising cannot be apprehended, it serves to negate and reveal the line concerning arising.
The second verse of the latter half concerns function, for its function is like a shadow.

There are three verses on the third [topic], clarifying the inexhaustibility of the true and the responsive: first, the inexhaustibility of the cloud of dharma; second, the inexhaustibility of the assemblies; and third, the inexhaustibility of the bodily marks.
The term "inexhaustible aspect" refers to both the true body (*dharmakāya*) and [the emanation body].
That it is ultimately inexhaustible is because it is entirely identical in essence.
Third, in the western direction is the Bodhisattva Fragrant Flame; his former name was Moonlight Fragrant Flame Universal Adornment.
In this context, "light" refers to moonlight, and "luminous wisdom" refers to the adornment of wisdom.

These ten verses praise the Buddha’s body as containing the oceans of all [beings], which answers the question regarding empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*); for through empowerment, one is able to enter [the state].
Within this, the first nine verses praise the ocean-like assembly, through which the Buddha’s virtues may be known;
the final one concludes by attributing those virtues to the Buddha.
Within the former group, the first verse is general while the remaining eight are specific.
Within the distinct [categories], there are two;
the former four are universally pervasive.
Among them, the first is the wisdom-body entering as many worlds as atoms in a land, and the second is the form-body manifesting its functions everywhere.
The latter two [verses] explain and establish the preceding meaning: first, because the conduct of Samantabhadra is perfected; second, because body and mind are equal.
The final four verses clarify how one enters subtly into the lands within a single pore and performs activities therein.
In the latter section on the "one bond," it is not merely a single assembly; rather, all bodhisattvas enter the Buddha-body before one can truly praise the Buddha.
Regarding the fourth Northern Bodhisattva, this is the same as the original name, with the addition of the character for "wisdom" (hui).

However, these ten verses praise the Buddha’s turning of the Great Wheel of Dharma by generating its function based upon its essence, thereby answering the preceding discussion on the Buddha’s practice; for the Buddha takes the transformation of sentient beings through the turning of the Dharma as his primary practice.
The text is divided into three parts:
the first two lines provide a general summary; the next eight and a half verses provide a detailed exposition; and the final verse provides a conclusion.

Within the detailed exposition, ten manifestations of the Buddha’s transformation are praised. The first two lines describe the manifestation of taking birth through transformation, as he takes birth everywhere, his clouds of bodies pervading all places.
The next verse praises the transformation through supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vikurvaṇa*).
Although the final phrase mentions "turning the Dharma," the intent is that it applies universally.
The three lines of the third [verse] praise the transformation through karmic fruition (*karma-phala-vikurvaṇa*).

Regarding the statement that "the names and titles of all lands are different," this is to show that they correspond to the names of the karmic retributions of those with similar dispositions and types.
The first three points concern the physical bodies upon which [the Buddhas] rely.

Fourth, "expounding the wondrous Dharma according to what is appropriate" refers to the manifestation of transformation; by being appropriate to the occasion, one is able to sever the doubts of others.
The five verses [of the first section] constitute the transformation through exhortation and encouragement, because they employ sublime sounds to inspire and urge them on.

The six verses [of the second section] constitute the transformation through consolation and rejoicing, because they universally rain down the rain of Dharma, causing those beings to advance in the cultivation of the dharma of non-arising.
The first three constitute verbal activity (*vākkarman*).
The seventh consists of one verse on the mental transformation of reception (*pratigraha-cittavikurvaṇa*); it refers to receiving and accepting questions in order to expound upon past conduct.

The eighth consists of one verse on the mental transformation of discernment (*viniścaya-cittavikurvaṇa*); it refers to being able to universally transform others only after discerning the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings and distinguishing the differing natures and characteristics of all phenomena.

The nine verses and one [additional] verse constitute the transformation through the arousal of intention; they arouse past roots of goodness and the great practices of the Three Vehicles in order to bring about skillful discipline.

The eleven verses constitute the transformation through the formation of intention; they establish the matters and meanings of the Buddha-dharma so that all may perceive them in their various aspects.
Function arising based on reality is precisely the nirmāṇakāya; therefore, it is said that the nirmāṇakāya has no separate mind or form.
These ten manifestations do not contradict the sequence in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, provided they are made mutually harmonious so as not to violate the intent of the sūtra.
The final verse concludes by returning to this assembly, as may be known.
Fifth, in the northeast, there was the Bodhisattva Dharmasāgara, who among the gathered assembly was named Anantaguṇakośa-jyotir-vijaya-pradīpa.
The Dharma Ocean may be regarded as the supreme radiance; its meaning is identical to that of Wisdom.
The name "Treasury of Merit" (Guṇaratanākara) is the same in both the preceding and succeeding titles.
As for the two characters "Inexhaustible" (Akṣaya), they appear in the former but are absent from the latter.

These ten verses praise the Buddha and his preeminent retinue, answering the inquiry regarding the Buddha’s powers; since the praise of the bodhisattvas is ultimately due to the Buddha’s power, they conclude by stating that [the bodhisattvas] "dwell within the stage of power."
In this passage, the first [point], that one attains the Dharma through the fulfillment of wisdom, constitutes the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding such a gateway of skillful means (*upāyamukha*), there are two intended meanings:
first, it refers back to what precedes, meaning that by possessing the transformations of the three wheels, one is able to pervade every single land.
The second [point] consists of the nine subsequent distinctions, which serve as such skillful means.
The remaining nine distinct characteristics collectively praise seven matters:
the first is the praise of the universally resounding great voice.
There are three kinds of greatness:
first, greatness of scope, because each individual land is included;
second, greatness of meaning, because it explains the conduct of the Buddhas.
Third is the greatness of essence, because it is heard throughout the ten directions.
Second is that praise never passes in vain, because in every thought-moment one contemplates the Dharma and realizes the ultimate truth.
Third is the ability to enter superior realms, because one cultivates pure lands within the bodies of all Buddhas.
Fourth, there is unimpededness regarding defilement, because one realizes the Dharma amidst sensory objects and acts with total mastery.
Fifth, one is able to enter the realm of the Buddhas, because one perceives the Buddha’s spiritual power and enters his sphere of activity.
There are two spheres of activity:
first, the sphere of wisdom, which refers to the domain of the ten powers;
second, the sphere of the Buddha's transformation, which refers to the receptacle world and sentient beings.
The sixth section consists of three verses on skillfully entering sounds: first, entering the great sound; second, entering the sublime sound; and finally, entering all sounds.
The seventh section consists of one verse on skillfully knowing the various stages (*bhūmi*).
"Proceeding from the ground" refers to the emergence of the mind.
"Attaining the ground" refers to abiding in entry.
"Within the ground of power" refers to the Buddha-ground.
The "Dharma obtained" refers to the concluding expedient means.
In the sixth direction, the southeast, is the Bodhisattva Prajñāpradīpa (Wisdom Lamp), whose name is identical to that mentioned previously.

With ten verses, he praises the various bodhisattvas for their realization and entry into the profound and vast; through the power of samādhi, he perceives the Buddha’s samādhi, thereby answering the questions concerning samādhi.

This section is divided into four parts; the first two praise the true body of the Buddha seen by the practitioner: first, seeing the Buddha as free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*); second, seeing the Buddha’s sovereign mastery.
Regarding being "free from all marks," the *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "To be free from all marks is what is called the Buddhas."

The *Maitreya-śāstra* states: "By merely departing from the four characteristics, one departs from all [phenomena]," namely name (*nāman*), object (*artha*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and distinction (*viśeṣa*).
As for "mastery," it refers to seeing the mastery of the Buddha through the Bodhisattva’s simultaneous cultivation of meditative concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā-yuganaddha*).

The following four verses clarify the realization of the Dharma: first, the manifestation of the profound principle of reality through the power of vows; second, the formation of the physical body through merit and wisdom by realizing the manifold practices; third, the penetration of the essence of the fruition-dharma as being all-pervasive; and fourth, the understanding that the teaching-dharma is profound, vast, and difficult to comprehend.
There are two verses in the third section praising the universal responsiveness of the physical body (*kāyakarman*): the first concerns its profundity, and the second its vastness.
Regarding the term "firm and dense" (*khan da*), it signifies being equal to the Buddha’s essence and function.
"Firm" refers to the Vajra-body; "dense" means being one of the three mysteries (*triguhyaka*).
Being one yet manifold, it pervades all things;
being great yet minute, it appears within a speck of dust.
As a response that requires no effort, it manifests without characteristics.
If we speak in terms of the Dharma-gate, this body is precisely the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
It is "solid" because it cannot be destroyed; it is "mysterious" because it is profound and difficult to perceive.
All sentient beings, despite their defiled minds, possess it without exception; it has been inherently present from the beginning, and is therefore called "unborn."
The essence is severed from all hundred negations; therefore, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).
The six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) of sentient beings are what are referred to as the various lands.
The four subsequent verses praise the attainment of the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*): first, the power of this Buddha; second, the power of other Buddhas.

In the seventh [direction], the southwestern quarter, the previously listed name of the place is *Samantakusumaprabhājvālācūḍa* (Universal Flower Light Flame Crest), which is slightly similar but mostly different [from the current name].
Ten verses praise the Buddha’s sovereign virtue in gathering and sustaining sentient beings, answering the previous question regarding sovereignty.

The text is divided into three parts: first, the six [verses] on gathering and sustaining sentient beings without omission; second, the two [verses] on the unimpeded nature of quiescence and function; and third, the two [verses] on the boundless great function. Now, for the first part, there are two sections: The text is divided into three parts: first, the six [verses] on gathering and sustaining sentient beings without omission; second, the two [verses] on the unimpeded nature of quiescence and function; and third, the two [verses] on the boundless great function. Now, for the first part, there are two sections:
The first two [verses] are able to encompass [the meaning], namely, the profundity and vastness of body and speech: the former verse refers to speech, and the latter verse refers to the body.
Within the section on the body, the upper half refers to its essence, because it is unstained by adventitious defilements;
the lower half refers to its function, because it appears differently according to objects.
This also serves to resolve doubts and manifests signs for the sake of sentient beings, without contradicting the nature of reality, which is like space.
This is subsumed within the latter four verses.
As for the first verse, who is it that can understand?
Regarding "internal faith and external restraint," the subsequent verse asks: with what eye does one see?
Only the superior, not the inferior.
What dharmas are clearly perceived by the subsequent verse?
It refers to the three minds of each stage (*bhūmi*) among all dharmas.
In what state does the following verse reach its culmination?
When the Bodhisattva stages are exhausted, one enters the ocean of the Buddhas.

Regarding the next two verses on the non-obstruction between quiescence and function: the first verse shows that while function manifests everywhere, the essence neither comes nor goes; the latter verse shows that through constant quiescence, function accords with understanding and appears as diverse.

Regarding the statement that "the three great functions are subsequently boundless": initially, each single hair universally manifests penetration; subsequently, each single body individually and pervasively turns the Dharma wheel.

The eighth Bodhisattva from the northwest was previously named Anantaprabhā-maṇirāja (Inexhaustible Light Maṇi King); here he is called Ojastejas-prajñā (Majestic Virtue Wisdom), which is the Maṇi King—the difference being merely between the dharma and its metaphor.

The ten verses praise the Buddha’s appearance in the world and his preaching of the Dharma as being all-pervasive in virtue; this is because he answers questions with fearlessness and his teaching of the Dharma is without distinction.
This section is divided into three parts:
the first two verses generally manifest that the light of his body responds universally; the next seven clarify his activities; and the final one concludes by returning the function to its source.
In the analysis of what is accomplished, there are two parts: first, three [verses] clarify that the light shines without omission;

second, four [verses] demonstrate the pervasiveness of the Dharma: (1) its pervasion throughout all dharmadhātu realms, both internal and external to the sensory objects; (2) its pervasion within all realms inside the Buddha’s body; (3) the clarification of the nature and characteristics of what is transformed; and (4) the clarification of the perfect voice capable of transformation.
The final binding returns to its source because it cannot be apprehended.
The Bodhisattva in the ninth lower direction was previously named Dharmadhātu-jvālā-prabhā; here he is called Samantaprabha (Universal Radiance), which refers to his former "Flame" (jvālā).

The ten verses praising the Buddha’s sphere and its supreme functions describe how Bodhisattvas are able to enter it and answer questions regarding supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); the text states that these are "manifested individually.
This section has two parts:

the first three [verses] reveal the Buddha’s sphere and its supreme functions. Within this, the first half-verse indicates their essence—namely, the wondrous physical form and marks (*lakṣaṇa*)—while the subsequent two and a half verses distinguish their functions.
The latter seven bodhisattvas are able to enter, meaning they enter the realm of the Buddha.
Among these, there are three parts:

the first two possess the qualities of knowledge and vision; the next three concern the benefits accomplished through knowledge and vision; and the final two summarize the swiftness of their function—all of which may be understood accordingly.
The tenth is the Bodhisattva from the Upper Direction; this differs from the preceding one only in name.

These ten verses praise the Buddha’s perfect voice, his manifestation of physical forms, and his mastery of supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), answering the question regarding the inability to encompass [all beings]. This means that the power of these vows is universally pervasive, such that nothing can prevent it from being taken up.
This section is divided into three parts;
the first three verses praise the Buddha’s virtue of raining down the Dharma with his perfect voice, which possesses ten characteristics:
first, it is the single, wondrous voice, because it is the Brahma-voice (*brahmasvara*).
Second, it is heard universally by all because it accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
third, this one is many because phenomena and principle are harmoniously integrated;
fourth, from each and every sound, there falls a rain of manifold teachings.
Fifth, each of those dharmas possesses all forms of expression;
sixth, each is identical to the voices of all sentient beings;
seventh, each of these voices pervades all places.
Eighth, each discourse elucidates the principle of the purity of nature;
ninth, each causes all beings everywhere to see and hear it;
tenth, each brings about ultimate benefit for all.

The ten meanings above are unfolded sequentially from a single "wondrous voice" (*svara*), and only when they are fully realized as the ten inexhaustible qualities can it be called the "perfect voice" (*pariśuddha-svara*);

this can be seen in the textual passages. Next, four verses praise the Buddha’s merit of unimpeded manifestation of his body: the first verse shows that through the power of liberation (*vimukti-bala*), the places of manifestation are pervasive yet subtle; the next verse shows that through the power of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-bala*), the manifested marks are identical with emptiness; and the final two verses employ the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*) to elucidate the preceding verses.
The first verse explains the latter half [of the stanza].

Regarding the term "image" (*pratibimba*), it is used to manifest that there is no fixed location; for when light is to the east, the shadow is to the west, and when light is to the west, the shadow is to the east. When the substance faces the image, the image arises without coming from anywhere; when the substance ceases, the image perishes without going anywhere. Therefore, this image is empty and lacks intrinsic substance.
The subsequent verse explains the first half [of the preceding verse].
To say "like space" means that it cannot be grasped and so forth.
Therefore, although it manifests form, it remains like the moon in water—equal to space.

The final three [verses] praise the Buddha’s virtue of sovereign mastery over miraculous transformations: first, the pores’ vast capacity; second, the universal reach of his vows; and third, using a small instance to illustrate the great.
Furthermore, the preceding brief correlation of ten phrases contains the meaning of forty phrases, which cannot be indicated in detail here.
Within the sixth major section, "The Conclusion that Pervades the Infinite," there are two parts:
first, the presentation of this [topic]; second, the analogy to that [preceding topic] starting from "It should be known."
Regarding the mention of "the four continents," the intent lies in Jambudvīpa; thus, while the words are general, the meaning is specific.
Since this serves to universally summon the gathering of bodhisattvas like clouds, it further highlights that the preceding praise refers specifically to those [bodhisattvas] from the ten directions.
The section on Remote Expedients is concluded.
Chapter Three: Samantabhadra Samādhi. Regarding the initial explanation of this chapter, the four gates are the same as before.

Regarding the meaning of the initial arrival: since the preceding assembly has already gathered and the light has manifested the Dharma Master, and as he is now about to preach the Dharma, the Dharma Master enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to receive empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as an immediate preparation; therefore, this [manifestation] follows next.
Second, regarding the explanation of the names: Samantabhadra is the "Enlightened Dharma-Master" because he expounds the Universal Dharma (samantadharma).
Samādhi is the "functional activity," for that which is not realized cannot be proclaimed; thus, these two—the person and the dharma—are raised together.
The samādhi of Samantabhadra is also this very samādhi, which belongs to Samantabhadra.

Furthermore, the realm of this samādhi is named Samantabhadra because the *dharmakāya* (body of the treasury of reality) of all Tathāgatas is Samantabhadra. Thus, Samantabhadra is identical to the samādhi; this distinguishes it from other meditative concentrations.
If one follows the Sanskrit original, this is the "Chapter on the Majestic Virtue and Spiritual Transformations of Samantabhadra’s Samādhi.
Since majestic virtue and spiritual transformations are all functions of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), by subsuming the function within the essence, it is simply called "samādhi."
Even though the Buddha bestowed light and praise, it was entirely due to his meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In other assemblies, he entered concentration to receive this empowerment and spoke immediately upon arising from it; these were thus treated as a single chapter.
In the present case, however, the text is extensive and the meaning is broad, intended to encourage practice and study.

Regarding the breadth of meaning, it is because the practices and vows of Samantabhadra are established; therefore, compared to other coarse characteristics, these four similarities and six differences are explained.
As for the four similarities, they are: entering, abiding, augmenting, and emerging.
Regarding the six differences: first, the difference in number; for while the arising of other assemblies is singular, the arising of this assembly is manifold.
Second, the difference in category; for its category is different from that of others.
Third, the difference in benefit, because its arising brings benefit to many people;
fourth, the difference in praise, because it is praised by the light from the pores of the Tathāgata;
fifth, the difference in the assembly’s request, because after arising from meditative concentration, he awaits the request of the assembly.

The six marks of certification differ: in other assemblies, the marks of certification appear only at the conclusion of the sutra, whereas in this chapter, they occur immediately after the benefit has been conferred, such as through the shaking of the earth and the falling of clouds.
Although the four and five types exist within the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmika*), they do not possess all six.
Now, because this [chapter] possesses all six [characteristics], it is established as a separate chapter; for while this explains the fruit (*phala*), the others all explain the causes (*hetu*).
Furthermore, it serves as the basis for all the assemblies and is comprehensive in nature.

Although the seventh, eighth, and ninth assemblies are meditative concentrations of the fruition (*phala-samādhi*), their exposition encompasses both cause and effect, and furthermore, they do not constitute the entirety [of the teaching].

Regarding the three essential purports (*abhiprāya*): entering the Dharma-realm concentration is the essential purport; the empowerment of the Buddha within the Dharma-realm is the essential purport; and causing the assembly of the Dharma-realm to accomplish the virtues of the Dharma-realm is the ultimate goal (*prayojana*). In relation to the subsequent chapters, the ocean of world-systems is also said to be the ultimate goal.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text, there are six sections:

first, the section on samādhi; second, the section on empowerment; third, the section on emerging from meditative absorption; fourth, the section on realization; fifth, the section on the praise of virtues through bodily light; and sixth, the section on the request for verses by the great assembly.
The first section has two parts:
first, clarifying entry into meditative concentration within this realm; second, categorizing [this practice] as being universal throughout the ten directions.
Regarding the first part, it is divided into three sections:
First, entering meditative concentration through the power of reception; second, revealing the name of the concentration; third, clarifying the essence and function of the concentration.
Now, for the first [section], there are six parts:
first, the time—namely, the time when the verses have been finished.
Second, regarding the lords: this reveals that the universal virtues of the Buddha belong solely to Samantabhadra.
Third, regarding the location: "relying on the Tathāgata" means he is constantly in the presence of the Buddha.

Fourth, regarding the seat upon which he relies: the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states, "Because the Bodhisattva has attained the Lotus Dhāraṇī, there are lotuses at every place where he preaches the Dharma. This symbolizes that the intrinsic nature of the samādhi he enters is untainted and contains all resultant dharmas.
The fifth is the causal basis of reliance, meaning that what is entered is profound and vast, which requires relying upon [the Buddha's] power.
The sixth is the actual entry into samādhi, because the mind and its object are in dark resonance.
From "This samādhi" onwards, the name of the concentration is revealed.
Vairocana has already been explained at length above.
Furthermore, there is another explanation which states:
"Extensive," "vast," and "nurturing"—possessing these three meanings, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha-body."
The "body" (kāya) is the essence and the basis.
This is of two kinds:
first, that which is accomplished through cultivation; second, the fundamental nature.
As for its fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), it is realized by both ordinary beings and sages alike.
As for that which is accomplished through cultivation, it exists only in the Buddhas.

That which exists in the Buddhas is called "vast" because their compassion is boundless; it is termed "great" because their wisdom is unsurpassed; and it is said that "birth has ceased" because the characteristics of arising have been exhausted.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Because he is eternally abiding and free from existence, he is called the Tathāgata; because he encompasses all myriad virtues, he is called the 'Treasury Body' (*garbha-kāya*). This refers precisely to the Dharma-body that has emerged from its entanglements.

Regarding the term "original nature" (*prakṛti*): it refers to the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) which contains all seeds and establishes the realms of rebirth; therefore, it is called "vast.
Because fundamental enlightenment (*mūlajñāna*) is equal to that of a Buddha through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is termed "great."
Because it arises anew at every moment, it is called "arising" (*jāti*).
Because it cannot be moved by defilement or purity, nor by suffering or pleasure, it is called "cessation" (*śānti*).

This aforementioned *dharmakāya*, when enveloped in bondage, is called the "womb" (*garbha*); it is termed both empty and non-empty, for emptiness acts as the container because the womb contains that which is non-empty.

If one understands Vairocana through the universal illumination of light, then Vairocana is the great wisdom that performs the contemplation, while the Tathāgatagarbha-body is the profound principle that is the object of contemplation.
Although these exist in principle for all beings, it is only through the Buddha’s wisdom that they are truly illuminated.

Furthermore, Vairocana also signifies that which is primordially present; because he is the true, primordial awareness that universally illuminates the Dharma-realm, this is precisely what is meant by "original enlightenment" (benjue).

Deluded and unaware, one fails to attain its function; only the Buddha awakens to this and is thus able to accomplish all that can be done. Therefore, it is said "all Buddhas," distinguishing them from ordinary beings as well as from those still on the causal path.
This reveals that regarding the environment and its inhabitants (*bhājanaloka* and *sattvaloka*), there is no separate self-nature apart from the *tathāgatagarbha*; therefore, one enters into this.
Xianshou’s commentary states:

"The Buddhas pervade all" means that it is revealed that the Buddhas are nowhere not omnipresent throughout the ocean of lands of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-kṣetrasamudra*), as well as all the lands within their atoms, and further, all the lands within the atoms of those lands—thus, in such successive layers, they are inexhaustible.

Regarding the term "Tathāgata-garbha-body" (Rulai zangshen): it clarifies that this very body, which pervades all lands, encompasses the ocean of lands throughout the entire Dharma-realm; because there is nothing that does not reside within the Tathāgata’s body, it is called the "Garbha-body."
Therefore, there are four propositions regarding this interpenetration:

first, the body pervades the ocean of lands; second, the lands are within the body; third, the body pervades the lands within the body; fourth, the lands enter and pervade the bodies within the lands.
The internal and the external, the primary body and its environment, are blended and fused without obstruction or hindrance; this is the function of this samādhi, and thus it is named as such.
Because he was about to expound this Dharma, he entered this meditative concentration.
Third, from "Universal Entry" (*pùrù*) onwards, the essence, characteristics, and functions are clarified.
These meditative states, characteristics, and functions are immeasurable and boundless, all of which are explained based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.
To briefly set forth their essentials, there are thirteen phrases and ten gates; the latter two gates subsume the five phrases.
These are subsumed into six pairs, as the latter two sections each constitute one pair.
The text contains four divisions, yet the underlying meaning consists of only three, which will be clarified below.
Regarding the six pairs: the first two phrases clarify the pair of essence and function.

This means that non-conceptual wisdom takes the realization of equality as its essential nature (*svabhāva*), while the manifestation of the *dharmadhātu* constitutes its preeminent function (*karman*).
That is to say, by means of the causal-nature of the cause, one realizes that causal-nature; thereby, the resultant-nature is established and the resultant-nature of the result is revealed.
Thus, the Buddha-nature possesses seven meanings:
first, truth; second, reality; third, goodness; fourth, permanence; fifth, bliss; sixth, self; and seventh, purity.
The nature of sentient beings and Buddhas is fundamentally no different from beginning to end; how much more so, then, is the fruit of Buddhahood not equal?
The equality of the Buddha is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore, merely entering the body of the Tathāgatagarbha is itself to have entered the equality of the Buddha.
This is the first gate of the perfect correspondence with Buddha-nature.
As for "superior function," it refers to the gate of manifesting all images for the multitude; that is to say, it is able to manifest and generate the images of bodies, lands, and wisdom.
Next is the pair of "profound" and "vast.
"Vast" means boundless, because it exists neither internally nor externally.
"Great" means unsurpassed, because it is the ultimate reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
"Unobstructed" means being without hindrance, thus being identical to empty space.
These three preceding meanings together constitute the "Gate of Vast Unobstructedness.
The subsequent phrase refers to the "Gate of Entering the Vortex of the Dharma-Ocean," where "vortex" signifies depth.
The third pair consists of two phrases concerning "expenditure" and "reception.

The first concerns the production of the gates of samādhi; that is to say, whether they be specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), all samādhis arise from this, for this is the foundation of all meditative concentrations.
The subsequent section on the "Gate of Embracing the Dharma-realm" concludes with this because it is the ultimate destination and the essential nature of the dharma-realm.
Within the four sections, there are two pairs of object and wisdom.
The first pair is the "Gate of Attaining Buddha-wisdom," which means that if one does not realize this principle, one does not possess Buddha-wisdom.
Subsequently, the gates for manifesting various objects are shown.
Now, regarding the term "establishment" (vyavasthāna), there are generally three kinds:
first, the world, which establishes the environment as retribution;
Second is the sacred teaching, which establishes sublime meanings;
third is contemplative wisdom, which establishes the characteristics of the truths.
All these are manifested and made present within the treasury of the dharma-realm.

The fifth section contains two phrases, which constitute the "Gate of Mutual Containment between the Primary and the Derived" (*yi- zheng han-rong men*), serving as the counterpart to the "Mutual Containment of Inner and Outer.

This means that internally, it contains the power of wisdom regarding cause and effect; externally, it causes the sensory objects (*rajas*) to contain the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This is because the sensory objects are entirely manifested based upon the treasury of the Dharma-realm, as they are identical to true nature (*tathatā*).
The sixth section consists of three phrases, which constitute the "Gate of Accomplishment and Sustenance. This serves as a counterpart to the person who accomplishes and sustains the Dharma.

That is to say, first, one accomplishes the great vows of merit; subsequently, one sustains the Wheel of Dharma so that it remains uninterrupted. It is because of this that the eye of the profound principle and the Dharma-eye are ever complete.

Regarding the aforementioned four sections: the first four lines clarify that there is no realm of obscurity into which it does not penetrate, thereby explaining the meaning of Vairocana’s universal illumination;
the next four lines clarify that there is no virtue that does not arise, thereby explaining the meaning of "all Buddhas";
and the final two lines clarify internal and external containment, thereby explaining the meaning of the "Treasury."
The final three phrases establish the virtue of upholding the Dharma, explaining the meaning of the aforementioned body [of the Buddha].
As for the statement that there are only three meanings, they are essence (*tattva*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and function (*vṛtti*).
Entering into the nature of equality is the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Vast and equal to space—this is the characteristic of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
All others are the functions of concentration.
These three are perfectly interfused, collectively constituting the unimpeded Samantabhadra-samādhi.
Second, from "In this way" onwards, the analogy extends to the ten directions and all realms of dust.
Within this section, there are two parts:
first, the presentation of the present case; second, from "In such a manner" onwards, the application of the analogy to those [other cases].
This is analogous to the two [sections] therein:
first, it clarifies that [the light] pervades the dharma-realm evenly; second, it clarifies its infinite layering.
Within the former, there are eleven phrases; the first one provides a general clarification, meaning that it reaches the ultimate limits of the dharma-realm.
The subsequent ten points specify [the scope] individually to demonstrate its exhaustive detail:

first, throughout the realm of empty space; second, within that space, throughout all locations of the ten directions; third, within the ten directions, throughout the time of the three periods; fourth, within the three periods, in the locations of subtle objects such as the tips of hairs; fifth, in all small gaps and unobstructed places; sixth, in vast places measuring hundreds or thousands of *yojanas*; seventh, in places such as the light of humans, devas, the sun, and the moon; eighth, throughout all places visible to the Buddha-eye; ninth, throughout all places reached by supernatural power (*ṛddhi*); tenth, throughout all places where the Buddha-body can manifest.
This tenth phrase has two meanings:
first, it concludes the preceding section, as the term "land" (kṣetra) applies throughout the eleven segments;
second, it introduces what follows, because these lands within the body are subtle.
Second, from the phrase "and this" (*ji ci*) onwards, there are briefly four layers within the pervasive [pervasion]:
first, the dust-particles of the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the phrase "and this land," it refers to the lands of the ten aforementioned locations.
Second, within each atom there are many lands;
third, within each land there are many Buddhas;
fourth, before each and every Buddha there are many Samantabhadras.

Since one enters this meditative absorption in all the aforementioned locations, the body of Samantabhadra is undivided yet pervades both the coarse and the subtle, being profoundly vast, level, full, and layered.
Since this is the case for the general category of entering absorption in these places, it is likewise so here.
The entry into meditative concentration within the *dharmadhātu* is likewise universal.
Thus, with respect to the primary concentration, there is only one Samantabhadra before each Buddha, because all are one.
If, however, one considers the universal class, there are as many as atoms before each Buddha, because each one is the totality.
Second, from "At that time, each one... onwards is the section on the empowerment (adhikāra), which has three parts:
first, empowerment by speech; second, empowerment by mind; and third, empowerment by body.
Within the first of these, there are four sections:
First, because all Buddhas manifest before them and bestow empowerment through this oral transmission, there is no subsequent need for further unification.
This is a general enumeration of the successive times and places, referring to each instance before Samantabhadra.
2. From "Those [beings]" onwards, he praises their attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Although this is a resultant concentration, because it is entered through the gateway of the Bodhisattvas, it is called the "Bodhisattva Samādhi.
3. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, he clarifies the cause by which this concentration is attained.
There are three reasons for this:
first, the shared empowerment of the Buddhas as companions, because the Way of each Buddha is identical;
second, the original vows of the presiding Buddha.
These two serve as conditions;
third is the vow of one's own practice.
These are the causes for entering meditative concentration.
Furthermore, regarding the three preceding meanings, each preceding one serves as the basis for each subsequent one; how could the others not also possess this characteristic?
This is because they are the masters of the Dharma-gates and because they manifest and explain the Universal Dharma (Samantabhadra).
4. From the words "That which is called" below, the purpose for which the empowerment is bestowed is explained.
This passage has two aspects: first, the explanation of the purpose for which the empowerment is bestowed; [the second is the explanation of the nature of the empowerment].
The second [section] reveals the characteristics of the superior vows of conduct; therefore, it says "so-called.
What is that which is so-called?
It is for the purpose of turning the wheel of Dharma.
There are eleven phrases: the first is general, while the remaining ones are specific.
Within the specific section, the first phrase generally subsumes the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), and the remaining nine are the ten oceans (*sāgara*).
The first is the Ocean of Establishment (*vyavasthāna-sāgara*).
The second is the ocean of sentient beings and karma;
the third is the ocean of worlds;
and the fourth is the ocean of Buddhas.
The fifth refers to the ocean of names, titles, lifespans, and liberations, as well as the great functions of transformation, all of which are merits;
the sixth refers to the ocean of *pāramitās*, because they reach the shore of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
the seventh refers to the ocean of turning the wheel of Dharma.
Eight is the ocean of faculties;
nine is the ocean of exposition, which, together with the ten [oceans] below, causes one to know these ten.
Second, from "At that time" onwards, the empowerment of the mind is clarified.
Within this, there are two parts: first, the application; second, the explanation.
In the former, there are also two:
first, this land; second, the general classification.
Regarding the ten kinds of wisdom bestowed in the preceding section, the first is general; it refers to the wisdom of bestowing the ocean of fruits.
As for the term "bestowal," it means that the power of the Buddha is infused to cause [the wisdom] to increase.
The nature of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the ocean of fruition.
This nature of wisdom is itself power, because it is unshakable and because it possesses the ten powers (*daśabala*).
The final character "wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to that which is able to enter [into this state].
The remaining nine constitute the distinct [categories], which are the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) found within the "Chapter on Attainment" (*Siddhi-paṭala*).
Because of these knowledges, one is subsequently able to explain those [other] knowledges and contemplate those ten oceans; however, the text is slightly incomplete and out of order.
The first is the third, the ocean-like wisdom of the established dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-vyavasthāna-sāgara-jñāna*), because it establishes that which is boundless and immeasurable.
The second is the fourth, the ocean of Buddhas (*buddha-sāgara*); the ocean of Buddhas is the exclusive domain of the Buddhas' own cognitive range.
The third corresponds to the first [ocean].
The fourth corresponds to the second, the ocean of the karma of sentient beings; because the causes of karma are subtle, it is described as "vast. The fifth contains two phrases:

the first corresponds to the eighth, the ocean of the Buddha’s supernormal transformations (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*). The functional activity of liberation is itself a supernormal transformation; since this transformation relies upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the term "samādhi" is added.
The second contains the knowledge of the three periods of time, as stated in the subsequent text:
"In a single thought-moment, one knows the three periods of time, by virtue of the Buddha’s inconceivable power of liberation.
Because this general phrase is added, these two sets of six are combined to form the fifth [set].
The seventh is the ninth;
the eighth is the seventh ocean of vows, by which, through the power of vows, one enters all worlds within the dharma-realm;
the ninth is the tenth, the establishment and exposition.
Furthermore, the faculties of a bodhisattva have many other meanings:
in cultivating the ten paths of wholesome action, there are three wholesome roots;
in cultivating the stages and the perfections, diligence serves as the faculty.
Upholding the True Dharma has faith and wisdom as its root;
nurturing sentient beings has compassion and kindness as its root;
and realizing the Buddha-way has compassion and wisdom as its root.
Because they thoroughly know the various distinctions.
Second, from "In this way" onwards, the application by analogy can be understood.
Second, from "For what reason? onwards, the explanation of the cause has two parts:
First, the objection:
The intention is to ask, "The Buddhas possess the power to bestow [benefits] and the compassion to do so universally; why, then, is the tenfold wisdom bestowed exclusively upon Samantabhadra?"
The commentary states:
When Samantabhadra attains this samādhi, it is the natural law that he should be granted [the empowerment].
Regarding the section beginning with "At that time," there are also two parts within the bodily empowerment:
First, this land; subsequently, from "In this manner" onwards, the categories are applied universally.
Within the former, there are again two parts:
first, the Buddha strokes [the crown of] the head with his hand, clarifying that he bestows upon them his protective inclusion.

Furthermore, according to the Sanskrit original, it is clarified that the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions do not actually come here; their outstretched arms need not be long, yet they simultaneously touch the crowns of the heads, each making full contact with the crown without obstructing one another—all of which are the sovereign manifestations of the Tathāgatas' karmic power.
Second, from "His hands" onwards, the function of the hand-marks is explained.
Within this section, there are ten phrases used to manifest their inexhaustibility.

The first five describe how his virtuous marks are perfectly complete—namely, being supple, slender, straight, and so forth—and thus it is said that he is "adorned with the primary and secondary marks."
The five subsequent phrases, beginning with "Furthermore, it emerges," clarify the sovereign mastery of wondrous function.

The intent is to clarify that this hand extends throughout the ten directions and encompasses the three periods of time; it gathers cause and effect and includes both persons and dharmas. Its profound and vast essence and function are boundless and sovereign, beyond what words can express.
The subsequent summary can be understood accordingly.
Third, from "At that time" onwards is the section on emerging from meditative concentration (*vyutthāna*), because the tasks to be performed have been completed.
This section has two parts:
First, this realm; later, the same category extends to the ten directions.
Within the former, there are also two parts:
first, the emergence from meditative concentration; second, the benefit to the assembly.
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, the arising of the primary concentration;
second, the arising of the attendant concentrations, which also has two parts:

The first part is the general overview, meaning that when one arises, all arise; for this wondrous samādhi is the ocean of all samādhis, and since all other samādhis enter it as its gates, they are entirely identical to it and thus also receive the name "ocean.
The second part, beginning with "That is to say," provides a detailed analysis; since the objects of perception are as numerous as atoms, ten are briefly enumerated:

the first is the samādhi of the wisdom that knows [all things], which means there is not even a single thought-moment of deviation, hence it is said that "thought after thought is without difference."
Yet, without abandoning universal knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), it constitutes skillful wisdom (*kauśalyajñāna*).
The second [pair] consists of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-viṣaya*).
Thus, there is one pair of subject and object.
Third, manifesting vast lands; fourth, manifesting dwellings; these constitute the pair of the general and the particular regarding the world.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata-garbha ālayavijñāna suddenly manifests all bodies, vessels, and various objects of enjoyment."
The "vessel" is the vast world-system (*viśva-kṣetra*).
"Enjoyment" refers to one's dwelling.

The fifth [knowledge], knowing the distinctions among mental states, and the sixth, knowing the characteristics and names of bodies, correspond to the pair of form and mind (*rūpa-citta*) in sentient beings.
Seventh is knowing the vast environment; eighth is knowing the vast body—this constitutes the correspondence between the primary and its support.
Although it speaks of "dust-like particles," the intent is to manifest that the Buddha is as vast as space and has no fixed location, appearing wherever there is a place for things to exist.

Only the *tathāgatagarbha* exists as a substantial reality; based upon this, the distinct locations are established, for there are pure and impure lands according to the conduct of bodhisattvas, and various destinies according to the karma of sentient beings.

Regarding the Buddhas within a minute particle, there is another meaning: the Tathāgatagarbha is the true body of the Buddha; its essence is vast and expansive such that no one can fully know it, yet it eternally abides within six or seven minute particles.
Each and every sentient being possesses an *ālayavijñāna*; therefore, it is said that each has an "infinite great body.

Regarding the ninth [point], "knowing the principles and modes (*naya*) of all phenomena": the preceding eight were explained by way of distinct categories of phenomena, whereas this one encompasses all phenomena through their underlying principles; hence, it says "all."

The "Section on the Essential Principles" (*Naya-parivarta*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states that all phenomena are empty, neither arising nor ceasing, devoid of intrinsic nature, and free from all marks such that they cannot be the object of aspiration or seeking.
However, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is serene and eternally abiding; one should know that this is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha.
The *Saṃghabhedavastu-sūtra* (or *Cintiprabhāsa-sūtra*) states that wherever one avoids emptiness, one never departs from emptiness.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* explains that there are six modes of reasoning (*naya*):
first, the mode of reasoning regarding ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), which refers to the true nature as it is practiced by the wisdom purified of the two obscurations;
second, the mode of reasoning regarding realization, which refers to attaining knowledge of ultimate reality exactly as it is.
Third is the principle of instruction, which means having personally realized [the truth] oneself and then revealing it to sentient beings.
These three constitute the basis, while the subsequent three provide their explanation.
Fourth is the principle of avoiding the two extremes.
That is to say, if someone were to ask:
"What is meant by the 'principle of the true meaning'?
one should answer them as follows:
Neither existent nor non-existent, neither eternal nor annihilated—
this is the fivefold inconceivable principle.
That is to say, there may be one who asks:
How is it realized?
One should answer them:
"It is inconceivable."

If one remains free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding all phenomena, at that time one realizes the nature of true ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); therefore, it is known that verbal expressions are not the true meaning.
Sixth is the principle of accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings.
That is to say, if someone asks:
"How does one provide instruction?
one should answer them as follows:
In accordance with the diverse inclinations of sentient beings, he skillfully reveals [the truth] by following their desires.
That ultimate reality is this very body of the treasury;
that which is inconceivable is this very samādhi.
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga explained the four intentions (*abhiprāya*) as the interpretation of all sūtras; this is also the *naya* (methodological principle), as argued in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Of the nine preceding phrases, only the third and fourth are named according to their manifestation, while the remaining seven are all designated based on the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
When all such categories, numbering as many as the atoms within all world-oceans, are combined into a single totality, one knows that this totality is indeed the totality of all concentrations.
Second, from the section on "Samantabhadra" onwards, the great assembly attains benefits.
The first part indicates the time of the benefit, which is also the cause for obtaining it;
the latter part, beginning with "Those various," correctly clarifies the attainment of the benefit, stating nine by omitting the number [ten].
The first five [verses] attain the Dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva; each phrase has a single meaning, yet all are contained within the preceding definitive state.
Furthermore, these five phrases successively establish each preceding one.
The latter four are the dharmas for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, namely the three karmas of the Tathāgata:
first, the attainment of the real wisdom that illuminates the treasury-body;
second, the attainment of the expedient wisdom regarding the power and function of the treasury-body.
Third, the manifestation of lands through the pores of the three bodies;
fourth, the descent of the eight signs [of a Buddha's life], which includes the meaning of oral transformation, as the *tathāgatagarbha* (the treasury-body) also encompasses this significance.
As for the benefit to others when Samantabhadra emerges from meditative absorption, it is due to the mutual resonance between the response and the stimulus.
Just as when the yang energy has long been full within the sprouts of spring, a single breeze from the east causes all the buds to open simultaneously;

so too, for the assembly of bodhisattvas who have accumulated goodness over a long duration and shared the same vows, what is there that cannot be achieved when, upon merely beholding the sublime realm, their myriad virtues are suddenly perfected and both the hidden and the manifest are simultaneously sustained?
Second, from "In this way" onwards, the application by analogy can be understood.
Fourth, from "At that time" onwards is the section on manifesting signs as proof.
However, because the mind gains benefit and rejoices, the earth shakes and various auspicious omens appear.
The other assemblies have already heard [the teaching] and attained benefit; therefore, the manifestation of signs occurs later for them.

Although this assembly has not yet heard it, they have already attained benefit beforehand; thus, the auspicious sign is manifested first, because in this assembly the excellence of the fruit is revealed through eloquence.
The text contains four sections.
First, the world slightly trembles, which simultaneously reveals the causal basis of the auspicious omen through the two powers of cause and effect.
As for the term "slightly trembles," it refers to the preceding sign.
Second, they are adorned with two kinds of jewel assemblies;
third, they emit sounds that preach the Dharma;

fourth, jewels rain down during the Buddha’s assemblies. These ten types are cited briefly to manifest their inexhaustibility: the first three are the treasures of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-ratna*), while the latter seven are the treasures of the transmission and penetration of the Dharma-transformation (*dharmaparyāya-prasaraṇa-ratna*). Both arise from supramundane roots of goodness.
The fifth section, following "Having universally rained down these ten kinds of clouds," is the Part Praising Virtues through the Light of the Hairs.
It consists of two parts:
first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent; second, the actual presentation of the verses.
The ten verses in this section are divided into three parts:

first, one verse that provides a general summary of the preceding meditative concentration; second, eight verses that specifically reveal its pervasive characteristics; and third, one verse that concludes by praising the reasons for this.
Within the specific revelation, there are two [subdivisions]:
The first two and a half verses directly state the aforementioned pervasiveness, while the subsequent five and a half verses demonstrate that pervasiveness by citing its causes.
This section consists of two parts:
the first half-verse concerns the pervasiveness of the power of conditions, and the latter five verses concern the pervasiveness of the power of causes.
Within this, there are four parts.
The first verse is "pervasive" because it expresses function through essence; the first half concerns essence and the second half concerns function.
The physical marks being like space refers to the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*).
Abiding in accordance with reality is the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*).
Responding universally according to the capacities of beings is the land of enjoyment and transformation (*saṃbhoga-nirmāṇa*).
Question:
Are the dharma-nature body and its land distinct or not?
If they were distinct, they could not be called "dharma-nature," for the nature is non-dual;
if they were not distinct, there would be no distinction between the supported and the support.
Answer:

The sutras and treatises offer differing explanations; when the dharmakāya is comprehensively categorized, there are briefly ten types. As for the lands, which manifest in accordance with the body, there are five levels:
first, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the dharmakāya is constituted solely by the pure dharma-dhātu, and the land is likewise constituted by that very dharma-nature.
Although its nature is of a single flavor, it is divided into two categories according to the characteristics of sentient beings and the insentient world.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Within the category of sentient beings, it is called Buddha-nature; within the category of non-sentient things, it is called Dharma-nature. While 'subject' and 'object' are provisionally posited, in reality there is no difference."

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Although there is no difference in essence between this body and its environment, they differ in terms of their nature and characteristics because they belong to the Buddha.
This means that the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) belongs to the Buddha, and thus constitutes the *dharmatākāya* (dharma-nature body).
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) belongs to phenomena and constitutes the Land of the Nature of Phenomena (*dharmatā-kṣetra*).
It is said thus because the nature varies according to its manifestations.

As for the present statement that it is "like empty space," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "This body and land are both not comprised within form (*rūpa*); although their dimensions—whether large or small—cannot be described, their extent is nonetheless boundless in accordance with their phenomenal characteristics."
"Just as space pervades all places.
This expression "like space" serves as a general metaphor for both the body and the land.
Alternatively, the Great Wisdom alone constitutes the Dharma-body, while the True Suchness realized therein constitutes the Dharma-nature Land.
Wu-xing’s *Compendium of the Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*) states: "Because stainless and unimpeded wisdom constitutes the Dharma-body.
If this is so, why is it said that its characteristics are like space?"
"Because the essence of wisdom is unimpeded and identical to empty space.
Third, that which is both wisdom and suchness constitutes the Dharmakāya; as the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* of the Liang dynasty state:
"Only suchness and the wisdom of suchness remain alone, and this is called the Dharmakāya."
In this state, the body contains both suchness and wisdom; at the highest level, there is only suchness.
When both the four objects and wisdom are simultaneously extinguished, they constitute the Dharmakāya.
As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is neither mind nor object; the Buddha-lands are likewise."

Based on this principle, all sūtras state that the body and land of the Tathāgata are non-dual; this indicates, through the phrase "relying on the truth" (*satya*), the absence of subject and object, whereby one speaks of "relying on the truth to realize the meaning of being like space."

5. These four preceding phrases combined constitute the single unimpeded Dharma-body (*anāvaraṇa-dharmakāya*); all [teachings] are obtained according to what is spoken, and the lands are likewise so. 6.

These five preceding phrases—both general and specific—are mutually fused and mutually sublated, such that these five modes of expression vanish; it is utterly non-reliant as the Dharma-body, and the lands are likewise so.
The above has been explained solely in terms of objects and wisdom.

The seven [categories] comprehensively include the five factors, as well as the immeasurable virtues of practice such as compassion and vows; there are none that are not subsumed within this dharmakāya, because the virtues produced through cultivation must necessarily realize the principle.
In its unhindered integration and inclusion, the very essence of the *tathatā* (suchness) realized herein constitutes the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*).
Based on this principle, the body and the land are fundamentally distinct.
Now, when it is said that the bodily marks are all meritorious virtues, and that [the body] is like space, this refers to the nature of the body itself.
The subsequent sutra also states: "Understand that the Tathāgata’s body is not like empty space, for it is perfected by all merits and immeasurable, wondrous dharmas.

This eighth [point] universally encompasses the merits of the physical marks of both the recompense-body (*vipākakāya*) and the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), as there are none that are not subsumed within this Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the thirty-two marks and so forth are all subsumed within the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
However, there are three meanings:
first, because the marks are identical with Suchness (*tathatā*), they are subsumed within the Dharma-body of Principle (*li*).
Because it is manifested by the two wisdoms, it belongs to the Wisdom-Dharmakāya;
because its three essential characteristics are all dharmas of merit, it is called the Dharmakāya.

As for its supporting land, it is universally unimpeded in its nature and characteristics, whether pure or defiled. My land is pure, yet you do not see it; sentient beings see a burning land, yet the pure land is not destroyed.
Form is itself suchness, and characteristics are themselves non-characteristics; body and land, phenomena and principle, mutually support one another. Generally, there are four propositions:

namely, the form-body relies upon the land of phenomenal characteristics; the form-body relies upon the land of the dharma-nature; and the dharma-body relies upon both the land of the dharma-nature and the land of phenomenal characteristics.

Furthermore, by mutually correlating the single and the double, five propositions are also established; that is, the body of phenomenal characteristics relies upon the dharma-nature, and one should apply this same principle to the lands of phenomenal characteristics and so forth.
This above [classification] still applies generally to all Mahāyāna teachings.

The nine penetrations encompass the three kinds of worlds as a single Great Dharmakāya; because they possess the ten Buddhas, the three bodies and so forth are all subsumed within the perfect awakening of wisdom herein.
The same applies to the lands: they are like the empty body manifesting as universal bodies.
What could possibly be lacking? This is unique to the *Avataṃsaka*.
Regarding the division of the ten lands into provisional and real, only the ninth belongs to this scripture.

If one relies on the principles of fusion and inclusion, as well as the inclusion of the same teaching, the preceding nine meanings are taken together as a single comprehensive statement; this is called the Tathāgata’s unimpeded body and land, and the same applies to Samantabhadra.
The meaning follows the concealment or manifestation [of the teachings] and cannot be fixed rigidly; those who have attained realization seek it within the text without being limited by narrow views.
As for the previous statement that there are five levels of lands: the first is the Dharma-nature alone, which belongs to the first three bodies;
the second is the simultaneous cessation of both [subject and object], which belongs to the fourth.
Third, the nature and characteristics of the three [realms] serve as the basis for the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth;
fourth, the integration of the three worlds belongs to the ninth;
fifth, the synthesis of all preceding meanings constitutes the tenth basis.

Second, from "Samantabhadra Abiding" onwards, the one and a half verses concern the universality of the Great Vows; they also manifest that [the vows] universally pervade the basis of the Correct Center.

They are layered and pervasive in every respect. As for why they are not seen now, it is because the faculties [of the beings] are not in resonance with them and thus do not see them; this is because they are the body of empty space (*ākāśakāya*), and thus they pervade even those places where they are not seen.
The first three and a half verses clarify the superiority of what is manifested.
The fourth verse shows that although the fruit-virtues are already perfected, he does not abandon the gateway of the causal stage.

The third single verse concludes by praising the reason for this: his sovereign power is inconceivable and manifests universally; while he is designated as entering a single concentration, in reality he wanders everywhere. How could anyone but the Buddha’s clouds of light be able to praise and describe him?
The sixth section, "The Great Assembly’s Praise and Entreaty.

In the preceding section, the assembly questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha manifested himself as the Lord of Dharma; now, as the assembly beholds his emergence from meditative concentration, they praise and entreat Samantabhadra.
Whereas the previous section involved only the original assembly, this one encompasses both the new and the old, and is therefore described as "all."
Since the questions are the same as those previously mentioned, they are here merely cited in brief.
The ten verses are divided into three parts:
the first eight verses praise the Master and request [his teaching], manifesting his capacity to expound it;
Next is the request by raising a single point of dharma, which formally presents the doubts;
following this is the request by praising the assembly, clarifying that there are those with the capacity to hear.
Within the former [the first request], there are two parts:
The first five verses praise the profound and vast virtues of Samantabhadra’s cause and fruit, clarifying that there is a teaching regarding the cause;
the final three verses praise his virtue of raining down the Dharma throughout all dust-motes and lands, clarifying that there is a teaching regarding the fruit.
Now, regarding the first section, each verse conveys a single meaning.
The first verse praises one's own pure *dharmakāya*; three lines clarify the cause, and one line clarifies the fruit.
Regarding the cause, there are three meanings:
First, it arises from the cultivation of the Dharma, where the meaning applies to both the conditional and the perfecting causes;
second, it arises from great vows, which constitutes the conditional cause;
third, by relying on the Tathāgatagarbha to realize true equality, this is the direct cause.
True Suchness (*tathatā*) is precisely non-emptiness, and empty space is the treasury of emptiness.
"Equanimity" and "treasury" both encompass these two preceding meanings.
Second, the praise of abiding pervasively throughout Buddha-fields.
The third phrase refers to the pervasive cause; all others are pervasive characteristics.
Because the cause is endowed with the adornment of wisdom, it is able to illuminate equally the adornments of all merits, ensuring that there is nothing not perceived.
Third, praising those who draw near to the Buddha;
fourth, praising those who are constantly in meditative concentration.
Regarding "within the realm of reality," it means not being subject to the fluctuations of conceptualization.
"Cao" (曹) means "a group" or "class.
The five hymns exhaustively describe the salvation of sentient beings.
As for "microscopic dust" (微塵), it is because there are many sentient beings within even the most minute particles.
The second section consists of three verses concerning the fruits of teaching the Dharma.
The first verse praises the constant proclamation of the Great Dharma;
the phrase "words like space" and following serves as a metaphor for its vastness.
The preceding analogy was inexhaustible and without distinction; next, one verse praises and explains the peerless Dharma.
There are two aspects to this "peerlessness":
first, the excellence of the power of the speaker, because they are endowed with the two types of adornment.
The second [verse] states that there is nothing equal to what is taught, because it describes the Buddha’s sphere of activity.
The final verse cites the cause and its resulting fruit, demonstrating that these virtues have their source.
Because the causes have been perfected over vast eons, he is thus able to rain down the Dharma through his preaching.

In the second verse, which presents the request for the teaching, although many aspects were previously inquired about in the preceding chapter, their essential convergence does not exceed the three types of worlds; therefore, each of the three lines now clarifies one of these.
Furthermore, while the previous question encompassed all the assemblies in general, this one requires an answer from within the present assembly.
The final verse praises the request of the assembly and is also termed "self-narration.
This has two meanings:
First, with reverence and a single-minded focus, one is inwardly capable of receiving the Dharma.
Second, because the Buddhas rejoice in it and there are superior external conditions, it should be taught.
If taught, it will above accord with the Buddha’s mind and below conform to the inclinations of sentient beings.
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Vaipulya, Scroll Ten;
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Vaipulya, Scroll Eleven.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang in the Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Four: The Manifestation of the World-Sphere.
Regarding the initial intent for this chapter:

Since the conditions have been fully set forth in the preceding section, what follows is the formal presentation of the subject matter. This chapter appears here to provide a general explanation of the characteristics of the fruit and to specifically answer the questions concerning the Ocean of the Establishment of the Dharma-Dhātu.
Second, regarding the explanation of the names: "world" (*loka*) refers to the three periods of time, as it falls within the past, future, and present.
"Sphere" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial divisions, as there is a distinction between this and that.
Furthermore, "world" implies concealment or obscuration, while "sphere" also implies a boundary; this refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) which are subject to destruction.
The world is concealed by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which is indestructible;
phenomena arise from true nature and, being identical to the unconditioned, are concealed by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), which is destructible.
The worlds are each distinct and do not intermingle; this is their respective boundary.

Therefore, those who perceive the Sahā world see the Sahā world in contrast to the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha), while those who perceive the Flower Treasury World see the Flower Treasury World in contrast to the Sahā world.
"Accomplishment" (siddhi) refers to the conditions by which accomplishment is achieved, namely the ten conditions and so forth; this is a designation that combines both the agent and the object.
If it is taken as the accomplishment of the world, it is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound).
According to the Sanskrit original, it says "the accomplishment of the world-ocean.
The subsequent section explaining the oceans was omitted by the translator.
The intended meaning is as follows:

The fruit of Buddhahood arises only through hearing and cultivation regarding the primary and secondary [receptacle] worlds; whereas the karmic retributions of sentient beings exist inherently from the beginning, it is for this reason that only the world-realm is specifically designated here.

Regarding the threefold thematic scope (*piṇḍārtha*): the purpose is to list the boundless supreme virtues and to provide an extensive explanation of the "Ocean of Worlds" (*lokadhātu-samudra*) as the object of knowledge. This constitutes the central theme.
However, its underlying intent is manifold:
first, it serves as the goal for causing all bodhisattvas to give rise to great faith and understanding and thereby enter [the path].

This means causing them to know that the ocean of the great compassionate conduct of Buddhas and bodhisattvas extensively covers the boundless realm of sentient beings without exception, so that they may emulate it in their own practice.
Because all worlds are boundless and must be entirely purified;
because sentient beings are boundless and must all be transformed and delivered;
because lands differ according to the mind, one should purify both one's own mind and the minds of others.
