first, the introduction; second, the verses.
Within the verses, there are three divisions:
The first verse indicates the essence and function of the benefit;
the subsequent eight verses reveal what is seen through that function, among which the first seven see the cause and the final one sees the fruit;
the third verse expresses a vow to emulate [the Buddha], which is precisely the cultivation of the great vow at the beginning of the preceding chapter.
The fourth section, "Transforming and Guiding Sentient Beings," is divided into three parts:
first, clarifying one's own awakening; second, from "For the sake of all... onwards, clarifying the turning of that awakening to others, which displays ten dharmas.
Together with the eleven previously attained by oneself, there are both similarities and differences, as can be understood from the text.
Third, the section beginning with "Now, like Mount Sumeru" describes the benefit of benefiting others.

In the fifth section, "The Tathāgata’s Encouragement and Exhortation," there are eleven verses. The first three praise the attainment of the mind [of awakening] and the realization of the Dharma, stating that the great fruit shall be accomplished;
the next four contrast the inferior with the superior, showing that the virtues of those who advance will be perfected;
the final two concern external conditions and internal wisdom, resolving that realization will be attained without doubt.
The latter two [sections] cite one case as an illustration for the remainder; the practitioner thereby attains [the realization].
The second [section], "Encountering the Second Buddha," is divided into two parts:
first, concluding the preceding and introducing what follows; second, the actual manifestation of the Buddha’s appearance.

Regarding the first point: it is because he is about to speak of a future Buddha that he discusses the kalpa-lifespan in general to clarify the number of intermediate kalpas (*antara-kalpa*). This is intended to manifest the appearance of many Buddhas.

As for the mention of human lifespan and the Buddha’s lifespan: since the Buddha’s lifespan was short while human lifespan was long, [the Bodhisattva] was able to serve three Buddhas throughout his life by means of his majestic radiance.
Second, from "That Buddha passed away" onwards, the text correctly reveals the arising of the Buddha.

The passage is divided into five sections: first, clarifying the arising of the Buddha after his passing; second, obtaining benefits upon beholding his marks; third, praising his virtues and exhorting others to visit him; fourth, the retinue collectively returning [to him]; and fifth, awakening to and entering [the truth] upon hearing the sutra.
This is the first [name].
Regarding the Buddha's name herein: his wisdom guides all practices so that they all reach the other shore.
Because he perceives the nature of reality with perfect clarity, he is named "Excellent Eye" (Sujāta).
The fruit is adorned by its cause; this is called "ornamentation.
Second, from the passage beginning with "At that time," there are two parts concerning how Vimalaprabha beholds the signs and attains benefit:
first, the beholding of the signs, which is the cause for immediately attaining benefit.
Second, from "immediately attains" (*ji de*) onwards, there is the actual acquisition of benefit, first presented in detail and then summarized.
There are ten items in the detailed presentation:

first, the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), which is explained first because it is the father of Bodhisattvas; thus, one does not depart from the mindfulness of the Buddha even up to the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
Regarding the "gate of the boundless ocean-treasury": "treasury" (*kośa*) refers to that which accumulates and stores, while "ocean" (*sāgara*) denotes its depth and vastness.
Briefly stated, there are three meanings:
first, because within this meditative concentration one perceives many Buddhas.

The subsequent text states: "Taking the Buddha as one's object of focus, maintaining exclusive mindfulness without relinquishing it, this person attains the vision of the Buddha; its magnitude is equal to the mind.
Because one is able to see through mindfulness, it is designated as a "gate."

The two hundred and eleventh: The virtues of the Buddha are an infinite ocean-treasury; because they can be known through mindfulness, they are called "gates. What is this infinite ocean? There is an ocean of practices and vows cultivated throughout oceans of kalpas;

there is an ocean of physical marks and signs that accomplish the form-body (rūpakāya); there is an ocean of eloquence that accomplishes the wisdom-body (jñānakāya); there is an ocean of names and titles established through the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna); there is an ocean of merit from cultivating the various factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma); and there is an ocean of pure lands for establishing sentient beings.
In this way, each of these oceans is boundless, and each gives rise to what is called a "treasury" (kośa) of accumulated [qualities].
Because these three boundless supreme virtues arise from the recollection of the Buddha, this single gateway is a profound and vast accumulation.

Why is this? By recollecting the Dharma-nature body, one accords with the principle of suchness; by recollecting the merit-body, one accomplishes boundless virtues; by recollecting the marks-and-signs body, one realizes boundless characteristics. There are no obstructions that are not extinguished and no virtues that do not arise—all these are subsumed in a single phrase through the general practice of Buddha-recollection. Because one attains universal awakening through this, it is called a "gate"; yet even this single gate cannot be fully described.
Second, the great wisdom of the two types of dhāraṇī, which enables one to penetrate the profound Dharma;
third, responding universally without conditions;
fourth, impartially eliminating the heat of affliction.
The profound ocean of merit of the five Buddhas accumulates power and function; the Bodhisattva, taking this as an object of focus, experiences joy that pervades both body and mind.

If compassion causes the mind to be dejected and joy leads to agitation, then by deeply acceding with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one becomes as vast as empty space, where both compassion and joy vanish, resulting in equanimity and purity.
The seventh [aspect of] *prajñā* is the awakening to the true nature of phenomena, which is free from conceptual discrimination.

To have something to be abandoned is not true abandonment; rather, knowing that self-nature is already free, one does not abandon it further. This abandonment of non-abandonment is the true *dharmadhātu*.

The true dharma-realm is primordially pure; the purity of the dharma-realm is the purity of prajñā, and the purity of prajñā means that all phenomena are fundamentally pure. When all phenomena are pure, there is neither purity nor impurity—this is true purity.

The *prajñā* of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the substance of all phenomena; because contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*) darkly accords with this, it is the locus where all virtues depend, and is thus called the "body.
Since it is conjoined with the eight universal wisdoms, it manifests unimpededly in accordance with conditions.
The nine entrances (*navāyatana*) penetrate the profundity of the Dharma and are free from the defilement of verbal expression.
The ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) illuminate the purity of the Buddha-dharma, purifying the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and containing all virtues.
In the second section, "Thus" and below, the conclusion clarifies the progressive advancement through successive stages; hence it is said to be "ten thousand."
The meaning of "thoroughly penetrating" is understood immediately from what precedes it.
From the third section, "At that time," onwards, the text praises his virtues and exhorts [the audience] to approach him; this passage is divided into two parts:
first, the recitation of verses, and second, the benefits derived from those verses.
The verses are divided into three parts:
first, one verse praising the rare and auspicious encounter;
second, seven verses praising the Buddha’s supreme virtues, which are further divided into three sections:
The first three [verses] concern bodily action (*kāyakarman*), the next three concern verbal action (*vākkarman*), and the final one concerns mental action (*manaskarman*).
There are two verses that exhort the assembly to follow together;
the benefit of the subsequent verses beginning with "O Sons of the Buddhas" can be understood accordingly.
The fourth section, beginning with "At that time, Mahātejas," describes the assembly returning together.
The fifth section, beginning with "That Buddha," describes hearing the sutra and attaining realization.
This text is divided into three parts:
First, the Buddha preaches the sutra; second, those who are receptive obtain benefit; third, the Tathāgata offers praise and exposition.
Now, first, regarding the subject matter of the sutra:
the essence and nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is "Great Vaipulya" (*mahāvaipulya*).
"Purity" refers to the Buddha;
"adornment" refers to the *Avataṃsaka*.
The mention of having many retinues demonstrates the perfection of this teaching.
Second, from the passage beginning "Those various," the benefits obtained by those present according to their capacity are described.
There are likewise ten benefits.

Since it refers to the "great assembly," some individuals may obtain one, others two, three, or four, while some may possess all ten; as their majestic radiance was first realized [by the Buddha], they are not specifically listed here.
The words of the Great Assembly have already encompassed this, and thus the Buddha’s praise follows below.
However, these ten matters can be briefly explained in two ways:
first, they are correlated respectively with the ten stages (bhūmi) and the ten perfections (pāramitā).
Whether taking the meaning of "ground" (bhūmi) or the meaning of "crossing over" (tāraṇa), to realize that all phenomena are fundamentally pure is called "pure wisdom.
Not grasping at the mark of purity is called "skillful means"; this is precisely the wisdom of realization upon entering the first ground.
Second, in the second stage (bhūmi), one is free from the defilement of breaking the precepts; this is the obstacle to be eliminated.
Illuminating all categories of wholesome qualities is the light of morality (*śīla*).
Third is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); patience is the supreme ornament, cherished by all.
There are no lands that it does not enter, no dharmas that it does not illuminate, and no visions that it does not purify; this is the expansion of all practices through diligence.

Explained according to the meaning of the stages (*bhūmi*), by means of the various factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), it burns away inexhaustible delusions and accomplishes boundless radiance.
The five inclinations toward all conditioned phenomena enable one to enter the mundane world.

Because the perfection of meditation increases, one’s nature is able to leave defilement behind; by engaging with the mundane to transform sentient beings, one forms clouds of merit and virtue, and by not being deluded regarding the true principle, one becomes a banner of light.
The sixth is the manifestation of *prajñā*, termed "entry through realization," which illuminates the profound arising of conditions and is called the "light of the ocean of Dharma.

The seventh is when effort has already receded and one is about to enter the state of non-effort; this is the profound advancement wherein the provisional and the real are unimpeded, constituting the "great adornment."

The eighth [ground] is the seeing of the true nature of phenomena; it is a cultivation that is effortless and is the most sublime vision, because through this wisdom one further attains consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "The latter three grounds equally dispel ignorance and are equally effortless. Therefore, it is not the ground of consecration itself, but rather the wisdom of consecration.
Ninth, clearly discerning the medicine and the illness is the mark of the ocean of merit; eloquence responds universally, like the flowing light of the moon’s reflection.
Tenth, when wisdom is perfected and obstacles removed, one then gives rise to faith and understanding regarding the Buddha’s vows; therefore, it is called "birth."
Second, these ten preceding sections establish their names according to each individual matter; they do not necessarily correspond entirely to the specific stages (*bhūmi*).

They may apply generally to all stages, or they may not follow a sequential order, because people are infinite and their realizations differ, and because the skillful exposition of Samantabhadra contains manifold meanings within its text.
Third, from "At that time" onwards, the Tathāgata provides a descriptive praise.
The ten verses are divided into two parts:

the first six praise his possession of supreme virtues and his future attainment of the ultimate fruit; in each case, the first half refers to what he has already acquired, while the second half refers to what he shall realize.

Regarding the fourth verse alone, the first three lines present the cause, while the latter four verses show that one's practice is equal to the Buddha’s cause and should lead to realization like the Buddha’s; in all these cases, the first three lines cite the Buddha’s practice, and the final line shows equality with the Buddha’s virtue.

However, regarding the descriptions and praises herein, they largely coincide with what was previously encountered through the light and what was attained before the great assembly; their meaning must surely be based on the former, and one may discern this for oneself through careful reflection.
The section on encountering the third Buddha is divided into six parts:
first, the time when the Tathāgata appears, which refers to the period following the parinirvāṇa of the preceding Buddha;
second, from "That maṇi... onwards, which correctly clarifies the present age.
One who establishes this title has fulfilled the ocean of merit; there is nothing further to surpass it.
3. From "At that time, Great Radiance" onwards, Great Radiance goes to make offerings.
4. From "At that time, that Tathāgata" onwards, the Buddha preaches the sutra for him.
Because it perceives the Universal Dharma, it is called the Universal Eye (*sarvākṣa*).
Because its nature is wisdom, it is termed "Radiance.
Furthermore, since one eye is itself ten eyes—fused without obstruction and with no phenomena existing outside the eye—it is only then that it is truly the Universal Eye.
When various conditions give rise to seeing, each condition individually acts as a root; because the cause is submerged within the effect, all conditions are designated as "the eye.
Thus, when the entirety of form constitutes the eye, one constantly sees form without [a separate] condition;
when the entirety of the eye constitutes form, one constantly refers to it as "seeing" rather than as a self.
5. From "At that time" onwards, the section on the benefits gained through majestic light (*vairocana*).
All five perfections are merits, but meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the greatest; its quiescence, which illuminates all without exception, is called "Universal Radiance."
The section beginning with "Having attained this" clarifies the function of this meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the terms "merit" (*puṇya*) and "non-merit" (*apuṇya*), there are briefly two meanings:
first, merit is that which is wholesome (*kuśala*), while non-merit is that which is unwholesome or sinful (*pāpa*).
The two types of merit are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while non-merit is the nature (*dharmatā*); this is because both nature and characteristics are fully understood.
The Sūtra states, "Merit is itself the non-meritorious nature"; this refers to its profundity. To fully understand all things is its vastness; hence the metaphor of the ocean.
That one encountered the first Buddha and obtained only ten was because their own power had not yet prevailed.
That the next Buddha obtained ten thousand was because the Way had become deeper.
That now there is only one is because the Way has already reached fulfillment.
The sixth section, from "At that time, that Buddha" onwards, consists of the Tathāgata’s prophetic declaration (vyākaraṇa) in eleven verses, divided into four parts: first,
four verses manifesting the possession of the bodhicitta— namely, the initial verse contains the aspiration (praṇidhāna),
and the subsequent verse contains compassion (karuṇā).
The fourth is the light of wisdom;
the third combines diligence, for by universally directing the three minds, the bodhicitta is perfected and one shall attain sublime wisdom.
The subsequent four [stages] involve ascending into the realm of the Buddhas.
The third section consists of one verse, which shows that the characteristics of its fruition are identical to those of all Buddhas.
The fourth section consists of two verses, praising its present capacity to benefit others by abiding in the practices of Samantabhadra.
The section on encountering the fourth Buddha is divided into four parts:
first, the Buddha’s coming and going; second, the heavenly kings making offerings; third, the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma; and fourth, the recipients of the benefit returning home.

Regarding the first [meaning]: in terms of its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it resembles a blue lotus; in terms of its virtue (*guṇa*), the mind is unstained. Because its characteristics and virtues are lofty and manifest, and its fame is proclaimed abroad, it is called a "banner" (*dhvaja*) as it subdues the heterodox and draws all beings to take refuge.
Second, from "At that time" onwards, the section on the Heavenly King’s offerings consists of two parts:
first, it clarifies that the Bodhisattva has advanced in practice and is now in his reward-realm heavenly palace—this city is the very one listed at the beginning of this chapter;
second, knowing that the Buddha is worthy of refuge, he takes flowers and goes to make an offering.
Third, from "At that time" onwards, the sutra is expounded.
Regarding the term "expedient means" (*upāya*), there are briefly three types:
first, the provisional bestowal of what is not real, which is a circuitous and skillful expedient.
Second, the principle is fundamentally beyond words; to speak by means of provisional words is a great skillful means.
Third, to have no obstruction between the provisional and the real is also a great skillful means. Only when both phenomena and principle are fully manifested can it be called the Universal Gate.

4. From "At that time, the Heavenly King" onwards is the section on attaining benefits and returning home. Having heard the aforementioned Samādhi of the Universal Gate and abiding therein, one experiences inexhaustible joy in the Dharma; thus it is called a "Treasury" (*kośa*), by means of which one realizes and penetrates the ocean of all true marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

Within this kalpa, there were Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in ten Mount Sumerus; yet here only four are mentioned, and furthermore, there is no record of the connection between past and present or of those who attained realization and benefit, because the transmission of this sutra has not yet reached its conclusion.
If one were to synthesize [the meaning], it should be stated that "at that time, the Bodhisattva Majestic Light" refers to Vairocana, and so forth.
This concludes the section on the assembly concerning the cause and effect of faith. Chapter Seven: The Names of the Tathāgatas.

This is the second section, titled "The Division of Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generating Understanding. It begins at the start of the second assembly and extends from here through the twelfth sutra; the thirteenth sutra, the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Illumination," is now about to be explained. This chapter will be analyzed according to five topical divisions.
Regarding the intent of the initial arrival, we first clarify its division into parts.

Since the preceding section presented the fruit to inspire faith and delight, the present section clarifies that which produces it; thus, it follows next as a matter of faith and understanding regarding cause and effect.
Regarding the arrival of the second assembly: among those who give rise to understanding, faith is the foremost.
Furthermore, while the preceding section presented the objects of faith, this section clarifies the practice of being able to believe; therefore, it follows in sequence.
Regarding the three sections: the preceding section set forth the cause to manifest the fruit, thereby establishing the object of faith;
the present section sets forth the fruit to discern the cause, thereby clarifying the practice of faith.
Among the three types of karma within the fruition, the body serves as the aggregate; therefore, it is presented first.
Furthermore, this is to provide a remote answer to the previous question regarding the ocean of names and titles.
Second, the explanation of the names also has three parts:
The first section is titled "The Section on Cultivating the Causes to Accord with the Result and Giving Rise to Understanding.
This means that by cultivating the perfect causes of the five stages, one accomplishes the full result of the ten bodies, thereby enabling all bodhisattvas to understand these characteristics.
This gives rise to the understanding that the cause of cultivation accords with the fruit; this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.
Second is the name of the assembly: regarding the location, it is called the "Assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance.
However, there are three interpretations of this:
First, because this hall is composed of jewels and its light shines everywhere;
second, because the Buddha emits universal radiance from within it;
and third, because the Buddha expounds the Dharma-gate of Universal Truth within the hall, illuminating the world with the light of wisdom, it is thus named.
Based on the first meaning, it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound; based on the latter two, they are *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compounds.
In terms of the dharmas, it is called the "Assembly of Faith and Practice.
The names of the three sections have already been explained in the "Chapter on the Tathāgata Manifesting Signs."
That which summons the essence is called a "name" (nāman), while that which expresses virtue is termed a "title" (abhidhāna); names distinguish, whereas titles are universal.

All Buddhas universally possess the ten titles; however, because names such as "Śākya" differ from one another, the title "Tathāgata" is but one among those ten. In this chapter, we shall correctly explain how these distinct names are established according to the capacities of sentient beings and their respective virtues.
Since it expresses the name of virtue, it is both a name (*nāman*) and a title (*abhidhāna*).
The name and title of the Tathāgata is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
Regarding the three fundamental tenets, there are likewise three:
First, the classification of the tenets (*mūla-vibhāga*):
this takes the cultivation of what is produced and the manifestation of what is cultivated as its tenet, with the aim of leading all bodhisattvas to practice and enter [the path].

Second, the convergence of the tenets (*samudāgama-vibhāga*): viewed from a general perspective, this takes the stages subsumed under faith, understanding, practice, and virtue as its tenet, with the attainment of the Buddha-fruit as its ultimate goal.
Because faith enables one to certainly reach the stage of the Tathāgata, in its proximate sense, faith alone is the principle (*zong*), and the attainment of the state is the goal (*qu*).

If one follows the long-term classification into ten divisions, these three lower grades constitute one division; therein, the fruit-function that universally responds to capacities throughout the Dharma-realm constitutes the principle, while giving rise to faith based upon this constitutes the goal. Therefore, this is also called the "causality of the primary retribution" (*zhengbao*), and it is likewise that which is believed.
What Dharma-gate does one believe?
One believes that the Buddha’s body and name are equal to those of sentient beings; thus, one knows that my name is like the Buddha’s name.
One believes that the Buddha’s Dharma-gates are established according to what is appropriate; thus, one knows that my deluded thoughts, suffering, and its accumulation are also entirely Dharma-gates.
When one believes that the light of the Buddha’s mental karma shines everywhere, one knows that there is nothing of which one’s own mind is not aware.
Therefore, the virtuous masters of antiquity also categorized the aforementioned three grades by means of the "division of the fruit" (phalabhāga).

Regarding the three categories of tenets: the first takes as its tenet the manifestation that the Buddha’s name is all-pervasive, and its purpose is the benefit of taming and transforming beings according to their capacities.
Alternatively, both of the first two may be taken as tenets, with the purpose being the generation of faith.
The fourth question and answer.
Question:
Since the five cycles of cause and effect differ in their distinctions and equality, why are they divided by name yet combined into one?
Answer:
Because it universally gives rise to the understanding of both differentiation and equality;
and because, apart from that which is produced through cultivation, what cultivation could be said to manifest it?
Question:
In the previous assembly, the fruits were presented primarily to inspire faith; why are the three categories, such as the Name and so forth, presented again here?
Answer:
In general, there are two meanings to generating faith based on an object:
first, to designate the objective phenomena to clarify their locus; second, to subsume them within the mind so as to bring about faithful practice.
The previous assembly was based on the former meaning, while this assembly is based on the latter meaning.
Furthermore, in the previous assembly, the fruit was extensive and the cause was concise; thus it was called "raising the fruit.
In this assembly, the cause is extensive and the fruit is concise; therefore, they are collectively subsumed as the cause.
The sequence of "first the basis, then the actual" is merely a stylistic abbreviation in the text.

If one considers this in terms of the "chain of causality" (*saṃkalana*), it belongs to the fruit of the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*) itself; thus, it differs from what was explained in the seventh assembly regarding the fruits achieved, as the present section specifically elucidates the basis upon which faith relies.
Question:
Why does one not enter meditative concentration?
Because, having not yet entered the [proper] stage, one's nature is not yet settled.
If that is so, are the ten meditative concentrations not mundane wholesome states?
However, the conventions for teaching the Dharma generally comprise four permutations:
first, teaching subsequent to [attaining] concentration, as in the various assemblies.
Second, the teaching after entering meditative concentration, as in the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra* and others.
Third, the teaching while within meditative concentration, as in the ninth assembly, because no words are uttered.
Fourth, the teaching without entering [meditation], as in this current *Śraddhā-bhūmi* and the seventh assembly.

The various texts are not uniform; the ninth [consciousness] serves as a manifest proof that it alone is capable of teaching, because once attained, it is eternally constant and does not obstruct the arising of its functions.
The seventh [consciousness] is intended to manifest that it is always in a state of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, entry is for the purpose of receiving empowerment; since that [attainment] does not require empowerment, it does not require entry.
As for the mention of "subsequent entry," it is said because it occurs during the course of practice and because it is about to arise subsequently.
Thus we know that movement and stillness are but the mind alone, and the sages have no fixed rule.

Therefore, in the subsequent text, when explaining the function of the ten stages of faith (*śaddhā*), it is shown that while one direction enters right concentration, other directions arise to deliver teachings; this is sovereign and unimpeded.
In other assemblies, the touching of the crown was performed after the teaching; in this assembly, it was performed after the teaching.
Thus we know that the structure and momentum of this sutra are both vertical and horizontal, and cannot be fixed by a single standard.
Fifth, the explanation of the text.
If categorized according to the meaning into ten divisions, these following three chapters constitute the "Division of the Universal Application of the Resultant Function According to Capacities.
If categorized according to the dharma into ten assemblies, this single assembly constitutes the second, the "Assembly on the Achievement of Virtues through Faith."
Now, regarding the structural outline of the fourfold questions and answers:
from this point until the end of the seventh assembly, it constitutes the second division, "Cultivating the Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generating Understanding.
If one follows the sequence of the assemblies, these questions and answers should be categorized directly according to them.
Now, in order to follow the textual structure, this single assembly is divided into three parts:
first, the introductory section (nidāna); second, the section on the request; and third, the section on the exposition.
We shall now begin with the introductory section.
It is exactly as at the beginning of the sutra, with the only slight difference being the addition of "Universal Radiance.
It is briefly divided into three parts:

first, the designation of the principal figure, the time, and the place; second, from "Just attained" (*prathama-abhisambuddha*) onwards, the specific manifestation of the three matters; and third, from "Together with ten Buddhas" onwards, the perfection of the supporting retinue.
Within the second [section], there are three parts:
first, the specific explanation of the time;
second, from "In the Universal Radiance" onwards, the specific explanation of the place.
Located approximately three *li* to the southeast of the Bodhimaṇḍa, at a bend in the River Hiraṇyavatī, this [stūpa] was built for the Buddha by the nāga of that river.
Here, the general encompasses the particular; the name of the country mentioned previously subsumes its branches.
Because the name of the site is cited above, the immovable bodhi-tree extends throughout the ten directions below.
3. From "Sublime Awakening" (*miāowù*) onwards, the specific virtues of the Lord are revealed, which also demonstrates the characteristics of attaining perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

According to the beginning of the eighth assembly and the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and other texts, it is taught that the Buddha possesses twenty-one kinds of merit; these shall be explained in detail in the "Chapter on Ascending to Tuṣita."
The first ten phrases of the present text are also merely a brief explanation.
Within these ten phrases, the first is general and the remainder are specific.

Regarding the general section, "sublime awakening is fully perfected": "sublime awakening" (miào wù) is termed "excellent awakening" (shàn jué) in the Jin translation and "right awakening" (zhèng jué) in the treatise translation. This is because the Sanskrit term *sū* contains the meanings of both "wondrously good" (*miào shàn*) and "right" (*zhèng*); thus, the translators adopted whichever term was appropriate.
Awakening (*wu*) is identical to enlightenment (*jue*).
Because it simultaneously illuminates both the ultimate truth (*zhen*) and the conventional truth (*su*), it is called "wondrous awakening" (*miaowu*).
Because it encompasses all subsequent phrases and differs from that of ordinary beings (*yinren*), it is further termed "fulfilled" (*man*).

Regarding "two courses are eternally severed" within the section on differentiation: afflictions and the objects of knowledge, as well as birth-and-death and nirvana, are all termed the "two courses. That neither of these manifests before one is called "eternal severance."
Second, regarding the realization of the signless dharma: pure *tathatā* (suchness) is called the signless dharma.
"Realization" (*da*) means thorough understanding.
Third, the Tathāgata eternally abides in great compassion, spontaneously benefiting and bringing joy to others.
Furthermore, because he constantly dwells in the sublime celestial abodes and the Brahma-abodes, it is said that he "abides in the Buddha-abode.
In these four aspects—the realized, the realization, and the transformative activity—he is equal to all Buddhas.
Fifth, they possess the path capable of counteracting [afflictions], because they have liberated themselves from obstacles.
Sixth, the teachings they proclaim cannot be overturned by non-Buddhists.
Seventh, whether acting in accordance with or contrary to worldly conventions, they cannot be hindered by Māra or his adversaries.
Eighth, because it establishes the teachings that transcend words and thought;
ninth, because it possesses unerring discernment and prophetic declaration regarding the objects of the three times, whether in terms of phenomena or principles.
Possessing these nine distinctions, the first general phrase is established.
The points regarding similarity and difference, as well as formation and destruction, may be understood by applying this principle accordingly.
The third [section] concerns the perfection of the supporting retinue.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the enumeration and definitive selection; second, the praise of his supreme virtues.
Within the former, "Bodhisattva" distinguishes him from ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle, while "Successor to the Throne" clarifies that he is not of a lower rank.
They have come from other directions and do not belong to the original assembly.
Regarding the term "one lifetime," there are two interpretations:
first, in terms of the manifested form (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), as in the case of Maitreya.
This further consists of three types:
first, one birth among humans; second, one birth in the heavens; and third, one descent [to earth]. Here, we specifically take the case of birth in the heavens.

Second, regarding the single birth of the true recompense body (*sambhogakāya*): this refers to the fact that among the four kinds of transformational death and rebirth (*pariṇāmikī cyuti*), there is only the final type, which is designated as being bound to the stage of "no more birth and death" (*acyuta*).
This passage mostly concerns the aspect of transformation.
Second, from "Universally Good" (*Samantabhadra*) onwards, there is a praise of his virtues.
Although his virtues are immeasurable, he is praised briefly for one universal quality.
"Skillful observation" refers to the wisdom capable of contemplation.
"Universally" has two meanings:
first, that all beings universally possess this virtue; second, that one universally contemplates the ten objects.
There are three meanings of "skillful" (*kuśala*):
first, skillfully knowing signs; second, skillfully knowing the signless; and third, skillfully knowing these two without obstruction.
The section beginning with "the realm of sentient beings" clarifies that all objects of observation possess these three aforementioned meanings.
Among these ten, the first is the general statement concerning the sentient beings to be converted.
The next [verse] asks: "Where do these beings come from?
They arise from the world-system through delusion regarding the dharma-realm."

I shall cause them to abide in the realm of nirvāṇa and purify the fruits of their karmic actions; therefore, it is necessary to understand the diseases of mental activity and the medicines of words and meaning, so that they may grow weary of the mundane world and rejoice in the supramundane, neither exhausting the conditioned nor dwelling in the unconditioned.
The preceding section distinguished the horizontal observation of the ten dharmas; now we shall vertically penetrate the three periods of time.

One observes *nirvāṇa* as having been realized, being realized, or yet to be realized; one observes various karmas as having been performed, being performed, or yet to be performed; one observes retributive fruits as having been received, being received, or yet to be received; and one observes mental activities as having been initiated, being initiated, or yet to be initiated. The remaining cases may be known by analogy, and they too are integrated through the six characteristics.
The second section, "At that time, the bodhisattvas... and below, consists of two parts within the section on the request:
first, citing the individuals to indicate their intention; second, from "If, World-Honored One... onwards, the actual presentation of the inquiry.
Although there are fifty phrases in total, there are only forty questions, because the twentieth phrase is an explanatory statement.

These forty questions share both similarities and differences when compared with those in the first assembly: the latter twenty phrases are identical, while the former twenty are largely the same but differ slightly.

Furthermore, there is a difference between the preceding and the following sections. The first ten phrases correspond to the thirtieth "sea" mentioned previously; in that prior assembly, the profound and vast nature of what is contemplated was explained in general terms.

Here, however, the *dharmakāya* (the Tathāgata’s reliance) and the *rūpakāya* (his environment) are explained specifically. This is because the previous assembly served as a general overview, whereas this assembly specifically reveals the basis upon which faith relies.
Therefore, while in the previous assembly all were referred to as "oceans," here only the "lands" and so forth are mentioned.
In the twentieth phrase, the former were termed the "ten oceans of bodhisattvas," whereas this enumerates the stages of practice, such as the "abodes."
The preceding section pervades all assemblies, collectively manifesting the causes for both the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*) and the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*);
this present section, however, pertains to their respective divisions, intending to manifest the characteristics of the causes for differentiation.
Although the subsequent twenty phrases are entirely identical [to those previously mentioned], the former was general while the latter is specific.

Furthermore, what was previously the object of faith is now analyzed as the result of accomplishment; since the essence of the object of faith and the result of accomplishment is non-different, the phrasing is identical.

If one were to distinguish them solely by their meaning, they could also be divided into three parts: namely, the first ten phrases inquire about the Buddha’s virtues and his unimpeded great activity in responding to sentient beings, thereby clarifying the basis of the cause and the fruit.
The next ten lines inquire about the stages of the bodhisattva’s practice, which are the causes that bring about the fruit.
The final twenty lines concern the supreme virtues of the Buddha-fruit, which manifest the results produced by those causes.

This means that one takes the Buddha as the condition (*pratyaya*) to give rise to the cause (*hetu*), and by means of this very cause, one realizes the fruit (*phala*); such is the general purport of this section.
Therefore, the Treatise says: "The permeation of extensive learning (*bahuśruta-vāsanā*) does not fail to flow from this Dharmakāya, nor does it fail to result in the realization of this Dharmakāya."
This is precisely that meaning.
Now, for the sake of both textual coherence and semantic convenience, the text is divided into two main parts:
the first ten phrases consist of direct questions, while the latter thirty phrases consist of inquiries by means of citing examples.

The meaning is no different from what preceded; however, the basis (*āśraya*) and the established (*sādhya*) should each appear in both texts. Their mutual presence is merely omitted by way of abbreviation, as there was no desire for prolixity. Thus, the direct inquiry raised in the first assembly is cited here as an example, and the example cited here is the direct inquiry from that [first assembly].
Furthermore, the preceding section clarified only the single layer of what is to be believed, and thus comprised thirty phrases of results;
now, in order to divide this into two sections, causes are interspersed between them.

Here, in the first ten phrases, the intent of the request is first revealed in general, and subsequently, from the words "reveal and show" (*kai-shi*) onwards, the specific points of doubt are enumerated.

Regarding the ten phrases concerning the inquiry into the relationship between the environment (*āśraya*) and the beings therein (*adhiṣṭhita*): because the primary retribution (*pratyaya-phala*) must necessarily rely upon a land (*kṣetra*) to respond to sentient beings, and furthermore, to symbolize that there is no obstruction between the environment and the beings, five phrases concern the environment:
first, the category of lands; second, adornment; third, purity; fourth, essential nature; and fifth, accomplishment.
The first five [points] are the same as the two preceding oceans, as detailed in the fourth and fifth chapters.
The five phrases beginning with "the Buddha’s dwelling" refer to the great function of the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
A single Buddha-body pervasively dwells in all lands, and the Buddha-mind eternally abides in great compassion.
Second, the qualities possessed and the nature of reality realized;
third, teaching the Dharma according to the capacities of beings;
fourth, the majestic power of their activity.
Through these five practices, one attains realization and manifests the attainment of Bodhi.

Furthermore, these five correspond to the seven seas mentioned in the preceding assembly: the first is the sea of Buddhas; the second is the sea of liberation; [the third is the sea of Dharma-nature; the fourth is the sea of wisdom; the fifth is the sea of vows; the sixth is the sea of practice; and the seventh is the sea of fruition].
Third is the ocean of expounding the Dharma;
fourth is the ocean of transformations;
fifth is the oceans of names and titles, lifespans, and *pāramitās*.
The ocean of sentient beings consists solely of those to be transformed; therefore, it is omitted here and is included within the various oceans [of phenomena].
Regarding these ten phrases, there are answers provided through verbal explanation and the manifestation of signs, which shall be understood when they appear below.
The second section, beginning with "Just as in the ten directions," cites examples to pose questions.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, ten phrases that indicate the intent of that teaching, clarifying that it possesses compassion;
The subsequent thirty phrases cite what was said by him to demonstrate his wisdom;
the final phrase concludes with a formal request.
Since it was so for that Buddha, it is likewise appropriate here.
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the text], the first phrase is general, meaning it causes the practices and vows of all bodhisattvas to be fulfilled.
The remaining nine are specific:
the first is to continue the lineage of the Buddhas above.
2. How does one succeed?
By means of saving sentient beings.
3. How does one save them?
It is for the purpose of causing them to become free from delusion.
How is the fourth [objection] resolved?
By knowing their faculties and conduct.
Fifth, by what means is one saved?
By means of the medicine of preaching the Dharma.
Sixth, what benefit is accomplished?

First, it eliminates the defilements of the Truth of Origination; second, it resolves doubts regarding the Truth of the Path; third, it uproots the longing for suffering; and fourth, it realizes the state of detachment from cessation.
Furthermore, it accomplishes the bodhisattva practices by perfecting both compassion and wisdom.
What is the purpose of possessing this compassion and wisdom?
It is to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not interrupted.
What are the characteristics of the uninterrupted lineage of the Buddhas?

This refers to the accomplishment of the three virtues: accomplishing the virtue of benevolence by rescuing and protecting sentient beings; accomplishing the virtue of cessation by eternally severing afflictions; and accomplishing the virtue of wisdom by thoroughly understanding all conditioned phenomena.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are of three kinds:
first, mental formations; second, the objects of formation; and third, that which is understood through formation.
That all formations are impermanent and signless is precisely what is understood.
What is meant by "providing protection"?
It is the exposition of all dharmas.
What is meant by "perpetual severance"?
It purifies all defilements,
eternally severing the afflictions so that both their seeds and manifestations are extinguished.
"Eliminating all defilements" refers specifically to the manifest afflictions.
How is wisdom accomplished?
It is said to be the permanent severing of the web of doubt.
What benefit does the accomplishment of wisdom provide?
Sever all hopes;
what benefit is there in merely removing delusions?
Extinguish all attachments and cravings.
All attachments refer to attachment to existence, attachment to emptiness, attachment to practice, and attachment to fruit.

To be unattached to all phenomena, for right wisdom to manifest before one, to compassionately rescue sentient beings, and to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed—this is the essential requirement of a bodhisattva and the fundamental intent of all Buddhas.
Each of the questions posed herein possesses this specific benefit.
Furthermore, it is explained that all bodhisattvas are those who have achieved [this].
How is accomplishment achieved?
By not severing the lineage of the Buddhas, one achieves it for oneself; by rescuing and protecting sentient beings, one achieves it for others.
How does one rescue and protect them?

This means being free from the two hindrances: having forever severed the afflictive hindrances so that there are no longer any afflictions, and fully realizing all things so that there are no longer any cognitive hindrances.
By what skillful means can these two hindrances be severed?
This refers to the teaching that these are the afflictive obscurations (kleśāvaraṇa) of all phenomena.
What are their characteristics?
They are craving (tṛṣṇā) and views (dṛṣṭi).
It eliminates all defilements and severs the afflictions of craving; it forever cuts the web of doubt and severs the afflictions of views.
What are the characteristics of this cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?
It is said to be: lack of understanding regarding objects, harboring expectations, not having forgotten the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), and giving rise to attachment in all things.
Now, since there are no marks that are not understood, what is there to hope for? Since one has realized that the nature of phenomena is empty, where could one possibly cling?

When the two obstacles are stilled and the two wisdoms manifest, one accomplishes Bodhi and Nirvana; this is called "not severing the lineage of the Buddhas," whereby the Bodhisattva achieves fulfillment.
The second section, "Explaining the Various Bodhisattvas," below, cites what was previously stated.
The text is divided into two parts:
the first ten lines inquire about the cause, and the latter twenty lines inquire about the fruit.
Regarding the first [section] now, there are nine phrases.
It was previously said that the ninth phrase, "the patience of the tenth stage," was missing.

Furthermore, because the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) do not constitute independent positions and are thus skillful means for abiding (*sthiti*), they are subsumed within the stage of abiding; therefore, they are not asked about separately.

Thus, the "Chapter on Teaching and Transforming" in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "The thirty persons of the noble embryo of the forbearance of subduing (*vinīyaka-kṣānti*) consist of the ten faiths, the ten cessations, and the ten firm minds. Therefore, faith and abiding are not divided.
One interpretation states:
For four reasons, faith does not enter the stages (*bhūmi*).
First, because progress and retreat are not fixed;...
Second, because there is no fixed sequence in the ten minds of mixed cultivation;
third, because one has not yet cultivated the vast practices in accordance with the dharma-realm;
and fourth, because one has not yet attained the dharma-body to manifest the Buddha-lineage.
Because the Ten Faiths are not opened here, this assembly and the third assembly together answer the questions regarding the Ten Abidings.
The Ten Practices are answered in the fourth assembly.
The ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are answered in the fifth assembly.
The ten treasuries (*daśa-kośa*) are answered within the fourth assembly; this is because the treasury has two meanings:

first, the meaning of gathering and encompassing, which refers to gathering and encompassing all practices for the purpose of dedication. Therefore, the answer regarding the treasuries occurs prior to that of the dedications.
Second is the meaning of "arising" (*niṣyanda*). Because it gives rise to the realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*) of the stages (*bhūmi*), it is asked after the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

The ten stages are answered in the sixth assembly; the ten vows are answered within the first stage; and the ten concentrations and ten masteries are answered in the seventh assembly, each having its own respective chapter.
Regarding the single category of the Ten Summits (*daśa-mūrdhan*), the answer in the text is not explicit, and there have been many ancient interpretations.
One school states:
according to the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, after the ten patiences (*daśa-kṣānti*) there is the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*citta-bhūmi*).
These ten "summits" (*mūrdhan*) can also be logically applied here;

however, that sutra describes eleven locations. It does not mention the assembly at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) at the outset, but rather speaks only of sitting upon the Thousand-Rays King Throne (*sahasraraśmirāja-āsana*) and preaching the ten world-oceans (*lokadhātusāgara*) in the Hall of Sublime Light (*Prabhāsaśrī-sabhā*).

The second, third, and fourth [stages] are entirely identical to this [stage's] third, fourth, and fifth meeting-points of the Dharma; the sequence of the ten stages of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is also the same.
However, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven speaks of the ten dhyānas, while the first dhyāna speaks of the ten vajra-minds;
the second dhyāna speaks of the ten vows.
In the third dhyāna, the ten patiences (*daśakṣānti*) are taught;

in the fourth dhyāna, within the palace of Maheśvara, the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi-dharmamukha*) as taught by Vairocana Buddha of the Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbhalokadhātu*), my own source, is proclaimed, without mentioning a successive series of assemblies such as those at the Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā*) or the multi-storied pavilion in Jeta Grove.
Furthermore, it is difficult to reconcile this with other interpretations.

Moreover, since there is a question regarding the cause here followed by a subsequent question regarding the fruit, that "Buddha-ground of the mind" (buddha-citta-bhūmi) refers to the subsequent "Tathāgata-ground" (tathāgata-bhūmi) and so forth, rather than the "Ten Summits" (daśa-śikhara).

Some say that the answer in the "Saṃghāṭī" chapter, when compared with the *Ratnakaranda-sūtra*, indicates that Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) has a distinct "Summit Stage" (*mūrdha-bhūmi*), as it represents the ultimate consummation of the causal stage.
Now, the *Mahāsāṃghika* [Vinaya] speaks of ten great numbers, which are the ultimate among all reckonings; hence they are called the "Ten Summits.

Although that question lists ten, the answer contains many more numbers; furthermore, as these correspond to the fixed supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), they do not belong to the same category, and thus it is not appropriate.
Some say: "The *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* provides the answer.
Within that, there are ten successive tiers of Buddha-lands, each being the summit of the one below it; reaching the Buddha-field of Bhadrasena is called the 'Ten Summits' (*daśa-mūrdhan*)."

Furthermore, because the second name of the Buddha takes these eleven worlds as its primary focus, by citing only these first and last eleven, it reveals that the number of world-ages exceeds one million asaṃkhyeya worlds.
This serves as the heading, for "heading" (śīrṣa) means the crown (mūrdhan).
However, since there is no separate question following it, there appears to be some underlying logic.
It merely indicates these ten realms as the opening of the inquiry; yet, they do not correspond at all to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth.

Now, it is said that neither the new nor the old Sanskrit manuscripts contain the term "patience" (*kṣānti*) in the question, yet it appears within the answer; therefore, we know that the "patience" mentioned there is precisely this "summit" (*mūrdhan*).
As for the "ten summits," they represent the ultimate limit of the stage of causes.

The ten concentrations (*samādhi*) and the ten penetrations (*abhijñā*) both belong to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). The ten patiences (*kṣānti*) follow at the end; furthermore, they receive the name "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).
In the question, the focus is on the ultimate limit of the stages, and thus it is called the "Summit.

In the answer, the basis is the patient acceptance of the Dharma-gates, which are determined by the seal of wisdom (*jñāna-mudrā*); therefore, they are called "patiences. It is not that one lacks the ten patiences unless one has reached the ultimate limit of the stages, nor is it that one does not reach the ultimate limit of the causal stages unless one possesses the ten patiences; these two passages clarify this further.

Therefore, at the end of the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences," it says: "Having thoroughly penetrated this gate of patience and accomplished unimpeded wisdom, one transcends all multitudes and turns the unsurpassed wheel," and so forth.
Since it is said that he has "surpassed," this carries the meaning of "summit" (*mūrdhan*).
This is because its meaning is analogous to the "Dharma-door of the Summit of Patience" (*kṣānti-mūrdha-dharmamukha*) among the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*).
Otherwise, if there were no separate question regarding patience, what would be the purpose of answering about emptiness?
If one intends to establish ten [stages], one should exclude the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Although the ten stages of faith have not yet attained a fixed position, they nonetheless cultivate vast practices in accordance with the *dharmadhātu*; their virtuous functions are so preeminent that they merit a separate assembly for an answer, as there must be a corresponding inquiry.

If one takes the four chapters from "The Ten Endurances" (*daśakṣānti*) onwards to collectively answer the question regarding the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), there is no logical flaw, as both constitute the ultimate stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
The second section, consisting of twenty phrases, concerns the fruit achieved and is entirely identical to that of the first assembly.
Within this, the first ten phrases clarify the fulfillment of internal virtues, while the latter ten phrases manifest the characteristics of the essence.
Regarding the former, the Tathāgata’s spiritual power is referred to as "Buddha-empowerment" (buddhādhiṣṭhāna) in the preceding assembly; this is because it is an empowerment through spiritual power.
"Supernormal powers (abhijñā) refer to the absence of obstruction in external application, while spiritual power (ṛddhi-bala) refers to internal capacity and efficacy.
In the 'Chapter on Leaving the World,' each has ten matters, and their characteristics are distinct."
Regarding "unimpeded speech," it means that there is nothing capable of obstructing what the Tathāgata does.
This is identical in meaning to the previous passage concerning "being incapable of being grasped" and so forth.
Regarding the latter ten [qualities], eloquence is vocal action (*vākkarman*), wisdom is mental action (*manaskarman*), and supremacy is bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
According to the previous assembly, there is only the omission of the single phrase concerning the Buddha’s radiance; the remainder is as explained previously.
The text of the response is also as previously cited from the "Manifestation," "Inconceivable," and "Ocean of Marks" chapters.
However, since those were cited as a general summary, this specific passage—which directly answers the present question—should be cited again by the expositor.
3. From "I pray that the Buddha... onwards is the conclusion of the invitation.
Since this invitation is identical to what was previously stated, the word "also" is employed.
The section on the invitation is complete.
The third is the Section on Exposition (*vyākhyāna-bhāga*).
Within this, the lower six assemblies provide the answers to these questions.
Following the length of the questions, this is also divided into three parts:

Of these, the first three chapters answer the question regarding the basis and fruit; from the second question downward, they clarify the answer to the question regarding the causes to be cultivated; and from the "Inconceivable" chapter (*Acintya-parivarta*) onward, they answer the question regarding the fruits to be accomplished.
Regarding this equality of cause and effect: the cause is the cause within the effect, and the effect is the function of this effect; therefore, it is subsumed under the category of the effect.
This initial section is divided into two parts:
first, the Tathāgata’s response by manifesting signs, because of the petitioner’s invocation and because the Tathāgata has realized the ultimate limit.
The subsequent discourse of Mañjuśrī’s response serves as an assistant to the Principal [Buddha], manifesting through provisional speech.
This first section is divided into two parts:
first, the Buddha manifests supernatural powers; second, the ocean-like assembly gathers.
First, "knowing their thoughts" refers to receiving their request;
"manifesting supernatural powers" refers to answering by displaying signs.
Regarding the phrase "according to the type," there are three meanings:

first, it varies according to what is appropriate for those who harbor doubts. This means that one may manifest form to be seen, employ sound to be heard, or provide silent assistance to bring about understanding; all of these are manifestations of supernormal powers, as the body of the Dharma-realm manifests instantaneously and perfectly.
Second, because it follows the different categories of those who harbor doubts;

third, because it follows the specific differences in what those who harbor doubts are uncertain about—meaning that if one doubts the ten faiths, one immediately sees the wheels on the Tathāgata’s feet emit light that pervades the entire dharma-realm, and so forth.
If one harbors doubts regarding the Ten Abodes, one will see the Tathāgata’s toe emit light, with bodhisattvas from as many lands as there are atoms in a hundred buddha-fields gathering there.
Just as it is with this single instance of emitting light, so it is with all other signs.

Thus we know that the manifestations of the first assembly pervade all nine assemblies, while the manifestations of this particular assembly pervade only one portion; the compilers have merely arranged them in sequence according to their respective meanings. Consequently, in each of the three subsequent assemblies, there is the statement that [the Buddha] did not rise from the Bodhi tree.
Second, from "Manifesting Supernatural Powers" onwards, the assembly gathers like an ocean of clouds; he then answers the initial ten questions by manifesting signs.
By manifesting light throughout the Buddha-fields, he answers the question regarding the Buddha-fields.

The fact that the buddha-fields possess golden colors and so forth constitutes the adornment of those fields; since they are composed of gold, this also answers the question regarding the substance of the fields.
The bodhisattvas in those fields likewise constitute the adornment of the fields, for they are adorned by the great jewels that are the bodhisattvas themselves.
Furthermore, the buddha-field is pure, for it is a purely immaculate buddha-field consisting solely of bodhisattvas.
It is accomplished through the pure cultivation of the brahma-faring, because it is the practice of purifying the land.
Moreover, the buddha-field is pure, because that which is cultivated is pure.
The above constitutes the response to the five questions regarding the basis (*āśraya*), while simultaneously answering the five questions concerning the primary retribution (*vipāka*) and the land.
The fact that there are Buddhas and that one sees Tathāgatas sitting within the Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*) is the answer to the Buddha’s dwelling (*vihāra*).
Manifesting supernatural powers and emitting light is the answer regarding majestic power;
being named Immovable Wisdom and so forth is the answer regarding the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
seeing the Buddha turn the wheel of Dharma is the answer regarding the preaching of the Dharma.
The Buddha’s attainment of perfect enlightenment is the answer to bodhi.
Although the text appears later, its meaning is fully contained herein.
This is because the manifestation of the light of awakening is precisely the manifestation of this.
The assembly from the ten directions is divided into ten sections.
Within each direction, there are eight items:

first, distance; second, the name of the land; third, the name of the Buddha; fourth, the chief disciple; fifth, the retinue; sixth, approaching the Buddha; seventh, paying homage upon arrival; eighth, being transformed into a seat and sitting down.

Regarding the phrase "at a distance from here of ten world-systems as numerous as atoms": in the previous assembly, the causes and effects of what is to be believed were explained as being profound and vast; therefore, it was necessary to gather from afar the oceans of world-systems in the ten directions beyond the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*).

Now, because the causes and effects for generating understanding are being explained as something to be cultivated gradually, only the world-systems adjacent to this Sahā world are gathered. Furthermore, since those whose practice of faith is most inferior are addressed, the number is specified as "ten."
Subsequently, these increase gradually until, in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," they again assemble into the ocean of lands.
The reason the initial number is not stated as one but rather as ten is to symbolize their inexhaustibility.
Those who seek to reach the number of atoms in a buddha-field are compared to others because they are superior;
levels are established to provide a symbolic representation, for those at the stage of initial faith and so forth do not represent a universal standard.
The formation [of the land] and its realization are proclaimed simultaneously throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, while "external" is a name following delusion and "coming" is a name for the place of awakening, in reality, the Buddha-lands have no distance or proximity.
That "the earth is entirely name-and-form" indicates that faith is coarse and manifest; it also indicates that it is clearly evident and can give rise to faith.
That "the Buddha is named the One of Equal Wisdom" is because having faith alone without wisdom increases ignorance, whereas within faith, the wisdom of original enlightenment arises.
Regarding the master whose name is "Śīra" (Shou), the Sanskrit term is *śrī*. It has four meanings:
first, head; second, victory; third, auspiciousness; and fourth, virtue.

For this reason, translators have used different equivalents at various times. Now, "faith" (*śraddhā*) is generally adopted as the equivalent for "head," because faith encompasses all stages, because among the practices in sequence faith is the most excellent, because it is extremely difficult to attain, because initiating faith within the cycle of birth and death constitutes auspiciousness, and because faith can increase wisdom, merit, and all other virtues.
These ten bodhisattvas collectively represent the gate of faith; therefore, they are all named Śrī.
Because each attains all dharmas through one particular gate, there are nevertheless distinctions among them, which shall be explained in the subsequent text.
There is also a tradition which states:
in Sanskrit it is *śrī*, which here means "Auspiciousness.
That *śrī* means "head" is likewise a valid interpretation.
That their retinues each numbered as many as the atoms in ten buddha-fields signifies that each and every practice encompasses inexhaustible virtues.
That they all went to the Buddha signifies their orientation toward him.
The rest is as in the previous assemblies.
Furthermore, the names of the bodhisattvas below, and so forth, all symbolize dharmas.
"Bodhisattva" symbolizes the practices performed; "original land" symbolizes the principle realized; and the "name of the Buddha" symbolizes the wisdom attained.

First, regarding the Easterners' description of it as "golden" in color: this is because the nature of the mind is unstained, serving as the very substance that becomes a vessel through its engagement with conditions.

Fundamental wisdom is like space; it is free from the distinction between the perceiver and the perceived, serene and immovable. Movement constitutes delusion, for movement is not what is called wisdom.
Furthermore, even if one attains the fruit of Buddhahood, it is not different from the ordinary state; thus, the wisdom of original enlightenment abides in the True Suchness of the mind.
As for the "wondrous virtue of the Bodhisattva," it refers to the wisdom that penetrates the realm of the Buddha—the Mañjuśrī who is present everywhere.
Because wisdom discriminates and accords with fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*), it distinguishes between cause and effect.
Regarding the two "heads of awakening": the first is the awakening to the nature of the mind.
That there is no inherent nature does not obstruct following conditions, and that following conditions does not obstruct the absence of inherent nature; this is unobstructed gnosis.
To be unstained yet stained, and stained yet unstained—both are difficult to comprehend, for they constitute wondrous form (*rūpa*).

As for the foremost of the three riches: the wealth of the Dharma through teaching is the wisdom that extinguishes darkness; it realizes the emptiness of sentient beings, remaining unattached like a lotus.
Regarding the "Four Jewel Heads": because the ultimate and conventional truths are non-contradictory and thus precious;
because one skillfully understands karma and its fruits and does not violate dignified decorum;
and because nature and characteristics are non-contradictory as the singular purport of the One Vehicle—this is what is meant by "scenting only the *campaka* flower."

The foremost of the five virtues is the thorough comprehension of the Tathāgata’s merit in manifesting and preaching the Dharma; this constitutes clarity regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, by comprehending the Buddha’s virtues, the mind becomes pure and enlightened.
If one possesses this wisdom, it is like the blue lotus, the most supreme.
The Six-Eyed Leader (Ṣaḍakṣa-mukha) is a field of merit that illuminates and guides, just as eyes lead the body.
This impartial field of merit constitutes ultimate wisdom; because it is most worthy of veneration, it is called "golden."
The Buddha is the field of merit; because he is taken as the object, it is the same as Mañjuśrī’s reliance upon the Golden Realm.
Seventh, the Head of Diligence: the sublime teaching is profoundly deep, and must necessarily rely upon diligence.
It can spur all practices and constitutes the most supreme wisdom; because it is perfectly luminous and worthy of esteem, it is further called a "jewel.

As the foremost of the eight dharmas, although there are many gates of Dharma, one must rely on correct practice; only by being able to practice the Dharma does one attain mastery. Attaining the firmness and sharpness of *prajñā* constitutes its adamantine nature.

Ninth is Wisdom Chief (Jñānamukha). Although the Buddha’s auxiliary paths to enlightenment are immeasurable in their gateways, wisdom is the foremost, capable of purifying all practices; thus it is called "Brahma-Wisdom.
When wisdom is pure, the essence is pure, like crystal—luminously transparent and untainted.
Ten, O Bhadrapāla: from the Buddhas of the past to the Buddhas of the future, the Way is one and pure; because it is virtuous by its very nature, it is called "noble" (bhadra).
To be able to know this nobility is the power of observation, for one observes that the fundamental nature is eternally equal.
Furthermore, when the ten Buddhas are compared to one another, Akṣobhya is the essence while the others are all functions.

When the ten Bodhisattvas are compared to one another, Mañjuśrī is the universal while the others are all the particular; since the universal guides the particular, the other nine Bodhisattvas do not depart from the Sublime Virtue (Mañjughoṣa).
I have briefly provided this explanation based on preceding and succeeding examples; one should simply empty oneself and seek its meaning therein.
If one does not believe in this principle, what concern does this profoundly deep dharma-gate have for me?

The second section, beginning with "At that time, Mañjuśrī," distinguishes the verbal response. It is divided into four parts: first, praising the rarity of the assembly;

second, from "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards, restating the question and offering a general praise; third, from "Why is this? onwards, investigating the praise and providing a general explanation; and fourth, from "O Sons of the Buddha, the Tathāgata" onwards, extensively revealing the inconceivable nature [of the teaching].

This is the first [section]. Regarding why the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to answer the questions posed by the assembly: it is because Mañjuśrī manifests his residence in this land while possessing ten signs of birth; he comes from other directions with a body containing myriad virtues; he subdues Māras and restrains outsiders, excelling in inconceivable eloquence; his transformations fill the dust-motes of the quarters and span the three periods of time; having perfected the Way in previous kalpas, he was already called the Honored King Dragon-Species (Nāga-jāti-rāja), and upon manifesting the realization of Bodhi, he is further named Maṇi-ratna-akṣaya; he is truly the Mother of the Buddhas of the Three Periods. How could he have come merely as a shadow or an echo to resolve the errors of Śāriputra? Thus, everyone beheld him, and for this reason, he spoke.
Why not wait for an invitation?
Because [the recipient] is revered as being equal to a Buddha.
Why not wait for a formal announcement?
Receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power and by the Buddha’s own consent, the assembly made their request;
only then did the Buddha manifest his signs. Were it not for such a supreme Great Being, how could there be such a profound resonance and secret communion?
Therefore, the former [passage] uses light to manifest Samantabhadra, while this [passage] represents the secret empowerment of Subhūti.
If that is so, why does Samantabhadra request further instruction after his meditative absorption?
It is to express that the object of faith is profoundly subtle.
Why does one not enter meditative concentration?
Because the fruit follows from the cause, it is identical to faith.
The rest is as explained above.
Why is there no further empowerment?
Because there is no fixed [limit], and because this is an "unseen empowerment" (adṛṣṭa-adhiṣṭhāna) received through the Buddha's spiritual power.
There are briefly five meanings for praising the rarity of the assembly:

Because the resonance between cause and effect is so remote that such an encounter is difficult to achieve; because their inner cultivation of virtue is so fully realized that it merits universal praise; because manifesting the Dharma through names is exceedingly rare; because the initial arising of faith and practice is unprecedented; and because this single assembly is itself an assembly equal to the Dharma-realm as vast as space.
In the second part, the citation of the question, the essence of the *kṣetra* (buddha-field) is omitted.
"The appearance of the Buddha" refers to the aforementioned majestic virtue (*vibhūti*).

*A* means "non-" (*na*), *nuttara* means "supreme" (*anuttara*), *tṛ* means "correct" (*samyak*), *yā* means "equal" (*sama*), and furthermore, *tri* means "pervasive" (*vyāpin*), while *bodhi* means "awakening" (*bodhana*).
This means that the Path cannot be further augmented, which is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
To know without distortion or partiality is "perfectly universal" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*).
Among the three interrogations and explanations, the interrogation refers to the aforementioned term "inconceivable."

The subsequent commentary states: "The capacities of those who can be inspired are infinitely diverse, yet the Tathāgata universally responds throughout the entire Dharma-realm"; this is vast and inconceivable.
The following concluding verse clearly elucidates this point.
Furthermore, he teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, with intentions that are difficult to conceive.
Moreover, regarding those who are equal to the Dharma-realm: by expounding a single teaching, they are equal to all other numerous gateways; these gateways are inexhaustible.
Their measure is equal to the Dharma-realm, and these Dharma-gates are inconceivable.
The fourth section extensively elucidates the inconceivable; it consists of two parts:
first, a general presentation of its many aspects; second, a detailed exposition according to specific categories.
This is the first part.
Taking the Sahā world as the foremost, ten kinds of diverse distinctions are briefly manifested.
According to the concluding summary below, these actually pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
These ten phrases do not go beyond the three karmas:
First, the single body is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), yet it manifests as the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) in their differences; hence it is called "various.
Second, names are used to summon the reality, which will be extensively analyzed below.
Third, there are differences in colors such as gold and silver, and distinctions in the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*).
Fourth, their physical forms vary in length, ranging from three feet or sixteen feet up to being boundless.
Fifth, their lifespans are limited; they may last for immeasurable kalpas, or less than a hundred years, down to appearing in the morning and passing away by evening.
Sixth are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which differ according to their transformation, defilement, purity, and so forth.
Seventh are the faculties (*indriya*), such as the eye and others, which manifest differently according to individual experience.
Eighth are the places of birth (*upapattisthāna*), which include distinctions such as the *kṣatriya* caste and others.
Ninth, regarding the function of speech: because it establishes various designations according to different regional dialects and sounds.
Tenth, regarding observation: looking around and surveying in order to respond to the diverse capacities of sentient beings.
Furthermore, by observing existence and non-existence, security and peril, one may not fail to employ wise illumination; the various manifestations of these realms are shown to be manifold.
The conclusion below states the intent: "It causes all sentient beings to each accord with their own capacity, so that through their own knowledge and vision, they attain subduing."
The second section, beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha," provides a detailed exposition according to the specific categories.
The text is divided into three parts:

first, this chapter concludes by distinguishing the various names of the bodies, answering the aforementioned question regarding the Buddhas' abodes, and extensively elaborating upon the eight phrases such as "various bodies" and so forth; for all attributes such as physical form (*rūpa*) and other characteristics belong to the body.

Second, the "Chapter on the Four Truths" (*Catuhsatyaparivarta*) elucidates the pervasiveness of the verbal teachings and answers the question regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, thereby extensively elaborating upon various types of vocal karma.

Third, the "Chapter on the Radiance of Enlightenment" (*Prabhāsa-bodhiparivarta*) clarifies how the circle of light illuminates all things exhaustively; it answers the three aforementioned questions concerning majestic power, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and enlightenment (*bodhi*), and extensively elaborates upon various types of contemplation.
Regarding these five phrases concerning the *paratantra* (dependent) retribution, there is only a response based on manifest signs, as the detailed explanation is found in the preceding assembly.
Now, for the first [point]:
to expand upon the aforementioned names—yet the Sages have no names; they establish designations for the sake of sentient beings.
If established according to its virtues, those virtues are boundless;
if names are established according to circumstances, they are equal in number to the realm of sentient beings.

Although there are many varieties, they are all established for the purpose of generating goodness and extinguishing evil as appropriate, based on the principle that the Ocean Seal manifests instantaneously; one should not give rise to attachment.
The text is divided into four parts:
first, the ten billion worlds within this Sahā world-system;
second, those adjacent to the Sahā world-system, which are beyond the ten billion.
The first three categories apply universally throughout the ten directions;
the fourth explains the reason for their differentiation, which is due to following the capacities of sentient beings.
Regarding the first [of these], it is divided into three parts:
