second, the simultaneous ascent without separation; third, each seeing the Buddha arrive; fourth, each adorning the palace and seat; fifth, all coming together to invite the Buddha; sixth, entering the palace at the same time; seventh, the musical sounds ceasing simultaneously; eighth, each recollecting their past causes; ninth, praising the Tathāgata in unison; tenth, the palaces all becoming vast, adorned, and pure.

The phrase "at that time" refers to the period of the preceding two assemblies, during which the primary teacher and his retinue together and universally expounded the teachings of those two assemblies.
This current clarification of "universality" constitutes the first of the ten successive locations of exposition.
Why is it necessary to cite this?
It is because one wishes to clarify that the previous assembly does not disperse, thereby forming the subsequent assembly;
and because the subsequent must necessarily carry forward the previous, so as to form a single, unobstructed assembly of the Dharma-realm.
Because each and every assembly proceeds without interruption;
because all subsequent assemblies occur simultaneously;
and because if a preceding assembly were to disperse, there would be no subsequent one.
The reason why [the teaching] is restricted solely to the assemblies at the Bodhi tree is that this is the primary site and the place where Buddhahood was attained.
In truth, the second assembly is likewise all-pervasive in this same manner.
If they were simultaneously pervasive, how could there be a sequence of nine assemblies?
If there are [distinctions of] before and after, how can they be called simultaneous?
One should say that the substance of that which is employed is simultaneously and instantaneously pervasive;
yet the function of that very substance does not destroy the sequence of before and after.
It is like the impression of a seal.
Second, from "At that time" onwards, it clarifies how they each ascended to the Śakra-heaven without departing from the Bodhi tree.
Question:
Movement and stillness are contradictory; going and staying are vastly different. Since it is said that they are not separate, how can one speak of "ascending"?
There have been many ancient interpretations. One says:
This Śākyamuni body did not rise from beneath the Bodhi tree; rather, a separate emanation was manifested to ascend to the heavens.
One source states:
"Not rising [from the tree] refers to the retribution-body (*vipākakāya*); ascending to heaven refers to the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*)."
One interpretation states:
"Not arising" refers to the Dharma-body, while "ascending to heaven" refers to the transformative function.
This is not the intended meaning of the text, because within this passage, both are the ten-fold body-clouds of Vairocana.
One interpretation states:

Because that which has already departed is not departing, it is called "non-arising"; because that which is not departing is indeed departing, one thereby ascends to heaven—just as with the phrase "coming with the characteristic of non-coming," and so forth.

If that were so, it would merely be a case of ascending while remaining detached from [the original location]; it would not mean that there is a separate body of non-ascension beneath the tree. Therefore, this is untenable. Some say:

This Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is the functional activity (*karmayoga*) of a single essence; thus, abiding is itself going, and going is itself abiding. Abiding is the pervasive essence, while going is the responsive function; the response is the essence responding. Thus, although he ascends afterward, he does not depart from his former place.

The essence is the essence of the "should-be" (the future); although it does not depart from the former [present] to ascend to the latter [past], if this were so, how would it differ from the third master?
For that master also maintains that this dharma does not arise, and explains non-arising by means of abiding.
If you say that abiding is the pervasiveness of the essence, how can he abide alone beneath the Bodhi tree?
When he ascends to heaven, how could that not be the pervasiveness of the essence?
Beneath the Bodhi tree, how could it not be the functioning [of the essence]?
Now the correct principle shall be revealed.
Indeed, when the Buddha attains Bodhi, his wisdom is all-pervasive and his essence is omnipresent; he is without dependence or abiding, and neither comes nor goes.

However, as the response is the very embodiment of sovereign freedom, the response pervades wherever that embodiment extends; yet, according to the sequence of conditions and stimuli, there is both abiding and ascending.
When there is a stimulus in Jambudvīpa, he is seen at the Bodhi tree;
when there is a stimulus in the celestial palaces, he is seen ascending to heaven.
It is not that the Buddha who sat at the Bodhi tree has moved to ascend to the celestial palace; therefore, it is said that he ascends to the Śakra-palace without leaving the Bodhi tree.
As the verse of Dharmamati states: "O Son of the Buddha, you should observe the Tathāgata’s power of mastery: throughout all Jambudvīpa, everyone says the Buddha is within their midst."
"This is not departing.
"We now see the Buddha dwelling upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
This is ascending.
The principles of this argument are well-founded; let me further clarify them through an analogy.

It is like the bright moon whose reflections appear everywhere in response to conditions. Suppose there is a single moon over a clear river, observed by three boats together. One boat remains stationary while the other two move—one south and one north. To the one moving south, the moon appears to travel a thousand li with it; to the one moving north, the moon appears to travel a thousand li with it; yet to the one whose boat is stationary, the moon does not move. Thus, this single moon does not leave the center of the stream to travel to either the north or the south.
Suppose a hundred thousand people were to look together; as each person in the eight directions moves away, a hundred thousand moons would each follow them as they depart.
Those with discernment understand this principle.
The ancient masters have explained this with approximately ten meanings:
First, regarding the entry through the aspect of the locus: because within one locus there are all loci, these celestial palaces and so forth originally exist beneath the trees;
thus, they need not be raised up. However, because they are employed [there], it is said that they ascend.

The second [interpretation] also relies on the gate of entering by way of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mukha*); because one enters all places through a single place, it is not necessary for the trees to actually arise throughout the heavens.
However, because the celestial palaces (*devakula*) are intended to symbolize the progressive advancement of the Dharma, it is said that they "ascend."
Third, because all is one, the deity is beneath the tree.
Fourth, because one is all, the tree is in the heavens; [the arguments regarding] non-arising and so forth follow the previous logic.

Fifth, regarding the Buddha-body: this body beneath the tree is, in fact, fully pervading the Dharma-realm and existing in all places; thus it has been there from the beginning and does not need to arise.
Because its manifestation is made possible when sentient beings' capacities ripen, it is said that he "ascends."
Therefore, the Tathāgata, by means of the body of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-kāya), is eternally here and is simultaneously there.

Sixth, regarding the Buddha’s sovereign and inconceivable liberation: it is said that sitting is itself walking, standing, and so forth; being here is itself being there, for all these states cannot be measured by those of lower stages.

Seventh, the gate of mutual dependence through dependent origination; eighth, the gate of the interpenetration of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); ninth, the gate of manifesting the Dharma through symbolic representation; tenth, the gate of the great assembly of the *dharmadhātu*.

However, regarding these ten interpretations: the first five constitute the profound gateways, the next four explain the underlying reasons, and the final one summarizes the overall intent. These are established so that the ten meanings may complement one another; although they appear somewhat disordered, they do not contradict the core tenets of the sutra and may all be employed accordingly.
Nevertheless, within this context, there are four pairs of dharmas that are mutually identical and unimpeded:
first, this place and that place; second, this body and that body; third, going and staying; and fourth, one and many.
Regarding the mutual identity of locations, there is no obstruction between this place and that place; this should be understood as being like the first four [of the ten] among the ten [powers].
Regarding the mutual identity of bodies, there is no obstruction; this should be understood as being like the fifth and sixth [powers], as well as what was previously explicitly revealed.

Furthermore, among the ten [categories], the latter four pertain to the locus of the body (*kāya-sthāna*). In terms of the locus (*sthāna*), there are only "this" and "that"; in terms of the body itself, one further adds "going" and "staying," meaning that this very body is that body, and the body that goes is the body that stays.
Whether regarding the body or the location, both are characterized by being both one and many; all the dharmas mentioned above coexist at the same time, without any sequence of before or after.
When comparing "one" and "many," four propositions should be established:
first, not departing from beneath all trees while ascending to a single celestial palace, as in the present passage.
Second, without leaving one tree, they ascend to all heavens;
third, without leaving all trees, they ascend to all heavens, as the Sūtra states, "All worlds in the ten directions are likewise";
fourth, without leaving beneath one tree, they ascend to a single heaven.
In the sutra, because it seeks to reveal the identity of the one and the many, it cites the first phrase.
Just as it is for ascending to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, so it is for ascending to the other heavens, as seen in the latter two assemblies;
and just as it is for ascending to heaven, so it is for going to other places.

Furthermore, one should consider each tree in relation to the others to form two propositions: namely, that while not departing from beneath a single tree, it is always present under all trees; and while not departing from all trees, it is always present under a single tree.

Furthermore, one should apply the principle of "not arising in other places" by analogy to "not arising under a tree," extending this mutual comparison until it encompasses all possibilities; thus, the sequence remains unimpaired, sovereign, and inconceivable.
Furthermore, since that which exists in one place exists in all places, there is also the sense of subtlety; because their functions differ, there is the sense of concealment and manifestation.
If one adds the distinctions of prior and posterior time to the preceding, there is the doctrine of the ten periods of time (*daśakāla*), yet only "abiding" (*sthiti*) is mentioned.
Furthermore, regarding other dharmas, there is the sense of being purely [distinct] or mixed.
Subsequent [dharmas] encompassing preceding ones carries the sense of Indra’s Net.
This deity, in relation to others, constitutes the sense of principal and attendant.
The Ten Mysteries are complete.
Question:
Since the principle that the preceding stage gives rise to the succeeding one should apply equally to both phenomena and noumenon, why is this specific teaching found only among the Three Sages?
Answer: It is for the purpose of clarifying their distinct meanings.

That is to say, because the first two assemblies are adjacent to one another, they do not require reference back to what precedes; however, because these three [assemblies] are separated by the realms of humans and devas, they must be connected by reference to what precedes.

Furthermore, these three assemblies equally elucidate the stage of the Sage (*bhadra*). Because the sixth assembly has already entered realization and does not require reference to what preceded it; because the seventh assembly establishes the stage itself where Samantabhadra is naturally present without requiring anything else; because the eighth assembly suddenly reveals that the essence and function of the five stages are already fused; and because the ninth assembly clarifies only the realization and entry wherein essence and function are of one flavor—none of these require further elaboration.
Third, from "At that time, the Lord of Devas" onwards, it clarifies that each perceives the Buddha’s arrival.

From the perspective of the Buddha, this is an emergence from his essential nature; from the perspective of the responsive capacity and its object, it is a manifestation from the mind. Because they are adjacent yet not yet immediate, it is said that they see him from afar.
The fourth section, beginning with "Thereupon," describes the individual adornments of the palace and the throne.
This represents the adornment of the palace of the faculties and desires, for the sake of becoming a vessel for the Dharma.
The placement of the lion throne symbolizes the dharma-gate of the ten abodes.
The text consists of ten phrases: the first is general and the remainder are specific.
As for the general statement "Universal Radiance Treasury," this refers to the wisdom of the stage of liberation, which illuminates the emptiness of phenomena and encompasses all virtues.
Because one first enters through faith, there is the statement regarding its placement.
Within the section on distinctions, the first phrase concerns the essence, while the remainder all manifest the adornments.
The reason they are all called "ten thousand" is that the myriad practices serve as the cause for such an inspiration.
Regarding the term "tiers" (*krama*): it is because the myriad practices have been cultivated and perfected.

A golden net provides protection, while a canopy of compassion and mercy nurtures and covers; the silken streamers of the four means of integration drape all around. Interwoven with the harmonious union of practice and vows, the myriad virtues form a lattice; gentle forbearance and a sense of shame cover the sky of the ultimate truth of *dharmatā*. Pure Brahma-conduct encircles this Dharma-body, and because each aspect is illuminated by wisdom, it is like the radiance of the sun.
Within the cycle of birth and death, it dispels the darkness of the long night; by manifesting these fruits and virtues, it causes sentient beings to practice the causal path.
In the lower stages and directions, the positions gradually increase, signifying that the Dharma is without difference.
Fifth, from "At that time, Śakra" onwards, [the text] describes the invitation for the Buddha to reside in the palace.
Within this section, the ritual of invitation is performed through the veneration of the three karmas (body, speech, and mind). Regarding the phrase "Welcome":

it is because he comes in response to the capacity [of beings]; it is because he comes despite having no appearance of coming; and it is because he comes accompanied by the assembly of the Dharma-realm.
The threefold exclamation of "Excellent! is due to the height of joy.
The citation of the three titles is for the purpose of briefly praising his virtues.
The prayer "May you deign to accept [this]" is because one hopes to rely upon the field of supreme merit to generate great blessings.

Sixth, from "At that time" onwards, they enter the hall simultaneously; this means that when the faculties and conditions coincide, the resulting benefit is not in vain, and it is thus throughout the ten directions.
This concludes the six preceding sections on the matter of entering the hall; therefore, there is a single summary to conclude them all.
The four sections of text below concern the events within the palace.

The seventh section, beginning with "At that time," describes the cessation of musical sounds; this signifies the withdrawal of distraction and the return to stillness, thereby attaining the benefit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Eighth, from "immediately [realizing] for oneself" onwards, each [section] describes how he recalled his past causes and obtained the benefit of wisdom.

Once distracted objects of perception have ceased, supreme virtues manifest before him; in a state of tranquil non-conceptualization, he gives rise to the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).
Those who plant roots of goodness are those who, as indicated below, have previously entered this hall with ten Buddhas to hear the Dharma and make offerings;
it also symbolizes that they perceive their own mind-nature as being identical to that of the Buddhas of the past.
The ninth chapter, "Kāśyapa," and those following, collectively praise the Tathāgata.
However, while all Buddhas of the three periods of time expound the Dharma of the Ten Abodes at this location,
the fact that only the ten are praised here signifies that they teach both the Ten Abodes and their inexhaustibility.
There are four meanings for this praise:

first, that because ten Buddhas have previously resided there, the hall is superior and worthy of habitation; second, that by citing the virtues of one [Buddha] in turn, one praises the Original Teacher by extension; third, that by recounting past roots of goodness, it expresses the joy of being worthy to encounter [the teaching]; and fourth, that by stating that past Buddhas likewise taught this, it signifies the permanence of the Dharma.
In this text, the nature of this realm is first clarified, followed by an analysis of its universal application.

Regarding the initial ten verses: in each, the first half-line provides the title and praises the virtues—the upper phrase being specific and the lower phrase being general—while the second half-line identifies the person and the locus.

Only the first phrase differs among the Buddhas; however, as most of the Buddhas' distinct names are established based on their virtues, those who offer praise take these virtues to explain the aforementioned titles.
Regarding the first, Kāśyapa, this is translated as "Drinker of Light" (Ābhāsvara); if established according to his clan, it indicates that he was born into that lineage.
Regarding the virtues of the Buddha, there are two aspects: first, his bodily radiance eclipses all other lights; second, the light of his compassion drinks up and obscures all deviant lights.
*Kanakamuni*—formerly called "Golden Immortal" (*Jinxian*) and also "Golden Silence" (*Jinji*)—is "Silent" because he is unimpeded, and "Golden" because he sees with clarity.
*Kālāma-kuṭa* is fully rendered as *Kālāma-kūṭa-vada*; this means "one who has already severed what ought to be severed," like gold that has been purified or a mountain that is immovable.
Furthermore, that which is seen as unimpeded is the merit of this Buddha, while that which is like a mountain of gold is the merit of the preceding Buddha.
Viśvabhū is also called Viśvabhu.
Viśva means "pervading all. Kula means "sovereignty.
It is also called "Pervasive Excellence," for because it is free from the three stains, there is nothing in which it does not possess sovereignty and by which it is surpassed.
The three impurities are the manifest, the seed, and the habitual tendencies.
Śikhin, also called Śikhiṇa, means "One with a Topknot" (Chiji) or "One Possessing a Topknot" (Youji).
Non-conceptual wisdom is the most supreme; it resides at the crown of the heart.
Furthermore, the bright jewel within the topknot signifies non-discrimination.

*Vipaśyin* has four translations: namely, Pure Contemplation (*viśuddha-vipaśyanā*), Supreme Contemplation (*viśiṣṭa-vipaśyanā*), Supreme Vision (*viśiṣṭa-darśana*), and Universal Vision (*samanta-darśana*).
The full moon represents the perfection of wisdom, which is universal vision; the waning of the crescent represents the extinction of delusion, which is pure contemplation.
Being both full and pure, it constitutes supreme contemplation and supreme vision.
Puṣya, also transcribed as Bóshā, means "increasingly flourishing" (zuòngshèng) in this language; it refers to the flourishing of clear realization regarding ultimate truth.
Tiṣya, also transcribed as Dǐshā, is explained in the Western Regions as *tīraṇa*, which means "crossing over" (dù).
*Śā* is *vāśā*, which here means "to speak"; it refers to preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, or simply "speaking.
"Unimpeded eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) is precisely this capacity to speak.
*Padma* means "red lotus" in this language; his body and mind are like a lotus, pure and free from dust and defilement.

Regarding *Dīpaṃkara*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "From the time this Buddha first appeared in the world until he attained Buddhahood, his entire body was suffused with light, as if a lamp were burning."
The radiance of his body and wisdom is universally pervasive and renowned as great.
However, among the ten [Buddhas], the latter seven were Buddhas of past kalpas; how then could they have entered the palace during the Bhadrakalpa?
There are two ancient interpretations:

first, that they are mutually inclusive with respect to the temporal kalpas; second, that they differ in coarseness and subtlety with respect to their location—whereas the coarse perishes along with the kalpa, the subtle remains eternally.
As in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, while gods and humans see it burning, my land is not destroyed.
Furthermore, while Brahmā sees it as pure, Śāriputra sees it as defiled.
Now, this Lord of Devas is a great bodhisattva; he perceives it in the same manner as Brahmā, and this is also due to the Buddha’s empowerment.
Second, from "In this way" onwards, it concludes by extending [the teaching] to the ten directions.
Tenth, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, the halls are all vast and expansive, thereby manifesting the sign of fulfilling all wishes.
The vast hall serves as a common locus to dispel narrow-mindedness, and it also manifests the expanse of great compassion equal to the realm of sentient beings.
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata enters the hall, awakened wisdom immediately appears before him.
Suddenly becoming vast and expansive, body and mind become boundless.
From "In the ten directions" onwards, the section on the inexhaustible concludes; specifically, only the final four [points] are concluded here, as the preceding ones have already been concluded.

Chapter Fourteen: The Chapter on Verses of Praise from the Summit of Mount Sumeru. Regarding the initial intent for this chapter: since it has already been clarified how the Master of Transformation responds to the calls of sentient beings, this chapter now distinguishes the assistance rendered through the glorification of his deeds.
Now, in order to expound the section on abiding, the essential nature is first presented.
This nature is the Buddha-wisdom; because the Tathāgata was previously praised, this chapter follows.
Second, regarding the explanation of the title: "Sumeru" refers to a location. Since the praise of the Buddha’s virtues is based upon his locus, this name is established accordingly.
"Also the praise at the summit" distinguishes it from other locations.

Regarding the three aspects of the essential purpose (*piṇḍārtha*): taking the assembly of the multitude, the emission of light, and the verses of praise as the essence (*piṇḍa*), and taking the accomplishment of the correct teaching as the purpose (*artha*).
Furthermore, it reveals the Buddha’s virtues as the primary theme, enabling one to know that abiding in the essence is the goal.
The fourth section, the explanation of the text, is divided into three parts:
first, the section on the assembly gathering; second, the section on the emission of light; and third, the section on the verse praise.
Now, regarding the first [section], there are ten points of commonality in the text and three points of difference in meaning, namely [the sections on] the fifth, sixth, and seventh.
First, the commonality of the cause for the compilation: because it is all due to the Buddha’s power, it is also identical in its assembly during the preceding period.
2. From "The ten directions" onwards, the leaders are identical.
3. From "Each one" onwards, the number of retinues is identical.
4. From "From a hundred Buddhas" onwards, the dimensions of their dwelling places are identical.
The preceding ten [stages] are multiplied by one hundred here, as their status has already increased.
Fifth, regarding "their names," the names of the dharmas they signify are the same.
"Wisdom" refers to the ten stages of understanding (*adhimukti*), for it is through this that one is able to perceive the dharmas.
The names of the bodhisattvas differ, which will be explained in the following verses.
Regarding the phrase "the worlds from which they come," the names are identical.
They are all named "Flower" (*Puṣpa*) because their stages have newly blossomed, and they have realized the fruit through non-attachment.
These are individually and sequentially assigned to the ten stages (*bhūmi*):
first, because the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) leads the world;
second, because the ground of the mind is purified and cleansed like a blooming lotus.
Third, because of the perfect purity of spiritual practice;
fourth, because of the nobility of that which is born from water;
fifth, because of the firm vow of skillful means.
Sixth, the correct mind is signless (*animitta*), because it is like the fragrance [of incense];
seventh, the non-retrogressive mind is joyful;
eighth, *aruna*—which here refers to the red-and-vibrant appearance at sunrise—is the state of the youthful (*kumāra*) who is luminous and pure.

The ninth is Nārada, which here is translated as "Supported by Humans" (*renchi*); because flowers and incense are worn by all people, the prince wears them as well, following the regulations of the Dharma King.
The tenth is that wisdom is all-pervading like space. Alternatively, one may separately clarify the ten superior dharmas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); this can be understood through reflection.
7. From "Each [of them]... onwards, the Buddhas they serve are identical.

They share the same name, "Moon" (Candra), which symbolizes the Buddha-fruit within this stage: their wisdom is luminous and darkness has ceased; their beneficent grace is cooling, and because they respond to those who are worthy vessels, they are all-pervasive.
These alternative names refer to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which are the fruits of the ten internal dharmas:
first, by means of the ten dharmas that are difficult to obtain, they may be called extraordinary;
second, the generation of the ten great minds is inexhaustible.
Third, contemplating emptiness and so forth, one is immovable.
Fourth, thoroughly understanding karmic actions, one realizes that birth-and-death and nirvana are like the wind, not remaining still.
Fifth, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, one is like water that universally moistens.
Sixth, by hearing the ten kinds of dharmas, the mind becomes settled and unwavering, thereby attaining liberation.
Seventh, by hearing the ten non-retrogressions, one may be called unsurpassed.

Eighth, when the three karmas are without fault, they are as bright and pure as the stars; one takes birth at will, radiantly filling the void, with supernormal powers as free and unimpeded as movement through space.
Ninth, because they thoroughly know the arising of afflictions and their habitual tendencies, they attain purity.
Tenth, they observe the mental states of the faculties, desires, and wisdoms of countless sentient beings; others cannot know these, but they alone understand them clearly.
By means of these ten causes, these ten Buddhas are established.
Above, I have provided this explanation by following the essential connections; a detailed clarification of their characteristics is as found in the text of the "Ten Abodes" (Daśabhūmika).
8. From "These [beings who have already... onwards, the expression of reverence is the same.
9. From "According to where they have come... onwards, the abiding in dignified deportment is the same.
10. From "In this manner... onwards, the conclusion regarding the ten directions is the same.
Furthermore, ascending through the ten directions in order from the east, as described in the "Chapter on Names" (*Nāmanirdeśa-parivarta*).
Question:
According to this concluding summary, it follows that there are bodhisattvas from all worlds throughout the entirety of space who have gathered for this assembly.

Furthermore, beyond the dust-motes of a hundred lands in the eastern direction, there is likewise an assembly; it is not known where that Indraloka world is located, and it is the same for the other realms as well.
Answer:
As in the "Chapter on Names and Titles.
The second section, beginning with "At that time," is the section on the Tathāgata’s emission of light.
The textual meaning consists of six parts:
first, the time; second, the principal figure; third, the location; fourth, the number; fifth, the characteristics; and sixth, the sphere of activity.

This means that with his two big toes, he touched the ground and remained standing with great power; he attained a state from which there was no regression and his walking was constant; as for the number, it exceeds the previous count by a factor of one thousand.
Their characteristics manifest through mutual expression; thus, they are called "wondrous colors.
Universally illuminating the ten directions, they reveal the Buddha’s great assembly.

When one light shines upon all, so too do all shine upon one; layered yet unobstructed, they are all seen within one another, constituting the Great Assembly of Perfect Clarity within the Single Dharma-realm.

Third, in the section on "Verses of Praise" beginning with "At that time, Dharmamati," the discourse by the ten bodhisattvas is divided into ten sections: the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific.

Because Dharmamati is the master of the Dharma discourse, he provides a general summary of the events and meanings from beginning to end of this assembly and collectively manifests the Buddha’s virtues; the remaining nine [bodhisattvas] praise the Buddha’s distinct virtues, so that both the general and the specific together reveal the Tathāgata’s unimpeded assembly.
The names of these ten bodhisattvas also symbolize the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the teachings they expound symbolize the progressive advancement through those stages.
There are two types of such advancement:
first, progressing toward subsequent stages; second, progressing toward the fruit of Buddhahood. Here, the reference is to the fruit of Buddhahood.

Regarding the first point: because the Dharma-wisdom of the eastern direction comprehensively understands all Buddha-dharmas, it is said in the section on "Superior Progression" that "one desires to cause the bodhisattva’s mind to become increasingly expansive with respect to the Buddha-dharmas."
In this passage, both the present application of contemplating the Buddha and the past cultivation thereof are shown to be all-pervasive.
The ten verses are divided into three parts:

the first five describe the causes; through the Buddha’s light, many magnificent events are seen. Of these, the first verse describes the emission of light in this chapter, the next one describes the request for praise in the preceding chapter, and the remaining three verses describe this chapter.
Next, the two [verses] encouraging the contemplation of the Buddha’s power further inspire a superior resolve; this constitutes the "rising without departing" mentioned in the preceding chapter.
The final three [verses] present the cause and its fruition: the first presents the cause, and the latter two present the fruition.
Because they practice vows equally in every land while on the causal stage, their bodies and wisdom respond universally and sever [all afflictions] universally upon reaching the resultant stage.
Second, regarding "All-Wisdom" in the south: this refers to the realization of the true nature of all phenomena through the Ground of Pure Mind.
The intent of these verses is to demonstrate the increase of great compassion toward all sentient beings, because one perceives the Savior in accordance with reality.
The ten verses are divided into six parts:

the first two concern how viewing the Buddha through irrational perspectives does not constitute seeing the Buddha; the following four clarify that perceiving the true nature of phenomena is the true seeing of the Buddha.
Verse three: One who is deluded regarding nature and grasps at dharmas does not see the Buddha.
Verse four: The Buddha is identical to the Dharma; this is the true Buddha. Verse five:
One who has realized the Dharma for themselves is said to see the Buddha.
The "Six-One Verses" trace the source of merit to the realization of the true Buddha.
Regarding the first and second [sections]: the preceding verse exposes false contemplation, employing the metaphor of a long duration to illustrate a brief glimpse;

the subsequent verse clarifies its detrimental effects, showing that by failing to rely on reality, one grasps at signs that deviate from truth, seeing only the net of accumulation that binds one to the prison of suffering, blind and devoid of the eye of wisdom, thus remaining in darkness and failing to see the Buddha’s Dharma-body.

However, because this negates the grasping of signs, it is provisionally designated as a long duration; yet there are no actual multiple kalpas, for it is not of definitive meaning, since it is seen that the Tathāgata increases wisdom thereby.
The second set of four verses clarifies that by realizing the true nature of phenomena, one truly sees the Buddha.
This section has two parts:
the first two verses concern True Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and the latter two concern True Quiescence (*śamatha*).
Regarding the preceding section: the first two phrases constitute the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because that which arises dependently lacks intrinsic nature;
the next two phrases constitute the contemplation of the conventional (*prajñapti*), because they are provisional names following worldly convention;

the subsequent two phrases constitute the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), because all phenomena produced through the aforementioned arising and ceasing are, by their very nature, devoid of intrinsic nature, such that their characteristic and essence are themselves non-arising and non-ceasing.

The latter two phrases concern the benefit of contemplation: the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena is the very suchness of the Buddha; since the essence of the Buddha is fundamentally eternal and devoid of arising or ceasing, when one’s contemplation accords with this suchness, the Buddha is constantly manifest.
How much more so when the three contemplations are unified within a single mind; then there is no aspect of the Buddha’s essence or function that does not manifest.

Within the latter two types of True Cessation (*zhenzhi*), because one uses contemplation to observe phenomena, the subject and object become agitated and restless; therefore, it is necessary to bring them to stillness.
The first phrase restates the preceding nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
the second phrase dissolves the duality of subject and object.
Since the nature of phenomena is originally empty, it is not made empty by contemplation; therefore, there is nothing to be grasped—how could there be a seer?
The following two lines state that because the mind is in profound accord with the Buddha-nature, one must cease all conceptual seeking.

Furthermore, while above it was taught that emptiness is used to dispel existence and the provisional is used to dispel emptiness, here both emptiness and the provisional are simultaneously dispelled; as form and substance mutually negate one another, both vanish. If one were to claim this is "neither," it would still constitute conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Therefore, it is clarified that the arising of thought is entirely delusive, whereas the cessation of thought is the truth. Since thought is fundamentally non-existent from the start, even this cessation is extinguished.
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The Tathāgata’s mark of quiescence cannot be conceptualized as existing;
likewise, within this emptiness of intrinsic nature, even contemplation is impossible."
By employing this text,
one subsequently attains the further benefit of manifest contemplation.
When the mind merges with the fundamental nature, how could delusions possibly arise?
This also contains the meaning of the three types of cessation (śamatha).

Furthermore, it universally concludes both cessation and contemplation (vipaśyanā): by observing in accordance with what has been stated above, one sees that the nature of delusive afflictions is empty and identical to Buddha-nature; how then could they defile?

In the third section, consisting of one verse on the nature of delusion (*moha*), the first half takes up the dharmas, the next line addresses the nature of delusion, and the final line concludes with the fault.
In the fourth section, consisting of one verse, the Buddha is identical to the *dharmatā*.

This means that because it is identical to the dharma of emptiness, it transcends the three periods of time; because it is identical to the dharma of conventionality, its characteristics are fully complete; because it is identical to the simultaneous negation of both, it is without abiding and without attachment; and because it is identical to the essence of suchness, it is omnipresent and immovable.
In the fifth section, consisting of one verse, he cites his own experience; this is his personal realization, intended so that the assembly may be free from doubt.
In the sixth section, consisting of one verse, he attributes his achievement to its source; this is not a matter of following one's own arbitrary mind.
Furthermore, he humbles himself and extols others, differing from ordinary sentiments; thus, the links of the Dharma, though following divergent paths, reach the same destination.
The following eight cases are to be understood by analogy.
Third is Western Śrīmati (Superior Wisdom): because she understands the Buddha’s supreme wisdom and her mind is pure through accordance with emptiness, she is named accordingly.

The intent of this verse is to clarify that it is intended to make the bodhisattva’s wisdom lucid, specifically because great wisdom realizes suchness (*tathatā*) and the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
These ten verses are divided into four parts:

the first praises wisdom as the basis of both delusion and awakening; the next four correctly manifest delusion and awakening; the following four provide metaphors for the aforementioned gains and losses; and the final one attributes the merit to its source.
Regarding the first [point], because it is inconceivable, confusion may occur for those who do not contemplate it, whereas awakening occurs for those who do contemplate it.
Within the subsequent four [points] concerning confusion and awakening, the first two refer to confusion and the latter two refer to awakening.
Within this state of delusion, in the first verse, because one takes external objects as real and gives rise to perceptions that contradict reality, one cannot see the Buddha who is without marks.
In the subsequent verse, because one grasps at the internal characteristics of the aggregates and fails to understand the true nature of the aggregates, one does not see the Buddha within the mind.
Furthermore, because this refers to the ignorant Dharma of the Hīnayāna, it is called "ignorance.
Among the latter two delusions, the former clarifies inverted perceptions, wherein both the internal and external are false;
now, with the presence of the cause of illumination, both the internal and external are awakened.

The first verse overturns the aforementioned external grasping; it means that one realizes all phenomena are the very nature of mind, and that this nature is itself no-nature. When deluded attachments are shattered and principle manifests, one beholds Śākyamuni; thus, in accordance with the dharma-nature, there is neither internal nor external.

The subsequent verse reverses the preceding internal grasping; by comprehending the nature and characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), one perceives the Buddha of one's own mind, who is neither identical to nor different from Vairocana, and is therefore inconceivable.
However, this single verse contains multiple layers of meaning:
first, by stating that there are only the aggregates and bonds and no self or person, it refutes the ordinary person’s grasping at the mark of a self;

second, by stating that the preceding and succeeding causes and conditions are a continuity lacking intrinsic nature, it refutes the grasping at the marks of phenomena held by both ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle.
This nature is precisely the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of the ultimate truth is itself the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Furthermore, the aforementioned nature of non-existence is the nature of the direct cause (*hetu-bhūta-dhātu*).
The previous explanations of this [nature] all pertain to the nature of the revealing cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*).
This continuity of the aggregates is the direct cause, and it is also called the generative cause.
What is termed the "direct cause" has the meaning of the Middle Way; the Middle Way is itself Buddha-nature.

This means that while the aggregates of the present life cease and the aggregates of the intermediate state arise, these present aggregates do not themselves transform into the five aggregates of the intermediate state; therefore, the present aggregates are impermanent.
Just as a seed produces a sprout, yet the seed does not migrate to the sprout; although it does not migrate to the sprout, it is nonetheless able to produce it.
In this same way, although these present aggregates do not migrate to the future, they are nonetheless able to produce them; thus, the present aggregates are not annihilated.

Furthermore, the five aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) do not arise from themselves, nor do they come from elsewhere; rather, the aggregates of the intermediate state arise conditioned by the present five aggregates.
Thus, these subsequent aggregates are not without cause, and therefore the subsequent aggregates are not eternal (*śāśvata*);
yet, since they can continue the preceding ones, the subsequent aggregates are not annihilated (*uccheda*).
Neither annihilation nor permanence is the meaning of the Middle Way; it is the nature of the true cause.
Because it can produce the fruit of Buddhahood, it is called the "producing cause" (*janakahetu*).
There are two kinds of causes for the Buddha-nature of sentient beings:
The first is the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), and the second is the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).
As for the direct cause, it refers to all sentient beings; therefore, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are themselves the direct cause.
As for the conditional cause, it refers to the six *pāramitās*; because they do not arise through the mutual production of the aggregates, they are called the conditional cause.
Now, because the revealing cause (liao-yin) reveals that fundamental cause (zheng-yin), it is said: "to fully understand this nature.
This "understanding" (liao) is precisely *prajñā*, and it is also the conditional cause (*yuan-yin*).
Regarding the third and fourth verses which illustrate the aforementioned gain and loss: the first three verses illustrate loss, while the final one illustrates gain.
The preceding section has two parts;
the first two analogies illustrate the fault of internal grasping.
Within this, the first analogy demonstrates that without an object of cognition, one cannot perceive the true cause.
The "jewel in the darkness" refers to the nature of the true cause (*tathāgatagarbha*).
It is called a "jewel" because it is perfect and precious.
Dwelling within the chamber of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of ignorance is like being in the dark.
The metaphor of the lamp illustrates the causes of conditions and understanding.
The latter half of the verse applies this to the Dharma:
if there is no one to explain it, the cause of conditions is lacking; thus, even with wisdom, one cannot comprehend it.
This meaning contains two aspects:
first, wisdom is the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), which corresponds to the "jewel" mentioned above;
however, because it lacks the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), it cannot bring about realization.

The two Buddha-dharmas are themselves the treasure. Because they lack the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), although wisdom exists internally, it does not function as the actualizing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*) and thus the true nature is not perceived.

In this regard, the contributory cause is indeed the actualizing cause, yet the actualizing cause is not necessarily the contributory cause, because there is a distinction between the proximate and the remote.
A virtuous friend is a conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), which must be understood as such.
Buddha-nature is termed the "cause of realization" (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*); it is not necessarily a conditional cause, as this refers specifically to the nature of wisdom.

If ultimate emptiness is taken as the Buddha-nature, it is solely a direct cause (*hetu*) and not a revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*); it is merely that which is revealed by a revealing cause, rather than something produced by a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*).
If wisdom is taken as the Buddha-nature, it is the "revealing cause" (了因).
If the five aggregates are taken as the Buddha-nature, they are called the "direct cause" (正因) and also the "generative cause" (生因).
Furthermore, arising must correspond to the *ālambana* (object), and correctness must correspond to the *pratyaya* (condition).

Now, the single analogy of the lamp serves as a double metaphor for both the *pratyaya* and the *ālambana*; the jewel in the darkness serves as a double metaphor for both the *samyak* (correct) and the *ālambana*. The full significance of these meanings is contained therein, as explained in detail in the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Furthermore, since the analogy of lighting a lamp is already the correct meaning, why did the Buddha not approve of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*’s Lion’s Roar [Parable]?
Therefore, the Lion’s Roar said:
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; this nature is like the curd within milk."
Because it possesses existence, it necessarily requires causal conditions.
Why is this? It is because one wishes to clearly perceive it.
The conditional cause is precisely the revealing cause; it is like when various objects already exist in the dark, and one uses a lamp to illuminate them for the purpose of seeing them.
If they did not originally exist, what would the lamp illuminate?
Therefore, the Buddha spoke with difficulty:
"If it were the case that the nature of curd definitely exists within milk, then it would be a revealing cause; if it is a revealing cause, why would it need to be revealed again?"
Furthermore, noble son!
If all sentient beings already possess the Buddha-nature, why is it necessary to cultivate immeasurable merit?
If you say that cultivation is the "revealing cause" (*vyañjana-hetu*), then it would be the same as [the process of] curd turning into butter.
Jie Zhengyi states:
"Regarding the fact that milk contains curd, it is because [the curd] is certain to be obtained; the Buddha-nature is likewise.
That sentient beings possess [it] is because they shall see it in the future."
However, these preceding points generally comprise two intentions:
first, the position that the lamp illuminates the jewel is established as the correct view based on the nature of the cause, which is why the Lion’s Roar proclaims it;
the Buddha’s disapproval is based on the nature of the fruit.
Second, regarding the correct analogy of the lamp: from the perspective of its essential nature, it is not different from existence;
that which the Buddha does not permit is because, from the perspective of manifest delusion, it is no different from non-existence.
Therefore, one should know that if one says it definitely exists, this is called attachment;
if one says it definitely does not exist, this is false speech. One should rather say that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings both exists and does not exist.
However, the wisdom of sentient beings is the cause of the Buddha-nature, while Bodhi and Nirvana are its fruit; thus, the Buddha-nature is neither cause nor fruit.

Since the central tenet of this sutra is based upon the Dharma-nature (dharmatā), it takes the Dharma-nature as the Buddha-nature; consequently, it is neither internal nor external, and the descriptions of "ascending" or "sinking" are merely provisional designations made according to the delusion or enlightenment of beings.
The essential meaning of Buddha-nature must be known; it is explained extensively in other chapters as well as in the "Lion’s Roar" chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and elsewhere.

Regarding the phrase in the subsequent verse concerning "one with cataracts," this is a metaphor for how the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) is accompanied by afflictions, such that vision is not pure; because it is impure, one does not perceive the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha-dharma is itself the vision of the Buddha-nature; thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "There are two kinds of Buddha-nature:
first, that which is form; second, that which is non-form.
That which is form refers to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; that which is non-form refers to all sentient beings."
That which possesses form is called "seen by the eye," while that which lacks form is called "seen by hearing.

The Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external; although it is neither internal nor external, it is not lost or destroyed, and for this reason it is said that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.
The twenty-first verse illustrates the aforementioned fault of external grasping.
"Blind" refers to being entirely devoid of eyes, like the skin of a drum; thus, one would not see the Buddha at all.
The stainless removal of obstructions constitutes the eye of clarity and purity; grasping at signs is consciousness, not the eye of wisdom, and therefore one does not see.

The third verse serves as a metaphor for the aforementioned awakening: by removing the cataract of grasping at signs and abandoning the images of flowers in the sky, one cuts off [dualistic] seeing and accords with suchness; thus, one sees as a Buddha.
The fourth single verse attributes the merit to a specific source, which may be understood by reference to what precedes it.
Regarding the fourth, Guṇamati of the North: he was born into the family of the Buddha and is well-versed in the Buddha’s virtues.

The meaning of this verse is to reveal that within the three periods of time, the mind attains equanimity and realizes its own nature, because it exhaustively understands the emptiness of all phenomena.
These ten verses are divided into four parts:

the first four clarify the false awakening of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles; the next four demonstrate their true awakening; the third consists of one verse on the dual perfection of the Buddha’s awakening; and the final verse traces the source of this achievement.
Now, for the first part, there are two sections:
the first verse explains how ordinary beings, deluded regarding dependent origination, lack intrinsic nature and wander in saṃsāra through attachment to signs;
the subsequent three verses apply to both ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle.

The first verse distinguishes the deluded attachment that interprets according to the literal expression; this may be called the false discrimination of those with limited wisdom who grasp at phenomena as being external to the mind.
The remaining two verses clarify the faults [of such views].
The first two lines describe taking a winding path toward tranquility while being lost to the direct road.
The subsequent half-verse [indicates that] the perversions such as the notion of permanence increase the evils of the world;
whereas [the notion of] impermanence and so forth increases the evil of ignorance.
In the latter half [of the *Śālistamba-sūtra*], since the two kinds of emptiness are not seen, one undergoes the suffering of the two types of death.
In the final half, as there is no contemplation of the true reality (*satya*), how could there be the Dharma-eye?
Even if the three vehicles were present, they would not be called "truth" (*satya*).
The following four verses demonstrate his true awakening. Among them, the first verse cites his own losses to exhort others toward achieving benefit;
the next verse teaches the true vision, meaning that seeing the Buddha without grasping is precisely seeing suchness (*tathatā*), and suchness is that which the Buddha knows;

the subsequent verse teaches the understanding of the conventional: the first half follows upon the preceding realization of the ultimate, while the second half is able to understand the conventional.

The subsequent verse dispels the two preceding views to establish the authentic view. This means that only when one forgets the grasping at the views of the ultimate and the conventional (in the first half) can one perceive the true principle of the ultimate and the conventional; the second half provides a reverse explanation, stating that while there are the ultimate and the conventional to be seen, one cannot see the true source of the ultimate and the conventional.
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If a person perceives prajñā, they are thereby bound"—this is the meaning of the second half [of the verse];
"If one does not perceive prajñā, one attains liberation"—this is the meaning of the first half.
If a person perceives Prajñāpāramitā, they are liberated; this is the meaning of the sixth and seventh verses.
If they do not perceive Prajñāpāramitā, they are bound; this is the meaning of the fourth verse.
Only those who have forgotten words can fully investigate this principle.
The third single verse reveals that the Buddha’s two types of awakening are both perfectly fulfilled.
Because he awakens by himself within that which cannot be awakened, it is called "How marvelous! (Aho).
Knowing that there are no sentient beings yet being able to awaken others, he is a great guide;
this fourth point may be understood.
Fifth, in the northeast is Vīryamati (Wisdom of Diligence), who, through diligent contemplation of ultimate truth, accumulates immeasurable goodness, for both are non-abiding.

The intent of this verse is to reveal that one should cause the mind to further apply itself with diligence and remain free from attachment; this is because, within the text, one perceives reality as it is by being free from conceptual discrimination.
The ten verses are divided into two parts:
the first nine contemplate the Dharma, and the last one attributes the merit [to the Buddha].
The first section has three parts.

The first three concern the signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*) regarding what is grasped; among these, the first presents the faults of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), while the latter two reveal the signless contemplation itself.

First, regarding the separation from the grasped object (*grāhya*): the first half [of the verse] indicates that it exists conventionally (*saṃvṛti*), while the second half indicates its non-existence in terms of ultimate principle (*paramārtha*). This is like mistaking a piece of wood for a ghost; knowing that the ghost exists only as a delusion is called "knowing the ghost as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
Knowing that the ghost is fundamentally non-existent and that its entire substance is merely wood is called "seeing the wood."
Second, it is free from the grasper because the grasped is empty.
The first half of the verse sets forth the error: just as when one sees a ghost, one does not see the wood;
the second half reveals the realization: only by being free from the perception of a ghost does one truly see the wood.
Next, the three clarifications on the contemplation of the non-arising of dependent origination:
first, the elimination of the object-condition (*ālambana*).
This involves two aspects of the other-dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*):
The first is illusory existence arising from discrimination, which corresponds to the first half [of the verse];
the second is the absence of intrinsic nature, which corresponds to the latter half.
Both eliminate the subjective perceiver; the first half reiterates the previous fault of arising, showing that views of existence and non-arising are both unreal, being merely conventional.
Seeing that the latter half [of phenomena] is equal to non-arising is called being a "true seer.
Third, the benefit of contemplation is distinguished; subsequently, the three [sections] clarify the contemplation of the perfected nature as being without intrinsic nature:
first, restating the two kinds of non-existence—namely, that both subject and object of discrimination are unobtainable—is because the perfected nature is pure.

Second, the correct revelation of true nature: the first phrase indicates that the essence exists, while the second phrase indicates that characteristics are non-existent; because these two are fused and identical, there is no one who can speak of them.
Third, the accomplishment of benefits through contemplation and the second [section] on attributing merit—the texts of both may be understood accordingly.
The sixth is the Bodhisattva Good Wisdom (Sudhīmat) in the southeast; he has accomplished the mirror-like wisdom of prajñā that is immovable, which may be called "good.

This verse is intended to manifest the desire for his mind to further progress and attain the non-retrogressive patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), because within the text, the liberation from defilement is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The ten verses are divided into four parts:

the first two concern seeing the Buddha; the next three concern seeing the Dharma; the next three concern the accomplishment of benefits through contemplation; and the final two concern inferring that what is seen has a basis.
Regarding the first part: the preceding verse praises that which is seen; its upper half provides the heading for the praise, while its lower half explains and establishes it.
Wisdom is detached from the objects of knowledge and the mind is liberated from afflictions;

because it accomplishes both self-benefit and the benefit of others, it is rare and courageous, for the two obstacles are difficult to eliminate and sentient beings are difficult to deliver, yet one exerts oneself with tireless vigor.
In the subsequent verse, "able to see" refers to seeing according to reality, as a great bodhisattva sees.
The following three [verses] regarding the vision of phenomena (dharmadarśana) are explained in terms of sentient beings.
The first verse correctly reveals that exhaustion is precisely the conditioned (saṃskṛta), because all conditioned formations (saṃskāra) are impermanent and arise and perish rapidly.
The nature of the conditioned is as profound and still as empty space; this is precisely the unconditioned, because its substance is eternally pervasive.

The next two verses clear away traces to enter the profound mystery: the first half clears away the preceding notion of the unconditioned, asking, "Since it is like empty space, how could there be any characteristic of the unconditioned?"

The next four lines dispel the preceding notion of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). This means that since inexhaustibility is discussed in terms of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it does not destroy exhaustion; therefore, it is called "inconceivable.
Since exhaustion is itself inexhaustible, there are no sentient beings.
The latter two lines concern the benefits realized when contemplation is perfected, which is the vision of the *dharmakāya*.

Within the subsequent three verses on the perfection of contemplation, the first verse reveals the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); because the second half clarifies that the perceived object and the perceiving subject are dependently originated and lack intrinsic nature, the perceiving subject and perceived object of the first half naturally vanish.
The next two lines reveal the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-nairātmya*): if even the phenomena of subject and object are empty, who is there to be the seer?

The final two lines reveal the reality: one merely eliminates the aforementioned afflictions without eliminating the true dharma; thus, the essence of the two kinds of emptiness and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) revealed thereby are the True Buddha.

The three verses together conclude the exposition on the benefits of knowing the Buddha-dharma; the meaning of the text is clear and may be understood accordingly. The four verses consist of two pairs.

The first pair, "inferring that there is a basis for views," means that because the Buddha taught the one path of purity, he is able to dispel existence (*bhava*); and because he further expounds immeasurable gateways through wisdom, he is able to dispel non-existence (*abhāva*). Only when conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) ceases and the principle manifests does one know that the Tathāgata abides at the limit where neither existence nor non-existence prevails.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the reality; realizing this reality is the limit (*koṭi*).
Ordinary beings possess this reality, yet they have not realized it.
Regarding the seventh [deity], the one of wisdom in the southwest: because he decisively resolves matters with immovability, he is named Wisdom (*jñāna*).
The intent of this verse is to demonstrate that one is able to transcend all phenomena, for within the text it states that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are well transcended.
The ten verses are divided into two parts:
the first verse cites the author’s own example to exhort the assembly;
The remaining verses hope that the multitude may accord with themselves; herein there are also two parts:
the first six demonstrate delusion, and the latter three initiate awakening.
Within the former, there are also two parts:
The first [of these views] is an adherence to the person (*pudgala-grāha*); in reality, there is no such person, yet through false conceptualization, it becomes a peril.

The remaining [views] are all adherences to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*); among them, the first two adhere to worldly phenomena, while the latter three adhere to both worldly and supramundane phenomena.
Now, first:
the first two phrases clarify "clinging," meaning that by reckoning the aggregates as real, one is unable to contemplate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the body;

the remaining phrases all clarify the faults: the first two phrases show that clinging to reality contradicts the principle and thus one does not see the Buddha; the next two phrases show that lacking wisdom one does not see the Buddha; and the final two phrases show that this only increases the cycle of transmigration.
The latter three pairs within the Middle Way are also divided into two:
the first two uphold [the view of] dharmas, and the last one upholds the Buddha.
Within the former [three], there are likewise two:
First, the establishment of the principle; second, the arising of dogmatic attachment.
Regarding the first: the first half [of the verse] establishes a designation, meaning that nirvāṇa is established in dependence upon the preceding cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Defilements (*kleśa*) are termed "contention" (*raṇa*).
Because it agitates the side of virtue and harms both oneself and others, it is called "dispute" (*raṇa*).
Since these contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are accompanied by and increase through such dispute, they are called "possessing dispute" (*saraṇa*), because that dispute exists within them.
Therefore, birth and death have outflows (*āsrava*) as their essence; because those afflictions (*kleśa*) are absent, it is called nirvāṇa.
The second half [of the verse] is a double negation, meaning that both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are provisionally designated by names based on afflictions; how could there be anything real?
Furthermore, because the two depend upon each other, both are empty; because the two negate each other, both are quiescent.
The subsequent verse gives rise to attachment: the first half expresses attachment, while the second half refutes it.
Regarding the latter position held within the [category of] Buddhas, there is also the "upper half" position and the "lower half" impairment.
This "position" (執) has three meanings:
first, comparing Buddha to Buddha; second, comparing the three bodies (*trikāya*) and so forth; third, comparing the mind to the Buddha.
Within the subsequent three sections on awakening, there are also two parts:
the first two concern attainment in accordance with principle, while the last one cites the Buddha to provide an explanatory proof.
Within the former [two], there are also two parts:
The first half-verse clarifies knowing in accordance with principle; the remainder reveals the benefits of such knowledge.
Within these benefits, there are also two parts:
one half-verse provides the heading, and one full verse offers the explanation.
What is meant by "transcending words"?
If one grasps at the knowledge that can know tranquility, one has not yet escaped words, for there is still an object of perception (*ālambana*).

Even if one says that knowledge knows itself, this is likewise not without an object; therefore, the subject and object must be equal. Because this equality does not lose its illumination, it is a knowing that is not like wood or stone; thus, it is called "the ability to see."
Regarding the subsequent verse that cites the Buddha as the explanation: the preceding section states, "The Buddha is thus. How is the Buddha thus?
The explanation says:
because he awakens to the three periods of time and is free from conceptual discrimination.
When the seeds and habitual tendencies are extinguished, this constitutes severing the roots.
Furthermore, being without mind and relinquishing discrimination is called severing the roots.
The eighth Bodhisattva from the northwest, Real Wisdom (Tathatājñāna), possesses real wisdom because his mind is not inverted.
The intent of this verse is to clarify that, in order to bring about further progress, one attains mastery in the linguistic expressions regarding all phenomena.
To be non-erroneous with respect to phenomena and to realize them as they truly are—this is the meaning of "mastery."
The ten verses are divided into two parts:
the first two clarify that names are established based on reality and that these names are capable of benefiting sentient beings;
the latter eight reveal the reality underlying the names and distinguish the reasons for their beneficial efficacy.

Regarding the first point: the preceding verse clarifies loss and gain, for those who undergo suffering are swiftly liberated upon hearing the name, whereas those who experience pleasure do not hear it and instead sink into further delusion;
the subsequent verse recounts past events to substantiate the present teaching.
The latter eight are divided into three parts:
the first three involve awakening to delusion and realizing the truth, which carries the meaning of "awareness";
the next one involves awakening to both truths simultaneously, which carries the meaning of "illumination."
The latter four [verses] concern awakening where there is no awakening; this is the meaning of "wondrous awakening" (*miao-jue*).
This is the first [section].

The initial verse establishes the name based on the realization of truth. The first line distinguishes it from fallacious inference (*tarka*): to conceive the impermanent as permanent, or the permanent as impermanent, and so forth, constitutes inverted cognition, which is termed fallacious inference.
The next phrase establishes true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is like seeing with the eyes.

The subsequent phrase excludes pseudo-direct perception and clarifies true direct perception; that is to say, seeing a "unified whole" (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*) such as man, woman, heaven, or earth is termed pseudo-direct perception.
Because a unified characteristic (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*) cannot be apprehended as a characteristic, it is called "detachment.
It is not only that what is perceived is detached from unification; there is likewise no wisdom external to suchness (*tathatā*) that could unite with suchness.
The first half-verse concludes the name;
the next verse illustrates the past and future;
the final verse establishes the clear observation (*abhisamaya*).
Next, regarding "awakened illumination": in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), things are real because they lack any composite nature;
in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), things are not real because they are merely provisional composites.
Their mutual fusion without confusion is called "ultimate liberation."
Now, one who possesses true vision does not even perceive reality, let alone what is unreal.

One who perceives the unreal knows that it is itself reality; thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "All phenomena are real, all phenomena are unreal, they are both real and unreal, and they are neither unreal nor non-unreal—this is called the Dharma of the Buddhas."

Regarding the latter four lines on "that which is not awakened yet is awakened": the first verse correctly reveals that the characteristics of suchness and wisdom are mutually detached, and thus it is called "unawakenable.
Because it is quiescent yet possesses exhaustive illumination, it is called "comprehending this."
That which cannot be apprehended is precisely true cultivation.
The following two verses explain this sequentially.
The first verse explains the meaning of "not one": the first half [of the verse] concerns existence through mutual dependence, encompassing both identical and distinct entities.
Because the latter half [of the verse] concerns dependent origination, it is empty; thus, the characteristics of unity and multiplicity are exhausted.

The first half of the subsequent verse explains the latter half of the preceding verse: because there is neither agent nor action, there is no basis for dependence; because it arises from the conceptualization of karma, it is a conditioned conjunction.

The second half [of the verse] explains and establishes the first half: how is it known that there is neither subject nor object? Because apart from the conceptualization of diverse karma, there is no "mine" (ātmīya).

There follows a single verse that concludes this sublime meaning: the first half refers to the "abode" (sthāna) and the second half to the "dweller" (sthātṛ); because there is no abiding, there is nothing in which one does not abide.
This means that one does not abide in existence because existence is itself emptiness; yet one is able to abide in existence because one accords with the reality of existence.
Nor does one abide in non-existence, for non-existence is itself existence.
It does not abide in both existence and non-existence, because there is no duality of substance.
It does not abide in the negation of both, because it does not destroy the two characteristics.
By this analogy, one should understand that which is capable of abiding.
Since one takes non-abiding as abiding, the mind is then free from all agitation and movement, thereby accords with the fundamental enlightenment that is profoundly still and eternally present.
The ninth section below concerns Supreme Wisdom; its title is the same as in the preceding verse.
Furthermore, because they are born from the teachings of the Dharma King and shall succeed to the rank of Buddha, they are called "unsurpassed.

The intent of the verse is to manifest the desire to cause further progress so that the mind is free from obstacles; the text states this because there is no attachment, no conceptualization, and no dwelling in phenomena.
The ten verses are divided into three parts:
the first explains the meaning of the title; the next eight manifest the Buddha’s supreme qualities; and the final one dedicates the merit and concludes with the benefits.
Within the middle eight verses, there are two further divisions:
The first six [qualities] are the virtues of internal realization, while the latter two are the virtues of external transformation.
Within the former, there are also two parts:
the preceding verse correctly clarifies the entry into realization, while the subsequent five illuminate the objects and manifest the principles.
Regarding the first point: it is precisely bodhi and nirvāṇa, because one attains bodhi through non-attainment.
"Abiding" refers to nirvāṇa; as original enlightenment is spontaneous, it is not something produced by effort.
Awakening is also a dark resonance; thus, wisdom is without discrimination, the three subtleties are already exhausted, and the six grossnesses are naturally absent.
Furthermore, because it cannot be known by consciousness, there is no grossness; because it cannot be known by wisdom, there is no subtlety.
Furthermore, that which possesses the duality of subject and object of realization is termed "coarse," while that which is devoid of such subject and object is termed "subtle.
Both are beyond the path of language and thus do not exist [as such], for Bodhi and Nirvana transcend all mental activity.
Among the latter five [verses], the first verse correctly elucidates the illumination of the object.
The "object" refers to the conventional (saṃvṛti) object, for it possesses both subject and object.
Because it is the conventional itself that is the ultimate (paramārtha), it is said to be "innumerable."
Because the mind is identical to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is said to be "far removed.
This is the true Dharma of the Buddha, which simultaneously binds together both the subject and the object.
The final four [verses] dispel appearances to reveal the principle; all of them follow the tracks of the preceding to eliminate obstructions.
The first verse uses a double negation to reveal the Middle Way, wherein the illumination of principle extinguishes hindrances, for Bodhi and Nirvana are free from existence and non-existence.
The following two verses explain the aforementioned double negation; one and a half verses explain the meaning of "non-illumination," the first line of which serves as the general statement.
The second line states that because the illuminating capacity is without attachment, it is called "thoughtlessness" (amanasikāra), and furthermore, it is not defiled by this thoughtlessness.
The next phrase indicates non-attachment in what is illuminated, because it takes the absence of a locus as its dwelling;
the following phrase does not destroy the subject and object;
the subsequent two phrases simultaneously dispel both nature and characteristics.
The next two lines explain that there is not an absence of illumination, because it is an illumination that accords with principle (*tattva*).
The subsequent verse clears away the traces of the preceding "non-duality.

To speak of "non-duality" merely means that there are no two; it does not mean that there exists a duality of existence and non-existence. If one maintains a view of non-duality, one has merely returned to the state of duality.

Because non-duality necessarily implies its opposite, duality, one must negate it and continue to negate until there is nothing left to negate; thus it is said that "all things in the three realms are empty.
This emptiness refers to the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā), which all Buddhas perceive in common.

Within the latter two [verses] concerning the virtue of external transformation, the preceding verse directly reveals the awakening that causes one to abide in non-abiding, while the subsequent verse provides its explanation.
Since the body is itself no-body, there is nothing to be awakened to.

To realize that the view of a self-body arises [from delusion], and that this view is like the body itself—when both the view of a self-body and the body itself are extinguished, this is the true Dharma-body.
To contemplate the true mark of the body is likewise to contemplate the Buddha; therefore, the conclusion is drawn in reference to the Buddha.
The merit [of this] can be inferred.
Regarding the tenth, the "Firm Wisdom" of the zenith: it is because the power of his wisdom is accomplished and indestructible.

The intent of the verse is to manifest the desire to cause the increase of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*); thus the text says that he has attained the pure eye of wisdom and perceives the realm of the Buddhas.
The ten verses are divided into four parts:
The first verse offers a general praise of his appearing in the world for the sake of sentient beings, his wisdom-light shining everywhere, and his courageous compassion.

The next four verses specifically demonstrate the characteristics of his compassion: the first verse observes the capacities of beings; the next two verses provide a counter-argument to establish this point; and the final verse correctly clarifies [his activity] while also manifesting the Jewel of the Sangha.
The next three and a half verses concern the benefits of seeing and hearing [the teaching], while the final one and a half verses conclude with the inexhaustibility of its virtues.
As this represents the ultimate point, the preceding ten items are summarized as a whole.

Chapter Fifteen: The Ten Abodes (Daśabhūmi). Regarding the intent for the initial arrival [of this chapter]: since the preceding causes and conditions have already been clarified, it is appropriate to manifest the main body of the teaching; therefore, this chapter follows.

Furthermore, while previously the virtues of the Buddha—the basis (*āśraya*)—were analyzed, now the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which depend upon that basis, are being analyzed; therefore, this follows in sequence.
Second, regarding the explanation of the name: wisdom abides in the principle (*tattva*), and having attained its position, one does not regress; thus it is called a "stage" (*bhūmi*).
The lower fascicle of the *Benye jing* states: "Upon first entering the realm of emptiness, one abides in the stage of the nature of emptiness; therefore, it is called 'abiding' (*sthiti*).
However, there are many types of meanings for "abiding," which are here explained as ten by way of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna*).
The general statement "ten abodes" (*daśavihāra*) is an explanation by means of a numeral.
