The fact that there are ten [chapters] in each of the subsequent sections may be understood by analogy with this.
Third, regarding the essential purport: the practice of the ten abodes is the essence (*piṇḍārtha*), while the attainment of the stages and their fruits is the goal (*prayojana*).
Regarding the fourth section, the explanation of the text, the four chapters are divided into two parts:
the first three concern the practices and virtues of their respective stages, while the last one concerns superior progress toward subsequent stages.
As for why there is no mention of superior progress in the preceding assembly, it is because that was merely a skillful means for entering the stage; the stage itself had not yet been accomplished.

In this stage of dedication, there is no further progression; for the fulfillment of the three stages of the ordinary person constitutes the overall expedient means for entering the grounds, it likewise manifests the non-conceptual nature of progression, as it is free from the characteristics of progression.
Now, for the first [section], there are three parts:
the first chapter distinguishes the stages, the second chapter distinguishes the practices, and the third chapter clarifies the virtues.
The first [part] is also called "Exposition"; its text is divided into seven sections:

First, the section on samādhi; second, the section on the empowerment; third, the section on arising; fourth, the section on the fundamental; fifth, the section on the exposition; sixth, the section on the realization of attainment; and seventh, the section on the verses of reiteration.
First: For what reason does one enter meditative concentration?
Briefly stated, there are six intentions:

First, because this samādhi is the very essence of the Dharma; second, because it is not taught unless realized; third, to reveal that this Dharma is not an object of discursive thought; fourth, to observe the capacities of beings and examine the Dharma; fifth, to receive the empowerment of the Buddha; and sixth, to perfect the ritual procedures. The remainder is as explained in the *Xuan* (the *Xuanzang Commentary*).
The text has three distinctions:
first, those who enter meditative concentration.

As for "the one who enters through Dharma-wisdom," this refers to the leader of the assembly; others would enter in a distracted manner because they are not yet disciplined. This is to manifest that the Dharma-wisdom of the Ten Abodes is capable of expounding [the teaching].
Second is the basis for entering meditative concentration,
which refers to relying on the power of the Buddha and attributing the merit to the primary teacher of the transformation, thereby manifesting an absence of pride.
Third is the name of the entry into concentration.
To distinguish it from the meditative concentrations of the fruits [of the śrāvaka path], it is called "bodhisattva.
Because one can know through innate capacity and possesses skillful understanding and insight, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Because each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) encompasses many doors of skillful means, it is called "immeasurable."
The mind proceeds toward the Dharma; therefore, it is called "entering.
Furthermore, all samādhis possess three phases: entering, abiding, and emerging.

When the five consciousnesses confront their objects, the mental faculty (manas) issues forth from its gateway; while guarding the sense faculties against distant objects, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) retreats and enters back within—this is common to both the provisional and the Hinayana.
Now, illumination within stillness is called "entering"; illumination within stillness is called "emerging"; and because it has not yet arisen after entering, it is called "abiding.
The other samādhis and so forth are all explained as previously stated.
Second, the section on "bestowing empowerment through samādhi" has three parts:
first, a general explanation of the causes and conditions; second, clarifying the purpose of the empowerment; and third, specifically revealing the characteristics of the empowerment.
Now, for the first [section], there are three parts:
first, indicating the cause of the special empowerment; second, the manifestation of the conditions for empowerment; and third, praising the causes and conditions for the discourse.
Regarding the first: it is because of the power of samādhi that the treatise states why Vajragarbha alone is specially empowered—it is because he has attained this concentration.

Previously, one was able to enter [the state] through the power of the Buddha; now, the Buddha manifests through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). These act as mutual conditions of sovereign influence (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
What is meant by "unconditioned samādhi" (*anabhisaṃskāra-samādhi*)?

It reveals that the wisdom of self-awakening is quiescent yet never loses its illumination; being in profound accord with the Buddha-mind, it evokes the manifestation of the Buddha’s three karmas (body, speech, and mind) as an empowerment.
Second, from "The ten directions" onwards, the Buddhas appear through the addition of conditions.
The reason the number of Buddhas coming from each direction is stated as "a thousand" is because [the practitioners'] practice is still inferior.

The inclusion of many Buddhas serves to manifest increased reverence for the Dharma and the Dharma-preacher; furthermore, it demonstrates that the Buddhas collectively add their support by preaching in unison.
Regarding the Buddhas who share the name Dharmamati (Dharma-Wisdom), it is because they have attained the Dharma without differentiation.
The *Śāstra* states: "When these Bodhisattvas hear that their names are the same as their own, their joy increases.
However, all Buddhas manifest with the name Dharmamati within this stage of abiding; this is due to the power of the Dharma and because such is the nature of the Dharma.
"Manifesting universally before them" means arriving without coming.
Third, from "Addressing Dharmamati" onwards is the praise and explanation of the causes and conditions.
This section has two parts:
First, there is the cause for further praise: because he is able to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
To say "you are able" is an expression of rare excellence; this concentration is difficult to attain, yet you are now able to enter it.

Regarding the mention of the name of the samādhi: previously, he entered it silently, and as the assembly did not yet know its name, he now mentions and praises it so that the multitude may look up to it in reverence.
Second, from "Good sons, in the ten directions... onwards, both the empowerment and the causes and conditions of the samādhi are explained together.
Within this, four causes are first explained individually:
first, the accompaniment of the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
When the Buddhas speak of themselves, it is to inspire reverence and admiration in the assembly.
First, the original vows of the primary Buddha;
second, the manifest majesty of the primary Buddha;
third, the roots of goodness of Dharmamati.
Briefly stated, there was no stimulus or response from the great assembly.
The two phrases, "later entering this samādhi and causing you to preach the Dharma," conclude the attribution of the cause.
This means that by virtue of the four matters mentioned above, the first three serve as conditions and the fourth serves as the cause; because cause and conditions conjoin, he enters this samādhi.
Therefore, the four preceding causal conditions cause you to preach the Dharma; this is precisely the augmenting condition. Thus, the Treatise says: "For what reason is there an augmentation?
It is for the sake of preaching this Dharma.
Consequently, within both the "Ten Practices" and the "Ten Transferences," it is stated: "It causes you to enter this samādhi and expound the Dharma."
Furthermore, this exhortation for you to preach the Dharma is also a general summary of the subsequent text.

However, since the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that all Buddhas, including Vairocana, bestow their empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) due to prior vows, these four sections are all causes for such empowerment.

In those sutras, while the various Buddhas merely speak of "adding their majestic spiritual power" (*adhiṣṭhāna*), Vairocana speaks of it as being "due to the power of his original vows. Consequently, ancient masters took the empowerment of the various Buddhas to be the cause for attaining meditative concentration, and thus transformed the latter three conditions into causes for that empowerment.
If it were the case that one could attain concentration without the latter three causes, then what would be the purpose of the word "also"?
Since the conclusion states, "it enables you to enter this samādhi," how can it be that the latter three do not serve as causes for concentration?
This not only contradicts the principles of the sūtras and their commentaries, but also deviates from what is explained in the śāstras.
According to the true meaning, these four causes apply to two senses:
first, as the causes for attaining meditative concentration, as distinguished above; [the second sense is...]
Second, the latter three [causes] further constitute causes of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-hetu*); the Buddhas employ their power of vows (*praṇidhāna-bala*) as these causes of empowerment.
To clarify this point, the author of the treatise states that those Buddhas previously made such vows and now further empower [the teaching] themselves.
Question:
Regarding empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which comes first and which later?

If concentration were prior and empowerment subsequent, then one should not say: "You are able to enter this samādhi; this is because the Buddhas of the ten directions collectively empower you," and so forth, up to "and because of the power of your own roots of goodness, you enter this samādhi."
If the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) were prior and the concentration (*samādhi*) subsequent, then it would not be appropriate to explain the empowerment portion only after the concentration portion.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "For what reason is there empowerment?"
"It is for the purpose of expounding this Dharma," it is said, and not "for the purpose of entering samādhi.
Furthermore, it is stated that only Vajragarbha is empowered and no others because this Bodhisattva has attained this samādhi.
Since both are supported by scriptural evidence, how are they to be reconciled?
An ancient master answered:
"The preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) occur simultaneously."
That is to say, if one applies effort before concentration is established, the distracted mind will be unable to sustain it;
if concentration is established before applying effort, one's own power will be insufficient to enter this profound meditative absorption. Therefore, they must occur simultaneously.
This interpretation also contradicts both scripture and reason.

For it is stated that after entering samādhi, the Buddhas then manifest their bodies to praise his attainment of concentration; furthermore, it is only after the explanation of the purpose of the empowerment is concluded that the empowerment of the three karmas is bestowed.
To claim they are simultaneous would it not contradict the text?
If one says they are simultaneous, the cause cannot be established, which would contradict reason.
Furthermore, one should not cite the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) as proof, because these two factors may be separated from one another.
If one explains it correctly, there are two kinds of "addition" (ādhāna):

if categorized according to the internal and external, that which consists of the secret assistance of the power of roots of goodness, majestic spiritual authority, and the power of vows, enabling one to attain meditative concentration, occurs prior to entering that concentration.

If one considers the bestowal of wisdom, the praise, the touching of the crown, and the exhortation regarding the three karmas as manifestations of manifest empowerment, then these occur after entering meditative concentration.
Since both textual passages are so clear, how can one be so deluded?
The second section, beginning with "for the sake of increase," clarifies the purpose of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
While the purpose of the empowerment is designated by the name of its cause, the actual purpose of the empowerment lies precisely in the preaching of the Dharma.
These ten points also constitute the purpose for which the Dharma is taught, forming a mutually reinforcing sequence.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the ten lines that explain each point individually; second, the final line that concludes the exposition.
Regarding the preceding section, the text contains two meanings:

viewed in relation to the purpose of the empowerment, it is a specific explanation; viewed in relation to the preaching of the Dharma, it carries the sense of preaching the Dharma—that is, the empowerment is for the sake of preaching the Dharma.
For what purpose is the teaching of the Dharma?
It is for the sake of increasing the Buddha’s wisdom and so forth.
However, the purpose of teaching the Dharma is itself the purpose of the empowerment.
Among these ten statements, the first is general and the remainder are specific.
"General" refers to the teaching of the dharma of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*).

This is because the present faith and understanding of all bodhisattvas causes the two natures—the innate and the acquired—to increase through practice, thereby giving rise to the wisdom of enlightenment (*bodhicitta-jñāna*).
Furthermore, this wisdom of causes is identical to the Buddha-wisdom and may also be said to increase.
What is the use of increasing wisdom?
It is for the sake of penetrating deeply into the Dharma-realm and so forth.
The nine phrases consist of five pairs:
the first two constitute the pair of realizing the ultimate truth and understanding conventional truth.
This means entering that which has no aspect of entry; hence it is called "profound entry."
Because they have thoroughly understood the characteristics and the nature [of phenomena], it is said that they "thoroughly understand.
Next is the pair of being unobstructed and unhindered.
By entering the Dharma-realm, they are free from the hindrance of afflictions.
By understanding sentient beings, one is freed from the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Next, the two [aspects] correspond to the perfection of the cause and the attainment of the fruit.

This means that because one skillfully establishes the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional, the cause is perfected; and because one enters into *sarvajñatā* (omniscience), the fruit is said to be fulfilled.
The next two [verses] concern the correspondence of the faculties (*indriya*) regarding the cognition of phenomena;
the final line, although not a textual correspondence, is a correspondence of meaning, namely: internally upholding all phenomena and externally teaching for the benefit of others.
The section beginning with "That which is called" summarizes what has been explained;
that is to say, if one speaks of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), then all that was previously mentioned is fully accomplished.
The third section, beginning with "Good son," correctly elucidates the characteristics of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is divided into three parts:
First is empowerment through speech, by exhorting and persuading to increase eloquence;
second is empowerment through mind, by secretly bestowing influence to augment wisdom;
third is empowerment through body, by stroking the crown of the head to enhance majestic power.
The first [point] can be understood from the beginning.
Regarding the second, from "At that time" onwards, within the section on the addition of mental power (*manas-kṛta*), there is first the bestowal and subsequently the explanation.

Within the former, ten kinds of knowledge are bestowed; the first is general, meaning the knowledge of the four analytical insights (*pratisaṃvid*), because this is the basis for preaching the Dharma.
The others are all the unhindered eloquence of delight in speaking (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Regarding "unattached" (*asaṅga*): this treatise calls it the "eloquence of non-attachment," because one does not dwell in attachment toward the Dharma being taught.
It is the "swift eloquence" (*tarka-pratibhāna*) among the seven types of eloquence; because one speaks immediately when speech is required, it is called "unattached."
Second is unimpeded knowledge (*anācchedya-jñāna*), which is unimpeded eloquence (*anācchedya-pratibhāna*); this means that because it is a continuous, linked succession, it never comes to an end.

Third is non-delusion (*amoha*), which is swift eloquence (*āśu-pratibhāna*); being clear regarding both phenomena and principles, the mind is free from the darkness of delusion, and one's speech is as rapid as a cascading torrent.
Fourth, "without distinction" refers to analytical exposition that is timely and appropriate to the faculties of the listeners, being free from any disparity.
Fifth, "without error" refers to analytical exposition that is free from mistake, for whatever is spoken accords with principle and is without deviation.
The six immeasurables (*ṣaḍ-apramāṇa*) refer to the eloquence of abundant meaning and flavor, for both name, number, phenomenon, and principle are immeasurable.
The seventh, "unsurpassable" (*anabhibhūta*), refers to the most supreme and wondrous eloquence in all worlds;

it possesses five virtues: first, its profundity is like thunder; second, its clarity is heard from afar; third, its tone is mournful and elegant like that of the *kalaviṅka* bird; fourth, it causes sentient beings to enter into a state of respectful love; and fifth, those who hear it rejoice without weariness. Because it possesses these five meanings, it is called "unsurpassable."
The first refers to the seven types of eloquence.
The eighth, "being untiring," means that one is free from weariness throughout the preceding seven.
The ninth, "being unassailable," means that because one possesses both the general and specific [qualities], no one can subdue or cause one to retreat.
The subsequent section beginning with "For what reason" provides an interrogation and explanation.
First, the intent of the interrogation is as follows:
Since the Buddhas possess the power to bestow and the compassion to grant universally, for what reason are the ten knowledges bestowed solely upon Dharmamati?
The sub-commentary explains:
When Dharmamati attains this samādhi, it is by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that he receives the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas.
Regarding the "at this time," there follows the empowerment of the body, which serves two purposes: first, to increase his majesty; second, to cause him to arise.

However, although the three empowerments occur simultaneously, they are arranged in sequence according to their meaning; because it follows the convenience of the preceding discourse, the empowerment of speech is mentioned first, while the empowerment of the body, which causes the arising of meditative concentration, is placed last.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, "The sūtras state that the Buddhas do not depart from their original place, yet their going and staying are unimpeded."
"Furthermore, his hand does not extend [beyond its reach], yet there is no obstruction to its extension or contraction.
Simultaneously touching the crowns of heads, there is no obstruction between the one and the many; therefore, this is extraordinary.

Regarding the necessity of touching the crown of the head, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "If there were anyone who could preach the Dharma without being established by the two kinds of supernatural powers of the Tathāgata, such a thing is impossible."
First is the spiritual power of bodily, facial, and verbal expression, which is the aforementioned empowerment of speech.
Second is the spiritual power of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), which consists of the empowerment of wisdom into the heart and crown, and the touching of the crown of the head with the hand.
"Receiving upon the crown of the head" means receiving from above by virtue of the power of the Honored One.
"The right hand" refers to the fact that the Dharma-wisdom (dharmaprajñā) speaks in accordance with the capacities of beings; for all Buddhas speak in conformity with the Dharma-wisdom.
The third section, beginning with "Dharmamati Bodhisattva," consists of four brief points:

first, the completion of the matter of samādhi; second, having already attained superior power; third, the arrival of the time for exposition; and fourth, the absence of verbal expression within meditative concentration. These four points are explained sequentially, each subsequent one clarifying the preceding.

The fourth section, "Announcement to All" and below, constitutes the Main Division (*maulabhāga*). The text is divided into three parts: first, a general manifestation of the essence and characteristics;
second, the formal announcement of the intention to speak; and third, the specific enumeration of their names.
First, regarding the essence of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), there are briefly three types:
first, in terms of their basis, which refers to the three samādhis, for it is based upon these that the dharmas of the ten stages are taught.
The treatise states: "Samādhi is the very essence of the Dharma.
Second, regarding its fundamental basis, this is what will be explained below.
Third, as for its essential nature: if considered in terms of its objects of focus, these are the two realms of the ultimate and the conventional.
If categorized by the subjective perceiver, these are the two practices of compassion and wisdom.
Since the two objects are integrated, compassion and wisdom are no longer distinct; when object and wisdom are in profound accord, they are one within the single Dharma-realm.
Now, regarding the fundamental substance (*dharmatā*):

if one examines the scriptural text directly, the two characters "dwelling place" (*vihāra*) collectively indicate its substance, while the passage beginning with "vast" and so forth briefly reveals its characteristics.
"Abiding in the family of the Buddhas of the three periods" indicates the place of abiding.

Now, following the categories of the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* (Dilun) for interpretation, the "place of abiding" serves as the general [category], while the others are all specific; the general indicates the essence, which here is called the "place of abiding," whereas the ten practices are termed "practices and activities."
The tenth stage (*bhūmi*) is named "Vow" (*praṇidhāna*); the tenth ground (*bhūmi*) is named "Perfectly Determined Vow" (*praṇidhāna-suviniścita*).
Since these are both the essential nature of their respective positions, why are their names different?
However, both the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood take the bodhicitta as their essence. There are three types of bodhicitta:
first, the direct mind, because it maintains right mindfulness of the dharma of suchness;
second, the profound mind, because it delights in cultivating all virtuous practices.
Third is the mind of great compassion, because it rescues and protects all suffering sentient beings.

The True Suchness that is contemplated is also the wisdom of original enlightenment, which is fundamental wisdom; the latter two [aspects] manifest the nature-merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
However, among these three minds, the presence of one necessarily entails the other two, though they vary in their degree of predominance or subtlety across the three stages of worthiness (*śaikṣa*).
Because the mind of straightforwardness (*ṛjukacitta*) increases during the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), it is termed "understanding" (*jñāna*).
Understanding is the foundation of practice and vows; therefore, it is explained first.
Because the profound mind within the ten practices increases, they are called "practices" (*caryā*); this is because one initiates practice based upon the aforementioned understanding.

The tenth stage is called "Vow" because great compassion increases; it involves dedicating the preceding stages of understanding, practice, and vows so that all sentient beings may be freed from suffering and attain happiness.
The ten stages and the three minds are termed "Certainty" because they involve direct realization; however, since great compassion is primary, the vow is specifically cited here.
Therefore, the Treatise states: "The vow for excellent determination is the arousal of the bodhicitta within the first stage.
This refers precisely to the vow within this section on the fundamental stages.

Since the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā) universally correspond to these three types of equal enlightenment and these three types of equal Buddhas, we know that the bodhicitta is the common basis for all stages.

Regarding the designation of this stage of abiding as a "place of dwelling": if considered from the perspective of preeminence, one abides in *tathatā* (suchness) by means of profound *prajñā* (wisdom); thus, it is precisely through this that it becomes the place where one's practices and vows abide.
If explained according to the general sense, it is because both abide in the household of the bodhicitta of the three higher [vehicles].
As for "abiding place," the Sanskrit original is *kula*, which here is translated as "household" (*jia*).
"Family" (jia) refers to a clan; thus, it was translated as "spiritual lineage" (zhongxing) in older versions, specifically referring to the "lineage of cultivation" among the four types of lineages.
Because this family is the dwelling place of Bodhisattvas, it is here translated as "abode" (zhuchu); the subsequent text concludes by returning to the "Buddha-family."
Within this distinction, there are two phrases but three meanings:
first, being as vast as the *dharmadhātu*, it is the supreme dwelling place.
However, regarding the general phrase in the *Bhūmi-sūtra*, one should certainly not study that.
In this context, "vast" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The term *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) encompasses four meanings:

first, it is the true suchness (*tathatā*) of correct mindfulness; it shares the same nature as the dharma-realm, being profoundly limitless and surpassing all ordinary beings, as well as surpassing the partial truth of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Second, the universal encompassing of the boundless aspects of a bodhisattva’s practice; because of their profound mind of great compassion, they share the same activity as the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) without limit or measure, thereby surpassing the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
Third, the non-obstruction of the three minds; because phenomena and principle are fused, they are identical to the unobstructed dharma-realm.
The fourth is the "Dharma-realm of Mutual Interfusion," because within each and every atom, nothing is not fully present.
This corresponds to the third [category], the "Superior Expedient Bodhisattvas," whose two types of space are equal; this refers to the causal dwelling place.
There are two kinds of causes:
first, the cause of impermanent, cherished fruits, which is like space; depending upon this, form arises, and because form is inexhaustible [it persists].
Second, the cause of permanent fruits; since this present stage is prior to the stages of the bodhisattva grounds (*bhūmi*), this latter cause is absent here.
An ancient worthy further said:
"Within each and every stage, it is like space containing boundless oceans of practice;
again, it is like space pervading everywhere, neither reaching nor not reaching."

Furthermore, just as space is unimpeded, the third dwelling is the abode of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. According to the treatise, this is called the "dwelling of non-cowardice. This means that the place where a bodhisattva dwells is precisely the place where a Buddha dwells; therefore, it is called the "Buddha-abode. To advance and dwell in the Buddha-abode is to be without cowardice.
If one were to explain the scriptural text directly, this would be the concluding indication.
That is to say, regarding the aforementioned "place of dwelling," where does one dwell?
It means dwelling in the family of the Buddha.

The Buddha-family is precisely the great bodhicitta, for all Buddhas abide in this to give birth to bodhisattvas; since the ultimate realization of true suchness, compassion, and vows can only be abided in by a Buddha alone.
The phrase "the three periods of time" is a praise of excellence.
Second, from "That bodhisattva" onwards, the text cites [the subject] to grant permission for the explanation; this may be understood accordingly.
Third, from "O sons of the Buddha, there are ten kinds of bodhisattva abodes" onwards, their specific names are enumerated.

The text has three distinct sections: first, stating the number and citing scriptural evidence; second, listing the names according to that number; and third, providing a summary to manifest their excellence. Regarding the first:

the fruits of Buddhahood attained by the Buddhas of the three periods have all been accomplished through these causes of the ten abodes. This is like the royal highway, a natural and eternal rule; therefore, they are spoken of in common.
Second, from the phrase "What is... onwards, the names are listed according to their number.

Regarding the first, the *Abhimukhī* (Initial Resolve) stage, the *Ratnakuṇḍala-sūtra* states: "These are individuals with superior progressive roots of goodness who, for one or two kalpas, or for one or two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, practice the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) in the presence of Buddhas. With minds that believe in the Triple Gem, they constantly abide in the eighty-four thousand *prajñāpāramitās* and cultivate all practices and all dharma-gates, even until they first enter the realm of emptiness and abide in the station of the nature of emptiness; therefore, it is called 'abiding' (*vihāra*)."

According to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith*, after ten thousand kalpas of cultivating the practice of faith have been perfected, one enters the stage of non-retrogression; having first given rise to the Great Mind, this initial resolve constitutes dwelling [in the path], which is called the "Dwelling of Initial Resolve."
Regarding the three types of generating the mind of enlightenment, this refers to the "generating the mind through the fulfillment of faith.

Second, as for "cultivating the ground" (*bhūmi-karman*), it means that one constantly accords with the emptiness of mind and remains pure; because the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates are cleansed and made immaculate, one refines and cultivates the ground of the mind so that compassion and wisdom increase and become luminous; this is called the stage of "Cultivating the Ground" (*bhūmi-pratisthā*).
Third, skillfully contemplating emptiness and existence in order to increase and cultivate correct practice;
fourth, being born into the family of the Buddhas because one’s lineage is noble;
fifth, conforming to worldly conventions while maintaining the truth, practicing immeasurable skillful means, and transforming beings without abiding.
Sixth, because they have accomplished *prajñā*, their minds remain unmoved whether hearing praise or slander regarding the true and the real.

Seventh, having entered the ultimate emptiness of non-arising, their every thought constantly practices emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; through the union of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), they cannot be destroyed by external conditions.
Eighth, the mind does not give rise to perversions, because it does not allow demons or malevolent spirits to destroy the bodhicitta.
Ninth, one generates understanding from the teachings of the Dharma King, for one shall succeed to the rank of a Buddha.

Tenth, because the contemplation of emptiness from the ninth stage upward results in the attainment of the mind of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which is supreme; and because the Dharma-water of all Buddhas is poured upon the crown of the heart.

Nevertheless, there are three ways in which the names of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are established: namely, the fourth, eighth, ninth, and tenth are named after metaphors; the seventh receives its title by virtue of being free from faults; and the others are designated according to their specific merits.
From the perspective of the metaphors themselves, they are all *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds;
from the perspective of the objects being metaphorized, they may be *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds.
The summary beginning with "This is called" [at the end of section three] is self-evident.
Regarding the stage of determination (*niyata-bhūmi*), there are briefly ten meanings.
First, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other texts, it corresponds to the first of the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*). As for the five stages:

first is the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), which refers to the three levels of worthiness (*tri-kalyāṇa-pudgala*). From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), one accumulates merit and wisdom as the provisions for the Path, and for the sake of sentient beings, cultivates the virtues conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).

Second is the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*): once the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) have been perfected, one again cultivates application in order to enter the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); this is also called the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*).
The stage of thorough penetration is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which refers to the two types of paths of seeing at the initial entry into the stages (*bhūmi*).

The stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) begins from the second state of mind in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) and extends up to the state of the diamond-like immediate mind (*vajropamasamantakacitta*); this is called the path of cultivation.

Fifth is the stage of ultimate consummation (*niṣṭhāgata-avasthā*); following the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), all [moments] until the end of the future are subsumed under this stage.
Second, according to the sixth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, four stages are taught, which correspond to the very beginning of the first stage mentioned above.

Regarding the four stages: first is the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), beginning from the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and ending before the [first] ground; the remaining three—the stages of seeing (*darśana*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and ultimate perfection (*niṣṭhā*)—are identical to the latter three among the five stages.
Third, based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter forty-seven, it speaks of the twelve abodes (*dvādaśa-vihāra*), which correspond to the beginning of the second [category].
Regarding these twelve: first is the abode of the spiritual lineage (*gotra-vihāra*), meaning that the nature of those bodhisattvas is inherently virtuous;
their nature is naturally accomplished in the merits of a bodhisattva, and they sustain the seeds of all Buddha-dharmas.
By nature free from coarse defilements, one is unable to manifest the entanglements of higher afflictions.

Second is the stage of dwelling in conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*); this refers to all bodhisattva practices from the initial generation of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*) until the pure intention (*viśuddhāśaya*) has not yet been attained.
The third is the dwelling of extreme joy; the fourth is the dwelling of higher ethics; the fifth is the dwelling of higher mind.

The sixth, seventh, and eighth are called the dwellings of higher wisdom, which are divided into three types: namely, the dwelling of higher wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) in the sixth; the dwelling of higher wisdom associated with the truths (satya) in the seventh; and the dwelling of higher wisdom associated with the arising and cessation of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) in the eighth.

Ninth, the dwelling of signlessness with effort; tenth, the dwelling of signlessness without effort; eleventh, the dwelling of analytical knowledge; twelfth, the supreme bodhisattva dwelling; and thirteenth, the supreme Tathāgata dwelling.
The preliminary statement regarding the twelve stages (*vihāra*) is spoken with reference to bodhisattvas; when the subsequent stage of the Tathāgata is added, they become thirteen stages.
The second [stage] corresponds to the three levels of the ordinary person (*tri-piṭaka-śaikṣa*).
From the third onward, they correspond respectively to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Fourth, based on both the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the seventh chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavāca-śāstra*, seven stages (*bhūmi*) are established among the thirteen abodes (*vihāra*): first, the stage of the nature of the lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*); second, the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*); third, the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), which comprises the first three abodes;
fourth, the stage of practicing correct conduct (*samyakpratipatti-caryā-bhūmi*), referring to the abodes from the fourth through the ninth;
and fifth, the stage of certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*), which is the tenth abode.
The sixth is the stage of definitive practice (*niyatacaryā-bhūmi*), which is the eleventh dwelling;
the seventh consists of the final two dwellings, which constitute the stage of reaching the ultimate (*nisthāgata-bhūmi*).
The first six stages pertain exclusively to bodhisattvas, while the seventh is established as a stage through the combination of both bodhisattvas and tathāgatas.

Fifth, according to the lower fascicle of the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), thirteen Dharma Masters each abide in a distinct stage; this corresponds to the first [section]. Regarding these thirteen: first, the nature of the cultivated seed (*śikṣāgotra*);

second, the nature of the innate seed (*prakṛtisthagotra*); third, the nature of the path-seed (*mārgagotra*); fourth, the Mahāyāna of Good Awakening; fifth, Virtuous Wisdom; sixth, Luminous Wisdom; seventh, the Knowable (*jñeya*); eighth, Supreme Penetration; ninth, Constant Manifestation of Reality; tenth, Mysterious Penetration; eleventh, Equal Awakening, which is the eighth stage (*bhūmi*); twelfth, the Light of Wisdom and Spiritual Transformation, which corresponds to the ninth stage; and thirteenth, the Meaning of Contemplating Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which corresponds to the tenth stage and Equal Awakening. However, the Buddha himself is not included within the count of these thirteen.
Sixth, according to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, Upper Scroll, among the five types of patience (*kṣānti*), this corresponds to the lower stage of the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*).

Regarding the "five patiences," they are: the patience of subduing, the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*), the patience of compliance (*anuloma-kṣānti*), the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*), and the patience of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*). Each has upper, middle, and lower grades, which correspond respectively to the three stages of worthiness (*tri-satpuruṣa-bhūmi*), the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and wondrous enlightenment (*prabhāsvara-bodhi*).
The seventh also relies on the fifty-two stages of the *Renwang jing*, corresponding to its second stage.

The eighth relies on the forty-two stages of the worthy and sage (*xian-sheng*) in the *Yingluo jing*, corresponding to the "Lower Worthies" among the ten abidings (*shizhu*), because the ten faiths (*shixin*) are not established as a separate category here; rather, the ten faiths are subsumed within the ten abidings.
Ninth, according to the *Ābharaṇa-sūtra*, there are six kinds of natures, which likewise correspond to the first [category].

These six natures are: first, the nature of practice; second, the nature of essence; third, the nature of the path; fourth, the noble nature; fifth, the nature of equal enlightenment; and sixth, the nature of wondrous enlightenment.
If one relies on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and other such texts, there are no longer distinct stages (*bhūmi*).

This scripture, however, speaks of forty-two stages based on these [ten], without employing separate designations such as "provisional equipment" (*sambhāra*) or "preparatory application" (*prayoga*). Nevertheless, the stages thus described are established according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), wherein both the sequential arrangement (*vyavasthāna*) and the perfect fusion (*yuganaddha*) are mutually unimpeded, as explained in the *Xuanwen*.
The opening and closing of the ten levels of faith have already been seen in the "Chapter on the Worthy Head" (*Bhadrapāla*).
The fifth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, what is...", explains the aspects of practice (*caryā-lakṣaṇa*).

This exposition of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) is divided into ten sections; within each section, there is first a formal inquiry followed by an explanation, and within the explanation, there is first a clarification of the stage itself (svabhāga) followed by a clarification of its further advancement (viśeṣagamana).
Furthermore, the former refers to the stage of abiding, while the latter refers to the arousal of practice.
Now, regarding the first, this is the Stage of Resolving the Mind (Cittotpāda-vihāra).
The preceding inquiry may be understood as it stands.
In the explanation of the "own-nature" (svabhāva), there are two parts:
first, clarifying the conditions for generating the resolve; second, correctly clarifying the generation of the resolve toward its objective sphere.
This is the first.
The text enumerates ten conditions, while its meaning encompasses four causes, namely: faith, compassion, wisdom, and spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, constitutes the first general characteristic;
the section beginning with "arousing bodhicitta" concludes the preceding and introduces what follows.
The ten intermediate phrases specifically manifest the distinctions:

first, physical form and deportment; second, the major marks of color; third, being endowed with secondary characteristics such that one is pleasing to behold—these three constitute the observation of external features.
Appearing only once every four eons, he is difficult to encounter because his appearance brings benefit; this applies to both the internal and external [teachings].
The five powers, ten powers, and fearlessnesses for subduing Māra and overcoming outsiders clarify internal virtue;
the six inconceivable supernormal transformations are the wheel of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), which pertains solely to external application.

Among the six superior matters, if one perceives even a single event and gives rise to pure faith and a joyful aspiration to seek it upward, thinking, "If this can be cultivated, I shall certainly attain it," this constitutes the seventh [matter]:
hearing the bestowal of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). This contains two meanings:

first, hearing the prediction of becoming a Buddha and aspiring to be included among those so numbered; second, hearing that one will become a Buddha and aspiring to obtain this knowledge. Both are recorded in the wheel of the mind.
Eighth is listening to the instructions, whereby one knows that evil can be severed and the good can be cultivated; this is the wheel of instruction.
In the cases above, faith and wisdom serve as the causes.

Ninth is seeing those undergoing suffering and giving rise to a compassionate mind; this does not necessarily require hearing the teachings, for it arises from the innate, natural compassion and forbearance inherent within one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*); this is the cause of compassion.
Tenth is hearing the vast Dharma, which refers to the merits of the Buddha; its meaning encompasses both the extinction of the Dharma and its transmission or protection.
Because it serves as the cause for the lineage of compassion and wisdom, its meaning extends throughout the preceding ten [categories].

These ten conditions differ from the four conditions cited in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* within the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*) only in their expansion and contraction; that is to say, the first six are conditions for seeing the Buddha, the next two are conditions for hearing the Dharma, the next one is the condition for seeing beings undergoing suffering, and the last is the condition for seeing the extinction of the Dharma.
Regarding the subsequent summary that links what precedes with what follows: "Only upon realizing Bodhi does one complete the preceding matter" summarizes the former;
"seeking all-knowledge" pertains to what follows, as it refers to generating the resolve by taking the dharma that is difficult to obtain as its object.
Second, from "This bodhisattva" onwards, the text correctly explains the arousal of the mind by taking an object as its condition.
It was previously stated that one seeks "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*); the ten powers of knowledge (*daśa-jñānabala*) are precisely what constitutes all-knowledge.
The text contains a heading, an enumeration of names, and a concluding count, yet the meaning is already evident in the first chapter.
It is largely identical to the first stage (*bhūmi*), for it is for the sake of attaining the ten powers (*daśabala*) and so forth.

Furthermore, these ten powers are opened up from a single, ultimate wisdom (*ekasatyajñāna*) into ten; since they suffice for the work of transforming sentient beings and encompass the meaning of both compassion and wisdom, they are mentioned briefly here, though this does not mean that other qualities of the Buddha are not taken as objects of focus.
The second [section], on superior progress (*viśeṣa-gamana*), is divided into three parts:
first, a general statement; second, an inquiry followed by an enumeration; and third, an inquiry followed by an explanation.
Regarding the first: one who seeks a superior state should encourage oneself and also exhort others to study.
Within this list there are ten items, none of which fall outside the scope of compassion and wisdom.
Making offerings to the Buddha constitutes the general category, encompassing both material wealth and the Dharma;
the remaining nine items constitute the specific categories, for practicing these nine matters constitutes true offering.
First, dwelling joyfully in birth-and-death because great compassion is foremost, and because wisdom realizes its emptiness and thus has nothing to fear;
second, dwelling as the master of the path to eliminate evil;
third, being able to lead by means of the Dharma of principle and teaching.
Fourth, manifesting the fruit to inspire aspiration, which is the ultimate reach of the teaching;
fifth, training in the Buddha’s virtuous conduct as the means to reach it;
sixth, generating birth in the presence of a Buddha by relying on the conditions for accomplishing virtue.
Seventh, it is the tranquility that calms the agitation of seeking higher goals while transforming those below;
eighth, it is the tranquility that necessarily brings one far from the cycle of birth and death;

ninth, because it does not lose its compassion, it constantly serves as a refuge for sentient beings—this also summarizes the preceding meanings, as all actions performed are driven by the predominance of great compassion for sentient beings.
Question:
Regarding the eight ways of distancing oneself from birth and death, which initially cause one to dwell in happiness—how is this to be reconciled?
Briefly, there are three points of meaning:
First, one exhorts others to distance themselves from [suffering] while remaining personally untiring;
second, one must be free from self-bondage to be able to gather in others;
third, because it is compassion arising from wisdom, one joyfully dwells in birth and death, yet because it is wisdom arising from compassion, one remains distant from cyclic existence.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The bodhisattva’s revulsion toward birth and death exceeds that of the two vehicles by hundreds of thousands of millions of times; it is not that they lack revulsion.

This means that while not severing birth and death, one enters nirvana; while remaining unmoved within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one constantly follows the flow of saṃsāra, thereby accomplishing the path of non-abiding.
Furthermore, since at the outset they took pleasure in dwelling within birth and death, how could they subsequently appear before all Buddhas?
There are three reasons for this:
first, to entice sentient beings; second, to seek means for gathering and guiding sentient beings; and third, because their compassion and wisdom are unimpeded.
Furthermore, the Ten Treasuries, based on ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), accord with relinquishment; thus, upon hearing of the various Buddha-fields, one does not aspire to be reborn there.
These [Treasures], however, rely on provisional means (*upāya*) without destroying phenomena; therefore, one is born in the various Buddha-fields.
3. From "Why" onwards is the interrogation and explanation.
Why must one study this?
Because it enables one to attain both the general and specific benefits.
"Distinct" refers to that which is superior, excellent, and vast; these distinct benefits all aspire toward subsequent stages.
According to the following verse, they also cause one not to regress.
From the phrase "having heard" onwards, the benefits of all stages are universal, because understanding arises from internal phenomena and thus does not depend on others.
He has three types: first, those external to others;
second, those external to the mind; and third, those external to nature.
His own understanding is likewise threefold:
First, because the nature is formed through habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), one is able to achieve self-liberation;
second, one realizes that all is mind-only (*cittamātra*);
third, because one realizes that all is nature-only (*dharmatāmātra*), it is said below: "One knows that all phenomena are the very self-nature of the mind."
If that is so, why does it further say that there is "that which is heard"?
This refers to hearing in a general sense, or to investigating for oneself.

"Hearing" pertains to the Dharma, while "awakening" pertains to its meaning; since one certainly does not depend on another person for detailed instruction, it is said to be "not derived from others."
The ultimate state is the Buddha’s teacherless wisdom (*asāsrava-jñāna*).
The same explanation applies to all the subsequent stages below. Some say:
To claim that [enlightenment] arises from one's own seeds and not from another is merely the first sense [of the teaching]; how is it worth esteeming?
Furthermore, he cites the following passage: "Although one knows all dharmas and realizes them without relying on a teacher, one never tires of seeking a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra)."
Nor is it that same intention, for the former is based on dual practice while the latter concerns self-awakening.
Within the second stage, the Dwelling of Purifying the Ground (*bhūmi-viśodhana*), there are also two parts:
first, the interrogation, which may be understood; [the remainder follows].
Within the second explanation, the internal text of the *svabhāva* (self-nature) section has four distinct parts:
first, the heading; second, the inquiry; third, the enumeration; and fourth, the conclusion.
All subsequent *svabhāva* sections should be understood as following this pattern.
Regarding the ten mental states within the list, there are two meanings: first, that one gives rise to these ten mental states toward each and every sentient being;

second, that they are distinguished in relation to eight types of sentient beings: (1) toward hostile sentient beings, not only does one refrain from seeking retribution, but one even bestows benefit upon them; (2) toward suffering and destitute sentient beings, one gives rise to compassion with the desire to cause them to be free from such conditions; (3) toward sentient beings who are endangered, fearful, and lacking joy, one causes them to obtain inexhaustible requisites for happiness; (4) toward sentient beings of evil conduct, one causes them to abide securely in virtuous conduct; (5) toward sentient beings who have attained happiness, one uses a heart of pity to prevent them from becoming heedless; (6) toward followers of external paths who have not yet resolved their minds [on enlightenment], one gathers them to inspire right faith and the resolve for awakening; (7) toward those who have already resolved their minds and practice together, one guards them so they do not regress; and (8) toward all sentient beings who have embraced the vow for bodhi, one regards them as if they were one’s own self.
Within this, two categories are distinguished: those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle path are regarded as teachers, while those who have accumulated perfected merit are revered as Buddhas.
These ten [practices] are explained in the second stage of the *Mahāsamaya* (*Dàtóng dì'ér dì jíyì*). By means of these ten minds, one remedies the ground of one's own mind.
Regarding the two types of superior progress, there are also three.
Among the ten dharmas listed therein, there are both general and specific applications.
The general characteristics can be understood [from the preceding].
As for the specific dependencies in their successive order:
first, seeking extensive learning in general serves as the basis for the two types of beneficial conduct.
Second, having heard [the teaching], one should contemplate and practice it in seclusion;
third, having heard it, one must rely upon a spiritual friend;
fourth, in requesting instruction from a spiritual friend, one’s speech must be harmonious and pleasant.
Fifth, he does not inquire at improper times;
sixth, he is not terrified by profound dharmas such that he cannot accept them, nor is he intimidated by the practice of the Dharma such that he cannot practice it;
seventh, through the power of the wisdom of reflection, he understands and penetrates the profound meaning, rather than merely possessing extensive learning while remaining ignorant of its meaning.

Eighth, practicing according to the teaching: the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that approaching virtuous friends, hearing the true Dharma, maintaining mindful reflection, and practicing according to the teaching are the proximate causes and conditions for Great Nirvāṇa; these are now expanded into ten stages.
Ninth, because one accomplishes practice and subdues delusions, one is free from ignorance and confusion.

Third, the inquiry and explanation:
As for the reason for this cultivation, the preceding ten [perfections] were primarily concerned with wisdom; by guiding compassion with wisdom, one causes it to increase further.
The universal benefit [of this] can be understood.
Regarding the third stage, the Dwelling in Practice (*caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*):
in the explanation, first the "self-perfected" (*svabhāva*) aspect is clarified, which is the practice of guarding against afflictions (*kleśa*);
subsequently, the "superior progress" (*viśeṣa-gati*) aspect is clarified, which is the practice of guarding against the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Regarding the preceding section: however, these ten types of impermanence are largely identical to those in the *Tri-svabhāva-nirdeśa*, which that treatise explains in detail.

Since the text and its meaning encompass much, I shall briefly cite one or two points.
The Treatise states: "The non-abiding of the formations of life is collectively termed impermanence. This is the general statement.
Furthermore, there are two [aspects]:
The first is moment-to-moment impermanence; the second is the impermanence of a single lifetime.
Regarding what is impermanent:
it is suffering because it is characterized by the oppression of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 34, states: "By means of the mode of impermanence, preceded by mental attention (*manasikāra*), one enters into the mode of suffering.
By means of the mode of the non-apprehensibility of suffering, one enters into the mode of emptiness; because it is empty, there is no self-mastery."
"Because of lack of autonomy, one enters into non-self.
These four are the four aspects of the truth of suffering.
Fifth, "there is no agent," because it merely conditions existence.

Because of the impermanence of every moment, there is no volitional construction; because all things are suffering, there is no flavor of pleasure—only a perverse notion of pleasure arising amidst inferior suffering.

This is the perception that the entire world is not to be delighted in; for since it is empty, the myriad phenomena lack intrinsic substance, and things possess no reality corresponding to their names.
Because there is no self, there is no location; it does not exist within form, nor even within consciousness.
"Non-discrimination" refers to the observation of the grasper;
"lack of solidity" refers to the observation of the grasped.
Question:

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha rebukes a bhikṣu for his delusion regarding the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*). How, then, can one enter and abide in the practice of contemplating impermanence?
Answer:
They merely grasp the name but do not grasp its meaning;
because they subsume nirvāṇa under impermanence and so forth, the Buddha rebuked them.
Now, since we are speaking only of saṃsāra, there is no error.
Furthermore, it is "impermanent" because the Dharma-body has not yet been realized;
it is "suffering" because nirvana has not yet been attained;
it is "empty" because it lacks the existence of goodness.
Regarding "selflessness," it is because one has not yet attained the eight masteries.
Thus, the first four phrases speak of saṃsāra by themselves;
the subsequent four, beginning with "effortlessness" (anabhisaṃskāra), speak of nirvāṇa by themselves.
Because it is eternal, there is no action; because it is blissful, there is no flavor; because it is self, it is not like a name; because it is pure, it has no location.
Yet these two principles do not illuminate [the object] one-sidedly, but accord with it, just as when a mirror is suspended in a high hall, the myriad forms are all reflected therein.

Furthermore, the first four phrases signify that arising and ceasing through causes and conditions is the meaning of impermanence; the subsequent four phrases signify that neither arising nor ceasing is the meaning of impermanence, and for this reason they are called "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
To penetrate thoroughly the five aggregates of clinging as empty and non-arising is the meaning of suffering.
Because suffering arises from arising, and since arising is itself non-arising, it is without flavor.

That all phenomena are ultimately non-existent is the meaning of emptiness; because both the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena are themselves empty, they do not correspond to their names.

The meaning of "non-self" is that self and non-self are non-dual. Although the Buddhas may sometimes speak of a self or sometimes speak of non-self, within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena there is neither self nor non-self; therefore, there is no fixed location.
Therefore, the *Antaśikṣā-sūtra* states that non-arising and non-ceasing is the meaning of impermanence, whereas arising and ceasing is, conversely, the meaning of permanence.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 46, asks: "How does a bodhisattva contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being entirely impermanent?"

This means that when one contemplates the nature of the verbal expression of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one finds that at all times they are eternally non-existent; thus, these conditioned phenomena are eternally unobtainable.
If one attains this understanding, one enters the Middle Way.

If one follows the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra* in explaining this according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), then the non-arising and non-ceasing of the first and last two natures constitute the meaning of impermanence, whereas for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), arising and ceasing constitute the meaning of impermanence, and so forth.
Furthermore, it has no agent, because it is neither permanent nor impermanent.
It is flavorless, because it is neither suffering nor pleasure.
It does not conform to names, because it is neither empty nor non-empty, being beyond the reach of words.
That which has no location is neither self nor non-self, for it does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
That which is without discrimination is so because of the absence of conceptual thought and recollection.
That which lacks solidity exists only through its dependence upon the real and the unreal.

In the subsequent stage of superior progress, this constitutes the protection of the practice of the Hīnayāna; for those of the Hīnayāna do not seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) nor desire extensive knowledge.

Among the ten [realms], the first three are the places where the Buddha's work is performed: sentient beings are those to be saved, the dharma-realm is that which saves, and the world is the place of salvation.

The subsequent four realms are the places where views arise: non-Buddhists reckon the Great [Element] as the root of all dharmas, while followers of the Lesser Vehicle reckon the Great [Element] as the cause of all forms and the substance of the body’s formation.
The latter three realms are places of bondage.
How are they to be contemplated?
First, one contemplates their characteristics, knowing them in minute detail; second, one contemplates their nature, which is profoundly deep and equal.
The meaning of the threefold inquiry is:
"If one simply contemplates impermanence in general, what need is there to know it extensively?

Because one contemplates emptiness without obstruction, possesses vast knowledge and vision, understands both essence and characteristics simultaneously, and the wisdom of phenomena becomes increasingly luminous, this is the fourth stage, the Dwelling of Noble Birth (*janmaja-vihāra*).
Within this stage, there are five parts: namely, the definition of the name, the thesis, the inquiry, the enumeration, and the conclusion.
"Born from the sacred teaching" refers to the fact that wisdom arises from the outflow of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) teachings through the cultivation of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).

Furthermore, the subsequent verse states: "The sons of the Buddha contemplate the Dharma in this way; born directly from the Buddha, they are called sons of the Buddha. This [latter phrase] refers to the person who is able to teach.

Each of the three preceding meanings can give rise to the single subsequent meaning, while simultaneously manifesting the locus wherein they are produced.

Furthermore, it can be explained that the speaker and the spoken, the signifier and the signified, constitute these three distinctions; from these three, all three types of birth are equally worthy of veneration.
The ten matters listed herein correspond to the ten kinds of knowledge regarding phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) of the fourth stage, differing only in their expansion or contraction.
Having been born from the holy teachings, one accomplishes the four wisdoms to transform sentient beings.
The first is the wisdom of one's own abode, which is also that which is produced because it is non-retrogressive.

Third, the wisdom of suchness: because of skillfully observing phenomena, it is also the locus of production; "phenomena" here refers to the dharma-dhātu.

The fourth is the wisdom that discriminates what has been taught, which consists of the remaining seven phrases; namely, the thorough understanding of the emptiness and existence of sentient beings, the provisional and real aspects of Buddha-lands, the defilement and purity of worlds, the goodness and evil of karmic actions, and the suffering and pleasure of retributive fruits.
The two types of birth-and-death and the four types of nirvāṇa are fully explained as in the regular commentaries.
Regarding the subsequent ten stages of superior progress: the first three involve understanding and realization, encompassing both teaching, principle, practice, and fruit;
the next three involve the cultivation and accumulation of the dharmas of practice.
The next three vows shall fulfill the fruit;
the final one specifically clarifies the principle of the Dharma.
This is followed by the interrogation and explanation.
The intention to advance to the subsequent stage arises because the ultimate and the conventional are equal;
one realizes their equality only after observing that they are no different throughout the three periods of time.

Regarding the fifth, the Stage Endowed with Skillful Means (*upāya-saṃbhāra-vihāra*): the ten mental states of self-perfection (*svabhāva*) constitute skillful means, and the ten mental states of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*) are likewise fully endowed with them.

Now, within this stage of self-reflection, it is precisely during the second dwelling that one gives rise to this mind; taking the roots of goodness now cultivated as directed toward the intended goal, the explanation follows the previous pattern, and the text is clear throughout.
Now, this is treated separately as a single category: the first is the general statement, because it saves beings from suffering and protects their goodness.
How does it protect goodness?

Second, to cause them to obtain the fruit of happiness, that is, for the sake of peace and bliss;
third, out of compassion for their attachment to false pleasures, not to allow them to remain clinging to them;
fourth, how to rescue them from suffering?
Because it delivers all from suffering and attains liberation.
What is suffering?
There are two kinds of suffering:
First, the three calamities and eight difficulties; second, the two kinds of birth and death.
How can one leave them behind?
First, by generating pure faith through the teaching.
Second, by means of pure faith, one is granted the three trainings, whereby all faculties and afflictions are brought under control.
How does one attain happiness?
It is said that the realization of nirvana—the ultimate cessation of suffering—is true and eternal happiness.
The first phrase consists of nine characters that flow down to this point.
Within the subsequent section on "Superior Progression," the first six meanings encompass both the profound and the vast, while the latter four manifest only the extremely profound.
How is it vast?

First, it is boundless; second, it has no limits; third, it transcends calculation; fourth, it is beyond the reach of words and thought; fifth, its colors and categories are not uniform; sixth, it cannot be fully exhausted by measurement.
That which is called "profound" is boundless, meaning it is neither existent nor non-existent, and neither annihilated nor eternal.
That which is "immeasurable" is eternally a single kṣaṇa, for it has no length or brevity.
"Incalculable" means neither one nor different, because it does not fall within the realm of numerical calculation.
"Inconceivable" means that it is both delusion and truth, for the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
"Immeasurable color" refers to the simultaneous manifestation of the physical body and the environment.
"Incalculable" refers to transcending the two measures [of subject and object].
Among the latter four [categories], the seventh serves as the general heading, because of the emptiness of persons and phenomena.
How is this empty?
Eighth, with respect to that which establishes [the self], it is empty because it is not produced by itself, by another, or by both together.

The ten [categories] lack intrinsic nature; this explains that because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty.
Because they lack intrinsic nature, who could create them?
Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are non-existent, yet this is not a nihilistic non-existence.
Furthermore, seven, eight, and nine constitute the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).
The three questions and explanations intend to clarify that when both depth and breadth are illuminated and their natures and characteristics mutually penetrate, they become increasingly superior.
Because both form and grasping have perished and there is no defiled attachment, one accomplishes *prajñā*.
Thus, it is the sixth stage, the Stage of Right Mind (*samyaktva-cittāvasthāna*).

Within its initial section, because one has accomplished *prajñā* and realized the characteristics of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), all things are immovable; therefore, it is called "Right Mind."

The first four [verses] concern the Three Jewels of veneration: because one realizes that phenomena are equal and that sounds are like echoes, one gives rise to neither joy nor distress toward praise or blame.
Furthermore, this is because what is conventionally held as blameworthy is, from the perspective of ultimate principle, worthy of praise.
Therefore, the *Sārthavāha-devaputra-sūtra* states: "There is no one who can attain liberation without destroying [the bonds of] speech.
Next, the three [subsequent points] concern the sentient beings to be pitied.
The extremes of the finite and the infinite are the extremes of annihilation and permanence; the bodhisattva does not fall into them.
The extremes of the defiled and the undefiled are the extremes of increase and decrease; the bodhisattva remains far removed from them.
The extremes of the easily crossed and the difficult to cross are the extremes of suffering and pleasure; the bodhisattva does not dwell therein.
Furthermore, it is difficult for those with defilements and easy for those without them.
Conversely, because they do not give rise to the aspiration [for enlightenment] and thus do not recognize defilements, they are termed "without" [defilements].
The latter three [categories] pertain to the dharma-realm as the object of knowledge.

The finite and the infinite are likewise [the extremes of] annihilation and permanence; the other two, increase and decrease, are likewise so. Because one has already attained the correct mind, one remains unmoved by all of them.

Furthermore, with respect to sentient beings, because great compassion and great vows are limitless, and because one realizes the nature of the dharma-realm as transcending both the measurable and the immeasurable.

Knowing that the characteristics of the dharma-realm form the world through conditions, one speaks of its formation and destruction, yet it is neither formed nor destroyed; for while the essence possesses characteristics, the characteristics are non-existent, and while the essence is non-existent, the characteristics are existent—all of which is sovereignly free.
Moreover, since both are by nature devoid of sound, how could they possibly cause any movement?

Within the subsequent ten stages of superior progress, although it is recommended that the student engage in hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, the verse mentions only "hearing" (śruta), as these constitute a single unified meaning.

Among these points: first, because the characteristic of a self-nature is unattainable; second, because it is established through the conception of dependent origination; third, because the perfected nature is pure; fourth, because that which can establish [it] does not exist; fifth, because that which is established has no reality; sixth, because self-nature is fundamentally empty; seventh, because emptiness itself is also transcended; eighth, because the metaphorical appearance of conditions arises; ninth, because the metaphorical conception is produced; and tenth, because one is universally free from the conceptions of grasping, abandoning, emerging, and submerging.
This passage is largely similar in wording to the section in the *Sixth Ground* that treats the antidote to the pride of discriminating between defiled and pure phenomena.
