From the tenth point, "all are excellent," onwards, the characteristics of the perfected contemplation are distinguished.
The phrase "all are one's own mind" is used because wisdom is in correspondence with the mind.

The cause is the training of the mind; the fruit is accomplished by the mind; objects manifest through the mind; power and function are states of the mind; supernormal powers arise from the mind; discrimination is the mind’s discernment; and what is attained is the mind’s realization. Since nothing is obtained apart from the mind, what is there to cling to?
11. From "In this way" onwards, the conclusion summarizes the benefits of the contemplation.

Regarding the three sections from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, which reveal the essential excellence of the stage, the structure—consisting of the heading, the inquiry, the explanation, and the conclusion—is clear throughout the text.
The third response addresses the question regarding the purity of great practice.
It consists of twenty phrases:
the first ten are causes, and the latter ten are results.
Regarding the first point: because practice is perfected and obstacles are eliminated, it is called "pure.
Although the numerical designations differ slightly, they are largely identical to the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and also correspond to the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*).
What is practiced within the ten practices is precisely the ten perfections.
Because one desires to excel and progress beyond that, this [practice] is cultivated first.

Furthermore, as will be explained below, by preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, one increases all the perfections (pāramitās) for oneself; therefore, it is explained extensively again.
Since the points of focus differ, there is mutual omission and inclusion between them.
The first seven are understandable.

The eighth is that one practices the bodhisattva path toward evil sentient beings with an unshakable mind; this is the meaning of "that which is difficult to attain," because it is due to the original vow to transform them.
Among the nine practices of wholesome dharmas, one serves as a pool of refreshing Dharma for sentient beings.
With firm great compassion, one universally gathers in sentient beings, acting as their shelter and refuge; this is the vast deliverance of sentient beings.
This is like the meaning of a bridge, because it possesses the power of capability.

Regarding the ten true practices, the text states: "This bodhisattva enters the essence-nature of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and becomes equal in merit-roots to all Buddhas of the three periods of time, because their wisdom is decisive and their essence is identical."
Second, from the passage beginning "Once the bodhisattva has attained," [it is shown] that one attains the fruit of supreme dharmas through the purity of causal practice.

These are: (1) superiority of others' power, (2) superiority of one's own goodness, (3) superiority of profound meditative concentration, (4) superiority of shared practice, (5) superiority of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), (6) superiority of true wisdom, (7) superiority of intention (*āśaya*), (8) superiority of observational insight (*vipaśyanā*), (9) superiority of cultivation, and (10) superiority of progress.
The fourth response concerns the question of the great vows.
It consists of twenty phrases:
the first ten concern the arousal of supreme and pure vows, while the latter ten concern the exertion of the will to bring them to fulfillment.
Regarding the first [set of vows], they are entirely identical to the ten vows of the first bhūmi:
first, the vow to bring sentient beings to maturity;
second, the vow to purify buddha-fields.
Third, making offerings;
fourth, protecting the Dharma;
fifth, serving [the teacher].
Sixth, the commonality of roots of goodness;
seventh, the preeminence in gathering the Dharma and the penetration of the Dharma up to Buddhahood, termed the "Gate of the Tathāgata";
eighth, the non-emptiness of the three karmas.
Ninth, the complete cultivation of all practices;
tenth, the manifestation of perfect enlightenment.
However, as that text is extensive, if one follows its sequence, the order for the present [treatise] is five, seven, one, two, six, eight, three, nine, four, and ten.

Second, regarding the phrase "O Son of the Buddha, may the vows of the Bodhisattva be fulfilled": by means of these ten phrases, one is able to fulfill the aforementioned ten [vows] as well as many other aspirations.

Among them, the first five profound mentalities (*adhyāśaya*) signify what is enduring, while the sixth, "complete accomplishment," signifies what is vast. What is enduring constitutes the virtue of the Bodhisattva, and what is vast constitutes the activity of the Bodhisattva; the remainder can be understood accordingly.
The fifth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," answers the question regarding the protection of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
This passage also consists of four parts:

first, it concludes the preceding section and introduces the following one; that is to say, because the preceding practices and vows have accumulated to form the "piṭaka" (collection), there are only ten phrases, and no others such as "maturation" and so forth.
The text contains five pairs [of questions and answers], all of which are clear and can be understood.
The sixth section, beginning with "The Bodhisattva attains this," answers the question regarding how he constantly preaches the Dharma according to those who are to be transformed.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the conclusion of the preceding section and the introduction of the subsequent one, which refers to the accumulation of merit and wisdom used to gather in sentient beings;
second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the inquiry that introduces the topic; [and third, the actual exposition].
Third, the section beginning with "That which is called" correctly explains its meaning.
This is divided into two parts:
first, knowing the vessel and bestowing the Dharma; second, possessing the requisite qualities to achieve benefit.
At the beginning and middle [of the path], one first knows that there are four types of vessels:
First, those whose actions are driven by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); for example, the son of a goldsmith who should be taught counting the breaths (*ānāpāna*) and so forth.

Second, knowing the causes and conditions of their spiritual lineage (*gotra*); hearing the Dharma and generating the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) serves as the cause, and according to that cause, their nature is established.
1) Encountering a teacher and hearing the Dharma serves as the condition; following these conditions, the seeds are formed.
2) Third, knowing the ailments of mental activity, namely, the prevalence of greed and so forth.
4) Knowing the distinctions among aspirations.
Second, the bestowal of the Dharma from "greed" (*rāga*) onwards.
The text contains ten phrases;
the first two are self-evident.
There are two kinds of delusion:
first, being confused regarding phenomena, principles, teachings, and contemplative methods;

second, seeking through evil and heterodox means while disbelieving in karmic causes, which leads one to observe the twelve links of dependent origination so as to abandon false attachments such as the notion of a self-nature (*svabhāva*).
The first three are exclusively remedies.
Regarding the "four equal parts" (*catur-bhāga*): "equal" refers to the three contemplations being similar [in intensity], such that they cannot be applied simultaneously.
If they are equally predominant, one is taught to contemplate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), namely, that sensual desire is itself the path (*mārga*), and so forth.
If one is of equal or inferior capacity, one may give rise to wholesome roots and be transformed by others.
This explanation of the four parts is fully detailed in the thirteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*.

Fifth, for those who seek the pleasures of gods and humans, one speaks of the three types of suffering in order to [discourage] their attachment to birth and death; this is because they are pursued even by the suffering of conditioning (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The subsequent four points may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the ten matters of quiescence (*śānti*), they cause the quiescence of principle (*li-ji*) to be realized; if one sinks into the quiescence of emptiness, they cause the functional application of phenomena (*shi-yong*) to be realized.
From "Bodhisattva" onwards, this is the summary of acting according to what is appropriate.
Second, from "When preaching the Dharma" onwards, it clarifies the fulfillment of virtues and the attainment of benefit, consisting of ten phrases and ten pairs:
first, the connection between the text and the correctness of its meaning;
second, the non-differentiation of the Dharma and wisdom—namely, relying on the Dharma and not on the person, and relying on wisdom and not on consciousness.
Third, having ascertained that there is no contradiction, one relies on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not on sūtras of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Fourth, by establishing the principles of the Dharma, one is able to universally sever all doubts.
Fifth, by understanding the faculties of sentient beings, one enters the Buddha’s teaching.
Sixth, through silent accord with the ultimate reality, one illuminates the source of the dharma-nature.
Seventh, by severing attachment to the true Dharma, one eliminates grasping at persons and phenomena.
Eighth, through mindfulness of the Buddha, one fully understands the sounds [of the teachings].
Ninth, through skillful speech that transcends words, although there is neither speaking nor showing, one skillfully accords with the fundamental cause.
Tenth, causing awakening according to what is appropriate so that all ultimately returns to equality; this is the benefit of such teaching.
The seventh section, beginning with "The bodhisattva thus," answers the question regarding never abandoning the various *pāramitās*.
This section has two parts:

first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent; second, the actual exposition of the teaching. At the time of practicing the Dharma, one is already endowed with the ten *pāramitās*; even when personally cultivating these, it is for the sake of benefiting others, because one is consistently moved by great compassion and realizes equality.
Because they lead all the way to the fruit of Buddhahood, they are all termed "paths" (*mārga*).
Second, from the section beginning with "At that time," the characteristics of not abandoning the [practice of] deliverance are correctly demonstrated.
The ten perfections (*pāramitā*) constitute ten sections; in each, the characteristic is first analyzed, and subsequently, from the phrase "This is then," the name is concluded.

Within the first four [sections] that distinguish the characteristics, the characteristics of giving (*dāna*) and the others are distinguished first, followed by the characteristics of the *pāramitās* such as non-attachment (*asaṅga*).
Giving and ethical discipline (*śīla*) are easy to understand.
Regarding the three types of patience (*kṣānti*), all evils pertain to both the internal and the external.
"Regarding 'that mind'": below this, by accords with principle and attaining equanimity, one accomplishes the *pāramitā*.
Among the four types of diligence (*vīrya*), universally initiating all activities constitutes "cultivation without remainder," which is also the diligence of benefiting and bringing joy.
To constantly practice without indolence is "long-term cultivation" (*dīrgha-kāla-bhāvanā*).
To never regress is "uninterrupted cultivation" (*nirantara-bhāvanā*).
The former refers to diligence in preparatory application (*prayoga-vīrya*).
"Courageous and unassailable" refers to the cultivation of valor and the donning of armor with diligence.
From "Regarding all... onwards, this clarifies the characteristics of the perfections (*pāramitā*).
Within the five dhyānas, there are eleven phrases in the text:
First, he rebukes the five desires.

The reason for this rebuke is that meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is empty, tranquil, and profound like a still ocean; even to aspire toward the sublime realms of the sages is still called deluded emotion—how much more so to let one's thoughts race after the five sensory objects? How could such a thing ever constitute the Way?
How does one censure them?
Form is like a glowing iron ball; to grasp it is to be burned.
Sound is like a drum smeared with poison; to hear it is certain death.
Its fragrance is like the breath of a putrid dragon; to smell it brings illness.
Its flavor is like boiling hot honey; to lick it causes burns and wounds.
Its touch is like lying near a sleeping lion; to approach it leads to being bitten.

Regarding these five desires, one can never be satiated with their acquisition; like adding fuel to a fire, they ruin states and destroy families, causing harm life after life that exceeds even that of a vengeful enemy. Therefore, one should not be attached to them.
How much more so for a Bodhisattva who realizes that this very body is suchness—what could they possibly be attached to?

Second is the sequential entry into meditative concentrations (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), which refers to the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*), constituting the nine sequential concentrations.
The ten lower stages are fully explained in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*), which constitutes the dhyāna of all gateways.

Third is the concentration that abides in principle (*tattva-vihāra-samādhi*): it is a dwelling in tranquility free from the savoring of attachment, wherein wisdom accords with reality without emerging; this is called right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), for one thereby perceives the nature of the mind.
This is also the mark of a true noble being (*satpuruṣa*).
The essence of the two higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of concentration, while the remaining six are its functions.
Since these four eliminate afflictions—including craving, views, and pride—they are said to be entirely the mark of purity.
The fifth is the production of various samādhis, as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*: "Attaining this samādhi of True Suchness (tathatā), one is able to give rise to immeasurable gates of samādhi.
This refers to what was said in the preceding passage: "A single samādhi gives rise to samādhis as numerous as motes of dust," and so forth.
This is the characteristic of difficult practice.
Sixth is the elicitation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which means that through the refinement of meaning one enters the divine to achieve practical application;
it is also the characteristic of fulfilling one's aspirations.
Mastery over the seven stages in both reverse and direct order is also a mark of difficult practice.

To emerge from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), proceeding down to the first dhyāna, is called "reverse.
To emerge from the first dhyāna and enter the second dhyāna, proceeding up to the meditative absorption of cessation, is called "direct."

Within this, there should be both regressive and progressive leaps, meaning leaping over one, leaping over two, and so on up to leaping over all; that these are not mentioned in the text is due to abbreviation.
This is also called the Lion’s Gait Samādhi.
Regarding the eighty-one types of mastery that encompass all meditative absorptions, there should be four permutations:
namely, mastery over one absorption in one; mastery over one absorption in all;
[mastery over all absorptions in one]; and mastery over all absorptions in all.
Entering one within all;
entering all within all, because one has attained their source.
These are the nine meditative states of total knowledge.
There are three aspects of the meditative state (*samāpatti*):
first, the objects of focus of all concentrations; second, the boundaries of all concentrations; and third, the functional efficacy of the objects of all concentrations—all of which can be known.
The tenth [point] summarizes that the essence and function are not in conflict.
Regarding "samādhi," this is translated as "equipoise" (samāhita); it applies exclusively to states with mental activity (*sacittaka*) while encompassing both concentrated and distracted minds.

"Samāpatti" is translated as "attainment" (samāpanna); it encompasses both states with and without mental activity, referring specifically to the essential nature of meditative absorption across all stages.
These two qualities are called "equipoise" (samāhita).
The first two phrases refer to the essence of concentration, which pervades these three;
the six phrases refer to the function of concentration, which is that which is induced.
Regarding the term "Wisdom Seal" (Jñānamudrā), it refers to the single true reality (ekadharmatā).

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, among the explanations of the one hundred and eight samādhis, the second is named the "Treasure Seal Samādhi" (Ratnamudrā-samādhi), which signifies its correspondence with the prajñā of true reality.
The former two are meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while this one is wisdom (*prajñā*); their union constitutes the simultaneous practice of both.
Now, whenever the bodhisattva abides in any one of these, it is not in contradiction with all the other samādhis or these three [qualities].
Eleventh, one swiftly enters the stage of wisdom, which is also the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Because the practices of a bodhisattva’s concentration are boundlessly exhaustive and their principles reach the ultimate limitlessness, they are able to swiftly arrive at the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).
It is both the aspect of difficult practice and the aspect of happiness in two lifetimes.

Furthermore, the first four among the higher [dhyānas] are dhyānas for dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), while the subsequent five are dhyānas that induce the production of meritorious qualities.
The five [types of dhyāna] are also dhyānas that benefit sentient beings; the latter two [of these five] apply to all three [categories], and they further apply to the ten kinds of purity.
First, by way of mundane purity, because they are free from all attachment to flavor (*āsvāda*); this refers to the third phrase.
Second, supramundane purity is also subsumed under this phrase.
Third, purity of application is the first phrase.
Fourth, purity of attaining the fundamental state is the second phrase.
The five fundamental purities of superior progress constitute the fifth phrase.

Sixth is the purity of mastery over entering, abiding in, and emerging from meditative absorption; seventh is the purity of mastery over returning to realization after having relinquished meditative absorption—these latter two correspond to the seventh phrase.
The purity of mastery in manifesting the eight supernormal powers (abhijñā) corresponds to the sixth phrase.
The purity of being free from all dogmatic views and the purity of all afflictive and cognitive obscurations (kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa)—these two together are subsumed under the fourth phrase.

The remainder is as explained in the forty-third and forty-ninth fascicles of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* regarding the nine dhyānas; its characteristics will be manifested within the ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*).

Within the six types of *prajñā*, there are likewise ten phrases: the first three phrases—listening to the Dharma and associating with spiritual friends—constitute the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
The first phrase provides the direct clarification;
the second, "tirelessly associating with spiritual friends," is the condition for the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
the third, "delighting in hearing without satiety," is the cause of the wisdom born of hearing, for if one hears only briefly, such wisdom will not arise.
The fourth is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); because one reflects after having studied, it is said to be "in accordance with what has been heard.
Because one applies correct mental attention internally, it is said to be "according to principle" (*yoniśas*).
The fifth is also the wisdom of investigation; furthermore, because it skillfully discriminates within the state of being free from afflictions and because it abandons the afflictions.
6. From "skillfully observing" (*suvicāra*) onwards, all constitute the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*); this phrase refers to the awakening entry into suchness (*tathatā*).
7. Because of the deliberation of long-standing habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), one realizes the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*).
Eighth, being fully equipped with the realization that one is identical to all, it is called the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*).
Ninth, entering the gate of the two wisdoms.
Tenth, as the summary is already complete, it is called "resting."
The latter three are linked in succession.
Within these, there are likewise the characteristics of the nine gates; fearing prolixity, they are not explicitly correlated here.
Although concentration and wisdom are present within them in alternation, because they mutually adorn one another, the gates are distinct.
If they are fully integrated as a pair, the *Awakening of Faith* combines the six perfections into five gates;
the subsequent application of skillful means follows this same principle.

To engage with existence without becoming confused by emptiness is called skillful means; to observe emptiness without reviling existence is termed prajñā. How could it be that prajñā is unable to know existence?
If skillful means (upāya) do not contemplate emptiness, how can they be called "skillful means"?
It is not only these three; all myriad practices are likewise so.
How much more so for Prajñāpāramitā, which can carry out the myriad practices—what dharma would it not employ?
When quiescent illumination reaches the ultimate limit of principle, there is not a single practice that does not exist therein.
Thus, when opened, the myriad practices are vast and boundless; when merged, even "one" is not one. If one grasps the underlying meaning, there is nothing to which one does not penetrate.
Within the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*), there are likewise ten kinds:
first, skillful wisdom manifesting in the present world as an expedient means;
second, compassion that is not based on views of endearment, whereby one transforms others without weariness—this is the expedient means of compassion and wisdom guiding one another.
Third, arising function based on essence;
fourth, being free from both rejection and acceptance, all things are undefiled;
fifth, the simultaneous practice of both the ordinary and the sage, due to the non-duality of both.
Sixth, the path of non-abiding through the six practices;
seventh, observation of progress;
eighth, manifesting signs without attachment.
Ninth, entering all realms of existence while manifesting birth within non-arising;
tenth, liberating sentient beings through the manifestation of non-transformation as transformation.
The first nine constitute deliverance, while the remainder are all dedicated toward [enlightenment].
According to the "Causes and Effects" chapter of the *Ābhūṣaṇa-sūtra*, each of the latter four perfections likewise possesses three aspects.
Regarding the three aspects of skillful means (*upāya*): first is the skillful means of progressive advancement, which corresponds to the seventh phrase;
second is the skillful means of skillfully uniting existence and non-existence, which—excluding the fourth phrase—is entirely subsumed under this category.
The third, "neither abandoning nor receiving," corresponds to the fourth phrase. Within the eight vows there are also ten vows:

the first five and the last three take the word "exhaustion" (*jin*) as their initial term. The sixth is that the body constantly abides throughout the ocean of kalpas; the seventh is that wisdom exhausts the ocean of the mind; the eighth is the thorough exhaustion of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*); the ninth is the exhaustive manifestation of lands; and the tenth is the ultimate realization of the wisdom of the Buddha-fruit.
This seeking of bodhi consists of nine prior benefits and joys.

If categorized according to the three vows, the second, third, fourth, and fifth constitute the vows for one's own practice; the sixth and seventh pertain to supernatural powers; the first, eighth, and ninth pertain to external transformation; and the tenth encompasses both types of benefit.
The statement that "all are exhausted" is because their source has been thoroughly investigated.
Within the nine powers, there are ten phrases, each consisting of two parts: the naming of the term and the explanation of its meaning.

First, regarding "conformity with reality": the profound mind is the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-bala*); when it is defiled, it lacks this power, and it exists because it is the opposite of that state.
The rest may be understood by analogy; they are all powers resulting from the force of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*).

The *Ratnakūṭa-vaipulya-sūtra* (Yíngluò) speaks of three types, all termed "powers of supernormal knowledge" (*abhijñā-bala*): first, the power of retribution (*vipāka-abhijñā*); second, the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-abhijñā*); and third, the power of transformation (*nirmāṇa-abhijñā*). Observing those [categories], they likely correspond to the ninety-two phrases.
Within the *Prajñāpāramitā*, diagnosing the illness and knowing its root, and bestowing the Dharma in accordance with principle, is called *prajñāpāramitā*.
It also consists of ten phrases:
the first four concern knowing the severity of the illness;
The next three know the faculties, desires, and inclinations: first, the stage; second, the conduct; and third, the mind.
The final three know the Dharma and its enjoyment: first, knowing the Dharma of principle; second, knowing the Dharma of fruition; and third, universally awakening to the Dharma-realm.
The first seven [perfections] bring sentient beings to maturity, while the latter three constitute dwelling in happiness in the present life.
According to the *Ratnavyuha-sūtra*, there are three types of wisdom:
first, the wisdom of signlessness, which is the knowledge of the true reality of phenomena;
The third is the knowledge of emanations, which is the power of the Tathāgata;
the remaining two are both the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā).
The other meanings are as explained in the first assembly.
The eighth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," answers the previous question regarding how all sentient beings may be brought to liberation.
This is divided into three parts:
first, concluding the preceding and initiating the subsequent; second, clearly explaining the transformation and deliverance; and third, concluding that this accords with the original vow.
Regarding the preceding section: first, "concluding the previous purity" refers to being free from hindrances;
"perfection" means possessing both phenomena and principle;
and "not abandoning" means being constantly in accord.
Regarding "abiding in the great adornment," this summarizes the ten perfections as adornments, which constitute the essence of the Mahāyāna.
The subsequent section beginning with "according to what they contemplate" follows later because it presupposes the preceding [section].
Second, from "falling into evil realms" onwards, the text correctly clarifies the process of transformation and deliverance.
There are ten phrases, which can be categorized into four groups:
the first two cause one to depart from evil retributions.
In the three miserable realms, all except those in the Avīci hell are capable of generating the resolve for enlightenment, as was the case with the girl Maitrakanyā.
Second, by diligently practicing, one will escape the eight difficulties, encounter a Buddha, and hear the Dharma.
The next three [teachings] cause one to depart from unwholesome causes.
Regarding greed (*lobha*), there are two types: the former refers specifically to greed for forms (*rūpa-lobha*), for which one is taught to cultivate the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*);
the present case refers generally to greed for wealth, fame, and so forth, and therefore it simply speaks of "showing the dharma of non-greed."
Regarding the dharma of non-attachment: it refers to the contemplation of impurity and emptiness, as well as having few desires and being content.
Hatred is likewise of two kinds; since the former primarily concerns speech that can cause harm and opposition, one cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Now, since the latter concerns hatred toward both sentient and insentient beings, one should contemplate them as being of the same essence and thus not harbor hatred toward oneself.
The three types of delusion are also of two kinds, as clarified above;
this refers to erroneous delusion, which leads one to contemplate dependent origination.
The subsequent three [delusions] cause one to abandon the cyclic flow through the three realms, for all [of these] are to be reviled.
First, regarding desire, ill-will, harmfulness, and so forth, their meaning is seen in the Third Ground.

Second, although concentration and wisdom are seemingly balanced in the Form Realm, it is nonetheless a stage of meditative absorption; fearing that practitioners might become stagnant in quiescence, contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is taught for them, and furthermore, the correct contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*) enables the attainment of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Because the three formless absorptions are predominant, he speaks of "sublime wisdom" for them; furthermore, he demonstrates that one can only achieve permanent transcendence through correct contemplation of the truths.

Regarding the latter two [absorptions], he teaches the Three Vehicles according to the capacities of beings; moreover, he leads those who rely on provisional means back to the ultimate reality, enabling them to realize primordial quiescence.
Third, from "Just as in the past" onwards, it concludes by showing that because [the Bodhisattva] acts according to his original vow, he is truly able to deliver others.
The "Lion's Roar" refers to the certainty of his deliverance.
Ninth, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, it answers the previous question regarding the succession of the Three Jewels so that they shall not be severed.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, a general statement based on the preceding; second, from "So that" onwards, an inquiry and explanation of the reason.
Because they transform sentient beings so that they enter the ocean of the Three Jewels, they are able to succeed their predecessors and ensure that the lineage is not severed.
The text consists of four sections to establish ten propositions:
the first nine provide specific explanations, while the last one serves as a general conclusion.
Within the first three sections, both the general and the specific are explained; however, each subsequent section is progressively deeper than the preceding one.

The "universal" refers to its presence throughout all stages, while the "particular" begins with the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), next resides in the three levels of worthiness (*tri-kalyāṇaka*), and finally pertains to the entry into the stages (*bhūmi*).
What is the distinction between these three types of Buddha-nature?
Initially, one is taught to generate the resolve so as to possess the causal nature, for before its generation, there exists only the primordially abiding nature;
subsequently, one is praised for making great vows so as to bring about the practice of the cause, thereby ensuring that the generated resolve does not regress.
Regarding "great vows," these refer to the vow to seek enlightenment and the vow to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is the vow to prevent evil, as explained in the *Śīla-sūtra*;
and there is the vow to advance in goodness, as commonly elucidated.
Third, planting the seeds of the Buddha causes one to attain Buddha-wisdom; that is, by realizing *tathatā* (suchness) and becoming free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
The above has been explained according to specific distinctions.

As for the general [classification], it consists of generating the bodhicitta, which comprises three minds: namely, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*), and great wisdom (*mahājñāna*).

The first section is the totality, which already encompasses great compassion; the second section is the vow; and the final section is wisdom—meaning that by revealing the sublime principle, it causes one to momentarily perceive the nature of the mind, thereby becoming a vajra-seed.

Regarding the characteristics of the threefold differentiation of the seeds of the Dharma: first, by opening the treasury of the Dharma, the teaching is made to remain uninterrupted; second, by explaining the causes and conditions, the meaning is made to remain uninterrupted; and third, by possessing the four kinds of protection, the teaching, the principle, the practice, and the realization are all made to remain uninterrupted.

Furthermore, although one initially receives the teachings, true understanding has not yet been awakened; subsequently, although one possesses both understanding and practice, realization has not yet been attained.
What are the differences between these three types of monastic lineages (*saṃgha-vamśa*)?

The first receives the Dharma without deviation and thus first enters the ranks of the Saṃgha; the second cultivates the six points of concordant respect (*ṣaḍ-ānuśaṃsā-saṃgha-kriyā*), whereby monastic conduct is perfected; the third governs and manages the great assembly, causing the Saṃgha to be pure.
Furthermore, although one may initially follow the teachings, if one's understanding and practice are not yet complete, one is not yet a true companion.
Next, although one may possess complete understanding, if one's practice has not yet transcended the various fears, one cannot exercise self-mastery.

Regarding the "six harmonies," these consist of the three karmas as three, plus harmony in precepts, views, and material benefits; that is to say: harmony of body in gathering together, harmony of speech in being without contention, harmony of mind in being without opposition, harmony of views in shared understanding, harmony of precepts in shared observance, and harmony of benefits in shared distribution.

Furthermore, with respect to the Bodhisattvas, their three karmas are identical to compassion and their six [faculties] are of one essence; this is true harmony. Through universal reverence, they cause the Sangha to endure for a long time.

The concluding summary states that by propagating the Dharma and upholding the precepts—cultivating the three trainings in tandem—one ensures that the Three Jewels are never severed and that the process of transformation continues without end.
The tenth section, beginning with "The Bodhisattva in this way," answers the previous question regarding how the roots of goodness and skillful means are entirely not in vain.
First the brief, then the detailed.
Within the brief section, there are three parts:
first, connecting the preceding with the following; that is to say, because one is able to continue the Three Jewels, one's conduct is without fault.

Second, from "according to existence" (*yathā-bhavam*) onwards, because it is not empty, the three types of action (*tri-karma*) are without flaw; that is to say, the dedication of what has been performed is an action that is not empty.
Third, from "because it is without blemish" (*nir-avadyatvāt*) onwards, because it is without blemish, it is not empty, and what is performed is mutually established through reciprocity.
The internal defects of jade are called *xiá* (flaws); *xiá* refers to a fracture in its substance.
The external defects are called *diàn* (blemishes); *diàn* refers to a stain in its color.
This is to manifest that the three karmas are without fault, both internally and externally.
"A flaw in white jade may still be polished away, but a flaw in the three karmas cannot be remedied.
The first phrase restates what preceded;
the subsequent section, beginning with "that which is done," demonstrates the characteristic of being without blemish.
The following passages all clarify the characteristic of non-emptiness below.
When skillful means possess wisdom, the skillful means are not empty;
when wisdom possesses skillful means, the wisdom is likewise not empty.
This explains that the sphere of activity is not empty;
through the wisdom of dedication, it explains that the pursuit of the fruit is not empty.
The second section, beginning with "The bodhisattva thus," provides a detailed exposition in two parts:
The first part clarifies that one's own karma is not in vain; the latter part distinguishes how benefiting others is not in vain.
Although the first part clarifies non-emptiness, its meaning also encompasses the absence of error, because all that is pure is free from afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, this absence of fault is precisely because one's own karma is not empty, as it accords with tranquility and stillness.
The text consists of a heading, an inquiry, an explanation, and a conclusion.
Within the explanation, each point first presents a heading followed by its exposition.
The first four [verses] concern the adornment of the primary and secondary [bodies], while the subsequent six concern the adornment of gathering and transforming beings.
Regarding the phrase "the ground of nirvāṇa," it means that the ground is adorned by nirvāṇa.
This indicates that wherever one attains enlightenment and enters nirvāṇa, that ground should be known as adamantine (*vajra*).
Now, since it is accomplished in all places, there is nothing that is not vajra.
The heading states "nirvāṇa," while the explanation says "attaining the Way"; this is merely a stylistic abbreviation in the text.
Fourth, the section beginning with "The bodhisattva’s accomplishment" is the concluding text, which can be understood [by itself].
Second, the section beginning with "If there are sentient beings" concerns the non-emptiness of benefiting others.
Within this, there are the elements of the thesis (*dharma*), the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*), which can be understood from the text itself.
Both the Buddha and the bodhisattvas benefit others without fail; as for why they are not seen now, it is because it is not appropriate for them to be seen at this time.
Regarding "seeing that which is not beneficial," this is because there is no power in practice and because it is remote from benefit.
The preceding section has completed the answers to the questions concerning the practices to be accomplished.
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this... onwards, the answers to the questions concerning the virtues accomplished by those practices are provided.

The preceding text consisted of two parts, and the present section likewise has two sections: first, answering by means of the virtues resulting from practice; second, answering by means of the virtues resulting from the cause.
Now, for the first part, all twelve questions are answered in full, each having two phrases:
the upper phrase answers the lower phrase.
The previous section asked what kind of cessation is cultivated; here, the answer is given in terms of wisdom.
All other instances should be understood accordingly.
Second, subduing Māra through the application of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Those who wish to harm others, conversely, invite harm upon themselves; whereas those who sincerely desire to bring peace to others find that both things and self are at peace. Thus, the supple overcomes the rigid, and the weak overcomes the strong.
By using compassion to pacify all malevolent māras, one leaves them with no means to inflict harm; the power of the roots of goodness born of such kindness is immeasurable.
Regarding the three blessings, he intimidates them with his majesty; regarding wisdom, he subdues them with his eloquence.
The texts for the subsequent four and the following four [sections] can be understood accordingly.
The eighth section, which states "giving birth through skillful means and wisdom," is the answer; the passage beginning with "all bodhisattvas" is that which was asked.
According to the preceding text, there are seven matters here; however, the phrase concerning *dhāraṇī* is missing below the section on "pāramitā.
Nevertheless, there are two types of skillful means (*upāya*):
if it is the skillful means of preparatory application (*prayoga-upāya*), it gives rise to the stages and perfections (*bhūmi-pāramitā*).
If skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) is present, it likewise gives rise to the various perfections (*pāramitā*) and the other five dharmas.
Wisdom (*jñāna*) also has two aspects:

if it is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), it constitutes internal realization; if it is subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it constitutes functional activity. Therefore, these two give birth to these seven.
Regarding the term "purification," it refers to the remediation of those obstacles.
Second, from the words "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the answer addresses the question concerning the attainment of the fruit through causes.
This section also consists of two parts:

First is the summary of the accomplishment of the fruit based on the cause, meaning that by diligently cultivating the various practices mentioned above, one can successively attain the fruit from the cause.

Second, from "In boundless worlds" onwards, is the direct answer regarding the virtues accomplished; this refers to the protection and upholding of the True Dharma. It means that by simply diligently cultivating the virtues previously practiced to form the cause, one will naturally accomplish the subsequent virtues such as protecting the Dharma and so forth; therefore, this is clarified by riding upon the previous summary of the accomplishment of virtue based on the cause.
The answer to the ten preceding phrases is divided into nine sections:
First, answering the initial general phrase, [it states that] the Tathāgata’s Dharma-treasury is protected and expounded.
Second, because it is protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness, this answers the point that neither Māras nor non-Buddhists can obstruct or destroy it, as it is shielded by the Buddha.
3. From "Guarding and upholding" onwards, the answer concerns the inexhaustible preservation of the True Dharma.

4. From "In the boundless" onwards, the answer concerns how, when preaching the Dharma throughout all worlds, the ten kings respectfully protect him—meaning that their superior bodies and skillful voices cause listeners to enter into wisdom.
5. From "Knowing all sentient beings" onwards, it answers [the question] by showing that he is universally admired and praised, and that he brings joy to others according to their capacities.

6. From "His body is upright and handsome" onwards, it answers [the question] because Bodhisattvas love and respect those who are upright, handsome, and virtuous; his consecration (abhiṣeka) occurs within the second section on the Buddha's protection mentioned previously.
7. From "Skillfully knowing the minds of the assembly" onwards, the answer concerns attaining the power of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and the increase of pure dharmas (*śukladharma*).

Within this, first the three types of action (*trikarma*) are explained in general; subsequently, from "attaining the mind" onwards, ten kinds of mastery (*vaśitā*), all of which are roots of goodness, are specifically revealed.
The capacity of these ten masteries is entirely for the increase of wholesome dharmas (*śukladharma*).
Section Eight, from "In this way, the bodhisattva... onwards, answers the question by expounding the Tathāgata’s profound treasury of the Dharma.

9. From "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva attains such [realization]" onwards, the text answers the question regarding how one adorns oneself by upholding the True Dharma (*saddharma*). Within this section, it first clarifies self-adornment, followed by an inquiry, and finally an explanation.
Because they encompass the True Dharma, there are ten phrases of virtue; these are also the very virtues previously established, which may be understood by analogy.
This concludes the second section, the Section of Verses.
The ten verses are divided into two parts:
the first six verses praise the essence of the ten types of practices accomplished, and the latter four verses praise the virtues accomplished through those practices.
Within the former, the first two verses praise the Buddha’s joy; therein, the first half-verse praises heedfulness (*apramāda*), while the remainder praises the Buddha’s joy.
Two verses describe entering the stages (*bhūmi*), as well as the great practices and great vows.
Three verses describe the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and the teaching of the Dharma for those to be converted.
The first four verses praise not abandoning one's own practice of the perfections (*pāramitās*) and ensuring that all sentient beings one has in mind attain liberation.
The fifth verse praises the non-interruption of the Three Jewels (*triratna*).
The first six and a half verses praise the skillful means of the roots of goodness, all of which are entirely non-empty.
Following the section beginning with "What the Bodhisattva Cultivates," the subsequent verses praise the virtues accomplished through practice:
the first verse praises the causal virtues of the initial practice, while the final three stanzas praise the resultant virtues achieved through those causes.
Among these, the first two verses generally summarize the preceding eight sections;
the final verse specifically summarizes the ninth response concerning the adornment of oneself by upholding the True Dharma, illustrating it through a metaphor:
"The physical demeanor is peaceful and composed," which summarizes the manifestation of the body.
Next, the majestic power of his virtues is distinguished: the first verse praises him through fearless eloquence;
the second praises him for stabilizing those who are timid and weak;
the third praises him through profound wisdom as deep as the ocean.
The five dharmas rain down to extinguish hindrances; having praised the preceding [section], he now preaches the Dharma.
Third, from "At that time, Dharmamati" onwards, is the section clarifying the conclusion of the preaching.
This means that because it accords with principle and suits the capacities of the audience, the Buddha rejoices and the assembly reveres it.
The Third Assembly concludes.

Chapter Nineteen: Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven.
This is the nineteenth chapter of the Sūtra, the third within the Middle Section, the Assembly on the Ten Practices of the Bhadramati Bodhisattva.
Regarding the intent of this initial passage: it serves as a response to the ten preceding lines of inquiry.
"It is not difficult to know; it is difficult to practice.
Having previously explained these practices, they are now like the mutual dependence of oil and light, or the complementary support of eyes and feet; thus, this section follows in sequence.
Regarding the subsequent sections that follow: this assembly’s four sections are divided into three parts:

the first two sections concern the causes and conditions of the assembly; the next section concerns the main body of the teaching for the assembly; and the final section concerns superior progress toward the subsequent stage.

Within the *Yūchì* (Expedient Means), the subsequent chapter elucidates the praise of virtues and the manifestation of the essence; this present chapter first clarifies the mutual resonance and interaction between the response and the stimulus.
As the preceding assembly has concluded and the subsequent discourse is about to be presented, this chapter follows accordingly.
Second, regarding the explanation of the names, there are three ways of designating this assembly.
First, it is named the "Assembly in the Palace of Yāma Heaven" based on its location.

*Yāma* is translated here as "time-period" (*kāla-bhāga*); it is the foremost among those who dwell in the void. This signifies that when the ten practices engage with the realm of existence to transform sentient beings, one must act appropriately according to the timing; speaking at the right time causes listeners to rejoice and submit, while acting at the right time causes observers to revere and follow.
Traversing existence by relying on emptiness and entering the profound through phenomena, he speaks based upon this.
With respect to the person, it is named the Forest of Merit; with respect to the Dharma, it is named the Assembly of the Ten Practices, as will be explained later.
All three [titles] are *tatpuruṣa* compounds.
Regarding the name of the chapter: it is largely the same as that of the assembly (*parṣad*).

However, in the Sanskrit manuscript, the character for "ascending" (*sheng*) is absent above, while "spiritual transformation" (*shenbian*) appears below; the translator has thus rendered "ascending" as "spiritual transformation."
Ascending as a divine transformation (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇā*) briefly comprises four meanings:

first, because one ascends to this state without departing from the preceding three; second, because ascending to one place constitutes ascending to all places; third, because having ascended, one expands that location; and fourth, because the preceding and succeeding moments are simultaneous and unimpeded.
This means that with his all-pervading body, the Buddha ascends to the celestial palaces of the *Tuṣita* heaven without rising from his seat.
"Ascending" refers to the Tathāgata, while "*Tuṣita*" specifies the location; this is an example of the *tatpuruṣa* (determinative) compound.
As it was previously stated that he ascended Mount Sumeru and subsequently ascended Tuṣita, this may be understood by analogy.
Regarding the three points of essential purport: the essential purport of each chapter is as its title indicates, and their underlying intent can be understood accordingly.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text: this first chapter is divided into ten sections.
The first is "The Fundamental Assembly’s Perfect Pervasiveness," which means that the subsequent assembly is explained without the preceding assembly being dispersed.

The first phrase constitutes the pervasive cause; from "the ten directions" downward, it constitutes the pervasive characteristic. It also includes the primary and attendant [deities] and so forth, all as explained above.
However, by adding Mount Sumeru to the location, the preaching of the Dharma extends throughout the three aforementioned assemblies.
The second section, from “At that time, the World-Honored One” onwards, describes ascending without departing.
The third section, from “At that time, the Yāma [Heaven]” onwards, concerns the celestial king seeing the Buddha; these are both as in the previous assemblies.
The fourth section, from "immediately" onwards, describes the individual adornments of the palace and the seats.
The first phrase indicates that the practice arises based upon emptiness; thus it says "transformed.
Because non-attachment guides the practice, it is called a "lotus."
A single practice contains many [elements], which is why it is called a "Treasury" (*piṭaka*).
The rest is as explained above.
From "one million" onwards, the characteristics of the adornments are specifically revealed; herein there are four parts:
First, the substance of the seat is clarified as being fully endowed with majestic virtues; all are said to number one million, because their positions gradually increase in scale.
Next, from "one million Yāma [gods]" onwards, the surrounding adornments of the seat's sides are clarified.
Third, from "One million" downward, the practice and virtue of the dharma-gates are adorned.
The text contains eight phrases, which are subsumed into four pairs:
first, causes and conditions;...
Second, merit and wisdom, because the profound mind accords with principle;
third, aspiration and practice;
fourth, essence and function, because they arise from the essence of the dharma of non-arising.
The fourth section, the final sentence, concerns the solemnity of the transmission of the Dharma teachings.
The fifth section, beginning with "At that time he," records the invitation for the Buddha to reside in the palace.
The sixth section, beginning with "At that time the Buddha," describes the Tathāgata’s acceptance of the invitation.
Seventh, from "At that time" onwards, each [section] recalls past causes.
However, as for the fact that the sound of music ceasing is present in the Jin translation but omitted here, it reflects the intention of the translator.

This means that it does not accord with the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*), which involve returning to principle through phenomena; nor does it speak of the cessation of pleasant sounds.
It does not reach the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), where phenomena and principle are without obstruction; nor does it speak of being "blazing."
The regressive [stages] may be understood as before, and the progressive [stages] may be aligned with what follows; therefore, both are abbreviated here.
The eighth verse praises ten Buddhas.

These ten Buddhas precede the ten Buddhas of the previous assembly; in successive order, these ten Buddhas clarify that their positions are gradually higher and their recollections of the past are more remote. In truth, however, all Buddhas of the three periods of time are described in this same manner.
The remainder is as in the previous assembly.
The text also has two parts:
first, clarifying this realm; second, distinguishing the universal application.
Each of the ten verses in the preceding section also contains four parts:

first, the initial line designates the name and praises its specific qualities; second, the next line generally reveals that it is endowed with auspiciousness; third, it recalls having previously entered this hall; and fourth, it concludes by establishing the location as the ultimate excellence.

Furthermore, the first line of each verse differs; the first two characters are specific names (*viśeṣa-nāman*), the next two characters are general titles (*sāmānya-saṃjñā*), and the final three characters are specific virtues (*viśeṣa-guṇa*).
In all cases, the specific virtues below explain the specific names above:
first, "renown throughout the ten directions" explains and establishes the name "Renowned."
Second, the meaning of "Jewel King" (ratnarāja) is explained by means of the "Lamp of the World.
Among jewels, there is the night-luminous pearl that can serve as a lamp; thus, it is the king among jewels.
Because the Buddha possesses the light of wisdom that illuminates the night of ignorance, he is called the Jewel King.
The meanings of [the numbers] three, four, five, and six can be understood accordingly.
Seventh, he is explained as the "Victorious Deva" (Jinadeva) by means of the "Lamp of the World," because the radiance of his body and wisdom surpasses that of the devas.
Eighth, he is explained as the "Hero of Treatises" (Śāstravīra) by means of being "One Who Does Not Depart" (Agantṛ), because he possesses courageous wisdom and eloquence and is unshakable.
The ninety [items] may be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, within this context, each pavilion is given a distinct name: the first indicates the essential substance of the adornment, while those below all denote specific qualities of the jewels. That is to say, these jewels are pure; being employed for adornment, they are preeminent and stainless.
This jewel emits fragrance; this fragrance must be exquisite.
This jewel that can adorn all things sees nothing it does not encompass, and may thus be called the Universal Eye.
Such adornment is sublime adornment; there is nowhere it does not adorn, and is therefore named Universal Adornment.
Furthermore, "well-adorned" means it arises from wholesome causes.
Ninth, from "At that time, the World-Honored One entered... onwards, the Buddha ascends the hall together with the assembly.
Tenth, from "This hall... onwards, the space suddenly becomes vast and accommodating, as in the previous assemblies.

Chapter Twenty: Verses of Praise in the Palace of Yāma. Regarding the intent of this initial section: it is for the purpose of assisting in transformation through praise and glorification, for explaining the essential nature of practice, and for clarifying that upon which practice relies.
However, the three celestial hymns of praise share the same fundamental intent and general purport; they differ only in their respective interpretations of practice and vows.
Their definitions and essential purports do not differ from those previously mentioned, though there are slight distinctions regarding their locations and modes of practice.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the text, there are also three parts:
first, the gathering of the assembly; second, the emission of light; and third, the praise in verse.
Within the first part, there are ten sections:
1. Clarifying the causes for their gathering, which also means that each manifests supernatural powers according to their respective categories.
2. From "In the ten directions" onwards, the subject is the Bodhisattvas.
3. From "Each one" onwards, it concerns the number of their retinues.
Fourth, regarding the scale from which "one hundred thousand" is derived:

it clearly shows that the numbers increase according to the stages; faith at the ten abodes is ten, at the hundred [abodes] it is one hundred, and at the ten dedications it is ten thousand. This should logically correspond to one thousand, yet it is stated as one hundred thousand; this may be an error by the translator, or perhaps an error in transcription where "ten hundred" was written instead.
5. "Their Names" lists the names of the bodhisattvas below.

Those who share the name "Forest" (Vana) represent the establishment of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*): because the types of practice are vast and manifold; because they are gathered together and manifested; because they are profound, secret, and uninterrupted; and because they provide shelter and shade like spreading branches.
These ten bodhisattvas represent the essence of practice, which can be understood through careful reflection.

Sixth, regarding the passage "these bodhisattvas" and below, the name of the land from which they come is the same—Wisdom (Hui)—because wisdom is that upon which the practice of the ten stages of understanding (daśabhūmi) relies.
7. "These various bodhisattvas each [serve]" and so forth clarifies the Buddhas they serve.
They are all named "Eye" (Cakṣus) because, by guiding their practice with wisdom, they perceive things with perfect clarity and thus become those who possess both eyes and feet.

This refers to the Buddha of the fruit at the stage of the Ten Practices; since all those who manifest at this stage are called "Eyes," one should explain it by contemplating the mutual correspondence between the Buddha of that realm and the Bodhisattvas of that same realm.
8. From "These various... down to "...having already paid respect.
9. From "According to what... down to "...participating without intermixture.
10. From "In this way... down to "...concluding with inexhaustible pervasion."
Second, from "at that time" onwards, light is emitted from below.
"Above the feet" refers to the tops of the heels, as movement necessarily involves the feet.
The backs [of the hands] depend upon the wheels and fingers to function; this symbolizes that practice depends upon faith and understanding to achieve its utility.
The remainder is the same as in the preceding assembly.
Third, from "At that time, Forest of Merit" (*Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha*) onwards, it clarifies the recitation of verses of praise.
Ten bodhisattvas speak, which constitutes ten sections.
Furthermore, beginning with the eastern direction and ending with the zenith, each has its basis for the recitation of verses, namely "relying on the Buddha’s power" and so forth.

Regarding the first bodhisattva here, speaking from the perspective of his capacity to teach: because he has accumulated practices within himself and his merits are perfected, he is named "Merit" (Guṇa).
If one considers that which is praised, it praises the Buddha’s supreme virtues; thus, it is called "The Forest of Merits.
There are twelve verses, which serve as the presiding master of this assembly to provide a general summary of the universal matters of this gathering.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, eight lines describing and praising his extraordinary qualities; second, four lines citing his virtues to provide an explanation and confirmation.
Within the former part, there are four sections:

The first verse describes the emission of light in this chapter; the next two describe the responsive manifestations of the preceding chapter; the following three describe the assembly of the multitude in this chapter; and the final two clarify the pervasive universality of sovereign mastery.
The final four lines explain and establish the preceding two through the elevation of their virtues:
the first two cite the causes to manifest the function, while the latter two distinguish the profundity and vastness of the resultant function.

Within this, the first [pair] concerns the mastery of essence and function: the upper half shows that without departing, one reaches everywhere; the lower half shows that the characteristics of contraction and expansion are both exhausted.

That is to say, if the one body were many, then the characteristic of oneness could not be apprehended; if the many were one, then the characteristic of multiplicity could not be apprehended. Therefore, it is eternally one and eternally many, yet eternally neither one nor many; by this, there is mastery.

Within a single atom, the body is omnipresent throughout the ten directions; bodies pervading the ten directions simultaneously reside within a single atom. These are all perfectly pervasive rather than partially pervasive, and are therefore inconceivable.

The latter [verse] establishes the characteristics of profundity and vastness: the first half reiterates the vast to distinguish the profound, while the second half explains the profound to reveal the vast. That is to say, because it does not abide, there is nowhere it does not reach; because it does not go, it does not depart from its original position. This is the explanation of the profound.
There is nowhere it does not universally penetrate, from a mote of dust to a hair; it is vast and boundless.

The first [section] clarified meritorious virtues, while this section distinguishes wisdom. Because one awakens to this wisdom that dispels darkness and is difficult to encounter, it is called the Forest of Wisdom (Prajñāvana).
In the verses, this is praised; the ten stanzas are divided into three parts:
the first clarifies that a Buddha is difficult to encounter;
the next six provide a detailed explanation of this difficulty, which is further divided into three sections:

The first two [verses] concern the difficulty of encountering the vast benefit; the next one concerns the difficulty of encountering the perfection of causes; and the final three concern the difficulty of encountering the profound fruit.

Within these, there are three verses that employ comparative measurement to reveal their excellence: the first compares them to great practices over a long period, the second compares them to making offerings to Buddhas over a long period, and the third compares them to offering superior objects to Buddhas.
The third section, "The Excellent Grove" (*Sudhana*), awakens one to the profound Dharma of ultimate truth; thus, it offers verses of praise for its boundless and vast virtues.
These ten verses are divided into two parts:

the first three clarify the Buddha’s virtues as being expansive and extensive, while the latter seven reveal the profundity of the essence of the Dharma, with the horizontal and vertical aspects mutually illuminating one another.
Regarding the preceding section, the first two [verses] provide metaphors, while the final one provides the doctrinal application (*dharma-saṃgīti*).
The expression "the month of early summer" is a free translation based on the intended meaning;
in the Sanskrit original, it is a direct correspondence translated as "the latter hot month."
In the Tathāgata’s holy teachings of the Western Regions, the year is established as having three seasons, namely: the hot, the rainy, and the cold.
The *Xiyuji* states: "From the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month constitutes the hot season."
Thus, the statement regarding the "hot month" refers to both the latter half of the fourth month of spring in this region;
the other two seasons each consist of four months, which can be understood by applying the same principle.
The words of the "Blazing Sun" merely take the long duration of sunlight as their basis, for its limits are difficult to exhaust.
In that region, there may be four seasons with names identical to those here, differing only in that they take the dark fortnight of the first month as the beginning.
Failing to see this text, they have erroneously offered divergent interpretations.

Regarding the latter seven [points], they are intended to cultivate the contemplation of the three natures of non-essence (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) with respect to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because the other two natures are not separate from the dependent nature and because the [other] two natures are established by means of the dependent nature.

This means that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the very essence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is merely a horizontal clinging to the dependent nature, which further arises from delusion regarding the true and its semblance. Thus, based on these three natures, the three absences of nature (*trisvabhāva-niḥsvabhāvatā*) are taught.
If even the three natures are ultimately one, how could there be three absences?

These three absences are simply the absence within existence; these three natures are simply the existence within absence. Existence and absence are non-dual as the single true nature; since existence and absence mutually negate their forms, even this nature is not a nature. Therefore, within the single dependent nature, one cultivates all contemplations.
The text is divided into three parts:

the first three [verses] cultivate the contemplation on the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of arising; the next two cultivate the contemplation on the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of the ultimate while concurrently practicing it; and the final two cultivate the contemplation on the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics.
Now, this first section is divided into three parts;
the initial verse correctly contemplates non-arising (*anutpāda*).

The first line concerns the emptiness of the fruit (*phala-śūnyatā*), meaning that the phenomena which are fruits produced through conditions do not possess a pre-existing essence that comes from the primal nature (*prakṛti*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), or the causal seeds within the future storehouse (*ālayavijñāna*) or the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*). If there were a place from which they came, they would already exist beforehand, like a bird coming to perch in a tree; how then could one speak of "arising"?
The second phrase concerns the emptiness of causes.
Since the effect does not exist, in relation to what could a cause be spoken of?
Furthermore, even the "nature of the world" (jagat-prakṛti) and so forth are merely falsely imagined as existing through causes and conditions.
The next line dispels both [possibilities].
That from which something arises is the cause; that which is produced is the effect.
Furthermore, the first line refutes arising from self, the second line refutes arising from another, and the third line refutes arising from both.

Furthermore, the first phrase [shows that] it does not arise from pre-existence; the second phrase [shows that] it does not arise from prior non-existence; and the third phrase [shows that] it is neither half-existent nor half-non-existent. Each of these three meanings uses the final phrase to still delusion and establish contemplation.
The subsequent verse explains non-extinction by means of non-arising, which briefly has three meanings:
first, because there is no arising that can be extinguished; second, because there is nothing to be depended upon or opposed; and third, by analogy with arising, which proceeds from conditions.

The subsequent verse observes the benefits of accomplishment; as the Sūtra says, "Non-arising is itself the Buddha," the Treatise states, "If one perceives the law of dependent origination, one is able to see the Buddha," because that which depends on others and conditions is precisely non-arising.

Regarding the next two verses, which concern the contemplation of the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) in conjunction with the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*): the preceding verse eliminates that which is to be contemplated. The first half of the verse distinguishes the contemplation, while the second half clarifies its benefit; because each contains two meanings, the term "conjunction" (*jia-xiu*) is employed.
First, establishing the preceding [point]: it means that not only is the arising of the characteristic of production itself non-arising;
the nature of the produced dharma, being devoid of intrinsic nature due to its dependence on conditions, is likewise non-existent.
This reveals that the non-arising of the dependent nature is the benefit of the perfected nature.
Why is it called "profound"? Because it is the truth within phenomena themselves.
Second, it is said that even the true nature of non-arising is non-existent; this is the benefit of the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
"Clouds are deep" means that true nature cannot be established.
The subsequent verse dispels the "observer," yet it carries two meanings:

first, it perfects what was previously observed; that is to say, because there is no intrinsic nature, there is no one who can cognize. This is like having no person who can cognize the length, shortness, largeness, or smallness of a tortoise's hair; knowing that there is nothing to be cognized is ultimate cognition.

The second [verse] correctly dispels the cognizer; since there is neither an object to be cognized nor a subject that cognizes, the simultaneous disappearance of both subject and object constitutes ultimate liberation.

Regarding the observation of the lack of intrinsic nature in characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), the first of the final two verses provides the direct explanation, while the latter verse provides the summary.
In the first half [of the verse], the first part reveals the grasping.
Because one does not understand that the country and so forth are dependent on others, one takes them to be directly perceived and falsely imagines them as being produced.
The Jin translation says: "That which is called 'having production' should be known to arise from that which is produced."
The second half clarifies contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); for if one knows the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), one is then free from the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The final verse provides a summary, describing how one contemplates the world and so forth in accordance with the reality of phenomena and principles; therefore, it is well-spoken.
The fourth [section] is named the Forest of Fearlessness (*Abhayavana*), because through the power of faith and aspiration, one hears the profound teachings without fear.
This is because the ten verses praise the virtue of deepening one's faith and inclination.
These ten verses are divided into two parts:

First, regarding the object of faith: it refers to the Dharma-body, which is itself the Dharma-realm; and the Wisdom-body, which realizes the ultimate Dharma-realm, thereby enabling the body of application to be omnipresent without moving.
Regarding the benefits of hearing and believing [the Dharma] in the latter nine sections, there are five divisions:
first, one leaves evil through hearing and believing;
next, two sections distinguish the difficulty of hearing it.

Next, three verses clarify that hearing and faith lead to Buddhahood, demonstrating what was already accomplished in the past, what is being realized in the present, and what will be attained in the future;
the fourth section, consisting of one verse, clarifies that there must be a cause for hearing [the Dharma], thereby exhorting beings to arouse their vows;
the fifth section, consisting of two stanzas, reveals the benefits of initiating practice.
The fifth section, "Rejecting the False and Honoring the True; Rejecting Delusion and Honoring Wisdom," is titled the Forest of Shame and Remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*).
It praises the supreme benefits of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom through ten verses, which are divided into three parts:
The first three verses explain the inconceivable nature of the Dharma; the next six use analogies to resolve doubts; and the final one concludes by ascribing these virtues to the Buddha.
Regarding the first section, the initial verse clarifies that hearing [the Dharma] produces supreme benefit, thereby inspiring beings to long for its hearing.
The "sovereign dharma" is none other than the Buddha's wisdom.
The subsequent verse states that the Buddha has exhausted all-encompassing knowledge (sarvajñatā), and thus his state is inconceivable to those in lower positions.
The following verse reveals from whence this wisdom arises; while the current passage expresses this through negation (via *paryudāsa*), it nonetheless carries two intended meanings:
First, establishing what precedes: this means that if one wishes to give rise to wisdom, one should seek it from the Buddha, for there is nothing the Buddha does not know;
one should not seek it from ordinary beings, for ordinary beings are shrouded in darkness.
It is like plucking a lotus flower, which must be done from deep water; how could it possibly be obtained from the tips of trees?
These two [types of wisdom] arise subsequent to their formation.
Wisdom arises from its own seeds through habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*); it does not arise from afflictions or ignorance.
Therefore, it is said below: "The two minds do not exist simultaneously, as they belong to the ignorant and the wise respectively. Thus, one should be careful regarding what one cultivates.
If this is so, why does the Sūtra say, "Within the mud of afflictions lies the Buddha-dharma"?
This is because it refers to the *tathāgatagarbha* while still enveloped in afflictions (*saṃkliṣṭa*).
However, this great wisdom arises from the virtues of the *garbha*, not from delusion.
If that is so, how can one reconcile the statement that "afflictions are themselves awakening" (*kleśā eva bodhiḥ*)?
In terms of their essential nature, they are distinguished by what they delude, like waves and moisture;
yet in terms of ultimate reality, they are true and false, or foolish and wise.
If considered in terms of their mutual formation, these two gates stand side by side.
If one examines them by way of their mutual negation, the two characteristics are quiescent.
The dual illumination of the two gates is neither identical nor separate: if one speaks of them as "one," they are separated to make them distinct, as in this chapter;
if one says they are "different," they are joined to make them the same, as in the subsequent chapters.
One must skillfully grasp the meaning and not be hindered by the words.

If one follows the Jin translation, it says: "It is not born from wisdom, nor is it born from the absence of wisdom; it thoroughly understands all phenomena and extinguishes the darkness of the world."
This reveals that the essence of wisdom is transcendent of both folly and [ordinary] wisdom; failing to realize it as it truly is is termed "lack of wisdom.
This verse clarifies both nature and characteristics together, while the subsequent analogy merely illustrates the difference between these two characteristics.
The second section consists of two parts:
first, five verses clarifying that the two natures are mutually exclusive; second, one verse distinguishing their unequal functional capacities.

Regarding the first part, only the three lines of the second verse constitute the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*); for the remaining verses, the analogy and its application (*dārṣṭāntika*) each occupy half a verse.

First, regarding the distinction between form and non-form: "non-form" refers to the mind, because its nature of objective apprehension and conceptualization differs from that of physical obstruction.
Second, within this there are two metaphors: "with characteristics" and "without characteristics," as principle and phenomena are mutually opposed.
Birth-and-death and nirvana are opposites in terms of reality and delusion.
Although they share the same essence, their conceptual gateways are distinct and not identical.
As for formation and destruction, they are differentiated based on their phenomenal characteristics.
Fourth, because the initial and subsequent moments of mind differ in time.
Fifth, because the functions of the various groups of consciousnesses are distinct; since the convergence of conditions differs, the eye does not possess the function of the ear.
Furthermore, this visual consciousness does not conjoin with other faculties; even within the same category of consciousness, they do not conjoin with one another.

How could that which is foolish and that which is wise give rise to each other when their natures are so different? As for the inequality of their functions, it is not merely that their two natures are distinct; rather, wisdom can extinguish folly while folly cannot extinguish wisdom, just as medicine can remove poison while poison cannot remove medicine, and likewise, light can extinguish darkness while darkness cannot extinguish light.
The three verses conclude by returning to the Tathāgata, who stands far beyond the world; thus, he is difficult to encounter.

The sixth [verse] speaks of diligently contemplating that principle and phenomena are equally without distinction, transcending the characteristics of body and mind; therefore, it is called diligence.
These ten verses collectively manifest these virtues of the Buddha through their general characteristics.
