Third, from "In this manner" onwards, the text generally distinguishes the long duration; this refers to the realm that is difficult to endure.

Second, from "When a Bodhisattva encounters this" onwards, it clarifies the practice of endurance; it first concludes the preceding section and introduces the following one, meaning that one encounters the aforementioned extreme suffering.
Second, from "He forms this thought" onwards, the characteristics of patience (*kṣānti*) are explicitly revealed through the loss of one's own commitment.
The text contains ten phrases:
the first is a hypothetical case of impatience, wherein mindfulness is lost and the will is easily swayed; therefore, it is described as "agitated and disturbed."

The remaining nine clarify the faults: first, failing to subdue anger; second, failing to guard the gates of the sensory faculties; third, being deluded regarding the dharma-gate of patience; fourth, failing to cultivate the practice of patience; fifth, turning outward following the wind; sixth, internal agitation and distraction arising; seventh, not cherishing roots of goodness; and eighth, not forgetting the distinction between self and other.
The first eight [types of patience] involve self-harm, whereby one is unable to benefit others;
now, because one is able to endure, by not rejecting what should not be rejected, these become the eight practices, whereby both self and others are benefited and both self and others are harmonized.
If one speaks of these benefits, one accomplishes the conduct of a true noble being (*satpuruṣa*).
Second, from the passage beginning "At that time, the bodhisattva," [the text] establishes the patience of accepting suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsana-kṣānti*).

Although it still follows the preceding text, its meaning corresponds to acceptance; therefore, it cites the sufferings previously endured as an analogy for the present suffering, with the intent of accepting it peacefully.

The reason for citing this is that "beginningless" reveals that the duration of past suffering was long, while "various sufferings" clarifies that the scope of those sufferings was vast; yet, despite this vastness and length of time, they were empty and devoid of both self-benefit and benefit for others.

Now, since time is brief and suffering is slight, one can accomplish the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) and thereby benefit both oneself and others; why then remain in a state of impatience?
Thus, the verse on refining the mind says: "You have already wandered through evil realms for many eons; you were able to transcend them even while undergoing useless suffering."
"Now that I have attained Bodhi by practicing even a small amount of goodness, I should not give rise to despondency regarding this great benefit.
Through these words, he again exhorted and encouraged himself, ensuring his mind was pure and undisturbed, joyful and free from sorrow or distress.
To regulate one's anger and obscuration and to guard the sense faculties is to abide in the dharma of patience oneself and cause others to likewise practice patience.
From "Furthermore" onwards is the third [section], the patience of discerning the dharma (*dharmānupaśyanā-kṣānti*).
Since it also arises following the previous [moment], it is said to "arise again.
This means that within a single patience (*kṣānti*), all three patiences are present; to indicate they are not entirely distinct, a single object is fully elucidated.
The text is divided into three sections.
First is the attainment of the patience regarding the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) by oneself;
this section consists of five sentences.

The first phrase provides a general heading; the section beginning with "non-self" (anātman) below explains the meaning of emptiness (śūnyatā), interpreting it through the four aspects of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
Inversion follows as the next [topic].
Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna, suffering, pleasure, and so forth are both negated:
first, because the self of persons and the self of phenomena are both absent;
second, because permanence and impermanence are not real, as they exist only in mutual dependence.
Third, because both emptiness and existence are quiescent, it is said that there are "no two";
fourth, because both suffering and pleasure are dispelled, it is said that there is "nothing whatsoever.
Second, from the section on "the emptiness of all phenomena" onwards, he causes others to achieve patience.
Sentient beings are deluded regarding emptiness; therefore, one should explain to them that all things are the patience of purity (*viśuddha-kṣānti*).
Third, from the words "For this reason" onwards, the practice to be cultivated is concluded.
However, according to the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, one is able to endure through three reflections and five contemplations:
First, reflect that others' insults and humiliations toward me are the result of my own karma;
second, reflect that both they and I are subject to the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*);
third, reflect that even Śrāvakas, who seek their own benefit, do not inflict suffering upon others.
These three texts are situated within the patience of acceptance (*kṣānti*), because one contemplates past sufferings and disciplines both oneself and others.
Regarding the "five perceptions" (*pañca-saṃjñā*): first is the perception of kinship, for since beginningless time there has been no sentient being who has not been a relative;
second is the perception of practicing the Dharma, for one cannot find anyone to strike or revile.

Third, cultivating the perception of impermanence; fourth, cultivating the perception of suffering; fifth, cultivating the perception of grasping—these are subsumed within this text, which may be considered in contrast to what precedes it.
Second, from "for the sake of compassionate mindfulness" onwards, the intention for cultivating patience is clarified.
The text contains ten phrases, whose meanings encompass both the general and the specific.
Generally speaking, all three types of patience (kṣānti) consist of these ten; this can be understood from their respective meanings.
Specifically, they constitute the first five [patiences] because one cultivates them for the purpose of enduring injury and harm.
Compassionate mindfulness is the foundation; next, one simply desires to benefit others and does not fear their lack of benefit.
Since one's original intent is to bring peace to others, how could one possibly seek retribution?
How could one harbor resentment when pitying those who are mired in delusion?
One should employ the practice of patience to restrain all anger.
Next is the patience of enduring suffering, because one follows after sentient beings without weariness or distress.
The next two lines constitute the practice of discerning the Dharma for the awakening of oneself and others.
The final two apply universally to the preceding three.
The one above flows down to this point; this is the happiness of the two periods within the ninefold [classification].
The fourth is the practice of being unyielding; "yielding" means to be crooked or weak, whereas this refers to firm and vigorous diligence.
The explanation of its characteristics has two parts:
first, a general manifestation of its characteristics; second, a detailed explanation according to specific difficulties.
The preceding Chinese text has three parts:

first, the actual manifestation of diligence; second, from "the nature is non-existent" onwards, the clarification of being free from faults; third, from "only for the sake of" onwards, the discernment of the purpose of progress.
Regarding these three sections: the first is a general enumeration;
the second explains "purity," meaning it is free from admixture;
and the third explains "progression," meaning it moves toward its objective.
Now, in the initial section that correctly reveals [the subject], the first phrase indicates the category to which the practice belongs;
the portion beginning with "namely" (yad uta) reveals its excellence by enumerating its names.
There are many names for diligence (*vīrya*), as they are designated in relation to its various functional activities.
Regarding "the first" (*prathama*), it also carries the meaning of "foremost. This meaning has three aspects:
first, it is foremost because it is great, meaning it is for the sake of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*);
second, it is foremost because it is superior, due to its qualities of radiance.
It is supreme because of its threefold excellence, meaning it transcends all else.
Its greatness is also characterized by three meanings:
first, it is great because it is most excellent, being the ultimate among the excellent, like a great king of the world.
Second, it is "great" because it is most sublime, for its phenomena and principle are interfused, like a great virtuous person of the world;
third, it is "great" because it is supreme, for the essence of its practice is loftily exalted, like the World-Honored One who is the eldest.
The third "Victorious One" (Jina) also has three meanings:
first, he is victorious because he is unsurpassed, for nothing can be added to him;
second, he is victorious because he is peerless, for there is no one who can match him.
It is superior because it is universal, for its essence pervades the entire dharma-realm and thus nothing can surpass it.
Second, regarding the absence of faults, this refers to the diligence of difficult practice (*duṣkaravīrya*), for its nature is uninterrupted and unmixed, which is the most difficult of all.

First, one is free from the fault of self-affliction; that is to say, the root and secondary afflictions do not arise spontaneously, and thus they are said to be non-existent by nature. In the Perfectly Integrated Teaching (Yuanrong jiao), this state is attained prior to the stages (bhūmi).
Following the phrase "Never for the sake of... and below, it clarifies the avoidance of causing affliction to others.

Third, in the analysis of the purpose of diligence, there are twenty phrases which fully encompass the three types of diligence; however, because they are for the sake of the four great vows of donning the armor, their practice constitutes the dharmas of skillful means and preparatory application, which are the virtues thus subsumed.
The text is divided into four sections:

the first three concern the severing of delusions; the next seven concern the cultivation of births; the next four concern the knowledge of dharmas; and the final six concern the seeking of Buddhahood—these being the Four Great Vows.
Now, regarding the first [stage]: first, one cuts off the active manifestations; next, one cuts off the seeds; finally, one cuts off the residual habits.
Among the two ways of saving sentient beings, this is for the purpose of accomplishing the wisdom of the ten powers.
The afflictions (*kleśa*) are the outflows (*āsrava*); the mind causes them to be exhausted.
The objective sphere (*viṣaya*) is the practice leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī pratipad*).

The meaning of "mental formations" (*citta-saṃskāra*) includes karma; the meaning of "birth and death" (*saṃsāra*) includes the powers of the knowledge of past abodes (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) and the knowledge of the possible and impossible (*sthānāsthānajñāna*); because these are comprehensive, they are not explained separately.
Regarding the three sets of four propositions for knowing the Dharma, the first is general while the others are specific.

Within the specific [categories], the first is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*): if one enters the Dharma for oneself, pure faith is the root; if it concerns benefiting others, compassion is the root, and so forth.
The second is the dharma-dhātu of principle, which is called the nature of equality.
The third is the dharma-dhātu of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle; the phenomena of the three periods of time are themselves the nature of equality.
Phenomena are harmonized through principle, and their meaning encompasses the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

Among the four sets of six propositions for seeking the Buddha, the first two constitute wisdom: the first phrase is the light of teaching-wisdom (*jiaozhi*), and the latter phrase is realized-wisdom (*zhengzhi*).
The next two [knowledges] concern the objects of cognition, the former being the ultimate and the latter the conventional.

The final two are both provisional wisdoms: the preceding phrase refers to knowing the capacities of beings and identifying the appropriate remedies, while the subsequent phrase refers to proclaiming [the Dharma] through the four analytical eloquences.
To analyze and expound upon them is "eloquence" (pratibhāna);
to speak of the meaning of the Dharma through phrases is "diction" (vākya).

The first four Great Vows—namely, knowing suffering and severing its accumulation, and cultivating the path and realizing cessation—constitute the realm of the Four Noble Truths of Non-action (anabhisaṃskāra).
The second section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva," provides a detailed explanation according to the specific difficulties.
This consists of two parts:
first, the explanation of armor-like diligence; second, the explanation of diligence for the benefit and happiness [of others].

Regarding the first point, it is entirely identical to the text of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; however, that treatise places "donning the armor" (*saṃnāha*) first, as it refers to the initial self-vow of the mind.
Among the three types of progress in the *Benevolent King Sutra* (*Bennyè jīng*), the first is termed the "Great Vow";
here, it follows "gathering wholesome dharmas," being established as a provisional designation based on encountering specific conditions.
The text contains two rounds of question and answer.
The first round is understandable.
In the second round, beginning with "Even if there were," the difficulty is even greater than before.

Regarding those who have attained great and wholesome benefit: I originally resolved my mind with the vow to vicariously bear the suffering of all beings, yet I only feared that such vicarious substitution would not be permitted.

Now, hearing that one can endure physical suffering and thus fulfill my original compassionate heart, I do not worry about the length of time, but only increase in joy and celebration. If one does not grow weary even through long kalpas, how much less so for the duration of a single lifetime?
If one does not feel regret for even a single thought-moment, one immediately forgets the self and enters the Avīci hell.
If one rejoices at having attained benefit, one immediately attains equal and universal penetration.
To possess such profound merit is what constitutes a difficult practice.
The second section, beginning with "The bodhisattva by this," concerns the diligence of benefiting and bringing happiness.

It means that one employs the previously mentioned preparatory practices of gathering wholesome qualities to benefit sentient beings, thereby causing them to attain the true peace and happiness of nirvāṇa.
The fifth is the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.
In the explanation of its characteristics, there are two parts:
first, a general manifestation of freedom from delusion and confusion; second, a specific clarification of freedom from delusion and confusion.

Now, first: although there are six phrases, there are ten meanings; the first is general, while the others are specific. Regarding the general statement, "one who has accomplished right mindfulness," it encompasses three meanings, all of which are termed "right mindfulness": 1. Mindfulness that is not distracted by external objects. 2. Mindfulness that does not forget the internal object of focus. 3. Mindfulness that is free from both distraction and forgetfulness. The second phrase, "dwelling in solitude," refers to the physical seclusion of dwelling alone in a quiet place, free from the five types of sensory distractions. The third phrase, "without desire," refers to the mental seclusion of being free from the five hindrances. The fourth phrase, "practicing with diligence," refers to the practice of right effort. The fifth phrase, "with clear comprehension," refers to the practice of right mindfulness. The sixth phrase, "with constant awareness," refers to the practice of right concentration. These six phrases encompass the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). The seventh phrase, "attaining the bliss of tranquility," refers to the fruit of the practice of the seven factors of enlightenment. The eighth phrase, "the mind is well-liberated," refers to liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*). The ninth phrase, "having attained the destruction of the taints," refers to liberation through the cessation of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-vimukti*). The tenth phrase, "realizing for oneself through direct knowledge," refers to the realization of these two liberations. Thus, the ten meanings are fully contained within these six phrases. This concludes the first section. The second section concerns the meaning of the term "Arhat. Although there are many names for this stage, they are subsumed under four categories: (1) the name based on the abandonment of afflictions, (2) the name based on the attainment of fruits, (3) the name based on the destruction of enemies, and (4) the name based on the exhaustion of outflows. The first category includes: the Arhat who has abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm, the Arhat who has abandoned the afflictions of the form realm, and the Arhat who has abandoned the afflictions of the formless realm. The second category includes: the Arhat who has attained the fruit of stream-entry, the Arhat who has attained the fruit of once-returning, the Arhat who has attained the fruit of non-returning, and the Arhat who has attained the fruit of arhatship. The third category includes: the Arhat who has destroyed the enemy of ignorance, the Arhat who has destroyed the enemy of craving, and the Arhat who has destroyed the enemy of views. The fourth category includes: the Arhat who has exhausted the outflow of desire, the Arhat who has exhausted the outflow of existence, and the Arhat who has exhausted the outflow of ignorance. These four categories encompass all the various names for the stage of arhatship. This concludes the second section. The third section concerns the meaning of the term "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*). Although there are many names for this title, they are subsumed under six categories: (1) the name based on the destruction of enemies, (2) the name based on the possession of qualities, (3) the name based on the breaking of bonds, (4) the name based on the excellence of merit, (5) the name based on the fulfillment of vows, and (6) the name based on the transcendence of the world. The first category includes: the World-Honored One who has destroyed the enemy of afflictions, the World-Honored One who has destroyed the enemy of karma, and the World-Honored One who has destroyed the enemy of birth. The second category includes: the World-Honored One who possesses the ten powers, the World-Honored One who possesses the four fearlessnesses, and the World-Honored One who possesses the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. The third category includes: the World-Honored One who has broken the bond of craving, the World-Honored One who has broken the bond of views, and the World-Honored One who has broken the bond of ignorance. The fourth category includes: the World-Honored One whose merit is supreme, the World-Honored One whose merit is vast, and the World-Honored One whose merit is inexhaustible. The fifth category includes: the World-Honored One who has fulfilled his original vow, the World-Honored One who has fulfilled his vow for the benefit of others, and the World-Honored One who has fulfilled his vow for the purification of the land. The sixth category includes: the World-Honored One who has transcended the world of desire, the World-Honored One who has transcended the world of form, and the World-Honored One who has transcended the world of formlessness. These six categories encompass all the various names for the title "World-Honored One. This concludes the third section. The fourth section concerns the meaning of the term "Tathāgata. Although there are many names for this title, they are subsumed under eight categories: (1) the name based on the arrival at suchness, (2) the name based on the departure from suchness, (3) the name based on the non-departure from suchness, (4) the name based on the non-arrival at suchness, (5) the name based on the non-duality of suchness, (6) the name based on the non-differentiation of suchness, (7) the name based on the non-obstruction of suchness, and (8) the name based on the non-extinction of suchness. The first category includes: the Tathāgata who has arrived at the suchness of all phenomena, the Tathāgata who has arrived at the suchness of sentient beings, and the Tathāgata who has arrived at the suchness of the Dharma-realm. The second category includes: the Tathāgata who has departed from the suchness of afflictions, the Tathāgata who has departed from the suchness of karma, and the Tathāgata who has departed from the suchness of birth. The third category includes: the Tathāgata who does not depart from the suchness of emptiness, the Tathāgata who does not depart from the suchness of signlessness, and the Tathāgata who does not depart from the suchness of wishlessness. The fourth category includes: the Tathāgata who does not arrive at the suchness of permanence, the Tathāgata who does not arrive at the suchness of self, and the Tathāgata who does not arrive at the suchness of purity. The fifth category includes: the Tathāgata who is non-dual with respect to the suchness of the subject, the Tathāgata who is non-dual with respect to the suchness of the object, and the Tathāgata who is non-dual with respect to the suchness of the knower. The sixth category includes: the Tathāgata who does not differentiate the suchness of the past, the Tathāgata who does not differentiate the suchness of the future, and the Tathāgata who does not differentiate the suchness of the present. The seventh category includes: the Tathāgata who is unobstructed regarding the suchness of the dharmas of the Buddhas, the Tathāgata who is unobstructed regarding the suchness of the dharmas of sentient beings, and the Tathāgata who is unobstructed regarding the suchness of the dharmas of the Dharma-realm. The eighth category includes: the Tathāgata who does not extinguish the suchness of the nature of phenomena, the Tathāgata who does not extinguish the suchness of the characteristics of phenomena, and the Tathāgata who does not extinguish the suchness of the function of phenomena. These eight categories encompass all the various names for the title "Tathāgata. This concludes the fourth section. The fifth section concerns the meaning of the term "Samyaksaṃbuddha. Although there are many names for this title, they are subsumed under nine categories: (1) the name based on the perfection of wisdom, (2) the name based on the perfection of compassion, (3) the name based on the perfection of power, (4) the name based on the perfection of skillful means, (5) the name based on the perfection of vows, (6) the name based on the perfection of practice, (7) the name based on the perfection of fruition, (8) the name based on the perfection of teaching, and (9) the name based on the perfection of liberation. The first category includes: the Samyaksaṃbuddha who has perfected the wisdom of the knowable, the Samyaksaṃbuddha who has perfected the wisdom of the path, and the Samyaksaṃbuddha who has perfected the wisdom of the fruit. The second category includes: the Samyaksaṃbuddha who has perfected great compassion, the Samyaksaṃbuddha who has perfected great pity, and the Samyaksaṃbuddha who has perfected great equanimity. The third category includes: the Samyaksa

First, within the category of śamatha, it is termed "right mindfulness" (samyak-smṛti); right mindfulness is itself concentration (samādhi). Because that concentrated mind is free from the distraction of deluded thoughts, it is called "right."
This is named according to its functional activity, and it is also designated by virtue of its proximity [to mindfulness].

Within the Eightfold Noble Path, right mindfulness subsumes concentration. As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "If the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately draw it back and cause it to abide in right mindfulness."
Secondly, within the category of *vipaśyanā*, it is also termed "right mindfulness" (*samyak-smṛti*), meaning that one observes without partiality and clearly comprehends the object.
Therefore, the sutra below states: "Rightly mindful of all phenomena, never forgetting them."

The path of the threefold union is called "right mindfulness" (*samyak-smṛti*). As the subsequent sutra states, "By means of right mindfulness, one skillfully understands the world," etc.; this means being clear regarding the object of focus, which is the sense of non-delusion (*amoha*);
not deviating from the object of focus is the sense of non-distraction (*avikṣepa*).
This refers precisely to the union of the two.
Furthermore, the subsequent sutra states: "Dhyāna-samādhi maintains the mind constantly on a single object; wisdom realizes the objects as identical to samādhi.
Although there are both vipaśyanā and the path of their union, these are all distinguished by way of the mind being one-pointed, and are thus termed the intrinsic nature of dhyāna.

Within these distinctions, the first phrase is further a general summary of non-confusion: because it does not shift according to objects, there is no distraction; because the three obstacles cannot destroy it, it is called "solid"; because the four conditions cannot pull it away, it is called "immovable"; because it transcends the inferior to manifest the superior, it is called "supreme"; and because it is untainted by other worlds, it is called "pure."
The first five [points] explain the absence of confusion; the latter four explain the absence of delusion through their meaning:

namely, the seventh is called "vast" because it accords with the *dharmadhātu*; the eighth is called "great" because it leads toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); the ninth is called "immeasurable" because it brings forth that which is difficult to measure; and the tenth is named "non-delusive" because it does not abandon great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

The nine superior phrases are subsumed under three categories of dhyāna: the first six pertain to dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), the next two lead to the production of merit, and the final one benefits sentient beings.
The second section, beginning with "By this," specifically elucidates the absence of delusion and confusion.
It explains the ten preceding meanings in successive order, forming ten distinct segments.
Furthermore, the first segment serves as a general exposition, explaining the aforementioned right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
This section is divided into two parts:
first, the conclusion of the preceding and the introduction of what follows; second, from "skillfully understanding" onwards, the manifestation of the capacity of right mindfulness.
This latter part is further divided into two sub-sections.
First, there is the simultaneous presentation of the two; second, the simultaneous explanation of the two.
This is the first part.
Because right mindfulness possesses contemplation, one is able to understand well.
Right mindfulness possesses stillness (śamatha), which enables it to maintain [the mind].
Worldly discourse is of no benefit; one need only understand it well.
Transcendental discourse is beneficial; it specifically concerns mindful retention.
If one does not understand the supramundane, one should not maintain its meaning.
If worldly speech does not maintain [its meaning], there should be no memory of it.
Therefore, although the text is abbreviated, the meaning must necessarily encompass both.
Because one understands both phenomena (*dharma*) and principles (*artha*), it is called "skillful understanding.
Regarding the second section, beginning with "That is to say," there is a dual explanation divided into two parts:

first, a general clarification of the absence of delusion and confusion regarding all objects; second, a specific clarification of the absence of delusion and confusion regarding that which is upheld, beginning with "This bodhisattva... and so forth.
This is the first [section].

Based on the absence of delusion and confusion, the text contains only nine [items]; however, when the first is divided into two, there are ten phrases as well, because the phenomena (dharma) and their meanings (artha) are distinct.
The first phrase is the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*); when combined with the aggregates, it forms two categories, namely matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
That which is non-material refers to the mind, which consists of the remaining four aggregates.
The second section, beginning with "capable of maintaining and establishing," concerns the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
Meaning is of two kinds, and intrinsic nature is likewise twofold: first, phenomena (*vastu*), and second, principle (*tattva*).

Phenomena consist of material obstruction, such as the nature of form (*rūpa*) and so forth; principle consists of the absence of intrinsic nature, which is the nature of form and so forth. Both are provisionally established and designated within that which is devoid of names and signs.
"Holding the words and their meaning" refers to the two types of retention (*dhāraṇī*): that of the phrasing and that of the meaning.
Now, being perfectly awakened to both principle and phenomena and being free from deluded discrimination is called "absence of confusion.
These two [terms] explain the aforementioned "ability to retain," while the following eight explain the aforementioned "skillful understanding."
Since these meanings must necessarily coexist, ignorance (*moha*) and confusion (*sammoha*) are mentioned together.
Third, one attains freedom from ignorance and confusion regarding the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) states: "Death has two kinds of karma:"
"First, because it can destroy all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); second, because there is no conscious awareness [of them], the continuity remains uninterrupted.
Now, this bodhisattva is tranquil regarding the principles of these two matters, and thus possesses no delusion or confusion.
The fourth type, the "partial speech" (*pralāpa*) womb-birth, clarifies the absence of delusion and confusion.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 2, explains four ways of entering the womb:
first, entering with full awareness but not remaining or emerging with awareness; this refers to a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
Second, those who are fully aware upon entering and abiding but not fully aware upon emerging, namely the Pratyekabuddhas;
third, those who are fully aware in both cases, namely the Bodhisattvas;
and fourth, those who are not fully aware in either case, namely other sentient beings.
The former two individuals still possess delusion and confusion.

As for the characteristics of the delusion and confusion of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*): those of inferior capacity see the place of their rebirth as being in a latrine or filth; those of middling capacity see it as being in a house or dwelling; and those of superior capacity see it as being in a grove of flowers.
If it is a male, he conceives love for his mother and hatred for his father because they compete for his mother;
for a female, it is the reverse of this.

This is fully explained in the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Mahāsāṃnipāta-sūtra*, the eighteenth and twenty-ninth fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and the ninth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
The third [set] of three and the ten [sets] can both be understood from the text.

Regarding the eighth and ninth [sets], each has both general and specific aspects. The specific aspects refer to the four māras, the ten māras, and karma, as explained in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*), the "Chapter on the Deeds of Māra" (*Mārakarmaparivarta*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra*.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, with the exception of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), everything else constitutes the Māra-work of a bodhisattva; every arising thought and movement of the mind is entirely the activity of Māra.
Now, by means of wisdom one observes and does not follow along with these movements, just as a person who has awakened recognizes a thief or a thieving dog.

Knowing that the suchness of the realm of Māra and the suchness of the realm of the Buddha are non-dual, because suchness is without duality, one who has awakened to this matter does not create its karma.
Second, from the passage beginning "This bodhisattva," the text specifically clarifies the absence of delusion and confusion with respect to the Dharma-gates he upholds.
The text has two distinct sections:
first, the formal exposition; second, the interrogation and explanation.
Within the former, there are three parts:

First, the preceding section establishes the heading; second, from "Next, that which is called" onwards, the actual content held [by the mind] is revealed; third, from "Bodhisattva" onwards, the absence of delusion and confusion is concluded.
Within the second part, the actual revelation, there are fifteen dharmas:
first, the essence of the realized principle, which is the profound meaning in its major aspects, namely emptiness, because phenomena are themselves reality.
Second, it is the dharma of essence, activity, and function.
Third, because it is endowed with the marks of virtue.
Fourth, because one contains all, it is called "various."
The first four are the dharmas of the principle (li) that are explained;
the fifth is the dharma of the teaching (jiao) that explains it—the meaning of which is seen in the first fascicle.
The sixth is the dharma of practice, because one adorns the fruit with causes.

Regarding the seven dharmas of fruition: the first seven comprehensively clarify four categories of dharma, while the latter eight pertain exclusively to the stages of realization (*bhūmi*) and are subsumed under fruition and practice.

Specifically, these eight refer to the great vows of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*); because one has already realized the principle (*tattva*), they are termed "correct aspiration" (*samyak-praṇidhāna*); and because they definitively resolve and sever the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), they are called "pure."
The ninth is fundamental wisdom and the tenth is subsequently attained wisdom; these two extend through to the seventh stage.

The eleventh is the vast and great Dharma, which refers to the realization of the profound patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) in the eighth stage, as it is identical to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The twelfth stage, the nine grounds (*navabhūmi*), constitutes the rank of the Dharma Master, because it involves discerning the capacities of sentient beings.

The thirteenth stage, the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), is so called because one knows the arising of the world, both common and uncommon; since [realizations] such as suffering and impermanence pertain to both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), they are termed "common," whereas the distinct categories of matter and mind are termed "uncommon."
Furthermore, the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) is called "common" because it is produced by common karma;
the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) is called "uncommon" because it is formed by their individual karma.
These two categories apply exclusively to the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Furthermore, practicing in accordance with the intentions of others is called "shared," while practicing in accordance with one's own intentions is called "unshared.

Moreover, although the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the four immeasurables (*brahmavihāra*), and the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are shared with ordinary beings and followers of the Lesser Vehicle, they are called "unshared" when practiced by Bodhisattvas as untainted (*anāsrava*) great compassion.
14. The wisdom of equal enlightenment;
15. The wisdom of the Tathāgata.
These [fifteen stages] vertically enumerate the various levels.

If categorized according to horizontal correspondence, the first [knowledge] is exclusively cause and the last is exclusively fruit; the six intermediate knowledges pertain to both cause and fruit, though their specific characteristics are made manifest through distinct meanings.
Regarding "the three fetters being without delusion or confusion": this means not forgetting, not being deluded, not losing [the object], and being undisturbed.
From "The mind constantly recollects" onwards, it generally concludes the continuity [of the preceding section].
The second section, from "For what reason," provides the interrogation and explanation.
In the explanation: because the cause is profound, one does not confuse sentient beings and thus attains the fruit of non-confusion.
Because one does not destroy the true Dharma and increases vast great wisdom, one attains the fruit of non-delusion.
Without severing the roots of goodness, one attains the fruit of continuity;
the influence between cause and effect is so subtle as to be without discrepancy.
Second, from the phrase "Furthermore" (*punar-aparam*) onwards, the preceding nine points are individually explained and subsumed under three meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
The first six [sections] explain the previously mentioned "abiding in happiness in the present life," which is divided into six parts.
Now, for the first [of these], explaining the previously mentioned "absence of mental distraction," the text has two sections:
first, the heading; second, the explanation, beginning with the words "That is to say."
The commentary further divides into two parts.
First, regarding the explanation of various sounds, seven types are briefly enumerated.

As for the phrase "obstructing and destroying the six sense faculties," it does not merely refer to the deprivation of the faculty of hearing; it also renders the other faculties unable to perceive their respective objects. Therefore, they are called "obstructed and destroyed faculties" (*indriya-vighāta*), as their essential meaning consists in the impairment of seeing and the other functions.

Furthermore, regarding "corruption," the *Cī-cán-bìng-jīng* (Sūtra on Treating the Illnesses of Meditation) states: "Due to external sounds, the six sense-faculties are stirred; the heart-vessels become inverted, and five kinds of evil winds enter through these heart-vessels."
"Because the mind is moved by the wind, one may sing or dance, performing various transformations.
This refers to the sense of destruction.
Once the mental body is destroyed, everything else follows in destruction.

However, while forms can be perceived with eyes closed, touch and taste are known through direct contact, and fragrance is only slightly expressed by language, sound alone acts as a thorn to meditative concentration; therefore, it is specifically mentioned to clarify that when one is free from delusion and distraction, the other four sensory objects cannot cause such disturbance.
Therefore, during the stage of "superior patience," even when encountering physical harm, the mind remains undisturbed.
Second, from the passage beginning "This bodhisattva" below, the text explains that [the bodhisattva] cannot be deluded or disturbed.
This section is also divided into two parts:

First, the state of being undistracted over a long period is explained in general; subsequently, from the words "That is to say" (*yad uta*) onwards, the specific characteristics of non-distraction are revealed.
There are eleven phrases: the first is general, and the remainder are specific.
There are five distinct pairs:
first, the object is examined and the mind is stabilized;
second, the teaching is mastered and practice is perfected.
Third, recollecting causes through mindfulness as a condition;
fourth, observing reality to give rise to its function;
fifth, externally purifying the delusions of others while internally resolving the gates of meaning, such that even when encountering evil sounds, none of these can cause harm.

The above constitutes all types of dhyāna, meaning that it is so designated because it encompasses both the general definitions of śamatha and vipaśyanā as well as the two benefits [of self and others].

The third section, beginning with "non-doing," explains the aforementioned steadfastness; that is, being unshakable by the four obstacles, which signifies that right mindfulness is firm. This also serves as the cause for the previously mentioned state of non-distraction.
Regarding the "obstruction to the Dharma," this refers to a lack of understanding of the Dharma, like that of cattle or sheep; it is precisely the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
These three obstructions are subsumed within the afflictions (*kleśa*), for their essence is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*).
This is also pure meditative concentration (*śuddha-dhyāna*).
The fourth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, as above," explains the preceding immovability (*aniñjya*), meaning that various adverse conditions cannot draw one away.

They are entirely capable of disrupting the bodies and minds of sentient beings; yet the faults of manifesting sounds cannot destroy the mind of this Bodhisattva, which is revealed as inconceivable in contrast [to others].
The fifth section, beginning with "The Bodhisattva enters," explains the aforementioned "supreme" state, meaning that it transcends the inferior to manifest the superior.
The following three sections likewise present the aforementioned absence of delusion and distracted conditions, correctly demonstrating the characteristics of dwelling in the bliss of the Dharma.
Regarding the term "surpassing," the first phrase identifies the person and distinguishes them from [ordinary] dhyāna.
It is said that "the Bodhisattva enters" because he differs from ordinary persons and those of the Lesser Vehicle.

From the phrase "abiding in" onwards, the text cites specific dharmas to distinguish the noble dharma; that is, it uses the untainted (*anāsrava*) to distinguish [the noble one] from the ordinary person.

Through contemplation and observation, one distinguishes oneself from the followers of the Two Vehicles; for those of the Two Vehicles, when entering dhyāna, they are unable to perceive external objects. Thus, Śāriputra was unaware of the hand that struck him, and Kāśyapa did not hear the sound of *nirvāṇa*.
The section beginning with "skillfully knowing" correctly reveals the superior characteristics, because it thoroughly understands both nature (*dharmatā*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
As for characteristics, they do not abide even for a single moment, and thus cannot be apprehended;
as for nature, its three characteristics are empty of intrinsic nature, and thus there is truly nothing to be obtained.
Since neither nature nor characteristics can be apprehended, upon what could compliance or opposition depend?
The sixth section, beginning with "Having heard this," explains the aforementioned purity, which is precisely the dhyāna of purity.

This is because, amidst objects of both compliance and opposition, the three poisons do not arise; one is unstained and correctly grasps [the truth], owing to the presence of concentration and wisdom.
Having realized both the characterized and the uncharacterized, it is called "skillfully grasping.
Possessing such right mindfulness, even if the great earth were made into a drum and Mount Sumeru into a mallet, how could they possibly disturb it?
The seventh section, "Knowing All," provides an extensive explanation, meaning that it accords with the dharma-realm and is like space.
It also serves as an immediate commentary on what precedes it.
The text contains six phrases:
The first part is general; the remainder is specific.

Within the specific section, there is the emptiness of non-attainment, the emptiness of the person of non-action, and the emptiness of the nature of non-limitation. When these three characteristics are exhausted, the principle of the dharma-realm manifests.
It is equal to the dharma-realm because phenomena are as they are in principle;
it is without differentiation because principle is itself phenomena.
The eighth section, beginning with "The bodhisattva thus," explains the aforementioned great meaning.
The following two sections explain the merit of producing [the dhyāna].
Here, it is called "great" because it leads toward omniscience without regression; this is precisely the dhyāna of difficult practice.
The ninth section, "Skillful Entry," explains the aforementioned immeasurables, meaning that they are capable of eliciting incalculable virtues.
The text is divided into three parts:

first, the introduction of virtues for one's own benefit, which consists of six phrases; the first marks "meditative absorption of all doors" (*sarvadvāra-dhyāna*), the next four specifically manifest it, and the final one concludes by categorizing many doors, such that what meditative concentration would not be included?
Furthermore, regarding "Gate" (Mén): samādhis are immeasurable in number, like space; because many are now subsumed within one, it is called a "gate.
It is like pulling a single corner of a garment, or like a queen bee approaching.
Next, from "increasing" (*vṛddhi*) downward, he cites the qualities of benefiting others.
Afterward, from "at that time" (*tasmin samaye*) downward, he concludes that there is no distraction.
It is not merely that there is no distraction; the original concentration increases further, like a boar rubbing against a mountain of gold, or like wind fanning a fire.
The tenth section, beginning with "Acting in this way," explains the absence of delusion.
To be attached to the flavor of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-rasa*) and fail to give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is what constitutes delusion.
Now, because compassion guides meditative absorption, there is no delusion.
This is precisely the dhyāna that benefits sentient beings.

Abiding in pure mindfulness constitutes happiness in the present life, and attaining the fruit of wisdom and abandonment constitutes happiness in future lives; this is called bestowing happiness upon two lifetimes.
The sixth is the practice of excellence (*sādhumatī*), whose essence is *prajñā*.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, all *prajñā* is also of three kinds:

first, the wisdom that can realize and penetrate the reality of the objects of knowledge; second, the wisdom that possesses definitive skill regarding the five fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) as they have been taught and the three collections (*piṭaka*); and third, the wisdom that can effect the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* takes the preparatory, fundamental, and post-attainment stages as its three [divisions], all of which clarify the meaning of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* takes the emptiness of birth, phenomena, and both together [as its three divisions], while the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* takes the illumination of the three truths [as its three divisions]; all of these clarify the meaning of the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*).
Although the sutras speak of ten perfections, one should rely on the *Mūlavyākhyāna* (Benye);
however, for the sake of following the current text, we shall rely on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Thus, both the provisional and the ultimate are unimpededly termed "Subhūti."

Although those [earlier stages] rely on the six perfections, the Bodhisattva who now practices them in their fullness cultivates all ten perfections simultaneously; yet, when distinguished according to their sequential arrangement, the auxiliary and the primary differ, and thus they do not overlap.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics, ancient masters also followed the *Bunyue jing* (Sutra of Original Karma) in dividing the three wisdoms into three parts:

first, they clarify the Middle Way; second, they take the contemplation of the non-arising of phenomena and so forth as the illumination of non-existence; and from "universally entering" onwards, they clarify the illumination of existence.
This results in attaining the three truths sequentially, thereby losing their perfect interfusion.

Furthermore, regarding the illumination of non-existence, the sutras state that the Buddha-dharma and worldly dharmas are neither different from nor confused with one another; how could it be that they are merely non-existent?

Now, based on the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), and relying upon the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* while also incorporating its correct interpretation, it is established that each [of the three wisdoms] possesses the three truths (*tisraḥ satyaḥ*).

Thus, that treatise explains the first wisdom as follows: "One awakens to the nature of equality in all phenomena, enters the great universal characteristic (*mahāsāmānyalakṣaṇa*), thoroughly investigates the limits of all that is knowable, remains far removed from the two extremes of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*), and accordingly enters the Middle Way."
The textual analysis is divided into two parts:
first, the clarification of the modes of practice; second, the manifestation of the benefits achieved.
Within the former, there are also two sections:
First a brief summary, followed by a detailed exposition.
Within the former, there are two parts:
first, a general heading; second, an explanation beginning with the phrase "is able to know."
This is the first point.
That the three karmas are pure is what can manifest the essence.
To manifest the three karmas is precisely the meaning of "manifestation" (xian).

Abiding in non-attainment is manifestation; manifestation itself is non-attainment. When quiescence and function are unimpeded, this is the Middle Way, which may be called "Excellent Manifestation" (Sudṛśa).
If one were to speak of the Middle by way of something other than the negation of posterior existence and non-existence, it would be a middle defined by mutual dependence.
In the second explanation: to know that the three types of karma are all non-existent is the meaning of abiding in non-attainment.
Not falsely grasping at existence and being free from the bonds of the two extremes is the meaning of purity.

All that is manifested is without intrinsic nature and without basis; it demonstrates the meaning of non-attainment, for since objects have no fixed nature and the mind has nothing upon which to rely, neither can be apprehended.
Because all three types of action are demonstrated, the common expression [“ordinary speech”] is employed.
Second, regarding the detailed analysis of the characteristics of practice from the section beginning with “Abiding in Suchness,” there are three parts:

first, the wisdom that correctly awakens to suchness; second, the skillful wisdom regarding the five sciences and so forth, as found in the section beginning with “O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva acts in this way.”
Third, from "At that time, the bodhisattva" onwards is the wisdom that acts for the benefit of sentient beings.
Regarding this first section, he manifests the three types of action by awakening to them as they truly are; herein, there is first a detailed explanation and subsequently a summary.
The three types of action—of body, speech, and mind—are divided into three sections.
Herein, the first is the mental action (*manas-karman*); because it is the root of the other two, it is explained at the outset.
"The mind as it truly is" refers to the basis upon which [action] functions.
"Abiding" refers to the essence of the mind being in profound stillness.
"Knowing immeasurable minds and so forth" refers to the unimpeded functioning [of that essence].
This is precisely what is indicated by the term "mental karma": within the manifold minds and manifold phenomena, there is the Truth (satya) in each and every one.
Since the objective realm is without marks, what can the mind apprehend?
This is precisely the absence of [conventional] truths.
Because existence and non-existence are non-dual, it is called "profound," which is the meaning of the Middle Way.
It cannot be observed through sequential contemplation; therefore, it is called "difficult to enter," for only those with the capacity of the Perfect Teaching (yuan-ji) can enter it.
Why is this? If one were to observe the three truths (san-di) in a biased manner as being either eternal or annihilated, they would be merely relative (xiang-dai).

If one views them collectively, the One would destroy the Three Truths; if one views them as distinct, one becomes confused regarding the Single Reality. Therefore, they are three within the One and the One within the three; they are neither three nor one, yet both the three and the one are simultaneously illumined. In terms of the objective realm, the Three Truths are perfectly interfused; in terms of the mind, the three contemplations operate together. Abiding and knowing are themselves contemplation.

The ancient masters, down to those who found [the teachings] difficult to enter, clarified the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), yet there was a reason for this, even though the full meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* was not yet fully revealed.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:

because the mind is not external to objects, there is nothing to be attained; because objects are not external to the mind, they possess no phenomenal characteristics. Since the mind is itself the object, it is profoundly deep; since the object is itself the mind, it is difficult to enter.
This is also one principle.
Second, from "Abiding in the Right Position" (*samyaktva-niyāma*) onwards, the bodily action (*kāyakarman*) is explained and demonstrated.
The "Right Position" and the other two [terms] indicate that which serves as the basis.

From "Expedient Means" (*upāya*) onwards, [the text] explains how function arises based on the essence: because this birth does not arise from afflictions or karma, arising and ceasing are themselves non-arising and non-ceasing.
Herein, the "correct position" (*samyagavasthā*) is a synonym for *tathatā* (Suchness).
This is not a matter of abiding in the Path of Seeing through the union of wisdom; therefore, it is called "abiding in non-abiding.
To "abide" means to abide in True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Third, the section beginning with "abiding in nirvāṇa" explains and demonstrates the verbal activity.
The first three phrases indicate the basis upon which it rests.
The "severance of the path of language" reveals that it is signless;
for when words themselves vanish, this is the severance of the path of speech.
The Jin translation states: "It is not existent, yet it is spoken of as existent; the path of language is severed.
Nevertheless, those aforementioned abodes comprise seven types in total, which are one in essence but differ in name.
These differences arise from distinctions in meaning:
The "one true mind" is the intrinsically pure mind; this constitutes the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Next, the three [stages] beginning with the "correct position" (*samyagavasthā*) constitute the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of that mind.
The "correct position" (samyag-avasthā) refers to that wherein phenomena abide.
True Suchness (*tathatā*), in its own essence, is real and eternal.
As for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is the fundamental basis of all phenomena; because one is deluded regarding this True Suchness, all phenomena arise.

Having brought all phenomena (*dharma*) to completion, they do not lose their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, it is called *dharmatā*. This is also the causal characteristic (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*).

The three [aspects], such as *nirvāṇa*, are the resultant characteristics (*phala-lakṣaṇa*). Abiding in the realm of *nirvāṇa* is precisely *tathatā* (suchness), because its essence is perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*) and because it transcends the two obstructions.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are bodhisattvas who, upon generating the mind of awakening, immediately contemplate nirvāṇa while practicing the path; fearing that this nirvāṇa might be confused with [the state] existing only at the fruit-stage, it is said they 'dwell in the nature of tranquility.'"

This means that, with respect to the essence of *tathatā* (suchness), the absence of deluded movement is itself *nirvāṇa*. Since this nature of suchness is neither existent nor non-existent, it is called "naturelessness" (*niḥsvabhāva*).
This nature of naturelessness is precisely the true nature; it does not mean a mere void of annihilation.
Therefore, by citing many names, the profundity of that which is dwelt upon is made manifest; by relying on this manifestation, it is clarified that what is manifested is virtuous.
Second, regarding the summary of the three karmas from "Entering Detachment" onwards: the first phrase summarizes the mind, thus there is no bondage or attachment;
the second phrase summarizes the body, namely the *tathatā* (suchness) and so forth in which one dwells.
The preceding phrase, "the three fetters," refers to the passage beginning with "transcending all worlds.
The final sentence summarizes that the three karmas are all quiescent yet functionally unimpeded; therefore, it is called "skillful means" (*kauśalya*).
It is from this that the name "Subhūti" (Excellent Manifestation) is established.

The second section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," elucidates the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*); because it concerns the wisdom of definitive skillfulness among the three aggregates, it explains worldly phenomena within this text.
This section is divided into three parts:

first, reconciling phenomena with principle through reasoning; second, from "The bodhisattva thus... onwards, the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle; and third, from "Never... onwards, giving rise to compassion in accordance with principle.
Now, regarding the first [section], there are six phrases:
first, because sentient beings arise through conditions, it is said that they lack intrinsic nature;
second, because phenomena arise based on the Truth (tathatā), they ultimately converge in the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
1. Because the three realms are the differentiated manifestations of the mind; 2.
Because the four seasons rely on phenomena as provisional designations; 3.
Because names lack the power to apprehend things—if a name were inherent within a phenomenon, one would see that the meaning should be known through the name itself.

Because the six categories of phenomena lack any reality corresponding to their names, if a phenomenon were contained within its name, then upon hearing the name, one should perceive its meaning; for instance, if one called out "fire," it ought to burn one's mouth.
Second, from "The Bodhisattva is thus" onwards, the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle is elucidated.
The text contains seven phrases:
the first one generally reveals the profound depth, while the remaining phrases specifically reveal the characteristics of that profundity.

However, worldly phenomena (*saṃsāra*) and Buddha-dharma (*dharmatā*) truly possess no dual essence; they are distinguished as two only by way of conventional designation regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*). Therefore, five propositions are used to clarify that they are neither identical nor different: 1.

Because the characteristics of the world are identical with emptiness, it is called "quiescent. 2. Because the Buddha-dharma is equal [to all things], there is no augmentation. 3. Since there is no principle that is not a phenomenon, the Buddha-dharma does not differ from worldly phenomena;
since there is no phenomenon that is not principle, worldly phenomena do not differ from the Buddha-dharma.
Fourth, this is the principle of the entirety of phenomena and the entirety of principle, yet phenomenon and principle are not conflated.
Fifth, each fully encompasses the other without omission; therefore, it is said that there is no differentiation.

The final phrase concludes that all preceding phenomena share the same essence as the *dharmadhātu*; thus, they attain a state of seamless fusion, universally entering the three periods of time and encompassing both the horizontal and vertical dimensions.
If categorized according to the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), they are described as mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*) and Buddha-phenomena (*buddha-dharma*).
Regarding the explanation according to both phenomena and principle: first, because birth-and-death is itself nirvana, it is said that "the world is quiescent";
second, because there is not a single dharma that is not the Buddha-dharma, what further could be added?
Third, although the two sets of dharmas differ in terms of defilement and purity, they are one and the same true nature, and thus are not distinct;
fourth, because their characteristics are indestructible, there is no confusion or disorder;
fifth, as all are phenomena that are identical with principle, each mutually encompasses the others without omission, and thus there is no discrepancy.
The sixth point, "the same single dharma-realm," collectively reveals the underlying cause.

The third section, beginning with "forever not," describes the arising of compassion in accordance with principle; that is, through non-referential compassion, one guides the aforementioned wisdom that has extinguished the objective conditions to enter into conventional reality in order to transform sentient beings.
The first phrase serves as the general statement: although one has deeply entered into wisdom, one does not forget the fundamental mind, unlike those at the eighth stage who wish to relinquish it.
The following three phrases provide the specific details:

first, not abandoning the wick of the vow; second, increasing the oil of great compassion; and third, combining these with the light of prior wisdom; therefore, one is capable of serving as a locus of reliance.
The third section, beginning with "At that time, the Bodhisattva," concerns the wisdom that effects the welfare of all sentient beings.
This section has two parts:
first, establishing the resolve to gather in and deliver sentient beings; second, placing others before oneself.
Now, for the first [section], there are five phrases:
"maturation" (paripāka) is the general term, because it refers either to the fruit of causes reaching maturity or to the encouragement provided from beginning to end.
The remaining phrases are the specific details:

First, subduing; second, gathering and transforming; third, causing [beings] to realize their original nature and achieve Great Bodhi; fourth, severing delusions, attaining purity, and obtaining the fruit of Nirvana.
Second, from "Furthermore, he acts... onwards, he places others before himself.

The text is divided into four parts: first, the hypothetical case of self-deliverance; second, from "But all sentient beings... onwards, observing that sentient beings transmigrate, possessing karma, afflictions, and suffering;

third, from "The Bodhisattva thus... onwards, concluding what should not be done because there are two faults: first, violating one's original vow; second, falling into the error of stinginess and greed—this is impermissible. Fourth, [the conclusion].
4. From "I shall" onwards, the resolve to first extract [beings from suffering] is determined.
Second, from "This bodhisattva" onwards, the accomplishment of practice and its benefits are revealed.
Within this, the three karmas are not in vain; this constitutes universal benefit.
"Ultimately reaching Bodhi" constitutes the final benefit; herein follow twenty sūtras.
*The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty-two.
*The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle Twenty.
3. Below this, twenty sūtras follow, compiled by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Monastery on Mount Qingliang of the Tang Dynasty.
Seventh: The Practice of Non-attachment (*asaṅga-caryā*), whose essence is skillful means (*upāya*).

By means of these two skillful means—through dedication, one does not abide in saṃsāra; through deliverance, one does not abide in nirvāṇa. Because one abides in neither, it is called "non-attachment."
In the latter four [stages] of the *Benye jing*, there are likewise three skillful means for each.
These three are: first, advancing toward the fruit; second, skillfully engaging with both existence and non-existence; and third, neither abandoning nor grasping at any dharmas.

The first is the dedication [of merit]; the second is that through skillful integration one is able to deliver others; not abandoning [sentient beings] yet not receiving [their suffering] is identical to Prajñā.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* establishes only the latter because it clarifies only the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). The *Bunyé jīng* differs in its inclusion of both the provisional and the ultimate; thus, there is no contradiction in these three being all skillful means. Since both are free from attachment, the compassion and wisdom—which are non-dual yet appear as two, and which are the single mind where duality is non-dual—constitute non-attachment.
There is this illusory existence and that which is non-existent, the true emptiness; illusory existence is not existent, and because it exists, it is precisely true emptiness;
true emptiness is not empty, and because it is empty, it is precisely illusory existence.
Because these two are unimpeded, they are called "skillful integration"; because they are thus mutually fused, there is no attachment.
Since there is that which can give rise to function and emptiness that can be observed, neither is abandoned.
If one accepts [existence], one is the same as ordinary beings; if one does not accept it, one is the same as those who have realized the goal. Therefore, one accepts neither.
In the second explanation of the characteristics, there are two major divisions:
first, clarifying non-attachment within one's own stage (*svabhūmi*); second, clarifying non-attachment in superior progress (*viśeṣa-gamana*).
What was previously explained is already contained within this section.
The two or three skillful means are divided into three parts in the text:

first, clarifying that one's own practice alone is free from attachment; second, from "Why? onwards, investigating and explaining the underlying reasons; and third, from "The Bodhisattva thus... onwards, illustrating the myriad practices by analogy.
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, clarifying non-attachment toward pure objects; second, from "seeing the impure" onwards, showing no aversion toward defiled objects.
Within the first part, there are three sections:
First, clarifying non-attachment to the adornment of the buddha-field;

second, from "goes to" (*yāti*) onwards, non-attachment toward the Triple Gem, which includes: first, reverently serving and making offerings to the Buddha; next, from "in this way" (*evam*) onwards, revealing the purpose of the offerings; and finally, from "in every thought-moment" (*kṣaṇe kṣaṇe*) onwards, specifically demonstrating the characteristics of non-attachment. This meaning encompasses both non-attachment toward the Triple Gem and toward one's own cultivation, while the term "thought-moment" indicates that it is both rapid and frequent.
Third, from "this bodhisattva" onwards, long-term non-attachment.
Second, the explanation that the defiled object is not to be loathed.
Regarding the single phrase, it is because defilement is easily abandoned.
Within the second section, which provides the inquiry and its explanation, the intent of the inquiry is as follows:
To delight in purity and loathe impurity is the common sentiment of ordinary people; how then can a Bodhisattva neither loathe nor be attached?
The meaning of the explanation is this:
based on the Buddha’s wisdom, "purity" and "impurity" are merely conceptual constructions; when one contemplates in accordance with the Dharma, where do these two characteristics abide?
Therefore it is said: "One observes in accordance with the Buddha-dharmas.
The Buddha-dharmas refer to the Dharma-realm and the Buddha-wisdom.
The third category reveals the myriad practices.

Whether for oneself or for others, there is no attachment whatsoever. Among these, the first phrase concludes the preceding section and introduces what follows; from "teaching and transforming" onwards, the various practices are enumerated in detail.
As for "the dwelling place of the Buddhas," this refers to the noble devas, Brahmā, and so forth; the rest may be understood accordingly.
The second section, "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" and below, concerns superior progress and non-attachment.
The text is divided into three parts:

first, the clarification of one's own practice; second, from "Having received the prophecy" onwards, benefiting others; and third, from "The bodhisattva contemplates the body in this way" onwards, concluding with the fulfillment of the practice.
Now, for the first part, there are two divisions:
first, restating the preceding stage of self-perfection;
second, from "In the Buddha-dharma" onwards, the actual manifestation of superior progress, which consists of eleven phrases—the first being general and the remainder specific.
In general, this refers to the thorough comprehension of the dharmas of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit.
Specifically, the first is the comprehension of the dharma of the fruit, which is the *bodhi* of the Buddha;
the second is the comprehension of the dharma of principle, which is the realization of the Dharma and Vinaya.
*Vinaya* is a Sanskrit term; in its full form it is *vinaya*, which is translated here as "extinction" (*nirodha*).
If it is designated by the name of the *Vinaya-piṭaka*, its meaning also includes "subduing" (*vinayana*).

Here, the term "the extinction of the Dharma" (*dharma-nirodha*) applies generally to all four kinds of Dharma, as each possesses the sense of extinction: because the teaching explains extinction; because practice extinguishes delusions; because the fruit is realized as extinction; and because the principle is fundamentally quiescent extinction.
Since the current text already contains the other three [aspects] throughout its upper and lower sections, this "extinction" (nirodha) refers to extinction as principle (li).
Furthermore, it accords with the meaning of "realization" (sākṣātkriyā), for in the Perfectly Integrated Teaching (yuanrong jiao), realization is permissible in this context.
Third, "abiding in the Buddha's true teaching" means that one understands the teachings and abides according to what has been taught.
Fourth, from "practicing the bodhisattva path" onwards, all are dharmas of practice.
These three phrases concern practice according to characteristics; "practice" refers to the myriad practices.
"Mind" refers to the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
"Liberation" refers to the various gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).
The subsequent two phrases refer to the locus of practice and abiding in signlessness (*animitta*), which corresponds to the aforementioned teaching, principle, and fruit.
The "practices" refer to the aforementioned myriad practices and so forth, all of which are free from defiled attachment.
Because of this, one is able to purify the bodhisattva path and become worthy of receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Second, regarding the benefit of others through great compassion, there are two parts:
First, one increases great compassion, and subsequently, one must resolve to deliver [beings].
Within the former, there are two parts:
first, observing the object of that compassion; second, increasing compassion while remaining free from attachment.
The preceding section also has two parts:

first, observing how one enters a perilous path due to delusion regarding the Four Noble Truths; second, observing how one enters a perilous path due to delusion regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This is the first.
The first two phrases introduce the moment of mindfulness.
From "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*) onwards, the objects of mindfulness are distinguished; there are thirteen phrases, the first of which is general and the remainder are specific.
In general, it is said that being deluded regarding the Four Noble Truths constitutes ignorance (*moha*).
Within the specific classification, the first five [ignorances] manifest the delusion, while the latter seven reveal its faults.
Among the former, the first is not knowing the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Second, not seeing the faults of the origin [of suffering];
third, not believing that the nature [of phenomena] is fundamentally quiescent;
fourth and fifth, being unable to cultivate the path, which consists of two parts: first, understanding, and second, practice.

The latter seven reveal the faults: first, because one does not perceive the fault of the origin [of suffering], one is stubborn, dull-witted, and greedily attached—this refers to delusion and craving.
Second, due to craving and attachment, one undergoes the suffering of birth and death.

Next, the four lines beginning with "not seeking to see" explain the failure to cultivate the path: the first three lack the conditions for the path, while the fourth is due to a lack of faith; thus, one becomes deluded regarding the correct path and loses the original understanding, taking what is false to be true, which is termed "error."
The latter [of the two] enters a perilous path and undergoes destruction due to the failure to practice previously;
the former is exclusively mundane (*pṛthagjana*).

From "lack of respect" (*agaurava*) onwards, it clarifies that because one is deluded regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one enters a perilous path, which applies to both the mundane and the Hinayana.
The first two phrases refer to being separated from superior conditions; the next two phrases refer to lacking superior causes; and the third refers to birth in emptiness as a place of dwelling.

Those who fear the emptiness of phenomena do so because they [fear it] will lead to annihilation. Therefore, at the conclusion of each assembly in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Subhūti, out of compassion for sentient beings who dread the emptiness of phenomena, raises the question:
"How can one cause all sentient beings to realize the emptiness of all phenomena?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not that a phenomenon existed previously and was later said to be non-existent.
Since it did not exist previously, it is likewise not non-existent now; its intrinsic nature is eternally empty—do not give rise to fear."
The section beginning with "Distant Separation" (*dūrībhāva*) comments upon the preceding meaning.
Because they fear emptiness due to their attachment to a locus, they distance themselves from the correct and dwell in the deviant; they abandon the level (*sama*) and enter the perilous.
Because they lack superior conditions, they turn their backs on the Buddha and follow Māra, clinging to existence without relinquishing it.
Māras delight in birth and death, whereas the Buddha dwells in emptiness.
Second, from "The Bodhisattva thus... onwards, the compassionate mind is increased and perfected as non-attachment.
Second, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva... onwards, he resolves to deliver [beings], following them through long kalpas with a heart of great compassion.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the arousal of practice; second, from "乃至" (even unto) onwards, the manifestation of non-attachment.
Within the former, there are also two sections:

First, it clarifies that the mind is free from weariness; because it is unattached, great compassion is firm and steadfast, such that one does not abandon those who are difficult to transform out of exhaustion.

Following this, the section beginning with "Furthermore" clarifies the vastness of that mind: transforming many sentient beings within a space the size of a single hair, and doing so throughout the entire dharma-realm—this is what constitutes vastness.
The second section, "Manifesting Non-attachment," has three parts:

first, using a small case to illustrate the many; second, extensively manifesting non-attachment from the phrase "In each and every... onwards; and third, questioning and explaining the reason for this from the phrase "Why... onwards.
Regarding the reason for non-attachment, the subsequent explanation contains two points:
first, because mindfulness is aroused toward the profound signlessness; second, because the preparatory application is initiated pervading the entirety of space.
Regarding the preceding section, the absence of marks (animitta) is difficult to clarify; thus, it is revealed by means of metaphors.
While these various metaphors generally illustrate all phenomena—as in the present chapter—here, for the sake of convenience in explaining the meaning, one is cited from each.
This demonstrates that all that was previously perceived is devoid of marks.

The first phrase constitutes the general observation of the dharma-realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*): because [phenomena] arise from conditions like illusions and lack substantial reality, one does not cling to them.
The remaining phrases constitute the specific analysis:
first, the Buddha manifests according to the capacities of sentient beings, just as a shadow follows its substance, and furthermore, he appears within the water of the mind.
Second, because the practices and thoughts of bodhisattvas have arisen, they have not yet attained great awakening.
Third, because it is a sound produced through conditions, there is speech according to what is perceived.
The remaining phrases of the sutra text, "All dharmas are like the limit of reality," serve as the summary.
Furthermore, the preceding clarification that the dharma-realm is like an illusion means that its very substance arises from conditions;
the subsequent conclusion that all dharmas are like the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) means that phenomena are quiescent within their own occurrence.

Ordinary people all claim that the limit of reality is unchanging while all dharmas are impermanent; because they use what they know as a metaphor for what they do not know, they employ the term "like" [to express this].

In truth, the phenomena of the world are perfectly interfused and are themselves eternally abiding; nevertheless, the ancients subsequently explained away doubts by means of seven successive metaphors.
The first doubt is as follows:
