This is a contentious teaching, like a poisoned arrow; it should not be pursued or investigated."
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also states: "All of these are worldly treatises; they are not what I have taught.

Regarding the mention of "fourteen," this refers to the four sets of four propositions mentioned above, wherein the fourth set of four is condensed into two: namely, that the body and the soul are one, and that the body and the soul are different.

Although various sutras and treatises frequently discuss the fourteen difficult questions (*caturdaśāvyākṛtavastūni*), their characteristics sometimes agree and sometimes differ; thus, I shall not labor here to reconcile them exhaustively.
This present sutra discusses them in detail, showing that they do not transcend the two attachments to self and dharmas (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).
The text is divided into five sections:
the first consists of four sets of four lines, which clarify the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature with respect to the self;
the second, beginning from "the past," discusses the relative numbers of ordinary beings and sages across the three periods of time.
3. From "What are... onwards, the sequence from beginning to end is discussed by distinguishing between ordinary beings and noble ones.
4. From "From what does the world arise... onwards, the origin of the three worlds is investigated.
5. From "What is" onwards, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is distinguished by way of the boundaries of birth and death.
Now, although there are sixteen [positions] in the first group, their faults do not exceed the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.

Regarding the term "the world," according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it encompasses the three worlds: namely, the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-loka*), and the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*).

The intent of this passage is primarily to clarify the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), while also elucidating the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-loka*); this is because sentient beings are the primary, conventional designations (*prajñapti-pudgala*), which non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) falsely conceive of as a self (*ātman*).

Regarding views such as "the world has an end," the first four propositions concerning having an end refer to the future life, while the four propositions concerning permanence and so forth refer to the past life.
Whether the Tathāgata exists or not arises based on nirvāṇa.
Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, in the "Chapter on False Views," states: "Was I in past lives existent or non-existent?
Views such as the permanence of the world all depend upon the past life."
"Regarding the future world, is it something created or uncreated?
Views such as 'having limits' and so forth all depend upon the future world.
The "Nirvāṇa Chapter" states: "Whether the Tathāgata exists or does not exist after his parinirvāṇa, these views arise based on nirvāṇa."
"The four propositions regarding the existence or non-existence of 'self' and 'sentient beings' are explained in reference to the present.
Having understood the root from which these views arise, the text is next interpreted section by section, divided into four parts.

Regarding the first tetralemma, those who speak of "having an end" are the non-Buddhist proponents of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*); they reckon that the self will no longer act in future lives and will perish along with this present body.
"Infinite" means that I shall have further actions to perform in future lives.
Regarding the third combined proposition: it is "finite" because the body has perished, yet "infinite" because the self is not different [from that which remains].
Regarding the fourth category, the "neither" position: this statement is also established because one perceives faults in the view that the self exists while the body perishes.
That is to say, because the body perishes, it is not infinite; because the self exists, it is not finite. Since both [of these views] are false views, [the Buddha] did not answer them.

If one wishes to refute this, the first two propositions fall into the error of denying the existence of future lives: that is, if there were a finite limit, then [the self] would perish together with the aggregates; if there were no limit, then it would be identical to the present body; therefore, in both cases, there would be no future life.
If there is no future life, what benefit is there in practicing the path and performing ascetic disciplines?
Regarding the third proposition—that there is both finitude and infinitude—if the body perishes while the self remains, are the body and the self one and the same, or are they different?
If they were one, there would be neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion; if they were different, by what characteristic apart from the aggregates could a self be known?

If you claim that when a person abandons their human state to be reborn in heaven, the human portion remains while the celestial portion increases, then one would be half-human and half-celestial; therefore, both positions are untenable.

Regarding the fourth alternative: if it is not finite, one does not escape non-existence; if it is not infinite, one does not escape existence. Why, then, do you insist on making such conceptual distinctions?
This concludes the four alternatives concerning the two [views of] permanence and so forth.
Regarding the past, if one holds that the self of the past is identical to the self of the present, this is called "eternalism.
If it were eternal, there would be a great error, as it would destroy the principles of cause and effect, nirvana, and so forth.

If you claim that the self is impermanent because it has only now arisen, then the self would be a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛta-dharma) and would likewise fall into the error of being causeless; if it were causeless, there could be no nirvāṇa and so forth.
The third view, seeing the faults of the two preceding positions, asserts that the self is eternal while the body is impermanent.
But apart from the body, where could the self exist?
Furthermore, this would incur the same two faults mentioned above.
The fourth [position] means that because the self is not different [from the body], it is not impermanent; yet because the body is different, it is not eternal.
This refutes the same [argument] as the third statement.
Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Since all phenomena are empty, how could there be views such as finitude, infinitude, or permanence?"
The remaining meanings are explained extensively in that treatise.
Regarding the four propositions beginning with "after the Tathāgata has passed away," there are two interpretations:
first, it clarifies that the term "Tathāgata" does not refer to a Buddha.
"Like" means similarity; "coming" refers to coming from the past limit (*pūrvānta*).
This refers to a certain proponent who asserts:

"Just as one comes from a previous life to be born in this world, so too is it when going toward a future life; therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata exists after death, because he exists just as he did when coming from the past limit."
This is because they reckon the self to be distinct from the aggregates.
Second, it is said:

"Just as one comes to this world from a previous life, after death there is annihilation; therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata does not exist after death," meaning that he does not go away as he came.
This is because they conceive of the self (*ātman*) as identical with the aggregates (*skandha*).

Thirdly, it is due to conceiving of the self as having both coarse and subtle aspects: the coarse self perishes together with the body, and thus they say it "does not go" after death; the subtle self is distinct from the aggregates and does not perish with them, and furthermore, it departs when the Tathāgata comes, and thus they say that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he both exists and does not exist.
The fourth [type of person] says: "I am like space, because my essence has neither coming nor going.
The Jin translation states: "After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he has gone, or he has not gone," and so forth; this is distinguished by referring generally to the three periods of time.
If one relies on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, the four propositions concerning Nirvāṇa take the Tathāgata as the Buddha.
Following the text of this sūtra, these are likewise the non-Buddhists establishing their own teacher as the Tathāgata.

Some say that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there must certainly exist something unchanging; others say that upon entering nirvana without remainder, he becomes identical to empty space; some say that because the dharmas exist, [the Tathāgata] should not be non-existent; and others say that from the perspective of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) he is not existent, while from the perspective of the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body) he is not non-existent.
Because all four propositions constitute frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and fail to perceive the Tathāgata’s mark of quiescent extinction, they are likewise considered false views.
This is something that even those of the provisional *Hīnayāna* followers have not yet been able to avoid.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 87, states: "Based on two principles, one observes according to reality that it is in both cases undeclared whether the Tathāgata exists or does not exist after passing into extinction."
Why is this? For, according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), that [Tathāgata] cannot be apprehended; how much less can he be said to exist or not exist after his passing away?
If, however, one relies on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), is the Tathāgata merely a provisional designation for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)?
Or is it for the sake of nirvāṇa?

If, regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), not a single phenomenon can be found to undergo transmigration after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, then at that time, where could one conventionally designate a "Tathāgata"?
Since there is no Tathāgata, how could there be "non-existence" and so forth?
If, regarding nirvāṇa, nirvāṇa is manifested solely by the absence of activity and is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),
then because it is personally realized within and is beyond conceptual proliferation, it is not reasonable to designate it as "existent."
Furthermore, one should not posit it as non-existent, lest one should undermine the positing of the sublime existence of the tranquil nirvāṇa.
Moreover, because this nirvāṇa is extremely difficult to know and most subtle, it is called "profound."
Because it is manifested by the severance of various and manifold conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called "vast.
Because it cannot be measured by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or valid scripture (*āptāgama*), it is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).

Regarding the four propositions concerning the existence or non-existence of the self and sentient beings: these all establish both [the self and the aggregates] as being sentient beings—that is, the five aggregates—rather than referring to a collective master. "Existence" implies definite existence, which leads to the attachment of eternalism;
"non-existence" implies definite non-existence, which leads to the attachment of nihilism.
Third, regarding the two faults mentioned above, if one posits both existence and non-existence simultaneously, one falls into contradiction.
Fourth, if one avoids this contradiction by positing a "neither-nor" category, it again becomes mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).

However, regarding these four propositions, there are also cases where one calculates that "the self exists but its attributes do not" or "its attributes exist but the self does not"; yet these do not depart from the first two propositions.
Furthermore, by combining the former two, the third is formed; and by mutually negating them, the fourth is formed—neither of which transcends the first two propositions.
Regarding the second gate, which clarifies the number of ordinary and noble beings of the three vehicles: because they are boundlessly vast horizontally, they cannot be recorded.
Regarding the third gate: because they are limitless vertically, they cannot be recorded.

Someone answered the question, saying: "There was a primordial Buddha who spoke of spontaneous awakening; even the otter’s sacrifice to Heaven was an instance of responding to capacity—how could one fail to bestow a prediction [of enlightenment]?
If there were such a primordial Buddha, the Tathāgata would surely have known him, and thus his name could have been mentioned."
As for the question "What are these phenomena?
they are all phenomena, such as those that are defiled or pure.
The fourth section investigates the origin of the world and contains six propositions:

The first two lines inquire about the world of sentient beings and the world of aggregates; the subsequent four lines concern the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) maintain that sentient beings have an initial beginning.
Some claim that [beings] come from the principle of primordial darkness (*avyakta-tattva*) and return to that same darkness.

Others claim that the world is composed of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), asserting that these most subtle forms are eternal and unchanging; they hold that when these atoms aggregate, they form the bodies and the receptacle-world, and when they disperse, they become subtle atoms once more.
These are all sources of wrong views; therefore, one should not provide an answer.

Regarding why the formation and destruction of the sentient world (*sattva-loka*) are not discussed, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "There are five differences between sentient beings and their environment (*bhājana*):

first, the environment arises from both common and uncommon causes for birth and death, whereas the birth and death of sentient beings arise solely from uncommon causes; thus, they differ in terms of cause."
Second, it refers to the difference in time, because while the receptacle world undergoes destruction and cessation, the flow of sentient beings continues without interruption.
Third, it refers to the difference in phenomena, because the three calamities bring about either destruction or non-destruction.
The fourth refers to the difference in the nature of cessation: the receptacle world has causes that are never permanently severed, whereas sentient beings are not so;

thus they are called "different in cessation. The fifth refers to the difference in continuity: the receptacle world ceases and then continues again, whereas once sentient beings have ceased, there is no further continuity; thus they are called "different in continuity."
For this reason, the formation and destruction [of the world] are omitted.
Regarding the fifth point, which concerns the prior and posterior limits of birth and death, there are only two phrases.
Question:
That the beginning is without origin is what is clarified in the holy teachings.
Is it not, then, the correct principle that birth and death have an end?
Answer:
Briefly, there are three meanings.
First, from the perspective of a single individual, one may say it has an end; yet, when viewed universally across all beings, there is no final limit.
Second, because they stubbornly cling to the long-lasting false view, one likewise should not provide an answer.
This means that if one admits there is an end, there must necessarily be a beginning; furthermore, eternal phenomena have neither beginning nor end.
Thirdly, because all three [extremes] cannot be predicated in terms of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "That which the Great Sage has taught is that a primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) cannot be found."
Birth and death have no beginning, nor do they have an end.
If there is neither beginning nor end, how could there be a middle?
Therefore, within this, neither priority, posteriority, nor both together exist.

Since it has been stated that the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is unattainable, one should not definitively assert that there is neither beginning nor end; how much less could there be the view of a beginning and an end?
Furthermore, a verse says: "Because the true Dharma, its teacher, and its hearer are difficult to find, therefore saṃsāra is neither finite nor infinite."
Most of the aforementioned false views belong to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), though some also involve the Hīnayāna.

When a Bodhisattva understands them well, they can engage in question-and-answer sessions without impediment; by then raising refutations, they cause both themselves and others to establish the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).
The second section, beginning with "Bodhisattva," clarifies the purpose of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).

It means that because sentient beings lack learning and thus remain submerged in birth and death for a long time, one vows to uphold the treasury of learning to realize it for oneself and to benefit others.
The sixth is the treasury of giving.
The three sections of the text are the same as before.
Within the explanation of its characteristics, there are two parts:
The first part enumerates the ten chapters; the second part, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," provides the detailed explanation according to those chapters.
Within this explanation, there are ten sections, each consisting of three parts: the heading, the exposition, and the conclusion.
Regarding these ten types of giving, the first six constitute the relinquishing of things—that is, body, life, and wealth;
the next three constitute the relinquishing of the mind—that is, non-attachment;
and the final one constitutes the relinquishing of both, which is termed the ultimate.
The first section, "Diminishing the Portion for Giving," has three parts within its explanation:
first, clarifying the characteristics of diminishing the portion;
second, from "If one eats oneself... onwards, clarifying skillful giving—wherein even when there is no external object of giving, one does not abandon the intention to give.
Third, the following section addresses the obstacles to giving.
Regarding the second type, "giving to the point of exhaustion," this means disregarding one's own livelihood and exhausting all that one possesses.

Nevertheless, while the intention to give must be perfected, the execution of the act must be measured; yet, if it serves to accomplish a great benefit, then one should have no stinginess regarding even body or life.
If they should seek only with insatiable greed, or with an evil mind desire to inflict great harm, one should employ skillful means to prevent such human wickedness.
For example, when King Candraprabha gave his head to his enemy, he robbed the people of their joy;
yet when he offered his life to two men, the king who was the enemy rejoiced at his death, while the beggar lamented it.
Although he possesses virtuous conduct, it cannot yet be taken as a complete standard.

Now, the term "exhausting [one's resources]" is used to demonstrate that the Bodhisattva’s mind of giving has been perfected; when faced with an appropriate object for giving, he never has any stinginess.
The internal, external, and both internal and external forms of giving should be understood according to this principle.
If it were otherwise, why would a bodhisattva—who can rain down the seven treasures to satisfy all beings—not practice such giving?
Furthermore, this is because one perceives that which is unsuitable for sentient beings.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics [of giving], there are three parts:

first, clarifying things that are difficult to give; second, from "At times... onwards, the objects of begging appear before one; third, from "The Bodhisattva thinks to himself... onwards, the actual practice of the act of giving.
Each of the four types of giving mentioned below possesses these three aspects.
The third is internal giving, which refers to one's own body.
The term "quǐng" means solitary or alone.
The *Yupian* states: "One without an elder brother is called *qiong*;
one without children is called *du*.
*Dun* means to diminish."
"Ji" (冀) means "to hope for.
The fourth external gift is the royal throne itself.
"Ju" (窶) refers to one who lacks the wealth to prepare the ritual offerings.
The fifth is the giving of both internal and external things: the royal throne is the external, while subjecting one's own body to service is the internal.
The sixth is the giving of all things: whatever objects one possesses.

The difference between this and the "exhaustive" or "internal and external" types of giving is as follows: the "exhaustive" type excludes partial or reduced giving and concerns itself solely with the necessities of life;
the "internal and external" type combines the previous two categories—namely, material goods and verbal services—and includes the royal throne.
The present mention of "all" encompasses the preceding various categories.
Furthermore, as this marks the conclusion of relinquishing these matters, it summarizes them all.
By citing the difficult to include the easy, a few items have been briefly listed; were they expanded, they would be boundless, as explained in the sixth dedication.

Regarding the seventh, giving in the past: although the general characteristics of giving throughout the three periods of time are all clearly explained as being without attachment, specifically, one does not give rise to longing for the past, preempts the pursuit of greed regarding the future, and maintains a mind free from defiled attachment in the present.
Now, regarding the past, the section on Śakra is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying non-attachment to the Buddha-dharma; second, from "Furthermore" onwards, clarifying non-attachment to all dharmas.
In the preceding section, the first two lines provide a general explanation;

the subsequent portion, beginning with "not giving rise to discrimination," provides a detailed exposition. First, it clarifies the characteristic of non-attachment: one who does not discriminate accords with the *dharmatā*.

Next, it explains that one neither becomes greedily stained nor seeks out flavors for enjoyment, nor does one employ skillful means to seek after these as personal virtues, nor does one initiate practice based upon them.
Next, from "seeing the Dharma" (*dṛṣṭadharma*) onwards, there is a broad explanation of having attained thorough understanding, which explains the reason for non-attachment.
Next, from "but for the sake of" (*kevalam...arthāya*) onwards, there is the resolution of doubts.
The doubt is as follows:
Since both are without attachment, how can one speak?
The commentary says:
It is for the sake of transforming sentient beings so that they may become free from attachment.

Second, regarding non-attachment to all phenomena: since they cannot be apprehended when sought through the wisdom of *prajñā*, even the objects currently manifest before one's eyes are understood to be empty by nature; how much more so, then, could one reckon them as existing among past phenomena?
The eighth is the giving for the sake of the future; the explanation is divided into two parts:
first, the formal exposition, and second, the resolution of doubts.
Within the former, one does not cling to the causes of practice, does not crave the fruit of a pure land, does not savor its excellence, and does not loathe its tasks.
"Not dedicating" explains the aforementioned "not relishing," because one does not seek superior pleasure by dwelling in self-complacency.
From "non-retrogression" onwards explains the aforementioned "not becoming weary," because one cultivates those practices.
Second, the section beginning with "merely desiring" (*but yu*) explains away the doubt.
The doubt is as follows:
"If one does not relish even purity, for what purpose is practice undertaken?"
This explanation has two intentions:
first, regarding compassion, it is solely for the purpose of gathering sentient beings;

second, from "However, this" onwards, regarding wisdom, one practices because wisdom realizes that things do not exist, because arising is non-arising, because there is no attachment or obstruction to phenomena, and because it is the arising of that which does not arise.
It is not that it has no location, because it is in profound accord with principle.
It is not that it has no location, because it possesses the forms and images of phenomena.

it is not near because of distinctions such as the hundred thousand [yojanas];

This is explained in reference to the Pure Land.
If one were to discuss future phenomena in general, it can be understood through the power of the mind.
From the phrase "furthermore, he acts" onwards, the meaning of relinquishment is again established by means of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, if one renounces even that which is directly perceived, how much more so that which has not yet taken form?
Regarding the ninth [type], giving in the present, there are three parts to the explanation:
first, clarifying the objects to be relinquished; second, from "Having heard" onwards, correctly clarifying the mind of renunciation; third, from "In order to" onwards, resolving external objections.
Regarding the first point: previously, the merits of the various devas were listed first, followed by those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).
In the preceding two periods, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas were cited; that now the various devas and the two vehicles are cited is merely due to the elliptical nature of the text.
Regarding the heavens, the first six belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as already explained in the first assembly.
From "Brahma Heaven" (*brahmāloka*) downward, the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are clarified.
However, there are slight differences among various accounts concerning the number of heavens included within the form realm.
Both the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Nyāyānusāra* state that there are seventeen; thus the verse says: "There are three in each of the first three dhyānas, and eight in the fourth dhyāna."
In the long prose section, sixteen [abodes] are established because the Brahmakāyika and Brahmapurohita heavens share the same celestial realm.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that "there are eighteen locations," referring to Mahāmaheśvara as being outside of Akaniṣṭha; it does not mention the Āsaṃjñika heaven, intending for it to be subsumed within the Bṛhatphala heaven.

Now, although there are twenty-two items according to the literal text, the first [item] of each of the four dhyānas is a general heading; thus, there are four for the first dhyāna, three each for the second and third, and eight for the fourth, which together total eighteen.
The *Nyāyānusāra* initially states that there are three [classes], and now the Brahmakāyika is added.
In the Jin translation, the name "Brahmaparṣadya" (Brahma-assembly) is rendered as "Brahmānucara" (Brahma-retinue).

If this is the case, since "kāya" (body/group) also carries the sense of a "multitude," then the Brahmakāyikas would be the external multitude led by him, while the Brahmaparṣadyas would be the internal retinue; the Brahmapurohitas would then be the attendants standing in the vanguard of the Great Brahmā.

The Great Brahmā (*Mahābrahmā*) is that very Heavenly King who has attained the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*). Because his majesty and virtue are superior both at birth and at death, he is called "Great.
Next, the "Luminous Heaven" (*Ābhāsvara*) and those below it comprise the three heavens of the second dhyāna: first, because within their own realm, the light of the gods is minimal;
second, because their radiance becomes increasingly superior and its extent is difficult to measure.
Regarding "Three Radiant Sounds," this refers to the emission of pure light from the mouth.
Following "Pure Heaven" (Śuddhāvāsa) are the three heavens of the third dhyāna; because they experience bliss on the level of the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*), they are collectively termed "Pure."
First, within its own stage, this purity is the most inferior, and is therefore called "limited purity" (parītta-śubha);
second, because the increase of purity is immeasurable;
third, because this purity is all-pervasive.
Next, below "Vipula" (Broad Heaven), the four dhyānas and eight heavens are explained.
The first three are mundane; because they are free from the eight calamities and afflictions, they are all termed "Vipula" (Broad).

Within their own respective levels, this merit is still inferior, hence they are called "Parītta-vipula" (Limited-Broad). This is because these three merits are difficult to measure, and among the fruits of the three types of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), this is the most excellent.

The realms above Avṛha are called the Five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). This means that the noble ones who have abandoned desire wash away the defilements of affliction with the water of the Noble Path; thus they are called "pure.
Because these are the dwellings of those with pure bodies, they are named "Pure Abodes."

Alternatively, because there are no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) mixed among these gods, and they are the dwelling place of pure sages (*ārya*) alone, they are called the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).

Regarding the first, the "Untroubled" (*Avṛha*): "trouble" (*vṛha*) refers to either confusion or vastness. This [level] is so named because it is the first among those free from confusion, and because it is the lowest among the vast heavens; this is according to the *Nyāyānusāra*.
If one were to apply this [explanation] to the present sutra in all cases, there would be no broad meaning.

Regarding the second, "Free from Heat" (Apariṇāda): because they have already skillfully subdued and eliminated the superior and middling grades of obstacles to the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, their mental dispositions are harmonious and supple, and they are free from the affliction of heat.
Alternatively, "heat" (*ūṣmagata*) has the meaning of being intensely blazing; this refers to the cultivation of superior dhyāna and its fruit, which have not yet been realized.

Third, "the stage of good manifestation" (*sudarśana*): having already attained the superior mixed cultivation of dhyāna, the qualities of its fruit are easily manifested; therefore, it is called "good manifestation."

Regarding the fourth, Sudarśana (Good Vision): because the remaining grades of obstacles to meditative concentration have been attenuated through mixed cultivation, vision is extremely clear and penetrating; thus it is named Sudarśana.
In the original sūtra, "vision" (jien) appears before "manifestation" (xiàn); this may perhaps be an error.

As for the ultimate limit of the five colors, there is no further state within the realm of form that can surpass this; or rather, because this has reached the final boundary of the body which serves as the basis for all suffering.
Regarding the phrase "up to the merits of the two vehicles," this is because one has transcended the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and so forth in the interim.

Second, in clearly explaining the mind of relinquishment: having heard of the aforementioned mundane and supramundane objects, one does not mistake them for reality, does not sink into craving, does not accumulate their causes of goodness, and does not waver through conceptual discrimination.
The phrase "but observe" (但觀) below explains the reason for this, which can be understood.
Third, regarding the resolution of difficulties: a doubt arises, saying:
"If it is stated that one does not accumulate wholesome causes, why then do you speak of the causes and effects of the five vehicles?"
The commentary states:

To rescue sentient beings from the intense sufferings of the three miserable realms and to provide rest for humans and devas; to cease the deluded attachments of inferior views and to employ the Two Vehicles as means of guidance—these are done solely for the sake of others, not because he himself would not relinquish them.
The tenth is ultimate giving; the text has three parts.
Regarding the inquiry into its name as before, there are briefly five reasons why it receives the designation "ultimate":

first, while the preceding six [types of giving] involve relinquishing wealth and life, and the next three involve relinquishing the mind of attachment, the present one encompasses both of these two approaches.
Second, because they give rise to great vows so that sentient beings may be free from attachment;
third, because they cause sentient beings to attain the ultimate fruit;
and fourth, because they do not give rise to even a single thought of craving or attachment, thereby being subtly free from attachment.
Fifth, because it is ultimately able to bring about real benefit for sentient beings.
For example, one who gives while lacking eyes and so forth is like an ordinary worldly person; how could such a person take another's eyes and place them upon themselves?
Now, by the power of the Bodhisattva’s merit—and specifically through the power of his roots of goodness characterized by kindness and compassion—he causes them to recover as before.
Just as the five hundred bandits were restored to their former state, it is therefore called "ultimate benefit."
In the explanation of the characteristics, there are three parts:

first, the manifestation of the objects of giving; second, the actual explanation of the practice of giving, beginning with "The bodhisattva hears..."; and third, the dedication for the sake of sentient beings, beginning with "As I... and so forth.
This section has two parts:
first, the actual practice of giving without stinginess;

second, from "But for oneself" onwards, the explanation of the reason for performing this practice, which arises from entering meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*), and this observation is precisely the meditation on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Regarding the statement that "all are called the body," one should observe that there are both general and specific perspectives. Specifically, observing each of the five aggregates individually as a "body," the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "This body is like a bubble; it cannot endure for long," and so forth.

By comprehensively observing that the five aggregates are all impermanent and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The five aggregates are themselves impermanent; impermanence is itself suffering; suffering is itself non-self," and so on.
Now, this contemplation of impurity refers specifically to the physical body (*rūpakāya*); the remaining three contemplations all pertain to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

Regarding the first, the contemplation of suffering (*duḥkhānupaśyanā*): it means that from the moment of entering the womb onwards, everything is subsumed under the category of suffering; old age and so forth are to be understood accordingly.
Second, the section beginning with "Furthermore, one contemplates" clarifies the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*), meaning that there is no real, sovereign master.

Regarding those who lack a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*): although they are provisionally sustained by bathing, clothing, and food, they may turn their backs on such kindness all at once, like small children.
That which is not a thing of the noble ones (ārya) belongs to the mundane world;
thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because of non-self, one causes the relinquishing of the mundane world.
Third, from the term "stench and filth" (*pūti-kutsita*) onwards, the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is clarified.
4. The section beginning with "Furthermore, he practices" clarifies the contemplation of impermanence (*anityatā*), because it contemplates [existence] as precarious and fragile.
Regarding the three types of dedication (*pariṇāmana*), they serve to distinguish [the Mahāyāna] from the Hīnayāna.

However, when a Bodhisattva cultivates this contemplation, since they take non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as their skillful means and because [all things] are identical with the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they have already transcended what is not shared with the Śrāvakas; how much more so, then, regarding the dedication?
The seventh section, the Treasury of Wisdom, is divided into four parts:
first, the inquiry into its name; second, the explanation of its characteristics; third, the conclusion regarding its name; and fourth, the praise of its benefits.
Within the explanation of its characteristics, there are two parts:
The first part clarifies the treasury of wisdom; the latter part explains its inexhaustibility. Within the former, there are three sections:

first, clarifying the knowledge of objects as they truly are; second, from "How... onwards, explaining the meaning of knowing them as they truly are; third, from "The bodhisattva accomplishes... onwards, summarizing various approaches to manifest skillfulness.

First, the wisdom of the Four Truths illuminates ten kinds of phenomena, which are subsumed into five categories: the first five are the five aggregates (*skandha*); the next two are the branches of existence (*bhavāṅga*); and the final three pertain to the three vehicles (*yāna*).
These five categories can be subsumed under two gates:
the first two pertain to the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the latter three pertain to the realm of the noble ones (*ārya*).

Furthermore, if the latter three are considered from the perspective of their fruition, then the first two constitute the four truths with conditioned activity (*sa-niṣyanda*) and the last one constitutes the four truths without conditioned activity (*a-niṣyanda*), because the causes and effects within and beyond the realms differ.
This is explained from the perspective of that which is observed.
If considered from the perspective of the Bodhisattva who observes, all are without volitional action (*anabhisamskāra*).
Furthermore, the first two [truths] pertain to the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*), while the latter three pertain to the process of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
The former, cessation and the path, constitute the beginning of the cycle of transmigration; by practicing them, one returns to cessation.
The latter, suffering and its origin, constitute the transmigration that has not yet been fully extinguished through such return.
Furthermore, the former refers to the phenomena that are known, while the latter refers to the person who knows.
The Dharma within humanity is precisely the aforementioned Dharma.
That which traverses the Four Noble Truths is the Dharma of the Śrāvakas;
that which takes the links of dependent origination as its object is the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas.
The five aggregates are the common dharmas of the three vehicles; knowing them all as they truly are is the dharma of a bodhisattva.
Regarding the phrase "knowing as it truly is," the subsequent sutra provides a general explanation, which shall now be briefly analyzed:
first, reality as fact (*yathābhūta*); second, reality as principle (*yathātathya*).

Among these ten, the first seven are suffering by their very nature (*lakṣaṇa-duḥkha*), because ignorance and craving possess the nature of being tainted (*sāsrava*), because they follow the nature of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and because they are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Conditionality constitutes origination; the absence of intrinsic nature is cessation; and the path is revealed as cessation, since it is manifested through its designation.
This is a general explanation and one according to the principle of cessation.
If explained specifically, the failure to comprehend impermanence, impurity, and so forth, which gives rise to craving and attachment, is called the "accumulation of form" (*rūpa-samudaya*).
If delusion and craving are extinguished, this is called the extinction of form (*rūpa-nirodha*).
Only serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) constitute the path to the extinction of form; through serenity one is detached from craving, and through insight one is detached from delusion.
If the auxiliary paths are included, there are also the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and so forth.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness may be understood by analogy with this.

As for the accumulation of ignorance, it arises from the improper guidance of others' speech and from one's own false conceptualization and incorrect reflection; the cessation of these is called "cessation."

Regarding the statement "the accumulation of craving," this refers to the feeling produced with contact conditioned by ignorance as its condition; likewise, the cessation of this is called "cessation.
The path of delusion and craving is explained in the same manner as the aggregates.

Among the twelve links, only two are singled out because these two alone initiate karma and moisten karma; furthermore, the first of each category is cited for that which projects and that which generates.
Ignorance and craving are mentioned because they are the source of the "disease" [of cyclic existence].
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 34, states: "From ignorance arises craving. One should know that this craving is itself ignorance. "From craving arises grasping";
one should know that this grasping is also ignorance. Other factors such as craving and so forth are likewise to be understood according to this principle.

Furthermore, regarding the three time periods, ignorance is the root, while craving and grasping constitute the limits; between these two lie the five factors beginning with consciousness, as well as birth and old age/death.

Now, one awakens to the fact that ignorance arises from being deluded regarding the five factors beginning with consciousness in the past; present craving is itself ignorance, and if it is not severed, the cycle of rebirth will not cease.
Now, by contemplating the severance [of these fetters], there shall be no further birth and death in the future.

Regarding the subsequent three [stages] as pure: for the śrāvaka, the person is the practitioner; the Four Noble Truths are the Dharma; the factors of the path practiced are the accumulation; and the fruit realized is nirvāṇa.
The twelve links of dependent origination are the dharma of the pratyekabuddhas.
The boundless dharma-realm is the dharma of the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, to know the śrāvaka is to know suffering; because the suffering of the śrāvaka is already known, only their stage is mentioned.
The Dharma is precisely that dharma which is practiced; it is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Accumulation (*samudaya*) refers to those afflictions; as long as accumulation is not yet exhausted, it constitutes the Truth of Accumulation (*samudayasatya*).
Because it has already been abandoned, the Dharma is mentioned after it.
Nirvana is precisely the Truth of Cessation; because cessation has already been realized, it is renamed "nirvana.
The cases of the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas may be understood by analogy with this.
The former explanation applies generally to the cause, while the latter explanation pertains specifically to the fruit.

If one were to determine that the first two [stages] constitute *fen-duan* (segmented birth) and the latter three constitute *bian-yi* (transformational birth), then those in the Small Vehicle who have not yet attained the third fruit would have to undergo transformational birth; furthermore, those below the seventh stage of the "directly proceeding" (*zhíwǎng*) class would not be within the scope of this knowledge. Therefore, this is untenable.

The second explanation concerns the meaning of "knowing as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). This does not merely refer to the ability to know the characteristics of the path, but also reveals the characteristics of that which is known.
First, there is the inquiry; second, the explanation.
The intent of the inquiry is as follows:
Is it through knowledge that conforms to characteristics? Or is it through knowledge that is free from characteristics?
If it were through knowledge that conforms to characteristics, how would it differ from that of ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle?
If there is no cognition of characteristics, and no characteristics to be cognized, one asks: "How is it known?
The subsequent explanation clarifies the meaning:
that the nature of the characteristic and its cognition is without obstruction is what is known by a bodhisattva; this cognition of non-cognition is the knowledge of a bodhisattva.
The text is divided into two parts:

first, regarding self-benefit, it clarifies the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*); second, regarding the benefit of others, it manifests the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*). These two sections are mutually abbreviated; each should actually contain all four [noble truths].
Furthermore, the second section contains the first five categories and fully reveals the three vehicles.

Now, within the first section, knowing that [phenomena] arise from karmic retribution is the characteristic of the five aggregates; that the accumulation of karma results in the suffering of retribution is the characteristic of the two truths; and stating that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are produced through causes and conditions.

The causal conditions of the various formations (*saṃskāra*) within the twelve links of dependent origination are the products of the characteristic of accumulation (*samudaya-lakṣaṇa*); this is the characteristic of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

The preceding section has distinguished the characteristic of knowledge (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*). From the word "all" (*sarva*) onwards, the characteristic of knowing non-existence (*abhāva-jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) is revealed as applying to both suffering and its accumulation.
The first two phrases describe the common characteristics of the three vehicles.

From "not-self" (*anātman*) onwards, the text explains the preceding section and distinguishes their specific characteristics: because they are not-self, they are empty and lack substantial reality; thus, the characteristic of the śrāvaka is that [the self] is merely a provisional designation based upon the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Because it is not solid, empty, and without reality, being merely a provisional construction dependent on conditions—this is the characteristic of a pratyekabuddha.
If not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended, being empty and without reality, but consisting only of illusory and provisional marks—this is the characteristic of a bodhisattva.
It is not the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*), because there is nothing that can be established.
Second, from the phrase "wishing to cause" onwards, [the text] next clarifies the knowledge of cessation and the path with respect to the benefit of others.
Being able to know the true nature is the characteristic of the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
The indestructibility of phenomena and their nature as objects of knowledge constitute the characteristic of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
This is explained extensively as being exclusively the characteristic of a Bodhisattva.
The text consists of two parts:
First, the intended meaning of the statement is indicated;
second, from "for the sake of explaining" onwards, there is a successive interrogation and explanation.
In total, there are three layers.
The initial inquiry asks:
"By teaching what Dharma can one come to know the true nature?
The explanation states:
It is said that they are indestructible;
this briefly indicates their thesis.
Next, it asks:
Is this "indestructibility" its nature (*svabhāva*) or its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)?
This is the point where the inquiry is addressed.
The commentary states:
Because their characteristics are identical in nature, the five categories of phenomena and so forth are all indestructible.
According to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, this applies universally to everything from form (*rūpa*) up to and including the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The subsequent objection states:
"We currently perceive all phenomena to be as unreal as a mass of foam, a bubble, a mirage, a plantain tree, an illusion, or a dream; how then can you say they are indestructible?
The following provides the reasons for this response, briefly summarized through three points:
First, the nature of form and so forth is empty because there is nothing that can be destroyed;
if emptiness were achieved only through destruction, it would not be primordial emptiness.
Second, emptiness is identical to reality because it is one with the dharma-nature.
If [the conventional] were destroyed to reveal the real, then phenomena would exist outside of principle;
thirdly, because it is emptiness itself, there is no need for destruction—
were it to be destroyed, it would result in annihilation.
In this passage, there are ten phrases comprising five pairs:
first, because it is without self and without agency, it is indestructible;
second, because it is free from the signifier and the signified.
Third, the producer neither produces nor is produced, because that which is produced does not arise;
fourth, the cause does not take up the fruit, because the fruit is not given to the cause;
fifth, its essence is without movement or change, because its function is without the characteristic of activity.

Third, the summary of various approaches to manifest skillfulness: there are further approaches wherein taking "non-apprehension" and so forth as minor expedients results in the exhaustion of the view of form and emptiness; with both "destruction" and "non-destruction" vanished, one does not follow after objects, which is termed "awakening not dependent on others."
The second [section] explains the meaning of inexhaustibility, consisting of a heading, an inquiry, an explanation, and a conclusion.
The explanation also comprises ten matters in five pairs:
first, causes and conditions; second, teaching and principle; third, merit and wisdom; fourth, retention and eloquence; fifth, knowledge and supernormal powers.

Regarding the statement in the *Fozhi jing* (Sutra on the Wisdom of the Buddha) that there is "one flavor": just as flowers of a hundred different colors together form a single sheath [of petals], so too, although the myriad dharmas differ, they are permeated by a single wisdom; it is also like the aforementioned ghee, into which nothing does not enter.
The three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the four exhortations (*anuśaṃsā*) can be understood from the text.
Regarding the eighth, the "Treasury of Mindfulness" (*smṛtinidhāna*),
there are four parts in the explanation of its characteristics:

First, a general indication of the essence of mindfulness; second, the distinctions of the objects of mindfulness; third, the superior characteristics of the subject that mindfully recollects; fourth, the characteristics of the benefits of mindfulness.

Within the second section, "Recollection," which concerns the distinctions of the objects of mindfulness, the clarity of memory is elucidated solely by means of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*), briefly citing ten matters to demonstrate its inexhaustibility.

First, the life-span; second, the eons; third, the names of the Buddhas; fourth, the bestowal of predictions; fifth, the exposition of the teachings; sixth, the assemblies; seventh, the explanation of the meanings; eighth, the faculties and natures; ninth, that which is to be remedied; and tenth, the remedies—the texts for each of these may be understood accordingly.
The twelvefold teaching shall now be briefly explained.
Formerly called the "twelve-part scriptures" (*dvādaśāṅga-sūtra*), this was renamed "twelvefold teaching" to avoid confusion with the physical volumes of the canon.
Each of these possesses two characteristics, except for the *sūtra*, which may have either two or three.
*Sūtra* (xiūduluó) is here translated as "Scripture in Accordance with Truth" (*qi jīng*), as detailed in the first fascicle.

Regarding the two characteristics: the first is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 15: "From the beginning, 'Thus have I heard,' down to the end, 'rejoicing and practicing accordingly,' all are *sūtras*."

Second is the *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic). The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, fascicle 11, states: "It refers to prose compositions that briefly explain the meanings that ought to be explained.
Furthermore, there are alternative names; these four are: first, *dharmapada*;
second, *nāmamātra-sūtra*; third, *vartamāna-vyākhyāna*; and fourth, *ārya-śāsana*.

Regarding the term "the root of the Dharma" (*dharmamūla*), Master Huiyuan explained it through five meanings: first, the teaching is the root of the principle; second, the sūtra is the root of the śāstra; third, the general is the root of the specific; fourth, the initial is the root of the subsequent; and fifth, the concise is the root of the extensive—this being because he established three types of *sūtra*.

First, the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); second, the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); third, the fundamental characteristic, also called the abbreviated characteristic (*saṃkṣepa-lakṣaṇa*).
The general characteristic is no different from what preceded.

"Specific" refers to the eleven [categories] derived by branching out from the aforementioned general characteristic; those not included elsewhere are again subsumed within the *sūtra*, which is termed the "specific characteristic."
Using these specific characteristics to examine the *geya* and other categories, because they serve as its basis, the former is called the "basis" for the latter.

As for what is meant by "characteristics of the basis": among those twelve divisions of the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), that which first briefly sets forth the titles is called the *sūtra*, while that which subsequently provides detailed explanations is designated according to its specific name.

To speak of "form" (rūpa) is the fundamental, concise characteristic; furthermore, to mention "blue, yellow," and so forth, is called the detailed characteristic. Therefore, it is said that the concise serves as the basis for the detailed.
However, the latter two [categories] do not contradict the prose commentary (*gadya*) of the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, which mentions "compilation" (*saṃgraha*) and so forth.

"Compilation" refers precisely to those works not included among the eleven categories, such as the passage in the "Bhadramukha Chapter" stating, "At that time, Mañjuśrī, having spoken on the great power of pure conduct free from turbidity and confusion," and other similar instances. These are compilations by the redactors (*saṃgītikāra*), not the direct teachings of the Buddha; therefore, they are said to be "not included among the eleven."

The meaning of what should be briefly explained is precisely the brief version serving as the basis for the extensive version; it is of the same category as, for example, that which is intended to manifest the merits of the bodhicitta.

This third summary of characteristics also accords with the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. The *Tattvasiddhi* is called "direct exposition" (*ṛju-nirdeśa*); it is termed "direct exposition" because its language speaks of general characteristics as a whole, whereas the analytical differentiation of many meanings within each individual expression is termed "non-direct exposition."
Thus, throughout all twelve divisions of the teaching (dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana), each possesses these three aspects.
Within the twelve divisions, the Sūtras generally encompass the first three;

however, as for the Sūtras within the Three Piṭakas, they are restricted solely to the general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa). It is only by opening up the specific meanings of the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* that the latter two [aspects] are established.

There are those who, being ignorant, falsely criticize the former sages, claiming that the *sūtras* rely only on general characteristics and functional applications; however, such a view contradicts the statements in the prose sections of various treatises concerning "compilation" and so forth.
Second, *geya* (祇夜) is translated here as "Verses to be Chanted" (*ying song*).
First, it refers to verses that correspond to the prose (*gadya*), because what was not fully expressed in the prose must be further explained through chanting.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "Sūtras of incomplete meaning (*neyārtha*) should be further explained through verses."
This is of the same category as the verses on the "Abiding in the Arising of the Mind" from the "Ten Stages Chapter.
Second, it is because one should further provide verses for those who arrive later.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the past, the Buddha finished expounding the sūtras for the bhikṣus."
At that time, there were also sentient beings of sharp faculties who, having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling later in order to hear the Dharma, immediately asked others:
"What did the Tathāgata speak about just now?"
The Buddha, knowing this, then recited verses based on the original sutra, saying:
"In the past, I and you were all ignorant of the Four Noble Truths; for this reason, we have long wandered through the great ocean of suffering of birth and death," and so forth.
Regarding the third, the "Prediction" (Vyākaraṇa): in Sanskrit it is called *vyākaraṇa*, also translated as "prediction.
"Prediction" (*ji*) means recording; "distinction" (*bie*) refers to differentiation.
The first type records the causes and effects of birth and death for disciples, and its texts are not uniform.
Second, there are predictions concerning the future buddhahood of bodhisattvas, such as the prediction for Maitreya;
the texts for both of these are found in this "Chapter on the Resolve for Awakening" and the "Chapter on Manifestation."
The four *gāthās* are here translated as "recited verses" (*fèngsòng*).
"Recited" (*fèng*) is itself "verse" (*sòng*, *geya*), referring to independent verses (*gūqǐ jì*).
This is for two reasons: first, to facilitate easy recitation and retention; second, for the sake of those who delight in verse.
The three-day verses of praise (*tridaṇḍaka-stotra*) all belong to this category.
The five *nidānas*—here translated as "causes and conditions"—are as follows:
first, those spoken only upon request, because of the gravity accorded to the Dharma, such as the instances of the three families making five requests and so forth.

Seventh, the *itivṛttaka* (Sanskrit: *itivṛttaka*).

One type describes the Tathāgata, such as the account of how he repeatedly took rebirth and encountered various Buddhas due to his majestic radiance.

the Jātaka (Birth Stories) primarily describes the taking on of a physical body.
Ninth, the Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings), which in Sanskrit is called Vaipulya:
first, because they provide vast benefit and happiness; second, because they extensively set forth the True Dharma.
This entire scripture bears this title.

First, because their virtuous deeds are extraordinary: for example, when the Buddha was first born, he immediately took seven steps; likewise, this sutra ascends to the four heavens without rising from its seat, and so forth.

First is profound wisdom: it employs semblances to enable the understanding of the ultimate reality. The first chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

As stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, bodhisattvas cultivate śamatha based upon the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 21, states: "The Buddha expounded each of the twelve divisions of the teaching individually for the sake of the śrāvakas.

As for the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* stating that there are only nine for the Mahāyāna, this is based on the minor characteristics within the three categories [of the twelvefold division]: taking the causal events from the *nidāna* (causal narratives) as the formulation of precepts; relying on the method of attraction within the *avadāna* (parables); and regarding those of non-definitive meaning within the *upadeśa* (expositions).

Regarding the nine classes of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, although they are minor in their specific forms, they are great in their three characteristics. Within the *Vyākaraṇa* (Prophecies), it takes up the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood; within the *Svayambhūbhāṣita* (Self-Explanations), it relies on the uninvited friend; and within the *Vaipulya* (Extensive Teachings), it relies on vast benefit and joy. Thus, its True Dharma is extensively set forth, encompassing both the Great and the Small Vehicles.

However, when the *sūtra* (契經) is compared to other categories, it is admitted that it may possess both general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and abbreviated characteristics (*saṃkṣipta-lakṣaṇa*), yet it lacks specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

The *geya* (應頌), *geyya* (諷頌), *itivṛttaka* (本事), and *jātaka* (本生) have no mutual correspondence with one another. The *udāna* (自說) and *nidāna* (因緣) may, however, have mutual correspondence, as in the case where a teaching is delivered due to a specific event rather than at the request of others.
Excluding those already excluded above, all others are mutually present.

Chapter Twenty-three: Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. From Sutra 22 to the midpoint of Sutra 25, this marks the fifth assembly, clarifying the Ten Dedications of the Superior Sages.
The four gates are the same as before.

Regarding the first, the intent of the coming [of this chapter]: first, to harmonize the preceding [material], it is precisely for the purpose of answering the previous question concerning dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). It dedicates the preceding practices of understanding and conduct (*adhimukti-caryā*) toward true realization (*bhūta-pramāṇa*), extensively benefiting oneself and others, so that one's practice may be all-encompassing and leave nothing incomplete.

The *Bodhisattva-mahāyānābhidharma-kośa-sūtra* states: "That which draws forth immeasurable fruits from a small root of virtue is the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*), for the mind of dedication constitutes a great benefit."
Therefore, it is explained subsequently.
Furthermore, as the previous practice has already been established, the present compassion and vows are now even more expansive.

As for the subsequent chapters that follow: since the preceding assembly has concluded and the subsequent discourse is about to be presented, this chapter first clarifies the location of the teaching to manifest the nature of the Dharma; thus, it is introduced here.
Second, regarding the explanation of the names: first, concerning the derivation of the name [of the assembly], there are also three meanings, identical to the two previous assemblies.

Second, regarding the explanation of the chapter title: Tuṣita is the place; because the Buddha, by means of his Dharma-realm body, responds to beings without arising from it, it is called "Ascending."
To speak of them as dwelling here indicates that their status is transcendentally superior, as this follows the sequential order.
Furthermore, while those above and below are heedless, these devas are content; this signifies the fulfillment of worldly conduct, and thus they dwell in the Heaven of Joyful Contentment (*tuṣita*).
Furthermore, because he is in his final birth before enlightenment (*ekajātipratibaddha*), it signifies that the merit and practice of the bodhicitta are complete.

Moreover, having accumulated merit and built up virtue, he realized that his own rank was still insufficient; thus, by transferring his merit to his son, he came to know that there was indeed a surplus.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: though he has diligently accumulated practices without finding any sense of surplus, it is only upon dedicating them to sentient beings that he knows true sufficiency.
Furthermore, among the six heavens of the desire realm, this [heaven] dwells in their midst, signifying the balanced equilibrium of compassion and wisdom, as it abides in the center.

Furthermore, those born in this heaven cultivate the three types of merit—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration—whereas others do not possess them all, or possess them unevenly and disproportionately; therefore, it is said that they dwell here.
Regarding the third point concerning the essential tenets (*zongqu*): the assembly takes the ten dedications toward the great vows as its tenet and the attainment of the stages (*bhūmi*) as its goal.
This chapter takes ascending to heaven and responding to conditions as its tenet and the exposition of the dedications as its goal.
Fourth, the explanation of the text.
This assembly consists of three chapters of scripture: the first two concern the causes and conditions leading to this assembly, while the last one constitutes the formal teaching itself.
As for why there is no further advancement [beyond these], it is due to two reasons:

First, because this assembly marks the conclusion of the stage of the three types of worthies (*tri-śaikṣa*), it subsumes the preceding stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) as a whole into the skillful means for entering the [first] ground; since the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) constitutes a superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*) in its own right, there is no separate category for it.
Throughout this sutra, there are four general patterns:

first, those concerning the transition from the fulfillment of practice to entry into the stages, such as in the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla-paṭala*), where the fulfillment of faith serves as the preparatory means for both entering and abiding.

Second, regarding the juncture of entering realization through the fulfillment of vows: such dedication serves as the preliminary means for entering the stages (*bhūmi*) upon the completion of the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.

Third, regarding the juncture of entering the state of non-effort through the fulfillment of effort: this is like the initial stage of the eighth *bhūmi*, which subsumes the preceding seven stages as its preparatory means; this marks the completion of the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.

Fourth, regarding the stage of fulfillment at the causal level: as in the first moment of the tenth bhūmi, which subsumes the preceding nine bhūmis as the preparatory means for entry; this refers to the subsumption at the point where the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas are completed.
In other cases, where positions are contiguous, there is a distinct expedient means; therefore, they are not of one type.
When one wishes to enter the stages from two directions, one must necessarily abandon the aspect of progressive advancement, as this serves as the expedient means for non-conceptualization.

Regarding the first two chapters: the former concerns the primary transformer responding to the needs of sentient beings, while the latter chapter assists in the transformation by praising the Buddha.
Within this first chapter, there are broadly ten sections: 1) the simultaneous manifestation of the original assembly;

2) ascending without departing; 3) beholding the Buddha’s majestic abode; 4) welcoming the Buddha and presenting offerings; 5) observing the Buddha’s supreme virtues; 6) requesting the Buddha to occupy the palace; 7) the Tathāgata accepting the invitation; 8) the heavenly kings obtaining benefits; 9) offering verses of praise through the power [of the Buddha]; and 10) the Tathāgata taking his seat.
This is the first [section].

The initial term "supernatural power" (*ṛddhi*) refers to the pervasive cause; it does not necessarily imply the arising of the supernormal power of the physical realm (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*), but rather denotes the power of mastery over the mind achieved through cultivation.
From the phrase "in the ten directions" onwards, the manifested appearances are distinguished; herein, there are both the primary transformers (*nirmātṛ*) and their assistants.

Looking forward to the fourth assembly, since it extends to the summit of Mount Sumeru, this [passage] should likewise state that he sat beneath a tree, on the summit of Mount Sumeru, and in the palace of the Yāma Heaven; the absence of such wording here is due to abbreviation.

In the second section, the preceding [sections] are carried forward; since the latter is fully presented, the former four are implied by shadowing, thereby revealing that all four are complete and pervasive.

The second section, beginning with "At that time," clarifies ascending without departing. This means that while the four assemblies in all ten directions previously mentioned remained solemnly without dispersing, [the Buddha] ascended to deliver this teaching. The intent is to clarify that [the Buddha’s presence] extends horizontally throughout the ten directions and vertically encompasses the nine assemblies, for the Dharma-body of the Buddha-pāramitā pervades all times and places.
The remaining meanings are fully detailed as in the beginning of the third assembly.

The "Deva of Skillful Reflection" (Sudhīmat) also encompasses all categories.
Third, beneath the "Bodhisattva Deva," there are twelve phrases that clarify the Bodhisattva’s activities of making offerings.
4. The four lines beginning with "The sons of the gods emerged from their celestial palaces" describe the offering of the bodies of the devas.
5. The ten lines beginning with "Contemplating the Bodhisattva" describe the offering of the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the Dharma, and also clarify the benefits obtained.

The reason why the bodhisattvas primarily clarify the attainment of benefits while the devas merely speak of making offerings is that the offerings of the devas are the cause of those benefits, and the attainment of benefits by the devas is itself the bodhisattva.
The third section, beginning with "a hundred trillion roots of goodness," extensively elaborates on the profoundness of the preceding causes; these ten phrases are thus to be understood.

As for why the adornments and services in this assembly are so numerous, it is because among these devas, many serve as kings of the stage of the Bodhisattva in his final birth (abhiṣeka-bodhisattva).
The two stages of the Sages have already reached their ultimate limit because Great Compassion is universally pervasive.
Thus, the Ten Abodes lack the adornments of Bodhisattvas to signify that ordinary beings are entering these stages;
whereas the Yāma Heaven does possess them because [the Sages] have already entered those stages, yet even there they are not yet extensive.

These supreme manifestations are all the sovereign, real virtues of the differentiation of the dharma-realm as manifested by the Tathāgata’s ocean-seal samādhi; they are the magnificent array in which persons and dharmas are unimpeded, and the environment and its inhabitants are harmoniously integrated.
The second section, beginning with "In this world," concludes by extending the application [of the description] to the ten directions, as should be understood.
The fourth section, beginning with "At that time," describes welcoming the Buddha and presenting offerings.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the welcoming and offering; second, from "At that time, by the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power" onwards, the seeing of the Buddha and the offering.
Within the former, there are two [subdivisions]:
First is the welcoming; second, from "With purity" onwards, is the offering.
Within this, first are the offerings made by the devas.

That they all emerge from their bodies not only manifests the power of the devas' merit, but also signifies that the body itself serves as the offering implement, and that the offering arises from the mind.
Regarding the section following "Tuṣita Palace," the offerings presented by the bodhisattvas can be understood [from the text].

Within the second part, concerning the offerings presented upon seeing the Buddha, there are two sections: first, the devas; second, the bodhisattvas, as clarified in the passage beginning with "hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas who had previously resided [there]."
The preceding section has three parts:

first, clarifying the seeing of the Buddha through the power of support, which includes (1) the manifestation of the Buddha’s supernatural power, (2) the power of past roots of goodness, and (3) the power of the Dharma-gate;
second, from "Together they arise" onwards, celebrating the encounter and welcoming [the Buddha].
Third, the section beginning with "Each with... correctly elucidates the offering.
This section has three parts;
first, ten lines describe the offering of garments scattered before the Buddha, symbolizing that by cultivating quiescence (*śamatha*), one proceeds toward the fruit of enlightenment.

Second, the ten phrases beginning with "hundreds of thousands of billions" clarify the arousal of the mind to rain down offerings that adorn space; they manifest that the myriad practices cultivated accord with the emptiness of the dharma-nature. That emptiness and existence are non-obstructive is the meaning of "adorning space."

Third, the nine phrases beginning with "three hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta-asamkhyeya* devaputras" present various offerings, signifying the integrated cultivation of the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*).
If "a mind that is disciplined, tranquil, and free from negligence" is divided into two, there will be ten phrases in total.
In the second section, "The Bodhisattvas Present Offerings," there are two parts:

first, clarifying the offerings of the supporting environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) resulting from their practice; second, following the phrase "those bodhisattvas," clarifying the offerings of the primary physical bodies (*mūla-deha*).
The first twenty-seven phrases of the middle section are divided into three parts:
the first ten phrases consist of offerings of multiple causes producing multiple effects;
the next eight phrases consist of offerings of a single cause producing a single effect.
Regarding the latter nine phrases, "one cause producing multiple effects," there should be four permutations;
however, the case where multiple causes produce a single effect is subsumed under the first section, because multiple causes are capable of producing each individual effect.
Furthermore, the first section consists of "one within all" and "all within all"; the second section consists of "one within one"; and the third section consists of "all within one."
Now, in the first ten lines, many causes are presented simultaneously; subsequently, these collectively establish all offerings.
Regarding the phrase "surpassing all devas," it is because [the Buddha] is superior and more numerous.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
In the second set of one cause and one effect, in each case the cause and effect are analogous:
first, the canopy is used to obstruct dust, just as wisdom can eliminate defilements;
second, the curtain is used for shelter, just as compassion serves as the realm of the Buddha.
The flowers bloom in full splendor, like the awakening and understanding of purity.
Through the harmonious joy of the three dharmas of patience, one adorns the Dharma-body.
Fourth, by unfolding the net of teachings, one vibrates the wondrous sound of the vajra; by contemplating the net of teachings, one perceives the principle without being obstructed by the words.

The five fragrances are such that they can be smelled but not seen; they can be seen but not grasped. They are like illusory phenomena (*māyā-dharma*), which can be seen but not seized, and though seized, cannot be obtained. One knows that illusion lacks solidity, yet through it, solid phenomena are established.
Sixth, the emptiness of pervasive phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*); this is the objective realm upon which the Buddha’s wisdom-body relies, and thus it has the meaning of a "seat.
Seventh, the destruction of the banner of indolence and pride, because one plants the supreme banner of the Dharma.
Eighth, all dharmas are like dreams; this is the place where the Buddha dwells.
Third, from "non-attachment" (*asaṅga*) onwards is the offering of many fruits from a single cause.

Non-attachment and non-arising (*anutpāda*) are but one meaning: non-arising refers to principle (*tattva*), while non-attachment refers to wisdom (*jñāna*); only when these two are in harmony do they constitute a single cause.
The nine phrases within the text may be understood as follows.
Regarding the second body, which emerges from the offerings of the primary retribution, there are ten phrases:
the first two clarify the magnitude of the manifested body’s virtues, meaning that each individual measure pervades the Dharma-realm and its virtues are equal to those of a Buddha.
Next, the three phrases beginning with "Because of following" clarify the causes of superior eloquence;
next, the four phrases beginning with "Endowed with" manifest the basis upon which superior eloquence relies;

finally, the single phrase beginning with "Because it cannot" formally expresses the praise of this eloquence. Since all these flow from the treasury of dharanis and eloquence, emotions are stirred within and thus take form in speech; yet even such speech is insufficient to fully express the height of this reverence.
Fifth, from "At that time, all... onwards, within the section on beholding the Buddha’s supreme virtues, there are two parts:

first, clarifying the supreme virtues of the clouds of the Buddha’s body; second, from "At that time, the Tathāgata’s great compassion... onwards, clarifying the intention behind manifesting these supreme virtues.
The preceding section is divided into two parts:
first, beholding the Buddha’s supreme virtues; second, from “At that time, the great assembly all saw” onwards, beholding the Buddha’s application of light.
The former pertains generally to what is seen by the ten eyes, while the latter refers specifically to what is seen by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
This is the first [section].

However, as for the text of this sutra, it sequentially and fully reveals the twenty-one kinds of the Tathāgata’s preeminent merits; because the wording is so vast and extensive, ancient commentators have all been equally confused.

However, although the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*) contains twenty-one phrases, the meaning of this text is both comprehensive and extensive; therefore, I shall cite it from various treatises as appropriate.
The text is divided into three parts:

first, a general contemplation of the Tathāgata; second, a specific contemplation of his virtuous marks and characteristics; and third, the conclusion that establishes the contemplative understanding.
Now, first, three qualities are briefly cited to manifest the One Hero:
the first is "Tathāgata";
the second, the term "Arhat," refers to the Worthy One (Arhat).
