Therefore, while the significance of these three requirements is boundless, I shall briefly set forth ten points: namely, because they rely upon the three dharmas; because they extinguish the three paths; because they purify the three clusters of precepts; because they manifest the three Buddha-natures; because they perfect the Three Jewels; because they harmonize the three bodies; because they possess the three virtues; because they attain the three types of enlightenment; because they realize the three nirvāṇas; and because they abide securely within the three kinds of secret treasuries.

Regarding "relying on the three dharmas": these are true nature (*tathatā*), contemplative illumination, and the supportive accomplishment; they correspond to the essence, attributes, and function (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-vṛtti*) of the *Awakening of Faith*. Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) relies on the essence, bodhi relies on the attributes, and sentient beings rely on the function.

Regarding the two extinctions and the three paths: only by perceiving the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) within suffering can one extinguish suffering; by illuminating the emptiness of afflictions, one immediately attains bodhi; and by transforming the karma of fetters and bonds, one creates the karma for benefiting sentient beings.

Regarding the three purities and the three aggregates: that which is directed toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) refers to the restraint that avoids transgressions; that which is directed toward bodhi refers to the extensive gathering of all virtues; and that which is directed toward sentient beings refers precisely to the gathering of beings.

Fourth, regarding the manifestation of the three Buddha-natures: the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is the direct cause (*dharmatā-hetu*), bodhi is the revealing cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*), and that which is directed toward sentient beings is the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

Fifth, regarding the accomplishment of the Three Jewels: the reality-limit accomplishes the Dharma, bodhi accomplishes the Buddha, and that which is directed toward those sentient beings accomplishes the Sangha of identical substance (*sahaja-kāya*).
Sixth, the three bodies in six assemblies refer to the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body.
Seventh, the possession of the three virtues refers to cessation, wisdom, and benevolence.

Eighth, the attainment of the three types of bodhi refers to the bodhi of true reality, the bodhi of true wisdom, and the bodhi of skillful means, because one manifests the attainment of Buddhahood beneath the Bodhi tree.

Regarding the nine proofs of the three nirvāṇas: these are the nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), the nirvāṇa of perfected purity (*pariśuddhi*), and the nirvāṇa of purity through skillful means (*upāya-viśuddhi*), which is like the extinction of fire when the fuel is exhausted.
If, according to the *Dilun*, there were only the latter two [stages], then how would the fulfillment of ultimate truth differ from the manifestation of parinirvāṇa? The same applies to bodhi.
The four preceding stages are to be correlated, respectively, with the dedication to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), bodhi, and sentient beings; this can be understood through reflection.

Regarding the ten ways of abiding in the three secret treasuries: by turning toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one abides in the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), for the Buddha takes the Dharma as his body, which is pure like space.
By inclining toward bodhi, one can accomplish prajñā, for bodhi possesses luminous discernment that abides in ultimate illumination.
By inclining toward sentient beings, one can accomplish liberation, for having oneself free from afflictions, one causes others to attain liberation.
Manifesting spontaneously in response to circumstances is also the liberation of unimpeded understanding.
Based on these ten meanings, the three types of dedication are established.
If one establishes the three kinds of bodhicitta, they likewise rely upon these ten.
Furthermore, within these ten, taking one as the primary leads to their successive interdependence.
Moreover, because these three establish two types of practice—tending toward actual self-benefit and tending toward the benefit of others—bodhi encompasses both.
Furthermore, the vow directed toward reality protects against afflictions, while the vow directed toward birth protects against the Lesser Vehicle; thus, bodhicitta encompasses both vows.
Moreover, in order to perfect compassion and wisdom—whereby wisdom illuminates both principle and phenomena—there are these three.
Furthermore, compassion and wisdom, as they are raised here, also each possess these three aspects.
Regarding the three aspects within compassion: it causes those sentient beings to know the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) so that they may together realize bodhi.
Regarding the three aspects within wisdom: they illuminate the exhaustion of the marks of arising, thereby becoming identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and realizing *bodhi*.
Furthermore, these three necessarily support one another; each one possesses all three aspects, and together they bring about the perfection of each individual one.

First, one dedicates [merit] to sentient beings for the sake of realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because by transforming sentient beings, one fulfills one's own benefit through the severing of hindrances and the realization of truth.

Furthermore, one directs it toward Bodhi so as to swiftly realize Bodhi; for only by possessing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and severing the two hindrances can one ultimately exhaust the limit of reality.

Second, for the sake of saving sentient beings, one dedicates [merit] toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) so as to swiftly realize that limit; for it is only by attaining mastery over delusions that one is able to transform others.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "If one is bound oneself, there is no possibility of being able to untie the bonds of others."
Furthermore, because one must swiftly realize bodhi and then be able to extensively benefit others, the *Bhūmi-sūtra* states:
"If one wishes to deliver sentient beings, one cannot be apart from the wisdom of unobstructed liberation."

Third, for the sake of attaining bodhi, one dedicates [merit] to sentient beings; yet, because one does not transform sentient beings nor realize a fruit, one also directs it toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
If one does not realize the limit of reality, how could one attain bodhi?
Therefore, these three matters are established through mutual support.

It is not merely that the three matters support one another; rather, each individual matter fully encompasses the virtues and functions of the *dharmadhātu*. Only when one enters into non-obstruction in this way can it be called the true dedication of the three matters.
Regarding the third, the essential nature (*svabhāva*), there are both general and specific aspects.
The general aspect is as previously explained, namely the great vows and so forth.
The specific aspect pertains to the section on exposition, where it is revealed according to the respective stages.
Regarding the fourth stage of determination (*niyāma*), there are differing explanations concerning its relationship to the five stages, such as the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*) and so forth.
One view states:

This stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) marks the conclusion of the stage of equipment for the Mahāyāna factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); this is because everything from the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) onward constitutes the stage of equipment, and because the stage of application (*prayoga*) is established separately after the ten dedications.
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states:

"Having completed one asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, one nurtures faith until it becomes predominant; with this predominant cultivation, one attains the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Furthermore, the ninth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "Once the provisions of merit and wisdom—the factors conducive to liberation—have been perfected during the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, one further cultivates the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) in order to enter the path of vision and abide in the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*)."
The *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* (Compendium of Abhidharma), fascicle 11, also states this. Some say:
"These ten dedications belong to the stage of application (*prayogamārga*)."
There are two further explanations. One says:

among the four aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), these are subsumed under the latter two; that is, the ten stages of understanding (*adhimukti*) constitute "Heat" (*uṣmagata*); the ten stages of practice (*caryā*) constitute "Summits" (*mūrdhan*); the first nine stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) constitute "Patience" (*kṣānti*); and the tenth stage of dedication constitutes the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "These four roots of goodness are also subsumed within the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
Although this passage does not provide explicit proof, Master Xuanzang’s intention lies in this interpretation.
One version states:

"The four stages of application (*prayoga*) are subsumed within the 'Supreme Worldly Dharma' (*laukikāgradharma*); therefore, Paramārtha’s translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says: 'Just as there are four preparatory means (*upāya*) prior to the path of the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), so too for the Bodhisattva there are four preparatory means, namely the forty minds.'"
If one follows this interpretation, there would be no five stages, as all forty minds prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*) constitute the stage of application (*prayoga*).
The remaining details concerning the four stages, the thirteen abodes (*vihāra*), and so forth, are all as explained in the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*).

The preceding sections were for the most part introductory gateways to the Mahāyāna, intended to guide those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) by establishing the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*) in accordance with their conceptual frameworks.

Some teachers maintain that the three stages of the "Noble Ones' Preliminaries" (*tri-kṣānti*) constitute the general means for approaching sainthood, without distinguishing between the distant and near stages of the provisions (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*).
This is stated according to the ultimate perspective. Others say:
the state of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is entirely ineffable.
This is explained in terms of the sudden revelation of true nature.

If one follows this particular school, all stages are suddenly subsumed within a single stage without obstructing their sequential order; thus, the point at which the stage is perfected is precisely the fulfillment of the cause.
Speaking in terms of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), yet intersecting with the preceding teachings, there should be four permutations:
first, those that refer exclusively to characteristics (xiang), such as the various preceding teachings;
second, those that refer exclusively to the intrinsic nature (ziti), such as the sudden teaching mentioned previously.
Third, the substance follows the characteristics; fourth, the nature integrates the characteristics—these two correspond to the present text.
That is to say: by following the nature through the characteristics, the nature remains undifferentiated while the positions are distinct;
by the nature integrating the characteristics, the characteristics are not destroyed because they are constantly identical with one another.

Within each and every stage, all stages are fully present; it is not merely that the cause is fused, but the fruit is also eternally fused, for only a cause that is fused with the fruit is a true cause.

Regarding the fifth point, the differentiation of the practices (*caryā*): as the practice varies according to the stage, there are likewise the differentiations of circular fusion (*yuanrong*) and provisional entrustment (*jifa*).
If one applies this to the preceding teaching, it likewise forms four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*);

these should be understood by analogy with their respective stages. Some assign the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) to the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), granting them names according to their predominant quality. Although all the perfections are present in every stage of dedication, there is also a sound principle in subsuming them under these specific names.
The enumeration of the four knots and the citation of scriptural evidence can be understood [from the preceding].
The fifth section, beginning with "How, O Son of the Buddha," is the Section on Exposition.
This exposition of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) consists of ten segments; within each segment, there is first a prose passage followed by a verse.
In the prose sections, there are two parts for each:
first, the practice of the stage; second, the fruit of the subsequent stage.
Should any [stage] be incomplete, this shall be understood from the relevant passages.
Within each of the stages and practices there are three parts:
first, citing the name and raising an inquiry; second, providing an extensive explanation based on that inquiry; and third, concluding the name based on the explanation.
These textual locations can be seen [in the source].
Now, regarding the initial dedication, the text lacks the section on the fruits of the stages.
Within the practices of the stages, the names are first cited as they appear in full in the "Original Section" (Benfen).

Furthermore, the *Benye jing* states: "Constantly, within the mind of signlessness, one constantly traverses the six realms while entering into karmic retribution; one undergoes all sensations without being subject to them, transforming and converting through the process of transference. For this reason, it is called 'Rescue and Protection' (*jiuhu*)," and so forth.
Within the second section, the detailed explanation, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the roots of goodness to be dedicated; second, the section beginning with "when cultivating roots of goodness," which correctly explains the dedication itself.
Now, the first part.
The ancients named this the "essence of practice.

If one follows the preceding terminology—where protecting sentient beings is compassion (*karuṇā*) and being free from the marks of sentient beings is wisdom (*prajñā*)—then compassion and wisdom constitute the essence of that practice.
Because this is the initial practice, the universal essence is taken as the particular essence.
If one cultivates various roots of goodness for the sake of dedication, then those very roots of goodness may also be called the essence.
The ancient commentaries rely upon this.
In the subsequent section, which correctly elucidates the dedication (*pariṇāmana*), there are two parts:
first, the dedication according to characteristics; second, from the passage "I should be like the sun" onwards, the dedication free from characteristics.
The former dedication—toward sentient beings and toward Bodhi—explains the protection and salvation of sentient beings;
the latter dedication—toward the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)—explains the departure from the marks of sentient beings.

Regarding the first two [sections], there is first a general explanation that causes sentient beings to leave suffering behind and reach ultimate bodhi; this simultaneously clarifies both compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*), as well as the two types of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Following this, from the passage beginning "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva," the text is specifically revealed in four parts: first, protection through benefit and happiness;

second, protection against being harmed by those who are not friends, starting from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva [encounters] those who are not friends..."; third, protection through sharing in their suffering, starting from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva sees all sentient beings..."; and fourth, protection through radical deliverance, starting from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva correctly dedicates all roots of goodness..."
The first part consists of three sections:
first, the general heading; second, the specific exposition beginning with "I shall..."; and third, the summary beginning with "O Son of the Buddha.
Now, the first section.

In the [text of the] Jin [translation], there are no words such as "bodhisattvas" and so forth, but rather the phrase "furthermore, he forms this thought," which more clearly demonstrates that he has already performed the dedication previously.
Within the section specifically clarifying the intermediate [state], there are ten phrases;
the first concerns the separation from the fruit of suffering.
The second is the cause for the departure from suffering;
the third is the convergence of cause and fruit, because the three paths are contained within the five fears.
The first three apply to both the deep and shallow levels, while the latter seven pertain exclusively to the ultimate stage.
Fourth, attaining bodhi;
fifth, attaining nirvana;
sixth, extinguishing the source of afflictions—fundamental non-awakening; if this is extinguished, it is like the great brilliance of heaven.

Seventh, it extinguishes the darkness of the knowable; thus it is said that all ignorance is precisely the failure to comprehend phenomena. If this is extinguished, it is like a person holding a torch, illuminating everything with complete clarity.

Eighth, it enables the attainment of liberation; as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "Stilled, tranquil, and pure is true liberation. Because one has already been freed from the heavy gloom, it is called a "lamp."
Ninth, it causes one to realize the Dharma-body; therefore, it is called the "True Dharma.
Tenth, it causes one to accomplish Prajñā—the wisdom that is free from the two-fold obstruction—which is likewise the wisdom of the unimpeded union of the provisional and the real.
Among the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), because the preceding ten phrases encompass both the shallow and the profound, they enable one to ultimately attain the One Great Matter.
Within the second section on providing protection against suffering, there are two parts:

first, clarifying the characteristics of experiencing suffering; second, from the passage beginning "O Son of the Buddha, by means of all the Buddha-dharmas," clarifying the characteristics of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, the principle (dharma), and second, the illustration (dṛṣṭānta).
Within the section on the principle, there is the thesis, the inquiry, and the explanation, which may be understood accordingly.
In the subsequent section on analogies, there are two:
first, the analogy of the great ocean remaining unchanged, which illustrates not altering one's fundamental mind even when encountering adverse conditions.
The ocean represents the Bodhisattva, because his capacity is vast.
The various poisons are a metaphor for evil sentient beings;
"unchanging" is a metaphor for the bodhisattva’s lack of confusion.
The metaphor of the sun’s orb universally shining illustrates that one continues to benefit others without ceasing, even when encountering evil.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the analogy; second, the application; and third, the inquiry and explanation.
Within the analogy, there are briefly two points:
Previously, the wheel possessed its virtues; subsequently, it encountered conditions that did not cease.
There are eleven adverse conditions, which combine with the intermediate combinations.
First, the combination possesses virtues; taking ten of these virtues to correspond with the sun, the shadow manifested on the sun likewise possesses ten virtues.

1. The wheel of merit has already reached full completion; 2. The application of wisdom is profound and vast, difficult to fathom; 3. Right mindfulness wanders through space without high or low; 4. The movement of the wind of compassion is tireless and never regresses; 5. The wheel of perfected merit and wisdom shines forth, illuminating the dharma of emptiness; 6. It universally illumines the mountain valleys of the three vehicles without partiality; 7. It causes the eyes to behold the myriad phenomena and realize the meaning of the ultimate and the conventional; 8. It causes those dwelling in their own vehicle’s karma to accomplish it through wisdom; 9. It constantly acts for the benefit of others, resting neither by day nor by night; 10. Even for those who are unworthy vessels or born blind, it does not speak of abandonment.

In the subsequent section, from "not by means of sentient beings" (*na sattvena*) onwards, this corresponds to the non-obstruction of non-conditions; herein there are four parts, with eleven matters combined through the negation "not by.
The first part, "not by," generally corresponds to those born blind; first is the direct correspondence, followed by the reverse correspondence starting from "but only by" (*kevalam tu*).

Therefore, the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Samantabhadracaryā-nirdeśa*) states: "Those who lack faith and lack understanding, who violate the precepts and violate right view," and so forth—all such persons are called "born blind.

If we categorize them separately: those of corrupt and evil nature are likened to the born blind; those with false views are likened to the city of the Gandharvas, for they cause people to falsely claim that which is unreal to be real.
The turbidity of anger joins with the hand of the asura; the sun serves as the vanguard for Śakra, yet it is obscured by that very anger.
Next, ignorance and volition join with the jambu tree, the lofty cliffs, and the deep valleys.

Next, the passage beginning with "not by the foolish and ignorant" correlates with the preceding dust, mist, smoke, and clouds; because those [elements] can pervade space, they are like the foolish and ignorant who dwell together in one place.

The subsequent section, "not arising according to the number of sentient beings," correlates with the previous discussion on the alteration of seasons; it refers to the frequent arising of excessive afflictions, being sometimes good and sometimes evil, just as the sun, moon, yin, and yang lose their proper measure during day and night.
3. Regarding the section beginning with "Why," in the process of raising an inquiry and providing an explanation: first, the intent of the inquiry is:
"Why does one not feel revulsion toward and abandon evil?
The intent of the explanation is as follows:
Because compassion and wisdom are balanced.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the analogy; second, the application.
There are two parts to the synthesis:
first, the general synthesis; second, the specific synthesis beginning with "not only.
Within this, there are two further sections:
Initially, Great Compassion is conjoined with the sun, and evil is its object.
Since it is fundamentally for the sake of all beings, how could it single out only evil people?
Just as the sun universally benefits all, how could it ever abandon even a withered log?
Second, from "In this way" onwards, wisdom is compared to the sun, because it illuminates both good and evil equally.
The second part clarifies the characteristics of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), which is divided into two sections:
first, the analysis of the mind of dedication; second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the analysis of the vows of dedication.
Regarding the preceding section, because one practices dedication based on the mind of compassion and wisdom, it consists of two parts:
first, the vastness of the objects of focus, which equals the mind of the Buddhas; that is, taking the dharma of the cause and fruit of Perfect Enlightenment as the object of focus.
Perfect clarity and luminosity are precious, and for this reason they are called "jewels.
Below the passage beginning with "The Bodhisattva thus," compassion achieves benefit and joy; this is the mind that rescues beings.
Within this section, it first restates what preceded to initiate the following.
Thereafter, two kinds of mind arise:
first, regarding those above as Buddhas, one attains pure faith;
second, regarding those below, one shares the essence of great compassion with sentient beings.
Based on these two, ten states of mind such as "profound" and so forth are established:

first, because it accords with reality; second, because of self-congratulation and congratulating others; third, because of being free from faults; fourth, because of surpassing the Two Vehicles; fifth, because of being associated with the joy of meditative concentration; the remaining five may be understood accordingly.
The section beginning with "Universally for" concludes the purpose of its application.
Because the mind accords with the speech, it is called "true reality.
The second part correctly expounds the vow of dedication.
The text has two parts:
first, the aspiration to cause sentient beings to become vessels for the Dharma; second, the vow "furthermore, may they act" so that they may attain the perfection of the Dharma.
Within this [second part], there are four sections:
First, a general summary of attaining the Dharma through encountering conditions;
second, from "In the presence of all Buddhas" onwards, the fulfillment of one's own inherent virtues, wherein the "seven riches" refer to the first seven of the ten treasuries;
third, from "Constantly following all Buddhas" onwards, the perfection of superior virtues.

4. From "causing all" onwards, the fulfillment of the fruit is clarified. First, the bliss of the Buddha is indicated; the following two lines provide the explanation. Therefore, the third dedication briefly clarifies ten kinds of bliss, namely, the inconceivable bliss in which the Buddhas abide, and so forth.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharma" briefly elucidates ten kinds of immeasurable abodes, namely, the constant dwelling in great compassion and so forth.
Within the third section, "Relieving Suffering through Generational Succession," the text is divided into three parts:

first, a general explanation of dedicating [merit] to relieve suffering; second, a specific explanation of the mind of dedication beginning with "He further thinks: 'That which I practice... and so forth; and third, a summary of the resulting benefits beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates all roots of goodness in this way, that is to say, according to what is appropriate... and so forth.
Now, for the first [section], there are two parts:
first, clarifying the prior rescue from grave suffering; second, from the passage "At that time, the Bodhisattva thought thus," onwards, clarifying the intention to universally rescue all sufferings.
Regarding the first [point], there are two parts:
first, seeing suffering and giving rise to compassion, with a mind firm and non-retrogressive.

Firmness has seven aspects, namely: not abandoning one's practice; not avoiding painful matters; not being startled by what arrives suddenly; not fearing delusion; not retreating from great compassion; not being cowed by much suffering; and having no weariness despite long-term suffering.
Second, the section beginning with "Why" interrogates and provides an explanation to establish the point.
This interrogation has two intended meanings.
First, it says:
"Birth is self-created suffering; why should it concern the Bodhisattva, such that he wishes to take its place on one's behalf?
The second said:
"Such intense suffering is unbearable; why do you not grow weary of it?"
The meaning of the commentary is:
"Because one has undertaken the original vow.
If one encounters suffering and feels weary, how could one possibly bear the burden?"
The second section, "Mindfulness Universally Saving from All Sufferings," has two parts.
First is saving from the eight sufferings, the eight difficulties, and other forms of suffering; thus there are various statements:
"Wandering according to karma is the suffering of karmic bondage; holding wrong views and lacking wisdom is the suffering of ignorance."
From "I ought to... onwards, the resolve to provide salvation arises.
Second, from "Furthermore, all sentient beings... onwards, there is the salvation from the suffering of ignorance regarding the Four Noble Truths.
This section is divided into two parts:
First is the contemplation of the state of suffering; second, from "The Bodhisattva sees" onwards, is the actual arousal of compassion for rescue.
Regarding the first [section], within it there is first the ignorance of the origin (*samudaya*): that delusion and craving are the root, which constitutes the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*).
The section beginning with "attachment" clarifies the path of action (*karmapatha*); it is called "attachment" because one engages in formative activities.
Following such karma, one enters into suffering, just as birds and beasts enter cages and traps due to their craving for food.
To engage in demonic activities indicates the presence of evil karma;
for merit and wisdom to be utterly exhausted indicates the absence of wholesome karma.

Furthermore, constantly harboring doubt means that one lacks the cause for the cessation of views regarding non-arising; thus, one does not perceive the peace of parinirvāṇa, nor does one know the Path Truth of deliverance, remaining instead within the Suffering Truth of birth and death.
Regarding the second [section], "arousing compassion to provide rescue": "arousing the mind of great compassion" is for the purpose of causing [beings] to be liberated from suffering and its origin;
"the mind of great benefit" is for the purpose of causing them to attain purity through cessation and the path.
Therefore, one employs the roots of goodness for dedication.
Regarding the *Mahāpariṇāmanā-sūtra*, Xianshou said:
"It is because it contains the universal dedication of Samantabhadra as taught in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*)."
"However, within the Tripiṭaka there is the *Mahāpariṇāmanāsūtra*; since this teaching is the very first [of its kind], one should not point to that.
If the compilers sought brevity, it would be reasonable to do so."

In the second section, the dedication of merit through vicariously undergoing suffering for others, there are five further reflections within the mind: the first three clarify the mind that vicariously undergoes suffering, while the latter two clarify the mind of dedication.
Now, the first section is divided into three parts:
first, it clarifies that he universally rescues others exclusively, without any thought of self-benefit;
second, it shows that he endures all manner of suffering without a mind of indolence.
Third, the resolve to protect [the Dharma] with a mind free from falsehood.
The first section is clear.
Within the second, there are again two parts:
First, the primary clarification; second, the interrogation and explanation.
Now, for the first:
as for the term "great abyss," it is like the abyss of the Tailgate (Wailu), for it drinks in and contracts sentient beings without a moment’s respite.
In the subsequent section on interrogation and explanation, the initial interrogation poses this question:
"For what reason do you alone undergo all manner of sufferings for the sake of sentient beings, and furthermore, why do you diligently cultivate [the path]?
The explanation states:
Because the suffering of a single body brings liberation to many, he vows to undergo it himself;
this reveals the depth of his compassion.
Question:

The suffering of sentient beings is summoned by their own karma and manifested by their own minds; how, then, can a Bodhisattva take it upon themselves? Answer: Generally speaking, there are seven meanings regarding the taking on of suffering: 1. Taking on the suffering of others through the power of great vows. 2. Taking on the suffering of others through the power of great compassion. 3. Taking on the suffering of others through the power of skillful means. 4. Taking on the suffering of others through the power of great wisdom. 5. Taking on the suffering of others through the power of great merit.
6. Taking on the suffering of others through the power of great samādhi. 7. Taking on the suffering of others through the power of great expedient means.
First, one binds oneself with suffering in order to increase compassionate concern.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 49, asks:

"When a bodhisattva enters from the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) into the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), how does he transcend all evil destinies? and so forth.
This question asks how a bodhisattva liberates themselves from the miserable realms (*durgati*). The subsequent answer is extensive, its meaning being as follows:

it refers to a bodhisattva who, having already well accumulated the provisions through pure meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) in the world, cultivates compassion (*anukampā*) for sentient beings who undergo much suffering, without any other thoughts.

Through this cultivation, one attains the mental disposition of compassion (*anukampā*) and the mental disposition of pity (*karuṇā*). For the sake of benefiting sentient beings in the miserable realms (*apāya*), one vows to dwell in those miserable realms as if in one’s own home; even while remaining in the miserable realms, one is able to realize awakening and endure it. To eliminate the suffering of others, one vows to take it upon oneself in their stead, ensuring that their evil karma never manifests again and that all wholesome karma may constantly manifest.

By the power of this compassionate vow, all the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) belonging to the category of afflictions within all evil destinies are eliminated from their respective bases, and one attains entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The commentary states:

In this regard, there is merely the intention and aspiration of compassion; the body cannot act as a substitute. Nevertheless, through the determination of compassion, one inevitably attains supreme benefit for oneself.

Second, regarding the Bodhisattva’s original practice of seeking the Dharma through asceticism for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, this is already termed "substitution. Furthermore, when one subsequently serves as a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for others, this is also termed "receiving [suffering] on their behalf."

Third, regarding Bodhisattvas who intentionally retain afflictions to undergo existence through shared activity (*sabhāgatā*), they assume bodies of suffering in order to teach the Dharma to sentient beings so that they do not create the causes of suffering; since the cause is extinguished and the fruit is lost, this is also called "vicarious suffering."

Fourth, if there are sentient beings who intend to commit an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) and so forth, the Bodhisattva transforms them to stop them from proceeding and prevents them from ending their own lives; the Bodhisattva then personally undergoes the bitter retribution of the evil destinies to enable those beings to escape the great suffering of the *ānantarya* hells—this is called "substitutionary reception."

This is based on the eleventh fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* translated during the Liang dynasty; the King of Senāyu in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also shares this same meaning, and it is not merely a matter of intention alone.

Fifth, by initially cultivating the correct vow to undergo suffering for the sake of birth, the Bodhisattva reaches the ultimate stage where their vows attain mastery; they constantly dwell in the evil realms to rescue and substitute for sentient beings, such as Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva and King Prabhāsa-vyūha, even to the point of becoming a great fish during times of famine—all of whom belong to this category.
Whether by illuminating and touching with light or through the secret empowerment of spiritual power, such instances are manifold.

Sixth, because the Bodhisattva’s vow is in accord with True Suchness (tathatā), the suffering of those sentient beings is identical to the nature of Suchness; thus, by means of a vow that accords with Suchness, it secretly permeates and reaches that very suffering which is itself True Suchness. Based on this interpenetration, it is also termed "substitution" (dai).

Seventh, because Samantabhadra takes the Dharma-realm as his body, and all sentient beings are the Dharma-realm, sentient beings who undergo suffering are at all times the Bodhisattva; therefore, this is called "substitution."

Regarding the seven meanings mentioned above: the first consists solely of the intentional aspiration; the next two concern only acting as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); the fourth and fifth meanings can actually take the burden upon their own bodies; and the sixth and seventh meanings involve the integration of principle and contemplation.
Question:
If one were to rely on the two meanings of the fourth and fifth [stages], one should be able to universally take their place; why, then, do sentient beings still undergo suffering?
Answer:
This has three meanings.
First, because there are those with whom one has a karmic connection and those with whom one does not: if one shares a karmic connection with a bodhisattva, it can be substituted for them.
Second, because karma is either determinate or indeterminate: that which is indeterminate can be substituted.
Third, if undergoing suffering is beneficial, the Bodhisattva causes it to be endured, for only through this can one ultimately achieve liberation from suffering.
Just as parents instruct their children by entrusting them to a strict teacher for discipline, such subtle benefit is beyond the comprehension of ordinary or inferior beings.
The third section, "Resolutely Vowing to Protect," has two parts:

What is meant by "not abandoning"?

First, it distinguishes [the Bodhisattva] from the Śrāvakas because they do not act for their own sake.

The reason for not seeking is that one perceives many faults [in seeking].

In this context, the essence of the text is that desire is itself suffering and is further capable of producing suffering; it closely obstructs celestial bliss, let alone the Great Bodhi in which both afflictions and habitual tendencies have been simultaneously extinguished.

First: Its merit exceeds that of the two realms of heaven and earth, yet it is not benevolent; its brilliance surpasses that of the sun and moon, yet it is ever more obscure. Therefore, among these qualities, it first clarifies its lack of partiality.

The latter three [points] are the avoidance of faults:

Within the section on avoiding the notion of a grasper (*grāhaka*), the first phrase corresponds to the "grasped" (*grāhya*) that was previously discussed, while the subsequent phrase specifically excludes the three inversions (*viparyāsa*).

That is to say, when one gives rise to mental discrimination regarding the aforementioned phenomena—such as [judging them] as permanent or impermanent—it is called a perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*).
When one grasps the delimited characteristics of objects such as permanence, it is called a perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).
To grasp at characteristics as being real is called a "perverted view" (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
Because it turns its back on correct faith, it is designated by the name "perversion.
Conversely, the absence of these three perversions is called "not giving rise to the three perversions. Thus, in the seventeenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Maitreya says to Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain enlightenment rejoices in the roots of goodness of all Buddhas and their disciples and dedicates them toward Bodhi, how can they avoid falling into the perversions of perception, mind, and view?"
Subhūti said:
"One does not give rise to the notion of those roots of goodness; one dedicates this mind toward awakening, and yet one does not give rise to the notion of this mind of dedication either."
"Such dedication is free from the inversion of perception, the inversion of mind, and the inversion of view.
If one dedicates while grasping at signs, it constitutes an inversion of perception, mind, and view.
The "Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance" says: "If, regarding all-knowledge, one gives rise to a mind of dedication and perceives that the mind has no arising, one shall obtain great renown."
This also lacks the three inversions.

If one follows the intent of the "Chapter on Rejoicing and Dedication" in the second assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, then all the aforementioned phenomena are utterly extinguished, detached from, and transformed; what, then, within this context, could be considered "phenomena"?

If a bodhisattva knows that all these things, up to and including enlightenment, are utterly non-existent, yet is still able to practice sympathetic joy and dedication, then they are free from the perversions of perception, mind, and view, because they employ the method of non-apprehension.

However, the Hīnayāna schools sometimes state that perception (*saṃjñā*), mind (*citta*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*) arise sequentially; or they state that while they occur simultaneously, they are distinguished as preceding and succeeding in meaning. In these views, perception and mind are not themselves erroneous; it is because of the confusion caused by the view that the name "error" is established for them.
Although all these explanations are identical in establishing [the mind] as the six consciousnesses,
there are also many different accounts within the Mahāyāna. One says:

Based on the meaning of the seven consciousnesses as mind, there are three types of inversion. That which is called the deluded mind of the seven consciousnesses has a nature that deviates from principle and is inverted;

this is termed "inversion of mind. Because one relies upon this mind, all deluded objective realms arise—just as dream-objects arise based on the dreaming mind—and one falsely grasps their characteristics within those realms; this is termed "inversion of perception."
To grasp at the grasped phenomena as being real and distinct is called a "view-inversion.
Based on these three inversions, one gives rise to eight types of inversions—such as permanence and impermanence—with respect to conditioned and unconditioned objects.
Fearing that the divergent theories of various schools would weary the reader with their prolixity, [I have omitted them].
Third, it is distinct from the names that express it.

Thus, for a bodhisattva who falsely grasps at objects, dedication does not exist; yet for a bodhisattva of true reality, dedication is not non-existent.

from "without attachment" onwards, one leaves delusion to accord with the truth, which is the meaning of leaving behind appearances.
The subsequent section beginning with "All Buddhas" concludes the preceding and introduces what follows.
The second section, beginning with "In accord with the nature of all phenomena," describes the characteristics of dedication, while simultaneously revealing the dedication toward Bodhi.
Within this, there are eleven phrases: the first six concern the separation from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-viveka*), and the latter five concern the following of characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvartana*).
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) onwards, the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-caryā*) is accomplished.
This section has three parts:
First, the accomplishment of practice following signs; second, from "by means of purity" onwards, the accomplishment of practice free from signs;
third, from "the bodhisattva is thus skillful" onwards, the simultaneous conclusion that these two practices are unimpeded.
Now, for the first [section], there are three parts:

First, the restatement of the preceding [point], which states that because one has previously detached from characteristics, it is not merely that one does not obstruct following after characteristics, but can also accomplish this following after them.
Second, from "Although one follows... onwards is the actual exposition, which contains ten phrases:
First, because it accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as previously explained, it remains unchanging throughout birth and death;
second, because one enters the state of non-activity while performing all activities, one never regresses in the pursuit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*);
third, because of the relinquishing of conceptual attachment and perception, one is unmoved by any form of existence (*bhava*).
Fourth, by abiding much in skillful means, they are able to deliver sentient beings;
fifth, because they have forever emerged from all realms of existence (*bhava*), they are not defiled by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
sixth, because they practice without dwelling on signs (*nimitta*), they do not lose their unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*).
Seventh, because they universally encompass all roots of goodness, their causal conditions are inexhaustible;
eighth, because they universally purify their great vows, they are unmoved by worldly dharmas;
ninth, because they give rise to the bodhicitta, they fully cultivate all the perfections.
Tenth, because of dwelling together with the roots of goodness, one is endowed with the ten powers (*daśabala*).
These are to be correlated respectively as follows.

The subsequent section, beginning with "The Bodhisattva thus," concludes the preceding and introduces what follows; it arises precisely from the aforementioned mind of supreme faith and understanding (*adhimukti*).
Second, the accomplishment of practice free from characteristics: because the preceding point—that phenomena do not obstruct principle—allows one to realize that all objects are as they truly are.
Within this, the first phrase is general, while the section beginning with "comprehending all" is specific.

Within this section, first, the contemplation of mind-only is accomplished; next, from "knowing karma" onwards, the contemplation of dependent origination as being without intrinsic nature is accomplished; and next, from "giving birth" onwards, the Dharma-eye perceives reality.

"Endowed with the bodhisattva [qualities]" refers to the non-attachment to sublime conduct, which is also correlated with the preceding points in sequence: first, because of realizing the nature of the mind; second, because of the non-action of karma; third, because of not giving rise to conceptualizations; fourth, because of skillfulness in practice; fifth, because of the dependent origination of all existences; sixth, because of practicing without abiding; seventh, because of universal inclusion without attachment; eighth, because of the vastness of all practices; ninth, because of realizing that the nature of bodhi is non-dual and is solely the one reality; tenth, because of dwelling together with roots of goodness, one is able to fulfill the bodhisattva practices; and eleventh, because of supreme faith and understanding, there is no abandonment of the untainted pure dharmas.
If one understands this through the preceding [explanation], it is easily comprehensible.

Within the section on dedicating [merit] by means of the non-obstruction between the three pairs of fetters and the two practices, the first part is general, clarifying that there is no delusion regarding either principle or phenomena; thus, it is called "skillful reflection.
The latter part, beginning with "not contradicting," is specific, and in all cases, the non-obstruction between phenomenon and principle can be understood.
The third section, "The bodhisattva-mahāsattva dedicates all roots of goodness in this manner," concerns the purpose for which the dedication is made.
The first phrase provides a general clarification, while the subsequent portion beginning with "uninterrupted" provides a detailed exposition.
Among these, the former—abandoning the deeds of Māra—applies to all evils;
the latter—the activities of Māra—apply to all appearances, for anything that contravenes the Seal of the Dharma is a matter of Māra.
Therefore, the subsequent commentary states:
"By universally sealing all karmas with the seal of equality, one becomes free from Māra.
The remaining phrases may be understood accordingly.
The second fruit is also like the fruit of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), such as pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

In the text, first the time of attainment is cited; next, from "attaining vision" onwards, the characteristics of the fruit itself are correctly analyzed; and finally, from "the bodhisattva" onwards, its category is summarized.
The second verse consists of twenty-five stanzas divided into three parts:
the first two stanzas concern the roots of goodness to be dedicated and the dedication of the first section;
Next, the eighteen verses constitute the practice of making offerings, which is then dedicated;
the final five verses concern the purpose for which the dedication is made.
Within these two sections, there are again two parts each:
The first eight verses concern the roots of goodness to be dedicated;
the subsequent ten verses concern the practice of dedication. This section consists of three parts:

first, four verses on the mind of dedication; second, two verses on the characteristics of dedication; and third, four verses on the purpose for which the practice of dedication is accomplished, as may be understood from the text.
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Extensive Radiance,
Scroll Twenty-Six Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha of Great Extensive Radiance,
Scroll Twenty-Seven Compiled by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang in the Tang Dynasty.
The third is the dedication equal to all Buddhas. The prose section also has two parts: first, the practice of the stage; second, the fruit of the stage.
Within the former, there are also three [sections]:

Regarding the initial designation of the name: if one follows the subsequent text, it refers merely to the path of dedication shared with all Buddhas of the three periods; according to what follows below, it also equals the roots of goodness. Therefore, the text says: "Just as all roots of goodness practiced by the Buddhas of the past, I likewise do so."
The *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Acts) also states: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time practice at all times.
This simultaneously reveals their continuity; therefore, the subsequent text says: "Even when together with his wife and children, he never for a moment abandoned the bodhicitta."
This name is established based on what it equals; that is, it is the dedication of all Buddhas, having as its nature the practice of universal-gate virtues through deep entry into the dharma-nature.
Second, regarding the detailed explanation based on the inquiry, there are two parts:
first, the general presentation, which is the explanation of the names;
second, the detailed explanation from "In this way" onwards, which also has two parts:
First, dedication is revealed; second, the accomplishment of benefit is clarified.
Within the former, there are two parts:
first, equality with respect to characteristics; second, equality with respect to the absence of characteristics.
Within the former section, there are again two parts:
first, clarifying the dedication by means of roots of goodness directed toward specific objects; second, the dedication by means of subsuming all virtues in their entirety.
Within the former of these, there are again two parts:
Regarding the initial dedication of roots of goodness and the subsequent section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," which correctly reveals the dedication:
first, when training in the practice of the Buddha, one cultivates four pure minds in relation to the six sense objects, whether they are adverse or favorable.
First, regarding favorable and unfavorable conditions, one achieves equanimity (*upekṣā*) in practice and is not led astray by objects; this is called mastery of mind.
Second, being distinct from ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle, one purifies all afflictions through the vastness of compassion and wisdom.
Third, because one is free from the fault of sorrow, there is joy, bliss, and equanimity, devoid of grief, suffering, and distress.
Because of the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of the fourth dhyāna, the mind and mental factors are supple; because one does not falsely grasp at objects, the sense faculties are cool and serene.
Within the second section on "Right Dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*), there is dedication toward the realms of the five vehicles, which is divided into five parts:
first, the Buddhas; second, the Bodhisattvas; third, sentient beings with virtue; fourth, those of the two vehicles; and fifth, sentient beings with evil.
The first two sections consist of:
first, citing the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, from "I pray that by means of me... onwards, the actual manifestation of the vows.
The first part is a general vow for the increase of joy.
However, although the Buddha’s virtues are already perfected, the reason for now wishing to increase them is to express sincere reverence and gratitude for his grace.
It is like offering wild celery to a superior or presenting incense and flowers to the Buddha; it is not that he stands in need of such things.
The section beginning with "That which is called" provides a detailed exposition consisting of ten phrases.
The first phrase is also a general statement in relation to the remaining nine, as it encompasses all the subsequent stages; for this reason, it is termed "inconceivable.
The second is the celestial abode (*devasthāna*), namely the ocean-seal and so forth.
The third is the Brahma-abodes;
the fourth is the Noble Abodes, namely the infinite liberations and so forth;
the fifth is the universal, effortless practice that is innate to all types.
The sixty sovereign joys, or the eightfold self-mastery:
seven consist in the boundless application of wisdom;
the eighth is the perfect stillness of detachment from conceptualization.
The nine great functions are eternally tranquil;
the twelve practices are forever extinguished.
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, there is the dedication for Bodhisattvas, which also has two parts:
First, the preceding section summarizes what was previously established and introduces what follows;
the subsequent section, beginning with "That is to say," provides the formal exposition. There are ten points: the first six concern one's own practice, and the latter four concern benefiting others.
Within the former [six], three meanings are contained:

First, because they fulfill [the practices] such as those of "willingly following" (*anuvartana*) by means of discerning the common characteristics; second, because of ultimate fulfillment; and third, because of fulfillment through successive stages.
First, within the stage of faith, there is the vow to follow conditions, as in the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Śīlaparivarta*);
second, it is for the sake of purifying the mind of understanding in the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*), which the Jin translation calls "not yet purifying the straightforward mind."
Third, they fulfill the ten practices;
fourth, they fulfill the ten transferences; therefore, the Bodhisattva precepts are named the Ten Vajras.
Fifth, having attained the first stage and above, they realize non-retrogression.

Attaining the effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) from the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) and above is called "great diligence" (*mahāvīrya*); spontaneously comprehending all phenomena is called the "wholesome root that guards the gate of bodhi.
Among the latter four [perfections] which benefit others: first, it causes [beings] to realize the arousal of the mind [of awakening], because they are free from the two kinds of self;
second, it universally establishes them in the various stages (*bhūmi*).
The third [dedication] attains the virtues within the stages;
the fourth causes one to realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the dedication is for sentient beings who possess virtue.

Furthermore, for those deluded sentient beings who are ignorant of the true meaning and possess only slight roots of goodness— seeking merely rebirth in the realms of humans or devas within the cycle of existence—
he now causes them to abide in the Buddha Vehicle, thereby accomplishing the ten benefits.

The first three [days] cause one to recollect the Three Jewels; the next three [days] involve recollecting the virtues already accomplished within oneself; and the final three [days] concern the benefits realized through those virtues. These are each assigned respectively to the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, because the *nienfo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi) is capable of giving rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
4. The section beginning with "Just as for... dedicates [merit] toward the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).
However, because sentient beings are prone to backsliding from the Buddha-dharma, he first dedicates [merit] toward them.
Since those of the Two Vehicles will ultimately turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], they are not abandoned; as in the previous case, this serves to bring about benefit.
5. "Furthermore, [the vow] below" is for the sake of those who possess evil.
This refers to not abandoning the icchantikas, who are also sentient beings deluded regarding maturation (vipāka) because they do not perceive the fruits of suffering.

First, one causes [beings] to leave behind the fruits of suffering and accomplish the causes of goodness; subsequently, with the words "forever not," one causes them to leave behind evil causes and accomplish the future fruits.
Of the five preceding sections, the first is dedicated toward Bodhi, while the remaining four are dedicated toward sentient beings.
The second section, "O Sons of the Buddha, all the roots of goodness possessed by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas," etc., generally subsumes the dedication of all virtues; it consists of two parts:
first, a general manifestation of its characteristics, and second, a detailed enumeration of each practice, beginning with "O Sons of the Buddha."
First: all roots of goodness, which are those that have been initiated and so forth, are all [perfected] by means of great vows, which are those that can initiate and so forth.
There are three distinct phrases:

First, as for roots of goodness not yet arisen, they are brought forth and caused to arise through the skillful means of great vows; therefore, the Jin translation renders this as "initiation" (*pravṛtti*).
Second, they are also accumulated and made manifold through great vows.
Third, following those roots of goodness already arisen, each is made increasingly superior and perfected until reaching the stage of Buddhahood.

Regarding the repeated phrase "properly initiating," etc., it means that according to its initiation, accumulation, and intensification, it necessarily proceeds toward three destinations and seeks nothing else.
Being free from all faults is what is termed "correct.
The passage beginning with "causing all to" concludes by establishing the benefits.
Because it is initiated correctly and so forth, it accords with compassion and wisdom; therefore, it is called "vast."
Because they are initiated and accumulated, all virtues are fully possessed.
Because they increase, each one fills the entire Dharma-realm and becomes equal to the Tathāgata.
There is no virtue that is not thus; therefore, it is said "causing them all to."
However, the Jin dynasty translations render it as "equal" (等), because the Sanskrit original uses the term *sama*, which encompasses both "correct" (正) and "equal" (等).
Furthermore, there are two meanings to "equal":
first, equality with the Buddha, meaning that one attains equality with the conduct of the Buddha through the practice of a bodhisattva; [the second meaning is equality with all sentient beings].
The second is "equal to the rest," which means that one formation is equal to the remaining formations.
Although ancient masters have offered various interpretations to conclude this section, none of them accord with the subsequent text.
If one takes "equal" (等) to mean "equality" (平等), it approximates the correct term but still fails to encompass the full meaning; thus, it is not what is intended here.
Second, the various matters are presented individually.
The various virtues are not limited to one; here, one or two are briefly cited to demonstrate that gathering virtue in accordance with conditions all constitutes dedication.
The text has two parts:
first, the dedication of increase; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, at that time the Bodhisattva... onwards, the dedication of accumulation.

The arousal of the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) pertains to both sections: the preceding section demonstrates compliance with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), while the subsequent section clarifies the profound depth of that great compassion; this is explained in terms of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
If we rely on the principle of dedication (pariṇāmanā), the preceding section clarifies dedicating toward enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings,
while the subsequent section dedicates toward sentient beings so that they may attain enlightenment.
These are all mutually complementary, intended to reveal that dedication occurs simultaneously toward these three points.
Now, within the first section on "increase," there are two parts:
first, a detailed explanation; second, a summary beginning with "In this way, the bodhisattva...
Within the former, there are three sections:

First, it clarifies the dedication that follows defilement without being stained: because of compassion, one follows defilement; because of wisdom, one abides in the path of purity and recollects *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Second, from the passage "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" onwards, movement accords with the Path, and the dedication is universal and uninterrupted.

Third, the section beginning with "for the desire" generally reveals the characteristics of dedication (*pariṇāmana*), specifically clarifying the meaning of the arousal and growth of the great vows mentioned in the preceding text.
This section contains two parts:
first, a general explanation, where the initial phrase indicates the underlying intention.
"Abiding securely" (anurakṣaṇā) refers to the ability to immediately give rise to aspiration.
"Gathering" (parigraha) refers to universally rescuing all beings through the roots of goodness that have been produced and increased; this constitutes the establishment of the definitive meaning.
Second, the section beginning with "permanently detached" provides a detailed exposition consisting of ten phrases:

(1) because of being free from afflictions; (2) because of proceeding correctly toward the goal; (3) because of not taking up other paths; (4) because of correct contemplation; (5) because of abandoning defilements; (6) because of possessing the cultivation of causes; (7) because of abandoning the two obstacles regarding the causes of enlightenment; (8) maintaining and reciting the stage of wisdom; (9) accumulating virtue through wisdom; and (10) remaining unstained by worldly conduct while receiving supramundane dharmas.
All ten are virtues of one's own that enable one to turn toward Bodhi.
If these are further integrated with the universal salvation of all beings, then all ten become "generative," causing others to attain this goodness.
In the second section, the summary, this passage serves as proof to explain the meaning of "increase," the logic of which is very clear.
Second, the clarification of the accumulation and dedication has two parts:
first, the specific explanation; second, the summary beginning with "The bodhisattva mahāsattva, in this way... and so forth.
The first section has two parts:
first, the explanation of subtle accumulation; second, from "When a bodhisattva first generates... onwards, the explanation of long-term accumulation.
Within the first part, there are also two sections:

First, the roots of goodness accumulated are explained: even if they are as minute as a single morsel of food or a single grain of rice, their merit is exceedingly subtle; and even if the field of merit is as inferior as giving to an animal, by accumulating such slight virtues, one causes them to be correctly initiated through great vows and brought to completion as acts of dedication.

Second, from "All together" (*xianzuo*) onwards, the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is clarified: first, it is explained in general terms as being free from suffering and attaining happiness; next, from "Forever crossing over" (*yongdu*) onwards, it is specifically shown as being free from suffering.
The text contains nine statements:
the first generally reveals its profundity and vastness, while the subsequent eight specifically clarify the characteristics of suffering.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is the very intrinsic nature of suffering.
The aggregates (*skandha*) are the basis of suffering, namely the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
The perception of suffering refers to the characteristic of suffering, which also includes the perception of encountering the unpleasant and parting from the beloved.
"Accumulation" refers to birth, old age, sickness, death, and the three types of suffering as well as the eight types of suffering.
"Practice" refers to karmic offenses; "cause" refers to the various delusions.
"Root" refers to craving and desire; "abode" refers to the three miserable realms.
This extends even to the basis of the transformation of existence, all of which can be abandoned—this applies throughout the subsequent five phrases.
The subsequent section, beginning with "In this way, the bodhisattva," concludes by showing how one attains bodhi.

Regarding the second point, the accumulation over a long period: it refers to the fact that one begins to accumulate [merit and wisdom] from the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
The text has two parts:
first, a general indication of the dedication of roots of goodness;
second, from "desiring to" onwards, the clarification of the intent of the dedication, which constitutes the characteristic of dedication, because the phrase "desiring to" expresses a mental vow.
The text consists of thirteen phrases. The first twelve form six pairs, which provide benefit according to their specific characteristics;
the final phrase provides benefit by entering the principle of equality. Within the former [twelve], the first pair—leaving behind the fruit of suffering and attaining the bliss of cessation;

the second—emerging from the cause of accumulation and cultivating the right path; the third—endowing oneself with compassion and wisdom to perfect the aforementioned cultivation of the path; and the fourth—protecting the wholesome and drawing near to the Buddha so as to emerge from the ocean of afflictions—these four pairs together establish the first [pair]. The remaining two pairs collectively complete the initial pair.
In the second summary, "a single lump" or "a single grain" refers to what is currently accumulated.
From the first moment of generating the bodhicitta, it has already been accumulated.

Although the merits to be accumulated have not yet arisen, through the power of one's vows, they will inevitably flow spontaneously toward these three places; how much more so when relying on this teaching, wherein the nine periods of time are perfectly interfused.

The second section, beginning with "Furthermore, he thinks: 'As in the past,'" and so forth, concerns the Buddha’s dedication that is free from marks, which is directed toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Synthesizing the preceding two [dedications], it is taught that although there is a sequence of before and after, the practice resides in a single mind.
The text has two parts:
the first corresponds to the past, and the second, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," corresponds to the present and future.
Within the former, there are two sections:
First, that which is equalized is presented; subsequently, from the words "Just as that" onwards, the means of equalizing is revealed.
Within the former [section], there are three parts:
first, the characteristic of following is indicated, which is precisely the absence of characteristics; therefore, the final phrase states, "yet there is no attachment."
Next, from "That is to say" (*yad-uta*) onwards, the specific characteristics of the state free from marks are revealed;
third, from "Thus deeply entering" onwards, their non-obstruction is concluded.
Within the second [section], first there is the detachment from delusion and the realization of *śamatha*, beginning with the aggregates (*skandha*) and followed by the sense bases (*āyatana*).
"Not abiding in worldly dharmas" refers to the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), because the presence of faculties, objects, and consciousness constitutes the world.
"Neither relying upon nor clinging" is precisely what transcends the world.
The section beginning with "knowing all" below explains the aforementioned non-clinging.
The reason for non-attachment is that one has formed contemplation through seeing reality.
The first phrase is the metaphor; the subsequent phrase, "having no point of departure," contains both the dharma and the metaphor.

By observing the metaphors employed, the subjects they illustrate can be understood; for all things, being devoid of intrinsic nature due to their dependence on conditions, the five phrases beginning with "no coming" explain one another in succession.
As the preceding text states: "All phenomena have no coming; therefore, there is no arising," and so forth.
From "Distantly removed" onwards, this concludes the formation of the contemplation.
Because the mind is free from conceptual discrimination, it is tranquil and unmoving.
Since external conditions do not turn [within it], it does not lose its illumination nor does it impair its stillness; therefore, it accords with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
What is the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi)?
It is the signless (animitta).
What is meant by "signless"?
Its essence is free from the ten marks; it is only a single mark.
What is this single mark?
It is precisely the absence of marks.
Furthermore, regarding "signlessness" (animitta) in terms of principle, it is because [all things] are fundamentally non-existent from the outset.
Regarding it in terms of wisdom, it is because one is detached from grasping at signs.
It is solely a single sign, for the mind and its objects are in profound union.

Regarding the "unimpededness of the three fetters": since one practices in accordance with the characteristics while abiding in the *dharmatā*, a single [characteristic] encompasses all; this is called the "virtue of the universal gate" (*samantamukha-kuśala*).
It consists in seeing all Buddhas; herein is briefly explained the accomplishment of benefit.
The second section, "Manifesting the Ability to Equalize," has two parts:
first, restating that which is to be equalized to generally manifest the ability to equalize;
second, from "Understanding thus" onwards, specifically manifesting the characteristics of equalization.
The first two lines express the aspiration to equal the Buddha’s realization and testimony;
the next two lines, “relying upon this to practice without contravention,” and those following, reveal the characteristics of practice.
Reaching the ultimate stage constitutes the fruit of cultivation.
The second section, "Equalizing the Present and Future," is divided into three parts:
first, the restatement of what is equalized, which cites the past as an example for the present and future;
next, from "I now" onwards, the general manifestation of that which is able to equalize.
Third: From "The First" onwards, the common characteristics of both subject and object are specifically elucidated.

In the preceding chapter on the past, these have already been extensively revealed through the negation of characteristics; here, within this text, we directly praise their excellence. The meaning is preserved in a concise manner, as I do not wish to produce prolixity.
There are nineteen phrases; the Jin translation contains twenty, namely, "vast and great" followed by "luminous and pure dedication.
In the present translation, this is omitted because it is considered identical to "pure."
Within this, the first nine points distinguish superiority through formal comparison:

first, it is designated as "the foremost" because it emerges preeminent; second, because it transcends the mundane and the Hinayana; third, because it surpasses the stage of causes; fourth, because it stands alone; fifth, because there is nothing added that exceeds it; sixth, because there is none with which it can be equaled; seventh, because it is solely the ultimate, such that no non-dual entity can be its equal; eighth, because it has no peer; and ninth, because it has no rival.
The latter ten [attributes] manifest excellence by way of their own essence: first, "venerable," because they are worthy of being highly esteemed;
second, "sublime," because they transcend speech and thought;
third, "in accordance with reality," because they are without deviation.
Fourth, because there is no other destination;
fifth, because it encompasses all virtues;
sixth, because it pervades the dharma-realm—formerly called "great vows."
Seventh, because it is free from the indeterminate;
eighth, because it is free from defilement;
ninth, because it is itself devoid of unwholesome conduct.
Tenth, because of not following evil conditions.
The above constitutes the formal explanation of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Second, the benefits accomplished by dedication are clarified; the text is explicit and can be understood as it stands.
Regarding the second fruit, there is a brief exposition of ten kinds of supreme virtues.
First, because one cultivates the deeds of a Buddha and dedicates them with an aspiration equal to that of a Buddha; for dedicating [merit] to sentient beings is the deed of a Buddha.
Furthermore, as in the "Chapter on Leaving the World," there are ten kinds of Buddha-activities:
second, the virtue of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, because it is directed toward bodhi;
third, the wisdom that enters into profound principle, because it is directed toward the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
The remainder may be understood.
The second verse consists of twenty-four stanzas, divided into three parts:
The first twenty-one verses explain the practices of the preceding stages; the next two verses describe the fruits; and the final one provides a concluding eulogy.
Within the former section, there are two parts:
the first verse provides a general outline and explains the name [of the stage].
The subsequent twenty verses provide a detailed commentary on the preceding [section], which is also twofold:
first, nineteen verses that correctly clarify the dedication; second, one verse that establishes the benefits.
Within the former, there are paired verses concerning both following signs and being free from signs; this section also has two parts:
The first six verses concern the dedication of roots of goodness arising from their respective objects.

Within this, the first two verses dedicate the roots of goodness being dedicated toward the bliss of the Buddhas; the latter four verses dedicate them toward sentient beings so that they may attain the peace and happiness of the Buddhas.
Second, there are thirteen verses that summarize all virtues for dedication, divided into three parts:

The first four verses correspond to the dedication for increasing; the second three verses correspond to the dedication for accumulation; and the third six verses correspond to the aforementioned dedication of roots of virtue toward the Bodhisattva as the object.
In this palindrome, the first four lines follow the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), while the latter two transcend these characteristics.
Within them, the first verse reaches the limit of reality (*dharmadhātu*): both duality and non-duality, being mutually dependent, are quiescent. The latter verse realizes the source of delusion:

by using thought to dispel objects, when objects are exhausted, thought perishes; when neither thought nor the dispelling of thought remain, their mutual dependence is simultaneously quiescent. Only when there is quiescence yet constant illumination can it be called the realization of thought.
The resulting benefits and the fruits of these stages can be understood from the concluding praise.
Fourth is the dedication reaching all places (*sarvatragāminī-praṇidhāna*).
The prose commentary also has two parts: first, the practice of the stage; second, the fruit of the stage.
The preceding section also has three parts: the citation, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Herein is the first: the citation of the name and the raising of the inquiry.
"Attaining" (*prāpti*) refers to the roots of goodness that can reach [the goal] as well as the requisites for offering.
"Everywhere" refers to all places where offerings are made.
This means that through great vows, these roots of goodness and offering requisites are made to pervade all times and places, providing for all fields of merit as appropriate.
The *Benye jing* (Sutra on the Original Vocation) states: "By the power of great vows, one enters all Buddha-lands and makes offerings to all Buddhas.
However, according to the subsequent text, both cause and fruit reach all things; ten matters are briefly cited:
first, the Dharma-body reaches all places, because the Tathāgatagarbha-body is universally pervasive.
Second, because the dharma-body is attained, the wisdom-body is attained;
third, because the wisdom-body is attained, the great vows are attained;
fourth, because the great vows are attained, the roots of goodness for offering requisites are attained.
Fifth is the arrival of seeing the Buddha and hearing his teachings;
sixth is the arrival of manifesting one's own body to bring about awakening;
seventh is the arrival of neither coming nor going.
Eighth, one can reach [all places] without emerging from a single pore;
ninth, one reaches [all places] with a single body and a single hair equaling all bodies and hairs;
tenth, one reaches [all places] in a single thought-moment equaling all kalpas.

If one defines it by its distinct substance, its essence consists of the roots of goodness dedicated to the Buddhas and the mind of resolute conviction; if defined comprehensively, it encompasses the entire *dharmadhātu*.
Within the second section, the detailed explanation following the inquiry, there are three parts:
first, dedicating toward the enlightenment of sentient beings; second, dedicating toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); and third, concluding with praise for the benefits accomplished.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, a brief explanation; second, a detailed exposition.
