Chapter Ten: The Dedication of All Firmly Established Roots of Goodness, from the twenty-fifth to the thirty-third sūtra, part six.
The prose section also has two parts: the practice of the stages and the fruit of the stages.
Within the practice, there are also three parts: the citation, the explanation, and the conclusion.

Now, for the first part, the names are cited and the inquiry is raised: because all the wholesome matters that are cultivated accord with and enter into the firm *dharmatā*, the subsequent text states: "This constitutes conforming to the true abiding in the fundamental stage; it is called entering into all impartial roots of goodness."
"Entering" means to accord with [the truth].
"Equanimity" means firmness, because the principle of equanimity cannot be destroyed.
If one accords with this principle of equanimity, one then accords with all roots of goodness; therefore, the subsequent text says, "This constitutes acceding to the Buddha’s dwelling," and so forth.

Furthermore, the *Benye jing* (Sutra on the Original Activities) states: "Because the cultivation of conditioned goodness and unconditioned goodness are non-dual, it is called 'conforming to all roots of goodness that are equal.

This means that it is not merely a matter of phenomena conforming to principle; rather, when phenomena and principle conform to one another, they receive the name 'equality. Only such equality can be termed 'firm and stable. This designation is established based on the roots of goodness being dedicated and the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) toward which they are directed."
It may also be called "firm roots of goodness," wherein firmness itself constitutes the roots of goodness.
If one regards these in relation to the roots of goodness that accord with them, they likewise encompass two meanings, taking the unimpeded roots of goodness as their essential nature.
The second part, the detailed explanation based on the inquiry, has two sections:
first, clarifying the body that serves as the basis for practice; second, from "Endowed with" (*samanvāgata*) onwards, the arising of practice based upon that body.
Within the former, there are again two parts:
First, the attainment of the stage is clarified; second, the possession of virtues is manifested.
Regarding the first:
because the body of a Bodhisattva practicing *dāna* manifests in ten thousand varieties according to what is appropriate, the word "or" (*vā*) is employed.

As for why the discourse focuses specifically on kings: first, because those at home occupy the position of donors; second, because they are able to relinquish what is difficult to give, thereby exemplifying the superior by exhorting the inferior; and third, because Bodhisattvas frequently become kings.

Because there are only two types of bodhisattva positions—the Dharma King and the Human King—the Dharma King teaches and transforms through the Dharma, while the Human King gathers and transforms through governance. Because they fully possess the bodhisattva precepts, they act as kings everywhere; because their proclamations and commands are never dared to be disobeyed, and because they are fully capable of bestowing material goods to fulfill all requests.
"Di" means sovereign;
"Wang" means king;
"Lin" means to govern.
The sovereign is also the ruler; when he governs a state of a thousand chariots, he is already called "Great.
As for the lower statement regarding the Wheel-Turning King, he may be called "Great" even with only one continent under his rule.
Second, regarding "majestic power" (*prabhāva*) and below, there are two parts within the section on possessing virtues:
first, the virtue of sovereign authority over governance; second, from "the bodhisattva" onwards, the virtue of a sublime physical retribution.
Now, the first section consists of twelve phrases:

the first two are general. If one possesses majesty, those below will inevitably stand in awe; if one possesses virtue, those below will inevitably cherish one; thus, one’s reputation is made to resound.
Next, the ten lines beginning with "All those who... distinguish the specific qualities; the first line explains *wei* (majestic authority).

An ancestral grievance is called a "vendetta" (*yuan*), while foreign tribes possessing territory are called "enemies" (*di*). Because majestic authority is extended to them, enemies submit and those harboring vendettas become compliant.

Next, following "Issuing Decrees," the text explains the aforementioned possession of virtue; by relying on the primary and secondary [aspects of the Buddha-body] to issue commands, sentient beings may take them as models.
The passage on "Holding One Parasol" and so forth further explains his presiding over and governing [the world].
There are three aspects to the single canopy (*eka-cchattra*): first, because it is impartial toward all phenomena;

second, because it equally teaches the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*). As stated in the section on the canopy of giving (*dāna-cchattra*): "In order to cause sentient beings to obtain the canopy of mastery, so that they may uphold all wholesome dharmas."
Regarding the third, the canopy of compassion, King Mahāprabha said:
"Just as the various bodhisattvas serve as a lofty canopy, their hearts of loving-kindness universally shade all sentient beings. Thus it is.
The term "Emperor" (Di) is explained as meaning "to release from defilement," while the term "King" (Wang) is explained as meaning "sovereignty over the Dharma.

From the phrase "without punishment" onwards, both majesty and virtue are revealed together: it means that one does not employ the majesty of execution or penal sanctions, but rather causes others to be moved by virtue and follow transformation; thus, there is majesty without ferocity.

Furthermore, adding suffering is called "punishment" (xing) and confiscation is called "fine" (fa). If one guides them with virtue and righteousness, none will dare not to submit, and thus the common people will be without punishment.
If one regulates them with ritual and music, none will dare not to be reverent, and thus the great officers will be without fines.
Next, the section beginning with "By means of the four means of integration" (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) reveals that this is a bodhisattva, distinguishing him from a worldly king.
As a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), he establishes his status and provides for all universally.
The phrase "possessing great wealth" refers to the fruit of wealth and status.
The second part concerns the excellence of the primary retribution that is peerless in virtue.
The first clause concludes the preceding section while its meaning simultaneously introduces the subsequent one.
"Having a great retinue" and below detail seven kinds of fruits:
first, the fruit of kinship;

second, the fruit of trustworthy speech, which consists in being free from the faults of the multitude, neither haughty nor arrogant, speaking with sincerity so that those who see one never tire of them, possessing both compassion and wisdom, and being trusted and followed by others.
3. From "merit" (*puṇya*) onwards, the great fruit of form (*rūpa-phala*) is revealed.
4. "Obtaining the body of Nārāyaṇa’s firmness" reveals the fruit of longevity (*āyus-phala*).
5. "The accomplishment of great power," etc., reveals the fruit of great power (*bala-phala*).

Sixth is the attainment of pure karma, which means attaining great mindfulness and wisdom and achieving *dhāraṇī*; thus, one never forgets what has been experienced and perceives even before it has sprouted. By virtue of this, one’s superior reputation resounds throughout the world; this is the fruit of renown.
Seventh, being free from all karmic obstructions manifests the fruit of human nature; for one who possesses obstructions regarding karmic retribution is not a true man (*puruṣa*).

Together with the aforementioned wealth and status, these eight maturations (*vipāka*) constitute a superior birth (*abhyudaya-janman*); such sovereignty constitutes a birth of great power (*mahānubhāva-janman*).
The second section, concerning the arising of practice based on the body, has three parts:
first, the dedication according to characteristics; second, the dedication free from characteristics; and third, the explanation of the term "dedication.
The first refers to dedication toward enlightenment and toward sentient beings; the second refers to dedication toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); and the final section applies to both.
Furthermore, the first is the vast dedication, the second is the profound dedication, and the last combines both the profound and the vast.
Now, within the section on "according with characteristics" (*xiāng*), it is divided into three parts:

first, the general enumeration of the dedication of roots of goodness; second, the detailed exposition of the dedication of roots of goodness based on that enumeration, beginning with the words "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, according to what he has bestowed..."; and third, the summary of the various gateways of dedication of roots of goodness, beginning with the words "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, according to all sentient beings..."
Now, the first [section] also has three parts:
first, listing the objects to be given;
second, from "Among them" (*tatra*) onwards, distinguishing the field of giving; third, from "O Son of the Buddha" (*jinaputra*) onwards, revealing the mind upon which the practice relies.
Now, regarding the first [section]: the first phrase is general, while "or gives" and what follows are specific.
Within the specific section, if one considers the subsequent dedication, there should be sixty items;
if calculated directly by the number of textual passages, there are eighty matters in total.
From food and drink up to the bed and seat constitutes the first group of ten;
this is because the "bed and seat" are collectively treated as a single item, whereas the text below separately lists the provision of seats.
Next, from the house up to the canopy constitutes the second group of ten.

The thirty [gifts] end with the royal parasol at the topknot; this is because the royal throne is considered weighty and serves to clarify the conclusion of the giving of external wealth. Thus, it concludes by saying "up to the royal throne.
Since the royal throne appears naturally in the subsequent text, and because this sequence is absent in the later section on dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), [the list here ends there].

Next, from the eyes to the feet constitutes forty; from the blood to the intestines constitutes fifty; from the thick skin to saving others from bodily injury constitutes sixty; from showing the Buddha’s appearance to the village constitutes seventy; and from the settlement to the end constitutes eighty.
Although among the acts of rescuing prisoners there are four matters, such as providing wives and so forth, they constitute merely a single practice of rescuing prisoners.
Among these, the first twenty-seven matters are the giving of external wealth (*bāhyadravyadāna*).
Next is the rescue of prisoners; this first [category] encompasses both internal and external substitution for the lives of prisoners.
The subsequent twenty-nine matters clarify only internal resources (*adhyātma-dhana*).
Among the various sections that follow, some encompass both internal and external, while others concern only the external; these can be understood through careful reflection.

Furthermore, among the aforementioned twenty-seven types of giving, those that lack [the recipient's] joy constitute the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); acts such as rescuing prisoners or sacrificing one's own life for another constitute the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
the remaining types may pertain to either practice, and when distinguished by their general characteristics, they all encompass both practices.
Furthermore, to take one's place in life to save a man from being harmed is the gift of fearlessness.
There are two ways of severing killing:
if it is done with regard to the victim, it is the gift of fearlessness; [if it is done with regard to the perpetrator, it is the gift of material wealth].
If one hopes for the ability to kill and yet causes [others] to uphold the five precepts, this constitutes the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*).
To announce the arising of a Buddha is likewise the gift of Dharma; the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣa-dāna*) is easily understood.
Furthermore, since these are all gates of the Dharma, they collectively encompass all three types of giving.
Regarding the second point, "giving equally to all within the field of recipients" means not discriminating between the worthy and the foolish.
"Causing them all to be satisfied" means granting whatever they request.

Third, regarding the manifestation of the mind that performs dedication through giving: in relation to what precedes it, this is the mind that practices giving, hence it says, "at the time of such giving, one generates a well-restrained mind";
in relation to what follows it, this is the mind of dedication, hence it says, "one generates a well-restrained mind."
All are dedicated [to enlightenment]; therefore, throughout the subsequent sections on dedication, this mind serves as the underlying thread.
The text consists of two parts:
first, a general explanation; second, a detailed exposition beginning with the words "That is to say."
Within this, there are five items included, which collectively encompass all that has been mentioned above: the donor, the recipient, and the gift.
The term "well-comprised" (*susaṃgṛhīta*) explains the meaning of "conformity."

This means that when this bodhisattva practices giving and dedicates the merit, their mind does not dwell upon or become attached to the five aggregates of themselves or others, nor does it allow them to scatter; therefore, it is said that they "skillfully gather [the mind]."
In this way, one accords with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and is thus able to conform to firm roots of goodness.

That is to say: by relinquishing attachment to dwelling, one conforms to the goodness of giving; by having no other seeking, one conforms to the goodness of precepts; by enduring the profound principle, one conforms to the goodness of patience; by being free from the marks of form, one conforms to the goodness of vigor; by not being distracted, one conforms to the goodness of concentration; and by realizing non-arising, one conforms to the goodness of wisdom.
In this manner, it continues until all [virtues] accord with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), spontaneously conforming to all goodness that accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Regarding the second section, "Extensive Elucidation Based on the Headings," there are briefly five differences when compared to the preceding [section], in terms of their coarse characteristics:

first, the *chattra* (parasol) and the *makuṭa* (crown) exist in the former but not in the latter; the *gṛha* (dwelling) exists in the latter but not in the former—this constitutes the difference between existence and non-existence.
Second, regarding guidance and transformation through the Dharma: previously it was "guiding and transforming," while later it is "prohibiting killing and causing one to abide in the five precepts";

thus, they differ in terminology. Third, regarding service and offerings: previously [the text] combined [the items] while later it separated them, such as the case of elephants, horses, and so forth; whereas previously it separated [the items] while later it combined them; thus, they differ in their combination and separation.
In the latter text, the tongue is placed after the teeth, the retinue before the wife and children, the bones below the intestines, and drinking after eating; thus, the sequence differs.
In five instances, the preceding is abbreviated while the subsequent is expanded, such that the wording is not uniform;
in all other cases, they are largely identical.
However, although there are only sixty gates in total, they are termed twelve sections due to their combination and opening: two by two are joined together.

First, elephants and horses; second, banners and streamers; third, precious crowns and bright pearls; fourth, ears and noses; fifth, teeth and tusks; sixth, hands and feet; seventh, marrow and flesh; eighth, thick and thin skins; ninth, fingers and toes; tenth, male and female servants; eleventh, gardens and groves; twelfth, wives and children.

Furthermore, there are two sections, each comprising five items combined: first, the four organs—intestines, kidneys, liver, and lungs—along with the large and small intestines, combined into a single dedication;
second, the royal position, the city, the village, and the palace, combined into a single dedication. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "the lands and all things."
These five matters comprise fourteen gates, totaling twenty items.
Although two items are missing, two others are added—namely, the inclusion of "dwellings" and the separation of "serving" from "attending"—thus resulting in sixty gates.

Formerly, Master Guangtong took the sixty gates established by his predecessors and added the middle section, thereby forming one hundred and twenty gates. Each of these possesses ten wholesome qualities, totaling twelve hundred; when multiplied by the seven types of giving, they become eight thousand four hundred. Each of these is further endowed with the ten dedications, resulting in eighty-four thousand gates.

Regarding the "seven kinds of giving," there are six according to their characteristics: namely, three types of mind, which correspond to the three times; three types of joyful matters, which are the three wheels; and one entry into principle, which is the illumination of the emptiness of the three wheels.

Furthermore, one may also attain it by means of the vehicle of the seven noble riches; as with the single practice consisting of eighty-four thousand [subdivisions], so it is for every other individual practice.
This above has been explained by way of the Dharma-gates, and there is indeed reason for this.

If explained in detail, the modes of practice (*ākāra*) are immeasurable—such as the distribution of requisites and the great assemblies—and cannot be described as singular; therefore, it is next designated as "immeasurable and boundless," and finally concluded as "asamkhyeya things. In reality, these are all the gate of the Great Dependent Origination (*mahā-pratītyasamutpāda*) of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), for they constitute the unimpeded and sovereign conduct of Samantabhadra.
To give all that exists to a single field of merit is to do so for all;
to give to a single speck of dust is to give to all sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm;
to accomplish this practice instantaneously in a single moment is likewise to do so throughout the limits of past and future.
This single Bodhisattva’s body, which fills the Dharma-realm, fully undertakes these practices, yet they remain both pure and mixed.

If considered from the perspective of purity, when focusing on the single act of giving eyes throughout all times and places, one perceives only the boundless giving of eyes throughout the ten directions, without beginning or end, while all other gates are like empty space.

When combined, each individual bestows the eye and fulfills all gates; the same applies to the others. Thus, purity and mixture are unimpeded, layering upon layer without end. Therefore, one should know that the numbers sixty-eight and eighty merely cite the general outline.
The text has two parts:
first, a general statement on the meaning of how the practice of giving becomes an immeasurable practice of dedication, which has already been explained above;
second, from the words "That is to say" (*yad uta*) onwards, each point is individually elucidated.
Within each of the sixty gates, there are four parts:
first, the practice of giving; second, the practice of dedication; third, the combined conclusion of these two practices; and fourth, the purpose for which the dedication is made.
If the object of the action (*prayojana*) is omitted, there are only three [sections].
Alternatively, the latter two sections may be combined to form a double conclusion regarding the object of the action; this classification should be noted.
Below, there are expanded and abbreviated versions, which should be understood from the actual text.
If the text were complete in four sections, it would generally not be divided into distinct chapters at the beginning.
Here, the first section concerns the offering of food; since food constitutes the worldly life upon which both the noble and the humble alike depend, it is explained first.
The text contains only three [sections].
First, it clarifies the practice of giving.
The statement that "the mind is pure" refers to being free from the faults of giving.
This means that one practices giving out of fear and so forth, rather than seeking the fruits of fame or profit.
"Without greed" refers to the volition of non-attachment.
"Without regard for parsimony" refers to the volition of non-stinginess.

Furthermore, when giving, one is without attachment; after giving, one has no lingering regret or stinginess. One shares whatever is practiced in the act of giving with all sentient beings, and by encompassing both the phenomenal and the principled aspects, it is called "complete."
This mind is present at the beginning and also runs through all the subsequent sections.
Second, from "May all... onwards is the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
However, that which is aspired for is precisely to cause sentient beings to attain Buddhahood; this is what it means to be directed toward Bodhi.
The following sections are all to be judged accordingly.
However, the *Āgamas* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra) and other texts state that there are four kinds of worldly nutriment (*āhāra*) in total:
first, contact (*sparśa*); second, volition (*manas-karma*); third, consciousness (*vijñāna*); and fourth, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
Regarding the supramundane foods, there are five kinds:
first, the joy of dhyāna; second, aspiration; third, mindfulness; fourth, liberation; and fifth, the joy of the Dharma.
Now, by reversing four [of these], they become five:
First, by transforming the thought of food into the food of wisdom, this is the "food of mindfulness," because mindfulness and wisdom are adjacent to one another.

Second, from the phrase "without craving" onwards, the food of contact is transformed into the joy of the Dharma; for contact functions as food by means of its capacity to receive and sustain joy and so forth.
I only wish for the joy of the Dharma; this is the food of renunciation, which is the food of liberation, because it completely transcends the [first] four types of nutriment.

Third, from "the abundance of wisdom" (*prajñā-puṣṭi*) downward, the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*) is overturned to become the delight of dhyāna (*dhyānārāma*). This is because: first, dhyāna is immovable; second, because the Dharma abides firmly, it draws forth meritorious qualities; third, by grasping roots of goodness, it can eliminate afflictions; and fourth, the purity of the two bodies is like the nutriment of consciousness in its ability to sustain and maintain.
4. From "Out of compassion" (*anukampā*) below, it is shown that he accepts solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) through the power of his great compassionate vows.
The current use of the term "lump" (*tuṇḍa*) still follows the ancient translation.
3. From "This is" (*idam... iti*) below, both practices are concluded together.
The second, the giving of drinks, also has three parts:
first, the practice of giving;
second, from "By this" onwards, the practice of dedication.
Within this, first the preceding section is restated to introduce the subsequent one.
Below the phrase "That which is called wishing for all," the characteristics of the vow are specifically revealed; all that follows is modeled after this.
Although these differ from the [five] nutriments (āhāra), they do not depart from the five nutriments.
Although the metaphors for water differ, they mostly share the same function as water.

Therefore, regarding the matters one wishes for, whether they are expressed through inversion or conformity, through direct opposition or through analogous categories, they are not strictly definitive.
In this text, it is as if one were drinking from an uninterrupted stream, easily attaining full satisfaction.
By practicing the method of drinking with diligent effort, one will swiftly perfect the Great Way.
All other matters may be understood accordingly.
The third is the practice of giving the flavor (*rasadāna*), which consists of four sections because it adds the specific purpose [of the gift].
The first, the practice of giving, is as previously understood.
The second, beginning with "By this," concerns the ten vows within the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Regarding the first vow, the Jin translation mentions the mark of "exquisite flavor" (*rasarasāgratā*), which is one of the thirty-two marks.
The sutras state that behind the Buddha’s large canine teeth there is a spring of nectar (*amṛta*), so that whatever food enters his mouth becomes entirely nectar.
The summary of the Dharma is also *nirvāṇa*, the nectar-like flavor of immortality.
The remaining text is clear.
Fourth, the gift of vehicles is divided into three parts:
Regarding the initial practice of giving, the meaning extends to horses and so forth, because the sixteenth [perfection] specifically mentions the giving of chariots.
The dedication toward the ten vows all concerns providing means of transport.
The first [vow] pertains solely to the fruit, while the others pertain to both the cause and the fruit.
However, the essence of the vehicle (yāna) pervades both wisdom and principle; names are established according to their respective meanings. First, its essential nature is all-inclusive;

second, it cannot be discarded or established [alternatively]; third, it transcends inferiority; fourth, it is free from fault; fifth, one does not traverse three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; sixth, the ten powers universally operate; seventh, it encompasses the five perfections and the myriad practices; eighth, it is in correspondence with the untainted (*anāsrava*); ninth, those who resolve their minds and aspire toward it are immediately called Bodhisattvas.

Regarding the fifth type of robe, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the gift of robes can bring about a beautiful complexion, because clothing wards off the cold and causes the skin’s color to become lustrous.

Question:

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle thirty-nine, states: "If there are sentient beings who come seeking various objects that incite frivolous pleasure or lead to what is meaningless, one should not give them."
"Now, giving away one's own beautiful form—does this not contradict [the previous teaching]?

Furthermore, it was said that 'when giving away one's wife and children, one should not give them to enemies, wicked people, yakṣas, rākṣasas, or those engaged in violent deeds'; yet now you speak of various fields of merit (puṇyakṣetra)—are they all to be given to?"
Answer:
There are two types of capability. First, if one knows for certain that giving will cause harm or distress, there is no fault in not giving;
second, if one does not know for certain, but acts with a mind intent on benefit and peace, there is likewise no fault in giving.

Moreover, a bodhisattva is able to know that there is no defilement; furthermore, the woman who shares his practice will certainly not give rise to any sensual attachment; and finally, the woman is able to transform him through the Dharma.

Therefore, in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is stated that there are three cases in which a bodhisattva does not engage: when there is benefit but defilement, when there is neither benefit nor defilement, and when there is defilement but no benefit.
Only when there is benefit and no defilement does a bodhisattva engage.
The second section clarifies [the distinctions] according to the field (*kṣetra*).
Based on five types of fields, it is divided into five parts; within each individual section, all four [aspects] are fully present.
Now, first is the giving to the Buddha.
The practice of giving can be understood from what precedes.

Within the practice of dedication, there are twenty vows: the first ten establish vows based on the field of merit consisting of the Buddhas to whom the gift is given, and the latter ten establish vows based on the vehicle to which the gift is given; both are clearly evident.
Regarding the statement that one merely practices the "Practice of Peaceful Bliss" (*anraku-gyō*), the "Peaceful Bliss Chapter" (*Anrakugyō-bon*) of the *Lotus Sūtra* explains four such practices:
first, the practice of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

The sūtra refers to these as the "place of practice" (*gyōsho*) and the "near place" (*kinjo*); because one has already entered into principle and acts in accordance with it, they are called the "place of practice."
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, while not engaging with any phenomena, one contemplates all phenomena as they truly are," and so forth.
Although one has not yet entered into the ultimate principle, because one is able to distance oneself from all evils and draw near to [the truth], it is called the stage of drawing near (*upaniṣad*).
The Sūtra states, "Do not associate with kings, non-Buddhists, and the like," which means to distance oneself from evil.
To contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena is to draw near to the principle.
The second is the practice of being free from faults in body and speech;
the third is the practice of a mind free from envy;
the fourth is the practice of great compassion.
It is as explained at length there.
However, regarding "peaceful bliss" (*sukha*), there are briefly two senses:
first, the fruit of nirvāṇa is called peaceful bliss, and this practice which can lead toward it is the practice of peaceful bliss.

Second, by abiding in these four practices, the body becomes tranquil and the spirit becomes concentrated; when the body is tranquil and the spirit is concentrated, external suffering does not disturb them, and thus they are called "peaceful and blissful.

Furthermore, it is observed that for non-Buddhists with the view of permanence, both cause and effect are suffering; for non-Buddhists with the view of annihilation, the cause is pleasure and the effect is suffering; for the followers of the Two Vehicles who analyze phenomena, the cause is suffering and the effect is pleasure; only for Bodhisattvas are both cause and effect blissful. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Those who practice fixed asceticism are called ordinary worldlings; those who practice both suffering and pleasure are called Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; those who practice fixed bliss are called Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
The simultaneous presence of cause and effect is called "peaceful conduct" (sukha-vihāra).
Within the three sections of the text, it further includes all stūpas and temples that exist after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa.
A stūpa is where the śarīra (relics) are enshrined; a temple is where images are placed.
"Stūpa" (塔) is correctly called *stūpa* (窣堵波), which here means "lofty and manifest," and is also termed "the place where one returns to the source.
As for the phrase "that which possesses [it]," it does not restrict [the term] to Buddhist stūpas alone.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that there are four types of persons for whom stūpas should be erected:
first, the Buddha; second, the pratyekabuddha; third, the arhat; and fourth, the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
The *Sūtra on the Twelve Conditions* states: "Eight types of persons should have stupas erected for them:

first, the Buddha, whose *āmalaka* (dew-dish) has eight or more tiers; the remaining seven—namely, the Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, those of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path, and the Wheel-turning Kings—have their tiers reduced by one in succession, with the Wheel-turning King having only a single tier."
"One should not prostrate before a single-storied stupa because it does not belong to an *ārya*," so it is said.

However, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that even ordinary monks are permitted to erect stupas; yet they must not be provided with a dew-basin (*lupan*), and they should be placed in a secluded location. These refer to four types: first, those who uphold the Vinaya; second, Dharma masters; third, administrators; and fourth, those of virtuous reputation.
Those who now construct stupas should carefully examine this text.
Generally speaking, there are six purposes for erecting stupas:

first, to manifest the excellence of the person; second, to inspire pure faith; third, to mark the location where the mind is directed; fourth, to generate merit through making offerings; fifth, to fulfill the practice of repaying kindness; and sixth, to produce blessings and extinguish transgressions.
If one constructs a Buddha stupa, it brings about Brahma-merit in the near term and liberation from birth and death in the distant future.
According to the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*, by making an offering to the Buddha’s relics even as small as a mustard seed, one attains ultimate liberation from the suffering of birth and death.

The latter ten points overturn the Śrāvakas:

first, they overturn the view that the Lesser Vehicle is not a method for the ultimate extinction of offenses; for while one who violates the disciplinary code (*vinaya*) may still repent and extinguish the offense, one who commits the four grave prohibitions (*caturmahāpatti*) is beyond salvation.
The supreme teachings of the Mahāyāna leave nothing unextinguished.
The *Buddhanāmasūtra* states that hearing the name of a single Buddha extinguishes the grave sins of immeasurable kalpas of birth and death.

The tenth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "If one has committed the four pārājika offenses or the five heinous crimes, or is possessed by malevolent spirits and poisons, upon hearing this sūtra, all such evils shall be completely extinguished."
It is further stated: "That one who has committed the four grave prohibitions would not be reborn [in the hells]—such a thing is impossible.
Passages such as these appear everywhere, owing to the power of this Great Sūtra, which had never been heard before.
Second, although the śrāvakas have heard from the Buddha, they have not yet realized the profound principle.
Third, because they are unable to propagate it extensively.
Fourth, because compared to the Mahāyāna, it is still considered erroneous.

Therefore, many sources state that there are ninety-five types [of heterodoxies], referring to the separate existence of ninety-five kinds of sūtras containing the erroneous doctrines of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
The present mention of ninety-six has two meanings:

first, according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, each of the six teachers of the outsiders had sixteen types of teachings they studied; one was for their own study, while the remaining fifteen were each taught to fifteen disciples. When masters and disciples are combined, there are ninety-six.
Second, there are two types of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*):
first, the external non-Buddhists, who are outside of the Buddha-dharma;
second, the internal-external non-Buddhists, which are further divided into three kinds:

First, those who affiliate with the Buddha-dharma and yet follow external paths (bāhyaka), originating from the Vātsīputrīyas and the Vaipulya; because they rely on their own cleverness to study the Buddhist scriptures and give rise to a singular view, they arise in affiliation with the Buddha-dharma and thus receive this name.

Vātsīputra studied the *Śāriputrābhidharma* and established his own distinct interpretation, asserting that the self exists outside the four propositions, within the fifth [category], the "Ineffable Store" (*avaktavyakalāpa*).
The Buddha said that such a person is no different from a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
All treatises reject them as not accepting [the teachings], and thus they are called non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, there are those who follow the Vaipulya school; relying on their own cleverness, they read the Buddha’s ten parables and formulate their own interpretations, saying:
"Neither arising nor ceasing, like an illusion or a transformation, with emptiness and illusion as its tenet.
Nāgārjuna rebuked him, saying:
"This is not the Buddha-dharma; it is the work of the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna], and is also the teaching of heterodox persons."

Second, those who study the Buddha-dharma but become heterodox practitioners (tīrthika) are those who cling to the gates of the Buddhist teachings and thereby give rise to afflictions, failing to enter into the principle.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one does not grasp the meaning of Prajñā, entering the Abhidharma leads to falling into existence," and so forth.
Third, the Great [Vehicle] refutes the Small [Vehicle].
Thus, the first fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* in seven fascicles states:
"Mahāmati, what are the evil views of the non-Buddhists?"

This means that they do not understand that objects are manifestations of their own mind’s conceptualization; regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they engage in verbal discourse by perceiving things as either existent or non-existent.
Furthermore, the second [section] states: "Again, there are those who say:
'Seeing all phenomena as existing because of a creator is what constitutes nirvāṇa.'"
Mahāmati! They have no liberation because they have not yet perceived the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya).
This is the lineage of the śrāvakas and non-Buddhists; within that which has not emerged [from saṃsāra], they produce the appearance of emergence.
"You should diligently practice so as to abandon these evil views.
When the Mahāyāna texts criticize those of the two vehicles as being the same as externalists, this is not intended to deprive them of their skillful means.
Now, combining the latter three into one category, they total ninety-six.
Based on this meaning, one makes a vow to be forever free from them.
Regarding those who "attain direct vision" among the seven [categories], it is because they do not rely on visionary hearing.

Regarding the five fields of merit,

Sixth, regarding the "ten paths of renunciation," these are the ten stages (*bhūmi*), because one renounces the ten layers of obstructions and the ten coarse [defilements] through the practice of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).
Seventh, regarding the "four wheels of the vehicle," they are listed in the text itself.
However, the sixth chapter of the *Śrīkāra-sūtra* (or *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*) is titled "The Four Wheels of Heedfulness.
To first distinguish their characteristics, each possesses five kinds of causal conditions.
First, the wheel of dwelling in a favorable land is called the wheel of the superior land.
Regarding the five conditions: first, ease of procurement, meaning that the four requisites are easily obtained;
second, a king who is well-protected, because he acts according to the Dharma;
third, an excellent location, because it is harmonious.
Fourth, good companions, because their precepts and views are identical;
fifth, good tranquility, because there is no clamor.
Second, the wheel of relying on virtuous persons has five conditions: first, extensive learning;
Second, seeing the truth;
third, skillful exposition;
fourth, compassion, because of not being greedy for profit.
The fifth is non-retrogression, because there is no weariness.
Regarding the third, the wheel for gathering supreme merit: that corresponds to the fourth [wheel], named the wheel of prior merit.
The first is "delightful," because it has dwelling in superior worldly states as its cause.
Second is being free from obstacles, due to the cause of encountering virtuous persons;
third is freedom from illness, fourth is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and fifth is wisdom—these three have the wheel of self-correction as their cause.
Fourth, he makes a great vow; this third [wheel] is therefore called the Wheel of Self-Correcting Resolve, which is why the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* names it the Wheel of Self-Initiated Right Vow.
First is the good condition, because the sublime Dharma serves as the condition;
second is the good accumulation, because of the possession of merit and wisdom.
Third, he is skilled in the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā, because he cultivates them in accordance with all practices;
fourth, he is skilled in preaching, because he seeks no profit;
fifth, he is skilled in relinquishing all possessions, because he respectfully aspires to cultivate the supreme Dharma.

However, while the first two [terms] are established by way of the result and the latter two are named according to their causes, although all four apply to both cause and result, they are presented through mutual abbreviation and implication.
The first two are external conditions and the latter two are internal causes; aspiration is the cause of wisdom, and merit is the cause of fortune.
For what reason are these four called "wheels"?
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, it is because these four wheels can destroy the eight unfavorable conditions (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*).

That is to say, first, by dwelling in a favorable place, one can eliminate five unfavorable conditions: namely, the three miserable realms (*durgati*), the northern continent (*uttarakuru*), and the long-lived heavens (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*).
Next, by relying on virtuous persons, one removes the obstacles of the Buddha’s presence and absence;
third, by making great vows, one removes worldly wit, eloquence, and cleverness;
fourth, by having planted roots of goodness in past lives, one removes the primary obstacles of blindness, deafness, and muteness.
The first five are unfavorable places, the sixth is an unfavorable time, the seventh is an unfavorable cause, and the eighth is an unfavorable result.
Having understood these four wheels, why are they collectively termed "vehicles" (yāna)?

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that dwelling in a favorable land—meaning one has obtained a human or celestial body and is free from the various states of adversity—constitutes the body of the chariot.
Second, by accumulating superior merit, one’s faculties are fully intact; this is like the hub, axle, rim, and linchpin of a chariot, which can be lubricated with grease.
Third, one makes great vows, like a fine ox drawing heavy loads to distant places.
Fourth, one relies on virtuous persons—namely Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—who are like skillful charioteers.
By possessing these four, one achieves Great Nirvana; thus it is said that "all pure brahmacarya is fulfilled," for when the causes are perfected, the fruit is necessarily attained.

According to this sutra, the "lands" refer to the ocean of ten lands; the "virtuous people" refer to the Tathāgatas of the ten bodies; "supreme merit" refers to the merits of the nature-arising (prakṛti-udbhava); and the "great vows" refer to the ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows. Together, these constitute the vehicle of the inexhaustible great dharma-realm dependent origination.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the two matters of giving elephants and horses, there are ten vows in total:
first, that they be naturally well-tamed and docile;...
Second, they go wherever they wish;
