Eighth, it is as swift as the wind;

ninth, the previous [version] mentions being "well-tamed" (*dānta*) and "manifesting increased merit," while the present [version] says "possessing the stage of a Bodhisattva, named the Most Excellent Tamed Elephant-Horse. Since each contains the sense of being tamed, they are divided into two vows;
tenth, it resembles the aforementioned "establishing a golden banner."
Within the dedication of the eighteen offerings of seats, the phrase "the three worlds" is explained according to the usual interpretation.
Master Bian states:

"The stage prior to the [first] bhūmi is called the world of aspiration and joy; from the first bhūmi to the seventh is called the world of effortful application; and from the eighth bhūmi up to Equal Enlightenment (samyaksaṃbodhi) is called the world of effortless spontaneity."
Some say: According to tradition in the Western Regions, within the realm of sentient beings there are three worlds:
first, the subterranean world, consisting of nāgas, asuras, and so forth;...
Of these two, there is the mundane world;
the three are the supramundane worlds.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the three worlds consist of sentient beings, the five aggregates, and the vessel-world.
In that regard, the emphasis on excellence carries no fault in meaning.
The rest may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the nineteenth [topic], the parasol of giving: the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* (or *Prātihārya-sūtra*) states that he wove grass to make a parasol, and the parasols made of the seven precious jewels followed after it.
How much more so when adorned with various jewels—how could the merit and retribution be limited?
Within the four [categories], there are ten [aspects], which, combined with the twenty [aspects of the previous], make forty.

Furthermore, it is because one desires to cause all sentient beings to have their causes perfected and their fruits fulfilled, and to touch upon and encompass all principles, that the profound and subtle compassion and wisdom of the Bodhisattva are revealed; this may be called conforming to all roots of goodness.
One may also seek this through contemplation; however, as the Dharma-gates are vast and expansive, they cannot be explained in full detail.

Regarding the two matters of the twenty banners and pennants combined into a single dedication: among the ten [verses], the first two concern the combined vows for the banners and pennants—first, establishing the good to overturn evil, and second, honoring the Dharma to overturn arrogance.
The next one concerns the pennant alone, because characters are written upon the pennant.
The latter seven are all distinguished by means of the banners.
Regarding the opening of the treasury to bestow jewels among the twenty-one practices of dedication,
as for what are called the "sixteen jewels of wisdom," Master Bianfa says:
"Before the stages (bhūmi), there are the four concentrations of *vidarśanā-labdha*, *vidarśanā-vṛddha*, *mudrā*, and *ānulomika*.
On the stages, there are the four concentrations of *āloka-saṃbhūta*, *puṇya-rāja*, *bhadra-śrī*, and *sudurjayā*."
"Each of these eight has its own basic and its superior development; based on these, the arising of wisdom constitutes the sixteen jewels of wisdom. Some say:
"The four wisdoms of the Buddha-ground each possess four [aspects], thus making sixteen, because at the stage of fruition they are sovereign and mutually interpenetrating."
Now, following Xianshou, these are the eight patiences and the eight knowledges.
However, there are two ways of establishing them:
first, sixteen are established based on the observation of the grasped and the grasper.

First is the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*): it contemplates the suchness (*tathatā*) of suffering within the three realms, correctly severing the views of suffering in the three realms and abandoning the discriminative latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are to be severed.

Second is the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*): this refers to the contemplation of the aforementioned suchness immediately following the patience, realizing liberation from the afflictions previously severed.

The subsequent patience regarding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) refers to the arising of untainted wisdom immediately following that knowledge, wherein one internally realizes each of the patiences and knowledges regarding the dharmas individually.
It is said that all subsequent noble dharmas are of this same category.

The subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) refers to the arising of uncontaminated knowledge immediately following this [subsequent patience of suffering], which definitively confirms and validates the subsequent patience of suffering.
The first two [moments] observe the suchness (*tathatā*), while the latter two observe the knowledge (*jñāna*).
There are four [knowledges] for each of the lower [realms], and the same applies to the three truths; thus, there are sixteen knowledges.
Second, these are established separately based on the distinction between the objects of the higher and lower truths as they are contemplated.

That is to say, when contemplating the suffering of the desire realm, there are dharma-patience (dharma-kṣānti) and dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna); the former is the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), and the latter is the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).

Next, one contemplates the suffering of the two higher realms as "subsequent patience" (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and "subsequent knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*), because their nature is analogous to that of the desire realm.
Just as it is with suffering, so it is with the remaining three [truths], constituting the sixteen knowledges.
This is explained in detail in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the ninth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*.
Regarding the tenth vow, the phrase "supreme jewel lord" refers to the Buddha, as he is the lord of the Dharma-jewel.
Among the twenty-two vows for adorning generosity, the first benefits others and the latter nine benefit oneself.
Within these, the first three pertain to the body, the next three to speech, and the final three to the mind.
Regarding the marks of the hundred merits (*śatapuṇya-lakṣaṇa*), the preceding text has already cited the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

According to the fifty-third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, they are termed "hundred meritorious actions" (*śatapuṇya-karman*); thus the treatise states: "Furthermore, by means of the discipline (*saṃvara*) comprised of one hundred actions—namely, abstaining from killing and so forth to a small extent constitutes ten;
second, abstaining from killing and so forth to a great extent [constitutes another ten];"
Third, complete separation;
fourth, temporary separation;
fifth, long-term separation.
Sixth, abstaining for as long as life lasts;
seventh, abstaining by oneself;
eighth, teaching others to abstain.
Ninth, praising and extolling renunciation through immeasurable gateways;
tenth, seeing renunciation such as abstaining from killing and feeling deep-seated joy and great rapture.
Each of these ten gateways contains ten aspects, which are collectively described as the "one hundred practices," and the measure of the merit produced is likewise the same.
This has been explained provisionally with reference to the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) possessing the thirty-two marks according to the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-dharma).
However, if one relies on this sutra, the ocean of the ten bodies' marks is formed by inexhaustible causes for each and every individual mark.

The verse by the water-governing spirit named Universal Cloud Banner Arising Above states: "Pure gates of compassion, as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field, together produce a single wondrous mark of the Tathāgata," and so forth.
The rest may be understood.
Twenty-third, the two matters of bestowing the jeweled crown and the topknot jewel are combined into a single dedication.
Regarding the "bright pearl of wisdom" and so forth: its substance is perfect and its virtues complete; it is penetratingly clear and free from delusion, thus it is the bright pearl of wisdom.
As it is the ultimate goal of all teachings, it is called the "Crown"; being secret and wondrous, none are able to see it.
Furthermore, because the provisional conceals the real, it is said to reside within the topknot.
By opening up the provisional to reveal the real, it is called "untying the topknot.
Although the text does not explicitly contain the meaning of "untying," it is included here for the sake of convenience.
If one does not understand this "untying," the Buddha possesses a secret treasury.
The preceding and following sections may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the twenty-fourth [type of giving], which is the giving of one's wife and children to save those imprisoned: all that has been explained above clarifies external giving (*āmiṣadāna*);
the two sections below clarify the giving of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*).

The first [type of giving] involves both internal and external wealth; since internal wealth is difficult to relinquish, the *Buddhacarita-sūtra* states: "In the past, five hundred sons of elders each renounced precious jewels and other possessions as offerings."
There was a poor man who was asked what boon he sought;
he replied that he wished to seek the path of Buddhahood.
He then thought to himself that he was destitute and had nothing, so he smeared his body with honey and cast it away among the graves.
The Heavenly Emperor tested him, and seeing that his mind remained unshaken, he recognized his pursuit of the fruit of Buddhahood and praised him, saying:
"This courage of yours exceeds by hundreds of thousands of billions of times the offerings made by those five hundred bodhisattvas; you shall become a Buddha first."
"That poor man was none other than myself.
Thus one knows that this is the most difficult among difficulties.
There are three ways of practicing giving:
First, one gives rise to compassion upon first beholding the object.

Second, from "Just as with Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) onwards, it refers back to the preceding example; "Great Compassion" here refers to Avalokiteśvara, because he specifically presides over this gate.
The examples cited in the following text should all be understood according to this principle.
Below the section beginning with "Having already delivered," he bestows both material wealth and the Dharma.
The dedication of merit through the practice of the ten vows should be easily understood through careful reflection.

Twenty-five: Sacrificing one’s own body to save a condemned prisoner; this refers exclusively to internal wealth (*adhyātmika-dhana*), and the four textual passages may be understood accordingly. From here below, we enter the twenty-seventh sūtra. Twenty-six:
"The fleshly protuberance on the crown of the head" (*uṣṇīṣa-śīrṣa*); this is the *māṃsa-uṣṇīṣa*.
The practice consists of three parts:

first, a general statement of the practice; second, "As in the case of Ratnacūḍa" and following, which points to the objects and shows their shared cultivation; third, "At that time, the Bodhisattva" and following, which correctly elucidates the practice itself.
Within this, there are six [points]:
first, "beholding the beggar and giving rise to joy," because one abides in the spiritual lineage (*gotra*);
second, from "and spoke" onwards, the purity of speech and intention, because of being free from the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
3. "Then he takes hold" refers to the excellence of his physical actions (*kāyakarman*), as they are correctly relinquished;
4. "With right mindfulness" refers to the excellence of his mental disposition (*āśaya*), as he aspires to the higher realms;
5. "Regarding all phenomena" refers to the excellence of his skillful establishment in the principles of the truths, as it is subsumed by the signless (*animitta*).
6. From "Therefore" onwards, he resolves to emulate [the Buddhas], because his reliance is superior.

This section, along with the dedication of merit, contains the seven types of supremacy that constitute the *pāramitās*; in the preceding and succeeding sections on various forms of giving, the text is mostly abbreviated and omitted.
Second, regarding the ten vows within the practice of dedication following the section on "Bodhisattva":
first, "one whose crown cannot be seen," because even if one were to exhaustively reach the upper realms, there would still be something above;
it is said to be "like a stūpa" because Bodhisattvas pay reverence to him.
Second, because it is firm and uninterrupted.
Regarding the fifth, the *Zhongjing fapin* (Sūtra on the Dharmas of the Middle) states:
"According to the Sanskrit original, two characteristics are obtained: the hair refers to the *śrīvatsa-svastika* hair-mark; its meaning is as previously explained."
Sixth, regarding the attainment of the Buddha’s mark of the *ūrṇā* (hair-treasure): according to the Sanskrit original, it is actually clockwise.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the purpose for which the dedication is made: because all the hair is gathered together to form a perfectly full topknot (*uṣṇīṣa*), it is described in this way.

Twenty-seventh is the gift of the eyes. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom), in its fourteenth fascicle, states that there are three kinds of giving: food and drink are the lowest; precious jewels are the middle; and one's head, eyes, and five viscera are the highest, as explained in detail therein.
Within the text, there are four sections:
first, the heading and citation of examples;
second, from "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva" onwards, the arousal of the superior mind.
3. From "For the sake of ultimate [attainment]" onwards, it clarifies the mental activities performed by the practitioner, which may be understood accordingly;
4. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, it manifests the ritual procedures for bestowal.

Regarding the second, the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), one vows to accomplish the ten eyes, which is largely the same as, yet slightly different from, that in the "Leaving the World" (*Lokottara*) chapter.

Regarding the twenty-eight acts of giving, such as those involving the ears and nose, two matters are explained together to clarify the practice of giving, while the dedication of merit is shown separately.
However, the text contains only three [sections].
Now, for the first, the practice of giving, there are two parts:

First, the heading and citation of examples; second, from "At the time of giving" onwards, abiding in the supreme mind: (1) possessing the Buddha-lineage is abiding in the most excellent; (2) from "Mindfulness of all... onwards, the excellence of activity; (3) from "Always diligent... onwards, the excellence of reliance; (4) from "In accordance with... onwards, the excellence of purification; (5) from "Rescuing and liberating... onwards, the excellence of intention; (6) from "Growing and developing... onwards, the excellence of skillful means.
Within the two types of dedication practices, the ten vows are first presented.

Regarding the fact that the first and the seventh are both termed "unimpeded" (*asaṅga*): according to the Sanskrit original, the first is named "unattached deafness," because [the bodhisattva] was deaf from birth.
Regarding the ear-king, it is because both hearing and not hearing are under one's mastery.
In the subsequent dedication of the gift of the nose, there are four parts;
first, the restatement of the subject.
The second [section] correctly reveals two vows within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); the former vow attains ten nose-ornaments (*anuvyañjana*).
Regarding the "ornaments" (*anuvyañjana*), it is because the two nostrils do not appear.

Regarding the "excellent marks" (*lakṣaṇa*), the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks" states: "The Tathāgata’s nose possesses a mark of a great man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) named 'Cloud of All Supernormal Powers and Wisdom'."
"Conforming to the nose" means that it manifests according to what is appropriate.
Regarding the latter vow to obtain ten faces: since the nose is situated in the center of the face and beauty or ugliness arise from it, the [other] marks are established in accordance with it.
"May all dharmas" means being correctly directed toward all phenomena.
Third, the section beginning with "This is for... is the conclusion.

Fourth, the section beginning with "In order to... is the dedication of merit toward specific goals; there are ten [reasons], because of the entry of fragrance through the nose, because of the grasping of fragrance, because of its thorough knowledge, because of abiding in awakening, because it is like seeing forms with the eye, because of knowing through conjunction, because of not impairing the faculty of the nose, because of not engaging in false discrimination, because of the purity and adornment of the fragrance, and because of the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body.
Twenty-ninth is the gift of the tusks.
Regarding the initial practice of giving, those who abide in the firm and sovereign state are those who have already ascended the stages (*bhūmi*).
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom), fascicle 14, states: "The elephant king’s gift of his tusks is an act of a Dharma-body Bodhisattva."
The details are as found in that [text] and the fourth chapter of the *Daśacakra-sūtra*.
Second, from "Bodhisattva" onwards, the practice of dedication consists of ten vows.
Only the third is explained solely in terms of the mind; it means that wisdom can subdue afflictions and lead one to the other shore, just as a tusk subdues food to nourish the Dharma-body.
The rest all refer to the teeth.
Regarding the accomplishment of the *svastika* (万字), according to the Sanskrit original, it merely says "spiral to the right" and "possessing bliss.
As for "emitting immeasurable light," this is as explained in the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks" (*Lakṣaṇasamudra-parivarta*).

Among the thirty vows regarding the offering of the tongue, the first is the mark of the broad and long tongue as described in the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks" (*Lakṣaṇasāgara-parivarta*); the remainder may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the thirty-first, the offering of the head, there are three parts within the initial practice of giving:
First, the chapter is introduced and supported by scriptural citations.
Regarding the citation of the King of Kāśī, the *Saṃghabhedavastu* (The Sūtra on Past Deeds) also recounts how King Candraprabha repaid his debt of gratitude;
the fifth instance, in which the Great Radiance King (*Mahāprabha*) gave his head to a brahmin, is explained in detail as it appears therein.

Next, the section beginning with "for the sake of desire" (*chandataḥ*) reveals the ten purposes for which giving is performed; all of these are based on Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*), differing according to their respective meanings.

First, entering into principle (*tattva*); second, guiding through compassion (*karuṇā*); third, perceiving phenomena (*vastu*); fourth, abandoning hindrances (*āvaraṇa*); fifth, harmonizing phenomena and principle; sixth, serving as the basis (*āśraya*); seventh, transcending the inferior; eighth, seeing that there is no mark of a beginning; ninth, manifesting mastery in function; and tenth, because it is true within phenomena themselves, it is indestructible.
Below the section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," the actual practice of giving is revealed, which likewise possesses the most excellent qualities and can be understood through reflection.
Second, from the section beginning with "Bodhisattva" onwards, the practices of dedication and so forth are to be understood.
Regarding the thirty-two acts of giving, the two matters of hands and feet are combined into a single vow; thus, there are only three [sections] in the text.
The first section, the practice of giving, also has three parts:
first, the heading and the citation of scriptural evidence.
Next, from "by means of faith" onwards, the causes are designated to pray for the fruits.
Faith is the cause that serves as the hand, whereby the fruit is able to rain down jewels;
conduct is the cause that serves as the feet, whereby the fruit is able to travel everywhere, and so forth.
Following this, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards is the pure-minded, correct giving.
Within this section, the first part concerns the giving of the hands;
from "By the power of the resolve of the mind" onwards clarifies the giving of the feet and the mind.
Just as the feet, by abiding on the ground, can support the body, may the vows, by abiding on the ground of wisdom, bring about the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*).
Because they are free from the defilements of the mind, they can manifest the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Since the Dharma-body is serene and profound, it is indestructible.
Because wisdom-realization is perpetual, there is no interruption.
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the practice of dedication is clarified.
The text has two parts:
First, the various functions of a single hand are explained in detail: the hand is able to rain down jewels, and the foot is able to travel through buddha-fields.
Next, from the passage beginning with "Furthermore, he causes," the various functions of all the hands are briefly enumerated.
Third, [the account of] destroying his own body to give blood.
The textual passages also consist of only three parts.
The application of the practice and the citation of examples, as well as the subsequent offering of marrow, are all as explained in the fourteenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Among the thirty-four instances of giving one’s body, marrow, and flesh, two matters are combined with the vow.
The first section, on the practice of giving, has three parts:

first, the heading and citation of evidence; second, the explicit exposition of the characteristics of the practice, beginning with "In all realms of existence"; and third, the demonstration of the immediate benefits of the practice, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha."
Second, the dedication to the ten vows.

Third, regarding the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*): the second fascicle of the seven-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states, "Just as the mind travels swiftly and without obstruction, it is called the mind-made body."
This is merely an illustration provided by the mind.
Nevertheless, there are three types of such bodies: first, the body of the bliss of samādhi;
second, the body that realizes the self-nature of dharmas; and third, the body that arises spontaneously from the nature of things and is free from volitional effort.
Regarding the first point, the fourth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "It refers to entering samādhi, being free from various mental states, and remaining tranquil and unmoving.
The ocean of the mind does not give rise to the waves of the evolving consciousnesses; one realizes that objects are manifestations of the mind and are ultimately non-existent."
What is the awakening to the intrinsic nature of phenomena?
It refers to realizing that all phenomena are like illusions and are devoid of any marks.

This is the basis for the transformation of the mind; by relying on the illusion-like samādhi and other meditative absorptions, one can manifest immeasurable sovereign supernormal powers, as swift and effortless as a flower blooming at will.

Like an illusion, like a dream, like a shadow, and like a reflection; neither created nor produced from causes, yet resembling that which is created; fully adorned with all marks of physical form, because they universally enter the Buddha-fields and thoroughly understand the nature of all phenomena.
What is the unconditioned practice that arises simultaneously with one’s spiritual lineage?
It refers to the thorough realization of the characteristics of the dharmas realized by all Buddhas themselves. Commentary:
The first body is named after its basis, which is meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
the second body is designated according to its basis, which is wisdom (*prajñā*);

and the third is the self-realized characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), whose meaning encompasses both concentration and wisdom as well as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatālakṣaṇa*); therefore, it is called the "category" (*jāti*).

Because of this, one is able to manifest various births simultaneously in accordance with the aspirations of sentient beings, accomplishing them spontaneously; thus it is called "effortless practice" (*anābhoga-caryā*).
If categorized by the stages (*bhūmi*), the first refers to before the fifth stage, the second to before the eighth stage, and the last to after the eighth stage.

If the eighth [consciousness] in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* is called "mind-made" (*manomaya*), it is because it is produced according to the mind's vows; "mind" clarifies that it is merely a transformation, not something newly generated.

Therefore, the treatise further states: "It is also called the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), because through the power of untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), it is transformed so as to differ from its original state, just like a magical creation.
The above all apply to the causal stage.
This is now one of the ten bodies; in terms of its meaning, it also extends to the final one, as detailed in a separate chapter.
The fourth is called the "Body of the Marks of a Hundred Merits," which cites the general cause for the thirty-two marks.
If they are distinct causes, it is as stated in the "Lion’s Roar" chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Regarding the five types of eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), it means that because they are all exceptionally sublime, they are designated by the name "minor marks."
This is fully as explained in the forty-ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the three hundred eighty-first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The remaining passages may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the tenth point, the "body that is the treasury of bodhi," it is as described in the "Chapter on Manifestation": when the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives within his own body all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment and so forth.
The thirty-five acts of giving the mind:
first, the practice of giving;
second, within the practice of dedication, there are twenty mental states that first distinguish the intention and subsequently manifest the vow.

Regarding the initial reference to "Vajragarbha," "garbha" (藏) signifies "firmness," just as the core of a tree is firm; likewise, the *vajra* is also firm. This refers to the wisdom of the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi-jñāna*), which cannot be destroyed by worldly phenomena, as described in the first of the ten kinds of heroic qualities in the "Inconceivable Chapter" (*Acintyavimokṣa-parivarta*).
On the exterior, it is marked with the svastika symbol, signifying the auspiciousness of myriad virtues;
internally, wisdom accords with suchness, and thus it is named the Vajradhātu.
*Dhātu* means "nature"; because one accords with this nature, it is as firm as a vajra and cannot be destroyed.
Because it accomplishes wisdom, its benefit is like a vajra that destroys afflictions difficult to destroy;
therefore, within the section on the conferral of office in the tenth stage, it is called the mark of the virtue of the "Vajra-Adorned Chest."
Both the "Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharma" and the "Leaving the World" contain this mind; thus, they are called "Greatly Identical.

Furthermore, the ninth dedication and the "Leaving the World" are also named the "Vajra-Domain Faculty" and the "Vajra-Flame Faculty. These are established as "faculties" (indriya) because the pure mind-king serves as the basis and the predominant condition for non-conceptual wisdom.
The "Great Banner of Valor" (*mahā-vīrya-dhvaja*) takes the sense of subduing.
The "Firm Banner" (*dṛḍha-dhvaja*) takes the sense of not being destroyed by others.
"Donning the adamantine armor" (*vajra-kavaca*) signifies the great vow (*mahā-pratijñā*).
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the thirty-six gifts of intestines, kidneys, livers, and lungs: these four items are combined into one for dedication.
Previously there were two types of intestines, large and small; now they are merged into a single intestine.
Regarding the "body that is a treasury of wisdom," it is because the body serves as the support for wisdom.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
[It consists of] thirty-seven joints and various bones.
It was previously stated that there are "marrow and bones"; since marrow has already been explained above,
the addition here of "the various bones of the limbs and joints" would,
if combined, constitute but a single matter— namely, the bones of the limbs and joints.

If one were to expand upon this, the various limbs and joints would each constitute separate matters, such as the "member-by-member dismemberment" and so forth, which were not included in the preceding list.
Regarding the phrase "unbound from the realms" within the context of the practice of dedication, it refers to the realm of nirvāṇa.
Regarding the statement that he possesses the great strength of Nārāyaṇa’s limbs and joints, it is as compared and measured in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Regarding the statement that his body appears universally illuminating, it is because, like a pure and bright mirror, there is nothing that does not appear within it.
The remainder may be understood.
Regarding the statement "attaining wisdom" within the middle [section], it is because wisdom serves as the backbone of all virtues.
Thirty-eight times he gave away his skin.
In the cited examples, no Bodhisattva named Qingjingzang (Viśuddhagarbha) is seen.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 16, it is recounted how a venomous dragon, having received the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*), was skinned of its five-colored hide and gave it away with forbearance, and so forth.
Regarding the statement about the Golden-Sided Deer King, it is explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the fourth fascicle of the *Bodhisattvapūrvapraṇidhāna-saṃcaya-sūtra*.

The Golden-Sided Deer rescued a drowning man; however, that man betrayed his kindness and informed the king to seize the deer. While the general title is the same, this does not refer to the offering of the skin.
Regarding the phrase "the skin of the marks and signs" in the vows, this refers to [the skin] being golden in color and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "purifying the Buddha-fields," it is because the skin constitutes the external appearance.
The thirty-ninth practice is the giving of the fingers and toes of the hands and feet, dedicated toward the ten vows.
The slender and long is its measure; the smooth and round is its shape; the red copper is its color; that which can grasp is its power.
Here, wisdom serves as the finger, and the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) are its excellence.
Regarding the "ten powers" (*daśabala*): each individual finger is capable of supporting all worlds and so forth.
"Equal" means they are not uneven.

Regarding the "wheel-mark" (*cakrāṅka*) and other signs: according to the Sanskrit original, it is said that one should wish that all sentient beings obtain the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the inner surfaces of the tips of their ten fingers; furthermore, on the inner surfaces of the remaining joints, there should be the *bhadraka* and *svastika* marks, adorning the spaces between them.
According to this principle, the term "complete" (*pūrṇa*) should be rendered as "full vessel," and the term "clockwise rotation" (*pradakṣiṇāvarta*) should be rendered as "possessing joy.
If one follows the *Buddhānusmṛtisamādhisāgara-sūtra*, twelve wheel-marks (*cakra-lakṣaṇa*) appear at the tip of each finger joint.

Regarding the eight [marks] therein, according to the Sanskrit original, one should wish to obtain the *nandika-vardhamāna* (the "joy-increasing") mark on the fingers, which indeed spirals to the right.
As for the karmic retribution of the Ten Powers, these are also the ten kinds of great *Nārāyaṇa-dhvajas* (Nārāyaṇa-banners), which are the qualities of heroic vigor.
The marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are fine and so forth, while the excellence (*anuvyañjana*) is sublime.
Some say that the "swastika spiral" refers to the Chinese script.

According to the *Samādhi-sāgara Sūtra*, each fingertip possesses the mark of the ten-thousand-character (*myriad-character*) seal; between the dots of these myriad characters, there is the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel.
Regarding the webbed fingers, the sūtra states: "When the fingers are contracted, they do not appear; when extended, they appear immediately, like a net of pearls, distinct and lovely."
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the purpose of "attaining a pure mind," it indicates that this is achieved by means of the mind.
Among the forty marks involving the flesh and nails, that which is called the "copper-colored mark" is a minor mark (*anuvyañjana*).
Regarding the five incomparables: the physical nail is unstained by dust and grime, while the nail of wisdom is unstained by the marks of objective phenomena.
It is called "well-born" because it is produced from virtuous karma.
Some say:
In the dialects of the Western Regions, "Sujāta" (善生) means "handsome" (端正).
The rest may be understood accordingly.
The reason why the search for the Dharma is specifically associated with the offering of one's nails is, first, because there is an actual precedent within the cited examples.
The subsequent entry into fire to seek the Dharma is also understood by analogy with this.
Second, there is that which is indicated: using the fingernail to tear it out signifies seeking it according to its meaning.
The subsequent entry into the fire to seek it signifies that it is difficult to grasp.

Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Prajñāpāramitā is like a great mass of fire; it cannot be grasped from any of its four sides; there is no grasping, nor is there anything to be grasped."
In the forty-first [chapter], "Seeking the Dharma and Entering the Fire," regarding the practice performed therein,
the term "seven *ren*" refers to one *ren* being seven feet.

Within the section on the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*), the first and ninth [vows] concern the seeking of the Dharma as the aspiration, while the remaining [vows] concern entering the fire as the aspiration.

Forty-second: those who seek the Dharma and protect the Dharma by undergoing manifold sufferings; such as [the Bodhisattva] at Gandhavatī who ground his bones to powder, or on the Snow Mountains who forgot his own person—instances of this kind are not one.
Forty-third: seeking the Dharma by relinquishing all that exists within the seas, which refers to relinquishing the royal throne and its governance.

Regarding the practice of dedication, the term "arrow of doubt" refers to what is taught in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: that if a person is struck by a poisoned arrow, it must be extracted immediately; for if one engages in false conceptualization, one will die before the matter is fully investigated.
Forty-fourth is the king’s practice of severing killing and so forth.
While engaged in such practices, he personally abides in the threefold pure precepts and causes others to abide in the five precepts; this constitutes the gift of Dharma.
Since killing is the first of the five precepts, this [text] speaks of it specifically.
From the perspective of the victim, this constitutes the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*).
[The remaining] forty-five [precepts] rescue those with physical impairments.
In the initial practice, one fulfills the three types of giving; therein are three stages:
first, observing the object and giving rise to compassion;
second, from "At that time, the Bodhisattva... onwards, using the Dharma to offer admonition through parables.

Below the phrase "Having spoken these words," there follows a dual rescue through both material wealth and the Dharma: material wealth rescues from the present suffering caused by harm, while the Dharma rescues from the future suffering that causes harm. This demonstrates the attainment of tranquil extinction, for by cultivating the path of pure karma, one extinguishes the causal conditions of *saṃskāra* (accumulation).
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
In the past, there was a eunuch who saved five hundred oxen; by the power of this root of goodness, despite his mutilated form, he came to possess the male organ in full.
Within the practice of the two types of dedication, one may cultivate various pure conducts (*brahmacarya*) without necessarily restraining the mind.
Later, once the mind is free from desire, there will certainly be no physical transgressions.
Possessing a male form merely distinguishes one from a female body; [it does not constitute a distinct category].
One who possesses the qualities of a great man will surely cause his mind to ruin the Way and its Virtue.
Among the four types of dedication, the first causes one to attain the fruit, while the latter, "constantly diligent," causes one to give rise to practice.
Regarding the "true man" (*puruṣa*) practitioner, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 18, states: "If all men and women possess four dharmas, they are called true men.
First, associating with virtuous friends; second, hearing the true Dharma; third, contemplating its meaning; and fourth, practicing according to the teaching."
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Four Marks" states: "One is called a 'great man' (puruṣa) because he possesses the four marks.
It also says: "Even though one is a woman, if she is able to believe that she possesses the Buddha-nature within herself, she is a great man."
Therefore, that which is not believed by men is precisely the woman.
To manifest the seven paths of the man, the word "path" (mārga) is used for the man; in the Sanskrit original it is called *kṛti*, which here means "activity" (*karma*).

The Jin edition reads "the path of the *puruṣa*," which is close to the meaning of "the Way. Regarding the seven types of *puruṣas*, there are several general explanations. First, according to the mundane perspective, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* sets forth seven meanings of a *puruṣa*:

(1) long-lived and enduring; (2) possessing exquisite and dignified physical form; (3) free from illness and having few afflictions; (4) being neither a servant, nor a woman, nor a *paṇḍaka*; (5) possessing sharp and penetrating wisdom; (6) speaking with majestic authority; and (7) having a great lineage and influence. One who possesses these seven qualities is called one on the path of a *puruṣa*, which refers to the causes for such a state.
The six phrases listed below involve slight variations in their expansion and contraction, which can be understood through careful reflection.
The previous requirement to possess the physical form of a male refers precisely to those who are not female and so forth.

Second, according to the Hīnayāna, there are seven types of individuals, namely the seven noble ones (*ārya-pudgala*): first, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); second, the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*); third, the one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*); fourth, the one attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*); fifth, the bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*); sixth, the one liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*); and seventh, the one doubly liberated (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). These will be explained in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*), and one should not aspire to achieve such Hīnayāna states.
Third, based on the Mahāyāna, the seven stages of the *Yogācārabhūmi* correspond to the seven noble persons (*āryapudgala*), as explained at the beginning of the "Ten Abodes" chapter.
Fourth, based on the *Ratnakaranda-sūtra*, the six stages and the stage of faith correspond to being born into the family of the noble ones.

Furthermore, there are those who say that it consists of the seven kinds of right knowledge: namely, knowledge of the Dharma, knowledge of the meaning, knowledge of the time, knowledge of moderation, knowledge of oneself, knowledge of the assembly, and knowledge of the honorable and the humble.
The Buddha is of the lineage of great beings (*mahāpuruṣa*), meaning that through his Great Compassion he has perfected the ten powers and other qualities to become a Buddha, a great being.
The authentic teaching of this great being consists of the three inner piṭakas and the five outer sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
The remaining text is easy to understand. From this point onward, we enter the twenty-eighth scripture.
