Second, one is forever free from the obstacles of the three poisons: "obscuration" refers to delusion (*moha*), while "turbidity" refers to greed (*lobha*); the term "various" (*zhū*) is used because it also includes other obstacles.

Third, the section beginning with "That mind" concerns the virtue of being free from poison; the first phrase serves as the general statement, while the phrases beginning with "upright and honest" provide the specific details.

Because it is free from hatred, the mind is upright, honest, and supple; because it is free from greed, it is without guile or crookedness; and because it is free from the cataracts of delusion, it is without confusion or folly.
Fourth, cultivating true concentration and wisdom constitutes the path to liberation.
Fifth, exercising compassion that shares the same essence constitutes the mind of equanimity.
Sixth, entering the cause of the outflow-free constitutes pure and white dharmas.
Seventh, by being free from the aforementioned faults, one does not afflict sentient beings; one’s own conduct is without error and is further capable of being dedicated [toward enlightenment].
Eighth, one benefits both oneself and others.
Ninth, one eliminates and eradicates the causes of evil.
Tenth, the practice of the roots of goodness.
Second, exhorting others toward dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), which has two parts:
first, causing compassion and wisdom to proceed together to accomplish dedication; second, from "In order to... onwards, clarifying the intent of dedication.

The "intention" (*āśaya*) encompasses both the subject and the object. With respect to the subject—the Bodhisattva—it is for this purpose that the teaching is given; with respect to the object—that which is to be taught—it is how they ought to act.
There are six phrases in the text; in two of them, "nature" (*prakṛti*) carries the meaning of "essential nature" (*svabhāva*), which thus connects both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*).
The third section, beginning with "Furthermore," concludes the dedication of merit.
While the preceding stages involved successive dedications that were adapted as appropriate— thereby encompassing both cause and effect,
as well as the mundane and supramundane— now that the dedication is finalized, there is only the aspiration to attain the ultimate fruit.
"Peaceful" (*kṣema*) means being free from obstacles and afflictions;
"blissful" (*sukha*) means being solely characterized by quiescent extinction (*śānti*).

In this second dedication to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), first the preceding [dedication] according to characteristics is restated, and subsequently, from the word "non-attachment" (*asaṅga*) onwards, the actual manifestation of the departure from characteristics is revealed.
The ten phrases consist of five pairs: first, the cause and effect of past karma;

second, one's own person and possessions; third, the methods and locations for initiating practice; fourth, the sentient beings to be transformed; and fifth, the dharmas to which merit is dedicated, which also apply universally to all.
"Not clinging to any phenomena" is because one realizes that phenomena are empty.
"Not clinging to the non-existence of all things" is because emptiness itself is also empty.
The third section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," summarizes these three types of dedication.
The proximate refers to what has arisen previously, namely that the aforementioned detachment from characteristics does not obstruct following along with characteristics.

The remote connects back to the preceding text: "universally bestowing upon the world" refers to sentient beings; "vowing to become a Buddha" refers to Bodhi; and the section beginning with "attaining a pure mind" refers to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
"Accomplishing the lineage of the Buddhas of the three periods" summarizes the capacity of the three types of dedication.
The second major section, "The Benefits Accomplished by Dedication," refers to the vast virtues produced by this practice.
There are four sons of the Buddha, which constitute four sections:
first, one son of the Buddha possesses the vast virtues of the causal stage;
second, one son of the Buddha possesses the pure virtues of the resultant stage.
The third assembly [demonstrates] the virtue of transcending the sovereign;
the fourth [demonstrates] the virtue of the equality of the exhaustion of marks.
The first two sections constitute benefit through following marks, while the latter two sections constitute benefit through departing from marks.
Furthermore, the first is the virtue of present accomplishment and the next is the virtue of future accomplishment; these two constitute one pair of cause and effect.

The third is the virtue of conforming to characteristics and the fourth is the virtue of attaining reality; these two constitute the pair of conforming to what is contrary and encompassing all phenomena.
Regarding the first point: previously, at the time of establishing the benefits, it was shown that these benefits are accomplished precisely during the time of correct cultivation.
Below the section beginning with "Transcending," the actual explanation is given, which consists of twelve phrases.
The first two serve as a general summary; the first phrase reveals that [this state] is profound and unsurpassed.
The subsequent phrase reveals its extensiveness, for it cannot be fully extolled.
The final ten phrases are categorized into five pairs:

the first two constitute a pair of "practice" and "vision. Within practice, the former refers to the initial practice, while the latter refers to what is seen upon arriving at the buddha-field. Regarding vision, the former refers to seeing the fruit, and the latter refers to seeing the cause.

Second is the correspondence of preaching the Dharma that is profound and vast, because of skillfulness regarding both phenomena and principle; the meaning of the Dharma is extremely deep, the dhāraṇīs are broadly inclusive, and the eloquence of speech is uninterrupted.
Third, from "for the sake of sentient beings" onwards, is the correspondence of manifesting the body to adorn the buddha-field.
Within the Adorned Realm (*vyūha-kṣetra*), the result comes first and the cause follows.

Regarding the fourth section, from "moment by moment causing" (*kṣaṇe kṣaṇe kārayati*) onwards, there is the accomplishment of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgraha-vibhāga*): the first part is the accomplishment, and the latter part, from "in that [realm]" (*tatra*) onwards, is the act of gathering them.

5. Regarding "Attaining Non-obstruction," the following sections correspond to "hearing from afar" and "swiftly proceeding. First, "hearing from afar" clarifies that hearing must be followed by practice;
subsequently, from "Abiding in Non-attainment" onwards, it concerns "swiftly proceeding," wherein all such proceeding is characterized by non-attainment.

Because it does not rely on meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), it is called "without support" (*anāśrita*); because it does not give rise to preparatory effort (*prayoga*), it is called "without action" (*akṛta*); and because it is not defiled by the objects of its supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is called "without attachment" (*asaṅga*).
By relying on this lack of support, it is able to manifest [all things] instantaneously and all at once.
Regarding those of the same view, although the lands they visit are many, their spiritual influence remains no different.
Second, the purity of the merit of the second fruit is divided into two parts:

first, citing the present situation to illustrate what is to come; that is, if the causal merit already attained is thus inexhaustible, how much more so will the resultant merit of the fruit be beyond measure?

Second, from "all Buddha-fields" onwards, there is a detailed explanation of the actual characteristics, which refers to the state of having attained fruition. Briefly stated, these ten are presented: the first six represent the complete perfection of the characteristics of fruition, while the latter four cite the causes to manifest the fruition; that is to say, this fruition is fulfilled because the causes are perfected.
Those who speak of "purity" do so because there is no defilement that has not been exhausted.
Those who speak of "equality" do so because there is no principle that has not been realized.
Since both defilement and purity are empty, they are called "equal"; since purity accords with principle, it is simply called "pure."

Regarding the virtues and functions of cause and effect above this: if these were not subsumed within the various stages of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), how could those prior to the [first] ground attain such unimpededness?
In the third assembly, there is a contradiction regarding the virtue of mastery;
this section has two parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent. This conclusion consists of two elements: [The text continues with the specific content of the conclusion.]

First, this is a proximate conclusion regarding the excellence of the fruit; since the excellence of the fruit is boundless and cannot be fully exhausted by the word "supreme," it is said that "all merits are pure.

Second, this is a general conclusion regarding both cause and fruit: having completed the explanation of the benefits according to characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one now seeks to clarify that attaining these benefits according to characteristics simultaneously entails the departure from characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa*). Therefore, it concludes generally by stating that one "attains all merits" up to "perfectly adorned," and for this reason, there is no contradiction and so forth.
Second, from the phrase "When dedicating in this way" onwards, the text correctly reveals the benefits of resolving contradictions.
There are fifteen pairs, which are broadly divided into four sections:

first, eleven pairs where phenomena are mutually consistent; second, two pairs where worldly matters are consistent; third, one pair where worldly phenomena are consistent; and finally, one pair where cause and effect are consistent, which serves as the summary.
The preceding section is divided into three parts:

first, six pairs concerning the non-contradiction between phenomena and phenomena; second, the two pairs beginning with "dharma-nature" concerning the non-contradiction between phenomena and principle; and third, the three pairs beginning with "the equality of lands" concerning the non-contradiction between principles and principles.
Now, first: one concerns the primary and its support;
second, karmic results;
third, the royal domain.
Fourth, the mental state;
fifth, karmic retribution—of these two, one is the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) and this is the completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*);
sixth, the absence of contradiction between the primary and auxiliary factors.
The volitional effort (*cetanā*) that precedes an action and initiates the formation of karma is merely called "karma";
however, the actions of body, speech, and mind that arise from that volition are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*), because they are what the volition traverses.
The title of the Jin translation is *Yejì* (Traces of Activity); "traces" (*jì*) are precisely the Way (*dào*).

The reason each of these matters is without contradiction is that they are fused according to their nature, because phenomena arise through mutual dependence (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and because they share the single principle of dependent origination; furthermore, this lack of contradiction is also brought about by the latter two sections.

Regarding the next two pairs concerning the non-contradiction between principle and phenomena: the first pair discusses the non-contradiction between nature and characteristics with respect to the phenomena that are characterized (*lakṣya*), while the latter pair distinguishes the non-contradiction between nature and characteristics with respect to the four characteristics that characterize (*lakṣaṇa*). Only one instance, "birth" (*jāti*), is cited here by way of illustration.
That nature does not contradict characteristics means that principle is able to accomplish phenomena.

That characteristics do not contradict nature means that phenomena are able to manifest principle; because one establishes all dharmas without moving from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); and because one speaks of the true mark (*dharmatā*) without destroying conventional designations.
There are three pairs in which principle and principle do not contradict one another:
first, the supported and the support; second, the person and the dharma; third, the subject and the object.

The limit of detachment from desire that is realized is the principle realized (*prameya*), while sentient beings abiding therein is the wisdom that realizes (*pramāṇa*). Because wisdom is in profound accord with principle, these two are not in contradiction.

However, there is no contradiction among the three preceding sections; the first and last two sections refer exclusively to the mutual comparison of different categories, because within the latter section, there are many forms of equality in taking phenomena (dharma) to realize principle (li).
Regarding the non-contradiction between phenomena and principle in the middle section, there are two meanings:
first, the mutual comparison of the same category, such as the equality of one land (*kṣetra*) with respect to another land.

Second, regarding the mutual observation of different categories: as a land is observed in relation to sentient beings, they are equal; this equality is the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
When this is unfolded, there are four propositions; if discussed in detail, there are five layers of four propositions.

Regarding the first set of four propositions: first, the land; second, sentient beings; third, the principle of the land’s lack of intrinsic nature; and fourth, the principle of sentient beings’ lack of intrinsic nature—these four constitute the foundation.
Regarding the second set of four: first, a single land is not identical to the land because it lacks intrinsic nature, as phenomena do not exist;
second, it is not non-identical, because phenomena are not destroyed.
The three lands are non-substantiality itself as the land, because they do not maintain their own inherent nature.
Fourth, they are not identical to the land, because that nature does not change.
Regarding the third and fourth [points], sentient beings and non-substantiality are likewise the same land; this explains the two preceding sets of four lines.
The first and third of each [category] refer to the mutual comparison of their own kinds within the second section, "the nature and characteristics are not contradictory.
The second and fourth of each, although not characterized by non-obstruction, are likewise not contradictory; the meaning is as explained above.

Regarding the fourth set of four points: first, the lack of intrinsic nature in a buddha-field is identical to the lack of intrinsic nature in sentient beings, because there is no duality between them;
second, they are not identical, because there is nothing that can be made identical;

third, the buddha-field is identical to sentient beings, because the lack of intrinsic nature constitutes sentient beings, and since the buddha-field lacks intrinsic nature, it is therefore identical to sentient beings.
The four lands are not identical to sentient beings, because there is no obstruction to their coexistence.

Herein, the first two phrases constitute the third section on the non-contradiction of principle with principle (*li-li wuwei*), for there is nothing with which they can be identified and nothing with which they can be in conflict;
the third phrase constitutes the first section on the non-contradiction of phenomena with phenomena (*shi-shi wuwei*).
The fourth phrase is neither non-obstructive nor contradictory. As for the fifth set of four phrases:

first, the land is not identical to the naturelessness of sentient beings; second, it is not non-identical; third, sentient beings are not identical to the naturelessness of the land; and fourth, they are not non-identical.

Among these, the first and third phrases refer to the mutual relation between different categories of phenomena and principle within the second section on the non-contradiction of principle and phenomena;
as for the second and fourth phrases, although they do not destroy the nature and characteristics [of phenomena], they likewise do not contradict one another.
However, because the gateways differ, there are many distinctions; in reality, all phrases are without exception mutually interpenetrating.
Second, [the classification] by way of time; third, by way of worldly phenomena; fourth, by way of cause and effect—the texts for these can all be understood accordingly.
The fourth is the virtue of the equality of the exhaustion of marks.
The text is divided into two parts:

first, the benefit of attaining equality and being free from marks; second, from "attaining the service of all Buddhas" onwards, the clarification of the benefit of attaining the indestructibility of all marks.
The third section, which relies on the commentary to explain the title, can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the second major heading, the distinction between the fruits of the stages (*bhūmi*) and their benefits: the attainment of benefits refers to the realization of the fruits within those stages.
Regarding the fulfillment of these stages, there are twenty-one phrases:
the first one introduces what precedes, the last one provides a general conclusion, and the nineteen in between are subsumed into nine fruits:
first, the fruit of severing defilement, which consists in vanquishing demonic adversaries—meaning to cease evil conditions by uprooting the thorns of desire and severing evil causes;
Second is the fruit of realization and entry, which is the attainment of the bliss of liberation and the correct realization and abiding in the cause of non-dual nature;
third is the fruit of benefiting others, which possesses great majestic power and is the cause for protecting sentient beings;
fourth is the fruit of internal and external transcendence, meaning internal virtues and external applications.
5. From "Going everywhere" downward: the fruit of unimpeded activity in tranquility;
6. From "Possessing all" downward: the fruit of the vastness of conduct and vows;
7. From "Discriminating" downward: the fruit of the excellence of wisdom and supernormal powers.
8. "Attaining Unimpededness" and below describe the fruit of mastery in seeing and hearing.
9. "Regarding all objects" and below describe the fruit of the perfection of practice; the former is accomplishment, while the latter is non-attainment.
The second section consists of twenty-one verses in *śloka* meter, divided into three parts:
the first eleven verses praise the dedication of merit; the next nine verses praise the accomplishment of benefits; and the final verse provides a concluding eulogy.
Now, for the first [section], there are two parts:
the first half-verse praises the roots of virtue to be dedicated;
the remainder praises the act of gathering what is to be dedicated. Within this, there are three [subsections]:

The first three and a half verses praise the dedication of one's own cultivated virtues as requisites to be bestowed upon sentient beings; next, the five verses beginning with "The Bodhisattva, for the sake of delivering... praise the further dedication of this giving so that sentient beings may be fully endowed with both material wealth and the Dharma; third, the two verses beginning with "The Bodhisattva’s words... praise the dedication toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Second, from "Knowing all worlds" onwards, the verses establish the benefits, which consist of three parts:

the first two verses concern the vastness of causal virtues; the next five verses concern the purity of resultant virtues; and the final two verses concern the equality of the exhaustion of characteristics.
The omissions, the non-versification, and the contradictions have already been explained in detail above.

However, these three sections in verse differ slightly in their rhetorical force from the preceding prose; they not only provide further benefit but also simultaneously manifest the causes for dedication.
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Scroll Twenty-Nine (of Thirty),
composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple at Mount Qingliang in the Tang Dynasty.
The eighth is the dedication of the aspect of true thusness (*tathatā*).
Within the prose section, there are two parts:
first, a detailed explanation; second, a concluding indication.
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, clarifying the practices of the stages; second, discerning the fruits of the stages.
Within the first part, there are also three sections:
First, the title is indicated.
Because the roots of goodness are combined to form the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the name is established based on its support; thus, its meaning applies to both the subject and the object.
Therefore, the *Benye jing* says: "It constantly illuminates the two truths of existence and non-existence, because all dharmas are a single unified mark."
If the Sanskrit original were complete, it would be titled "The Dedication of the Self-Nature of the Characteristics of True Thusness" (*Tathatā-lakṣaṇa-svabhāva-pariṇāmanā*).

"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the marks of virtue (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*), and "nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the essential substance (*tattva-svabhāva*); because these two are neither identical nor separate, they are mentioned together.
While the text primarily discusses the marks of virtue, the Tang translation provides a single title, taking the Seal of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-mudrā*) as its very nature.

The difference between this and what precedes and follows it is as follows: the seventh stage clarifies that phenomena (dharma) tend toward principle (tattva), and thus it is called "equality"; this [eighth] stage clarifies that phenomena are exhausted and principle manifests, and thus practice is identical to suchness (tathatā). The ninth stage clarifies the arising of function from essence, while the tenth stage clarifies that function is identical to essence and functions while being identical to essence. The rest is as explained in the commentary on the fourth *Parivarta* (Chapter on Dedication).
The second part, the detailed explanation based on the inquiry, has three sections:

first, the dedication according to characteristics; second, the dedication free from characteristics, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of these roots of goodness..."; and third, the benefit accomplished through dedication, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates in this manner, he attains all... and so forth.
The first part, the introduction, is divided into two sections:
first, the dedication of accumulated merit; second, the dedication upon encountering objects, beginning with the passage: "O Son of the Buddha, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sees... and so forth.
The preceding section also has two parts:

first, clarifying the essential nature of the practices to be dedicated; second, from the passage beginning "At that time, the Bodhisattva’s eye of wisdom," on the appropriation and dedication of those practices.
Within the first part, there are also two sub-sections:
First, there is the accumulation of the provisions; subsequently, from "accomplishing the immeasurables" onwards, the accomplishment of qualities is concluded.
Regarding the first [section], there are ten phrases:
the first serves as the general [summary], namely, right mindfulness that is firm and lucid.
The final nine [verses] constitute the distinct section, which has three parts: First, the initial three verses concern the correct mindfulness of Bodhi.

"Being far removed from delusion" refers to the explicit meaning (*nītārtha*); focusing one's intent on practice constitutes correct mindfulness. Correct mindfulness is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and being explicit in meaning is wisdom (*prajñā*); the union of concentration and wisdom is the source of the Path.

Second, because one accords with reality and remains unmoved, it is called the "profound mind" (*gambhīracitta*). Since external conditions cannot obstruct it, it accomplishes indestructible karma; this is the firm abiding in one's own stage (*svabhūmi*).
The third, "seeking Buddhahood without regression," refers to the firm abiding of superior progress.

The subsequent four phrases concern the transformation of birth through right mindfulness; the first phrase serves as the general principle, for one courageously seeks to bring universal salvation for the sake of the Great Dharma.
The last three phrases are distinguished as follows:
first, the simultaneous application of compassion and wisdom constitutes "clarity," because *prajñā* (wisdom) is the foundation of all virtues;
second, advancing in goodness and eliminating outflows constitutes "right mindfulness."
Third, compassion increases wisdom and perfection constitutes firm abiding.
The final three are the right mindfulness of the Triple Gem:
first, mindfulness of the Buddha; second, protection of the Dharma; and third, increase of faith.
The first phrase establishes right mindfulness, while the second phrase secures firmness; these two briefly encompass the entire scope.
This concludes the section on the accomplishment of virtues.
The text consists of four phrases:
The first three fetters were previously discussed; the first is not merely the cessation of the ten [defilements] above, hence it is called "immeasurable.
The second and third encompass and subsume these, such that they do not transcend merit, wisdom, and great compassion.
The final phrase refers to the subsequent dedication of merit.
The second section, "The Compendium for Dedication," has two parts:
first, observing the roots of goodness with the intention of dedication; second, from "With all roots of goodness" onwards, the actual explanation of dedication.
Now, for the first [section], there are three parts:
first, a general heading; second, a detailed exposition from "Those various virtues" onwards; third, a summary from "In this way" onwards.
Within this [third part], there are two sections:
First, regarding the many categories of the "types" (jāti), there are ten phrases; that is to say, there are numerous distinctions following the aforementioned conditions for seeking and so forth.
Since the single roaming is not singular—just as with a single entry—is it for the sake of a door of function?
Is it by means of the gate of emptiness?
Or even up to the immeasurable? Therefore, the maiden Maitrīcaryā said:
"Each of the Buddhas has led me into this Gate of Universal Adornment through their own distinct approaches."
Second, whichever gate one follows, what serves as the object?
Is it the Buddha, or the Dharma, and so forth?
Third, on whichever single object [one focuses], the characteristics (nimitta) differ.
1. The entities that serve as the basis for the four characteristics, namely form, mind, and so forth;
2. the fact that many states exist upon each individual entity;
3. the ten thousand practices, such as generosity and the rest.
Seventh, the names that express;
eighth, analytical discernment;
ninth, the generation of extensive knowledge and vision.
Tenth, whether it be concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), there are superior, middling, and inferior levels of cultivation.
The subsequent section, beginning with "Among these," concludes the original intent of this cultivation.
Since the original intent is thus established, how could one not dedicate [the merit]?
The second [section], the actual explanation of the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), has two parts:
first, the dedication toward enlightenment; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, just as a bodhisattva mahāsattva [acts] for his own body," etc., the dedication for the sake of sentient beings.
The preceding twenty vows are divided into three parts:
the first ten vows concern the accomplishment of the practice of wisdom, which constitutes the cause and fruit of bodhi.

The second four vows, beginning with "Attaining Samādhi," concern the universal benefit of sentient beings; these constitute the cause and fruit of transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-karma*). Specifically: first, the basis for transformation; second, the time and place of transformation; third, knowing the medicine and its treatment; and fourth, recognizing the nature of the illness and what is appropriate for it.

Third, "Attaining Sovereignty and Below" consists of six vows for the universal adornment of Buddha-fields, which constitute the cause and fruit of the Pure Land: first, the adornment of the phenomenal land through the wisdom of supernatural powers; second, the adornment of the dharma-nature land through the wisdom that enters into principle, which is an adornment by way of non-adornment; third, the adornment of the Indra’s Net land through the wisdom of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle; and fourth, the transformation of sentient beings through the application of these three types of adornment.
The first four [stages] represent the perfection of causes, while the latter two represent the fulfillment of the fruits.
Regarding the second dedication to sentient beings, the text has three parts:
first, the restatement of what precedes to introduce what follows; this consists of restating the preceding three sections in reverse order, starting from the end.
Second, from the words "That is to say" (*yad uta*) onwards, the actual dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is clearly revealed in eight phrases:
the first two vow the abandonment of the three obstacles—the term "obstacle" here carries the dual sense of hindrance and affliction (*kleśa*);
the next four bring about the four wisdoms (*jñāna*).
The latter two knots have two fruits, namely *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
Since *bodhi* is not limited to the four wisdoms alone, it is described as "immeasurable.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, is the summary of the purpose for which this was done.
The second section concerns the dedication of the contact with objects; it is largely identical to the vows made in the presence of objects found in the "Purifying Conduct" chapter.
This section contains five parts:
first, a listing of the objects perceived.
2. From "Seeing this matter" onwards, one observes the objects to accomplish virtue, namely, increasing compassion and wisdom;
3. From "With the roots of goodness of the Buddha" onwards, there is a general explanation of dedication, which is also the virtue of dedication;
4. From "At that time, the Bodhisattva" onwards, there is a specific explanation of dedication.
5. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards is the dedication for the accomplishment of benefit.
The first three [sections] are understandable.
Regarding the fourth: the first phrase is a general heading, indicating that the specific details are about to be explained.

In the section on "The Superior Practice" (*adhimātra-pratipatti*), it says: "By means of skillful means, one dedicates all roots of goodness. However, the characteristics of this dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) are not yet known;
therefore, it is said: "At that time, one dedicates in this manner."
Below the phrase "That which is called," there is a specific exposition clarifying such statements.

Regarding the fact that all thirty-one vows state that one "shall attain what is lovely and desirable": because one gives rise to wholesome states that are lovely and desirable by perceiving objects that are lovely and desirable, these vows result in the attainment of lovely and desirable virtues.
In explaining these various vows, there are generally two intentions:

first, to issue flow-on vows (nisyanda-praṇidhāna) that correspond horizontally to the aforementioned objects; second, to correlate them vertically with the stages of the path (bhūmi) to manifest the comprehensive vow.
"Comprehensive" means that upon seeing any single object, one immediately gives rise to many vows, as these encompass both cause and effect.
Regarding "corresponding horizontally": the first ten vows correspond to the aforementioned pure lands. First, if one sees a land, one should vow for sentient beings to see the Dharma-nature land;
second, the requisites of that land; [and so forth].
The three supernormal powers involve the enjoyment and transformation of pure lands;
all other matters are simply events within those lands and can be understood through reflection.

Regarding the ten vows made in relation to this single realm, one may take this as a model for others, as there should be many more; however, to avoid excessive prolixity, the subsequent sections will gradually become more concise.
Next, the three vows beginning with "attaining fearlessness" correspond to the aforementioned groves and gardens.
Because they are free from fear due to the forest of untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), and because they take *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi* as their parks and gardens.
Next, one vow corresponds to the grasses and trees above, because one skillfully contemplates the five vehicles through the wisdom that distinguishes the three types of grass and two types of trees.

Next, three vows correspond to the flowers; for dharmas such as the supernormal powers are like flowers in full bloom, and when they are expounded among the assembly, they all manifest like blossoming flowers.
One type of fruit will be left for clarification later.
From the phrase "arousing great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) downward, one makes a single vow to correspond with a single object.
That is to say, great compassion permeates the mind to correspond with the superior incense, causing the faculties to rejoice, just as with that superior garment.
Born into the family of the Tathāgata, one obtains a share of rare jewels; the practice of discipline serves as sacred wealth, and unimpeded eloquence serves as an ornament.
The delightful world is like a village; the entry through many gates is like a city; and being unimpeded and without basis is like a hamlet.
Ultimately there is no duality, just as a kingdom cannot have two kings.
One attains mastery only upon realizing the limit of detachment from desire; the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) constitutes freedom from clamor and confusion.
The final three phrases correspond to the aforementioned fruits.
Regarding the second point, the correlation of the two uprights with the stages (*bhūmi*), the text is divided into two parts:
the first reveals the perfection of the cause, and the latter three reveal the fulfillment of the fruit.
Within the former, there are three sections:

In the first seven days, those who have not yet entered the Dharma are caused to enter it; this refers to the stage prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*). First, the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is identical to the Buddha’s vision of principle; second, the practice of making offerings through the Dharma—these constitute the twenty stages of faith (*śraddhā*).
Third, being born before all Buddhas; fourth, the liberation of the mind and the vision of the Dharma—these constitute the twenty stages of abiding (*vihāra*).
Fifth, practicing according to what has been taught—this constitutes the ten practices (*caryā*).
Sixth, seeing with virtuous friends; seventh, no contradiction in contact with objects—these are the twenty aspirations for the stage of approach (*prayoga*).
Second, from "attainment" (*prāpti*) downward are seventeen aspirations, which cause those who have already entered the Dharma to attain entry into the stages (*bhūmi*).
In the first three stages and the first bhūmi, there are three aspects: first, realizing the principle of suchness; second, attaining the light of the teachings;
and third, accomplishing the practice of conduct. Next, in the second bhūmi, because one’s conduct is free from the concern of erring or transgressing, there is no fear.
Because loving speech is predominant, one is able to preach the Dharma.
Next are the practices of the second and third stages, wherein one cultivates various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and seeks extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).

Following this are three vows corresponding to the three stages: namely, Blazing Wisdom (*arcismatī*), which contemplates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*); Hard to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), which possesses supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); and Manifesting Presence (*abhimukhī*), which is profound *prajñā*.

Next, the two vows following "Skillful Means" pertain to the practice of the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). This is because skillful means predominate; thus, although one has skillfully cultivated emptiness and signlessness, one does not abandon sentient beings through compassion. Therefore, it is called "equanimous great compassion."

Next are the practices of the second and eighth stages: because the Buddhas exhort one to arouse the great mind for the benefit of others, which constantly manifests before them with perpetual joy; and because one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), becoming truly born into the family of the Buddhas.

Next are the practices of the two [stages] of the ninth ground (*navamī-bhūmi*): because they are able to tame [beings] through skillful knowledge of the dense forest [of afflictions], and because they skillfully teach the Dharma through the forty kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).

Next are the practices of the tenth ground (*daśamī-bhūmi*): because they attain the wisdom that enters into eons (*kalpa*), enter worlds as numerous as motes of dust, and so forth to bring about vast benefit and happiness, and because they are able to receive the great rain of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.

In the third dhyāna there are four vows: for those who have already entered the stages, they shall accomplish the rank of Samantabhadra. First, to attain unimpeded vision within all objects, because one awakens to the fact that the source of phenomena has no root;
second, to attain the non-dual dwelling, because one has severed the two obstacles;
third, to dwell in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because one is equal to the Tathāgata.
Fourth, one attains the patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*) because of the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Regarding the fulfillment of the results in the second and third vows, these are the three virtues (*triguṇa*): first, the adamantine wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*) acts as the agent of severance; next, the separation from the two obstructions (*dvayāvaraṇa*) constitutes that which is severed—these two constitute the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*);
finally, the single path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) realizes and manifests [the result], for wisdom pervades the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Using the two preceding interpretations, the textual intent is well-supported and the sequence remains unerring; this is the skillful discourse of Vajradhvaja, not the mere contrivance of a speaker.
Within the fifth dedication regarding the accomplishment of benefits, first the time of attainment is clarified;
subsequently, from the phrase "attaining wisdom" onwards, the ten phrases are correctly revealed and subsumed into five pairs.
First, causes elicit conditions: through internal clarity of wisdom, one is externally embraced by spiritual friends.

Second, by means of conditions that respond to causes, one externally receives the illumination of wisdom and internally extinguishes the darkness of ignorance; this is the benefit of removing hindrances.
Third, through diligent cultivation, one enters the activity of the three types of wisdom; this clarifies the benefit of study.
Fourth is the benefit of the realization-wisdom of the four higher trainings, which spontaneously and universally suffuses one’s own goodness;

this is the benefit of entering into realization. Fifth is the benefit of perfecting the two adornments by exhausting the source of wholesome merit and entering the ocean of true wisdom; this is the very basis for heading toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because one exhaustively enters it through wisdom.
The second is the dedication that is free from marks (*animitta-pariṇāmanā*), which is directed toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

This differs slightly from the previous dedications: whereas the former mostly involve subsuming marks back into their nature (*dharmatā*) with little arising of marks based on that nature, the present one predominantly manifests the non-obstruction between nature and marks as the "mark of suchness" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*).
The aforementioned headings all refer back to the time of following the characteristics;
now, since it is not necessary to correlate with what preceded in order to establish non-obstruction, the word "time" is omitted.
The text is divided into two parts:
First, the direct clarification of dedication; second, the detailed analysis in contrast with the Tathatā (Suchness) from the passage beginning with "For example.
Now, the first section is divided into two:
first, practice in accordance with Suchness; second, the benefits of practicing in accordance with Suchness, from the passage beginning with "In all Buddha-dharmas."
The preceding section also has two parts:

first, clarifying it in terms of the mind, which involves the simultaneous cultivation of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā-yuganaddha*), remaining neither attached to existence nor non-existence;

second, from "Although he is skillful... onwards, clarifying it specifically in terms of practice, which involves the simultaneous application of the provisional and the ultimate (*upāya-paramārtha-yuganaddha*), without contradicting nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*).
Now, the first [section] further has two parts:
first, quiescence that stills false grasping, which does not contradict essence and function;
second, from "Equal Contemplation" (*samadarśana*) downward, contemplation that penetrates emptiness and existence, wherein faith and wisdom are both perfected.
In the preceding section, the first two lines present the thesis;

the subsequent two lines, beginning with "its mind," provide the explanation. The former line [indicates] the absence of an object of apprehension (*grāhya*), while the latter line [indicates] the departure from a subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*).
"Non-abandonment" below clarifies its non-contradiction: first, non-contradiction with the cause; second, non-contradiction with the dharma; third, non-contradiction with the fruit.
The reason it is not contradictory is that there is no attachment to non-existence.
In the contemplation section, the first part contemplates true emptiness; from "skillfully conforming" (*shan shun*) downward, it contemplates wondrous existence.
Within the section on the simultaneous practice of the provisional and the real, the first phrase establishes the thesis, taking non-obstruction as the thesis;
the second phrase provides a corroborative analogy, for just as illusory appearances exist, their substance is ultimately void.
Below the section "Knowing All," the text synthesizes [the preceding] and sets forth its underlying causes:

first, because no single dharma possesses intrinsic nature; second, from "Contemplating All" onwards, because one contemplates non-attachment, these two accord with the *tathatā* of emptiness (*śūnyatā-tathatā*);
third, from "Knowing Reality as It Is" onwards, because one knows the single reality, this accords with the *tathatā* of non-emptiness (*aśūnyatā-tathatā*).
4. From "knowing all dharmas" onwards, the section concludes with non-contradiction;
5. From "bestowing upon all" onwards, the section concludes with what is accomplished, meaning one is able to enter horizontally into the single path and vertically into the single gate.
Within the second section on "Conforming to Suchness and Benefiting Others," there are ten phrases arranged in five pairs that cause the four minds to become increasingly firm.
First, establishing others in the profound Dharma above while purifying sentient beings below constitutes the "vast mind.
Second, the non-arising of self and other leads to the severance of worldly views, which constitutes the "non-perverted mind."
Third, being unstained by objects, one diligently cultivates supramundane practice;
fourth, not relying on the mundane, one remains steadfast solely in the right path.
The first two correspond to the first mind, for non-abiding nirvana is considered the foremost.
When these five false views are stilled and one realizes that their actual substance is identical, this is the "constant mind," because it never abandons the compassion of the same essence.
This second pair is as explained at length in the *Yuxiang Huixiang* (Dedication of the Aspect of Suchness).
The composition of this section is briefly analyzed by means of five gates:
first, the explanation of the name.
"True" (zhen) signifies reality, indicating that it is not false or illusory.
"Suchness" (tathatā) means "as it is," signifying the absence of change;
this is the perspective of the Dharma-character school (Faxiang zong).
In the Dharma-nature school (Faxing zong), that which does not change is called "true," while its conformity with conditions is termed "suchness."
Because it is unchanging, it is not identical to conditioned phenomena;
because it accords with conditions, it is not different from conditioned phenomena.

Yet, the *Awakening of Faith* states, "That which is without negation is called 'True' (zhen), and that which is without establishment is called 'Suchness' (ru)"; this speaks of the truth directly through exclusive negation (*paryudāsa*).
Second, the clarification of its types:
it may be of a single flavor without distinction,
or it may be divided into two, namely the true suchness of the emptiness of persons and the true suchness of the emptiness of phenomena.
Furthermore, there are two: the established and the non-established;
and two: the empty and the non-empty.
Both are explained as is customary.
Alternatively, it may be divided into three according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), as in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts.
Alternatively, it may be divided into seven: first, the *pravṛtti-tathatā* (tathatā of phenomenal evolution), which is the actual nature of the evolution of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*);
second, the *lakṣaṇa-tathatā* (tathatā of the true characteristic), which refers to the non-dual self-nature of all dharmas when contemplated.
Third is the suchness of consciousness-only, which is the very nature of consciousness-only;

fourth is establishment, fifth is erroneous practice, sixth is purification, and seventh is correct practice. The first four correspond respectively to the essential natures of the Four Noble Truths, as explained in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
Alternatively, they may be divided into ten, as will be clarified in the *Ten Stages Sūtra* (*Daśabhūmika-sūtra*).

Or there may be a hundred gates, each set of ten being inexhaustible, as distinguished in the present sūtra; thus, all that has been listed above is but a single meaning within this system. Even if one were to say it applies to all phenomena, it would still be but a single meaning.
Third, the analysis of its virtuous functions:
first, it functions as the support for all phenomena, because it is that which can sustain them;

second, it functions as the object of contemplation, meaning it serves as the object of realization for the contemplation of the noble ones, and is thus one of the virtues among the "one hundred gates."
The *Awakening of Faith* speaks of three great aspects:
first, the greatness of essence (*tair-mahātmya*), meaning that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is equal and neither increases nor decreases;
second, the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahātmya*), meaning that it is fully endowed with immeasurable inherent merits.
Third is the greatness of function (*vṛtti-mahattva*), because it is able to produce all mundane and supramundane wholesome causes and effects.
However, those three greatnesses are explained in reliance upon the mind; true suchness (*tathatā*) is one of them, for by unifying the one with the two, both are subsumed within suchness.

However, that which contradicts reality is called "evil," while that which accords with suchness is extinguished; that which conforms to reality is "good," and that which accords with suchness is "great. Based on the meaning of goodness and conformity, suchness is therefore said to be the cause of goodness.
However, although opposition and compliance differ, there is nothing that can be opposed apart from *tathatā* (suchness); therefore, even evil takes *tathatā* as its essence.

If one understands this sutra, whether it be essence or characteristic, function or a combination thereof within the hundred gates, in reality each and every one of them universally penetrates essence and so forth. Thus, these hundred gates harmonize principle and phenomena, making them infinitely layered and interpenetrating like the net of Indra.
Fourth, regarding the differences in the teachings, one may reflect upon and apply them accordingly.
Fifth, as for the commentary on the text:
however, there have been many ancient interpretations of these "One Hundred Gates."

The Dharma Master Ying divided [the stages] into ten parts and assigned them respectively to the ten positions: first, the stage of the Worthy Head; second, the stage of Abiding; third, the stage of Practice; fourth, the stage of Orientation; fifth, the stage of the Pure Mind-ground; sixth, the stage of Traces of Practice; seventh, the stage of Certainty; eighth, the stage of Ultimate Realization; ninth, the stage of Equal Enlightenment; and tenth, the stage of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, various virtuous masters each divided [the stages] into ten sections, but Xianshou rejected them all.
Master Yuanceng divided them into three:
the first ten correspond to the stages prior to the bhūmis; the next eighty-eight phrases correspond to the bhūmis; and the final two phrases correspond to the Buddha-bhūmi.
In principle, all these [explanations] are difficult to reconcile.
Why does the Buddha-ground lack the qualities of the former "suchness" (tathatā)?
If suchness—as defined in the second gate—has reality as its nature, why can it not be present throughout all stages?

If one were to establish the name "Tathatā" (Suchness) by taking its qualities according to their respective stages—such as the ten *tathatās* of the ten stages—the principle would indeed be applicable; yet, it still does not reveal its essential characteristic.
In reality, while the qualities of the hundred gates must all be permeated by a single suchness, how could the qualities that constitute this capacity for suchness lack distinct characteristics?

The distinct characteristics are difficult to perceive; for now, let us proceed without differentiating them, as there is no fault in doing so. Thus, the final sentence states: "Ultimately pure, its meaning is identical to the fruit.
For now, we shall categorize them by tens to correlate them with the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*).
The first [characteristic], "pervading all" and "having signlessness as its characteristic," refers to the meaning of the pervasive *tathatā* (suchness).
The second, "incomparable" and "beyond analogy," refers to the meaning of the supreme (*paramārtha*).

Among the three [kinds of unimpeded knowledge], the unimpeded knowledge regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) serves as the eye for all dharmas; this is the meaning of "supreme flow" (*prabhava*).
Among the four [kinds of mastery], being without attachment and without dwelling, etc., is the meaning of "non-appropriation" (*aparigraha*).
Among the five [aspects], ultimate inexhaustibility and the absence of change constitute the meaning of "no distinction in kind.
Among the six [aspects], the absence of discrimination and the non-arising of essential nature constitute the meaning of "neither defilement nor purity."
In the seventh [point], being omnipresent and abiding in both existence and non-existence means that phenomena have no distinct meanings.
In the eighth, the purity of essential nature and the equality of essential nature mean that there is neither increase nor decrease.
Among the nine [mastery powers], the mastery over all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) is the Buddha’s domain; it is the meaning of mastery over knowledge (*jñāna-vaśitā*).
Among the ten [stages], abiding in all stages and accomplishing all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth, is the meaning of mastery over action (*karma-vaśitā*).
The remaining meanings therein may be inferred by analogy.

As each stage is specifically revealed, it is taught that "one suchness possesses all ten"; ten times ten makes a hundred, intended to manifest that the virtues of suchness are immeasurable and boundless. Before the stages, one practices them universally; at the stage of Equal Enlightenment, one attains them pervasively; and in the Tathāgata stage, they are fully realized.

However, while distinctions arise from differences in meaning, their essence is fundamentally and eternally integrated. It is simply that by acceding to the single suchness (*tathatā*), one naturally contains all virtues; this does not result from deliberate mental effort.

By conforming to the suchness of differentiation, one is able to equally dedicate [merit]; thus, being harmoniously inclusive and unimpeded, one acts in accordance with suchness, and the very essence of this practice is itself suchness.

However, although people believe in the nature of suchness (*tathatā*), they still remain deluded regarding dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); therefore, the quality of suchness is used as a metaphor for the quality of dedication.

If one were to adopt a more literal interpretation of the meaning, it should be stated that the essence and characteristics of true suchness pervade all places, and thus roots of goodness are dedicated because they are identical to suchness.
It also pervades all things without limit or boundary, and by pervading all directions, it attains identity with Suchness (*tathatā*).

Within each of the hundred gates there are two phrases: the former is the virtue of Suchness that is the object of identification, while the latter, beginning with "roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla*), is the virtue of the capacity to identify and dedicate.
Among the first ten [verses], the first gate reveals that [the nature] is present within conditions; therefore, it is not non-pervasive.
The second clarifies its immutability, hence it is called "real.
The third clarifies that following conditions is itself immutability, hence it is said to "constantly maintain its original nature."
Fourth, it demonstrates its nature;
fifth, it demonstrates its characteristics.
These five points are exclusively explained according to the *Tathatā* (Suchness).
The next two pairs are explained in terms of wisdom, and therefore constitute the objects of wisdom.

The eighth [pair] clarifies that True Suchness (tathatā) is not an object [in the conventional sense], yet it is taken as an object; this is because one must forget all objects to accord with the object of Suchness, and because the fundamental nature of Suchness is non-conceptually-constructed (apraṇihita).
The ninth is precisely the conceptually-constructed Suchness.
The tenth [point] refers to the meaning of "as usual.
The remainder may be inferred accordingly; they shall be explained as the difficulties arise.

Regarding the twelfth point, "pervading all": this means that whether it be matter or mind, whether large or small, and even down to the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*) and the moment (*kṣaṇa*), all are perfectly complete, for there is no partial fulfillment.

Just as it is indivisible, to divide it would entail many fallacies; this is because of this very principle, and because, as explained below, the forty [aspects] are not separate from all phenomena, because all phenomena accord with suchness and pervade within a single atom, because this gate is attained within the fruits discussed below, and because a single hair-pore can contain all lands, and so forth.
Fourteenth, regarding the incomparable counterpart: because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) does not coexist with the ultimate truth.
Fifteenth, both are indestructible persons, yet their delusions differ.
Seventeenth, it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, for wisdom is the functioning of suchness itself.
22. Since its essence is illumination, why would it lack the eye that gazes?
Furthermore, because seeing suchness constitutes the Dharma-eye, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* states:
"All Buddhas of the three periods of time take the emptiness of intrinsic nature as their Buddha-eye."
Regarding the statement in [Section] Thirty that there is "no root," it means that because there is nothing prior upon which to rely, there is no fundamental basis for abiding.
Regarding the statement in [Section] Thirty-Seven that there is "abiding," it means that by virtue of having no place of abiding, one abides in reality.
Forty-first, "ultimately inexhaustible" means that although it exists within all phenomena (*dharma*), its essence remains constant even when those phenomena are exhausted.
Furthermore, while it is precisely within phenomena, it cannot be grasped as something exhaustible, for it is like the space within a mustard seed.
Fifty-one, its nature is eternally awakened, because it can internally permeate [the mind] to give rise to weariness with and seeking for [samsara].
Fifty-two, it is indestructible, because while abiding in birth and death, it is stained yet remains unstained.
Fifty-three: because it signifies the great light of wisdom universally illuminating the dharma-realm.
Fifty-four: ineffable suchness.
Sixty-one: "being omnipresent" means that while previously it was described as pervading all things without limit, now it is shown to be fully contained within each and every phenomenon.

Regarding the sixty-two [views] existing from day and night up until the end of the future: because each thought-moment and each long eon are respectively gathered within suchness and respectively based upon suchness, thought-moments and eons are able to mutually contain and mutually enter one another.
Regarding the seventy abodes of existence and non-existence, there is no delusion or conceptualization in principle, because existence and non-existence are not permanent realities.
The seventy-second is the awakening of nature as clarity; it is purity through the departure from discursive thought.
The eighty-ninth [point], "not to be cultivated," is because there is nothing to be attained;
it is "not not to be cultivated" because it is the objective realm of the noble ones (*ārya*).
The ninety-fifth, "abandoning all outflows" (*sarvāsrava-prahāṇa*), according to the Sanskrit manuscript reads *anāsrava*, which here means "without outflows" (*anāsrava*).
Now, regarding what is called "abandonment" (śeṣa): because its nature is fundamentally one of abandonment, it is like the essence of the mind being free from thought. As verse 96 states:

"There is not even the slightest dharma that can cause disruption or confusion such that even a small portion would not be awakening. If this were so, then just as with insentient things (*aprakṛta*), there might be some small portion that is not awakening; yet how much more so when the Sūtra says, "Buddha-nature excludes tiles and stones," and the Śāstra says, "That which is counted among insentient things is called *dharmatā*, while that which is counted among sentient beings is called Buddha-nature"? It is clear, therefore, that insentient things do not possess the nature of awakening. Thus, one should explain it as follows:
when the nature conforms to conditions, then the distinction between sentient and insentient arises, and their natures likewise differ, as is the case with *nirvāṇa* and other such categories.

When conditions are extinguished and one follows nature, then neither awakening nor non-awakening exists; fundamentally, the hundred negations are severed and words vanish beyond the four propositions.
If the two natures are mutually fused, then there is nothing that is not awakening.

The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because the nature of form is identical to the nature of wisdom, it is called the Wisdom Body; because the nature of wisdom is identical to the nature of form, it is called the Dharma Body that pervades all places."
The *Śāstra* states: "Both 'bodhi' and 'the abandonment of bodhi' are called *bodhi*.
Both 'knowledge' (*jñāna*) and 'the locus of knowledge' (*jñeyāyatana*) are called *prajñā*.
This may also serve as proof for this point.

Since the two natures are mutually identical, and conditions are further identical to that nature, there is not even the slightest portion that is not awakening; how much more so when the mind serves as the universal characteristic, encompassing and integrating them in ever-deepening layers.
The ninety-seventh [verse] states that "the past is not a beginning," and so forth. The initial limit of the past is called the "beginning" (*ādi*);
the future is the "end," and is thus termed the "unmanifested" (*anāgata*);
and the present appears to exist, yet because it lacks even a momentary duration between the past and the future, it is called the "different" (*anyathātva*).

Now, it is clarified that although True Suchness (tathatā) pervades the three periods of time, its essence transcends the characteristics of beginning, middle, and end within those three periods; therefore, it is said to be "not" [existent] in each case.

Dedication (pariṇāmanā) is likewise: although one generates new vows for sentient beings moment by moment, these are identical to True Suchness in pervading the three periods of time, yet they cause one to forever leave behind the characteristics of birth and death within the three periods; only then is it called pure.
However, the Jin edition states: "The past is not the same; the future is not because of [existence]; the present is not different.

If one reconciles this with the current text, "not the same" does not refer to the beginning of the past; rather, although it exists in the future, it is not something that exists by virtue of being the original nature (*prakṛti*).

Furthermore, the Jin translation erroneously conflates the "three periods of non-discrimination" from the subsequent section into this present section; consequently, one hundred items are missing, leading to various confused interpretations, which I shall not detail here for fear of prolixity.

Regarding the statement that there is no discrimination regarding the three periods of time: previously, this was explained through the method of negation (*paryudāsa*) as being distinct from the three periods; now, it is explained through the method of affirmation (*vidhi*) as being eternally without discrimination. Since the underlying intent is similar, the Jin translation combines these two points.
Furthermore, the preceding section showed that [the nature] is not the same as the three periods of time, thereby generally demonstrating its non-existence;
now, by means of non-discrimination, it is also clarified that it does not exist.
Thus, while essence and attributes mutually integrate such that it can be both new and old, when both the new and the old are simultaneously transcended, [the ultimate state is realized].
The third dedication, which establishes the benefits and provides the concluding title, is clearly intelligible.
In the second major section, from "When the bodhisattva dwells in this" onwards, the fruits of the stage are elucidated.
The first part restates the cause for attainment, while the section following "realization" (*prāpti*) correctly reveals that which is attained.
The text contains ten phrases: the first is general, and the remainder are specific.
All are described as "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) because they are equally vast, expansive, and inexhaustible like *tathatā*.
The statement that "all have attained Buddhahood" is because they share in what the Buddha has realized and because they perform the deeds of a Buddha.
The second major section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," serves as a general conclusion and demonstration.
The second section is the Geya (Verses).
The twenty-nine verses are divided into four parts:
first, six verses on the characteristics [of dedication], among which the first two concern the essence of the practice to be dedicated, and the latter four concern the practice of dedication itself;

Second, there are sixteen verses on the dedication that transcends characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vivikta-pariṇāmanā*). Within these, the first nine verses extensively analyze [the dedication] in relation to the Tathāgatas, while the latter seven verses directly clarify that the Bodhisattvas abide in the inconceivable and so forth; one should reflect well upon this.
Third, the six verses beginning with "Those sons of the Buddha" eulogize the benefits accomplished by the dedication.
Fourth, one verse concludes the intent of the dedication; all of this may be understood as leading from here into the thirty-first scripture.
The ninth is the dedication of liberation that is unattached and unbound.
Within the prose commentary, it likewise first clarifies the practice of the stage and subsequently reveals the fruit of the stage.
Regarding the former, there are also three parts; here, first, the title is cited and the inquiry is raised.

This means that when wisdom and principle are without dependence, one is not bound by the delusions of grasping at the characteristics of subject and object; for this reason, it is called liberation. This is an explanation based on the essential nature of practice.

Therefore, the *Benye jing* (Sutra on the Original Activities) says: "Because all dharmas are non-dual, prajñā is unborn, the two truths are equal, and the three periods of time are a single unified mark."

Furthermore, liberation also possesses sovereign activity, such as that which is inconceivable; this refers to its functional application, because it encompasses all roots of goodness and dedicates them toward the boundless, sovereign power of the three karmas of Samantabhadra.
In what is there no bondage or attachment?

It refers to the ten [categories] beginning with the mind. This is because there exist within oneself the fruits of mental, physical, and vocal karma; the performance of Buddha-activities; world-systems and Buddha-fields; and sentient beings, dharmas, wisdom, and so forth.
By what is one bound and attached?
Briefly, it is as explained above.
Specifically, there are ten matters consisting of five pairs:

First, by departing from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one is not bound to birth and death; by transcending the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), one does not cling to the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Second, by abandoning the grasping of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*), one is not bound to external objects; by abandoning the attachments of the seventh [consciousness], one does not cling to the internal.
Third, being free from the bondage of manifest activity and the attachment to seeds;
fourth, not grasping at the bondage of existence and not clinging to the attachment to emptiness;
fifth, being free from the bondage of the afflictive obscurations and the attachment to the cognitive obscurations—these all refer to the coarse bondage and the subtle attachment.
If considered with respect to a single matter, one is bound due to attachment; the meaning is as explained in the general section.
Alternatively, "binding" and "attachment" share the same sense; this is designated according to its unimpeded great function, encompassing both the subject and object of dedication.
In terms of liberation from the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it is without bondage and without attachment; this is precisely liberation.
In terms of its function, it is liberation that is itself free from bondage and attachment.

If one considers it in relation to the mind and so forth, it is likewise a mind without bondage or attachment; thus, both the aforementioned essence and function are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The second part, the detailed explanation, is divided into three sections:

first, clarifying the roots of goodness to be dedicated; second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the practice of dedication; and third, from "When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dedicates in this way, as in the three periods of time" onwards, clarifying the benefits accomplished through dedication.
Regarding this, first, there is a general indication of respect, because even a single hair’s breadth of goodness is a cause for Buddhahood and none of it fails to flow from the Buddha;
next, the section beginning with "That is to say" provides a specific explanation;
finally, the section beginning with "In such a way as this" offers a summary—all of which may be understood accordingly.

Within the second dedication practice, there are two parts: first, proceeding forward to cultivate the practice intended for dedication; second, from "By means of all... onwards, the explicit clarification of the vows of practice.
In the first part, there are also two sections: first, a general reference to what preceded; second, from "Ultimately... onwards, the specific manifestation of the characteristics of cultivation.

The text consists of ten phrases; the first five cultivate the preceding [section], specifically explaining the words "the World-Honored One" and so forth: (1) because of joyful aspiration, one respects; (2) because of faith and understanding, one accepts; (3) one conforms to it oneself; (4) one causes others to conform; (5) the fifth generally reveals non-attachment to encompass the preceding four.

The five subsequent advancements are: first, the accumulation of superior progress; second, the aspiration for the boundless virtuous functions of Samantabhadra; third, ascending entry into the realm of the Buddhas; fourth, the increasing power of the roots of goodness; and fifth, the further clarification of knowledge and vision.
The second section, which correctly elucidates the meaning within the practice of aspiration, consists of ten gates. The text is divided into two parts:

first, a detailed exposition of their characteristics; second, a summary of the various gates beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates those roots of goodness in this way, namely, with a mind that is unbound."
The preceding section is divided into two parts:

first, the dedication of sentient beings and bodhi; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates with a mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated, without discrimination," onwards, is the dedication to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

The preceding section clarifies the vastness, while the subsequent section reveals the profound depth. There are sixty gates within the vast dedication, twenty gates within the profound, and another twenty gates for the previously mentioned respect and further progress; totaling one hundred gates, these manifest the infinite, deep, and expansive non-obstruction of perfect integration as the Great Dedication.
Regarding the extensive exposition of the sixty gates that broadly manifest the sovereign power and function of Samantabhadra’s virtues, there are two major divisions:
the first four gates provide a general manifestation, while the remainder clarify them individually.
Regarding the first point: the first three [perfections] establish the three types of action (*trikarma*), because none of the subsequent categories transcend these three;
the last one, diligence (*vīrya*), serves as the universal catalyst for all practices.

Within this, the mind that is unattached, unbound, and liberated is the mind capable of dedication; the accomplishment of the physical karma of Samantabhadra is precisely the object toward which it is dedicated.
All other cases follow this pattern: the previously mentioned roots of goodness are what is dedicated, and therefore the phrase "all roots of goodness" flows downward into the eighty gates within.

Regarding this dedication that does not aspire to become a Buddha but aspires to become Samantabhadra: because Samantabhadra encompasses both the stages prior to and subsequent to [attaining] the position, one does not abandon causal practices even after attaining the Way, and exhausts the realms of sentient beings to bring them benefit and happiness; therefore, the aspiration to become Samantabhadra includes both types of dedication.

In the subsequent detailed exposition, each individual section encompasses the sovereign power and function of the *dharmadhātu*. Whether it be principle or practice, wisdom or object, one's own cultivation or the transformation of others, essence or function, cause or fruit, person or dharma—each universally subsumes all phenomena. Therefore, they cannot be categorized separately from one another; they are briefly divided into two parts:
the first twenty-three sections reveal the ultimate state of Samantabhadra’s own cultivation (*svabhāva*), which is Samantabhadra within the stages (*bhūmi*);
the latter thirty-four sections reveal the ultimate state of Samantabhadra’s superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*), which is Samantabhadra beyond the stages (*bhūmi*).
The non-obstruction of these two aspects is the virtue of Samantabhadra.

The former refers to the perfection of the cause and the fulfillment of the fruit; the latter refers to attaining the Way while not abandoning causal practices. Thus, both sections encompass both cause and fruit.
Now, for the first part, there are three sections:

first, four [verses] that establish the merit of Samantabhadra’s dhāraṇī; second, twelve vows that establish the sovereign power and function of Samantabhadra; third, seven vows that aspire to accomplish the practices of Samantabhadra.

However, while the virtues of the various gates are mostly categorized according to the three types of action (trikarma), this initial gate of dhāraṇī likewise possesses all three: first, the dhāraṇī of vocal action; second, the dhāraṇī of bodily action, which consists in seeing the Buddha; and third, the dhāraṇī of mental action, which consists in understanding and realization.

Regarding the latter [set of] three, when discussing the activity of the three karmas, the names are designated according to time and their functions are distinguished according to place; thus the texts mutually clarify one another.
Within the second section on power and function, there are again two parts:
first, the mastery of encompassing the one and the many through nine vows, for which the textual descriptions of the times and places of transformation by the three karmas can be understood.
The latter three [aspects]—vastness and mastery—may be understood accordingly.
Within the third section, "Accomplishing the Conduct of Samantabhadra," there are two parts:
first, the accomplishment of supernormal powers through four vows; [the second follows].
The second [section] contains three vows, which aspire to the accomplishment of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). The first [vow] collectively possesses all four analytical knowledges;
the subsequent two specifically manifest the dharma and its meaning—the former being the dharma and the latter the meaning—which thus reveals the ultimate fulfillment of the fruit.
The second section, beginning with "From this it arises," clarifies the ultimate stage of progressive advancement (*viśeṣa-gamana*).
As for the term "cause" (*hetu*), it refers to a cause within the state of fruition.
This is divided into three parts:

First, there are nine gates that encompass the virtue of vast and sovereign mastery of phenomena; next, there are fifteen gates that reveal the virtue of mutual identity and interpenetration in successive layers; and finally, there are ten gates that clarify the virtue of profound containment and support in subtle detail.
The first section is divided into six parts:
the first three are vows that accomplish wisdom;

the first of these is the wisdom of ultimate reality (*bhūta-jñāna*), and the latter two are the wisdoms of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*). Of these two, the first is the skillful means of illuminating practice, and the last is the skillful means of illuminating those very skillful means.
The second [type of person] possesses two vows that make the three karmas of body, speech, and mind fruitful and non-empty;
the third possesses one vow for the vastness of the three karmas.
Those who are "vast in terms of sentient beings" possess the great resolve.
The fourth [category] consists of one vow to bring the three karmas into purity.
The fifth consists of one vow regarding the faculties and the three karmas.

There are fourteen distinct faculties, all of which are designated by the name "faculty" (indriya) because they possess the sense of being preeminent, dominant, and luminously manifest through their superior functions.

First, regarding the three faculties beginning with *prajñā* (clarity), they are categorized according to the six [faculties] such as the eye, together with the five faculties of feeling. "Clarity" (*prajñā*) refers to the swift and keen capacity for comprehension.
"Tranquility" (*praśrabdhi*) refers to the absence of internal rigidity or harshness.
"Masterful" (vibhu) means that one is not led away by external objects.

Regarding the other [faculties], they refer to the five faculties beginning with faith; the first is the faculty of faith, because the mind of faith is inexhaustible, and it also includes the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
Next is one advancement.
Next is one moment of mindfulness, because mindfulness is solely the equality of recollecting the Buddha.
Next is one concentration and diligence, because non-retrogression is the meaning of concentration.
The remaining seven are all wisdom (*prajñā*).

As for the faculty of the Vajra Realm, its meaning encompasses both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom: this is because the Vajra Samādhi is concentration, and Vajra Right Knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is wisdom.
The realm (*dhātu*) is itself the nature (*prakṛti*); because wisdom that realizes the nature of the mind is called the "supreme concentration" (*uttama-samādhi*).
It is also the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), for it is attained as indestructible within the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

Regarding "Vajra-flame" (*vajrajvālā*): because the flame penetrates both phenomena and principle, as well as the subject and object, it is already the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*), which has become wisdom (*jñāna*).
Therefore, the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*) states: "Like the vajra-faculty, because it realizes and knows the nature of all dharmas."
