Thus, it is known that among the eight [sections], the first seven are universally applicable, while only the last one is restricted.

Furthermore, although it is stated below that from this point onward the exposition of the first bhūmi begins, since there is an exposition of the first bhūmi, there must likewise be expositions for the second through the tenth bhūmis.
Alternatively, it is divided into eight parts, because the exposition on the benefits of the stages is distinct from the formal teaching.
Alternatively, it is divided into nine parts, because the "reflected image" is distinguished from the preceding [section], and the "dharma" is distinguished from the "analogy."
Alternatively, it may be divided into ten parts, which correspond to the ten stages (daśabhūmi).
Or, one may add the subsequent verses to the preceding nine.
Regarding this sequence of ten, there are three meanings:

First, the general exposition regarding the mode of transformation; second, the general demonstration regarding the intention behind the transformation; third, the dual analysis of scriptural testimony and logical proof according to the essential tenets of the school.
Regarding the first of these points, it is fully contained within the commentary on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* itself, as explained in accordance with the text.
Now, this shall be briefly explained:
first, because it sets forth the causes and conditions for the teaching, there is the Introductory Section (Nidāna);
second, because it reveals the capacity of the speaker, there is the Samādhi Section.
Third, because it demonstrates that the teaching is not in vain, there is the "Section on Additional Benefits" (Prabhāva-bhāga);
fourth, because meditative concentration is beyond verbal expression, there is the "Section on Arising" (Utpatti-bhāga);
fifth, because what was previously briefly presented is now elaborated, there is the "Section on the Main Body" (Mūla-bhāga).
Sixth, because upon hearing the name one feels thirst and yearning, there is the "Section on Requesting";
seventh, because it is for the purpose of extensive exposition, there is the "Section on Explaining.
These seven [sections] follow the sequence of the treatise.
The eighth [section], consisting of detailed explanations, is difficult to understand; it is therefore clarified through general illustrations in the "Section on Reflected Images.
The ninth, following the completion of the exposition, reveals its excellence and exhorts practice in the "Section on Benefits."
The ten scattered explanations are difficult to comprehend; there is a section consisting of verses.
Second, regarding the manifestation of proof: the first part manifests the means for proof, while the remaining nine parts correctly manifest the characteristics of proof.
Among these, the first three demonstrate the realization through their characteristics: first, demonstration by way of entry;
second, demonstration by way of empowerment, wherein realization is shown to be non-false because one has obtained empowerment;
and third, demonstration by way of emergence, for that which does not arise cannot be expressed in words, and thus it cannot manifest quiescence.

Next, the four [sections] explain the evidence of manifestation: the "Fundamental Section" provides a brief explanation of the evidence of manifestation; the "Request Section" clears away characteristics to reveal quiescence; and the "Explanatory Section" and the "Section on Images" employ the characteristics of cultivation as metaphors to represent its virtues, though the dharma and the analogy differ.
Next, one part clarifies the realization in terms of its benefit, while the final part reiterates the qualities of that realization.
Regarding the three pairs of arguments: the first serves as the reason, and the subsequent nine correctly manifest the characteristics of the scriptural authority and the realization.
Among these, the first three manifest realization through meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
the latter eight manifest the teaching, because from the stage of application (*prayoga*) onwards there is already discourse.
Within these eight, the sequence is the same as that explained in the initial section.

Alternatively, they are divided into forty-eight parts: namely, the first through tenth stages each comprise eight parts; the second stage comprises two parts; the third, fourth, and ninth stages each comprise four parts; the fifth and sixth stages each comprise three; the seventh stage comprises five parts; and the eighth stage comprises seven parts; thus, there are forty-eight.
Question:

Among the eight [aspects] of the first stage, the first seven pertain to the ten stages; among the eight [aspects] of the eighth stage, the latter two encompass the ten stages. Why, then, does the treatise judge them as belonging specifically to the first and the tenth stages? Answer: [Because they represent the initial entry and the final consummation.]
The topical outline (*ko-wen*) of the *Dilun* contains four types of structural principles:

first, the principle of subsuming the subsequent within the preceding; because the "Preface" and other sections are proximate to the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), they are judged to belong to the First Ground.

Second, the principle of subsuming the preceding within the subsequent; because the latter two [grounds] are proximate to the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), they are subsumed under the "Cloud of Dharma" (*dharmameghā bhūmiḥ*), which does not mean that they do not pertain to the others.
Third is the method of analyzing the textual divisions, as seen in the intermediate sections;
fourth is the method of demonstrating the comprehensive inclusion of the stages (*bhūmi*), meaning it demonstrates that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the *dhāraṇī* dharma.

Although the textual passages in the various stages (bhūmis) may appear either implicit or explicit, their meaning necessarily encompasses them all in their entirety; thus, within each individual stage, there are forty-eight [factors].

Just as the first six divisions are assigned to the first stage while it is admitted that they also pertain to the remaining nine, this analogy demonstrates that the other divisions likewise have no point of non-penetration.
Question:
If the precepts are not first explained, those two purities do not exist.
If the factors of dhyāna are not explained, the arising of revulsion and so forth do not exist.
How is it that all factors (aṅga) are common to every stage (bhūmi)?
Answer:
The meaning of the explicit statement is universal, whereas the citation of the text is restricted.
Does not the Sūtra state that "within each stage, all the virtues of every stage are fully present"?
How, then, could one allow that the first stage does not possess morality and the other perfections?
This has been briefly examined.
Next, the text is formally explained.
Based on the *Daśabhūmika*, it is divided into ten sections.
The first is the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), which consists of eight parts; seven are as previously explained, and the eighth is called the "Section on the Measurement of Superiority."
The demarcation of the text’s divisions is clearly explained below.
First is the introductory section (*nidāna*).

While the *Śāstra* treats the sūtra as a separate work and includes all six accomplishments (*siddhi*), here, as it is subsumed within the great collection (*mahāsaṃnipāta*), the two of "faith" and "hearing" are omitted; thus, there are only the remaining four: first, the time; second, the principal [teacher]; third, the location; and fourth, the assembly.
Although there are four factors, the treatise mentions only the comparison of time, place, and so forth to demonstrate its superiority.
Because this Dharma is supreme, it was taught at the initial time and in a preeminent location.
As for not mentioning the "Victorious One who Presides over the Assembly," the intention is to clarify that in other sūtras, there may well be such a presiding figure.

If we follow the principle of mutual correspondence, since the "presider" consists of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*), the "assembly" cannot be definitively stated; yet it may also be termed "victorious. Therefore, the treatise employs the term "equal" (*sama*).
Regarding "Now, at that time" (*atha khalu tasmin samaye*): this refers to the excellence of the time, for it is called excellent because it is the initial period.
Thus, the treatise states: "Not long after the Blessed One had attained enlightenment, during the second seven-day period."
Since the treatise discusses the separate circulation of the sutra, it specifies "two sevens" (fourteen assemblies).

In the present sutra, as it is subsumed within the Great Collection (Mahāsaṃnipāta), it simply says "at that time," which refers to the very beginning of the first assembly when he had just attained perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, according to the treatise, if the first [set] were superior in its manifestation, why would the first seven [days], being the very beginning, not have been mentioned?
The treatise states: "Because one contemplates the causal conditions for conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*)."

The "cause" refers to the wisdom capable of teaching, and the "condition" refers to the receptive capacity of those to be transformed; because one wishes to employ the sublime Dharma attained to suit the capacities of beings, it is called "contemplating and practicing."
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The wisdom I have attained is subtle, wondrous, and supreme.
This refers to the cause as an object of contemplation.
"The faculties of sentient beings are dull," and so forth, refers to the conditions as objects of contemplation.
The treatise says: "Originally, he sought to attain enlightenment for the sake of benefiting others; why then did he contemplate for seven days without preaching?
It was to manifest his own delight in the great Dharma-bliss.
The intent of this question is as follows:
In the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), one perceives that sentient beings are capable of being transformed and only then manifests as a Buddha; what further need is there for deliberation?
The intent of the present response is this:
it is not that one knows through deliberation, but rather because one spontaneously experiences the bliss of the Dharma.
The "great joy of the Dharma" refers to the joy of tranquility attained through wisdom.
The treatise states: "For what reason does he manifest his own joy in the Dharma?
It is to cause sentient beings to increase their love and reverence for the Tathāgata."
Furthermore, having relinquished such sublime bliss, he acts out of compassion for sentient beings in order to preach the Dharma to them.
Why does he practice only the path of dependent origination?
It is to manifest the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).

This means that his wisdom is ultimate and reaches its consummation, illuminating the capacities of sentient beings without omission; since no one except the Buddha alone can equal him, this is called an "unshared quality" (*āveṇika-dharma*).
Furthermore, the causal conditions are themselves the profound principle realized; because only the Buddha has reached their ultimate limit, they are unshared.
Regarding the second, "the World-Honored One," it refers to the excellence of the master; the meaning is as explained previously.
Third, "in Paranirmita-vaśavartin" refers to the excellence of the location.
The Treatise states: "Because the palaces in this place are superior."
The palace is the palace of Īśvara, for it surpasses the palaces of the five lower heavens.
The hall is composed of pure jewels from the Maṇi-treasury, for it is adorned with superior gems.
The Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven represents how terrestrial wisdom accomplishes transformative deeds without deliberate thought;
the mani-jewel palace likewise represents how compassionate protection exhausts itself in the production of inexhaustible function without deliberate thought.
If it were held that the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is superior by virtue of its desire, then the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) would be even more superior; why then is it not taught there?
The treatise states: "Because the fruition is experienced in this place.
This means that the karmic conditions for such fruition exist here.
Furthermore, the form realm (rūpadhātu) is subject to the obstacle of the long-lived devas (*dīrghāyu-deva*), whereby one cannot bring about the fruition [of the path];

the body capable of bringing about superior fruition must be that of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Therefore, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* clarifies that this place is where Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) constantly travel.
The *Mahāyāna-samatā-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Because there is the pure land of the Reward Buddha (saṃbhogakāya) in this place, it is taught here.
If one were to consider this solely in terms of the responsive capacity of the audience, the underlying symbolic meaning would be lost.
IV. "Endowed with Greatness" and below concerns the excellence of the assembly; the text is divided into five parts: first, identifying the categories of the assembly;

second, praising their superior virtues from "Abiding in All... onwards; third, listing names based on those virtues from "Their names... onwards; fourth, concluding that the number is immeasurable from "In this way... onwards; and fifth, designating the speaker of the Dharma from "Vajragarbha... onwards.
Now, this first section further has three parts:
first, distinguishing the Great [Vehicle] from the Small, because they are alike as Bodhisattvas;
second, from "As for all those... onwards, distinguishing the Honored from the Lowly, meaning that from the eighth stage upward, they possess non-retrogressive mindfulness.

The *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "That which is firm in its own nature is called 'non-retrogression' (*avaivartika*); that which is invulnerable to superior progress is called 'non-turning-back' (*anivartya*).

According to the treatise and the sūtra, it further says: "All shall attain unsurpassed bodhi in a single lifetime. This implies they are all at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), for Equal Enlightenment also encompasses the non-retrogression of mindfulness.
Furthermore, the *Renwang jing* states: "In one lifetime, one correctly attains the lower stage of *śānti-kṣānti* (patience toward quiescence).
It is called "non-retrogression" because one no longer regresses into [the state of] *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena).
Although the manifest text is thus, its fundamental and derivative aspects (*honjaku*) are difficult to measure, for it is mostly that which has been transformed by various Buddhas.
Third, from the phrase "all [have come]" onwards, the new is distinguished from the old, as they have assembled from other directions.

Within the second section, the "Praise of Virtues," there are twenty phrases: the first two provide a brief clarification, the final two offer a summary, and the middle ones provide an extensive praise.

Regarding the initial brief section, the first phrase concerns the fulfillment of one's own practice (*svabhāga-pratipatti*), which refers to the unimpeded wisdom of the provisional and the ultimate. This abides in a realm where the true and the conventional are fused; as realm and wisdom are of one suchness, it is an abiding that is non-abiding.
The latter phrase refers to the fulfillment of superior progress; having realized what the Buddha has realized, one is called a bodhisattva because the Tathāgata’s diligent practice is unceasing.
Second, from "skillfully able" onwards is the extensive praise, consisting of sixteen phrases, which is divided into two parts:
the first thirteen phrases extensively explain the stage of self-benefit (*svabhāga*), and the final three extensively explain superior progress.
The preceding section also has two parts:

first, the three [aspects] that demonstrate the perfection of the cultivation of practice—first, skillfulness in supernatural powers; second, timely adaptation in training and transforming others; and third, the pervasiveness of vows across time and place.

The remaining ten phrases describe the perfection of his virtuous functions: first, the inexhaustible benefit of both merit and wisdom; second, although his provisional and ultimate knowledge and insight have already reached the ultimate, he does not abandon cultivation through the path of non-abiding; third, his internal realization of meditative concentration and wisdom is penetratingly luminous; and fourth, his external application of skillful means is sovereign.

Among these seven, if they accord with the characteristics of the Three Vehicles: "dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas; "samādhi" refers to the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); and "liberation" (*vimokṣa*) refers to the eight liberations.

"Samādhi" is here translated as "equipoise" (*samāhita*), because it evenly holds the mind so that it proceeds toward a single object; it thus refers to the three samādhis and all mental states of meditative concentration.
*Samāpatti*, here translated as "equilibrium" (*tingzhì*), refers to reaching a state of one-pointedness by being free from dullness and agitation.

It is restricted to the meditative stages (*dhyāna-bhūmi*) and extends to mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), such as the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

"Supernormal powers and clear wisdom" refers here to all the merits induced by states of meditative concentration—whether involving a mind or devoid of a mind; this bodhisattva is now able to skillfully enter and skillfully induce them all.

If explained according to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), "meditative concentration" refers to the ten dhyānas; "liberation" refers to the inconceivable samādhis and so forth; the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) each have immeasurable hundreds of thousands; and both "penetrating clarity" and "wisdom" each have ten. These ten times ten inexhaustible qualities are what is attained by Bodhisattvas at the stage of Samantabhadra.

Ninth, attaining mastery and capability within; tenth, being able externally to universally request the Dharma in a single thought-moment; eleventh, protecting the Dharma; twelfth, making offerings; and thirteenth, diligently cultivating the two benefits for self and others.
The latter three [stages] are extensive, superior, and progressive; that is, the vastness of the three types of action, as well as the concluding text below, can all be clearly understood.

Among the enumeration of names, the reason the first thirty-eight are all termed "Treasury" (*kośa*) is to indicate that the factors of these stages contain and encompass all virtues and possess the functional capacity to produce fruits.

The one named Vimukticandra (Moon of Liberation) who follows is the foremost petitioner of the Dharma; he removes the darkness of doubt from the assembly and brings them refreshing clarity, just like the moon at night.

Furthermore, the "Treasury" (*pitaka*) symbolizes the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which contains and gives birth [to all things], while the "moon" symbolizes the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which benefits sentient beings with its refreshing clarity.
*Sūrya* means "moon" in this [language].
*Kusuma* means "delightful," which is a name for a flower.
Other specific names may be explained according to their respective meanings.
The enumeration of the four [sections] can be understood.
Fifth is the designation of the master of the Dharma.
The treatise asks: "For what reason does the Bodhisattva preach this Dharma-gate?"
"It is for the purpose of increasing the powers of all bodhisattvas.
Since those of his own kind are capable of doing so,
why is it that only Vajragarbha speaks, given that there are many bodhisattvas?

The treatise answers: "All afflictions are difficult to destroy, yet this dharma can shatter them; its roots of goodness are as firm and solid as a vajra, and therefore it is described by a name that is not different [from 'vajra']."
This "Vajra" (Diamond) commentary means that the wisdom of the ground (*bhūmi-jñāna*) possesses two meanings—solidity and sharpness—just as a vajra does.
Its ability to destroy afflictions (*kleśa*) is the meaning of sharpness; the following explains the meaning of "treasury" (*kośa*).
The treatise first asks: "For what reason is he named Vajragarbha?
The intent of this question is:
Is he called Vajragarbha because the treasury (garbha) contains the vajra? Or [is it otherwise]?
Is it that the *vajra* constitutes the "store" (*kośa*)?

In the former case, it is "possessing wealth" (*sadhana*), while in the latter, it is "possessing the activity" (*karman*). The treatise follows both formulations, yet it accords with the latter formulation, stating: "The 'store' is called 'firm,' just as the core of a tree is its store."

This means that just as the heartwood of a tree is firm and dense, enabling it to grow branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit, so too does the wisdom of the ground (bhūmi-jñāna) give rise to cause and effect; because it is capable of such containment, it is called a "store" (garbha).
Next, following the preceding phrase, it says: "Furthermore, it is like being pregnant within a womb; therefore, it is as firm as a vajra, like a vajra-treasury.
This means that when a child is conceived within the embryonic treasury, it is sustained by wholesome karma and is so firm that it cannot be destroyed, yet it continues to grow.
This is called a "repository" (*garbha*) in the sense of that which is stored within it.
Both metaphors share the meaning of growth and production.

The treatise later provides a detailed synthesis, stating: "These roots of goodness possess the most supreme power among all other roots of goodness; they are like a diamond (*vajra*), capable of producing the practices leading to the realms of humans and gods, and cannot be destroyed by any other roots of goodness. Therefore, they are named the 'Diamond Repository' (*Vajragarbha*)."
This single synthesis applies to the two preceding metaphors.
These roots of goodness refer to untainted (anāsrava) goodness;
all other roots of goodness pertain to the stages prior to those of the Two Vehicles.
Now, among all other wholesome states, untainted goodness is like a fetus within the womb;
its power is supreme, and it combines the two metaphors in the sense of firmness.
Furthermore, it is capable of bringing about birth and growth, combining the two metaphors in the sense of development.
Its power is supreme, like a vajra; its essential nature is termed "firm.
Because nothing else can destroy it, it is termed "firm" in relation to others.
Second, from "At that time" onwards, the section on samādhi is explained.
"At that time" means when the assembly had already gathered.
"Vajragarbha Bodhisattva" identifies the person who has entered meditative absorption, as he is the leader of the assembly.
"Relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power" indicates the basis for his eloquence; it reveals that the depth and mystery of this samādhi can only be fully realized by a Buddha.
To attribute merit to others is to be free from *māna* (self-conceit).
"The Samādhi of the Bodhisattva’s Great Wisdom Radiance" is the designation for the meditative absorption entered;
"samādhi" is a general term, while all other terms are specific names.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the essence, while radiance is its function; it illuminates the two kinds of selflessness.
Realizing suchness is termed "wisdom," while illuminating phenomena is termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Because these two are unimpeded and can destroy the delusions of views as well as ignorance, they are called "radiance."
The term "Great Being" (Mahāsattva) has two meanings:
first, it distinguishes [the practitioner] from ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle;

second, because they are able to sever great delusions and realize the Great Principle, thereby accomplishing the Great Fruit, yet they do not manifest as being fixed in that fruit, they are called "Bodhisattvas."
It is the illumination of stillness; therefore, it is called *samādhi*.
Wisdom and principle are merged in obscurity; therefore, it is termed "entering.

In the treatise, this sūtra is titled the "Mahāyāna Radiance Samādhi"; thus, radiance is itself wisdom. This corresponds to the ninth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, where the names of the four dhyānas and the first dhyāna are identical.
However, its essential nature does not exceed three aspects:
first, concentration; second, wisdom; and third, the suchness that is realized. This is because it possesses both the subject and object of realization, and unites quiescence with illumination.

Regarding the ways of entry, there are briefly six meanings in the intent, though only two are discussed in the treatise. The first is called "indicating profundity," as the treatise states: "It is shown that this Dharma is not the sphere of discursive thought."
The second [point] clarifies that [the Buddha] does not preach because there is no proof [of the capacity to understand], based on this very principle.
The remaining four [points] are as described in the "Ten Stages" chapter.
Third, from "Entering into this" onwards is the section on the bestowal of empowerment (*adhikāra*), which consists of six parts:

1. Distinguishing the cause for the empowerment; 2. From "At that very moment" onwards, the manifestation of the empowering Buddha; 3. From "He spoke thus" onwards, praising his attainment of meditative concentration; 4. From "Good son, this is" onwards, distinguishing both the causes and conditions for the empowerment and the concentration; 5. From "I now wish to" onwards, distinguishing the purpose of the empowerment; 6. From "Good son" onwards, specifically revealing the characteristics of the empowerment.
First, regarding the phrase "having entered this samādhi": if one has not yet entered meditative concentration, the Buddha does not bestow his empowerment.

Therefore, the treatise below states: "The reason he specifically empowers Vajragarbha is that he has attained this samādhi," and the Ten Abodes Assembly (Daśabhūmika-parivarta) says, "By the power of samādhi."
Regarding the second [point], there are five aspects to the Buddha’s manifestation through empowerment:
first, the time of the Buddha’s appearance, which refers to the moment he enters meditative absorption;
second, the distance from which he descends, indicated by the passage beginning with "the ten directions."
3. From "Each [had]... onwards, it indicates the number of Buddhas who bestow empowerment;
4. By stating they share the same name, "Vajragarbha," it reveals that those empowered have identical names;
5. By stating "they appeared before him," it shows the manifestation of their bodies to inspire faith.
In the first two of the three [categories], the intention is to clarify a great number, as they surpass the preceding stages.
If that is so, why does it not say "immeasurable worlds," but rather "ten billion world-systems as numerous as atoms"?
The treatise states: "This is because expedient means manifest many Buddhas.
This means that although [the number] is vast, the expression remains general, and people do not consider it to be many.
Now, by provisionally using the atoms of a world-system (*kṣetra-rajas*)—where each atom is a world-system and each world-system is a Buddha—one considers it minute and unfathomable.
If that is so, merely mentioning "dust motes of a world-system" (*kṣetraparamāṇu*) would already suffice to indicate their great number; why then specify "ten billion"?
There are two reasons: first, it is for the purpose of explaining the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*);
second, this sutra frequently employs the number ten to manifest inexhaustibility.
Precisely for this reason, it does not say "immeasurable," because "immeasurable" cannot manifest "inexhaustibility.
Why is it necessary to manifest this addition of many Buddhas?
The treatise states: "To manifest the Dharma and the teachers of the Dharma, so as to increase the mind of reverence; and furthermore, to indicate that all Buddhas speak in the same way."
"Why is it necessary for them to share the same name?
Regarding this, the treatise offers two interpretations:
first, it is due to the power of their original vows.
For what reason does the Tathāgata make such a vow?
It is to manifest the multiplicity of Buddhas.

This samādhi is the essence of the Dharma; when he was formerly practicing as a bodhisattva, he was always named Vajragarbha and taught this same Dharma together with others. Now that he has attained perfect enlightenment, he is likewise named Vajragarbha; therefore, he adds his name without distinction.
The intended meaning of this treatise is as follows:
While still in the causal stage, the Buddhas attained the concentration named Vajragarbha and subsequently made a vow, saying:
"When I attain Buddhahood, may I likewise bear that same name."

Regarding the phrase "those who act in the same way," this is intended to show that the dharma-body attained by the Bodhisattva is identical to that of many Buddhas, clarifying that although persons differ, their paths are the same.
Such is the true meaning of the treatise.

If taken from the perspective of its meaning, it also accords with the fundamental vow of Vairocana; for since the Buddha attained this samādhi while on the path of causes and preached the Dharma, both the bestower of empowerment and the recipient of empowerment are identical in name as that which is naturally so (dharmatā).
He also made this vow to manifest that his path was identical [to theirs]; thus the subsequent scripture states: "This is also due to the power of the original vows of Vairocana Tathāgata.
The second *Yìlùn* (Treatise on Meaning) states: "Furthermore, because this Bodhisattva, having heard that the names of all Tathāgatas are the same as his own, increases his courage and joy."
The preceding section concerned the principles of the Dharma; this section concerns the methods of transformation.
In the third [section], they jointly praise the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), revealing the presence of an augmenting cause.
In the fourth [section], which analyzes both the augmenting cause and the conditions for concentration, there are four causal conditions:

First, because the accompanying Buddha exerts his power together [with the practitioner]; second, because of the original vow of the presiding Buddha; third, because of the manifestation of the presiding Buddha’s majestic power; and fourth, because of the power of wisdom of the one in meditative concentration.
Of these four, the first alone is the cause for attaining concentration, as one must first rely on the Buddha’s empowerment to be able to enter it.
Therefore, the treatise states: "That Buddha previously made such a vow, and now he further bestows his own empowerment.

The latter three matters pertain to both causes; for it is by these that one can enter meditative concentration, and it is by these that one obtains empowerment, as they do not constitute the actual characteristics of empowerment itself.
The treatise states: "Because there is subsequent empowerment by other Buddhas, it says, 'by the power of the original vows of Vairocana Buddha.

The intent of this treatise is that the characteristics of the empowerment by all Buddhas are revealed only in the subsequent passage; since this occurs precisely through the power of the original vows herein, these [vows] constitute the cause of the empowerment."

If one considers that the attainment of meditative concentration arises through the empowerment of the Principal Buddha, then the aspirations and so forth herein already manifest the characteristics of such empowerment; however, because this is an inconceivable mental empowerment, it is simply what was previously described as "receiving the Buddha's spiritual power."

Thus, there are four causes for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and likewise four auxiliary causes (*pratyaya*). Although the auxiliary cause consisting of the Buddha’s accompaniment may be lacking, because there is still the single cause of attaining concentration, there are four [causes].

Therefore, in the third assembly, the latter three causes are preceded by the words "also" (*yāpi*), and in both the fourth and fifth assemblies, it is likewise stated "also"; thus, one cannot take the first cause as the primary basis for addition.
If this has already been explained as the conferral [of empowerment], what is the purpose of the subsequent section that explicitly reveals the characteristics of the conferral?
The remainder is as argued in the third assembly.
The fifth [section] clarifies the purpose of the conferral; thus, the treatise asks: "For what reason is there a conferral?"
However, if one follows the scriptural text directly, it should be divided into two parts:
first, a general explanation; second, a detailed exposition beginning with the words "That is to say.

Since the treatise lacks the two characters "so-called" (suǒwèi), the phrase "entering the stage of wisdom" from the detailed section is taken to be included within the initial general sentence. Thus, when the general and specific explanations are combined, there are exactly twenty [points].

The first ten rely on practice for one's own benefit, while the latter ten rely on practice for the benefit of others; although their meanings apply to both, they are distinguished according to the predominant aspect in order to clarify the distinct characteristics of these two types of benefit.
Now, according to the commentary on this treatise, within the first ten lines, the treatise explains them through two approaches:
first, a direct explanation of the scriptural text; second, a reconciliation of the fundamental and the derivative.
Within the first approach, the general statement is explained first.
That sutra states: "Furthermore, all bodhisattvas are enabled to enter the stage of wisdom through the inconceivable, luminous teachings of the various Buddha-dharmas.
Since this takes a specific phrase and incorporates it into a general category, the sutras and śāstras differ in their methods of expansion and condensation.
The treatise states that "illumination" (*prabhā*) refers to the "light" (*prabhā*) in the present sutra; the difference lies merely in the degree of elaboration versus brevity.

That [treatise] speaks of "illumination," while this [sutra] speaks of "inconceivable exposition"; since the former has not yet adjusted its phrasing, there is simply a difference in the dialectical terminology of the sutra and the treatise.
Having already understood the similarities and differences between the two sutras, we shall next provide a formal commentary on the text.
First, regarding the phrase "desiring to cause you to act," this indicates the headings of the chapters and generally reveals the intent behind the empowerment.
What is the purpose of this intent?
This refers to the passage beginning with "all bodhisattvas" and so forth.
Within this, there are three meanings:

first, all bodhisattvas are the intended audience; second, the light of the inconceivable dharmas of the Buddhas is the teaching to be expounded; third, causing them to enter the stage of wisdom is the benefit of the teaching.
By what capacity [of audience] is this addressed?
The *Śāstra* states: "In this context, 'all bodhisattvas' refers to those dwelling on the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*).
This applies to two categories:

The first refers to the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), when one has not yet realized *tathatā* (suchness) and practices solely by relying on faith; this is likewise designated as such in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*.

The second applies throughout the grounds, such as when the preparatory stage (*prayoga-avasthā*) of the first ground is called the "ground of practice through faith" (*śraddhā-carita-bhūmi*), meaning that the preparatory stages of each successive ground are all termed "practice through faith."

Since the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the non-conceptual contemplation of mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) extends across all four stages, we know that there is also practice through faith (*śraddhācaryā*) on the stages beyond the first.

Furthermore, as explained below regarding the "stages of wisdom entered" (*praviṣṭajñānabhūmi*) and the "distinct entries," these pertain to all ten stages; thus, it is clear that those for whom this teaching is intended are not limited solely to those prior to the [first] stage.

Moreover, within the section on the "request for the distribution [of merit]," the treatise states: "Those who have not yet entered the stages shall attain the pure mind; those who have already entered the stages shall attain the ten powers.
This must necessarily apply universally to all.
Regarding what dharma is taught in the two [middle] sections,
there are two kinds:
first, the dharma that is realized.
The treatise states that the "inconceivable dharmas of the Buddhas" refer to the supramundane factors of enlightenment (*lokottara-bodhipakṣa*).
This clarifies that the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is untainted (*anāsrava*), and is therefore termed "supramundane."
It is called the "Path" (*mārga*) because it gives rise to the fruit of Buddhahood.
The various categories of the practices throughout the ten stages are termed "Chapters" (*varga*).
Since these are the causes of Buddhahood and are what the Buddha has realized, they are called the "Buddha-dharma."
When the paths of mind and speech are cut off, it is called "inconceivable.
These two explanations can serve as proof.
The Treatise says: "That which is luminous is seen through wisdom and realized through attainment."

This means that the subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) which observes the differentiation of phenomena is called "vision" (*darśana*), while the fundamental [attainment] which observes the single characteristic of principle is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
Vision is termed "attainment" (*prāpti*) when it penetrates phenomena, and wisdom is termed "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*) when it accords with principle.
Because it speaks directly of the essence of wisdom, it is called "seeing wisdom" (*jñāna-darśana*); because wisdom is conjoined with its object, it is called "attaining realization.
Although the dharmas of the stages (*bhūmi*) are numerous, they do not transcend these two.
Although "seeing wisdom" is broad in scope, this explanation is most appropriate here.
Therefore, the third chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "I have taught wisdom and vision through immeasurable gateways; I shall now briefly explain their characteristics for you.
That sublime wisdom which arises from cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā by taking general phenomena as its object is called 'wisdom' (*jñāna*)."
"If the sublime wisdom that arises from cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā by taking specific dharmas as objects is called 'view'";
this is precisely that meaning.
What was stated above regarding "the teacher" is intended to cause one to discern the aforementioned dharmas of the subject and object of realization.
What is the benefit of explaining this among the three [categories]?
It causes one to enter the stage of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*).
The treatise states: "To 'enter' means to have faith and delight, and to attain realization."
In this context, "faith and aspiration" refers to that which is realized by the recipient of the teaching; it is the convergence of the two aforementioned wisdoms.
Into what dharma does one enter?
It is called the stage of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*).
The Treatise states: "The stage of wisdom refers to the wisdom of the ten stages.
As explained in the *Mūla-vibhāga*, this is precisely the aforementioned inconceivable Buddha-dharma.

Regarding the aforementioned subject and object of realization, the intended meaning is to cause Bodhisattvas to enter the dharma realized by the Buddhas by means of the realizing wisdom; this is the general purport.

The general statement regarding the characteristics of entering the stages has already been explained; next, the following nine statements reveal the specific distinctions of entry by expanding upon the branches based on the root.
The treatise states: "In this sūtra, there are nine kinds of entry based on the fundamental entry."
These nine types of entry are assigned to four stages: the first four belong to the stage of aspiration and joy (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*);
the next one belongs to the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*); the next three belong to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*); and the final one belongs to the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*).
Because the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) also belong to the stages (*bhūmi*), and because the subsequent superior progress leads toward the ultimate, all are subsumed within the ten stages.
Regarding the "nine entries," the first is the entry by inclusion, meaning that within the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are included.

Second is entry by means of reflecting on the meaning, because the wisdom of reflection constitutes the skillful means of knowledge (*jñānopāya*) among all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
This "skillful means of knowledge" refers precisely to the excellent discernment of the factors of enlightenment, which is itself the Buddha-dharma.
Third is the mutual inclusion of the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), because within each respective meaning there is immeasurable and manifold knowledge.
Those "respective" [meanings] are precisely all dharmas, and "manifold knowledge" is extensive knowledge; this is the accomplishment of the contemplated dharmas.

Regarding the four modes of conversion through teaching: because they are fully endowed with the names and meanings according to what is contemplated, they are able to explain them well; this is known as the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Cultivation benefits both oneself and others; since a bodhisattva’s benefiting of others is itself the fulfillment of their own Buddha-dharma, it is subsumed within the category of self-benefit.
The five modes of entry consist of the wisdom of equality regarding all phenomena, because it is thoroughly purified at the time of the path of seeing.
What is called "equality" is precisely non-conceptuality.
Non-conceptual wisdom directly realizes suchness and is free from the marks of the two grasps; therefore, it is called "equality.
Because the latent tendencies of dualistic self-discrimination do not arise, it is termed "perfectly pure."
Initially, according to principle, the name "Path of Seeing" (darśanamārga) is established.

Because one enters the six states of non-negligence during the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), one remains far removed from all afflictive obstructions; therefore, one is not defiled by worldly dharmas.
The transition from stage to stage occurs in the seventh ground because the supramundane factors of enlightenment and the roots of goodness, such as non-attachment, are purified.

This clarifies that within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one realizes the principle by abandoning hindrances; as wisdom and practice advance, one simultaneously abandons two types of ignorance within each respective ground.

This untainted goodness (*anāsrava-kuśala*) is able to purify that which is known; by means of these three untainted roots of goodness, it is called the purification of afflictions (*kleśa-viśuddhi*).

The Treatise states: "Furthermore, there are roots of goodness that can serve as the causes for the factors of the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārgāṅga*). This clarifies the purification of the preparatory roots of goodness (*prayoga-kuśalamūla*) within the various stages (*bhūmi*).

The eight bodhisattvas all enter [this stage], because within the tenth ground they enter the secret wisdom of all Tathāgatas; this refers precisely to the entry into the ten kinds of secret wisdom of the Tathāgata as described in the section on the "Great Exhaustion" (mahāparikṣaya).
The secret of the Tathāgata cannot be fathomed by those on lower stages; thus it is called "inconceivable.
If one enters that which is entered, this is the realm of wisdom.
If one enters that which is the means of entering, then wisdom itself is the realm.
Attainment is itself entry; therefore, the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) was praised as saying, "There is no secret treasury of the Buddhas that one cannot enter.
All nine Buddhas have fully entered, because they have entered into the wisdom of omniscience.
The upper [part] explains "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā) and its entry.
The lower [part] concerns the character "knowledge" (jñāna); "knowledge" refers to the realm of wisdom, and "entry" means attainment.
The direct explanation above is now complete.
From here on, the treatise synthesizes the beginning and the end.

First, it brings the end back to the beginning: the aforementioned nine types of entry are intended to measure the progressively superior characteristics of the distinctions in the wisdom of the stages; they do not constitute the actual distribution of practices within the fundamental entry.
The subsequent section clarifies the non-obstruction between the fundamental and the derivative;

it seeks to reveal that while the preceding process of the derivative arising from the fundamental constitutes a "differentiation within non-differentiation," the subsequent process of the derivative being subsumed back into the fundamental constitutes "non-differentiation within differentiation. Therefore, these six characteristics are harmonized so as to be without obstruction.

The treatise states: "In all that has been taught within the ten phrases, there are six kinds of distinct categories. This is a general heading intended to demonstrate universal applicability; therefore, it says that "all" possess these [six categories].

Regarding the statement, "One should know that this verbal explanation excludes the [substantial] entity," this reveals the underlying intention: namely, that these six characteristics are intended to manifest the dharma of the perfect interfusion of dependent origination, and one must not grasp them through the substantial characteristics of the aggregates, elements, or sense bases.

Regarding the "six characteristics," they are: the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), the identical characteristic (*tulya-lakṣaṇa*), the different characteristic (*visama-lakṣaṇa*), the formative characteristic (*siddhi-lakṣaṇa*), and the disintegrating characteristic (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*). This is the enumeration.
The subsequent explanation states: "'General' refers to the fundamental entry (*mūla-praveśa*)," because there is nothing that the first entry does not encompass.
The "distinct" refers to the remaining nine bases (*āyatana*).

Regarding the phrase "based on the distinct foundation to fulfill that foundation," this means that by relying on one [base], the other nine are opened; since neither a totality nor individuality could be established otherwise, it is called "relying."
Because the general is established through the particular, it is said that they "fill" that [totality].
Regarding the phrase "as for the common characteristic, because they enter," this means they are called "entry" by virtue of having the same name.
Regarding the phrase "as for the distinct characteristic, because of the increasing characteristics," this means that the nine characteristics gradually increase and are thus not identical.
Regarding the phrase "the characteristic of formation is explained briefly," this means that by gathering the nine conditions into one, it is expressed concisely to manifest the mark.
Regarding the phrase "the characteristic of disintegration is explained extensively," this means that one is divided into nine, such that apart from these nine, there is no "one."
These nine causes and conditions each abide in their own characteristics and do not mutually establish one another.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "like the formation and destruction of the world," it is just as the world is formed through many concurrent conditions; if one were to examine each individual thing therein, what exactly would be designated as the "world" that undergoes destruction?

It is also like beams and other materials together forming a single house: in its totality it is one house, yet individually they are the various conditions. When they are the same, they do not contradict one another; when they differ, the conditions remain distinct. When established, the conditions accomplish the fruit; when disintegrating, each remains within its own dharma.
All other ten phrases should be understood according to their respective categories of meaning, as they are extensively elucidated in a separate chapter.
The second section, beginning with "Furthermore, causing them to obtain," consists of ten phrases based on altruistic practice; these constitute an increased enumeration of ten.

The Sūtra contains twelve phrases; because the Śāstra combines two phrases from the Sūtra (the seventh and eighth), there are only eleven. The first phrase serves as the general [heading], while the remaining ten constitute the particulars.
Within the general heading, "beginning" refers to internally giving rise to faith and aspiration, and externally approaching virtuous friends and listening to the Dharma.
"End" refers to the recollection and maintenance of the dharmas of the stages as they were heard; since this applies to each stage, it is called the "beginning and end of the ten stages.
This is according to the perspective of teaching and practice (*śikṣā*).

Furthermore, there is the view where the *āgama* (scriptural transmission) is the beginning and realization (*adhigama*) is the end; in that case, everything preceding [realization] constitutes the teaching.
This exposition of the meaning of the teaching consists of nine general points:
first, the correspondence between the teaching (*śāsana*) and practice (*pratipatti*).
Here, "sound" is the teaching, and "virtuous conduct" is the realization; this is analogous to the two categories of "words" and "meaning" within the Tripitaka.
Second, the contrast between those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and those on the stages themselves.

As in the "Request" section where the assembly is praised, that which consists of hearing, reflection, and cultivation prior to the stages is taken as the purity of the teaching (*śāsana-viśuddhi*), while the virtues of practice on the stages are taken as the purity of realization (*adhigama-viśuddhi*).
Third, regarding the contrast between the true and the false:

within the stage [of practice], the understanding that arises through the illumination of the conditions of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as the consciousness and gnosis born of karmic maturation, is called *āgama*; the emergence of true gnosis and its verbal expression constitute the realization (*pramāṇa*).
The lower treatise states: "Hearing, contemplation, and cultivation can be spoken of, but the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi*) transcends words.
This refers to the relative distinction between the four types of cultivation.

Throughout all the stages, the combined cultivation of the true and the false constitutes the teaching (*śāsana*); abandoning the false to accord with the true constitutes realization (*adhigama*). This is like the two great meanings explained below.
The five marks correspond to the true reality (*dharmatā*).

Within the world, one cultivates and attains the realization of those marks; this is called "teaching" (*śāsana*), while accords with the fundamental true reality as "realization" (*adhigama*). This is like the "Dharma-gate of the Radiance of the Sublime Dharma of Superiority" explained below: radiance is the teaching, and superiority is the realization.
Sixth, the correspondence between essence and virtue:

within the practices accomplished by departing from characteristics, the fundamental dharma-nature is revealed as the realization (*pramāṇa*), while the virtues accomplished based on that nature serve as the teaching (*upadeśa*). This is like refining gold: the essence of the gold remains constant, whether it takes the form of a bracelet or other ornaments.
Seventh, the relative nature of essence and function:

the preceding [sections on] essence and qualities all pertain to realization (*sākṣātkāra*); the function of the wisdom that arises from the essence to initiate the teaching constitutes the teaching (*deśanā*). This is like a jewel below emitting light; the light is a metaphor for the teaching, while the substance of the jewel is a metaphor for realization.
Eighth is the pair of self-perfection and further progress (*viśeṣa-gāmitā*).

One realizes both the essential qualities and the functions accomplished within oneself; furthermore, one receives the Buddha’s teachings as instruction. Herein, praising the two powers of Vajragarbha’s wondrous wisdom and eloquence is termed the power of realization (*adhigama-bala*), while firmly maintaining mindfulness of the teachings is termed *āgama*.
Ninth, regarding the relationship between the expression and the reality:

the essence of true wisdom serves as the realization (*pratyakṣa*); based on words, it is divided into ten as the *āgama*. This is like the metaphor of footprints left below in space to illustrate realization: the footprints in the space represent the *āgama* of the stages (*bhūmi*).

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "The locus of the body of syllables (*vyañjana-kāya*) is subsumed under realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*). It is not that there is no wisdom regarding the stages (*bhūmi*), nor are there no names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*); these names, phrases, and syllables are precisely the *āgama*."

Now we come to the fourth [section], wherein the teachings and proofs are frequently cited within a single sutra; the underlying principles must be understood as a whole, so do not weary yourself with the repetitive text.
Next, according to the fundamental beginning and end, there are ten stages of beginning and end:
the first three concern the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi, where one benefits sentient beings through reflection and cultivation.
Next is the single path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
the remaining six are the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

This [distinction] is made because one enters [the path of seeing] previously; that is to say, the former lacks the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), while the latter lacks the wisdom of the Buddha’s exhaustion [of outflows]. In reality, however, both are equally pervasive. Since these two are not the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*) themselves, they have already been explained previously, and thus are omitted here.
First, it encompasses the beginning and the end.

As the Sūtra states: "Because it explains the distinct characteristics of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Bodhisattva as they truly are. This means that one upholds what has been heard through the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), and proclaims it in accordance with that reflection; therefore, it is called "as it truly is" (*yathābhūtam*).
Second is the beginning and end of aspiration (*chanda*).
This refers to the intention to cause sentient beings to realize the Buddha-dharma through mindfulness; this is the superior grade of seeking within the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Third is the beginning and end of practice (*pratipatti*).
Because one cultivates wisdom through this, it is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).

As for the statement regarding the "discrimination of untainted phenomena" (*anāsravadharma*), it refers to the fact that on the stages (*bhūmi*), one gives rise to mental-linguistic discrimination (*manojalpa-vikalpa*) regarding the contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) of the untainted path-factors (*anāsrava-mārgāṅga*).

Because it has not yet been realized, this is merely the stage of contemplation where the mind is observed while still bearing signs; since one has not yet awakened to signlessness, it is called "discrimination.
This concludes the fourth section on the beginning and end of realization.
This refers to the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). "Great Wisdom" refers to the True Path of Seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*).

It is called "great" because its fundamental wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmānātma-jñāna*) transcends that of the Lesser Vehicle; it is called "light" because it counteracts ignorance (*avidyā*).
This wisdom directly realizes suchness; being perfectly equal and free from the characteristics of the two grasps, it is called "thorough observation.
Because it truly severs the latencies of conceptualization regarding the two obscurations, it is called "thorough discernment."
"Skillful adornment" refers to the path of vision through its aspects (*lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*).
Because this is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the treatise calls it "skillful means" (*upāya*); "skillful means" is itself "skillful.
The true path of vision (*tattva-darśanamārga*) is established in various ways, which is termed "adornment."
Furthermore, "adornment" refers to the accomplishment of virtue through the two types of wisdom.
Because one attains these two and thoroughly penetrates the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), having gained mastery over many hundreds of gateways, it is called "adornment."
Therefore, the treatise states: "Because one thoroughly knows both within this matter and at this time.
Due to the path of insight (*lakṣaṇa-mārga*), there are further two types:
first, contemplating the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*), which is termed "within this matter."
The two contemplations of the non-established truths are called "at that time.

Because the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) directly realizes suchness (*tathatā*), it cannot be designated as a [conventional] entity; since it is viewed in relation to the preceding true [path], it is termed "that."
Regarding the beginning and end of the fivefold path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the treatise states:

"Because one enters into the dharma and its meaning through the power of supramundane wisdom. This is because, having subsequently attained the conventional by virtue of realizing the ultimate truth, it is termed "supramundane wisdom" (*lokottara-jñāna*).
Wisdom, by virtue of realizing the ultimate truth and penetrating conventional reality, is called "skillful entry.
Since wisdom is able to enter into phenomena, it is termed a "gate.
The preceding section concludes the account from the second stage through the seventh stage.

The following five phrases contain five "beginnings and endings," which, by being applied from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) up to the Buddha stage, remedy the five obstacles to bodhi for the Bodhisattva.
These five obstacles reside in the seventh stage and extend through to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The sūtra text contains only the remedies, while the obstacles lie outside the text.
Now, the first two phrases immediately serve as the means to break through the obstacle of heterodox treatises from beginning to end.
That which cannot break through the obstacle of heterodox treatises is precisely what is to be remedied.
"Wherever it dwells" refers to the place where the mind of false doctrine adheres.

"Explaining clearly in sequence" means employing the means of valid cognition—thesis, reason, example, direct perception, inference, and authoritative scripture—to manifest one's own correct doctrine and treat the afflictions according to their specific ailments.
The above all discusses what is relied upon.
To speak of "fearlessness" is the adornment of the treatise.
The subsequent phrase, "eloquence," is the essence of the treatise, and it is also the adornment of the treatise.
This refers to the perfection of speech, characterized by being compliant, eloquent, and dignified; hence it is called *pratibhāna* (eloquence).
Furthermore, the preceding sections primarily discuss the various functions [of eloquence];

these functions are threefold: first, skill in one's own and others' tenets; second, courageous fearlessness; and third, inexhaustible eloquence—their correspondence with the text may be understood accordingly.
Regarding "light," it is because its nature is not dark.

This refers to the discourse on transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*), meaning that one skillfully examines gain and loss and so forth. Because one possesses the aforementioned meanings, one does not incur defeat; by destroying these hindrances, one enters the eighth stage.
Second, being able to skillfully answer difficult challenges from beginning to end.
The preceding section clarified the ability to refute; this section reveals the ability to establish [one's own position].
The ninth, excellent wisdom, is eloquence (*pratibhāna*); abiding on this stage is its realization.
Third, the beginning and end of the antidote to attachment to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*): because one does not forget bodhi, seeking it above while transforming others below.
Fourth, the beginning and end of the antidote to indolence in transforming sentient beings: because one achieves tirelessness.
Fifth, there is the beginning and end of lacking skillful means as an antidote.
One who has thoroughly mastered the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) is able to awaken others in all circumstances; thus, one is capable of skillful transformation.
Furthermore, regarding the aforementioned five obstacles, the first is the inability to refute heterodoxy.
Second, although they are able to refute [others], they are unable to establish [their own position];
third, although they are able to both refute and establish, their inclination favors the Hīnayāna;
fourth, although they do not favor the Hīnayāna, they do not diligently strive to transform others.
Although the fifth stage involves transformation without weariness, it lacks the skillful means for such transformation.
By governing these five stages, the practice of transformation is roughly complete.
The sixth stage correctly reveals the characteristics of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
The treatise says: "It has already been explained why there is empowerment.
Furthermore, how is one empowered?
There are three aspects of empowerment, namely: those of speech, mind, and body."
Speaking according to specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), the mouth is empowered with increased eloquence, the mind with the bestowal of wisdom, and the body with the enhancement of majesty.

Speaking according to reality (*yathābhūta*), the agent of empowerment is restricted while that which is empowered is universal; however, following the sequence of the preceding discourse, the empowerment of the mouth is mentioned first.

Having attained wisdom, one is capable of preaching; for this matter, it is necessary to arise from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and cause the body to experience tactile sensation so that awareness arises; therefore, this is done.
Following this, the discussion proceeds by way of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
If we consider Vairocana, first the mind must be brought to attain concentration, and then there shall be that which is to be preached.
Next, the light from his body shines upon him, increasing his majestic power;
finally, the Cloud Terrace speaks a verse to prompt him to expound.
This is also a sequence of meaning, not a matter of superiority or inferiority.
In the initial "Oral Empowerment" (*mukha-adhiṣṭhāna*), there are eleven phrases: the first is general and the remainder are specific.

Within the general section, [the Buddha] commands that one should expound the distinctions of the names and characteristics of the Dharma-gate of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) with eloquence (*pratibhāna*), so that it may be skillfully accomplished without contradicting facts or principles; therefore, it says, "You should expound with eloquence," and so forth.
Regarding the ten distinct phrases that follow "so-called," based upon fundamental eloquence (*pratibhāna*), there are two kinds of eloquence:
first, eloquence through the power of others, which corresponds to the first phrase, meaning to rely upon the power of the Buddha.
By what power is this sustained? It is by the power of the Tathāgata’s luminous wisdom.
Second is the eloquence of one's own power, which consists of the subsequent nine phrases, because speech occurs only through the causal conditions of both self and others.
These nine powers are subsumed under four kinds of purity because there are four meanings within the causal stage:

first, having power to act; second, lacking power and thus not acting; third, possessing both capacities to induce and produce; and fourth, the merging and integration of the preceding three, which accords with principle and constitutes a virtue. Therefore, they constitute the four purities.

First, "purifying one's own roots of goodness" refers to the purification of conditioned wholesome dharmas; this is the practice of teaching, and because it relies on signs (*nimitta*), it is called "conditioned.
Second, "universally purifying the dharma-realm" refers to the purification of unconditioned dharmas; this concerns the practice of realization (*adhigama*).
It is also called "unconditioned" (anabhisaṃskāra) because it refers to its essential nature (svabhāva); for it is spoken of in reliance upon this characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
The first two [aspects] are both for one's own benefit (svārtha).
Regarding the third, "universally encompassing sentient beings": purifying sentient beings through teaching and transformation is precisely benefiting others (parārtha).

The remaining six phrases of the sutra are all termed "purity of body," which are subsumed into three kinds of "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*). These all manifest the fulfillment of the two benefits, thereby constituting the virtues of accomplishment.
There are two meanings to these virtues of accomplishment:

first, the "exhaustion of bodhisattvas" which manifests benefit within their own respective stages; second, the "last two exhaustions" which are established by way of contrast to demonstrate superiority.
Regarding the "initial exhaustion" of the bodhisattva, it refers to the ultimate culmination of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).

This encompasses three phrases from the sutra: the first phrase concerns the fulfillment of the stages, meaning that through the progressive advancement of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one destroys the synthetic consciousness (*saṃghāta-vijñāna*) and manifests the *dharmakāya*. This is not attainable by mind, thought, or consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*); rather, it is the support of suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*) that constitutes the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*).
Because the Bodhisattva illuminates quiescence, it is said that he has "entered deeply.
The latter two phrases establish the benefits: first, they establish the benefit of present retribution, as he receives the Buddha’s consecration and attains the rank of a Buddha;
second, they establish the benefit of future retribution, wherein he gathers the rewards of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and is born with great mastery, which is described as a "lofty and vast body."
The two meanings of "vast and great" (*mahān*) are as follows:
first, it is the ultimate within form and appearance, for its magnitude is greatest and it dwells at the summit of existence (*bhavāgra*);
second, with respect to the three vehicles, this constitutes the stage of the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is supreme and universally pervasive; thus, it is called "vast and great."
The treatise states: "Because it arises from the locus of Maheśvara’s wisdom. Regarding this "locus of wisdom," there are two meanings:
first, that Maheśvara possesses mastery over wisdom; second, that through the fulfillment of the wisdom resulting from karmic retribution, he achieves the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

Regarding the second section, "Manifesting Superiority by Contrast," there are two parts: first, contrasting with those below to demonstrate the transcendence that distinguishes it from the Two Vehicles, which exhausts all [limitations].
This encompasses two phrases from the Sūtra: first, "surpassing all worldly paths" means crossing over the five destinies; thus, "path" (mārga) carries the sense of "cause" (hetu).
Regarding the second point, the supramundane wholesome roots of purity, the *Śāstra* states: "Furthermore, because the path to Nirvāṇa is pure.
This means that although those of the Two Vehicles have crossed over the five destinies, their Nirvāṇa is not yet pure because they still possess the three remaining traces (*traya-avaśeṣa*).
Since these [Bodhisattvas] now lack the three remaining traces, it is said to be "further purified."
Because it possesses these two qualities, it differs from the Two Vehicles.

The latter [quality], looking upward, reveals its similarity [to the Buddhas]; it is called the "exhaustion of Buddhahood" because the Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) equally fulfill the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Regarding the many meanings clarified through the power of self-exertion (*svātman*), they are presented because each subsequent stage is shown to be superior to the preceding one.
Within the second section on the addition of mental application (*manasikāra*), there are two parts:
first, the actual presentation; second, the inquiry and explanation regarding the reason for the partial application.
Of the ten phrases in the preceding section, the first is general and the remainder are specific.
Within the general section, there are two kinds of bodies:
first, the body of unsurpassed and supreme majestic power, which, like a king in an assembly, cannot be eclipsed by others.
The second [type of body] is the body that cannot be eclipsed by eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
The former is the excellence of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), while the latter is the excellence of the name-body (*nāmakāya*).

The section following "endowed with unimpededness" (*asaṅga*) is distinct; it separately enumerates the name-body as nine types of bodies, because the attributes added therein apply to all three [types of bodies].

It augments the physical body; when residing in the mind it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*), and when expressed through the mouth it is termed "eloquence. While the Sūtra says "bestowing wisdom," the Śāstra judges this to be "names"; these two texts are mutually abbreviated, and only when combined are the meanings fully revealed.
First is the eloquence of non-attachment: because one’s preaching of the Dharma is uninterrupted and free from obstruction, it is called "unimpeded joyful speech.
This means that because there is no biased dwelling or attachment, one is not hindered by either phenomena or principles; hence, it is termed unimpeded joyful speech.
Second, it is called "purified" because it possesses the analytical capacity to discern the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and can explain them correctly.
The *Śāstra* states: "The wisdom of excellent purity and capability is of four kinds:

first, objective condition (*ālambana*); second, phenomena (*dharma*); third, activity (*kriyā*); and fourth, accomplishment (*niṣpatti*). This is because one thoroughly knows the characteristics of success and failure regarding these meanings."
Regarding these terms: "condition" refers to phenomena produced through dependent origination, which is also termed "contingent observation.
"Two phenomena" refers to the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
"Three agents" refers to the functional activity of these two.
Regarding the "four proofs" (*siddhi*): by citing correct reasoning and examples, one establishes the three [criteria] mentioned above.
If these four are followed, they are termed "characteristics of proof" (*siddhilakṣaṇa*); if they are not followed, they are termed "characteristics of non-proof" (*asiddhilakṣaṇa*).
Because Bodhisattvas possess excellent knowledge, they are capable of discourse; this is termed "capable eloquence" (*pratibhāna*).
Furthermore, these four are frequently elucidated in the sūtras and śāstras.
In the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, they are referred to as the "four accomplishments."

The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (also known as the *Saṃtati-vimokṣa*) is the same text as the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, though translated at different times; in the fifth chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, it is titled "The Four Principles."

However, the two preceding sutras are extensive in their prose and obscure in their meaning; I shall now explain them according to the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* (Treatise on the Compendium of Abhidharma), chapter eleven, where the sequence of names is identical to that in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.

That treatise states: "The principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*) refers to the fact that when conditioned phenomena arise, they necessarily depend upon a multitude of conditions, just as, for example, the arising of a sprout depends upon the seed, the season, water, soil, and so forth."

Second, regarding function: this refers to the distinct functions of various phenomena characterized by difference. For example, the sense organs such as the eye perform the function of serving as the supports for consciousnesses such as visual consciousness, while objects such as visible form perform the function of being the focal objects for visual consciousness and so forth.
The three means of proof (*sādhana*) refer to the proclamation of statements that do not contradict valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in order to prove the meaning that is to be proven.
The meaning to be proven refers to the meaning to be proven as comprised by the specific distinctions of its own nature (*svabhāva*).

"Words that do not contradict the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) refers to statements such as the proposition (*pakṣa*) that are not contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of valid cognition.

"The four natural principles" (*dharmatā*) refers to the established nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) that exists naturally within all phenomena—whether characterized by specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—from beginningless time. This includes, for example, the fact that fire has the capacity to burn, or that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are impermanent.

That the sequence of those sūtras and śāstras is thus means that the dharmas of dependent origination possess this functional activity, which is established and proven by reason; subsequently, it concludes that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are eternally so.
Regarding the sequence of the present discussion on the meaning, it has already been explained as before.

Third is the power of eloquence that is spontaneous and unrestrained; one speaks without waiting for a sequential order, the flow of speech is uninterrupted, one proceeds at will through all matters, and does not forget names or meanings. Therefore, it is called the power of skillful recollection and non-forgetfulness.
This means that although various approaches are taught according to different gateways, the fundamental tenet is never forgotten.
Fourth is the eloquence of exposition, which, by employing various analogies as appropriate for those to be converted, is able to sever their doubts.
It is called "definitive" because it severs doubts according to the capacity of the listener;
it is called "clearly manifest" because it can respond appropriately to each case.
It is the "unmixed eloquence of the five," because the three types of identical wisdom are constantly present before him.
The three identical wisdoms are: the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and the non-dual characteristic (*advayalakṣaṇa*).
The specific characteristic refers to the distinctness of form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth.
The common characteristic refers to their shared nature of impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and non-self (*anātman*).
The non-dual characteristic is the single reality-principle.
Furthermore, the specific characteristic is the conventional truth, the common characteristic is the ultimate truth, and their non-duality is the Middle Way, the supreme truth of the primary meaning.
The various treatises, such as the *Vajrasamādhi*, all clarify that these three dharmas are not otherwise; therefore, they are said to be "pervasive.
They are what all bodhisattvas realize; therefore, they are said to be "awakening."

Sixth is the eloquence of manifestation, which, through the wisdom of the ten powers, transforms beings with mastery; because it severs delusions and attains the fruits [of the path], it is called "attaining enlightenment with mastery.
Seventh is the eloquence of fearlessness, because one is not timid or weak when speaking before others.
The eighth is the eloquence of the immeasurables, because it expounds the six kinds of right views regarding the Dharma of the sūtras and so forth in accordance with all-knowledge.
These six right views are themselves the gateways to the Dharma.
The *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* states: "First, the right view of true reality (*tattva-jñāna*), which is able to know the dharma of principle;
second, the right view of practice (*caryā*), which is able to know the dharma of practice."
Regarding these two doctrinal principles:
the third is the correct view that enables one to know the teachings;
the fourth is the correct view that transcends the two extremes, whereby one knows that the aforementioned rational dharmas are not to be grasped according to emotional attachment.
Fifth is the right view of the five inconceivables, which knows that the dharmas of prior practice accomplish virtue and transcend ordinary sentiment;
sixth is the right view of the faculties, desires, and natures, which knows that the teachings of prior instruction are expounded in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
The sixty-four names of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* are categorized under six types of logical gates (*yukti-mukha*), and their general purport does not differ [from this].
Regarding the nine points on "identical transformation" (*samāna-nirmāṇa*): it is because all Tathāgatas equally transform by means of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*).
Because the three karmas are preeminent, they are called "adornments.
The preceding ten sections have already explained the power of others.
From the second section, "For what reason," onwards, the text explains the reason for the partial bestowal of grace, thereby manifesting that one's own power is capable of receiving such grace.
To explain specifically in terms of mental karma (*manas-karman*), it is because the mind is the fundamental basis.
The initial inquiry regarding the mind states:
