"If the compassionate power of the Buddhas were to follow [the conditions] and be deficient, one might allow for partial application."
Since he possesses the power to bestow and the compassion to be universal, why is it that the aforementioned ten [qualities] are applied exclusively to Vajragarbha and not to others?
The following explains these ten phrases:
the first is general, while the remainder are specific.
This generally clarifies that those who attain this samādhi are entitled to receive special empowerment as a matter of course.
This is because Vajragarbha has attained it, whereas others have not.
How did he attain this samādhi?
The following section specifically reveals two causes for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*): first, it is brought about by original vows, which is indicated by the first phrase;
second, from "well-purified" (*suviśuddha*) onwards, it is because the body of samādhi encompasses meritorious qualities.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of purity based on self-benefit and the benefit of others; that is to say, the first four pertain to self-benefit and the latter four to the benefit of others.
First, the thoroughly pure profound resolve is the purity of cause, for through the ultimate degree of faith and aspiration, one is able to proceed toward the bodhisattva stages.
Because all are completely pure, it is called "well-purified" (*suviśuddha*).
This first [point] is the foundation of all practices; therefore, it is termed the "cause.
Next, the three [points] clarify the virtues of practice for one's own benefit.

This refers to the second [purity], namely the purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi*). It extends throughout the bodhisattva stages; as one cultivates the path, the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness) becomes like the full orb of the sun, universally illuminating the *dharmadhātu*. This is the quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*).
The three bodies are purified through transformation, meaning they become increasingly superior with each birth because of the accumulation of merit that aids the path.

Fourth is the purification through the subduing of the mind; because the habitual tendencies of the afflictions are skillfully severed, it is called "cultivation and treatment," which constitutes the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
The first three also serve as aids for realizing non-abiding.

Among the latter four [perfections] that benefit others, the fifth—pure hearing—is the means of benefiting others, for by being able to hear and retain the Buddha’s Dharma, one becomes a vessel for the Dharma.
The essence of the remaining three types of altruistic conduct consists of the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Sixth is purity of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because through superior supernormal powers one generates faith and understanding in sentient beings.

Seventh is purity of eloquence (*pratibhāna*); by the power of dhāraṇī, one encompasses all words and phrases within a single syllable, and because there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows, there is no error.

Eighth is purity through freedom from pride: this means that although one transforms sentient beings, one seals them with the seal of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna-mudrā*) so as not to violate the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*);

thus, there is no pride regarding transformation. Among these eight phrases, the first four are causes for self-benefit: first, the cause of diligence; second, the cause of non-forgetfulness; third, the cause of power; and fourth, the cause of non-attachment thereto.
These are to be assigned respectively to the preceding four lines, meaning that through the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*), one is able to initiate practice and so forth.
The latter four are the causes for benefiting others; specifically, five are the causes for severing doubt, because of the knowledge of the Dharma.
Sixth is the cause of reverent respect, because one causes others to enter through faith by means of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Seventh is the cause of the principle for turning the Dharma, because when the Dharma is in decline, one relies on other venerable teachings to recite and uphold it.
The eighth instruction concerns the cause for renunciation; the treatise states: "Thus, when the transformer attains self-benefit, they do not forget it.

This meaning clarifies that if, at the time of transformation, one apprehends signs and seals them with the *dharmadhātu-mudrā*, then self-benefit will not be forgotten, and one is thereby able to achieve renunciation.
Because the third body increases its majestic power and causes [the earth] to rise, it is said that "each extends [their hand].
This extension occurs without leaving their original positions; thus, there is no obstruction to prolonging or shortening [the reach].

Since all Buddhas touch [the earth], it is called "each extends," which signifies the non-obstruction of the one and the many. This is the supernormal power of mastery over the mind (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*) among the four unhindered powers (*pratisaṃvid*).
The remaining meanings are as explained previously in the third assembly.
The fourth section, beginning with "Touching the Head," constitutes the section on the arising [of the teaching].
The reason it arises is that the matters of the samādhi have been concluded.
What is meant by "concluded"?
It is because one has already attained superior power.
Although one has attained this power, why not remain in meditative concentration for a while?
The time for this explanation has arrived.
Why is it not explained within the context of meditative concentration? Because there is no verbal expression within concentration.
The fifth section, "Universal Announcement," constitutes the lower portion of the fundamental division (*mūla-bhāga*).
It briefly indicates the essential outline for the sake of the extensive version, and also serves as the basis for the subsequent request [for teaching].

As for speaking without being requested: if one does not personally state the basis [of the teaching], the assembly will not know whether it is to be taught or not, nor will they know what dharma is intended to be taught.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the six determinations are explained as the essence of the ground;
second, from "O Son of the Buddha, what are they? onwards, the ten names are listed to manifest the characteristics of the ground.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha, I do not see... onwards, the passage cites the simultaneous proclamations of the ten directions to manifest the essential excellence of this stage.
Regarding the essence of the first stage, it has already been analyzed as before.
Within the text, the first sentence serves as the heading, while the section beginning with "Addressing all Sons of the Buddha" constitutes the formal exposition.
Within this, the first phrase provides a general explanation, while the subsequent section beginning with "unmixed" provides a specific exposition.

Regarding the general explanation, the statement that "the Bodhisattva’s vow is well-determined" identifies the person and enumerates the dharmas; thus it is said that because a Bodhisattva establishes a vow to seek great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), it is called a "vow," which refers to the arousal of the bodhicitta in the first stage (*bhūmi*) mentioned below.
The reason this vow is called "well-determined" is that it is embraced by true wisdom.
That is to say, it guides and encompasses this vow so that all things accord with principle through decisive discernment and definitive establishment.
True wisdom is itself goodness, and goodness is itself determination; thus, it is named according to its essential function (*dharmatā-nirukti*).
Therefore, the treatise states: "That which is wholesome determination is precisely wholesome determination."
This distinguishes [the vow] from that which receives its name based on the *paratantra* (dependent nature).

This refers to having already entered the first stage (*bhūmi*), which is the certainty of realization; it is not the name of a "vow-reception" belonging to the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) prior to the stages.
If discussed comprehensively, there are six meanings of "determination" (*niyata*):

first, determination regarding the essence of practice, which is firm and stable; second, determination regarding that which is to be realized, meaning it must necessarily be realized; third, the certainty of being able to sever afflictions; fourth, decisive faith without doubt; and fifth, the certainty of the noble ones in saving sentient beings.
Sixth is the certainty of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood.
Within the subsequent section on distinctions, this "certainty of goodness" (śubha-niścaya) is of six types, corresponding to the six phrases in the Sūtra.
Both the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* explain these six; while their names differ slightly, their essential meaning is no different.
Regarding these six aspects of practice, the first five constitute the stage of self-perfection (*svabhāga*), while the last one constitutes the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa*).
Among the five, the first four pertain to self-benefit (*svārtha*) and the last one pertains to the benefit of others (*parārtha*).

Among the four [of the self-benefit category], the first three clarify the essential qualities of the practice (*caryā-svabhāva-guṇa*), while the last one reveals the functional efficacy of the practice (*caryā-kriyā-śakti*).
Among these three, the first two encompass the essence of conduct, while the last one is fully endowed with its virtues.
Within the former two, the first clarifies the intrinsic nature of conduct, and the second reveals that conduct is free from faults.

Therefore, taking the self-nature—which is free from faults and encompasses virtues—as the cause, one perfects the practices for the dual benefit [of self and others] to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood; this is the aspect of these practices.
"Undifferentiated" means that the characteristics of contemplation are well-determined, because the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness) is of a single-taste characteristic.

This means that when the fundamental essence takes suchness as its object, the identity of object and wisdom constitutes the characteristic of contemplation; thus, there is no admixture of conceptual signs.
Second, regarding "the invisible": this is the true, virtuous, and definitive state, which is not the domain of any worldly being, because it is supramundane.
This means that this true wisdom transcends the destructible phenomena of the world; therefore, it is called "ultimate reality" (*tattva*).
Because it is ultimate reality, it is not seen by worldly wisdom.
Third, "vast as the dharma-realm" refers to its supreme goodness and certainty.
The general commentary on the treatise states: "Because it is the great dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and because it is the root of all Buddhas.
Herein, the former phrase identifies the dharma-realm as that which is to be realized, and also explains the meaning of "great" (mahā).
The second phrase reveals the wisdom that is capable of being like the earth, and it also explains the broad meaning [of "dharmadhātu"].
As for why the *dharmadhātu* is called a "realm" (*dhātu*), first, it has the sense of a cause, because it is the root of both delusion and awakening;
second, it has the sense of nature, because it is the fundamental nature of all phenomena.

Now, the wisdom that is like the earth serves as the root of Buddhahood; thus, one attains "suchness" (tathatā). How much more so when the essence is conjoined with suchness, wherein there is nothing to which one conforms?
Below follows the exegesis of the meaning.
The Sūtra sets forth "vastness," and the commentary explains it through "supreme goodness."
In what way are these identical?
The treatise explains in summary: "Great, supreme, lofty, and vast are synonymous names for a single essence, because they refer to the meaning of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
To say 'single essence' means that it is of one and the same flavor."
Regarding the alternative names: they follow the meanings of the characteristics of the dharmas.

Because its essence is omnipresent, it is called "Great" (Mahā); because its marks cannot be grasped by the mundane mind, it is called "Supreme" (Vijaya); because its principle transcends the realm of calculation, it is called "High" (Uccha); because its function encompasses all things without exception, it is called "Vast" (Viśāla).
The above explains the two characters "vast" (guang-da).
Next, the name "Dharmadhātu" is explained as being because all phenomena (dharmas) are such by their very nature (dharmatā).
Regarding "all phenomena," this explains the character "dharma."
"Dharmatā" means the sense of "element" (*dhātu*), because its nature is inherently so.
All subsequent instances of the term "dharmatā" should be understood according to this principle.
The above explains the *dharmadhātu* as that which is thus.
The following section explains that the wisdom which is capable [of such realization], like the earth, also receives four names.
First, the *Great Commentary on the Ultimate Meaning* (*Mahā-artha-vyākhyā*) states:
"Furthermore, the contemplation of the Great True Suchness of the Dharma-realm surpasses the wisdom of ordinary beings and the two vehicles."

Regarding the statement that "the pure dharmas are thus pure by their very nature," this purity differs from the previously mentioned essence of *tathatā* (suchness), as it encompasses both the defiled and the pure.
This is the ground of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

It is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*) because its essence is such; it is called "Great" (*mahā*) because it is all-pervasive; and it is called "Supreme" (*viśiṣṭa*) because, in contrast to ordinary and inferior states, it transcends them.
The second commentary explains the broad meaning as follows:

"Furthermore, it is the stage of the Great Collection of Dharma-realm Expedients; this means that because the Mahāyāna teachings are established by the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one realizes the ultimate truth while thoroughly understanding conventional reality, thereby extensively gathering great practices."
Since it penetrates both types of wisdom, it is called the Mahāyāna.
The third explanation of its lofty meaning states:
"The great white dharma-dhātu is wholesome because all dharmas are such by their very nature."
This means that because untainted wholesome dharmas manifest as supramundane, they are the wholesome qualities accomplished by the two types of knowledge.
Four [categories] are established according to their meaning, yet they do not transcend the identity of object and wisdom.
The fourth is ultimate reality, which is like space and extends to the end of the future; this is the cause for the definitive determination of goodness.
This has two aspects:
first, it is the cause that produces the fruit of impermanent craving; as for this cause being like space, it is by depending upon it that all forms arise, and because these forms are inexhaustible.
Second, it is the cause of the eternal fruit, because one thereby attains the path to nirvana; thus the sutra says, "until the end of the future.
One interpretation states:
first, it acts as the generative cause (*janakahetu*), because it gives rise to the conditioned fruit of bodhi.
Second, it serves as the cause of comprehension (*parijñā-hetu*), because it comprehends the unconditioned fruit of nirvāṇa.

This conforms to the characteristics of dharmas (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), but does not conform to the tenet of the Sūtra, because according to the tenet of the Sūtra, permanence and impermanence are neither identical nor different.
Now, to provide a direct explanation of the treatise, it clarifies that the wisdom of this stage possesses two capacities:

first, because it is quiescent yet constantly active, it serves as the cause for non-eternality; although its activity waxes and wanes, the wisdom itself has no arising or ceasing, just as the space upon which it relies is not non-eternal. Thus, the Sūtra clarifies that this wisdom is ultimately like space.

Because it functions in two ways while remaining eternally quiescent, it serves as the cause for the eternal fruit; although nirvāṇa is forever still, the essence of wisdom is not non-existent—otherwise, how could one reach the end of the future limit?
If one synthesizes the three bodies, then activity constitutes the nirmāṇakāya, quiescence the dharmakāya, and wisdom the saṃbhogakāya; thus they are not impermanent.
Furthermore, even if wisdom is taken as the cause of realization (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*), it simultaneously realizes both bodhi and nirvāṇa.
The treatise states: "The path to nirvāṇa—the path is itself bodhi.
If these aspects are mutually integrated and subsumed, they certainly do not depend on words.
As for speaking of "craving for impermanence," it is employed to suit the capacities of those to be taught.

Regarding "pervading all Buddha-fields and rescuing and protecting all sentient beings": because it is a great, virtuous, and definitive resolve that accords with and performs deeds for the benefit of others, it is called "great" by virtue of its universal coverage.

The treatise further states: "Next, regarding 'well-determined,' this vow does not abide exclusively in either the mundane world or nirvana. This means that by virtue of the excellence of prior causes, great wisdom does not abide in saṃsāra;
and by virtue of this great goodness, great compassion does not abide in nirvana.
Although there was previously mentioned the application [of the cause], it is likewise accomplished by wisdom. Some say:

because one grasps the aforementioned causes for the eternal fruit, one does not abide in saṃsāra; because one grasps the aforementioned causes for the impermanent fruit as well as this great goodness, one does not abide in nirvāṇa.

This does not contradict reason; however, from the perspective of the dual negation (*dvaya-niṣedha*), both do not abide, whereas from the perspective of the dual illumination (*dvaya-avabhāsa*), both abide—meaning that because of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one constantly dwells within saṃsāra and so forth. Therefore, the treatise states that it is "not abiding exclusively."
Sixth: "For the sake of all" and below refers to the excellence of being free from timidity, because one enters the stage of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*) without timidity.
The *Śāstra* omits the phrase "protected by all Buddhas," stating only that one enters the stage of wisdom without timidity.
If one follows this sutra, it is because of protection that one enters wisdom without timidity.

Regarding "protection by the Buddha," it means that through wise action one enters the realm of the Buddha; because the Buddha’s wisdom illuminates it, the protection afforded by the Buddha and the entry into the stage of wisdom mutually reinforce one another.
The discussion below on the six aspects being perfectly interfused can be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Within the characteristics of the second stage, there are four parts:

first, the inquiry that introduces the subject; second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the enumeration of the number and the manifestation of their commonality; third, from "What are they? onwards, the inquiry into the number and the listing of the names; fourth, from "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva" onwards, the conclusion of the names and the manifestation of their excellence.
The first [point] is easily understood.
Regarding the second, because it pertains to generation, maintenance, and abiding, it is explained in the same way for all three periods of time.
The phrase "explained in the same way" appears in the text as part of the characteristics of earth (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), but its meaning encompasses the essence of earth (*dharmatā*) as well.

Within the list of names for the three [categories], in order to counteract the ten obstacles, realize the ten suchnesses, and accomplish the ten supreme practices, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are explained and various treatises are cited; these are all analyzed as they are set forth in detail in the subsequent extensive commentary.
Now, based on the root treatise, I shall briefly explain the names of the stages.

The treatise states: "Because one accomplishes the supreme practices for one's own benefit and the benefit of others, and experiences great joy upon first realizing the state of a noble one, it is therefore called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*)."
This has two meanings:

first, because the twofold benefit has been newly accomplished; second, because the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*) has been newly attained, one gives rise to joy as the original aspiration is fulfilled.

Second, because one is free from the stains of afflictions (*kleśa*) that give rise to erroneous thoughts and the violation of precepts, and is thus endowed with pure morality, it is called the "Stainless Stage" (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
This has three meanings:
first, separation from the cause, which refers to being free from the afflictions that give rise to transgressions of commission;
second, separation from the conduct of the fruit, which refers to being free from the evil karma of violating the precepts; hence the term "and so forth."
The third is "separation through antidotes," which refers to the fulfillment of pure ethical discipline.
It is called the "Luminous Stage" because the Dharma appears through the illumination of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
This has but a single meaning: that the three types of wisdom illuminate the Dharma heard on that very stage.

If one follows the subsequent treatise, there is another interpretation: it refers to attaining the characteristic of the light of wisdom (*jñāna-āloka-lakṣaṇa*) of the fourth stage, such as the concentration of "attaining light" (*āloka-labdha-samādhi*).

Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "The wisdom of that which is without activity and without the activity of arising is called 'light'; because one relies upon this light, it is named the 'Stage of Light' (*prabhākari-bhūmi*)."

However, both the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and this sutra name this stage "Luminous" (*Prabhākari*), because by accomplishing supreme meditative concentration and the great dhāraṇīs of the Dharma, one is able to emit the boundless light of wondrous wisdom.
This involves three meanings:

first, concentration (*samādhi*) acts as that which initiates; second, retention (*dhāraṇī*) acts as that which maintains; and third, the light of wisdom (*prajñā-āloka*) of the subsequent stage acts as that which is initiated and maintained.
However, because the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) pertain to the initial [stage] while the "Radiant" (*Prabhākari*) pertains to the subsequent [stages], their designations differ.
"Because the fire of wisdom can burn the fuel of the four afflictions that cause forgetfulness, it is called the 'Blazing Ground' (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
Blazing refers to the flame of wisdom; therefore, this is named the Ground of Blazing Wisdom."

This also encompasses the meanings of the two lower stages; it refers to how the fire of fundamental wisdom can now burn away the afflictions of the preceding stage—those involving the pride of relying on hearing, retaining, and not forgetting the teachings.

Second, regarding the arising of function from subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), the subsequent treatise states: "Within the light of the mani-jewel of the dharma-illumination of that realized wisdom (*sākṣātkṛta-jñāna*), it emits the light of the *āgama*; it enters into the meanings of immeasurable dharma-gates, and its light and wisdom universally illuminate and manifest throughout."
For this reason, the name of this stage is explained as "Blazing" (Arciṣmatī).
Question:
According to the first meaning, do not the various preceding and succeeding stages also burn away the afflictions?
For two reasons, this stage alone receives this name:
first, in terms of its provisional stationing, it is said that this stage provisionally takes the place of supramundane, untainted [wisdom];
second, in terms of the three trainings, this stage corresponds to wisdom, as it is where wisdom is first attained.

"Because one attains five types of supramundane wisdom and, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), is able to deliver those who are difficult to deliver, it is called 'Difficult to Conquer' (*Sudurjaya*).
This has but a single meaning: that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are non-contradictory, and thus are exceedingly difficult to conquer.

Because those on the third stage remain within the mundane world and have not yet attained liberation, while those on the fourth stage, though liberated, cannot conform to the world, remaining largely stalled at the two extremes and finding it difficult to transcend them.

Now, having attained transcendence of the world and yet being able to conform to worldly conventions, skillfully mastering the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), and being able to bridge the gap between the ultimate and the conventional to overcome partiality and stagnation—this is truly "Difficult to Conquer" (*Durjayā*).
Because this is first attained, it alone receives that name.
"The sixth is called the Ground of Presence (Abhimukhī) because the great wisdom of the uninterrupted practice of the six pāramitās manifests before one."
This means that skillfully penetrating dependent origination and inducing non-conceptualization is called the practice of *prajñā*.
To perceive it as if directly before one's eyes is called "manifest" (*sammukhībhūta*).
It is termed "interrupted" (*sāntara*) in contrast to what follows, because in the seventh stage one remains constantly in contemplation.

"Because one exerts effort in the practice of the signless (*animitta*) through the sevenfold cultivation of goodness, ultimately surpassing both the mundane and the supramundane paths of the two vehicles, it is called 'Far-Going' (*dūramgama*).
This may have three meanings:
first, because one skillfully cultivates the signless and reaches the limit of the signless, it is called "Far-Going."
Second, because its effort reaches its ultimate limit, it is called "Far-Reaching" (dūraṅgama);
third, because it surpasses what preceded it, it is called "Far-Reaching.

These two points together constitute a single meaning: the phrase "skillfully cultivating signless practice" explains the character *xing* (practice), while the section beginning with "effort" explains the character *yuan* (far).
However, there are two meanings to "skillfully cultivated" (*su-bhāvita*):

first, in the preceding stage, because there were intervals [of distraction], it was not called skillfully cultivated; now, because one is constantly in contemplation, it is called skillfully cultivated.

Second, abandoning existence for the sake of non-existence is not skillful cultivation of non-existence; now, because one is free from both existence and non-existence, it is called skillfully cultivated.
What is meant by "simultaneous detachment"?
It means that because there is skillful means within emptiness, one is detached from existence; because there is sublime practice within existence, one is detached from non-existence.
The following explanation of "distance" clarifies the meaning of distance through the ultimate perfection of its application.
Since it is as remote as the very limit of a single world-system (*dhātu*), what further distance could there be?
The first three stages are similar to the mundane realm; having transcended them, one has already gone far.
While the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages were expected to be similar to those of the Two Vehicles, they now also transcend them.
In the fifth stage, the ultimate and the conventional are not in conflict; how does this differ from here, where both existence and non-existence are simultaneously transcended?
Briefly, there are three differences:
first, they are still unable to transcend the two vehicles;
second, although they enter the conventional through the ultimate, they are not yet masterful in the simultaneous practice of both.
Third, because they have not yet attained the profound *prajñā*, their dual practice is not yet deep and subtle.
"The eighth is called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) because the maturation of its retributive conduct is signless (*animitta*) and uninterrupted."
This also has three meanings:
first, because one abandons the activities of the triple world that produce the fruit of transformation through rebirth, it is called "retributive activity" (*vipākakarma*).
Because one initiates activities based on this [state] such that they are accomplished spontaneously, its functional power is unshakable.
Second, having attained the wondrous wisdom of signlessness (*animitta*) and the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one is unmoved by signs.
Third, immediately following these two, one is unmoved by afflictions (*kleśa*).

Taken together, this constitutes a single meaning: that while the signlessness of the preceding stage has already been attained without interval, and even afflictions cannot move it, it is still moved by the activity of effort; thus, it does not yet possess the name "unmoving."
Now, because of the absence of effort (*anābhoga*), the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*) proceeds spontaneously and uninterruptedly; therefore, the three cannot disturb it.
This can be verified by the analogies of the lower wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*) and the Brahmā-king.

"Because one attains the nine unimpeded powers (*anāvaraṇa-bala*), accomplishes the teaching of the Dharma, and fulfills the practice of benefiting others, it is called the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
The attainment of unimpeded wisdom alone is not yet termed 'excellent'; it is only when one teaches universally and benefits all universally that it is designated as 'excellent'."
"Because one attains the great Dharma-body and achieves complete mastery, it is called 'Dharma-Cloud' (dharmameghā).
This has two meanings:

first, attaining the essence of the great Dharma-body and the Dharma-cloud, and achieving complete mastery—this explains the meaning of 'Dharma-Cloud. It refers to the sovereign function of raining down the teaching; thus, this name is applied from the perspective of the speaker."
"Second, attaining the great Dharma-body" clarifies the meaning of "Dharma," as this refers to being a great vessel for the Dharma.
"Endowed with mastery" explains the meaning of "cloud," as it is able to receive the rain-like teachings of the Tathāgata.
The subsequent section on the "Explanation of Names" will provide a detailed exposition of these terms.
Briefly stated, there are four pairs of reasons by which these ten stages receive their names:

first, regarding the relationship between the phenomenon (*dharma*) and its metaphor (*upamā*), the stages of "Blazing Wisdom" (*Arciṣmatī*) and "Dharma Cloud" (*Dharmameghā*) employ both phenomena and metaphors together, while all others rely solely on the phenomena themselves.
Second, regarding essence and function: *Pramuditā* (Joy) and *Sādhumatī* (Good Wisdom) are named according to their essence, while all others are named according to their function.

Third, regarding self and other: *Vimalā* (Stainless) and *Acalā* (Immovable) receive their designations from the perspective of others, while all others are established by name according to their own intrinsic meaning.

Fourth, although they are superior when compared within their respective stages, only the "Far-Reaching" (Dūraṅgamā) receives its name from its relation to others; all the remaining stages receive their names based on their own specific characteristics.
These ten stages are perfectly interfused, and each stage possesses them all.

If one considers them according to their sequential arrangement (*xingbu*), then the name of each preceding stage should encompass those that follow, while the designation of each succeeding stage would not encompass those that precede it.
For example, the meaning of the name "Joyful" (*pramuditā*) encompasses all ten stages, whereas the title "Dharma-Cloud" (*dharmameghā*) does not include the preceding nine.
Now, in order to manifest their distinct characteristics, each is named according to its initial attainment; these will be further elucidated in the subsequent text.
The fourth [section] concludes by naming them to manifest their excellence, which may be understood.
Regarding the third [section], which demonstrates the essential superiority of the stages (*bhūmi*), it is intended to inspire a sense of longing and veneration in sentient beings.
The text has two parts:

first, it clarifies that [the Buddha] neither sees nor speaks [in a specific way], thereby conversely revealing that both the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* throughout the ten directions do indeed speak.
Second, it investigates and explains the reason for this.
The objection states:
"Since the Buddha-lands differ, their modes of transformation and teaching are also diverse; why then must the ten stages be taught in all of them?
The intent of the response is as follows:
This is because it is the most supreme.

That is to say, all phenomena are suchness; when their substance is realized as suchness, one becomes a sage. Apart from this realized wisdom, all else is merely provisional; therefore, this is essential and supreme.
The text consists of four phrases:
the first two phrases provide a general heading to manifest its excellence.
The first phrase concerns realized practice (*pratyātma-pratipatti*), meaning that the Buddhas realize this as the cause for attaining *bodhi*.
All others assist the path; therefore, this is the most supreme and most excellent.
Regarding the second phrase, "the dharma-gate of the Āgamas," it is called the essence of the Dharma.
"Radiance" refers to its illuminating all other dharma-gates.
The latter two phrases specifically clarify its characteristics.

The first phrase explains the aforementioned *āgama*, stating "discriminative exposition," which clarifies that the light of the preceding dharma is the functional essence (*kārya*) of the teaching. This phrase refers to the dharma-gate illuminated by that teaching; thus, the treatise states: "To discriminate the matters of the ten stages is to reveal the dharmas known by worldly knowledge."

The latter phrase clarifies that the aforementioned realized path is not something known by the worldly knowledge (*loka-jñāna*) prior to the stages; it is called "inconceivable. Therefore, the treatise states: "Because it reveals supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*), one speaks of the realization and then remains silent; thus, one addresses them as 'Son of the Buddha' (*buddhaputra*)."
The Fundamental Section has been explained.
*The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 31.

Chapter Six: "At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva spoke. This section below, concerning the requests, consists of three parts:

first, his remaining silent after having spoken; second, from "At that time" onwards, the five requests made by the three families; third, from "At that time, Vajragarbha observed" onwards, the section on granting the scope of the discourse.
The reason for his silence is that he intends to expound [the teaching]; he must first remain silent so as to cause the great assembly to feel a thirst for it and entreat him to speak.
There are briefly two reasons for awaiting such an entreaty:
first, to increase the reverence for the Dharma among the bodhisattvas; [and second, to demonstrate that the Dharma is not easily obtained].

Second, in the preceding section on the "Stages" (*bhūmi*), the excellence of the stages was extolled as an increase in bliss; this was intended to give rise to correct understanding within this request.
How is such understanding produced?

It is by means of the request that the reasons for both speaking and remaining silent are obtained, thereby revealing that the essence of the stages is profoundly deep and transcends speech and thought, so that the assembly may first gain comprehension.
Later, when hearing the exposition of the divisions, one does not grasp them according to the sounds, because this avoids erroneous understanding.
Precisely for this reason, there is a third stage consisting of the demonstration and exposition of the limits [of the teaching].
The first stage, characterized by silence, can be understood accordingly.

In the second section on requests, there are three distinct types of requests, which are divided into three parts: first, the request by Vimukticandra; second, the request by the great assembly; and third, the request by the Tathāgata.
The reason for involving these three families is to manifest the profound and subtle nature of the Dharma so that those who hear it may understand it.
When the leaders of the assembly proclaim it, those present are inspired with longing; when the Master of Transformation further exhorts them, the task is finally brought to completion.
The Way is great and encompasses all; it is because the Dharma ought to be requested.
To comply with the requester, this assembly is capable of hearing it, for the words shall not be in vain.
To fulfill the request, the Tathāgata protects and mindful of them, they will give rise to faith and acceptance, for the words possess verification.
This refers to the request based on causes and the request based on arising; it also follows a sequential order.
Furthermore, the "request by the Buddha" is termed an "empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
This means that although the assembly has already made their request, it is only through the majestic light of the Principal Buddha that they become capable of preaching.
It is also called "Instruction" (*śāsana*), because it reveals the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata and transmits the Buddha's doctrine.
Furthermore, the requests made by the first two families demonstrate that the dharmas of this stage are cultivated by individuals;
the request made by the last family demonstrates that the dharmas of this stage are what have been realized by the Buddha.

The first two requests may be found in other sutras, whereas the final request is unique to this scripture; the three requests in the *Lotus Sutra* belong exclusively to this single school, precisely because the Dharma of the Grounds is so profoundly deep that it is difficult to explain while remaining within the stages of spiritual development.

Furthermore, regarding the sequence of the three requests: the first request was made by Vimukticandra because he was the leader of that assembly; otherwise, other questions would have caused confusion.
For what reason did the great assembly not ask their questions in a disordered manner?

Because the assembly was well-disciplined—due to the two preceding periods of silence and the three formal requests that regulated the assembly at the appropriate times—next, the assembly made their request to manifest their devotion;
yet this was not a contentious uprising, for they followed the protocol of the previous requests by making the request in unison, and thus there was no disorder.
Later, as they were weary of hearing the principles to their limit, the Tathāgata exhorted them to speak.
Now, within the initial request made by the leader of the assembly, there are three requests in total.

The reason for there being three is to accord with worldly etiquette: too few would lack earnestness, while too many would lead to confusion; thus, the middle way is attained. Furthermore, because there are three instances of cessation [of the discourse], it serves to balance the occasion and to subdue the capacities of the disciples.

Although each of the two families assists in accomplishing only a single request, one should divide it into three sections based on the three requests; if the three instances of silence are included, it should be divided into six. Since the silence of remaining in stillness at the outset serves as the basis for all five requests and cannot belong exclusively to the first, the phases of silence and requesting are combined to form five sections.
First, the expression of wonder and the request to dispel doubts;
second, the refusal based on the difficulty of receiving the profound Dharma;
third, the praise of the assembly’s capacity to hear it and the subsequent request.
Fourth is the cessation due to incapacity for harm, meaning that although there are those who are capable, there are also those who are incapable;

fifth is the request by praising both the person and the Dharma, meaning that because the Dharma is profound, even those incapable of hearing it receive the Buddha’s protection and thus it ought certainly to be taught; at this point, Vajragarbha’s reasoning was exhausted, and he could no longer refuse the request.
Regarding the first request, it is divided into two parts:
first, the great assembly perceives his silence and conceives doubt; second, from the words "Vimukticandra," the doubt is voiced as a formal request.
Now, the first part.
As for the question of "what is the cause and what is the condition," these are words of doubt and wonder:
is it because the speaker is unable to speak, or is it because the listener is incapable of hearing?
From "Vajragarbha" onwards, the matters of doubt are set forth.
Second, the raising of these doubts as a request for instruction has two parts:
first, the description of the cause for the request, which refers to his leading the assembly's doubts.
Second, the formal request is made by means of verses.
This passage consists of five stanzas which demonstrate that there is no fault in preaching or listening, and thus it is appropriate to speak.
This is divided into two parts:
The first verse states that the speaker is without fault, thereby dispelling the assembly's doubt as to the cause;
the latter four [verses] state that the listener is without fault, thereby dispelling the assembly's doubt as to the condition.

Although the first two [cases] appear similar, the inquiry into the reasons for the silence serves to dispel the doubts of the assembly; whereas the latter three requests for instruction serve to fulfill the desires of the assembly. The text merely indicates this concisely.
It is not that they do not interpenetrate one another; therefore, the previous judgment is maintained.
Regarding the first point, this praises the purity and faultlessness of the speaker’s awakening.
The first two characters of the verse and the final three characters are combined to form a phrase of inquiry, meaning that there exists an intermediate state of pure awakening free from fault.
Why is it not explained? Although the noble virtues are manifold, the specific praise of "pure awakening" (*viśuddha-vitarka*) is because it is stated to be the cause.
Awakening here refers to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), for it is by means of these that one attains the preliminary mental application (*vāk-prayoga*) of speech.
Possessing both the capacity for practice and that which is to be remedied, yet speaking without deliberation, it is therefore called "Pure Awakening" (*viśuddha-bodhi*).
One who possesses this pure awakening is termed a "person of pure awakening.
These three characters constitute the general [definition], while all the others are specific [details].
Furthermore, the praise of pure awakening possesses two superior capacities:
first, the inclusion of remedies, which refers to the possession of mindfulness and wisdom.
Mindfulness refers to the four foundations of mindfulness; wisdom refers to suchness-wisdom (*tathatājñāna*).
Second, being free from all faults, which refers to the remaining ten syllables.
Each syllable has a dual function: first, because there is that which can counteract, that which is to be counteracted does not arise.
There are two types of that which is to be counteracted:

The first is miscellaneous awareness (*vikalpa*), which refers to the discursive thought and investigation of ordinary beings associated with the four inversions; this is the inversion regarding phenomena, for which the four foundations of mindfulness serve as the remedy.

The second is the cause of miscellaneous awareness, which consists of recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination; this refers to revolving according to names and signs, which is the inversion regarding principle, for which the wisdom of *tathatā* serves as the remedy.
The former refers exclusively to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the latter applies to both ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Regarding the phrase "free from faults," it means being free from three kinds of faults:
first, because one is endowed with virtues such as non-hatred (*adveṣa*), one is free from the faults of stinginess and envy.
This means that non-hatred (*adveṣa*) counteracts envy (*īrṣyā*), while non-attachment (*alobha*) is included by extension.
Non-attachment counteracts stinginess (*mātsarya*); non-delusion (*amoha*) does not [counteract] inequality, because non-delusion is already subsumed under the aforementioned "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
Second, because the superior and sublime stages have already been explained previously, there is no fault of indolence regarding the teaching of the Dharma.
Third, because he possesses the power of eloquence for joyful exposition, there is no fault of lack of delight in speaking.
However, mindfulness and wisdom are specifically designated as "remedies" because they serve to counteract discursive thoughts and the like; thus, they receive the name "remedy.

In contrast, non-aversion and the others do not primarily intend to remedy envy and so forth; rather, since those [defilements] naturally cease in their presence, they are simply called "freedom from faults."
The second section, consisting of four verses praising the faultlessness of the audience, is divided into three parts.
The first two verses praise the assembly of co-born beings; the *Śāstra* states: "Because they are determined in the Dharma and because they delight in hearing it."
The next verse praises the assembly of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); the commentary states: "It further demonstrates that the minds of the others are pure.
The final verse praises both groups together; the commentary states: "Furthermore, it reveals that this entire assembly is capable of hearing the Dharma."
Regarding the first two verses now: the former verse praises the faculties, hence it says "determined";
the latter verse praises the desire, hence it says "desiring to hear.
If one has the desire but lacks the faculties, although one hears, one will not understand.
If one possesses the faculty but lacks the aspiration, even if they hear [the teaching], they will not accept it; therefore, both must be praised.
Here, "having the same Dharma" (samānadharma) refers to being of the same birth (sahaja), distinguishing them from those of a different birth.
"Certainty" (niyata) refers to the spiritual capacity (indriya), distinguishing them from those who merely possess aspiration.
The first phrase serves as the general definition; the treatise states: "Determination (*niścaya*) means being discerning (*medhā*) and clear-sighted (*prajñā*).
Discernment is the faculty (*indriya*); for through discernment one can understand the teaching, and through wisdom (*prajñā*) one can enter into realization.
The next two phrases distinguish [the specific types]. The *Śāstra* states: "There are three kinds of certainty:
first, the certainty of the superior vow for great enlightenment, which is why it is called 'courageous';
second, the certainty of renown, wherein others respect one's goodness, which is why it is called 'without timidity'."
Because they are internally free from cowardice, they are externally renowned for their great fame.

Third is the certainty of being well-received: this refers to the fact that the speaker possesses excellent knowledge; as the Sūtra says, "The Dharma is taught only when one is capable of receiving it."
The meaning of the subsequent line’s inquiry regarding silence can be understood accordingly.

In the following verse, which praises desire, the first line refers to the phenomena that are desired; the next two lines explicitly clarify the existence of desire; and the final line concludes with a request.

The treatise states: "In this regard, if there is only the certainty of scripture (*āgama*) and no certainty of realization (*adhigama*), there is only the certainty that is not manifest (*aparokṣa*) and no manifest certainty (*parokṣa*)."

Thus, because those who are determined vessels for the Dharma are not yet fully satisfied, they are unable to hear and receive [the teaching]. This is because what is present here is the arising of desire to see it manifest; it is not that the sense-faculties (indriya) are present, but rather that they are merely latent equipment (sāmagrī).
The meaning here clarifies that one who possesses the faculties but lacks desire is incapable of hearing the Dharma.

Now, the preceding verse refers to one who possesses both types of certainty—certainty regarding the teaching through decisive understanding and certainty regarding the principle through decisive realization—and thus represents the faculties that are not present before one [in the sense of lacking desire].

Furthermore, there is the present desire manifested by this verse; since the teaching and its realization are definitive, it possesses complete certainty and is thus capable of receiving [the dharma].
As for the mind being free from timidity, the *Śāstra* states: "The sons of the Buddha possess fearless wisdom. Fearlessness is precisely the absence of timidity.
The mind that accords with principle is called wisdom (*jñāna*); however, there are two kinds of wisdom:
first, that which realizes the Dharma, which belongs to the preceding faculties;
second, that which is currently experienced, which belongs to the present desire.
Since desire must also be accompanied by wisdom, one’s mind remains free from timidity when wishing to hear [the teaching].
Summarizing the two preceding verses: possessing both the faculties and the desire, I pray that you will explain the sublime meanings of all the stages (*bhūmi*).
The second section consists of one verse praising the assembly of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Since it simply refers to them as the "assembly," it praises both their faculties (*indriya*) and their inclinations (*ruci*).
The first line serves as the general statement; because their minds are free from turbidity, they are called "pure."
The three phrases constitute a distinction, specifically distinguishing them from the six turbidities:
first, the turbidity of lack of desire, which refers to having no intention to partake; this is remedied by abandoning indolence.
Second, the turbidity of improper deportment, which arises from a lack of reverence and solemnity; this is remedied through rigorous discipline.
First is the turbidity of the three poisons; because of greed for fame and the like, it is purified by means of cleanliness.

Second is the turbidity of divergent thoughts; arrogance-defilement, contemptuous defilement, and so forth are all termed "divergent thoughts," which are now treated by means of firm and immovable practice.
Third is the turbidity of insufficient merit; because one's roots of goodness are meager, the mind does not delight in dwelling amidst those teachings, which is treated by means of possessing merit.
The sixth is the turbidity of delusion (*moha-kaṣāya*); because it is characterized by ignorant darkness and a lack of clarity, it is countered by wisdom (*prajñā*).
The third verse praises both assemblies together by referring to them as "all."
Mutual gazing is the general [category].
The Treatise states: "They gaze at one another together" indicates the absence of defilement.
All others are specific [categories].
All are respectful and so forth, free from the defilement of contempt or negligence.
The second half of the verse uses a metaphor to show that their reverence for the Dharma becomes ever deeper; how, then, could there be any defilement?
The *Śāstra* quotes the Sūtra as saying: "Like bees desiring the ripened honey."
An ancient commentator explained:
"To direct the mind toward realization is like bees gathering mature honey;
to focus the intent on seeking the teachings is like one parched with thirst longing for nectar."
Now, if we simply speak of "mindfulness of honey," then both phrases encompass both the Teaching (śāsana) and the Realization (adhigama).
However, the bee’s mindfulness of honey and the thirsty person’s longing for the drink serve as metaphors for the aspiration for the joy of the Dharma;
the taste of liberation is further described as "excellent honey."
He further contemplates the nectar [of the Dharma], manifesting the subtlety of the teaching; his longing and thirst for it are profound.
The second section, beginning with "At that time, the one of great wisdom," addresses the point that the Dharma is so profound it is difficult to receive.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the statement of the intent; second, the response in verse. Within the former, causing the assembly to rejoice is the general form of the response.
This means that the original purpose of reciting the verses was to eliminate the preceding doubts and afflictions, thereby enabling the mind to attain joy.
There are two kinds of responses:
first, a response that is capable, because one possesses great wisdom oneself;
second, a response that is not timid, because one does not fear that the great assembly will be unable to comprehend it.
The treatise states: "These two [verses] demonstrate that there is no fault regarding oneself or others.
Therefore, the meaning of the subsequent verse clarifies that the Dharma is difficult to expound; it does not mean that one cannot expound it due to a lack of personal wisdom."
"It is merely said that it is difficult to hear; it does not mean that the great assembly is entirely incapable of hearing it.
Within the verses, the five stanzas are divided into four parts:

the first two stanzas clarify that the Dharma is difficult to expound, thereby dispelling the doubt raised by the previous question "For what reason? and establishing that [the Buddha] possesses wisdom.
The following verse reveals that the Dharma is difficult to hear, thereby dispelling the doubt as to the reason for the aforementioned [silence] and establishing the preceding fearlessness.
Three verses employ metaphors for the difficulty of preaching and hearing;
the final verse cites the difficulty to conclude with silence.
The first part is divided into two sections:
the preceding verse reveals the dharma that is difficult to express, while the subsequent verse clarifies the reason why it is difficult to express.
This is the first section.
The difficult characters at the end of the verse constitute the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), meaning that it is "difficult to obtain.
The reason why it is difficult to obtain is clarified in the subsequent verse.
This difficulty is of two kinds:
First is the most difficult [to realize], because its essence transcends names and forms; thus the Sūtra calls it "the foremost.
Second is the unprecedented difficulty, because it does not exist among [ordinary] characteristics; thus the Sūtra calls it "rare."
The preceding two [verses] clarify the characteristics of the objection.
What is the essential nature of this objection?
It is the first two lines of the verse.
The practice of the Bodhisattva is supramundane wisdom, which refers to the Path of Realization (*adhigama-mārga*).
Because the realizing mind engages with its objects, it is termed the "stages of practice" (*bhūmi-caryā*).

As for "phenomena" (*vastu*), this refers to the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which constitute the Path of Teaching (*deśanā-mārga*) due to the distinctions between their characteristics.
"Supreme" refers to the general explanation of the two superior [stages] above.
"The fundamental source of all Buddhas" explains the reason why the wisdom of realization is given the name "bodhisattva practice.
"Practice" (caryā) carries the meaning of "cause" (hetu).
One is called a Buddha because of awakening to the Buddha-wisdom; since this realized wisdom (pramāṇa) also awakens to the Buddha-wisdom, it serves as its basis.
"Basis" here means the cause.
Wherein does the difficulty lie regarding the establishment of this teaching and realization?

This means that while it is displayed through analytical exposition, it is difficult to display because the path of realization transcends the mind; likewise, the path of instruction, which relies upon realization, is also difficult to analyze.
Regarding the reason for this difficulty in the second explanation: the reason why the prior practices of the bodhisattvas are difficult is that they abide in subtle and profound meanings.
Therefore, the treatise states: "The meaning of that bodhisattva’s practice and abiding cannot be explained in such a manner.

In the verse, the first two lines contrast the inferior to manifest the profound; the next line reveals the sublime by way of the superior; and the final line demonstrates the difficulty of explanation by citing the confusion caused by hearing it.
Within this context, "difficult" refers to the general characteristic.
Why is it difficult?
Because it is difficult to attain and difficult to realize.
There are four ways in which it is difficult to obtain:
first, it is difficult to obtain because of its subtlety, as it is revealed to be beyond the scope of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
second, it is difficult to see and difficult to obtain, as it is not seen by the "eye of the mind" of the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

Third, it is difficult to attain because it is free from conceptualization; furthermore, it is not the object of the mundane wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). This is because the wisdom of the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) constitutes true cultivation, whereas it is not the object of the analytical cultivation through mental factors (*caitta*) of the stages prior to the first.

The four transcendental stages of the mind are difficult to attain; they are not merely beyond the realm of those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), nor are they the realm of the wisdom attained through cultivation by those born of retribution who have already ascended the stages. That which arises from the transformation of the basis (*pariṇāma*)—namely, the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*)—is called "born of retribution. Because one is able to know impermanence and so forth upon birth, it is called "well-attained wisdom of the path of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārgajñāna*). However, because this is not the wisdom that illuminates reality (*tattva*), it does not fathom the wisdom of the [ten] stages.

The state in which the knowledge of impermanence and so forth has not yet been forgotten within the mental sphere is called the "ground of mind" (*cittabhūmi*), because from the seventh ground downward, all stages still permit emerging from contemplation (*vyutthāna*).

Furthermore, this "skillfully attained wisdom of the path of cultivation" refers to the wisdom obtained subsequent to preparatory application (*prayoga-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), and not the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); therefore, it is distinguished [from the latter].

Therefore, within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the fifty-fifth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there is both the supramundane path of abandonment and the mundane-supramundane path of abandonment.
Since it also pertains to the mundane, [the latter] is not its object.
Since it is not the object of the four minds, whose object is it?
It is the object of Buddha-wisdom.
What is this wisdom?
Because one perceives the true meaning.
There are two senses in which it is "produced":
first, it gives rise to that Buddha-wisdom; [the second is...]
The second [point] is that it is a departure from birth, because it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
The final sentence states that it is difficult to explain because listeners become deluded by grasping at whatever they hear.

The second single verse reveals that [the teaching] is difficult to hear. The *Śāstra* states: "Having already explained that it is difficult to expound, we now further reveal that it is difficult to hear.

However, by citing within the verse those who possess the qualities and capacities to hear, the difficulty of hearing is revealed by contrast; this is also intended to lead people to train in the capacity to hear."
Among these, three phrases enumerate the virtues, while the final phrase establishes the capacity for hearing.
Within the first [section], the initial phrase serves as the general statement: that is, by maintaining a resolve to hear the Dharma as firm as a vajra, one is able to hear it.
The latter two phrases are distinct.
Firmness is of two kinds:
first, firmness of decisive faith, which corresponds to the second phrase; for without this firmness, one cannot enter into the dharmas belonging to others.
Second is the firmness of realization, which corresponds to the third phrase; for if there is no firmness of realization, one cannot enter into the dharmas of one's own level.
What are the characteristics of profound faith?

This means that regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, even if one's own mental wisdom cannot reach it, one looks up to and infers that the Buddha’s wisdom is not within one's own domain; this is the characteristic of profound faith.
It is precisely the "wisdom of looking up and inferring" among the three kinds of correct wisdom mentioned in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
What is that which is to be believed?
It is the supreme wisdom of the Buddha, because the wisdom of this stage is superior and identical to the Buddha’s wisdom.
There are two kinds of Buddha-wisdom:
First is the wisdom of enlightenment (*bodhijñāna*), which is the Dharma realized through one's own practice; it accords with the nature of reality and is boundless.

Second is the expedient wisdom of transformation (*nirmāṇajñāna*), which is the teaching for benefiting others; it manifests various distinctions according to the capacities of beings, appearing or remaining hidden as appropriate. This is precisely the "wisdom of all Buddhas" and the "gateways of wisdom" mentioned in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Because one is able to have faith in both of these two depths.
How is firmness realized?
This also has two aspects:
First, "knowledge" is that which realizes; second, the "mind-ground" is that which is realized.
The term "selflessness" applies to both the realizing subject and the realized object.
The mind-ground is the true reality of the two kinds of emptiness; the phenomena upon which it relies are the characteristics of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). As the treatise states:
The retributive results experienced within the three realms according to the mind are the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation consciousness).

Furthermore, all objects traversed by the mind are also termed the "mind-ground" (*cittabhūmi*); these consist of the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), as well as all internal and external objects that constitute the *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect) of the eight consciousnesses.
By understanding these two categories as they truly are—the emptiness of self and phenomena—one achieves the wisdom of non-self.
The subsequent phrase provides the conclusion:
having understood this meaning so difficult to hear, and thus possessing the two aforementioned firmnesses, one is finally able to hear the subtle and supreme wisdom described above.

The third section consists of one verse concerning the difficulty of explaining and hearing [the Dharma]. The first half is the simile, and the second half is the application to the Dharma (*dharmasama*).
Here, the meaning of the simile does not take empty space alone, because space where there is no painting cannot serve as a metaphor.
Nor should one take only the painting, because a painting on a wall cannot serve as a metaphor;
rather, one should take the painting in the sky.
The same applies to the metaphor of the wind.
Among these, the wind-painting that depends [upon it] serves as a metaphor for the *āgama*, while the empty space upon which it depends serves as a metaphor for realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*).
Nevertheless, the wind-painting within the empty space cannot be said to be non-existent, because if it were supported by a tree or a wall, it would be visible.
Nor can it be said that they exist, for they do not abide in emptiness.
Because they are neither existent nor non-existent, they are inexpressible; such is the intended meaning of the text. The treatise consists of three sections:

first, the explanation of the characteristics of the analogy; second, the explanation of the characteristics of the application; and third, the distinction between the analogy and what it does not resemble.
The beginning and middle [of this section] have three parts:

first, the individual explanation of two metaphors to clarify that it is not existent; second, the combined explanation of the two metaphors to clarify that it is not non-existent; third, the dual conclusion of the two metaphors to establish that it is inexpressible.
Regarding the two types of metaphors illustrated in the preceding section:

first, the actual manifestation of the metaphorical characteristics. As for the statement in this verse, "It demonstrates that colors painted in space are like those on a wall," this means that the colors painted in space are no different from the colors painted on a wall; therefore, it says they are "like a wall."
If that is so, why is it not seen?
The two [preceding points] demonstrate its non-existence; the treatise states: "Because it does not abide therein, it cannot be seen.
This means that a painting on a wall can be seen because there is a wall for it to abide upon.
A painting in the sky has nothing upon which it can rely for support, and therefore it cannot be seen.
The metaphor of the wind below also consists of two parts:
first, it is said that the wind in the sky is like a tree leaf; this precisely clarifies the characteristics of the metaphor.

The second [explanation] states that because it does not abide therein, it cannot be perceived; this demonstrates its non-existence. That is to say, wind upon tree leaves can be perceived because there are leaves for it to rely upon, whereas wind in the sky cannot be seen because there is nothing for it to abide in or rely upon.
The second section explains the two metaphors through a combined interpretation to demonstrate that they are not non-existent.

It says: "As for this 'mover,' it is not the case that these two things do not exist within emptiness. The intent of this treatise clarifies that one cannot perceive them simply because there is nothing upon which they can rely; it does not mean that the substance of the wind or the painted figure is entirely non-existent.
The three knots form the meaning of the "unspeakable": it is said that the phenomena of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśāyatana*) cannot be described.
As for "sphere," it refers to the sphere of infinite space; this is the emptiness upon which the painting of wind depends.
The phenomenon of space is the mark of wind-painting within emptiness.

According to the former sense, it cannot be said to exist; according to the latter sense, it cannot be said not to exist. Therefore, the location of this empty space, the painted phenomenon, and the phenomenon of wind are all ineffable.
In the second explanation of the application of the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), the three preceding sections are applied in sequence, yet they are combined only in pairs.
Regarding the initial treatise’s statement, "This painted wind is like the speaker," this applies the characteristics of the preceding analogy.

The subsequent treatise states: "Because it is not of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it cannot be perceived; because it does not abide and because it is adventitious (*āgantuka*)," this combines with the preceding "non-existence.
That is to say, "not being of intrinsic nature" combines with the preceding "non-abiding."
Regarding the phrase "because it is a guest": this refers to the reason why names lack intrinsic nature and do not abide.
That is to say, a name is a subordinate to reality; therefore, it has no place of abiding and lacks self-nature.
Second, combining with the preceding [point], it is not that there is nothing; it is said that within this [context] there is no such verbal expression.

Third, combining with the preceding, the conclusion is established as "inexpressible. Regarding the statement, "Thus, the differentiation of the excellence of the stages as revealed by the verbal expressions of Buddha-wisdom is difficult to perceive," Buddha-wisdom is itself the object of differentiation, which, when combined with the aforementioned [analysis], occupies the space of emptiness.
The statement "manifesting through verbal expression" refers to that which is capable of conceptual differentiation; it joins with the aforementioned matter within emptiness.
Because the expression follows from the intended meaning, it is likewise difficult to perceive; it joins with the aforementioned point of ineffability.
However, when discussing the Buddha’s wisdom, it is precisely what this sutra calls the Muni’s wisdom.
"Muni" here is translated as "Silent One," because the characteristic of wisdom is identical to the nature of wisdom.
That this is the wisdom of the stages yet is named the Buddha’s wisdom is because there is no duality in their essence.
Furthermore, this is merely because the translator, seeing the word "Muni," assumed it referred to Śākyamuni.
Thirdly, regarding the difference in the metaphors used for exclusion: the reason two metaphors are cited is that their underlying purposes are distinct.

The Treatise states: "Painting" is a metaphor for names and phrases because they are explained based on signs (*nimitta*). That is to say, painting possesses forms and characteristics, just as names and phrases possess their own syntactic structures; these are able to manifest the characteristics of the ground.
The wind is used as a metaphor for sound; like the nature of the wind, sound has no curvature or distortion.
Since the provisional and the real are distinct, both are mentioned together.

Furthermore, the provisional and the real depend upon one another, and it is impossible to lack either; thus it is said that "it is further explained" by means of these two matters. The speaker explains by means of these two matters, and the listener hears by means of these two matters; therefore, two metaphors are raised to simultaneously illustrate both speaking and hearing.
If one employs these two metaphors to illustrate that which is signified, there are still two layers of meaning:

first, the reason why the characteristics of the ground cannot be seen through the metaphors of wind and painting is that they share the same nature as the cognition of the ground, just as wind and painting merge with space;
second, wind and painting are further used as metaphors for the cognition of the ground.

The reason the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi*) cannot be spoken of is that it is identical with the fruit-stage (*phala-bhāga*) and is thus free from the characteristics of verbal expression, like wind and a painting merging with space.

If one proceeds from the fruit back toward the cause, it can indeed be spoken of; for when wisdom follows its characteristics, the stages possess distinctions, and when the ultimate meaning follows its expressions, it can be heard and spoken. This, then, is a hearing and speaking that is devoid of hearing and speaking.

The fourth section, consisting of one verse, raises an objection regarding the conclusion of silence: according to the principle established above, if [the teaching] is spoken by means of two matters and heard by means of two matters, then it can indeed be spoken and heard.
However, it is difficult to perceive; why then is it not explained?
Therefore, there is this verse.
Its meaning is as follows:
It is said that hearing is fundamentally for the purpose of realization and vision; what benefit is there in speaking of that which is difficult to see?
Moreover, since it is further compounded by being difficult to believe, I remain silent.
The first phrase refers to the Dharma realized and seen.
The second phrase refers to that which is difficult to realize; because it is the most difficult among difficulties, it is called "supreme.
The third phrase refers to that which is difficult to believe; because it is not realized or believed by those prior to the [first] stage, it is called "worldly."
The first three phrases raise the difficulty, while the final phrase concludes with silence.
Thirdly, Vimukticandra praises the assembly as being capable of hearing and requests [the teaching].

Although he has already offered praise previously, he praises them again here because, having heard the preceding words, it is difficult to find those who possess both realization and faith; thus, he demonstrates that this assembly possesses faith, realization, and the capacity [to understand].
First the prose, followed by the verses.
Within the former, there are two parts:
first, the narration of the request; second, from the words "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the formal articulation of the request.
This section has three parts:
first, the description of the assembly’s gathering; second, the praise of the assembly’s endowment with virtues, beginning from "well-purified" (suviśuddha);
and third, the summary request, beginning from "excellent" (sādhu).
Within these two [sections], there are ten phrases: the first is general, while the remainder are specific.
"General" refers to the thoroughly pure profound mind (*adhyāśaya*) being free from the faults of reliance on teaching or realization; thus it is called "thoroughly pure.
There are two aspects to this profound mind:
First, because one cultivates all virtuous practices, there is purity regarding the teaching (*śāsanaviśuddhi*);
second, because it accords with principle, there is purity regarding realization (*adhigamaviśuddhi*).

Within the nine subsequent distinctions, the first five constitute purity regarding the scriptures (*āgamaviśuddhi*) and the latter four constitute purity regarding realization (*adhigamaviśuddhi*). That is to say, practicing in accordance with the teachings is called purity regarding the scriptures, while giving rise to practice through the realization of principle is called purity regarding realization.
The teaching extends to those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), while realization occurs only from the stages onward.
Regarding the first five [factors] therein:

first, "thoroughly purifying recollection" refers to the purity of desire; that is, according to what one contemplates within the *āgama*, one attains the purity of the awakening of skillful means through recollection. This means that upon attaining skillful means, one does not grasp at the characteristics of recollection, which is termed "thorough purification."
Second, those who have well-cultivated all practices seek purity, because they respectfully and compliantly initiate the practice of seeking the Dharma through the three types of action.

Third, they skillfully accumulate the aids to the path, thereby attaining birth-purity; they aspire to attain increasingly superior births for the benefit of sentient beings, and upon being born, they immediately obtain the superior mindfulness of compassion and wisdom to assist the right path.

Fourth is being able to equalize the wholesome, which is the purity of reception and retention; it consists in drawing near to many Buddhas with the intent to hear much and to memorize and uphold [the teachings].

Fifth is the accomplishment of roots of goodness, which is the purity of practice; it consists in cultivating the roots of goodness that abandon attachment, such as fewness of desires and the dhūtas, for the sake of seeking the true realization of the stages (bhūmi).

Regarding the four kinds of subsequent clear realization (*pratyakṣa-śraddhā*), first, "the abandonment of delusion and confusion" refers to attaining pure direct knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*) because of its excellent determination.

That is to say, within the Path of True Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); since this is not a knowledge derived through inference, it is termed "direct knowledge."

Within the path of insight (*darśanamārga*), one uses subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) to scrutinize the wisdom of principle (*tattva-jñāna*); therefore, there is certainly no delusion.
This may also be understood as applying to both the path of insight and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
It is also termed "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*).

Within the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one is certain of the principles and free from delusion, having destroyed all ignorance; therefore, it is said that "one abandons and leaves behind delusion.
Second, "there is no defilement" means that there is no practice of purification, because all afflictions (*kleśa*) do not function within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

From the subsequent path of vision (*darśanamārga*) up to within the diamond-like uninterrupted path (*vajropamasamādhi*), all constitute the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Because one repeatedly cultivates non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*) therein, it is called the path of cultivation; it eliminates the two types of heavy burdens (*dausthulya*) so that they no longer function.
Because it refers to the initial abandonment of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is called "defilement" (*mala*).

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states: "Regarding the seeds of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), all are abandoned simultaneously at the moment the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests."

Those hindrances manifest before the stages (*bhūmi*) and are gradually suppressed; from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, they can be suddenly and completely suppressed so that they never again arise. Just as an Arhat, through the power of intentional effort, may allow them to manifest temporarily during the seven stages without it being a fault, from the eighth stage upward they never arise at all. Thus it is said.
Afflictions (*kleśa*) are precisely defilements; their non-occurrence is precisely their absence.
However, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is not that delusions are severed, but rather that the realization of the meaning of the principles increases.

Within the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is careful deliberation and repeated contemplation, wherein the sense of removing hindrances is predominant; therefore, this is what is emphasized here.
