this present mention of "contemplative practice" (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) refers to the practice that accords with the ultimate.

The subsequent phrase states that the *dharmakāya* is the characteristic of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); that is to say, by transforming the basis of impermanence, it is said to transcend the three periods of time. Therefore, this subtle wisdom relies upon the eternal *dharmakāya*.

The treatise states: "It is not like impermanent mental consciousness and cognition, which rely upon impermanent causes and conditions. This distinguishes the state prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); it refers here to that which constitutes the transformed basis.
The impermanent consciousness-cognition is that which depends [upon others], while impermanent causes and conditions are their support.

The fundamental consciousness that sustains seeds is the impermanent cause; the various defiled and pure seeds it sustains are the impermanent conditions. Based upon these causes and conditions, impermanent consciousness arises.

Now, the consciousness of discernment is transformed into the wisdom of wondrous observation, and the mental consciousness is transformed into the wisdom of equality as the supporting faculties; these rely upon the fundamental consciousness—the Tathāgatagarbha nature and the Dharmakāya of True Suchness—as their support.
The treatise states: "That which is definitively taught within the sūtras is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: 'By transforming the consciousness of non-perception, one attains the consciousness of perception.'"
The texts of the various Mahāyāna sūtras are not uniform.
Question:
That which exists as the fundamental basis may be considered eternal.
If that which depends [upon it] arises through cultivation, how could it be without arising and ceasing?

According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, because the basis is eternal, that which depends upon it is also said to be eternal; however, this is not eternal by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*), as it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If, as in the *Awakening of Faith* and other texts, initial awakening (śikṣā-bodhi) is identical to original awakening (mūla-bodhi), it too is eternal.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "Because all dharmas are eternally abiding."

Third, its characteristic is like empty space; it is the characteristic of liberation. Unlike the śrāvakas, who still possess the obstruction of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), here both obstructions have perished, and thus it is unimpeded like space.
The meaning of the three virtues has already been seen in the preceding text.
However, while perfection resides in the Buddha, it is permitted that they be manifested even at the stage of the tenth abode (*daśabhūmi*) in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*).
Here, from the perspective of the cause, it is said that they are "partially attained."
The fruit of the basis, such as the ocean of the Buddhas, is without distinction; the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is likewise so.
From the perspective of the causal gate, this refers to the transformation of seeing and cultivation.
When distinguished according to the fruit, it is the ultimate, vast transformation.
This characteristic of difference arises from attaining the aforementioned identity;
this difference establishes that very identity and is able to manifest it.
It causes one to leave behind obscurations and attain purity, such that there is no separate difference, just as when molten gold is cast into an image, the image is not external to the gold.

The conclusion of the latter five sentences in the treatise states: "By such contemplative wisdom, one thus abandons the afflictions; by such contemplation of reality (tathatā), one thus relies upon it;
relying upon it, one attains liberation through such liberation. Contemplating reality means relying upon it in this manner, and by so relying, one attains liberation.

Regarding the fact that the latter three [sections] all employ double statements: the first part restates what preceded, while the second part constitutes the conclusion, namely, "observing in this manner" and so forth.

The reason these latter three alone have double statements is that the preceding text’s final three sections contrasted the false with the true; therefore, it was necessary to restate the truth and thereby conclude.

The second section consists of one verse concerning the subtle practice of the stages (*bhūmi*). Within it, the first half restates the wisdom of the preceding stage as being beyond words to serve as the means of analogy (*upamāna*), while the second half formally cites the practice of the stages to serve as the object of analogy (*upameya*).
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the passage]: this means that the wisdom of the preceding stage reveals two types of nirvāṇa, both of which are said to be surpassed [by the present one].
"Quiescence" refers to the *pariśuddha-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of pure nature) as a common characteristic, because its intrinsic nature is quiescent.

Cessation is the "purified nirvana through skillful means" characterized by dissimilar characteristics; it requires wisdom to take cessation as its object, for it is not a cessation based on intrinsic nature.
Since these two types of nirvana are the domain of the Buddhas, it is said that [the bodhisattvas] do not reach them.
The practitioner is one who realizes [this].
To say that it is "beyond words" means that both speaking and listening are difficult.
Why not simply speak of the wordless, rather than saying it is "beyond what words can reach"?
If there were absolutely no words, by what means could one attain awakening and understanding?
One is led to seek the principle through words, only to realize that while the principle is perfect, the words are partial; therefore, it is simply said that words do not reach it.

Regarding the categories of the latter half [of the verse]: it is not only that the realized wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) is thus profound and mysterious, but even the conduct of its associated wisdom-factors (*jñāna-parivāra*) is difficult to describe and receive.
The Treatise says: "The 'ground' (*bhūmi*) refers to the object of observation (*ālambana-darśana*); the 'conduct' (*caryā*) refers to the wisdom-factors."
The "retinue of wisdom" refers to those who practice together (*sahāyaka*).
Those who practice together refer to the various *pāramitās*, such as generosity (*dāna*) and the rest.

Regarding "contemplation of the objective sphere": when one takes an object as the sphere and illuminates and penetrates it, this is called contemplation; this is precisely the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
If "ground" (bhūmi) refers to the essence of the ground, the intention here is to cite the ground in order to include its practice; thus it is called "ground-practice.

Since one employs this wisdom of the ground to cultivate generosity (*dāna*) and the other perfections, it is termed "concordant practice," because one practices in accordance with those [perfections].
This is precisely the subsequently attained [wisdom], serving as the retinue of the wisdom of realization.
Regarding the third single verse, which "manifests the subtle by means of contrast": it is so called because it reveals the subtlety by contrasting it with hearing, reflection, and so forth.
The first phrase identifies the essential nature of the phenomenon.
"Wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to the ground-wisdom that is produced, which is precisely the fundamental wisdom elucidated in the preceding five verses.

"Produced" (*utpāda*) refers to both the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); both contemplate suchness (*tathatā*), and since suchness is the realm of the Buddha, they both serve as the means of production.
Therefore, the treatise asks: "By what contemplation and by what concomitant practices can this wisdom be generated?
This refers to the preceding verse: "What is the contemplation?
It is the contemplation of the preceding object."
What are the co-existent practices? They are the preceding practices such as giving (*dāna*) and so forth.

All [the questions] begin with "what," because whichever contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) one follows, it is not a singular statement; for since the preparatory applications (*prayoga*) differ according to the stages (*bhūmi*), the objects perceived in the subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) are each distinct.
The next two phrases clarify that it is difficult to describe. Among them, the first phrase states that it is difficult to describe because it is not a mental factor (*caitasika*).
"Not recollection" means it is not within the sphere of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
"Beyond the path of the mind" means it is not within the sphere of consciousness or wisdom born of retribution (*vipākaja-vijñāna*).
Regarding consciousness born of retribution (*vipākaja-vijñāna*), it has been analyzed above in the section on the "contradiction of the request.

The subsequent phrase clarifies that it is distinct from the three categories (*triskandha*); because it possesses both matter and mind, as well as faculties and objects, it cannot be definitively described [as belonging to any one category].

The *Śāstra* on the Sūtra states: "It is not taught as the aggregates, elements, or sense bases. The commentary explains that "not taught" means it is free from words; thus, in the present sūtra, the word "taught" (*śāsana*) is omitted in brief, and the "gate" (*mukha*) itself constitutes the teaching.
Therefore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, speaking is presented as a gateway to wisdom.
The subsequent phrase clarifies that it cannot be heard.
As for "wisdom-knowing," it refers to knowing through the wisdom of realization alone.
Regarding "the mind does not reach it": because one takes up [the teaching] upon hearing it, this means relying on wisdom (*jñāna*) rather than consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The fourth verse, consisting of a single stanza, uses a metaphor to clarify the subtlety of the stage; the first half is the metaphor and the second half is the application.
Regarding the analogy here: it does not refer exclusively to emptiness, for empty space in other contexts is not used as an analogy;
nor does it refer exclusively to tracks, for tracks in sand or soil are not used as an analogy; rather, it specifically refers to the tracks of birds in the sky.

The treatise states: "The traces of a bird flying through the air cannot be described as having a fixed form, nor can they be seen. This passage generally clarifies the characteristics of the analogy.
"Place" refers to the space where the traces occur; "form" refers to the traces within that space.
It cannot be shown as having length, shortness, largeness, or smallness for one to see, nor can it be described as being existent, non-existent, or the like.
Within this, the emptiness of the locus of traces serves as a metaphor for realized wisdom (*pratyātmajñāna*).
The traces of birds in the sky are used as a metaphor for the Āgamas.
Therefore, the treatise states: "In this way, the abodes of birds' tracks are the abodes of names, phrases, and syllables.
Why is it that they cannot be described?
The treatise states: "Because the traces of birds in space cannot be distinguished.
The meaning is this:
when a bird's feet tread upon sand, there are both tracks and a location; however, because it treads upon empty space, the location and the tracks are difficult to distinguish.
The same applies to the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables; because they are subsumed within the realized wisdom of Bodhisattvas, they cannot be spoken or heard.
Whether one speaks or listens, the mind and consciousness cannot comprehend them.

Therefore, by means of realization (pramāṇa), one subsumes the teaching, just as space subsumes its traces; this causes names, phrases, and so forth to not be of the same nature as sound, because they are names and so forth belonging to realized wisdom.
The preceding section clarified that coarse characteristics do not exist, and thus they cannot be described or heard according to the analogy;
the subsequent section clarifies that subtle characteristics are not non-existent, and can therefore be verified by means of an analogy.
The treatise states: "It is not that there is no trace of movement within space."
This means that the emptiness of the trace-locus differs from other forms of emptiness; it is a metaphor for the fact that there is no absence of the cognition of the ground.

The trace of the locus of emptiness differs from being traceless; it is a metaphor for the fact that there is no absence of the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables, because wherever there is the flight of a bird, there must be a trace.
The Treatise states: "It is not that the bodies of phrases, names, and syllables lack the wisdom of the ground"; this is a double conjunction.
This means that because the various sages have personally realized suchness, even their realization is not non-existent, let alone their verbal teachings.
Furthermore, when the trace is subsumed by emptiness, the trace cannot be pointed out;
when emptiness is subsumed by the trace, emptiness is likewise not non-existent.
It is like using realization to subsume the teaching: the teaching cannot be pointed out.
By means of teaching, one gathers [practitioners] toward realization; realization can be expressed through words.
The meaning of the analogy is precisely this.

If one wishes to distinguish the bird from its tracks, then the bird represents the verbal expression and the tracks represent the characteristics of the distinct stages. Thus, there are three elements, with the tracks situated between them; since the tracks follow the bird, the characteristics of the tracks are not non-existent.
Just as footprints follow upon the void, yet the characteristics of the footprints do not exist;
so too, by analogy, particular distinctions follow upon their designations, yet the distinctions are not non-existent;
while the characteristics of the stages follow upon realization, yet the distinctions [between them] do not exist.

If one further distinguishes the emptiness of the provisional traces (jìkōng) from the ultimate empty space (tàikōng), then the emptiness of the traces is a metaphor for realized wisdom (zhèngzhì), while the ultimate empty space is a metaphor for the ocean of fruition (guǒhǎi).
When the emptiness of the traces follows the traces, the wisdom of the stages (dìzhì) can be described;
when the emptiness of the traces follows the ultimate empty space, the wisdom of the stages transcends all words.
Although this meaning is generally understood, there is no explicit textual authority for it in the treatise.

If one uses the analogy of footprints to illustrate wisdom, as was analyzed previously in the discussion on wind and drawings, then by reflecting upon the text concerning the ten stages (*bhūmi*) through the metaphor of bird tracks, every word and phrase—whether concerning the varying depths of assigned stations or the factors of giving, morality, and meditation—will be seen as profoundly profound and mysterious.
How could it be said that the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) is profound while the stages of the grounds themselves are shallow?
Therefore, the treatise concludes by stating: "Because this is profound herein, the manifestation of its meaning brings great joy.

Herein, the tracks of birds serve as a dual metaphor for both teaching and realization being difficult to explain and difficult to hear; how does this differ from the metaphor of wind-drawn figures mentioned in the request [for instruction]?
Therefore, the treatise says: "How, then, should one explain the treatise?
The answer is:
You should not grasp the meaning according to the literal sound."
The meaning of this is as follows:
the preceding metaphors and the Dharma were intended to manifest the principle of remaining silent and not speaking;
here, however, through metaphors and the statement that it is difficult to explain, he admonishes the assembly to abandon attachment and grants permission to proclaim the teaching.
The intention is different.
If one follows the sound with an attached mind to grasp the meaning, there are five faults:
first, incorrect faith, because the understanding follows the words rather than corresponding to reality.
Second, they lose their courageous vigor because they cannot forget conceptual signs and thus fail to proceed toward the true principle;
third, they deceive others by explaining their own erroneous interpretations to them;
fourth, they slander the Buddha by claiming that their own erroneous interpretations are the Buddha’s teaching.

Fifth is the disparagement of the Dharma, which arises from interpreting its profound intent through shallow and superficial understanding, or by treating the Dharma as being merely literal and failing to regard it with reverence.
The intention is to ensure that the great assembly recognizes these five faults for themselves; this is why the difficulty of explaining and hearing [the Dharma] is clarified.
Those of today who consider the mundane world to be shallow all fall into these five faults; therefore, they lament that it is difficult to explain and hear.
By reversing these five faults, one accomplishes the five virtues.
Having already explained the profound meaning to engender right faith,
from here below is the second section, which further elucidates the greatness [of the Buddha] to engender right faith.
This consists of five verses divided into three parts:
The first one and a half verses correctly reveal the meaning of the accomplishment of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā);
the second set of three verses demonstrates one's own faultlessness and admonishes the assembly to eliminate defects;
the third set of half a verse indicates the limits of the exposition, which serves merely as the cause for the teaching.

Now, regarding the first point, the "three greatnesses of accomplishment": First is the greatness of the accomplishment of the cause (*hetu-sampad-mahattva*). This refers to compassion, vows, and power as the foundation for initiating practice; thus, it is called the "cause.

Second is the greatness of the gradual accomplishment of the cause (*hetu-kramika-sampad-mahattva*). This refers to the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*) as the causes for supramundane knowledge; since these do not arise instantaneously, it is called "gradual."

The "Exposition through Teaching" refers to the great accomplishment of cultivation, which is to say, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*). It is so called because true cultivation accords with reality as it is realized in direct realization, and thus can be expressed through verbal explanations; hence, it is termed the "Exposition through Teaching."
The two characters "teaching" (jiao) and "explanation" (shuo) specifically distinguish [this] from the "Great Meaning" (yida), for it is not like the fruit-stage which is ineffable.

The preceding two [stages] do not resemble direct realization; their essence is not profound or wondrous, and they do not require verbal distinction. Rather, they serve as causes for supramundane wisdom; therefore, both are termed "causes" (yin).
When one attains [the fruit] according to its respective portion, all three are accomplished.
In which stage do these three positions reside?
Regarding this, there are two interpretations:

First, regarding the first stage (*bhūmi*), the former two may be included in the stage prior to the grounds (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) because they are the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the grounds; the latter one resides exclusively on the grounds.

Second, regarding the general explanation, within each ground, the cultivation of compassion and the power of vows through preparatory practice constitutes the accomplishment of the cause; the wisdoms of hearing and reflection constitute the gradual development of the cause; and both the fundamental realization and the subsequently attained wisdom are taught as cultivation.
Question:

Regarding the explanations of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and hearing (*śruta*), these are easy to understand from the text; however, in what specific location do the characteristics of their actual realization (*sākṣātkriyā-lakṣaṇa*) reside?
Answer:
This has two meanings.

First, the essence of the ground is profound and subtle, such that it cannot be directly manifested; it is displayed by relying upon phenomena, which constitute its characteristics—namely, the ten wholesome actions, the factors of dhyāna, the limbs of the path, the various truths, and so forth.

The fulfillment of the two causes constitutes actual realization (*samyak-sākṣātkriyā*). As it is said regarding the first stage (*bhūmi*): "It is called dwelling in the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) because of its correspondence with immovability.

Regarding the eighth stage, it is said: "One enters into the nature of all phenomena being like space; by accomplishing this patience (*kṣānti*), one is said to enter the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*)," and so forth.
This is precisely that text.
Because the true and correct realization cannot be expressed or demonstrated,
both of these categories are explanations of cultivation.
If that is so, why do the various Buddhas speak of "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*) regarding the three higher gradual stages?
It is because those [stages] are named "realization" due to the greatness of the meaning they signify;
whereas in the present case, since it is merely from the perspective of what can be expressed, one can only say "explanation."
The preceding treatise states: "Because it is said that by means of this, the Great [Vehicle] is able to attain that meaning.
Having already understood the general purport, we shall now correctly explain the text.
The accomplishment of the Great [Vehicle] corresponds to the first two lines.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the benefit of others;
the vow (*praṇidhāna*) encompasses both benefits;
and power (*bala*) encompasses the preceding three. Because its cultivation of these two benefits differs from that of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), it is called "power."
The latter phrase refers to the merit of the two benefits (self and others); the "arising" (*janman*) of the stages and practices is precisely the meaning of "cause.
The gradual fulfillment of these two causes into greatness corresponds to the second character, "succession" (*krama*).
The treatise states: "The sequence of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and so forth is taught because they serve as the causes for accomplishing supramundane knowledge.
Regarding the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), it carries two meanings: first, it includes the preceding items;
however, it does not include the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), as this constitutes the third major category and thus is not considered equal [to the others in that specific context].
Second is equal cultivation (*samabhāvanā*). There are two kinds of cultivation:
first, cultivation by means of conditions (*ālambana-bhāvanā*), which is subsumed under this gate;
second, true cultivation (*bhūta-bhāvanā*), which is subsumed under the third [gate].
Because the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) contains an inclusive sense, it is simply called "and so forth.
Otherwise, why would one not merely say "hearing, reflection, and cultivation," but instead substitute "and so forth" for "cultivation"?
Third, from "perfection" (*paripūri*) onwards, it clarifies that the teaching explains the accomplishment of greatness through cultivation.
This consists of two types:
first, cultivation through fulfillment, which refers to the first eight characters;
second, cultivation through contemplation, which refers to the final two phrases.
When the stage of true cultivation reaches its ultimate limit, mundane concerns are entirely stilled; being able to fulfill the wisdom of the stages is called "cultivation of fulfillment.
When true wisdom arises within, its tranquil illumination is distinct and clear; this is called "cultivation through contemplation."
The former refers to being quiescent in accordance with the nature; the latter refers to being quiescent yet capable of illumination.
It is like a polished, bright mirror: that no impurity remains uncleaned is like the cultivation of fulfillment;
that nothing is not reflected through to its depths is like that cultivation of contemplation.
These two types of cultivation, when compared to true realization, are like that [stage] relative to the Sublime Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*);
while Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddhatva*) is merely the perfection of causes, Sublime Enlightenment involves the relinquishing of practice and is thus called the fulfillment of the fruit.
This case is likewise.

The two types of cultivation, as they pertain to the supramundane, merely constitute the conclusion of the causal stage; it is only when one attains direct realization and abandons cultivation that it is designated as the resultant stage.
May all who possess wisdom examine this principle.

In this passage, "contemplation" (*lǜ*) refers to hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī* wisdom), "knowledge" (*zhì*) refers to the knowledge of true cultivation, and "mind" (*xīn*) refers to the essential substance of the mind of true cultivation.

This means that only when the mind of contemplative consideration based on hearing and reflection is absent can it be called the perfection of the mind of true cultivation; therefore, it is accessible only through the knowledge of true cultivation.
If one follows the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra*, the mind is that which conforms to suchness (*tathatā*), because it is the supramundane mind.
The *Sūtra* states: "The wisdom of the non-mind-ground is the fulfillment of suchness, the pure mind.
The commentary on the *Śāstra* explains: "Regarding 'fulfilling cultivation,' the verse says 'the non-mind-ground'."

Regarding the phrase "not the sphere of mind," this sentence indicates that while the spheres of mind such as the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*) serve only as causes for the arising of supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*), they cannot fulfill that supramundane wisdom. This clarifies that the wisdoms of hearing and reflection are mental objects and thus cannot fulfill the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi-jñāna*); by contrast, it reveals that true cultivation, which is not a mental object, alone can fulfill the wisdom of the stages.
Next, a verse is cited, which says: "The verse states that wisdom is fulfilled because it is like the pure mind.
This is then explained by restating the point:
"Like the pure mind" means it is like the supramundane pure mind, for it is able to fulfill the wisdom of that stage.

This clarifies that the container and its lid must correspond; that is to say, the wisdom that fulfills the ground cannot be achieved by any other state of mind, but can only be fulfilled by a mind of true cultivation and tranquil contemplation, which is identical to the supramundane wisdom-mind.
The mind that accords with the world-transcending state is precisely the wisdom of the stage of correct realization (*samyag-abhisamaya-bhūmi-jñāna*).
This statement is truly direct.
Regarding the phrase "the realm within the subsequent contemplation and cultivation," this refers to the object of true cultivation.
"Difficult to see" means it cannot be seen through hearing or reflection.
"Knowable" means that only through true cultivation—the tranquil illumination of one's own mind—can it be known.
To know is precisely to see.
Therefore, the treatise on the sutra states: "It is difficult to explain; one knows it through one's own mind.
The commentary explains:
"The purity of one's own mind can be seen."

Since it is difficult to perceive and difficult to explain, it is nevertheless explained in accordance with practice within the section on the Great Vehicle; this differs from the section on the fruits, which concerns only profound meanings.
Second, demonstrating one's own faultlessness and admonishing the assembly to eliminate their failings, which consists of two parts:
first, a general clarification in the first half-verse; second, a detailed exposition in the subsequent two and a half verses.
First, regarding this point:
because both the speaker and the listener each have two faults, they are unable to attain realization; therefore, both are shown to be free from them.

As for the two faults of the speaker: first, the Buddha does not grant his approval (*anumodana*) to their teaching. Since it is now said that "the power of the Buddha has opened and expounded [this]," we know that the Buddha has already granted his approval.
Second is the teaching on inequality. Now it is said, "You all should receive [this]," whereby there is no distinction of self and other in one's disposition.

Regarding the two faults of listening: first is the fault of contention through views, which is to say, "My dharma is correct, while their dharma is incorrect," thus adhering to various kinds of views.
Second, regarding those who do not give rise to reverence for the teacher of the Dharma, this now causes them to receive it with respect;
thus both faults are abandoned: because one respects the Dharma, there is no fault of contentious views; because one respects the person, there is no second fault.
In the second section, which provides a detailed exposition, although the preceding [section] was free from the four faults, there were only three matters:
first, receiving the power; second, expounding and teaching;

and third, respectfully receiving. Now, these three segments expand upon them: the first verse expands upon the expounding and teaching; the next verse clarifies the respectful reception; and the latter half-verse clarifies the receiving of the power.
Now, first:
the previous section merely spoke of "opening and expounding," without clarifying whether it was extensive or concise; now it is shown to be concise rather than extensive.
The first half of the verse reveals that the practice of entering through wisdom is profound and mysterious, such that even a detailed exposition could not exhaust it.

Regarding the statement "wisdom enters into practice": the dharmas of the stages (bhūmi) are that which is entered, and realized wisdom is that which enters. By practicing this course of wisdom, one enters the dharmas of the stages.
Furthermore, "wisdom entering" refers to realized wisdom, while "practice" refers to the practice of activities.
Although the latter half has now been explained briefly, it encompasses the extensive teaching without omission.
"Reality" refers to the entry of wisdom into practice.
"Without remainder" means that there is nothing—whether in terms of phenomena (*dharma*) or principle (*tattva*)—that is not fully contained therein.
The second [section] clarifies the recipient’s respectful reception, which demonstrates the aspect of veneration.
The first phrase explicitly clarifies this, while the [subsequent] three phrases provide the reasons.
There are two types of veneration:
First, one waits with physical reverence, abiding in proper deportment so as to be worthy of receiving the teaching of the Dharma.
Second, one waits with mental reverence, with a mind of firm resolve so as to be capable of retaining it in memory.
When the mind is respectful, the body will necessarily be reverent; therefore, the verse mentions only the mind.
The following explains the cause of such reverence: it is because of well-spoken words that beings are led to show respect and deference.
The first phrase clarifies one's own excellence in preaching for the sake of others.
Regarding the single character "preaching" (shuo), it is termed "excellent preaching" (shan-shuo) in the treatises and sūtras.
"Excellent preaching" means that, in relation to those who are the appropriate audience, one is free from flattery and free from arrogance.
"Relying on the Buddha's power" indicates that he himself is free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*), as he does not claim to be equal to the Buddha.
The next two phrases demonstrate his own skillful exposition in contrast to the Dharma.

The two characters "supreme Dharma" (*jina-dharma*) refer to the signified (*vācya*); the subsequent six characters refer to the signifier (*vācaka*); and the two characters "their correspondence" (*tatsaṃprayukta*) apply to both the signifier and the signified.
Although the text consists of three sections, its meaning comprises four layers:
first, what is it that is being elucidated and manifested here?
It refers to the dharmas of the supreme stages; therefore, they are called "supreme dharmas."
Secondly, he further interrogates:

"That which is expressed is the ground (*bhūmi*), while the means of expression are manifold; whether it be color and fragrance, or deportment and movement, all may serve as the means of expression. By what specific dharma, then, is it expressed?"
Therefore, the treatise states: "By what means?
The answer is:
I employ the eight kinds of sublime Brahma-sounds as the expressive medium, rather than fragrances and so forth; thus the Sūtra speaks of 'sublime sounds'."
He questioned him again three times, saying:
"This sound has many varieties; is it used in its literal sense, or is it employed as a metaphorical illustration?"
Therefore, the treatise says: "What is the subject matter?
The answer is:
it is not merely revealed directly; rather, it is clarified by means of analogies, and is thus called 'parable' (dṛṣṭānta)."
"Furthermore, there are two kinds of metaphors:
first, those that use a concrete object as a metaphor, such as the examples cited below regarding the ornaments made of gold from each joint, the jewels of the great ocean, and so forth."
Second, borrowing the characteristics of phenomena and events to illustrate a principle, thereby clarifying it for the listener, is also called an analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*).
This [section] now encompasses both of these.
Fourth, he further inquires:

Although it is known that metaphors are used for clarification, there are many kinds of metaphors: are they metaphors based on the unwholesome letters of the mundane world, or are they metaphors based on the wholesome letters of the supramundane?
Therefore, the Treatise says: "Upon what basis does it rely?
The answer is:
it relies upon the word 'good' (kuśala)."
The Sūtra omits the word "excellent," whereas the Śāstra includes it in its exposition of the Sūtra.
How do these correspond to both the means of expression (*vācaka*) and that which is expressed (*vācya*)?
First, the correspondence with the metaphor through sublime vocal sounds pertains to the means of expression.
Second, regarding the word "wholesome" (kuśala), it corresponds to the underlying principle and thus serves as the general referent.
Therefore, the treatise states: "The word 'wholesome' has two aspects: first, it conforms to local dialects and sounds, because it accords with them."
"The two-word phrase is perfect, neither increasing nor decreasing, because it accords with principle.
Furthermore, when it accords with the three factors that constitute the expressive signifier, it then accords with principle.

Regarding the third point, the power of receiving [the Buddha’s] empowerment, the treatise states: "It was previously mentioned that one receives the Buddha’s spiritual power, but it was not yet explained what kind of power this is;
therefore, this is now stated. As for the "immeasurable Buddhas," there are briefly three categories:
first, the presiding Buddha; second, the Vajragarbha Buddhas of the ten directions; and third, all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Regarding the third point, the demonstration of the limits [of the teaching]: this merely refers to the cause.
Within the second half-verse, the latter line—in both the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra*—concerns the "Great" (*mahat*).
At the beginning of the five verses, it says, "I have spoken only one part," which precisely constitutes the limit.
Whether it is due to the translator’s use of a palindrome or because there are variations in the Sanskrit manuscript, the essential meaning does not differ; thus, what harm is there in the sequence?
Within this, the preceding phrase restates the request made earlier and simultaneously concludes the two great points of the preceding doctrinal exposition as the subject matter for this section.
The meaning of "difficult to proclaim and demonstrate" has been extensively analyzed above.
The subsequent phrase permits the teaching of a small portion.

The commentary on the preceding section states: "It was previously said that the ten stages are thus impossible to speak of or hear; now it is said that I shall speak but a single part. What is the meaning of these words?"
That which is subsumed under this stage is twofold:
first, the causal portion (*hetubhāga*); second, the fruitional portion (*phalabhāga*).
The commentator states that explaining one part [of these] constitutes the causal portion, because it is a single part of the fruitional portion.

Regarding the two divisions of cause and effect, there have been many ancient interpretations; those that completely deviate from the intent of the text are not discussed here, while those that are coherent are adopted in their corrected form.
To directly examine the intent of the treatise: it refers to the "Great Meaning" (mahārtha) as the resultant portion (*phalabhāga*), and thus it cannot be spoken of;
when the "Great" is spoken of as the causal portion (*hetubhāga*), then it can be spoken of.
Furthermore, if we take this according to its meaning, there are briefly two kinds:

First, this is explained solely in terms of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Taking realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*) as the fruit-division, the skillful means (*upāya*), the provisional dharmas, and so forth, are all taken as the cause-division.
This further has two meanings:

first, when contrasted in terms of cultivation and realization, the application of skillful means and the process of cultivation constitute the cause-division, while the cessation of cultivation and the accord with reality constitute the fruit-division.

Second, in terms of the relationship between the expressive and the expressed, the provisional reliance on dharmas to manifest the distinctions of the stages constitutes the causal portion (*hetu-bhāga*), while the true realized wisdom constitutes the resultant portion (*phala-bhāga*).

For instance, the first three stages rely upon worldly analogies, while the subsequent three rely upon the Two Vehicles, the factors of dhyāna, the path-factors, and so forth, enabling sentient beings to understand the meaning of the stages through these symbolic expressions.

The realized wisdom manifested by causes is the fruit of these causes; as all such realized wisdom is beyond the reach of verbal expression, it cannot be described—just as the tracks of birds in the sky are identical to the sky itself.

Expedient means rely upon dharmas that can be revealed through speech, and thus are said to be "expressible"—just as the tracks of birds in the sky are distinguished by reference to the birds themselves.
Therefore, this single trace comprises two aspects: that which can be spoken and that which cannot be spoken.
Second, when considered in relation to the cause of Samantabhadra against the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood, its meaning extends throughout the entire treatise.

This means that when this realized wisdom (pramāṇa-jñāna) becomes one with the ocean of the ultimate fruit, it constitutes the "fruit-portion" (phala-bhāga); it is like the space within a footprint being no different from the great expanse of space.

The causal aspect of the ground (bhūmi-lakṣaṇa-hetu) is identical to the cause of Samantabhadra; for if explained extensively, there are immeasurable varieties of phenomena, and because his sublime power of aspiration (praṇidhāna-bala) exceeds even this.

This implies that there is also a sense in which the traces of the locus of emptiness follow from the emptiness of the locus; for even the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi-jñāna*) can be indicated by means of provisional words.
Question:
The preceding treatise states, "That which is subsumed under these stages is twofold. How, then, can this be described as the ultimate fruit?
Answer:
Is it not the case that it was previously stated they are identical in the ocean of fruition? Therefore, the preceding treatise says: "By whom is this wisdom realized?
The verse states: 'It is the sphere of the Buddha's activity.'"

Furthermore, the "Section on Additional Qualities" speaks of the "inconceivable Buddha-dharmas," while the "Section on the Reflections of the Grounds" states: "Those ten great mountains derive their names from the great ocean, and the great ocean likewise derives its name from those ten mountains."

The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of a bodhisattva are likewise: they all reside within omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), receive their names by reason of omniscience, because the cause and the fruit accord with one another.
Thus we know that the author of the treatise also includes the ultimate fruit within the ten stages.

Some say: "That [text] states that the ten mountains rely upon the ocean, but it does not state that the great ocean is itself the mountains. [Yet] how could the ten virtues of the great ocean be separate from the ocean?
How could the ten meanings of the precious jewel be separate from the jewel?
Those who knowingly raise these objections have not perceived the purport of the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi-jñāna*).
Furthermore, based on the principle that a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) cannot be pointed out or described, they speak of both the unspeakable and the speakable.

If there are causes and conditions by which the fruit may be expressed through words, yet the phenomenon itself enters the profound mystery such that even its cause cannot be described, it is therefore said that "only a small portion is taught"; one must not hold to this as a fixed limitation.
From here on, in the seventh major section clarifying the "Exposition," there is a threefold analysis:

first, the purpose, which means that once the ritual of request has concluded, the limits have already been shown to manifest the reality of the stages (*bhūmi*); since the reality of the stages is difficult to clarify, it is manifested by relying upon its signs (*nimitta*), and these signs constitute the causal portion.
From this point onward, the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) are explained in detail so that by investigating these characteristics one may attain the reality; thus, this section follows.
Furthermore, the request for the divisions [of the stages] gives rise to correct understanding, and what follows thereafter reveals their practice and cultivation; hence, it comes next.
Second, the explanation of the names:
because it elaborates upon and proclaims the distinctions of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), it is called the "Section of Exposition" (*nirdeśa-vibhāga*).

Since the preceding "Section of Request" (*adhyeṣaṇā-vibhāga*) universally requests [instruction on] the ten stages, and since the principle of providing an exposition in response to such a request must necessarily be universal, this section is so named as a collective title for the joy experienced at the very beginning of receiving [the teaching].
The Treatise states: "From this point onward, the first stage (*bhūmi*) is formally expounded.
Since there is a section for the exposition of the first stage, it is known that all ten stages likewise possess sections for their exposition.

Furthermore, within the first stage, all [aspects] should be designated as "sections" (*bhāga*) because they constitute the fulfillment of the stage, distinguishing them from the initial dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*); therefore, following the ten vows, further distinct names are provided to examine and evaluate their excellence.

Furthermore, while the commentators' structural outlines (ko-wen) merely present the general framework, they do not concern themselves with the underlying logical continuity (xue-mai); these should arise and conclude according to the context rather than being fixed rigidly.
Third, regarding the explanation of the text: the ten stages (daśabhūmi) constitute ten sections.
The first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) is analyzed through seven gates:

first, the purpose; second, the explanation of the name; third, the abandonment of hindrances; fourth, the realization of principle; fifth, the accomplishment of practice; sixth, the attainment of the fruit; and seventh, the commentary on the text.

First, regarding the purpose of its introduction: it is because, among the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one first abandons hindrances, realizes the principle, and attains the nature of a noble one (*āryatva*).

Second, regarding the explanation of the title: the explanation provided by this treatise has already been seen in the "Fundamental Section" (*mūlabhāga*); the explanation found in the corresponding sūtra is fully contained in the following text. For now, I shall cite another school to establish the correct meaning.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle nine, states: "At the initial attainment of the noble nature (*āryagotra*), one fully realizes the twofold emptiness and is able to benefit both self and others, thereby giving rise to great joy.
This involves three meanings:
first, attaining the stage; second, realizing the principle; and third, accomplishing the practice."
"Because of these three reasons, it is called 'Supreme Joy' (*pramuditā*).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, fascicle seven, states: "Because, for the first time, one attains the supreme merit capable of accomplishing the welfare of both oneself and others."
This is explained solely in terms of the meaning of "accomplishing practice" based on the third stage.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: "Because one has first attained the flavor of the Dharma and gives rise to great joy."
This is stated solely in reference to the meaning of realizing the principle.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 78, citing the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, states: "Because one accomplishes the great purpose, attains the unprecedented supramundane mind, and gives rise to great joy."

This is based on two meanings: the "great meaning" refers to the accomplishment of the practice of the two benefits and the arising of the supramundane mind, which constitutes attaining the stage of an ārya; this is explained in the same manner as in the "Main Section" (Mūlaparivarta) of this treatise.

Regarding the three obstacles to be abandoned, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle nine, states: "The obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is what is abandoned here; that is to say, among the two obstacles, those arising from conceptual construction (*vikalpita*) are established as the nature of an ordinary being based upon their seeds."
"When the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the two vehicles manifests, one attains the nature of an ārya by severing only one type [of affliction].
When the path of seeing of a bodhisattva manifests, one attains the nature of an ārya by severing both types."
This term "ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*) refers to the commoner; in the Liang translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is termed "the nature of the commoner.
In the "Fundamental Section" of this treatise, it is termed "the obstacle of the self-characteristic of the ordinary person," and this obstacle obstructs the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Since that which gives rise to afflictions is the root, it is said that the two obstacles are severed; however, if explained in full, one also severs the various karmas and their fruits in the evil destinies. For this reason, it is said in the first bhūmi that the two delusions and their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) are severed.
First is the delusion of attachment to a self and phenomena, which is the obstacle of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
second is the delusion of affliction in the miserable realms, which refers to the various karmas and their fruits in those realms.

Although these karmas and fruits are not themselves delusions, they are categorized as such because they belong to the class of delusion; the same principle applies to the delusions in the nine lower stages.
The meaning of "abandonment" is as explained previously in the section on the limits [of the path].
Regarding the four principles realized: by abandoning the aforementioned hindrances, one realizes the all-pervading *tathatā* (suchness).
That is to say, this *tathatā* is manifested through the two kinds of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), for there is not a single phenomenon that does not abide within it.

In the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty, this is termed "pervasive," because it pervades all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). This is intended to clarify that there is not a single dharma that is not [encompassed by] the two kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
In this stage, one first partially realizes universal pervasiveness.
Regarding the five practices to be accomplished, there are briefly four types:
first, the practice of giving (dāna) accomplished through cultivation based on its preeminence;
Second, regarding what is accomplished, there are the ten great vows;
third, regarding their cultivation and accomplishment, there are the ten practices such as faith;
fourth, regarding actual practice, it refers to the fact that all practices, such as the ten perfections, are cultivated without exception.
The remaining points regarding the practice will be clarified by the explanation of the text itself.
Sixth, as for the fruits obtained, there are briefly four kinds:
first, the four fruits such as pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and so forth, attained when the stage is fully perfected.
Second, by attaining the practice of giving (*dāna*), one achieves the fruit of great wealth;
third, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, by penetrating the emptiness of obstructions, one attains the fruit of the extinction of all obstructions;

fourth, through a comprehensive discussion, one attains the wisdom and insight (*jñāna-prajñā*) regarding the three natures and three non-natures of *Vijñaptimātra*, as well as the fruits of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

However, while the various gates mentioned above mostly rely on sequential progression (xingbu), if we consider them in terms of perfect interfusion (yuanrong), then with one severance all are severed; with one realization all are realized; with one practice all are practiced; and with one attainment all are attained.
The seventh section, the explanation of the text, is divided into two parts:
first, the prose; second, the verses.
Within the former, if one were to follow the sutra text directly, it should be divided into two sections.

The first part clarifies the dharmas of the stage; the latter part, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he mostly becomes a king of Jambudvīpa," explains the fruition of the subsequent stages.
Within the former, there is first an extensive explanation, followed by a summary beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this is called... and so forth.
The preceding section has three parts:

first, the explanation of the mind of entry; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva takes great compassion as the foremost" onwards, the explanation of the mind that abides in the stages; and third, from "O Son of the Buddha, once the bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi), by the power of his great vows he beholds many Buddhas" onwards, the explanation of the mind of emergence.
The texts concerning the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) are for the most part all like this.
Therefore, according to the treatise of Maitreya, each of the ten grounds contains three types of mind.

The *Renyō-kyō* (Śūraṅgamasamādhi-sūtra), in its first fascicle, also states: "On each ground there are thirty patiences—superior, middle, and inferior; within each ground, the initial arising, the abiding arising, and the final arising are unobtainable. This principle is necessarily so.
The treatise establishes that the fruit of mental flexibility arises from this [state of mind], as will be clarified below.
For now, we shall follow the treatise in analyzing the long prose section into two parts:
first, the section explaining the first stage (*bhūmi*); second, the section on the comparative excellence, beginning with the words "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this..."
Regarding the preceding section, according to the treatise, there are one hundred phrases in total, divided into three parts:

first, forty phrases clarifying the "Abiding" (sthiti) section; second, thirty phrases from "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells on the Stage of Joy" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) onwards, explaining the "Exposition of Names" (nāma-nirdeśa) section; and third, thirty phrases from "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva, by means of great compassion" onwards, clarifying the "Abiding in Stability" (pratiṣṭhāna) section.
If one takes the comprehensive comparison of excellence as the basis, it constitutes the four parts of the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the first part, "abiding" (*sthita*): because the supramundane bodhicitta has arisen and one firmly maintains the first stage without further falling back, it is called "abiding"; this refers to the initial mind of entering and abiding.

Although one initially dwells in the stages (*bhūmi*), it is not yet called "virtuous"; when one further gives rise to faith and so forth and dwells virtuously within those stages, it is termed "abiding" (*vihāra*). Thus, both the correct dwelling within the stages and the subsequent portion constitute the mind of abiding.

Regarding the explanation of the names, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) should be treated uniformly; however, for the sake of clarifying their specific meanings, only three stages are explained in detail—namely, the first, the eighth, and the tenth—while the others are omitted. This is because the first stage marks the beginning of attaining sainthood, the eighth stage is the commencement of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), and the tenth stage, the Bodhisattva stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*), represents the completion of countless eons; thus, these three are specifically explained.

Since the three minds are realized simultaneously within each of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), each stage encompasses the three preceding positions. Herein, the "Stage of Abiding" (*vihāra-bhāga*) subsumes the "Abiding in the Initial Resolve" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*);

the "Explanation of the Name" (*nāmanirukti-bhāga*) subsumes the "Practice of Joyful Regard" (*pramuditā-caryā*); and the final two sections subsume the "Dedication for the Protection of Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings" (*sattvārakṣa-sattvanimitta-viveka-pariṇāma*). All of these correspond respectively to the text and its meaning; one should reflect upon them according to the text.
Now, regarding the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), the text is divided into two parts:
first, the specific exposition of the dharmas of this stage; second, from "The Bodhisattva dwells thus" onwards, the summary of dwelling and entering the stage.
The first forty phrases of the middle section are divided into four parts:
first, ten [phrases] concerning which body; second, ten [phrases] concerning for what purpose; third, ten phrases concerning by what cause; and fourth, ten phrases concerning what characteristics.
The first refers to the deeply planted roots of goodness, which serve as the basis for the body [of the bodhisattva].
The second refers to the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood, which serves as the object of focus.
Both of the above are objects of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*).
Third, taking great compassion as the cause for generating the resolve;
fourth, taking the transcendence of the ordinary state and the attainment of sainthood as the characteristics of the benefits of generating the resolve.
The forty-seventh fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also contains these four characteristics; since the treatise was composed based on the sūtras, it is identical to this.

Furthermore, these four matters are themselves the three types of bodhicitta: planting deep roots of goodness is the profound mind (*adhyāśaya-citta*); next, seeking enlightenment is the straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*); and third is the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*). Possessing these three minds constitutes the sign of subsequently entering the stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, each of these four sections contains three mental states, which may be inferred through reflection.
Now, regarding the first section concerning the ten phrases on the basis of what body: the first is general, while the remainder are specific.
The general statement, "If there are sentient beings," refers to those who possess [wholesome] practice.
According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, this refers to one who practices through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*).
When such a mind arises, one enters the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmi*); having entered, this mind constantly manifests before one.
The first ten minds in each of the subsequent stages should be understood by analogy with this.
The phrase "having deeply planted roots of goodness" is precisely the general statement.
In the treatise, the scripture refers to this as "thickly accumulated"; "thick" means "deep," and "accumulated" means "planted.
If considered according to the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), there is no fixed number of time periods.
If one relies on the sequential progression (*paryāya*), it means that the provisions have already been accumulated over one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*; hence, it is said that they have "planted deeply.
Separately, there are nine types of accumulation: the first six protect against the activity of afflictions (*kleśa*), and the latter three protect against the activity of the two vehicles (*yāna*).

The preceding three constitute the three higher trainings (*adhiśikṣā*): the first is ethical discipline (*śīla*), the second is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and the remaining four are wisdom (*prajñā*).

Within wisdom, the first three correspond respectively to that derived from hearing (*śruta*), reflection (*cintā*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*); the last one is the supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*) that is fully accomplished.

Among the latter three, the first two protect the minds of those of the Two Vehicles—namely, protecting narrow-mindedness through great resolve and protecting small intelligence through great understanding;
the last one protects the practices of those of the Two Vehicles.
Having understood their meaning, what are the nine accumulations?

First is the accumulation of conduct (*caryā-saṃgraha*), which refers to the thorough cultivation of various practices and the proper formation of one's retinue through the observance of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Because the three clusters are not one, it is called the "Samādhi of Not Producing All Impure Śīla"; thus, it is clarified first.
Second is the "Accumulation of Concentration," which refers to the Samādhi of Skillfully Accumulating Aids to the Path and Skillfully Forming Retinues, as stated in the Sūtra.
This refers to the "attainment of illumination" (*ālokalabdha*) and so forth, as well as the four dhyānas; because concentration directly supports wisdom, they are called "aids to the path.
They are all termed "retinues" because wisdom is the sovereign.

Third is the accumulation through proximity, which refers to the sūtra’s statement on "skillfully making offerings to all Buddhas," for one makes offerings to the Buddhas with the desire to accumulate the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*).

Fourth is the accumulation through gathering, which refers to the sūtra’s statement on "skillfully gathering pure dharmas," for one gathers the wholesome dharmas such as the perfections (*pāramitā*) through the skillful reflection of the wisdom of contemplation (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*).

This means that by relying on hearing and reflection, because their names, meanings, intrinsic natures, and specific characteristics possess degrees of superiority and inferiority, one achieves the stages of *ūṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit), which counteract all obscurations and outflows; therefore, they are called "pure white."
The fivefold gathering of protection constitutes being well-guided by a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Because one attains external instruction through internal practice and realization, there is the practice and realization [of the Dharma].

That is, the knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) is also divided into superior and inferior levels, established as the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
The five superior [levels] are all identical to the stage of application (*prayoga*), while the four inferior [levels] have all already entered the stages (*bhūmi*).

The sixth is the accumulation of the pure mind, which is the thoroughly purified profound resolve; by attaining supramundane right knowledge, one realizes through non-conceptual wisdom that there is absolutely nothing to be apprehended within the objects of perception.
Because one does not grasp at the various marks of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is called "thoroughly pure.
Because wisdom accords with reality, it is called "deep mind" (*adhyāśaya*).
"Extensively gathering" refers to establishing a vast resolve, because the deep mind seeks extensive benefit for others.
The eighth is the assembly of the eightfold faith, which gives rise to vast understanding for the sake of seeking the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The ninth is the manifest assembly, which refers to the manifestation of compassion; because one practices compassion extensively and never abandons it even for a moment, it is called "manifest."

However, because the Hīnayāna lacks the intention to seek Buddhahood, the aspiration for omniscience within the self-benefiting mind is clarified while maintaining the Hīnayāna perspective; this is because the Hīnayāna also possesses the practice of the three trainings for one's own benefit.
Now, within the context of protecting [sentient beings] through practice, only the compassion that benefits others is mentioned.

Among these, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is based on the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), because one contemplates and aspires for their happiness while they are currently in a state of suffering.

Compassion relies upon the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) to uproot the delusive pleasure [of beings], for they do not realize that they are being transmuted by the suffering of conditioned existence.
Since the three realms are never free from the three types of suffering, they constitute the object of compassion.
Furthermore, since clarity (*vidyā*) and bliss (*sukha*) can directly uproot suffering,

loving-kindness (*maitrī*) relies upon the two types of suffering [the suffering of pain and the suffering of change], for by uprooting suffering it bestows true bliss; whereas compassion (*karuṇā*) relies upon the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
It is already known that the general and specific collections constitute the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

As for the distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) such as morality (*śīla*) and so forth, they are briefly described as "accomplishment" (*saṃsthiti*) and extensively described as "disintegration" (*vibheda*), as fully clarified above.
Regarding the purpose of the second [section], it is for the sake of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood (*buddhatva-phala*).
First, the characteristics of seeking the fruit are specifically revealed; subsequently, from the words "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the generation of the mind is summarized.
Regarding the initial ten phrases, the first is general and the remaining ones are specific.

Collectively termed "Buddha-wisdom," it refers to the supreme wisdom that knows, abandons, realizes, and cultivates; therefore, these four distinctions are explained in relation to the unconditioned Four Noble Truths.
Because it is the ultimate cultivation, it is also called "cultivation."
This wisdom has nine kinds of differentiated activities, all of which it seeks to accomplish.
First is the Buddha-wisdom of power (*bala*), whose activity is that of answering questions; for by means of the ten powers, he responds to sentient beings according to their individual capacities.
Second is the Buddha-wisdom of fearlessness, which destroys the karma of false views; it is called "Great" because it distinguishes itself from that of bodhisattvas.
Third is the Buddha-wisdom of equality, which realizes the selflessness of persons and phenomena, and functions as the teaching for sentient beings to realize and enter [this truth].
The fourth is the Buddha-wisdom of rescue, which is the activity of transforming sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
The fifth is the Buddha-wisdom of purification, which functions as the causal activity for rescue and integration, because compassion purifies hatred.

Sixth is the wisdom of non-remainder (*anavaśeṣajñāna*): the Buddha-wisdom that constantly observes the karma of sentient beings in the world with the Buddha-eye; it is called "non-remainder" because it observes universally throughout the ten directions.

Seventh is the defiled Buddha-wisdom (*saṃkliṣṭabuddhajñāna*): according to this present sutra, it adorns its *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment) with unobstructed wisdom, spontaneously manifesting through transformation to cause others to have faith and joy, which constitutes its function.
The treatise notes that the sūtra omits the Buddha-wisdom of the pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*).
The eighth is the Buddha-wisdom of the eight awakenings, whose function is to know in a single thought-moment the minds and mental factors of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
The ninth is the Buddha-wisdom of turning the wheel of Dharma, which functions through skillful means in liberation.
Skillfulness in speech refers to the simultaneous turning of the Great Wheel of Dharma across ten billion Jambudvīpas;
the Wheel of Dharma is precisely the skillful means that enables sentient beings to attain liberation.

However, in these nine preceding phrases, each first indicates the essence of wisdom and subsequently manifests its activity; the first three concern self-benefit, while the latter six concern the benefit of others.

Within the benefit of others, the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are the practice for benefiting others, compassion and loving-kindness are the mind for benefiting others, and the final four are the wisdom for benefiting others.

In the second section, the summary of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), the phrase "arousing such a mind" refers, according to the direct reading of the sūtra text, to the ten preceding types of mind; however, the treatise states that this is precisely what was described in the "Fundamental Section" as the "firm determination of the vow," because the upward-seeking of Buddha-wisdom is itself the vow.

In the previous section on the "Original Ground" (Mūlabhūmi), it was stated: "May they be well-established in their resolve. This refers to the generation of the bodhicitta within the first stage (prathamā bhūmi); that which is referred to here as the "vow" (praṇidhāna) within this very section on the Original Ground points specifically to this passage.
The arising of the mind is precisely the arising of the bodhicitta, because it seeks the Buddha-wisdom above; the vow is thus a vow for enlightenment.
Since the two entities are not distinct, they may be designated interchangeably.
The former refers back to this, which subsumes the ten preceding phrases on the Buddha’s wisdom;
this refers forward to the former, which subsumes the six definitive meanings from the preceding text.
That [refers] to this within the general statement, for this concluding summary subsumes the particulars within the general.

Furthermore, when it simply says "arising of the mind," "mind" (citta) is the general term; it thereby encompasses knowing, abandoning, realizing, and cultivating. Therefore, it does not say "arising of wisdom" (jñāna).
Because it also encompasses all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), it does not say "arising of other mental factors" (caitasika).
The purpose for which [this mind is generated] has already been explained.
Third, from the phrase "by means of great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) onwards, it clarifies by what cause such a mind is generated.
The intention is as follows:
For what reason does one seek great enlightenment?
It is because of great compassion for the sake of sentient beings.

Just as in the third stage, one contemplates the deliverance of beings without departing from the Buddha-wisdom; therefore, the general concluding statement in the treatise and the sūtra says, "This mind takes great compassion as its foremost. This "mind" refers back to the previously mentioned mind that seeks Buddha-wisdom.
Among these ten phrases, the first is general and the remaining nine are specific.
There are nine kinds of greatness in the specific section:
first, the greatness of supremacy.

Subtle practice is suffering because wisdom arises as predominant; that is to say, if one merely understands the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), wisdom is not predominant.

The treatise further states: "Wisdom is so called because it contemplates cause and effect, the adverse and the favorable, and defilement and purity. This refers to wisdom by way of discerning phenomena (*vastu*).

The Treatise states: "Wisdom (prajñā) is so called because it observes the distinctions between specific and general characteristics. This defines wisdom as that which comprehends the universal principle of the two truths; furthermore, this constitutes another specific interpretation from a particular perspective.
Regarding "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*): it is because the existence of causes and conditions constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this dharma.
Regarding "common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*): it is because the two kinds of emptiness, true suchness (*tathatā*), and so forth, are of a single flavor.

Beings give rise to delusion regarding these; therefore, one arouses the mind of compassion. This is like the predominance of great compassion in the sixth stage, wherein one contemplates their adversities and harmonies, as is extensively explained in the sixth stage.
The two skillful means (*kauśalya*) and so forth encompass "greatness" (*mahat*);
the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*) encompass "skillfulness in adaptation" (*vaicakṣaṇya*), because they attract beings according to what is appropriate.

Regarding the section beginning with "supreme" (*parama*): "purity of intent" (*adhyāśaya*) is the meaning of "supreme," referring to having previously resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) and vowing to provide inexhaustible benefit for as long as the realm of living beings endures; therefore, it is called the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*).
Because compassion increases through these conditions, reaching a state of profound sincerity, it is called "supreme.
One should always sustain this bodhisattva by means of these two.

Regarding the "four immeasurable powers of the Tathāgata": they are called immeasurable because they encompass the immeasurable spiritual powers of the Tathāgata in order to inspire faith in sentient beings.

The five kinds of skillful observation and so forth constitute the greatness of determination (*niścaya-mahattva*). To possess firm faith and understanding toward the sublime Dharma is called "skillful observation and discernment" (*sudarśana-vibhāga*).
To be firmly capable of delivering all sentient beings constitutes "heroic power" (*vīrya-bala*).
It possesses the power of wisdom because it is definitively able to counteract the obstacles that are to be remedied.
The phrase "unimpeded wisdom manifests" connects with the preceding sentence.
Sixth is the conformity to spontaneous wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), which is the conformity to the Great [Vehicle].

The seven [qualities], beginning with "able to receive" (*śakta-grāhaka*), constitute the greatness of receiving and upholding (*udgrahaṇa-mahattva*). This is because they are able to take up the great and supreme Dharma and bestow it upon sentient beings.

"Great" (*mahat*) means encompassing all; "supreme" (*viśiṣṭa*) refers to the Buddha-dharma; and "bestowing" (*pradāna*) refers to teaching and transforming. It is through wisdom that one is able to bestow it.
Eighth, "vast as the dharma-realm" refers to the greatness of the most sublime, because it encompasses supreme and wondrous merit.
Ninth, from "ultimate" downward, it is the greatness of the exhaustion of abiding, because it reaches the limit of nirvana where the causes for immeasurable fruits of affection are exhausted.
To complete the ten phrases, these two are combined.

The latter two great [categories] are as explained in the "Original Section" (Mūlabhāga); however, while the former speaks of "impermanent affection" (*anitya-sneha*), this speaks of "immeasurability" (*apramāṇa*), because their superior functions are not identical.
Among the nine types mentioned above, the first seven constitute the essence of compassion (*karuṇā*), the next one its quality, and the last one its capacity.
Within the seven, the first three are the self-referential [compassion]:
first, the wisdom that uproots suffering; second, the practice that uproots suffering; and third, the mental state that uproots suffering.
The latter four [verses] concern superior progress.
From the fourth verse, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva," there follows the characteristic that correctly reveals the signs of the benefits of attaining this stage.
The text contains nine phrases: the first is general, while the remainder are specific.
The general statement, "one who first gives rise to such a mind," refers to the preceding two sections.
The phrase "immediately transcends the stage of ordinary beings" means that one attains the supramundane noble path; thus, "transcendence" (chao) carries the sense of "passing beyond" (guo).
Second, following the section "Entering the Stage of Bodhisattvas," there are eight distinct types of faults; in the treatise, for each, the principle is presented first, followed by a simile.

Because entering this noble stage means being born into the family of the Tathāgata—just as a prince is born into a royal house—each sentence contains a statement regarding the correspondence between the dharma and the simile.
First is the fault regarding the stage of entry.
Because the initial formation of the supramundane mind is analogous to the state of first dwelling in the womb,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, "Chapter on Dwelling," refers to this as the Bodhisattva’s entry into the state of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*).
Regarding "being born into the family of the Tathāgata," this refers to the excellence of the family; it is a teaching on the analogy of being born into a family.

That is to say, although worldly people may receive the retribution of conception, if they are born into an ordinary family, it is not considered superior; it must be into a royal family that one is truly distinguished and eminent.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: if he were to renounce the world within the teachings of non-Buddhists, it would not be considered superior; only now that he has attained the Dharma realized by the Buddha does he become truly noble and preeminent.
The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states: "Born into the family of the Dharma-king, he is fully endowed with nobility and excellence."
The subsequent phrases all follow this pattern of building upon the preceding to distinguish the superior.
Third, from "incapable" onwards, it concerns the fault of the lineage (*gotra*).
This is because the practices of the Mahāyāna arise as something analogous to a seed; that is to say, the great practice is established.
Just as one who has obtained a portion of the royal body is fit to succeed to the lineage of the Buddha—this is the meaning of "son"—for such a person is neither low-born nor a guest.
The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states: "Because they transcend the lineages of the two vehicles and the mundane world."
4. "Transcending the World" refers to the path beyond [the mundane].
Because it is not *āsrava* (tainted), it transcends worldly destinies, just as one who is not a ghost or an animal cannot possess the essence of a king;
because it constitutes the *anāsrava* (untainted), it enters the supramundane path, just as one must possess the constituent parts of the essence of a human king.
The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states: "Because one never again commits wrong actions such as killing.

Fifth is the attainment of the Bodhisattva-dharma, which is the transcendence of the dharma-body (*dharmatā*), because great compassion of the same essence (*sahaja-mahākaruṇā*) constitutes the very body of the Bodhisattva.

Since the work of transforming others is itself one's own work, if great compassion were absent, the *dharmakāya* would be incomplete, just as it is when one excludes something that is deficient or damaged.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Suppose someone were to ask:
'What constitutes the essence of a bodhisattva?'"
"One should answer that its essence is great compassion.
Regarding the "abiding place" of a Bodhisattva in the sixth stage, this refers to transcending abiding.

That is to say, the path of non-abiding is their dwelling place; it is not like ordinary people or Hinayanists who, being defiled by the world or abandoning the world, remain stuck in the two extremes—just as a prince does not dwell in a base or lowly place.
Regarding the seventh point, "entering the equality of the three periods of time," this refers to transcending karma.

That is to say, one realizes the equality of true suchness (tathatā) to sustain the life of wisdom; if one lacks this essential flavor, one's lifespan will be prematurely shortened by celestial forces, rendering one incapable of continuing the lineage.
This is the analogy of life.
From "In the Tathāgata" onwards, it concludes with certainty.
That the Buddha-seed is not severed demonstrates the certainty of the cause.
Having attained the Unsurpassed Way, the manifestation of the fruit is certain, like a prince of the world.
Although one may rely on correct vigor and excellence, if one's resolve is not established, what is undertaken will not be accomplished;
