Now, to further briefly demonstrate the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one contemplates that form is itself emptiness and the mind rests in emptiness; this is the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Next, one knows that both emptiness and form do not transcend the mind; this is the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Next, when both mind and objects are extinguished, it is called "nothingness.
Next, one also extinguishes the perception of nothingness and dwells in the focus on non-perception; this is named "neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
If one does not take this non-conception as an object, then all outflows (āsrava) are eternally stilled.

This third entry into the mind merely accords with the method for transforming sentient beings; it is not like the ordinary, inferior attachment to flavors and so forth, as has already been explained previously.
The fourth major section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva’s mind follows," clarifies the fruit of renunciation.
Because it is induced by the aforementioned eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), it is termed a "fruit."
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the four immeasurables, which are the fruits of the skillful means of practice;
second, the five supernormal powers, which are the fruits of the functional efficacy of practice.
III. "This Bodhisattva, regarding all dhyānas," and so forth, summarizes his mastery. This is the first [section]. The reason for explaining this first is as follows:

ordinary beings, relishing meditative absorption (*āsvādita-samādhi*), transmigrate through the three realms; those of the Two Vehicles, ascending, mostly tend toward extinction (*nirvāṇa*); whereas Bodhisattvas, by means of meditative concentration, give rise to compassion and extensively benefit sentient beings, thereby perfecting their Bodhisattva nature.
However, the reason for this inclusion has already been clarified in the preceding treatise.
To correspond with the dichotomy of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the four immeasurables are divided into two pairs.

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, these four immeasurables are directed toward four types of sentient beings: that is, one arouses loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward those seeking happiness, compassion (*karuṇā*) toward those in suffering, sympathetic joy (*muditā*) toward those who possess joy, and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—remaining untainted by delusion—toward those possessed of confusion.
Furthermore, these four should universally take all things as their objects; when guided by wisdom, one remains unattached.
Because these four all take immeasurable objects, they are called the "four immeasurables" (catvāry apramāṇāni).
If explained in general terms, all [immeasurables] take concentration and wisdom as their essence. If explained specifically:
loving-kindness consists of bestowing happiness and takes non-hatred as its essence; compassion consists of removing suffering and takes non-harming as its essence;
sympathetic joy consists of rejoicing in others' welfare and takes non-envy as its essence.
Abandoning delusion regarding self and others is itself "skillful relinquishment.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the specific manifestation of the practice of loving-kindness; second, from the phrase "abiding in compassion" onwards, the other three [immeasurables] are manifested by analogy.
In the beginning and middle [of this section], there are twelve phrases.
"The mind follows loving-kindness" is the general statement.
Regarding "follows," there are two meanings:
First, the mind does not incline toward quiescence, but every movement accords with compassion;
second, this compassionate mind follows after all beings, like a calf following its mother.
The subsequent ten phrases are distinct [from these two].
There are three general categories of loving-kindness (*maitrī*):

first, there are seven phrases and eight meanings, consisting of loving-kindness directed toward sentient beings; next, one type directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambana*); and finally, two types that are objectless (*anālambana*).
"Condition" refers to mental attention.
First, one takes as an object a conventional person, desiring to bestow happiness upon them.

Next, one takes as an object the emptiness of persons, [realizing] that there are only the aggregates and so forth; one then employs the dharmas of wholesome and unwholesome conduct to teach and transform them.
Subsequently, because the essence of sentient beings is empty, [the Buddha] desires to lead them to awakening and entry [into the truth].
The first [of these three gates] applies to ordinary people, the next applies to those of the Small Vehicle, and the last applies exclusively to the Great Vehicle.
Now, regarding the first eight meanings, there are further four subdivisions:
The first four [immeasurables] bestow happiness, which primarily reveals their mental modes (*ākāra*).
"Vast" refers to bestowing the happiness of the desire realm, because the objects of desire are vast and manifold.

"Great" refers to bestowing the joy and happiness shared with others; that is, because the first and second dhyānas are accompanied by the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*), they are termed "great" due to their eminent transcendence.

"Immeasurable" (apramāṇa) means giving joy and happiness that is not shared with others; from the third dhyāna upward, because one is free from both suffering and joy, it is called "immeasurable" due to its profundity.
"Non-dual" (advaya) means giving the three types of happiness equally.
The above constitutes the general meaning of the argument.
There is, however, another principle:

"Extensive" means there is no bliss that is not bestowed; "Great" refers to Bodhi and Nirvana; "Immeasurable" means it extends to the furthest reaches of the future; and "Non-dual" means there is nothing whatsoever that is not bestowed.
The next two [verses] treat the obstacles.
Since one bestows happiness even upon hateful enemies, there is no obstacle of resentment;
since one bestows happiness even upon beloved kin, this is not a matter of partiality, and thus there is no obstacle of obstruction.
Ordinary people have neither love nor non-love; therefore, these are not obstructions.

Next is "purity," which means being free from the obstructions such as the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) and the lack of harmony between body and mind; this is the practice of pure loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

The latter one subsumes the realms: the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) arises as the direct fruit (*vipāka-phala*) in the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), while the residual force of that loving-kindness arises as the habitual fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) in the desire realm (*kāma-dhātu*). In both cases, there are no matters of suffering or affliction; therefore, the *Maitrī-bhāvanā-sūtra* states that there are fifteen benefits to cultivating loving-kindness: namely, peace in sleep and peace upon waking; protection by devas and protection by humans; no evil dreams during sleep; constant joy upon awakening; inability to be swept away by water; inability to be burned by fire; inability to be wounded by weapons; inability to be harmed by poison; constant rebirth in auspicious places; perpetual experience of happiness; the primary retribution of birth in the Brahma world; the residual retribution of becoming a king among men; and the distant fruit of attaining Buddhahood—all of which are the fruits of loving-kindness.
However, within this there are several kinds of fruits:
first, the fruit of retribution in the present life;
"born constantly" and below refer to the fruit of retribution in subsequent lives.

Taking the primary retribution (*vipāka-phala*) of the Brahma-world as the standard: in relation to the higher rebirth-retribution and the lower primary retribution, the residual retribution of being a human king is the fruit of cultivation (*abhyāsa-phala*).

Furthermore, regarding the first seven [stages], the fact that one is not swept away by water and so forth is the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*); being constantly born there is the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*); the residual retribution and so forth are the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*); and becoming a Buddha is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*).

By cultivating a single mind of loving-kindness, the threefold retribution is uninterrupted and the five fruits are all perfected; without expending so much as a hair’s breadth, the merit and reward are infinite. I hope that future students will reflect upon this and practice accordingly.
Next, it pervades all places; this is the compassion that takes phenomena as its object (dharmālambana-maitrī).
It extends horizontally throughout the ten directions and vertically through the three realms, being able to take as its object and bring to mind all phenomena contained therein.
However, there are two kinds of dharmas:
first, the dharmas of the five aggregates belonging to both noble ones and ordinary beings; second, the dharmas of discriminative karmic activity possessed by sentient beings.
These constitute the distinctions among those to be transformed; thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The dharma that takes sentient beings as its object is called 'dharma-object' (dharmālambana)."
Regarding the absence of objects for the latter two lines, there are two kinds of objectlessness:
first, objectlessness in its own nature.
Vertically exhausting the emptiness of all phenomena, it is said to pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
The second [verse], "pervading everywhere without an object," reveals that emptiness has no boundaries, extending horizontally to the very limits of space.
The final phrase, "pervading all worlds," summarizes the preceding loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to establish its meaning as immeasurable (*apramāṇa*).
The remaining three categories may be understood by analogy.

Section Two: “The Sons of the Buddha” and below, which clarifies the fruit of the application of spiritual practice (*prayoga*) that attains the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Previously, he inwardly harbored a mind of compassionate salvation; outwardly, he manifested the function of saving sentient beings. This is explained from the perspective of the majority of cases as being solely for the purpose of guiding those who have turned toward heterodoxy.
Inconceivable wondrous function is called "spiritual" (shen), and sovereign freedom without obstruction is called "penetration" (tong).
Within this section there are five [powers]:

first, the power of spiritual transformations; second, the divine ear; third, knowledge of others' minds; fourth, recollection of past lives; and fifth, the divine eye. Because these are presented in parallel with worldly phenomena, only these five are attained.
External forms and the internal body are both objects of the mind; they undergo various transformations and are thus specifically designated by the term "mind" (*citta*).
It is also called "basis of supernormal power" (*ṛddhipāda*), because it is accomplished through reliance on desire, effort, mind, and investigation.
It is also called "according to wish" (*yatheṣṭa*), because it accomplishes things according to one's will.
The other names are easy to understand.
As for its essential nature, it generally belongs to the category of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*); specifically, the first four are knowledge (*jñāna*) and the last one is vision (*dṛṣṭi*).
Vision (*darśana*) is also a form of knowledge; because it clearly illuminates and accords with the function of the eye, it is specifically designated by the name "vision.
In other contexts, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is categorized under the supernormal power of the basis (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*).

As for the sequence [of the supernormal knowledges], this reveals the practitioner's own cultivation: first, one perfects the superior function of one's own faculties; next, one knows the minds of others; and finally, one knows past karma.
Now, based on the three types of action for the benefit of others, the divine eye is placed last.
First is bodily action: reaching the place where those to be converted reside.

Next are two types of vocal action: with the divine ear, one hears the Buddha preaching the Dharma and hears the various dialects of the multitude; having fully understood all these diverse sounds through the knowledge of others' minds, one then takes the Dharma previously heard and, according to the differences in their dialects, determines which specific linguistic variation would be most appropriate to bestow upon them.
The latter two are mental actions:
through the knowledge of past lives, one knows which realm or seed they belonged to in the past;
through the divine eye, one perceives their future benefits, whether near or far, and accordingly transforms them.
The remainder is as explained in the "Chapter on the Ten Supernormal Powers" (*Daśābhijñā-parivarta*).
Here, regarding the first, the supernormal power of the body (*kāyābhijñā*), the text has two parts:
first, a general explanation; second, a detailed exposition beginning with the words "capable of moving."
Regarding the statement "attained" in the general [section], it means that one practices collectively and attains collectively.

However, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Triṃśikā-bhūmi), after having attained the four dhyānas, if one practices each individually and all involve conceptualization (*parikalpa*), then it is individual practice leading to individual attainment.
Since the sequence of the stages has already been established, there is no contradiction in this distinction;
however, they all generally rely upon the four dhyānas, with most relying specifically on the fourth.
Within the subsequent section on the distinctions, one attains three kinds of mastery:
1. Mastery over the world (*loka-vaśitā*), because he causes the great earth to tremble;
2. Mastery over the body (*kāya-vaśitā*), as indicated by the phrase "with one body";
3. Mastery over action (*karma-vaśitā*), as indicated by the phrase "stone walls."
The second day concerns the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*).
First, its essence is generally defined as the "purified divine ear.
This purification has two meanings:
First, one attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by being free from the phenomena of the desire realm, because it is produced by the great elements (*mahābhūta*) derived from pure [elements];
second, one is free from obstacles through listening with careful discernment.
For this reason, it is said that [this power] "surpasses that of humans.
The section beginning with "hears everything" clarifies its function and explains the meaning of "surpassing humans," because he knows all things, even those distant and subtle.
Third, within the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, there are three parts:
First, the general knowledge of others' minds applies to the king's presence;
next, from "That is to say" onwards, it is specific;
finally, from "The Bodhisattva thus" onwards, it is the conclusion.

Within this classification, although the mental aspects (*ākāra*) of the twenty-six minds differ from one another, with the exception of the four minor minds and so forth, all others clearly manifest as alternating between obstacles and their remedies, or as opposites of good and evil.
These are summarized into nine categories:

first, the initial six mental states clarify the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). They are called "secondary" because they arise in accordance with conditions in association with the primary afflictions; this designation as "secondary" does not refer to them being minor afflictions (*upakleśa* in the sense of *paryavasthāna*).

Regarding those "possessing greed," they are so called because they are bound by the fetters of greed toward attractive objects; those "free from greed" are so called because they have distanced themselves from such fetters of greed.
The following four cases should be understood by analogy.
That is to say, the three unwholesome roots and the three wholesome roots serve as the remedies (*pratipakṣa*).

However, since the treatise now considers that even these remedies arise from afflictions (*kleśa*), they are all termed secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); the same applies to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) discussed below.
Second, regarding the two minds associated with afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, it clarifies that the proclivities (*anuśaya*) are themselves the latent tendencies.
Third, the four minds—small and so forth—are termed "arising" (*jāti*), referring to the neutral resultant (*vipāka*) mind. The human mind is small;

the desire-realm devas are broad; the form-realm devas are great; and the two liberations of the formless realm are immeasurable, because they function through the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the infinite space and infinite consciousness.
The latter two are not thus; therefore, they are not "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).

Although the treatise does not explicitly clarify the two higher spheres of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana* and *vijñānānantyāyatana*), its intention is to clarify that [the sphere of nothingness] is non-existent and [the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception] is dull and inferior; alternatively, it may be a case of omitting what is included within the non-omitted.

Regarding the four modes of existence, there are four types of mind that practice the cultivation of samādhi. "Concentration" (samkṣepa) refers to the practice of calm abiding (śamatha), because by means of it, the mind is bound to an internal object of focus.
"Non-concentration" (asamkṣepa) occurs because [the mind] is either overly dull and obscured, or because it does not remain fixed on a single object of focus.
"Distracted" refers to excessive elevation, because the mind flows and scatters in accordance with the objects of the five types of sensual desire.
"Not distracted" refers to the clear and vivid manifestation of the sublime object of focus.

The first two are defined in terms of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the latter two are defined in terms of wisdom (*prajñā*). When concentration and the other factors are equal, it is termed "equipoise" (*samāhita*). Since the treatise and the sutra combine these into two categories—namely "comprehended" (*saṃgṛhīta*) and "not comprehended" (*asaṃgṛhīta*)—the treatise explains them by means of "distracted" (*vikṣipta*) and "undistracted" (*avikṣipta*).
Regarding the fifth point, there are two types of mind: those that clarify the attainment of samādhi, because they correctly enter the fundamental concentration;
and those that are not fixed, because they have not yet entered it or have emerged from it.
Regarding the sixth point, there are two types of mind that clarify the attainment of liberation: those with bondage and those without bondage.

There are two types of mind among the seven; the rest are categorized as the same class as the ordinary persons with overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Furthermore, those who attain the four dhyānas and claim them to be the four fruits are called "superior" because their habitual practice is coarse; those who lack this are called "unsurpassed" because their habitual practice is subtle.

Regarding the eight [types of persons], there are two types of mind: those who practice erroneously and those who practice correctly; in the treatises and sūtras, these are termed "seeking" and "not seeking.
A mind that yearns for fame and reputation is defiled; the opposite is non-defiled.
The ninth category consists of two types of mind. In the Mahāyāna, the attainment of both compassion and wisdom constitutes "extensiveness" (vaipulya); if either is lacking, it is not extensive.
This treatise excludes these two [types of mind].
The nine aforementioned categories do not transcend three kinds:
The first two are afflictions;
the next one is suffering;
the remainder are all karma, which is either wholesome or unwholesome.
This is also the Four Noble Truths, wherein liberation is opened up as Cessation and wholesome karma as the Path.
"Knowing all as they truly are" means examining the facts of phenomena and perceiving the reality of principles.
Furthermore, it is not that phenomena are perceived outside of the mind, nor is it that there is no object to be known.
If the distinctions between self and other are severed, then one’s mind is of the same substance as the minds of all sentient beings; therefore, there is nothing outside of the mind.
Because subject and object are not destroyed, one is able to know.
Furthermore, the mind of another is the general, while all others are the particular.
The six characteristics are perfectly interfused; this is the true knowledge of the One Vehicle.

Regarding the fourth supernormal knowledge, the knowledge of past abodes (*pūrvanivāsajñāna-abhijñā*): first, there is a general indication of who is able to recollect, which refers to the knowledge of past abodes;
next, the section beginning with "That is to say" provides a detailed exposition;
finally, the section beginning with "In this way, the past... offers a summary.
Within the specific [analysis], what is the object of the first moment?
It refers to events from one lifetime up to many kalpas; this clarifies the temporal duration of the recollection.
Next, regarding the phrase "I once... and so forth, how does one recollect?
This refers to the distinctions between names and characteristics.

"Names" refers to the different appellations within those causal conditions; "clan" (*gotra*) refers to the family surname of one's parents, such as the *Kāśyapa* lineage, as well as the social status of the caste, such as the *Kṣatriya* and so forth—the rest can be understood accordingly.

The fifth is the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*); in the treatise it is called the supernormal power of knowledge regarding birth and death (*cyutyupapādajñāna-abhijñā*), as they differ according to their faculties and objects.
First, the capacity to see is generally revealed. Who is it that can see?
It is called the "divine eye" because it is pure;
it is "clearly seeing" because it perceives with precision;
it is "surpassing that of humans" because it sees at a distance.
Next, from "He sees all" onwards, the specific objects of his vision are revealed.
First, he sees the fruit that has existed fundamentally within birth and death, as well as the causes that follow from karma.
Regarding the section beginning with "If those sentient beings," how does he see?
The distinct views regarding the differences between cause and effect are as analyzed in the section on the "Precepts for Gathering Virtue" in the second stage (*bhūmi*).
The section beginning with "Bodhisattva" below serves as a conclusion.
The third section, beginning with "This Bodhisattva," provides a summary of mastery.
The proximate result of aversion is bound, while the remote result of prior aversion is also bound.
In what does this mastery reside?
It resides in the aforementioned dhyānas and so forth; "dhyāna" refers here to the four dhyānas.
"Samādhi" refers to the samādhis of the four immeasurables, such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and so forth.

Regarding "samāpatti," the treatise states it refers to the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*); however, this is likely a translation error by the commentator, as it should read *samāhita*. This is translated as "equipoise" (*samāhita*), for the five supernormal powers are that which are induced by equipoise.
Samāpatti is here translated as "equilibrium" (dengzhi), for it is not a supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
How is there mastery?
When wisdom can enter and emerge [from it], then discursive agitation cannot bind it.
Because at the very moment the mind arises, it functions in accordance with that mind, as it manifests before one.
If the skillful means of great compassion did not follow along with rebirth, they would certainly be unable to bind [the bodhisattva].
If they do not follow along with birth through dhyāna, then where would they be born?
Without discriminating between the pure and the impure, one is born wherever the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) can be fulfilled.

The Master of the Treatise speaks from the perspective of excellence and self-benefit, stating that the place where Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwell together is the locus for fulfilling these factors; this is because those who possess the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) are not born through the bondage of karma.
The second fruit.
The three fruits constitute three distinct categories.
Within the first, the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), there are three:

First, the essence of the practice of initial flexibility; second, the specific characteristics of the stages from "This bodhisattva, regarding the four means of integration" onwards; third, the summary of the characteristics of the stage from "O Son of the Buddha, this is called" onwards.
In the preceding section, there are the thesis (*dharma*), the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*).
Within the thesis, there are three parts:

first, the conditions for refining practice; second, from "all by means of" (*sarvam etena*) onwards, the clarification of the practice that refines; and third, from "the bonds of views" (*dṛṣṭibandhana*) onwards, the clarification of the purity resulting from refinement.
Within these two [categories], first is the practice of merit, next is the practice of dedication, and finally is the practice of cultivating wisdom.
To speak of contemplating all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing refers precisely to the contemplation of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because one does not perceive increase within pure dharmas, afflictions do not arise;
because one does not perceive decrease within delusive thoughts, causes and conditions do not cease, yet they exist.
This has two meanings:
first, it establishes that because pure dharmas arise from conditions, there is nothing to be added;
and because delusive dharmas cease due to conditions, there is nothing to be subtracted.

Secondly, with respect to its indestructible characteristic: although its essence is neither arising nor ceasing, it is not obstructed by arising and ceasing. It is said to "cease" because it is free from afflictions and delusive conceptualization through the conditions of remedial practice; it is said to "arise" because the increasingly superior and pure *prajñā* manifests before one.
Because the non-arising of all dharmas gives rise to prajñā, one knows that all dharmas do not cease, for it is only deluded thought (*vikalpa*) that ceases.
By applying this principle to what follows, one sees that the bonds of views and so forth are extinguished; this is the extinction of that which does not truly cease.

Furthermore, because these three stages are filled with worldly phenomena, one performs this contemplation of reality within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This gives rise to the wisdom of non-arising practice (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) regarding the subsequent stage, which is precisely the skillful, decisive analytical knowledge (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

Among the three types of purification through cultivation (*pariśuddhi*), the first clarifies the severance of delusions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), followed by the distinction between the subtle and the coarse.

Within the former, the "five bonds" (*pañca-bandhana*) refer to the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsika-kleśa*); if combined with the realm of form-existence (*rūpabhava*), they constitute the "four bonds," so called because they bind sentient beings.
They are also called the four floods (*ogha*).

Regarding the prior cessation of the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-bandhana*), it is because the delusions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*) have already been severed through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in the first stage (*bhūmi*).

As for "all [afflictions] such as desire" (*sarva-kāma-ādi*), the *Śāstra* states: "In all paths of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), the three fetters and their causes, together with the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), are all rendered extremely subtle."
This refers to the active manifestations and seeds of the three bonds of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*); thus, they are called "their causes.

Because they are extinguished simultaneously with the seeds of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of that same stage, they are said to be "identical to the habitual tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*)."

The meaning of "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) is that of "seeds. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 48, states: "Because one abandons desire and greed, there is no bond of desire; because one relinquishes meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and concentration (*samādhi*), the bond of existence (*bhava-bandhana*) is severed."
The subsequent passage, beginning with "In the immeasurable," distinguishes the subtle from the coarse.

This refers to the severing of the subtle, because for many eons one has not accumulated the three unwholesome roots; thus, the subtle seeds are gradually severed and the wholesome roots become increasingly pure.

Regarding the phrase "many kalpas," the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states that the first bhūmi requires four asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the second five, and the third six; as the subtle obstructions are difficult to sever, the required kalpas increase accordingly. Because these many kalpas are not accumulated [as a single duration], perverse greed and other such afflictions are severed.

However, this merely severs subtle habitual tendencies and does not sever the coarse ones; for coarse obstacles to the Path of Seeing have already been severed at the first stage (bhūmi), and coarse obstacles to the Path of Cultivation have already been severed from the second stage onward.
The roots of goodness become increasingly purified; these are the same as the faith and other virtues mentioned previously.

The metaphor of the scale not losing its weight means that because one’s revulsion for the world surpasses the faith and other virtues of the preceding stage and enters the fire of revulsion, one’s mastery is neither lost nor diminished.

Within the third [section], there are two parts: first, the general explanation of the purity of practice; second, from "This bodhisattva" onwards, the specific revelation of the purity of patience (*kṣānti*).
Because patience increases in this stage, it is explained in particular detail.
There are thirteen states of mind.
The first two phrases constitute the general summary: first, one is able to endure insults and humiliations inflicted by others;
second, one skillfully protects the minds of others, meaning that when others treat me with arrogance and harshness, I respond to them with gentleness and flexibility.
The subsequent phrases provide a detailed explanation of these two.
Regarding the first, there are two types of mental states for skillfully protecting the minds of others.
First is the "harmonizing mind": when others commit evil against a bodhisattva and suspect that the bodhisattva harbors resentment, the bodhisattva manifests as a companion to harmonize with them.
Second, regarding "pleasing and beautiful," this refers to instructing and guiding others with loving speech.
Next, one should distinguish [this practice] by means of three mental states.

First, enduring harm: when physical harm is inflicted, one does not become angry; when verbally insulted, one’s mind remains unmoved; and even when subjected to jealousy or malice, one cannot be turbidized by grief or vexation, for one's capacity is like that of a ten-thousand-acre pond.
Next, there are three mental states that arise from the two aforementioned causes.

Regarding "being without superiority or inferiority": because one has long since abandoned arrogance in the past, one does not exalt oneself or disparage others; by means of this, one is able to be gentle and protect others.
The latter two [factors] add the causes for not ceasing even when confronted with evil:
first, one benefits others without expecting gratitude and endures being insulted;
second, one constantly remembers kindness received and repays even small favors with great generosity.
Sentient beings have been kind to me; it is the natural law that I should practice patience toward them.
The latter three mental states clarify the former two.
Although they are compliant in being free from hindrances, they protect others without guile, for their true purpose is to bring about benefit.
Because his mind is not deceptive and he is free from concealment, flattery, and sycophancy, he is without crookedness.
"Crookedness" refers to flattery and sycophancy.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Second, from "The Bodhisattva abides in this" onwards, the fruit of the maturation of rewards (*vipākaphala*) is subsumed.
In all subsequent passages concerning the maturation of rewards in these various stages (*bhūmi*), the text is divided into two parts:
first, the superior body; second, from "He is able to... onwards, the superior fruits.

Within the section on the fruition (*phala*), there are three parts: first, the practice of one's own sphere (*svabhūmi-pratipatti*); second, the practice of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gamana-pratipatti*) from the point where it says "Furthermore, he thinks" onwards; and third, the summary verses (*uddāna-gāthā*).
These eighteen verses are divided into five sections:
the first verse initiates the section on the practice of weariness (*udvega-caryā*).

The second section consists of twelve verses on the stage of practice characterized by weariness (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipatti*). Among these, the first two verses concern the practice of guarding against afflictions (*kleśa*); the next three concern the practice of guarding against the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); and the final seven concern the practice subsumed under skillful means (*upāya*).
Three verses summarize the stage of revulsion and its fruit;
four verses summarize the fruits of the stages;
one verse concludes the exposition of the three stages. From this point downward, we enter the thirty-sixth sūtra.
The fourth is the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
The reason for its inclusion is that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 78, citing the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, explains that four kinds of purity can encompass all the grounds.

The preceding three—namely, the three purities of superior intention (*āśaya*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), and meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—have been concluded. Below this, from the fourth [purity] up to the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), the purity of superior wisdom (*prajñā*) is elucidated; therefore, it follows next.
Furthermore, wisdom is of many kinds; since this stage clearly elucidates the dwelling in superior wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), it follows next.

Moreover, although the preceding stage attained worldly meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs, one had not yet attained the factors of enlightenment; having now abandoned attachment to concentration and attachment to phenomena, one cultivates and realizes those practices, and thus it follows next.
According to the root treatise, the first three [stages] are based on the mundane world, while this present one is supramundane; it follows in sequence for this reason.
If viewed in proximity to the preceding stage, this realized wisdom is generated through hearing based on the prior meditative concentration (dhyāna); therefore, it follows immediately after.
Therefore, the treatise states: "Relying upon that pure samādhi, one possesses the wisdom of hearing and retaining as it truly is, because of its pure manifestation.
Regarding the term "Blazing Wisdom" (Arciṣmatī), both the dharma and the metaphor are presented together, and there are three meanings:
first, the explanation based on the initial entry into this stage.
Upon first entering the realization of gnosis (*pramāṇa-jñāna*), one is able to burn away the firewood of pride regarding the understanding of the dharmas of the preceding stage.
As the *Mūlabhāga* states: "The fire of wisdom can burn the firewood of the afflictions that have not yet been forgotten."
Second, the explanation according to the *bhūmi*s.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Because one abides in the most excellent factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the flames of wisdom increase as they burn the fuel of afflictions."
Since one only begins to cultivate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) upon completing the fourth stage, it is clear that these [factors] belong to this stage.
If one were to take only this as the definition of wisdom, then the stage prior to cultivating the path-factors (mārgāṅga) would not be the "Blazing Stage" (arcismatī-bhūmi).
Since this stage clearly elucidates the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), it encompasses both the beginning and the end; most treatises rely on this interpretation.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Because all factors conducive to enlightenment burn away all obstacles."
"Obstructions" refers to the two obstructions.

The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "Taking the wisdom of the factors of enlightenment as the nature of the flame, and taking the two obstructions—of afflictions and of knowledge—as the nature of the fuel; because a bodhisattva on this stage can give rise to the flame of wisdom to burn the fuel of these two obstructions, it is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*)."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 78, quotes the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* in a manner largely identical to this explanation. It states:
"The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that have been attained are like flames—the fire of wisdom capable of incinerating the afflictions."
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* do not differ from this intent.
Third, it is categorized by the perfection of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Because it emits the light of the *āgama* from the mani-jewel of realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*), it is called "Flame" (*arcis*); the lower treatise provides a detailed account of this.

However, the afflictions that are burned away are precisely the subtle manifesting obstacles of the afflictions to be abandoned; these consist of a portion of the innate aspect of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and they also include attachment to meditative concentration and attachment to the Dharma.

The factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) are specifically opposed to those [afflictions] and are thus able to incinerate them; for this reason, it is said that on the fourth stage one abandons two delusions along with their corresponding coarse residues (dauṣṭhulya).
First is the delusion of attachment to meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), because of relishing the eight dhyānas;
second is the delusion of attachment to dharmas, which is precisely the pride of intellectualizing the Dharma.
Now, having attained untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) and untainted instruction (*anāsrava-śāsana*), one thus opposes that [previous state].

By this, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) free from grasping; that is to say, this *tathatā* has no point of attachment, because it is not the basis for the appropriation of the ego-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) and so forth.
Having attained this True Suchness (tathatā), how could there be any attachment to fixed dharmas?
Thus one is able to accomplish the practices for the stage of Bodhi and the practice of the non-abiding path, exerting diligence without regression.
By realizing the suchness that is free from grasping, one attains the fruit of gathering in sentient beings.
Next is the formal explanation of the text, which also consists of three parts:
first, the praise and request; second, the formal exposition; and third, the summary verses.
Now, regarding the first part, the six verses are divided into two sections:
the first two and a half verses constitute the prologue composed by the compiler of the sutra.
As for "the shaking of the earth and the oceans," this symbolizes that the thick earth of ignorance and the ocean waters of great compassion can both be overturned and exhausted.

The final three and a half verses explicitly clarify the praise and the request; therein, the first two and a half verses constitute the request by the Heavenly King, and the final one verse constitutes the request by the leaders of the assembly.
Within the second section, the "Section on the Actual Exposition," there are two parts:
first, the elucidation of the characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*); second, the elucidation of the fruits of the stages.
The preceding section is divided into four parts:

first, the part on the causes for the growth of the cultivation of the antidotes for purification; that is to say, "purification" and so forth constitute the next two parts, wherein the skillful means for entering the stages (*bhūmi*) serve as their cause.

Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Blazing Wisdom" onwards is the part on purification, because it concerns the practice of emerging from obstacles upon first entering the stage.

3. From “O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this fourth [ground]” onwards is the section on the increase of remedial practice (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā-vṛddhi*). This refers to the correct dwelling in the ground and the practice of the *caryā-pratipatti* and so forth; it is called "remedial" because it is capable of eliminating [defilements], and the progressive training in ever-higher stages is termed the "increase of practice.

4. From “O Son of the Buddha... as far as all views of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*)” onwards is the section on its fruit (*phala*). This constitutes the fulfillment of the ground (*bhūmi-paripūri*), which is the fruit of these two preceding sections.

Furthermore, these four parts correspond to the four paths: the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the path of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
Moreover, among these four, the first pertains to the mind of entry (*praveśa-citta*), while the latter three pertain to the mind of abiding (*sthiti-citta*).
The "emerging mind" (niryāṇa-citta) resides in the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

Within the "abiding mind" (*sthiti-citta*), three parts subsume the first three stages: the first, the "part of purification" (*viśuddhi-bhāga*), subsumes the stage of noble birth (*janma-kulīna-vihāra*); the second subsumes the dedication that reaches all places (*sarvatraga-pariṇāmanā*); and the third subsumes inexhaustible conduct (*akṣaya-pratipatti*). These should be understood as they appear in the text.
Now, regarding the first section on the causal stage (*hetubhūmi*), the text is divided into three parts:

first, the conclusion of the preceding section and the introduction of the subsequent one; second, the inquiry and enumeration of the specific names beginning with "What are they?"; and third, the conclusion of the practice and entry into the stage beginning with "The bodhisattva, by means of this..."

First, regarding the "ten dharma-gates of illumination" (*daśa-dharmāloka-mukha*): "gate" (*mukha*) carries the sense of a passage for entry; therefore, the treatise and the sūtra refer to it as "entry. Here, "illumination" (*āloka*) is the gate that enables entry, and "dharma" is the locus into which one enters. Thus, the treatise states: "Having attained the light of wisdom pertaining to the stages of realization, one relies upon that illuminating wisdom to enter into the teachings expounded by the Tathāgata."
The phrase "knowledge of the realization of the stage" refers to the knowledge of realization of the fourth stage (*caturthī-bhūmi*).
"Radiance" refers to the light of wisdom of the third stage (*tṛtīyā-bhūmi*).

This means that within the third stage, one attains the precursor to this knowledge of realization of the fourth stage; therefore, the knowledges of both stages are cited together to explain "clarity," just as the "attainment of clarity" (*āloka-labdha-samādhi*) occurs prior to the stages.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that "the wisdom therein is called 'light' (*prabhā*)"; this is precisely its meaning.

Regarding the "Dharma being taught," it refers to having previously sought extensive learning and heard from the Buddha the ten kinds of dharmas, such as the *dharmadhātu* of sentient beings; one then enters into them repeatedly by means of the light of wisdom.

Entering through play is itself spiritual practice; spiritual practice consists of downward observation. Because this observation increases and reaches ultimate perfection, one is finally able to realize and enter the fourth stage.
Within the enumeration of the two inquiries, there are ten types of distinctions.
To observe these ten, they may be briefly explained through three layers:
first, the initial phrase serves as the general heading, because it is fundamentally for the sake of sentient beings.
The remaining nine are distinct because they all pertain to the affairs of sentient beings.
Second, among these, the first eight are defiled and the latter two are pure.
Third, the first five infer the supported (the faculties) back to the support (the physical bases), while the latter five establish the supported based upon the support.
Regarding the preceding section, first one contemplates the conventional designations (*prajñapti*) of the distinctions among sentient beings.
There are three types of conventional designations:

first, the conventional designation of causal formation (*hetusamutthāna-prajñapti*); second, the conventional designation of continuity (*santati-prajñapti*); and third, the conventional designation of relative dependence (*apekṣā-prajñapti*).
Since "provisionality" (prajñapti) is a designation for "emptiness," one first contemplates it.
There are two ways in which it is established:
first, when the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) are combined and provisionally named "so-and-so," one enters the emptiness of sentient beings (sattva-śūnyatā).
The two aggregates also exist through causes and conditions, and thus one enters the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
That which is revealed by these two kinds of emptiness is *tathatā* (suchness). Without destroying conventional designations, the non-duality of emptiness and existence is itself the Middle Way.

Regarding "continuity" (*saṃtati*): because the preceding aggregates (*skandha*) cease and the subsequent aggregates arise in succession, they continue moment by moment; this is a provisional designation and not substantial reality.
It also enters into the true reality of the two kinds of emptiness.
Regarding "mutual dependence": it is by depending on what is not a sentient being that one speaks of a sentient being;

entering into reality is likewise so. This is one instance of pushing through the conventional to enter the real; the remaining nine cases should be understood by analogy. Therefore, the treatise merely clarifies the characteristics of their distinctions.

Regarding the second, the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*): it corresponds to the third [topic] in the treatise and is the cause of both the basis (*āśraya*) and the based (*āśrita*). This refers specifically to the defiled dharma-realm.
If, however, the pure dharma-realm is taken as the universal basis for all ten, then the ten and the dharma-realm are ultimately without distinction.
The three worlds refer to the provisional names for the dwelling places and environmental retributions (*āśraya-vipāka*) where sentient beings reside.

The fourth is the space upon which both the environment and its inhabitants depend; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* calls this the "equal ultimate truth" (*samatā-paramārtha*), as it is the emptiness of principle (*li-kōng*) that is entirely inexhaustible.

The fivefold basis for defilement and purification is this fundamental consciousness-element (*ālayavijñāna-dhātu*). The subsequent five [consciousnesses] are established based upon this support as the supported; therefore, this consciousness-element has two orientations: looking forward, it serves as the primary support (*āśraya*), and looking backward, it serves as the support for defilement and purification.

The first three phrases indicate that, due to the latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) becomes defiled, resulting in the distinctions of the three realms. This is because of attachment to desire, attachment to sensation, and attachment to perception; for the three realms are nothing but mind (*citta-mātra*).

The latter two, the vast and great resolute beliefs (*adhimukti*), constitute the purified dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Regarding these, the treatise and the sūtra state that the former is the basis for the superior mind of resolute belief, which is untainted by afflictions and thus identical to that of the śrāvakas;
the latter is the basis for the great mind of resolute belief, which does not abandon sentient beings and is therefore distinct from that of the śrāvakas.
The present sutra is what was previously called "extensive," which clarifies a mind that protects the narrow while simultaneously providing universal succor;
the latter is the "great mind," which means protecting those of small capacity while seeking great bodhi.

Thus, these two states of mind both differ from those of the Two Vehicles: the former involves contemplating sentient beings with the great compassion of shared essence, while the latter involves contemplating that sentient beings possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, vowing to cause them all to attain it together.
Furthermore, all that is called "dhātu" (element/realm) encompasses both phenomena and principle.

Phenomena refer to the exhaustive manifestation of distinctions; principle refers to each and every thing entering into reality, which is the Pure Dharma-realm. Therefore, they all serve as gates of illumination.
Regarding the third stage of practice, the entry into the levels:
when one’s observation is perfected and accords with the ten principles, one enters the fourth bhūmi.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (48) states: "Previously, while dwelling in the stage of superior mind (*adhicitta-vihāra*), by means of the superior power of seeking extensive learning..."

Having attained the ten entries into the light of the Dharma, because these ten entries into the light of the Dharma have become superior and perfectly complete, one enters the first stage of the dwelling in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-vihāra*).

The second major section, the Section on Purity (*viśuddhi-bhāga*), subsumes the Dwelling of Birth in Nobility; therefore, the preceding text states, "born within the holy teachings of all Buddhas. How is it pure?
Because one gains increasing power within the family of the Tathāgata.
The text has three parts:
first, a general explanation; second, a detailed inquiry and exposition beginning with "What are they?"; and third, a summary concluding with "These are the ten."
Regarding the beginning and middle, the text contains three phrases:

the final phrase, "the family of that which is produced" (*janyapakṣa*), is the general characteristic; the first phrase, the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*), is the productive cause; and the second phrase, internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*), is the family of that which is produced (*janyapakṣa*).
Because one observes the ten dharmas, such as the lower formations (*saṃskāra*), by means of the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), one attains maturation.

Through this maturation, the cognitive obstructions regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) pertaining to the three stages are eliminated; one gathers the supramundane superior wisdom of the fourth stage and accords with the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is said that "one attains those internal dharmas."
"Internal dharmas" indicates that which is not external in appearance; these dharmas are precisely the teachings for transformation spoken by the Tathāgata, and are thus called the "Tathāgata family.
Since this stage marks the beginning of transcendence from the world, it is named "Birth."
However, there are briefly three kinds of the Tathāgata family:
first, the family of the bodhicitta, which arises upon the initial dwelling;
second, the family of the Great Teaching, which arises upon the fourth dwelling; [and third, the family of the ultimate fruit, which arises upon the tenth dwelling].
Regarding the three dharma-realms, [the Bodhisattva] is born because they are realized in the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Now, this [stage] subsumes the four abodes; therefore, by means of wisdom one accords with the teaching and unites it with the dharma-realm. Because it possesses the ten meanings mentioned below, it is called "birth."

If the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* merely states that one "grows in the Tathāgata family," and the commentary on the sūtra likewise merely states that one "increases in power within the Tathāgata family," the intent is to clarify that although one has already been born into the family from the first bhūmi onward, it is only upon entering the second and third bhūmis that one initiates the cultivation of skillful means and thus acquires such power;
now, based on the extensive learning of the third bhūmi, one accomplishes supramundane wisdom, and therefore it is said that one "further increases" [in power].
In this context, the "conformity of wisdom" (jñāna-yukti) refers to the light of wisdom consisting of non-practice and the practice of non-arising.
Within the enumeration of the two inquiries, there are ten phrases.
The *Śāstrasaṃgraha* condenses these into four:

The first phrase refers to the ultimate wisdom of abiding in one's own place; that is to say, the Mahāyāna is the place in which the bodhisattva himself abides. To abide means to be in correspondence with the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*); "ultimate" (or "final") means non-retrogression.
Second is the ultimate wisdom of equal reverence for the Three Jewels, which means realizing that the Three Jewels are of one essence and thereby accomplishing indestructible faith.

Regarding the preceding two [wisdoms], they are distinguished by their practice and qualities: the former is the stage of self-perfection (*svabhāga*), while the latter is the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa*).
Below are two types of wisdom, distinguished by their modes of understanding: first, realization; second, teaching.
This refers to the two phrases concerning the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness), which means that by seeing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one realizes the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
First, because there is only the arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) such as the aggregates (*skandha*), there is no self of persons (*pudgala-ātman*).
Second, because these very phenomena such as the aggregates are fundamentally unarisen, there is no self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*).
The remaining six phrases clarify the wisdom of analytical exposition (*vibhāga-deśanā-jñāna*); that is, it is the wisdom of teaching, and is thus called "exposition.

Because it knows the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is called "analytical"; because it distinguishes between defilement and purity, the first two phrases refer to defilement, while the latter three phrases refer to purity.
The third phrase possesses both defilement and purity, each having its own cause and effect, as these constitute the Four Noble Truths.

Specifically, the first two phrases are termed "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*); "defilement" refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), which consists of the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—since they arise from the causes that accumulate secondary afflictions.

This means that the first phrase refers to the environmental retribution (*pariṇāma-vipāka*) and the second phrase refers to the personal retribution (*nirmāṇa-vipāka*); hence it says "there is birth.
Since both share the same cause—karma—and since karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) together constitute the causes for their accumulation, the treatise and the sūtra state this by way of mutual ellipsis.

In the first part of the third sentence, one first contemplates birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); in the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra*, this is termed the "world," which refers to the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa*).
The preceding sentence reveals the effect by means of the cause, stating that "birth arises from karma as its cause";
this sentence reveals the cause by means of the effect, and thus speaks of "birth-and-death."
Since birth and death have afflictions as their essence, they are the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*); this accords with the intent of the treatise.
Next, one contemplates that nirvāṇa is all that is pure, which is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

If one proceeds directly according to the scriptural text, the arising of existence due to karma constitutes the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); furthermore, birth-and-death and nirvana are respectively observed as suffering and cessation.
The final three phrases correspond to what is purified, which is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), because they accord with the aforementioned cessation.
Among these three, the first is the practice of benefiting others. As the treatise states: "In the worlds of all Buddhas, they transform sentient beings because their own karma has matured.

According to the intent of this treatise, this first phrase should be translated as "observing the karma of transforming sentient beings in various lands"; thus, it will not be confused with the previous [discussion of] karma giving rise to existence.

The latter two phrases concern the practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha-caryā*), namely, contemplating the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the purity of nirvāṇa as the path conducive to cessation.
The first phrase refers to phenomena (*vastu*): because afflictions have no beginning, they constitute the "prior limit" (*pūrvānta*);
because nirvāṇa has no end, it constitutes the "subsequent limit" (*aparānta*).
The latter phrase accords with principle: one contemplates that afflictions are fundamentally empty and thus subject to no diminution, so there is nothing that can be exhausted;
nirvāṇa is pure by nature and involves no new addition, for its self-nature is already exhausted—therefore, both are termed "exhaustion of non-existence."

The reflection of afflictions grasps at birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), while the reflection of nirvāṇa grasps at awakening (*bodhi*); because the wisdom of awakening also accords with principle, it is nevertheless conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Because it is the Middle Way, it is like the aforementioned wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*).

Furthermore, the latter two lines refer to "that which existed previously but is now absent. The intent of the verse is likewise to contemplate the dharma of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), wherein ignorance and volitional formations constitute the prior limit, and birth, old age, and death constitute the subsequent limit.
With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; because they cease by their very nature, this is called the "exhaustion of non-existence," as in the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī-bhūmi*).
From here begins the third major section, the "Part on the Growth of Counteractive Cultivation," which has two parts:

first, guarding against afflictive conduct, and second, the bodhisattva’s cultivation. The section beginning with "In this way" clarifies the guarding against the conduct of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
The former is great wisdom, which distinguishes self-benefit from that of ordinary beings; the latter is great compassion, which distinguishes benefiting others from that of the Lesser Vehicle.
These two guide one another to form the path of non-abiding, reaching everywhere; therefore, they comprise the dedication "reaching all places."
Regarding the first point, this concerns the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
Since the Master of the Treatise has composed a separate *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Treatise on the Factors of Enlightenment), it will not be explained here.
Now, I shall briefly present four sections:
First, the explanation of the names:
*bodhi* means awakening (*jñāna*), and *aṅga* has the sense of "factor" (*hetu*). These thirty-seven [factors] are the causes for the awakening of all vehicles.
They are also called the "limbs of the path" (*mārgāṅga*); *aṅga* here means "category" (*jāti*), as they are the categories that constitute the fruit.
The alternative names will become clear from the text itself.
Second, the similarities and differences are clarified:

*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 44 states that there are many types of Mahāyāna bodhipakṣa-dharmas; the thirty-seven factors are but one specific category among them, applicable to both the Great and Small Vehicles.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also states that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are causes for nirvāṇa, but not causes for Great Nirvāṇa, because immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* categories of the path are the causes for Great Nirvāṇa.

In the five lower stages, the "Chapter on the Immeasurables" (*apramāṇa-paṭala*) and the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*lokottara-paṭala*) speak of the path and its auxiliaries as all being "immeasurable"; however, here, because we are dealing with the provisional stations [of the bodhisattva], there are only thirty-seven factors.

If one follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are only thirty-seven [factors], yet nothing is not subsumed within them; thus, even the immeasurable factors of the path (*apramāṇa-mārga*) are included therein. This is like how the four noble truths are analyzed as having immeasurable aspects; it is simply that the mental activities differ in their magnitude.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are the site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for they are the cause of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* names them the "Bodhisattva Jewel-Torch Dhāraṇī.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "If a person can contemplate the Eightfold Noble Path, they will immediately see the Buddha-nature; this is called attaining the 'cream of cream' (*sarpis-manda*)."
All of these are explained in terms of the Great Vehicle.

Regarding the essential nature of the three knowledges (*vidyā*), although there are thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, they are rooted in ten dharmas: namely, faith (*śraddhā*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), diligence (*vīrya*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), equanimity (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), relinquishment (*upekṣā*), and reflection (*manasikāra*).

Based on faith as two factors and ethical discipline as three, mindfulness is expanded into four; diligence, concentration, and wisdom each comprise eight factors, while the remaining four each comprise one. Thus, they constitute the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

Furthermore, these ten [factors] are subsumed under three aggregates as their substance: namely, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*); the factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*) is feeling (*vedanā*); and all the rest belong to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Among the five categories of phenomena, they consist of only two as their substance: namely, matter (*rūpa*) and mental factors (*caitta*).
If one takes its accompanying factors (*sahāya*), it comprises all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); if one takes its objects of perception (*ālambana*), it comprises all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).

For a detailed exposition of these distinctions, see the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicles 20, 21, and 53; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicles 20, 28, 29, and 45; and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, fascicle 10.
The following explanation relies upon these various treatises.
Fourth, the correct interpretation of the text:
namely, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) as aspects of practice, which comprise seven categories in total.
First, the path that counteracts distortions consists of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Second, the path that abandons all forms of indolence consists of the four right efforts.
Third, the path that brings forth the supernormal powers consists of the four bases of power.
The fourth is the path of the means for clear realization (*abhisamaya-upāya-mārga*), namely the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
The fifth is the path of proximity to clear realization (*āsannābhisamaya-mārga*), which is the five powers (*pañcabala*).
The sixth is the path of the essence of clear realization (*svabhāvābhisamaya-mārga*), namely the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
The seventh is the path arising subsequent to the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*), namely the Eightfold Noble Path.

Regarding the sequence of these seven: having heard the Dharma, one should first maintain it through mindfulness; next, one should practice with diligence; through diligence, the mind is gathered and made pliant; through pliancy, faith and the other faculties become established as faculties (*indriya*); when these faculties increase, they become powers (*bala*); next come the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) for discernment; and finally, the eightfold noble path for correct practice.
Sometimes, when the eight [limbs] are present before one, that which is not yet accomplished is called the Path (*mārga*), and that which has already been accomplished is called Awakening (*bodhi*).
However, the above still refers to the stages (*avasthā*).
If we consider the practitioner, the initial mind universally cultivates [all factors], let alone the Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages (*bhūmi*).
First, the path that counteracts distortions is called the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
"Four" refers to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.

"Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to mindfulness-wisdom (*smṛtiprajñā*); because the body and so forth serve as the bases upon which this mindfulness-wisdom is established, they are also termed "foundations of mindfulness."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "That in which one abides is the body and so forth; that by means of which one abides is mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Its actual substance is wisdom, for it observes and guards the object through wisdom. Because one abides by means of mindfulness, and because it is closely associated with mindfulness, it is termed 'mindfulness' by virtue of its proximity."
The *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* states: "All factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are established by way of five gates:

first, the object of focus (*ālambana*); second, the essential nature (*svabhāva*); third, the accompaniments (*sahāya*); fourth, the cultivation (*bhāvanā*); and fifth, the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanāphala*). Although these may be omitted in the text, their meaning must necessarily be complete."

Now, first, regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): the body and so forth are their objects; mindfulness and wisdom constitute their essential nature; the contemplation of the body and so forth constitute their cultivation; the destruction of the four inversions and the entry into the Four Noble Truths constitute their function; and liberation from attachment to the body and so forth constitutes their fruit.

Regarding these four objects beginning with the body, the first three correspond to the three aggregates; yet, the inclusion of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*) within the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is intended to clarify, respectively, the object that is the basis of the self, the object of the self's enjoyment, the object that is the self's own essence, and the object of the self's defilement and purification.
The purpose of these four is to remedy the four inversions.

Specifically, contemplating the impurity of the body remedies the inversion of purity; contemplating sensation as suffering, the mind as impermanent, and phenomena as selfless remedies the [remaining] three [inversions], respectively.
This sequence proceeds from the coarse to the subtle for the purpose of providing the appropriate antidotes.

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Since this body is thus impure, those sentient beings who crave it perceive it as pleasant because they give rise to various sensations through their sensory faculties (*viṣaya*) and mental objects (*dharma*)."
"Who experiences this pleasure?
Therefore, one next contemplates that the mind arises and perishes from moment to moment, and subsequently contemplates that both aggregates (skandhas) lack self-mastery.
By destroying these four inversions and practicing the four right practices, one opens the gateway to the true nature of reality (dharmatā).
If that is so, why are permanence, bliss, self, and purity presented as the sequence among the four perversions?
This is because the order is established according to what is more grave preceding what is lighter.
However, in these four bases, each can give rise to all four inversions; yet, speaking according to what is most prevalent, each base mentions only one.

Furthermore, the contemplation of impurity and so forth is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (45) states: "The Bodhisattva understands the factors of the path of the Śrāvaka as they truly are."
As in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*. How does one understand the Mahāyāna as it truly is?
It is through ultimate cultivation (*paramārtha-bhāvanā*) and conventional cultivation (*saṃvṛti-bhāvanā*).
Worldly cultivation refers to practices such as the contemplation of impurity, yet one does not regard these as real.
Ultimate cultivation refers to the nature that is free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Texts such as the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* and the *Prajñāpāramitā* all involve the simultaneous contemplation of both nature and characteristics; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is likewise the same, even extending to the point of not recollecting body, sensation, mind, or phenomena.

The *Caryā-apratipatti-sūtra* states: "Contemplate that the body is ultimately empty; contemplate that feelings are empty both internally and externally; contemplate that the mind is non-existent; and contemplate that phenomena are merely names."
This refers to reality as it is (*yathābhūta*).
However, there are two intended meanings:
first, that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is serene and characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity, which serves to dispel inversions such as impermanence and so forth.

Second, this entry into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) simultaneously dispels the eight inversions; the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* also states that the four foundations of mindfulness can eliminate the eight inversions.

Once the eight inversions are eliminated, the eight modes of practice (*aṣṭākāra*) are established; thus, the four pairs and eight individuals at the twin trees in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, as well as the four withered and four flourishing trees, precisely symbolize this.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness through all modes (*sarvākāra*).
What is meant by "cultivating through all modes"?
One should contemplate the form of this body: because its dharmic nature (*dharmatā*) arises through conditions, a single form is all forms.
Because that which arises through conditions is emptiness, all forms are one form;
because they exist within the *dharmatā*, they are neither one nor many, yet simultaneously illumine both the one and the many.
Furthermore, they are neither form nor non-form, yet simultaneously illumine both form and non-form.
As it is with the mindfulness of the body, so it is with the other three.
How do withering and flourishing illustrate this foundation of mindfulness?
It means that the form of the dharma-nature is in reality not pure, yet ordinary beings reckon it to be pure; this is called perversion.
In reality, it is not impure; it is the followers of the Two Vehicles who conceive of it as impure, which is called a perversion.
Now, when one contemplates that the elements of form are themselves empty, and all things are empty, there is no purity within emptiness—how, then, could one be stained by attachment?
Thus, when all impurities, inversions, and breaches are purified, the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are perfected.
When the seeds of form are not destroyed, provisional names remain; thus, all things are merely provisional, and the differentiation of names and characteristics is inexhaustible.
Conventional wisdom is eternally pure; why then would one stagnate in emptiness and grasp at the annihilation of ashes?
To say that form is impure is called the "inversion of impurity" of the Two Vehicles, which is overcome by the establishment of the mindfulness of glory (*śrī-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Therefore, the eight inversions are simultaneously subverted, and withering and flourishing stand together. When one contemplates that the ultimate limit of form is neither empty nor provisional, then all things are neither empty nor provisional. Because they are not empty, there is no inversion of impurity; because they are not provisional, there is no inversion of purity. Being free from these two extremes is what is called the Middle Way.
The Buddha, having realized this principle, entered parinirvāṇa in the interim.
The remaining three cases are similar to this.

Thus, there are four categories of remedial medicinal dharmas: the wisdom that contemplates the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is termed "mindfulness" (smṛti); the single truth and the three truths are termed "bases" (sthāna).
All is emptiness; among all delusions, whether withering or flourishing, there is nothing that is not empty and quiescent.
All is provisional; within the twin trees of the two extremes, there is nothing that is not established.
All is the Middle Way; there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.

A single thought-moment is as vast and far-reaching as this; therefore, by deeply contemplating the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one immediately sits upon the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) without needing anything else.
Because capacities and dispositions differ, other categories are taught.
Since this first section is thus profound and subtle, the remaining six may be understood by analogy with it.
In the subsequent text, only the characteristics will be briefly explained; those who preach should have the power to reveal each one in detail.

In this sutra, it simply says "contemplating the body" without mentioning whether it is pure or impure; this is spoken from the perspective of its general characteristics to demonstrate its comprehensive nature.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the specific contemplation of mindfulness of the body; second, from "In this way" onwards, the other three [foundations of mindfulness] are illustrated by analogy.

Now, regarding the initial contemplation of the body, there are three types of contemplation, namely the internal and so forth; the characteristics of these three are explained extensively in the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi*, and here I shall briefly cite one or two examples.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "That which is one's own sentient form is the internal body; that which is external insentient form is the external body; and that which belongs to other sentient beings is the internal-external body."
First is one's own body, because it is the object of self-love.
Next are the requisites and so forth, because they are the objects of "mine-ness" love.
Finally are the retinue, wife, and children, because they are both the objects of self-love and "mine-ness" love.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 28, also explains this extensively.
Furthermore, fascicle 53 states: "One's own body is called 'internal,' while another's body is called 'external.

Although it does not explicitly define internal and external, according to the intent of the following explanation, these two [categories] are simply combined to form what is termed "internal and external."
The reason these three cases exist is to refute three kinds of wrong conduct.
There are those who are deeply attached to internal emotions; they sacrifice their wives and wealth to preserve their own lives.
There are those who are deeply attached to external things; out of greed for wealth, they lose their freedom and give up their lives for the sake of a wife.
There are two types of attachment.
By destroying these three perversions, one accomplishes the three correct practices; this is explained according to the distinct remedies for three different types of persons.

If, however, it is explained according to the beginning and end of the contemplation arising within a single person, it means that one first contemplates one's own body and finds that purity and so forth cannot be obtained, or that they might exist externally.
Next, when he observes the external and again finds it unobtainable, doubt arises within him, thinking:
"When I observed the internal, I may have been mistaken regarding the external; when I observed the external, I may have been mistaken regarding the internal."
Next, one contemplates both the internal and external together, yet [the self] is still not to be found.
The first two [contemplations] are specific, while the last one is general.
Through these two explanations, it is clearly understood that the "internal and external body" is simply a combination of the preceding two.

Now, first one contemplates the internal body. The initial statement identifies the specific object of focus, while the subsequent "contemplation following the body" (kāyānupaśyanā) generally reveals the characteristics of the practice.
As the *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa* states: "By searching and following along with observation, one knows it to be impure," and so forth.
However, "investigation" (anuvicāra) has two meanings:
first, the sense of "seeking," because one thoroughly seeks out the five kinds of impurity;
second, the sense of "conforming," because even with eyes closed, one clearly perceives the image of the body in accordance with its similarity to the actual substance.

The previous heading stated that the internal body is the essence (*svabhāva*), while the present passage says that "following the body" (*anuparivartin*) is the reflection (*pratibimba*); this is the intended meaning of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*.
Next, "diligent mindfulness and awareness" (*ātāpī saṃprajānan smṛtimān*) reveals the procedure for cultivation.
