Because worldly affairs such as greed arise from beginningless evil habits, they are extremely difficult to abandon—more so than a worldly father’s separation from a filial son; therefore, one must apply diligent effort to be able to eliminate them.

"Diligence" (*vīrya*) refers to the desire to exert effort; "courage" (*utsāha*) means being valiant and tireless; "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is clear recollection without forgetting; and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is decisive discernment without regret.

Furthermore, if the mind wanders and scatters, one should reflect upon the suffering of old age, sickness, and death; the suffering of the three evil realms; the impermanence of body and life; and the impending extinction of the Buddha-dharma—this is termed "mindful knowledge."
Thus, one is able to lash the mind so that it returns to the original contemplation; thereupon, diligence and vigor arise, and by possessing the aforementioned meanings, one is not negligent.
Next, the phrase "removing worldly greed and sorrow" refers to the fruit of contemplation, because there is something from which one is liberated.

For one who practices the contemplation of the impurity of the body as a remedy for greed, having already abandoned the worldly pleasures of the five desires but not yet attained the bliss of meditative concentration, sorrow may occasionally arise.
Like a fish that delights in water, such a person constantly seeks pleasurable things and returns to recollecting their former desires.
These two [afflictions] arise most frequently; therefore, they are specifically eliminated.
Furthermore, craving is the foremost of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*); once craving is removed, all five hindrances are completely dispelled, like splitting the first node of a bamboo stalk.

Among the five types of sensation (*vedanā*), sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is particularly capable of obstructing meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Just as one eliminates a great threat first when destroying malevolent bandits, it is therefore singled out for mention.
Its details, such as the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth, are extensively explained in the two treatises.
The observation of characteristics as they truly are has been explained above.
Next, one observes the external body and the internal-external body; while the objects of observation differ slightly, the characteristics of the observation are largely the same.

Regarding the subsequent application of this to the remaining three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), according to the intent of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, since feeling, mind, and phenomena arise based on the aforementioned three types of bodies (internal, etc.), feeling, mind, and phenomena also possess the qualities of being internal and so forth, corresponding to their respective bases of arising.
The intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is largely the same as this.
The treatise asks:
"Among the four foundations of mindfulness, the mind is exclusively internal, while sensation and dharmas are exclusively external; the body pertains to both the internal and the external."
How is it that all four have both internal and external aspects?
Answer:
Feeling is of two kinds: first, bodily; second, mental.
"Mental feeling is called internal, while bodily feeling is called external.
Furthermore, feeling associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called internal, whereas feeling associated with the five [sensory] consciousnesses is called external.
Although the mind is internal, it is called external because it takes external phenomena as its object.
The five consciousnesses are invariably external.
Furthermore, the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) is internal, while the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*) is external.

Although mental objects (*dharma*) are external, those mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) that take internal phenomena as their object are called internal; those mental factors that take external phenomena as their object, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), are external.
The latter three foundations of mindfulness likewise combine with the former two to constitute the internal and external; the remainder is as explained in the two treatises.
As for the characteristics of the sequential observation, they are as previously stated in the general exposition.

Second, regarding right effort (*samyak-vīrya*): if the fire of the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness obtains the wind of effort, there is nothing it will not consume; therefore, it is explained next.
Since diligence (*vīrya*) constitutes its essential nature, it is collectively termed "effort" (*vīrya*).
It is called "right" because it is distinguished from the ninety-five types of discordant diligence;
although it is a single form of diligence, it is divided into four according to its meaning:
the first two types of diligence involve abandoning the two kinds of evil, which constitutes the practice of ceasing evil.
The latter two involve diligently cultivating the two types of goodness; this constitutes the performance of wholesome conduct.
Both the two types of goodness and the two types of evil serve as objects of focus (*ālambana*).
Among these, one restrains unarisen evil so that it does not arise, and one cuts off arisen evil so that it does not continue.
The latter two cause unarisen wholesome states to arise and those already arisen to increase; these are also called the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Although the latter two refer to cultivation (*bhāvanā*), they are termed "efforts" (*prahāṇa*) because the wholesome is the locus of abandonment.
Regarding "abandonment through correct cultivation," this refers to abandoning laziness.

Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "First, abandonment through restraint; second, abandonment through abandonment; third, abandonment through cultivation; and fourth, abandonment through protection."

However, regarding good and evil, there are both general and specific distinctions. Specifically, within the aforementioned contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), indolence, the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and so forth are taken as unwholesome; that which can serve as their antidote is what constitutes the arising of the wholesome.
Speaking according to the Mahāyāna, one diligently contemplates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); apart from the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), everything is termed "evil.
Within each instance of such diligent practice, the text contains four elements.
First, "the non-arising of unwholesome states not yet arisen" indicates the object of focus (*ālambana*).
Second, "for the sake of their non-arising" clarifies the intention for practicing meditation (*vipaśyanā*).
Third, "desiring them to arise" refers to the arousal of a mind of aspiration; this is the basis for cultivation, namely the perfection of the superior resolve (*adhyāśaya*).
4. "Diligent Exertion" and below correctly reveal the practice, which is the perfection of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Regarding "diligent exertion": it refers to constantly self-urging oneself to generate the resolve (*cittotpāda*).
Right exertion (*samyakprahāṇa*) refers to the uplifting of the mind and the sustaining of the mind.
The texts concerning the other three instances may be understood by analogy with this.

If the two types of unwholesome states that have not yet arisen are abandoned, and the two types of wholesome states that have already arisen are increased and expanded, this is the fruit of right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*).

Third, regarding the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): because diligence may exceed the point of non-distraction and the fire of wisdom be weak, one must establish fixed concentration; thus, that which is desired will be mastered with sovereignty.
"Divine" (*divya*) refers to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and "feet" (*pāda*) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Just as one who has feet is able to go and return, leap and bound with vigor and strength, and is able to attain and realize the supreme dharmas of the world."
The world’s preeminent qualities are called "supernormal powers" (*ṛddhi*).
Because one can reach [the goal] by means of them, they are named "bases of supernormal power" (*ṛddhipāda*).
This is an illustration.
Because they possess supreme mastery over supramundane dharmas, they are the "supreme powers" (*ṛddhi*).
Since the four meditative concentrations, such as desire and so forth, can realize this, they are called the "bases of power" (*ṛddhipāda*).
They are also called the "bases of psychic success" (*ṛddhipāda*), because that which is desired accords with the mind.

The objective referent (*ālambana*) of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) consists of various transformative feats; the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the bases of supernormal power is meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and desire, effort, mind, and investigation are all their auxiliary companions.
"Desire" refers to intense aspiration;
"effort" refers to uninterrupted diligence.
The mind itself is concentration (*samādhi*), meaning that one focuses the mind exclusively upon an object;
contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), as it involves internal discernment based on hearing the teachings.
Through the predominant power of desire (*chanda*), one realizes one-pointedness of mind; this is termed "concentration through desire" (*chandha-samādhi*).
The same applies to the remaining three.
Diligently observing the nature of the mind is called "supreme concentration" (*adhimātra-samādhi*); all these derive their names from their preparatory application (*prayoga*).

These four applications are precisely the desire, diligence, vigor, and right exertion (*samyak-prahāṇa*) for the arising [of wholesome states] within the aforementioned right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*).

In the stage of arousing the mind, the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) can give rise to concentration (*samādhi*): because if the application is too exalted, it gives rise to the concentration of exertion (*vīrya-samādhi*);
and because if the application is too depressed, it gives rise to the concentration of discernment (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Therefore, for each application of mindfulness there are four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and for each right effort there are four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*).

In this passage, the desire-concentration (*chanda-samādhi*) is first explained specifically, while the section beginning with "practicing diligence" (*vīrya*) below clarifies the remaining three collectively.
Regarding the initial point, the phrase "practicing desire-concentration" identifies the nature of the auxiliary factor being cultivated.
The two characters "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) and "practice" (*caryā*) collectively manifest the characteristics of cultivation as well as the fruit of that cultivation.
What are these characteristics of cultivation?
They are further of two kinds:
First, one cultivates concentration through desire (*chanda-samādhi*) because it can sever the active manifestations of all afflictive entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).

Second, in order to permanently eradicate all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one cultivates the eight formative acts of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*), namely: desire, exertion, faith, pliancy, mindfulness, clear comprehension, volition, and equanimity.
How can it also be a fruit?

If the practice of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*) is subsumed under the accomplishment [of the bases], then the accomplishment of the practice of abandonment is also the fruit of the bases for supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Subsequently, the accomplishment of the bases for supernormal power is exclusively its fruit.
Following the section on "relying on revulsion," the characteristics of cultivation are further revealed, while also identifying the objects of focus.

According to the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, from the five faculties onward, one takes the four truths as the objective sphere; it is only from the seven factors of enlightenment onward that there are the characteristics of cultivation such as relying on revulsion.

Now, the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) in this sutra is cultivated by taking the Four Noble Truths as its object; that is to say, cultivation based on the truth of suffering necessarily relies on revulsion toward suffering; cultivation based on the truth of origin necessarily relies on detachment from desire; cultivation based on the truth of cessation necessarily seeks the realization of cessation; and cultivation based on the truth of the path necessarily proceeds toward the practice for the extinction of suffering, thereby enabling one to abandon suffering.

When one encounters these objects, one must necessarily seek to cultivate them; therefore, they are called "dedications" (*pariṇāmanā*), which also comprise the four paths such as the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
The subsequent passages concerning reliance on revulsion (*nirveda*) and so forth are all explained in this same manner.

Fourth, the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) constitute the path of the means for clear realization (*abhisamaya*). They are called "faculties" (*indriya*) because they possess predominance (*ādhipatya*).
The intrinsic nature of these five faculties consists of the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*); these five exercise predominance over the arising of supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*).
The first four are further able to give rise to the latter [four], thereby receiving the designation of "predominant" (*adhipati*).
Among them, faith is the foremost and is able to give rise to the other four.
In the text, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is first explained individually, followed by a general exposition of the remaining four.
Within each of the two sections, the object of cultivation is first stated, followed by a detailed explanation of the characteristics of cultivation, such as the basis of reliance.
The three subsequent categories should be understood according to this same pattern.

Regarding the present object of cultivation: it consists of profound patience and aspiration toward the reality of the truths. The remaining four consist of exerting effort based on what was previously believed, practicing with clear mindfulness so as not to forget, binding the object to a single point of focus, and discerning right from wrong; the rest is as explained before.
However, although one may first enter the Buddha-dharma with faith, it cannot yet be called a "faculty" (indriya) as long as concentration and wisdom are absent.
Now, by virtue of the preceding three categories, this faith becomes unshakable.

In this context, mindfulness is the mindfulness within the foundations of mindfulness; diligence is right effort; concentration is the bases of spiritual power; and wisdom is the wisdom that takes the Four Truths as its object. These first three, when reaching this stage, are collectively designated as "faculties" (*indriya*).
If one considers this according to the stages, prior to the Path of Seeing, it takes the swift manifestation of insight as its fruit;
now, being in the fourth stage, it should take the manifestation of the subsequent stage as its fruit.
Fifth, the five powers (*pañcabala*).
These are the aforementioned five faculties (*pañcendriya*) when they have increased to the point that Māra, Brahmā, delusions, and the like cannot subdue them; thus they are called "powers.
Furthermore, because they can diminish obstacles such as lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), they are also called "powers."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because it can destroy afflictions and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), it is called 'power.
Sixth are the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
"Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) means thorough awakening and comprehension.
If explained according to their stages, they are the wisdom that realizes the self-nature of the truths as they truly are, which awakens to the self-nature of phenomena.
The essential nature of the factors of enlightenment consists of mindfulness and the others.
Within the seven topics, there are likewise two [aspects]:
First, mindfulness as an awakening factor (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is explained individually; subsequently, the remaining six are revealed collectively.

Regarding these seven factors of awakening, while all seven constitute the essence (*svabhāva*), their distinction lies in this: awakening itself is the essence, whereas the other six are all branches (*aṅga*) of awakening.
That is to say, mindfulness is the limb of support; because of the binding of mindfulness, all wholesome dharmas are prevented from being forgotten.
The investigation of dharmas is the limb of essential nature, because it realizes their specific characteristics.
Vigor is the factor of departure, because by its power one is able to reach the destination.
Joy is the factor of benefit, because through mental exhilaration the body becomes pliant.
The three factors of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are the untainted branches.
Pliancy is itself lightness (*praśrabdhi*); because it is untainted, it is so called, for through this lightness one is able to eliminate heaviness (*dausthulya*).
"Concentration" (samādhi) refers to being undefiled by virtue of relying upon it; that is, by relying on concentration, one attains the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti).

"Equanimity" (upekṣā) refers to its essence being undefiled; that is, as the equanimity of practice, it eternally eliminates greed and sorrow, having the state of non-defilement as its intrinsic nature.
Taken as a whole, the seven factors of enlightenment are subsumed within three categories:
mindfulness encompasses both concentration and wisdom; the next three are wisdom; and the final three are subsumed under concentration.

Although these [latter six] were previously categorized as the former [three], they increase at this stage; thus, according to what is clarified by their respective positions, they are able to sever the delusions of views, which constitutes their fruit.

Furthermore, although these seven factors arise simultaneously in a single moment, their respective functions are described according to their modes of activity: mindfulness eliminates discursive thoughts; discernment eliminates incorrect awareness; and the remaining factors eliminate indolence, lethargy, heaviness, distraction, and restlessness.

The above is a general explanation. Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) of the Mahāyāna: because one does not dwell upon any phenomena; because discernment (*vīmaṃsā*) is unattainable; because one is free from the marks of exertion and indolence; because sorrow and joy are cut off; because the objects of mental tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) are all ungraspable; because within the nature of concentration (*samādhi*) there is neither fixedness nor distraction; and because one does not perceive either the subject or object of relinquishment (*upekṣā*).
Seventh, the Eightfold Right Path (*aṣṭāṅga-mārga*).

If explained according to the stages, it refers to the path that arises subsequent to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), for the purpose of abandoning the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Because it is free from the eight wrongs (*mithyā*), it is called the Eightfold Right Path.
Because it opens up and leads to nirvāṇa, it is called the "Path" (mārga).
It is also termed the "Eightfold Noble Path" because it is the path of the noble ones (ārya).
The essential nature of the eight right factors consists of right view and the others.
In this passage, the correct view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) is first explained specifically, and subsequently the remaining seven factors are revealed collectively.
As for the "correct view," it is the factor of discernment (*viniścaya-aṅga*), because it involves the analytical selection (*pravicaya*) based on the reality previously realized.

Right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is the limb that instructs others; it consists of establishing the means according to what has been realized, because one gives rise to speech by reflecting upon names and meanings.
The next three [limbs] are the limbs that cause others to have faith.
"Right speech" means that, by relying well upon what has been realized, one provides answers and definitive resolutions to questions, thereby causing others to believe in the purity of one's views.
"Right action" means that one’s physical conduct—whether moving or remaining still—is fully endowed with correct practice, thereby causing others to believe in the purity of one's ethical discipline.

Right livelihood means begging for sustenance in accordance with the Dharma and abiding by the noble lineages, being free from the five types of wrong livelihood, so as to inspire confidence in others regarding the purity of one's livelihood.
Right effort is the factor that purifies the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because through it all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are permanently severed.

Right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) is the factor that purifies the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), because by not forgetting the signs of correct tranquility (*śamatha*) and exertion (*pragraha*), it forever refuses to admit sinking (*laya*) or agitation (*auddhatya*).

Right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) is the factor that can purify the obstacles to supreme qualities (*guṇa*), because through it, immeasurable and superior qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are induced.
If one can provide such analytical instructions as described above, this constitutes the fruit of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

Furthermore, among these eight, three—vocal action, livelihood, and [right speech]—are subsumed under the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*); mindfulness and concentration belong to the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*); and the remaining three belong to the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*).
Concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are largely identical to those in the various preceding chapters, differing only in their degree of excellence;

as for ethical discipline (*śīla*), there were no factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) previously mentioned. Although there was a subtle, unmanifest form of restraint associated with concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara-avijñapti*), it is newly established here because it constitutes the primary practice (*samyak-pratipatti*); this is explained by way of its specific stage.
According to this sutra’s "Chapter on Transcending the World," the Eightfold Rightness constitutes the bodhisattva path.

First is right view, which distances one from wrong views, up to the eighth, right concentration, which is skillful means; from within a single samādhi, it gives rise to the inconceivable dharmas of a bodhisattva. All other samādhis differ vastly in their essential purpose from what has been explained here.

The preceding seven categories are collectively illustrated through metaphors: the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is like the great earth; the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are like seeds; right effort (samyakprahāṇa) is the planting; the bases of spiritual power (ṛddhipāda) are like the emerging sprouts; the five faculties (pañcendriya) are like the taking root; the five powers (pañcabala) are like the growth of stems and leaves; they blossom into the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga), and bear the fruit of the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga).
In the second section, regarding the ten phrases on protecting the practice of the Hīnayāna, the first is general and the remainder are specific.
Within the general part, "such merits" refers back to the preceding *bodhipākṣika-dharmas*.
"For the sake of not abandoning sentient beings" clearly elucidates the meaning of protection, as it differs from the solitary excellence of the two vehicles.
Within this distinct section, since both compassion and wisdom are fully present, one has already transcended the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), let alone using these as a guide.
The preceding nine phrases are divided into four parts:
first, the beginning; second, the benefit; third, the aspiration; and fourth, the practice. The former three protect against a narrow mind, while the latter one protects against narrow practices.
First, regarding the beginning: great vows serve as the foundation for initiating practice.
Second, compassion benefits sentient beings.
The former two protect a narrow-minded [self-centered] heart.
Third, one reflects that the possession of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is rare; this protects against the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Fourth, within the section on practice there are five phrases; the first four concern self-benefit:

the first two seek the fruit—first, by practicing the cultivation of the pure land, one seeks the Buddha’s *parivṛtti* (the environmental support); second, by practicing the cultivation of the arising of the Buddha-dharma, one seeks the Buddha’s ten powers and other qualities of the *anuparivṛtti* (the primary retribution).

The latter two seek the cause; the third seeks the practice of tireless application toward the skillful means of those stages—namely, the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages—and is therefore called the "superior path of the highest excellence";

the fourth is the practice of entering the stage of non-retrogression, which is the realization of the intrinsic nature of dharmas and conformity with the Buddha’s liberation from the eighth stage upward.
The latter, benefiting others, refers to the necessity of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) in the practice of teaching and transforming sentient beings.

In the fourth major section, the "Fruit Portion," it encompasses inexhaustible practices;
having abandoned hindrances and perfected virtues, it extends throughout the entire realm of sentient beings for the sake of their benefit and happiness.
There are two kinds of fruits:
first, the fruit of freedom from obstacles, which arises from guarding against afflictions;
second, the fruit of the accomplishment of virtues, which arises from guarding against the Lesser Vehicle.
The former section also has two parts:
first, the fruit of distancing arising from the defilement of afflictions, which is the removal of the obstacle of afflictions;
second, the fruit of distancing arising from the defilement of karma, which is the removal of the obstacle of karma.

The statement that "all are born" refers to afflictions and defilements being like raw food; now, as this is the initial stage of entering the supramundane state, one is able to leave behind such birth.

Here, at the outset of leaving behind delusions, the objects to be left behind are first mentioned, and subsequently, from the phrase "In this manner," the capacity to leave them behind is established.
Regarding that which is abandoned, the arising and subsiding of attachment therein is its general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); all else is particular (*viśeṣa*).
Attachment to this general characteristic is the pride of having understood the Dharma (*dharmāvabodha-māna*) in the preceding stage.
The treatise states: "I know" and "great knowledge. "I know" refers to the attachment that "I am able to know"; "great knowledge" refers to the attachment to the great dharmas that are known.
"Emergence and submergence" refers to the pride of meditative absorption (*samāpatti-māna*) in the preceding stage.
"Emergence" (*udaya*) has the meaning of arising from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), referring to the cultivation and arising of that concentration.
"Disappearance" (*astaṅgama*) has the meaning of the cessation of meditative absorption, referring to what is eliminated by that concentration.
Now, one conceives: "I am able to cultivate this concentration," and "this concentration is what I have cultivated. Therefore, the treatise says: "I cultivate; I cultivate what belongs to me."
The general statement has already been explained.
Specifically, there are five kinds:
first, the basis; second, the origination; third, the practice; fourth, the protection; and fifth, the transgression.

Fundamentally, this refers to all forms of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) up to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). Among these, *satkāyadṛṣṭi* is the general category, while "self" (*ātman*) and so forth are the specific instances.

Within the specific instances, the four—self (*ātman*), person (*pudgala*), and so on—constitute the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) regarding persons; the three—aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—constitute the conceit of self regarding phenomena (*dharma*).
Regarding the term "fundamental" (*mūla*), there are two meanings:
first, this self serves as the basis for the two types of pride—the pride of being liberated from the teachings and the pride of meditative attainment;
second, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) further serves as the basis for the two selves and the sixty-two views.
There is this distinction.

Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) herein, if we consider its actual status according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this stage eliminates the innate (*sahaja*) view of a self-identity within the sixth consciousness, along with the faults it gives rise to, because it is counteracted by supramundane path-factors (*lokottaramārgapakṣa*). Since that which is conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*) is abandoned in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), the *Yogācārabhūmi* refers to this as the "subtle view of a self-identity."

If we consider this in terms of the provisional stages (*yiji*), according to the *Renwang jing*, the fourth stage corresponds to the level of a *srotāpanna*; because it serves as the initial point of entry into the supramundane, one is thereby able to sever the conceptual view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Second, "reflection" clarifies arising, meaning that pride arises from improper reflection (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).

Third, "observation" clarifies activity, meaning that within the objects of mental activity, one frequently observes what has been attained—whether it be a dharma or a meditative concentration—in order to seek out superior characteristics and make them known to others.

Fourth, regarding the three phrases beginning with "because of cultivation," they clarify the protector who cultivates through remediation. This refers to one who repeatedly observes and cultivates what is seen as "mine"; such a person gives rise to the notion of a self (*ātman*) because they grasp at those superior characteristics as belonging to their own self.
"Material wealth" refers to the enjoyment and protection of accumulated possessions.
Through these three matters above, one guards what one has acquired.
The "five attachments" clarify the faults, meaning that the mind is firmly established in two matters: meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Dharma.
Among these five, the first three constitute the preliminary application for giving rise to pride, while the latter two assist and support the mind of pride.
The preceding summary and the explicit characteristics represent that which is precisely what arises.

In the subsequent conclusion regarding detachment, through the attainment of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) as both primary and auxiliary means, there is nothing with which one is not detached.
The second section, beginning with "This bodhisattva," clarifies the departure from the defilement of karma.

In the preceding section on the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), one correctly abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*); once the afflictions have departed, karma likewise perishes along with them. Having eliminated unwholesome karma, one cultivates wholesome karma.
In this passage, one first abandons evil and subsequently advances toward good.
There are two reasons why one should not commit evil:
first, because it is not praised by the Buddha, one does not perform it out of reverence for the Buddha; [the second reason follows].
Regarding the second point, the defilement of afflictions: one refrains from [non-virtue] out of fear of an ill reputation, for an ill reputation obstructs the path of benefiting sentient beings.
The two meanings of progressing toward virtue should be understood as the reverse of this.
Furthermore, one does not create karma defiled by afflictions, which differs from the karma of ordinary beings;
rather, one creates karma that accords with the bodhisattva path, which differs from that of the two vehicles.
Within the second [section], the "Fruition of Accomplished Virtue," there are four parts:

First, the fruit of generating a resolute mind of aspiration toward supreme qualities; second, the fruit of giving rise to a sense of gratitude toward the Honored One who teaches the Dharma; third, the fruit of exerting diligent effort within those skillful practices; and fourth, the fruit of fulfilling the fundamental realm of the mind through that superior aspiration.
Regarding these four fruits: the first three arise from the preceding [stages], and the last one further arises from these three fruits.
Within the former [three], the first two are the fruits of protecting a small mind, while the last one is the fruit of protecting small conduct.

Regarding the first of the three fruits mentioned previously: because one originally sought higher [realms] for oneself and sought to save those below, one now acts for the sake of sentient beings, seeking higher [realms] again and again;

thus it is called "increasing" (*adhimātra*). The text has two parts: first, a restatement of the previously practiced causes; second, from "In this way, he attains... onwards, the manifestation of the fruit obtained.
Regarding the first point: this refers back to the general statement within the preceding section on protecting those of the Hīnayāna.
"Exercising the wisdom of skillful means according to what arises" refers back to the preceding [point] regarding not abandoning any sentient beings.
To cultivate the factors of enlightenment without abandoning sentient beings is to possess skillful means; this is the wisdom-liberation of the factors of enlightenment.
To practice the path and its auxiliaries is precisely the prior cultivation of such merits.
The Path refers to the realized wisdom of the four stages, while the factors conducive to the path refer to the bodhipakṣa-dharmas.
These two manifest the fruits attained, which consist of ten phrases: the first is general, and the remaining ones are specific.
The general statement regarding "moistening" (*ārdratā*) refers to a profound desire for love and respect.

This means that by practicing the two paths, one personally experiences moistening and thus develops a deep desire to respect those above; likewise, by practicing for the sake of others, one moistens all living beings and thus develops a deep desire for love toward them.
The nine phrases in the middle section below explain that there are three kinds of excellence in its moisture:
first, "one with a supple mind" clarifies the excellence of delighting in practice, meaning that the realization of the Dharma is harmonious with the spirit.
Second, regarding "harmonious compliance": being harmonized, well-compliant, and unimpeded amidst conditions constitutes the excellence of mastery over samādhi.
The first two [points] constitute the essence of practice.
Third, the seven phrases beginning with "benefiting" clarify the excellence of the antidotes that eliminate faults.
This is the application of practice.
Within this, the first phrase is general: "benefiting" because there is no fault in benefiting others, and "bringing peace and happiness" because there is no fault in benefiting oneself.
The following six phrases specifically clarify [the benefits] according to their respective faults.
If one does not rely on these opposites, it is difficult to manifest the virtue of the purity of nature.
These six phrases eliminate the six faults; in the sutra, they all serve as remedies.
First, a mind free from defilement remedies the fault of seeking food for one's own benefit and the fault of jealousy regarding fame.
Second, it remedies the fault of having few virtues despite having few desires;
third, it remedies the fault of not seeking superior wisdom.
These three [remedies] above are all for one's own benefit.
The fourth [perfection] remedies the fault of being indolent and failing to gather sentient beings.
The first four [perfections] all remedy faults arising from conduct;
the latter two remedy faults arising from teaching. Specifically, the fifth remedies the fault of adhering to one's own views and failing to follow the superior teachings.
The sixth fault is that of prioritizing equanimity over practice as taught.
As it is said, practicing according to the teaching is the foremost among hearing and reflection; now, by abandoning that priority, this constitutes a fault.
Furthermore, "saving sentient beings above" is the fruit of the aforementioned compassion; "seeking sublime wisdom" is the fruit of the aforementioned seeking.
From the second section, "This bodhisattva," onwards, it describes the fruit of giving rise to a mind of gratitude within the Honored One who preaches the Dharma.
This means that in the preceding stage, one heard the Dharma from the Buddha; thus, the Buddha was the honored one who preached the Dharma.
Now, by giving rise to the mind to transmit the Dharma and practice it, one thereby repays the kindness of all Buddhas.
Above, one aspires to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā) because of recognizing the Buddha’s kindness; thus, now one contemplates repaying that kindness and seeks the supreme fruit.
Within the text, there is first an individual explanation, followed by a summary.
Regarding the first section, there are ten phrases: the first is general, while the remaining ones are specific.
As for the general statement, "knowing gratitude," it means that if one practices acts of repaying kindness in accordance with the teacher’s instructions, only then is one truly "knowing gratitude."
Within the section on distinctions, those practices are of nine types, which are subsumed into seven categories:
first, knowing how to repay kindness, which means giving rise to a mind of gratitude toward those who are venerable.
"Venerable" refers specifically to the Buddha; as he is the primary benefactor, this is specifically termed "repaying kindness."
The second pair of phrases concerns giving rise to a mind of gratitude based on shared qualities; this is called the intention of a virtuous friend who acts in accordance with one's practice.
The third pair of phrases, "upright and gentle," concerns initiating practice based on the Dharma.
This means that by following the instructions received and not contradicting the teacher’s commands, one is called "upright.
By initiating the practice of cultivation and being able to endure suffering when encountering it, one is called "pliant.

Regarding the fourth point, "one who does not act with dense forest-like concealment": this refers to not concealing one's own faults from donors while relying upon their offerings of food and clothing.
Fifth, although he truly possesses virtues, he is not conceited.
Sixth, he properly receives instruction and attains the teacher’s verbal explanations.
Seventh, he is unerring regarding the teaching and grasps the teacher’s intended meaning.
Within the first seven chapters, the first two rely on persons, the next three on practice, and the final two on the teaching; although their bases differ, they are all alike in repaying kindness.

Second, from "This bodhisattva thus... onwards is the summary, which states that these ten phrases do not transcend these three types of patience: namely, the mind being extremely harmonious and gentle, dwelling together in peace and happiness, and being pliant, which means being upright and sincere.
"Suppleness and tranquility" (mṛdu-śānti) serves to connect with and conclude the remaining phrases.
The third section, "Thus, through patience and gentleness," and so forth, describes the fruit of exerting diligent effort (*vīrya*).

This means that because one practices the two types of beneficial conduct (*dvividha-hitakriyā*) with tireless diligence, one exerts effort in cultivating the previously mentioned non-abandonment of sentient beings and the protection of minor practices; therefore, within the context of skillful means (*upāya*), this is precisely the characteristic of inexhaustible practice.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the restatement of the time of attainment; second, from "attainment is unceasing" onwards, the actual exposition.
Within this, there are ten phrases: the first is general, and the remainder are specific.
There are nine further meanings of "uninterrupted practice": first, being undefiled.
This is because that energetic practice flows forth with equanimity.

As for defilement, it consists of being accompanied by indolence and passion; passion leads to attachment and excess, while indolence leads to falling short and deficiency. It is like the strings of a lute: if they are too tight or too loose, they do not produce sound; only when one is neither overly diligent nor indolent does there arise an even flow.
Second, not regressing from one's own vehicle;
these two [points] are for self-benefit.
Third, giving rise to a mind of vast concern for the benefit of others.
The fourth is the vow to bring benefit to infinite sentient beings, giving rise to the practice of gathering them in.
The [first] two are for the benefit of others.
The [first] four above are all of the nature of self-benefit (*svabhāga*), while the four below are of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).

That which is called "the five blazing ones" refers to constantly being intent on practicing in accordance with the Way; it is like a blazing fire that advances upward and cannot be extinguished. In the sutras, this is termed "radiance," as it simultaneously illuminates other stages.
Sixth, cultivation transcends others;
seventh, one cannot be corrupted by the delusions of Māra.
The first three [perfections] pertain to self-benefit.
The eighth, "gathering in sentient beings," is precisely benefiting others.
Of the eight [perfections] mentioned above, all are practices; the last one is understanding.
This means that through the ninth [perfection], one personally severs doubt and resolves what is right and wrong.
It is able to subdue the speech of others because it is like fearlessness.
If one is able to possess this, it constitutes correct cultivation.
The fourth section, beginning with "This bodhisattva," describes the fruit of the fulfillment of the fundamental mental realm of that superior aspiration.

The mind of the factors of enlightenment is the fundamental realm of the mind; by maintaining right mindfulness of *tathatā* (suchness) and cultivating the higher path-factors (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), it is said to be "fulfilled" due to diligence.

Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 48, following upon the preceding discussion of diligence, states: "By these causes and conditions, all intentions, superior intentions, and the nature of the realm of resolute belief (*adhimukti-dhātu*) attain fulfillment."
Thus we know that this fruit arises from the preceding two fruits: namely, the *āśaya* (intention) is the first fruit, and the *adhyāśaya* (resolute intention) is the second fruit.

The nature of the *adhimukti-dhātu* (element of resolute conviction) is precisely this *citta-dhātu* (mental element); because the third, *vīrya* (diligence), causes the growth of the preceding two fruits, it is said to be "fulfilled."
In this passage, there are ten phrases: the first is general, while the remaining nine are specific.
There are nine such specific types:
first, "not losing the profound mind," because the mind of those factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) is cultivated and increased through practice.
First, this is a stage of self-perfection (*svabhāga*), while all subsequent stages are of superior progress (*viśeṣa*).
Second, it is because from the fifth ground upward, within the realization of the increasingly superior, there is clear discernment and decisive resolution.

Third, it is the cause for that aforementioned superior realization; that is to say, because the roots of goodness of the remedies and the practice of roots transcend what preceded, it is called "increase" (*vṛddhi*).
Fourth, one eliminates the stains of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that are to be countered.
Fifth, one severs and removes the secret points of doubt within this stage, which constitute the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Subtle pride regarding the Dharma constitutes these secret points of doubt; by means of non-appropriation (*anupādāna*), one is able to eliminate them.
The first two remove internal obstacles;
the sixth clarifies the severance of contact with sense objects;
and the seventh relies on superior bliss to practice samādhi and harmonize the spirit.
The eighth [point] is based on the Buddha’s power to transform sentient beings.
The ninth treatise states: "By relying on the mind of immeasurable samādhis, the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are purified.
This refers to the removal of cognitive obscurations within meditative concentration.
If one proceeds directly according to the scriptural text, it is shown in general that all original vows are fully accomplished.
Within the second stage, the fruit, there are also three parts;
first, "pliancy" (mṛdu-karmaṇyatā), followed by four [subdivisions]: [The text continues with the four subdivisions.]

1. The practice of harmonious flexibility; 2. From "Like a mani jewel" onwards, clarifying the purity of the wisdom of teaching; 3. From "This bodhisattva" onwards, the specific characteristics of the stage's practice; 4. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, a summary of the characteristics of the stage.
The first three sections are as follows:
first, the conditions for training; second, from "all with reverence" onwards, clarifying the ability to train; third, from "furthermore" onwards, clarifying the purity that is trained.

Among these two [sections], the first is the practice of merit through making offerings to the Buddha; the second, from "By this" onwards, is the great practice of dedication; and the third, from "In that" onwards, is the practice of wisdom through hearing the Dharma.
Within this, first is the stage of being a householder, and subsequently, from the words "Furthermore" (*fù yú*) onwards, is the stage of renunciation (*chūjiā*).

However, once one has ascended to the stages [of the Bodhisattva] (*dì*), one possesses a body that embodies the ten dharma-realms (*shí fǎjiè shēn*); whether emerging from or remaining within [the world], what could possibly be impossible? Nevertheless, according to the meaning, there is a shifting of prominence and concealment, presence and absence, and priority and sequence; for the first three stages are provisionally aligned with the mundane world and thus still rely upon worldly laws.
In the first two stages, they exist because they are kings;
in the third stage, they do not exist because they are celestial kings;

from the fourth stage upward, they are again clearly shown to exist because they serve as the leaders of those who have transcended the world, signifying their departure from the household life; therefore, they are elucidated within the context of the practice of harmonious flexibility (*saṃvṛti-caryā*).
If one wishes to accord with the non-existence of heaven, renunciation is not distinguished within the retribution of karmic accumulation.
From the sixth stage upward, one realizes the equality of dharmas; because there is neither emergence nor abiding, there is no renunciation at all.
Regarding the three aspects of purification— thesis, example, and application—
the "ornament of gold" refers to the fact that the refined gold of the third stage is manifested as these ornaments of realized wisdom of the fourth stage.
"All other gold" refers to gold that has not yet been fashioned into ornaments.

Regarding "the purity of both teaching and wisdom," this passage is specifically included because on this stage, the purity of realization is accomplished, whereby the function arises from the essence.
Previously, because the teaching was established by means of the realization, gold was used as a metaphor for the ornaments;
now, because the teaching arises from the realization, the mani-jewel emitting light is used as a metaphor.

The mani-jewel is the essence of realized wisdom (*pratyātmajñāna*): its stainlessness is called "purity," its tranquil illumination is called "light," and its perfection is called the "wheel. Because it possesses these three meanings, it is termed "realized wisdom."
To say that it can emit radiance means that it emits the light of the Āgamas;
this refers to entering into the realization of the meanings of immeasurable dharma-gates through the wisdom of this limit (*koṭi*).
Therefore, that which is able to illuminate—the radiant light—is itself realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*), while the teachings illuminated therein serve as the locus of wisdom.

Realization is able to universally illuminate and manifest within the teachings; having attained the radiance of the teachings, it gives rise to flames based upon realization. Thus, this stage is named "Blazing Wisdom" (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
The phrase "not other jewels" contrasts with what preceded it to demonstrate its superiority.
The fact that it cannot be destroyed by wind and so forth demonstrates its solidity in contrast to other things.
All else is as explained previously.
The third section consists of seventeen verses in *śloka* meter, divided into three parts:
first, twelve verses praising the practices of the stages; second, four verses on the fruits of the stages; and finally, one verse revealing the name and concluding the exposition.
The preceding section has four parts:
the first verse concerns the stage of increasing the cause;
the subsequent two verses concern the stage of purification.

The third section, consisting of four verses, praises the stage of increasing cultivation; therein, the first verse praises the protection against afflictions, while the latter two verses praise the protection against the Lesser Vehicle.
The fourth section, consisting of five verses, praises the fruit of increasing cultivation.
The rest may be understood as before.
Regarding the fifth stage,
the Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjaya*), there are briefly four reasons for its name:

First, regarding the provisional assignment of stages: the fourth, fifth, and sixth grounds are provisionally assigned to the supramundane; the former (the third ground) is assigned to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), while this (the seventh ground) is assigned to the *arhat*.

This is because their meanings follow a sequential order. Although there are four fruits, by citing the beginning and the end, the intermediate stages are subsumed. This is based on the *Mūla-śāstra* regarding the characteristics of the observed practices: since the latter six grounds observe dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are provisionally assigned to the same category as the *pratyekabuddhas*; therefore, only two grounds are provisionally assigned to the *śrāvakas*.

The lower fascicle of the *Renwang jing* and the upper fascicle of the *Yingluo jing* assign stages according to persons; because those of the seventh stage have not yet abandoned the *pindabandhana* (segmented existence), they are provisionally associated with the śrāvakas at the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh stages.
Second, whereas previously the wisdom associated with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) was clarified, now the wisdom associated with the truths (*satya*) is being distinguished.

Third, whereas previously one had attained the supramundane but was not yet able to conform to the mundane world, now one is able to gather and transform others by means of the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*); therefore, these are explained next.
The first four [sections] previously established the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; now, the factors of enlightenment subsumed under skillful means (*upāya*) are being distinguished.
These latter three points originate from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Regarding the term "Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*), the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "Because the skillful cultivation of those very factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) is extremely arduous, it is called 'Extremely Difficult to Conquer'."
This is because it is taught from the beginning.
In the first section, the Sūtra states, "Because one has well-cultivated the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)," and so forth.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Because the wisdom of ultimate truth (*paramārthajñāna*) and worldly wisdom (*lokajñāna*) are mutually contradictory, one brings these two difficult-to-unite [wisdoms] into correspondence."

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* agrees with this; Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Because in this stage, the knowledge that realizes ultimate truth is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), while the knowledge of worldly arts and crafts is conceptual (*savikalpa*), these two are contradictory and should be cultivated until they are unified. Because it can unify what is difficult to unify and bring them into correspondence, it is called 'Extremely Difficult to Conquer' (*sudurjayā*)."
This applies to the beginning, middle, and end [of the stage].

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "In this present stage, it is revealed that the bodhisattva’s definitive and sublime wisdom regarding the noble truths is extremely difficult to surpass; therefore, it is named the 'Difficult to Surpass' Stage (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*)."
This refers exclusively to the stages (*bhūmi*).
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "Regarding these five stages, there are two kinds of difficulties:
first, the difficulty of being untroubled while exhorting and transforming others; second, the difficulty of being untroubled when [beings] are born according to their own inclinations."
"Bodhisattvas on this stage are able to overcome two difficulties and achieve victory amidst them.
This primarily refers to the completion of the stage (*bhūmi*).

The *Vyākhyāyukti* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*) states: "Having realized the subtle wisdom that takes the objects of knowledge—the truths—as its extremely pure conditions, which is most difficult to accomplish, and having attained the noble path of tranquility that does not abide in saṃsāra, it is called 'Extremely Difficult to Conquer' (*Sudurjayā*)."
This is largely the same as the original section.
Although various sutras and śāstras above frequently cite "difficult-to-surpass" dharmas, it was not known what it is that cannot be surpassed.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Because the power of merit is perfected, no māras whatsoever can destroy it."
This [distinction] reveals superiority in relation to persons, while also encompassing the delusions and the māra of afflictions.
Nevertheless, although various sūtras and śāstras differ in their phrasing, they are identical in intent: all of them elucidate the non-obstruction between the ultimate and the conventional truths.

If one were to rely on the actual stages according to the *Renwang jing*, a Bodhisattva of the first stage and the Four Heavenly Kings both simultaneously illuminate the path of the equality of the two truths.

Now, however, we are considering the provisional assignment of stages: whereas the former [the Heavenly Kings] were provisionally assigned to the supramundane, they now enter back into the mundane; hence it is said that there is no obstruction.

Therefore, regarding the phrase "in this stage, one cuts off the obstacle to parinirvāṇa by means of the lower vehicles": this refers to the preceding four stages where one transcends the world, grows weary of the suffering of saṃsāra, and seeks to enter nirvāṇa; this constitutes the obstacle to the fifth stage.
Now, by entering the path in which the ultimate and the conventional are undifferentiated, one is able to sever them.
This severing of delight and aversion constitutes the two delusions.
Through this, one realizes the suchness of non-differentiation in kind, because, from the perspective of a single principle, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equal.

The practices accomplished therein also consist of two kinds: namely, the practice of higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) regarding the Truths, and the practice of teaching through the five fields of knowledge (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*).
Because these two are unimpeded, one attains the fruit of the undifferentiated Dharma-body; thus, all meanings and principles are mutually consistent.
Next is the formal explanation of the text, which also consists of three parts.
Within the first part, the section on praise and request, there are nine and a half verses, divided into two:
the first eight and a half verses consist of offerings and praise, while the final one verse is the request for the teaching.
The first section has three parts:
the first is a Bodhisattva making offerings and offering praise; the second is a host of celestial kings; and the remainder are all celestial maidens.
Within this [second part], there are three sections:
The first verse provides the heading, and the subsequent four and a half verses offer praise.
Within these, the first two verses concern the beauty of the response to conditions.
The repeated use of the word "long" indicates that the Buddha’s response depends upon the spiritual capacity of beings, and such capacity is difficult to encounter.
"The great ocean moves" means that he moves the ocean of Buddha-wisdom in order to exhaust the ocean of suffering.
The final two and a half verses praise his possession of virtues: the first verse is complete in wisdom and abandonment, while the subsequent half-verse is complete in grace.
The latter [Buddha] possesses these three virtues; therefore, he is worthy of offerings.
The three verses [in the following section] concerning the conclusion of the praise and the request can be understood accordingly.
Within the second part, the "Section on the Correct Exposition," first the practices of the stages are clarified, followed by the discernment of the fruits of those stages.
Regarding the preceding section, the treatise is divided into three parts:

first, the antidote to excessive pride; second, the excellence of the practice of the non-abiding path, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows as it truly is..."; and third, the excellence of its fruit, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this..."
The first refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the initial stage;
the second refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the stage of formal abiding;
and the last refers to the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) at the completion of the stage.
Regarding the initial mention of "pride of superiority," there are two types of pride:

first, pride of other stages (*bhūmi*), which refers to attaining supramundane knowledge within the four stages and grasping its superior characteristics—this is called the pride of superiority; it is now countered by the ten kinds of pure mind.
Second is conceit regarding one's own level (*svabhūmi-māna*), which refers to seeking a superior state within these ten mental states and, based on that, giving rise to conceit.
Because it accords with the path as it leads toward this [superiority], these two are collectively termed "conceit of superiority" (*abhimāna*); thus, this single category possesses two paths.
The treatise states: "Regarding the antidote to superior pride, the ten kinds of profound and pure equanimous minds refer to the 'antidotes' in the preceding section.
It further states: "The mind of non-retrogression through shared mindfulness refers to the 'antidotes' in the subsequent section."
The phrase "identical in thought" refers to the subsequent general statement, as it accords with the identity and oneness of a single moment of thought (*ekakṣaṇa*).
The term "non-retrogressive" refers to the final sentence of the latter section; by briefly citing the beginning and the end, it encompasses the middle.
The preceding stage remedies the pride of conceptualizing the dharma;
this stage remedies the pride of conceptualizing the purity of the body. Because the objects remedied differ, it does not overlap with the preceding stage.
Regarding "purity of the body," it means that having attained supramundane wisdom, one is no longer defiled by the body.
The text has two parts:
first, the remediation of pride regarding other stages; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this... onwards, the remediation of pride regarding one's own stage.
Within the former, there are three sections:
First, the summary of what precedes and what follows; second, the interrogation and the formal exposition; third, the summary of the ability to enter the stages.
Regarding the first, "equality" has two meanings:
first, that which accords with reality (*yathābhūta*); second, the pure dharmas of cause and effect.
The fact that a thousand sages share this same standard is called the "profoundly pure mind," for this is the contemplative understanding (*vipaśyanā*) of this stage.
The *Śāstra* states: "Because the mind attains purity within equality.
How does this differ from the observation of the ten dharmas of equality in the subsequent stages?
There are three differences here:
first, because on this stage one previously gave rise to pride regarding the pure [dharmas], it specifically clarifies the equality of pure dharmas;
whereas on the subsequent stages, by relying on the true [nature] to enter into the conventional, one universally contemplates that all dharmas, both defiled and pure, are entirely equal.

Second, this [stage] reveals the purity of mind through the principle of exertion (*pragraha*) and so forth, whereas the subsequent stage enters into that same principle by means of observation (*vipaśyanā*).

Third, this [stage] encompasses both principle and phenomena (*dharma*), while the subsequent stage is exclusively concerned with principle to harmonize the two truths (*satyadvaya*); in all these cases, each successive stage progressively excels by transcending the characteristics of its predecessor.
The second part, the actual exposition of the ten minds, is divided into two sections.
First, the three [verses] clarify the qualities of the Buddhas.
Regarding the treatise’s statement, “namely, the powers of the three times and so forth,” this refers to the ten powers (*daśabala*) and other qualities at the stage of fruition.
The latter seven clarify the practices that accord with the qualities of all Buddhas, because these causal practices for the two benefits lead to the attainment of the result.
Among them, the first six pertain to self-benefit, and the last one pertains to the benefit of others.
The preceding [three] and the middle [one] are combined to form the three trainings: first, morality; next, concentration; and the remaining four, wisdom.
Separated, they constitute the seven purities:
first, purity of morality;...
Second, purity of concentration;
third, purity of view;
fourth, purity through overcoming doubt—since the characteristics of view and doubt are distinct, these two are combined into one phrase in the sutra to complete the ten [purities].
The five paths are not the path of purity.
These aforementioned five purities share the same names as those in the Hīnayāna.
The sixth is called the purity of practice;
The seven practices are "abandonment and purification" (*prahāṇa-viśuddhi*), because in that school [of the Śrāvakas], one proceeds toward the exhaustion and cessation [of defilements].

Now, in the Mahāyāna, these six are called "abandonment through practice" (*pratipatti-prahāṇa*); as the Sūtra says, "cultivating knowledge and vision," the word "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) is omitted for brevity.

The seventh is called "the supreme purification through reflection on the factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣadharma*), because by relying on practice and abandoning [faults], one gives rise to superior aspiration.

If categorized according to the stages (*bhūmi*), the first two belong to the period prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); for one has just begun to turn away from the faults of an ordinary person and should guard against them with ethical discipline (*śīla*). Furthermore, since one desires to give birth to true wisdom, it is necessary to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*); yet, as this has not yet conformed to the principle [of the supramundane], they are judged to belong to the mundane realm.

The next three [knowledges] exist in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because within the path of seeing one abandons the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), abandons doubt (*vicikitsā*), and abandons attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Attachment to precepts and rituals is not the true path; one knows that untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) is the true path.

When entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), all ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned simultaneously; yet the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks specifically of three because it describes these three as being particularly heavy.

Furthermore, among the ten underlying tendencies, the five views and doubt only obstruct the Path of Seeing, whereas the remaining four pertain to both the Paths of Seeing and Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); therefore, they are omitted here.

Among these six, there are three fundamental and three derivative views; here we speak specifically of the fundamentals: extreme views follow the view of self-identity, false views follow doubt, and the grasping of views follows the grasping of precepts and rituals.
When the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are severed, the three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are also severed; however, only three purities (*viśuddhi*) are established.
For the five higher [fetters], both the Great and Small Vehicles are the same.

In the Lesser Vehicle, the purity of practice (*pratipad-viśuddhi*) occurs during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because it involves the arising of the practice of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipad*).
The practice of abandonment occurs in the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), because one realizes abandonment by relying on this practice.
In the Mahāyāna, the latter two [practices] both occur in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); because they involve abandoning hindrances and accomplishing virtues, there are these two.

Regarding the simultaneous nature of practice and realization: if categorized by stages, from the seventh stage downward it is termed "practice" because one severs afflictions through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and abandons fetters;
from the eighth stage upward, having entered the stream of the Dharma and being in accord with *bodhi*, it is termed "contemplation of the progressively higher."
The remaining text is easy to understand.
Second, it clarifies "abiding like the practice of the Way.
Furthermore, in accordance with the meaning of the sutra, the preceding section clarified "entering the mind," while from this point onward, all clarify "abiding in the mind."
This should be divided into three parts:

first, this encompasses the "abiding in the perfection of skillful means," where the practice of the ten mental states constitutes the meaning of skillful means, and "non-retrogression" constitutes the meaning of abiding;
second, the superior encompassment of the practice of the path of non-abiding, which is free from delusion and confusion because wisdom is pure and thus devoid of delusion and confusion.
Third, the excellence of its fruit consists in its encompassing an inexhaustible treasury of merit, because it encompasses inexhaustible virtues through dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
For now, following the treatise, this clarifies the practice according to the path.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the designation of the stages, which serves to show that one has already entered the fifth stage in accordance with suchness;
second, the general exposition beginning with "By means of goodness" and so forth.
The latter is explained separately under "the power of vows.

Within the general [classification], the four phrases all refer to the correct cultivation of various practices; therefore, they are collectively termed "conforming to suchness" (*yathābhūta-anuloma*).

This means that the first two phrases constitute the objects of remediation—namely, the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) in the fourth stage—and through the ten preceding mental states, one is able to thoroughly purify them and enter the fifth stage.
To seek superior characteristics within this pure mind is itself a form of pride; because pride lies beyond the literal text, the latter two lines serve as the remedy.
The first line serves as the remedy by turning toward the pursuit of the superior practice of the non-abiding path.
This means that one initiates various practices without dwelling in a [self-congratulatory] pure mind, thereby counteracting the pride of dwelling in purity.

Although the latter phrase mentions initiating various practices, one does not lose the previously attained profound and pure mind of equanimity; thus, one can accord with True Suchness (*tathatā*), for equanimity is itself Suchness.

In the subsequent detailed explanation, it is shown that there are eight kinds of practice in accordance with suchness (*tathatā*). Although the sūtra contains nine phrases, the first seven each constitute one kind, while the final two are combined as one.
Among these eight, the first two constitute the mind that initiates practice: first, the vow for one's own benefit, which is the cultivation of the bodhicitta;
second, compassion for others, which is the mind free from weariness.

The latter six are practices: namely, (1) the power of attaining the three roots of goodness; (2) not abandoning the various practices; (3) skillful cultivation; (4) because of being insatiable, illuminating the higher and highest stages; (5) attaining the superior power of others; and (6) attaining one's own superior power.
This consists of two phrases. The first phrase possesses the mindfulness of the three types of wisdom; it comprises the wisdoms of hearing and reflection, which is itself the wisdom of cultivation.
The second phrase refers to superior progress and the ultimate goal.
Within the six lines above, the first three constitute self-perfection and the latter three constitute superior progress; each of these has its own beginning, middle, and end—contemplate this.
The second, the excellence of the practice of the non-abiding path, has two types of contemplation:

first, the excellence of the purity of wisdom regarding the objects of knowledge; and second, the excellence of the diligent application of skillful means for the benefit of sentient beings, beginning from the passage "O Son of the Buddha, having attained such truths... and so forth.
The former refers to self-benefit, for by guarding against the activity of afflictions, one does not dwell in the world;
the latter refers to benefiting others, for by guarding against the practice of the Lesser Vehicle, one does not dwell in nirvana.
Simultaneously guiding one another is called the "Path of Non-abiding.
Now, the first section, "Superiority of Wisdom," is divided into two parts:

first, clarifying the analytical discernment of the real dharmas of the Four Truths; second, from the passage "skillfully knowing the conventional" onwards, further clarifying the distinctions in the transformative teachings for sentient beings through the ten contemplation gates based on these same four truths.
This refers to contemplating the Four Noble Truths through ten aspects; it does not mean contemplating fourteen truths.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the "Chapter on Abiding," states: "In this stage, one understands the Four Noble Truths as they truly are by means of ten modes of contemplation."

Now, regarding the first point, as for what are called "real dharmas": whether a Buddha appears or not, the essence of the two truths of suffering and its origin consists of the causes and effects of deluded conceptualization and defilement; the essence of the two truths of cessation and the path consists of the causes and effects of supramundane purity.
This is an explanation based on the meaning of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

If explained according to the meaning of conventional examination (*saṃvṛti*), if the former two [truths] did not exist, there would be no Buddha who could know that "this is suffering" and "this is its origin"; how then could the latter two—the cessation and the path—as cause and effect, exist?
The remainder is as in this chapter. Regarding the ten subsequent contemplations (*vipaśyanā*), four gates are briefly introduced:

First, the establishment [of the categories]: The meaning of the Four Truths encompasses the entire *dharmadhātu*. The Bodhisattva’s exhaustive illumination leaves nothing unexhausted; though the various explanations according to their wisdom are difficult to fathom, ten are briefly cited to illustrate their inexhaustibility. However, these ten are all the Bodhisattva’s own wisdom. Because the characteristics of wisdom are difficult to clarify, the treatise explains their distinctions by means of the beings to be converted (*vineya*). By this, they are collectively termed "the purity of wisdom regarding the knowable phenomena" (*jñeya-dharma-viśuddhi-jñāna*).

Second, the explanation of the opening and closing [of the categories]: these ten, in total, are merely a single manifestation of differentiated birth (*upapāduka-vibhāga*). If categorized according to the magnitude of those to be transformed, they are divided into two: the first nine transform those of small capacity, while the final one transforms those of great capacity.

If categorized according to the arising of the transformative teachings, they are divided into three: the first five produce understanding, the next four give rise to practice, and the final one brings about realization.

When distinguished according to the different types of persons, they are further divided into seven; from the first, for those whose faculties are not yet mature, up to the seventh, for those who can be transformed by the Mahāyāna—this should be understood as the text proceeds.
Third, the general and specific [aspects] are clarified by means of real dharmas.

These ten, in relation to the preceding four truths, involve the first five as a general contemplation of the four truths: first, contemplating the characteristics of the four truths as conventional phenomena; second, contemplating their emptiness of intrinsic nature; third, contemplating the non-obstruction between nature and characteristics; fourth, contemplating the distinctness of nature and characteristics; and fifth, contemplating how these four are integrated through dependent origination.

Next, there are four distinct contemplations of the Four Truths; that is, the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth [stages] contemplate suffering, origin, cessation, and the path respectively, while the final one contemplates only cessation and the path, because it is the cause for attaining Buddha-wisdom on the Bodhisattva grounds.

The latter five [stages] of Master Yuan’s system also involve the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths: that is, because one is deluded regarding the Four Truths, there arise suffering and its origin; because one awakens to those Four Truths, there are cessation and the path; and finally, by thoroughly exhausting the true nature of the dependent origination of the Four Truths, one realizes the pure Dharma-realm and achieves the Mahāyāna path.
There is also this principle.
Fourth, the correct explanation of the text, which is divided into two parts:
first, the listing of the ten names; second, the sequential explanation beginning with "This bodhisattva... and so forth.
Within this, there are briefly two interpretations:
first, based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; second, based on the present treatise. Regarding the first:
the ten phrases of the *Yogācāra* are abbreviated such that their phrasing is not explicit, and the meanings they express are incomplete.
The tenth [topic], the knowledge of the bodhisattva stages, also consists of ten phrases, which are divided into three sections.

The first three are termed "the statement of this" (*idam-vacana*), because they refer to the purpose for which it is taught: first, one knows conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) based on the awakening of others;
second, one knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) based on one's own internal wisdom.

Third, the truth of characteristics is known by virtue of their co-locating basis; that is to say, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the conventional, while the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is the ultimate. Because these two essences are not divided, they are said to be co-located.

Next, regarding these two phrases of the present sutra, it should have three names based on this explanation; that is to say, because they are taught by means of the teachings of the Three Piṭakas, it is said: "Based upon the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās, their names are explained by this."
The distinctions of stages within the sūtras should be understood as the Vinaya; the meaning of the aggregates, elements, and bases should be understood as the Mātṛkā;
and herein, the tenth [category] corresponds in meaning to the Sūtra.

The three existences (bhava) are explained by four propositions as follows: because the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths are known individually, one should understand them in sequence—namely, the truth of facts (*vastu-satya*) based on the intrinsic nature of present suffering; the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*) based on the nature of the cause for the arising of future suffering; the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) based on the nature of the exhaustion of that cause and the non-arising [of suffering]; and the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) based on the nature of the means for abandoning that [suffering] through cultivation.
Second, according to the *Mūla-śāstra*, the ten categories are subsumed into seven:

the first is for sentient beings whose faculties are not yet mature—meaning those who are not yet capable of entering the Mahāyāna—and for them, the Four Truths and the sixteen aspects are taught; this is called "knowing the conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
