The distinctions between these characteristics will be understood from the text itself.

However, these three contemplations all encompass both self-benefit and benefit for others: the contemplation of the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) is self-benefit when analyzed according to their specific marks; next, the contemplation of great compassion clarifies benefit for others; and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) pervades both benefits.

Within this, the distinctions are further differentiated as follows: the first five concern self-benefit; the next two concern benefiting others; and the final two concern the maturation of both benefits.

Among the first five, the first two pertain to both the defiled and the pure: the first reveals the characteristics of the defiled and the pure, and the second reveals the basis of the defiled and the pure.

The latter three observe only the defiled; among these, the first two establish the phenomena of defilement—the first being the cause of defiled phenomena and the second being the conditions for defiled phenomena—while the last one observes the faults within defilement.
Next, regarding the two types of benefiting others, the first transforms ordinary beings and the second transforms those of the Lesser Vehicle.

Regarding the latter two, which concern the maturation of the two benefits: the former is called "beginningless" because the True Truth (paramārtha-satya) observation sees that the collection of conditions for phenomena lacks an intrinsic nature;
the latter is called "various" because the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya) observation sees that things merely revolve according to conditions.
Having already grasped the general meaning, we shall next provide a formal commentary on the text.
We shall explain it according to the ten sections of the Sūtra, following the sequence of the three contemplations as presented in the Śāstra; there is no other underlying principle.

In these ten sections of the sutra, the first five concern the "sons of the Buddha"; the next three consist of further repetitions; and the final two are distinguished by the use of the word "again" (you). Only within the first section does the term "son of the Buddha" appear once in the middle.

Now, regarding the first section, the Gate of the Continuity of the Links of Existence (*bhavāṅga*), one first contemplates according to the distinctions of the Truths of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇasatya*).
Among the three sections, the three characters "Answering the Characteristics" (*dengda xiang*) shall be explained; this is thus divided into three parts.

Upon first arriving, one establishes the non-arising of a place of birth and definitively discerns non-self; this is immediately clarified in the treatise, which means that by simultaneously presenting both delusion and awakening, it explains and establishes non-self. Thus, one knows that the collection of conditions is merely a false self.

Second, from "Again, he thinks thus" onwards is the section on the conditions for the arising of delusive inversion; this is the explicit answer provided by the treatise, as it explains and resolves the objection regarding the meaning of non-self (*anātman*).

Third, the final section concerns the sequence of conditions for the arising of delusion through the confusion of true reality; this is the explicit description of the characteristics provided by the treatise.
If these three are viewed in light of the ten gates, they all reveal that the false self does not exist.
When the three are compared with one another, they may be condensed into two: the first two reveal the causes and conditions [of arising], clarifying that the conditions are without self;
the latter one reveals the sequence of the conditions for arising, clarifying that the conditions possess characteristics.
Based on this meaning, the Sūtra inserts the phrase "a son of the Buddha" between [the preceding and following sections], as both [the subject and the object] possess both defilement and purity.

Here, for the sake of initial establishment, one is about to contemplate dependent origination; first, however, one explains the establishment of non-self (*anātman*) to definitively identify the fundamental tenet that "one principle runs through all. Thus, it is revealed that all ten gates establish non-self, which constitutes the direct refutation of the habitual tendencies of the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha-vāsanā*).
The text contains two sentences.

The first states that "all worldly rebirths arise from attachment to a self," which serves as a counter-argument to raise the nature of delusion; it clarifies that the self is irrational, being merely the origin of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*).

"If one is free from this attachment, there is no place for rebirth" means that this directly follows the text to raise the mind of understanding, clarifying that the principle is not-self because it is the path to cessation.
Thus, by merely following the scriptural passage, the meaning of non-self is established.

The treatise states that regarding birth in the various stations of embodied existence, the habitual tendencies of the grasping at a self merely cause the distinction between self and other; therefore, the treatise says: "All the distinctions of birth and death within the five destinies."
"If there are distinctions among the five destinies, they are merely summoned by karma.
Furthermore, the Master of the Treatise counters by interrogating the deluded mind to demonstrate the non-existence of a self.
First, he interrogates the attachment to a self, clarifying that ordinary beings would otherwise incur the fault of being identical to the sages.
If it were the case that there truly existed a mark of self within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), this would be the mind that fixates upon and clings to such a self;
it would then be the wisdom of the ultimate truth itself, established here by way of concession, because it would be known as a self that accords with reality.

Next, regarding the statement that "one should not be born in a place where one receives a body in the world," this is a correct inquiry based on principle: if the principle were that the self is extinguished and attachment to the mind is the path, then ordinary beings should likewise attain nirvana just as the sages do; why then would they remain attached to a self and receive birth in the world?
In this context, one should formulate the following critique:
"If, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there were a truly existent self (*ātman*), then ordinary beings would necessarily be identical to noble ones"—this constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*).
"Because they possess the cognition that realizes a truly existent self in the ultimate sense"—this constitutes the reason (*hetu*).
If all those whose births have ended were taken as the noble ones (ārya) to serve as the corroborative example (dṛṣṭānta),
then ordinary beings would necessarily be identical to the noble ones.
If ordinary beings were identical to the noble ones, there would be no such thing as an ordinary person, which would constitute another fallacy.
Next, reversing the latter part of the argument, it clarifies the fault that the Sage would be identical to ordinary beings:

"Furthermore, if there were truly a mark of self within the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), then even one who is free from attachment to a self would constantly be born in the world; for such a state would not accord with reality, being equivalent to false clinging and not the wisdom of the ultimate sense."
In this context, one should formulate the following critique:
"The thesis is that, according to the actual nature of reality, the self must exist, because the noble ones would otherwise be identical to ordinary worldlings;
the reason for establishing this is that the noble ones’ realization of non-self contradicts reason, as it would be a perverted delusion rather than noble wisdom."
Ordinary worldlings serve as the corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
This would then establish the fallacy that the noble ones (*ārya*) must be identical to ordinary worldlings.
If the noble ones were identical to ordinary worldlings, there would be no noble ones at all; this constitutes another fallacy.
Therefore, the Sūtra states: "If one is free from this attachment, there will be no place of birth. This, in turn, clearly demonstrates that deluded sentiment is certainly a fault.
Once these two faults are established, the principle of non-self becomes manifest and evident.
The second [point] concerns the conditions for the arising of inverted delusions; this is precisely what the treatise clarifies in its response, as it answers external challenges and objections.
There are two challenges and two responses:
first, the challenge that interrogates principle based on biased attachments, and the response that shows such attachments to contradict correct principle.
Second, the objection concerning the attachment to signs while seeking the real, and the response that signs do not depend on a self.
First, the objection states:
"If there is truly no self, why is there attachment to a self?"
If there were no person in space, how could one conceive of a person being there?
Since you are attached to a self and not attached to non-self, it is clear that you believe a self exists.
He replied:
Due to ignorance, one clings to a self where there is no self; it is not because a self exists.
It is like seeing flowers in the sky due to an eye disease; how could there be flowers in the sky?
The second objection states:
If there were truly no self, why would one be attached to a self? How could the sequential order of taking birth in the world function as a causal condition?
It is clearly known that only by having a self can there be a sequential arising of conditions.
The answer says:

It is precisely because of the non-self that one conceives of a self; with delusion and craving as the root, one creates karma through inverted confusion, leading all the way to old age and death—so what need is there for a "self"?
The meaning of the answer is exactly this.
The textual analysis is divided into three parts:
first, an explanation of how deluded confusion gives rise to the conditions for defilement;
second, from "Because of these causes and conditions" onwards, the correct wisdom contemplates in reverse order, concluding with the response regarding non-self; third, [the remaining section].
3. "The Bodhisattva is thus," and so forth, concludes the contemplation with respect to persons.
This is the first [section].
Now, the twelve links constitute twelve distinct parts, yet they are also without interval.
In various treatises, these are mostly subsumed into four categories:
first, the projecting factors (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*), namely ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), because they project the seeds of the five results, such as consciousness (*vijñāna*);
second, the projected factors (*ākṣipta-aṅga*), namely the five beginning with consciousness, because they are brought forth by the preceding two factors.
Third are the factors that produce, namely craving, grasping, and existence, because they closely give rise to future birth, aging, and death;
fourth are the factors produced, namely birth, aging, and death, because they are what is closely produced by craving, grasping, and existence.
This is based on two lifetimes and a single set of cause and effect, clarifying the distinction between "arising" (*janman*) and "projecting" (*ākṣepa*).
If one relies on three lifetimes and two sets of cause and effect, then "arising" and "projecting" are mutually interpenetrating.
This sutra contains both.
Furthermore, based on the twelve phrases, this is divided into five sections.
From the beginning up to "existence and non-existence" distinguishes the factor of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Lack of wisdom is delusion (*moha*); constantly seeking existence and non-existence is precisely craving for existence (*bhavarāga*).

However, based on the three periods of time, all afflictions that have passed away are collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*); this is stated briefly because it refers to the fundamental factors of the branches of existence (*bhavāṅga*) that project and moisten [rebirth].

If restricted to two periods of time, although all afflictions are capable of projecting and moistening, ignorance is designated as such because its power is predominant at the stage of projecting karma; thus, its essence is taken solely as those factors capable of projecting karma that directly brings about good or evil results in future lives.
The desire for permanence is "existence" (bhava), because one wishes to abide eternally in pleasant things.
The seeking of cessation is "non-existence" (vibhava), because one vows to bring about the extinction of painful things.

Next, regarding the section from "improper reflection" up to "the increase of the factors of clear conduct," there are seven phrases: the first three phrases concern the transgressions, the next three concern the essence, and the final one constitutes the conclusion.
The initial mention of "improper reflection" refers to the ignorance that co-arises with mental formations.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that this is the cause of ignorance and is itself subsumed under ignorance.
Stepping on the former to give rise to the latter, cause and effect are thus presented in tandem.

The second phrase reveals the fault with respect to the person: it means that one who gives rise to deluded practice must be an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*), for they take ignorance as the cause and create karma in pursuit of existence.

Therefore, the First Stage (Prathamā Bhūmi) states: "Whatever karma one performs is associated with perversion. This is presented as a counter-demonstration of the Bodhisattva’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha*): although a Bodhisattva acts within existence and initiates wholesome deeds, because these are caused by wisdom (*vidyā*), they do not seek the creation of existence and thus are not called deluded actions.
The second phrase reveals the fault in relation to the Dharma; the treatise states: "Because it demonstrates incorrect practice regarding the state of liberation.
Only by walking the path to nirvāṇa does one follow the true path.

The next three phrases distinguish the essential characteristics of the nature of action (*karma*), because volition (*cetanā*) associated with the three types of activity (*trikarma*) creates the three kinds of conduct.

That is to say, due to delusion regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*) and its opposition to correct faith and understanding, one gives rise to evil karma that brings about rebirth in the three miserable realms (*durgati*), as well as karma that brings about the suffering of distinct retributions among humans and devas; all of these are termed "meritorious misconduct" (*apuṇya-karma*).
However, while the specific [factors] necessarily include the general, only those that induce specific retribution are not considered "formative factors" (*saṃskāra*).

Due to delusion regarding the true nature of reality, one fails to recognize that the three realms are all suffering and falsely deems them to be happiness; the arising of wholesome karma in the desire realm is called "meritorious formative action," while the pure karma of the eight dhyānas is called "immovable formative action."

The subsequent phrase concludes the branch of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), meaning that having performed [an action], one has no regret; because it accumulates, increases, and involves a process of flux, it is so designated.

Next, from the words "regarding all formations" (*saṃskāreṣu*) onwards, the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is clarified: once the formations have been set in motion, they infuse the mind; thus, this fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is able to attract future birth, aging, and death, and is therefore termed a "seed."
If there were no perfuming by formative forces (*saṃskāra*), the seeds would ultimately not be established.

Therefore, it is said that "the seed-syllable of the mind is planted within the various formative forces. This refers to the five types [of aggregates], such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth, which are gathered by the formative forces in a single moment, without any sequence of before or after.
That which serves as the seeds for the six faculties as their maturation is called the limb of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
That which serves as the seeds for maturation-contact and feeling is called the limbs of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
Excluding the seeds of the fundamental consciousness constitutes the essence of the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Furthermore, these three types of seeds and all other remaining seeds of the ripening aggregates (*vipāka-skandha*) are collectively termed the "limb of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa-aṅga*); therefore, there is no sequence [of cause and effect].

Because the causal stage is difficult to discern, one speaks of the five distinctions based solely on their future states of arising. These five do not exist apart from the mind; they are merely called "seeds of the mind. Moreover, because the other four [aggregates] are concealed and the present state is emphasized, [the term "name-and-form"] is used.
However, in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, only the seeds of consciousness and so forth are taken as the "projected" [factors].

Yet, in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it is stated that this member of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*) extends to the "projecting" [factors] as well, because it takes the seeds of karma as its primary constituent for the member of consciousness; thus, the seeds of consciousness are actually subsumed under the member of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-aṅga*).

The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that [the term "consciousness"] applies to both the inducing and the induced, because both the seeds of karma and the seeds of consciousness are termed "consciousness";
however, since the seed of consciousness is merely the support for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and is not itself name-and-form, this differs from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

The intent of the present sutra is the same as that explained in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*; since it takes both [aspects] together, it mentions both "formations" (*saṃskāra*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).

The treatise states: "In this context, the seeds of the arising mind demonstrate the essential nature of birth and old age/death," meaning that the two future fruits take these seeds of consciousness as their direct cause.

Next, regarding the meaning of "having outflows" (*sāsrava*) and "having grasping" (*sopādāna*) as constituting the superior seeds: this refers to the seeds of linguistic designations (*nāma-vyañjana-bīja*), such as formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), which generally pertain to both the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the tainted; however, because they are currently associated with the three outflows, they are termed "limbs of existence" (*bhavāṅga*).
As in the case of the first stage (*bhūmi*), because the seeds of the mind arise through the four floods (*ogha*) such as desire (*chanda*) and so forth:

that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and that which is with grasping (*sopādāna*) is clinging (*upādāna*); because craving and clinging provide moisture, they are able to summon a future existence (*punarbhava*).
Next, the section beginning with "Furthermore, it arises again" explains the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The first two lines of the text contain two meanings:
first, they establish the sense of "seed" mentioned above; because it gives rise to birth and death, the mind receives the designation of "seed."

Second, this is a general indication of the subsequent meaning: because the manifest names and so forth all constitute birth, old age, and death, they are identical to the sprouting of the shoots of suffering once again within the field of the three realms at the first stage.
Regarding the section beginning with "That which is called," there are two further meanings:
first, it generally refers to the twelve [links]; from this point up to the arising of the sprout of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it signifies that consciousness gives rise to name-and-form.

Second, in order to demonstrate that the ten causes previously established result in the production of the branches of existence (*bhavāṅga*) within saṃsāra—wherein name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) occupies the initial position—they are explained in successive order.

That is to say, because the five preceding types of outflowing and grasping states (*sāsrava-sopādāna*), moistened by craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*), give rise to subsequent existence, this indicates the production of the two fruits of the branches of existence; it is now specifically to reveal the characteristics of these branches of existence.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The seeds of karma that project [a future existence] and the causes projected therefrom, when moistened by the conjunction of craving and grasping, are designated as 'existence' (*bhava*), because together they are capable of bringing about the fruit of a future birth."

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its tenth chapter, states that only the seeds of karma are designated as "existence" (*bhava*), because these are what directly bring about the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*),
as explained in the subsequent section.

Furthermore, among the thirty-eight [factors], the five beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) are said to be "existent" because they directly produce the five [factors] such as consciousness in the future.
In reality, however, eight members in total are collectively established as "existent"; excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), there are nine when including those that are "existent" in general.
Now, if ignorance (*avidyā*) is further added to the sūtra, then the preceding ten causes collectively bring about two fruits.
If the twelve [links] are considered to be the two fruits of a previous life, then a single lifetime would possess all twelve.
Furthermore, regarding the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the text sets forth six conditions:

first, karma serves as the field; that is, it is the seed of formative action (*saṃskāra*), which, with respect to the fruit to be produced, functions merely as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
The two consciousnesses serve as seeds; that is, the five constituents beginning with consciousness act as the direct causes for future birth and death.
This is like planting in the world, which depends on whether the field is fertile or barren, yet the beans and wheat grow according to their own respective seeds.
The general commentary on the treatise states: "Because karma is the ground for the practices that conform to and appropriate [the results of] demerit, merit, and so forth.
This precisely clarifies that by conforming to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), one appropriates the seeds of the preceding consciousness and thereby constitutes the link of existence (*bhava*).

Regarding the third point, "obscured by the darkness of ignorance," the Master of the Treatise takes up the "ignorance" mentioned in the preceding sutra; therefore, he says, "as previously stated, there is the obscuration of the darkness of non-knowledge, because it is shrouded by ignorance.

This is based on the fact that [ignorance] can equally act as a remote auxiliary in initiating [the process], and it also serves to cite a precedent from a previous life to illustrate the present life.

According to the intent of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the ignorance that initiates action (*karmasamutthāna-avidyā*) is not identical to the ignorance that conceals action (*karmasaṃvartanīya-avidyā*).
It is also subsumed under craving (*tṛṣṇā*), specifically the delusion regarding external dominant fruits (*bāhya-adhipati-phala-moha*).
Furthermore, because all afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of moistening [the seeds], they share the same temporal period (*adhvan*) based on ten causes.

The "water of craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) acts as the moisture; the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) refers here to the aforementioned craving that constantly seeks existence and non-existence. This is an illustration, and it is also what was previously designated as "contaminated" (*sāsrava*) within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), since it is subsumed under craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).
The "irrigation by the five forms of *asmimāna*" refers to the link of grasping (*upādāna*); it is only through repeated irrigation that the sprout of existence (*bhava*) can arise.
This is because the grasping of "self-identity" (*ātman-vāda*) and so forth constitutes *asmimāna*, and if one realizes selflessness (*anātman*), such [grasping] would not arise.
The proliferation of the six nets of views is also the limb of grasping (*upādāna*), because they are subsumed under the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭy-upādāna*).
Since all views arise with the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as their root,
and because they prevent one from destroying the outflow-free dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), they are called "nets."
The general commentary on the treatise states: "Thus abiding and thus arising of the mind" refers collectively to the arising of the sprout of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
This is because ignorance and craving cause the seed of consciousness to abide upon the ground of karma, whereby the mind of name-and-form arises.

Next, the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) is explained. That sutra says, "My mind irrigates," and the treatise states, "I, mine, and the notion of 'I' and 'mine' are conceit. This explains the word "I" as meaning "I" and "mine," because one not only clings to a self but also clings to the actions performed, thinking, "This is what I have cultivated."

Next, regarding the statement "the notion of self is pride," this explains the term *citta*. Here, *citta* carries the meaning of "notion" (*saṃjñā*). Because one gives rise to the notion of self based on the [notion of] "I" in order to look down upon others, it is called pride (*māna*).
This is exactly as in the present sutra.
Next, regarding the explanation of the "net of views," it says: "My birth is non-birth. Here, "birth" refers to permanence (*śāśvata*), while "non-birth" refers to annihilation (*uccheda*).
With annihilation and permanence as the basis, the sixty-two views are fully encompassed.
The final phrase states, "Such various views.
As in the case of the first bhūmi, everything from ignorance (avidyā) at the beginning up to the link of consciousness (vijñāna) at the end is termed false view (mithyādṛṣṭi).

However, Master Huiyuan and the other virtuous ones all say that regarding "self" and "what belongs to the self": at the time of taking birth, one perceives one's own body as the "self," and perceives the semen and blood of the parents as "what belongs to the self."

Furthermore, it is said that when one's parents are regarded as one's own spouse, and at the time of conception one competes with the parents for their sexual favors, thinking that one has won the contest and giving rise to a sense of superiority—this is therefore called pride (*māna*).
Regarding "I am born," it means that I am born only in this place and not in any other;
this includes, without logical error, both the craving for rebirth and the craving of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

However, all the preceding phrases clarify that which is capable of producing; the "sprout of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa-aṅkura*) that is produced is precisely the five fruits of retribution (*vipākaphala*) that are to be experienced.

The initial aggregate at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi-skandha*) is the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Here, whereas previously the seeds of consciousness were distinguished as being latent within the other four members, the present discussion distinguishes the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) while omitting the basis of the total retribution (*sāmānyavipāka*), in order to reveal the principle of the sequential production of consciousness and name-and-form.
Furthermore, because one wishes to clarify that [the seeds] pervade both the latent (bīja) and the manifest (vartamāna), there is this alternation of concealment and manifestation.

However, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth must necessarily have a supporting basis, which is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); thus, the First Stage (*prathamabhūmi*) states: "In the field of the three realms, the sprouts of suffering grow once again, namely, name-and-form arise together."
The *Śāstra* states: "Because it arises together with the ālayavijñāna. This refers to what is later stated as "arising simultaneously with consciousness.
Next, from the phrase "the increase of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) onwards, the eight members beginning with the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are explained, as clarified in the subsequent section.

However, this section intends to answer the reason for taking birth; therefore, it fully sets forth the distinctions among the various afflictions regarding their concealment and manifestation, rather than focusing on their manifest characteristics.
The manifest characteristics are addressed in the subsequent section.
Second, regarding the contemplation in reverse, the response concludes that there is no self.
The first two phrases clarify non-self in relation to arising: it arises solely through the accumulation of ignorance and so forth, not through the accumulation of a self.
Furthermore, the first phrase excludes the absence of a cause, while the second phrase excludes false causes.
The latter two phrases clarify non-self (*anātman*) with respect to cessation:
things perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇikatva*), and there is no agent that causes them to do so.
Third, the contemplation on the formation [of afflictions] in relation to persons:
one who contemplates in this manner accords with the principle of dependent origination.
Third, regarding the sequence of the conditions for delusion regarding reality and the arising of falsehood, this refers to the distinctions among the characteristics of the discourse.
The treatise states: "If conditions are without self, by what characteristic do they abide as the collection of formative forces (*saṃskāra*)?

That is to say, abiding refers to their own characteristic, while 'arising' refers to subsequent activity; therefore, the intent of the sūtra is that one merely gives rise to the collection of characteristics through delusion regarding the principles of the truths."

However, while the three modes of answering establish that these are generally part of the continuity of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*), what is the distinction between their two layers of conditional characteristics?
Briefly, there are five differences:
first, the former concerns the arising of conditions based on a false self, which is precisely the delusion of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*).
This refers to the arising of conditions through delusion regarding the truths, which is precisely delusion regarding the meaning of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*).
Second, the former [section] concerned dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), whereas this concerns the sequence of conditions.
The former takes all ten causes and one basis collectively to give rise to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); [this section does not].
In this context, the sequence is explained exclusively as singlefold.

Three [factors] pertain to three time periods or two time periods, because it is accepted that the ten causes belong to the same time period; in terms of their meaning, they also pertain to five time periods.
This [set] pertains only to the three time periods, because name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth refer only to the present; in terms of their meaning, they also pertain to one time period.
In the preceding passage, it was intended to clarify that the three time periods are fully present; for therein, craving is mentioned within ignorance, and ignorance is mentioned within the present.
In this context, the three time periods have mutual concealment and manifestation, and it is not permitted for them to interpenetrate one another.
The preceding five [sections] served as responses to objections;
this section serves to distinguish the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), in accordance with the intent of the treatise.

Because there are these five differences, although the conditions (*pratyaya*) are distinguished in two places, they together clarify the continuity [of the causal process]. Thus, they collectively refute delusion and inversion, and are therefore bound together as one of the ten gates.
The text also consists of two parts:
first, the direct order (*anuloma*), and second, the reverse order (*pratiloma*).

Within the direct order, regarding the first member, ignorance (*avidyā*), it says "not understanding the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*); however, all twelve members arise based on reality (*tattva*) and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, the subsequent verse states: "When observing the true meaning of all dependent origination, they are empty."
However, ignorance (*avidyā*) is primary; it directly deludes regarding the principles of truth and gives rise to formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Since it arises horizontally from emptiness and cannot be traced back to its origin, ignorance is specifically designated by the term "delusion."
The *Śāstra* on the Sūtras states that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) among all truths is precisely the Four Noble Truths.
Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* says: "Ignorance regarding the true meaning refers to delusion concerning the Four Noble Truths."
That which is deluded is the actual reality, while that which causes delusion is ignorance (*moha*).
Ignorance is a distinct obscuring phenomenon; it is not merely a negative designation (*paryudāsa*) indicating the absence of knowledge.
The second is the "fruit of the karma performed," which refers to the member of "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*).
Karma consists of the three types of action, such as unwholesome deeds (*pāpa*) and so forth, because it is the fruit arising from that ignorance.

Thus, the verse states: "The volitional karma performed is the fruit of delusion. Furthermore, when the commentary says, "Among these, the fruit of the karma performed by ignorance is what is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)," this is identifying the essential substance of the fruit.
"Substance" refers to the substance of formations (*saṃskāra*), which is precisely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Master Huiyuan’s *Commentary on the Treatise* states: "Formations consist of three types of karma:
mental karma constitutes 'name,' while bodily and vocal karma constitute 'form.'"
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "There are two kinds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*):
first, preparatory name-and-form; second, actualized name-and-form.
If it is said that name-and-form conditions consciousness (*vijñāna*), this refers to preparatory name-and-form."
If it is said that consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), then this is designated as name-and-form.
Here, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) serve as the preliminary means for name-and-form.
Third, the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is that which depends upon volitional formations.
The treatise states: "Among these, consciousness [is so called] because it is that which relies upon them.
"Them" refers to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Here the word order is inverted; it should rather say "because it relies upon them."

The *Śāstra* on the Sūtra states: "Based on formative forces (*saṃskāra*), there is the initial consciousness; that is to say, because the mind is perfumed by formative forces, there exist seeds for future fruits as well as their actual manifestations.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "With consciousness as a condition, the resultant consciousness continues in a sequential succession from one moment to the next."
4. "Bestowing Consciousness" refers to the member of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

The first character, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), is the consciousness member as it manifests; as a seed, this consciousness is exclusively the *ālayavijñāna*, whereas in its state of manifestation, it encompasses all six consciousnesses.

Now, to exclude what is manifest and not the seed, it is said that the four aggregates arise together; this is because the aggregate of consciousness already belongs to the supporting consciousness (*āśraya-vijñāna*).

If one were to say that the four aggregates are "name" (*nāman*) and the *kalala* and so forth are "form" (*rūpa*), then the supporting active consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) would likewise be nothing other than the *ālayavijñāna*.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The sense faculties that serve as simultaneous supports are called 'form' (*rūpa*); the sense faculties that serve as immediately antecedent supports are called 'name' (*nāman*).

Thus, their substance comprises all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), referring specifically to the stage prior to the completion of the faculties during the first four weeks [of embryonic development].
The *Śāstra* states, "Name-and-form and consciousness arise together," which is intended to eliminate ambiguity, for one might otherwise mistakenly believe that name arises together with form.

It further states, "Consciousness and name-and-form depend on each other reciprocally," which explains the meaning of their co-arising: namely, that consciousness arises by virtue of name-and-form, while name-and-form exists by depending upon consciousness. This is like water and sediment, which mutually support one another to form a lump of mud, or like a bundle of reeds; thus they continue to depend upon one another until the end of life.
Therefore, in the preceding response, the resultant suffering is collectively termed the "sprout of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa-aṅkura*).

Regarding the branch of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*): after four weeks, when the faculties have reached full development and the six bases are clearly manifest, the mental base (*manāyatana*) is said to be "increased and perfected," while the other five are said to be "increased and perfected" in terms of form (*rūpa*).
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "From the arising of the faculties such as the eye, the three [faculties] precede the six sense bases.
The preceding section was intended to clarify the existence of the fundamental mind; it merely stated that the five faculties are established.
In the eleventh fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa*, among the five fruits, the first three occur within the womb, while the remaining two occur outside the womb.

The "six contacts" (ṣaṭ-sparśa) refer to the act of touching; although there is a conjunction of the three [elements], at this stage one has not yet fully understood the causes of the three types of sensation, but is merely able to touch them.
The seventh link, the branch of feeling (*vedanā*), refers to the experiencing of the three types of sensation through contact; this is termed "arising together with contact.
The preceding four links are explained solely in terms of their active manifestation (*samudācāra*).

The eighth link, the branch of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), involves the persistent longing for pleasant sensation among the three types of sensation; thus it is called "defiled attachment," which constitutes greed of middling and inferior grades.
Although this [craving] generally takes both internal and external fruits as its objects, most treatises maintain that it refers to the arising of the dominant fruit of craving for external objects.
While the ninth link, "appropriation" (*upādāna*), subsumes other afflictions, because the moistening power of craving is predominant, it is said to be the increase of this craving.
However, the aforementioned two links (birth and aging-and-death) pertain to both the manifest and the seeds.
As for the ten links of existence (*bhava*), they are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) because they consist of various karmas arising from the four types of grasping (*upādāna*).
These karmas are termed "existence" (*bhava*) because they directly bring about their future fruits.

This is based on the three periods of time; it differs from the preceding section where craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) together moisten karma and so forth, which is termed "existence" (*bhava*). This is because the karma prior to that has already been separated by the manifest name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and other factors.
Regarding the eleventh link of dependent origination, from the perspective of the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is said to arise from karma.
Beginning from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) until the onset of decay and transformation, all of this is termed "birth" (*jāti*).
The twelfth link, old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), is a designation for the state of various decays and transformations because it constitutes the ripening of the aggregates (*skandha*).

While the entities of these latter two links pertain to all five aggregates and exist only as actual manifestations (*samudācāra*), they are combined into two by aggregating the five aggregates in order to induce revulsion; this is done to manifest the three types of suffering (*duḥkhatā*).
Old age is not invariably present; it is established as a link in conjunction with death.
Although the five links such as separation and so forth exist at other times, they are specifically discussed in relation to death because they most frequently occur at that time.
Nevertheless, this particular set of links is also established by spanning the beginning and end of a single lifetime; the other links may be understood accordingly.
Reflect on this: it is simply that one type of birth universally takes up what precedes it.

In the subsequent contemplation of the reverse order, a single fetter is the tree of suffering: namely, ignorance and formations induce consciousness through to feeling as the sprout of suffering; craving conditions the induction from feeling through to becoming as the nurturing; and birth, old age, and death constitute the tree of suffering.
To guard and nurture the sprout is the meaning of growth.

Furthermore, within this present life, karma created by ignorance serves as the seedling of suffering; if it is moistened by craving and grasping, it attains growth, whereas if it is not moistened, it will even perish—how much more so if it is further increased?
Furthermore, the first two constitute the roots, the next two the trunk, the next three the branches, the next three the flowers, and the final two the fruits.
The absence of self and what belongs to self constitutes non-self; the absence of agent and recipient constitutes emptiness.
The passage beginning with "Again, he thinks thus" uses the self as an analogy for the Dharma to establish the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Dependent origination is profound by way of ten aspects."
The six meanings rely upon impermanence:
one meaning relies upon suffering, one meaning relies upon emptiness, and two meanings rely upon non-self.

Regarding the first [of these], there are four points: first, arising from its own seed while also depending on other conditions; second, arising from others while also depending on itself; third, both [arising] from that which lacks functional activity; fourth, the nature of these two causes is not non-existent. These four meanings correspond to the previous section’s statement that because it is merely through causes and conditions that things arise, there is no agent who causes them to arise.

Fifth, although they have no beginning, their characteristics are established and yet they perish moment by moment; sixth, although they perish moment by moment, they appear to remain stable—these two [aspects] are both spontaneously extinguished as before, and there is no agent of extinction.

Regarding the single meaning based on suffering: because it has the single flavor of the characteristic of suffering yet appears as if it had three characteristics, it is summarized as the "tree of suffering.

Regarding the single meaning based on emptiness: this refers to being free from sentient beings, agents, and experiencers; yet, while appearing as if not separate from them, it is presently without action and without experience.
Regarding the two meanings based on selflessness: first, although in reality there is no self, a semblance of a self appears; this refers to the present absence of "self" and "mine.

Second, although according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) it is inexpressible, one speaks of the expressibility of the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all phenomena; this refers to the scriptural passage beginning with "Again, he thinks... and so forth.
The ten meanings are complete, because all preceding conditions and characteristics are merely semblances of meaning.

In the contemplation of reversal, one directly reveals that the true nature and characteristics are non-obstructive; therefore, the profound contemplation of dependent origination resides precisely here.
Furthermore, the absence of an agent and an action reveals that [phenomena] arise dependently and are not created by gods or humans;
for whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, they abide in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti), and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
This single contemplation is already extremely profound; how much more so when the latter two are added.

Regarding the second point, the contemplation that accords with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), among the four contemplations, this first gate corresponds to the first: the contemplation of delusion and inversion (*moha-viparyāsa*).
The general commentary on the treatise states: "Because one contemplates this matter—the delusion and inversion regarding whatever object of attachment.
This means that the twelve links of dependent origination are the objects of attachment.

The passage beginning with "Deluded regarding the nature and characteristics, erroneously grasping at 'mine'" provides a detailed explanation of the meaning. It clarifies that ignorance establishes two types of inversion according to what it is deluded about:

first, from the beginning up to "there is no place of arising," it clarifies that one is deluded regarding the selflessness of dependent origination, and by grasping at a self, one forms an inversion.
Because of attachment to a self, the world arises; thus, this [attachment] is clearly an inversion.
If one were free from this attachment, there would be no place for arising; conversely, this demonstrates that such attachment must necessarily be an inversion.

Second, from "Furthermore, he acts" down to the end of the first section, one gate clarifies the conditions for the characteristics of delusion, which give rise to doubt and inversion. This means that because of a lack of wisdom, one constantly seeks after existence and non-existence, becoming stuck in the two paths of annihilationism and eternalism; therefore, it is called "doubt."
The continuity of the characteristics of conditions is clarified as being inverted;

causing the Bodhisattva to accord with the ignorant and inverted affairs of those sentient beings and to give rise to compassionate observation is called the "contemplation of affairs" (vastu-vipaśyanā).
Third, regarding the contemplation of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*):

among the nine types of contemplation, this section encompasses the entirety of the first contemplation and half of the second. That is to say, the two passages concerning the initial establishment of the answer are termed the "contemplation of the distinction between defilement and purity. This has two meanings:
first, attachment to a self is defilement, while being free from a self is purity; [the second meaning follows].
Second, because of attachment to a self, the arising of conditioned marks (*nimitta*) constitutes defilement; because of detachment from a self, the cessation of conditioned marks constitutes purity.

The subsequent passage of the *Lakṣaṇasūtra* belongs to the second [section], that on the basis of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). This means that although one relies upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), if one does not know it, various conditions (*pratyaya*) arise, which constitutes the basis of defilement;
when one perceives the ultimate truth, those conditions cease, which then constitutes the basis of purity.

Because one does not know [the truth] while contemplating characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they become the conditions for characteristics; because one does not know while contemplating great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), it becomes a perversion (*viparyāsa*).
Nevertheless, although this single gateway of continuous succession has no division in the scriptural text, it is divided into three according to its meaning:
first, clarifying that the arising of delusive perversions is conditioned by the fact that, in reality, there is no self, thereby accomplishing the contemplation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Next, one follows the objects of delusive inversion to accomplish the contemplation of the knowledge of aspects (*ākārajñatā*);

subsequently, one thoroughly investigates the nature and characteristics of affliction and purification regarding understanding and delusion to accomplish the contemplation of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Furthermore, the first [contemplation] accords with the fundamental [wisdom], the second accords with the subsequently attained wisdom, and the last is unimpeded; although there is no sense of "mine," the characteristics are not destroyed.
One gives rise to great compassion, wherein subject and object are fundamentally empty;
through compassion that is free from attachment, one thoroughly investigates both nature and characteristics, remaining unimpeded regarding self and other.
When the three contemplations are unified within a single mind to form unimpeded wisdom, how could the profound *prajñā* not manifest before one?
If even one gate is thus, how much more so when the remaining nine are added.

Section Two: The Gate of Being Subsumed within the Single Mind. Now, this gate contains many meanings and shall be divided into two parts:

First, the section on "tracing the derivative back to the fundamental gate"; second, from "The Tathāgata herein" onwards, the section on the mutual support of the fundamental and the derivative. Regarding the first:

according to the three contemplations of the *Śāstra*, this first part concerns the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasatya*), which corresponds to the second contemplation, that of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* raises the question: "What is the distinction regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
It is because by thus realizing the ultimate truth, one attains liberation through that contemplation.
This clarifies the purpose of cultivating contemplation.

Since the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), one who perceives this nature of conditions is liberated from the bonds of conditions; therefore, one cultivates that contemplation.

Although the treatise and the sūtra both state that "all are produced through mental attention (*manasikāra*)," they take the capacity to produce a single mind as the primary factor; hence, it is called the "contemplation of the ultimate truth."
The treatise states: "It is simply the one mind" because all three realms are merely the transformation of mind.
This statement is general in scope.
"Transformation" (pariṇāma) carries the meaning of arising and activity, as well as the meaning of transmutation.
However, this single passage is cited by various teachings alike as proof that all is but mind-only (*cittamātra*).
How does a single mind produce the three realms?
Briefly, there are three meanings:
Those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) maintain that external objects exist as real entities and do not realize that they are merely mind.

Even if they hear of the "one mind," they regard it only as the single ultimate truth, or they claim that while things arise through the transformation of the mind, they are not all exclusively mind itself.
Second, the *ālayavijñāna* of maturation is called "one mind," because it is taught as one mind to distinguish it from the absence of external objects.
Third, the intrinsically pure one mind of the *tathāgatagarbha*, because in principle there is no duality of essence, it is called one mind.
Regarding this first single mind, the Bodhisattva does not perform this contemplation.

As for the latter two single minds, the intent of the sutra clearly indicates that they apply to all three contemplations: taking the pure single mind as the first contemplation, and applying these two minds [together] as the latter two contemplations.
The latter two [teachings] regarding the single mind are summarized as in the *Wenming* (Exposition of Questions); their detailed exposition comprises ten sections.
The first section provisionally posits a "single mind," asserting that while external phenomena truly exist, they are merely manifestations resulting from the fluctuations of the mind.
The nine gates described below are in reality nothing other than the single mind.

Because both the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) and the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) coexist, they are spoken of as "one mind. This encompasses all eight consciousnesses along with their associated mental factors (*caitta*), including the transformed objective aspects and their corresponding original images, all fully present.

Due to the power of the perfuming of the members of dependent origination (*bhavāṅga*) and so forth, the retributive fruits of the triple world—both the environment and its inhabitants—are manifested, as explained in detail in various treatises such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Because the three [aspects] are subsumed within the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), they are said to be "one mind. This also applies to the sovereign consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) and its mental factors (*caitta*); however, the transformed object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) does not arise from separate seeds. Rather, the perceiving consciousness arises carrying the image of that object. This meaning is fully explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*.

Because the four types of grasping are subsumed within the sovereign mind (*citta*), it is said to be "one mind"; this applies exclusively to the eight consciousnesses. This is because those mental factors (*caitta*) lack an independent substance, as they too are transformations of that sovereign mind, as stated in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.

Fifth, because the derivative returns to the root, it is taught as "one mind. This means that the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are all merely differentiated functions of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), having no separate substance.

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The ocean of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) abides eternally; moved by the winds of objective spheres, the various waves of consciousness surge forth and arise in succession."
It further states: "For example, as in the vast ocean waves, there are no distinct characteristics; so it is with the various consciousnesses and the mind—difference cannot be found.

Since it says that apart from water there are no separate waves, it clarifies that apart from the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna), there are no separate [entities] for the preceding seven consciousnesses.

Because the six [consciousnesses] are subsumed within their characteristics and traced back to their fundamental nature, they are said to be the "one mind. This means that these eight consciousnesses all lack intrinsic substance; they are merely the manifestation of the Tathāgatagarbha in its state of equality, wherein all other secondary characteristics are exhausted.
The Sūtra says, "All sentient beings are themselves the mark of nirvāṇa," and so forth.
The *Laṅkāvatāra* says, "There are eight unchanging marks; even the markless is itself markless."
There are many such passages that serve as authentic evidence.

Because the seven natures and their characteristics are both fused, it is called "one mind. This means that while the Tathāgatagarbha, in its entirety, follows conditions to accomplish all phenomena, its own nature is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing. Thus, principle and phenomena are thoroughly fused and unimpeded; for this reason, the one mind and the two truths are both free from obstruction.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Based on the dharma of the one mind, there are two gates, which are not mutually separated.
Furthermore, the *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* states: "The Buddha taught that the Tathāgatagarbha is the ālayavijñāna," as well as the analogy of gold and a ring, and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "The intrinsically pure mind is undefiled yet defiled, which is difficult to comprehend;
it is defiled yet undefiled, which is likewise difficult to comprehend."

All are clearly understood as follows: when the intrinsically pure nature follows defilement such that its entire substance becomes the conventional, this is the Gate of Arising and Ceasing; when the defiled nature is eternally pure and fundamentally true purity, this is the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Thus, defilement which is identical to purity does not obstruct the True while remaining perpetually conventional; purity which is identical to defilement does not destroy the conventional while remaining perpetually True. Therefore, without obstructing the One Mind, the Two Truths coexist—this is profoundly worthy of deep reflection.

Eighth, because phenomena interpenetrate through their fusion, it is called "one mind. This means that because the nature of mind is perfectly interfused and unimpeded, the nature gives rise to phenomena, and phenomena likewise melt together without mutual obstruction.

Entering into one, one understands the equality of the immeasurable within that one; within each and every atom, one perceives the entire dharma-realm, wherein devas, humans, and asuras do not exist apart from a single atom.
These passages are not singular.

Ninth, because phenomena and their characteristics are identical, it is said that they are one mind. This means that the phenomena based upon the nature are not distinct from the nature itself; since the mind-nature has no distinction between self and other, all phenomena are likewise identical to the one.
The preceding text states: "One is many, and many are one," and so forth.

Because the tenfold Indra-net is unimpeded, it is described as the "one mind. This means that within one there is all, and within all there is again all, in infinite layers without end; this is because the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is consciousness, is perfectly interfused and inexhaustible.

Regarding these ten gates above: the first one pertains to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna); the next three involve the provisional (upāya); the next three pertain to the ultimate reality; and the final three concern the unique [teachings] of the Perfect Middle Way.
If these are applied downward to accord with the various vehicles, all ten are universally unimpeded.
This major section is not limited to this single chapter alone; the contemplations formed according to each individual gate differ, and these may be sought through emptiness.
Second is the Gate of the Basis and Support of the Fundamental and the Branches.
From here below, ending with the ten gates, all are distinctions of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Since the characteristics of conditions are fundamentally quiescent, one should only contemplate the ultimate reality (*tattva*); why then further contemplate the distinctions of conventional truth?
The Treatise states: "By observing the conventional truth in accordance with reality, one immediately enters the ultimate truth.
Thus, the conventional serves as the means for elucidating the ultimate; only by realizing that the conventional lacks intrinsic nature does one truly perceive the ultimate.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If one does not know conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one cannot attain ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This contemplation has six aspects:
first, the contemplation of what constitutes defilement and its basis, which simultaneously examines both the dependent and the basis, encompassing this half-gate.
Second is the contemplation of causes, which, because it contemplates the causes of defilement, subsumes the following two gates.
Third is the contemplation of the inclusion of faults, as it pertains solely to suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*).
Fourth is the contemplation of guarding against faults, as it guards against the false views of ordinary beings.
Fifth is the contemplation of non-disgust, which serves to prevent minor conceit.
The first three [contemplations] each encompass one gate in their respective order.
Sixth is profound contemplation, which reveals the subtle principle of dependent origination by transcending emotional grasping.
This summarizes the latter three gates.

Among the six, the first two establish the characteristics of defilement; the next one examines the faults from the perspective of defilement; the following two correctly observe and prevent transgressions; and the final one represents the ultimate depth of contemplative practice.

Now, this "half-gate" refers to the contemplation based on defilement; because the factors of dependent origination are defiled, and because this basis for defilement relies upon the one mind, the Treatise states: "This is the distinction between the two truths."

"Because pure truth does not arise alone and delusion cannot be established by itself, the truth of the one mind and the conventionality of defilement—these two—in their union constitute the collection of causes and conditions.
This passage from the Sūtra has three parts;
the first is the general summary, which means that based on the one mind, the twelve [links] are distinguished, and thus the twelve are sustained by the one mind.
The specific mention of "the Tathāgata says" is because [this teaching] is suddenly and fully possessed within a single mind, something that no one other than a Buddha could know.
It is said to manifest that the Tathāgata’s past awakening of the nature of conditions has arisen in continuous succession, being transmitted from one to another.
The subsequent inquiry states:
"The twelve links of existence (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) are arranged across the three periods of time, arising through mutual succession and induction.
Why, then, is it now said that they all depend upon the single mind?"

In later commentaries on the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, there is no distinct interpretation; the various masters of antiquity merely state that apart from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), nothing at all can be established.

Their explanation of the characteristics [of this consciousness] as persisting through births and transcending worlds, while not failing to preserve the sense of it being the basis and support, has nonetheless failed to capture the intended meaning.
Now, it is said that the Teacher skillfully demonstrates that not only are the three periods of time inseparable from the true mind;

now, a single thought-moment suddenly possesses all twelve [links], further manifesting that the preceding and succeeding moments are inseparable from the one mind. This is identical to the explanation of the twelve links of dependent origination within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) found in the ninth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Therefore, this single section contains multiple types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):
it includes the two kinds of dependent origination from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Its second [section] states: "If explained briefly, there are two kinds of dependent origination:"
"First, the dependent origination of the discrimination of self-nature refers to the arising of all phenomena based on the *ālayavijñāna*"; this refers to the present "single mind as the support.

"Second, the dependent origination of the discrimination of the agreeable and disagreeable refers to the twelve links of dependent origination; because they serve as the causal nature for various individual existences that can discriminate between the agreeable and disagreeable within the good and evil realms of rebirth," this encompasses both the current commentary and the nine preceding sections.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter nine, explains four types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):
first, momentary (*kṣaṇika*); second, continuous (*sāmbandhika*); third, situational (*āvasthika*); and fourth, remote (*prākarṣika*).
The latter three [sections] pass over the remaining nine gates; here, the first one alone is appropriate.
It says: "What is a moment (*kṣaṇa*)?
It refers to the duration of a moment during which, due to greed, one commits killing and so forth, possessing all twelve [factors]."

The detailed explanation of their characteristics is largely identical to this; therefore, it is not necessary here to follow the sequence. The intention is to reveal that a single mind is suddenly endowed with all [factors].
Regarding "craving for objects arising together with the mind," this refers collectively to the objects being engaged.

The objects of craving are not singular; taking any one such object, within a single moment of thought, all twelve links are present. This is because the performance of this act of craving necessarily arises dependent upon the mind, and furthermore, it involves the discernment of the preceding object; thus, the mind constitutes the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding "the object is the activity": the object of craving is itself the activity of mental karma (*manas-karman*); if it manifests through body or speech, it is likewise twofold activity.
Not knowing that the fault of craving can bring about suffering is called being deluded regarding activity.
Regarding "name-and-form arises together with ignorance and mind": name-and-form is the totality that serves as the basis for these two; thus, "name" arises together [with them].
Therefore, the Jin translation states: "Because the locus upon which consciousness relies constitutes name-and-form."
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The three aggregates co-arising with consciousness are collectively termed 'name-and-form' (*nāmarūpa*).
This is intended to clarify that the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is itself the limb of feeling (*vedanā-aṅga*).

Regarding the statement that "the growth of name-and-form constitutes the six sense bases": when the five consciousnesses have not yet arisen, there are only the ten elements (*dhātus*); once the five consciousnesses arise based upon them, they are called the ten bases (*āyatanas*).
The manifestation of the characteristics of the support for consciousness is precisely what is meant by "growth"; thus, the term "growth" should be translated as "manifestation."

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "That which abides in name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is called the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana). This means that while the six faculties are distinct, they are established as six by distinguishing them from their common basis; thus, they are said to "abide in name-and-form."
Craving necessarily has an object as its contact; feeling necessarily experiences contact. Craving is itself attachment, which is termed "insatiability regarding feeling.

The grasping that involves not relinquishing what one craves constitutes the "grasping for sense-pleasures" (*kāmopādāna*). Because craving and grasping moisten the preceding six links, they form "becoming" (*bhava*).
However, the arising of the preceding factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) is precisely the meaning of "existence" (*bhava*).
That which arises is the emergence of those aforementioned phenomena; this is the meaning of "birth" (*jāti*).
That which has matured through birth is "aging" (*jarā*), because as soon as a thing is born, it undergoes change.
That which decays and perishes is what is called "death," because it ceases moment by moment.

Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna, it is because its own characteristic is subject to destruction; as the Sūtra says: "That which arises is immediately extinguished; this is not taught to the foolish."
If this is not severed, it is called "continuous bondage.
The five aggregates at each stage of the twelve links are all termed "stages" (*avasthā*).
This very sequence, which follows on from the past and has existed since beginningless time, is called "distant continuity."
The reasoning regarding the large and small [vehicles] is generally consistent; the difference lies merely in the six versus eight consciousnesses.
If this were not the authoritative measure of the holy teachings (*āgama*), who would believe such a principle?
That the author of the treatise did not understand it seems almost like an oversight.

This text precisely analyzes the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) as being simultaneous and distinct in nature. If they were simultaneous and identical in nature, they would likewise possess all twelve links:

delusion regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is itself ignorance (*avidyā*); the presence of outflows and grasping is termed formative action (*saṃskāra*); its substance is consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is also name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); its engagement with objects through the sense bases is contact (*sparśa*); the experiencing of objects is feeling (*vedanā*); the defiling of objects is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); the attachment to objects is grasping (*upādāna*); the summoning of retribution is becoming (*bhava*); the manifestation of the body is birth (*jāti*); and its transformation and cessation is aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Based on these twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), when explained in terms of time, there are generally six types.

First, the twelve links are explained according to five periods: namely, past ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, these arise from past-past afflictions (*kleśa*); thus, afflictions give rise to delusion and karma.
If two past causes produce five present fruits, then afflictions and karma give rise to suffering.
If the present produces the future, and the future further produces the future, then suffering gives rise to further suffering.

These five are provisionally established by inferring causes and examining effects based on the three periods of time; they do not refer to a sequential progression, nor do they fall into infinite regress.

The second [classification] relies on the three periods of time, the third on two periods of time, and the fourth on one period of time; their anterior and posterior arrangements are all explained as analyzed in the first section.
Fifth, simultaneous difference of substance; sixth, simultaneous identity of substance—this is as stated in this very text.

Second, regarding the contemplation in accordance with great compassion, it corresponds to the second [point]: seeking liberation elsewhere. This refers to the delusion and perversion of ordinary beings, who constantly seek liberation from elsewhere—in the *ālayavijñāna* and the *ādānavijñāna*, as well as from elsewhere in terms of "self" and "what belongs to self."

Since the sutra clarifies that there is only the single mind, there is no self or phenomena outside of the mind; one should seek them within this single mind. This is likewise like the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which states: "The liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings."

Regarding the term *ālaya*, this is translated as the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*). It is so called because it can store all factors belonging to the category of defilement so that they are not lost, and because it is grasped and stored as one's own internal self by means of self-view, self-love, and the like.
This name applies only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*).
As for *ādāna*, it is translated here as "grasping" or "sustaining," because it grasps and sustains the seeds and the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*);
this name applies to all stages.

These two are alternative names for the mind; since the master of the treatise intends to clarify that the mind encompasses both defilement and purity, he cites both names together to explain the meaning of the single mind.
What is the meaning of "seeking"?
If there is grasping at a self, it constitutes the *ālaya*; if grasping at a self ceases, one abandons the name "ālaya.
When only the *ādāna* holds the untainted seeds, the deluded mind is extinguished and the true mind manifests.
Therefore, the following verse states: "If the mind is extinguished, birth and death are exhausted. This refers to the extinction of delusion, not the extinction of the essence of the mind.

Third, regarding the contemplation of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), this corresponds to the second reliance on contemplation; it clarifies that this dependent origination relies upon two types:
first, reliance on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), as already explained above.
The second [type of] reliance on mind-consciousness is precisely what is presented in the current text.
While the former refers exclusively to the pure, this one encompasses both the defiled and the pure; the meaning of "reliance" is as explained previously.
Furthermore, while the former describes the arising of delusion based upon the True, this one clarifies that delusion relies upon the True.
Within the third section, "Assisting through One's Own Karma," there are also three parts.
First, regarding the contemplation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the following two gates correspond to the contemplation of causes (*hetu*).
There are two types of contemplation of causes:
First, the contemplation of external causes; second, the contemplation of internal causes.
Master Huiyuan said:
"Because the practice differs from ignorance, it is termed an external cause."
The arising of subsequent ignorance from preceding ignorance is called its "own cause" (*svahetu*).
The "other cause" (*parahetu*) is of minor relevance, whereas the own cause presents a difficulty.

For the treatise states: "Regarding the observation of the own cause, there is no subsequent member apart from the preceding member," and the Sūtra says: "With ignorance as a condition, volitional formations arise."

Now, regarding what is called "other-causality" (paratantra-hetu), it refers entirely to the arising of subsequent factors depending upon preceding factors; this serves to exclude intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Within the contemplation of great compassion, one excludes the primordial essence (prakṛti); the contemplation of all marks is termed "skillful means" (upāya).

Because volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise solely from ignorance (*avidyā*), it is called their "own cause" (*svahetu*); this distinguishes them from other causes that could produce such formations.
It is just as curd is invariably produced from milk and does not emerge from stone.

The Great Compassion Contemplation refutes causes such as Īśvara and others, because the Knowledge of All Aspects (sarvākārajñatā) reveals the characteristics of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Although the intended meanings of these three contemplations differ slightly, their textual purports are largely the same; thus, various masters who do not seek out the original treatises have erroneously provided divergent interpretations.
This present section concerns the contemplation of the causes of others.
The Sūtra clarifies that each has two functions: first, its own function, and second, its auxiliary function.

Yet, they are both referred to as "others" because it is specifically due to ignorance being deluded regarding the object-condition (*ālambana*) that it becomes the cause for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); if one were to fully understand the object-condition, how could false formations ever arise?
Furthermore, the first [link] clarifies one's own karma, thereby manifesting the meaning of being "other";
the second clarifies subsequent birth, thereby manifesting the meaning of being a "cause.
The remaining eleven links should be understood by analogy in this manner.

However, the cause of arising is precisely the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); since "condition" (*pratyaya*) is used as a synonym for "cause," this is stated according to its general meaning, because among the four conditions, the relationship of dominance exists with certainty when the various members are viewed in relation to one another.

In the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* and in this text, only one [condition] is explicitly clarified; as for the other three conditions, their presence or absence is not fixed, and thus they are omitted here.

That is to say, with respect to *upādāna* (clinging) and *bhava* (existence), there is the sense of being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for *tṛṣṇā* (craving) and *vijñāna* (consciousness), because craving increases into clinging and consciousness increases into existence.

If it is said that the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the seed of karma, then volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) also act as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for consciousness; however, there is no sense of being a causal condition among the other links relative to one another.

As for the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* stating that ignorance (*avidyā*) is a causal condition for volitional formations, this is said because ignorance is associated with the karmic latencies (*vāsanā*) at the time of ignorance; thus, ignorance is metaphorically designated [as the cause], whereas in reality it is the seed of volitional formations.

When the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the various members [of dependent origination] lack the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) when viewed in relation to one another, this is based on the teaching that craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) consist solely of karma.

Regarding the mutual relationship between the four higher stages, it is clarified that they possess the causal condition; among these, the first two are actual, the next one is indeterminate, and the final one is a provisional designation.
