Third, the Attainment of Superior Practice, which has two parts: first, clarifying the superiority of profound practice, which is presented as emerging from what precedes;
second, from “O Son of the Buddha, in this stage the Bodhisattva... onwards, clarifying the superiority of the arousal [of resolve], which is presented as entering into what follows.
The preceding section also subsumes the stage of the Youthful (kumārabhūmi).
This passage consists of two parts:

first, concluding the previous section and introducing the subsequent one. The entry into the eighth stage constitutes the conclusion of the preceding entry into the stages, as it serves as the basis for the profound practices that follow.
Second, from "for the sake of profound practice" onwards, the profound practice itself is correctly revealed; first by means of the Dharma, and subsequently by means of a simile.
Within the section on the Dharma, there are eight phrases:
the first is a general characteristic, because the stages and practices are profound and mysterious.
The remaining seven distinct characteristics are as follows:
First, "difficult to know" refers to the difficulty of entering the profound; this specifically highlights its distinction from the lower stages.

Second, "without differentiation" refers to the profundity of shared practice; because it is identical to the various bodhisattvas of the untainted pure stages, it is difficult to discern any difference, just as barley within a heap of barley.

Third, the phrase "free from all" indicates that the objective realm is profound, because its boundaries are transcendent; this is due to the departure from the characteristics of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the non-manifestation of the characteristics of the grasper (*grāhaka*).
Furthermore, it is said that "being free from all attachments" refers to guarding against the conceptualizations of all obstacles to be remedied on this stage.
The four immeasurables are "boundless" because their cultivation is profound; self-benefit is without limit, and benefit for others is boundless.
The "fivefold all-equality" clarifies the depth of non-retrogression, for the two vehicles cannot destroy its supremacy.
While the preceding phrase should be distinguished by its specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), this phrase clarifies it by means of contrast.
Sixth, being free from all clamor and contention, which is the profundity of being free from hindrances; that is, because one is free from the hindrance of effortful application (*prayoga*).
Seventh, the manifestation of quiescent extinction, which is the profundity of the manifestation of the remedy; for by realizing *tathatā* as the remedy, all things are extinguished.

Within the seven specific [stages] above, they are grouped into three parts according to their characteristics. These enable one to abandon the four kinds of afflictions and hindrances of the preceding stages: First, the three [stages] clarify that the objective realms of this ground are exceptionally distinct, thereby abandoning the fourth hindrance—the subtle fault of conceptualization and mental formations—namely, the failure to cease the seeking of Tathāgata-knowledge;

Next, the two [stages] clarify the vastness of correct practice, thereby abandoning the third hindrance—the fault of diligent application toward emanated births—namely, the persistence of effort in practices such as the ten immeasurables;
Finally, the two [stages] clarify the tranquil cessation that is free from obstacles, thereby abandoning the first two hindrances.

First, it is free from the fault of lacking diligent application on the second pure stage; that is, one previously cultivated effortless practice, constantly practicing day and night, and giving rise to the Path during all activities—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
Second, it is free from the fault of intermittent effort characteristic of the first [stage] of existence.
These four faults are as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, they are termed the "four calamities," and their sequence of meaning is likewise the same.

In the second analogy, there are three similes; they follow the order from last to first to correspond with the preceding three sections. This is because, in accordance with the treatment of obstacles, one proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, whereas within the Dharma itself, the profound is revealed by proceeding from the coarse to the subtle.
Each of the three [categories] contains both an analogy and its application.
Here, first is the analogy for the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), which serves as an analogy for the previously mentioned "freedom from hindrances.

Within the analogy of "quiescent extinction" (*śānta-nirvāṇa*), many who have attained the liberation of mind—namely *anāgāmins* and *arhats*—are able to enter it; as it constitutes the ninth among the nine successive absorptions (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpattayaḥ*), the text says "up to and including" (*yāvat*).

"Movement of the mind ceases" means that the six or seven mental kings (*cittarāja*), which serve as the basis, have already ceased, and thus the mental factors (*caitta*) dependent upon them—such as recollection and conceptualization—spontaneously vanish.
Abiding immovably within this state of union, one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
"Immediately relinquishing" and below correspond to the cessation of the moving mind.
"One who immediately relinquishes all functional effort" has transcended that which is to be remedied.
"Attaining the state of non-functional effort" clarifies that one has attained the remedial dharma.

Regarding the cessation of body, speech, and so forth: because one has attained the practice of effortlessness (*anābhoga*) which proceeds spontaneously, it is identical to the aforementioned state of non-attachment; thus, one is free from the fault of intermittent arising in the practice that transcends the "summit of existence" (*bhavāgra*).
Regarding the phrase "dwelling in the practice of fruition" (*vipākacaryā*), the text contains two meanings:

first, it also establishes the aforementioned manifestation of a state contrary to effortful practice (*sābhisaṃskāracaryā*), namely, because one has attained the stage of effortless mastery (*anabhisaṃskārabhūmi*).
This refers to the path of teaching (*śāsanamārga*), which, like the previous [stage], is free from grasping and attachment.

Second, it means being well-established within the *tathatā* (suchness) of the *ālayavijñāna*; this refers to the path of realization (*adhigamamārga*), which, like the previous [stage], enters into the nature of all phenomena as being like space, thereby departing from the fault of exerting effortful skillful means on the second pure stage (*śuddhabhūmi*).
Because it differs from the preceding stages in that cultivation is now effortless (*anābhoga*), it is called "fruition-conduct" (*vipākacaryā*).
Regarding "fruition-conduct," this refers to what was cultivated in the preceding stages now manifesting as the fruition has matured.
As for "abiding in *tathatā*," this is because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) possesses two aspects:
The first is the defiled portion, wherein ordinary beings abide;
the second is the truly pure portion, wherein this stage abides.
Because one abides in suchness, the name "ālaya" is relinquished.
Furthermore, while the stage of Buddhahood abides solely in *tathatā* (suchness), it is not said to abide in the *ālaya-tathatā*;

this is because the retribution of transformation (*pariṇāma-vipāka*) still persists there. Therefore, both are mentioned together: the term "ālaya" refers to the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*), whereas the Tathāgata is designated as the stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*).
The second metaphor, that of awakening from a dream, illustrates the vastness of the preceding correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*).
The treatise states: "To demonstrate that this practice guards against the notion of faults [in others] means that it is free from the faults of exerting effort through artificial means."
One who possesses the perception of right knowledge does not lack this stage, because there is no absence of the wisdom of accomplishment.
It is like awakening from a dream: although the dream-perception is absent, it is not that the perception of waking is absent.
However, because this practice is quiescent, it is said that "all that is to be done has ceased.
Within the synthesis, "courage" refers to the mind and "diligence" refers to practice; these, along with the aforementioned "skillful means," are all functional efforts.
The passage beginning with "the two modes of activity" (*dvividhā caryā*) below sets forth the obstacles that are stilled.
Based on the purity of internal realization, the two mentalities of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa do not function; this is termed "the non-manifestation of the two modes of activity."

Just as when one awakens, there is no dependence on this shore or the other shore; because the mental engagement with external conditions, objects, and enjoyments does not function, it is said that "characteristics and activities do not appear," which means one is detached from conceptualizations such as those regarding transformation-birth or the noble path.
Just as upon waking, neither the person nor the boat exists;

so too, in the analogy of seeing a person fall into a river during a state of meditative union, the body falling of its own accord signifies that the illness of sentient beings is itself the illness of the Bodhisattva.
The third analogy, that of being born in the Brahma Heaven, illustrates the extreme distinction of the objective realm.
Within the section on "correspondence," the first part correctly corresponds to the lower realms:
the non-manifestation of mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) corresponds to the non-occurrence of the mental states of the desire realm.
The reason one does not practice [the former] is that one has attained the practice of retribution (*vipāka-caryā*).
Because this is free from the fault of subtle conceptualization and activity, the treatise states: "This is called the excellence of detachment."
Below the passage beginning with "This bodhisattva," the superior is used as a standard to illustrate the inferior:

it means that even a single moment of mind that does not conform to the ways of the world is not present in Buddhas and others, let alone a single moment of mind that conforms to the ways of the world.
"The Buddha-mind being equal" refers to the mind that seeks the wisdom of the Tathāgata in the seventh stage.
Here, it merely uses the mundane as an illustration; one should likewise use the great to illustrate the small—if even the great do not practice it, how much less so the Small Vehicle?
Thus, whether mundane or supramundane, whether persons or phenomena, whether causes or fruits, whether wisdom or abandonment—none of these are practiced.
Second, the excellence of the initiation of practice is clarified.
The following section also subsumes the causes for the practice of respect, as it exhorts one to initiate practice with a sense of reverence.
"Superiority" also carries the meaning of being respected.
This passage consists of four parts:

First, the proponent provides a general summary; second, from "acts in this way" onwards, he explicitly presents the words of exhortation; third, from "O Son of the Buddha, all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones" onwards, he reveals the purpose for which the exhortation is made; fourth, from "O Son of the Buddha, if all Buddhas" onwards, he demonstrates the benefits of the exhortation.

Now, the first vow is precisely the cause of exhortation; as in the third section on exhortation, when the treatise says, "because one abides by the power of the original vow," the phrasing is incomplete and should rather be stated as, "because one abides by the power of the original vow."
The phrase "All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones" below generally reveals the aspect of exhortation.
The reason the Buddhas provide this exhortation of wisdom is to transform that mind which delights in profound practice and contentment, causing it to enter the gateway of the stream of Dharma.

As for the "flow of the Dharma," it breaks through the stagnant waters of non-arising and causes the river of effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) to arise, spontaneously proceeding toward the ocean of Buddha-wisdom; thus, that which enables this progression serves as the gate.
Furthermore, the "flow of the Dharma" is the ocean of practice.
Regarding the phrase "bestowing upon the wise," there are two meanings:
first, manifesting it to their awakening-mind, which is like that [Buddha's] mental empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Second, because it causes one to initiate the practice of grasping [the Dharma], it is called "bestowing.
The seven subsequent exhortations are all subsumed within Buddha-wisdom; therefore, they are simply referred to as "bestowing wisdom.

Since this patience (*kṣānti*) was not yet purified in the preceding stage, it is only now bestowed. Because one attains this patience which encompasses the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*), once it has been bestowed, one no longer wishes to sink back into [lower states].
The second section, which clearly presents the words of exhortation, contains two parts:
first, the praise, which follows the principle that "one who intends to take must first firmly give";
second, the exhortation beginning with the words, "Furthermore, good son."

Within this, there are seven [sections]: first, exhorting the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of skillful guidance; second, exhorting compassion for sentient beings; third, exhorting the fulfillment of one's original vows; fourth, exhorting the pursuit of unimpeded wisdom; fifth, exhorting the attainment of the Buddha’s external retribution; sixth, exhorting the realization of the Buddha’s internal illumination and immeasurable superior practices; and seventh, exhorting the comprehensive cultivation without omission to achieve the knowledge of all paths.
Master Yuanfang subsumes these seven into two categories:
the first six illustrate those who have mostly not yet acted, thereby transforming their mind of abiding;
the latter one clarifies those who have already acted to some extent, showing how they can achieve the increase of their mind of departure.
This passage does not appear in the Sūtra, yet it seems to have a basis in the Śāstra and does not contradict the underlying principle.
Now, these are subsumed into three categories:

the first three exhort him toward downward transformation (*adhaḥ-pariṇāmanā*); of these, the first concerns the method of transformation, the second is the actual transformation, and the third is the vow for transformation.

Next, three [verses] exhort him to seek the higher; the first refutes that what he has attained is not supreme, while the latter two lead him toward seeking the supreme fruit of Buddhahood, whether external or internal.
The final one of the three summarizes the various approaches collectively, because the practices to be performed are boundless and would be difficult to exhaust through individual explanation.
However, all seven [stages] contain the aspects of turning, abiding, increasing, and departing.
Now, for the first [stage], there are three points:
first, it clarifies that much remains to be done, because one has not yet attained the ten powers or the methods for instructing sentient beings.
Second, from "You should" onwards, he exhorts them to practice;
third, from "Do not again" onwards, he instructs them not to abandon the gate of patience. Furthermore, there are two meanings to "abandoning":
[the first is to give up the practice, and the second is to give up the patience itself].
First, if one were to dwell in this gate of patience by abandoning the body and mind, this would be improper; therefore, it says "do not do so again.
Thus, the Treatise states: "If one does not relinquish this practice of patience, one will not achieve all the Buddha-dharmas."
This is intended to cause one to abandon attachment.
Since it is improper to completely discard [the practice], the treatise states: "Because it relies on that power to act, one must not again let it go."
This causes one to rely upon it.
In the second exhortation, there are three parts:
first, clarifying the patience attained by oneself; second, from "However, all... onwards, clarifying the faults arising when others lack patience.
Those who live at home have many afflictions (*kleśa*), while those who have left the home life have much discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); both are matters of no benefit to sentient beings.
Third, from the words "You should... onwards, there is an exhortation to arouse compassion; this compassionate mind proceeds based upon the aforementioned [realization].
In the third exhortation, there are two kinds of vows:
first, "relying on the expansive mind" to transform sentient beings through downward engagement; second, "causing all to attain" and so forth, relying on the great mind.
However, there are two meanings:
first, causing others to attain it; second, causing oneself to attain it.
By attaining the Buddha’s wisdom for oneself, one can extensively benefit others by acting in reliance upon this wisdom.
The fourth exhortation has three parts:
first, the true permanence of the *dharmatā* establishes what is to be esteemed;
next, from "All Buddhas" onwards, it refutes the notion of being distinct from the Buddha and exhorts one to seek the supreme goal.
Because he possesses profound and unimpeded wisdom, his great functioning is boundless; it is only thus that he is not shared with the two vehicles.
The subsequent section beginning with "all" suppresses the tendency to equate him with the two vehicles, ensuring that they do not abide in their patience.
The three animals crossing the river share the same engagement with principle (*tattva*).
Since the exhaustion of effortful practice leads to the defilement of seeking quiescence (*śānti*), one should not abide therein.
In the fifth exhortation, the six aspects beginning with the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are cited; these are all the activities of transformational birth (*nirmāṇopapatti*).
If one accomplishes this dharma, one possesses the power to manifest through transformation; therefore, one is exhorted to practice for its accomplishment.
Within the sixth exhortation, there are three parts:
first, clarifying that what has been attained is not yet extensive; second, from "Good son" onwards, demonstrating the Buddha’s immeasurable and superior practices.
"Immeasurable entries" refers to the distinctions among the dharma-gates entered.
"Acting" refers to the functional activity of these dharma-gates.
"Transforming" refers to the uninterrupted progression of this functional activity to ever-higher levels.
The subsequent section, beginning with "You should," concludes with an exhortation.
Within this seventh exhortation, there are two parts:
first, it cites three kinds of immeasurables, which are the three practices of mastery within the Pure Land; [the second part follows].
The subsequent section, beginning with "all should," concludes the exhortation, clarifying that even a small amount of practice suffices.
Since it states that one "should all attain thorough penetration," it clarifies that through even a partial observation, one can achieve success; thus, one is not far from Buddhahood.
This is because the Bodhisattva Sagaramati exhorts Sudhana not to become complacent with minor practices; therefore, it is said to be "immeasurable.
Third, this reveals the purpose of the exhortation: to cause the arising of the activity of wisdom.
The fourth section, which clarifies the exhortation to the benefits, is likewise for the sake of those to be exhorted; it is for this reason that the exhortation is given.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, it clarifies the harm incurred by failing to exhort, and thus one cannot help but exhort.
Below the section beginning with "By means of all Buddhas," the benefits of exhortation are revealed; therefore, exhortation is necessary.
Now, for the first part, there are two aspects:
first, regarding self-diminution—since wisdom is not bestowed, one would immediately enter *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it must be bestowed.
Therefore, the treatise states: "The two who enter nirvana do so by means of the manifestation of wisdom.
This is because the second [type] harms others and does not benefit sentient beings.
Question:
Those who have only recently entered the path still value the cultivation of non-abiding; how could those on the ground of profound wisdom take extinction as their goal and require such exhortation?
Is there even a single person whom the Buddha does not bestow wisdom upon before they take extinction?
Answer:
There are four reasons why it is necessary to exhort them.

First, to lead away and refute those of fixed nature among the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), clarifying that even at this stage of great quiescence, the bodhisattva is still exhorted to arise; how much more so, then, could what they have attained possibly be ultimate?
Second, it is to awaken Bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment from their habit of delighting in quiescence;
third, it is to inspire those at the beginning of their practice to seek the supreme goal with tireless diligence;
fourth, it is to demonstrate that this stage is profoundly deep and mysterious, difficult to relinquish, and thus requires such exhortation.

Wherever this profound stream of the Dharma exists, there must be the Buddhas who construct the bridge of the seven exhortations; therefore, not a single person attains eternal quiescence on their own.
Furthermore, even if the Buddhas did not offer these exhortations, there would still be no movement toward quiescence;
thus, these words are spoken provisionally to manifest the benefit of the exhortations.
In the second section on "Exhortation to Benefit," there are the three parts of the Dharma, the Simile, and the Application.
Within the Dharma, there are three points;

first, it reiterates the aforementioned bestowal of wisdom to demonstrate the cause of benefit, as the treatise states: "Because the causes for the accumulation of merit within those practices are superior."
"How is it superior?
Because all Buddhas collectively provide this instruction.
Second, from "In one... onwards, it concerns the swiftness of initiating practice.
3. From "Why" onwards, the reason for the illness is explained: previously there was only a single body, and thus it was inferior over a long period;
this present momentary body on this stage is equal to the immeasurable [bodies].
There are eleven phrases concerning the sudden transcendence in a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-ksana*): the first ten clarify this individually, while the last one summarizes it as a whole.

Within the ten, the first six rely on the transformation and education of sentient beings; the next two rely on the personal accumulation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*); and the final two rely on the purification of hindrances.
Among the ten [aspects], the first is the manifestation of many bodies.
As for why there are many, the *Śāstra* states: "Because all bodhisattva bodies are perceived through faith and understanding as being like one's own single body."
This means that because wisdom accords with the single essence (*ekātmatā*), it is able to manifest the one as many.
This capacity for actualization belongs to the *sambhogakāya* (recompense body) and differs from the transformations (*nirmāṇa*) of the preceding stages.
This is contrasted with the "single body" mentioned previously.
Other sounds and so forth, when contrasted with the preceding, give rise to practices that are likewise immeasurable.

[These are: first, following the utterance of the perfect voice; second, following the wisdom of what is known; third, following the category of beings to be taken in; fourth, following the appropriate country; fifth, following the category of sentient beings to be taught; sixth, following the accumulation of merit through offerings as an aid to the path; seventh, following the entry into dharma-gates as an aid to the path for accumulating wisdom; eighth, following the purification of the hindrances to supernatural powers; ninth, following the purification of the hindrances to wisdom; and tenth, because of these purifications, being able to dwell amidst immeasurable assemblies and preach the Dharma according to their capacities.
The phrase "all say 'according to'" means that there are many ways of being appropriate; it is used to explain immeasurable expressions.
How great is the significance of "according to the occasion"!
In the subsequent summary and explanation, first comes the summary: although the practices undertaken are numerous, they do not depart from the three types of action (trikarma).
Regarding the phrase "later, by virtue of the immovable dharma," this is the explanation:
because it is signless, effortless, and uninterrupted, its characteristics and functions are immovably and spontaneously perfected.
In the analogy, the ship represents the swiftness of that practice.
When the *Śāstra* states, "One should know that this is a manifestation of the excellence of the cause," it explains the reason for that swiftness.
The ship is swift because it enters the ocean; likewise, the practice is swift because it enters the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Regarding the correspondence within the text: the initial stage of the correspondence, before reaching the ocean, corresponds to the preceding seven stages (*bhūmi*).
The subsequent section, beginning with "The Bodhisattva Arrives," corresponds to reaching the ocean, which is the non-arising wisdom (*anutpāda-jñāna*) of the eighth stage.
Because it is also a practice, it is called the "ocean of practice.
Furthermore, because it can suddenly arise universally—being both profound and vast—it may also be named an "ocean.
Non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) corresponds to the aforementioned wind.
The realm of omniscience clarifies the path toward its fruition.
What was absent in the preceding metaphors is now present here; because the wisdom of non-arising is identical to the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom, the metaphors are not differentiated.
The section beginning with "originally existing" correlates with the preceding comparison.
The fourth major section, the "Pure Land Portion," poses the following question:

The sutra merely states that through the wisdom of great skillful means, one observes all things and knows them as they truly are, providing an extensive explanation of the manifestations and activities of those born by transformation.

In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, regarding the ten masteries (*vaśitā*), the former section introduces them through the gateway of wisdom (*jñāna-mukha*), while the latter merely mentions "attaining the wisdom of the transformation body" (*nirmāṇakāya-jñāna*).
Why, then, does the Master of the Treatise classify this as the section on the Pure Land (*viśuddhabuddhakṣetra*)?
Answer:
There are two kinds of pure lands: first, the cause that purifies; second, the fruit that is purified.
These consist of two pairs:
First is the pure fruit of a single characteristic, such as the Array of Jewels and so forth, which takes practice and action as its cause, namely, the straightforward mind and so forth;
second is the pure fruit of mastery, such as the perfect interfusion of the three worlds and so forth, which takes virtuous deeds as its cause, namely, the samādhi of the pure land and so forth.
Now, according to the latter correspondence:

the practice for the Pure Land begins among ordinary beings and reaches fulfillment at the tenth stage; the merit and activity of the Pure Land begin at the Immovable Stage (Acalā) and culminate in the state of a Tathāgata.
The text is divided into three distinct sections:
first, mastery over the vessel world; second, mastery over the sentient world; and third, mastery over the world of wisdom and perfect enlightenment.

The first is the place of transformation, the second is that which is transformed, and the third is that which performs the transformation; only when the latter two purities are complete is it called a "Pure Land.

However, the first is mostly concerned with the agent of purification, while the latter two are mostly concerned with the object of purification; this is merely an elliptical abbreviation in the text.
The first section is divided into two parts:
first, a general presentation.
Non-conceptual wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) is the observing wisdom; the object traversed by that wisdom is the observed; and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) is the cause of non-conceptuality.
Having cultivated effortlessness (*anābhoga*) in the seventh stage, one now attains mastery.
Below the phrase "That is to say," its specific characteristics are individually revealed.
There are five kinds of mastery:

First, according to the mind’s desire; second, according to whatever is desired; third, according to the time’s desire; fourth, according to the desire for expansion or contraction; fifth, according to the mind’s desire for a certain measure. Regarding the first:
when observing the formation and destruction of the world, the treatise states, "according to what the mind desires."
Regarding the phrase "because it can manifest or not manifest," this refers to the capacity for purification.
Regarding the phrase "knowing according to one's own mental inclination," this refers to the object of purification.
The treatise states that according to the inclinations and desires of sentient beings, [the world] appears as either formed or disintegrating;
to those who do not desire to see it, it does not appear. Therefore, when the sutra speaks of "contemplative knowledge," it refers exclusively to the causal aspect.

The author of the treatise wishes to demonstrate that the meaning encompasses both the cause and the result; therefore, he says "manifesting according to [desire]," which refers to mastery over transformation.
The following four sections should be understood by analogy as "manifesting according to [desire].

Second, from the passage beginning "By this karma," it clarifies "according to whatever desire": that is, because one can manifest whatever karma—whether of formation or destruction—that beings wish to know.
3. "In how much time is it accomplished? The following clarifies the desire according to the occasion, meaning that because one can manifest [the result] according to the length of the occasion.
If considered in terms of what is able to purify, it is the wisdom according to the occasion.
In this manner, the formation of this world takes twenty kalpas: during the first kalpa, the receptacle world is formed; during the remaining nineteen, sentient beings are formed.
Its destruction likewise takes twenty kalpas: first, sentient beings are destroyed; finally, the receptacle world is destroyed in one kalpa.
To know both in accordance with phenomena and in accordance with principle is called "knowing as it truly is.
Fourth, from the passage "Furthermore, he knows the stages" onwards, [it is shown that] he can manifest them according to the desires for their broadness or narrowness.
This section contains three parts:
First, knowing the distinctions among the four great elements is the knowledge of their extensive characteristics;
second, from "knowing the subtle atoms" onwards is the knowledge of their narrow characteristics;

third, from "whatever earth and water exist in any world" onwards is the knowledge of that which constitutes the subject and the object, thereby clarifying both the extensive and narrow characteristics together.
Now, regarding the minor and intermediate marks (*lakṣaṇa*), they are not the objects of the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) of the meditative states (*samāhitabhūmi*).
As for the major marks, they are the objects of the meditative states, because [the consciousness] takes the three thousandfold world system as its object up to the fourth dhyāna.
The "immeasurable" refers to the realm of the Tathāgata.
The first three [categories] are the limits of phenomena (*vastu-paryanta*), all of which are known through the wisdom of the realm (*viṣaya-jñāna*).

As for their "distinctive characteristics," because these are the limits of dharmas (*dharma-paryanta*), they are known through the wisdom of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-jñāna*), as one knows the distinctions between their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common-characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
The subsequent categories are easy to understand.
Second, regarding the knowledge of subtle objects: this refers to the *suvarṇaraja* (gold-dust), because it can pass through [a lattice].
As for the "coarse characteristics" mentioned next in the treatise and the sūtra, these refer to the *vātāyanaraja* (dust motes in a sunbeam).
The distinctions are the same as before.
Regarding "immeasurable distinctions," this is because many dharmas are contained within a single atom (*paramāṇu*).
Since the coarseness or subtlety of an atom applies to both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the distracted state, the terms "small" or "large" are not used.
Regarding the three knowledges that accomplish both the subject and the object, there are two parts:
first, a general knowledge of the internal and external; second, from "knowing the hells" onwards, a detailed explanation of the six realms of existence.
This corresponds to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*’s critique of what was not asked, intended to reveal the exhaustion of the most profound mysteries.
It is also said, "Because of the absence of intrinsic nature.
The fifth section, beginning with "Furthermore, knowing the desire realm," clarifies that according to the extent of one's desire, one can immediately manifest [the form].
This passage consists of two parts:
First, regarding mastery through knowledge:

previously, "great" and "small" were discussed in terms of the mutual comparison between the three realms; now, they are discussed in terms of the internal distinction between great and small within a single realm.
Within the desire realm, the human environment is small and the celestial environment is great.
Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the presence of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) is considered "small," while their absence is "great.

Regarding the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the treatise states that within the Buddha-dharma, ordinary realms are "small" and those of the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas are "great. This is specifically referred to as "Buddha-dharma" in order to distinguish it from the false grasping of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who mistake [such states] for *nirvāṇa*.
All that the Tathāgata knows within the three realms is termed "immeasurable characteristics.

In the second section, beginning with "The Buddha-son Bodhisattva again arises," it clarifies, through a general perspective, how he manifests transformations according to beings with sovereign mastery.
The text consists of three parts:
first, manifesting transformations according to the capacities of beings.
Within this, the initial section designates the wisdom of the transformer, while the subsequent section beginning with "That is to say" clarifies the capacities of those to be transformed.
There are three points:

first, knowing that the categories of bodies differ; second, knowing that the application of skillful means varies according to what is appropriate for each body; and third, knowing which realm one is born into so as to be able to benefit sentient beings.
The section following "according to" (*suǐ qí*) below correctly clarifies the manifestation of transformation according to circumstances.
Although it speaks of manifesting a body, the intent lies in the place of birth; therefore, it belongs to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
Second, the section beginning with "this bodhisattva, within a single trichiliocosm" below clarifies the scope of the transformation.
Third, from "This bodhisattva accomplishes... onwards, it clarifies the manifestation of mastery, meaning that while remaining unmoving, he is omnipresent, like the moon entering a hundred rivers.
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva, according to the bodies and minds of all sentient beings... onwards, it clarifies the practice of mastery over the world of sentient beings.
This means that because he is sovereign in responding to and taming sentient beings according to their needs, there are three parts:
first, a general explanation of response and resonance; second, a specific manifestation of response and resonance, beginning with the words "That is to say."
Within this, the manifestation of transformative birth (*upapāduka*) involves two kinds of mastery:
first, manifesting a body identical to that of others, such as appearing in the form of a śramaṇa among śramaṇas; this constitutes "acting in concert with others through one's own body."

Second, "Furthermore, one should" refers to the mind that responds to beings through downward transformation; for while the body need not necessarily be identical to those being transformed, the mind itself acts in concert with them. Thus, the treatise says: "When they practice the transformation of sentient beings, their body and mind act in concert."
3. "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva is thus... and so forth, which concludes the section on responsive manifestation.
The repetition "thus and thus" indicates that the manifestations are manifold; whether in body or mind, the response is impartial and instantaneous.
The commentary’s conclusion states: “He manifests as one whose body and mind are in equal measure.
Third, from the passage beginning “O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva is far removed,” the text elucidates the practice of the World-Master’s Perfect Enlightenment.
Master Yuan said:
"If one proceeds from the perspective of the sphere of activity, it should be called 'the sovereign practice of the two truths.
Now, proceeding from the perspective of the essence of practice, it is named 'wisdom and perfect enlightenment.'"
"Wisdom is called 'sovereignty' because it possesses unimpeded, perfect awakening regarding the two truths.
Now, another interpretation:

since the ten bodies of the objects of knowledge are all the essence of Vairocana’s perfect awakening, wisdom may also be termed "perfect awakening" from the perspective of its object; this is because it can also exercise sovereignty over their mutual manifestation.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the elucidation of the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*); second, from "This bodhisattva" onwards, the elucidation of the wisdom of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Regarding the first part: the upper phrase [indicates] the departure from delusion, while the lower phrase [indicates] abiding in reality.
Because there is no discrimination between one's own body and the bodies of others, one abides in equanimity.

The term "non-discrimination" does not merely refer to the illumination of a single nature; it also signifies the disappearance of both the subject that illuminates and the object that is illuminated.

The Treatise states: "This differs from the ultimate wisdom manifested by the Two Vehicles because they do not attain the emptiness of dharmas and cannot realize the true within the conventional; thus, it is neither identical nor different."
Second, regarding the wisdom of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are three parts:

first, the general knowledge of the ten bodies; second, from "This bodhisattva... onwards, the manifestation of the mutual functioning of the ten bodies to demonstrate sovereign mastery; third, from "This bodhisattva knows the bodies of sentient beings... onwards, the specific revelation of the characteristics of knowledge to manifest the sovereignty of wisdom.
Now, regarding the first ten bodies, the treatise subsumes them into three categories:
the first three belong to the defiled portion (*saṃkleśa-bhāga*), the next six to the pure portion (*vyavadāna-bhāga*), and the final one to the non-dual portion (*advaya-bhāga*).
All are termed "portions" (*bhāga*) because the single Great Dependent Origination of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is divided into these ten.
This is because both the defiled dependent nature and the pure dependent nature rely upon the same single reality.
Regarding the three within the defiled [nature], the first is the world of sentient beings, and the second is the world of the environment.
Regarding the retribution body (*vipākakāya*), it has two causes for its arising: namely, karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).
While the Sūtra mentions karma briefly and omits the afflictions, this treatise provides them both.
It is called "retribution" because karma is capable of summoning retribution; thus, the name is established from the perspective of the result.
If these are what is summoned, how could they differ from the two mentioned above?
Nevertheless, while the bodies of the lands may generally pertain to the pure, for the time being we shall judge them as defiled according to one class [of opinion].

Next, the six [realms] are collectively categorized as the pure portion by way of the three vehicles; among these, the first four consist of humans, *bodhisattvas*, and Buddhas, differing only in terms of cause and fruit.
The first of these is the wisdom that realizes;
the last is the dharma that is realized.

Therefore, the treatise states: "Whichever wisdom and whichever dharma among these three vehicles [are involved], they manifest purity. This means that the distinctions between the three vehicles are manifested by the differences in their respective dharmas and wisdoms.
The subsequent "space-body" (ākāśakāya) is not a single part, as it serves as the support for both [the defiled and the pure], since it is neither defiled nor pure.
This will be specifically clarified below; for the most part, it concerns the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), while its meaning also encompasses that of principle (*tattva*).

Second, regarding the manifestation of all bodily characteristics (*kāyalakṣaṇa*), it first clarifies the reasons for such manifestation, which arise from adapting to the capacities of sentient beings (*yathābhavyatā*).
This section contains two parts:
first, the specific explanation of the manifestation of characteristics.
Briefly, there are four aspects of this transformation.
How does the Dharma-knowledge take empty space as its own body?
Because one enters into the Dharma-knowledge and naturally manifests one's own body therein, causing one to suddenly perceive one's own body within empty space; therefore, it is called "acting."
The same applies to the other [transformations] as well.
The second section, beginning with "following all sentient beings," serves as a summary that extends the principle to the remaining cases.
Above, only four transformations were cited; logically, there should be ten, thereby forming one hundred bodies.

However, one's own body is itself the Bodhisattva; yet, if one regards one's own self in contrast to the Bodhisattva, there are separately one hundred and ten bodies. Therefore, it is said that they manifest in this way.
The reason why they are able to act in mutual interpenetration without obstruction is explained in detail in the *Xuántán* (Introductory Discourse).
For the present text, there are briefly three points:
first, because one realizes that phenomena themselves are the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Phenomena have no existence outside of principle, for phenomena are harmoniously integrated in accordance with principle.
This chapter first clarifies the ultimate truth (paramārtha); second, because phenomena arise through mutual dependence; and third, because their karmic functions are sovereign.

The verse in the Jin translation of the sutra states: "The Bodhisattva has mastery over causes and conditions within their convergence; even unto the point of being able to manifest the body of a Buddha according to his will.
This verse is omitted in the present translation.

The Master of the Treatise merely explains the intent behind the term "manifestation through creative action," stating: "Regarding 'the various manifestations of the actions of grasping within that sovereignty,' this means that because one performs the actions of grasping sentient beings within the sovereignty of perfect enlightenment, one manifests various forms according to the inclinations of their minds."
In the third section, which specifically elucidates the characteristics of knowledge (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), the ten bodies (*daśakāya*) are reduced to eight because three bodies are combined.
However, according to their respective categories, each should possess ten; perhaps the text is abbreviated, and for now, we follow what is explicitly stated.

Initially, the body of sentient beings has five characteristics. The first three concern the differentiation of afflictions and delusive thoughts arising from karma; this explains the three realms in general.
The latter two concern the two upper realms, distinguishing them specifically according to their retributive fruits.
If one were to comprehensively open up the three realms and five destinies, there would then be ten [kinds of bodies].

Regarding the two types of body of the land, they possess ten characteristics: the first eight are the characteristics of all-aspects, and the latter two are the characteristics of the ultimate reality.
Regarding the preceding section, first is the characteristic of the threefold demarcation, namely the small, medium, and great chiliocosms;
next are the two distinctions of defilement and purity;
next is the distinction of breadth, which here is presented briefly without the narrow [measure].
Next, regarding the two distinctions of abiding and dwelling within the ultimate reality (*tattva*):
the first is called "universal entry" (*samanta-praveśa*), because one enters all at once; it is termed a "network of directions" (*dig-jāla*) because the ten directions interlace.
Furthermore, because it manifests in successive layers, it is for the most part similar to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).

Regarding the statement that the two sections, the third and fourth, together comprise four bodies, all of which are said to be "differences of provisional names": this means there are only differences between self-characteristics and common characteristics; these are distinctions made by provisional names, for in reality there is no self or person.
The rest are likewise provisional designations; yet, since even the causes—karma—are merely provisional, it can be known that their effects—suffering—are as well.
If even the sages are merely provisional, how much more so the ordinary beings?
Furthermore, while the noble ones of the Three Vehicles are only able to understand [the Buddha-body] as provisional, the Buddha’s virtues are so transcendent that they cannot be called provisional.
Regarding the five ways of knowing the Buddha-body, there are ten characteristics inherent in each.

Since the remaining nine bodies are all Buddha-bodies, each possesses these [ten characteristics], which already amounts to one hundred. If these further interact with one another, they become infinitely layered and inexhaustible.
The *bodhi-kāya* (enlightenment body) is so called because it manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment;
second, because of the vow to be born in Tuṣita;

and third, because it is the Buddha’s response-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), which distinguishes it from transformations such as those of monkeys, deer, or horses—hence it is termed a "response-body," specifically referring to the physical body born in the royal palace.
Fourth, because it abides as the preservation of one’s own bodily relics (*śarīra*).
The aforementioned four are all subsumed under the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) among the three bodies.
Fifth, there is the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body) of actual recompense.

The "ocean of infinite marks" and so forth distinguish [this body] from the thirty-two marks and the like; thus it is called the "True Reward," which refers to the Reward Body (*sambhogakāya*) among the three bodies.
Because the six kinds of radiance subdue and convert sentient beings, it is called "majestic power," which refers collectively to both the Reward and Transformation Bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Regarding the "seven types of mind-born bodies," the treatise states: "Because one attains mastery over all similar and dissimilar mundane and supramundane minds and achieves liberation. "Similar" refers to those of the same class; "dissimilar" refers to those of different classes. "Mundane" refers to the stages prior to the bhūmis; "supramundane" refers to the stages of the bhūmis.

This refers to whether one is an ordinary person or a noble one, and whether they are similar or different; because they have attained mastery and liberation, [the body] arises simultaneously with the mind according to one's will. This is the "mind-made body" (manomaya-kāya) that arises simultaneously with its kind and is characterized by effortless activity (anabhisamskāra). It encompasses both the transformational body (nirmāṇa-kāya) and the body of enjoyment for others (para-sambhoga-kāya).

Regarding the eight merits: because all merits not shared with the two vehicles serve as the cause for performing vast benefit, one who plants even a small root of goodness will necessarily attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Regarding the ninth, the Dharma-body: because it is the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) of all Tathāgatas, it is the very essence of the realized Dharma.
In the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*), among the ten Buddhas, this is named the Dharma-realm Buddha (*dharmadhātu-buddha*).
All outflows (*āsrava*) are eternally exhausted, and no outflows increase therein; its nature is pure, perfect, and luminous, and is therefore called the "outflow-free realm" (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
It has the meaning of a "repository" (*garbha*) and the meaning of "giving birth," for it contains boundless virtues and gives rise to all mundane and supramundane sources of happiness.

Regarding the "body of the ten knowledges," it refers to all unobstructed wisdom, namely the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), because it has emerged from the stains of hindrances and realized the nature of equality.
Next, that which is said to be able to perform all activities is the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
That which is able to know all the distinctions of phenomena is the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (the wisdom of wondrous observation).
This penetrates the four bodies (*kāya*), yet it differs from other teachings because each of the two sets of ten bodies is perfectly interfused.
The sixth is the knowledge-body of knowing (jñānakāya), which possesses eleven aspects and is subsumed into three categories:

the first two are distinguished according to their substance; the first is common to both hearing and reflection, while the second is precisely the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanā-prajñā), both of which pertain to both principle and teaching.
Next is the aspect of the fruit and its practice, which is the differentiation between cause and effect.
Practice is the cause, which encompasses the three types of wisdom;
the fruit consists solely of realization and entry, and its characteristics are distinct from the preceding three.
There are eight remaining types of knowledge, all of which are distinguished according to their respective stages.
Among them, the first is general: mundane conventional knowledge is termed "worldly," while the noble knowledge of the three vehicles is termed "supramundane."
Furthermore, that which precedes the Path is called "worldly," while that from the realization of the Path onward is called "transcendent.

Regarding the five vehicles of the three vehicles, within the transcendent there is a distinction between the Great and the Small: the Small Vehicle comprises the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and so forth; the Middle Vehicle comprises the seventy-seven knowledges and so forth; and the Great Vehicle comprises the immeasurable provisional and ultimate [knowledges].

Regarding the coarse and subtle distinctions between the two sets of six and seven marks within the Mahāyāna: profound *prajñā* is unique to the [Mahāyāna] and not shared with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), whereas similar *prajñā* is what is termed "shared."

The first eight or nine [consciousnesses] are distinguished according to the three vehicles in terms of bondage and liberation, because they concern whether the nature of newly perfumed seeds has been cultivated or not.
The latter three are distinguished according to the components of cultivation within the three vehicles.
Regarding the seven knowledges of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*): while the preceding [knowledges] are the wisdom that is able to know, the objects known by them apply universally to all things.
However, as for the wisdom of the Buddha (*buddhajñāna*), it differs from these; the aforementioned Buddha-wisdom is restricted exclusively to the Tathāgata.
The text has five characteristics:
first, the characteristic of equality, which is the principle-dharma (*dharmatā*).

As the *Śāstra* states, "The immeasurable dharma-gates clarify the single Dharma-body," this means that although the dharma-gates differ, they all equally expound the equal Dharma-body; since there is no duality between the Buddhas and sentient beings, [the text] distinguishes the principle from phenomena, as the latter are all subsumed under the gate of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The second is the characteristic of non-destruction, which is the practice of the Dharma.
The *Śāstra* states: "Because one takes [the teaching] according to what was heard. This means that initiating practice in accordance with principle is called "taking according to what was heard.
When such practice accords with principle, it merges with Bodhi; this is termed "indestructible."
The third is the teaching (dharma), which refers to the various distinctions taught according to the time when they correspond to the capacities and dispositions of those to be converted.
Although the principle is fundamentally beyond words, the principle is manifested through provisional speech; whether expedient or ultimate, all are conventional designations following worldly usage.

The fourth [characteristic] further elucidates the realm pervaded by the principle-dharma; this encompasses both the defiled and the pure, because the equal *dharmakāya* pervades both sentient and insentient beings.

The fifth is the dharma of the fruit, which pertains exclusively to the pure; thus the treatise states: "Regarding the distinction of the first characteristic, the three vehicles equally realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)."
"Because there are differences according to wisdom, there are three distinct types; therefore, the principles revealed are also said to have varying degrees of depth.
If one considers the differences in terms of merit and so forth, it is as has been commonly explained.
Eighth, the knowledge of the body of space has six characteristics:
first, the characteristic of being immeasurable, because even the space within a mustard seed lacks any measure;
second, the characteristic of pervading all places, whether material or non-material.
Third, because it is invisible.
Those who see it today merely perceive the mental image of the single manifest color of emptiness and claim they "see" it; therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* extensively refutes the view of emptiness.
Furthermore, because this [space] contains the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and is empty, it is also invisible.

Regarding the fourth point, "the absence of distinct characteristics": because there is no obstruction; that is to say, unlike material phenomena (rūpadharma), which possess mutual distinctions and obstructions.
Fifth, it has the characteristic of being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because it lacks the boundaries of beginning, end, arising, and ceasing.
Sixth, it is capable of universally receiving and sustaining the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) and that which is sustained by form.
Therefore, the sutra below states: "For example, space is vast and non-material, yet it can manifest all forms."
Since one distinguishes that as "space" by means of form, it is known that one manifests that as "form" by means of space.
The fifth major section, the Section on Mastery, is divided into two parts:
first, taking the preceding as the cause, because one practices the three kinds of mastery over the world, one attains the ten masteries.
This explanation is based solely on the general teaching regarding the supernormal power of wisdom (*jñānābhijñā*).
If one follows the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are taken as the causes, as will be explained separately below.
Second, from "attaining life" onwards, the fruit of mastery (*vaśitā-phala*) is revealed.
Mastery over life means abiding and maintaining life for unspeakably unspeakable eons;
mastery over the mind means entering into the wisdom of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya samādhis.
"Wealth" refers to the manifestation of the maintenance and adornment of all worlds with infinite ornaments.

The first three [perfections] have giving as their cause, because one gives at all times, in all places, and with all things; "karma," however, is like the present life, because it is the manifestation of the maintenance of karmic retribution at a later time.
Regarding birth, it is because one manifests birth in all worlds.
The two preceding types of morality serve as its cause, for morality disciplines body and speech, thereby accomplishing superior karma.
Furthermore, through the purity of morality, one is born according to one's wishes.
Aspiration is that which accords with whatever the mind desires;
because it manifests the attainment of *sambodhi* within a Buddha-field at the appropriate time, this arises from diligence that is spurred by exertion and free from indolence.
Because when one understands, Buddhas manifest as filling all worlds;
thus, what is called "faith-understanding" (*adhimukti*) in the *Śāstra* and "supreme understanding" (*adhimokṣa*) in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* are of one and the same meaning.

Taking patience as the cause—because when practicing patience one accords with the intentions of sentient beings—one attains the power for all things to revolve according to one's will; that is to say, such as transforming earth into gold and so forth.
As for "according to wish," it is because one manifests transformations at will throughout all Buddha-fields.

With meditative concentration as the cause, wisdom consists in the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and the marks and signs of physical excellence, as well as the three types of awakening (*bodhi*).
The Dharma is the gateway of neither middle nor extremes, because it is clearly manifested.

In the preceding two [stages], both take Prajñā as their cause: by inwardly illuminating the objects of knowledge, one attains mastery over wisdom; by proclaiming the teaching in accordance with the faculties [of beings], one attains mastery over the Dharma.
Among these ten, because both knowledge and supernormal powers are entirely unimpeded, they are called "mastery.
This treatise uses these ten to counteract ten fears:
first, the fear of death; [and so forth].
Second, the fear of the defilements of affliction;
third, poverty;
fourth, evil karma.
Fifth, the five evil realms;
sixth, the failure to obtain what one seeks;
seventh, the karmic offenses of slandering the Dharma.
Eighth, when seeking, it binds one from being unable to sustain life;
ninth, mastery over phenomena (dharmavaśitā) remedies doubts such as "how" or "what";
tenth, mastery over knowledge (jñānavaśitā) remedies the lack of majestic authority among the great assembly.
These two are as explained in the treatise.
Following these ten, there are also the five fears of the first bhūmi; because they are subtle, they are gradually differentiated.
Among these, the second, fourth, and seventh are identical to ill-repute, for ill-repute is their root.
The three [factors] and six [factors] belong to non-sustenance;

the nine belong to the tenth, and thus are categorized according to cause. This stage may also be categorized according to fruit, which is perfected in the Buddha; this refers to the sequential arrangement (*paryāya*).

Both the lower section, "Leaving the World," and the upper section, "The Chapter on Worthy Leaders" (Bhadrapāla), contain these ten [perfections], yet they are applied here to the stage of Samantabhadra as it pervades the beginning and the end.
The sixth major section, from "Having Attained This" onwards, clarifies the Greatly Victorious Division.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the greatness of wisdom, because the understanding of wisdom is preeminent;
second, the greatness of action, because the conduct of practice is vast.
Third, the greatness of the merit abiding in those two is due to its being accomplished through wisdom and activity.

Regarding this first point, the text contains five phrases: the first phrase cites the preceding as the cause, while the section beginning with "then it becomes" correctly elucidates the point itself.
It is revealed that there are four wisdoms:
the first is the general [wisdom], which refers to neither abiding in saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa; its quiescence and function are difficult to fathom, and it is thus called "inconceivable.
This inconceivability has three aspects:
First is the inconceivability of the completion of practice, which refers to the realization of nirvāṇa because it is without measure;
second is the inconceivability of the object of knowledge, because it illuminates the worldly realm extensively;
third is the inconceivability of the removal of hindrances, because it causes true suchness to emerge from the cognitive hindrance so that neither celestial māras nor non-Buddhists can destroy it.
The second section, "This bodhisattva" and below, concerns the greatness of activity (*karmamahātmya*), which has three parts:
first, the initial two phrases cite the preceding [qualities] as the cause—namely, (1) mastery of entry and (2) the accomplishment of wisdom;
next, from "obtaining the ultimate" onwards, the greatness of activity is explicitly revealed.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards is the summary of the many gates.
There are twelve phrases that correctly reveal this:
the first three clarify the purity of the three karmas, distinguishing the karmas according to their essential characteristics;
The latter nine [verses] distinguish the activity based on cultivation, subsuming it under four characteristics.

The first line clarifies "arising"; the *Śāstra* states that there is "that which can cause arising. Simultaneous with that which can cause arising—namely, body, speech, and mind—are the objects caused to arise, while wisdom is that which causes them to arise.
Since these three types of karma arise, they must necessarily exist simultaneously with that which gives rise to them; as the Sūtra says, "Wisdom is the leader that guides conduct.
Regarding the four lines beginning with "Prajñā" (2): wisdom encompasses non-defilement and performs deeds such as benefiting sentient beings.
This means that because great compassion is embraced by wisdom, one is untainted by craving and views, and is thus able to initiate skillful means for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.

Third, the two lines beginning with "skillfully arising" are subsumed under the cause; that is, the internal purity of the great vow serves as the cause for both one's own practice and the practice of others.
Furthermore, being externally encompassed by the Buddha, one achieves two causes.
Regarding the latter two phrases, they concern what is sustained by karma: the first phrase refers to benefiting sentient beings, and the latter phrase refers to purifying the buddha-fields.
The concluding summary at the end may be understood accordingly.
Third, regarding the section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells here," the greatness of the merits of those two abodes consists of three parts:

first, the designation of the scope of the dwelling; second, the manifestation of the merits of the dwelling, starting from "He attains goodness" (*śubha*); and third, the conclusion of the attainment of these merits, starting from "This Bodhisattva."

Within the second [section], there are ten phrases based on seven kinds of merit. That is to say, the first four constitute the first merit, "well-established in the path," which is the essence of these merits, because the practices of the two benefits constitute the bodhisattva path.

The first two [aspects] concern self-benefit: the former, characterized by accord with principle and freedom from hindrances, is termed the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*); the latter, characterized by firmness in its antidotes, is termed the "superior mind" (*viśiṣṭa-citta*).
The final two concern benefiting others through compassion and loving-kindness.

The latter six each consist of one [verse], which, in terms of cultivation, distinguish their virtues: the first three concern the benefit of others through the transformation of the three wheels, cultivating superior altruism;
the latter three involve the harmony between aspiration and practice, externally invoking the protection of the Buddhas, cultivating superior self-benefit.
Regarding the threefold conclusion: the proximate conclusion pertains to this section, while the remote conclusion pertains to the preceding three.
Having attained such wisdom, one concludes that the preceding wisdom is great; for by means of wisdom one realizes the principle, thereby attaining freedom from both hatred and attachment.
Next, from "capable of manifesting" (*nirmāṇa*) onwards, it concludes the greatness of the activity performed, because it acts with equanimity.
Afterward, from "in all" (*sarvatra*) onwards, it concludes the greatness of the qualities in which one abides, because one attains the seven qualities free from fault.

The seventh major section, the "Analysis of Names," also encompasses the dedication according to reality (*yathābhūta*), because it is designated as being "unmoving according to reality" and so forth. This Analysis of Names has two parts: first, the explanation of names by way of the stages (*bhūmi*), which clarifies the positions through the Dharma; second, the explanation of names by way of the meaning, which clarifies the distinctions between the stages. Regarding the first part, the explanation of names by way of the stages: this refers to the stage of dry insight (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*). Why is it called "dry insight"? Furthermore, because at this stage one practices insight without yet having attained the moisture of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), it is called "dry insight.
