Regarding the second point, the explanation of the names, this reveals the virtues in relation to the persons.

Now, for the first ten phrases, the *Śāstra* subsumes them into six categories; Master Huiyuan further subsumes these six into two, such that the first two constitute the "self-benefit" (*svabhāga*) stage and the latter four constitute the "superior progress" (*viśeṣagamana*) stage.
Within the progression toward excellence (*viśeṣagamana*), there are again three stages:
first, the arousal of cultivation that is free from faults;

next, the two [stages] where cultivation accomplishes virtues—first, the accomplishment of the path of teaching (*deśanā-mārga*), and second, the accomplishment of the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*); finally, the stage where one relies on these virtues to establish the [spiritual] positions (*avasthā*). There is likewise this underlying principle.

Regarding the statement that there are six aspects: first, the initial two phrases are named "the antidote to defilement. First, because it remedies the functional activities of lower stages, the vows of the Hīnayāna, and all demonic activities, it is called the "Immovable Stage" (Acalā-bhūmi).
Second, because it remedies the activity of the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśa-vāsanā*), it is called "Non-retrogressive" (Anivartana).
The first two [lines] refer to the characteristics and functions; afflictions cannot disturb them.
The second line and the following one can be understood as referring to the attainment of the profound.
The third section has two lines, concerning the purity of the practice of setting forth.

The preceding phrase describes the "arousing of purity," which means attaining true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), ensuring that the three karmas are without fault, not breaking the contemplative mind, and being able to initiate the practice of advancement.

However, while the eighth stage should correspond to the eighth abode and be collectively termed "Candala" (the Youthful), the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* names it the "Prince," which seems inconsistent with the textual tradition.
The second line concerns the purity of practice; for when one is engaged in correct practice, one is free from obstacles and possesses mastery.

Regarding the four sets of two lines, they are called the "superior purities of the conditioned" pertaining to the mundane and the supramundane: the first line refers to the mundane conditioned state, which follows worldly conventions out of compassion while remaining personally unconditioned;
the second line refers to the supramundane conditioned state, which, through wisdom, skillfully discriminates and thus purifies the cognitive obscurations—all of which carry a definitive meaning.

The fifth phrase refers to the two types of "unconditioned purity" (*anabhisaṃskāra-viśuddhi*): namely, those pertaining to the mundane and the supramundane, which are designated as "the two. Because they manifest through the power of vows and transformations without stagnating in quiescence, they are called "unconditioned," which is precisely *apratisthita-nirvāṇa*.
The sixth stage has two phrases concerning the superiority of the Bodhisattva-bhūmi, which distinguishes its specific stages.

The first phrase indicates superiority over the [first] six stages; for while the contemplation of emptiness in those six stages is subject to movement by others, here one initiates superior practices in every moment of thought. The second phrase indicates superiority over the seventh stage.
Based on the preceding commentary, I shall now further point to the text to provide a distinct interpretation:

these various names are established in relation to the preceding sūtra; the first two derive their names from the stage of "pure patience" (*śuddhakṣānti*), because one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) and enters the state of immovability (*aniñjya*).
This phrase serves as a general summary: because this wisdom is manifest, there is no falling back or destruction.

The following two points concern the attainment of superior practice and receive their names accordingly: first, because it is unknowable even to Bodhisattvas of profound practice; second, because it is free from all faults such as the perception of signs (*nimitta*).

The next three [stages] are designated according to their reception of purity within the Pure Land. "Birth-place" refers to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*); it constitutes a stage because one is born there at will according to one's pleasure.
"Sentient-being world" refers to mastery over the physical form; it constitutes a stage because one manifests a body in accordance with objects, being free from self-effort.
The wisdom of the ultimate stage perfectly awakens to the world by definitively discerning the two truths.
Next, the single [stage] concerns the aspect of mastery; it is only when one’s vows are accomplished accordingly that it is termed "mastery."
Next, one [aspect] is categorized according to the great and superior portion, because it attains the ten kinds of sustaining powers such as the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).
The latter, the effortless (*anābhoga*) stage, universally encompasses both the beginning and the end.
According to this interpretation, it appears as though the commentator has omitted a clear indication of the textual basis.
Second, regarding the section "The Bodhisattva Sons Accomplish... and below, the wise explain the names; this consists of three parts:

first, citing the preceding as the cause, because they have attained the stage of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*); second, from "Entering the Buddha... onwards, the actual manifestation in terms of persons; third, from "In the immeasurable... onwards, the summary of that which is dwelt in.
Regarding the manifestation [of this stage] for the sake of persons, by what meaning is a bodhisattva said to have attained the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*)?
There are two meanings:
first, it is unshakable in its single direction, meaning that their practice proceeds in accordance with the higher stages.
The second is "the immutability of the single essence," meaning that its essence is identical to the practice of all bodhisattvas.
In the text, this is first explained in general terms, and subsequently clarified in detail from the phrase "constantly for" onwards.
Regarding the first [section], there are four phrases, each containing two meanings; the treatise explains them collectively by stating, "Because Buddha-nature is the conforming cause.
Buddha-nature corresponds to the first phrase; since the Sanskrit term is *dhātu*, its translation as "element" (*jie*) or "nature" (*xing*) is comprehensive.
The *Śāstra* on the Sūtra states: "To attain entry into the Buddha-nature is precisely the fruition-nature of the Dharma-body.
The *Śāstra* further explains that "Buddha-nature" refers to the excellence of the fulfillment of the *dhātu*.
Because one ultimately perceives this nature, it is called "fulfillment."
This constitutes the boundary of the scope.
By attaining the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi*), the bodhisattva is able to ascend into it.
As for "conforming to the cause," this refers to the following three phrases; because these three serve as causes, one is able to conform to the realm of the Buddha.
First, regarding the inclusion of merits: "The illumination of the Buddha's merits" refers to the sense of being thoroughly purified.
That is to say, to illuminate the Buddha's virtues well with stainless wisdom is precisely the meaning of inclusion.
Second is practice, meaning correct conduct and deportment, because it accords with and conforms to that of the Buddha.
Third is proximity, meaning that the realm of the Buddha is present before one, being as close as if it could be seen.
In the subsequent section explaining the distinctions, we first clarify those who are exclusively immovable.
The treatise cites ten phrases from the sutra, whereas the present sutra lacks one.
The first phrase generally reveals the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*): because his understanding penetrates the ultimate mystery and supreme virtue is bestowed upon himself.
Since they are constantly sustained by the Buddha’s empowerment, they are called "unwavering in every respect.
The remaining phrases separately manifest this unwavering nature based on five kinds of merit:
first, the merit of making offerings, namely those of Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
In the sutra, following the word "king," there is the phrase "welcoming with reverence.
Second is the merit of protection, meaning that [the Buddhas] manifest forms such as Vajrapāṇi to guard [the practitioner].
Third is the merit of reliance, meaning that they never abandon samādhi.

Regarding the fourth, the merit of the purification of the lands: it is able to manifest the various distinctions of bodies; since it can manifest accordingly for both the environment and sentient beings, it is called "immeasurable."
5. The merit of teaching and transforming sentient beings, as described from "In each and every [one]" onwards.
This further consists of five types: the first three are of the nature of self-perfection (*svabhāva*), and the latter two are of the nature of superior progress (*viśeṣa*).
First, he vows to take up existence within the various realms of being and frequently acts as a leader; therefore, it is said that he possesses great power and influence.

Second is the power of the knowledge that subdues the faculties and mental tendencies, which is the supernormal power obtained as a result of maturation, because it exhaustively understands the faculties and inclinations of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
Third is the power of the Dharma of the immeasurables, because of the mastery over samādhi in turning the wheel of Dharma.
Fourth is the power of reception (*anubhava-bala*); as that sūtra states, "Because it is able to receive immeasurable predictions," this [power] is omitted in the present sūtra.
Fifth is the power of teaching (*deśanā-bala*), which means manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment according to those who can be transformed, for one is truly able to teach.
After this, the Sūtra has one additional sentence which concludes by saying, "This Bodhisattva thus penetrates," while the Śāstra explains, "Because he is unshakable in every respect."
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, it clarifies the immovability of the single essence.
The text contains ten phrases: the first is general, and the others are specific.
The general statement, "entering the assembly of the Mahāyāna," means entering the ranks of the homogeneous multitude of the Mahāyāna.
To "enter the number" means the sense of non-disruption, because one is harmonized as one.
There are nine distinct types; possessing these nine types, one is fit to enter the number of the assembly.
First, the non-destruction of wisdom, because of attaining the supernormal power of the knowledge of phenomena;
second, the non-destruction of teaching, because of emitting the light of the knowledge of instruction;

third, the non-destruction of liberation, because of dwelling neither in conditioned practice nor in realization, entering the unimpeded dharma-realm of both emptiness and existence with unobstructed karmic function.
Fourth, the purity of the Buddha-fields is indestructible, because of mastery over worlds;
fifth, entry into the Mahāyāna is indestructible, because wisdom can manifest great merits;
sixth, the supernormal powers are indestructible, because of mastery according to one's will.
7. "Skillfully able" and below explain that the meaning is indestructible, for it accords with the teachings of the three periods of time;
8. "Universally subduing" and below concern the indestructibility of sitting at the site of enlightenment, for one subdues Māra and the heterodox under the tree of bodhi through the myriad practices;
9. "Perfectly awakened" concerns the indestructibility of entering the realm of the Tathāgata, for one’s awakening is identical to that of the Buddha.
The third section summarizes the unimpeded practice of abiding in the middle way, because one does not sever, does not turn back, and does not regress from mindfulness.
This constitutes the second stage, the fruit.

Regarding "gentle flexibility" (*saṃvartanīya*), there is first the practice of gentle flexibility; within the explanation of the Dharma, this includes the differentiation of world-systems and so forth.
"Immeasurable illumination of the Dharma" means that one equally embraces all sentient beings through the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
Regarding the statement in the treatise, "it is named for its characteristic as the cause," this is because the Dharma received [from the Buddha] serves as the sovereign cause.
In the analogy, the pure gold fashioned into the crown of the Lord of Jambudvīpa symbolizes the attainment of the Pure Grounds (*śuddhabhūmi*), because the body and mind therein are superior.

Since within these grounds the practice of retribution (*vipākacaryā*) is fully matured and one possesses mastery over the three worlds, this ground is specifically distinguished as being "added" to the king.
"Having no equal" is a metaphor for the light of the roots of goodness becoming increasingly bright and pure.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha, it is as if... onwards, it teaches the purity of wisdom.
Regarding the Brahma King universally emitting light: it surpasses the light of the sun for three reasons: first, because it is manifold; second, because it is pure; and third, because it is vast.
Within the third section, the Section of Verses (Gāthā-varga), the twenty-two verses are divided into three parts:

first, eighteen and a half verses praise the practice of the stages; second, two and a half verses praise the fruition of the stages; and finally, one verse concludes by defining the limits of the exposition.
Now, first, the seven sections above [in the verse] are divided into seven parts:
the first one and a half verses correspond to the section on "compiling the ground" (*saṃgraha-bhūmi*).
The second, one and a half verses, corresponds to the section on "purifying patience" (*kṣānti-viśuddhi*).

The third section, consisting of seven verses, concerns the attainment of superior practice. Within this, there are two parts: the first two verses concern the superiority of profound practice, while the latter five verses concern the superiority of initiation.

Regarding the phrase "merely by means of profound and unimpeded wisdom," this is not found in the prose commentary; therefore, we know that if one merely contemplates the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), it would be identical to the practice of the Two Vehicles regarding both principle and phenomena.
However, when every single phenomenon is entirely without obstruction, this is the training of a Bodhisattva.

The entire Chinese translation of the *Jin jing* contains one verse which says: "Only by attaining unimpeded, profound, and subtle wisdom, and thereby penetrating the three periods of time, is one named a Buddha."
Furthermore, this single line may also serve as a general summary for the remaining exhortations.
There are six verses summarizing the section on purifying the Buddha-fields, which consists of three parts:

the first two concern the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*); the next three concern the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*); and the final one concerns the world of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*jñāna-saṃbuddha-loka*).
Five and a half verses praise the ten masteries (*vaśitā*);
the Jin translation states: "One is able to attain the ten kinds of wondrous and great mastery-wisdom.
One verse praises the section on Great Excellence (*mahāviśeṣa*).
The seventh chapter is the "Section on Explaining the Names" (*Nāmanirdeśa*).
Regarding "Guhyapada" (Miji), it was translated as "Malla" (Lishi) in ancient versions.
The remainder of the text is self-evident.

The Ninth Ground, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*). Regarding the reason for its arrival, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

Although one has previously abandoned effort within the dwelling of signlessness (*animitta-vihāra*) and attained mastery over signs, one has not yet attained great mastery in teaching the Dharma through the distinctions of synonyms, various characteristics, etymologies, and all categories. Therefore, this ground follows in order to bring this aspect to full completion.
Regarding "Excellent Wisdom" (*sādhumati*): the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states, "Because one has attained the most supreme unimpeded knowledge.

As Vasubandhu explains in his commentary: "This refers to attaining the four most supreme analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Since the wisdom of analytical knowledge is the most excellent among all forms of wisdom, and wisdom is itself insight (*prajñā*), it is therefore called 'Excellent Wisdom'."
This refers to the ten kinds of fourfold analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) mentioned in the subsequent text.
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "Among the nine stages, the fourfold analytical knowledge is most preeminent."
In what way is it superior?

In a single kṣaṇa, all humans and devas within the trichiliocosm may question this bodhisattva with diverse categories, diverse sounds, and diverse meanings; he is able to answer all these questions universally with a single voice, thereby severing all doubts.
This is the same as the passage below.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Because one possesses mastery in preaching the Dharma, there is no affliction or entanglement.

Regarding the phrase "increasing wisdom with mastery and unimpededness," this simultaneously reveals that being free from hindrances constitutes excellence; the intent of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* is also the same.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* differ slightly in their phrasing, yet there is no difference in their essential meaning.
The title *Benevolent Kings* (*Renwang*) as "Wisdom Light" (*Hui-guang*) combines both the Dharma and a metaphor.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* names it "Excellent Characteristics" (*Shanxiang*), deriving the name from that which is understood.
Although the subject and object differ, both clarify the wisdom of expounding the Dharma.
Regarding the obstacles to be abandoned: one abandons the obstacle of being unwilling to engage in the benefit of others because of possessing the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The obstacles to the four unhindered knowledges are divided into two types of delusion:

the first three constitute one, called the "delusion regarding mastery over the dhāraṇīs of the immeasurable teachings spoken, the immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables, and the subsequent analytical wisdom. Here, the teachings spoken refer to the meaning (*artha*); the names, phrases, and syllables refer to the phenomena (*dharma*); and the subsequent analytical wisdom refers to the eloquence (*nirukti*) and dhāraṇī. This "delusion regarding mastery" applies collectively to the aforementioned three.
The second is the delusion regarding mastery over eloquence (*pratibhāna-vaśitā-moha*), which is the delusion regarding the fourth unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).

Therefore, the *tathatā* realized therein is called the basis for mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā-adhiṣṭhāna*). This means that once this *tathatā* has been realized, one attains mastery over the unimpeded knowledges; consequently, one becomes proficient in the practice of skillfully discerning the capacities of disciples as vessels for the Dharma and teaching the Dharma with mastery.
The *Liang-lun* states: "By penetrating the ultimate True Suchness, one attains the fruit of the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
This is identical in meaning to the attainment of the Wisdom-Treasury Samādhi (*jñānagarbha-samādhi*) mentioned in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. Both refer to the same principle.
Next, the text is formally explained.
Within the three sections, the first—consisting of the praise and request—comprises thirteen verses divided into three parts:
the first two concern the Tathāgata’s manifestation of signs to reveal his effortless practice; because this unmoving movement is inconceivable, he specifically manifests these supernatural powers.
Next are ten verses of individual praise;
finally, one verse of the concluding request.
Within the individual praise, there are also three parts:
First, there is the offering of a bodhisattva; next, the offering of a celestial king (*devaputra*); and finally, the offerings and praises of eight celestial maidens (*devakanyā*).
Within this section, there are two parts:
first, the single offering, and second, the praises of the remaining seven.
Within the section on praise, there are two parts:
the first is the brief statement of praise, and the latter six clarify the words.
Within this [latter part], there are also two sections:
The first two [verses] praise the Bodhisattva’s supernormal powers (abhijñā) as pertaining to the eight stages (*bhūmi*) and the Master who expounds the Dharma;
the latter four pairs praise both the Buddha and the Bodhisattva regarding the beneficial activity of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*).
Furthermore, these are called the "illusory wisdom" (*māyājñāna*) of the Bodhisattva, for the concluding statement says, "because the Buddha has already been praised."
The text generally praises the eighth and ninth stages as being like the moon appearing universally, because they exist prior to this stage.
This is the rank of the Dharma Master, who expounds the provisional and the real according to the capacities of sentient beings.
The text consists of three parts:

first, the body being without mind yet universally responding; second, the two [sections on] the mouth preaching according to the capacities of beings; and third, the concluding metaphor showing that the mind is ever in accord with the Middle Way.
Since it specifically states that the mind of supreme wisdom reveals the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the provisional and the ultimate are clearly distinguished.

Thus, in the *Sutra of the Garland* (*Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*), ten kinds of goodness are taught; the first nine correspond to the three vehicles, each leading to the respective attainment of the three vehicles, while the tenth is named the seed-nature of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna-gotra*).

This means that upon first hearing the Buddha-dharma, one immediately gives rise to the bodhicitta; one contemplates only suchness and cultivates buddha-wisdom, never allowing compassion and vows to entangle the mind, and never giving rise to the mental orientations of the two vehicles.

The ninth [point] is because his mind is enveloped by the vow of compassion; as it is clearly stated here that he "delights in benefiting others through loving-kindness and compassion," how can one not believe it?
This concludes the second section: the Section on the Correct Exposition.
First, the practice of the stages (*bhūmi*) is clarified, consisting of four sections:

first, the accomplishment of the skillful means of the Dharma-preacher (*dharmabhāṇaka*), meaning that this stage is able to give rise to eloquence for preaching the Dharma; it is called the "Dharma-preacher stage" because the practice established for entering the stage is termed "skillful means";
second, the accomplishment of wisdom, meaning it possesses the wisdom capable of knowing the Dharma.
Third is accomplishment through entering [the mind], because one penetrates the mental activities of those to be converted;
fourth is accomplishment through teaching, because one imparts instruction correctly according to their faculties.
Among these four, the first is the stage of "entering the mind," while the remaining three are all stages of "abiding in the mind."
This also encompasses three stages, as will be understood below. However,
while in the eighth stage one merely purifies Buddha-fields and teaches sentient beings,
in this stage, by the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), one teaches sentient beings so as to accomplish all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), for one is thus able to teach them.
Regarding "all aspects" (*sarvākāra*): this is because they possess the four aforementioned divisions.
Within the first division, there are three parts:
first, citing what precedes to introduce what follows, because one has previously attained the knowledge of the two truths and so forth;
Next, the section beginning with "desiring further" (*yùgèng*) correctly reveals the skillful means;
third, the section beginning with "attaining entry" (*dé rù*) concludes the practice of entering the stages.
Within the section that correctly reveals [the means], there are ten phrases, which do not deviate from the two benefits [of self and others].

The Treatise states: "Regarding the manifestation of 'one by one' and 'five and three phrases': the first phrase refers to benefiting others and the second phrase refers to benefiting oneself; hence it is called 'one by one.
The next five phrases refer to benefiting others and the final three phrases refer to benefiting oneself; hence it is called 'five and three.'"
The term "manifestation" applies generally to the preceding four sections.

In the first phrase, based on the perception of liberation attained through the formless realm, one benefits others by transforming those sentient beings who are capable of being converted, leading them to attain Great Parinirvāṇa; therefore, it is said to be "superior."
The author of the treatise states that because a bodhisattva does not seek their own extinction, he offers this explanation.
However, since the sutra says they "further seek cessation" (śānti), why should it be forbidden for them to seek it for themselves?

Because the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages equally attain non-arising—wherein the eighth stage attains patience (*kṣānti*) and quiescence manifests—one relies on exhortation to initiate cultivation;
this seeking of the superior grade is called "transcendently superior," for it is the true liberation that is active yet quiescent.

If one follows this interpretation, although the first two [stages] pertain to self-benefit, it is also logically consistent that all ten phrases may apply to both self-benefit and benefit for others; thus there is no error in principle.
For now, let us explain according to the treatise:
because the ultimate self-interest has not yet been attained, one further cultivates the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Third, based on bodhisattvas whose faculties are matured, they transform beings by entering the secrets of the Tathāgata, because the three mysteries bring about transformative benefit.

Fourth, based on sentient beings who can be transformed through practice based on erroneous thoughts, they cause them to observe inconceivable wisdom so that they may attain right mindfulness; this means observing non-thought to perceive the nature of wisdom.

Fifth, it is based on turning the wheel of Dharma for sentient beings who have not yet known the Dharma, so that they may come to know it; for the dharanis and samadhi-doors of tranquil purity are all the basis upon which the Dharma is taught.
Sixth, for the sake of sentient beings who have taken refuge in what is false, he possesses vast and great supernormal powers in order to cause them to enter the True Dharma.
Seventh, for the sake of sentient beings born in the heavens through faith, he causes them to enter the pure lands of Buddhas in various worlds.
Within the first five [aspects], there is: first, no realization; second, no practice; and third, no understanding.

In the latter three aspects of self-benefit, beginning with "the two kinds of faith," one enters into reliance upon perfect enlightenment and internally realizes the virtue of wisdom; therefore, the power of cultivation and so forth are present.
Ninth, based on the merit of external transformation through turning the wheel of Dharma;
tenth, based on the merit of abandonment through non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells here" onwards, is the accomplishment of wisdom.
The following two or three sections subsume the "Abiding of the Prince," because knowing the dharmas and knowing the faculties are both the standard protocols of a Dharma King.

First, according to the text on the "Accomplishment through Wisdom," there is initially a general knowledge of the three natures, namely that the pure and the defiled are non-dual; this non-duality is itself the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Subsequently, from the section beginning with "outflowing" (*sāsrava*), they are progressively and specifically differentiated.

First, regarding pure phenomena (*śukla-dharma*), they are divided into those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*). This means that when practices such as giving and ethical discipline are cultivated by a mind that grasps at signs, they are associated with outflows and are thus called "with outflows"; the opposite is "without outflows."

Second, regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*), that which prior to the opening of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) is called "mundane" (*laukika*), while that from the path of vision onward is called "supramundane" (*lokottara*).

Third, based on these two categories of mundane and supramundane, their distinction is termed "conceivable" (*cintya*), whereas the state of being both mundane and supramundane is termed "inconceivable" (*acintya*).

Furthermore, within the supramundane, with respect to the two paths of teaching and realization, that which is capable of definitively entering into realization amidst the out-flowing and conceptualizable is called "concentration" (*samādhi*); that which is moved by conditions is called "non-concentration."

Furthermore, it may be said that the Buddha-nature is definitively existent, whereas all other dharmas are entirely indeterminate; this is because the three categories of the definite and so forth will be explained in the subsequent text.

Fifth, the various virtues mentioned above are expanded into the Three Vehicles—namely, the Truths (satya), the Conditions (pratyaya), and the Perfections (pāramitā)—because these all pertain to the aforementioned four [categories].
Only the fruit of Buddhahood is singular; it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and so forth, yet it belongs to the fruit of the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Sixth, within the teachings of the three vehicles, it demonstrates the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), based on practicing in accordance with them.
This is the essence of goodness; therefore, it is explained last.

That is to say, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), its objective condition (*ālambana*), its nature (*svabhāva*), the further shore (*pāra*), and ultimate reality (*tattva*) are all termed unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), its objective condition, wisdom (*jñāna*), that which can be realized, and that which is cultivated and arises, are all termed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). All [qualities] of the Tathāgata are entirely unconditioned; this is because the conditioned wisdom of a Buddha is not taught as ultimate, and because the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* instructs one to conceal the characteristics of the conditioned.
The noble beings of the three vehicles initiate their practice based on this and differentiate themselves based on this; therefore, it is called "conforming practice.
The third section, beginning with "This bodhisattva, by means of such... and so forth, clarifies the accomplishment of entering into practice.
This section has three parts:

first, the general presentation of the headings; second, the detailed explanation based on those headings, beginning with "This bodhisattva knows as it truly is..."; and third, the concluding summary of abiding, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the bodhisattva follows in accordance with..."
First, there are eleven forests:

the first is "the mind of sentient beings," which is the general [category]; as the treatise states, it is "based on the common," because this [mind] serves as the common basis for the ten subsequent [forests], both defiled and pure.
The Bodhisattva knows by relying upon this; therefore, it is called "reliance.
The subsequent instances of reliance should be understood by analogy with this meaning.
The remaining ten are specific categories, as they do not transcend the three types of defilement.
The treatise states: "Birth arises dependent upon afflictions and karma;
birth is the fruit of suffering. Now we come to the ninth [section].

The treatise explains the remaining seven [factors] as follows: "Dependent upon common defiled afflictions, defilement and purification, etc., and depending on whether the time is fixed or unfixed. This means that the subsequent four factors, such as the faculties (*indriya*), are collectively termed "common" because they share the same nature as karma.
The *anuśaya* (latent dispositions) are the seeds of affliction; they are called "defilement" because they lie dormant within the *ālayavijñāna*, causing the mind to be defiled.
Rebirth (*upapatti*) is simply birth, as has already been explained previously.
The remaining two [categories] pertain to all three [realms], and thus are not excluded from the three.
Second, how are they reconciled?
It is because habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have no separate substance, as they are merely the functional aspects (*dhātu*) of defilement, purity, and so forth.
The three aggregates (*skandha*) are merely designated according to whether they are fixed or unfixed in terms of time.

The treatise further provides a separate explanation of the meaning of the similarity between faculties (*indriya*), faith (*śraddhā*), disposition (*āśaya*), and nature (*gotra*), stating: "They are further categorized as determined or undetermined, according to the sequence of faculties and so forth.

Regarding the similarity of the faculties and so forth to faith and so forth, since the subsequent scriptural passage uses the faculties as an analogy for the three [categories], this section re-explains the meaning of their similarity.
It must also be determined by time; therefore, it is said: "Furthermore, that is either fixed or unfixed in time.
By what is time discussed?
It is also discussed according to the sequence of the four matters, beginning with the faculties (indriya).
What is the sequence?
It refers to the similarity of the faculties and so forth.
To what are they similar?
This refers to faith and the other [faculties].

Just as that which has been habitually practiced from the past is called a "faculty" (indriya), that which confirms and maintains [an object] is called "understanding" (adhimokṣa). Because understanding arises based on the faculties, they are said to follow in sequence; because understanding must necessarily correspond to the faculties, they are said to be "similar."
Habitual understanding forms one's nature, and that nature necessarily resembles the understanding.
Based on this nature, desire arises, and that desire in turn resembles the nature.
When this resemblance is not yet matured, it is termed "undetermined"; when it is matured, it is termed "rightly determined," for there is then no possibility of "wrong determination" at all.
At that time, based on the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, the Sūtra and the Śāstra explain "understanding" (*adhimukti*) as faith (*śraddhā*), because it is an understanding through faith.
As for why all ten are called "dense forests" (*gahana*): they are called "forests" because they are numerous, and they are called "dense" because they are difficult to know.

In the treatise on the Ten Forests (*Daśa-vana*), each instance contains the character "conduct" (*xing*). This refers to the conduct of improper faith; thus, they are called the "dense forests" (*gahana*) of mental conduct (*citta-saṃskāra*).
If mental conduct is severed, one realizes perfect and luminous faith; this is no longer the conduct of the dense forest.
However, these ten names are for the most part as explained in the "Chapter on Arousing the Mind.
As for the term *vāsanā* (habitual tendency), it applies to two meanings:
first, residual habit; second, the perfuming of seeds, as will be explained below.

The second part, the chapter on the basis (*āśraya*), provides an extensive explanation divided into nine sections, as it serves to clarify the unification of the dispositions (*śakti*) and the desires (*ruci*).
Now, for the first [section], there are three parts within the mind: namely, the general, the specific, and the conclusion.
Within this section, ten categories are briefly presented and subsumed into eight, because the second and third, as well as the last two, are combined.
First, the characteristic of differentiation, due to the sixfold distinction between mind (citta), thought (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna).
These eight [mental factors] are admitted to arise simultaneously when taking an object; therefore, they are called "arising in combination" (*miśra*).
Furthermore, that which arises in combination must necessarily be accompanied by others, for at its very minimum, it still possesses the five universal factors (*sarvatraga*).
Second, the two lines beginning with "swiftly shifting" clarify the mode of activity (*ākāra*), because the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) involve constant flux.
"Swiftness" is itself abiding; for the essence of abiding is precarious and swiftly proceeds toward change.
"Transformation" refers to change; "destruction" is cessation, while "non-destruction" is arising.

Although the sutra contains only a single phrase—stating that "lightness transforms into the characteristics of arising and non-arising"—the treatise explains it as "because of the activity of abiding, changing, arising, and ceasing."
Regarding the three that are formless: from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one contemplates that mind is devoid of mind.
How is it devoid?
It means that neither mind nor body can be apprehended.
"Body" (kāya) refers to the essence; it carries the meaning of a collection upon which [qualities] depend, which is equivalent to the "essence of mind free from thought" in the *Awakening of Faith*.
It has four boundless limits, because it apprehends immeasurable objects in accordance with its own characteristics and its harmonious functioning.
Because the objects apprehended differ, they are termed "self" (*sva*).
Of the four characteristics mentioned above, the first is the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the second is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); these two are both characteristics of the mind.
The third is the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the mind; since its nature and its characteristics are distinct, they together constitute the essence of the mind.
The fourth is the function of the mind.
These four are common to both the defiled and the pure.

The latter four clarify how the pure mind follows conditions: through the fifth, it becomes the sixth and seventh by following the conditions of secondary afflictions; through the eighth, it is formed by following the conditions for birth according to karma.

That which is called the fifth purity is the characteristic of being unstained by its own nature; it is the non-empty nature that serves as the basis for both true and false, as well as for the noble wisdom of self-awakening. Being stained yet unstained is termed "purity of self-nature."

The following two lines refer to being "stained while unstained," meaning that although the six defilements appear as if they possess defilement, they are in fact not identical to afflictions; for while they manifest defilement according to conditions, their inherent nature is eternally free from it.

Regarding the seven fetters (*bandhana*) and non-fetters: the meaning of their being associated with the proclivities (*anuśaya*) or not is no different; it is merely that there is a distinction between their seeds and their manifestation.

Regarding the eighth [category], there are two phrases sharing the name "causal characteristic" (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*): because birth is received according to causes, Bodhisattvas are born through the power of their illusory wisdom and vows, whereas other sentient beings are born into the various realms of existence according to their karma.

The second explanation concerns the dense forest of afflictions (*kleśa-gahana*), which also consists of three parts. Within the specific section, nine phrases are subsumed under three types of matters, because the final seven are combined.
First, from "entering far" up to "the peak of existence" (*bhavāgra*); this refers to the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the four abodes.
"Down to the vajra" refers to its own specific category.
"Long-lasting" means that it has constantly followed [the being] since beginningless time.
"The second, the arising of the boundless," refers to its difficult-to-know characteristic.
"Boundless" refers to the cultivation of immeasurable roots of goodness.
"Inducing" refers to inducing afflictions.
Because afflictions coexist with goodness, they are difficult to discern; these are the "afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" mentioned in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
The preceding section clarified the vertical depth; this section distinguishes the horizontal breadth.

The seven phrases beginning with "simultaneously arising" (*sahaja*) are combined to form the characteristic of defilement, namely the three types of defilement (*saṃkleśa*). This is because these afflictions (*kleśa*) also arise simultaneously with both karma and birth.
This is divided into three parts:
the first three phrases clarify the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa*) by way of their essential nature.
First, "simultaneously arising and inseparable" clarifies that which is bound; this phrase generally clarifies both the subject (the binder) and the object (that which is bound).

That which is bound is precisely the deluded mind; this means that the afflictions and the deluded mind mutually share a common activity, and thus they are said to be "co-arisen," where "arising" refers to their activity.
However, apart from the afflictions, one cannot be called the deluded mind, because if the mind were separated from the afflictions, upon what would the afflictions depend?
When they mutually clothe one another in turn, it is called "not abandoning.
Regarding the single meaning of sleeping and waking: by what are they bound?
It is said that the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) act as the binder.

Latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are precisely what arise as active manifestations (*samudācāra*); because active manifestations stem from latent dispositions, one cannot attain liberation from them, for the manifest and the seed share the same nature as a single affliction.

However, while it will be explained below that latent dispositions do not necessarily coexist with active manifestations, in this context, active manifestations must necessarily depend upon latent dispositions.
Just as there may be seeds without necessarily being sprouts, yet if there are already sprouts, they must depend upon seeds; therefore, it is said that these share one meaning.
As for the third point, regarding those things associated with or dissociated from the mind: these are the objects to which one is bound, and these objects are precisely the True Mind.
If it is defiled by delusion, it is said to be associated with [the afflictions].
This is bondage, not liberation; because the nature of the mind is pure, it is said to be dissociated [from them], demonstrating that liberation is possible.
Second, regarding the two lines following "following the destinies" (*yathāgati*), they clarify the defilement of afflictions with respect to birth.

The treatise states: "Because it is the cause for the arising of the path and realms of bodily phenomena. The term "arising of bodily phenomena" refers to the origination of the accumulation of suffering retribution.
The first phrase refers to the cause of the Path (*mārga-hetu*), and the second phrase refers to the cause of the realms (*dhātu-hetu*).
Regarding the two phrases following "craving and views" (*tṛṣṇā-dṛṣṭi*), they clarify the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*) in terms of karma.
The first of these phrases clarifies that among the three factors [of suffering, origin, and cessation], the causal factor of karma obstructs liberation.

Regarding the "three parts": craving refers to those who, within the pursuit of sensual desires, seek present rewards and practice the pursuit of sense-pleasures; views refer to the pursuit of false asceticism; and delusion refers to those who, within the pursuit of sensual desires, seek present rewards and habitually practice various evil deeds. Therefore, the treatise states: "Sentient beings without precepts, for the sake of slight pleasure in the present, habitually practice various evil deeds; their folly and delusion are extreme."
Pride (*māna*) extends across the upper three realms and is predominantly associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*).
The "seeking of existence" (*bhava-īṣaṇā*) is subsumed under the defilements of birth (*jāti-kleśa*); therefore, it is omitted here.

The [first] three [types of craving] all obstruct liberation; their faults are difficult to uproot, like an arrow embedded in wood. Thus, even when non-Buddhists attain the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), they still remain associated with views and pride.
The first part refers to the general meaning of the treatise.
It may also be understood that attachment (*tṛṣṇā*) and other afflictions pervade the seven consciousnesses; therefore, it is said they "penetrate deeply.
The second line clarifies that these delusions accord with the worldly actions of body, speech, and mind, thereby constituting the cause for their uninterrupted arising.

Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) are clearly explained in the "Chapter on the Minor Marks" (*Anuvyañjanaparivarta*); their characteristics also appear in the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*.
Thirdly, regarding the explanation of karma, within its three distinct divisions, ten phrases constitute nine types of distinctions, as the final two are combined.

First, regarding the distinction of the causes for the paths: it is said that the three natures are generally taught as the causes that lead to the six destinies; these are exclusively either wholesome or unwholesome, each having three grades.

Second, it has already been stated in the [Abhidharma] section on the *bhūmis* that completing karma (*pūrṇakarma*) pertains to all three natures, and that the perfuming of names and words (*nāma-vāk-vāsanā*) also pertains to all three natures, as they are admitted to be causal seeds.

Furthermore, in the seventeenth [chapter] of the *Abhidharmakośa*, the three natures as causes are correlated with five kinds of results, because even the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) can induce results.

Since the Master [Vasubandhu] generally treats all three as causes for the path, his statement—given that the indeterminate does not induce maturation (*vipāka*)—is general in wording but specific in intent.
Regarding the phrase "the two that possess expression" (*savyañjana*) and so forth, this refers to their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and their differentiation.

However, in both the treatise and the sūtra, this passage speaks of "the characteristics of what has been done and what has not yet been done"; this is because, in both cases, volition (*cetanā*) is taken as the intrinsic nature.
The treatise states: "This is of two kinds:

first, at the time of deliberation, this occurs in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), because there is only the single type of volition (*cetanā*) consisting of investigation; thus it explains the meaning of 'not yet having acted.'"
Regarding the second [type], at the time of performing the action, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains that the term "action" (*karma*) refers to determinative volition (*niścaya-cetanā*).

If it pertains to body or speech, it refers solely to impelling volition (*preraka-cetanā*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The volition that moves the body is called bodily action (*kāyakarma*); the volition that initiates speech is called vocal action (*vākkarma*)."

However, since it is now stated that there are "informative" (*vijñapti*) actions and so forth, both informative and non-informative (*avijñapti*) karma each pertain to all three types of action. Regarding informative action, all three are volition (*cetanā*); regarding non-informative action, it is neither mind nor matter (*na cittaṃ na rūpaṃ*).
Alternatively, it is said that they are subsumed under form (*rūpa*); the meaning is as explained elsewhere.

Regarding the three [factors] arising together with the mind and not being separate from it: they arise simultaneously with the mind through the differentiation of skillful means (*upāya*), because they permeate the mind and do not produce fruits separately from it.

This means that this volition of karma arises simultaneously with the motivating mental consciousness; once it has arisen—whether wholesome or unwholesome—it immediately perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) to form seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*).
Because these seeds resemble their perfuming agents, it is said that they do not produce fruits separately; this refers to the sense of non-separation.

Regarding "the four causes, self-nature, and so forth," this refers to the complete exhaustion of the distinctions of the fruit. That is to say, because the causal karma of beginningless time is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), its self-nature perishes moment by moment; therefore, it is said to be "exhausted."

This demonstrates that [the continuum] is not eternal, yet it maintains and carries forward until the fruit is attained; since its efficacy does not perish, it is said that "the accumulated fruit is not lost," which demonstrates that it is not annihilated.
Although the preceding moment ceases, the succeeding moment continues to exist; therefore, it is called "successive."
Furthermore, the cause is immediately perfumed while the fruit arises sequentially, as is the case with the five [consciousnesses] such as the visual consciousness.

Regarding the five, some possess retribution while others do not; the *Śāstra* states: "There is a distinction between those that have already received their fruit and those that have not yet received their fruit."
Karma from past lives that has already been experienced in the present is called "having retribution.
Karma whose subsequent retribution has not yet been experienced is called "without retribution," which does not mean it is entirely non-existent.
There is yet another principle: it is admitted that karma already repented has no retribution, whereas that which has retribution can be known.

Regarding the various retributions of the six types of "black-black" and so forth, this refers to their distinctions; that is, because they are distinguished by being contrasted with four types of karma: the first two are contrasted as black-and-white, and the latter two are contrasted as tainted and untainted.
Regarding the term "black-black," it refers to the first of the four types [of karma], because both its cause and its fruit are evil.
Furthermore, because both its cause and its fruit are associated with ignorance, it constitutes the karma of the three miserable realms.
The term "and so forth" (ādi) applies equally to the remaining three.

That is to say, two are called "white-white karma" because both cause and effect are wholesome, and both are associated with wisdom and clarity; these are the wholesome karmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Third, black-and-white karma refers to the wholesome karma of the desire realm; because its causes consist of a mixture of good and evil, the retributions it receives are likewise a mixture of the desirable and the undesirable.
Fourth, non-black-and-non-white karma refers to all untainted (anāsrava) karma, as it lacks ripening (vipāka).
Regarding the aforementioned black and white karmas, the designation "neither" (ubhayathā) is established.
As for the phrase "the characteristics of manifold retributions," because the three higher realms involve retribution, the treatise states: "Because karma is accumulated and brought to completion."

According to the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa*, black and white karma are explained in terms of their continuity; for there is no single karma or single maturation that is both black and white, as the five characteristics are mutually exclusive.
Regarding "continuity" (*saṃtati*): it refers, for instance, to having a black intention but white means, such as performing acts of respect and service in order to deceive others;
or having a white intention but black means, such as manifesting harsh speech out of compassion for one's disciples.
If one infers by way of meaning, it is precisely because one performs acts of respect with a deceitful mind that [the two] may also occur simultaneously.
For further details, see the eighth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* and the sixteenth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Seventh, regarding the immeasurability of the field: this refers to the differentiation of causes and conditions.
That is to say, with consciousness as the seed and karma as the field, according to the differences in the field’s elevation and depression, the seeds likewise undergo manifold distinctions.
The treatise on the Sūtra states: "The field of karma has immeasurable characteristics.

Regarding the distinction between the eight types of ordinary beings and sages, this refers to the distinction between those who have already accumulated [karma] and those who have not yet accumulated it; for while worldly karma has already been accumulated, supramundane karma has not yet been accumulated.
The ninety-two phrases distinguish between the determinate and indeterminate [karmas].

The preceding phrases clarify the three types of karma regarding the determination or indeterminacy of their timing and retribution: that which is performed in the present and experienced in the present is called "experienced in the present" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*); that which is performed in the present and obtained in the immediately following life is called "experienced upon rebirth" (*upapadyavedanīya*); and that which is performed in the present and only obtained from the third life onward is called "experienced later" (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).

Within these three [types of karma], each has both determinate and indeterminate aspects: that is to say, for the first two [types of] time, the timing is determinate while the retribution may be either determinate or indeterminate;
for the last one, both the timing and the retribution are equally determinate or indeterminate.
The tenth phrase clarifies the certainty or uncertainty regarding vehicles and non-vehicles.

"Vehicles" refers to the three vehicles; practicing exclusively the practices of one's own vehicle is termed "certain," whereas practicing this vehicle at one time and that vehicle at another is termed "uncertain."
"Non-vehicle" refers to the mundane world, because it lacks the sense of being conveyed out [of suffering].
Those with fixed [destiny] are difficult to deliver, whereas those without fixed destiny are easy to deliver.
Regarding the mention of eighty-four thousand within the context of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), since this is the case for the causes—the afflictions—it is likewise so for the karma they give rise to.
The gates of the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth all amount to eighty thousand; conversely, this reveals the gates of the *pāramitās*, the gates of *samādhi*, and so on.
Fourth, the explanation of the faculties consists of two parts:
first, the individual exposition, and second, the conclusion.
Within the distinctions, the ten aspects constitute nine differentiations because the five and six are combined.

One explanation concerns the distinction of the vessel: this refers to the vessels to whom the Dharma is taught. Because the five faculties—faith and the others—are of inferior, middling, and superior grades, they are also categorized as dull, middling, or sharp; that is to say, there are differences in the slowness or speed of their reception of the teachings and principles, as well as the extent of what they receive.

Regarding the distinction of the transformation of the two faculties (*indriya*): the past and future constitute the prior and subsequent limits (*pūrvānta* and *aparānta*), while the present is already fixed;

thus, their difference is discussed in relation to one another. That is to say, among the prior [faculties] of superior, medium, and inferior, they transform in mutual relation across the three time-periods. If the subsequent transforms into medium or superior, the prior faculty is then inferior;
if the subsequent transforms into inferior, the prior faculty increases—this is the meaning of "distinction."
When there is no shifting, there is equilibrium; thus, there is no distinction.
Therefore, the treatise states: "Regarding the preceding and succeeding faculties, the preceding faculty is inferior because it increases toward equilibrium.
This refers to the distinctions among the three natures.

This means that, with respect to the faculties and dispositions of the three vehicles—such as those of the bodhisattvas and others—they differ because they are distinguished as superior, middling, or inferior; the first [category] applies to all three vehicles.

Fourth is the distinction of defilement by the four afflictions, which refers to the five feeling-faculties, such as joy and so forth, because they attain predominance in accordance with the afflictions such as greed and so forth.
The fifth and sixth [verses] clarify the distinction between the determinate and the indeterminate.
In the first phrase, both "vehicles" and "non-vehicles" are explained in terms of being matured or immature.
Within the Mahāyāna, those who are matured are determinate, while those who are immature are indeterminate.
Within the Hīnayāna, those who are mature are not fixed, as they may turn toward the Mahāyāna;
those who are immature are fixed, as each attains liberation according to their own vehicle.
If one considers the mundane world to be a non-vehicle, those who are mature are not fixed, as they may be transformed and led into the Path.
Because the retribution for those who are not yet mature is already fixed, one temporarily sets them aside.
This is the "pure relinquishment" mentioned in the *Lokottara-parivarta*, wherein one awaits the proper time before transforming them.
The latter phrase, "purely matured and pliant," refers exclusively to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding "the six [faculties] that follow the net of the faculties, turning lightly and perishing," this refers to the differentiation of conforming activity.
This is because one knows that the eye and other faculties conform to their respective objects, thereby attaining predominance (*adhipatya*).
Within this, there are three kinds of conforming practice (*anuloma-caryā*):

first, conforming practice based on the body (*kāya*). This refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) being mutually and successively bound to one another, like fish or birds in a net from which they cannot escape; thus they are called the "net of the faculties" (*indriya-jāla*). This constitutes the internal object (*adhyātma-viṣaya*).

Second is the conforming practice of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya-anuloma-carita*), which means that its substance is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); because it arises and abides for only a brief time, it is called "light," and because it is easily subject to change and extinction, it is called "transforming and decaying.

Third is the conforming practice of grasping signs through contemplative cultivation (*bhāvanā-carita-nimitta-grahaṇa-anuloma-carita*). This practice takes external objects as its domain; as the treatise and the sutra state, this is "grasping signs. This [third category] is omitted in the present text, or it may be subsumed within the "net of the faculties" (*indriya-jāla*).
Seventh is the distinction of the purity of the śrāvakas.

Because they are superior to the practices of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, and because their faculties of the two vehicles are capable of achieving [liberation] through the extinction of hindrances, afflictions are unable to destroy them.
The eighth is the distinction of the purity of the bodhisattvas; this applies to all three types, whether subject to regression or not.

Regarding the ninth, "following from afar" and so forth, this demonstrates the distinction of the inclusion of all faculties, meaning that the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) collectively subsume all faculties.
Third, there are two stages: first, the initial practice, which is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*);

second, the preparatory application (*upāya*), which is the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), so called because it is precisely during the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*) that it is termed "preparatory application."

As for the maturation of the three retributions, this refers to the faculty of one who possesses full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*); that is to say, it arises together with the preceding faculties of faith and so forth, along with the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*). Because it follows [the preceding states] through their varying degrees of superiority and inferiority from beginning to end, it is called "remote following" (*dūranusārin*).
These three faculties are so designated because they exercise predominance over the cultivation of the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and the attainment of nirvāṇa.
Among the nine faculties mentioned above, the first two pertain to faith and the others;
the third, fifth, and seventh pertain to all three vehicles and thus apply to all faculties.
The fourth is based on the five feelings;
the sixth is based on the eye and so forth;
the ninth is based on the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).

Of the twenty-two faculties, nineteen have already been clarified; the male, female, and life faculties need not be further distinguished here, while the remainder are explained in brief according to the "Faculties Chapter" (*Indriya-nirdeśa*) of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Since these can be further subdivided into immeasurable categories, the text concludes by stating "up to eighty-four thousand.
Fifth, there are three types of "dense forests," namely: views (*dṛṣṭi*), dispositions (*gotra*), and desires (*chanda*).
These three accord with the nature of the faculties (*indriya*) in their entry [into the path]; by citing one, the other three cases may be inferred, and thus all are briefly illustrated.
Sixth, the explanation of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*): first the general, then the specific.
In general, both the *Jin* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) and the treatises on the sūtras designate these as "proclivities" (*anuśaya*).
The treatise explains that they are called "conformities" because their meaning is that of pursuing and binding.
Just as a public official’s messenger pursues people and seizes them when finding an opportunity to bind them, so too are these proclivities.
Because the latent store-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) follows and entangles [the mind],
this refers exclusively to seeds (*bīja*) and differs from the Lesser Vehicle schools.
There are twelve distinct phrases, which the treatise subsumes into two categories:
The first six [verses] clarify where [the afflictions] follow along; the latter six clarify by what means they follow along.
Now, for the first [section], there are five parts.
First, combining the first two lines, it clarifies the locus with respect to the mind.

The first phrase follows along with the retributive mind (*vipākacitta*), precisely manifesting the latent storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is the place where one has long been in deep sleep.
It is called "profound" because it has existed since beginningless time and is subtle and difficult to perceive.
The latter phrase follows upon the non-retributive mind (*avipāka-citta*), which is precisely the discrimination of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

Since the phenomenal consciousness (*sūtra-vijñāna*) arises without departing from manifest phenomena, it is simply called "mind" (*citta*), referring to the point where there is a temporary turning back.
Regarding the two aspects of association and non-association, these are clarified in terms of the three realms (*dhātu*).

[Each realm] is associated only with the mind of its own respective realm and not with the mind of another realm; therefore, the treatise states: "The desire, form, and formless realms are distinguished as superior, intermediate, and inferior."

Because the afflictions of the formless realm are subtle, they are designated as "lower" [in intensity]; although their nature as latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is fully present, there is also the sense of non-concomitance with respect to their manifest activity.
Regarding the third aspect, "following for a long duration," this is clarified by way of the stages (*bhūmi*).
The treatise states: "Because it conforms [to the mind] up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Now, the term "Peak of Existence" carries two general meanings:
First, reaching the summit of the vajra; second, reaching the summit of the three realms of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Here, taking the meaning common to both the Mahayana and Hinayana, it is simply called "summit of existence" (*bhavāgra*).
While the sutras merely speak of "entering from afar," here it is said "for a long duration," because from time immemorial one has ascended as far as the summit of the ninth stage.
Fourth is the characteristic of being unextracted since beginningless time; this clarifies the locus in terms of time.
Since the locus is boundless, time is likewise without beginning.

Only wisdom can terrify the enemy of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); however, because one has never yet possessed the wisdom born of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one is unable to extract them.
Regarding the fifth point, "being contrary to all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and so forth," this clarifies the locus in terms of practice.

Because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) persist and follow along, they prevent worldly meditative concentrations from extinguishing craving, views, and other such mental states, and thus fail to accord with correct cultivation; for these reasons, they are termed "contrary."
Therefore, the following verse states: "The objects of meditative concentration are dispelled, yet one still regresses.
Below the section on the "Three Realms," it clarifies by what [factors] one is pursued, thereby revealing the characteristics of that pursuit.
Due to these characteristics, they are called *anuśaya* (latent tendencies).
There are six kinds:
first, they persistently follow along without being severed within the three higher realms of existence (*bhava*).

The reason why the three realms of existence (tridhātu) continue in a similar succession without interruption is that these latent tendencies (anuśaya) act as fetters; it is like a person who has fallen asleep and is unable to rise from bed.

Second is "persistence over a long duration," which means that from beginningless time as mentioned above, it causes the mental continuum to arise without limit, just like the dream-consciousness of one who is asleep.

Third, regarding the opening of the gates of the various sense bases: first, there is the arising and following along [of consciousness] within the body, which means that upon the aforementioned body, the resultant mind and the non-resultant mind clearly follow along, just as one who sleeps sees and hears things in a dream.
Within this, there are two meanings:

first, when the six types of consciousness arise through the gathering [of conditions] at the gates of the various faculties such as the eyes, it causes [the mind] to arise simultaneously with them; thus it is called "opening the gates," which clarifies that [the mind] externally pursues the expedient mind.
The second treatise states, "and because of the perfuming of the ālayavijñāna. This clarifies that the retributive mind is internally perfumed.
In the sutra, following the character "gate" (mù), there is additionally the character "accumulation" (jí); this refers to the ālayavijñāna as the mind that accumulates and gives rise [to phenomena].
However, because these various points apply universally, the meaning is implied in this sutra.
Fourth, "solidity that is difficult to cure" refers to unrealities that persist; this means that when practicing dhyāna and so forth, one does not attain the true antidote.
The unreal is as solid as deep sleep; because one cannot experience deep touch, a great sound has no way to arise.
Regarding the five stages, locations, and so forth, they are subtle and follow along.
This is because, within the nine stages from here up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the body of afflictions follows along with the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Now, these nine stages have two meanings:
first, regarding the nine stages of the three realms, although [the afflictions] are all fully present, they are not perceived because they are subtle.
The degree to which they are established is termed "non-attainment," just as one who is asleep in the world might claim to be awake within a dream.
Second, because they take wholesome wisdom as their basis across the nine stages, yet still persist even in the tenth stage, they are termed "subtle."
It is not accomplished because within this stage there is still a portion to be severed;
thus, the following verse states: "Only upon the extinction by the vajra-path is it finally completed.

Sixth is the absence of the persistence of suffering, meaning that only non-conceptual wisdom and the supramundane noble path can extract one from it, just as one must touch a sleeping person to wake them.
The seventh [section] explains the ten phrases regarding the "dense forest of taking birth," first in general and then in detail.
The treatise summarizes these into eight points:
first, the variety of bodies, meaning that their forms and types are manifold;...
Second, the diversity of karmic causes;
third, the diversity of abodes;
fourth, the diversity of the upper and lower realms regarding form and perception as expressed in the four and five pairs of categories.
Fifth, the variety of external causes of form, namely the field and so forth, because they take external things as a common analogy;
sixth, the variety of the self-substance, wherein name-and-form and consciousness arise together, being mutually dependent and inseparable, as this is the retributional self-substance;
seventh, the variety of the fundamental causes that conform to rebirth, namely ignorance and craving as the basis, which conform to rebirth by seeking existence and causing existence to continue.

The last two phrases of the eighth [section] collect the various aspects of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). That is to say, the three types of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*) are all causes of origination (*samudaya*), yet they merely accumulate the fruit of suffering; therefore, it is said to be "various."
The preceding line reveals that desire has two types of seeking:
"desiring to receive" is the seeking of desire, because one pursues it incessantly through craving and grasping;
"desiring to be born" is the seeking of existence, because once craving arises, one spontaneously attains a superior body within the three realms of existence and further gathers a retinue.
The phrase "beginningless attachment and delight" reveals the faults of the two aforementioned types of seeking.

The subsequent phrase refers to the "seeking of a false holy life" (*mithyā-brahmacarya-paryeṣaṇā*); because the mind grasps with attachment, one does not understand the saṃsāra of the three realms. Out of craving, one seeks the various marks of the three realms—whether small, large, or immeasurable—and falsely claims them to be *nirvāṇa*. This is because some consider slapping their bellies to be the Way, while others reckon the non-perception (*asaṃjñi*) or neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) realms to be *nirvāṇa*.
In the eighth section, the explanation of *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies), there is also first a general treatment followed by a specific one.
Since the term "habitual tendency" generally encompasses two meanings, it cannot be restricted solely to the residual habits of Arhats.
Although "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) is the general designation, within the specific [explanations] all speak of "perfuming" (*bhāvanā*).
"Perfuming" means to imbue or infuse, like an external fragrance;
"habituation" means to practice or learn, which applies exclusively to sentient beings.
Habitual practice necessarily perfumes [the mind], thereby forming a latent disposition; thus, it is called "habitual energy" (*vāsanā*).

That is, the *ālaya-vijñāna* serves as the object of perfuming, because it constantly abides in a single category, is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), and is therefore susceptible to being perfumed.

The preceding seven evolving consciousnesses act as the perfuming agents (*bhāvakas*); because they possess the power of arising and ceasing, characterized by increase and decrease, the perfumer and the perfumed are mutually conjoined, and thus it is called "perfuming" (*vāsanā*).
This is as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the second chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

According to the *Awakening of Faith*, true suchness (*tathatā*) can also act as an internal perfuming influence, while Buddhas, spiritual friends, and so forth serve as external perfuming influences; through the conjunction of these internal and external factors, the "fragrance" (or predisposition) is formed.
In the preceding section, although hearing the teaching and so forth are also capable of being received through consciousness, consciousness was judged to be the perfuming agent (*bhāvanā*).

Now, this applies to both; since the text mentions both the cause as perfuming and the result as equal [to it], we know for certain that the meaning of "perfuming seeds" is the formation of a constituent part (*dhātu*).
Within this [section on] distinctions, there are ten types of differentiation:
first, the distinction between giving rise to results in the present versus not giving rise to them in the present.

This means that when past causes of wholesome or unwholesome karma give rise to present results, they are termed "active" (*caryā*); when they do not so give rise, they are termed "inactive" (*acaryā*).
For example, when a person practices giving, they now obtain a human body and continue to delight in giving; this is "habituation through causes.
Second, "pervasion according to the realm" refers to the distinctions in the permeation of the paths.

As if descended from heaven, it remains fresh and pure even now; it extensively elucidates the cultivation of the Way, as in the *Mahāteja-pradīpa-ṛṣi-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, which constitutes the cultivation of the fruit.
The first two [points] above are all spoken in contrast to past faults.
As for the third, "following the conduct of sentient beings," it refers to the differentiation produced by associating with sentient beings and their habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*).

Since this constitutes the conditioning of conditions, one ought to distance oneself from evil and draw near to the good, being careful regarding what one habituates oneself to. This is why kings of old did not establish stables within monasteries, but established them at slaughterhouses.
Regarding "the four [factors] following karma and so forth," these refer to the distinctions in the perfuming of meritorious deeds and afflictions.
"Meritorious deeds" explains the character *karman* (karma) in the sūtra; it refers to the performance of activities and serves to distinguish them from the causes of karma.
Just as the son of a goldsmith should be taught counting the breaths and so forth;
regarding the habit-energies of afflictions, it is like a person who is fond of sleep, such that sleep increases when practiced;
regarding the five wholesome and unwholesome [actions] and so forth, they are the distinctions of the perfuming of wholesome karma and the like.
This karma is itself the cause of karma, because it is designated as "karma" in relation to its future fruit by virtue of its three natures, such as being wholesome and so forth.
For example, in one who has practiced giving for a long time, the mind of giving becomes increasingly intense.
The first three [categories] clarify habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) solely in relation to the present life.
Regarding "the sixth follows into subsequent existence" (*ṣaṣṭhaḥ punarbhavānugataḥ*): this refers to the differentiation of perfuming (*vāsana*) within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Since the intermediate state follows immediately after the fundamental existence (*pūrvabhava*), even those practicing the holy life (*brahmacārin*) remain free from defiled desire while within that intermediate state.
Regarding the sevenfold sequence, it refers to the sequence of the ripening of fruits and the differentiation of perfuming.
That is to say, having cultivated wholesome or unwholesome karma, one experiences the sequence of those fruits within the various realms of existence during subsequent states of being.
The sequence of the cultivation and its fruit is likewise without discrepancy.
The preceding two cases explain the perfuming (*vāsanā*) by referring to the present in relation to what follows.
Regarding the "eight non-interruptions" and so forth, these distinguish the causes of worldly meditation through their differences in perfuming.
That is to say, all untainted concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*) are called "world-transcending dhyāna" (*lokottara-dhyāna*), and the cultivation and study of the untainted is their cause.

Because afflictions (*kleśa*) have not yet been severed, even though one cultivates the untainted, one is still pulled by and follows after afflictions; reaching the untainted is termed "distant travel," where "traveling" also carries the sense of "entering."

Regarding "the nine that are both real and unreal": this refers to the distinction between the practice of those within the same Dharma and that of outsiders, as well as the differentiation of liberation and perfuming.
"Real" is explained as being within the same Dharma, because the three vehicles share the same Buddha-Dharma.
The explanations of the heterodox schools are not real; they are called "heterodox" because they lie outside of the Buddha-dharma.
Practice is the cause of the former two [liberation and nirvana].
Liberation is the fruit of the former two.
Each possesses its own habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), because they were accustomed to practicing their original method.
