Having previously cultivated the Hīnayāna, even though they now study the Mahāyāna, their prior Hīnayāna habits will first manifest; the rest may be understood by analogy.
This thus clarifies both the deviant and the correct simultaneously.
When explained in terms of cultivation and realization, it also contains the characteristics of residual habits from the three vehicles.
The ten modes of cultivation and their distinctions pertain exclusively to the correct [path], as they are based upon its vision and hearing.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in its section on the "Peaceful Practices" (*anuvartana*), instructs that one should not associate with those of the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*), for fear that such association will lead to the formation of seeds [of those dispositions].

Of the ten types mentioned above, the first seven concern time; by examining the three periods and the three realms of existence in relation to one another, it is clarified that the cultivation [of habits] applies to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
The eighth clarifies that evil follows upon the wholesome.
The latter two [stages] concern the various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of persons;
they are able to fully comprehend these, thereby bringing about the Tathāgata’s wisdom of habitual tendencies that are free from habitual tendencies.
The ninth [section] explains the "dense forest" (*gahana*) of the three clusters (*triskandha*); this also proceeds first by way of a general summary and subsequently by way of specific details.
The treatise generally establishes five categories.

The first is the general category of those with the nature for nirvāṇa and those without the nature for nirvāṇa. Within the three vehicles, there is the distinction of being exclusively determined: "without" refers to the wrongly fixed (*mithyātva-niyata*) and "with" refers to the rightly fixed (*samyaktva-niyata*), as each is determined within its own respective vehicle.
Apart from this indeterminate [category], the treatise does not explain it in detail.

This is explained by way of stages according to spiritual lineage (*gotra*): those outside the ranks of the ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) lack *nirvāṇa*; the noble ones (*ārya*) of the three vehicles definitely possess it; and those within the ranks of the ordinary person are indeterminate.
Furthermore, regarding the duration of a single lifetime, they are not ultimately non-existent.

Second, there is the distinction between the causes of wholesome and unwholesome conduct; this classification of the three groups (*tri-nikāya*) is based on the differentiation between understanding and delusion. That is to say, right view is the cause of wholesome conduct, while wrong view is the cause of unwholesome conduct; because these two views invariably give rise to their respective two types of conduct, they are termed "determined" (*niyata*).

Regarding the statement that both are indeterminate: because there is no decisive discernment through right wisdom, yet one does not deny cause and effect, if one follows [the path] one may ascend to purity, but if one indulges [in negligence] one will fall into degradation; therefore, they are called "indeterminate."
The lower indefinite [factors] may be understood by analogy with this, and thus the treatise does not explain them.
The distinction between the causes for the three evil destinies and the wholesome destinies is made here in terms of karmic actions.

Regarding the distinction between the four types of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and *śrāvakas*, this is categorized according to their respective stages. The "eight wrongs" (*aṣṭa-mithyātva*) are established as the opposite of the "eightfold right path" (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). The stage of the non-Buddhists is fixed in error, while the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*) is fixed in the nature of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*), because they have already entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The first three roots of goodness are termed "indeterminate.
The five distinctions among bodhisattvas are categorized here according to the gains and losses of those who practice the Mahāyāna.
Attachment to the false constitutes loss, namely the six hindrances.
The "noble path" (*āryamārga*) refers to the attainment [of the stages], namely the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and so forth.
The third section provides a summary of abiding; the text belongs to the entry into practice.
Since the intent of the treatise summarizes the preceding three, it states that only when these three kinds of matters are accomplished can one abide in this stage.
The fourth major section, beginning with "Having dwelled in this stage," clarifies the exposition of accomplishment.

It also subsumes the practice of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-karma*), because its eloquence and benefits are for the most part similar to those [of the aforementioned practices].
The text consists of two parts:
first, a restatement of the preceding section to provide a general clarification, namely that one must understand the mental activities before being able to speak well;
second, from the words "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, a detailed exposition on how such speech is accomplished.
There are three kinds of accomplishment:
first, accomplishment of wisdom, which refers to knowing the Dharma, knowing the vessel [of the disciple], and knowing the appropriate means of transformation;
second, accomplishment of vocal action, which is the ability to initiate speech.
Third, the accomplishment of mastery as a Dharma Master, because one attains dhāraṇīs and so forth to perfect those virtues.
Each is distinguished by the title "Son of the Buddha.
Now, for the first [of these], there are two parts:
First, the explanation of the dharmas according to what is known; second, from "all" onwards, the explanation according to the vessel that serves as the support.
How do these two differ?
In the preceding text, wisdom was established and entry was established, such that the first three were each known individually.
Now, this [section] summarizes [the preceding material], applying the Dharma to the capacities of those who receive it.

First, regarding the "objects of knowledge" (*jñeya-dharma*): these refer to the distinctions in liberation among the three vehicles and the one vehicle, each encompassing both the teachings (*śāsana*) and their realization (*adhigama*).
The Path of Teaching (*śāsana-mārga*) is so called because it transforms sentient beings, causing their capacities to ripen.
The Path of Realization (*adhigama-mārga*) is so called because it delivers sentient beings, enabling them to attain liberation through the correct essence of deliverance.
Within the section concerning what these two depend upon, the text consists of three parts:
First is the general explanation; next, from "able to follow" onwards, is the specific manifestation; and finally, from "causing to arise" onwards, is the conclusion regarding the benefits.
The Master of the Treatise comprehensively categorizes these as seven kinds of vessels:
first, the teaching of the Dharma in accordance with the vessel, which he himself explains by saying that one bestows remedial teachings according to those who are to be delivered.
Regarding the two lines in the general [section], the latter line explains the Dharma that is taught, while the former line refers to the vessel [of the recipient].

Within the specific [section], the initial part concerns the one who is able to follow and subsequently teach the Dharma; this corresponds to what was previously described as the Dharma being taught. The intermediate section concerning the various groves of faculties and so forth refers precisely to the vessels [of the recipients].
In this context, according to the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra*, the word "mind" (*citta*) follows "sentient beings" (*sattva*), referring thus to the "dense forest of mind.
This generally constitutes five types of vessels:
first, the minds, faculties, dispositions, natures, and inclinations of sentient beings clarify the completion of the vessels for the Dharma to be taught.

That is to say, among the eleven forests, these five specifically manifest those who have already become vessels for faith and so forth; they are distinguished because they can be taught according to their faculties and inclinations.
Second, there is a difference in their conduct, which contains two meanings:
first, regarding the practice that is performed, they are called "vessels for various different practices," which refers to the practitioners of superior faculties and so forth.
The second is the sphere of practice, namely the sphere of those with superior faculties and so forth, which is called the "vessel of analogy.
This is because it serves as a general analogy for the aforementioned five [faculties].
It is like the cultivation of crops in the world, which, when provided with five causal conditions, results in the growth of the planted things until they are fit for use.

First, it is a sentient being; second, it possesses faculties that augment its power of growth; third, it has the nature of being capable of arising; fourth, it contains moisture and is ready to manifest; fifth, its arising is certain.
Because it illustrates the superior mind and so forth, it is called "analogy" (*aupamya*).

Fourth, regarding the distinctions among the various aggregates: this refers to the transformation of the faculties, whether fixed or unfixed, as well as the receptacle [of the body], which also includes those of superior faculties and so on.

5. The phrase "also following" (*api-anu*) below refers to the eloquence regarding the capacity [of the disciples] (*vibhakti-vaśitā*). Because the afflictions and karmic latencies produced by them are difficult to abandon, one must employ skillful eloquence in acting as a companion (*sahacara*) in order to be able to transform them.
The third section, "The Formation of Benefits," refers to the vessel capable of being carried forth by means of the causes corresponding to the respective vehicles (*yāna*).
This is because the various meanings discussed above do not transcend the liberation of one's own vehicle.
The second part, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells here," concerns the accomplishment of verbal action (*vāk-karman*).
The section is divided into two parts:
first, a general clarification of the virtues of complete exposition; second, from "By means of the immeasurable" onwards, the actual clarification of the accomplishment of verbal karma.
Regarding the first part, it is also the accomplishment of wisdom, because possessing the conduct of a Dharma teacher is itself wisdom.
As for "preaching," it refers to protecting the Tathāgata’s treasury of Dharma through the act of teaching.
This means internally upholding wisdom while externally expressing it through speech.
What is meant by being "endowed with the practice of a Dharma-preacher"?
Because the profound and subtle meaning possesses twenty kinds of merit:

(1) knowing the proper time; (2) correct intention; (3) suddenness; (4) continuity; (5) gradualness; (6) sequence; (7) the progressive sequence of the meaning of the phrases; (8) demonstration; (9) gladdening; (10) exhortation; (11) possession of virtue; (12) non-defamation; (13) non-confusion; (14) accordance with the Dharma; (15) conformity to the assembly; (16) a mind of loving-kindness; (17) a mind of peace and security; (18) a mind of compassion; (19) non-attachment to fame and profit; and (20) not praising oneself or disparaging others. A detailed explanation is as found in the treatise.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that one who possesses the seven kinds of skillful knowledge is called a Great Dharma Master; this is largely the same as the present [text].
The treatise of Maitreya says that one who possesses ten virtues is called a Great Dharma Master, which fully encompasses the meaning:

(1) skillfully knowing the meaning of the Dharma, (2) being able to proclaim it extensively, (3) being fearless in the midst of the assembly, (4) possessing uninterrupted eloquence, (5) teaching with skillful means, (6) practicing in accordance with the Dharma, (7) being complete in dignified deportment, (8) being courageous and diligent, (9) having no weariness of body or mind, and (10) achieving the power of patience. When these are compared, they are likewise the same.

In the second section, which correctly elucidates verbal action (*vākkarman*), there is first a brief explanation, followed by a detailed exposition beginning with the passage "This bodhisattva, by means of the Dharma...

Regarding the former, the names and essences are first revealed: externally, the manifestation of the meaning of the Dharma through the bodhisattva’s exquisite speech is called the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);
internally, their arising from wisdom is called the four unhindered cognitions (*jñāna*).

Next, to define its essence: this wisdom has the untainted subsequently attained wisdom (*anāsrava-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as its essence; therefore, it is called "skillful," which refers to the aforementioned wisdom that knows the Dharma and knows the capacities of beings.
As for the unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), it may be understood as encompassing both the fundamental and the subsequently attained wisdoms.
Next, from "This bodhisattva" onwards, the superiority [of this stage] is revealed by way of its position;
because it is attained spontaneously at this stage, having been partially acquired at the first stage, there is no temporary relinquishing of it.
Following that, from "What are they? onwards, the names are interrogated and listed.
Because wisdom takes phenomena as its object without obstruction, both phenomena and equality are the domains of wisdom.
From the perspective of their objects, they are divided into four:

first, "phenomena" (dharma) refers to the essence of phenomena, meaning the intrinsic nature of phenomena; because it possesses the functions of maintaining and upholding, it is the conventional reality subsumed within the two types of emptiness, which is the true conventional object.
The treatise states: "It is comprised of the dharmas that arise while remaining far removed from the two extremes, such as the characteristic of resistance in form," and so forth.
Regarding the "two meanings," these refer to the essence of the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*).

They are termed "distinctive objects" within the essence of the dharma because they constitute the realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) subsumed under the aforementioned two kinds of emptiness.

The treatise states: "Because it is the objective realm of the wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūtajñāna*), which is comprised within the phenomena arising from the very abandonment of the two extremes.

Now, as for attaining this true wisdom: because the Bodhisattva abides in wisdom regarding the objects comprised within the dual grasping at arising and phenomena, they seek to realize that form and so forth are merely illusory; thus, while being conventional, they are the ultimate. This is the distinct meaning within those very forms and so forth.
This is precisely the intention of Master Huiyuan.
It is like the principle that "neither arising nor ceasing" constitutes the meaning of impermanence.
Furthermore, one may not restrict this to the two truths; here, "dharmas" refers to their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), while "meanings" refers to their specific distinctions.
This refers to the eleven characteristics of false discrimination regarding form and so forth; these constitute the specific meaning.
As for the term "knowledge of reality as it is," it means to accord with the facts.
Regarding the three terms, they refer to correctly attaining [it] and bestowing it upon sentient beings.
This means that having acquired the local dialects, one speaks them for others.
Therefore, the treatise states: "Within the sphere of knowledge as it truly is regarding those [dialects], one possesses correct awareness in accordance with what others prefer."
This explanation is correct.
Because one gives in accordance with the speech of others while maintaining full awareness, this explanation is given to sentient beings.
As for the fourth, "eloquence" (pratibhāna), it refers to correctly seeking to provide [teachings] through immeasurable gateways.
This means that eloquence (*pratibhāna*) refers to a specific sense within speech; the seven types of analytical exposition (*saptavidha-pratisaṃvid*) are termed "infinite gateways.

The *Śāstra* states: "It is because one possesses correct knowledge regarding the speech preferred by others in various circumstances, and thus provides it according to their understanding through infinite varieties of meaningful discourse."

Regarding the second part, the extensive exposition: in reality, these four [categories] encompass all things; however, for the sake of a complete enumeration, ten gates are listed, each of which has further subdivisions.
The treatise states: "The latter five are pure, meaning they refer to the practices and fruits of the three vehicles."
This reveals that the preceding five [categories] constitute the doctrine and principle of the Three Vehicles, which apply to both the defiled and the pure.
As for the statement "ten," the first is based on specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), meaning that one knows the essential bodies of phenomena (*dharmas*) are each distinct.

Second is the basis of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which refers to knowing the principles of phenomena (*dharma*), because both their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) each possess a commonality of principle.
Third is the aspect of activity (*ākāra*), which distinguishes phenomena according to time, because they undergo transition and flux throughout the three periods of time.
The first three types of knowledge refer to meaning, which is that which is explained;
the fourth is the knowledge of characteristics, which refers to the teaching.
These four all pertain to the objects of knowledge.
1. The characteristic of the five wisdoms, which refers to that which knows;
2. The characteristic of being free from the conceit of "I," which clarifies purity in terms of what is abandoned;
3. The characteristic of the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna, which refers to the practice undertaken.
The first two [verses] comprehensively explain the practices and fruits of all vehicles, while the latter three specifically concern the One Vehicle.
The characteristics of the eight bodhisattva stages pertain to causal practice;
the final two [verses] concern the knowledge of the fruit.
The ninth, the mark of the Tathāgata-ground, is defined by its essence; the tenth, the mark of performing and maintaining [the Dharma], is defined by its function.
Nevertheless, among these ten, while the meanings of the dharmas differ, the latter two are largely the same.
All [of these] involve *pratibhāna* (eloquence) in explaining the meaning of the Dharma, whereas *pratibhāna* specifically refers to a distinct aspect within eloquence.
Furthermore, there are cases where one uses eloquence (*nirukti*) to explain the Dharma, and *pratibhāna* to explain the meaning.
Among the ten [powers], each possesses four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), which constitute four kinds of characteristics.

First: regarding the four kinds of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*): first, the specific characteristic of the arising of phenomena, which refers to knowing that form has the characteristic of being subject to change and obstruction, and so forth.
Second, the specific characteristic of differentiation, which refers to knowing that form consists of eleven bases (*āyatana*), and so forth.
The first two [of these four aspects] distinguish the phenomena and their meanings based on the general and the particular;

the latter two distinguish them based on the meaning of having a single essence. Regarding the third, the "firm conception of specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇasaṃjñā*): it is the basis for the arising of speech, and it also involves the mind of wisdom grasping those two kinds of characteristics: first, the characteristics of all phenomena as they are personally realized; second, the characteristics appropriate to the various verbal expressions suited to those to be converted.
To explain the dharmas one has realized to others using their own terminology, speaking for them without error, is called "firmness.
As the *Śāstra* on the Sūtra says regarding "indestructible," "destruction" refers precisely to error.

Fourth, regarding the differentiation of those perceptions (*saṃjñā-viśeṣa*), the meaning is the same as above; however, by means of an uninterrupted sequence and numerous diverse names, one makes that meaning firm so that others may find delight in it, which is called "uninterrupted and inexhaustible."

This first gate of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) is comprehensive; thus, it was also relied upon for explanation within the preceding general overview of this treatise, and it is frequently relied upon in various sūtras and śāstras.

Second is the gate of common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which distinguishes between the nature (*svabhāva*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) regarding the meaning of phenomena (*dharmārtha*).

First, the common characteristic of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the fact that all phenomena share the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) as their own nature.

Second, the common characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*): they share the same arising and ceasing. This means that by contemplating the gate of impermanence (*anityatā*), one enters the first phrase through the characteristic of arising and ceasing; because of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), the sphere of the wisdom of selflessness is established. Thus, arising and ceasing are themselves the meaning of permanence.
Third, because all phenomena share the common characteristic of being conventional designations (*prajñapti*), they are said to be "established.

Since the phenomena thus established are already conventional designations, to further discuss them by means of verbal expressions that are themselves conventional designations is called "uninterrupted discourse."

The fourth is the common characteristic of conventional designations (prajñapti), which means that without destroying the preceding conventional designation, one can further express it through various and boundless other conventional designations; therefore, the term "conventional designation" is repeated.
Within the third aspect of manifestation, the meaning of phenomena is distinguished according to the three periods of time.
First, regarding the aspect of arising:

because it is dependently originated within the present life, even if one knows the past and future, they are also termed "present," since all three periods of time are, in fact, the present of their respective eras.
Therefore, the treatise states: "Because the past and future are subsumed within their respective worlds.

Regarding the characteristics (*ākāra*) of that which has already arisen and that which has not yet arisen, even if one knows the present, it is termed "past" or "future," because the present is the home of the past and the home of the future.

This refers to the names and dharmas known in the present world; to perceive them as contrary or erroneous is what has not yet been understood regarding the present, and this is precisely the meaning of the "object-sphere of Bodhisattva wisdom.

The three types of entities are provisional designations for the modes of activity (*ākāra*); they are so called because, when taken collectively, the entities of the three periods of time are explained without error.

The fourth explains the characteristics of the phenomena being discussed; however, since the phenomena explained do not fall outside the general characteristics of things within the three periods of time, it says "each and every period.
It merely provides a detailed elucidation of various distinct phenomena and dharmas, and thus it is called the "elucidation of boundless dharmas."
In the fourth section on the exposition of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the dharma and its meaning are distinguished based on the fundamental interpretation:
first, the characteristic of the sūtra (*sūtralakṣaṇa*), which merely indicates the dharma;
second, the characteristic of explanation (*vyākhyānalakṣaṇa*), which concerns the names and meanings.
Third is the characteristic of conformity, because it accords with the speech and sounds of each respective type.

Fourth is the characteristic of corresponding exposition, which means that according to what dharma a person’s mind desires to hear and what kind of analogy is appropriate for them, the teaching corresponds to that mind.
The fifth is the characteristic of knowledge (*jñānalakṣaṇa*), which distinguishes the meaning of phenomena (*dharmārtha*) by way of their categories (*dharmajāti*).
First is directly perceived knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*).
Second is inferential knowledge (*anumānajñāna*); "inferential" (*anumāna*) is equivalent to "categorical" (*anvaya*).

However, the objects of knowledge are precisely the phenomena of the two truths, while the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are their unimpeded essence; thus, the designations established based on this essence differ from those used previously.

Furthermore, while the knowledges such as dharma and inference (*anumāna*) are common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, the four analytical knowledges are restricted solely to the Mahāyāna; hence the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "Only bodhisattvas possess them."
"Even if they exist among the śrāvakas, they are called 'non-existent' because they are so few.
If one considers them from the perspective of what is observed by the two types of wisdom, they apply to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
however, if one considers them from the perspective of the observing wisdom itself, they are restricted exclusively to the Mahāyāna.
Within the Mahāyāna, based on the contemplation of the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*), the categories of phenomena are established.

First, regarding "dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna*), it is called "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) because it contemplates suchness (*tathatā*); that is, one contemplates that the two truths, though distinct, are identical in their suchness and not different.
Second is the wisdom of inference (*anvaya-jñāna*), which is the wisdom that observes and correctly discerns the aforementioned subject of observation.
Other [types of] inference are likewise.
What is it that is being inferred?
The preceding knowledge is as explained before;
its distinction lies in its being "as-it-is" (*yathābhūta*).

Third is the wisdom of skillful means for attainment, which refers to this Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*); it is conventionally designated as "true" based on the conventional truth, and because it is subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it is called "worldly wisdom."
If one wishes to attain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), provisional designations (*prajñapti*) are employed as skillful means (*upāya*).

Regarding the "attainment of wisdom through the fourfold": although explained by means of worldly knowledge, it accords with the ultimate truth and is not inverted or divergent; only then is it termed "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*), and thus called "skillful" (*kauśalya*), because through it one can realize the ultimate truth.

The remainder is as explained in the ninth fascicles of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā*, and in the sixteenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; this was already briefly clarified above in the commentary on the "Chapter on Dedication."
Within the sixth characteristic, the absence of ego-conceit (*nirmāna*), the Dharma and its meaning are distinguished according to the ultimate and conventional truths.
First, because there is no self in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is called "one characteristic.
As for the term "indestructible," it means that this absence of self is indestructible.
If one says, "I know non-self" or "I realize non-self," then one destroys non-self, because there is a distinction between subject and object.
Since both conventional and ultimate truths are non-self, it is said to be "the aggregates and so forth."

One is deluded regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and clings to them as a collection that constitutes a self; one is deluded regarding the elements (*dhātu*) and clings to them as distinct causes for a self, because one reckons them according to their different lineages.
One is deluded regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*) and clings to them as a self of desire, because one reckons them as gateways for birth through which [objects] are received and entered.

Those who, being deluded regarding the truths and dependent origination, compose treatises on a self—all of which clarify that cause and effect involve volitional activity—are thus [clinging to] both the *dharma-ātman* and the *pudgala-ātman*.

Now, by conforming to the observation that phenomena arising through conditions in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) lack substantial reality, one employs this as an antidote to enter the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) of the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*); this is called skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
Therefore, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth are the objects of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom that serve as the counteragents to the self.
It is said thrice that "non-self" (*anātman*) is exquisite;
it is pleasing to the mind and thus praiseworthy, and it accords with reality and is therefore sublime.
The fourth explains the unsurpassed non-self; thus it is said to be "superior.
Because there are distinctions within the terminology, it is called the "name of boundless dharmas.
Regarding the seventh point, the characteristics of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, the meaning of the Dharma is distinguished according to the provisional and the real.
First is the aspect of contemplation (*ekābhisamaya-lakṣaṇa*), meaning that contemplation is non-dual because there is but one single reality.
Second is the aspect of nature (*gotra-lakṣaṇa*), meaning that within those spiritual capacities (*indriya-gotra*) there are the three vehicles.

Third is the aspect of liberation (*vimukti-lakṣaṇa*), meaning that the three vehicles are realized as equally returning to the single reality, for within the aspect of liberation there is no differentiation.
The Treatise states: "Relying on identical liberation, one is without fear," because the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Now I rejoice and am fearless; I shall preach only the unsurpassed path."
The four applications of mindfulness open the gate of skillful means; as mental recollections differ according to individual capacities, their mental activities vary.
Although various dharmas are used to clarify the teachings of the vehicles, they all serve a single purpose; thus, the treatise states that they "accord with liberation."
Within the characteristics of the eighth bodhisattva stage, the principles of the Dharma are distinguished according to the essential characteristics of that stage.
First is the characteristic of wisdom; this is a general heading for all practitioners of the bodhisattva path.
What are these? They are the practice of the dharma that is realized and the practice of the wisdom that realizes it.

Because wisdom accords with suchness,

As the *Śāstra* states in its commentary on the Sūtra: "The meaning being immeasurable refers to the distinct differences of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Fourth is the aspect of the teaching:

The tenth is the characteristic of performing the act of abiding. This distinguishes the meaning of the Dharma by means of the Buddhas’ quality of being able to teach and the vocal teachings that are taught.
First is the characteristic of awakening, which is the quality of performing the act of sustaining; it is so called because one awakens to the characteristics of the *dharmatā*.

Regarding speech: it consists of speech according to one's own intention, speech according to another's intention, and speech according to both one's own and another's intention, for this is that which is able to expound the Dharma.

Although he has attained great mastery in teaching the Dharma across all its categories, he had not yet attained the full realization of the perfect Dharmakāya; now, through diligent cultivation, he has attained it in its perfection, and for this reason he has come here.

This means that because one attains mastery over the performance of supernatural powers, the gates of *dhāraṇī*, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one then accomplishes the practices such as receiving the [Bodhisattva] position and fulfills the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). One thereby attains the fruits such as the *nirmāṇakāya-samādhi* (transformation-body samādhi), which is the ultimate fulfillment of the Buddha-body through the rain from the clouds.
Furthermore, both that which is realized and suchness are likewise pervasive throughout space; their essential meaning is one and the same.
Next is the formal explanation of the text.
The text consists of three parts:
Within the section on the preliminary praise and invitation, there are sixteen verses: the first thirteen are praises and the final three are the invitation.
Within the former [the praises], there are also two parts:
the first three verses merely express offerings, which can be understood as being of three types.
The final ten verses consist of the goddesses' offerings and praises.
These also comprise two parts:
the first verse provides a general heading for the offerings and praises, while the remaining nine verses specifically manifest the words of praise.
Within this, there are also two parts:
the first eight verses praise the Buddha’s virtues and powers, while the final one exhorts practice for the sake of benefit.
Within the former, there are also two parts:
The first five verses praise the sovereign power of the great function, while the latter three reveal the basis for that sovereignty.
Within the former section, there are also two parts:
the first two show that the beneficial function is universally pervasive, while the latter three show that it is not uniform according to how it is perceived.
Within this, there are also two parts:
first, a general clarification; second, the manifestation of the eight characteristics.
Within the latter, there are also two parts:
The first wisdom realizes that the world is an illusion; thus, the text contains both the metaphor and its application.

The latter two [wisdoms] realize the ultimate nature and characteristics; therein, one half-verse realizes the essence, one half-verse gives rise to function, one half-verse shows that function does not depart from the essence, and one half-verse demonstrates the total transcendence of both essence and function.
Among the three subsequent requests, the first is a silent request made through meditative recollection, while the latter two are verbal requests made by the leaders.
Second is the actual exposition, which the treatise divides into eight sections:

first, the section on the preparatory practices for fulfilling the ground, which subsumes the cultivation of the preceding nine grounds as preparatory practices because they bring this ground to fulfillment.

Second is the stage of attaining samādhi, wherein the practices and virtues of the initial dwelling on the stages are immeasurable; this is cited specifically because it is the basis for receiving the office [of a Buddha].

Third is the stage of attaining the position, which consists of the practice while correctly dwelling on the stages, whereby one gathers the Buddha-wisdom through the power of the aforementioned meditative concentration.

Fourth is the section on the Great Exhaustion (*mahāparikṣaya*), which refers to the practice that fulfills this stage; for while the practices of the preceding stages have already been exhausted, this stage now reaches the ultimate limit of such fulfillment.
Fifth is the section on the Explanation of the Name, because the learning of this stage is perfected, its qualities are distinguished, and its designation is made manifest.

The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) comprise both superior and unsurpassed categories; once the stages (*bhūmi*) are perfected, their wondrous functions become sovereign. This is because the form [of the lower stages] is inferior to that of a Buddha, even though it is positioned before one.
The seventh stage is the "category of reflected images" (*pratibimba-bhāga*), which reveals the Dharma through metaphors, just as one knows the physical substance by means of its reflection.
The eighth section, on "Benefits," elucidates the excellence [of the stage] in order to encourage its cultivation and entry.
The final two sections apply universally to all ten stages; since the former subsumes the latter, it is said that this stage possesses eight [sections].
If one follows the previous long-format outline, wherein the latter two sections are combined, then this stage (*bhūmi*) is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the practice of the stage (*bhūmi-caryā*);
second, the manifestation of the fruits of the positions (*pada-phala*). Within the practice of the stage, there are six sections, as listed above.
Among the six [stages], the first is the mind of entry (*praveśa-citta*), while the remaining ones are the minds of abiding (*sthiti-citta*).
The mind of emergence (*niṣkramaṇa-citta*) is the fruit of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-phala*), as already explained previously.
Now, within the first section, there are two parts:
First, there is a general explanation; subsequently, from the phrase "excellent fulfillment" (*sukṣema*) onwards, there is a detailed exposition.
Regarding the first part: "immeasurable wisdom" (*apramāṇajñāna*) refers to the extensiveness of the *āgama* (scriptural transmission);
"contemplative realization" (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) refers to the profundity of realized wisdom (*adhigamajñāna*).
In the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, bodhisattvas on the stages engage in two types of practice:
first, that which is termed "practice according to reality" (*yathābhūta-pratipatti*) with respect to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which is this very wisdom of realization;
second, that which is termed "universal practice" (*sarvatraga-pratipatti*) with respect to subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which is this very extensive wisdom (*vipula-jñāna*).

On all the stages (*bhūmi*), both of the two aforementioned types of practice arise; now, regarding these two superior [practices], one contemplates and cultivates them through definitive discernment (*viniścaya*).
Within the ten distinct phrases, they are subsumed into seven aspects, because the first three and the seventh and eighth are combined into two locations.
Among the seven [points], the first is the common characteristic (*sādharmya*) because it is well-practiced;
that is to say, the first three phrases clarify the non-abiding of realization and its aids, as these are practiced identically across all stages (*bhūmi*).
The first phrase refers to the realization of the Path, because it consists of untainted, pure dharmas.
How is this realization attained?
It is through the assistance of the Path provided by the subsequent phrase.
By what cause is assistance accomplished?
It is because, through the subsequent phrase regarding the non-abiding path, one does not abide in the unconditioned by increasing merit, and does not abide in the conditioned by increasing wisdom.
The latter six are the specific characteristics, namely:
second, the extensive practice of great compassion, which is the characteristic of universally conforming to both self-benefit and benefiting others.
This [characteristic] combines the preceding seven stages into a single one, because the distinct characteristics of the seven stages have already been analyzed at the beginning of the eighth stage.

This is a general summary; it explains extensively in accordance with the practice of universal liberation, whereby great compassion benefits others and thereby accomplishes one's own task—hence it is called "self-benefit.
The third line, "purifying the Buddha-field," refers to the characteristics of the eighth stage.
The latter three aspects correspond to the nine stages (*bhūmi*); because these are directly realized therein, they are frequently cited.

Specifically, the aspect of teaching and transforming sentient beings through a single phrase refers to the stage of self-maintenance in the ninth stage, as it involves entering the eleven dense forests.

The fifth has two phrases concerning the skillful understanding of characteristics: that is, because one understands and penetrates suchness as the sphere of the Buddha’s activity, and because one skillfully accords with the Tathāgata’s practice capable of realizing nirvāṇa.
The sixth is the characteristic of insatiability, because one constantly observes the powers and so forth in order to enter [the path].
The preceding phrase explains [theoretical understanding], while this phrase concerns practice; both constitute the superior progress of the ninth stage.
The preceding stage [the sixth] states that one applies oneself with exclusive diligence day and night, having no other thoughts, because one enters the realm of the Buddha alone.

The seventh stage reaches the culmination of entering the marks (*lakṣaṇa*), meaning that the realization of the ten stages is perfected. Since the concluding practice of the preceding stages and the entry into the position already belong to the tenth stage, it is said: "It is called the stage of receiving the office."
The second section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, by means of this," clarifies the stage of samādhi.
This section has two parts:
first, the restatement of the preceding to introduce the subsequent; second, the actual exposition, beginning with "he immediately attains."
Within this section there are four parts:

first, the individual listing of the ten names; second, the summary of the number obtained from the phrase "such as these" onwards; third, the demonstration of the fulfillment of entry from the phrase "the bodhisattva therein" onwards; and fourth, the revelation of the final name from the phrase "its last" onwards.
Now, within the first ten [stages], the first is general and the remainder are specific.
It is called "Free from Defilement" (*vimalā*) because it is free from the defilements of afflictions; as this is the stage where obstructions are exhausted, it specifically receives this name.
Among the nine successive concentrations (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), one is free from eight kinds of defilements:

first, the "entry into the secret and stainless," which refers to understanding entry into the profound and secret locus of the dharma-dhātu of both phenomena and their principles, as it is not accompanied by afflictions (*kleśa*).

The second [stage] is "near to the stainless" (*anāsrava*), because the myriad practices have already been perfected and the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is thus near, as explained in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
Of the preceding sections, the first is the initial interpretation; the next one line concerns the practice; and the following three constitute the perfection of virtue.

Third is the Stainless Radiance of Light, which means that the light opens the lotus flowers of the mind so that one may perceive reality; it also enables one to sit upon various great jewel lotuses, for there is no place this light does not illuminate.
The fourth is the stainlessness of the four *dhāraṇīs*, which is like the ocean that contains all within it.
The fifth is the stainlessness of the arising of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), wherein they manifest instantaneously without deliberate thought.
These five above are all the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) that give rise to the *dharmakāya*.
The sixth [verse] has two parts: first, the purity of the Buddha-land is stainless;
second, the upper phrase concerns "immeasurability," which encompasses the entire domain of the Dharma-realm;
the lower phrase concerns "correct contemplation," which exhausts the essential nature of all lands.
The sixth stage is self-benefit;
the seventh is birth through transformation free from defilement.
These two benefits of the upper stages are both the practice of one's own level.

The eighth is the stainless perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi-vimala*), which refers to the time when the supreme, progressive, and superior awakening is about to achieve *bodhi*; for at that moment, all Buddhas appear before one another and provide witness and knowledge.
As explained in the section on receiving office, this is because fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) is about to manifest.
Regarding the second point, the enumeration of the numbers, these are also the retinues.
That they all appear before one is because, having long practiced and achieved realization, they manifest spontaneously without the need for further exertion of effort.

Third, regarding the manifestation of entering into fulfillment: that which is able to enter refers to the general skillful means, the essence of meditative concentration, and the characteristics of its arising; because it manifests through concealment and appearance without fixed direction, it is called "skillful."
"Thoroughly understanding what is to be done" means knowing the functional application of karma.
Regarding the fourth point, "manifesting the final name," this is because the section on receiving the position is about to be explained.
"The Omniscient One" refers to the Buddha’s non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
In the treatise, the repeated mention of "wisdom" includes both [the fundamental wisdom] and subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
The equality of these two wisdoms is termed "receiving the position.
The third section, beginning with "This samādhi manifests before one," clarifies the stage of receiving the position.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, the principle; second, the analogy; third, the application; and fourth, the conclusion.
Now, for the first [the principle], there are six sections:
First, the seat; second, the body; third, the retinue; fourth, the marks; fifth, the place of origin; and sixth, the attainment of the stage.
Among these six, the first five comprise the complete virtues of one's own level, while the last one subsumes the fruit of Buddhahood from above.

Regarding the preceding section, the first three positions constitute the essence (*tī*), the next one position constitutes the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and the final one position constitutes the function (*vṛtti*).
The first three are the support (*āśraya*), the principal [deity], and the retinue (*parivāra*).
This is the first [of those].
What kind of seat?
It is the Great Jewel Flower King Seat.
Within this, there are two parts:
First, the primary lotus itself has ten characteristics:
first, the characteristic of the primary [lotus], which is the precious lotus;
second, the characteristic of its dimensions, beginning with the phrase "that flower."
3. From "By means of various wonders" downward, it refers to the possession of qualities through superior characteristics;
4. From "Transcending" downward, it refers to the place where the characteristics of the lower stages arise;
5. From "World-transcending" downward, it refers to the causal characteristics.
6. "Knowing all" and below: the characteristic of accomplishment;

7. "Constantly emitting" and below: the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because through correct contemplation one universally illuminates the phenomena appearing within the *dharmadhātu*, just as in the world a blooming lotus with its full-blown buds is considered supreme;
8. "Not [attained by] the various devas" and below: the characteristic of merit, because it is summoned by the virtues of the bodhisattva.
9. "Vaidūrya" and below describe the characteristics of the lower part;
10. "Its flowers" and below describe the characteristics of adornment.
"Twenty or thirty" and below clarify the flowers of the retinue.
The second section, from "At that time" onwards, concerns the marvelous body according to which [the Buddha] accords with the seat.
The third section, from "Immeasurable" onwards, concerns which retinue [he accords with].
The fourth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this great," explains the characteristic by showing how it performs its activity universally according to various characteristics.
The fifth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva sits upon that," explains the source from which it emerges.
Light issues forth from ten locations, causing those in the evil realms to attain liberation, as the Bodhisattva increases his practice.
The text is divided into four parts:
first, the activity of emitting light; second, all the sages’ collective knowledge; third, the rushing wind-like descent of lower classes of beings; and fourth, the resonance of identical sounds.
Now, regarding the first point: the emission of light from the ten locations has three types of function:
first, the function of benefiting; second, the function of awakening; and third, the function of subduing.
Following a similar classification for the sake of convenience, these shall now be divided into four.
First, the seven rays preceding it possess only beneficial karma: the first five benefit ordinary beings, while the latter two benefit those of small capacity.
Second, the single ray of the eighth [emanation] possesses two and a half types of karma:
the first is beneficial, as it benefits bodhisattvas from the ninth stage downward.
Second, it is for the purpose of awakening and causing [beings] to know;
the term "half" refers solely to the sense of gathering, as it gathers them and causes them to come.
Third, the single ray of the ninth [light] also has two functions and is half:
First, because it benefits bodhisattvas at equal stages; as the subsequent text states that since those rays have already benefited these [bodhisattvas], these rays must likewise benefit them.
Second, because they awaken them so that they may know.
Regarding the statement that "one half" is not manifested in the palace of Māra, this is because it is a karma of subjugation.
The fourth [section], the "Light from the Tenth Crown," consists only of the awakening; its text is divided into three parts:
first, the scope of the illumination;
second, from "circumambulating to the right" onwards, the actual manifestation of the activity, which refers to the arising of offerings and the accomplishment of benefit for others.
Regarding the term "non-retrogression from bodhi," the treatise sets forth four meanings:

first, because of attaining certainty upon ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*); second, because of entering the assembly of those correctly established in rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*); third, because of being certain to abandon negligence and evil; and fourth, because of being certain to accumulate wholesome deeds.
3. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the matter concludes and the light is withdrawn.

Regarding the phrase "entering through the soles of the feet," if explained according to the characteristics of the teachings (*śāstra-lakṣaṇa*), the light from the crown of the head entering the soles of the feet signifies the manifestation of profound reverence.
If one considers it in terms of the ultimate wisdom that realizes the truth, it is because one enters the domain of the Buddhas from below.
Therefore, the commentary on the latter section states, "because of being subsumed in equality," which reveals that realizing the Buddha-domain is itself self-realization.
The second section, beginning with "At that time," shows that all the sages were fully aware;

the third section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, at that time," shows those of lower stations rushing toward the wind to prostrate and receive benefit—the texts of both may be understood accordingly.

Fourth, "At that time," and so forth, refers to the mutual resonance of sounds; because they cultivate the practice of equal causes and mutually support one another, it signifies that the internal virtue of profound and vast auspiciousness has perfected the adornment of the mind, and thus externally, at this stage, the signs emit light to mutually benefit one another.
Furthermore, when [the light] above illuminates that [below], the emission of light from between the eyebrows signifies that the Middle Way has already been illuminated;
now, when that [light] illuminates this [here], its appearance upon the chest signifies that the minds of the two are in profound accord.
When virtue is perfected and Māra is exhausted, it is called "destroying the enemy Māra.
The sixth section, beginning with "At that time, in the ten directions," clarifies the attainment of the respective stages.
This contains two parts:
First is the emission of light.
Within this, there are ten types of karma.
The first light is named "Karma of Immediate Benefit," because it benefits all-encompassing wisdom and causes one to attain Buddhahood.
Second, the light of the retinue is the karma of cause;
third, manifesting the Buddha is the karma of reverence;
fourth, awakening others is the karma of realization.
Fifth, the karma of causing vibration;
sixth, the karma of ceasing evil;
seventh, the karma of subduing Māra;
8. The activity of manifestation;
9. The activity of expansion and contraction, beginning with "In this way" at the end of the scroll;
10. The activity of transformation, which manifests various forms.
Second, from the passage "Having manifested these things" onwards, it concerns entering the summit (*mūrdhan*) to achieve benefit.
Regarding "entering the summit": if considered in terms of the phenomenal aspect of transformation (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*), it means the higher [stages] subsuming the lower.

If considered in terms of the ultimate meaning, the illumination of the ultimate source of the mind is called the "summit of wisdom" (*jñāna-mūrdhan*); that the fruit is realized within oneself is termed "the light entering."
The treatise states: "Because the light of all Tathāgatas is mutually received through the equality of the wisdom of those Bodhisattvas.
This means that when the light from the crown of the Bodhisattva enters the Buddha’s feet, it signifies advancing from the cause toward the fruit.
The Buddha’s light enters the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head; this is the fruit gathering the cause.
Furthermore, when the cause gathers the fruit, there is no trace of entry; when both cause and fruit are simultaneously extinguished, it is called equality.
"At that time" refers to the attainment of benefits, which is termed the "concluding stage.
"Entering the realm of the Buddha" means that what is realized is identical [to the Buddha's].
"Possessing the ten powers" means that the qualities of practice are identical [to the Buddha's].
Regarding "falling into the category of Buddhas," it is like falling into the category of the Saṃgha immediately upon first leaving the household life.
The second section, beginning with "The Buddha’s son is like a wheel-turning [monarch]," provides analogies for the six matters mentioned above;
however, the text is somewhat abbreviated and out of order.
First, the analogy refers to whichever body [is assumed].
Second, from "That wheel-turning [king]" onwards, the analogy refers to whichever seat [is occupied].
Third, from "Grown tall" onwards, the analogy refers to whichever marks [are manifested].
4. "Taking up the four great elements" below serves as a metaphor for the positions attained.
The king represents the true body (dharmakāya), the hand represents the response body (nirmāṇakāya), the flask represents the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa), and the water represents the light.
There must be a third [condition], namely, what kind of retinue there should be—referring to the civil and military officials who serve as assistants and counselors.
The fifth section, beginning with "is able to," clarifies from what kind of source [of birth] it arises.
The third section, "The Bodhisattva’s Reception of Office," corresponds to the subsequent [stage].
It merely corresponds according to the respective positions attained, as the primary intent lies therein.
The fourth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," provides a summary, concluding this specific portion.
The fourth major section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Dharma-Cloud [Stage]," clarifies the stage of entering Great Perfection (*mahāparyanta*).
Within this, there are five kinds of greatness:
first, the greatness of wisdom; second, the greatness of liberation; third, the greatness of samādhi; fourth, the greatness of dhāraṇī; and fifth, the greatness of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
These five [bodies] rely upon five kinds of meanings:
first, they rely on the meaning of the true wisdom of perfect enlightenment, because it is free from the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);
second, they rely on the meaning of mastery over the mind, because it is free from the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Third, based on the arousal of the mind, one accomplishes all purposes and meanings through the power of mental concentration;
fourth, based on the purpose of benefiting sentient beings in accordance with all worldly needs, because the mind can universally sustain and the speech can universally comply;
fifth, based on the capacity to deliver sentient beings, because the body and the various supernormal powers can extensively transport them.
The first two [perfections] benefit oneself, while the latter three benefit others.
Within this text, there are three parts:
the first two are explained individually, and the latter three are treated as a collective example.
Now, regarding the first, the greatness of wisdom, it is divided into two parts:
first, a detailed explanation; second, a summary.
Regarding the first, there are seven kinds of wisdom:

First, the greatness of the wisdom of gathering; second, the greatness of the wisdom of transformation and emanation; third, the greatness of the wisdom of empowerment; fourth, the greatness of the wisdom of entering the subtle; fifth, the greatness of the wisdom of the secret places; sixth, the greatness of the wisdom of entering eons; seventh, the greatness of the wisdom of entering the paths. These seven arise sequentially from one another.
Now, first is the wisdom of collection (*saṃgrahajñāna*), which, by relying on the power to sever doubt, realizes that phenomena arise from the collection of conditions.
In the text, there is first a detailed explanation and subsequently, under the heading "Summarizing the Essentials," a concluding summary.

The preceding section contains twenty collections, all of which clarify the collection of causes and conditions; however, as these encompass both the true and the delusive, as well as their synthesis, they are divided into three parts:
first, the defiled part; second, the pure part; and third, the cessation part.
The text contains six layers:
first, those that are exclusively defiled, namely the first four [categories], as well as the collection of sentient beings and the collection of various views and afflictions;
second, those that are exclusively pure, namely the collections of the śrāvakas and those below them.
Third, those that are exclusively cessation, namely space.
Fourth, those where the pure and the defiled are spoken of together, namely consciousness and the formation and destruction of the conditioned world.

Fifth, those where the pure and cessation are spoken of together, namely the unconditioned and nirvana; herein, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as an unconditioned phenomenon is "pure," non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is "cessation," *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvana by nature) is termed "cessation," and the remaining three types of nirvana are termed "pure."

The six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) involve the cessation of both the defiled and the pure; this refers to the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Thus, the treatise states: "In accordance with what is correct or incorrect, the dharma-realm permeates the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)."
Furthermore, all the phrases in this treatise possess that which corresponds to their expressed meaning, because they are able to know whatever specific distinctions exist.
Second, from the words "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the wisdom of responsive transformation is clarified; this section has three parts.

First, it reiterates the preceding to introduce what follows, because the function of transformation arises based on the previously mentioned accumulation of the body of wisdom; thus, the treatise says, "The power arising in dependence upon that body."
Next, from "as it truly is" (*yathābhūtam*) onwards, the actual manifestation is shown;
finally, from "in this way" (*evam*) onwards, the summary is given.
Within the detailed exposition, there are ten phrases:

The first three [lines] concern the sovereign transformation of the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), wherein the sovereign power manifests the wholesome and unwholesome karma of sentient beings as well as their sharp or dull latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), causing sentient beings to perceive these as if they were truly created;
the next line concerns the sovereign transformation of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*);
and the subsequent five concern the sovereign transformation of the world of the perfectly awakened ones (*samyak-saṃbuddha-loka*), because of the perfect awakening of the three vehicles.
The transformation of the single dharma-realm constitutes the teaching and practice for the three vehicles;
the remaining four transformations constitute the persons and fruits of the three vehicles.
The final one pervades the three worlds: sentient beings possess discrimination while the vessel-world lacks it; wisdom and perfect enlightenment pervade the latter two.
Third, "Furthermore, knowing the Buddha’s sustaining power as it truly is" refers to the wisdom of sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

The treatise states: "By the power of such and such transformative activity. This means that relying on those manifestations of transformation, which constantly transform without ceasing, constitutes the practice of sustaining power.
The matters are not limited to these alone; they are reiterated as such.
There are eleven phrases:

the first three concern the uninterrupted continuity of the Three Jewels, which constitute the "retention of the objective realm" (viṣaya-dhāraṇa); the remaining eight concern practice, which constitute the "retention of conduct" (caryā-dhāraṇa).
Among these, the first two are perverse practices.

The practice of Ugra-tāpana (the "Fierce One") who scorched his body without weariness, the practice of Śabarī who indulged in lustful passions, and the practice of Paryanka who frequented improper places—all of these are instances thereof.
The latter six are practices conducive to attainment; the former four are practices that give rise to causes.
"Time" refers to the time when the causes arise; "aspiration" and so forth constitute the essence of the causes.
The latter two refer to the time when the fruit is attained.
"Time" refers to long kalpas; "wisdom" is the essence of the fruit, meaning the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The fourth section, beginning with "Furthermore, knowing all Buddhas as they truly are," concerns subtle wisdom.
This refers to knowing that the Buddha’s transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-prayoga*) is subtle and sovereign.
The *Śāstra* states: "Because, based on those [three], through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the emanation (*nairmāṇika*), they are well-integrated into a non-dual functioning.
This means that by relying on the aforementioned three wisdoms—such as the wisdom of emanation—they are unified into a non-dual wisdom, thereby performing this subtle transformative activity.
Each single matter already encompasses the preceding three;
it is not merely the eight aspects, for each one possesses the remaining seven, as can be understood from the text.
The fifth section, beginning with "Furthermore, entering," concerns the wisdom of the secret place.

Relying on sentient beings whose faculties are not yet mature, so as not to cause them alarm or fear, the coarse is manifested while the subtle is concealed, such that both the manifest and the secret are simultaneously established.
The first three [lines] collectively reveal the three secrets.
The next three [verses] specifically reveal the secrets of manifesting transformations: first, knowing the time for transformation through the mind;
second, bestowing predictions through speech—namely, giving a prediction later to those who are indolent, and giving a prediction sooner to those who are timid and discouraged.
Alternatively, it may refer to those śrāvakas who practice according to the true path, bestowing predictions upon them alongside those who are emanations.

Furthermore, whereas in the past only bodhisattvas were predicted, the predictions for śrāvakas were considered secret; thus, their manifestation or concealment was adjusted according to the capacities of sentient beings.

The subsequent "secrecy of gathering sentient beings" (攝眾生密) is referred to in the *Śāstra* as "gathering and subduing" (攝伏), meaning both gathering [through kindness] and subduing [through discipline], which apply to both body and speech.

Next is the "secrecy of teaching" (教密): from the perspective of ultimate reality, there are no three, yet the teaching of three is itself secrecy; this is solely for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas.
From the perspective of the diverse capacities of sentient beings, there is no one, yet the teaching of one is also secrecy.

The final three [teachings] clarify the "mystery" (guhya) in relation to the objects of knowledge: knowing the various types of faculties, knowing the myriad differences in karma, and knowing the practices of both the contrary and the compliant, through which all attain Bodhi; therefore, they are termed "mysterious."
The sixth section, beginning with "Furthermore, he knows," introduces the wisdom regarding eons (*kalpa*).
Based on the empowerment of the formations of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), one relinquishes the notion of mastery.
This means that the shifting flow of time within an eon is termed the "formations of life."
To encompass all within one is called empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
To enter all within one is termed relinquishment (*tyāga*), because it involves abandoning oneself to follow others.
That the kalpas revolve according to the mind is called mastery (*vaśitā*); this is also the gate of the distinct formation of phenomena separated by the ten periods of time.

Because they have attained inconceivable liberation, they do not perceive length or shortness, nor do they see the mutual inclusion of the one and the many, the large and the small, and so forth, all as described in the "Chapter on Arousing the Mind."
Seventh, "Furthermore, knowing the Tathāgata" and below introduces the knowledge of entering the paths (*mārga-jñāna*).
The Treatise states: "This is spoken with reference to the meaning of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*).
That is to say, one enters all paths; whether in reverse or in forward order, they all serve as counteractive measures, for there is nothing that does not constitute entry into the path."
This refers to knowing the path of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
If it refers to knowing the path for transforming ordinary beings, then these very [states of] contrariness and conformity are themselves the Buddha-path.
Within this, there are fourteen phrases:

The first phrase refers collectively to those to be converted; that is, because ordinary worldlings (*bāla*) are as unstable as the wind, the *Śāstra* and the *Sūtra* state, "entering the path of ordinary worldlings," and the *Śāstra* states, "relying on the stage of ordinary worldlings."
The remaining phrases separately reveal the types of those to be converted, which are briefly of three kinds:

first, for those who act out of pride in the self (*asmimāna*), they are led to enter the wisdom of atoms (*paramāṇu-jñāna*), so that by observing and breaking down the aggregate, they realize there is only dust and no self.
Regarding the second point, those who seek rebirth in heaven based on faith enter pure lands because they have transcended what was previously believed.

As for the remaining cases where all rely on vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought): among these, the first phrase gives rise to the body of vitarka and vicāra; the next two phrases correctly reveal the distinctions in the mental activities of vitarka and vicāra; and the subsequent phrase clarifies the objects of that awakening.
The first four [lines] refer to the *vitarka* and *vicāra* of those to be transformed;

the subsequent four lines concern the practice of the transformer. The first line generally reveals its universal application (*sarvatraga*); the next two follow circumstances, whether in reverse or in accordance with the flow; and the final line distinguishes between the profound and the shallow.
The latter four phrases transform [beings] to lead them into the fruits of the three vehicles.
The second section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, all... and so forth, provides a summary.
The preceding seven [points] are all the wisdom of the Buddha; because Bodhisattvas are able to enter them, they are called the "Greatness of Wisdom."
The second section, from "O Son of the Buddha, reaching this stage" onwards, clarifies the greatness of liberation; it contains three parts:
first, the designation of attaining the rank;
second, from "He immediately attains" onwards, a brief demonstration that there are ten [qualities]:
First, regarding the sphere of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is characterized by mastery in transformation that transcends the reach of words and thought, as attained by Vimalakīrti.
Second, one is able to reach immeasurable worlds, because the power of one's vows and wisdom is free from all obstruction.
Because the three types of higher knowledge (trividyā) are liberated from hindrances, they are called "pure contemplation" (śuddhadarśana).
There are two ways in which these hindrances are abandoned, both of which are fully understood:
first, in terms of the stages (bhūmi), there is a difference between what is abandoned in the mundane and supramundane realms.

Second, regarding the distinction between those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) within the supramundane, both these categories of training and beyond-training pertain to all three vehicles.
Among the three mentioned above, the first two are categorized by way of commonality, while this one is categorized by way of wisdom; together they form a pair.
The general characteristics are clarified as follows: by reference to the body, the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is elucidated; by reference to the person, wisdom (*jñāna*) is manifested.
Next, there is a pair of three: first, the supernatural power; second, the wisdom.

The fourth [point] clarifies the supernatural power by reference to the mind: it universally illuminates the capacities of sentient beings, transforming according to their inclinations and responding universally at once, just as Avalokiteśvara manifests through the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*).

The next two [perfections] are explained in terms of wisdom regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*): the fifth is the *dhāraṇī* of phenomena, because it reveals that within the Tathāgatagarbha there are aggregates of virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
the sixth is the ability to refute the arguments of others, because it is unimpeded and perfect in refuting those arguments according to their own words.
The next two pairs involve the mutual interpenetration of the marks and the penetrating wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*).
Regarding time, they clarify "penetration" because one attains mastery over the three periods of time and abides within them according to one's will through their mutual interpenetration.
Regarding the gathering of causes and conditions, they manifest "wisdom," because the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is contained within the *dharmadhātu*.
The latter two pairs clarify the pervasive wisdom by way of mutual identity.
Clarifying the pervasive by way of the body, because it universally illumines without departing from the single body’s wheel of light, it is the wheel of liberation-light.
Because "approximate time" (*samvṛta-kāla*) is a single entity that can nevertheless cognize many things, the subsequent section beginning with "These ten" concludes the detailed exposition.
Third, the section beginning with "In this way, up to... provides a general illustration for the remaining three; thus ends the section on the Great Exhaustion (*mahā-parikṣaya*).
The fifth major section, "Buddha-sons, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas thoroughly penetrate thus... and below, is the section explaining the name [of this stage]. It consists of three parts:
first, it is called *dharmameghā* (Cloud of Dharma) because one is able to receive the great rain of the Tathāgata’s Dharma;
second, from "Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattvas on this stage, by their own vows... and below, it clarifies that it is called *dharmameghā* because one is able to pour down rain to extinguish delusions.

3. "O Son of the Buddha, on this stage, the Bodhisattva in a single thought-moment... and so forth, clarifies that it is called the *Dharmameghā* (Cloud of Dharma) because it pours down rain that gives rise to wholesome qualities.

The subsequent two sections derive their names from what [the Bodhisattva] experiences themselves; this present section establishes its name based on what is received. The *Śāstra* states: "The cloud and the Dharma are similar, because both pervasively cover."
"In this stage, the hearing of the Dharma is analogous [to space], because it is like a body that pervasively covers all;

that is to say, the clouds of the Buddha’s body pervade the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the rain of Dharma is likewise vast. Only those at this stage can receive it; therefore, it is named 'Dharma-Cloud' (*dharmameghā*)."
The text has two parts:
first, a general explanation of the virtues of the one who receives [the teachings].

Because the preceding seven knowledges accomplish the power of mindfulness, they are able to receive many dharmas; since these knowledges truly accomplish manifold virtues, it is said that there is "immeasurable bodhi. This is merely a proximate explanation of the meaning of receiving and upholding [the teachings].
Second, from "The ten directions" onwards, the specific characteristics of receiving the Dharma are revealed.
This section has three parts:
first, a general revelation of the multiplicity of those who receive; second, a detailed enumeration to reveal the multiplicity; third, a series of questions and answers to reveal the multiplicity.
Now, for the first [section], there are the dharma, the analogy, and the application.
Within the dharma, there are three parts:

first, clarifying the abundance of the Dharma received; second, from "The Great Dharma-illumination" (*mahā-dharmāloka*) onwards, clarifying the excellence of the Dharma received; therefore, the subsequent application refers to it as the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyagarbha*).
The text consists of three phrases.
The first two phrases concern its nature (*svabhāva*); that is to say, they refer to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the phenomena known by the three types of wisdom.
"Great Dharma-illumination" refers to hearing and reflection, as it is subsumed within wisdom (*jñāna*).
"Shining" refers to cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), because it is that which is embraced [by it].
The phrase "acting" means that one speaks to and bestows [teachings] upon sentient beings like clouds, raining down the rain of Dharma for others.
Third, from "In a single thought-moment" onwards, the qualities of the recipient are revealed.
A "single thought-moment" (ekakṣaṇa) is so called because it is swift; being swift, it is both manifold and sublime.
Furthermore, its swiftness is displayed through successive progression to manifest its excellence.
"Capable of settling" means being able to settle and receive the text.
"Receiving" means receiving with faith.
These two refer to receiving the text.
"Comprehension" (*saṃgraha*) refers to the grasping of meaning through reflection.
"Retention" (*dhāraṇa*) refers to the upholding of those [meanings] and their texts; since these constitute two types of retention, this [section] merely explains them in accordance with that.
In the subsequent analogies and their applications, both the inability [to comprehend or retain] and its opposite are revealed; the texts are all easily understood.

In the second section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, it is like the great ocean," the text enumerates and demonstrates their multiplicity, first through a simile and subsequently through its application.
That the ocean is able to provide stability is because it receives all waters; that it receives them is because it does not become turbid.
"Turbid" is like a lack of faith.
"Gathering" means that other waters enter and thus the original name is lost.
"Sustaining" means that its use is inexhaustible.
In the third section, "Vimukticandra," the questions and answers reveal the multiplicity [of dharmas]. First comes the question, followed by the answer.
Within the answer, there are two parts:

first, a comparative calculation that demonstrates the vastness and abundance of the Dharma received by a single Buddha; second, from the phrase "As with one Buddha," the analogy is extended to reveal the same for many Buddhas.
Regarding the "treasury of the dharmas of the three periods," this refers to the treasury of the Buddha-dharmas of the three periods.

As for the statement in the treatise that there are "three kinds of treasuries of phenomena within the dharma-realm," the intention is to indicate that the aggregates of illumination, rain, and accumulation of phenomena reside within the dharma-realm.
Because that sutra refers to the "Dharmadhātu-garbha," this commentary provides this explanation.
Second, the rain is noted as extinguishing delusions.

Regarding the names [of the metaphors] herein, such as the clouds and so forth, they are explained in detail in the "Chapter on Manifestation": because the clouds of compassion universally cover all, because the thunder of the Dharma startles those hibernating in ignorance, and because it universally clarifies fearlessness, illuminating the capacities of beings with swiftness to cause them to see the Path.
