Their names are as listed at the end of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, with the exception of Mount Sumeru and the two mountains of Snow and Fragrance (*himagandha*).

Between these mountains lie the seven fragrant seas (*gandhasamudra*); just as the reflection of the sun appears in the seas, the reflection also appears upon the mountains because they are made of pure gold.

Second, the passage from "On that mountain of jewels" below clarifies how two reflections appear to one another; this serves as a direct metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s mutual entry into self and others. Because those reflections are clear and pure like a present-day mirror, they are able to manifest one another.

Third, the section beginning with "Or it is said to be a shadow of the sun" correctly distinguishes the different ways the name is derived. This means that when the original shadow in the water appears as a shadow on the mountain, this manifested shadow emerges from the mountain and enters into the space between the mountains.

When the original shadow on the mountain appears as a reflection in the water, this manifested reflection passes through the space between the mountains and out onto the seven golden mountains; therefore, at the very moment it enters, it is also said to be exiting.
The analogy can be understood accordingly.
Fourth, the passage beginning with "But this shadow" clarifies that reflections appear infinitely, serving as an analogy for the Bodhisattva’s net-like bodies and lands.
Fifth, the section beginning with "Essential nature" clarifies that the essence is free from the two extremes; therefore, they can manifest mutually without confusion.
This means that because it cannot be apprehended, it is not existent; because its reflection appears clearly, it is not non-existent.
"Not abiding" establishes the aforementioned non-existence;
"not departing" establishes the aforementioned non-non-existence.

If there were fixed abiding, they could not interpenetrate; if they were separated, there would be nothing to interpenetrate. Therefore, it is only by being neither separate nor abiding that they can interpenetrate.
In the subsequent section on the "conformity of dharmas," it directly clarifies that there is neither destruction nor abiding;

thus, they are able to enter one another without confusion. The first two phrases clarify the nature of non-destruction: if the nature and characteristics were subject to destruction, there would be nothing that could mutually enter.

The next two phrases clarify that if one abides within or outside, mutual entry is impossible: if one abides within the mundane world, one cannot encompass the world with one's body; if one abides outside the world, one cannot pervasively enter the world. Because there is no abiding in either case, mutual entry is possible.

The passage beginning with "In all worlds" explains the reason for this: because through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) there is no conceptual differentiation and thus no destruction of characteristics, while through wisdom (*prajñā*) one contemplates the single characteristic and thus does not destroy the manifold; since one traverses both phenomena and principle simultaneously, one neither destroys nor abides.
If one does not destroy [phenomena] and does not abide [in them], then one abides in *tathatā* (suchness) and never departs from it.
Since one does not abandon phenomena as they are, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are thus integrated with their nature (*dharmatā*).
Because there is nowhere it is not present, it is identical to *tathatā*, such that the internal and external mutually penetrate one another.
The latter [section] on the analogy of the illusion has two parts:
first, the general analogy; second, the specific analogies beginning with "As if there were a magician.
Regarding the first, there is first the analogy and then the application.
The analogy has three parts:
first, a general explanation of the capacity for illusion;

second, from "dwelling at the crossroads" onwards, an explanation of the time and place based on the original and the time and place manifested as illusion, illustrating their mutual interpenetration.
Below the section "not manifesting," the beginning and end do not obstruct one another, serving as a metaphor for the non-destruction of characteristics.
Below the section "Bodhisattva," there is the application [of the analogy], which consists of five parts:
first, clarifying that the one and the many are mutually inclusive yet distinct, corresponding to the aforementioned manifestation of multiple times and places.
2. From "The bodhisattva, in this regard... onwards, it clarifies that wisdom is discerning and not obscured, corresponding to the aforementioned skill of illusion.
3. From "Not by means of that... onwards, it corresponds to the non-destruction of the characteristics of the fundamental and the derivative.
4. From "Why" onwards, the text investigates and explains the underlying reasons.
First, the intent of the inquiry is as follows:
Why is it that they enter into one another while maintaining their indestructible characteristics?
The explanation of this meaning has three parts:
first, because one realizes the non-self of persons; the characteristics of the self of persons have already been discussed above;
second, from the passage "the Bodhisattva knows the intrinsic nature of all phenomena" onwards, because one realizes the non-self of phenomena; [and third, ...].
Third, from "The Bodhisattva Diligently Cultivates" onwards, it is because he attains the great compassion of identical essence (*sahaja-mahākaruṇā*).
By means of this, he is able to harmonize phenomena and principle.
Fifth, from "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva is thus" onwards, the preceding meaning is summarized and established.
Within this, there are three parts:

first, the section beginning with "Furthermore, many enter into one" concludes the preceding point; second, the section beginning with "yet they do not abandon" concludes the preceding nature and characteristics of non-destruction; and third, the section beginning with "one should diligently" concludes the preceding clear discernment.
Within the second section on specific analogies, there are three inverse analogies comprising three sub-sections in total:
first, the analogy that illusion does not destroy its basis, which serves as the specific analogy for the non-destruction of characteristics;

2. From "In this way, the illusionist... onwards is the analogy of the necessary locus of the illusion, specifically illustrating the original time and place of dependence versus the many times and places where it manifests;
3. From "Just as that illusionist performs various illusory feats... onwards clarifies the analogy of the illusionist’s lack of delusion, specifically illustrating the one who performs the illusion.
Regarding the first [section], there is first the simile and then the application (*yoga*).
Within the application, there is first the formal application and then, from the words "The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands" onwards, the explanation of its underlying reason.
Second is the simile of the illusion necessarily depending on a basis; here too, there is first the simile and then the application.
In the analogy, the phrase "necessarily depending on time" is omitted, yet it ought to be present according to the logical correspondence.
The correspondence is divided into two parts:
first, the correspondence regarding the locus; second, the correspondence regarding the time.
In the preceding section, first there is a general synthesis: because objects are manifested through cognition, they are empty; that is, phenomena themselves are empty. Next, from "Why is this so?
onwards, the reason is investigated and explained: it is because, according to principle, there is no differentiation.
Finally, from "Abiding in the world" onwards, the mastery [of the Buddha] is established.
Second, the section beginning with "In a single thought-moment" correlates with the temporal basis.

Within this, first there is the direct exposition, followed by the explanation of its underlying cause starting from "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains... and so forth, because by attaining illusory wisdom, he becomes equal to the Buddha.
Regarding the simile of the third illusionist not becoming deluded, the text may be understood as before; below this, it enters the forty-first sūtra.
Within the explanation of the third dhyāna, there are three parts: the teaching (dharma), the simile (upamā), and the application (anusandhi).

Within this section on the Dharma, there are five parts: first, explaining the entry into meditative concentration throughout all lands; second, from "Or in a single kṣaṇa" onwards, explaining the sequence of entering [concentration]; third, from "If for a long time" onwards, summarizing the various approaches; fourth, "The Bodhisattva therein," explaining the realization of the essence of concentration; fifth, "Although detached from this," explaining that the arising of supernormal powers is not abandoned, along with analogies and their applications. The texts are clear and may be understood accordingly.
Within the fourth dhyāna, the explanation of the internal [states] is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying the practice of the profound mind within the dhyāna; second, clarifying the practice of the profound mind upon arising from the dhyāna.
Now, for the first part, there are two subdivisions:
First is the practice of application (*pratipatti*), followed by the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).
Within the former, first the internal [mind] is raised, and subsequently, from the phrase "In each and every one of those," the practice of application is initiated.

Within that, first the practice of making external material offerings is clarified, followed by the practice of making offerings through the three types of action—reverence and so forth—in each and every instance.
Second, from "However, regarding all Buddhas" onwards, the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*) is elucidated, which consists of two parts:
first, an explanation by way of the Dharma; second, an illustration by way of analogy, beginning with "like distracted movement.
Within this, there are two analogies, each consisting of an analogy and its application (*upanaya*).
First, the metaphor of deluded thought being devoid of cognition illustrates that one accords with reality through non-thought;
second, the metaphor of a mirage appearing as water illustrates that one realizes the delusive is identical to the true.
The texts can both be understood accordingly.

In the second section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this samādhi," the profound mental conduct arising from meditative concentration is elucidated; first through the Dharma, then through a simile, and finally through an application.

Within the application, the former portion clarifies the practice of self-benefit through making offerings, while the present portion clarifies the practice of benefiting others through exposition; the text is merely abbreviated for stylistic brevity.
"Expounding the profound principle" refers to the arousal of practice from the profound mind.
Regarding the fifth determination, there are five parts within the commentary:
first, distinguishing wisdom according to its object.
Second, the explicit manifestation of wisdom and knowledge each has ten phrases, all of which are dharmas within the past treasury.
Third, regarding the temporal periods of the objects of knowledge, there are fourteen layers, which explain the meaning of the past.
The fourth clarifies the characteristics of knowing.
"Not extinguishing the present" means not abandoning it.
"Not taking objects in the past" means not grasping them.
This means that by relying solely on the perspective of the past, it is revealed that [the mind] takes as its object without either grasping or rejecting.
Each of the four preceding sections has one Buddha-son.
Fifth, the explanation of the benefits obtained upon emerging from meditative absorption has three parts:

First, the enumeration and definition of the characteristics are presented in ten phrases. The first phrase is general; it refers to the final stage of the position where the fruit is realized, which is called the "Method of Receiving Empowerment" (*abhiṣeka*).

The remaining phrases are specific: (1) belonging to oneself, (2) purifying obstacles, (3) ultimate completion, (4) initial entry, (5) correct realization, (6) final fulfillment, (7) maintaining so as not to lose it, (8) knowing through non-knowing, and (9) purifying the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*), which collectively encompasses the preceding nine.
Regarding the differentiation of the three wheels by way of wisdom: this refers to the absence of a knower, an object known, and the act of knowing itself; the rest may be inferred accordingly.
From the section beginning with "What are... onwards, their names are interrogated and enumerated.
The first four are the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence;
the next two pertain to self-benefit, being fearless regarding profound dharmas and being able to act according to one's words;
the final two pertain to benefiting others, serving as a reliance for those who do good and a rescue for those who do evil.
The final two [verses] collectively clarify the excellence of the two benefits.
Third, from the words "O Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*) onwards, the attainment of swiftness is concluded;
this consists of the teaching, the simile, and the application. *Kalala* means "thin curd" in this language.
The remainder may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the sixth samādhi, the Treasury of the Radiance of Wisdom, the commentary is divided into two parts:
first, it clarifies the functional application of the meditative concentration; second, it reveals the benefits of the meditative concentration.
The first part is divided into six sections: first, a general knowledge of all Buddhas;

second, from "If it has already been said" onwards, knowledge of their many names and titles; third, from "They shall appear" onwards, knowledge of what they will do in the future; fourth, from "Those Tathāgatas have cultivated" onwards, knowledge that their causes are perfected and their fruits are fulfilled; fifth, from "The names and surnames of those Tathāgatas" onwards, knowledge of what they are doing in the present; sixth, from "This Bodhisattva, in a single thought-moment" onwards, knowledge of the limits of their realization.
Within this, the great trichiliocosm is itself a buddha-field.
As for the repetition of the term, it is mostly for the purpose of elimination; one should rather say "a hundred buddha-fields.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Second, from "by thoroughly knowing" onwards, the benefits of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are demonstrated.
This section has four parts:
the first two concern self-benefit, and the latter two concern the benefit of others.

This means that one causes the mind to enter into and maintain its benefit: namely, because of the aforementioned knowledge, one maintains it without loss; and because one maintains it without loss, one obtains the benefit of such maintenance.
By maintaining the Buddha within a single moment of mind, one obtains the benefit of the Buddha’s protection.
The second mind enters into upholding the Dharma, attaining the benefits of dhāraṇī and eloquence.
The remaining phrases are to be understood by analogy with this.
As for "there are twelve," it is an increase of ten from the previous number.
One who is born as a lion does not fear the suffering of birth and death.
By demonstrating the true nature of birth and death, one is said to open the bolt of the Dharma; by realizing that birth and death are fundamentally empty, one emerges from the mire of desire.
"Maintaining through the power of wisdom" refers to the simultaneous cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and insight (*prajñā*).
Entering the maintenance through the power of non-abiding means that great eons (*mahākalpa*) do not depart from a single thought-moment.
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha... abiding in this samādhi" onwards, it clarifies the benefit of attaining skillful means, consisting of the dharma, the analogy, and the application.
However, there are two kinds of skillfulness:
first, skillfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmas*), because the clouds of Dharma are unspeakably immeasurable, which is illustrated by the metaphor of seeing various objects;
second, skillfulness regarding principle (*yukti*), as expressed by the phrase "the sunlight is impartial."
Furthermore, it is only by virtue of these two kinds of non-obstruction that one is termed "skillful"; therefore, they are combined in the phrase "non-conceptually knowing.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha... thus understanding" onwards, it clarifies the attainment of the benefit of non-emptiness.
IV. From "O Son of the Buddha, reaching and abiding in this samādhi" onwards, there is the section on the benefit of the ten kings' reverent offerings.
Regarding the seventh samādhi, the commentary has two parts:
first, clarifying the essence and function of the meditative concentration; second, clarifying the benefits of the concentration.
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, the inquiry; second, the explanation.
The reason for this repeated inquiry is that the former was a general inquiry regarding "certainty," whereas this is a specific inquiry regarding "ornamentation."
The subsequent section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva," provides an explanation in two parts:
first, the explanation of all worlds, which—being present—are referred to simply as the ten directions;
second, the explanation of their adornments, beginning with "They all see the various Buddhas."
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a general enumeration of the ten gates, all of which constitute adornments.
Among these, the eighth specifically clarifies adornment: namely, adorning the mind with merit and wisdom, and adorning the body with physical form and radiance.

Following the section on "The Purity of the Assembly," the characteristics of adornment are specifically revealed below to expand upon the preceding two points: first, expanding upon the assembly; second, expanding upon the adornments.
Regarding the first [expanding upon the assembly], there are three parts:
first, seeing others; second, seeing oneself; third, the capacity to see.
Regarding the first [section], there are also three parts:

first, seeing the essential characteristics of the assembly; second, from "He also sees the assembly" onwards, clarifying the extent of what is seen; and third, from "He also sees the Buddhas therein" onwards, seeing the activities of the Buddhas.
2. From "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" onwards, the seeing of oneself is clarified, which may be understood.
3. From "When seeing in this way" onwards, the seer is clarified; it contains the [threefold structure of] the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*).
In the Dharma, it is clarified that one sees through non-discrimination; in the analogy, it is clarified that there is the signifier and the signified.
It does not say of itself, "I am the signifier and the signified," yet it does not abandon the signifier and the signified, for it is known through the analogy of non-discrimination.
In the section on "Synthesis," first the synthesis of "not abandoning" is presented; subsequently, from "and yet" (*er yu*) onwards, the synthesis of "non-discrimination" is presented.
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" up to "seeing the Buddha’s immeasurable light and color," the preceding adornments are explained in detail, which consists of two parts:
first, an explanation by means of the Dharma; second, an elucidation by means of analogies.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, the presentation of the topical headings, briefly citing four kinds of adornments, all of which are clearly and fully realized;
second, the detailed explanation according to the headings, beginning with "Or one may see the Buddha-body" and so forth.
This is divided into four parts:
first, the explanation of immeasurable light and color;
second, from "Or one may see the Buddha's body as being of such a magnitude" onwards, the explanation of immeasurable physical forms.
3. From "The Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattvas, see thus" onwards, the text explains the aforementioned "perfect accomplishment," thereby manifesting the fulfillment of the former two perfections;
4. From "Furthermore, they see the Buddha" onwards, it explains the aforementioned "equal purity," which simultaneously encompasses the two internal adornments.
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva perceives the Buddha in this way" onwards, the meaning is revealed through analogies, which consist of three parts:
first, the analogy of emptiness being without increase or decrease, which illustrates that the *dharmatā-kāya* (Dharma-nature body) is incapable of increase or decrease.

The magnitude or minuteness of space depends upon whether it occupies a world-system or a mustard seed; it is not that the substance of space itself is so. This is like the body of *dharmatā*, which appears differently according to the capacity of the vessel.

The analogy of the second moon neither increasing nor decreasing illustrates that the true, eternal form-body (*rūpakāya*) does not change; yet, there are near and distant realizations, appearing differently according to the mind.
The previous analogy illustrated only the Buddha’s body; this analogy illustrates both the radiance and color as well as the perfect accomplishment.
The third analogy, that of appearances manifesting in accordance with the mind, illustrates the aforementioned purity.
When the bodhisattva’s mind is pure, he perceives the Buddha as pure; as for the Tathāgata, what purity or defilement could there be?
The second section, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "abiding in this samādhi," clarifies the benefits of meditative concentration.
Briefly stated, there are seven kinds of benefits, each distinguished by the term "sons of the Buddha.
First is the benefit of swiftly accomplishing practice and vows, which may be understood through its heading, inquiry, and explanation.
The second Dharma-seal is identical to that of the Buddha’s benefit and consists of ten phrases in five pairs:

the first two concern the identity of merit and wisdom; the next two concern the identity of the objects and cognitions of the two truths; the next two concern the identity of essence and function; the next two concern the identity of the two benefits; and the final two concern the identity of skillful means and impartiality.
The third [benefit], the benefit of maturing others through virtue, is clear.
The fourth, the benefit of encompassing wisdom and virtue, consists of two parts:
first, the analogy, and second, the application; each contains ten phrases.

In the section on "Correspondence" (*saṃgraha*), the general heading indicates that what was first obtained is now attained; ten phrases correspond to the ten preceding matters. Only the eighth and ninth are out of order because, although wisdom (*jñāna*) is singular, it is distinguished according to its objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
First, the merging of the physical characteristics of a buddha-field;
second, the merging of the physical forms of sentient beings;
third, the manifestation through the display of transformations.
Fourth, entering the Buddha’s assembly together with his retinue, for they mutually serve as leaders and companions like members of a family;
fifth, penetrating the Buddha-dharma as the necessary provisions for the path;
sixth, universally gathering pure dharmas, thereby manifesting the perfect voice to all people.
Seventh, causing all to enter the Dharma is true supernatural power;
eighth, the universal eye is pure, transcending and harmonizing with wisdom and understanding;
ninth, mastery is withdrawn and yet harmonizes with mastery.
The tenth dwelling is the application of wisdom in accordance with the Dharma.
The fifth [dwelling] concerns the benefit of the physical majesty that is preeminent; it contains both the heading and the explanation.
The sixth concerns the benefit of bringing others to perfection; first, it cites the preceding to introduce the subsequent, and then it interrogates and enumerates the names and characteristics.

The seventh turning brings about the benefit of performing Buddha-work; this also first restates the preceding section to introduce the subsequent one, followed by an inquiry and the enumeration of names and characteristics, the text of which can be understood as before, and below this it enters the forty-second scripture.
The eighth is the Samādhi of the Differentiated Bodies of All Sentient Beings.

Its explanation is divided into five parts: first, clarifying the wisdom capable of entry; second, revealing the characteristics of entering and emerging; third, clarifying the benefits of entering meditative concentration; fourth, clarifying mastery over the objective realm; and fifth, a concluding summary of the ultimate state.
First: by attaining ten kinds of non-attachment, one achieves mastery over subsequent entry and exit.
"All stages" refers to the Buddha-stage, the Bodhisattva-stage, and so forth.
Regarding the two aspects of entering and exiting, there are two parts: first, the interrogation that introduces the topic; second, the explanation of the characteristics.
Within this, there is first the teaching and then the analogy.
In the teaching, ten categories are briefly distinguished to represent their inexhaustibility:
First, the entry and exit are clarified through the mutual correspondence of the primary retributions (*vipāka*) of various classes;
second, from "Entering among the Gods" downward, the entry and exit are clarified through the mutual correspondence of the secondary environments (*upabhoga*) of the six destinies;
third, from "Entering with a Thousand Bodies" downward, the entry and exit are clarified through the mutual correspondence of the one and the many.
4. From "Jambudvīpa" downward, the four continents and the great oceans correspond;

5. From "all ocean deities" downward, the phenomena of the great primary elements correspond, as the vehicle of the non-arising dharma comes about through the arising of the four great primary elements;
6. From "all exquisite incense and flowers" downward, the various directions correspond.
7. From "All four continents" downward, the relative quantities of the various assemblies are contrasted;
8. From "Entering into the assembly of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings" downward, defilement and purity are contrasted;
9. From "The sense-base of the eye" downward, the various elements (*dhātu*) are contrasted.

10. From "A Single Atom" onwards, various categories are explained in contrast to one another—such as the coarse and the subtle, the ordinary and the sage, thought-moments and eons, and the real and the false.
The principles regarding their entry and emergence are as described in the "Chapter on Worthy Leader" (Bhadrapāla-parivarta).
The second section, "Illustrating by Simile," contains four similes, each of which corresponds to one of the ten preceding categories through a doctrinal application (*dharma-saṃgraha*).
First, the simile of a person sustained by a ghost’s power illustrates the first and fourth categories, primarily in terms of the physical body;
second, the simile of a corpse raised by incantation illustrates the second, fifth, and sixth categories, primarily in terms of the objective environment of dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
The third analogy, that of the arhat manifesting supernatural powers, illustrates the third and seventh [categories], as these primarily concern numerical frequency;
the fourth analogy, that of a single sprout on many plants, illustrates the latter three gates, as they variously clarify diverse matters.
The metaphors and the subject matter reflect one another, so that the principles and the phrasing reveal themselves naturally.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "abiding in this samādhi," there follows the benefit of entering meditative concentration (*samāpatti*), which contains three parts:
first, the benefit of receiving praise equal to the fruit of Buddhahood; in each case, the upper phrase clarifies the meaning and the lower phrase provides the name.

In the exposition of the meaning of the Ten Powers (*daśabala*), "the perfection of mental resolve" clarifies the power of self-benefit; "the accomplishment of meaningful benefit" manifests the power of benefiting others; "having accomplished all that was to be done" demonstrates the perfection of the power; "abiding in unimpeded wisdom" generally reveals the essence of the power; and "discerning and knowing all phenomena" comprehensively elucidates the function of the power.
The remaining text is self-evident.

Regarding the second [section], the benefit of the light of the wisdom of the two bodies; and the third, the effortless benefit of the activity of the three karmas—both contain the phrase "sons of the Buddha," and their textual characteristics are clearly manifest.

In the fourth section, from "Sons of the Buddha... abiding in this samādhi of immeasurable realms" onwards, the mastery over the objective realm is elucidated, first through the Dharma and subsequently through metaphors.

Regarding the first point: whereas the preceding second section only clarified entering and arising, this section additionally clarifies the presence or absence of the forward and reverse sequences as various objective spheres (*viṣaya*).
As for "entering" within the context of "arising," it refers to the quiescence that is the very nature of that arising.
As for "entering and arising therein," this is because it is the function of quiescence.

Thus one knows that the samādhi of a bodhisattva is characterized by constant entering and constant arising, constant simultaneous entering and emerging, and constant being without entering or emerging; only then is it truly sovereign.
To manifest sovereign mastery (*vaśitā*), it is clarified by means of the interlacing of various objective spheres (*viṣaya*).
Within the two metaphors used for this manifestation, there are six similes, each with its own application (*anugama*).
The first is the simile of the illusory manifestation of the six objects, which illustrates the aforementioned identity and difference.
The second is the parable of the asuras fleeing and hiding, which illustrates the preceding two pairs of coarse and subtle, and small and large.

If one considers the relationship between principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), then non-differentiation is the subtle and differentiation is the coarse, because principle is subtle while phenomena are coarse.
Alternatively, that which is without differentiation is "coarse," because it enters through general characteristics;
that which is differentiated is "subtle," because it enters through specific characteristics.
When undifferentiated, it pervades the entire dharma-realm; when differentiated, it becomes small according to the particular circumstance.
If one explains the "great" and "small" solely in terms of phenomena (*vastu*), both are subsumed under the category of differentiation.

The third analogy, that of farmers sowing seeds, illustrates the combined discernment of superior and inferior, as well as unity and multiplicity; the phrasing is merely abbreviated for stylistic brevity.
The fourth is the analogy of conception and growth, which illustrates having a body and being bodiless, because it is like that which arises from non-existence.
The fifth is the analogy of clouds descending and rising, which illustrates having marks and being markless.

The analogy of the universal manifestation of the six Brahma palaces illustrates entering the middle from above, arising within that which has arisen, and the mutual relationship of the forward and reverse orders; therefore, they are collectively termed "various.
The fifth section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha... reaching the other shore of supernormal powers," concludes the ultimate state and its manifestations are clearly evident.
The ninth is the Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharma-realm. Its explanation has four parts:

first, revealing the essence and function of the concentration; second, clarifying the benefits accomplished by the concentration; third, using a metaphor to illustrate it; and fourth, summarizing the dual practice.
The first section is now divided into three parts:
First, a general exposition of the names and essence, which refers to attaining mastery over the dharma-realm of the eyes and so forth.

Second, from "The Bodhisattva, within his own body" onwards, it demonstrates the locus of entry into meditative concentration; that is, entering concentrations of the eyes and so forth within the pores of the skin, thereby manifesting mastery in their mutual functioning.
III. Below "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*), the function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is clarified, which is divided into four parts:

first, comprehending the three periods of time; second, below "the bodhisattva therein," practicing for many eons; third, below "furthermore," entering and emerging without obstruction; fourth, below "because of the dharma-realm," concluding with the attainment of mastery.
This has two meanings:
first, because of mastery over the principle-dharmadhātu, one is able to skillfully discern the dhātus of the eye and so forth;
second, skillfully discerning the eighteen dhātus of the eye and so forth constitutes mastery over the phenomenal dharmadhātu.

Because these two are unimpeded and there is the unimpededness of phenomena with phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratighāta*), it is said that "these various kinds" exhaust the limits horizontally and reach the furthest bounds vertically.
Second, from the passage beginning "The Bodhisattva thus," the benefits accomplished by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are clarified, distinguishing ten kinds of benefits:
first, the benefit of generating manifold merits, which consists of twenty-one phrases, each numbering ten thousand *koṭis*.

Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "furthermore there are countless," this section fully explains the benefit of inexhaustible virtues, because each preceding matter leads to the inexhaustible.
Within these twenty phrases, the first ten describe the multiplicity of what is possessed, while the latter ten describe the characteristics of that which possesses them.
"Pure" means because it removes defilements.
"Luminously transparent" means because it brings forth the light of fundamental wisdom.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha... abiding in this samādhi" onwards, there is the benefit conferred by all Buddhas; herein, there are three parts:

First, the reception [of sentient beings] is clarified; next, from "Those Buddhas" onwards, the manifestation of the body and the preaching of the Dharma are shown; finally, from "Causing them to practice" onwards, they are led toward cultivation and realization. Fourth, from "O Son of the Buddha...

abiding in this dharma-realm" onwards, there is the benefit of the Buddhas' protective mindfulness (*anubhāva*). "Reception" refers to being gathered in, which belongs to the Buddhas' protective mindfulness—that is, the empowerment of the Buddhas' power being bestowed.
Fifth, one attains the benefit of the profound and vast ocean-like increase; sixth, one attains the benefit of supreme transcendence—both of which may be understood.

Seventh, one attains the benefit of the capacity for various powers (*bala*); herein, the ten powers are first enumerated, and subsequently, from the passage "O Son of the Buddha, these ten kinds of powers," their surpassing excellence is revealed.
9. Following each of the aforementioned powers, all are endowed with these thirty-eight powers.
Eighth, from "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva... onwards, it concludes the benefit of being able to bring [the teachings] to perfection.
Ninth, from "The merit of this bodhisattva... onwards, because his own virtue is boundless, others are unable to describe its benefits.
10. From "O Son of the Buddha, when one abides in this samādhi" onwards, the boundlessness of the samādhi itself brings benefit that is never uncomprehended.
Among the ten preceding sections, the first seven provide specific explanations, while the final three serve as a summary.
The third analogy, appearing within the section on "Manifestation," correctly elucidates the preceding essence, function, and benefit.

It also clarifies what was not previously revealed; therefore, it does not entirely resemble the preceding text. This section consists of two parts: 1. The primary manifestation of the essence, function, and benefit. 2. The clarification of what was not previously revealed.

First, the general body of the metaphors is presented; subsequently, from "O Son of the Buddha, just as [the Lake] Anavatapta... onwards, there is the specific application of the metaphors to their meanings.
There are thirteen sections, each first presenting the metaphor and then providing its corresponding application.

In the analogy of the single confluence of sands entering the ocean, the initial general explanation of the metaphor’s application mentions four rivers; however, the underlying intent lies in the fact that sand issues forth from four mouths.
Below, in the ninth section, the four rivers are explained individually.

Below the section beginning with "As the Ganges," the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are explained in detail; these correspond to the four mouths, while what is spoken corresponds to the four grains of sand.
If the four analytical knowledges are expanded by dividing them into general and specific categories, there are seventeen gates.

Second, the section beginning with "Just as the four great rivers" provides the analogy of the rivers encircling the lake and entering the ocean; herein, the analogy comes first, followed by the application.

Within the application, the encircling of the lake is addressed first: the wisdom-mind of bodhi is called the "lake," and the three karmas following along with that wisdom constitute the meaning of "encircling."
Below the section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," the four directions are unified.
Third, from the passage beginning "like the four great rivers surrounding [it]," the analogy of seeing jewel-lotuses in the pond is unified:
the preaching of the Dharma carries the sense of causing them to bloom, while samādhi possesses the power to evoke their fruition.
"Adorned and pure" are both specific meanings of "upon the flowers.
The fourth corresponds to the metaphor of precious trees surrounding the pond;
the fifth corresponds to the metaphor of the great pond's purity, which constitutes the very substance of the pond.
The metaphor of the six directions of sandalwood incense banks and the ten kinds of jewel-like wisdom have two meanings:
first, the ten kinds of jewel-like wisdom within the transcendence of the world; second, the ten kinds of wisdom such as the knowledge of others' minds.

The metaphor of the sevenfold bottom spread with gold and jewels is as follows: wondrous wisdom corresponds to the golden sand; liberation corresponds to the mani-jewel; unimpeded radiance corresponds to the two kinds of light emission; abiding where the Buddhas abide and entering the profound corresponds to spreading the bottom; and each of the four preceding sections takes the Great Lake Anavatapta as its primary illustration.
8. "As with the *anā* [dragon]" and below correspond to the parable of the Dragon King Anavatapta; this corresponds to the name of the lake, as its name was derived from that dragon.

9. This corresponds to the parable of the four rivers providing moisture; 10. This corresponds to the parable of the four rivers being inexhaustible; 11. This corresponds to the parable of entering the ocean without obstruction; 12. This corresponds to the parable of entering the ocean without weariness. In each of the above four parables, the phrase "like the four great rivers" serves as the opening of the metaphor.
In the ten preceding metaphors, each concludes with the application to the Bodhisattva.

From the thirteenth metaphor, "O Son of the Buddha, like the light of the sun," onwards, the metaphor of the mutual reflection of various jewels is presented, first providing the simile and subsequently the application.
The application [of the analogy] consists of two parts:
first, the formal application; second, from "Why... onwards, the investigation and explanation of the reasons for their mutual interpenetration.

Fourth, from "O Son of the Buddha... although they are able in meditative concentration" onwards, there is a summary of the dual practice, meaning that the provisional and the real, as well as concentration and dispersion, are without obstruction.
Within this, there are three parts: first, the Dharma; second, the analogy beginning with "O Son of the Buddha"; and third, the application beginning with "The Bodhisattva.

However, while the Dharma section clarifies that within stillness there is function, the analogy and application clarify that within function there is stillness; the text is merely abbreviated for stylistic reasons. This concludes the forty-third scripture.
The tenth, the Samādhi of the Unhindered Wheel, also consists of three parts: first, the introduction; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are three sections:

first, clarifying the skillful means for entering [the samādhi]; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi" onwards, clarifying the application of one's own wisdom upon entry; and third, from "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the abode of Samantabhadra" onwards, clarifying the benefits of the completion and fulfillment of the concentration.
Regarding the first section, there are twenty-two phrases that also clarify the name of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
The first eleven phrases concern the unimpeded application of causes, which constitutes the meaning of "unimpeded" (*asaṅga*);
the subsequent eleven phrases, beginning with "universally entering," concern the perfection of abiding in the fruit, which is the meaning of the "wheel" (*cakra*).
In this first section, this very state of being unimpeded and all-conquering is also the meaning of the "wheel. The first three phrases refer to the unimpededness of the three types of action;

the next phrase refers to the unimpededness regarding the container-world (*bhājanaloka*); the following two phrases refer to the unimpededness regarding the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*); and the remaining phrases refer to the unimpededness of the perfect awakening of wisdom.
Subsequently, while abiding in the fruit, the two wisdoms penetrate both the provisional and the ultimate; thus, it is called "universal abiding.
Third, one performs acts that bring benefit and happiness;
fourth, one purifies the seeds of the two obstacles.
The seven wisdoms accord with the Buddha’s realm; the remaining seven may be understood accordingly.
Within the second section, "Entering One's Own Wisdom-Function," there are four parts:
first, encompassing the Buddha’s merits; second, realizing and entering all dharmas; third, the inexhaustibility of universal virtue; and fourth, the concluding summary and exhortation to practice.
The initial and middle stages encompass the twenty-one kinds of sublime qualities of the Tathāgata, for within these stages, the virtues are equal to those of a Buddha.
Among them, some aspects are entirely identical to the characteristics of a Buddha, while others correspond through similarity in their causal factors, following a sequential order without deviation.
Within this section, there are three parts:

first, a general clarification that the wondrous awakening is fully perfected; second, a specific manifestation of the twenty-one virtues; and third, a manifestation of the superior power of these virtues.
Regarding the first part, there are ten phrases: the first phrase indicates the time of perfection, while the remaining nine manifest the characteristics of that perfection.

However, regarding "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā): if contrasted with "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā), it is the fundamental [wisdom]; if spoken of directly as the Buddha's wisdom, it encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate. Here, it is shown to encompass both.
Within this, the first three phrases concern the initial contemplation.
"Regarding the phrase 'observing all-knowledge,' this is the heading.
How does one observe?
There are two kinds of observation:"
First is the general contemplation, which means contemplating the provisional and the real simultaneously;
second is the specific contemplation, which means clearly discerning and illuminating that "this is the real" and "this is the provisional," as well as the many distinctions within the provisional.
In the subsequent three phrases, the sequence likewise begins with the first phrase as a heading;
the next asks, "How does one accord?
and the answer is: "By virtue of the preceding general contemplation."
It can be manifested all at once; because of the previous individual contemplations, each takes its respective object as a focal point.

The final three phrases reach a definitive realization, which is explained as being identical to the previous contemplation, differing only in that what was previously observed is now clearly realized through direct perception.
Second, from "Regarding Samantabhadra" onwards, twenty-one distinct types of merit are specifically elucidated in twenty sections, as the final two are combined.
Herein, first, the initial section clarifies that the two types of conduct are eternally severed; this is the merit of functioning with unimpeded transition toward all objects of knowledge.
However, there are two meanings:

first, it means that [the bodhisattva] does not lack the wisdom regarding existence and non-existence as do those of the two vehicles; second, it means that they do not manifest the cycle of birth and death to give rise to various defilements like ordinary beings, nor do they manifest nirvāṇa to abandon matters of benefit and happiness like those of the two vehicles.
The World-Honored One was without that [duality], and now the Bodhisattva likewise is without it.
In this text, the extensive manifestation of benefit and happiness shows that he is not the same as those of the Two Vehicles;
that he is always accompanied by wisdom shows that he is not the same as ordinary beings.
The textual analysis is divided into two parts:

first, a general explanation of the constant and eternal great function; second, a specific manifestation of one function, beginning with the passage: "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva has a lotus flower... and so forth.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, the explanation by way of the Dharma; second, the clarification by way of analogy.
Now, for the first part, the explanation by way of the Dharma, there are two sub-sections:
First, there is the explicit clarification; second, the interrogation and explanation.
Regarding the first: first, the essence of the practice is clarified; subsequently, from the words “uninterrupted” onwards, its permanence is distinguished.
Within the second section (the interrogation and explanation), the intent of the interrogation is as follows:
Why is it that this wisdom is perfected and its practice constant?
The explanation of the meaning is:
because the vows and practices have been successfully accomplished and wisdom has become skillful.
The second analogy clarifies the middle four [points]:
first, the analogy; second, the application; third, the inquiry; and fourth, the explanation.
Now, the first.
Placing a maṇi jewel within colored clothing serves as a general metaphor for placing the bodhisattva’s mind and wisdom within the Buddha-wisdom.

Although it takes on the color of the clothing, this is a metaphor for the preceding wisdom being fulfilled through the ten phrases; thus, they are combined and described as "contemplating all-knowledge," and so forth.
Not abandoning one’s own nature is illustrated by the twenty phrases on constant practice as previously explained.
The combination of these two is analyzed according to the illustration.
Third, the intent of the inquiry is: how can one, having already attained the fulfillment of wisdom, continue to practice without interruption?
The fourth explanation states:
It is because it is the natural law that a Bodhisattva’s vow is free from obstruction;
and because they benefit the entire realm of sentient beings without ever becoming weary.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the explanation by way of the Dharma, which is self-evident; second, the application of analogies as illustrations.
Within this, there are three analogies, all of which illustrate tirelessness in benefiting sentient beings, each consisting of a scriptural citation (dharma) and its application (yoga).
First, the analogy of space sustaining lands, which illustrates that great vows are naturally inexhaustible;
second, the analogy of universal extinction in nirvana, which illustrates that one never tires of purifying sentient beings.
The first two metaphors illustrate compassion (*karuṇā*).
The third metaphor, that of the universal accomplishment of the Buddha’s wisdom, illustrates that because the subject and object are non-dual, there is no weariness.
This one metaphor illustrates wisdom (*jñāna*); since this is not a compassion born of attachment or biased views, how could there be any weariness?
The second part specifically elucidates a single function, which consists of two sections:

first, clarifying the excellence of the *niṣyanda-phala* (concordant fruit); second, from "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, regarding this flower... onwards, it explains the mastery over the *vipāka-phala* (retributive fruit).
The preceding section has two parts:
first, the clarification of the adornment of marks, which surpasses the ten stages [of the *Daśabhūmika*] and thus reaches the limits of the ten directions;

second, from the phrase "This great lotus" onwards, the distinction of the adornment of virtues: viewed from within, its magnitude encompasses the entire Dharma-realm; viewed from without, it is permitted for sentient beings to see it—this is precisely the transformation of the small into the great.
Within the second section on the primary retribution, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the dimensions of the body; second, from "All Buddhas" onwards, the explanation of the Buddhas' empowerment through the emission of light.

There are twenty layers, each subsequent layer being multiplied by a factor of one million billion nayutas of unspeakable numbers of atoms of Buddha-fields compared to the preceding one; thus, the number is difficult to measure.

The second section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattva reaches this samādhi," clarifies the realization of the signless dharma; that is, the merit of being able to enter the most pure *tathatā*, which is identical to that of all Tathāgatas.
The first section concludes the preceding [discussion] and leads into the subsequent; because one realizes the signless (*animitta*), one is undefiled.
In the latter part, from "abiding securely" (*anusthita*) onwards, it correctly reveals that "abiding" is precisely the meaning of "entering.

That is to say, this *tathatā* (suchness) is neither existent nor non-existent, and is therefore called "boundless" (*ananta*); for that which is definitively existent or definitively non-existent constitutes a limit (*anta*).

The ineffable Dharma is precisely suchness free from verbal expression; its reality-mark (dharmadhātu-lakṣaṇa) and its unobstructed limit (anāvaraṇakoṭi) are all alternative names for suchness. As for what is called the "Tathāgata-lineage," it is that which takes the suchness of non-nature (abhāva-tathatā) as its nature.
Thus, the "Chapter on the Manifestation" states: "All are of one and the same nature, namely, the nature of non-nature.
The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Knowing that phenomena are eternally without nature, the Buddha-seed arises from conditions."
"Without coming or going," etc., further clarifies that True Suchness is itself the Middle Way; therefore, it is profoundly bottomless.
"Direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) and what follows specifically elucidate the meaning of the capacity for entry.

The third section, beginning with "For the sake of the past, future, and present," clarifies the virtue of abiding in the Buddha-abode; that is to say, because the Buddha dwells eternally in the noble, celestial, and Brahma-abodes without effort (*anābhoga*).
In this passage, the initial praise of the Buddhas of the three periods of time applies to both preceding and following sections.
From the phrase "The power of all Buddhas" onwards, the true meaning is revealed: namely, entering the realm of all Buddhas, which is the realm inhabited by the noble ones, devas, and others.
In the section following "Direct Realization by the Pure Eye," the characteristics of that which abides are clarified, because one dwells with the ten eyes perfectly clear and luminous.
The text explicitly mentions the five eyes; the others are merely implied by their meaning.
The fourth section, "Accomplishing the Bodhicitta," clarifies the attainment of the Buddha’s qualities of equality, as there are three types of equality when comparing one Buddha to another.
This passage consists of three parts:
first, it clarifies the equality of the basis, because all Buddhas rely upon pure wisdom.

In this text, beginning with the initial arousal of the bodhicitta and ending with the perfection of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), the arising of the functions of wisdom is that upon which everything depends.
Next, from the section "The Dharma of Birth Transcending the World" onwards, it clarifies the equality of intention (*āśaya*), because they share the same intention of taming sentient beings.

Following this, the section beginning with "Supernatural Powers and Transformations" explains the equality of activity, because [the Buddha] equally performs the activities of enjoyment and transformation.

Fifth, the section beginning with "Virtues, Understanding, and Aspirations" clarifies the virtue of reaching the state free from obstructions; because he has cultivated the remedies for all obstacles, both merit and wisdom are purified.

In the passage concerning "being free from the two obstacles," the first two lines concern merit and the next two lines concern wisdom; in each case, the upper line refers to the purification of the obstacle and the lower line to the fulfillment of the virtue.
The subsequent two lines further clarify merit, while the remaining four lines further clarify wisdom.

The sixth section, "Tranquility of Practice," clarifies the quality of the irreversible Dharma; that is, the two dharmas of teaching (*śāsana*) and realization (*adhigama*) cannot be overturned by others.
Within the text, the first two lines briefly indicate these two—teaching and realization—the latter being the realization of tranquility.
The passage beginning with "In all the Buddha-dharma teachings, he always... specifically clarifies the teaching.
The section beginning with "the power of mindfulness" provides a further clarification.
Since his realization is like space, free from attachment and so forth, how could others possibly turn him?

The seventh section, beginning with “In all worlds,” clarifies the virtue of unimpeded conduct; that is to say, although one performs acts of benefit and happiness for the world, the eight worldly dharmas cannot obstruct them.
In the text, the passage beginning with "the bodhisattva abides in the bodhicitta and achieves firm power" refers to the cause of non-obstruction.

The eighth section, starting from "all buddhas," clarifies the establishment of inconceivable virtues; that is, the establishment of the true dharma (saddharma), which ordinary and ignorant beings are unable to conceive.

In this passage, the initial section generally demonstrates that all teachings are established through the majestic power of the Tathāgata and that bodhisattvas are able to know them; by contrast, it implicitly reveals the inconceivability of ordinary beings.

The section beginning with "Entering Non-duality" separately elucidates the inconceivable characteristics of its formal establishment; that is to say, because it is extensively taught based on the signless (*animitta*), and because it possesses manifold aspects according to the various inclinations of those seeking understanding, both are inconceivable.

The ninth section, "Taking the Dharma-realm as the Body," clarifies the universal vision of the three periods of time; because body and mind are equal to the Dharma-realm, his prophetic declarations regarding the events of the three periods are without error, as can be seen in the text.

In the tenth section, "Revealing All Dharmas," it is clarified that the body is eternally pervasive throughout all lands; that is to say, for the purpose of revealing the Dharma, the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) and Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) are manifested, pervading all worlds to bring about benefit and happiness—the textual evidence for this is also clear.

Eleventh, "Attaining the Buddha’s Wisdom": below this, it is explained that his wisdom is ever-luminous and thoroughly penetrates all dharmas; this means that because he is skillfully decisive regarding objects and capable of severing the doubts of others, the meaning of the text is also clearly evident.

The twelfth section, "Possessing Great Majestic Power," clarifies the mastery of all practices; that is, being endowed with superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), one is able to understand the dispositions and behaviors of sentient beings and manifests a body accordingly, which is precisely what constitutes majestic power.

Thirteenth, "Furthermore, for the sake of revealing" and below clarifies the removal of all doubts. This refers to those śrāvakas who claim that they lack even the slightest portion of roots of goodness; now, [the Buddha] is able to reveal [this truth], enabling them to know that they shall give rise to the sublime wisdom of the Tathāgata, and thus their minds are no longer obstructed.
The fourteenth section, "The Mind is Unmoved Regarding All Dharmas," clarifies that the body is unfathomable.
This contains two meanings:
first, because his body does not arise from false conceptualization and is free from the defilements of afflictions, karma, and birth, it is unfathomable.
The first line of the verse clarifies this:

although his body is without discrimination, like a mani jewel, it appears as golden in color and so forth due to the sovereign power of the Buddha and the superior resolve (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings, yet the Buddha himself remains without discrimination.
This is clearly demonstrated by the subsequent scriptural passage beginning with "Thus, one does not destroy the various realms of existence.

The fifteenth section, beginning with "Although following worldly convention," clarifies the wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas and others; that is to say, bodhisattvas tame sentient beings through immeasurable syllables, yet they must first rely on the Dharma heard from the Buddha to attain sublime wisdom. Therefore, all bodhisattvas and others seek this wisdom, as the meaning of the text is very clear.

The sixteenth section, "Comprehending All Dharmas," clarifies reaching the Buddha’s ultimate, non-dual shore. This means that comprehending the emptiness of all dharmas, the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and so forth, is precisely the Buddha’s non-dual *dharmakāya*. By relying on this *dharmakāya* to cultivate practices such as the *pāramitās*, one attains their fulfillment and is thus born from the *dharmadhātu*.

Seventeenth, “Like Space,” clarifies the possession of the Tathāgata’s impartial liberation. This means that the bodies and lands manifested by each and every Tathāgata pervade the entire Dharma-realm like space; they are without marks or form, do not obstruct one another, and yet do not intermingle, appearing as distinct entities according to the conditions of those to be transformed.

Therefore, the text says: "Expounding in accordance [with reality], one gives rise to all-knowledge within a single gateway of objects," meaning that one accords with each and every object individually.

Below the eighteenth section, "Contemplating the Stage of the Ten Powers," is the realization of the Buddha’s stage of equality, which is without middle or extremes; this means that the three bodies of the Buddha are equal and all-pervasive, as there is no distinction between middle and extremes.
Reaching *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) is the wisdom of self-enjoyment;
serving as a bridge is the penetration of transformational manifestations;
seeing phenomena without obstruction is the Dharma-body.
The concluding statement, "skillfully entering the various stages," refers to the ten stages of the Buddha.

Under the nineteenth [section], "Knowing the Various [Aspects]," it clarifies that [the wisdom] extends throughout the entire dharma-realm; this means that because this dharma-realm is most pure, it is able to give rise to the flow of dharmas such as the sūtras.
Pervading this entire dharma-realm, they shall bring about the appropriate benefit and happiness of all sentient beings in future ages.
In the present text, only that which is produced is mentioned, while that which produces it is omitted for brevity.

The twentieth is that all great vows are accomplished without exception; because they are equal to the realm of empty space and reach the limits of the future without end, they are then said to be "accomplished."
The above has been a brief exposition; for a detailed citation from various treatises, one should refer to the "Chapter on Ascending to Tuṣita.
Third, regarding the section beginning with "The Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, by means of this reveal," which clarifies the excellence of their virtuous capacities, there are two parts:
first, a general clarification; second, a specific elucidation beginning with "Although all... and so forth.

First, the initial section provides a preliminary indication: that which reveals the Buddha’s nature of equality by employing the virtues of the events of this assembly, because they equally possess twenty-one kinds of merit;
subsequently, from the words "This is... onwards, there is a general praise of the aforementioned virtues.

Within the second section, "Detailed Manifestation," while the other nine [categories] are not explicitly mentioned, the meaning of the first "non-obstruction" (anāvaraṇa) is extensively elaborated through forty-one propositions.
The first proposition states that "existence does not obstruct non-existence," because existence is the existence of non-existence;
the subsequent forty propositions clarify that "non-existence does not obstruct existence," because non-existence is the non-existence of existence.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the preceding section clarifies how these two are non-dual, while the subsequent section clarifies how this non-duality is dual, as well as the mutual identity of quiescence and function, and so forth.
Regarding the second part, beginning with "The Buddha-sons, the Bodhisattvas enter thus," which concerns the realization and entry into the functions of all phenomena, there are four sections:
first, the clarification of realization and entry; second, the departure from the marks of realization; third, the inquiry; and fourth, the explanation.
Regarding the first ten phrases here, the first phrase clarifies the meditative concentration that serves as the means of realization.
"Samādhi-jñāna-cakra" follows the original Sanskrit phrasing; strictly speaking, it should be rendered as "Jñāna-cakra-samādhi."
Because his meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is most supreme, he is named "Great Majestic Virtue" (*mahātejas*).
The phrase "is then able to" and following reveals the dharmas realized, namely, the realization of the dharma of the Buddha-fruit (*buddhatva*).
The first phrase is general; the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*) is termed "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*), while the conditioned fruit (*saṃskṛta-phala*) is termed "attainment" (*prāpti*).
The remaining phrases are distinct:
"entering" explains realization, while "accomplishing" explains attainment; "perfection" applies to both.
"Accumulation" refers to the completion of causes, whereas "purity" means the exhaustion of hindrances.

Concentration can bring about stable abiding, while wisdom can bring about thorough penetration; when both concentration and wisdom are transcended, one enters realization through the correspondence with self-nature.
Second, from "And this" onwards, it clarifies the departure from the marks of realization.

Because realization occurs precisely through non-thought (*amanasikāra*), one does not even think of the object of unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*); how much less so for the various phenomena that constitute the realized dharma?
There are three points regarding the intent of this third inquiry:
first, why is it that there is no thought despite the act of realization?
2. Why is it that one necessarily attains many fruits?
3. Why is it that the causal factors necessarily result in the attainment of the dharma of the fruit?
4. Explanation, in two parts: [The first part is omitted in the source].
First is the brief, specific explanation, followed by the extensive, general explanation beginning with "This samādhi.
Regarding the first, there are three interrogations for specific explanation:

(1) because its essential nature is free from conceptual thought; (2) because although the substance of concentration is one, its functions are infinite; and (3) because it is preeminent, it serves as the cause for attaining the dharmas of the fruit.
Regarding the subsequent "Extensive Explanation," this means that the text is extensive and the meaning is comprehensive, thoroughly clarifying the three preceding phrases.
This section has two parts:

first, a general outline: the object is the focal point of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); "deep penetration" is the realization and attainment of concentration; and "power" is the function of concentration.
All three are determinate in essence, as each is described as being "of various kinds";
since the preceding text spoke of them as "boundless," and they possess all three qualities in abundance, they are called "extraordinary.
Below the phrase "That is to say," there are twenty-eight specific items, each of which possesses the aforementioned three meanings.

As in the first phrase, "entry" (*praveśa*) carries the sense of "profound entry. "Inexpressible," etc., carries the sense of "boundlessness. "Gateway of wisdom" (*jñānamukha*) carries the sense of "objective sphere" (*viṣaya*).
In some instances, the sense of boundlessness may appear to be missing; this is merely due to the brevity of the text.
Knowing that wisdom resides in speech, and that speech is the gateway to wisdom;
entering the twofold adornment of merit and wisdom as non-dual;
and realizing that the six sense bases are not empty, being the Tathāgatagarbha.
Seventh, the sphere of compassion and wisdom is observed and delivered without ceasing;
the rest may be understood accordingly.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in Samantabhadra... onwards is the inexhaustibility of universal virtue.
Within this, there are four parts;

first, the actual manifestation of inexhaustibility: it is not only the aforementioned various functions that are inexhaustible, but also the ability to enter numerous samādhis in every moment of thought, which likewise cannot be exhausted.
Second, the interrogation: the intent of the interrogation is to ask, "Since one enters [the meditative state] in many moments of thought after thought, why does it not reach its end?
Third, the explanation: the intent of the explanation is as follows:
Because the objects of this samādhi are ultimately inexhaustible, there are ten phrases in the text:
the first is general and the remaining ones are specific, both of which can be understood.
Regarding the four similes, three of them illustrate the aforementioned inexhaustibility; each consists of a simile followed by its application (*upanaya*).
Within the synthesis of the preceding two [analogies], further inquiry (*vicāra*) and explanation (*vyākhyāna*) are added.
First is the analogy of the wish-fulfilling gem that grants all requests, which illustrates how the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) responds accordingly to produce inexhaustible dharmas.
The intent of the inquiry is as follows:
Why is it that the Dharma emerges inexhaustibly and without depletion?
The explanation of this meaning is as follows:
One realizes that the many illusory phenomena are all identical to reflections; they arise when conditions meet—how could there be any exhaustion?
Since its essence neither increases nor decreases, how could there be exhaustion or cessation?
Second, the analogy of two minds arising separately illustrates that the objects of perception are inexhaustible; this can be understood.
Third, the analogy of the dragon king’s rain illustrates the inexhaustibility of entering the Dharma.
Within this, there is first the simile and later the application (*upanaya*).
The application is divided into three parts;
first, the actual clarification of entering the Dharma, which corresponds to the drop being like a chariot axle, meaning that one enters the vast Dharma.
The first phrase is the gateway of universal wisdom; as for the subsequent phrases all being called "gateways," it is because both self and others enter and traverse through them.
As for the "Illusory Net," all things are illusory, for they mutually function as conditions for one another, intersecting and reflecting each other.
The world is without essence because its nature is emptiness; it possesses essence because it undergoes defilement and purity according to conditions.
Furthermore, it possesses essence as the land of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-kṣetra*); it is without essence as the land of phenomena (*vastu-kṣetra*), which arises from conditions.
Furthermore, because the pure lands accord with principle, they possess substantiality; because the defiled lands are falsely constructed, they lack substantiality.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Second, from "In a single thought-moment" onwards concerns the temporal duration of entering the Dharma, which corresponds to the time of the preceding rain-fall.

3. Regarding the section beginning with "Thus, at the time of entry," this clarifies the characteristics and functions at the time of entry, which correspond to the previously mentioned boundless, inexhaustible, and unconditioned realm.
This section contains three parts:

first, ten phrases clarify its characteristics; second, the section beginning with "seeking all-knowledge" clarifies its functional activity; third, an inquiry and explanation of the underlying reasons.
Now, first:
the first two phrases correspond to "clouds being boundless" and "rain being inexhaustible.

From "without weariness" downward corresponds to the realm of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*); since non-action is precisely the absence of effortful application (*anābhoga*), the body does not grow weary and the mind does not become despondent, neither undergoing permanent cessation nor momentary rest.
Because that which has not yet entered is constantly entering, there is no regression; because that which has already entered is eternally constant, there is no loss.
Since there is no dharma that is not the gate of entry, one does not abide in improper places;
since there is no mind that is not in accord, one always maintains right reflection.
Neither sinking nor uplifting is precisely the characteristic of entry (*praveśa-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the second point, the functional activity (*karmopayoga*): following this entry, each and every gate possesses such activity; these gates are inexhaustible, as can be understood from the explicit wording of the text.
Within the threefold inquiry and explanation, there are two points of inquiry.
The first asks:
"How could it be that a bodhisattva does not attain Buddhahood through the fulfillment of practice; why, then, would their karmic activity be without limit?"
The second person says:
"It may be granted that they are inexhaustible when displayed collectively.
Why, however, are they inexhaustible within each individual gate?"
The subsequent explanation of this intent also has two parts.
First, it is said:
Because the Bodhisattva fundamentally acts for the sake of sentient beings, and since these beings are inexhaustible, his application [of means] is likewise inexhaustible.
The second explanation clarifies the latter intention as follows:
Since both sentient beings and the world are like empty space, one may employ them inexhaustibly through any single gateway, just as there is space within a mustard seed.
By this, not only does a single gate become manifold, but a single moment can also accomplish many tasks.
This passage consists of three parts:

first, the metaphor clarifies that fire follows the conditions of its fuel; where there is much fuel, the fire persists. This illustrates that because the conditions for a Bodhisattva’s birth within the realms are vast, their activity is boundless.
The subsequent combination can be understood accordingly.
The following section provides a critical inquiry and its explanation.
The intent of the inquiry is as follows:
Why does a bodhisattva give rise to manifold karmic activities?
The explanation of this intent states:
it is for the sake of universally delivering sentient beings and fulfilling universal vows.
The fourth section, "Therefore, all Bodhisattvas... and below, concludes and indicates the exhortation to practice; it consists of two parts:
first, the conclusion and exhortation to diligent cultivation; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra in this way" and below, the summary and manifestation.
Regarding the first [point]: it means that because the Bodhisattva’s mind exhausts the realm of sentient beings and its application is certainly boundless, one should cultivate it.
The text has two parts:
first, the presentation of the dharma to be cultivated; second, from "diligently apply" onwards, the demonstration of the manner of exhortation to cultivate.
Now, first:
the five characters "Therefore, all bodhisattvas" encompass the following two sections.

The dharmas to be cultivated consist of eleven phrases; the final phrase cites the name and essence of the samādhi, while the preceding ten phrases specifically clarify the functional activity of the unimpeded wheel (*anāvaraṇa-cakra*), in which the preceding texts are cited in reverse order.

First, regarding "categories" (*jāti*): because their functional activities are not uniform, they are like the analogy of damming a dragon; therein, the multiplicity of factors entering the dharma constitutes the meaning of "category.
Second, regarding "objects" (*viṣaya*): these are the focal objects of meditative concentration, as in the preceding analogy of the deluded mind taking an object as its focus.

Third, regarding "majestic power" (*prabhāva*), this refers to the universal manifestation of the function of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as illustrated by the previous analogy of the jewel being able to produce [all things].
Fourth, these three aforementioned types are all vast and expansive, each being limitless, because—as previously stated—one cannot perceive a prior limit to this samādhi.
Fifth, their number cannot be exhausted, for as previously stated, they enter the gates of ineffable wisdom and so forth, which are thus boundless.
Sixth, they are both beyond mind and speech, for as previously stated, they do not form such thoughts as "there are a certain number of bodhisattvas" and so forth.

All seven are accompanied by wisdom; as previously stated, although one knows that all phenomena are without activity, one is able to manifest all types of activity, because this is the clear illumination of the provisional and the real.

Eighth, when the eight aspects of essence and function are equalized within the Buddha-realm, all Buddhas appear before one, because—as previously explained—one has contemplated the stage of the Ten Powers up to *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Ninth, one is protected and remembered by the Tathāgatas, because—as previously explained—one is sustained by all Buddhas and has already entered the reckoning of future Buddhas.

The ten [perfections] not only exercise mastery in their present application but also fulfill past virtues, because—as with the previously mentioned qualities—their resolve and desire are entirely purified.
The second part demonstrates the characteristics of cultivation, which consists of two sections:

first, a brief demonstration of transcending faults and advancing in virtue; second, a detailed demonstration of transcending faults and advancing in virtue, beginning from the words "not relying on... and so forth.

Within this, first is the abandonment of faults, and subsequently, from the section beginning with "Regarding all phenomena" (*sarvadharmeṣu*), is the advancement in virtue; both passages can be understood accordingly.
This is the second summary.
As for "manifesting," it distantly summarizes the preceding sections in general, and proximately summarizes the aforementioned passage on the advancement in virtue.
If one were to correlate each detail individually, I fear it would result in overly cumbersome text.
This third major section concerns the perfection of the benefits of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*);
while the text specifically pertains to this particular absorption, its intent encompasses the preceding nine as well.
Within this, there are four parts:

first, the benefit of externally receiving the Buddha’s empowerment; second, the benefit of internally perfecting virtuous qualities; third, the benefit of being superiorly subsumed within the fruit of Buddhahood; and fourth, the benefit of correctly becoming identical with the fruit of Buddhahood.
The first five [points] of the beginning are as follows:
first, identifying the basis for the empowerment, which refers to being in a state of meditative concentration;
second, from "the ten directions" onwards, revealing those who bestow the empowerment.
3. From "Bestowed by the Tathāgata" onwards, the characteristics of the empowerment are explicitly revealed;
4. From "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva" onwards, the function of the empowerment is established; the texts for both can be understood accordingly.
5. From "Why" onwards, the text investigates and explains the underlying reason.
The intent of the investigation is as follows:
