Since universal practice has already been fulfilled, why is it necessary to continue practicing the conduct of harmonizing sentient beings until the end of the future?
The commentary explains:
This is because the nature of unobstructed vows is thus, and because having already perfected the great vows, they are truly capable of taming [sentient beings].
Second, regarding the section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva attains such... which concerns the benefit of the perfection of internal virtues, there are four parts:
First, the initial section restates the completion of the causes for abiding in concentration, summarizing the preceding text so that it may be clearly understood;
second, from "His mind constantly abides" onwards, the specific fulfillment is demonstrated, with the number ten signifying inexhaustibility;
third, from "O Son of the Buddha, this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has already reached Samantabhadra" onwards, the ultimate consummation is summarized.
4. From "Why" (*katham*) onwards, the text investigates and explains the underlying reasons.
The intent of the investigation is as follows:
Why is it that a bodhisattva is able to fulfill such a multitude of virtues?
The meaning of the commentary can be understood.

Regarding the third section, from "O Son of the Buddha" down to "by means of this samādhi," it summarizes the benefits of the Buddha-fruit; this middle portion has three parts, the first of which is the formal explanation.
Next, for what reason? This is an inquiry.
The intent of the inquiry is as follows:
"The aforementioned are the virtues of the Buddha; how can they be encompassed?"
Below the term "Bodhisattva," the commentary explains the meaning as follows:
Abiding in this samādhi, one is capable of all actions without exception, for one is identical to the Tathāgata.
This section consists of three parts:
First, it correctly reveals that there is no further karma remaining; therefore, all [kinds of karma] are referred to as "all.
Second, from the phrase "In this Dharma" onwards, it clarifies the characteristics of the performance of karma.
The first sentence generally shows that one acts based on the preceding [teaching], and no longer performs other insufficient karmas.
The phrase "dwelling in non-satisfaction" and so forth clarifies the meaning of its activity.
The section beginning with "Thus having... summarizes the aforementioned activities.

Thirdly, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the difficult points are addressed through a further explanation; that is, it elaborates on the aforementioned activities by stating that such karma is performed and no other karma is performed.
The text consists of three parts:
first, a brief presentation; second, the manner of practice, which extends to both body and mind;
and third, an inquiry. The intent of the inquiry is as follows:
Why is it not otherwise?
The subsequent detailed explanation clarifies that if one were to act differently from what precedes, one would no longer be a bodhisattva.
The text contains ten similes, which constitute ten sections, each with its own application (*yoga*).
First is the simile of the indestructible diamond, illustrating that the essence of practice is firm and solid.
Second is the simile of the exquisite color of pure gold, illustrating the external adornment of virtuous karma.
The analogy of the three wheels of light symbolizes the perfect clarity of wisdom.
The analogy of the four peaks of Mount Sumeru symbolizes the transcendence of the roots of goodness.
These four peaks do not correspond [directly] to the four [Bodhisattva] practices; however, they may be correlated with them if one so chooses.
The analogy of the five great earths being able to support illustrates the bearing of great compassion;
the analogy of the great ocean containing water illustrates the universal nurturing of great vows;
and the analogy of a military general clarifying battle illustrates the cultivation of meditative concentration to ward off enemies.
The eighth is the analogy of the Universal Monarch protecting the world, which illustrates how meditative concentration clears away the delusions of beings.
The ninth is the analogy of planting seeds and their growth, which illustrates how practice increases the virtues of beings.
The tenth is the analogy of seasonal rain bringing forth seeds, which illustrates how the rain of the Dharma universally brings all things to fruition.
First the analogy, then the application.
Within the application, there are two parts:
first the formal application, then the interrogation and explanation.
Regarding the phrase "up to" (*yāvat*) used previously: it signifies that one bypasses the initial stages of production and proceeds directly to the final accomplishment.
Because [the rain] falls at the appropriate time, one obtains these fourteen kinds of benefits:
first, the attainment of the fruit of wisdom, because the two obscurations are purified.
Second, one attains the fruit of abandonment, because of realizing the signless dharma.
Third, one attains the fruit of gratitude, because of abiding in great compassion.

Fourth, one attains the fruit of the ultimate perfection of the purity of the basis; of these four, the first four pertain to self-benefit, while the remaining ones all pertain to the benefit of others.
Fifth, by understanding the conduct of sentient beings, one causes others to rejoice; by personally remaining free from the ten fears, one rejoices oneself.
Sixth, one attains the severance of doubt.
Seventh, one becomes worthy of offerings.
The subsequent phrases below are established on this basis, and their meaning can be understood from the text itself.
In the subsequent section of inquiry and explanation, the intent of the inquiry is as follows:
By what power of practice does a bodhisattva preach the Dharma to achieve such great benefit?

The first part is the heading; the subsequent section beginning with "That is to say" is the explanation.
Within the explanation, there are three parts:
first, a listing of the merits to be purified;
Second, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the vastness and multiplicity [of the dharmas] are summarized, because they cannot be fully described through individual exposition;
third, from "In such as these" onwards, the causes capable of purification are revealed.
Regarding "concordant roots of goodness," it means that each individual root of goodness is dedicated to the *dharmadhātu* so as to become a principal with its retinue.
Regarding "surpassing all worlds" and so forth, it means that because the merit cultivated is in accord with the *dharmatā*, it transcends the world.
Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) does not coexist with reality, it has no counterpart.
The remainder is easily understood.
From the fourth section, "The Buddha-son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in this samādhi," onwards, it is identical to the benefit of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the actual manifestation of the commonality, which includes the heading, the inquiry, and the enumeration.
It is by virtue of these that the name "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambodhi) is established.
Second, from "At that time, Universal Eye" onwards is the section on questions and answers for clarification.
Within this, first comes the question and subsequently the answer.
In the question, first the preceding state of being identical to the Buddha is restated, and then, from "For what reason" onwards, the speaker sets forth his own doubts.
Within this, the initial doubt is not termed a "result," while the subsequent question does not abandon the "cause.
The answer begins from "At that time, Samantabhadra... below, which is divided into two parts:
first, praising the question and restating the doubt; second, the formal answer to the question, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this bodhisattva... and so forth.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the exposition of the Dharma; second, the illustrative analogy; and third, the application of the Dharma.
Now, regarding the first part, there are eleven sections that sequentially answer the eleven preceding questions.
The phrasing is easy to understand, yet the meaning remains difficult to perceive: how is it that one has already entered the Ten Powers and yet practices universally without ceasing?

To clarify this in general through analogy: it is like a person who, though having mastered a text through recitation, continues to rehearse it repeatedly rather than resting content with long-term proficiency alone.
The following parable of the fragrant elephant illustrates that while their appearances may be similar, their essential natures are different.
Thus, the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* states: "Equal Enlightenment is illumination within stillness; Wondrous Enlightenment is stillness within illumination."
This also resembles the stage of perfected effort, yet it is here effortless (*anābhoga*).
It further demonstrates that one realizes the fruit without abandoning the cause, for until the end of the future, one remains in the universal stage of Samantabhadra following the [initial] stage.
The analogy has three parts.
First, the description of the Elephant King’s excellence in both his physical form and environment:
Airāvaṇa—here translated as "Fragrant Leaf"—resides constantly on the flank of the foremost Golden Mountain.
Second, from "If, O Lord of Devas" onwards, it clarifies the sovereign spiritual transformations of the Elephant King.
Regarding the "seven tusks," according to the "Bhadrapāla Chapter," there are only six tusks; perhaps the translator, following the subsequent pattern of "three sevens," simply stated "seven."
If it is intended as a metaphorical expression, why would it be unacceptable?
There is no one capable of distinguishing whether this is an elephant or a celestial being; the true intent is to take this as a metaphor for the meaning of bodhisattvas being equal to Buddhas.
Third: "O Son of the Buddha, that Airāvaṇa... and below clarifies how one can manifest without destroying the fundamental [reality].
Within this third section on the application of the Dharma, there are four parts.
First, the perfection of various practices as adornments corresponds to the preceding discussion of the environment and its inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*).

2. From "In order to establish [them securely]" onwards, it clarifies the non-obstruction between cause and fruit, which corresponds to the aforementioned sovereign spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi*).

3. From "O Son of the Buddha, the original body of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva" onwards, it concludes by establishing that the fruit manifests from an indestructible cause, which corresponds to the aforementioned ability to manifest while the fundamental nature remains indestructible.
4. From "For what reason" onwards, there is a combined interrogation and explanation. The first part may be understood as it stands.
In the second part, there are two [sections]: [The text continues: ...the first of these two may be understood as it stands. Regarding the second, there are two [points]:...
First, clarifying the purpose for practicing unimpeded conduct.
Within this, that which precedes [the section on] "increasing" constitutes the fruit, while that from "not abandoning Samantabhadra" onwards constitutes the cause.
Second, from "not abandoning Samantabhadra" onwards, the actual characteristics of unimpeded conduct are revealed.
Within this, first there is a general clarification, because the causes and effects of the *dharmadhātu* are unobstructed;
subsequently, from "manifesting the unspeakable" onwards, there is a specific exposition.
This is divided into three parts:
First, the section on the causes and the practices of the fruits is revealed.
This passage contains four types of fruits:
first, the fruit of wisdom; second, the fruit of teaching the Dharma; third, the fruit of being conjoined with prajñā; and fourth, the fruit of abandonment.

Next, the section beginning with "and manifests birth" reveals that the fruit arises from causal practice, as well as the different times of its attainment, because it manifests according to sentient beings.
Finally, the section beginning with "furthermore, in all... reveals the causal practice of the gateway of the fruit.
This can also be understood.

Third, regarding the explanation of the indestructible cause within the manifestation of the fruit: the original body being indestructible is itself the indestructible cause; thus, it remains unchanging while conjoined within the cave.
The manifestation in all places is precisely the manifestation of the fruit; this is subsumed under the supernormal power of the devas.
Regarding the fourfold inquiry and explanation within the section on mutual inclusion: first, the intent of the inquiry is as follows:
since cause and fruit are mutually distinct, how can the fruit manifest through the gateway of the cause, and how can the fruit in turn become the cause?

The meaning of the commentary is that the method for disciplining sentient beings should be thus. The text consists of two parts: 1. The teaching on the method of disciplining sentient beings. 2. The teaching on the method of disciplining oneself. First, the teaching on the method of disciplining sentient beings has two sections: A. A general explanation of the method of disciplining sentient beings. B. A specific explanation of the method of disciplining sentient beings. Regarding the first section, the general explanation of the method of disciplining sentient beings, it is said: "If one wishes to discipline sentient beings, one must first discipline oneself. This means that if one wishes to subdue sentient beings, one must first subdue oneself. Why is this so? Because if one does not subdue oneself, one will be unable to subdue others. Therefore, one who wishes to discipline sentient beings must first discipline oneself. This is because the mind is the master of all phenomena; if the mind is subdued, all phenomena are subdued. Furthermore, the mind is the root of all dharmas; if the mind is subdued, all dharmas are subdued. Moreover, the mind is the sovereign of all dharmas; if the mind is subdued, all dharmas are subdued. For these reasons, one who wishes to discipline sentient beings must first discipline oneself. This is called the general explanation of the method of disciplining sentient beings. Second, the specific explanation of the method of disciplining sentient beings has three points: A. The method of disciplining sentient beings through the four immeasurables. B. The method of disciplining sentient beings through the six perfections. C. The method of disciplining sentient beings through the three gates of liberation. Regarding the first point, the method of disciplining sentient beings through the four immeasurables, there are four types: 1. The immeasurable of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). 2. The immeasurable of compassion (*karuṇā*). 3. The immeasurable of sympathetic joy (*muditā*). 4. The immeasurable of equanimity (*upekṣā*). Regarding the first type, the immeasurable of loving-kindness: what is loving-kindness? Loving-kindness is the wish for all sentient beings to obtain happiness. What is the immeasurable of loving-kindness? It is the cultivation of the mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings without limit or obstruction. How does one cultivate the mind of loving-kindness? One should first cultivate the mind of loving-kindness toward those who have benefited oneself, then toward friends, then toward neutral persons, and finally toward enemies. Cultivating the mind of loving-kindness toward those who have benefited oneself means generating thoughts of loving-kindness and wishing them to obtain happiness. Cultivating the mind of loving-kindness toward friends means generating thoughts of loving-kindness and wishing them to obtain happiness. Cultivating the mind of loving-kindness toward neutral persons means generating thoughts of loving-kindness and wishing them to obtain happiness. Cultivating the mind of loving-kindness toward enemies means generating thoughts of loving-kindness and wishing them to obtain happiness. If one can cultivate the mind of loving-kindness in this manner toward all sentient beings, this is called the immeasurable of loving-kindness. Regarding the second type, the immeasurable of compassion: what is compassion? Compassion is the wish for all sentient beings to be free from suffering. What is the immeasurable of compassion? It is the cultivation of the mind of compassion toward all sentient beings without limit or obstruction. How does one cultivate the mind of compassion? One should first cultivate the mind of compassion toward those who are currently suffering, then toward those who have previously suffered, then toward those who are currently happy, and finally toward those who are currently peaceful. Cultivating the mind of compassion toward those who are currently suffering means generating thoughts of compassion and wishing them to be free from suffering. Cultivating the mind of compassion toward those who have previously suffered means generating thoughts of compassion and wishing them to be free from suffering. Cultivating the mind of compassion toward those who are currently happy means generating thoughts of compassion and wishing them to be free from the suffering of change. Cultivating the mind of compassion toward those who are currently peaceful means generating thoughts of compassion and wishing them to be free from the suffering of conditioned existence. If one can cultivate the mind of compassion in this manner toward all sentient beings, this is called the immeasurable of compassion. Regarding the third type, the immeasurable of sympathetic joy: what is sympathetic joy? Sympathetic joy is the rejoicing in the happiness and merit of all sentient beings. What is the immeasurable of sympathetic joy? It is the cultivation of the mind of sympathetic joy toward all sentient beings without limit or obstruction. How does one cultivate the mind of sympathetic joy? One should rejoice in the happiness of those who are currently happy, rejoice in the merit of those who possess merit, rejoice in the virtues of those who possess virtue, and rejoice in the liberation of those who have attained liberation. If one can cultivate the mind of sympathetic joy in this manner toward all sentient beings, this is called the immeasurable of sympathetic joy. Regarding the fourth type, the immeasurable of equanimity: what is equanimity? Equanimity is the mind that is impartial toward all sentient beings, neither favoring nor disliking. What is the immeasurable of equanimity? It is the cultivation of the mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings without limit or obstruction. How does one cultivate the mind of equanimity? One should cultivate the mind of equanimity toward those who have benefited oneself, toward friends, toward neutral persons, and toward enemies, regarding them all as equal. If one can cultivate the mind of equanimity in this manner toward all sentient beings, this is called the immeasurable of equanimity. If one can practice these four immeasurables, one will be able to discipline sentient beings. This is called the method of disciplining sentient beings through the four immeasurables. [The text continues with the remaining sections on the six perfections and the three gates of liberation.]
First, the meaning of the fruit acting as the cause is explained; this can be understood through ten phrases.
Following this, from "O Son of the Buddha, you should... onwards, the meaning of the cause manifesting the fruit is explained.
This section contains four parts:
First, the teaching of the Dharma: this refers to the manifestation of the fruit without abandoning the cause.
Second, from "Like Airāvaṇa" onwards, the preceding metaphor is cited to clarify this.

Third, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, it is again conjoined with the Dharma; herein, first, the manifestation of the fruit without abandoning the cause is explained, and subsequently, from "Although one knows that all dharmas are equal," the manifestation of the cause without destroying the fruit is explained.
The four Buddhas [state] "From 'the son arrives' down to 'abiding securely'" as a praise of excellence.
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the characteristics.
The third part, the summary of the title, is self-evident.
The individual explanations of the ten concentrations are hereby concluded.
Finally, the "Son of the Buddha" summarizes the ten numerical categories;
this constitutes the third major section of the *Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Fascicle 45.
Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Fascicle Forty-Six, composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Monastery at Mount Qingliang, Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Ten Pervasions. From the "Ten Pervasions" chapter, twenty-eighth, onwards, one enters the forty-fourth scripture.

The purpose of this initial arrival is to answer the ten questions concerning supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) from the second assembly; two chapters are used to clarify the vastness of their karmic function, as this chapter on supernormal powers follows the preceding chapter on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in accordance with the sequential logic of the teachings.
Furthermore, these are developed through reliance on meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Second, regarding the explanation of the names: "penetration" (*abhijñā*) refers to supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). That which is wondrous in its application and difficult to fathom is called "spiritual" (*śen*), while that which is sovereign and unimpeded is called "penetration" (*tong*).
The wondrous function is infinite, yet it is manifested through the ten [knowledges] to reveal its perfection.
Both the Jin-period translation and the *Bunyé jīng* refer to them as the "ten clarities" (*shímíng*), because they illuminate all things exhaustively without omission.

However, the distinction between "penetrating knowledge" (*tōng*) and "clarity" (*míng*) differs across various sūtras and śāstras; thus, the third fascicle of the *Dàzhìdù lùn* states: "To simply know the events of one's past lives is penetrating knowledge; to know the causes, conditions, and karmic actions of the past is clarity," and so forth.
Now, because this sutra penetrates and illuminates exhaustively, it may also be called "clear," as explained at length in the text.
Therefore, the subsequent sutra states: "This is not the sphere of penetration and clarity for all bodhisattvas."
The intent of the Jin translations was to preserve the meaning with fluency; in this current translation, the priority is to remain faithful to the literal text.

As for the three essential principles: the principle is the sovereign mastery of the function of wisdom; the goal is to fulfill equal enlightenment through boundless, skillful transformation and guidance.
Next, the actual explanation of the text is divided into four sections:

first, citing the number and providing the formal announcement; second, interrogating the number and enumerating the explanations; third, praising the superior capabilities in general; and fourth, concluding the number and distinguishing the results.

Now, for the first [section]. Regarding the "ten," they are: (1) knowledge of others' minds; (2) the divine eye; (3) knowledge of past eons and former abodes; (4) [knowledge] reaching to the end of future eons; (5) unimpeded and pure divine hearing; (6) traveling to all Buddha-fields without substantiality or movement; (7) skillful discernment of all speech and terminology; (8) immeasurable form-bodies; (9) wisdom regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma-jñāna*); and (10) entry into the samādhi of the cessation of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-nirodha-samādhi*).
These ten are all called "wisdom-penetration" because they all take great wisdom as their essential nature.

If explained according to their specific characteristics, the first eight are wisdoms of measure and the final two are wisdoms of principle; yet in reality, they constitute a single, unimpeded great wisdom.

These ten also expand upon those six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because the divine eye, divine ear, psychic power (*ṛddhi*), and the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) are each divided into two.
The divine eye is divided into four based on seeing the present and the future;
the divine ear is divided into five or seven based on sounds and speech, as it also pertains to hearing the sacred teachings and various types of speech.
The bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) are divided into six or eight based on their functional application and their constituent material parts;
the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is divided into nine or ten based on the distinction between wisdom (*prajñā*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
since the single and the threefold are not further subdivided, six becomes ten.

However, the wisdom and function of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) in the Hīnayāna are partial; even the universal application of the three vehicles does not exhaustively encompass all things. Now, the wisdom and function of the ten supernormal powers in the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) are layered and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm; because they are as perfectly interfused as the net of Indra (*indrājāla*), they already transcend those [powers] in terms of clarity, let alone in their general utility.
To manifest the perfect purport, ten types of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are established.

In the second section, beginning with "What are they?", the enumeration is questioned and then explained; first, there is a general inquiry, followed by a specific explanation of the ten supernormal powers starting from "O Son of the Buddha."
This is divided into ten sections, each consisting of three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Now, for the first:
regarding the heading "other-mind," it is because wisdom takes the minds of others as its object of cognition (*ālambana*).

If it were simply based on its object, it should be called "knowledge of the differentiation of minds," because it is able to know various types of objects and various categories of kings; thus, it takes its name from both [the possessor and the object] according to the *tatpuruṣa* compound.
However, regarding the cognition that takes another's mind as its object, various explanations differ.
The master Sthiramati states:
"When the Buddha’s wisdom takes another's mind as its object, it apprehends the actual entity (svabhāva); all others [of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas] merely perceive a reflected image."

The Dharmapāla masters, however, maintain that even the Buddha manifests as a reflected image; for if one were to apprehend external dharmas by taking the primary object (bimba) as the basis, it would contradict the doctrine of Vijñaptimātra. Rather, [the reflection] merely resembles the primary object most closely due to causes of difference.
According to the Yogācāra school, Dharmapāla’s interpretation is correct.

From the perspective of the present sutra, however, the former [position] is also not lost; for while it subsumes objects within the mind, it does not destroy the objects themselves, and while both subject and object are extinguished, their existence is not obstructed.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is mind-only, neither identical nor different, because when it correctly takes another as its object, that very other is itself.

This is because the sentient being’s mind, which is the Buddha’s mind, is not the Buddha’s mind as the sentient being’s mind, serving as the object (*ālambana*); and the Buddha’s mind, which is the sentient being’s mind, is not the sentient being’s mind as the Buddha’s mind, serving as the subject (*ālambaka*). Since they are thus fused and integrated, they are neither identical nor different.
If one were to posit that sentient beings exist separately outside of the Buddha and must further project reflections, this would instead lose the meaning of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
Second, the section beginning with "knowing one" explains the characteristics, which has two parts:
first, knowing a single land; second, from "as with one," classifying the few by analogy with the many.
The preceding section has three parts: first, a general summary; second, a detailed exposition beginning with "That is to say"; and third, a conclusion beginning with "In this way.
Within the detailed exposition, there are thirty categories of mind, which lack the third category, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); however, this is fully present in the Jin translation.
Within this, the first ten [categories] generally manifest [the types of mind] by way of their characteristics, while the latter twenty minds specifically manifest them by way of individuals.
Among the former, the first two concern nature, encompassing all minds in general;
the next two concern practice, because they include both altruistic service and solitary cultivation.
The next two [categories] are distinguished by their retribution (*vipāka*): because the former is large while the latter is small.
The first four are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).

The next two are distinguished by their orientation (*mukha*): those that are "conformable" (*anuloma*) pertain to all three natures, whereas those that are "contrary" (*pratiloma*) are exclusively wholesome and may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

In distinguishing [the stages] according to persons, the first six are categorized by vehicle (*yāna*): the first three are the fruit and the latter three are the cause; these correspond respectively to the previously mentioned mind that turns away from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the minds of broadness and narrowness.
Next, the eight classes are categorized by type; these correspond to the previously mentioned minds that follow birth-and-death and those of greatness and smallness.
Regarding the hells and so forth, these are categorized according to the realms of existence (*gati*); they also conform to birth and death and are thus unwholesome states of mind.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Second is the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
The heading states "unimpeded" because of mastery in vision;
"pure" because it is free from obstructions;
and "divine eye" because it is a supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
Second, the explanation beginning with "seeing the immeasurable" is divided into three parts:

first, a general clarification that the characteristics of the many realms are distinct, and that the various states such as the good and evil destinies unfold successively, as described in the "Chapter on Questions and Clarifications";

second, beginning with "that is to say," a specific clarification that there are not merely one but many types, and that within each individual type there are the aforementioned offenses and so forth; [and third, the conclusion].

3. From the phrase "In this way, these various [aspects]" onwards, there is a detailed and clear illumination; whereas previously one merely beheld their manifest appearances, here their causes and conditions are illuminated.
It is from this that the titles of the Ten Clarifications (daśa-vyākaraṇa) are established.
Among these, the first [section] is able to see clearly;
the next, from "according to what" (*yathā-yathā*) onwards, details that which is seen—the phrase "according to what" is used because the objects of knowledge are not singular;
and the final section, from "all of them" (*sarvam*) onwards, concludes by affirming its freedom from error.
The text may be understood accordingly.
Third is the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
Among the headings, "past" (*pūrva*) refers to events that have already passed; "recollecting" (*anusmṛti*) refers to the clear and mindful remembrance of those things in the past.
This refers to the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) and the supernormal power of the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtyabhijñā*).
Regarding the second part, "capable of knowing" and below, which explains the characteristics, there are two sections:
first, knowing all matters, within which there is first a general statement, and then a specific explanation beginning with "namely."
Second, from "Furthermore, recollecting the past" onwards, one knows the Buddha’s deeds.
This section also has two parts:
first, by means of the realms (*dhātu*), it reveals their multiplicity, whereby one merely knows their fruit; [the second part follows].

The subsequent section, beginning with "Furthermore, he recollects," clarifies the multiplicity [of his visions] by way of the individuals involved and reveals their causes; this is because the Bodhisattva has attained the eye of the nine periods of time, whereby he perceives them as if they were present.
If it were not so, then a past phenomenon that has not yet ceased would not be called "past," and if it had already ceased, there would be no phenomenon that could be known.

If you claim that one remembers and knows because a seed or a reflection once experienced in the mind appears before one, then one is merely seeing one's own mind and not seeing that external phenomenon.
Furthermore, that which one has never experienced should not be remembered or known.
Moreover, if one perceives only the present and not the past, how can it be called "past lives" (*pūrvanivāsa*)?
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
The fourth is the supernormal knowledge of knowing kalpas, which is also named after its object.
Second, the section beginning with "knowing the ineffable" explains its characteristics; this consists of two parts:
first, knowing ordinary beings, and second, from "furthermore, knowing" onwards, knowing the Buddhas.
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, the clarification of the aeons (*kalpa*) upon which it relies.
These are merely designated by means of many world-systems (*dhātu*) to manifest the vastness of many aeons; they do not possess names that denote actual limits.
The subsequent sections extend throughout the future, for the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) in this stage are identical to those of a Buddha.
The following section, beginning with "each and every," clarifies the phenomena that serve as the basis; its meaning is as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
However, according to the Mahāyāna school, the essence and function of dharmas in future ages are both non-existent; how, then, can they be known?

Relying on the provisional teachings, one perceives only the present causal seeds and thereby knows the characteristics of the future fruit, but does not perceive the actual essence of future dharmas.
In the One Vehicle school, within the nine periods of time, the essence and function of the present exist together within the future; this is known as it truly is.
However, because it is not the "present of the present," it is termed the "future."
If this existence were existence by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would be identical to the Hīnayāna.
If it were existence by way of conditions (*pratyaya*), those conditions do not yet exist; how then can one say it exists?
If one examines the present moment, both conditions and intrinsic nature are absent, because in the present, the future is certainly non-existent.
If one examines it from the perspective of future time, because this [present] is the present of the future, it is just as if it were presently existing now.
Fifth is the supernormal power of the divine ear.
First, the name is stated; the supernormal power of knowledge is omitted for brevity.
If one simply speaks of "divine ear" (*divya-śrotra*), it receives its name based on its essential nature.
If one takes up the unimpeded and pure divine ear, it receives its designation based on its possession of virtuous qualities and functions.
Second, the section beginning with "Perfected" explains the characteristics [of the Buddha's activities], which is divided into three parts:

first, a general manifestation of the mastery of virtuous deeds; second, a specific demonstration of the activity and function in one direction, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha"; and third, an illustration of the remaining directions by means of one example, beginning with "Just as in the eastern direction."
Now, the first nine phrases all distinguish the virtues by way of their functions; the preceding designation of names constitutes the general statement.
First, "perfection" means the ability to employ [the senses] interchangeably;
second, "pervasive hearing" refers to hearing throughout the ten directions and the nine periods of time.
Third, because one simultaneously comprehends and perceives, thereby penetrating its source;
fourth, because one is free from the two obstacles;
fifth, because one clearly understands all that is to be known.
Sixth, because it cannot be obstructed by conditions;
seventh, because it is not like the limited understanding of those of provisional or small capacity who do not exhaustively realize its layered profundity;
eighth, because it has already been realized.

Ninth, because one possesses mastery over all things: that is to say, if one wishes to hear, even what is subtle and distant cannot escape; if one wishes not to hear, even what is near and loud does not disturb. Therefore, it is called "mastery."
The second part specifically demonstrates the function [of the teaching] in one respect, which has two sections:
first, citing many Buddhas to manifest the breadth of what is heard; second, from "These Buddhas... onwards, manifesting the hearing, recollection, and retention.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the hearing and upholding of the teachings, which can be understood through a word-by-word commentary;
second, from "Furthermore" onwards, the manifestation of perfect upholding, which is the characteristic of that which is able to uphold.
This section has two parts:

first, the presentation of what is upheld, wherein the preceding text generally reveals the Dharma taught by the Buddha, while the present passage distinguishes the specific differences of that teaching;
second, from "In that regard" onwards, there is the analysis of the characteristics of those who uphold it, while also clarifying their transformative activity.
The remainder of the text may be understood.
Regarding the sixth, the supernormal knowledge of the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva-jñāna-abhijñā*):
within the initial presentation of its names, there are fourteen; the first is a general designation, namely "absence of intrinsic nature," while the others are all specific.

Among these distinctions, there are: first, the absence of effortful activity; second, equality in principle; third, the capacity for universality; fourth, the difficulty of knowing its measure; fifth, not being said to arise from a substance as a function; sixth, manifesting form simply by following thought; seventh, the actual presence of functional activity; eighth, remaining unmoved from its original location; ninth, the certainty that its action reaches completion; tenth, the continuity of its activity without interruption, which also ensures the non-severance of the Buddha-lineage; eleventh, the inability of others to destroy it; twelfth, the capacity to generate roots of goodness; and thirteenth, proceeding wherever one goes.

Among these thirteen, the first two, the fifth, and the eighth pertain to the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), while the remainder pertain to the meaning of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); because these two are unimpeded, they receive this name.
Second, the section beginning with "This bodhisattva" explains the characteristics, which consists of three parts:
first, it clarifies vastness, meaning that upon hearing the names of many Buddhas in many lands, one immediately perceives one's own body within those many lands;

second, the section beginning with "Those various worlds" clarifies the meanings of being immeasurable and non-arising, meaning that by again hearing the names of the Buddhas in those lands, one immediately proceeds to pay respect, serve them, and receive the Way without attachment.
Third, the section beginning with "Thus, this sutra" clarifies the meaning of non-interruption; that is to say, because its essence and function are unimpeded over a long period of time.

Regarding the seventh [topic], the "Skillful Differentiation of Speech and Sound," first the name is designated: if named according to what is understood, it is established as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound);
if named according to what is produced, it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).
Second, the section beginning with "knowing that it is ineffable" explains the characteristics; this consists of two parts:
first, the knowledge of verbal expressions, which includes the headings, the enumeration, and the conclusion;
second, the section beginning with "this bodhisattva," which clarifies the utterance of words, meaning that one speaks according to the distinctions of their inclinations.
The thesis, the example, and the application are all clear from the text.
The eighth is the wisdom of the supernormal power of the adornment of the form-body (*rūpakāya*).
It is named according to what it manifests; that is, the designation is established based on its possession [of attributes].
Second, the explanation of the characteristics from "knowing all" onwards has three parts:
first, knowing formlessness, because form is itself emptiness;
second, from "the bodhisattva thus" onwards, clarifying the ability to manifest form, because emptiness is itself form.
Third, from "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, both the formless manifesting as form are clarified, because their activity does not obstruct compassion.
First, because one realizes that the dharma-realm has no fixed or substantial form, its entire substance is emptiness, yet it is not a nihilistic void.

In space there is no form, because it does not obstruct form; because it is able to exercise mastery over existence and non-existence, as well as concealment and manifestation, it can manifest various forms according to one's inclinations; therefore, this is explained first.
Among these, there are six phrases:
the first one generally understands that the nature of form is free from characteristics, because there is no dharma that constitutes emptiness;
the remaining five specifically clarify what kind of characteristics it is free from.
First, it is free from differentiated characteristics, because coarse and subtle, long and short, and so forth, are identical in their essence of non-arising.
Second, various distinct characteristics are empty.
Third, immeasurable manifold characteristics are detached.
Furthermore, there is neither large nor small, for all measure and quantity are severed.
Fourth, these are merely false discriminations, for they cannot be found when sought.
Since both the views of form and emptiness are equally objects of grasping, the distinction between identity and non-identity is transcended.
The preceding section encompasses both form and appearance.
Fifth, it distinguishes the characteristic of appearance, because [form] exists in dependence upon appearance.

Second, regarding the ability to manifest color: the first part summarizes the preceding section and sets forth the heading, while the latter part explains that color which is itself emptiness constitutes wondrous color.

Furthermore, the non-duality of emptiness and form constitutes the aforementioned true emptiness; though non-dual, they appear as two in this wondrous form. When form and emptiness are fused and identical, they become the true Dharma-realm; when dependent origination is inexhaustible, the one manifests as the many.

Below the phrase "That which is called," there is a detailed exposition of one hundred and three distinct types; these are established either by way of their physical characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) or by way of their qualities and functions (*guṇa-kriyā*), and may be sought through careful reflection.

However, all these are designated as "form" (*rūpa*) because they are the color-aspect of the *dharmadhātu*; they do not differ from that which undergoes transformation and obstruction, but rather the name "form" is established according to what is manifested.

Within the section clarifying the purpose through three pairs, the first summarizes the preceding [section], while the subsequent portion beginning with "that which is now to be converted" reveals the purpose; it contains ten phrases, all of which can be understood.
The ninth is the supernormal knowledge of the cognition of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-jñāna-abhijñā*).
First is the designation of its name, which receives its title from the phenomena known, such as the ultimate and conventional truths.
Second, the section beginning with "knowing all" explains its characteristics; this consists of two parts:
The first part, "clearly knowing the Dharma," clarifies internal realization of both phenomena and principle;
the latter part, beginning with "this bodhisattva," clarifies the exposition of the Dharma, which externally benefits sentient beings.

This is also because the former clarifies that phenomena are eternally the principle, while the latter clarifies that the principle is constantly manifested as phenomena, for there is no obstruction between quiescence and its functioning.
Now, for the first [section], there are two parts:
first, revealing reality by means of transcending words; second, from "non-self" (*anātman*) onwards, revealing reality by means of the two emptinesses (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).
Herein, the first three lines exclusively reveal reality:
First, because there is no merit in obtaining anything; second, because that which arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature; third, because its essence is devoid of coming and going.
Below, three phrases follow in pairs to reveal reality.
However, there are three meanings for explaining these three pairs:
first, if considered solely in terms of revealing reality, they are empty because they are mutually dependent;
since their distinct characteristics are mutually non-existent, it is said that they are not different.
To negate the statement that they are not different is itself not to find non-difference; thus, it is said they are "not non-different.
Second, regarding the simultaneous manifestation of their essence: the characteristic of non-difference is not non-different.

Third, regarding the simultaneous negation of identity and difference: because essence is not [identical to] characteristics, they are not different; because essence is identical to characteristics, they are not non-different.
Furthermore, because characteristics are not characteristics, they are not different; because essence is not essence, they are not non-different.
Therefore, one departs from the two extremes and does not abide even in the middle way.
The following two pairs should be understood by analogy.
Second, the middle way is revealed in relation to the two emptinesses; likewise, the first three pairs exclusively reveal the ultimate reality.
"Without peer" means there is nothing that possesses "mine-ness" (mamakāra) with which it could be compared.
The other two [terms] may be understood accordingly.
Regarding "without reality" (*asadbhūta*) and those following, they also admit of three interpretations; these should be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Furthermore, let us explain this by means of the provisional and the ultimate:
first, both the unreal and the real are manifested through conditions;

second, because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) does not coexist with the conventional, it is "one-marked"; yet since even this "one" is not established as one, it is "markless"; and since both existence and non-existence are merely dharmas that exist in mutual dependence, they are "non-existent."
Dharma and non-Dharma are merely provisional designations; when sought according to reality, both the remedy and that which is to be remedied are entirely quiescent.
All other cases are to be understood by analogy with this.
Second, the external benefit of expounding the Dharma, which has three parts:
First, restating the previously established wisdom, as it serves as the basis for the arising of activity;
second, from "not abandoning" onwards, correctly clarifying the manifestation of the Dharma;
third, from "although knowing the true nature" onwards, the non-obstruction between quiescence and activity, which contains three parts:

First, quiescence does not obstruct function; next, from "although there is verbal expression" onwards, function does not obstruct quiescence; finally, from "in non-duality" onwards, quiescence and function are non-dual.
The tenth is the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti-jñāna-abhijñā*). This section has three parts;
first, the designation of its name.

Regarding the phrase "the extinction of all phenomena" (*sarvadharmakṣaya*): it means that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are all quiescent in their very essence. This is the extinction of principle (*li-mie*), which differs from the extinction of other schools' systems of meditation on cessation, which merely clarifies the extinction of phenomena (*shi-mie*)—extinguishing only the sixth and seventh consciousnesses and their mental factors (*caitta*), but not extinguishing the eighth consciousness and so forth.
However, because phenomena are extinguished, one cannot immediately employ them while remaining in meditative concentration;

because the realization of principle is extinguished, there is no obstruction between concentration and dispersion. Since principle is identical to phenomena, extinction does not obstruct it; since phenomena are identical to principle, activity does not obstruct it. Therefore, the text says: "Although he enters [meditation] in every thought-moment, he does not abandon the Bodhisattva path," and so forth.

Nor is it that the mind remains fixed while the body initiates activity; nor is it simply a matter of clarity where both concentration and distraction are severed. Rather, it is because phenomena and principle are unimpeded. As stated regarding the seven higher stages:
"Though one practices within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one does not realize it as a final attainment; thus one can enter it moment by moment and arise from it moment by moment."
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one manifests all modes of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
Both of these passages convey this same meaning.

Because phenomena and principle are not identical, yet the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) of the extinction of all dharmas is not something separate, the state of cessation is itself the supernormal power; thus, both interpretations are valid.
Second, from "In every thought-moment" onwards is the explanation of the characteristics, which has two parts:

first, clarifying the sovereign mastery of the essence and function of samādhi itself; second, from "When this bodhisattva dwells in samādhi," onwards, clarifying the sovereign mastery over the duration of entering samādhi.
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, the heading that marks entering meditative concentration; second, from "also does not regress" onwards, the clarification of unimpeded function.
Within this, the first two lines are general: "not regressing when not yet acting" and "not abandoning when currently acting" specifically distinguish true cessation from the cessation of phenomena.
The remaining phrases are explained individually; the text is clear and can be understood on its own.
The second section clarifies mastery over the timing of entering meditative absorption, which has three parts:

first, the duration follows the mind; second, from "When the Bodhisattva enters this... onwards, his deportment is never faltering; third, from "Although amidst existence and non-existence... onwards, he is not hindered in the arising of activity, as concentration and dispersion proceed simultaneously.
Within this, first the principle is presented, followed by the analogy.
Light and shadow appear everywhere yet remain tranquil and mindless; they wax and wane according to the vessel, while their essence neither comes nor goes.
From the words "This is called" below, the name is concluded.
The third major section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva," is a general praise of their superior capabilities, which consists of two parts:
first, manifesting superiority through inferior form, because those of inferior capacity cannot fathom them;
second, from "except for" onwards, manifesting superiority through superiority, meaning that only Buddhas and the like can fathom them.
The fourth major section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, this is," concludes the enumeration and distinguishes the fruits; the text is clear and may be understood as such. Chapter 29:

The Chapter on the Ten Patiences (Daśakṣānti-parivarta). Regarding the initial intent for its inclusion: it is to answer the ten questions posed by Samantaprabha concerning the "Ten Summits"; the meaning is as explained previously.

The first two [stages] have already clarified their pervasive application to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and their broad utility; now, this section distinguishes the profound depth of their wisdom (*prajñā*), which is why it follows immediately after.

Second, regarding the explanation of the names: "Patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to patient acceptance, understanding, and confirmation; that is, the illumination and penetrating observation of wisdom, which, by relying on the Perfect [Teaching], manifests the ten stages.

Regarding the three aspects of the fundamental principle (*tātparya*): its principle is profound wisdom and practice; its goal is to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, which is unimpeded and inexhaustible.

As for this practice of forbearance (*kṣānti*), in terms of the stages, it corresponds to the mind immediately following the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), for the purpose of severing subtle ignorance.

If considered from the perspective of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), it actually encompasses all five stages; yet, speaking from the standpoint of the ultimate culmination, its essence is itself wisdom (*jñāna*).

This differs from other schools where the causal stage of patience (*kṣānti*) and the resultant stage of wisdom, though being one and the same wisdom, are explained differently according to their respective meanings—such as the various teachings of two, three, four, or five [stages]. Because this is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it speaks of the ten patiences (*daśa-kṣānti*).
Fourth, the correct explanation of the text.
The text consists of prose and verse.
Within the former, there are four parts:

This section consists of four parts: first, enumerating and praising the excellence; second, listing the names to reveal their essentials; third, providing detailed explanations based on those names; and fourth, summarizing their names. Regarding the first part:
first, the enumeration is given, and subsequently, from the words "If one attains... onwards, the excellence is praised.
Reaching the stage of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇabhūmi*) signifies the perfection of the causes inherent to one's own nature (*svabhāva-hetu*).
The non-obstruction of the Buddha-dharma signifies the fulfillment of the fruits of supreme progress (*viśeṣa-phala*).

Regarding the second section, "What are the ten?", which lists the names to reveal their essential significance: first, the inquiry into the number; second, the listing of the names; and third, the revelation of their essential significance.
Regarding the names, the first three are based on the dharmas and the latter seven are based on metaphors.
Among the three [categories], the first is based on the teaching; that is, patience toward the sound of the teaching, which is named after its object, and is thus "patience regarding sound."
Next, one [aspect] is defined by practice; because it accords with all dharmas, this "accordance" is itself patience (*kṣānti*).
Regarding the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*): if it is defined according to the principle of the non-arising of phenomena, it is the patience regarding non-arising;
if it is defined according to the wisdom of non-arising and the non-arising of afflictions, then non-arising itself is patience. Thus, both explanations apply.

Furthermore, regarding these three types of patience, if explained according to their general characteristics: the first two are both the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), tending toward it; only the last one is the actual realization of it.

If one considers them according to their respective stages, the three types of patience (*kṣānti*) are distinct and separate, because it is only when one has not yet reached this stage that there is "patience in accordance with non-arising" (*anuloma-anutpatti-dharma-kṣānti*).
This "accordance" refers merely to accordance with the principle; it is not the same as "patience in accordance" (*anuloma-kṣānti*).
If that is so, how does it differ from non-arising (*anutpāda*)?
Because compliant patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*) accords with both phenomena and principle, it is not the same as non-arising.
As the Sūtra says: "One also complies with and knows that dharmas exist," and so forth.
Furthermore, while the stages according to the five *kṣāntis* (patiences) correspond to *śānti-nirvāṇa* (quiescent extinction),
here the meaning is clarified in terms of the three *kṣāntis*, and thus they correspond to *anutpāda* (non-arising), as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Regarding the latter seven [patiences] among those based on metaphors, all are *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compounds), meaning they are "the patience that is like an illusion," and so forth.
Guangtong said:

"Regarding the four metaphors for sound, the metaphor of lightning and transformation illustrates compliant patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*); the metaphor of emptiness illustrates non-arising; and 'lightning' is precisely the present metaphor of the shadow.
Furthermore, he said that 'illusion' refers to the characteristic of arising without arising."
The flame has no characteristic of an object within its objective field;
the dream has no characteristic of cognition within its cognition;
the echo has no characteristic of hearing within its hearing.
"Electricity" refers to abiding in the mark of non-abiding.
Since it is now called "shadow," it should be said to manifest the mark of non-manifestation.
"Transformation" refers to existence within the mark of non-existence.
"Emptiness" refers to the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
While this [term] as a metaphor is restricted to a single characteristic, the meaning it represents applies to many phenomena.
Although this is not explicitly stated in the text, there is no error in principle.
Furthermore, an ancient master said:
"Contemplate consciousness as an illusion, perception as a mirage, feeling as a dream, sound as an echo, mental formations as lightning, and form as a magical transformation.
Because one contemplates all aggregates, elements, and sense bases collectively as ultimately empty, they are like space."
This explanation accords with the subsequent verses; therefore, the present metaphor of the shadow also represents formative activity (*saṃskāra*).

According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, all eight metaphors in the fifth [section] represent the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); however, because the doubts to be dispelled differ, the metaphors employed likewise vary.
First, when others hear that the dependent nature exists only as a product of false discrimination and is not a real object,
they immediately give rise to doubt, thinking:
"If there is no real object, how can there be any sphere of activity?"
Therefore, it is said that they are like illusions; for if an illusionist creates an object of perception through magic, how could the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) possibly possess reality?
Second, a doubt arises:
"If there is no reality, how can the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) continue to evolve?"
Therefore, it is said that like a flickering mirage, which is not water but appears as water, the mind revolves through delusion.
A third doubt asks:
"If there is no reality, how can there be the experience of the pleasant and the unpleasant?"
Therefore, it is said that just as in a dream there are no actual men or women, yet there is the experience of pleasant and unpleasant objects, so it is during the waking state.
Fourth, a doubt arises:
"If there is no reality, how can there be the proliferation of conventional discourse?"
Therefore, it is said that [all things] are like echoes; in reality there is no sound, yet the listener perceives it as existing.
The fifth doubt asks:
"If there is no reality, how can there be the fruits of good and evil karma?"
Therefore, it is said to be like a shadow; that is, like a reflection in a mirror, and thus it is not real either.
The sixth doubt asks:
"If there is no reality, why does the Bodhisattva perform acts of benefit and happiness?"

Therefore, it is said that they are like transformations (*nirmāṇa*); that is to say, although a creator of transformations knows them to be unreal, he still performs transformative acts, and the Bodhisattva is likewise.

However, while that treatise lacks the analogy of emptiness, the analogy of a reflection refers to a mirror image; furthermore, there is the analogy of a shadow cast by an object, which illustrates that the various consciousnesses lack reality.
Furthermore, there is the analogy of the moon in water, which illustrates that the objects of the meditative stages lack substantial reality.
Since the present sutra treats them as being of similar category, they are combined within the discussion of reflections; this shall be understood when the text is reached.
When Master Yuan saw that [the interlocutor] did not understand emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he used the analogy of emptiness to illustrate the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
While this was not without reason, it contradicts the subsequent scripture, which states: "Because sentient beings and all dharmas are all like emptiness."
If that is so, how is the analogy of space explained?

It means that although their doubt has been dispelled, they still believe that all phenomena possess an unreal characteristic; therefore, it is said that "like space, there is ultimately no substance."
The remaining meanings are explained extensively in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and in other chapters.
The nine similes in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* all metaphorically represent conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*);
however, the ten similes in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* apply universally to all things, as does the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

In this sutra, the prose (*gadya*) largely accords with the preceding general exposition, yet the metaphors used in the verses (*gāthā*) are also sometimes restricted; this is because the manifestation of meaning is not limited to a single method.
The enumeration of the names has already been explained.
From the words "These ten kinds" onwards, the essential points are revealed; because they are essential, they are treated together.
The third major section, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, how... and so forth, provides an extensive explanation according to the names, which consists of ten parts.
The first seven all contain three elements: the posing of the question, the explanation of the meaning, and the conclusion of the name.
Regarding the first patience (*kṣānti*), the commentary explains eleven phrases:
the first one generally enumerates what is heard, namely the dharmas such as the three natures (*trisvabhāva*);

the remaining ones reveal the capacity to hear and enter into these dharmas, meaning that upon hearing of signlessness (*animitta*), one is not startled, because one understands that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent.
One does not fear hearing of non-arising because one understands that the dependent nature is necessarily without arising;
one does not dread hearing of the absence of intrinsic nature because one understands that suchness has the absence of intrinsic nature as its very nature.
Another explanation:
regarding the dharma of true emptiness, one is not startled when hearing it, does not continue to fear when contemplating it, and does not remain in a state of dread when cultivating it.

Furthermore, hearing that there is nothing existing does not cause alarm; hearing that emptiness is nothing existing does not cause fear; and hearing that both of these are non-existent does not cause dread.
This is as explained in various *Prajñāpāramitā* treatises.
Profound faith is the beginning of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*),
while realization is its culmination, because what was initially believed is long since understood.
"Delightful affection" (*preman*) is the beginning of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), because one delights in and contemplates the Dharma.
"Tending toward" (*abhimukhībhāva*) is its end, because one has long reflected and is directed toward cultivation.
"Single-minded recollection" (*ekāgrasmṛti*) is the beginning of wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), because one initiates applied practice (*prayoga*).
"Cultivation as the culmination" clearly indicates that the practice reaches the fundamental basis of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Abiding securely" means that, relying on concentration, one gives rise to wisdom and realizes the principle through its corresponding application.
This is fully as described in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Regarding the second, the "patience in accordance with reality" (*anulomikī kṣānti*), the commentary explains that there are four stages of śamatha and vipaśyanā:
first, the initial cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā, which refers to śamatha as focusing the mind on a single object and vipaśyanā as contemplating both phenomena and their underlying principles.
Second is gradual *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: *śamatha* means settling the mind upon the objective realm; because it accords with the principle, it is called "equilibrium without contradiction.
*Vipaśyanā* means penetrating both the phenomenon and its principle; it is called "conformable comprehension."
As the verse says: "One correctly knows that phenomena exist, and one also correctly knows that phenomena do not exist.
Third is the full maturation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; that is, when delusions cease to arise through *śamatha*, it is called "purifying the mind."
Thoroughly observing the external object is "correct abiding" cultivation.
When the four [factors] harmonize with śamatha and vipaśyanā, becoming quiescent and dark within the realm of principle, it is called "entering.
Because wisdom manifests within the mind, it is termed "accomplishment."
The first four stages all involve the concurrent practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā; only in this way do they constitute true *anulomikī-kṣānti* (patience in conformity).
Regarding the third, *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena), there are two parts in its explanation:
First, there is a general clarification; second, from "Why... onwards, there is an interrogation and explanation.
Regarding the first:

if [the text] were complete, one should have interrogated each [quality] such as inexhaustibility and so forth; however, since these two serve as the general headings, they are merely indicated here briefly.
These are all specific meanings contained within the explanation (*vyākhyāna*).
Regarding the two points of inquiry within the subsequent interrogation and explanation:
the first is as follows:
"How is it known that there is neither arising nor ceasing?
The second [disciple] said:
"Since you call this the 'patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas' (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), why do you further say that one does not perceive the cessation of dharmas?"
In the commentary, the explanation of the initial inquiry states:
True dharmas are fundamentally non-arising; because dharmas arising from conditions lack intrinsic nature, they do not arise.
Since there is no arising, how could there be cessation?
This explains non-arising by means of the collection of conditions, and explains non-cessation by means of non-arising.
Herein, the collection of conditions is omitted for brevity, though it is fully present in the verse.
How does non-arising explain non-cessation?
There are two intentions here.
One says:
if something first arises, it must necessarily be subject to cessation later.
Since the fundamental [nature] is originally unarisen, it is now without cessation.
The second point states:

since that which is identical to conditions is devoid of intrinsic nature and is thus termed "unarisen," it does not wait for cessation to occur before becoming non-existent; therefore, it is next described as "without cessation."
These two serve as the general [categories], and the others may be inferred accordingly.
The explanation of the intent behind the second inquiry states:
Now, the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) is not merely non-arising; it must be the total quiescence of all phenomena.
Now, following the primary sense, the designation "non-arising" (anutpāda) is established; thus, "non-cessation" and so forth are subsumed within the meaning of non-arising.
If one follows an alternative sense, it may also be designated as "patience regarding non-cessation" (anirodha-kṣānti) and so on.

Therefore, the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra* clarifies that this patience can purify the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), stating: "First, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and also causes others to abide therein."
It further states: "The patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) refers to the realization of quiescence (nirvāṇa).
Second, one attains the patience of non-extinction (anirodha-kṣānti), and likewise causes others to abide therein.
It also states: "The patience of non-extinction refers to the realization of non-arising."
This text may be relied upon as authoritative.
Furthermore, each of these phrases possesses two meanings:

first, explaining the subsequent by means of the preceding, and establishing the preceding by means of the subsequent; and second, that because the preceding exists, the subsequent exists, and because the preceding is absent, the subsequent is absent.

Second, each and every phrase resides within the phrase of non-arising; at the very moment of non-arising, all meanings are instantaneously complete. This is because the principle that is identical with phenomena is not a state of annihilation, and the wisdom that is identical with this principle is devoid of subject and object.
However, as the meaning of the text is comprehensive, it shall be briefly explained in three ways:
first, according to principle alone; second, according to both principle and wisdom; third, according to wisdom alone.
Now, the first.
How is it that because there is a preceding existence, there is a succeeding existence? It is said: once a phenomenon has arisen, it ceases; having ceased, it comes to an end.

This ending is a defiled phenomenon (*saṃkleśa-dharma*). Being defiled, there is differentiation between the preceding and succeeding moments. Because they are differentiated, their locations differ. Where there is a location, the subject and object are not quiescent. When they are not quiescent, there is desire. When there is desire, there is purposeful activity (*abhisamskāra*). When there is activity, there is seeking and wishing. When there is wishing, the mind dwells upon the object of its wish. When it dwells [upon it], there is going and coming.

Now, because each preceding stage is absent, each succeeding stage is quiescent; thus, by means of the succeeding stages, non-arising is manifested and established. This accords with the prose section.
Regarding the two pairs concerning wisdom and principle: the first two are general, encompassing both wisdom and principle;
the subsequent four manifest that principle is non-arising.
The latter six [verses] reveal the non-arising of wisdom;
thus the verse says, "His mind is free from attachment," and so forth.
The harmonious convergence of principle and wisdom is termed the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Regarding the third point, "exclusively in terms of wisdom": because one realizes that there is no arising from conditions, wisdom itself does not arise; therefore, it is called "non-arising.
This patience regarding non-arising is profound and immutable, and is thus termed "non-extinction."
Because there is no cessation, its function is never exhausted. Next, it is free from all defiled thoughts; it is eternally without differentiation.

It has no spatial location, yet its illumination is ever-quiescent. Encountering objects, it remains unstained; though acting, it acts without fabrication; though compassionate, it is without longing; it dwells in the world without abiding; it is equal to the *dharmadhātu* without coming or going. All subsequent points are explained by preceding ones, and all preceding points are established by subsequent ones.
When words cease and thought is extinguished, such that there is still illumination in profound stillness, this is called the Patience of Non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
If one were to define the Patience of Non-arising merely by the knowledge of the principle of non-arising, it would not be sufficiently profound or mysterious.
The fourth is the patience like an illusion (*māyopama-kṣānti*).
In its explanation, there is first a brief summary and later a detailed exposition.
Within the brief summary, there are two parts:
First, one comprehends the characteristics of illusory conditions; subsequently, from the passage beginning "This bodhisattva," the practice of patience is accomplished.
Regarding the former [the comprehension of illusory conditions], there are three parts:
first, pointing to the phenomena as being identical to the analogy.
Next, that which arises from causes and conditions reveals the source of the illusion, because it is produced through conditions and is therefore unreal;
subsequently, the section beginning with "In a single dharma" manifests its illusory characteristics.
To begin with, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are the objects of the analogy; whether these objects are universal or limited has already been seen in the preceding text.
This point clarifies their universality, as they encompass both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Even if there were a single phenomenon that surpassed nirvāṇa, I would say it is like a dream and like an illusion."
Although *nirvāṇa* is real, it is manifested through conditions and serves to dispel the mind of attachment.
In the extensive [explanation], it is said that understanding the world as like an illusion makes it appear to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);

yet there is a "world of phenomena" (*dharmaloka*) that also extends to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Because this [unconditioned] is concealed and covered by the conditioned, it is therefore called a "world."
Therefore, it is said later: “Even bodhi and nirvāṇa are not perceived, because one has realized their equality.
Within the dharma and its metaphor, five factors are each distinguished, such as when a single cloth is knotted to magically create a horse:

(1) the cloth upon which it depends; (2) the magician’s artifice; (3) the illusory horse manifested; (4) the birth of the horse being identical to its death; and (5) the deluded and small-minded who claim it exists.
First, the cloth represents the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
second, the magic represents the causes and conditions that give rise [to appearances], namely karma, afflictions, and so forth;
third, it represents the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is sentient beings and the like.

The four similes illustrate that the dependent nature lacks intrinsic existence because it is, in fact, the perfected nature; thus, extensive explanations all state that [the dependent] is not [inherently existent].
The fifth simile illustrates grasping at persons and phenomena.
Now, the Bodhisattva acts contrary to this, and therefore it is said that he "understands."
The present sutra states that [the dharmas] arise from causes and conditions: that which can give rise [to them] is the second, and that which is given rise to is the third.
By taking the second as the cause, one is led to realize the third, thereby establishing the fourth and eliminating the fifth affliction, so as to return to the principle of the first.
However, since conditions themselves also arise from conditions, both the condition and its fruit are illusory.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "It is like a magically conjured person further creating another magically conjured person"—this is precisely that meaning.
However, each of the five aforementioned meanings possesses both existence and non-existence:
first, the nature of the cloth exists while its appearance does not, because it is concealed by the horse;
second, the function of the magic exists while its substance does not, because it depends upon the insubstantiality of the cloth.
Third, the three horses exist in appearance but lack reality, for they manifest despite being unreal;
fourth, birth is non-existence and death is existence, for there is no obstruction between them;
fifth, they exist emotionally but lack principle, for they are merely false perceptions.

Furthermore, within each of the five [categories], there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), which can be understood by applying the same reasoning; however, all of these possess virtuous qualities and are not like the four types of false accusation (*caturvidha-abhyākhyāna*).
If one were to interweave various categories to form many sets of four propositions, they may likewise be inferred through the same principle.
The subsequent manifestation of illusory appearances is briefly explained in two ways:

first, by way of analogy, which means that if one understands that a single thing lacks reality, one knows that all things are likewise so, because they all arise from conditions; hence it is said, "in understanding one, one understands many," and so forth.
Second, regarding the aspect of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), there are again three meanings:

first, because one follows principle through phenomena, one speaks of characteristics; that is, just as the cloth on the horse’s head is not different from the cloth on the feet, speaking of the head is itself speaking of the feet, such that one is many and so forth.
