Looking to the praise of Sudhana by Maitreya, it says that while other bodhisattvas can only fulfill their bodhisattva vows and practices after hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, Sudhana is now able to purify buddha-fields and so forth in a single lifetime; this is an instance of revealing the ultimate reality through provisional means, not a mere hypothetical assumption.
If such a person of non-faith truly exists, in what stage do they reside?

The text provides no definitive judgment, but by implication, they should belong to the three stages of the Sages-in-training (śaikṣa), for upon entering the realization of the noble ones (ārya), faith must necessarily be perfected.
If one considers the path of teaching, even after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* one has not yet entered the profound mystery.
That ordinary beings are suddenly able to believe is because their past causes—the cultivation of hearing—have served as distinct seeds.
If one does not believe now, how could one hear it in the future?
The second section, "If one is able to hear," below, provides a sequential explanation in two parts:

first, clarifying the benefit of hearing, believing, and being born into the family; second, from "O Son of the Buddha... having heard this Dharma, one is then able" onwards, clarifying the benefit of faith and hearing leading to the accomplishment of practice.
Now, for the first part: first, hearing and faith are clarified; subsequently, from "One should know" onwards, the accomplishment of benefits is shown.
Being born into the family of the Tathāgata serves as the general [principle], while the remaining phrases serve as the specific [details].

Among these specifics, the first takes the reality-as-it-is (*yathābhūta*) as the family. As the *Nirguṇa-śāstra* states: "To be born into the family of the Tathāgata means that the Buddha-dharmadhātu is what is realized and experienced; therefore, it is called being born into the family."
Second, they take the practice of the Dharma as their home, because they possess the qualities of a true household.
Third, they take the mundane realm as their home; as Vasubandhu’s commentary explains: "Because this ensures that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed."
"Fourth, dwelling far removed from the non-home;

fifth, taking the conduct of the Buddha as one's home. The first fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: 'Now this bodhisattva practices the path of the Tathāgata, because it continues in an uninterrupted succession.'"
This is explained at length in that commentary.
Sixth, the *dharmatā* of the bodhisattvas is their home, because it is also the lineage (*gotra*) of the Buddhas, and because it is identical to the single realm of the Tathāgata.
The seventh purity is the family of the Buddha;
the eighth is abiding in the fundamental family of the Buddha;
the ninth is the family that comprehensively clarifies the non-obstruction between cause and effect, as well as phenomena and principle.
The first six stages constitute the family of self-perfection, while the latter three constitute the family of superior progress.
Because one previously perceived the nature of the mind during the first stage, it is called the "family of birth";
because the fourth stage is associated with the supramundane, it is called the "family of the factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*).
Because the eighth stage is characterized by effortlessness (*anābhoga*), one is born into the family of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Now, this [stage] encompasses all three, further revealing that even the mind of understanding belonging to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is called "birth," because cause and effect are unimpeded.
The second [section] concerns the benefit of accomplishing practice through faith and hearing;
it consists of ten phrases, divided into five pairs of unimpeded [realizations]:

first, contemplation does not obstruct *śamatha*; second, seeing the Buddha does not obstruct entry into the Dharma; third, wisdom and practice within the *dharmadhātu* do not obstruct the arising of merit; fourth, wisdom being unstained by the world does not obstruct compassionate engagement; fifth, the essence being transcendent of the three periods of time does not obstruct the dedication of activity.
"Entering without entering" explains the meaning of "entering" mentioned above.
The passage beginning with "not in" further explains "entering without entering.
The essence of wisdom is itself suchness (*tathatā*); since there is no dharma external to suchness that can be grasped as an object of cognition, there is nothing into which one can enter.
Where the movements of the mind cease, there is stillness and no entry.
Because its illuminating function is never lost, one constantly observes all phenomena through the single suchness; therefore, this is called "entry."
When these two are unimpeded, one may truly be said to have entered.
Furthermore, since the one is itself suchness (tathatā), within that one, all is already seen.
The third section is a concluding summary, which can be understood accordingly.
The second verse pertains to the tenth benefit, that of seeing and hearing.
It does not eulogize the "receiving and upholding by name," as this will be eulogized later in the main text itself.

This verse should appear prior to the "exclusion of the dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*) in the analysis of phenomena; for the preceding prose section establishes the names through a linked sequence, as these too are beneficial through being seen and heard.
If this verse were moved to follow the "manifestation of omens," its connection with the subsequent verses would be highly consistent in both logic and literary style.
The four verses are divided into two parts:
the first verse provides the doctrinal exposition (*dharmadeśanā*), and the subsequent three verses correspond respectively to the three preceding metaphors.
This concludes the sixth major section: Manifesting Auspicious Omens as Proof of Accomplishment.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the manifestation of auspicious omens; second, the establishment through proof.
Now, for the first part: first, within this world-system; second, the universal application of these types.
Regarding the phrase "the number of moving lands and so forth are all vast and numerous," this is because the Dharma is inconceivable.
Second, from "At that time, in the ten directions" onwards is the section on "Proof and Establishment," which has two parts:
first, proof by those who have attained the fruit; second, proof by those who follow the path.

The reason for possessing both [the cause and the fruit] is that the Dharma is profound and subtle; it is the Dharma in which cause and effect mutually penetrate, and the Dharma in which the cause is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled.
As for the previous assemblies consisting solely of Bodhisattvas, they were concerned exclusively with causal practice.

In the "Chapter on Generating the Resolve," only the realization of the fruit is mentioned because it is the foundation of the fruit; furthermore, the idea that the initial resolve brings about Buddhahood is difficult to believe and accept.
Since these meanings are distinct according to their respective contexts, they do not appear together in those other sections; only here are both present.
Now, for the first [section], it is divided into four parts:
first, manifesting the body;
second, the praise and exposition beginning with "and he acts... and so forth.
3. From "O Sons of the Buddha, we... onwards, the text cites teachings to provide proof and establishes the connection to what has been taught, because it expresses one teaching as all teachings.
4. From "Now, in this assembly... onwards, the benefits are raised to provide proof.

Among these four, one attains the fulfillment of the fruit at the causal stage, because one gives birth to bodhi; and the supernormal powers and samādhis are precisely the ten powers and the ten concentrations.
Second, from the phrase "dust-motes of Buddha-fields" onwards, one obtains the benefit of generating the bodhicitta.
Regarding those who receive predictions for a distant time, it is because they do not expect swift accomplishment.

Furthermore, while the preceding section clarified that "one life" is itself "many," this section distinguishes how "many kalpas" are themselves "one. Since "one" and "many" are thus perfectly interfused, how could there be a fixed number of kalpas?
Though many kalpas may falsely elapse, the sun of wisdom does not shift;
if one stubbornly clings to distinctions of long and short, one will not expect to achieve Buddhahood.
That which is termed the "Excellently Superior Realm of the Buddha" is so called because it is the realm in which the Buddha appears.
3. From "We" onwards, the benefit of long-term preservation is shown.
4. From "In this way" onwards, the conclusion regarding the vast and universal benefit is presented.
Second, from "At that time, in the ten directions" onwards, the testimony based on persons is provided.
Within this, there are four parts;
first, the explanation of the causes for the arising [of the fruit].
As for the person who realized the previous fruit, because they inherited the causes of the preceding manifested omens, these are briefly not recounted.
Now, because this passage clarifies the distinction between cause and effect, it extensively sets forth the causes for their gathering; the text is explicit and thus easily understood.
Second, from "In each of the ten directions, beyond... onwards, the manifestation of bodies is explained.
Although they come from the ten directions and pervade the Dharma-realm, their coming is itself no-coming.
Third, from "Manifesting as Bodhisattvas" onwards, their virtuous functions are distinguished; the meaning of the ten phrases is clear.
4. From "By the Buddha's spiritual power" onwards, the words provide a sincere testimony.
That they are all identical to the Universal [Dharma] is because the Universal Dharma is the same.
That the names of the Buddhas differ across realms is so that the primary and attendant [Buddhas] are not lost.
"Universal Radiance" (Puguangming) refers to the fact that the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light pervades everywhere without exception.

The Buddha is named "Sovereign Universal Banner" (Putang Zizai) because his fundamental wisdom rises loftily, subduing all that stands before it, as phenomena and principle are unimpeded; this also serves to synthesize and connect what has been taught.
The seventh major section, beginning with "At that time, Samantabhadra," summarizes the preceding content in verse.
This section has two parts:
first, the introductory statement; second, the actual verses.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, the description of the ritual procedure;
second, from "desiring to reiterate" onwards, the clarification of the intent, which aims to further manifest the ten gates previously presented.
The text contains ten phrases, each representing a distinct gate; however, their sequence is not uniform, as they are arranged according to the benefit of sentient beings.

First is the attainment of perfect enlightenment; second is the turning of the Dharma wheel; third is the arising of wholesome roots through seeing and hearing—these three primarily manifest the benefits [of the teaching];
fourth is the manifestation of the Dharma itself, which serves as the general gateway for the preceding [three].
The fifth is the mind itself, as it is manifested by means of wisdom;
the sixth is the perfect voice;
the seventh is the objective realm, which is immeasurable, and thus the light produced is also manifold.
The eighth is *nirvāṇa*, because the Great Parinirvāṇa serves as the adornment of the Buddha, being the mastery over both movement and stillness;
the ninth is the "body," because it is spoken of as one from the perspective of its fundamental nature;
the tenth is "practice," because the cause is spoken of within the state of the fruit.
In the subsequent verses of the main body, there are four stanzas:
the first stanza explains the concluding response within the section, as it encompasses the meaning of all ten segments;
the latter three stanzas clarify the title and encourage its upholding—the first line clarifies the title, while the remainder all constitute exhortations to uphold it.
This may be divided into three parts:

first, a verse praising its profundity and difficulty to hear; second, a verse clarifying that the text arises from manifold roots of goodness; and third, a verse citing its excellence to encourage its upholding.
Indeed, the meaning of this chapter is vast and profound; it is both sudden and complete, investigating the fundamental source of sentient beings and exhausting the oceanic depths of all Buddhas.

Within the inner sphere of the fundamental wheel of Dharma, that mind arises within the lineage of the Golden Wheel; it is further the legitimate heir, the most sublime among the sublime, the most profound among the profound.
Sharing the same mind as ordinary beings, yet with little effort being able to realize [the truth] so swiftly—
how could one deceive oneself by refusing to accept this and remain long submerged within the cycle of birth and death?
Now that you have heard this explanation and can rejoice in it, you must especially congratulate yourself on your past roots of goodness.
The "Chapter on Manifestation" concludes.

Chapter 38: Leaving the World (Lishi-jian-pin). Above, the introductory meaning of the fifty-third scripture has been clarified.
There are three reasons for this introduction:

first, regarding the sequential order of the meaning. In the preceding section, "The Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generate Understanding," one gives rise to understanding regarding the Dharma;

now, in "The Section on Entrusting Oneself to the Dharma to Advance in Practice and Accomplish Conduct," one gives rise to practice based upon that understanding. This is because the meanings follow a logical sequence.

Regarding the arrival of the second assembly: the first assembly concluded with the generation of understanding through the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of fruits; this assembly concerns the correct practice of remaining unstained while dwelling in the world, which applies to both the beginning and the end, and is therefore the next to arrive.

Regarding the arrival of the third section: while the preceding section presented the excellence of the manifested fruit, this section clarifies how practice arises from that basis in a state of perfect fusion; thus, it follows next.
Although they are identical in being a single part, a single assembly, and a single section, because their respective objects differ, the purpose of their arrival is also distinct.
Second, the explanation of the names also has three distinctions:

first, regarding the partial names, these omit the names of those specific stages and instead manifest only the dharmas of practice. This is intended to reveal that the stages of practice are unimpeded and that the preceding and succeeding elements are perfectly interfused; therefore, they are designated by these names.

Regarding the names of the two assemblies: in terms of the Dharma, they are not distinct and thus share the same name; in terms of location, they are called the "Third Assembly" and the "Assembly in the Universal Radiance Hall.
As for the seventh assembly, it is because the end of the assembly returns to its beginning.
Although they transcended the four heavens, they were likewise gathered for the purpose of generating understanding;

now meeting once more, they universally correspond to the beginning and end of those respective stages, and because they rely on understanding to accomplish practice, they assemble at the Universal Radiance.
In the preceding section, there was a differentiation in the arising of understanding; therefore, the stages were traversed one by one to reveal their relative depth and shallowness.

In the present section, the arousal of practice is perfectly integrated; thus, a single assembly encompasses both cause and fruit, also signifying that the fulfillment of practice is not separate from the Wisdom of Universal Radiance.
In this context, since there is no interval between locations, how could there be the sense of "re-encountering"?
If considered in terms of sequence, the preceding and succeeding moments constitute the meaning of "repetition.

If considered in terms of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), it is called "repetition" from the perspective of its significance; thus, one ascends to the fourth dhyāna heaven without departing from the first two.

When the two groups of seven are viewed in relation to one another, what separation could there possibly be? It is clearly understood that, according to the underlying principle, they interpenetrate without obstruction like the light of lamps, and resemble the wick of a lamp repeatedly producing light again and again.
Regarding the persons involved, it is titled "The Assembly of the Questions and Answers between Samantabhadra and Samantamati.
As for the three chapters, there are two parts:
first, the naming of the title; second, the explanation of the title.
Regarding the first [section], there are again two parts:
first, the alternative names.
The ten meanings discussed in the subsequent text shall be analyzed in their respective places.
There is another separately circulated version titled the *Dushi jing* (Sutra on Transcending the World); "transcendence" (*du*) here carries the meaning of "detachment.

Furthermore, there is another separately circulated version titled the *Puxian pusa dan nan erqian jing* (Sutra of the Two Thousand Questions Answered by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva), which is so named because it focuses on the person who can detach from both phenomena and the self.
Second, the formal definition of the title itself: it receives its name primarily because it transcends all worldly defilements.
Specifically, there are three meanings:
first, in terms of the Dharma; second, in terms of practice; and third, in terms of the stages.
Within the summary of the Dharma, there are first the world of past lives and second the world of separation from life.
There are three categories:

first, regarding phenomenal characteristics, there are two worlds, namely the receptacle world and the world of sentient beings; this is a division based on the distinction between the environment and its inhabitants.
Secondly, regarding the coarse and the subtle, there are also two types:

first, the conditioned world (*saṃskṛta-loka*), and second, the unconditioned world (*asaṃskṛta-loka*). These are distinguished based on the *pariccheda-vipariṇāma* (segmented) and *pariṇāma-vaśitā* (transformational) modes of existence.
Because the transformational mode is not subsumed under the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), it is termed "unconditioned."
Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "There is conditioned birth-and-death and unconditioned birth-and-death.
Although they differ in being coarse or subtle, their essence does not transcend these two.
Thirdly, regarding the threefold division according to defilement and purity:

Regarding the first two [categories], the addition of "wisdom" and "perfect enlightenment" indicates that while they appear identical to the mundane world, they are in fact not mundane, as explained in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages).
Second, regarding "detachment," there are two meanings:
first, detachment by nature (*prakṛti-viveka*), because the emptiness of the nature of the mundane world is itself the supramundane.
Second, it clarifies the separation from phenomena, because practice is accomplished without defilement.
The *Balakāraṇḍavyūha-gāthā* states: "The dharmas of the five aggregates throughout the three times are called the 'world.
Their cessation is not the world; such [a world] is merely a provisional designation."

"Cessation" (*nirodha*) has two general meanings: cessation from phenomena (*dharma*) and cessation from reality (*tattva*). Within the former, there are further distinctions between partial cessation and total cessation, which will be analyzed below.
Second, regarding the practitioner, there are briefly four categories:
1) following, 2) separation, 3) conjunction, and 4) merging.
Regarding "conformity": ordinary beings are submerged in the worldly aggregates; they neither transcend nor conform.
Those of the Two Vehicles lack compassion and thus cannot conform to the world; although they have transcended it, this is not the ultimate truth.
Only when a bodhisattva is able to accord with [reality] can they be said to truly transcend; therefore, "accordance" is used to explain "transcendence.

Regarding the two types of transcendence: because they possess great wisdom, they realize that the nature of the world is transcendent; thus, while dwelling within it, they remain unstained, which distinguishes them from ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle.
Regarding the three being simultaneous: because of compassion, one constantly acts within the world; because of wisdom, one is not defiled by worldly phenomena.
Since one takes the non-duality of the world and its nature as the object of focus, one takes the non-duality of compassion and wisdom as the practice.
The integration of objective realm and practice consists of three propositions:

first, where there is compassion, there is no lack of wisdom; thus, there is nothing in the world that is not transcended. Therefore, one constantly abides within the world, yet never fails to transcend it.
Because the two wisdoms are not without compassion, they do not depart from the mundane world; thus, while they constantly transcend the realm of the world, they never cease to roam within it.
Because these two are fused as a pair, movement and stillness are non-dual, being but a single thought—what is called "no-thought."
Because there is no conceptualization and so forth, there is no obstruction between the mundane and the supramundane.

Regarding the "fourfold simultaneous dissolution": since the object has already departed from both the mundane and its intrinsic nature, and both form and negation have vanished, it causes compassion and wisdom to merge completely, such that the two types of thought are simultaneously severed.
Furthermore, when objects, mental activities, characteristics, and forms are mutually sublated and equally transcended, they become free from all relativity and beyond words.
Only when the preceding four positions are thus harmonized without obstruction does one truly transcend the world.

Third, regarding the stages: ordinary beings are defiled and do not transcend [defilement]; those of the two vehicles transcend and separate from it, yet this is not true transcendence—meaning they have transcended the segmentary existence of the fruit, while their cause is merely a separation of phenomena. This is not what is clarified here.
A bodhisattva who possesses the aforementioned true practices may be said to have attained detachment, yet it is not ultimate.
Only a Buddha is truly detached; thus the Sūtra says: "The Buddha constantly dwells in the world, yet is not defiled by worldly dharmas."

However, in this present text, the practice of the six stages is fully contained within "separation through practice" (xing-li), and the stages upon which practice relies constitute "separation through position" (wei-li). Therefore, whether in terms of phenomena or principle, or cause or fruit, all are termed "separation."
Second, regarding the explanation of the name: if analyzed according to the separation of phenomena and activities, there is no other designation [to apply].
This is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound, as it is distinct from worldly conventions.
If analyzed according to the separation of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

Regarding the four phrases concerning practice (*yoga*), the first three phrases both apply to the *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) and the *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-appositional compound), because the phenomena (*vastu*) and their principles (*dharma*) are distinct.
The phrase of "extinction" (*nirodha*) is not any of the six types of compounds.
Alternatively, it may be a *karmadhāraya*, because extinction is itself separation.
Third, the essential tenet (*siddhānta*):

it establishes as its tenet the simultaneous manifestation of the six stages wherein both principle and phenomena are mutually detached; it takes as its ultimate aim the immediate realization of true detachment through the detachment of their intrinsic natures, culminating in the final perfection.
Fourth, the explanation of the text.

The long version is divided into ten parts: first, the introduction; second, the section on samādhi; third, the section on the incitement; fourth, the section on the arising [of the teaching]; fifth, the section on the request; sixth, the section on the exposition; seventh, the section on the conclusion and exhortation; eighth, the section on the manifestation of auspicious signs; ninth, the section on the testimony of realization; and tenth, the section on the summary verses.
Now, regarding the first [section], there are three parts:
first, the perfection of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), the meaning of which has been explained as before;
second, from "wondrous awakening" (*mi-ao*) onwards, the perfection of the world of the correctly awakened intellect (*jñāna-sambuddha-loka*).
"Endowed with the three inexpressibles" refers to the perfection of the world of sentient beings.

Within the second [section], twenty-one extraordinary merits of the Buddha are elucidated; these have been extensively cited from various treatises and are already seen in the "Chapter on Ascending to Tuṣita."

Now, I shall briefly clarify this: the first phrase serves as the general statement, encompassing all twenty-one kinds of merit mentioned below; therefore, it says, "wondrous enlightenment is fully perfected.
The section beginning with "the two practices" follows as the specific explanation.
Among these, the first four pertain to self-benefit, while the remaining ones all pertain to the benefit of others.

Within the former group, the first is the quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), the second is the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), the third is the quality of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*), and the fourth is the quality of impartiality in activity (*samaprayoga-guṇa*).
First, the two types of conduct are forever severed; this is the merit of functioning with unimpeded engagement toward all objects of knowledge.
In the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, this is termed "non-dual manifestation."
The character "not" (*bù*) here should be understood as "non-existent" (*wu*), which carries the sense of eternal severance.

This means that the Buddha’s wisdom and virtue are free from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); it is not like that of the śrāvakas, who possess ignorance regarding extremely distant times, places, and so forth.
To have both knowing and not-knowing constitutes dualistic practice; since there is now no "not-knowing," it is said to be eternally severed.
To penetrate the two aspects of signlessness is to enter the supreme, most pure merit of *tathatā*, which is free from the two marks of existence and non-existence.
That sutra is titled "Entering the Dharma of Signlessness. "Entering" means to penetrate; it carries the sense of realization.
Now, the essence of the dharma of signlessness is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
Because it lacks the two signs of existence and non-existence, it is called "signless."
Supreme among all dharmas, pure and free from adventitious defilements, it causes both oneself and others to enter [enlightenment] and excels the two vehicles; thus it is called "supremely pure.
Regarding "the third abiding in the Buddha-abiding," this refers to the merit of effortless buddha-activities that never cease.
Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "That is to say, dwelling in the dwelling-place of the Buddhas, which is a place of non-dwelling. This explains the sutra;
that within this dwelling one constantly performs buddha-activities without rest explains the treatise.
The fourth is the attainment of equality with the Buddhas, which refers to the merit of non-differentiation regarding the basis, intention, and activity within the *dharmakāya*.
This means that all Buddhas are non-differentiated in three respects:

first, their wisdom as the basis is identical; second, their altruistic intention to benefit others is identical; and third, their activities of *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya* are identical; therefore, they are said to be equal.
Fifth, having reached the state of being unobstructed, one cultivates all meritorious qualities that serve as antidotes to obstacles.
Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "This means that at all times one constantly cultivates awakened wisdom (*buddhi*), because it serves as the antidote to all obstacles."
This clarifies that awakened wisdom (*bodhi-prajñā*) is the remedy;
all obstacles, namely the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), are that which is to be remedied.
The six unshakeable qualities (*avivartya-dharma*) are the merit of subduing all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This refers to the two paths of teaching and realization, which cannot be shaken by others.
Seventh is unimpeded conduct, which is the merit of being born in the world without being obstructed by worldly dharmas.
This means that one cannot be constrained by the eight worldly dharmas, such as gain and loss.
The establishment of the "inconceivable" refers to the establishment of the merits of the True Dharma;
that is, the establishment of the twelvefold teaching, which others are unable to conceive.
Ninth is the merit of universally perceiving the three periods of time,
which refers to the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), because the past and future are both manifested as if they were the present.

Tenth is the merit of the body being eternally pervasive throughout all lands, which refers to the manifestation of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) in all worlds.
This means that because the two kinds of bodies pervade the two kinds of realms, the eleven knowledges constantly and clearly penetrate all phenomena; this is the merit of severing doubt.
That is to say, because one has achieved excellent certainty regarding all objects oneself, one is able to resolve the doubts of others.
The twelfth is "comprehending all modes of conduct," which causes one to enter into the merit of various modes of conduct.
There are two commentaries; since the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* is easy to understand, it is not explained here.
The intended meaning is as follows:

Thirteenth is the exhaustion of all doubts, which is the merit of generating sublime wisdom regarding future phenomena; this is because one universally understands the dispositions and conducts of all sentient beings and causes them to enter [the path] according to their faculties.
This means that while śrāvakas claim he is entirely devoid of roots of goodness, the Tathāgata knows that because of his subtle roots of goodness from long ago, they will eventually arise.
Regarding the fourteenth, the "unfathomable body," it refers to the manifestation of merit according to the specific inclinations [of beings].

This means that according to the various inclinations of sentient beings, he manifests bodies such as those of golden color; yet although he manifests these bodies, they are free from conceptual discrimination, and because they are like mani jewels and the like, they cannot be fathomed.
Fifteenth is the wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas and others, which consists of the meritorious applications for the purpose of training sentient beings based on immeasurable supports.
That is to say, by means of the immeasurable supports of bodhisattvas, they initiate applications out of a desire to train all sentient beings.
Through the sovereign power of the Buddha, with the hearing of the Dharma as the precursor, one attains sublime wisdom.
This is received and entrusted by bodhisattvas of various classes, transmitted from one to another in an uninterrupted succession, whereby one realizes the wisdom sought by all bodhisattvas.
The meaning is this:
because the Buddha-wisdom is that which is sought by all bodhisattvas and others;
reaching the sixteenth stage, the non-dual ultimate further shore of Buddhahood, is the perfection of the merit of the fulfillment of the equal *dharmakāya*.
Equality is the meaning of non-duality; the non-dual *dharmakāya* serves as the basis for the *pāramitās*.
The seventeenth [perfection] is the Tathāgata’s perfect liberation of equality, which is the merit of manifesting diverse buddha-fields in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings.
In this context, liberation is itself resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), which accords with what is appropriate for the resolute convictions of sentient beings.
Just as the Tathāgata’s resolute conviction can manifest lands of gold, silver, and so forth, and this is true for every Buddha, it is therefore said to be "equal."
The eighteenth is the realization of the Buddha’s stage of equality, which is without middle or extremes; this refers to the merit of the three bodies of the Buddha being without spatial limitation.

Vasubandhu states: "That is to say, the Buddha’s Dharma-body cannot be partitioned such that its enjoyment and transformation [bodies] are restricted to a certain number of locations, nor can it be said to exist within only a certain number of worlds."
19. "Exhausting the Dharma-realm" refers to the merit of constantly manifesting benefit and happiness for all sentient beings until the very limits of saṃsāra.
20. "Equal to the realm of empty space" refers to inexhaustible merit.
This means that because the Buddha’s true wisdom is like space and inexhaustible;
now, this sutra lacks the final phrase "reaching the limits of the future," so that in total there are twenty-one phrases, both general and specific, the meaning of which is as previously explained.
However, while the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* refer to the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), this [text] refers to the Ten Bodies.

The reason for knowing this is that although the location in the kingdom of Magadha is a Transformation Land (*nirmāṇabhūmi*), it praises the merits of the Enjoyment Body; thus, we clearly know that the two bodies and the two lands are fundamentally fused.
Furthermore, it is not restricted to those before or after the stages (*bhūmi*), as all five positions are universally perceived therein.
The third is the perfection of the world of sentient beings, which has two parts:
first, citing the number and praising their virtues; second, listing their names and praising their virtues.
In the former, many people possess these virtues; in the latter, preeminent individuals possess them.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, citing the number to distinguish and define;
second, from "All fully possess bodhisattva... onwards, praising their possession of superior virtues, which is divided into three parts:
First is the general heading; second, from "That is to say" (*yad uta*) onwards, is the detailed exposition; and finally, from "Accomplishing" (*siddhi*) onwards, is the summary.
Within the detailed exposition, the nineteen phrases do not go beyond skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
This is divided into two parts:
the first ten lines praise his own inherent virtues (*svabhāva-guṇa*); the latter nine lines, beginning with "In a single thought-moment," praise his transcendent virtues (*viśeṣa-guṇa*).
Regarding the former, the first eight lines all possess both wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), because they manifest function based upon the essence.

The first five take "skillful means" as their opening phrase; the sixth knows emptiness without destroying the causality of karma and retribution; the seventh knows the distinctions among faculties to clearly identify the illness; and the eighth upholds the Dharma to transform others.
The final two clarify the presence of skillful means and wisdom, all of which return to reality through phenomena.

In the subsequent section on "Further Progress," the first sentence generally clarifies the swift attainment of the fruit-wisdom (*phala-jñāna*); all subsequent passages describe the functions of that fruit-wisdom, as well as the final summary—the text for each of these can be understood accordingly.
The second section is titled "Praising Their Virtues," which consists of two parts:
first, listing their names and stating the total number; second, from "All of them... onwards, praising their virtues.
This passage contains ten phrases: the first is general, while the remaining ones are specific.
Among these distinctions: first, the vow is in accord with principle and fulfilled because the Universal Eye is perfected;
second, they are leaders in gathering the Dharma for the sake of universal transformation;
third, they uphold the true Dharma because they possess universal wisdom.
Fourth, not severing the lineage of the Buddha, because one universally perceives the existence of the Buddha-nature;
fifth, knowing the ritual of the Buddha’s transformations, because light universally penetrates all;
sixth, manifesting the attainment of Buddhahood, because one perceives that [the Buddha] is ultimately non-existent.
Seventh, it purifies defiled capacities by illuminating their source.
Eighth, it destroys the obstacles of others because it possesses the banner of wisdom.
Ninth, it realizes the dharma-realm because it awakens to the nature of phenomena.
The nine preceding phrases are explained individually: the first phrase constitutes the vow (*praṇidhāna*), while the remaining eight constitute the practice (*caryā*).

From a comprehensive perspective, however, they are all the vows of Samantabhadra; because his ancient oaths have now been fulfilled, as seen in the case of the Ten Great Vows, which are both Samantabhadra’s practices and actions performed in response to present conditions. Therefore, the general phrase states: "Accomplishing the practices and vows."

Furthermore, these ten phrases are possessed in common by all ten persons, as the text states that they "are all fully accomplished"; yet each phrase also reveals the virtue of a single person, as it is intended to explain their respective names.
Therefore, the general term is Samantabhadra; the remaining nine have already been explained in sequence above.
The second major section, beginning with "At that time, Samantabhadra," is the section on samādhi.
Samantabhadra is the one who enters because he is the presiding master of this assembly and because he expounds universal practice.
The Buddha’s Flower Ornamentation (Avataṃsaka) refers to the unfolding of the myriad practices that adorn the Dharma-body.
It takes as its essence the ocean of mind consisting of the practice-gates of the Dharma-realm, because it sustains the infinite;
it takes the manifestation of teachings as its formation of practice and their arousal as its function, because of this capacity.
The third major section, beginning with "When entering this samādhi," clarifies the Section on the Arising [of the Teaching].
First, the shaking of the earth is explained to awaken the various capacities of sentient beings;
subsequently, the manifestation of sound is revealed to enable them to hear the Dharma.

The former cases all involve empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) but lack initiation (*samutthāna*), whereas this case involves initiation but lacks empowerment. This indicates that while understanding (*adhimukti*) can be derived from others, thus involving the empowerment of another;
here, conduct (*caryā*) is established by oneself, and thus it is initiated through one's own power.
Furthermore, since the manifestation of conduct arises based on understanding and there is no separate dharma [for it], it is not added.
To subsume understanding and bring about conduct, one must likewise enter meditative concentration.
The Sage’s intentions are manifold; they cannot be standardized by a single rule.
The fourth major section, beginning with "Thereafter," is the section on the arising [of the questions]; its three meanings are as previously explained.
The fifth major section, beginning with "At that time, Samantabhadra," is the section on the request; it is divided into three parts: first, the general statement of the intent of the inquiry;

second, the actual presentation of the opening of the questions, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha"; and third, the conclusion of the request for the teaching to be given, beginning with "Excellent, O Son of the Buddha."
First: The assembly of those whose capacities are suited has gathered, and the time for the preaching of the Dharma has arrived; this constitutes the intent of the question.
Why is it that in previous assemblies the questions were asked first and the definitive teaching followed later, whereas now the order is reversed?
This has two meanings:
first, it says that ritual procedures are not fixed.
In the former case, one emphasizes the Dharma, so that there is a response after being moved by the rite.
This clarifies that his compassion is profound and he intends to preach according to the capacities of the audience.
Since the assembly has already gathered, he first enters meditative concentration to let them know who the teacher is.

Second, regarding what is symbolized: the preceding section clarified entering the reality from the phenomenal marks in order to establish correct understanding; [this section clarifies]... [the reverse].
In this context, the arising of function based on the essence serves to establish correct practice; therefore, it is not the same [as the previous case].
As for the questioner, Universal Wisdom (Samantamati), he is so called because his wisdom accords with the dharma-realm and is capable of initiating practice.
As for the "Single Questioner," this refers to one who has already achieved solitary practice and does not yet possess the understanding [of the subsequent stages].

The second part correctly reveals that within the opening of the inquiry there are two hundred phrases; in the separate edition of the *Dushi jing* (Sūtra on Transcending the World), these are arranged into six rounds of question and answer. Within each round, there is first the question, followed by the answer, and finally the shaking of the earth and the manifestation of auspicious omens, which serve to manifest the benefits and provide verification.
Since ancient times, all virtuous masters have relied upon that text to categorize this sutra into six sections: first, twenty phrases concerning the inquiry into the practice of the ten faiths;

second, from "Generating the Mind of Samantabhadra" downward, twenty phrases concerning the inquiry into the practice of the ten abidings; third, from "Powerful Sustenance" downward, thirty phrases concerning the inquiry into the practice of the ten practices; fourth, from "Abiding Like a Jewel" downward, twenty-nine phrases concerning the inquiry into the practice of the ten dedications; fifth, from "Physical Action" downward, fifty phrases concerning the inquiry into the practice of the ten stages; and sixth, from "Contemplation" downward, fifty-one phrases concerning the inquiry into the practice of the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of the fruit.
In its fourth section, although there are thirty phrases, because one phrase regarding unimpeded function serves as a general heading for the empty phrases, there are thus twenty-nine phrases.

This sutra explains the six stages in three general cycles; this present section is the second, which explains them in terms of practice (*caryā*), because the practices of Samantabhadra encompass all six stages.

Thus, at the beginning of the *Dushi jing* (Sutra on Transcending the World), the request states: "I only pray that you will explain the practices of all bodhisattvas, from beginning to end, so that there may be no doubt."

Although that sūtra does not explicitly correlate [the stages] with faith and the other [faculties], since it speaks of "from beginning to end" and finally clarifies the attainment of Buddhahood, one knows for certain that this refers to the practice of the six stages.

The reason this sutra does not alternate between questions and answers is that its intent is to take up the practices within the stages (*bhūmi*) rather than the stages themselves; thus, it is as perfectly integrated as described below.
If one were to definitively fixate upon the stages, how would this differ from the causal progression of distinct, differentiated stages?

This sutra, its preceding and following sections, as well as the *Benye jing* and other texts, all establish six stages; in each case, those who have not yet entered the stages through faith are placed first, followed by the ten abodes, the three levels of worthiness, the ten sages, and so forth, up to the wondrous enlightenment.
Why, then, do you not open up the Perfect Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) and instead accept [the teachings] on faith?
There is a profound meaning here.
Both that and the preceding [passage] intend to refer to the stages (avasthā); they establish their discourse by taking these stages as the basis.
Now, this "intention" (manas) clarifies the stage of practice; therefore, the practice of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) properly resides at the very beginning of practice.
Regarding the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*sam-bodhi*), there are three meanings: it may be subsumed under the preceding ten stages as their "superior progress" (*viśeṣa-gati*);
or it may be subsumed under the subsequent stage, for it is then designated as "Buddha."
Alternatively, one might distinguish this as a separate stage because it is the "Stainless Ground" (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

However, since we are now explaining that these practices are subsumed within the perfection of the cause, among the fifty-one phrases, only the final four belong to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbuddha*), while the remainder all belong to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samaya-saṃbuddha*).
If that is so, then since this section relies on the "reliance" [upon] the bodhicitta and so forth, would it not be the Stage of Generating the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*)?
This objection is even more untenable;
for at the beginning of the second stage, one generates the Universal Good Mind (*samantabhadra-citta*), so would that not also be the Stage of Generating the Mind?
Is it not the case that at the very beginning of the ten stages of faith there is the arousal of the mind?
Therefore, Master Xianshou said:
"When a bodhisattva arouses the intention to seek bodhi, it is certainly not without causes or without conditions; these are precisely what the arousal of the mind relies upon."
Failing to investigate this essential meaning, they pointlessly cite external authorities.
In the sixth major section, from "At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed... onwards, the Section on Exposition consists of two parts:
first, the general address; second, the formal response beginning with "O Son of the Buddha."

In answering the two hundred questions of the preceding section, one question was answered with ten responses to manifest inexhaustibility, thereby accomplishing the two thousand sublime practices of Samantabhadra. Thus, Lord Ying said:
"The clouds arise as two hundred questions; the vessel pours forth two thousand replies."
To explain these two thousand [verses], they are briefly categorized into five sections:

first, concerning cause and effect; second, the distribution across stages and positions; third, manifesting the universal and the particular; fourth, clarifying the comprehensive inclusion; and fifth, discerning the characteristics of practice. The preceding questions follow this same pattern.
Now, there are four initial points:
first, regarding the major divisions, the first five are causes and the last one is the result;
alternatively, the latter four gates are the results and all the others are causes.

Second, when distinguished according to their subtlety, each and every one penetrates all the way to the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, at the conclusion of each section, it is stated that one attains Buddhahood. Thus, these two thousand [teachings] both encompass cause and fruit.
Third, they may all belong to the cause, because the practices of the stage of Samantabhadra demonstrate the attainment of Buddhahood.
Fourth, they may all belong to the fruit, because the subsequent text frequently states, "Although one has attained Buddhahood, one does not cease the bodhisattva practices."
Regarding the stages of the two types of practice (*dvividha-caryā*), there are also four meanings:
first, the establishment of stages through the accomplishment of concentrated practice, because it is divided into six parts;
second, the inclusion within the total category of stages, because these practices are all contained within the stages.
Third, all are collectively subsumed under practice, because the essence of Samantabhadra’s practice does not depend on specific stages.
Fourth, a single practice pervades all six stages, because cultivation is universal across every stage.
Only when there is such non-obstruction can it truly be called the practice of Samantabhadra.
However, the text explicitly clarifies the latter two [stages], because while the stages are established by gathering the practices, the stages are provisional while the practices are real.
Therefore, the questions and answers are presented together without dividing them into six sections; the intention lies herein.
Regarding the three aspects of universality and particularity: it means that while a single mode of activity necessarily pervades all things, it remains eternally unmixed.
Because it is unmixed, the meaning of "particularity" is distinctly differentiated;
because it necessarily pervades, the meaning of "universality" encompasses and subsumes all.
It is like a brocade pattern, where various colors form a design; it is both universal and particular, with every thread interpenetrating the others, unlike a piece of embroidery.
The practice of the Dharma is likewise: the universal is itself the particular, and the particular constitutes the universal, all without obstruction.
If this is so, then this practice possesses both the universal and the particular; why, then, is it called specifically "the conduct of Samantabhadra"?

It is not that one maintains the universal while being unable to act particularly, nor is it that one acts particularly while losing the universal. Rather, it is because one can act particularly without destroying the universal that it is named "the conduct of Samantabhadra."

Furthermore, the universal must necessarily involve the particular; however, the mention of the one and the particular does not necessarily entail the universal, just as a single thread is not brocade, for it is not the thread within the brocade.
Regarding the fourfold comprehensive inclusion, there are again four levels:
first, the inclusion of stages by means of stages, because each of the six stages individually includes all stages.
One [aspect] possesses two thousand, which constitutes the twelve thousand practices.
As stated above, within a single stage all the merits of every stage are fully present.
Second, by using gates to subsume gates, there are two hundred gates; each of these individually subsumes all gates, resulting in two hundred times two hundred, which forms forty thousand practices.

Third, by subsuming practices within practices: a single practice encompasses all practices. Thus, two thousand individual practices constitute four trillion practices. Fourth, by subsuming the broad through the concise:

regarding these two thousand practices, the subsequent verse concludes by stating, "like a single speck of dust on the great earth. By means of this brevity of a single speck of dust, it describes the vastness of the earth throughout the ten directions; therefore, even in subsuming the broad, nothing remains unexhausted.
This is the Dharma-realm of ultimate equality, which transcends the boundless void.
As the following verse says: "The void may be measured, but the virtues of the Bodhisattva are inexhaustible"—this is precisely what that refers to.
Fifth, the analysis of the modes of practice (*ākāra*) follows the textual exposition.
The explanation of the distinctions based on the provisional characteristics (*nimitta*) is divided into six sections:
first, the two hundred phrases answer the twenty questions concerning the stage of faith and practice (*śraddhācaryā*).
The textual divisions are threefold:
first, nine sections clarify the fulfillment of one's own practice; second, from "Entering the Bodhisattvas" onwards, eight sections clarify the perfection of superior practice;
third, from "Discriminating Wisdom" onwards, three sections clarify the culmination of both practices.
Now, for the first [section], each gate and category consists of nine segments.
The opening segment clarifies the "basis," because it is the basis upon which practice arises; that is to say, it is by relying on bodhicitta and so forth that the myriad practices are accomplished.
The "Chapter on the Wise and Virtuous" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*) states: "When a bodhisattva resolves to seek enlightenment, it is not without cause and without conditions," and so forth.
Nevertheless, these two hundred gates are for the most part divided into five sections:

first, the general heading; second, the inquiry into their number; third, the enumeration and explanation; fourth, the summary of their number; and fifth, the manifestation of the superior benefits of cultivation.
Alternatively, the last two may be missing, or the fifth may be missing; this should be understood from the relevant passages.
In the present case, based on the middle [classification], all five are present in the text.
The first two are easily understood.
Regarding the ten phrases within the section on "Classification," each first presents its name and subsequently explains its meaning.

First, "relying upon the bodhicitta": all ten are termed "reliances. Since [bodhicitta] is already the foremost of all practices, and furthermore, it is the very first among these ten, being the root of the myriad practices, it thus runs through the beginning of the two thousand [verses].
The commentary states that "not forgetting" means that if one forgets the bodhicitta while cultivating various roots of goodness, this constitutes a demonic activity.
Relying on this non-forgetfulness, one is able to accomplish the myriad practices.
This sentence serves as a general summary.
Although one may possess a superior mind within, if one does not rely externally upon a virtuous friend, one's practice will not reach fulfillment.
Therefore, the Great Sage said to Sudhana:
"To seek a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) is the primary causal condition for unsurpassed bodhi.
The commentary explains that "as one" means: if one's mental conduct does not accord with another's, how could they be my friend?
Third, if one does not cultivate the roots of goodness further, what benefit is there in meeting a spiritual friend?
Fourth, according to whatever goodness one cultivates, one must reach the other shore.

Fifth, it is not only the ten perfections that engage with objects; rather, all [perfections] universally apply to them. Of these, the first four pertain to self-benefit, while the sixth—vow—and the seventh—practice—pertain to both self and others.
The first eight rely on the Dharma, while the latter three rely on the person.

The eighth, "Victorious Companionship through Shared Wisdom," and the ninth and tenth, "Exclusively the Buddha’s Culmination," serve as the bases of reliance; thus, one offers pure devotion to cultivate merit and receives the compassionate instructions over time to cultivate the adornment of wisdom.
Furthermore, the first five [perfections] constitute the "self-benefit" (*svārtha*), while the latter five constitute "superior progress" (*viśeṣa-gati*).

The sixth [perfection] extensively elaborates upon the bodhicitta; the seventh extensively elaborates upon the second, fourth, and fifth [perfections]; and the final three extensively elaborate upon the second [perfection].
The four concluding sections are as can be understood.

Fifth, regarding the manifestation of the supreme benefit of cultivation: by relying on the aforementioned ten [perfections], one attains the great wisdom of a Buddha, which serves as the support for all things; this is the supreme benefit.
How could one not cultivate it?
Therefore, it is also called "exhortation to practice.
Regarding the second, the perception of the extraordinary: previously, one established all practices by relying on causes and conditions;

now, one gathers roots of goodness by relying on superior perceptions. Because this follows the source of deluded thoughts and serves as the subsequent basis for reliance, it transcends the perception of permanence and receives the name "extraordinary."
This refers to the aforementioned thought of benefiting all sentient beings by constantly wishing for their welfare and happiness.

Among the ten [aspects], the first—regarding others' goodness as one's own—is to rejoice in others because there is no sense of "self" or "other," because they mutually serve as hosts and companions to support and benefit one another, because they share the same essential nature, because it is what I myself practice, and because self and other are interpenetrating; this is likewise true for the fourth, sixth, vows, and practices.

Second, because even the slightest bit of subtle goodness is a cause for Buddhahood, the *Lotus Sūtra* states that those who merely raise their hands or bow their heads have already attained Buddhahood.
Third, because all beings down to the icchantikas possess Buddha-nature.
Fifth, because the *Saṃcodana-sūtra* states: "To know detachment is called the Dharma.
Seventh, because all dharmas of intrinsic nature and characteristics are what the Buddha has realized.
Mañjuśrī said:
"I do not see a single dharma that is not the Buddha-dharma, for all are ultimately unattainable.
All rules and rituals are emanations from the Buddha; as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Even the teachings of non-Buddhists are remnants of the Tathāgata’s true Dharma."
Eighth, although words accord with principle, principle is not itself words; therefore, it is called the "path of names.
Ninth, because the Buddha brings awakening to others to perfection, he is the compassionate father.
Tenth, the Tathāgata is the very meaning of the suchness of all phenomena; therefore, there is no duality.
Among the benefits, the perception of non-perception is called the "skillful perception.
Regarding the thirtieth type of practice, one undertakes great practice based on the understanding of superior perception.
Perception resides solely in the mind, whereas practice extends throughout the three karmas.
If one merely engages in empty conceptualization without practice, there will be no accomplishment.
This refers to the section on training in the aforementioned text.
Regarding the mention of "only nine" in the commentary, according to the Jin translation, this [version] omits the third point: "thoroughly training in all precepts."
Possessing these ten constitutes five pairs:

first, transforming those below while seeking [enlightenment] above; second, ceasing evil and advancing in goodness; third, wondrous stillness and profound contemplation; fourth, cultivating causes and adorning the buddha-lands; fifth, honoring friends and serving teachers.
Regarding the fourth [topic], the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*): since the arising of practice must necessarily rely upon virtuous friends, they are explained next.
Because they cause one to know what was unknown and recognize what was unrecognized, all who provide benefit and support are my spiritual friends; thus, all ten are beneficial.
The preceding statement, "one immediately attains intimacy with spiritual friends," refers to this.
Regarding the fifth [perfection], diligence (*vīrya*): once one has fully equipped oneself with a companion for practice, one must exert effort.
Within these ten matters, one practices without distraction, free from the conceptual marks of body and mind; therefore, the preceding text says, "diligently cultivate the merits of the Buddha."

Sixth, the mind attains peace and stability; because one advances toward accomplishing the two benefits, one obtains peace of mind: through self-benefit, there is the peace of mind of wisdom (*jñāna-citta*); through benefiting others, there is the peace of mind of compassion (*karuṇā-citta*). This is precisely what was referred to above as the "superior and most excellent mind."
Among these ten, the first line constitutes the fundamental basis.
The next two lines eliminate faults: first, the *araṇā-samādhi* (concentration free from strife), which eliminates all contention;

second, transcending both the ordinary and the small—where "ordinary" refers to common worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), and "foolish" refers to those of the Small Vehicle who adhere to the Dharma for the ignorant.
Next, two [stages] involve the advancement of goodness;
next, three involve realization and entry: first, entry into the stage; second, entry into the Dharma; third, entry into benefit.
Regarding "denial," it has two meanings:
The first is coarse, such as saying, "This was not spoken by the Buddha," and its fault is exceedingly great.
The second is subtle, meaning that what is taught does not accord with reality, and its fault is slight.
If there were no subtle slander, one would be able to realize the truth.
The latter two [causes] involve the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of fruits.
Among the benefits received, ultimate peace and security refers to *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the seventh [point], the accomplishment of sentient beings: while the preceding section generally clarified the peace of mind through the twofold benefit (self and others), the present section specifically clarifies the accomplishment of benefiting others; therefore, it was stated above that "one is then able to compassionately deliver sentient beings."

However, there are two meanings: first, these ten are used universally to bring all sentient beings to accomplishment; second, each brings a specific class of sentient beings to accomplishment, namely:

first, those who are stingy, greedy, and impoverished; second, those who rely on their physical appearance and are arrogant; third, those who doubt the Dharma; fourth, those who are perverse and stubborn; fifth, those who are greedily attached; sixth, those who delight in the Two Vehicles; seventh, those who do not delight in adorning the Buddha-lands; eighth, those who do not rejoice in the fruit of Buddhahood; ninth, those with false refuges; and tenth, those with false wisdom and deceit.
These ten dharmas are established in sequence within the sutra.
Regarding the eighth precept: to bring sentient beings to maturity, one must personally cease evil and practice goodness.
Among these ten, if one forgets the bodhicitta or even transgresses against the objects of the sense faculties, it is all termed a violation of the bodhisattva precepts.
Therefore, it was stated above that "the firm mind of great compassion is not destroyed.
These thirteen aggregates should be contemplated accordingly.

Regarding the ninth method of receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*): since one has already abandoned faults and perfected virtues, and because one has personally verified that one's own practice will necessarily bring about the future fruit, one knows for oneself that one has received the prediction.
The preceding passage states: "If one attains the profound *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*, one will receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from all Buddhas.
This is precisely one meaning within this context.

When one perceives the profundity of the principle and gives rise to deep compassion, the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) becomes sublime, and there is no doubt regarding the attainment of the fruit.
If one practices out of weariness with suffering due to others, it is not sublime and one has not yet attained the prediction of enlightenment.
Second is cultivation without weariness;
third is cultivation over a long period of time.
Fourth is cultivation without remainder;
fifth is cultivation in accordance with reality.
The remaining five can be understood accordingly.
Among these ten, if one possesses even a single one, one knows for oneself that one has received the prediction (vyākaraṇa).

This explains the conduct by which one receives the prediction; it does not reveal specific differences in the characteristics of receiving the prediction, as is done in works such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Furthermore, this [stage] possesses the ten faiths horizontally (*tiryak*), whereas the others possess them according to vertical stages (*ūrdhva-bhūmi*).
The above concludes the section on the practice of self-maintenance.

Second, within the eight sections clarifying the practice of superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*), since the practice of self-maintenance has been accomplished, one proceeds to enter the various places to be entered; these constitute eight segments.
Regarding the first point, "entering the bodhisattva path," there are two meanings of "entry":
first, the meaning of realization; second, the meaning of penetrating insight.
As for the cause of entry, it involves both realization and penetrating insight; as for the fruit of entry, it involves only penetrating insight and not yet realization.

The five gates below are all "entrances by wisdom" (*jñāna-praveśa*); the fourth and fifth gates also pertain to the "entrance by body" (*kāya-praveśa*). Herein, this refers specifically to the cause of entrance.
The reason they constitute an entrance is that what those [beings] cultivate is precisely what I cultivate; because we mutually benefit one another, we are fellow practitioners (*sahāyaka*).

Therefore, the *Dushi jing* (Sūtra on Transcending the World) is titled "Not Seeking the Shortcomings of Others," which can be understood through the ten phrases mentioned above, beginning with "the profound and secret application of supernormal powers.
Second, "entering all Tathāgatas" refers to the entry into the fruit.
The reason for entering is that one must necessarily realize and enter [the state].
As stated above, "One thereby adorns oneself with the virtues of a Buddha.
Third is the entry into the conduct of sentient beings.
The first two entries concern the capacity for transformation; this [entry] clarifies the entry into the mental activities and so forth of those to be transformed.
As stated above: "Capable of fully taming all sentient beings," and so forth.
In the question, the character "activity" (行) was omitted; there are many kinds of activity, as can be seen from the text.
The ten "times" and "non-times" refer to such states as being ripe or unripe.
One who does not know these times is not a great Dharma Master.
Fourth is entry into worlds; in relation to the Buddha, this is the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive support), while in relation to sentient beings, it is the place of transformation.
The preceding passage states, "Universally manifesting bodies in accordance with all realms of existence.
The concluding statement, "universally entering," means that because one does not depart from these ten [realms], one enters them all at once and simultaneously, rather than sequentially.
The fifth entry into the kalpa refers to the time of transformation.
The following three gates all serve to establish the aforementioned "knowing all in a single thought," leaving nothing further to be said.
Among the ten [entries], the first five enter directly, while the latter five enter by way of their characteristics.
This "simultaneous entry" (ji-rū) has two meanings:
first, because the characteristics of that eon are simultaneous, wisdom enters into them;
second, because the characteristics of that eon involve mutual inclusion and entry, one enters only what can include, which is precisely entering into what is included therein, and so forth.
The rest is as previously stated in the "Chapter on Arousing the Mind.

Regarding the sixth [point], which speaks of the three periods of time: the preceding kalpas and this present world differ in their duration; yet they are all equally temporal divisions, and all are established through the distinct formation of the ten periods of time.
Among these ten, the first nine are specific and the last one is general.
Within the specific category, there are three for each of the three time periods, thus constituting nine time periods.
Because that which is yet to come is a phenomenon that continues to arise, the "future of the future" is termed inexhaustible.
Because the past has already arisen, the past of the past is not called inexhaustible.
The present of the present is directly visible as a fact; by taking this as an analogy for the "present" of the past and future, it is said to be equal.
Because the present of the past and future cannot be perceived, the designation "present" is established only in relation to what precedes and follows it.
However, how do these three times constitute nine?
An ancient master explained:
In terms of their meaning, they are explained as nine, yet as jewels, there are only five.
The intention is this:

just as when five days are viewed in relation to one another, taking the first three constitutes the three periods of the past, taking the last three constitutes the three periods of the future, and taking the middle three constitutes the three periods of the present.

If one follows this interpretation, there would be no substance to the nine time periods when advancing [the argument], and it would exceed the count of the three time periods when retreating; how then could a single moment possess all nine?
Now I say:

if one does not require nine [periods] for the mutual dependence of dependent origination, but simply allows the three time periods to mutually depend through dependent origination, then the nine time periods are established.

This means that because the past is the cause for the present and future, the present and future exist within the past; likewise, since the present and future are each causes for the two other periods, there are thus three [periods] within each of the three times.
Thus, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "Whatever phenomenon arises from a cause, that phenomenon is not different from its cause.
While the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* refutes attachment [to extremes], it treats the presence of three within one as a fault;
here, however, clarifying the function of being free from such faults, the presence of three within one is treated as a virtue.
To turn illness into medicine—is this not excellent? As for the general statement regarding "a single thought-moment" (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*):

the preceding nine lifetimes were established in relation to one another; now, by subsuming the derivative into the fundamental, they do not depart from a single thought-moment. This very present single thought-moment is the past and future, and it is the future and past; it inherently possesses the three periods of time.
The three periods of time are mutually dependent, completing the cycle of nine;
thus, by unifying the one within the nine, though there are nine, they are eternally one;
by unifying the nine within the one, though there is one, it is eternally nine.
The nine realms are one and unimpeded; when the fruits of existence vanish, words are cut off, and the provisional ten realms are taken as the entryway for their perfect interpenetration.
Furthermore, since the world is formed by the accumulation of thoughts, is there any world apart from thought?
Furthermore, because of the absence of thought and so forth;
and because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is identical.
These consist of four points, the latter three of which apply to other schools as well.

Regarding the seventh point, "knowing the three periods of time": the preceding two sections clarified the time within which phenomena exist; this section distinguishes the phenomena within that time—namely, the phenomena of transformational birth (*nirmāṇopapatti*). Because these are manifested in accordance with their established conditions, they constitute the phenomena known by the aforementioned [knowledge].

The *Jing* (Sūtra) of the Jin dynasty is titled *The Three Worlds*, while the *Du Shijing* (Sūtra on Deliverance from the World) is titled *Entering the Three Bases*; both intend to capture the essential matters therein.
Among the ten [categories], the first seven concern the knowledge of the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*);

the next one applies to both, completing the aforementioned established matters so that they are inexhaustible, and giving rise to the non-established nature (*avyavasthāna-svabhāva*) which is likewise inexhaustible.
The latter two know that [the afflictions] are not established as real entities.
Regarding the eighth, the mind free from weariness:
since those to be converted are infinite, one seeks the Dharma to convert them without ever becoming weary or indolent; it is because of this that one knows afflictions have no basis for arising.
Among these ten, the first four concern the upward-seeking [of enlightenment];
the next four concern the downward-transforming [of sentient beings];

and the final two pertain to both: that is, because they involve traveling to buddha-fields to draw near to Buddhas and undergo birth by transformation, as well as contemplating the dharmas of practice for the dual benefit [of self and others].
The eight preceding sections on the superior progression are concluded.
The third [section] consists of three parts, clarifying the culmination of the two preceding practices.
Now, the first of these clarifies the culmination of the differentiated wisdom that is sustained.
The preceding passage states: "By the power of wisdom and eloquence, one transforms and guides according to the minds of sentient beings.
The second *dhāraṇī* refers to the ability to maintain ultimate reality.
The preceding passage states, "Practicing the various perfections leads to supreme liberation," and so forth.

Among these ten [points], the first concerns the retention of what is heard; the next four concern the retention of meaning; the following four concern the function of extensively retaining what is heard; and the final one summarizes the aforementioned retention of meaning.
Furthermore, the first four [verses] correspond, in order, to upholding the teaching, the practice, the principle, and the fruit;
the next two reiterate the upholding of practice, namely concentration and wisdom;
and the final one upholds the principle, because it is inconceivable.
The next two [verses] further clarify the teaching;
the final one further clarifies the fruit.

In the third [section], ten kinds of Buddhas are taught; whereas previously it was shown that both the support and the supported are all Buddha-dharma, here we now know the ultimate nature of the Lord of Dharma.
The text above states, "One then receives the consecration and ascends to the rank," and so forth;

for it is at the fulfillment of the mind of the ten stages of faith that one attains Buddhahood. Thus, these ten Buddhas are identical in both name and meaning to the ten kinds of Buddhas seen [in the preceding section]. While their names share similarities and differences with those of the ten bodies mentioned previously, their meanings are likewise no different.
First, because it demonstrates the attainment of perfect enlightenment, it is identical to the aforementioned body of bodhi.
Second, because it involves the vow to be born in Tuṣita, it is entirely the same as the preceding one.
Third, because it is the result induced by the causes of myriad practices, it is the aforementioned body adorned with the marks and signs of excellence.
Fourth, because the bodily relics (*śarīra*) abide and maintain [the Dharma], it is the body sustained by power.
Fifth, because the Buddha of Nirvāṇa must manifest extinction through transformation, it is the aforementioned *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
The Buddha of the six dharma-realms is, because he is the truly untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), none other than the aforementioned Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The seventh [Buddha] is, because it relies solely on mind-only (*cittamātra*), the Body of Sovereign Power (*vaśitākāya*).
Although light can also subjugate, the subjugation by the mind is supreme, as in the case of the subduing of Māra through a compassionate mind.
Eighth, because it is always in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is the body of merit; for concentration is the supreme form of merit.
Ninth, because it realizes the fundamental nature, it is the aforementioned body of wisdom; for both the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the Wisdom of Equality are inherently present.
Therefore, it is stated below: "One clearly perceives the ten [stages]; according to what one desires and delights in, there is nothing that does not manifest.
This is because it is the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body).
The Jin translation refers to it as the "Will-like Buddha" (*yìyì fó*).
However, because the Buddha focuses on internal realization while the body mostly concerns external characteristics, their designations differ.
The details are as explained in other chapters; a summary is found in the Eighth Stage (*Aṣṭamabhūmi*).

The second major section, "Generating the Mind of Samantabhadra," contains twenty gates that answer the previous twenty questions, clarifying the practices of the ten stages of practice (*daśacaryā*).
The ancient masters likewise divide this into four parts:
first, six sections specifically clarify the meaning of the "Abiding in the Generation of the Mind" (prathamacittotpādavihāra);
second, the six sections beginning with "the ten kinds of pāramitās" clarify the internal virtuous practices accomplished within the remaining nine abidings.
Third, from "ten kinds of preaching the Dharma" onwards, three sections clarify the external transformative practices within the various stages (*vihāra*).
Fourth, from "ten kinds of mastery" onwards, five sections clarify the unimpeded and extraordinary practices; it is not without reason that these are explained.

Now, following the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), I shall clarify the practices of the ten stages according to the twenty gates of the sūtra text in their proper order; however, these differ from the preceding sections in being mutually more detailed or concise, as they serve to reflect and reveal that the practices within the stage of realization (*praveśa*) are vast and inexhaustible.

If one relies on the principle of perfect interfusion, every practice universally permeates all others; yet, if one does not destroy their distinct characteristics, they do not obstruct sequential progression.
