The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, in its "Chapter on the World," clarifies that a Wheel-Turning King possesses non-confusion only during the act of entering [meditative absorption], while a Pratyekabuddha maintains it throughout both entering and abiding; only a Buddha, however, remains free from confusion throughout all three phases—entering, abiding, and emerging—because his merit and wisdom are both preeminent.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* agrees with this.
The three aforementioned conditions are also taught in the Hinayana;
the four subsequent matters pertain to both the provisional Mahayana and the definitive Mahayana.
Fourth, expounding the Dharma to benefit sentient beings;
fifth, transforming and delivering beings through the power of vows;
sixth, shattering the pride of those born from wombs.
Who could rely upon the Buddha’s lineage?
Because the seven-fold womb-obstructions do not separate them, they enable those of great resolve to behold him together.
As for the latter three conditions, they exist only in the True Teaching (Saddharma).
Eighth, the collective assembly of those of similar type is called the treasury of wisdom, for it serves as the womb.
Ninth, the manifestation of adornments through the power of meditative concentration is so called because the stainless treasury serves as the womb.
The tenth [perfection], making offerings and hearing the Dharma, takes the *dharmadhātu-garbha* as its *garbha*; thus, this one is the general [category].

The eighth and ninth are the specific meanings of the *dharmadhātu*: the quiescence of the *dharmadhātu* is the meaning of being free from defilement (*vimala*), and its constant illumination while remaining quiescent is the meaning of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, the former two are the means of realization and the latter one is that which is realized; because the Buddhas arise from the profound union of the means and the object of realization.

Moreover, the former two do not destroy their smallness yet possess vast capacity, while the latter one remains unmoved within this state yet is omnipresent; such mastery is the arising of the Buddha.
The fourth, the subtle course, elucidates the ten matters concerning dwelling in the womb.

The first pertains generally to the stage of manifesting the ground; the subsequent eight clarify the manifestation of the seven signs, because dwelling in the womb constitutes the capacity for manifestation, and the stage of childhood belongs to the sign of residing in the palace.

The final section summarizes multiple approaches, wherein all [characteristics] manifest simultaneously within a single characteristic; because it is profound, dense, and difficult to know, it is termed "subtle.
The last three sections, beginning from the fifth section on the "ten kinds of arising," clarify the characteristic of initial arising.
Now, first, the correct explanation: this refers to the time of birth from the right side.

The first [moment] is the time of emergence without confusion; the last [moment] involves movement that produces merit throughout the world-systems; the eight intermediate moments may be understood accordingly.
Second, he manifested a smile because, while taking his seven steps, he said:

The *Sūtra of Auspicious Response* states, "When the Bodhisattva manifested birth, he immediately took seven steps; pointing with one hand toward heaven and with the other toward the earth, he declared: 'In all that is above heaven and below heaven, I alone am the most honored.'"
This refers to his own vow.

The first three [verses] express self-congratulation; the subsequent six express the joy of being able to universally benefit all classes of beings, meaning that he can crush the four types of ignorant arrogance.
Fifth, because although one’s former goodness may now decline, I am able to sustain it.
Sixth, because I can serve as a fertile field of merit for sentient beings.
Seventh, because I see that hearing the teachings from those who have been born [into this world] is of no small benefit.
Eighth, because it would harm those practicing together and prevent them from attaining Buddhahood;
ninth, because it takes pity on those in the same assembly who remain stagnant in the stage of ordinary beings;
and finally, because one obtains the empowerment of the Buddhas.
"Taking three steps and walking seven paces" means that immediately upon being born on the ground, he walked seven paces in each of the ten directions to manifest his sovereign and marvelous nature.
The number seven exceeds three; thus it is called "transcending the three realms," and wherever his feet treaded, the ground everywhere manifested as vajra.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Under the sixth stage, "The Stage of the Youth" (*kumārabhūmi*), there follow two sections clarifying his conduct as a layperson in accordance with worldly customs while residing in the royal palace.
Although the youth was already in the royal palace, this section specifically clarifies that from a young age he possessed virtue and artistic skill, manifesting his transcendence.
The nobleman of the rear gate was of the highest rank yet remained untainted, thereby manifesting his lofty virtue.

Now, regarding the eighth day of the first month, it is said that those who delight in the Dharma—having practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) since childhood with virtues and deeds far surpassing others—will surely find joy in the Dharma once they have realized the Path.
The remaining nine [examples] may be understood accordingly.

Second, in the explicit explanation of the ten types of palaces (*bhavana*), first is "transforming into those of like practice" (*samāna-pratipatti*), because she dwells in a palace of like practice; thus she is like Gopā.
This is because in the four turbid worlds (*kaṣāya*), people delight in what is noble.
The remaining eight [categories] may be understood accordingly.
The seventh section, beginning with "Leaving Home," consists of two gates that clarify the practice undertaken by one who has renounced the household life for the sake of the Path.
First, leaving home is explained; subsequently, the cultivation of practice is revealed.
Regarding the first point: although one is able to enter the Way and leave the household life from within the deep palace, these ten intentions are demonstrated.
The first two cause one to feel weary of and abandon the fruits of suffering;
the next two inspire one to rejoice in and exalt the supreme Path.
The following two [verses] cause one to abandon the assemblies of the sharp and the dull.
Those who cling to the view of eternalism regard permanence as supreme, and thus do not leave the household life;
those who cling to the view of annihilationism believe that once the body is extinguished without remainder, what need is there to leave the household life?
Since it is neither eternal nor annihilated, it is clear that it can be cultivated and advanced; thus, it is said to be free from the two extremes.
Furthermore, it is neither suffering nor pleasure, and so forth.
The next two [lines] reveal the cessation of the fetters belonging to the realms.
The latter two demonstrate that the fruit is identical to the cause.
Regarding the second point, which shows that practitioners experience both suffering and pleasure,
there are ten underlying intentions for why those who practice universal suffering do so:
First, it serves as an essential teaching for the Hīnayāna, because it demonstrates that the Way is attained only through diligent asceticism.

Second, it reveals the distinction between the correct and erroneous paths in order to subdue heterodox views; that is to say, by first practicing self-starvation for six years and then receiving milk gruel, he demonstrated that fasting is not the true path.
Third, because he reviled the Buddha with a single word and suffered hunger for six years;
this account is as found in the second fascicle of the *Mahāyānopāya-kauśalya-sūtra*.

Sentient beings in the four or five turbidities all possess heavy karmic offenses, and their minds are so shrouded by anxiety and distress that they cannot attain the Way. To cause them to think: "If even one who slanders the Buddha can still attain liberation, how much more so for us! [is the purpose].
Because it immediately causes remorse and eradication, it is also as stated there.
Fifth, because it urges on sentient beings who are indolent.
Sixth, because it causes them to know that for the sake of the Dharma they may forget hunger.
Seventh, to demonstrate that attachment to pleasure is not the path;
eighth, because of diligent effort from beginning to end;
ninth, according to the Jin translation, it is "to cause future sentient beings to arouse diligence."
Now, the phrase "vigor" (*vīrya*) should have been placed in the preceding sentence, yet this one line is missing.
The statement that "the ten ascetic practices await the opportune moment" is intended to manifest the profundity of his compassion.
From the eighth section, "Approaching the Site of Enlightenment," the following five gates constitute the practice of realizing and entering [enlightenment] once the Way has been accomplished.
This is divided into five parts:

first, clarifying the progress toward the state of peace. This refers to proceeding from ascetic practices toward the Bodhi tree, manifesting the abandonment of the heterodox and the pursuit of the orthodox; it signifies the perfection of causes leading to the fruit, and the final stage of all practices.
The ten phrases may be understood as follows:

second, "sitting upright at the site of enlightenment" clarifies the peaceful abiding through one's own power; first, four phrases describe the adornment of the site, and next, three phrases describe the manifestation of signs through the three karmas.
Regarding the observation of the lion throne, it is because one knows that [the Buddha] is about to preach.
The Jin translation says: "Observe the lion’s roar of all Buddhas.
The latter three constitute the perfection of virtue: first, being fulfilled, one is able to realize it for oneself; clear wisdom manifests and delusions perish.
Second, receiving the Buddha’s dwelling place signifies that one is about to accord with the Dharma-realm;
third, because great compassion is of the same essence, it is able to bestow grace universally.
Third, regarding the ten extraordinary wonders: these clarify the rare and marvelous external responses, as they are the precursors to the great fruit.
Regarding the fourth point, the "subduing of Māra": this refers to the fact that when the Perfect Enlightenment was about to be manifested, he first crushed the heterodox.

All say "demonstrated" because [the subduing] had already been accomplished long ago; furthermore, because the Māra kings are mostly great Bodhisattvas, there were no evil Māras capable of disturbing the Buddha.

It is also like a jackal; how could it ever display its prowess before a lion? The *Mahāyānopāya-kauśalya-sūtra*, lower fascicle, states: "If they were not summoned by the power of the Buddha, how could those evil Māras approach him?"
Māra is the sovereign of the desire realm because he has successively subdued all others. Among the ten [sections], the first demonstrates the dispute over virtue;

the second resolves whether the Buddha or Māra is superior; and the third describes how Pāpīyān’s army, numbering thirty-six *yojanas* in circumference, surrounded the Bodhi tree intending to create obstacles, but the Bodhisattva, abiding in compassion and wisdom, pointed to the earth with his finger, and they were all dispersed and destroyed.
The eighty-four thousand assemblies of the eight classes of beings all gave rise to the great bodhicitta; therefore, it is said that his teaching and subduing were vast.
This is as explained in the *Upāya-kauśalya Sūtra* and the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha*.
Sixth, "not yet being free from Māra" means not to be indolent.
Seventh, "once subdued" refers to even turning to protect the Dharma during the final age.
The remaining five can be understood accordingly.
Fifth, there are ten kinds of accomplishments that constitute the powers of a Tathāgata, which is the manifestation of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

The first two gates correspond to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*); this [fifth gate] corresponds to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); and the preceding two gates correspond to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).

Among these ten [aspects], the first obstructs nothing from being tranquil; the next two cause nothing from being perfected; the next two result in nothing from being incomplete; the next three ensure that no virtue is not universal; and the final two mean that no Buddha is not identical. Therefore, they are collectively designated as "Tathāgata."
The ninth section, "Turning the Great Dharma Wheel," consists of two gates that clarify the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
This is because, when the Way is perfected and the capacity of sentient beings is matured, the gate of ambrosia is opened.
Within this, the first gate clarifies the essence and function of the wheel of Dharma being turned, while the latter gate clarifies the causes and conditions for turning the wheel of Dharma.
Regarding the preceding section: the continuous flow and perfect penetration is termed "wheel" (*cakra*); from oneself toward that [other] is termed "turning" (*vartana*).

In the Hīnayāna, the four practices of eye, wisdom, clarity, and awakening are bound to the Four Truths; here, the inexhaustible ten practices are revealed, which should be bound to the Ten Truths to constitute one hundred practices.
The rest is as explained in the "Chapter on the Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra-varga*).

Among these ten, the first two are capable of turning [the wheel] and are complete; the next two are what is turned and are profound and subtle; the next two generate faith and uproot suffering; the next two have a deep cause and a vast measure; and the final two involve a distant time and a lofty benefit.
The two kinds of pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) consist of ten matters; these are the causes of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharma-cakra*).

As for the "pure dharmas," they constitute the essence of the wheel that is turned: namely, the Buddha’s untainted (*anāsrava*) and pure *dharmadhātu* enters the minds of sentient beings and becomes the seeds of hearing-perfuming (*śruta-vāsanā*); therefore, it is called "seeds."

His teachings accord with the needs of the occasion, his words are never uttered in vain, and because they give rise to untainted noble wisdom (*anāsrava-āryajñāna*), they do not pass away fruitlessly.

This is the meaning of what is stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*: that the cultivation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) flows forth from the most pure Dharma-realm (*suviśuddhadharmadhātu*) to produce untainted actualization (*anāsrava-saṃmukhībhāva*).
This is precisely what was referred to in the previous chapter as "unimpeded liberation.
That one is able to plant these seeds is due to ten factors; the first is a past cause, while the remaining ones are all present causes.
Among these, the first six virtues are complete in their essence, while the latter three excel in their function.
Within the former group, the first two are complete in compassion: the first is internal sustenance, and the second is external gathering.

The subsequent four are complete in wisdom, which corresponds to the four *siddhāntas*: first, because the inclinations of people differ; second, because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) brings awakening when the time is right; third, because remedial measures are applied according to what is appropriate for each ailment; and fourth, because worldly conventions are understood and accorded with.
The tenth is *nirvāṇa*, meaning that one should exhaust [suffering] and return to the source.
There are ten such points of intent:
the first two clarify the faults and afflictions of birth and death—first, because it is impermanent; second, because it lacks bliss—and thus it is not peaceful or secure.
Third, the three knowledges (trividyā) and nirvāṇa are bliss; this reverses the aforementioned lack of bliss, because the quiescence of nirvāṇa is true bliss.
Fourth, it reverses the impermanence of the form body (rūpakāya), because the dharma-body (dharmakāya) is permanent.
Therefore, the Jin edition of the sutra states: "To cause the seeking of the eternally abiding, pure Dharma-body.
Here, the character for "eternal" (cháng) is missing.
Since the Dharma-body is one of the three virtues (triguṇa), its nature has existed from antiquity and its essence is without change; thus, it is specifically described as "eternal."
Now that they have emerged from the entanglements, they are termed "pure.
The next three phrases clarify that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is without self because it lacks sovereignty.
Since each individual period is impermanent and lacks sovereignty, it is said to be "irreversible."
Second, specifically clarifying that moment-to-moment impermanence entails a lack of sovereignty, which pertains to the death-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-śīti-bhava*);
third, even within the death-rebirth of segmentation (*bheda-śīti-bhava*), one cannot remain steadfast and likewise lacks sovereignty.
The eighth clarifies that nirvāṇa is firm, which is the self (ātman) and also carries the sense of permanence.
The ninth reverses the conditioned to clarify pure virtue;
for that which is impure is precisely the conditioned dharmas.

Regarding the purity of gathering and dispersal: the True Dharma of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is called "non-arising"; yet, this very nature-purity of *nirvāṇa* that accords with conditions within *saṃsāra*—the nature of its phenomenal marks—is precisely what constitutes the True Dharma.

However, the second turning of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* refutes the four virtues of ordinary beings and the Śrāvakas, thereby encompassing all Buddha-dharmas; thus, it takes the Tathāgata as the self (*ātman*), which precisely reveals *nirvāṇa*, and likewise clarifies the self with reference to *nirvāṇa*.
The rest are all mutually consistent.

Although the four virtues, such as permanence and so forth, pervade all Buddha-dharmas, they each manifest differently according to their specific meanings. Above, the four prosperities were used to overturn the four withered states, thereby completely dispelling the eight inversions.
It is the natural law of the ten stages and the constant rule of all Buddhas.
The preceding section on the "Analysis of the Teachings" is concluded.
The seventh major section, beginning from "O Son of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate," is the section on the Conclusion and Exhortation to Practice and Study.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the summary of the meaning with an exhortation to practice; second, from "O Son of the Buddha, all these Bodhisattvas... onwards, the summary of the title with an exhortation to study.
Within the former, there are also two parts:
First, the names are raised to establish their meaning; subsequently, from "If there be a son of the Buddha" onwards, there is the exhortation to believe and practice.
Within this section on concluding the names and exhorting study, the ten names are first revealed.

First, regarding the first [basis], it is called a "basis" (*āyatana*) because it serves as the support for the arising of the designating [mental] activity; whereas the preceding [basis] refers only to the essence of the designated activity itself as "pure activity," the remaining nine are established by name according to their designated functional capacities.
Second, because they definitively determine the meaning of that activity such that it is certain to produce results;
and third, because they realize what is to be realized.
Fourth, because they are able to realize with clarity;
fifth, because their wisdom is transcendent and supreme;
sixth, because compassion gives rise to the myriad practices.
Seventh, because of the perfect interfusion of all things;
eighth, because of the fulfillment of the rules of conduct;
ninth, because principle itself involves phenomena.
The tenth [point] is that phenomena are themselves reality;
thus, from "should be honored" onwards, the exhortation to study can be understood.
The eighth major section, from "having spoken this" onwards, is the section on the manifestation of auspicious omens, which can be understood.
The ninth major section, beginning with "At that time, in the ten directions," is the Section on Verification.
It consists of two parts:
first, the verification by praising the Dharma; second, the verification by extolling the person, beginning with "O Son of the Buddha, you have already..."
The tenth major section, beginning with "At that time, Samantabhadra," is the section consisting of verses.
It comprises a total of two hundred and fifteen and a half verses, divided into three parts:
first, there are eight seven-syllable verses praising the profound and vast virtues and clarifying the scope of the teaching;

2. From "That mind" downward, one hundred and thirty-one and a half verses collectively demonstrate the virtues of practice, briefly revealing their depth and breadth; these two preceding sections are both *gāthā*.
3. From "Relying upon the Buddha’s wisdom" downward, seventy-six verses are a versification of the preceding prose, and thus constitute *geya*.
Now, for the first part, there are four sections:

first, four [verses] granting permission to speak extensively and deeply; second, two [verses] citing virtues and exhorting the audience to listen; third, one [verse] reiterating the general permission to speak; and fourth, one [verse] indicating the scope of the discourse.
Within the second section, which provides a general demonstration of the virtues of practice, there are three parts:

first, two verses that briefly present the teachings through metaphors; second, fifty-five and a half verses that clarify the depth and breadth by using phenomena to symbolize the Dharma; and third, fourteen verses beginning from "The Bodhisattvas are equal to the Buddhas," which demonstrate the vastness by clarifying practice through the Dharma.
The initial heading is self-evident.

Regarding the second section, which uses phenomena to symbolize the Dharma, there are fifty similes in total that are difficult to categorize; for now, they shall be grouped according to their thematic similarities and divided into ten sections.
The first four and a half verses contain two similes, clarifying the practice of providing joy and shelter to sentient beings.
Second, the ten verses beginning with "Lion" describe the practice of destroying the heterodox and guiding the deluded;
the meaning of the lion's roar was explained at the beginning of the "Dharmadhātu" chapter.
Third, there are eleven verses that clarify the practice of loftiness, profundity, firmness, and density.
4. The six verses beginning with "Garuḍa" concern the practice of observing capacities and illuminating benefits.
5. There are six verses concerning the practice of sovereign governance.
6. The two verses beginning with "The mind of wisdom" concern the practice of inclusion and non-attachment.
Verse 72: The practice of universally accomplishing benefit for others.
Eight: "Like precious jewels," and the following six verses: The practice of restraining and cultivating the body.
Nine: Two verses: The practice of taming, governing, and transporting [beings].
10. The six verses beginning with "The Udumbara Flower" concern the practice of wandering and dwelling externally.
The third section concerns the practice of the illumination of the Dharma, which has two parts:
first, ten verses that generally clarify its profundity and vastness, granting permission to speak and admonishing the listeners;

The subsequent sixty-four verses, beginning with "A single body can manifest," separately clarify the profound and the vast to fulfill the previous promise. Within this section, there are three parts:

the first three [verses] show how [the Bodhisattva] is equal to the Buddha's awakening; the next three show how he transcends all other classes of beings; and the final four grant permission to speak and exhort the audience to listen.

Within the second section, which specifically elucidates the profound and vast [practice], it is condensed into ten types of conduct: first, the six verses on the profound and vast conduct of the three karmas;
second, the five stanzas beginning with "The Bodhisattva’s Body" on the unimpeded conduct of the two adornments;
third, the three stanzas on the conduct of fulfilling [the path] through both regressive and progressive stages.
4. The ten verses beginning with "Or manifesting through practice" describe the conduct of universal manifestation;
five verses describe the conduct of the perfect integration of time and place;
six verses beginning with "The Bodhisattva knows" describe the conduct of teaching the Dharma according to the faculties [of beings].
The seventy-four verses [from the beginning] describe the practice of swift activity within tranquility;
the ten verses from "Just as a skilled illusionist" (*tadyathā māyākāra*) downward describe the practice of compassion that does not lose wisdom;

the fourteen verses [thereafter] describe the practice of wisdom that does not lose compassion—meaning that while the final two lines express not losing compassion, all preceding lines demonstrate the perfection of the virtue of wisdom.
The twelve verses conclude the practice of inexhaustible virtue.
Regarding the third section, which comments on the prose portion, it consists of two parts:
first, there are thirty-nine verses that comment on the preceding "Explanatory Section"; [the second part follows].
Following this, the thirty-seven verses beginning with "Although he commands" (*suī lìng*) constitute the section on the conclusion and exhortation to practice and study.
Now, for the first part, these verses summarize the preceding six stages into six sections. The first four verses praise the practice within the stage of the Ten Faiths (*śraddhā*);
the second set of four verses praises the Ten Abidings (*vihāra*).
The third [chapter] has six verses, praising the ten practices;
the fourth has five verses, praising the practice of dedication;
the fifth has nine and a half verses, praising the practices of the ten stages.
The sixth [chapter] consists of ten and a half verses, which describe the practice of the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of results.
The first two characters, "the practiced" (*su-carita*), belong in meaning to the preceding section.
Regarding the second verse, which concludes the exhortation to practice and study, it differs slightly from the previous momentum; it is divided into four parts:
The first verse concludes that what has been previously explained is but a small portion;
the second section consists of thirty verses, which specifically reveal the vastness and profundity of its qualities and functions;
the third section consists of four verses, which provide a comprehensive summary of its depth and breadth.
The fourth section consists of two verses that conclude by exhorting practice.
Within these two [sections], there are two parts:
the first twenty-one and a half verses conclude by summarizing the practice through the Dharma; [the remainder concludes by summarizing through analogies].
The subsequent eight and a half verses conclude by correlating the narrative with the revealed Dharma.
Now, for the first part, there are five sections: first, five verses on the practice of mastery over the buddha-fields;

second, six verses on the practice of mastery over the three types of action; third, three verses beginning with "In the past" which clarify the practice of mastery over the three worlds; fourth, five verses clarifying the practice of mastery over body and wisdom; and fifth, two and a half stanzas summarizing the inconceivability [of these practices].

Regarding the subsequent section on the manifestation of the matters of association within the Dharma: some points were not previously mentioned, while others involve similar facts with different meanings; these can all be understood through reflection.

In the third part, the summary of the profound and vast, the first two items summarize what has already been explained, while the latter two summarize that the end of the discourse is difficult to fathom.
The fourth [section], the exhortation to practice, may be understood.
The "Chapter on Transcending the World" is concluded.
*Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary*, Fascicle 53.

Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya, Scroll Fifty-Four, composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of the Great Huayan Temple on Mount Qingliang, Tang Dynasty. Chapter Thirty-Nine:
Entering the Dharma Realm. From Chapter Thirty-Nine, "Entering the Dharma Realm," onwards, one enters the sixtieth fascicle of the scripture.
Regarding the intent of the initial arrival, we first distinguish the partial arrival.

Generally, practice is established based on realization, and realization depends upon the profundity of practice; this is because the preceding section relied upon the Dharma to bring practice to completion.
This [section], however, relies upon the person to enter realization, and it also serves as a remote response to the "ocean of liberation."
Regarding the "Chapter on Assemblies," it does not arise from a different division, as there is no separate category of assemblies.
Second, the explanation of the title has three parts:

Regarding the names of the first section: because one relies upon Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and various excellent spiritual friends to deeply realize the *dharmadhātu*, it is called "entering realization by relying on persons.
When the realized Dharma resides within oneself, it is termed "accomplishing virtue."
Regarding the names of the two assemblies: in terms of location, it is called the Assembly at the Multi-storied Hall in the Jeta Grove.
The grove is named "Victorious" (Jeta) to represent the person upon whom it depends;
the park is named "Anāthapiṇḍika" (Givaka) to represent his profound compassion.
The meaning of "multi-storied pavilion" (gopura) manifests the mutual adornment of the two wisdoms;
furthermore, compassion and wisdom together constitute the means of realization, which also carries the sense of "redundancy" (repetition).
If one takes the name of the city as well, it also signifies that the object of renown depends upon the person.
Regarding the summary of the principles, it is as explained in the titles of the chapters.

As for the titles of the three chapters: "Entry" refers generally to both the subject and the object—that is, the names for awakening, understanding, and realization. "Dharmadhātu" is the dharma that is entered, referring to the distinctions between principle and phenomena, and so forth.
However, while "dharma" (fa) contains the meanings of upholding (*dhāraṇa*) and norm (*vidhi*), the term "dharmadhātu" (fajie) possesses multiple significations.

The *Liang* commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, fascicle 15, states: "In order to manifest that the dharmakāya contains the five meanings of the dharmadhātu, it is renamed 'dharmadhātu'."
First is the meaning of "one nature," which takes the absence of a dual self as its nature, because all sentient beings do not transcend this nature.
Second is the meaning of "cause," because the dharmas such as the four foundations of mindfulness of all noble ones arise by taking this as their object-condition.

The meaning of the "Threefold Treasury" (Tripiṭaka) is that it is concealed and covered by all false and illusory dharmas, and thus cannot be taken as an object of cognition by ordinary beings or those of the Two Vehicles.

The meaning of the "Fourfold Reality" is that it transcends worldly dharmas; since worldly dharmas are subject either to spontaneous destruction or to destruction through their antidotes, this reality is free from these two forms of destruction.

Regarding the five profound meanings: if they correspond with this [nature], their intrinsic nature becomes pure and virtuous; if they do not correspond externally, their intrinsic nature becomes a husk.
These aforementioned five meanings are all the principle-dharmadhātu (*dharmadhātu-nīti*). Furthermore, there are the meanings of "sustaining," "lineage," and "delimitation."
However, there are three ways of maintaining [the object]:
first, maintaining its essential nature;
second, maintaining the distinctions among all phenomena.
The three types of "holding" (dhāraṇī) preserve their own respective categories without mutual confusion, which is identical in meaning to the term *dharma*.
"Lineage" (*kula*) refers to a family or class, namely the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
Both of the preceding two [terms] apply to both the phenomenal (*vastu*) and the principial (*tattva*) levels.
Regarding the "delimitation" (*prabheda*): because the phenomena of the dependent origination of events do not intermingle.

Within this, the [first] nature (*svabhāva*) is common to both *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound) and *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound); the cause (*hetu*) is exclusively *tatpuruṣa*; and the latter six are exclusively *karmadhāraya*.

The convergence of mind and object is termed "entering the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*). Initially, they are distinct; ultimately, they function as a single entity, for that which enters is itself the Dharma-realm.

Regarding the third point, the clarification of the fundamental tenet: since the chapters are categorized together and "entering the Dharma-realm" serves as the designation, it is likewise established as the primary tenet.
Within this, there is an analysis by way of three gates:
first, by way of meaning; second, by way of category; and third, by way of stage.
Regarding the first, there are two parts:

First, we clarify that which is entered: in total, it is the single, true, unobstructed Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Regarding its nature and characteristics, they do not transcend phenomena (*vastu*) and principle (*li*).
Manifested separately according to their meanings, there are briefly five gates:
first, the conditioned Dharma-realm; second, the unconditioned Dharma-realm; third, both; fourth, neither; and fifth, non-obstruction.
However, each of the five [dharmas] has two aspects. Regarding the first, there are two:

first, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) which is able to sustain the seeds of all phenomena is called the *dharmadhātu*. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The *dhātu* from beginningless time," etc.; this refers to the sense of cause, yet the essence of this *dhātu* does not refer to the *dharmakāya*.

Second, the distinct limits of the phenomena of the three periods of time are called the *dharmadhātu*. As the "Inconceivable" chapter states: "All Buddhas know all *dharmadhātus* of the past without exception," etc.; this refers to the sense of boundaries or divisions.
The two gates of the unconditioned dharma-realm are:
first, the gate of intrinsic purity, because its nature is eternally pure even in the stage of ordinary beings, and because it is the single flavor of true emptiness without differentiation;
second, the gate of freedom from defilement.
This is because purity is manifested through its antidotes, and because it is divided into ten types according to the depth of their respective practices.
Regarding the third point—that the *dharmadhātu* is both conditioned and unconditioned—there are two aspects.

First, the gate of following characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvartana-mukha*): this refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, the five kinds of form, and the eight unconditioned phenomena. These sixteen dharmas are known solely by the mind; within the eighteen *dhātus*, they are termed the *dharmadhātu*.

The second is the gate of non-obstruction, which means that within the single dharma-realm of the one mind, two gates are fully contained: first, the gate of the true suchness of the one mind; second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of the one mind.

Although these two gates each comprehensively encompass all phenomena, their respective positions are never intermingled; this is because the waves that comprise water are not still, while the water that comprises waves is not moving.
The fourth dedication states: "Within the realm of the conditioned, one demonstrates unconditioned dharmas, yet without destroying the characteristics of the conditioned;
within the realm of the unconditioned, one demonstrates conditioned dharmas, yet without conceptualizing the nature of the unconditioned."
This clarifies the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle.
Regarding the two gates of the dharma-realm, which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned:
first is the gate of mutual negation (xingduo), meaning that there are no conditions that do not accord with principle; therefore, it is not conditioned.

In principle, there is no reason that does not serve as an object of cognition; therefore, it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The essence of phenomena is equal, such that form and negation both vanish together.
In the thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"This equality of dharmas—is it conditioned?"
"Is it conditioned or unconditioned?
The Buddha said:
"It is neither a conditioned dharma nor an unconditioned dharma."
Why is this? Apart from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) cannot be found;
apart from unconditioned phenomena, conditioned phenomena cannot be found.
"Subhūti! This conditioned nature and this unconditioned nature—these two dharmas are neither conjoined nor dispersed.
This is what that means.
Second is the gate of non-reliance: this dharma-dhātu is devoid of characteristics and devoid of intrinsic nature; therefore, it is neither of these two.
Furthermore, because it is not the two truths, and because it cannot be reached by the two types of conventional designation, it is thus "neither."
The first chapter of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "All phenomena are, in brief, of two kinds: namely, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Among these, the conditioned is neither conditioned nor unconditioned."
“Unconditioned, yet neither unconditioned nor conditioned,” and so forth.
Regarding the two gates of the fivefold unobstructed dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*):
first is the gate of universal inclusion, which means that within the aforementioned four gates, any single one subsumes all the others.
Therefore, Sudhana, whether he beholds mountains and seas or sees the character for "hall," all are termed "entering the Dharma-realm.
This refers to the second gate of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), which means that because principle (*li*) fuses with phenomena (*shi*), it causes phenomena to be without boundaries.
A minute atom is not small, for it can contain ten lands;
an ocean of lands is not large, for it can secretly enter into a single atom.
Because phenomena manifest principle, this ensures that principle is not without parts; thus, one and many are unimpeded.

Some speak of the "one dharma-realm," while others speak of the "various dharma-realms"; yet because the one is not one, it is the various, and because the various are not various, they are the one—extending thus in infinite, overlapping layers.

Thus, it is like when Sudhana held [Mañjuśrī’s] hand for but a moment yet passed through many kalpas, or when he entered the pavilion and saw the infinite in an instant—all such cases are of this kind.
The five gates and ten meanings presented above collectively clarify the Dharma-realm that is entered; all of these should be harmonized by means of the six characteristics (ṣaḷlakṣaṇa).
Second, the explanation of the means of entry, which also comprises five gates:
first, pure faith; second, correct understanding; third, cultivation; fourth, realization; and fifth, perfection.
Regarding these five, there are two modes concerning the previously mentioned dharmadhātu:
first, each of the five capacities for entry corresponds to all five objects of entry, and each of the five objects of entry pervades all five capacities for entry.
Second, these five [practices] are able to enter; according to their respective order, each enters one gate.
These ten gates concerning the two meanings of the superior mind and objects are perfectly interfused through the six characteristics, forming as a single aggregate the unobstructed Dharma-realm.
The second category, the classification of the Dharma-realm, also consists of five gates:
first, that which is entered; second, that which enters; third, non-duality; fourth, the simultaneous submergence of both; and fifth, the unimpeded freedom between existence and non-existence.
The first entry also contains five stages:
first, the dharma-dharmadhātu; second, the person-dharmadhātu; third, the mutual fusion of both; fourth, the simultaneous sublation of both; and fifth, non-obstruction.
The first part consists of ten items:
first, the *dharmadhātu* of phenomena, referring to the ten layers of dwelling places and so forth;
second, the *dharmadhātu* of principle, referring to the single flavor of profound stillness and so forth.
Third is the dharma-realm of objects, referring to the limits of what is known and so forth;
fourth is the dharma-realm of practice, referring to the vastness and depth of compassion and wisdom and so forth;
fifth is the dharma-realm of essence, referring to quiescence, non-arising, and so forth.
Sixth is the application of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which refers to supreme mastery, universal penetration, and so forth;
seventh is conformity to the dharma-realm, which refers to the correct practice of the six perfections and so forth;
eighth is opposition to the dharma-realm, which refers to the fivefold heat asceticism without weariness and so forth.
Ninth is the dharma-realm of teaching, which refers to the verbal expressions one hears;
tenth is the dharma-realm of meaning, which refers to the intended significance that is elucidated.
These ten dharma-realms share a single dependent origination; they are unimpeded and fused together, such that each contains all.
The Dharma-realm of these two types of persons also has ten gates, namely: humans, devas, males, females, householders, renunciants, non-Buddhists, various deities, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.

These are all aspects of the dependent origination of the phenomenal marks (*nimitta-bhāga*), which are interpenetrating yet distinct; because Sudhana, upon seeing them, immediately enters the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is called the "Human Dharma-realm.

As for the "Dharma-realm in which the three persons and the dharmas are mutually fused," this means that the ten persons and ten dharmas of the preceding section share a single dependent origination, such that according to their respective meanings, the phenomenal marks are harmoniously integrated without duality.

Regarding the "Dharma-realm where the four categories of persons and dharmas are simultaneously extinguished": this refers to the ocean of the fruit of equality, which transcends words and numbers; both the nature and characteristics of dependent origination are inexpressible.

Regarding the "Dharma-realm of fivefold non-obstruction": this refers to the synthesis of the preceding four statements; therein, there is no obstruction regarding the identity or difference of persons and dharmas, and existence and non-existence are unimpeded, freely and perfectly interfusing. Contemplate this according to the principle.
Second, the clarification of the capacity for entry also has five stages:
first, the body; second, wisdom; third, their union; fourth, their dissolution; and fifth, their perfection.
This refers to entering the towered pavilion and returning, which is the realization through the integration of the body.
To mirror the boundless principles and phenomena is the realization of wisdom (*jñāna*).
To be universally pervasive like Samantabhadra is the realization of equality (*samatā*).
For body and wisdom to be mutually identical and both vanish is the simultaneous cessation of both.
Oneness and difference, existence and non-existence, coexist without obstruction, being freely and perfectly interfused.
The rest may be understood by analogy.

Third, the subject and object are blended into a single unity without boundaries or divisions; though distinctions are made for the sake of explaining their meanings, in principle they remain unmixed.
These five aspects of subject and object—both specifically and universally—can be understood through reflection.
The four aspects of subject and object are perfectly interfused, such that their mutual negation results in their simultaneous vanishing.
The five aspects of identity and difference, existence and non-existence, are unimpeded and complete; contemplate this according to the principle.
The preceding section has completed the analysis by way of categories.

Third, regarding the clarification of entry into the *dharmadhātu* by way of stages: according to the subsequent text, there are two major divisions of the *dharmadhātu* entered, namely cause and fruit.

Regarding the preceding persons and dharmas, there are none that are not encompassed within the fruit of Buddhahood; this is precisely the sovereign mastery over the dharma-realm manifested through the Tathāgata’s Lion-Stretching Samādhi.

Furthermore, regarding the dharmas of the former person, there are none that are not subsumed within the stage of the cause; these are precisely the dharma-gates of the dharma-realm manifested by Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. Within the causal stage, there are distinct variations in the dharma-realm corresponding to the five stages, such as faith and so forth.
Second, the clarification of the "ability to enter" (praveśa) also consists of two parts according to the text:

first, clarifying how the various bodhisattvas enter the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) instantaneously from the perspective of the preceding stage of fruition; second, illustrating through the perspective of the preceding stage of cause how Sudhana enters the dharma-realm gradually, thereby revealing the causal process.

Since there is no obstruction, the gradual and the sudden are likewise perfectly integrated; they differ only in that the teachings are established through exposition and are assigned to these distinct stages.
Next, the text itself will be formally explained.
The first major section is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the primary assembly; second, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī emerged from the Well-Abiding Pavilion" onwards, the explanation of the final assembly.
Furthermore, the former clarifies the resultant dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the latter clarifies the causal dharma-realm.
Moreover, the former involves an immediate entry into the dharma-realm, while the latter clarifies a gradual entry into the dharma-realm.
Additionally, the former is general and the latter is specific; thus, the general and the specific are perfectly interfused, and the fundamental and the derivative are mutually unimpeded.
Furthermore, the former refers to practicing sudden realization upon death, which is the ultimate of the orthodox teaching;

the latter refers to entering through practice by means of a person acting as a vessel, intended to distinguish and facilitate its circulation. Thus, the orthodox and the accommodated are universally interfused, and there is no obstruction between the middle and the final stages.
Within this assembly, the main section is divided into ten parts: first, the introductory section; second, the section on the invitation;

third, the section on the manifestation of samādhi; fourth, the section on the gathering of new assemblies from afar; fifth, the section on exposing faults to reveal excellence; sixth, the section on verses praising virtues; seventh, the section on Samantabhadra’s unfolding of the teaching; eighth, the section on the light from the ūrṇā-hair revealing benefits; ninth, the section on Mañjuśrī’s description of virtues; and tenth, the section on boundless great function.
First: Although its meaning extends through the subsequent assemblies, it is categorized as being in the first assembly alone based on its distinct location.
The text is divided into three parts:

First, the perfection of the world through the initial awakening to true wisdom; second, the perfection of the receptacle world (the physical environment), as indicated by the passage beginning with "In Śrāvastī"; and third, the perfection of the world of sentient beings, as indicated by the passage beginning with "Together with the bodhisattvas."
First: Regarding the term "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*), the Sanskrit is *Bhagavat*, which encompasses six meanings as explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
The first is the meaning of sovereignty, because he is forever unbound by any afflictions (*kleśa*).
Second, the sense of blazing intensity, because it is refined and tempered by the light of fierce flames of wisdom;
third, the sense of sublime adornment, because it is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man;
fourth, the sense of renown, because all supreme merits are perfected and there is nothing unknown.
Fifth is the meaning of auspiciousness, because all those in the world draw near to offer worship and universally praise him;
sixth is the meaning of nobility, because he possesses all merits, constantly employs skillful means to benefit the world, and tirelessly brings peace and happiness to all.
Now, by mentioning the latter, the former is encompassed; this also indicates the person and takes up the Dharma.
Because he possesses inexhaustible virtues, he is called the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*).
Second, the perfection of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), which has three parts:
First is the city of Śrāvastī (literally "The Hearer").
The *Xiyu ji* states: "In ancient times, there was an elder immortal who resided in this place. Later, a junior immortal named Śrāvaka came to study under him."
After the Elder Immortal passed away, the Junior Immortal established a city and its walls here, hence it took his name.
It is also called "Famous Things" (Munmo), because this city produced many people of intelligence, broad learning, and renown; it is thus within the domain of Central India.
2. Regarding "Jetavana" (逝多), the following clarifies the grove and garden.
"Jeta" is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "Victorious in Battle," which is the name of the Prince.

"Anāthapiṇḍada" (給孤獨) is, in Sanskrit, Sudatta; its literal meaning is "one who provides relief to the destitute," and its translated meaning is "Provider for the Orphans and Solitary," which is the title of the Elder.

The elder was benevolent and quick-witted; he accumulated wealth yet was able to disperse it. He rescued those in want and relieved the poor, showing compassion for the orphaned and providing succor to the elderly. Because people of the time praised his virtue, this title was established for him.
The elder purchased the land with gold and the prince donated the trees; together they accomplished this meritorious deed.
The two men held it in high esteem and jointly established it as a monastery.
The Triple-Gate Pavilion was the place for preaching the Dharma, symbolizing the Dharma-realm that has been realized.

That its essence is all-pervading is called "Great"; that its virtues are fully complete is called "Austere"; and that it gives rise to function based upon this essence is the "Multi-storied Pavilion.
The third, the world of sentient beings, is the "Supporting and Assisting Perfection."
Within this, there are three:
first, bodhisattvas; second, śrāvakas; third, world-protectors.
Regarding the first of these, there are also three:
First, the enumeration; second, the listing of names; third, the praise of virtues.
Now, regarding the first:

although the bodhisattvas in this assembly are few when their names are merely enumerated, they are many when their names are listed in detail, because this serves a specific symbolic purpose. Within the enumeration, it is intended to reveal that those in the five stages have equally realized and entered [the truth].
Each stage consists of ten degrees, and as each is mutually integrated, they form five hundred;
furthermore, the sixth stage, Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), is that which is entered.
Moreover, this symbolizes that those who practice through understanding are many, while those who realize it through direct experience are rare.
Second, the listing of names following "Samantabhadra" is divided into three parts:
first, the designation of the principal leaders; second, the listing of individual names; third, the summary of their number.
This is the first part, because these two great sages are the primary assistants in the work of transformation.
Furthermore, there is that which is indicated, which will be clarified below.

Second, within the detailed enumeration following "Their names were," there are fourteen ranks, each rank containing ten members; although there are some increases and decreases among them, they total one hundred and forty-one persons. Each name has its own specific meaning, and all possess profound significance.
For now, I shall briefly present this table, which is broadly divided into two parts:

the first forty-one positions generally represent the four stages beginning with "Abiding" (vihāra), while the subsequent ten positions—beginning with "Celestial Crown"—individually represent the ten stages (bhūmi) and ten perfections (pāramitā).
First, the ten banners represent the orientation [of practice], for their virtuous conduct rises high above all.
Second, the nine powers represent the actual practice, for they enable one to advance in cultivation.
Third, the ten treasuries represent the stages (*bhūmi*); their meaning is as explained previously.
Fourth, there are twelve eyes, which represent understanding, for they are able to illuminate all phenomena (*dharma*).
The reason they are not presented in sequential order is that it is intended to represent the state of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), wherein there is no before or after.
Within the subsequent ten positions, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and ten perfections (*pāramitā*) of the sequential and distributive (*vipaśyanā*) path are respectively represented.
First, regarding the "ten crowns": the first stage crowns the beginning of all stages, just as the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) precedes all other practices.
Furthermore, each individual stage possesses ten aspects, because within a single stage all the merits of every stage are fully present.
Within a single perfection (pāramitā), the ten perfections are fully present for the sake of adornment.
2. The Ten Topknots (Daśa-śikha) means that his precepts are stainless and he is noble in his self-restraint.
3. The Ten Radiances (Daśa-raśmi) means that he emits the light of hearing and retention to illuminate the patience regarding dharmas (dharma-kṣānti).
Fourth, the ten [stages] are also called "Pillars" (*dhvaja*) because the wisdom of the blaze and diligence transcend the world and rise loftily;
alternatively, it is because the factors of the path subdue afflictions and diligence subdues pride.
Fifth, the ten sounds refer to the arising of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because it is difficult to surpass and delights the faculties.
Sixth, the ten superior ones refer to the manifestation of wisdom (*prajñā*), because they are most venerable and supreme.
7. The ten excellences refer to the superior practices within the stage of Far-reaching Skillful Means (*dūramgamā*).
8. The eleven sovereign kings refer to the immovability of their marks and functions, due to the unimpeded nature of their great vows.
9–10. Furthermore, those named "Sound" (Ghoṣa) are so called because they skillfully expound the Dharma through the power of their own realization. 10.
There are nine persons who share the name "Awakened" (Buddha): because they have received the office of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā) and thus entered the ranks of the Buddhas;
and because their wisdom awakens to all phenomena without exception.
However, the banners and other items also possess a general sense [of application], which can be understood through a similar explanation.
Third, from "In this way" onwards, the number is summarized.
Thirdly, from "These various" onwards, there are eleven phrases extolling their virtues.

The first phrase serves as the general heading; the preceding names were established by manifesting specific qualities according to what was appropriate, with each name being based on a single virtue.
Now, these virtues are established by referring to the reality that internally encompasses all, and therefore it is said that they "all fully accomplish the practices and vows of Samantabhadra."

The remaining ten phrases are distinct; among them, the first six clarify that the function of wisdom is universally pervasive, while the latter four clarify that the function of wisdom is free from obstructions.
These collectively form five pairs:
first, the pair of "object" and "pervading the body," which is multiple, because it exhaustively investigates the basis, the near, and the correct.

Second, the correspondence between the function of the two kinds of vision and reality: the ten eyes see without going because they are free from obstructions, and in a single thought-moment, they accord with reality such that body and mind pervade everywhere;
third, the correspondence between internal illumination and external manifestation;
fourth, the correspondence between the purity of wisdom and the conformity of form.

The fifth [verse] contrasts profound compassion with vast wisdom: because compassion is identical to wisdom, there is no obscuration regarding sentient beings; because wisdom is not external, its illumination is equal to empty space.
While the preceding [verse] contrasted [wisdom] with empty space to take up the meaning of purity, the present [verse] takes up the meaning of vastness.
The second section, beginning with "and also," distinguishes the assembly of śrāvakas.
The text has two parts:
first, the enumeration of their numbers and categories; second, beginning with "all awakened," the praise of their virtues.
The text contains ten phrases.

However, these śrāvakas are all bodhisattvas; wishing to manifest the profound Dharma, they rely upon the guise of śrāvakas. Therefore, the virtues praised herein contain both their original and provisional identities.
Now, this explanation is divided into two sections:
first, regarding the manifest traces from the perspective of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), all ten phrases refer to the virtues of a śrāvaka.
First is "attaining clear observation" (*abhisamaya*), because of their excellent awakening and comprehension of the Four Noble Truths.
Second, because they have already realized the entry into the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) through wisdom that lacks skillful means;

third, because their training has reached its consummation, it is said they have "entered deeply. As the *Lotus Sūtra* states, "We have entered equally into the dharma-nature," which is like the three animals crossing the river: though their modes differ, the principle is non-dual.
The ancients also correlated the aforementioned three [types of Arhats] with the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, respectively.
Since their four types of birth have already been exhausted, they emerge from themselves forever due to the lack of great compassion.
Fifth, because the virtues of the five conditioned and unconditioned states are accomplished by relying on the Buddha, one immediately attains one's own benefit.
Sixth, the fetters of existence are exhausted, meaning that the nine fetters and ten proclivities have ceased their active manifestation.
Seventh, they are free from the obstruction of afflictions, because the seeds [of affliction] have been extinguished.
Eighth, because their minds are well-liberated, they are as tranquil as space.
Ninth, because their wisdom is well-liberated, they have no doubts regarding the Buddha.
First, it clarifies that those of no fixed nature can all turn their minds [toward enlightenment], and thus they believe and enter the Buddha-wisdom.
Second, regarding the "Original Gate," this is because the praise is directed toward the bodhisattvas.

The *Tathāgatācintyaguhyanirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas appearing in the forms of śrāvakas, who also came to sit in the assembly; their names were Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and so forth."
The details are as extensively explained therein.

Since it is clarified that all these are provisional (*upāya*), [the Buddha] subsequently had Śāriputra lead Haijue and others to contemplate the ten virtues of Mañjuśrī; among these, the first is awakening to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Second, having fully perfected the skillful means, because they are well able to enter the limit of the limitless;
third, because they have thoroughly investigated the source of the true principle of the two emptinesses;
fourth, because they are endowed with great compassion and are able to enter without defilement, thereby finally attaining eternal transcendence.
Fifth, by relying on the ten powers and so forth, one is free from inferior views;
sixth, because one can abandon [defilements] through neither severance nor simultaneous presence;
seventh, because the objects of knowledge have already been purified and there are no two-fold obstructions.
Eighth, the eight bases of mastery are eternally quiescent because they are understood to be fundamentally empty;
ninth, the unique qualities of a Buddha, for even though they have not yet been realized, one has no doubt regarding them;
tenth, the knowledge of all modes, because one enters through realization and faith.

Third, regarding the assembly of world-protectors (*lokapāla*) beginning with "and immeasurable," they are also first characterized by their number and categories, and subsequently praised for their virtues in the section beginning with "all have formerly.
Among these ten [praises], the first praises their merit; the following four praise their compassion.

Within these, the first phrase is general while the remaining three are specific: first, responding universally without a specific object; second, protecting and mindful of the initial resolve; and third, vowing never to abandon those in evil.

The next two phrases praise the virtue of wisdom: first, wisdom enters the gate of skillful means; second, practice protects and maintains the teaching. This is because the True Dharma encompasses both principle and practice, and protection encompasses both maintenance and application.
The preceding seven [phrases] all concern practice.
The eighth is the stage of aspiration, because it is the perfection of both aspiration and practice.
The ninth is the entry into the position.
These nine constitute the stage of self-benefit.
Tenth is "Superior Progression.
The preceding section on the introductory framework is concluded.

The second major section, beginning with "At that time, the bodhisattvas... and following, is the "Section on the Request," as the assembly has gathered primarily for the purpose of hearing the sutra.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the announcement of the assembly’s request; second, from the phrase "the realm of the Tathāgata" onwards, the manifestation of the Dharma requested.
This is the first part.
"Śrāvakas" are like those who are deaf and blind.
Regarding this "one who is able to remember," there are two interpretations:
first, in terms of the fundamental and the provisional, they are able to remember from the perspective of the fundamental, yet they do not know from the perspective of the provisional.
The second [category] is explained solely in terms of their outward manifestations. Master Fashi said:
"Because their principles and positions are not separated, they may share the same doubts;
however, because they have not yet accumulated the Great Mind (mahācitta), they do not rank among the latter."
This also has its道理 (principle): it is like Yegong’s love for dragons; when a true dragon appears, it is difficult to behold.
Though dwelling together in the Dharma assembly and equally aspiring toward the Dharma gate, that which is manifested here transcends all others, and thus [the others] are as if deaf and blind.

Within the second section on what is contemplated, there are sixty-one phrases; the first and last thirty phrases concern the Dharma requested, while the middle thirty-one phrases pertain solely to the ritual of the request.

The thirty requests for the Dharma are for the most part identical to the forty phrases of the first assembly; taking the first assembly as the general framework, this teaching is brought to its conclusion because the assembly returns to its original state.
Regarding the textual analysis, there are two parts:

the first thirty phrases contemplate the inconceivable virtues, while the latter thirty-one phrases, beginning with "I only pray," request that [the Buddha] teach according to the capacities of beings.
The first ten phrases clarify the perfection of the self-nature, manifesting by extension that the ocean of fruition transcends all words.
The final ten phrases clarify that the transformative function is universally pervasive, causing the fruit to be manifested through provisional words.
Because of this, the text contains both explicit and implicit meanings; in truth, the principle encompasses both aspects as requested, as was analyzed in the first assembly.

Now, within the section on the virtues of the first recollection: the first ten phrases correctly clarify the resultant dharmas that are recollected; the next ten clarify their profound and wondrous nature, which is difficult to conceive; and the final ten clarify that they can be understood through the convergence of conditions.

Now, within the first ten [categories], the first eight encompass the initial assembly; the first ten phrases therein represent the virtue of the perfection of internal practice, because the Tathāgata’s mastery subsumes those supernatural powers as well as the power of being incapable of being grasped.
First, regarding the "single objective realm" (ekaviṣaya), this refers to the delimitation of the focal object (*ālambana*), as explained in such chapters as the "Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva*).

Second, regarding the "practice of wisdom" (*jñānacaryā*), this refers to the effortless practice (*anābhogacaryā*) in which compassion and wisdom are non-obstructed, also as explained in the "Manifestation Chapter."
The third empowerment refers to the sustaining power of supreme strength that enables the performance of activities, as explained in the "Chapter on Inconceivable Dharmas.
The fourth refers to the ten powers and so forth.
The fifth consists of the fourfold and tenfold fearlessnesses and so forth.
The sixth consists of the lion’s sport and so forth.
The seventh, that which is "dwelt in," refers to the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) of the first assembly, for it is the ground wherein the Buddha dwells.
If explained separately, these refer to the eternal abiding in great compassion and so forth, as in the "Inconceivable Chapter.
The eighth refers to the ten masteries and so forth, along with the inclusion of two phrases, as previously analyzed.
The extensive citation of various texts to explain the meaning is identical to that of the first assembly.

As for the latter two phrases, they subsume the ten subsequent phrases of the first assembly; while the "essence" (*tattva*) and "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) were previously manifest, the "virtues" (*guṇa*) included the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) and the three types of action (*trikarma*).
Now, the "body" (*kāya*) subsumes the six sense organs and two types of action, while "wisdom" (*jñāna*) corresponds to the mental action (*manaskarma*).
Mind and consciousness are both unknowable, being known only through wisdom (*jñāna*).

The reason they are combined is that one wishes to manifest the body as encompassing the ten bodies; thus, the six sense organs and the three karmas are unified. Since they are guided by wisdom, they are referred to simply as "wisdom."
Second, the ten phrases beginning with "All" clarify that [the Buddha's state] is profound and wondrously inconceivable, such that humans and devas cannot fathom it.

Among these, the first two phrases generally clarify that [ordinary] understanding and practice cannot reach it; that is, wisdom cannot penetrate it thoroughly, and mental activity cannot arrive at its realization.
The next five phrases clarify that the three types of wisdom cannot fathom [this reality], and thus self-benefit cannot be accomplished.
Specifically, the first three phrases indicate that the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) cannot fathom it:
first, because it is subtle, one cannot grasp and maintain the object.
Second, because it is profound, the mind cannot clearly comprehend it;
third, because it is vast, it cannot be accepted or fully encompassed.
As for the next phrase, because it is mysterious, the wisdom of cultivation cannot observe it with thorough illumination.
Because the latter phrase [of "contemplation"] implies integration,
the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is unable to discern their relative superiority or inferiority.
In the Jin translation, "discernment" (*vicaya*) is rendered as "reflection" (*sīmānā*), which is placed above "observation" (*vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the latter three phrases, the four types of eloquence cannot be proclaimed; therefore, one is unable to accomplish the benefit of others. That is to say:

the eloquence of Dharma and meaning cannot extensively open up or provide detailed instruction; the eloquence of words cannot proclaim and clarify; and the eloquence of delight in speaking cannot cause others to understand.

Third, regarding the ten phrases beginning with "except for," which concern the conditions through which [the meaning] can be understood: the first four refer to the Buddhas' power being added as the contributing condition (*pratyaya*), while the latter six refer to one's own faculties being capable of receiving it as the cause (*hetu*); when these are complete, it can be known.
Regarding the first six [of the ten phrases], the first three refer to present conditions and the last one to past vows;
regarding the latter six, the first refers to past goodness and the remaining five to present virtues.
Within these ten phrases, there is partial knowledge and complete knowledge, as well as partial existence and complete existence.
Furthermore, these ten phrases have two general meanings:
first, to complete the preceding section by manifesting its profundity; second, to initiate the subsequent request for the teaching.
Within the second [meaning], the request for the teaching to be expounded according to the capacities of beings has two parts:
The first eleven phrases request [the teaching] according to the suitability of the occasion; the latter twenty phrases, beginning with "Manifesting," request the Dharma to be taught.
This is the first part.
Previously it was said that [the truth] can be known through the convergence of conditions; now, he requests that the conditions be applied according to the capacities of the vessels.

Among these, the first three concern the distinctions of the internal vessel of the mind; the next one concerns the differences in external types of sounds; the [following] four apply universally to both ordinary beings and sages;

and the final seven mostly concern bodhisattvas: (1) the distinctions in material wealth and so forth; (2) the superiority or inferiority of spiritual stages; (3) the reliance on faculties and the removal of hindrances; (4) the differences in activities performed; (5) the different objects of focus; (6) the particular virtues upon which they previously relied for cultivation; and (7) the specific teachings they previously heard as seeds.

Furthermore, regarding the sixth [point], by what qualities should one be transformed; and regarding the seventh, by what degree of detail—whether extensive or concise—should the various differences be taught: in all these cases, please act in accordance with our request.
Second, the request for the Dharma to be taught has two parts:
first, the listing of what is requested; second, the summary of the request, beginning with the words "In this manner, etc."
Now, for the first part, there are two sections:
the first ten lines request an explanation of the causes from the past, and the latter ten lines request an explanation of the functions of the present fruit.
This is the first section.
Among these ten phrases, seven are identical in both name and meaning to those in the first assembly.
"The various paths" refers to that ocean of the aids to the path (*bodhipakṣa*).
The "skillful means" herein is the aforementioned ocean of wisdom; thus, while the names differ, the meanings are the same.
In that [other] version, there is a "Vehicle" (yāna) but no "Original Matter" (pūrvayoga); thus, both name and meaning differ.
Because that version universally requests [the teaching] for all Bodhisattvas, it reveals the differences between the vehicles;

whereas here, as the question is addressed specifically to the Original Teacher, the "Original Matter" is added. Consequently, while the "Vehicle" applies throughout the various phrases, it is omitted here for the sake of completing the number ten.
Alternatively, the "original basis" (*pūrvayoga*) itself is the vehicle for crossing the ocean, as it was that which was previously mounted.
The remainder is as in the first assembly.

Regarding the ten phrases following "and the accomplishment," which concern the request for the function of the fruit (*phalavṛtti*): these ten, when compared to the thirtieth phrase of the third section of the first assembly, share much the same meaning while differing largely in wording. Because one wishes to manifest that the functions of the fruit are boundless, the wording has been abbreviated through such elliptical representation.
First, the perfection of causes resulting in the accomplishment of the fruit, which is the ocean of Buddhas;
second, the necessity of expounding the Dharma upon such accomplishment, which is the ocean of exposition;
third, the Dharma’s elucidation of pure lands, which is the ocean of worlds.
The four [aspects] all serve to harmonize and transform sentient beings; this is the Sea of Names and Titles.
The fifth pair opens the way to the citadel of the fruits of Bodhi and Nirvana; because Nirvana prevents error and stops evil, this is the Sea of Liberation.
The sixth demonstrates that the practices and deeds of birth are the causes for the ultimate fruit; this is the Sea of Sentient Beings.
Seventh, entering the spheres of sentient beings' faculties and establishing their lifespans according to those faculties, which is the ocean of lifespan;
eighth, acting as a field for sentient beings so that they may attain eternal life, which is the ocean of *pāramitās*, because giving (*dāna*) is the foremost among them;
ninth, expounding the various *pāramitās* in order to establish the formal methods for the oceans of worlds.
The thirteen transformations of the wheels are like the moon in water or a reflection in a mirror; this is the ocean of transformations.
The formal invitation may be understood accordingly.
The third major section, beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One," is the division on the manifestation of signs through samādhi.
This is because he responds to the request of his previous thought by manifesting signs in answer.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, clarifying that samādhi is that which manifests; second, from "Entering this samādhi" onwards, clarifying the pure land that is manifested.
Regarding the first point: because the great functioning that is without spatial direction arises based upon the essence, he first enters meditative concentration.
It is for this reason that the entry into concentration is explained first, followed by the gathering of the ocean-like assembly.
The previous assemblies were intended to clarify the entry from the phenomenal into the real; they proceeded from gathering to concentration, which differs from this case.
That the Buddha himself enters [the samādhi] signifies that the realization of the Dharma-realm is exhausted only in the Buddha.
The reason for not providing a verbal response is to manifest that realization transcends words, and furthermore, to cause others to witness it for themselves and realize it directly.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, entering meditative absorption, which involves taking the preceding thought as its object;...
Second, from "Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*) downward, the causes for entering meditative absorption are clarified;
third, from "Entering the Lion" downward, the actual entry into meditative absorption is clarified.
Within the section on the causes for entry, there are four kinds of compassion, which serve as the foundation for entering absorption to benefit sentient beings.
Each has two meanings: first, the body;
second, the meaning. Regarding the "body": first, it is the body that serves as the basis for entering meditative concentration, because it is permeated by compassion;
second, the "body" carries the meanings of essence and reliance, because when one intends to enter profound concentration, one takes great compassion entirely as its essence.

Regarding the two gates and two meanings: first, the Buddha possesses gates such as great wisdom, great meditative concentration, and great compassion; now, desiring to benefit sentient beings, he relies solely on the gate of compassion to lead them to entry.
Second, meditative concentration is that which is entered, while compassion is that which enables the entry.
Regarding the three verses and two meanings: first is the initial meaning, which holds that whatever benefits sentient beings is invariably preceded by great compassion;
second is the superior meaning, which means that it does not fail to employ the gateways of wisdom and meditative concentration, as these are further enhanced.

Regarding the two meanings of the four skillful means (*upāya*): first, compassion and wisdom guide one another and serve as mutual skillful means; here, compassion is taken as the skillful means for entering meditative concentration to benefit sentient beings.

Second, because this is compassion that is identical with wisdom and concentration, it does not stagnate in attachment or biased views and is thus called a "skillful means"; only then can it cause sentient beings to universally enter the *dharmadhātu*.
Furthermore, these four types of compassion also represent the gradual progression from the Buddha toward sentient beings.
Each of the four aforementioned compassions pervades all of space, for two reasons:
first, because they are vast and all-encompassing; second, because they are objectless (anālambana).
