Second, in the section beginning with "At that time, Sudhana," regarding the act of seeing and respectfully inquiring, the mention of one who gathers sand refers to the fact that merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are accumulated through the observance of the precepts.
The third section, "The Words of the Sovereign Lord," correctly demonstrates the *dharmadhātu*.
It consists of two parts:
first, the presentation of the name and essence of the dharma-gate; second, from "Good son, because of my cause... onwards, the clarification of its functional activity.
First: that which Mañjuśrī studies is wisdom, because it can protect the precepts;
that which is written is the means of expression, because it clearly distinguishes between what is to be ceased and what is to be practiced.
"Enumeration" (shu) signifies the four grave offenses, the ten precepts, and even the three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices.
"Calculation" (suan) signifies how many fruits are induced by each individual cause.
"Seal" (*mudrā*) refers to the fact that the results of upholding or violating precepts—whether good or evil—are determined.
"And so forth" (*ādi*) includes other medical arts, thereby completing the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
The preceding clarifies what is studied; the following distinguishes what is realized.
The supernormal powers of craftsmanship are all produced by wisdom; they also signify the cultivation of precepts that gives rise to meditative concentration and wisdom.
The second section, clarifying their functional applications, has three parts:

first, a general clarification; second, a miscellaneous explanation of various clarities (vidyās) beginning with "Furthermore, they can also heal..."; and third, a detailed exposition of knowledge of calculation beginning with "Good son..."
Within this, the first section distinguishes the numbers capable of being calculated;
the subsequent section, beginning with "Good son, by means of this," calculates that which is to be calculated.
The remaining three sections may be understood accordingly.
The third Upāsikā, Samudrapratiṣṭhānā, represents the practice of non-opposition.
The city named Samudrapratiṣṭhānā is so called because it is situated near the sea.
She dwells securely in patience, just as the ocean contains all things within it.
The friend named "Endowed with Fulfillment" (Pūrṇa) is so called because within her single vessel nothing is lacking, and because her vessel of patience universally contains all virtues.
Since patience is gentle and supple, she is represented by a woman.
In this passage, the first part—relying on the teaching to seek [the goal]—is clear.
The second part, beginning with “Having heard this, Sudhana,” concerns seeing, paying respect, and inquiring.
Within the section on seeing, there are four parts:
First, one sees the external retribution of the environment;
second, one sees the primary retribution of the companions.
That they are upright and pleasing to behold is due to the fruit of patience.
"Plain clothing and so forth" refers to the endurance of [rejecting] ornamental finery.
Third, from "In his residence" onwards, one sees the internal dependent retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Fourth, from "Furthermore there were" onwards, it clarifies that his retinue’s myriad practices all accord with patience (*kṣānti*).
The second [section on] "respect" and the third on "inquiry" can both be understood accordingly.
Third, from the words "He then... onwards, the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is correctly demonstrated.
This section contains two parts:
First, the names and essences of the dharma-gates are presented;
because objects emerge from within the vessel and the arising of merit is inexhaustible, it is called that which is summoned by the merit of the *dharmadhātu*.

Following this, from the passage "One is able, in such a manner... onwards, the functional activity is distinguished, consisting of three parts: [The text continues with the three parts of the functional activity.]
First, the functional activity is correctly revealed; second, it causes [beings] to see its common benefit; third, it causes them to verify it through direct observation.
Within the first [section], there are three parts:
first, benefiting sentient beings; second, benefiting those of the two vehicles; and third, benefiting bodhisattvas.
Regarding the first [section], there are also three parts.

First is the general clarification: because these are implements that accord with the nature (*dharmatā*), even a single small vessel is fused with and identical to the *dharmadhātu*. Since it is an inexhaustible dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), its function is such that there is nothing to which it does not respond, and its response is such that there is nothing that does not benefit; yet, the essence of this *dharmadhātu* neither increases nor decreases.
Furthermore, it expresses that patience must necessarily be humble, and thus it is the patience regarding minor dharmas (*kṣānti*).
Being identical and of a single flavor, it constitutes the "one.
Internally empty and externally provisional, it serves as the vessel.
Because patience can encompass all without exclusion, it gives rise to inexhaustibility.
Next, from "giving birth" (*janana*) onwards, the specific emergence of the flavor is clarified.
Finally, from "like food and drink" onwards, one instance is cited as an analogy for the remainder.
Second, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, son of good family, even if" clarifies the benefit for those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Although the Two Vehicles do not establish the name of "patience" (*kṣānti*), they likewise must endure the principle of the exhaustion of birth and non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) before they can achieve fruition.
Third, the section beginning with "Furthermore, good son, in the eastern direction" benefits bodhisattvas.
In terms of concrete events, this refers to receiving the milk gruel;

in terms of the Dharma, it refers to partaking in the supreme patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*) and thereby attaining *bodhi*. Thus, it is largely identical to the account in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* regarding the Gandhavyūha world.
2. "Good son, you see... and so forth, which causes those below to see and benefit equally.
3. "Wait a moment... and so forth, which causes them to witness it with their own eyes.
As for the subsequent three sections, the texts may be understood accordingly.
The fourth, the wise householder, relies on the practice of being unyielding.

Within the initial reliance on the teaching for seeking [the teacher], there is first the reliance on prior cultivation, and subsequently, from the section beginning with "gradually," the reliance for seeking the subsequent friend.
The city is named "Great Arising" (*Mahābhyudaya*) because it gives rise to great diligence (*mahāvīrya*).
The friend is named "Clear Wisdom" (*Pratibhāna*) because the advancement of one's feet must necessarily rely on the guidance of the eye of wisdom.

In the second section, beginning with "At that time, Sudhana," regarding the act of seeing, paying respects, and inquiring: first, his seeing [the friend] at a crossroads in the marketplace symbolizes that he is not disturbed by the clamor of the place, for there is nothing he does not penetrate.
The respectful inquiry may be understood.
The third section, beginning with "The elder said," praises and bestows the Dharma; it consists of three parts:
first, extolling the superior capacity of generating the bodhicitta.
2. From "Good son, you see" onwards, [the text] indicates the retinue of those he has transformed who have resolved their minds [on enlightenment].
Those "born into the family of the Tathāgata" are identical to those born during the four abidings (*catur-vihāra*).
Third, from "Good son, I have attained" onwards, the Dharma-realm is correctly demonstrated.
This section has two parts:
first, the names are presented.
Wealth and Dharma are inexhaustible, stored within the void; they are bestowed according to one's wishes, and thus it is named the "Treasury of Merit that Produces Whatever is Desired.
It also symbolizes the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), for there is nothing therein that is not complete.
Following this, the section beginning with "In general" (*fanyou*) reveals the functional activity (*karmayoga*).
This section has two parts:
first, a brief enumeration; second, from "Good son, wait a moment" (*shanzan qie dai*) onwards, citing specific instances as empirical verification.
Within this, first there is the assembly of the multitude;

subsequently, from "At that time, the householder" onwards, there is the extensive bestowal of wealth and Dharma, wherein he first bestows wealth and subsequently, from "Then" onwards, bestows the Dharma.
By giving a single meal, one brings about eight aspects:
the first two pertain to the act of giving, and the remaining six pertain to the food itself.
There are five fruits of such eating:
First, attaining that which is like all dharmas is the life of wisdom;
second, attaining joy is constant peace and happiness;
third, being endowed with the marks and signs of excellence is the eternal form.
The fourth and sixth are the power of permanence;
the fifth is constant discernment.
Regarding the mark of the supreme flavor: it is because there is a spring of ambrosia within the tooth-sockets.
The remainder may be inferred accordingly.
Fourth, from "At that time, the householder" onwards, one may understand how he humbles himself and defers to the superior.
Fifth, from "Good son" onwards, he points out the subsequent friend.

As for the city named Siṃhāsana (Lion Throne), it signifies that one’s meditative concentration is undisturbed; because one dwells therein like being within a deep inner palace, what is spoken is definitive and one acts with fearlessness, hence it is so named.
The friend named Dharmaratnacūḍa (Dharma-Jewel-Crest) gathers and restrains all that is disordered, for he dwells upon the crown of the mind.
His concentration contains brilliant wisdom; thus, by adding the name "Jewel" as a metaphor to illustrate the Dharma, he is called Dharmaratnacūḍa. The following sixty-six sūtras [begin with this].
The fifth is Dharmaratna-śikhin, who is entrusted with conduct free from delusion and confusion.
Regarding the six sections, the first text is easily understood.
The second, beginning with "Seeing this elder," concerns seeing, paying respect, and inquiring.
That those who see him in the marketplace represent his state of mindlessness amidst the clamor, for he remains constantly in samādhi within the midst of disorder.
Third, from the passage "At that time, the elder... onwards, he bestows his own dharma-realm.
Within this, there are four parts:

first, taking the hand and leading [the disciple] away, which is the expedient means for bestowing the Dharma; it reveals that the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) returns to correct realization.
Second, from "Acting in this way" onwards, he shows the place where one dwells; this is the actual bestowal of the *dharmadhātu*.
3. From "At that time, Sudhana saw his... onwards, he directly realizes the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
4. From "At that time, Sudhana saw this... onwards, the sequence of questions and answers constitutes subsequently attained wisdom (prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna).
The first two [sections] are clear.
Regarding the third, there are two parts:
first, the general; second, the specific, beginning with "After Sudhana had entered."
First, regarding the ten tiers and eight gates: they are shaped like an octagonal pagoda. Each tier and each gate has three meanings, which will be explained individually below.
As for the three meanings of the gates: first, in terms of the path practiced, the Eightfold Path serves as the gate, because the Eightfold Path provides universal access to all stages.
Second, regarding the path upon which one relies, one takes the eight consciousnesses as the gateway;
for by entering right concentration within the eye-faculty, if the faculty can enter, the object can then be known.
Third, the manifestation of principle through the classification of teachings involves entering the Dharma via the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Since there are four aspects for both teaching and principle, there are eight gates.
That is to say, if one loses the intended meaning, when both existence and emptiness are simultaneously negated, one falls into the four types of false views (*catur-nāstika-dṛṣṭi*).
The successful entry through penetration is collectively termed a "gate.
Attaining understanding by following the teachings refers to the four gates of the teachings;
attaining understanding regarding the principle refers to the four gates of the principle.
Regarding the three ten-layered sections within the distinct [sections], the first represents the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
First, the offering of food manifests the practice of *dāna* (generosity) in the first stage.
Second, the maintenance of precepts takes shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*) as one's clothing.
In the third stage, the practice of patience serves as its ornament.
In the fourth stage, the factors of enlightenment serve as its inner retinue; diligence is to be prized.
In the fifth stage, the phrasing is explicit.
The sixth stage [is so called] because Prajñā manifests therein.
The text has three parts:
first, the general [explanation].

Next, from the words "That is to say" (*yad uta*) onwards, fifteen specific gates are revealed: first, the essence of illumination is itself quiescence, yet nothing is not encompassed; second, this illumination within quiescence reflects all capacities without exception; third, external conditions do not cause it to turn; fourth, internal illumination seeks nothing; fifth, delusive objects cannot destroy it; sixth, it universally destroys all delusions; seventh, it encompasses supreme virtues and is profoundly deep; eighth, it universally perceives the *dharmadhātu* without obstruction; ninth, the one is inexhaustible; tenth, skillful transformation is boundless; eleventh, it internally realizes the mundane world; twelfth, it externally manifests supreme eloquence; thirteenth, it follows the desires of beings with flexibility; fourteenth, phenomena and principle interlace; fifteenth, it observes conditions and bestows the Dharma.
The section following "Thus it was said" serves as the conclusion.
Because the seventh stage possesses extraordinary practices and one understands the various teachings, it is said that one "attains the patience like an echo."
Within the eighth stage, two positions are contained:
first, the effortless supernatural powers (*anābhoga-abhijñā*) of the eighth stage and mastery over the three worlds;
second, the Dharma-preacher of the ninth stage, who is able to expound the teaching with a single voice.
The nine layers also consist of two stages, as both the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*) can each constitute a single lifetime.
The ten layers represent the stage of the Tathāgata.
The number two represents the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), because the ten practices are identical to the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*).

The first seven texts are manifest; the eighth is because it consists of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth accomplished through the eight great vows; the ninth is because its power is supreme as it pertains to those bound by only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*); and the tenth is because it reaches fulfillment only upon attaining the wisdom of a Tathāgata.
This means that each respective stage inherently encompasses all stages;
for when the ten stages are encompassed, all subsequent stages are thereby included.
Ten layers of pairs represent these two meanings, just as when the stage of Sāgaradhvaja has finished encompassing all ten stages, it is said that he attains Buddhahood.
The former was subsumed under the sixth stage, while this is subsumed under the fifth stage.

The former was categorized in terms of the primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*), whereas this is categorized in terms of the environmental retribution (*bhājanaloka*); both cases demonstrate that the stage is superior to the preceding one.

Third, these do not collectively indicate specific stages; rather, this bodhisattva, through practice adapted to the capacities of beings, manifests abiding in superior retributions that gradually increase in excellence.
The ten [perfections] manifest inexhaustibility: the first four involve giving material things, each subsequent one being more difficult than the last;
the next two involve the giving of the Dharma, the former being shallow and the latter deep.
The next two [verses] concern the attainment of the Dharma: the former is narrow and the latter is vast;
the final two manifest superior virtues: the former is the cause and the latter is the fruit.
Collectively, these three meanings—cause, fruit, practice, and stages—constitute the house of the elder.
Within the fourfold sequence of questions and answers, the question comes first, followed by the answer.
Regarding the dedication toward the three places, this refers to the departure from poverty and the summoning of the retributions of the preceding four levels.
The two or three fruits are precisely the latter six stages.
As for the subtle cause of "one" and "nine," the retribution is superior due to the power of the vow.
Furthermore, when manifesting that the myriad practices are harmoniously integrated and initiating them toward Buddhahood, then within each single practice, nothing is not fully present.
Which fruits are not attained?
The fourth section, beginning with "Good son," expresses self-humbling and the recommendation of others' excellence.

Regarding the self-humbling statement that [the author] is equal to Bodhisattvas and so forth: because he is like a treasure of the world and the Three Jewels accumulated within the ten stages, he is called a "Treasury of Jewels."
Being constantly used without exhaustion constitutes immeasurable merit.
This is because, among the subsequent categories of excellence, it is the dharma that demonstrates superiority.
That "the treasury of merit is entirely inconceivable" is the summary statement.
The section beginning with "Entering into non-conceptuality" explains this specifically.
Because all phenomena are possessed through non-conceptuality, it is inconceivable.
The latter two [points] can be understood.
The sixth, the Elder Universal Eye, represents the stage of the practice of good manifestation.
Regarding the kingdom named "Creeper Root": as for a creeper root, it penetrates deeply into the earth and sends forth flowers and sprouts above.

The outer manifestation represents the practice of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) that realizes the profound, which is capable of generating subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Because this subsequent attainment functions in accordance with all things, it is likened to a vine.
The city is named "Universal Gate" because the *prajñā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) penetrates everything without obstruction.
The elder named Universal Eye (Puyan) is so called because through the wisdom of contemplative observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*), there is nothing he does not see.
Regarding the phrase "profoundly entering the immeasurable knowledge and vision of all Buddhas" within the section on seeking according to the teachings, "immeasurable" has two meanings:
first, it refers to multiplicity, which is the realm of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Secondly, because they are without measure, they are the actual objects of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Since the objects are immeasurable, wisdom is also immeasurable.
Furthermore, "knowledge and vision" (*jñānadarśana*) also has two meanings:

First, the distinction: this means that "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is itself wisdom (*jñāna*), and "vision" (*darśana*) is itself insight (*prajñā*); it refers to the wisdom that illuminates two objects. Second, the commonality:
this means that both the terms "knowledge" and "vision" are the Tathāgata’s capacity for realization; because he knows those meanings as they truly are, it is unobstructed wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*).
If that is so, why employ these redundant terms?
The term "seeing" (*darśana*) is used to distinguish it from inferential knowledge (*anumāna*).

The term "knowing" (*jñāna*) is used to distinguish it from seeing with the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). This is as explained by Vasubandhu in his *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding the phrases "completely knowing" and "completely seeing."
"Entering" (praveśa) means realization and penetration; the remaining phrases are easy to understand.
In the second section, "Thereafter he was able to... and so forth, regarding the seeing, honoring, and questioning, he first beheld the primary and secondary [receptacle] worlds.
"Surrounded on all sides by hundreds of thousands of villages" refers to the *prajñā* of one's retinue.
"The battlements are lofty and steep" means that *prajñā* wards off what is non-virtuous; it is high and unsurpassed.
Five boards make one *du*; five *du* make one *zhi*.
The *die* refers to the battlements (or *nǚqiáng*).
As for the broad and level thoroughfares, they are the paths constantly traversed by the various Buddhas of Prajñā and not the provisional tracks; therefore, they are vast and boundless.

The third section, beginning with "The Elder’s Address," is the praise and bestowal of the Dharma. It consists of two parts: first, the praise; second, beginning with "Good Son," the bestowal of his own Dharma-realm.
Within this, there are two further points:
first, the ability to heal illness, which refers to the downward transformation of sentient beings.
Below the passage beginning with "Furthermore, son of good family, I also," it is explained that one can blend incense to make offerings to the Buddhas.
This section has two parts:
first, the removal of physical illness; second, the treatment of mental illness.
The preceding section also has two parts:
first, treating the inability [to benefit others]; second, from "Good son, in the ten directions" onwards, all [passages] treat both [the physical and mental] while also bestowing physical bliss.
Second, from "Then, combining them as one" onwards, there is the treatment of the mental illness, which also has two parts:
The first part, clarifying the removal of delusions, applies in meaning to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
the subsequent part, "in order to cause them to... and so forth, which aims to bring about benefit, pertains exclusively to the Mahāyāna.
It consists of sixteen phrases:
The first five [verses] manifest the practices and vows of the Great Mind;

the subsequent ten specifically clarify the causes of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) that evoke the fruit of the ten bodies. Because giving fulfills the minds of others, his physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) bring joy to all beings.

Because the precepts universally cease all evil, the purification of the body is all-pervasive; because patience encompasses both the principle and its endurance, it is inconceivable; because diligence encourages the myriad practices, none can surpass it; because dhyāna is focused on a single mind, there is nothing equal to it; because prajñā illuminates the principle, it reveals the Dharma-body; because skillful means manifest their function, the form-body is visible to behold; because vows exhaust the limits of the future, they abide through kalpas without end; because power cannot be shaken, it transcends all things; and because wisdom exhausts all phenomena and events, it assumes bodies in accordance with sentient beings.
The final phrase is ultimately pure and sublime because it completely transcends all evils.
Regarding the second [section], the practice of making offerings to the Buddhas above, there are two parts:
first, knowing the substance of the incense.
"Siṃdhu" refers to the Indus River.
"Pāra" means "bank," referring to the fragrance on that riverbank.
"Aruṇavati" is translated here as "extreme redness."
*Uragas* are the names for snakes in the Western Regions; these snakes possess venom, which is why they coil around this sandalwood tree.
"Harmonious integration" (*saṃyoga*) refers to the seamless fusion and unimpeded unity of morality, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth.
Next, the arousal of offerings and vows is followed by the ability to accomplish great offerings; these textual passages are all clearly evident.

Within the fourth section, on humbling oneself and deferring to the superior, regarding "humbling oneself through knowing one thing": this means that because the illnesses of body and mind are removed, one achieves happiness in both worlds and thus rejoices in all things. By universally making offerings with incense, one attains the ten bodies of a Buddha; thus, what Buddha would not see [this]?
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the seventh king, "Insatiable" (Anala), he is associated with the practice of non-attachment (*asaṅga-caryā*).

Within the first section on "Seeking by Relying on the Teachings," there are two parts: first, reflecting on how the teachings bring about benefit; second, from the words "gradually" (*krameṇa*) onwards, seeking the subsequent spiritual friends.
Having entered that land, one must certainly hear its governance.
"Tāra" means "luminous purity. A "banner" (dhvaja) signifies establishment;
it represents the practice of non-attachment based on the purity of *prajñā*, as it establishes superior conduct through clarity.
The king named Anala (No-Contentment) employs illusory skillful means; because his transformations are without attachment, he has no mind of weariness or exhaustion.
Regarding the second section, "Seeing from Afar" and below, within the context of seeing, paying respect, and inquiring, there are first four parts:

first, seeing the superior environment and inhabitants (*āśraya-dharmatā*); second, "Having before and behind him... and below, observing his transformative manifestations; third, "When Sudhana had seen this... and below, failing to understand and giving rise to doubt; fourth, "At the time he was thinking thus... and below, the celestial beings providing clarification.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, causing [the audience] to recall the reality of the previous teaching so that doubt does not arise;
second, from "Good son, the bodhisattva’s skillful means" onwards, elucidating the profound and mysterious nature of the subsequent practice, thereby enabling them to enter with faith.
However, although Sudhana constantly recalled their instructions, he still gave rise to doubts because their counter-intuitive actions were difficult to comprehend.
He did not doubt Vāsantī, as she appeared to benefit this world;
yet, because her greed and delusion manifested as harm, both Śūra and this king gave rise to suspicion and wonder.
Regarding the term "profound and mysterious," it refers to the thorough mastery of what is not the [conventional] path.

In the section on the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* translated during the Liang dynasty, it is explained that a bodhisattva may perform "contrary acts" such as killing and so forth, thereby generating immeasurable merit and attaining unsurpassed bodhi.
Only great bodhisattvas are capable of this matter.
There are two kinds:
first, those of actual practice; second, those who are emanations.

Regarding "one who truly acts": it is understood that the person before one will certainly commit an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*). Since there is no other expedient means to cause them to abstain from this evil, one may only take their life so that they do not commit it.
Furthermore, he knows that if the person before him should give up their life, they will certainly be reborn in a good realm.
Moreover, the Bodhisattva reflects to himself:
"If I commit this killing, I will surely fall into hell and undergo suffering for his sake."
"Although he currently undergoes slight suffering, he will certainly obtain a pleasant result.
This is also stated similarly in the "Chapter on Ethics" (*Śīla-paṭala*) within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Regarding the term "transformation" (nirmāṇa), it refers precisely to this passage.
Below, the King himself speaks.
Second, from "At that time, Sudhana... onwards, the respectful inquiry may be understood.
Third, from "At that time, Anala... onwards, the bestowing of one's own dharma-realm consists of two parts:
first, the bestowing of the skillful means of the Dharma.
By taking his hand and sitting together, the ritual of intimacy is demonstrated, signifying that he is to be gathered through preparatory practice and led toward the Truth.
Second, from "He said" onwards, the Dharma-realm is correctly revealed to enable realization through correspondence.
This section has four parts;
first, presenting the fruit to induce entry.
2. From "At that time, King Anala addressed Sudhana" onwards, he reveals the provisional through the real.
3. From "Good son, I have attained... onwards, he demonstrates what has been attained.
Within this, the first part, titled "Like an Illusion," clarifies that birth is like an illusion and thus uses illusion to transform illusion;
next, from "In this land of mine" onwards, it clarifies the functional application of the dharma-gate;
finally, from "I, by means of such [a dharma-gate]" onwards, it clarifies the supreme benefits of the dharma-gate.
4. From "O son of good family, my body and speech... onwards, the text directly reveals his actual virtues and the depth of his compassionate mindfulness.
However, as all stages up to the seventh are expedient means, Śāntarakṣita, Avalokiteśvara, and Kovidāra all primarily emphasize compassion.
The fourth [point] is the humility of deprecating oneself and extolling others.
Regarding the extolling of others as "the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*): it is because one realizes this patience only by understanding that all things are like illusions;
furthermore, it is because this [patience] corresponds to the stage immediately following [the present one].
The eighth, King Mahāprabha, is entrusted with the practice that is difficult to attain.

Within the first section, "Relying on the Teaching to Seek [the Goal]," one first contemplates the preceding and subsequent stages; from "Gradually" (*kramaśas*) downward, one proceeds toward the latter.
Among these, the first is known through investigation:
the city named "Exquisite Light" (Prabhāsa) signifies that while in the preceding stage one increased compassion, now one has attained non-abiding exquisite wisdom to transport sentient beings.
The king named Mahāprabha (Great Light) possesses the wisdom of the samādhi of loving-kindness that encompasses all things, and his vast vows are thoroughly illuminated throughout.
In the subsequent section beginning with "At that time, the youth Sudhana," he expresses his own joy regarding his future benefit.
The second section, from "Having formed this thought" onwards, concerns seeing, paying respect, and inquiring.
Within the initial section on seeing, there are three parts;
the first concerns seeing the *pariṇāmanavipāka* (the environment), which has two sub-sections:
Regarding the previously mentioned "extraordinary" [measure] of ten *yojanas*, this is intended to clarify its perfection.
Since there are already ten billion thoroughfares, each with immeasurable sentient beings, how could these be accommodated within the mundane measure of ten small *yojanas*?
Therefore, within this context, all phenomena should be understood as being perfectly interfused and manifesting the Dharma; reflect upon this according to the principle.
Below the passage beginning with "At that time, Sudhana," [the section on] "being able to see without defilement" follows.
Second, from "Gradually" (*jiàn-cì*) downward, we see the king’s primary retribution (*zhèng-bào*).
Regarding "at a crossroads": it is because he employs the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) and the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) to gather in sentient beings.
Regarding the twenty-eight marks, they are incomplete because their causes have not yet been fulfilled.
Third, from "In front of the royal throne" onwards, the primary figure and his retinue gather and sustain sentient beings.
Within this section, there are also three parts:
First, the objects of giving are enumerated, encompassing both sentient and insentient things;
the sixty-four skills are explained as in other sections.
Next, from the phrase "each and every path" onwards, the giver is clarified, who is the assistant.
Below the section beginning with "In order to universally encompass," the intention of his giving is clarified.
The first two [sections] regarding respectful inquiry can be understood accordingly.
Third, from the passage beginning "At that time, the King said," he bestows his own Dharma-realm; this consists of three parts:
First, a general presentation of the dharma-gate: it is said that great compassion is foremost because it emerges from and is perfected by being free from defilement.
Second, from the passage beginning "Good son, I... onwards, the causes and conditions for attaining the dharma are clarified.
Questioning and challenging [the teaching] constitutes the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); these three types of wisdom adorn this compassion.
The section beginning with "I, by means of this" clarifies its functional activity, which is divided into five parts:

first, gathering and transforming through the Dharma; second, gathering through fearlessness, starting from "In my land"; third, gathering through material wealth, starting from "If there are sentient beings"; fourth, gathering universally according to individual capacities, starting from "This city of Sublime Light"; and fifth, gathering through samādhi, starting from "Good son, within this land."
Within this section, there are two parts:
first, an announcement by means of words;
second, from "At that time, King Mahāprabha" onwards, the actual demonstration through meditative concentration, revealing the functional efficacy of that concentration.

"That both sentient and non-sentient beings all achieve supreme benefit" means that through the great compassion of the same essence (*samatā-mahāmaitrī*), there is no duality between self and others.
It is like a worldly king whose virtue accords with Heaven and Earth; then the qilin and phoenixes come to attend him, and precious jade and jade-discs manifest as auspicious omens.
How much more so, then, would the supramundane power of compassion not cause even grasses and trees to bow their knees?
The fourth section, beginning with "At that time, King Mahāprabha emerged from samādhi," expresses humility regarding oneself and defers to the excellence [of others].
First, humility is knowing oneself;
second, compassion is fundamentally for the sake of others, which is called "conforming to the world.
Because it rises above all other practices, it is named the "foremost," which carries the meaning of a banner (*dhvaja*); the rest may be understood accordingly.
The ninth is the Upāsikā Acalā, who relies upon the practice of wholesome dharmas.

Since she first resolved her mind [on enlightenment], there is no dharma among all dharmas in which she has not attained meditative concentration; for neither afflictions nor those of the Two Vehicles can move her, and because she causes the minds of sentient beings to be unshakable and cultivates loving-kindness through wisdom, she manifests as a woman dwelling in the household life.
"Abiding securely in the royal capital" refers to the status of a prince.
"Wisdom accords with the true Dharma and is not destroyed by conditions" is what is meant by "abiding securely.
Regarding the first reliance on the teachings for pursuit, there are two middle [sections]:
First, one relies on the teaching; subsequently, one seeks it out.
Within the former [stage], there are five parts:
first, contemplating and cultivating the preceding dharmas.
Second, from "giving rise to joy" onwards, [the text] explains the benefits gained through cultivation.
"Untroubled" refers to the absence of others' interference, while "pure" refers to one's own essence.
Third, from "reflecting thus" onwards, the merit is attributed to the spiritual friend.
Regarding the phrase "herein, one who is particularly compassionate," this is because the cultivation of compassion is about to reach fulfillment.
Fourth, from "Furthermore, he thought" onwards, there is an extensive praise of the friend's capability.
Fifth, from "The youth Sudhana, thus filled with sorrow" onwards, there is the exhortation through the seal of the superior conditions.
Regarding this, there are first the seals.
The term "heavenly" (deva) is used in two senses; thus, the Jin translation states: "the heavenly beings who are messengers of the Tathāgata, and the heavenly beings who follow the Bodhisattvas.

The heavenly beings who follow the Bodhisattvas are deities of one's own past karmic actions, while the heavenly beings who are messengers of the Tathāgata are deities who sustain sentient beings through the power of the Buddha. However, once the stage of cultivation has been established, both types of heavenly beings constantly accompany the person.
Following this, the section beginning with "You should go to... encourages him to visit the subsequent friend.
Second, the section beginning with "Then the youth Sudhana from there... describes his pursuit of the subsequent friend; these points are clear.
The second section, "Entering His Residence," and below, concerns seeing [Mañjuśrī] and paying respects and inquiring.
Within this section on seeing, there are two parts:
first, seeing [him] as a basis for obtaining benefit; second, from "The youth Sudhana approached... onwards, seeing [him] as truly transcending all peers.
Second, from "At that time, Sudhana bowed his body" onwards, the respectful inquiry may be understood.
Third, from "Then Acalā... onwards, there is the praise and the bestowal of the Dharma.
Within this, first there is the praise; subsequently, from "Good son, I have attained... onwards, is the formal bestowal of the *dharmadhātu*.
This section has two parts:
first, the presentation of the name and essence of the dharma-gate; second, the inquiry into the scope of its functional activity, beginning with the words "The youth Sudhana said.
Now, the first part.
The reason five dharmas are cited here, differing from previous examples, is that they correspond to the stage of a Dharma-preacher in the Ninth Ground, where extensive knowledge is required.
Among these five, the first two represent the internal virtues that are sustained:
the first is wisdom free from obstruction, which is specifically termed "liberation."
When there is wisdom, afflictions cannot destroy it;
because attachment cannot overcome it, it is said to be "difficult to subdue.
Since this wisdom encompasses all, it is called a "treasury" (garbha).
Second is firm upholding, which specifically receives the name "practice.
This means being able to endure when encountering evil sentient beings and remaining undeluded in mind while traversing all realms of existence; therefore, it is called "firm."
Third, it is the ability to uphold and penetrate deeply into the Dharma-gates; once the stage of the Dharma-nature is attained, there is nothing that is not upheld.

Fourth, it is external transformation: by correctly contemplating the Buddha-dharma and clearly illuminating its distinctions, one attains eloquence (*pratibhāna*) and is able to turn the wheel of Dharma according to the inclinations of sentient beings.

The fifth [point] concerns the upward-seeking [aspiration]: because one seeks the Dharma with a single mind, it is called *samādhi*; this is because one draws near to the Buddha without weariness and receives the Dharma without satiety.
Second, the investigation into the scope of its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*) consists of four parts:
first, the inquiry; second, the manifestation of its difficulty; third, the earnest request; and fourth, the detailed response.
The answer consists of two parts:
first, clarifying the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma to demonstrate its profound depth, thereby explaining the aforementioned difficulty of knowing it;
second, from "Good son, I have attained the Bodhisattva’s seeking of all... onwards, manifesting its functional activity to respond to the initial question.
Now, for the first part, there are six sections:
First, citing the past encounter with the Buddha as the condition for generating the resolve.

Second, from "Then, from the tower" downward, the internal arising of contemplation and mindfulness as the cause for generating the resolve; this consists of first observing and subsequently recollecting.
"Mindfulness of merit, wisdom, and so forth" refers to the causes of the aforementioned five dharmas.
"Mastery of the supernormal powers" refers to the firmness of practice.
Third, from the passage beginning "Good son, at that time," the Buddha exhorts the arousal of the bodhicitta.
There are ten kinds of mind that can accomplish the first five [perfections]:

the first two accomplish wisdom (*prajñā*); the next one accomplishes dhāraṇī; the next two accomplish supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); the next two accomplish meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and the last three accomplish eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
The preceding ten phrases explain the five dharma-gates.
Fourth, from "Good son, as for me at that time... onwards, it correctly clarifies the firmness of the resolve to awaken.
Fifth, from "Since I first gave rise to this mind... onwards, it shows that there has been no violation over a long period of time.
Sixth: "From that time onward" and below demonstrates the superior benefits of generating the resolve for enlightenment, which is the fruit of the five aforementioned causes.
This section has two parts: first, it reveals its functional activity, which consists of four sub-sections;
the first is the granting of a present manifestation, which cites two of the five dharmas.
Second is the request;

third is the actual manifestation, wherein entering ten thousand samādhis means that within a single "insatiable seeking of the Dharma" samādhi, one enters ten thousand [others], clearly showing that the remaining liberations (*vimokṣa*) and so forth likewise encompass many gateways;
fourth is the emergence from concentration, which is then described.
This can be understood accordingly.
Fourth, from the words "The upāsikā said" onwards, she humbles herself and defers to her superior.
Fifth, regarding the instruction toward the subsequent friend: *Tuṣita* (都薩羅) means "Joyfully Born," so called because immeasurable causes for joy arise within this city.
By means of the perfection of wisdom, one is able to give rise to nothing that cannot be produced.

This friend is named Universal Pervader (*Samantagāmin*); because his skillful wisdom accords with the capacities of beings such that there is nothing he does not practice, he is named True Practice (*Bhūtacara*).
"To demonstrate to the non-Buddhists" means that they are able to practice what is not the Path.
Because they are untainted by what is not the Path, they are called "those who have left home.
The remaining sixty-seven sūtras can be understood accordingly.
The tenth is the Pervasive Heretic (Sarvagata-tīrthika), who relies on true practice.
First, he seeks it by relying on the teachings;
second, from "To the east of the city there is a mountain" onwards, he encounters, pays respect to, and consults [the teacher].
Regarding the vision within the middle watch of the night: it is because wisdom enters into birth and death, and because Sudhana is about to enter this stage.
The previous mention of "the sun setting and entering the city" refers to this.
As for "at the mountain peak," it symbolizes that the stage has reached its ultimate limit.
"Radiant Illumination" refers to the destruction of the darkness of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the two extremes by means of the light of wisdom.

In the third section, beginning with "The Universal One replied," there is the praise and bestowal of the Dharma: first, the praise for generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*), and subsequently, from "Good son" onwards, the formal bestowal of the *dharmadhātu*.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, regarding the manifestation of the names and essences, there are four because wisdom is all-pervasive knowledge.
Although the four meanings are distinct, they function in mutual support.
First, because the sphere of transformation is universally pervasive, the name "universal application" (sarvatraga) is established on this basis;
second, he enters meditative concentration to observe sentient beings' capacities;
third, by virtue of his unconditioned supernormal powers (anabhisaṃskāra-ṛddhi), he is able to reach all those aforementioned places.
Fourth, by virtue of universal *prajñā*, one is able to universally contemplate while in meditative concentration.
If distinguished specifically, it is without fabrication and without dependence; it functions yet remains non-abiding.
Universal *prajñā* exhaustively penetrates all phenomena without exception.
Second, from "Good son, I universally... onwards, the four types of karmic functions are revealed, which are divided into four parts:
first, clarifying the function of reaching all places;
second, from "Or dwelling amidst various views... onwards, clarifying the function of universally observing the world, for it observes what is appropriate and teaches according to what is suitable.
3. Furthermore, from "Moreover, son of good family, this *sāra*... below, it clarifies the function of non-action and non-reliance; therefore, it says, "one does not know from where it comes.
4. From "Son of good family, within Jambudvīpa... below, it clarifies the function of the Universal Gate Prajñā, for it is able to exhaust all ninety-six types [of paths].
The preceding sections have assigned [the stages] according to their predominant characteristics; in reality, however, their meanings are universally applicable.
In the fourth major section, there are ten types of spiritual friends, which correspond to the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
This is the first.

The Elder Nīlotpala entrusts this dedication to rescuing and protecting sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a "sentient being," because he has newly entered into this dedication within the Land of Vastness.

It is "vast" because it is dedicated to sentient beings; it is "great" because it is dedicated to Bodhi; and its dedication to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) means that its significance pervades both the vast and the great.
As for the term "seller of incense," "seller" means one who sells.
Although the substance of the incense is small, its fragrance spreads far and wide;
although the roots of goodness are minute, their dedication is universal.
Furthermore, whether one sells it or buys it, both parties obtain the fragrance.
One may dedicate both one's own and others' roots of goodness.
As for the blue lotus, it dwells in the mud yet remains unstained; likewise, one protects sentient beings while remaining free from attachment to signs.
The blue lotus flower is the most excellent among those in water; providing rescue and protection is the most honored way of entering the cycle of birth and death.
The text is also divided into six parts.
First, regarding seeking according to the teaching: first, one arouses vows based on the teaching, because this constitutes the foremost of the great vows of dedication.
Third, from "Gradually" (*krameṇa*) onwards, he seeks the subsequent stage.
Second, from "He went to the elder" (*upasaṃkramya gṛhapatiṃ*) onwards, he sees, pays respect, and inquires.
Third, from "The elder said" (*gṛhapatir uvāca*) onwards, there is praise and the bestowing of the Dharma; first the praise, then the bestowal.
The bestowal of the middle [level] has two parts:
first, a general indication of what is attained; second, a detailed explanation of its functional activity, beginning with the words "That is to say.
Now, the first part.

One knows that all worldly fragrances represent the fragrance of the Dharma; that is to say, by means of the fragrances of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, compassion, and so forth, one perfumes and cultivates the arising of wholesome qualities and the eradication of unwholesome habitual tendencies.
"Skillfully knowing all fragrances" refers to the practice of differentiation (*vibhāga*).
"Also knowing how to blend them" refers to the practice of unification (*samprayoga*).

By pulverizing them with the vajra-pestle, they are harmonized by the *prajñāpāramitā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), so that the pure and the mixed are without obstruction, and compassion and wisdom are perfectly integrated, thereby accomplishing the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*).
Second, the specific manifestation of its functional activity has two parts:
first, the general manifestation of its knowledge; second, the specific manifestation through illustrative examples.
Within the first part, there are four sections:
First, knowing that the substance of fragrance is distinct;
second, from "Furthermore, he thoroughly understands" onwards, distinguishing differences by way of categories;
third, from "Furthermore, he skillfully discriminates" onwards, knowing the difference in power and function—while the former two pertain to the mundane world, this includes the supramundane as well.
4. From "In this way, etc. onwards, it clarifies the thorough investigation of the beginning and the end.
Reflect upon how each of the four preceding sections possesses both phenomena (事) and principle (理).
2. From "There are [scents] among humans" onwards, it specifically reveals the middle by citing concrete examples; herein, there are ten kinds of incense.
First, regarding the "Elephant-Treasury Incense," it possesses the ten matters of the preceding root and branches:
first, whenever the name of the incense is mentioned, it must necessarily have a physical form;
second, the battle of dragons constitutes its origination.
Third, the rising of clouds is manifestation;
fourth, the falling of rain is accomplishment;
fifth, the golden color is purity.
Sixth, joy and bliss constitute tranquility;
seventh, freedom from illness and so forth constitute the means;
eighth, a mind of loving-kindness and so forth constitute the objective sphere.

The ninth, purity of intention (*āśaya-śuddhi*), constitutes its majestic power (*prabhāva*); its functional activity (*karmakriyā*) is of one kind, as its meaning extends through the preceding seven stages.
The tenth, "I know" and below, constitutes the fundamental; it is fundamental because it is the bodhicitta.
If one explains the ten meanings by way of the bodhicitta, the fragrance of the bodhicitta is like the *tathāgatagarbha*, arising from the mutual conflict of good and evil.

If one gives rise to the cloud of compassion and pours down the rain of Dharma upon a single thought of awakening, all those reached by that mind shall be led back to true purity; they will attain the joy of the Dharma, become free from afflictions, karma, and suffering, and successively give rise to compassion until their vows and aspirations are purely refined.
The remaining nine fragrances should all possess the ten aspects of both dharma and simile; they are abbreviated here to either two or three.
"Mālaya" is the name of a country, so called because that country abounds in this fragrance.
This is the fragrance of patience, by which the fire of anger is not burned.
Third is the fragrance of diligence, by which the armies of Māra are repelled and dispersed.
The subsequent five are, in order, the fragrances of the fivefold Dharma-body.
Nine is the Incense that Accords with the Dharmadhātu.
*Sindhuvara* has four meanings for a single name; here it refers to salt, as this incense resembles it in quality.
Ten is the Incense that Forgets Subject and Object; therefore, it is named "Captivating the Mind."
The remaining three can be understood accordingly.
Second is the boatman Vasiṣṭha, who represents the non-regressive dedication.

"Vasiṣṭha" means "sovereign" (Skt. *vaśitā*); this refers to one who has already attained thorough mastery over the ocean of the Buddha-dharma, is able to skillfully transport others across the ocean of birth and death, and possesses indestructible, profound faith in all dharmas; therefore, he is named "Sovereign."

Regarding "those in the city of towers," this refers to the fact that through such dedication, the bodhicitta increases even further, as compassion and wisdom support one another to bring about excellence.

Within the first section of the text, "seeking by relying on the teachings," one first contemplates the path according to the teachings, because at the very beginning of the path of dedication, one attains what is indestructible.
The Buddha-way is high, while all others are low.
Birth-and-death and nirvana constitute the rugged and the level; hindrances and their absence constitute the defiled and the pure.
The two vehicles are crooked, while bodhisattvas are straight, and so forth.

Subsequently, through the section beginning with "gradually," one seeks the subsequent stages and gives rise to superior resolve; that is, because the path of the bodhisattva is attained by means of others, one gains indestructible faith in the Dharma-preacher who is a bodhisattva.
Within this section, the sequence is clear: first the correct elucidation, followed by the inquiry and explanation.
Second, from the passage "Having arrived there" onwards, it concerns seeing, paying respect, and inquiring.

Regarding "seeing those on the shore": if the Dharma of the Buddha is likened to an ocean, then birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) constitutes this shore, because [the Bodhisattvas] do not abandon birth-and-death.
If the ocean of birth and death has the cultivation of great compassion as its near shore, it is because one abides in great compassion to bring about the cessation of its causes.
Third, the section beginning with "The boatman said" praises and bestows the Dharma, which is divided into two parts:
first, praising the inquiry, which praises his generation of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Subsequently, one is able to inquire about the Dharma.

The text contains ten phrases: the first five are capable of inquiring about the causes of the fruit, while the latter five are capable of inquiring about the causes of those causes; therefore, they are called the "causes of the Path."
Regarding "the whirlpool of samādhi," "whirlpool" refers to deep stillness—sinking without flowing.
The two vehicles sink into quiescence for eighty thousand kalpas; therefore, they are able to remain far removed from this path of the bodhisattva.
2. "Good son, I am here" and below, the bestowal of one's own dharma-realm, which has two parts:
first, the designation of its name and essence—namely, that Great Compassion transcends all and serves as the refuge for sentient beings;
second, from "I observe Jambudvīpa" onwards, the clarification of its functional activity, which also has two parts:

First, it clarifies birth by transformation on land so that one may know there is an ocean; subsequently, from the passage "I know the ocean," it explains how one thoroughly knows the characteristics of the ocean regarding birth by transformation in the ocean.
This section has two parts:
first, the clarification of thorough knowledge; second, the demonstration of the benefits achieved through such knowledge.
First: This jewel island and so forth possess the meaning of the ocean of the phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); for now, they shall be explained by way of the ocean of birth and death.
Within the text, five kinds of matters to be known are briefly set forth:
First is the knowledge of the jewel, because the jewel is itself wisdom.
If one does not enter the great ocean of birth and death, one cannot obtain the jewel of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Within this, there are twelve phrases:

1. The ocean of birth and death, profound and tranquil and unmoving, is called the "Jewel Island. 2. The Tathāgatagarbha, which is empty yet not empty, is the "Jewel Mine. 3. The merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all "types of jewels. 4. Buddha-nature is the "seed of jewels. These four points above are all based on what is inherently existent (*pratyutpanna*).

The next four points concern what is accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanā-samudāgata*): taking pure precepts and ascetic practices (*dhūta*) as the means of purification; taking the wisdom of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-jñāna*) as the means of drilling; taking the arousal of the mind for omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) as the cause of extraction; and taking hearing the Dharma (*śruta*) as the instrumental agent. The final four points concern the "uses of the jewels": namely, that the vessels of the Three Vehicles differ in their wisdom; the functions used to illuminate reality and sever delusions are each distinct; the objects of perception (*ālambana-viṣaya*) consist of ten thousand varieties with differing stages; and the breaking of ignorance and the manifestation of clarity are each unequal.
Second, "I know all the nāgas" refers below to the three poisons of hatred, greed, and delusion within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
*Bhūta* here means "self-born"; they are similar to yakṣas, but because they are not born from parents, they serve as a metaphor for those with much delusion.

Third, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, he skillfully discerns the eddies and whirlpools" refers to knowing the characteristics of consciousness (*vijñāna*). This includes knowing that the realms of form and formlessness depend upon the mind of consciousness, determining the duration and depth of kalpas; it involves knowing the distance of the defiling habits of the seven consciousnesses' waves, and how the color of the water of the mind varies according to wholesome or unwholesome conditions.

Regarding the fourth point, "skillfully discerning the sun, moon, and so forth," this refers to the ability to know the time—that is, the ripening of the practitioner's faculties—and to understand that during such times it is appropriate to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and so on.

Fifth, one also knows the boat; that is, one knows that the myriad practices are not the same: those with skillful means are firm, while those without skillful means are fragile; those previously cultivated are smooth, while those not so cultivated are rough.
The "greatness and smallness of the waters" refers to the finitude and infinitude of birth and death.
The "favorable and adverse winds" refer to the eight winds—four favorable and four adverse—and also signify that spiritual practice may involve abiding or non-abiding.
If one opens up the third and fifth [categories], each having three matters, then they collectively total twelve.
The passage beginning with "I have accomplished" demonstrates the benefits of manifesting these qualities.
Since the ten oceans have been listed, one should understand that the preceding oceans should be considered according to this same principle.
The first four [perfections] benefit oneself, while the latter six benefit others.
The final three texts are explicit.
The third, the supreme and unsurpassed elder, represents the dedication equal to that of all Buddhas.
Because they have attained supreme supernormal powers that are unsurpassed;
because they are equal to all Buddhas, with none superior to them.

As for "dwelling in the Land of Delight," it is because, through the dedication of merit equal to that of the Buddhas, they perceive neither beauty nor ugliness, as all things have become pure and they experience joy and delight.
The first part of the text is clear.
Regarding the second part, from "seeing the unsurpassed excellence" downward, it concerns seeing, paying respect, and inquiring.
As for the initial "seeing," the reason he was located to the east of the city was to inaugurate the Buddha-sun.
Those who dwell in the Forest of No-Sorrow (Aśoka-vana) share the Buddha’s dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*), for they are free from love and hatred.

As for those merchants and others surrounding him: the Buddha is the caravan leader (*sārthavāha*) and the Bodhisattvas are the merchants; because the external benefit of the wealth of the Dharma results in merit returning to himself.
Next, from "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, he pays respect;
subsequently, from "He said," onwards, he poses his inquiry.
As for the mention of his name, it is because his reputation has long been heard of, signifying him as a vessel who values the Dharma, and it is hoped that [the teaching] may be heard by him.
The third section, beginning with "At that time, that elder," praises the conferral of the Dharma.
Within this conferral of the Dharma, the name and essence are first indicated: because it is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) and independent (*anāśrita*), it is able to reach everywhere.
Pervasive arrival signifies its vastness; being without dependence signifies the excellence of its essence.
"Without dependence" means not relying on others.
"Without an agent" means being free from deliberate effort (*prayoga*).
Second, from "Good son, how... onwards, there is an interrogation and explanation of the function [of the teaching].
Within this explanation, it clarifies reaching all places by extensively expounding the Dharma.
In the text, first the three thousandfold world system is cited, and subsequently, from "As in this three thousandfold world system," the ten directions are illustrated by analogy.

Within the fourth section on humbling oneself and deferring to the superior, the addition of the "Dharma-gate of Purity" is for the purpose of reaching everywhere to preach the Dharma; this is precisely what was explained previously.
The final two [sections] may be understood accordingly.
The fourth is the dedication reaching all places.
The good friend named Siṃhavijṛmbhitā (Lion’s Stretch) is so called because she extends with mastery, reaching everywhere.
The bhikṣuṇī is so called because her pure compassion is perfectly integrated and universal.
The name of the country is Śūna, which translates here as "Valiant.
It is called Valiant because its power enables roots of goodness to reach everywhere;
furthermore, according to the meaning clarified by the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), its significance corresponds to "progression."
The city named Kaliṅgavana is translated according to its meaning as "the time of mutual combat," because the city was established following victory in battle.

This dedication expresses the vow that, through the great power of faith and understanding and by means of vast, unobstructed wisdom, may the cultivation of roots of goodness reach everywhere—its significance being identical to that of the time of combat.
In the text, the first section concerns seeking [the Dharma] in accordance with the teachings.

Regarding the statement that King Prasenajit donated the Jeta Grove (Sūryaprabha Garden): according to the Vinaya, the dhūtas among the bhikṣuṇīs mostly reside in the king’s groves because they rely upon external protection.
This is because the manifest cause is the supreme light of the *bhūtakoṭi*, which causes one’s roots of goodness to pervade the garden of the *dharmadhātu*.
Since all these are identical to wisdom, they are given the name "light.
Second, from "At that time, the youth Sudhana immediately went to... onwards, regarding the section on seeing, paying respect, and inquiring, there are three parts:
First, one sees; next, one pays respect; finally, one asks questions.
Within the first [section], there are two parts:
first, seeing the basis; second, seeing the actual [object].
Now, regarding the first [section], there are six [points]:
first, the "Forest of Outflows-free [Dharmas]," because it is established through the practice of outflows-free dharmas.
Within this passage there are eight [subsections], each of which has its own symbolic significance; reflect upon them.
Second, the passage beginning with "Within the garden there is further... explains the flowing springs of the eight liberations.
As for the eight meritorious qualities (*aṣṭāṅga-guṇa*), they are: lightness, coolness, softness, sweetness, purity without odor, and being temperate and free from affliction.
Third, beneath the "Immeasurable Jewel Trees," Dharma-thrones are spread, which differ according to the adornments of the Dharma.
Within this, there are the introduction, the enumeration, and the conclusion, which may be understood accordingly.
4. From "This great garden" onwards, various adornments are explained in detail, because the myriad practices are not of a single kind.
5. From "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, their causes and conditions are set forth.
Sixth, from "Three Thousand" downward, it clarifies the sovereign function of the fruition.
Second, from "At that time, Sudhana saw the Lion" downward, it clarifies the vision of the primary retribution (the physical body), which is divided into four parts:
first, a general description of sitting everywhere, wherein his supreme virtues are manifest.
Second, a detailed explanation of the objects pervaded, showing that the manifestations of the Dharma differ;
third, a summary of the various types of those who hear the Dharma and resolve their minds [toward enlightenment];
fourth, a comprehensive clarification of the causes, establishing the attainment of mastery.
First: *Varuṇa* means "water" in this language, for this deity can fulfill the wishes of people.
Second, in the section beginning with "Or seen seated," which specifically clarifies the places where [the deity] pervades, there are thirty locations, divided into three parts:
The first sixteen [deities] are for the eight classes of humans and non-humans; the next two are for the Two Vehicles; and the final twelve are for Bodhisattvas.
Now, within the first section, there are seven locations for devas:
the first is for the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) devas.
The teaching on "the inexhaustible" is intended to remedy the desire of those *anāgāmins* to exhaust their physical and cognitive faculties.

Regarding the two Brahmā kings, while they might ordinarily respond only to their own retinues, when the Universal Gate is extensively applied to the trichiliocosm, there is nothing to which it does not respond.
The Brahma-sound is pure and subtle, yet it remains merely worldly; only when it is the sublime flow of the Dharma-realm does it become truly pure and subtle.
This is because the third heaven, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, enables beings to attain supramundane pure minds and achieve mastery that transcends the world.
Fourth is the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*), because its array of instruments of pleasure does not equal that of the [Heaven of] Goodness (*Sudharmā*).
Fifth is returning to the Tathāgata-garbha mind, for therein one attains true contentment.
Sixth is universally adorning the Dharma-realm, which only then exhausts the pleasures of time and portion.
The seven gods of the Śakras are placed first because their indulgence in sensual desires is extreme.
Next is one for the nāgas, because they possess the power of transformation and can adorn the world with lightning and rain.
Third are the yakṣas, because by nature they delight in flying through the air and harming living beings.
The fourth is the host of gandharvas, who are able to perform music because they delight in joy.
The three [realms] above are likewise the hosts of the Four Kings; since the intention here concerns the eight classes of beings, the southern and western [directions] are omitted.
Fifth are the asuras, who are skilled in illusions for the sake of adornment.
Sixth are the garuḍas, who agitate the ocean to terrify the nāgas.
Seventh are the kiṃnaras, who are deities of song; they are [present] so that the light of the Buddha’s conduct may shatter their attachments.
Furthermore, he has a single horn on his head, also called the "Doubt-Spirit," because it causes him to awaken equally with the Buddha by means of the light that dispels doubt.
Eighth are the mahoragas, because they possess much wrathful poison.

Of the eight classes mentioned above, with the exception of the first, the seventh, the yakṣas, and the mahoragas—which are explained in terms of their specific antidotes—all others are explained according to what is most appropriate for them, as they are able to enter the supramundane through the mundane.
The assembly of *kiṃnaras* encompasses two meanings.

The fifteenth seat represents humans; since most people practice unwholesome deeds, and even if they were to practice benevolence and righteousness it would not be superior, [the Buddha] causes them to give rise to supramundane, superior practices.
The sixteenth seat represents the rākṣasas; these are non-human beings (*amanuṣya*) because they likewise inflict much injury and harm.

The next two represent those of the Two Vehicles: the wisdom of the śrāvakas is inferior, and the pratyekabuddhas cultivate merit for only a hundred kalpas; thus, the light of their wisdom regarding dependent origination has not yet been able to eliminate objective conditions.
The final twelve [verses] concern the Bodhisattva, which is divided into three parts:
the first one concerns the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), explaining the light of meditative concentration and wisdom;
the subsequent ten concern the stages on the grounds (*bhūmi*).
The "initial arousal of the mind" refers to the realization-arousal of the mind, because it involves the arousal of the ten great vows.
Regarding the "Wondrous Flower Treasury of the Fifth Stage," "flower" refers to the ten kinds of pure minds of equality; thus, the Jin translation calls it the "Pure Mind Flower Treasury."

As for "Flower Treasury" (Kusumatalagarbha), it is so called because it contains as its cause the cultivation of both the ultimate and conventional truths, thereby attaining excellence in what is difficult to attain.
The remaining eight [realms] may be understood accordingly.

The final meaning corresponds to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samatā-jñāna), where the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi) is taught, because it shatters and disperses the habitual tendencies of the afflictions.
Since this was spoken by one who has already attained Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi), it is clear that this stage is not that of a Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
The mention of "dedication" (pariṇāmanā) refers merely to a provisional stationing [of the stages].
All other cases should be understood accordingly.
The third section, beginning with "The youth Sudhana saw thus," concludes by showing how various types of beings hear the Dharma and resolve their minds [on enlightenment], as can be understood.
The fourth section, beginning with "For what reason," generally reveals the causes and explains the accomplishment of mastery.
There are two [reasons]:
first, because the emanator is endowed with *prajñā*; second, from the words "this sunlight" onwards, because the faculties (*indriya*) of those to be converted have already matured.
Second, from the words "at that time, the youth Sudhana," [the text] describes the offering of respect.
Within this, there are three parts:

first, beholding the excellence and generating the resolve; second, the emission of light and the act of gathering [beings] through empowerment; and third, formally presenting the ritual of reverence.
From the words "He addressed [the Buddha]" below, he inquires about the Dharma.
Third, regarding the section beginning with "The bhikṣuṇī says," which concerns the bestowal of one's own dharma-realm, there are three parts.
First is the designation of the name:
"Omniscient One" (sarvajña), because her wisdom is identical to that of a Buddha.
2. From "Sudhana said" onwards, the nature [of the samādhi] is examined and explained, because it universally illumines in a single thought-moment.
3. From "Sudhana addressed [the Buddha]" onwards, its functional activity is distinguished; first there is the question, followed by the answer.
The answer has two parts:
first, clarifying the general function; second, clarifying the function of wisdom.
Within the former, there are also two parts:
First, we distinguish the basis for its function: it is because one enters the King Samādhi by means of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Regarding this "King Samādhi," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle eight, states: "Because all samādhis enter into it."
The essence is suchness (*tathatā*); the essence of suchness is fundamentally quiescent. Because true wisdom accords with this, it is called samādhi.
Regarding the term "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*), there are two meanings:
first, the thorough knowledge of all phenomena throughout the three periods of time.
Second, with respect to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is called "fundamental wisdom" (*mūla-jñāna*), because it knows that all phenomena are of one true reality.
Since this is the wisdom of reality within the provisional, it accords with the true principle within phenomena; thus, all samādhis enter into it.
Furthermore, because the essence of the King Samādhi is all-pervasive, the mind-born body can manifest according to the various types [of beings].
Second, from the section "Going to the Ten Directions" onwards, the functional activities based upon this [essence] are distinguished; these may be understood accordingly.
Second, from "Good son, I see" onwards, his intellectual function is clarified.

Furthermore, the former [passage] refers to the function of differentiated wisdom (*pravicaya-jñāna*), whereas the present [passage] refers to the function of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); thus, there are sixty-eight sūtra passages beginning with "touching objects without grasping."
The fifth is the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.

The name of the virtuous friend is Vasumitra, which in this language means "Friend of the World" (Shiyou) or "Friend of Heaven" (Tianyou), as he transforms beings through skillful means according to the capacities of worldly humans and devas.
The land is named "Perilous" because those who follow contrary paths and non-Dharmas are unable to practice there due to their low station.
The city is named "Jeweled Adornment" because, though following worldly ways in opposition [to the Dharma], it can give rise to an inexhaustible treasury of merit.
First, seeking by relying on the teachings; this has two middle parts:

first, the benefits accomplished by relying on the teachings. This means that because one hears the light of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), through reflection and cultivation one enters into it and attains two kinds of benefit:
first, the benefit of seeing the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which arises from the aforementioned wisdom of reality (*bhūtajñāna*).

Second, from "attaining thorough knowledge" downward, one attains the benefit of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), because of the aforementioned wisdom that exhaustively discerns the distinctions of the three periods of time.
Second, from "gradually" downward, one seeks the subsequent stage; herein there are four parts:
first, seeking with single-minded devotion.
Second, from "Within the city" onwards, those of shallow understanding raise doubts because [the bodhisattva's] counter-flowing practice is difficult to comprehend.
As for not doubting oneself: because one’s craving conforms to compassion, the obstacles to practice are inferior; thus, this is not the same as the previous two cases.
Furthermore, because they have already been tamed by the preceding two [sections], there is no doubt regarding this part.

Third, from "Among them, some people know beforehand" onwards is the praise of the teaching through profound wisdom; first comes the praise, and subsequently, from "Good son, Vāsuki... onwards, is the instruction on the location.
The marketplace is noisy and chaotic;
the North is characterized by cessation.

One’s own home is ultimate emptiness and stillness; thus, it is said that one practices dhyāna while amidst desires and remains constantly tranquil even in the midst of clamor—hence the reference to being in the marketplace or north of the city walls.
4. From "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, he proceeds according to the instructions.
Second, from "He saw him" onwards, there is the seeing, honoring, and inquiry.

Within the section on seeing, he first beholds the *pariṇāmanā-vastu* (the environment); since within ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) there is no quality that is not fully present, its adornments are extensively manifested.
Below the section beginning with "At that time," the primary retribution is seen, which fully possesses the virtues and functions of both the principal and its attendants.
Second, from "At that time, Sudhana went forward" onwards, he respectfully inquires; this is understood from what follows.
Third, from "He then said" onwards, the Dharma-realm is bestowed;
herein there are three parts:
first, the title is presented.
Regarding the limit of detachment from desire: ordinary beings are defiled by desire;
those of the Two Vehicles see desire as something to be abandoned;
whereas Bodhisattvas attain liberation without severing desire, for through wisdom they realize that its nature is empty, and thus desire itself is the Way.
In this way, being stained yet unstained is precisely the ultimate state of freedom from desire.
Second, the section beginning with "according to" reveals the functional activity.
Within this, first, he manifests in a body identical to that of his own kind.

Below the section beginning with "If there are sentient beings," within the context of benefiting others through the Dharma, there are ten kinds of samādhis; all of these are to be attained according to one's inclinations and capacities for desire. Contemplate how one may attain these profound samādhis.
Third, from "Sudhana said" onwards is the section on the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma, consisting first of a question and then an answer.
Regarding the gift of a single precious coin, there are two meanings:
because one can relinquish that which is precious, one thereby attains freedom from greed.
Second, although a single coin is minute, through the power of the bodhicitta, it becomes such a source of mastery.

The sixth is the dedication of roots of goodness that enter into universal equality. The spiritual friend named Viśṭhira—this is translated as "enveloping"—carries the meaning of "comprehensively including," because within the stūpa, all Buddhas are comprehensively included.
Some say it is called "Inclusion" because it includes all roots of goodness by bringing them into equality.
The city is named "Excellent Deliverance" because there is not a single root of goodness that is not delivered to the ultimate state.
