Regarding those who constantly make offerings to the Buddha-stūpa, it is because this is the most excellent among all roots of goodness.
It is not yet clear for what reason they specifically offer to this stūpa. Some say:
Because within the stupa there is a sandalwood throne, intended for the universal offering to inexhaustible Buddhas—
this is likewise a logical principle.
In the text, the first section relies on seeking according to the teachings, yet it lacks the contemplation of the Dharma.
The second section, "Approaching the Householder," shows paying respects and inquiring;
the third section, "The Householder Speaks," correctly imparts the Dharma-realm.
Within this, there are four parts:
First, the designation of the name:
"The limit of non-parinirvāṇa. Here, *pari* means "to enter," referring to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all Tathāgatas, which does not enter into nirvāṇa.
Thus, the "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "As is the nirvāṇa of the reality-limit, so too is the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata."

2. From "Good son, I do not give rise to a thought" onwards, the essence [of the Tathāgata] is revealed; that is to say, the mind accords with the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), knowing that the Buddha is eternally abiding.
3. From "Except for... onwards, doubts are resolved, as explained in detail in the "Chapter on Manifestation" (Avatamsaka-sūtra, Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata).
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also states: "There is no Buddha in nirvāṇa, and there is no nirvāṇa in the Buddha.
Fourth, the section beginning with "I open" reveals its functional activity (*karmayoga*).
Within this, there are two parts:
first, identifying the basis of its function, which also serves as proof for the preceding point that [the Buddha] does not enter parinirvāṇa, because it cites what is currently perceived.
Regarding "the Buddha-seed being inexhaustible," the Buddha-seed arises from conditions.

The Buddha arises from conditions based on principle; seeing that principle is profound and still, he perceives that the Buddha does not undergo extinction, because the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is itself the eternal body of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Following this, the section beginning with "Sudhana said" records the questions and answers concerning the realm of experience.
Fourth is the practice of humbling oneself and deferring to the superior.

Within this deferral to the superior, although the elder knows that the three periods of time are not extinguished, he is not yet able to know them in a single thought-moment, nor has he attained the equality of subject and object.
Fifth, regarding the section "To the south of this," which indicates the subsequent spiritual friends, there is first the prose (*gadya*) and then the verse (*śloka*).
Because the assembly of Great Compassionate Bodhisattvas is held in such high esteem, they are treated with particular emphasis in the verses.

The statement that there is a mountain upon the sea refers to the Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) which, in accordance with sentient beings, enters the ocean of birth and death while remaining on the mountain of nirvāṇa;
this is located to the south of South India.
The seventh is the dedication that accords with all sentient beings.

The spiritual friend named Avalokiteśvara possesses the three karmas of body, speech, and mind that necessarily respond to conditions through the six supernormal powers; his inconceivable gathering and benefiting of others is called "Avalokiteśvara," and by means of this, he is able to accord with all sentient beings everywhere.

Regarding "Mount Potalaka," this is translated as "White Flower Tree Mountain. This mountain abounds in such trees, whose fragrance is perceived from afar; that one must rejoice upon hearing or seeing it conveys the meaning of "conformity" (anuloma).
Furthermore, as for Avalokiteśvara, he is sometimes called Guanshiyin.
In Sanskrit, it is *avalokita*, which means "to observe";
*īśvara*, which here means "sovereign. Thus, he is the Sovereign who Observes.
If one says "Śabdavāda," this means "sound.
However, within the Sanskrit originals themselves there are two different versions, and thus the translators followed these variations accordingly.
In the "Avalokiteśvara Chapter" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it says, "By observing his voice, all attain liberation"; this refers to Avalokiteśvara.
If one gathers and transforms others through the three types of action, this is because one is Avalokiteśvara.

Among these, first, through vocal action, invoking his name removes the seven calamities; second, through physical action, prostrating fulfills the two vows; and third, through mental action, maintaining mindfulness purifies the three poisons.
Now, those who frequently invoke Avalokiteśvara do so because of the great utility of their vocal karma (*vākkarman*) and because many people recite his name.
Here, however, we adopt the sense of "perfection" (*pariniṣpanna*), and thus he is called "Sovereign" (*svayambhū*).
However, "contemplation" (guan) is itself the capacity for contemplation and pervades all forms of contemplation.
"The world" (shi) is the object of contemplation and pervades all worlds.
If one speaks of "sound," it likewise pervades the objects of contemplation, namely all sentient capacities to be saved.
If one speaks of "sovereign mastery" (*īśvara*), it pertains to the function of the transformer.
Within the text there are only five sections; the sixth, the words of salutation and departure, is missing.
The first section concerns seeking according to the instructions.
The second section, "Seeing [the Buddha] from the West" and below, concerns seeing, paying respect, and inquiring.
Regarding the initial act of seeing, there are three parts; first is seeing the supreme support (the environment) and the supported (the Buddha).
Regarding those on the western side: since the west presides over killing, this [manifestation] reveals compassionate salvation.
Furthermore, it causes them to turn back toward their original objective.
Second, from "When Sudhana saw him" onwards, the benefits of seeing [the Buddha] are shown, because he has attained superior mindfulness that permeates his mind.
"A virtuous friend is indeed the Tathāgata" means that they lead one to the ultimate goal, for they are identical to the Buddha.

Third, from "At that time, Avalokiteśvara" onwards, it shows how the Friend bestows praise and embraces [the practitioner] with profound and deep great compassion, thereby providing guidance and support in accordance with their needs.
Second, from "At that time, Sudhana... onwards, the respectful inquiry may be understood.
Third, from "The Bodhisattva said... onwards, there is the praise and the transmission of the Dharma; first the praise, then the transmission.
The bestowal of the Middle [Vehicle] has three parts:
first, the designation of its name;
second, from "I, by means of this" onwards, the general revelation of its essence and characteristics, which also serves as an explanation of its name.
Impartial teaching is precisely great compassion; it is called "impartial" because it arises from the compassion of shared essence (*samatā-karuṇā*).
Its uninterrupted continuity is the gate of practice; furthermore, this gate is the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*), for it manifests universally to provide salvation to all without exception.
Third: "Good son, I abide here" and below extensively reveal the activity; herein there are two parts:
first, revealing the activity by way of the universal gate, and second, by way of great compassion.

In the preceding section, first there is a general clarification: because [the Buddha] shares the same wondrously enlightened true mind as all Tathāgatas, he is ever-present in the abodes of all Tathāgatas;
and because he shares the same essence of great compassion with sentient beings, he universally manifests before all sentient beings.
"Universally manifesting" refers to the universal gate of manifestation (*samantamukha-prakāśana*).
Although the Great Sage attained perfect enlightenment long ago and is titled "Light of the True Dharma," he manifests as a bodhisattva; in meaning, this is simply equivalent to being a Buddha.

The subsequent section, beginning with "Or by means of giving," separately clarifies the meaning of universal manifestation through eleven phrases. While these appear fewer than the thirty-five modes of response in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at first glance, they are actually more numerous in their underlying significance; those thirty-five responses are merely instances of manifesting the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and preaching the Dharma within this very context.
Second, from "Good son, I practice" onwards, the functional activity is revealed by way of the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), because it rescues all who are terrified.
This section has three parts;
first, the removal of worldly fears, which consist of eighteen types:
The first three are categorized according to the afflictions (*kleśa*), which constitute the cause of fear;
the remaining ones are all categorized according to their results.
Among these, the three—bondage, killing, and greed—are established as distinct from the fear of being unable to make a living (*ājīva*).
From "The darkness has already subsided" onwards, all concerns the matters within the five fears.
The preceding section summarizes what is to be abandoned;
the subsequent section, beginning with "Furthermore, one acts," concerns the causes by which one is able to abandon them.
Mindfulness is itself the mental faculty, for it benefits all three types of action.
From the passage "I by this... onwards, one now advances toward the Great Mind, which alone can ultimately bring about liberation from the fear of the two deaths.
The fourth section, beginning with "I alone," expresses self-deprecation and the recommendation of a superior;
even though he has long since attained perfect enlightenment, he does not lose his humility.
The fifth section, beginning with "At that time, from the east," indicates the subsequent spiritual friend.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the entry of the subsequent friends into the assembly.
Those who come from the east occupy the rear position, as their wisdom and clarity must be realized according to their respective characteristics.

They are called "those who proceed correctly" because they universally transform sentient beings through the True Dharma and proceed correctly toward the characteristics of *tathatā* (suchness) by means of wisdom.
They are said to "come from emptiness" because the essence of wisdom is non-reliant, thereby attaining accord with suchness.
"Surrounded by the wheel of wisdom" means that it manifests based on delusive afflictions.
"The realm of moving feet" means that one eliminates various evils through the feet of meditative concentration and wisdom.
"Assembling as before" means that by not departing from following sentient beings, one attains the mark of suchness.
Furthermore, because wisdom is united with compassion, one achieves non-abiding.
Regarding the passage beginning "At that time, Avalokiteśvara," since his former friend pointed him out as being present in this assembly, the formal salutation and departure are omitted.
The eighth, the Bodhisattva Rightly Directed (*samyak-pratipanna*), relies upon the dedication of the aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*).
Within the section on "virtuous friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*), six points are fully contained.
The first two are easily understood.
Third, from "The Bodhisattva Samyaktvagāmin said" onwards, the bestowing of his own dharma-realm is divided into two parts:
first, the designation of its name and essence.
Because it is boundless throughout the ten directions, it is called the "Universal Gate" (Samantamukha); because it transcends many [eons] in a single thought-moment, it is called "Swift" (Kṣipra).
Second, from "Sudhana said" onwards, his activity is revealed.
This section has four parts;
first, the presentation of the inquiry.
Although there are three questions, their intent is to prompt a swift response.
Second, from "He said" onwards, the profundity [of the teaching] is revealed.
Third, from "Sudhana" onwards, he receives the power [of the Buddha's grace] and requests that it be explained.
4. From the words "The Bodhisattva Samyaktvagāmin said" onwards is the direct answer to the preceding question, which consists of five parts.

First is the answer regarding the locus from which the Dharma is attained: it means that all myriad virtues are universally produced from the Tathāgatagarbha-dhātu of one’s own fundamental wisdom; because they proceed from original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣājñāna*), practice can swiftly become universal. One knows that all phenomena do not depart from the nature of the mind, and thus the myriad practices are instantaneously perfected.
2. From "From that he sets out" onwards, the duration of time is answered.
3. From "In each and every thought-moment" onwards, the distance of the location is answered.
Since many steps are taken over a long period of time, one knows it is far; this is precisely what is meant by swiftness.
4. From "Each and every Buddha-field" onwards, its accomplishment and benefits are revealed.
5. From "As from the east" onwards, the ten powers are analogously revealed.
The final three [sections] are understandable.
The ninth is the dedication of liberation free from bondage and attachment.
The spiritual friend named Mahādeva is so called because he manifests a great body;
he is called a "Deva" (Heavenly One) because his wisdom is pure, unattached, and sovereign, being free from all bonds.
It is called "Great" (Mahā) because it accords with principle and responds universally;
it is called "Divine" (Śrī) because its wondrous function is difficult to fathom.

Regarding the city of Dhānyakaṭaka, this is translated as "Possessing Gates," meaning that it possesses subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates such as "having this" and "being unbound," for the sake of the Dharma Master.
The first two [sections] may be understood as before.
Regarding the third, from "At that time, Mahādeva" onwards, he bestows his own *dharmadhātu*; this consists of two parts:
first, the bestowal of the method for the Dharma, and second, the actual bestowal of what is attained.
Regarding the first point: manifesting signs to praise the difficulty of encountering a spiritual friend, thereby causing [beings] to joyfully enter [the path].

As for "stretching out [the arms]" and so forth: in terms of actual events, it refers to the difficulty of generating the resolve [for awakening], because one gazes with pure eyes and makes offerings by scattering flowers.

Regarding the symbolic representation: it means extending the hands of the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) to grasp the Dharma-gates corresponding to the superior stream of realized phenomena; one should first purify oneself to cleanse the body and mind, and subsequently scatter flowers for the sake of benefiting others.
It also signifies that the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) extend far and wide, as they encompass the fourfold assembly.
Second, from "I have already accomplished" onwards, the actual bestowal of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) consists of two parts:
first, the name and essence.
This means that by means of the six perfections and great compassion, one covers and moistens like a cloud and gathers [beings] like a net;
subsequently, from "Sudhana" onwards, the question-and-answer section concerns the activity of function, as one gathers sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
First the question, then the answer.
Within the answer, there are two parts:
first, manifesting jewels to induce giving, thereby teaching through the inclusion of *dāna* (generosity); second...
The subsequent passage beginning with "As I have done for you" includes the remaining categories of the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-yāna) and those subsumed under beneficial conduct (arthacaryā).
Such statements also encompass kind speech (priyavāditā) and collaborative conduct (samānārthatā).
The final three sections are easy to understand.
Regarding the tenth, the "Infinite Dedication of Entering the Dharma Realm":

the spiritual friend named the Earth Goddess Anvaya (Abiding in the Ground) is so called because the earth is that upon which all phenomena depend; it is precisely the Dharma Realm into which one enters.
"Abiding securely" means entering into the meaning.

"Being at the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) refers to the fact that the very dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) entered therein is the place where enlightenment is attained; therefore, enlightenment is the fundamental basis.
The south mentioned previously has a symbolic significance: it is the south from the perspective of the fundamental source.
Now, because this is the Dharma-realm in which the branches are gathered back into the root, it is not called "South. Furthermore,
since the realization of Suchness by those on the stages is likewise identical to the root,
and as this dedication has now reached its conclusion, all is gathered and returned to this.
The text also consists of six parts.
First is the pursuit according to the teaching.
Second, from "One million grounds" (*śatasahasra-bhūmi*) onwards, is the section on seeing, honoring, and requesting the Dharma.
Within this, there are five parts;
first is "the friend's view being praised.
Since it is called "the friend's view," the act of viewing the friend is already implicitly included.
2. From "At that time, Abhirati... onwards, the section on "adorned places" and "gathering beings" reveals his supreme virtues.
3. From "At that time, Abhirati addressed... onwards, the section on "granting permission to reveal past goodness" introduces the opening of the inquiry.
4. From "At that time" onwards, he pays respect and makes his request.
5. From "With his foot pressing" onwards, he correctly reveals the past causes.
Third, from "Good son, I have attained" onwards, he reveals his own *dharmadhātu*.
Within this, there are four parts.
First, the designation of its name, essence, and function: when the wisdom of a single thought-moment merges with the *dharmadhātu*, it becomes indestructible.
Within this state, there is nothing that does not arise; therefore, it is called a "treasury" (*garbha*).
Because the stage of the worthy (ārya) has been fulfilled, the three stages of worthiness are collectively gathered as the cause for entering the [Bodhisattva] grounds.
This demonstrates that Sudhana’s merit constantly follows the wisdom of the earth-deity, which is indestructible; thus, his former causes are not lost, and he is able to enter into realization.
The section beginning with "Always by this" briefly clarifies its function.
The second section, beginning with "Good son, I recall," specifically reveals its karmic activity.
Because wisdom is indestructible, one constantly recollects and so forth.
3. From "In ages long past" onwards, the time and place where the Dharma was attained are revealed.
4. From "I, in this [place]" onwards, the mastery [of the practice] is summarized.
The final three sections may be understood accordingly.
The Ten Dedications are concluded.
*The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll 57.
*The Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll 58.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Mount Qingliang, Great Huayan Monastery, Tang Dynasty.

This section, from the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter within the sixty-eighth fascicle, constitutes the fifth major division of the text, consisting of ten virtuous friends who correspond to the ten stages of the bodhisattva path; it is thus divided into ten sections.
The first night goddess, Vāsantī, is associated with the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
The city named Kapila means "yellow," for it was here in the past that the Rishi Yellow-Head (Kapila) resided.
Yellow is the color of the center, signifying that it accords with the Middle Way.
Furthermore, as this is the city where the Buddha was born, it signifies being born into the family of the Buddhas at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
*Vasanta* means "spring" in this language.
*Bhāvanī* means "presiding lord" (*zhǔdāng*); it is so called because in the springtime one presides over the growth of crops.
This signifies that upon first entering the stage [of the bodhisattva], one is able to bring forth and grow the myriad practices and protect sentient beings.
The reason night deities (*rātridevatā*) are frequently seen on the earth is that their realized wisdom is profound and subtle, as they dispel darkness through various manifestations.
According to the Sanskrit original, the nine celestial deities (*devatā*) of the lower [heavens] are all female deities.
"Gopā is also a woman" means that she has realized the compassion of the same essence (samatā-karuṇā) on the stages of the bodhisattva (*bhūmi*), and thus possesses the form of a woman.

Regarding the first section, "seeking according to the instructions," there are two parts: first, seeking based on prior cultivation and realization; second, from the words "gradually" (*kramaśas*) onwards, seeking the subsequent companions.
Within this, she first arrives at the time and place.
Entering through the eastern gate signifies the beginning of illumination and the commencement of manifesting entry into realization.
Seeing the sun set indicates that she is a night goddess, signifying that all differentiated perceptions of the sun have already vanished.
Following this, under the section "mental reflection," there arises a mind of longing and yearning.
Second, under the section "when making this reflection," it clarifies seeing, honoring, and inquiring.
This section contains two parts:
Regarding the initial vision of the friend’s reliance on both the environment and its inhabitants within emptiness:

the "city" represents the path of teaching (śāsana-mārga), while "emptiness" represents the path of realization (adhigama-mārga). Thus, the school’s doctrine and its exposition are both fully integrated, like the sun situated in the sky.
Those who wear vermilion robes do so because their realized wisdom is manifest and clear.
The constellations and images of the Dharma-gate are not separate from a single body, just as the functioning of physical transformations does not depart from the nature of a single hair.
Second, from "The youth Sudhana sees and hears" onwards, he pays respect and inquires.
Third, from "At that time, that night goddess" onwards, she praises him and bestows the Dharma; this section has two parts:
first, the praise, and second, from "Good son, I have attained... onwards, the bestowal of her own dharma-realm.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the designation of the name and essence; second, the manifestation of its activity and function; third, the duration of time since the Dharma was attained.
Now, the first.
"All sentient beings who are shrouded in the darkness of delusion" refers to the two types of ignorance that are to be destroyed.
"The light of the Dharma" refers to the wisdom of the two kinds of selflessness that serves as the means of destruction.
Furthermore, destroying the darkness of sentient beings constitutes compassion (*karuṇā*), while the light of the Dharma is wisdom (*prajñā*); thus, both compassion and wisdom are fully present.
Second, from "I [possess] evil wisdom" onwards, the functional activity is clarified; this section has two parts:
first, the prose, and second, the verse.
Within the first part, there are two sub-sections:
First, the arousal of the mind to rescue sentient beings; second, from "In the darkness of night" onwards, the explicit clarification of rescuing and gathering others in response to conditions.
Within this, there are ten sections:
the first clarifies the matter in general, while from "For those in peril at sea" onwards, it reveals it specifically.
Regarding the first [section], there are four types:

first, saving [beings] by means of time, such as at night; second, saving [beings] by means of place, such as at sea; third, those who are saved, such as those encountering robbers; and fourth, the various skillful means that serve as the saviors.
Within the subsequent section that separately elucidates the nine gates, each passage contains two parts:
first, relieving the world’s suffering so that it may attain worldly happiness; second, employing dedication through great vows so that beings ultimately transcend suffering and attain bliss.

Among these nine [sections]: first, saving sentient beings in peril at sea; second, from "for those on land" onwards, saving sentient beings dwelling on dry ground; third, from "all sentient beings" onwards, saving those who seek but do not obtain and those traveling through mountainous wilderness; fourth, saving sentient beings who delight in their native lands; fifth, saving sentient beings attached to villages; sixth, saving sentient beings in the darkness of night; seventh, from "these sentient beings lack wisdom" onwards, saving sentient beings bound by delusion and karma; eighth, from "or afflicted by illness" onwards, saving sentient beings suffering the eight types of suffering; ninth, from "entering the dense forest of views" onwards, saving sentient beings with evil views. The texts for each are readily intelligible.
The twenty-one verses within these two stanzas are divided into four parts:
first, one verse on the name and essence of the dharma-gate;
second, four verses exhorting practice by citing its causes, namely the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*).
The third section contains ten verses that manifest the fruit and lead [beings] into it, namely the excellence of the six sense bases;
the fourth section contains six verses clarifying the vastness of its karmic function.
Within the third section, regarding the duration of attaining the Dharma, two questions are first raised, followed by two corresponding answers.
The answer consists of two parts:
first, the response regarding the timing of the arousal of the mind; second, the response regarding the duration of attaining the Dharma.
Now, for the first part, there are six sections:

1. First, a general manifestation of the causal conditions of the original event; 2. Second, from "At that time, to the east of that city," below, the appearance of the first Buddha in the world is explained; 3. Third, from "Within the city of Padma," below, the exhortation and inspiration by the virtuous friend; 4. Fourth, from "Causing the King’s consort," below, the actual generation of the Great Mind (bodhicitta); 5. Fifth, from "At that time, the King’s consort," below, the identification of the past with the present; 6. Sixth, from "I, under that Buddha," below, the benefits achieved through generating the mind.
Second, the section beginning with "After this kalpa has passed" answers the question regarding the duration of time since he attained the Dharma.
This consists of two parts:

first, a general indication of the causes and conditions for attaining the Dharma; second, the section beginning with "As soon as I saw the Buddha," which specifically clarifies the attainment of the Dharma.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, attaining the samādhi of skillful means, which refers to seeing the Buddhas above and transforming sentient beings below;
next, from the passage beginning "Because of hearing the Dharma," one attains this liberation.
The section following "Having attained this liberation" extensively reveals its functional activity (*karman*).
The fourth [section] consists of a humble deferral, which may be understood accordingly.
The fifth indicates the subsequent friend.
Regarding the phrase "within the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*), there is no error in its application because it accords with the principle;
the principle itself is the site of enlightenment.
As for the name of the friend, "Universal Virtue" (*Samantaguṇa*), it is because within the most supreme *dharmadhātu*, there is no virtue that is not fully present.
“Pure Light” (*viśuddhaprabha*) refers to the entry into right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), because it is free from the defilement of transgressions.
Since this is the aforementioned “Pure Moon,” it is said that it originates fundamentally from the initial resolve (*cittotpāda*).
From the sixth section, “At that time, Sudhana...,” onwards, [the text] describes his longing for the virtues [of the teacher] and his respectful departure.
Within this section, there are two parts:
first, a eulogy in verse to express the depth of one's devotion to his virtues.
Within these ten verses, there are four divisions:

The first four verses praise the transcendence of his body and mind; the next three clarify that his great functions are boundless; the following two show that his benefit to sentient beings is never in vain; and the final one concludes that his virtues are inexhaustible.

2. From "At that time, Sudhana" below, through the prostrations and departure, there follow sixty-nine sūtras concerning the second night goddess, Samantagambhīraśrīvimalaprabhā, who is associated with the Vimalā Stage.
The meaning of "virtuous friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*) is as previously explained.
As for the text, it comprises six parts, which are here divided into four:
first, seeking according to the teaching; second, seeing, honoring, and inquiring; third, praising and bestowing the Dharma; fourth, longing for his virtue and taking leave.
First, regarding the initial section:

first, one recollects the preceding dharmas, which consist of eleven phrases; the first phrase concerns the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), while the remaining ten concern the attainment of the dharmas.
Second, from "Prostrations" (*namas*) onwards, there is the seeing, honoring, and inquiry.
The third section, "The Night Goddess’s Response," concerns the praise and the bestowal of the Dharma; first the praise, then the bestowal.
Within the bestowal, there are two parts:
first the prose, then the verse.
The prose section has three parts:
first, the formal bestowal of the Dharma-gate; second, humbling oneself and deferring to others' excellence; third, pointing out the subsequent spiritual friends.
Within the first part, there are two sections:
First, there is a general response to the question, followed by a specific presentation of one's own teaching.
Regarding the first part, there is a heading, an inquiry, an explanation, and a conclusion.
Within the explanation, there are ten phrases: the first is general and the remaining ones are specific.
Within the detailed explanation, three [aspects] are the light of the dharmas of wisdom, the fourth is the benefit of emitting light, and the fifth is the constant radiance of flames;
the remainder may be understood. Second, from "Good son, I have attained... onwards, there is a specific demonstration of his own dharma, which consists of two parts:

first, the designation of the names and essences—namely, being in accord with principle and free from attachment is "quiescence" (*śānti*); the dual cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is "meditative concentration" (*dhyāna*); dwelling in the joy of the True Dharma is "bliss" (*sukha*); and having boundless great function is "universal stride" (*samanta-vikrāmin*).
Following this, from "Universally Perceiving the Three Times" onwards, the extensive manifestation of its functional activity is presented in four parts:

first, the explanation of the *yathābhūta-pratītya-dhyāna* (meditation on reality as it is), which is identical to the Tathāgata’s pure meditation and constitutes the functional activity of tranquility;
second, the *dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra-dhyāna* (meditation dwelling in happiness in the present life), which constitutes the functional activity of meditative concentration.

The two types of meditative concentration—namely, the concentration that induces merit through the three knowledges (*traividyā*) and the concentration that benefits sentient beings (*sattvārtha*)—constitute the universal stride of activity.
Regarding the first, the text contains a thesis, an inquiry, and an explanation.
The title indicates that because one sees the Buddha without attachment, there is tranquility.
The commentary explains that the reason for non-attachment is that one has thoroughly realized the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the Tathāgata.

There are ten points, which are not entirely the same as the "Eight Negations" in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. Specifically, "neither going nor coming" and "neither arising nor ceasing" constitute four negations. "Neither real nor false" corresponds to "non-eternal" (*aśāśvata*); "neither shifting nor perishing" corresponds to "non-terminating" (*anuccheda*); "one mark" corresponds to "non-different" (*anānārtha*), and "markless" corresponds to "not one" (*anekatva*).

Second, from "Good son, I have thus realized" onwards, the meditative absorption for dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra-dhyāna*) is explained; first, the preceding section is restated to introduce the subsequent one, and then, from "contemplating" onwards, the four dhyānas are explicitly revealed.
Within the first dhyāna, reflection and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*) constitute the factors of counteraction; their firm adornment is likewise the characteristic of reflection and investigation.
Next, the non-arising of all conceptual constructions and discriminations constitutes the obstacle to be abandoned.
However, while worldly dhyāna merely abandons desire and unwholesome states, this One Vehicle is profound and subtle, and thus abandons all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

Next, the great compassion that rescues and protects all sentient beings constitutes the factor of benefit; that is to say, by abandoning one's own anxiety and attending to the anxieties of sentient beings, joy and bliss arise.

Following this, "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekāgratā*) constitutes the factor of support; that is to say, based upon those two [factors], one brings all mental activity to rest within the second dhyāna, thereby extinguishing applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Next, gathering all sentient beings is the state of one-pointedness of mind; the courageous power of wisdom is inner purity, free from applied and sustained thought.
Next, the heart’s joy and gladness is the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
Cultivating the second dhyāna relies upon those two [factors]; the lower and third dhyānas follow this principle accordingly.

Within the third dhyāna, one first contemplates the intrinsic nature of all sentient beings, which consists of the two factors of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*). This means relinquishing the joy (*prīti*) previously associated with gathering in sentient beings, while not losing mindfulness within this state of equanimity.

Disenchantment with birth and death constitutes the two factors of wisdom and happiness; that is to say, because one correctly knows that birth and death are not to be relished, through disenchantment one attains the bliss of true tranquility.

Within the four dhyānas, two phrases universally possess three factors; that is, suffering, joy, grief, and pleasure are all forms of manifold suffering and feverish affliction, for one falsely gives rise to the perception of pleasure within the suffering of the lower realms.
Because the four feelings have all ceased, it is said that they can all be extinguished; this is the purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
Since there is neither suffering nor pleasure, this is the neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Third, from "increasing and perfecting" onwards, the dhyāna that draws forth meritorious qualities is introduced.
"Playing with spiritual powers" (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*) carries the meaning of "universal wandering.

All that has been discussed above is based on the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), as it differs from the provisional teachings associated with the [first] three stages; hence it is said that one "universally enters the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*).
4. "Good son, I cultivate this" and so forth clarifies the dhyāna that benefits sentient beings.
It means that through various skillful means, there is nothing that does not benefit them; it also carries the sense of universal roaming.
The text consists of three parts:

first, it instructs on the practice of the contemplations of the four foundations of mindfulness; second, from the passage beginning "If there are sentient beings," it clarifies the causes and conditions for practicing the Path; and third, from the passage beginning "Furthermore," it instructs on the practice of the four right efforts.
The second section, beginning with "I alone," expresses self-deprecation and the recommendation of a superior;
the third section, beginning with "Not far from here," indicates the subsequent friend.
The phrase "not far from here" means that they both likewise reside within the mundane world.
Regarding "to the right of the Bodhimaṇḍa": this refers to the Radiance of Arising According to Principle, for its meaning is easily understood.

Regarding "Joyful Eye Contemplation": it is called "Joyful Eye" because it endures looking upon things with an evil gaze; it is called "Contemplation" because it emits the radiance of hearing and retaining [the Dharma].
The subsequent verses consist of thirteen stanzas divided into three parts:

the first ten stanzas praise the dharma-gate of direct instruction; the next two stanzas express self-effacement and deference to the superior; and the final stanza indicates the subsequent spiritual friend.

Regarding the first ten dharmas in the preceding verses, the textual order is slightly disordered: the first four verses correspond respectively to the first four dharmas; the fifth verse skips ahead to praise the seventh dharma; the sixth praises the sixth; the seventh returns to praise the fifth; the eighth praises the tenth; the ninth praises the eighth; and the tenth praises the ninth.
The fourth section, the ritual of salutation and departure, may be understood as before.
The third [section], the Night Goddess Who Observes Sentient Beings with Joyful Eyes, is associated with the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).
This text contains six segments in full.
The first section concerns seeking [the teacher] in accordance with the instructions; it has two middle parts:
first, relying on the previous friend’s instruction, one contemplates how that friend brings about benefit;
second, from "Having made this reflection" onwards, one seeks the subsequent friend and attains the latter’s empowerment.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, seeking a companion for the future journey;

second, from "At that time, the deity Pramuditanetra" onwards, receiving the empowerment of a companion, which refers to the empowerment that causes one to know the benefits of associating with a spiritual friend.

Third, from "At that time, the youth Sudhana suddenly aroused [his resolve]" onwards, the benefits achieved through empowerment are added; this refers to the fact that one gives rise to mindfulness based on the aforementioned empowering factors.
Accordingly, these ten phrases correspond to the four [categories] of the preceding ten phrases.
From "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, the text properly clarifies the progression toward the subsequent stage.

In the second section, from "He saw him" onwards, within the context of seeing, paying respect, and inquiring, the act of seeing is briefly explained, which already implicitly includes the respectful request.

The third section, "Entering the Banner of Universal Joy," below, demonstrates his own dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This means that by provisionally presenting the characteristics, it serves as the response to the questions.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the designation of the name and essence; second, the manifestation of its functional activity; and third, the revelation of its cause.
First, there is nothing that is not subdued, for it possesses great power.
Because it universally accords with the capacities of all sentient beings, it is called "Universal Joy."
It is called a "banner" (*dhvaja*) because it crushes and subdues while remaining lofty and prominent.
The second section, beginning with "Upon its body," clarifies its functional activity (*karmaprayoga*), which is divided into three parts:

first, the manifestation of its boundless function; second, from "At that time, Sudhana saw and heard" onwards, the witnessing of its function and the attainment of benefit; and third, from "At that time, Sudhana obtained this" onwards, the celebration of the benefit and the offering of praise.
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the text]: this refers to the inexhaustibility of the clouds of bodies from the pores.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the emergence of the body of practice explained in general; second, starting from "Furthermore, within each and every pore," the emergence of the body that expounds past practices.
The preceding section has three parts:
first, a general heading, which also serves as an etymological explanation;
second, the section beginning with "That is to say," which specifically elucidates the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*).
Corresponding to the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) respectively, each has further distinctions for the sake of differentiation.
The profound meaning therein should be contemplated according to principle.
Below the section "As it is said regarding the bodhisattva's various perfections," the same applies to other dharmas.
Regarding the various methods of practice, these include the supernormal powers for liberating sentient beings, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), and so forth.

Second, there is the manifestation of the body that explains the original conduct, which consists of four parts: first, the manifestation of the body that is capable of explaining; second, the manifestation of the body that explains the original conduct; third, the manifestation of the body that explains the profound meaning; and fourth, the manifestation of the body that explains the vast meaning. First, the manifestation of the body that is capable of explaining: [text follows].
2. From "toward all those sentient beings" onwards, the sound of preaching the Dharma is clarified;
3. From "with such sounds as these" onwards, the Dharma being preached is revealed;
4. From "when speaking in this way" onwards, the benefit of the teaching is manifested. The first two and the last one may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the three types of teachings expounded, there are two middle sections:
first, the teaching on the dharma of the ten perfections (pāramitās) of former practices; second, from "Furthermore, he taught" onwards, the general application to the remaining dharmas of practice.
Now, within the first patience (*kṣānti*), misconduct belongs to the body and improper speech belongs to the mouth.
Within the dhyānas, there are six points:
first, the essence; second, the supporting conditions; third, the cultivation; fourth, the attainment; fifth, the remediation of obstacles; and sixth, the arising of function.
The five phrases for the lower [vehicle] vary in length and brevity, but they may be understood by analogy with this.

Within the Prajñāpāramitā, the "sun" metaphor refers to the dispelling of darkness, while the "cloud" metaphor refers to the expounding of the Dharma; the "Treasury" (pitaka) signifies its comprehensive inclusion.
Within the context of skillful means (*upāya*), its essential nature (*svabhāva*) pervades both phenomena and principle; "principle" (*naya*) refers here to the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*).
One should reflect upon how the subsequent categories pervade the remaining practices, wherein the four bodhisattva practices are fully present.
Second, witnessing the function and obtaining benefit, one immediately realizes and enters the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This section has three parts:

first, revealing the causes and conditions for realization; second, from "Then one obtains" onwards, correctly clarifying the realization and entry; and third, from "Why? onwards, investigating and explaining the underlying reasons.
Within the threefold section on "Praising the Benefits," the ten verses are divided into four parts:

the first verse reveals the cause for the present teaching; the next verse reveals the purpose of the present teaching; the following six verses reveal that the essence and characteristics of the teaching are all the function of quiescence; and the final two verses summarize the unimpeded nature of the present teaching.
Third, from "At that time, Sudhana" onwards, it clarifies the cause for his emergence.
Within this section, he first poses two questions;
subsequently, two answers are provided. In these answers, he first responds with verses and later correlates the past with the present.
Regarding the preceding section, the ninety-one verses in total are divided into two parts:

the first seventy-nine verses answer the question concerning the duration of the initial resolve (*cittotpāda*), and the final twelve verses answer the question concerning the timing of the attainment of the Dharma.

In the preceding section, there are ten successive cycles (*anukrama*). The first, the *Śāntasvara* eon, is precisely the time of the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*). It consists of thirty-one verses, divided into six parts: first, one verse that provides a general summary;

second, eight verses that manifest his previous births (*jātaka*); third, ten verses that clarify the fundamental events of the arousal of the mind; fourth, one verse that explicitly manifests the arousal of the mind itself; fifth, six verses that clarify the virtues following the arousal of the mind; and sixth, five verses concerning his subsequent encounters with other Buddhas.
Those who have not yet attained the eye of wisdom have not yet attained the clear, correct wisdom of the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-vyākhyāna*).
Within the second *deva-jaya-kalpa*, there are four and a half verses.
To calculate that which is non-existent as being existent is due to not yet understanding that the self-nature is precisely the mind itself.
The number of verses for the remaining eight kalpas can be known from the verse count.
During the three Brahmā-prabhāsa kalpas, those who were unable to clearly understand the Dharma did so because they had not yet realized the ten practices of the true dharma of practice.
The fourth is the Guṇacandraprabha kalpa, because one has not yet attained the profound wisdom of skillful dedication that leads toward the ocean of Buddha-wisdom.
The fifth is the Śāntamati kalpa, because one has not yet attained the pure dharmas of the two kinds of emptiness and suchness belonging to the stages (bhūmi).
The sixth is the Kalpa of the Manifestation of the Six Virtues, because the obstacles to the path of cultivation have not yet been purified.
The seventh is the Kalpa of the King of Firmly Accumulated Power, because one has not yet attained the profound, compliant patience regarding dependent origination at the sixth stage.
In the eon of the Eight Sublime Lords, those who cultivate the most supreme path do so because the Prajñā of the sixth stage constitutes that supreme path.
In the eon of Nine Thousand Merits, they have not yet attained the pure patience regarding non-arising of the eighth stage.
The ten "Unattached Adornment" eons consist of four and a half verses; they speak only of making offerings because the subsequent section clarifies the attainment of the Dharma.
Furthermore, while the preceding stages all state that [the Dharma] has not yet been attained, each succeeding stage indicates that what preceded it has already been attained.
Reflect on this:

it may also be that during the first kalpa one attains the first bhūmi but not the second, and so on up to the ninth bhūmi without attaining the tenth, because it is only during the tenth kalpa that one finally attains perfection.
The name of that kalpa also accords with the meaning of "ground" (bhūmi); reflect upon this according to the text.

Regarding the second section, beginning with "Next, there appeared a Buddha named Guṇaketurāja," which answers the question concerning the timing of attaining the Dharma: it is precisely during the aforementioned *Anāsaṅga* kalpa that one attains this Dharma.
Within this, there are two parts:

first, four verses concerning the attainment of the three stages of effortlessness—namely, the eighth stage of great vows free from dependence, the ninth stage of the samādhi of cessation and dhāraṇī, and the tenth stage of accomplishing the powers of a Tathāgata;
second, eight verses concluding the stage of Samantabhadra’s practice, which consists of three sections:
The first four and a half verses cite the beginning of the Great Resolve;
the next two and a half verses clarify the culmination of the perfection of virtues;

and the final verse provides a summary of its fulfillment. Since cause and effect are thus harmoniously integrated and the beginning and end are thoroughly encompassed, one enters the path of Samantabhadra.
Second, the reconciliation;
fourth, the humility of oneself and the recommendation of others, both of which can be understood;
fifth, the pointing out of future companions.
Because they share the same stage of realization, it is said, "within this assembly.
Initiating the practice of vigor for the sake of universally saving sentient beings, he whose auspiciousness is the flame of wisdom is called Mañjuśrī; this concludes the seventieth sutra.
The fourth night goddess, Samantasattvatrāṇojaḥśrī, is associated with the Bhūmi of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī).
The text consists of only five sections, as the second and third [subsections] are combined.

Within the first section, "Seeking according to the Teaching," there are two parts: first, practicing the entry into the preceding dharmas; and second, from "With a single mind, I vow to attain" onwards, seeking the subsequent spiritual friend.

Second, from "At that time, those two deities" onwards, one hears and sees the *dharmadhātu*. This integrates the second and third [aspects]: namely, with respect to Sudhana, it constitutes seeing and paying homage; yet with respect to what is manifested by the night deities, it is the functional activity (*karmaprayoga*) of liberation, which thus silently bestows the *dharmadhātu*.

If one were to analyze this according to the two textual divisions, one would first clarify the seeing, reverencing, and inquiry, followed by the response regarding the causes and conditions as the formal bestowal of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Now, following the combined topical outline, it is divided into four sections:

first, the manifestation of light and empowerment; second, receiving the light and attaining benefit; third, reverent praise through the three karmas; and fourth, the dialogue on causes and conditions.
First: The liberation of taming sentient beings is that upon which the light relies; this is one's own dharma-gate, and its name and essence may be known.
Second, from "At that time, Sudhana... onwards, it describes receiving benefit through the light, meaning that he attained samādhi and beheld the great function [of the light].
Within this, there are two parts;

first, the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This refers to the fact that the three types of action and the six sense faculties are all free from obstructions, which is called "ultimate purity," meaning the perfection of pure wisdom.
Because it crushes hindrances to serve as a wheel, that which is perceived is without obstruction.
In the section following "Attaining this," the great function of vision is clarified; herein there are two parts:
first, the locus upon which the function of vision relies; second, from "Within each and every atom" onwards, the phenomena that are perceived are clarified.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the place of those to be transformed; second, the benefit provided by the transformer; and third, the intention of those to be transformed.
Within the first [of these], there are two: [End of segment]
First, a general explanation of the categories of locations;
second, from "Furthermore, he sees" onwards, a specific explanation of the lands within the sensory objects.

Regarding "entering into impurity and so forth": this refers to transforming toward defilement; they are called "impure" because they are pure [in essence], while those that are "pure" are so called because they abound in defilement.
The subsequent phrase is the reverse of this.
"Exclusively pure" is stated in contrast to the preceding two [phrases].
The first two phrases constitute a general clarification.
Second, from "In this way" onwards, the benefits of the transformative power [of the Buddha] are clarified, which is also twofold:
first, a general clarification; second, a specific manifestation from "Causing those in hell" onwards.

Within this, there is first the transformation of the five destinies, followed by the clarification of the transformation of the nine classes of beings from "Furthermore, seeing all sentient beings" onwards.

Third, regarding the section "In order to accomplish" and below, which clarifies the intent of the transformation, it serves to accomplish all dharmas, encompassing both the transformer and the transformed.
Third, regarding the section "At that time, the youth Sudhana saw this" and below, which concerns the veneration and praise through the three karmas, there are three parts:

first, veneration and respect through body and mind; second, "At that time, that night goddess... and below, revealing the friend's mastery; third, "At that time... and below, praising with verses through speech.
The twenty and a half verses are divided into two parts:
the first verse provides a general summary, while the remaining verses provide specific details.
Within the section of specific details, there are two further divisions:

The first nine and a half verses clarify that the function of light is boundless; the subsequent section, beginning with "I have received," describes the benefits obtained from being graced by that light.
This section has three parts:
first, the half-verse dedicates the merit to its source; second, the two and a half verses describe the attainment of samādhi; and the remainder describes the vision of the great function.
The fourth section on the causes and conditions of the question and answer consists of two parts:
first, the question; second, the answer.
Within the question, there are three points:
First is the question regarding the name; since the name was previously indicated by the compiler of the sutra, it is now specifically questioned here.
Second is the question regarding the duration of attaining the Dharma, intended to manifest that his cultivation has been long-standing and his merit far-reaching.
Third is the question regarding the purification of the causes for practice, seeking the path of entry.
The subsequent section, beginning with "The Night Goddess said," provides the answer, which consists of two parts:
first, a praise of its profundity and difficulty to explain; second, from "I rely upon" onwards, the reliance on power to provide the explanation.
This is the first part.
What are its profound characteristics?
If considered in terms of the time of attainment, it is because that time is remote rather than near.
If considered in terms of the cultivation of causes, it is because the causal practices are vast.
If it applies to both of the preceding [categories], it is because it accords with the profound principle.
If explained according to its name, the name is like the essence and function;
for the name is a subordinate to reality, and thus reality is difficult to exhaustively fathom through it.
The text consists of a heading, an inquiry, and an explanation, which may be understood accordingly.
Within the subsequent section on "speaking by the power of reception," there is first the prose and then the verse.
In the former, there is first the heading of consent, followed by the actual exposition beginning with the words "Good son."
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a general response to the three questions; second, a specific response to the question regarding the practice of purifying through remedial cultivation.
Now, for the first part, it is divided into three sections:
First, the answer regarding the duration since he attained the Dharma; second, clarifying the beginning of his resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); third, correlating the ancient and the modern.
Now, for the first [section], there are ten parts:
first, a general enumeration of the kalpas, lands, and the appearance of Buddhas, which has already briefly addressed the question of the duration.
2. From "That Buddha-world" onwards, the general characteristics of the land are revealed;
3. From "At the eastern limit of this world" onwards, the specific place of birth is revealed;
4. From "There was a wheel-turning king" onwards, the parents of his previous life are clarified.
5. From "She had a daughter" onwards, it clarifies the body of his past life;
6. From "At that time, the sentient beings" onwards, it shows how sentient beings give rise to evil as the cause for the Buddha’s manifestation;
7. From "At that time, to the north of the city" onwards, it describes the Buddha’s arising to benefit all things.
8. From "At that time, Samantabhadra" onwards, it clarifies the guidance provided by the spiritual friend;
9. From "At that time, the daughter of the Wheel-Turning King" onwards, it clarifies the cultivation of causes by the virtuous girl;
10. From "Universal Wisdom Jewel Flame" onwards, it clarifies the benefits gained from hearing the sutra.
The first six [points] can be understood as before.
Regarding the seventh point, the Buddha’s arising to benefit sentient beings, there are three parts:
first, clarifying the site where he attained the Way.
2. From "Mount Sumeru" onwards, the number of Buddhas is revealed in general.
3. From "The first one" onwards, the initial Buddha is specifically elucidated, which consists of seven parts:
the first is a general explanation of his attainment of enlightenment;...

Second, from "That Tathāgata" onwards, the signs prior to his attainment of the Way are presented; that is, the emission of light to harmonize sentient beings consists of eleven stages, and within each stage there are distinct functions of radiance that bring benefit. One may infer the corresponding names by correlating them with the benefits they confer.

If categorized according to the manifesting dharma, the first ten constitute the light of the ten pāramitās in sequential order, while the final one constitutes the light of the ten pāramitās in their perfect fusion; when these illuminate the mind, self-cognizing wisdom manifests.
3. From "When the seven days had passed" onwards, [the section] on the shaking of the lands and the gathering of the assembly.
4. From "At that time, in that world" onwards, [the section] on the manifestation of signs and the revelation of virtues.
5. From "Good son, this Universal Radiance" onwards, [the section] clarifying the primary and secondary environments of the attainment of enlightenment.
Six: "Good son, that Universal Wisdom Jewel Flame" and below marks the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, because when one is perfected, all are perfected.
Seven: "According to the minds of sentient beings" and below marks the turning of the true wheel of Dharma; herein there are three parts:
first, the general indication of the turning of the Dharma.

Second, "In each and every one" reveals its benefits; therein, the first benefits ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the next benefits those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), and the last benefits bodhisattvas.
Among the bodhisattvas, first the practices are established, and subsequently, from "arousing the bodhicitta" onwards, the stages (*avasthā*) are established. Bodhicitta is the stage of abiding;
the bodhisattva path is the stage of practice.
The "Purity Perfection" (śuddhi-pāramitā) refers to the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), because it purifies the preceding stages through the great ocean of vows;
the final two phrases refer to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Third, from "Good son, that Universal Wisdom... onwards, the conclusion is summarized as being without interruption.
Eighth, guidance by a virtuous friend, which has six parts:
first, knowing the occasion for the arising of evil;
second, "manifesting a wondrous body," and so forth, regarding the manifestation of a superior form.
3. From "At that time, all sentient beings" onwards, the objects and their faculties are struck with wonder;
4. From "At that time, Samantabhadra" onwards, he announces the appearance of the Buddha;
5. From "At that time, the daughter of the holy king" onwards, the girl generates the Great Mind, which is also the cause for entering the Dharma.
Six: "At that time, the noble son, the Wheel-Turning King" and below describes the father king approaching the Buddha.
This section has four parts:
first, his body abides in mid-air;...

Second, the praise by means of verses: within these ten verses, the first one is a general exhortation; the next five explain the exhortation; and the final four conclude with the exhortation that one should go because it is superior.
Third, from "At that time" onwards, there is the extensive arising of clouds of offerings.
Fourth, from "Having arrived" onwards, there is the cultivation of reverence upon reaching that place.
The ninth is the daughter of virtue, who cultivated the causes.
This section has three parts:
first, she offered ornaments to the Buddha, which symbolizes the cultivation of the myriad practices directed toward the fruit of Buddhahood.
2. From "At that time, the adornments... onwards, one sees the Buddha manifest transformations, signifying that the cause is small while the fruit is great;
3. From "Having seen this... onwards, one beholds the transformations and attains benefit.
The tenth section, "Gaining Benefit from Hearing the Sūtra," has three parts:
first, the Buddha preaches the sūtra, which is titled according to its general characteristics;
second, from the passage "At that time, that woman... onwards, the actual benefit of hearing the teaching is clarified, which also contains three sub-sections:
The benefits of first attaining samādhi are presented both collectively and individually in the text;
next, from "attaining such as these" onwards, are the benefits of attaining the Great Mind, namely the mind of compassion and wisdom;

finally, from "contemplating with a single mind" onwards, are the benefits of fulfilling one's vows, which consist of taming sentient beings—since all three matters [of taming] are methods for subduing.
Third, from "At that time, that Tathāgata again... onwards, the former causes are revealed.
Second, from "Good son, furthermore, prior to this... onwards, the beginning of the arousal of the mind of enlightenment is clarified.
The phrase "prior to this" refers to the period before attaining the Dharma-kalpa; it demonstrates that his prior attainment of the Dharma was not without cause.
The third section, beginning with "Good son, what do you think?", concludes by correlating the past with the present.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the identification of the body at the time of attaining the Dharma;
second, from "At that time, I... onwards, the identification of the beginning of the arousal of the bodhicitta; [and third, the identification of the duration of the practice].
Below the section beginning with "Next, he further guides," the attainment of the dharma is formally concluded; this finally fulfills its name, namely the three prior benefits.
Second, from "Good son, beyond that Vairocana... onwards, there is the specific response concerning the purification through practice.
The preceding section on hearing the Dharma and practicing it pertains to the time before attaining the Dharma;
this present section pertains to the time after attaining the Dharma.
Within this, there are two parts:
First, the specific mention of the Mahāprabha Kalpa; second, from "Good son, in this world" onwards, the general manifestation of all kalpas.
Regarding the first [the specific mention], it is divided into three parts:
first, the general explanation;...
Next, from "The first Buddha among them" onwards, the individual manifestations are specifically revealed; therein, the names of the sutras shall be expounded by the speaker.
Afterwards, from "Good son, in this way" onwards, their finality is revealed.
The second section, which generally reveals all the kalpas, has three parts:

first, a general heading; second, from "Those Tathāgatas... onwards, attaining the Dharma and practicing; and third, from "Good son, based on my reliance... onwards, seeing the Buddhas and completing the practice.
The second verse consists of forty-one stanzas, divided into three parts:

the first two stanzas introduce the teaching and exhort the audience to listen; the next thirty-eight stanzas versify the preceding formal exposition; and the final stanza cites the cause and exhorts practice.
Now, first of all, this verse reiterates the preceding heading and promise.
Within the main body of the verses, there is a general summary of the duration for attaining the Dharma and the purity of its cultivation; herein, there are two parts:
first, thirty-six verses summarize the initial eon, expanding upon the preceding prose.

There are one hundred and ten Buddhas, representing the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), each with the first Buddha as the principal and the remaining nine as companions;
reflect upon this.
The final two verses praise the preceding section by manifesting all kalpas in general, also symbolizing that because wisdom is perfected and conduct is complete, there is nothing that is not Buddha.
The fourth section, "Not far from here," below, indicates the subsequent friend, also by way of attestation through sameness.
Furthermore, because dhyāna arises based on exertion (*vīrya*), it is said to be "not far."
Because of dhyāna, there is tranquility; because one enters the mundane world to expound the Dharma and transform sentient beings with profound breadth, it is called the "Ocean of Sound.

Now, this spirit is the mother of Universal Salvation (Samantabhadra); she represents true diligence arising from meditative concentration, for the stirring of thoughts and the movement of the mind are delusion and not diligence.
The remainder may be understood as follows; hereafter we enter the seventy-first sūtra.
The fifth night goddess, Silent Ocean of Melodious Sound (*Śāntasvaranirghoṣasāgaravatī*), is associated with the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*).
Within the text, there are six complete sections.
First, seeking the teaching according to the instructions;
second, from "prostrating at her feet" onwards, seeing, honoring, and inquiring;
third, from "at that time, that night goddess" onwards, praising and receiving the Dharma.
Within this, there is first the praise, followed by the formal transmission of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) from "Good son, I have attained...
onwards. This section has two parts:
first, a brief indication of its name and essence.
The preceding passage contains two meanings:
first, joy arises because the aspiration for transformation has been fulfilled, which constitutes the adornment of merit;
second, joy arises from contemplating the superior functions of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which constitutes the adornment of wisdom.
Since the contemplation of transformation is without interruption, joy likewise arises in every moment of thought.
Below, starting from "Sudhana said," its characteristics are extensively revealed.
This section consists of three parts:

First, the function of activity is explained; next, the causes for liberation are clarified; and finally, the duration of the initial resolve is revealed. Each of these sections contains questions and answers.
Now, regarding the first [section], there are four preliminary inquiries:

first, an inquiry into the activity that is initiated; second, an inquiry into the object traversed; third, an inquiry into the skillful means that initiate [the activity] so as to accomplish what has been initiated; and fourth, an inquiry into the contemplation that observes [the object] so as to accomplish what has been traversed.
The subsequent response is divided into four parts:
first, answering the question of what means are employed to initiate [the resolve], by which the mind that unifies compassion and wisdom serves as the initiating means.
Second, from the passage "Having generated this mind" onwards, it answers the question of what activity is undertaken, for the primary activity is indeed the transformation of sentient beings.
3. "Furthermore, good son, I constantly observe" and so forth answers the question of what is observed; that is to say, observing the bodhisattvas and the Tathāgatas. 4.

"Moreover, good son, this liberation is boundless" and so forth answers the question of what realm is traversed; it takes as its objective sphere the boundless, inexhaustible, profound, and vast non-duality of subject and object.

In the questions, because the intent is to clarify the distinction between the object accomplished and the means of accomplishment, the object accomplished is questioned first, followed by the means of accomplishment;
in the answers, because the intent is to demonstrate how the means and the object mutually establish one another, the sentences are connected across an interval.
Furthermore, because the agent of cognition arises by means of the object, the agent is analyzed first.
Moreover, although there is an object of observation within the act of contemplation, the intent lies in the observing subject.
Although the sphere of activity consists of that which is traversed, its meaning encompasses both the subject and the object; therefore, these four questions are entirely distinct.

Therefore, regarding the *Jingxing* (Practice and Vow): what is its sphere of activity, what is its name for that sphere, and how does it simultaneously encompass the boundaries of the limits of practice, rather than being merely the object of contemplation?

Regarding the first [section], there are twenty mental states that can give rise to skillful means (*upāya*). The first ten are the mental states that give rise to the superior aspiration for great wisdom; the latter ten, beginning with "I initiate [the resolve] to cause all sentient beings to transcend," are the mental states of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) directed toward downward transformation.
In the second response concerning the activities to be performed, there is a thesis, an explanation, and a conclusion.
The initial thesis is easily understood.
Second, the detailed explanation beginning with "That is to say" consists of thirty-seven sections, which are divided into three parts:
The first fifteen gates follow what is appropriate to transform and treat the ten obscurations by means of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).
Among these, the first five gates clarify both relinquishment (*tyāga*) and precepts (*śīla*), because when all attachments are relinquished, the precepts become pure;
the subsequent ten mental states clarify the remaining eight perfections, with *prajñā* (wisdom) and *praṇidhāna* (vow) each having two gates.

Next, following "Lacking Physical Marks," there are twelve sections which transform sentient beings who lack merit, enabling them to attain the causal and resultant merits of Buddhahood and perceive the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
Following this, the ten sections beginning with "Those who predominantly act out of greed" employ the gate of counteractive measures solely to shatter their delusive obstructions.
Third, the section beginning with "Good son, by means of these... summarizes the intent behind the transformation.
Seeing that things have become beneficial, he experiences great joy; this is the first meaning within the explanation of the name.
The third part, the answer to the question regarding observation, has two sections:
first, observing the realm of the Bodhisattva; second, from the words "Good son, I observe this place of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) onwards, observing the supreme functions of the Buddha.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the summary of what precedes and the introduction of what follows, because the meaning from "knowing the Buddha’s spiritual power" onwards is intended to follow;
second, from "I contemplate Vairocana" onwards, the ten gates are explicitly revealed; [third, the conclusion].

The subsequent section, beginning with "Having seen this, in every thought-moment," serves as a general conclusion. It concludes proximately the preceding ten gates and, more distantly, the previous contemplation of the Bodhisattva's objects, because all observed objects accord with the nature (*dharmatā*).
Within this, first the joy that accomplishes benefit is indicated.

Following the section beginning with "Why," the source of that benefit is investigated and explained: because the great wisdom capable of contemplation accords with the essence and characteristics of the *dharmadhātu*, the faith and other qualities it engenders are equal to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

The fourth response addresses the question regarding the spheres of practice, which encompasses two types of objects: as it is said, "entering the gateway of the Dharma-realm" refers to the object of contemplation, while "arousing the mind of the nature of omniscience" refers to the delimiting object.
The remainder may be inferred accordingly.
This text is divided into three parts:
first, ten gates of Dharma-exposition;...
Next, the twenty-two similes beginning with "It is like a shadow" are taught because their profound and vast characteristics are difficult to comprehend;
finally, the single phrase beginning with "I shall now for your sake" serves as a concluding summary and an exhortation to practice.
Second, from "At that time, the youth Sudhana" onwards, the cause for attaining liberation is explained; first there is the question, followed by the answer.
The answer—that the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) serve as the cause—is readily understood.

The third section, beginning with “Sudhana said, ‘O Noble One,’” clarifies the duration since he first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], intending to manifest that his roots of the Path are profound.
This is presented first by way of a question and subsequently by way of an answer.
The answer consists of two parts:
first, the prose section, which itself has three sub-sections:

(1) generating the bodhicitta and practicing within other buddha-fields and oceans of worlds; (2) from "Then, at the end of his life" onwards, practicing and attaining the Dharma within the Sahā world-system; and (3) from "Good son, you ask me" onwards, concluding by responding to the question.
Now, for the first [section], there are two parts:
first, practicing during the first eon as numerous as the atoms of a *kṣetra*; second, practicing during the second eon as numerous as the atoms of a *kṣetra*.
Within the former, there are five subdivisions:
First, a general manifestation of the ocean of lands;
second, from "In this world" onwards, a specific indication of time and place;

third, from "There is a Buddha named Non-retrogression" onwards, a manifestation of how one attains concentration by generating the mind toward the first Buddha, which directly answers the question regarding the generation of the mind.

From this point onward, all [passages] reveal the attainment of the Dharma through practice; thus, it should be understood that the previous questions also implicitly inquire as to how long or recently they have attained such Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "the name Śrīsaṃbhava" and so forth, this also symbolizes the entry into the mundane world at the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*), because one’s merit and wisdom are then exceptionally sublime.
4. From "In this place of enlightenment, next there was a Tathāgata" onwards, the nine preceding Buddhas are briefly enumerated.

5. From "O son of good family, Pure Light" onwards, the brief summary is concluded by revealing the extensive; here it is shown that within a single eon, as many Buddhas as there are atoms in a world-system were all served and honored.
Second: "From here, at the end of life, he immediately returns" and so forth refers to practicing for as many eons as there are motes of dust in a buddha-field.
Since the realm is no different from the previous one, it says "immediately returns.
While the realm is the same, the duration of the eons differs; thus, it says "passing through as many eons as there are motes of dust."

Although it was previously stated that there were numerous deaths, the current mention of "the end of the preceding kalpa" indicates that the aforementioned *Samantaprabhāketu* kalpa is a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*), which already contains as many small kalpas (*antarakalpa*) as atoms in a buddha-field;
here, however, only the small kalpas numbered by atoms are clarified, omitting the name of the great kalpa, such that the two texts are mutually elliptical.
Therefore, the concluding summary below states: "He cultivated the bodhisattva practices for as many eons as there are atoms in two buddha-fields.
This implies that the appearance of each Tathāgata mentioned in the preceding section corresponds to one eon.

If one were to take the *Samantaprabhā* eon as a single atom of that buddha-field, then the phrase "at the end of this life" would result in a total of [only] atoms of eons; thus, the character "two" (*er*) is missing. Therefore, the Jin translation states, "In that world, passing through eons as numerous as the atoms of two buddha-fields," which alone accords with the mention of "two eons" in the subsequent text.
If there have already been as many Buddhas as atoms in a land in a single kalpa, then the Buddhas are even more numerous.
Second, regarding the practice and attainment of the Dharma in the Sahā world, there are two parts:
first, citing these three preceding Buddhas; [the second part follows].

Following this, the section beginning with "Next, he encountered Vairocana" reveals that by meeting his original teacher, he attained his present liberation; thus, all that was previously obtained is viewed as causes for this [present state].
This section has two parts:
first, the names and essence; second, from "Having attained this liberation" onwards, the clarification of its functional activity (*karmayoga*).
Regarding the "karmic function" herein, it does not refer solely to activity; this is because the preceding four questions all concern karmic function, and thus this term encompasses them all.
This section has two parts:
first, the enumeration of the number of oceans entered.
Below the passage "He saw all those," the text clarifies that what is seen within the ocean [of worlds] becomes increasingly profound and subtle.
This is summarized into four stages:
